# A.D. 355–358. Saint Felix, Pope II

*(From Labbe, Councils, vol. II, cols. 843–859.)*

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009]

## Biographical Notice Concerning Saint Felix, Taken from the *Pontifical Book* of Pope Damasus

[Col. 0009A]

[Note: **Felix.** Felix, a faithful and Catholic deacon of Liberius, was appointed by the Arians in the place of Liberius, who had been exiled and banished. If he held the pontifical see legitimately—as the *Pontifical Book* says—while Liberius, the true pontiff, was still alive and enduring exile for the faith, he could have held it only as a chorepiscopus, lest one body of the Church should have two heads. But if, as is more consistent with the more common opinion of the Fathers, he was thrust into it by the Arians and ordained bishop by their contrivance through Epictetus, then, as a kind of schismatic, he must have occupied it more by a right usurped than owed.

From the time when Felix himself raised the banner of faith by excommunicating Constantius, Ursacius, Valens, and the other Arians—and when Liberius, because of his manifest communion with heretics, was judged utterly excluded from communion with Catholics, since it is as though impossible for the same person to communicate simultaneously with heretics and Catholics—Felix began, in the judgment of all Catholics, to be regarded as the legitimate pontiff of the Catholic Church, although previously he had been a schismatic. See what we have said in the notes on the Life of Liberius, on the Councils of Milan and Sirmium. —Severinus Binius.]

Felix was a Roman by birth, the son of Anastasius. [Note: **He sat one year, three months, and three days.** That is, doubtless, from Liberius’s lapse until Felix’s death. So, approximately, Sozomen, book IV, chapter 14, saying that after Liberius’s return he held the see only for a short time. This view is also consistent with the statement that he performed only one ordination, in the month of December.

Marcellinus’s statement that Felix met his death after the death of Constantius and remained alive until the consulship of Valentinian and Valens—namely, for eight years after Liberius’s return—and that, when Liberius was sent into exile, the Roman clergy swore that they would appoint no pontiff until Liberius himself was restored, though some of them became perjured and installed Felix, was written and spoken with greater partiality toward Ursacius than truth. See Baronius, year 357, nos. 61 and 67. —Severinus Binius.]

He sat one year, three months, and three days. [Note: **Here he declared Constantius to have been rebaptized a second time by Eusebius of Nicomedia.** It is utterly false that Constantius was rebaptized a second time by Eusebius of Nicomedia: first, because Athanasius, *On the Synods*, and Socrates, book II, final chapter, affirm that at the time of his death he was initiated into baptism by the Arian Euzoius; secondly, because Hilary, in *On the Synods*, written after these events, reproaches him for daring, though unregenerate, to prescribe a form of belief to the churches. See Baronius, year 357, no. 62. —Severinus Binius.]

He declared Constantius, son of Constantine, a heretic, and said that he had been rebaptized a second time by Eusebius of Nicomedia at the estate called Aquilone near Nicomedia. [Note: **And for this declaration, etc., he was crowned with martyrdom.** The *Pontifical Book* differs remarkably here and in the Life of Liberius concerning Felix’s death. The Roman Martyrology testifies that he died by martyrdom. Because his entry into office was faulty and unjust, and because the written accounts of his death conflict with one another, in the time of Gregory XIII, in the year of Christ 1582, the learned men appointed to correct the Martyrology long and seriously debated whether this Saint Felix ought to be entered in the revised Martyrology.

His name would have been erased, had not a marble coffin been found in the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian on 28 July, that is, on the day before the day on which the commemoration of this Felix was customarily celebrated. It bore this inscription, carved in ancient letters into the marble: “Here lies the body of Saint Felix, pope and martyr, who condemned Constantius the heretic.” Since all reasonably believed that this discovery had occurred by divine providence, they deservedly reconsidered the opinion they had formed and turned it to the greater glory of the martyr. See Baronius, year 357, no. 63; Bellarmine, book IV, *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 9. —Severinus Binius.]

Reader, pause with me briefly here and consider the supreme providence of God, by which He has always governed the Roman Church itself. When Liberius had been shaken—not by participation in heresy, indeed, but solely by communion with the Arians—God raised up Felix, who had previously been joined to that same communion, to oppose him. At once He set Felix himself against those very Arians through whose assistance he had gained the Roman chair, strengthened him with mighty support against his adversaries, and fortified him for battle so that, after assailing all the Arians and striking their leader Constantius with anathema, he was rewarded with the crown of martyrdom. [Col. 0010C]

After Felix’s death, no one was substituted in his place; for Liberius, having wholly broken off the communion with the Arians into which he had entered for the purpose of recovering his see, was recognized and accepted by all as the legitimate pontiff of the Roman Church, as he had been before. Therefore it is worthy rather of laughter than refutation—the invention of certain recent historians, gladly followed by the Magdeburg Centuriators—who say that a certain Arian Leo was appointed as Felix’s successor, hostile to Saint Hilary; that he ordered Hilary, who had arrived late at a synod, to sit on the ground as punishment; and that, consequently, he suffered the same punishment from God the avenger as Arius, expiring with his entrails together with his soul. But since, by the testimony of all the most ancient authorities, Leo I sat at the time of the Council of Chalcedon, and since, without any mention of this matter, all authorities place Damasus after the deaths of Liberius and Felix, you may know that it is not history but a tale, perhaps devised by recent writers because they wrongly supposed that Liberius, after Felix had been expelled a second time, had raged against Catholics in Leo’s manner. See Baronius, year 357, no. 69; Bellarmine, book IV, *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 9. —Severinus Binius.]

] And for this declaration he was crowned with martyrdom and beheaded by the same Constantius, son of Constantine Augustus. [Col. 0010A] While exercising the office and honor of the presbyterate, he built a basilica on the Aurelian Way, at the second milestone from the city. He also bought land around the site for that basilica and offered it to the church which he had built. He performed one ordination in the city of Rome during the month of December: twenty-one presbyters, [Col. 0011A] five deacons, and nineteen bishops for various places. He also [Note: **Beheaded.**] suffered martyrdom in the city of Corona, together with many clergy and faithful, secretly near the walls of the city [Note: **Beside Trajan’s aqueduct.**] at Trajan’s lakes, on the third day before the Ides of November . From there his body was taken away by presbyters and clergy at night, together with [Col. 0012A] Damasus the presbyter, and buried in the aforementioned basilica, which he himself had built on the Aurelian Way, [Note: **On the seventeenth.**] on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December , at the second milestone. The episcopate was vacant for thirty-eight days.

[Col. 0011]

# Letters and Decrees (S)

[Note: **Letter.** This letter, written under Athanasius’s name to Felix from the Synod of Alexandria by the bishops of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Libya, is suspect concerning the faith—or authenticity—[Col. 0012D] both because, at this time, Athanasius had escaped by flight and was hiding in the desert, while, together with Liberius, all the orthodox bishops had been driven from their sees by decree of the emperor and of the conventicle of Milan, so that neither place nor time could have permitted the convening of a synod; and because this letter, written to Felix, informs Felix himself about his own ordination.

Let others judge whether Felix’s reply perhaps suffers from the same defect. Certain very learned men have held that the letter, fragments of which survive under Felix’s name in the Council of Chalcedon, was written by Felix II, for the reason that the aforementioned fragment is appended in the Council of Chalcedon, session 1, and in Cyril’s Apology, after the letter of Pope Julius. But we refuted that opinion above from the argument and title of the letter itself, in the notes on the fourth letter of Felix I. —Severinus Binius.]

[Note: Therefore all the other pieces “of the same stamp” (*ταυτοῦ κόμματος*) were likewise drawn from the same workshop.]

[Note: Baronius and other learned men consign these trifling scraps of an inept medley to the bad wares of a merchant.]

## Letter of Saint Athanasius and of the Egyptian Pontiffs to Pope Felix II, Concerning the Attacks of the Arians

[Col. 0011A]

[Col. 0011B]

To the most blessed and honorable lord, holy father Felix, pope of the holy apostolic see of the city of Rome: Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Libya, assembled by God’s grace in the holy Synod of Alexandria.

We lay before your holy apostolate (Maurus, bishop of Caesena, to Saint Martin; session 1 of the Lateran Council, A.D. 649) the request that, according to your most prudent wisdom, which is clearer than light to all, you may deign to take care for us in your customary manner. For your Blessedness, moved by apostolic compassion (Deusdedit, bishop of Cagliari, to Saint Martin) at our tribulation, exhorted us all to assemble together for the protection of the Catholic and apostolic Church and to deliberate canonically and unanimously concerning our oppression, since it is evident that you say compassionately with the blessed Apostle Paul: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29), striving that none of the rational sheep entrusted to you may be seized by beasts.

Therefore, most blessed Father, because our predecessors and we ourselves have always drawn help from your holy apostolic see, and have recognized that you take care for us, we seek that aforementioned apostolic and supreme see in accordance with the decrees of the canons, that we may receive assistance from the source from which our predecessors received ordinations, doctrines, and support. We also flee to it as to a mother, that we may be nourished at her breasts, because a mother cannot forget her infant. Thus do not you forget us, who have been committed to you; for our enemies have entangled us in no slight afflictions [Col. 0012A] and daily devise means to do so. They threaten to seize us or bind us in irons (Stephen of Dora to the same pope, session 2 of the same synod), unless we consent to their errors—something which we do not presume to do without consulting you. For the canons command that, in major causes, we ought to decide nothing without the Roman pontiff.

Therefore, returning to our purpose and hastening toward the prize, we implore the aid of your apostolic see. For we believe that God has not despised the prayers of His servants offered to Him with tears; but for this reason He placed you and your predecessors—the apostolic bishops—in the ark of supreme authority, and commanded them to have care for all churches: that you may come to our aid and, protecting us, not neglect to deliver us from our enemies, since all judgment concerning bishops has been entrusted to you.

For we know that the great Nicene Synod of three hundred and eighteen bishops unanimously confirmed that councils must not be held without the judgment of the Roman [Col. 0012C] pontiff (Socrates, book II, chapters 8 and 17; Sozomen, book III, chapter 9), nor bishops condemned. Yet these synodical chapters, along with many other necessary provisions, have been burned and taken away from us by the heretics who attack us daily and endeavor to destroy us, so that they may seize us more easily. Hence, having found this opportunity, they disregard all canonical and apostolic authority and unlawfully drive us by force from our own sees without consulting you. They invade the sheep entrusted to us by the apostolic grace of Christ the Lord; they deprive us of our ranks; and, what is worst and hostile to every Christian law, they strive to kill us.

Therefore, as has always been the custom of your holy see, come to the aid of those in danger; strengthen the oppressed; extend your hand to the afflicted; forbid such conduct [Col. 0012D] and impose laws, so that apostolic doctrine, which is in God, may quickly bring our judgment to victory [Col. 0013A] and, with Peter the prince of the apostles lending his aid, deliver us from imminent dangers.

For we know that in the aforementioned Nicene Synod it was decreed generally (and this is also contained in Pope Julius’s decretal letter against the Easterners on behalf of Athanasius, chapter 7) that no one may rashly and indiscriminately assail bishops, or presumptuously accuse them; nor may anyone dare to defame those who are not of upright faith, good life, or honorable conduct. Rather, if anyone has a complaint against bishops or leaders of the Church, he should first approach them gently and charitably, that the wound in question may rightly be healed by them; otherwise, should he act differently, the accuser is to be excommunicated. If he can obtain no just satisfaction from them, then only then should he approach the chief primates, who at a suitable time must summon them canonically (ibid., chapter 17).

If the bishops have been stripped of their goods, driven from their own sees, exiled, oppressed, or unjustly treated, they must first be rescued and canonically restored (ibid., chapter 8), and everything taken from them must be restored to them most fully under the laws (Hadrian, collection 35). For before this is done, as was established in the aforementioned council, they can neither be canonically summoned nor [Note: Perhaps: “constrained” (*distringi*).] be subjected to a judicial determination by anyone, since not even secular laws permit such things; much less do ecclesiastical laws.

Likewise, the aforementioned Fathers unanimously defined that if any bishop, metropolitan, fellow-provincial bishop, or judge is suspected, he should appeal to your holy Roman see, to which the power of binding and loosing (Matt. 16) has been granted by the Lord Himself above others by a special privilege. For it has received (Sergius, bishop of Cyprus, to Pope Theodore, session 2 of the Lateran Council) a foundation established by God and immovable, because the Lord Jesus Christ made your apostolic see the most brilliant standard of all titles. It is the sacred [Note: The Greeks say *polon* (*πόλον*) from *polein* (*πολεῖν*); from this etymology one should not infer that the text was written in Latin rather than Greek.] summit around which all churches revolve, are sustained, and are raised up.

[Note: **And just as.** It seems that the text should read: “And as Christians are renewed in Christ, so churches are renewed in the rock, that is, Peter.” The sense is that the pontiff of the Roman Church both can and ought, by his authority, to correct whatever has been corrupted or depraved in other churches. —Severinus Binius.]

And as Christians are renewed in Christ, and Peter in the rock—that is, Christ—so the churches of Peter are renewed. For you are Peter, as the divine utterance truly testifies; and upon your foundation the pillars of the Church—that is, the bishops, who ought to sustain the Church and carry it upon their own shoulders—are established for you. To you He entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven and proclaimed the authority to bind and loose whatever is on earth and in heaven (Matt. 16). You stand as the deposer of profane heresies, of accusers, and of all assailants, as prince, teacher, and head of all orthodox doctrine and unblemished faith.

Therefore, Father, do not disdain the piety and good intention of your fathers. As they delivered our fathers and predecessors from many [Col. 0014A] oppressions and distresses, so deign to deliver us. For your holy and apostolic see has always possessed authority to restore, by its own power, those unjustly condemned or excommunicated; to return all things to them; and to punish by apostolic privilege those who condemned or excommunicated them, as we know has been done in our own times and in earlier times.

Moreover, the primates themselves, who ought to take up cases concerning bishops and the highest ecclesiastical affairs, were enumerated in the specified Nicene Synod, lest contention should arise over this in the future. O most holy father of fathers (the same Bishop Sergius, just cited), cut off the blasphemies and boasting of empty talkers and the hostile attacks of plotters who oppress and wish to destroy us and our brethren. We flee to you as to the head, that, supported by your aid, we may be delivered and that, with the Lord’s help, we may rescue before they are swallowed the sheep of Christ entrusted to you and to us from the mouths of wolves.

For it is not lawful (Saint Pope Martin, in the same place) to despise prayers offered to the apostolic see by petitioners, in writing or without writing. Rather, as is fitting and as the privilege of your see requires, both we and they should be canonically summoned, and before you we should canonically contend with all uprightness concerning our accusations, as our predecessors did before your predecessors, and as the canonical institutions in the aforementioned holy synod teach. Thus, like those clothed in the words [Note: “of words.”] of the Word, through the winnowing-fan of canonical examination, standing in a common hearing, we may obtain full vindication concerning the mature and nourishing doctrines of the Catholic Church, [Col. 0014C] which strengthen the human heart, by participation in the institutions of the Fathers.

For ancient regulations established (the African Fathers, in their letter to Pope Theodore, session 2 of the Lateran Council held in A.D. 649) that whatever might be done, even in distant or remote provinces, concerning complaints or accusations against bishops, was not to be handled or received before it had been brought to the knowledge of your gracious see, so that by its authority [Note: According to whatever judgment had been made, it should be invalidated.] the decision made might be invalidated or confirmed. From that see they were to take their norm, from which the churches received the beginning of preaching, lest the pillars of the Church be indiscriminately overthrown by plotters.

For it is certain that the decrees of the Fathers, in honor of the most blessed Peter, assigned to that same holy see of yours a special reverence of God for investigating and determining matters which it is proper that the apostolic summit of bishops should examine diligently and justly. Its concern always was and is both to condemn evils and to approve what deserves praise.

Accordingly, rendering most humble obedience to your apostolic eminence, as the Lord Himself commanded and the decrees of the holy Fathers established, we make known with tears what we cannot keep silent without groaning of heart. For we are persecuted by the persecutors of God’s holy Church and by our enemies to such an extent that we are more weary of living than of dying. Therefore, above all things we confess that our heart is wounded so deeply (Victor of Carthage, in his letter to Pope Theodore) that we desire that prophetic lament, saying: “Who will give water to our head, or a fountain of tears to our eyes, that, sitting, we may weep day and night?” (Jer. 9).

For behold, the Church of God is not slightly disturbed; its pillars are grievously attacked and are being driven away by wicked men. The cries and groans of Christians and bishops resound far and wide; innovations arise, calumnies increase, persecution rages, and peoples perish. It is yours to extend your hand to us, because we have been committed to you. It is yours to defend and deliver us; ours to seek help from you and obey your commands.

Because of excessive sorrow and groaning, we cannot necessarily recount and communicate to you everything that presses upon and harasses us. [Note: “Necessary matters.”] Therefore we beseech your gracious apostolate to restore concerning these matters the law promulgated in the aforementioned Nicene Synod, although it has been suppressed through the corruption of the aforementioned plotters and of other wicked people, who thereby can more easily ensnare bishops and ministers of God. By the authority of your holy see, instruct us and all the brethren in whatever you recognize as necessary, so that, supported by your authority, we may, with the Lord’s help, escape unharmed the plots of wicked people. [Col. 0015C] For it belongs not to sheep to foresee the snares of wolves, but to shepherds (Third Roman Council under Symmachus).

For we know that you—as the bishops of your see have always done, first the apostles and then their successors—ought to care for the universal Church and especially for bishops, who are called the Lord’s eyes because of their contemplation and watchfulness, and ought constantly to meditate upon our revelation and law, as it is written: “Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1). This meditation (Victor of Carthage, cited letter) is known not merely through reading perceived by the form of letters, but through the grace of Christ abounding in you, implanted immovably in your conscience; and the most holy law of Christ, God and Lord, never departs from your heart, as the prophet says in the psalm: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment; the law of his God is in his heart” (Ps. 36). It is written in your inmost parts, not with ink but by the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts (2 Cor. 3), as the letter of the most blessed Apostle Paul sent to the Corinthians teaches us.

Having stated these matters, we inform your fatherhood, pleasing to God, [Col. 0016A] that on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August [16 July], in the fourth indiction, our humility, by divine grace and through His gift going before us as He commanded, received consecration and the stole of pontifical honor in the holy Roman Church, through your holy and God-worthy prayers.

[Note: **In the year 646**, so that the impostor’s fraud, by which he wished to deceive the world, may be more apparent.]

[Note: He substituted “Roman” for “Carthaginian.” Add that Athanasius, ordained at Alexandria, I believe in January A.D. 316, was in the fourteenth indiction.]

In this summit of dignity, we ask, commending ourselves to your holy and God-acceptable prayers, that we may be governed by God Almighty, the Most High, and delivered from every evil; that, by the protecting help of Christ the Lord our God, we may possess not merely the name of priestly office but also its merit; and that, strengthened by your prayers poured out to God for us and instructed by good teachings, we may be made worthy, together with all the Christian people entrusted to us, to be preserved unharmed under the divine covering.

Therefore, in our stead, for the greeting of your holy and venerable fatherhood, [Note: The plagiarist changed the proper names so that he might not be detected in theft.] we have sent Benedict, your humble brother and our bishop; Alexander likewise, a presbyter; and Crispinus, a deacon—your servants. We request that they may speedily be returned to us by your Blessedness, so that, strengthened by your exhortations and instructed by your rules, and with our enemies suppressed, we may prudently return, comforted, to our own churches before winter, God being favorable.

For it is yours, most holy Father, diligently to oppose, by canonical severity (see the end of Victor’s same letter), those who resist ecclesiastical rule and plot against the brethren, and not to allow newly to be asserted what the authority of the venerable Fathers did not at all decree. For we, humble in heart and, with the Lord’s help, understanding what is right, are bound with you by one bond of charity, courageously defending the true faith and Catholic religion in all things.

Accordingly, Catholics must strive more diligently and rightly to resist wicked persons, lest, oppressed by the torpor of negligence, we be held guilty of culpable silence and be judged to be granting favor when we neglect to repel what is hostile to the Catholic faith. Hence it has been said: “To neglect, when you can overthrow the perverse, is nothing other than to encourage them. Nor is one free from the stain of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.”

It is clear, most holy teacher, that the poisonous cunning of serpents is without simplicity when the deceitful fraud of enemies is manifest. Come to the aid, we beseech you, of the oppressed; deliver us from the hand of persecutors, that you may sing with blessed Job: “The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow. I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my judgment was as a garment and a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and the cause which I did not know I investigated most diligently. I broke the jaws of the wicked man, and from his teeth [Note: “His.”] I snatched the prey” (Job 27), and the rest.

For we, whom your greatest care awaits (Innocent, letter 18 to Alexander of Antioch)—that is, all bishops—ought especially to deserve your judgment and not be devoured by others. Rightly, therefore, does the Lord take account of us priests if we favor error through silence (Celestine, letter 1 to the Gauls). Such persons must indeed be corrected, nor should they be free to render judgment as they please. Let novelty cease to attack antiquity; let unrest cease to disturb the peace of the churches.

For, so that all metropolitans and other bishops might be unable to exercise their hatreds or acts of vengeance against other bishops, the primates who ought to hear and judge the other bishops were expressly designated by name in the Nicene Synod, lest any fraud should intrude into the judgment of bishops. Therefore, you who have been placed by God’s grace upon the highest watchtower ought to heed and suppress those who stir up seditions and scandals among the brethren (Stephen of Dora to the Lateran Synod, A.D. 619).

Therefore we beseech you not at all to despise the afflictions [Col. 0017B] and tearful prayers of our humility and of all the orthodox priests and peoples of the East. [Note: The forger removed the names of Sophronius, Apollinaris, and Severus.] Rather, as lights for the whole world, holding fast the word of life, extinguish the darkness introduced by the most impious plotters, which has also sprung up brazenly in our times. Thus, when such darkness has been wholly extinguished, may the light-bearer shine upon us through you, most holy Father, and may the dogmatic definition, gladdening all people everywhere, shine forth—that definition which the glorious Fathers of the holy Church are known to have proclaimed through their own most pious teachings as a firm inheritance of eternal life.

[Col. 0017C]

May the Lord preserve you forever, most holy father of fathers, safe and pleasing to God, as you pray for us. Amen.

[Note: You may with the fullest right also call this letter false.]

# Letter I of Pope Felix II: Reply to the Bishops Assembled in the Alexandrian Synod

I. That no one may accuse a bishop before secular arbiters. — II. If anyone has a case against a bishop. — III. On the same matter. — IV. On bishops stripped of their goods or expelled from their sees. — V. Persons of bad repute and sacrilegious persons are not to be admitted as witnesses. — VI. If a bishop summoned to a council is unable to go. — VII. On cases not contained in the laws, or known to be prohibited. — VIII. On accusations against bishops and restoration of their property taken away. — IX. Those who may not accuse or testify. — X. On the same matter. — XI. On the persons of accusers. — XII. On primates and metropolitans. — XIII. On accusations against bishops and the incapacity of accusers. — XIV. Those who ought not be admitted to make an accusation. — XV. On the same matter. — XVI. That in ecclesiastical affairs, once a case has been stated and concluded, it is permitted to withdraw—a thing not permitted in secular affairs. — XVII. On accusations against bishops. — XVIII. That bishops’ cases are not to be decided without the authority of the Roman pontiff. — XIX. If a bishop thinks himself oppressed by fellow-provincial bishops or by a metropolitan. — XX. On bishops’ trials and the period allowed for preparation and appearance. — XXI. On judges and accusers, what kind they ought to be.

To the most reverend and beloved brethren Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Libya, assembled in the holy Synod of Alexandria: Felix, bishop of the gracious city of Rome and of the universal Church, and the holy synod which assembled in the city of Rome, greetings in the Lord.

We gladly received your sacred synodical letter, composed through the grace of the Holy Spirit and with zeal pleasing to God, by the favor of your holiness, worthy of honor from God; and we immediately ordered it to be read aloud point by point in the synod, and commanded all to attend carefully to its words. While we hoped and desired to rejoice over these, “our harp was turned to mourning, our song into weeping,” and all the joy of the entire synod was changed into sorrow (Job 30): for it was unfitting that those who daily fashion the body of Christ with their own mouths (St. Jerome, Letter to Nepotian) should suffer so great a persecution. For the Lord our God, providing salvation for the human race, commanded that persecutions should not be carried out, disturbances inflicted, laborers in the Lord’s field envied, or the stewards of the great King harassed or driven out.

“Be at rest,” says the holy great Council of Nicaea (6, question 1), “and do not persecute those who minister perfectly to God, who keep with sincere will the commands of God on high, and are subject to our laws”; for neither is it fitting, nor does order permit, that the wicked and carnal should persecute the spiritual. For everyone who resists another, now by twisting, now by concealing the truth, lies against the person with whom he contends. And whoever is hostile to another acts in every respect as an enemy and, moreover, strives to speak against him.

We therefore admonish you, brethren, that you must remain watchful, so that, insofar as you can and the Lord gives help, you may resist such persons by our apostolic authority and your own. Let none of you withdraw himself from helping his brother, but let him provide assistance according to his strength [Col. 0018D]. For although you are few, if you are of one mind, you shall by no means be overcome, justice supporting you and the Lord also bringing aid; for “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccles. 4). For if human law comes to the aid of secular offices (St. Gregory, Letter 120, Book VII), how much more ought divine and catholic law to support ecclesiastical persons and the priests of the Lord—especially bishops, who are called the pupils of the Lord’s eyes! For the divine utterance says concerning bishops: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” [Col. 0019A] (Zech. 2).

And if secular persons are examined in many ways under human law, and its investigations and postponements [Note: *Eis.*] extending over many months are granted, lest they be condemned unjustly, how much more should far longer periods be granted to bishops, who are nearer to God, set over others, and stationed in the heavenly militia, lest they be burdened, oppressed, or suddenly condemned by certain persons!

Let us therefore begin (Innocent, Letter 2), with God and St. Peter the Apostle assisting us—through whom apostleship and episcopacy received their beginning in Christ—since many cases have often arisen which in some instances were not cases but crimes, because, as we have learned, they were imposed upon brethren more through malice than charity [Col. 0019B]. And, so that henceforth there may be care that such things do not happen, let us set down certain chapters established by the holy Fathers both in the Nicene synod and in this See. Strengthened by them, our brethren and fellow bishops may, with the Lord’s help, escape the snares of enemies. And, insofar as the Lord grants ability, let us make a brief compendium of so many evils (the same pope, Letter 7), review succinctly what we have learned from the volume of your letter, and add certain other matters necessary for the present time, as you request.

I. For it is decreed by synodical enactments (Carthage III, c. 9; Milevis 19; Agde; Orleans; etc.) that no one accuse a bishop before secular arbiters, but before the supreme primates.

II. If anyone has a case against a bishop, he must not first approach certain bishops to accuse him, but must privately make his complaint known to him and receive from him either a just correction or a reasonable excuse. Truth itself instructs us: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. 18). “If he hears you, you have gained your brother. If he does not hear you, take two or three with you; and if he does not hear them, tell the Church” (Luke 17)—that is, accuse him publicly [Note: Then], but not before that; and so forth.

III. If anyone thereafter chooses to accuse a bishop, let him present his case to the supreme primates of bishops, and not to secular persons. Let the primates call them back to peace rather than judgment (Carthage IV, c. 26), so that charity may be preserved in all things and by all persons. If the primates [Col. 0019D] (5, question 2) cannot privately reconcile the bishop’s accusers with him, then at the lawful time let them canonically summon them to a canonically convened synod—not within a cramped period—and not before they have notified them in writing what is alleged against them, so that they may arrive prepared to answer.

For if they have been driven out by force (Fifth Roman Council under Symmachus), or by fear, or stripped of their goods, they can neither be canonically summoned to a synod nor ought to answer their opponents, until they have been canonically restored and all their possessions legally returned to them.

IV. If any bishop has been stripped of his goods or expelled from his church by force or fear—which is hostile to every Christian name—it is necessary and fitting [Note: “The purpose of bishops must always proceed foremost”; or, “the holy purpose must always advance in the forefront.”] that the bishops’ purpose should always take precedence, so that everything taken from him may legally be restored to his control; that the bishop be first restored; and that afterward, not immediately but after a long and ample period in which he has authoritatively arranged all that is his and prepared what he requires, he may come at the appointed time to his case. If it seems just, he may then answer his accusers [Note: The same is found in the Decrees of Julius, c. 35].

V. No infamous person (from Anianus) or sacrilegious person may, in any affair whatever, give testimony against a religious Christian, even if the latter is a lowly person or a slave; nor may he prosecute a Christian concerning any matter, action, or written accusation [Col. 0020B].

VI. If any bishop has been lawfully accused and canonically summoned to a council in the aforesaid manner, he must go without any apprehension; and if he cannot go (Hadrian, c. 5), let him send an envoy to the synod in his place.

VII. No cases shall be heard by ecclesiastical judges (the same, c. 11) which are not contained in the laws or are known to be prohibited.

VIII. If anyone will not be satisfied unless he accuses a bishop, he must proceed in the manner stated above, since otherwise the accusation cannot stand. Let the accuser first canonically bring the accused person’s case before the primates (Carthage III, 7). Nor may the accused be excluded from communion unless, having been canonically summoned to the judgment of chosen judges, he delays for three, six, or more months in coming to render an account of his conduct. But if he can prove that he was unwilling not to come but was unable to come, it shall not harm him.

But one driven from his see by force or fear, or stripped of his goods, must not be summoned to a synod before everything has been restored to him according to law. And he shall remain in his own see, peacefully and with full authority administering all things (Rome V under Symmachus), for as long as he appears to have been deprived of his goods by expulsion or despoiling (3, question 2; and in Ivo’s Decrees, Book XLIII, question 3). When he comes to judgment, if he wishes and if necessary, postponements established by the Fathers shall be granted to him on request without impediment; and judges chosen by himself shall be granted, so that, in the place from which the accused comes—or, if elsewhere he fears the violence of some reckless multitude, in a suitable place chosen by him—he may, without fear, have his witnesses if necessity requires (African Council, c. 30), and may bring his canonical judgment to completion without hindrance; for many things are wont to happen by stealth.

IX. The right of giving testimony or making accusation shall be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, and the standard of their own law or profession, or matters regularly prohibited (Anianus on c. 1, title 7, Book XVI of the Theodosian Code).

X. Detraction has great force when the detractor is believed (Tripartite History III.8; from Socrates I.31). Therefore a primate ought not to be shaken by diverse calumnies and accusations, but rather strengthened by the rules of the Fathers (Damasus, Letter to the Illyrians in Theodoret II.22). Nor should he presume readily or indiscriminately to receive accusations, the Lord saying: “Do not entertain a false report” (Exod. 23); rather, he must first test the suspicion and the case, and the intention with which the person acts, and afterward give heed. For the motive of kinship, enmity, fear, love, hatred, and greed is accustomed to impede a profession of truth (Anianus, Book V of the Sentences of Paul, title 45, sentence 2) and to inflict wrongs upon brethren.

XI. The persons of accusers (Hadrian, 4 and 15) must be such that their faith, conduct, and life are trustworthy and beyond reproach, and they are free from every suspicion. For, as you well know, this too was decreed by all in the Nicene synod in your presence, on account of the attacks of evil persons—although these and very many other things have been destroyed by the snares of wicked men [Note: Observe here that certain decrees made in the Nicene synod have been destroyed].

XII. The primates must be those, and no others, who were established in the Nicene synod. The others who hold metropolitan sees (Hadrian, collection 23) are called archbishops, not primates, while the dignity of the Apostolic See remains unimpaired in all respects: a dignity granted to it by the Lord himself and afterward confirmed by the holy Fathers.

XIII. In every accusation of bishops, the life, person, and conduct of the accusers must always first be examined thoroughly (the same, c. 15); afterward the allegations must be faithfully considered. For nothing should be done otherwise [Note: “is fitting”], except that the faith of the accusers first be investigated and their persons, lives, and actions examined; since the life of the innocent ought not to be torn apart through the ruinous malice of wicked or plotting persons. Certainly, good persons are very often persecuted by evil ones, who never cease, through their calamities, to disparage others by their calumnies [Note: “to blacken others”]. Therefore the greatest care must be taken lest these things occur.

XIV. No slave (Carthage VII, c. 2), freedman, unfaithful person, person entangled in crimes, calumniator, person devoted to enmities, person who frequently litigates (Hadrian 11 and 50; from Carthage IV.58 and VII.2), or who is quick to accuse or disparage; no infamous person; nor any of those whom public laws do not admit to accuse public crimes [Col. 0021D], may be permitted to accuse bishops. For I cannot discover on what grounds the priestly order ought to receive accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not receive, since these things were prohibited also in the Nicene synod; and bishops ought rather to judge such persons than be judged by them. And the apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (2 Cor. 2).

XV. Heretics, by whom we are exceedingly oppressed, and excommunicated persons, murderers, evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, borne false witness, or resorted to diviners and magicians (Hadrian, collection 63), shall by no means be admitted either to accusation or testimony.

XVI. Ecclesiastical affairs must not be conducted as secular ones are (St. Leo, Letter 54). For in secular matters, after someone summoned under the laws has appeared and begun to contend in court, he may not withdraw before the case is concluded. In ecclesiastical matters, however, after the case has been stated, it is permissible to withdraw if necessary or if he sees that he is being overburdened.

XVII. Whenever a bishop is accused of specific crimes (Hadrian 27), if the accusers are such as ought justly and canonically to be received, he shall be heard lawfully in a synod assembled at its proper time by all the bishops who are in the provinces. But if the accusers are not lawful, the bishop shall not be wearied; for priests ought to be free for sacrifice, not litigation. Nor should those called the thrones of God (Council of Toledo XI, c. 5) be disturbed by the snares of wicked persons, but serve Christ the Lord freely.

XVIII. Although fellow-provincial bishops together with their metropolitan may charitably and harmoniously deal with the cases of bishops in their province, they nevertheless may not—as was decreed in the aforesaid synod in your presence—give a final decision without the authority of the Roman pontiff. If some persons presume otherwise, those who have done this shall bear the penalty of their presumption. And those whom they have wrongly excommunicated or condemned shall be absolved and restored by the authority of this holy See and the power of blessed Peter, our key-bearing teacher. For the Lord himself says: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16).

XIX. Whenever bishops believe themselves burdened by their fellow-provincial bishops (Hadrian 6 and 18, from canon 7 of the Council of Sardica), or by their metropolitan, or hold them suspect, they shall immediately appeal to the Roman See, to which they may freely go without any delay or loss of their possessions. And while they have appealed to the aforesaid Roman mother Church, or requested to be heard by it, no one may presume to excommunicate them, seize their sees, take their possessions, or inflict any violence upon them [Col. 0022D], until their case has been concluded by authority of the Roman pontiff. If anyone presumes otherwise, it shall be null and without force.

For we do not presume this improperly; rather, you know well, Athanasius, that this was itself established in the Nicene synod and practiced by our predecessors. When you, Paul of Constantinople, Asclepius [Note: *Asclephas and Lucius*] of Gaza, and Lucian of Adrianople had been condemned by the Eastern bishops without consulting our predecessor Julius of holy memory, and fled to him as to the head of the whole world—as it has always been lawful for this holy See [Col. 0023A]—after he learned of their wickedness (Tripartite History IV.15, from Sozomen III.7) and your justice, he received you into communion. Caring for you all and acting by reason of the dignity of his own See, he restored to each of you his church.

He wrote to the Easterners, blaming them because they had not dealt rightly with innocent men, expelling them from their churches and failing to preserve the enactments of the Nicene Council. He ordered certain of them to appear before him on a specified day to give a clear account of such presumptions, and to demonstrate before them that he had issued a just decree concerning them. He also threatened that the brethren would no longer endure such actions, and that, unless they ceased from these presumptions, they would be removed from their own ranks.

By such a privilege of this holy See, you and your brethren recovered your own churches with all that belonged to them. From these and very many other proofs it is evident that no bishop who has appealed to this holy See or enlisted it as his defender ought to be condemned or stripped of his possessions until he has received judgment concerning himself from our apostolic authority (Martin I, session 2 of the Lateran Council)—that is, from Peter, prince of the apostles. For Christ Jesus alone entrusted this function to this holy See, that is, the Apostolic See, since he alone, before all others, was acknowledged as the aforesaid prince of the apostles and deserved to receive from Christ God, King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 16).

XX. Concerning the postponements for bishops [Col. 0023C], about which you have consulted us, we find various rules established by the Fathers. Some ordered that a year or six months be granted for repelling the machinations of accusers, preparing answers, securing witnesses, and seeking the counsel of bishops and friends; others ordered a year, and most agree with this. But I find no period shorter than six months accepted (see Council of Carthage III, c. 7), since these concessions are granted even to laypersons—how much more to the priests of the Lord!

For our predecessors and the other holy Fathers have repeatedly prohibited anyone from directing detractions against the priests of the Lord; how much more accusations not brought forth from the root of charity [Note: Above, at the beginning of this decretal, where the Nicene Council is cited]! “Be at rest,” they say, “and do not persecute those who perfectly minister to God, by whose prayers earthly wars are calmed, attacks of angels departing from God are repelled, and all corrupt demons are confounded through the constancy of prayer” (Tripartite History VII.9).

Postponements, therefore, must be granted not for a narrow time but for a long interval, so that the accused may prepare themselves, meet all those in communion throughout the provinces, prepare witnesses, and arm themselves fully against plotters.

XXI. Judges and accusers must be free from every suspicion (Hadrian 15) and desire to deliver their judgment from the root of charity. Therefore, after these things have been set forth both legally (Tripartite History IX.14, from Theodoret V.9) and canonically, we ask that the reverence of all Christians may rejoice together, with spiritual love and fear of the Lord intervening. Through this, human offense is removed and the building up of the churches is preferred above all things, so that all may labor more for the edification of brethren than for condemnation. For the Lord says: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

We have now given the rule (Damasus, Letter 2, from Tripartite History IX.15; from Theodoret V.10), and we know that it was given by our predecessors: that if anyone recognizes himself as a Christian, he should preserve what is known to have been handed down by the apostles. The apostle Paul says: “If anyone proclaims to you anything beyond what you have received, let him be accursed” [Col. 0024B] (Gal. 1).

For Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, granted the human race complete salvation through his own suffering, in order to free us (Rom. 8). And if God loved us so greatly that he did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all in order to free us, why do we not love brethren, or rashly judge them, when the aforesaid apostle says: “Do not judge one another, but rather judge this: not to put a stumbling block or an occasion of offense before a brother” (Rom. 14)?

For if those who love brethren are born of God and see God, what then shall those be who persecute them and endeavor to condemn them through disparagement, plotting, accusation, and hostility? If the former are children of God, then undoubtedly the latter are children of the devil, who always, “like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5), and so pursues brethren as to destroy them. Those, however, who refuse to help brethren acquire a greater burden of sins and become guilty of withholding the consolation of brotherhood.

“Woe,” says the prophet, “to him who gives his friend drink, adding his gall” (Hab. 2). And again Solomon, most wise, says: “For one who speaks iniquity cannot hide, nor shall the judgment which reproves him pass him by. For the wicked man’s thoughts shall be examined, and the hearing of his words shall come to God for the correction of his iniquities; because the ear of jealousy hears all things, and the tumult of murmurers shall not be hidden” (Wis. 1) [Note: Deusdedit of Cagliari, session 2, Lateran Council of 649].

Had they wished to embrace these things with their own sound understanding, they would not at all fall into reprobation. Rather, guarding against their words by fear of God [Col. 0024D], they would surely observe the devout definition of the holy Fathers without any presumptuous injury. For sacred utterance says: “Good counsel shall preserve you, and sound judgment shall guard you” (Prov. 2).

Such accusations and disparagements do not proceed spiritually from salutary springs toward the attainment of eternal life (Maurus of Cesena, letter in the same council). Therefore Blessed Paul fittingly admonishes us: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly” (Rom. 12). Let us persevere in the definition of piety. For those who pass it over are not merely falling away from their own support; they have also left a memorial of their folly for all, so that they could not remain concealed in the very matters in which they sinned. “For glory and disgrace are in speech, and a person’s fall is in his tongue” (Ecclus. 5).

Therefore it is fitting that this exposure of their reproaches be incorporated into our acts, so that you may no longer suffer such things while they sow tares and scandals, but may deserve to rejoice in your offices and doctrines [Col. 0025A]. Let those who do such things therefore be ashamed and hasten to withdraw themselves from such blasphemy [Note: “from this kind of blasphemy”], unless they wish to be separated from our priestly fellowship and torn away from the communion of the Christian people.

Although we could have spoken and written much more, and much that is necessary, concerning these matters—things found established in the decrees of the Apostolic See and by the apostles and their successors, namely our predecessors—nevertheless, it has seemed better to us to conclude the letter with prayer (Julius to the Church of Alexandria, Tripartite History IV.29).

May Almighty God, and his only-begotten Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, grant you this encouragement: that you may aid with all your strength all our brethren and fellow bishops suffering whatever tribulations; that, sympathizing with them, you may bear the cross of the same Lord and Savior; and that you may appear before all as his true disciples. Thus you and those with you may possess, here and in the future, the better things “which eye has not seen, nor has it entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2), through our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0025C] through whom and with whom be glory to Almighty God the Father unto ages of ages. Amen.

I wish you well, dearest brethren. Given on the Ides of February, in the consulship of Agarius and Julianus, most illustrious men. [Note: A fictitious name.]

## LETTER II OF POPE FELIX II TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS AND TO THE OTHER PRIESTS OF THE LORD

### On patiently enduring persecutions and tribulations

Felix, pope of the holy universal Church and, through the grace of God, bishop of the catholic and apostolic Church of the city of Rome, together with our holy council of most reverend priests assembled here with us (Pope Martin I, in the synodical letter of the Lateran Council), for the confirmation of the most devout doctrines of the catholic Church and the vindication of oppressed brethren—namely, our fellow bishops who hold the right faith of the Nicene Council and do not harass their brethren—to all our spiritual brethren, to the others consecrated to the Lord in the priestly college, and to the entire fullness of the catholic Church.

May grace and peace be multiplied to you in strengthening and communion of the Holy Spirit, so that, advancing in him from glory to glory, we may proclaim the virtues of him who called us from darkness into his marvelous light (1 Pet. 2), with whom there is no change [Col. 0026A] nor shadow of variation [Note: “of an instant”].

Brethren, we exhort you (Jas. 1) to bear persecutions and tribulations patiently, that you may be found sons of him whom you daily call Father, God in heaven; and that in him you may conquer all things, for he conquered all things for us: “He did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). Those who imitate God ought in every word and deed to imitate God (Maximus of Aquileia, session 4 of the same Lateran Council, held in 649). Therefore we ought to say what the Lord himself testified concerning himself: “The prince of this world is coming, and he shall find nothing in me” (John 14).

Those who persecute you and us have also come, since they cannot persecute you without us; for we are members of one God and, through his sanctification, possess one priesthood. In us they found nothing of their own; for whatever we are, we are by the grace of God. Yet they have irrationally endeavored to calumniate us for this very reason, as enemies are accustomed to do, hastening to conceal their madness in this way so that they may be able to overshadow truth with falsehood.

“For,” says the blessed apostle, “I wrote to you through many tears, not that you should be saddened, but that you might know how abundant is my love for you” (1 Cor. 2). Indeed, to disparage those who disparage us (Deusdedit of Cagliari, letter in the same place) is not good, lest, stirred by what is written, we make a contest out of injury [Note: “lest”]. We ought not at all to fear the reproach of men (Martin I, session 3 in the same place), nor be overcome by their insults; for the Lord commands us through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose hearts is my law” (Isa. 51). “Do not fear the reproach of men, nor dread their blasphemies” (Ps. 43).

Consider also what is written in the psalm: “Will not God search this out? For he knows the secrets of the heart,” and knows that the thoughts of such persons are vain. “Each has spoken vanity to his neighbor; with deceitful lips and a double heart they have spoken evil. The Lord shall destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks proud things; those who say, ‘Our lips are our own; who is lord over us?’” (Ps. 11). For if they kept these things in mind, they would never rush into such great wickedness.

For they do this not through sound and fatherly instruction (words of the same pope), but in order to exercise their vengeance upon the servants of God. It is written: “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes”; and, “There are ways that seem right to a man, but their end leads to death” (Prov. 12, 14). We who suffer these things must reserve them for God’s judgment (Third Roman Council under Symmachus), for he “will render to each according to his works” (Jer. 15). He also thundered through his ministers, saying: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. 12).

For your part, assist one another in right faith and with pure and good will; let none withdraw his hand from supplying his brother’s need. For, says the Lord, “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13). Hence he himself speaks through the prophet: “Behold how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132).

I mean a spiritual dwelling (Paul of Constantinople, letter of a Monothelite to Pope Theodore, session 4 of the Lateran Council): concord that is in God and unity of this delightful faith, according to the truth of the dwelling [Note: Other readings: “who”; “which”] that was especially adorned in Aaron and in those wearing priestly dignity, “like ointment upon the head,” irrigating the governing intellect and descending to the very furthest knowledge. For in this dwelling the Lord promised blessing and eternal life.

Embracing, therefore, the force of this prophetic utterance, we have set forth this present fraternal discourse, seeking nothing for ourselves through love, nor intending to seek it. For it is not good to disparage those who disparage us, or, according to the common saying, to drive out one stake with another stake. Far be it! Such things are not ours; may divinity therefore avert them. Our habits have not been taught to conquer in this way, but through patient long-suffering and a spirit of humility. For just as *nigella* is not cleansed by hardness—as we may speak prophetically (Dan. 3)—so neither is the soothed fruit of peaceful understanding pressed out by harshness.

For this reason we have endured the blows of words, so that at least gradually we may imitate him who deigned to humble himself for us, and by this wound may avoid the words of that final vengeance. Let us therefore hear and obey the preacher of the Church, who cries out with the clear voice of the Holy Spirit: “Let all things be done among you in love” (1 Cor. 16). Therefore, whether we inquire, merely speak, or merely are heard, let love intervene. Let there be some art for composing harmonious good and joining it together.

For, as we seek concerning God, it is necessary that, in a spirit of uprightness, reckoning the intentions of our minds, we dwell peacefully in the temple in him for the Lord’s sake, who spoke through the prophet: “Seek by seeking, and dwell with me” (Isa. 21, according to the Septuagint). For God has given us as a mirror to his people, and those appointed by God to obtain the priesthood ought so to move toward one another in humility of mind that those who look to us may be built up for the better, rather than—as it pains me to say—have the pathway of their feet shaken by our discord.

Let us bend ourselves toward concord [Note: “so that”] and be of one mind in love. Let us revere humility, through which loftiness of spirit is usually attained. If until now we have loved silence more than the chattering of words [Note: “have loved”], we considered this good, lest our written replies to yours should foster the fuel of injury and we should be judged faint-hearted by him who declared that all things must be directed toward love.

We prayed then that a guard might be set over our lips in the circumstance, and that we might conceive an unspoken rather than a spoken word [Note: “and attend to a word”]. Yet this too is a gift to me from the Lord, and “I became like one who does not hear, and who has no rebukes in his mouth” (Ps. 17). But because “there is a time to speak and a time to be silent” (Eccles. 3), I open speech and close the door through silence, appropriately praying: “Lord, you will open my lips, and I shall answer those who reproach me with a word” (Pss. 50, 118).

For although we were silent, we shall not always be silent, once the Lord opens to us the keys of speech. Therefore the *apocrisiaries*—envoys—sent at present by the blessedness of your brotherhood, after many conflicting discussions had been held between us concerning ecclesiastical inquiry, finally came to this: they urged and exhorted us to interpret the meaning of the one will of Christ our true God, and to send such an interpretation to your most sacred veneration.

We, accepting the admonition of the aforesaid venerable men in good conscience, and knowing also what the supreme authority of the apostles teaches—namely, to be ready to give an answer to everyone asking us for a reason for the hope that is in us (1 Pet. 3), tempering knowledge with the fear of God and gentleness—set forth our understanding concerning this inquiry alone through these words. We avoid and guard against superfluous exercise and wrangling over words [Col. 0028C], because of their weariness and the inappropriateness of the present time. We understand, utter, and say absolutely nothing other than what we have heard and learned from the holy and universal great apostles and their successors, and what our fathers related to us, and what we have preached after hearing it, as we press toward the heavenly calling.

Our purpose is that, where the establishment of peace abides for those who are in the contest of piety, the one good glory of an intercessor and a crown may be granted. We have been made manifest to God, who judges and approves all things. We do not stand quarrelsomely, do not look toward contradiction, and do not embrace empty favor. Rather, we acknowledge that we have made a resolution of this inquiry in the proposed word of God, trusting that the Lord God of peace will preserve our unity and love for one another in the glory of his most gracious majesty.

We and those with us send many greetings to all the brotherhood existing in Christ together with your blessedness. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Philemon [Note: A name unknown to the Roman fasti] and Atticus, most illustrious men.

## A.D. 368–384: FAUSTINUS AND MARCELLINUS, PRESBYTERS

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0029]

[Col. 0029A]

## ON FAUSTINUS AND MARCELLINUS

*(From Galland, Bibliotheca, vol. VII, pp. XIII–XV.)*
I. Among the earlier writers, Gennadius mentions the presbyter Faustinus [Note: [Col. 0029C] Gennad., *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 11.], whom he reports to have written seven books, addressed to the Empress Flaccilla, against the Arians and Macedonians. It is indeed surprising that, despite the clear and well-attested testimony of an author by no means insignificant, who was separated from the age of the Faustinus of whom we speak by only one century, there should have been writers—even of the first rank—who ascribed to Gregory of Baetica, bishop of Elvira, the work here praised by Gennadius. But in our own and the preceding age the true parent of the work has at last been recognized as our Faustinus [Note: [Col. 0029C] Tillem., *Mem. eccl.*, vol. VII, p. 767, note 6, on Lucifer; *Hist. des Emper.*, vol. V, p. 727, note 3, on Theodosius.]. Moreover, since he was a Luciferian, as we shall shortly say, he sufficiently reveals at the end of his work that he himself favored the tenets of that [Col. 0029B] sect [Note: [Col. 0029C] Faustin., *On the Trinity*, ch. VII, § 4, below, p. 459.]. This is Tillemont’s observation [Note: [Col. 0029C] Tillem., *Mem. eccl.* vol. VII, p. 526.]; although our Baronius understood the cited passage otherwise, supposing the author of the work to be Gregory of Elvira, on the basis of the title in the Roman edition published in 1575 by Achilles Statius [Note: [Col. 0029C] Baron., under the year 371, § 124.].

Faustinus, therefore, wrote seven books according to Gennadius—or rather, one book divided into seven chapters—against the Arians. He dedicated his work to the Empress Flaccilla, the first wife of the great Theodosius; and from the cited Baronius we learn that she died in the year 385 [Note: [Col. 0029C] Id., under the year 385, § 32.], an opinion accepted by Pagius [Note: [Col. 0029C] Pagi., under the year 385, § 6.] and Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0029C] Tillem., *Hist. des Emper.*, vol. V, p. 740, note 25.]. On coins she is called both Aelia Flacilla and Flaccilla [Note: [Col. 0029C] Patin., *Impp. Rom. Num.*, p. 491;—Mediob., *Impp. Rom. Num.*, p. 519;—Bandur., *Num. Impp. Rom.*, vol. II, pp. 515–517.], as in Gennadius; yet Gregory of Nyssa [Note: [Col. 0029C] Greg. Nyss., *Funeral Oration on Placilla*, works, vol. III, p. 524.], Theodoret [Col. 0029C] [Note: [Col. 0030C] Theodor., *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 19.], and Zosimus [Note: [Col. 0030C] Zosim., *New History*, book IV, p. 264, Oxford ed.] call her Placilla; while Socrates [Note: [Col. 0030C] Socrat., *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, ch. 31.] and Philostorgius [Note: [Col. 0030C] Philost., book X, ch. 7.] call her Placidia. Both are less correct, as Valesius shows [Note: [Col. 0030C] Vales., notes on Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, ch. 31.]. I would suppose that this gave rise to the error which crept into certain manuscript and printed copies, in which the work of the presbyter Faustinus is said to have been dedicated to Galla Placidia, who was apparently thought to have been the second wife of the elder Theodosius. [Col. 0030A] Yet writers call her only Galla, never Galla Placidia; on this matter Bandurius, after Du Cange, has written more [Note: [Col. 0030C] Bandur., *Numismata Imperatorum Romanorum*, vol. II, p. 566, note 1.].

II. However the matter may stand, the work of Faustinus of which we are speaking appeared at Rome in 1575 under the name of Gregory of Baetica. Of that edition Baronius says [Note: [Col. 0030C] Baron., on the *Roman Martyrology*, under 24 April, note f.]:

> “Our Achilles Statius, of praiseworthy memory, cleansed and published these commentaries of Gregory, encrusted with decay, buried in oblivion, and weakened by errors.”

This Roman exemplar was repeatedly printed under the same Gregory’s name. Yet in various older collections of the works of the ancient Fathers, the same work was restored to its author Faustinus. A letter to the Empress Flaccilla is prefixed; it survives entire [Col. 0030B] in both Basel *Orthodoxographi* and other libraries of the Fathers, as well as in the latest Lyons edition. Consequently, the care of the Oxford editor seems less commendable: when he brought Faustinus’s works before the public from the Sheldonian Theatre in 1678, he presented that same letter mutilated for the most part, apparently following the Paris edition of 1644, where only the final portion of that letter occurs.

III. Faustinus’s *Faith Offered to the Emperor Theodosius* follows the book against the Arians. The Oxford editor, whose edition (*ekdosis*, “publication”) we have followed in preference to the others, took it from the Code of Canons which Quesnel appended to the works of St. Leo [Note: [Col. 0030C] *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*, ch. 38.], giving it this title: “A Code of Ecclesiastical Canons and Constitutions of the Holy Apostolic See.” Learned men, however—Coutant [Note: [Col. 0030C] Coutant, preface to the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, part II, § 3, p. LXVII ff.] and the Ballerini brothers [Note: [Col. 0030C] Baller., works of St. Leo, vol. III, pp. 753 ff.]—have clearly demonstrated that this was not a code of the Roman [Col. 0030C] Church, and consequently that the title prefixed to it by Quesnel in no way suits that code. Accordingly, these words must be corrected: “The Faith . . . received into the Code of Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church,” which are appended to the title of Faustinus’s tract on the faith [Note: [Col. 0030C] Faust., see below, p. 460.].

Moreover, this [Col. 0031A] tract is assigned to Faustinus on the authority of the Thuanus and Vienna manuscripts; and it also survives in an old Reichenau manuscript examined by Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0031D] Ballerin., cited place, p. 278, n. 1.]. The editor of that code thinks that it was written between 379 and 381, when Faustinus was living at Eleutheropolis, where he complains that he was harassed by Turbonus, bishop of that city [Note: [Col. 0031D] Marcellinus and Faustinus, *Petitionary Tract*, § 30, below, p. 472.]: “From this,” he says, “perhaps arose the occasion for composing a confession of faith and sending it to Theodosius, whose name and authority one may readily suppose that the bishop employed against the schismatics.”

IV. “Faustinus also wrote a book which, with a certain presbyter Marcellinus, he presented to the Emperors Valentinian and Arcadius in defense of his own party. From it it is shown that he agreed with the Luciferian schism. [Col. 0031B] For in their book he censures Hilary of Poitiers and Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, as though they had served the Church badly by receiving back into communion and the priesthood, for the sake of recovering peace, bishops who had broken faith. This displeased the Luciferians as much as it displeased the Novatians to receive repentant apostates.” These are the words of Gennadius [Note: [Col. 0031D] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 16.]. Concerning Marcellinus, see the uncertain author who appended a supplement to Isidore and Ildefonsus [Note: [Col. 0031D] *Tract on the Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 12.].

This tract, addressed to the Emperors Valentinian II, Theodosius, and Arcadius, is learned from the context to have been presented at Constantinople, and thus to Theodosius. For these Luciferian presbyters, speaking of Bishop Alexander, through whose prayers the impious Arius died [Note: [Col. 0031D] Marcellinus and Faustinus, *Petitionary Tract*, § 3, below, p. 463.], say: [Col. 0031C] “Not that Alexander who was bishop in Alexandria, a man of divine faith, . . . but this Alexander who was in THIS CITY OF CONSTANTINOPLE, himself also a remarkable bishop,” etc. This circumstance of place is confirmed by the rescript of Theodosius alone appended at the end of the tract.

As to the time when this tract was written, it seems to be confined to the years 383 and 384. First, Arcadius, one of the three emperors to whom this petitionary tract was offered, had not yet been proclaimed Augustus by his father Theodosius before the year 383, as Pagius demonstrates after Baronius [Note: [Col. 0031D] Baron., under the year 383, § 22; Pagi., under the year 383, § 12.]. Next, it appears to have been written while Damasus, Roman pontiff, was still alive, from these words read in it [Col. 0031D] [Note: [Col. 0031D] Marcellinus and Faustinus, cited place, § 23, p. 470.]: “But even RECENTLY,” say the Luciferian presbyters, “he [Damasus] attempted grievously to persecute the most blessed Ephesius,” etc. This is the opinion of Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0031D] Tillem., *Mem. eccl.*, vol. VII, p. 525.] and Mazocchi [Note: [Col. 0032D] Mazoch., *Commentary on the Neapolitan Calendar*, vol. II, p. 581.]. Since holy Damasus died at the end of the year [Col. 0032A] 384, the same tract could readily have been offered in that very year; or at least, to speak with the learned man [Note: [Col. 0032D] Mazoch., *Commentary on the Neapolitan Calendar*, vol. II, p. 581.], it was presented in 383, but the rescript of Theodosius found at the end of the tract, addressed to Cynegius, praetorian prefect, happened to be deferred until the following year, 384, when Cynegius held that office from the middle of January [Note: [Col. 0032D] See the *Prosopography of the Theodosian Code*, vol. VI, part I, p. 47.]. This is especially likely if the emperor thought that such a business required some examination of the case and ought not to be dispatched summarily; this is the bearing of Digest IX, § 1, *On the Office of Proconsuls*. Thus, whether in 383 or 384, Marcellinus and Faustinus presented this tract in defense of the Luciferian cause.

V. We must now speak of the preface prefixed to that [Col. 0032B] tract, which is wholly concerned with the Ursinian schism against Damasus. Tillemont conjectures concerning this preface [Note: [Col. 0032D] Tillem., *Mem. eccl.*, vol. VII, p. 766, note 5 on Lucifer.] that it has nothing in common with the tract, and accordingly suspects that it is either the preface of another work or, if it does belong to this tract, a later addition by an altogether different author. But Mazocchi, a most learned man, considered these conjectures less sound; having shown their weakness, he summarizes his own opinion thus [Note: [Col. 0032D] Mazoch., cited place, pp. 583 ff.]:

> “The style, which is exactly the same in both parts, plainly cries out that the preface proceeded from the same authors as the tract. Yet it was not written and prefixed to this tract before Theodosius, having received it, finally issued his rescript in favor of Marcellinus and Faustinus. [Col. 0032C] For then those two men, rejoicing at their successful outcome, since they judged it advantageous to themselves that the tract should be circulated publicly together with the appended rescript, thought that readers should be prepared by this very preface with an account of the beginnings of their calamity, so as to accomplish this more fittingly. For everyone knew at that time that these presbyters were Luciferians, and the tract openly professes it. But not everyone knew that they had formerly been Ursinians and had contended against Damasus twenty years earlier; and those who did know it, especially now that the schism had been quieted, were more favorably inclined toward the cause of Damasus than of Ursinus.
>
> “Therefore, in this prologue they repeat the whole matter from the beginning, and throughout the preface weave a lengthy narrative, though embellished in their own manner, of events long ago enacted in the rupture between Damasus and Ursinus, in which they themselves had taken part. [Col. 0032D] For that was the beginning of their calamity. Finally expelled from Rome, they joined themselves to the Luciferians, as a last resort—unless you prefer to think that [Col. 0033A] they had been Luciferians even before, while they were still at Rome. However this may be, the continuity (*synecheia*) of the preface with the tract—that is, the connection of the Ursinian rupture, of which the preface alone treats, with the Luciferian cause, which alone they defend in the tract—makes itself more than sufficiently clear to the reader at the end of the preface; I am surprised that Tillemont did not notice it. ‘Thereafter,’ they say [Note: [Col. 0033D] Preface to the *Petitionary Tract*, § 4, below, p. 462.], ‘the presbyters of the Ursinian party were afflicted in diverse ways and scattered through exiles and foreign places. From among them, the presbyters MARCELLINUS and FAUSTINUS’—that is, the authors both of the tract and of the preface, formerly Ursinians but now Luciferians, as what follows sufficiently makes clear—‘offered petitions to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, as follows, concerning the confession of the true faith’ (from which the Luciferians excluded others, as though they alone were Catholics), ‘the presentation’ (that is, the granting) ‘of sacred [Col. 0033B] communion’ (namely, to whom communion ought to be granted and to whom denied), ‘and the persecution of those opposing the truth.’ Thus far the preface, after which the tract begins. What could be adduced more clearly to join the preface to the tract now extant? Could an author by these words, which certainly contain the essence of Luciferian poison, have prefaced some other tract setting forth the petitions of Ursinians against the Damasian party?”

Thus far the learned man.

VI. Although from what has been said thus far concerning the petitionary tract offered to Theodosius and the other partners in imperial rule, it is sufficiently established whose composition are the things recounted in it by the Luciferian presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus, nevertheless, in order that anyone approaching its reading may become more cautious and circumspect, [Col. 0033C] it will not be useless to set forth what Sirmond, a distinguished man and its first editor, prefaced concerning the same tract. His words are as follows:

> “Those who once stirred up the schism at Rome against Damasus with Ursinus were either Luciferians, or the Luciferians joined themselves to them, and troubled the Church with a double rupture. How turbulent they were in the cause of Ursinus, and how importunately they wearied the ears of magistrates and emperors, is declared by the rescripts preserved in the ecclesiastical annals: those of Valentinian to Praetextatus, Olybrius, and Ampelius, prefects of the City, and of Gratian to Aquilinus, the vicar. The synodical letters of the Councils of Aquileia and Rome, published in the appendix to the Theodosian Code, also bear witness: [Col. 0033D] they assert the innocence and integrity of Damasus and do not conceal the fury and intrigues of Ursinus. This book of two of their presbyters displays no less shamelessness and insolence in the Luciferians. By their deceitful representation they not only insinuate themselves into the favor of the Emperor Theodosius, but with their dog-like eloquence, as Jerome calls it, so tear to pieces all orthodox persons who opposed them that some will not be lacking who judge it unworthy for that reason to be brought into public light. But you, reader, will, I hope, think otherwise; and by experience [Col. 0034A] will discover that even an unpraiseworthy work has its value, since its authors teach not a few things about themselves and others which it is useful to know and which are not known from elsewhere.”

Thus far he. Baronius had previously expressed nearly the same judgment [Note: [Col. 0033D] Baron., under the year 367, § 14.]. We too have touched upon certain points on this subject elsewhere, where we spoke of St. Damasus [Note: [Col. 0033D] Prolegomena to vol. VI of the *Library of the Fathers*, ch. 4, § 2, p. IX.]. Finally, the learned editor of Sirmond’s works compared the same *Petitionary Tract* with a manuscript in the Colbertine Library and supplied variant readings from it; likewise, he supplied some readings from the Remigian manuscript, which the eminent Mabillon made available to him. Among these readings may be seen a few observations by the distinguished Mazocchi. As for the remaining annotations on the works of Faustinus, let the fair and learned reader judge.

[Col. 0034B]

## ON FAUSTINUS

From Schoenemann, *Library*, vol. I, pp. 547–554.

### § 1. Life

A Luciferian presbyter, who, together with Marcellinus, likewise a presbyter, defended the cause of his sect in a tract presented about the year 384 to the Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius. About twenty years earlier he had also stood against Damasus with the Ursinians, with whom the Luciferians were then closely allied.
