For this reason the tract—or rather the preface prefixed to it—bears manifest traces of hatred toward Damasus and accuses him and his associates of many disgraceful and unjust acts; how far such charges accord with truth is commonly questioned. But this I know for certain: reading this writing itself will diminish the esteem and credibility of its authors among all fair-minded [Col. 0034C] and honorable persons.

### § 2. Writings

Besides the *Petitionary Tract* already mentioned, of which some parts are said also to belong to Marcellinus, the Preface which usually precedes it undoubtedly proceeds from the same authors. For although it appears to have nothing in common with the tract, and Tillemont thought it should be separated from it as the preface of another work or the product of a different author, nevertheless an explanation of this difference is not lacking; nor is Gallandius unjustly considered to have embraced Mazocchi’s acute opinion.

Faustinus’s *Faith Offered to the Emperor Theodosius*. Written, in Quesnel’s view, [Col. 0034D] between 379 and 381, when Faustinus was staying at Eleutheropolis, where he complains that he was harassed by Turbonus, bishop of that city.

Faustinus’s seven books *On the Trinity, or On the Faith against the Arians, to the Empress Flaccilla*—or rather, one book divided into seven chapters. Written before 385, the year in which Flaccilla, first wife of Theodosius the Great, is known to have died. Gennadius expressly assigns it to Faustinus [Note: [Col. 0034D] *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 11: he says that he “wrote seven books against the Arians and Macedonians, addressed to the person of Queen Flaccilla.”]; although there were some in more recent times [Col. 0035A] who attributed it to Gregory of Baetica, bishop of Elvira.

### § 3. Editions

Faustinus’s minor works appeared gradually and separately, and were gathered together rather late in the Oxford edition and in Gallandius’s recent edition. First, in 1555, Faustinus’s books *On the Trinity* were published by Johann Herold of Basel; afterward, under the name of Gregory of Baetica, they were issued partly in a separate volume by Achilles Statius and partly in certain Libraries of the Fathers. They were soon received into other collections under the name of their true author. The *Petitionary Tract*, with its preface, was finally edited by Jacques Sirmond in 1650; and half a century later Quesnel published the *Faith Offered to Theodosius* among the Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church.

### SIXTEENTH CENTURY

[Col. 0035B]

**1555.** Basel, at the press of Heinrich Petri, folio. Faustinus’s book *On Faith against the Arians*, in the *Orthodoxographi* of Basel’s Johann Herold, no. 31.

**1569.** Basel, from the same press, folio. The same book among the *Monuments of the Orthodox Writers* of Johann Jacob Grynaeus, pp. 1998–2028.

**1575.** Rome, in the buildings of the Roman People, quarto. *The Book on the Trinity, or on the Faith, of Gregory of Baetica, bishop of the see of Elvira*, now first published through the efforts of Achilles Statius; Catalogue of the Bunau Library.

Paris, at the press of Michel Sonnius, folio. *The Book on the Trinity and Faith of Gregory of Baetica*, in vol. VIII of Bignon’s *Library of the Fathers*, p. 766, occupying the final place. But Ittigius noted that in the same [Col. 0035C] Library, vol. V, p. 716, exactly the same book exists under the name of Faustinus himself, titled *The Work of Faustinus on Faith against the Arians* [Note: [Col. 0035D] *On the Libraries of the Fathers*, p. 37; cf. p. 44.].

**1577.** Cologne, through Maternus Cholinus, octavo. The same book from Achilles Statius’s edition; Catalogue of the Bunau Library.

**1589.** Paris, folio. *Book of Gregory of Baetica, bishop of the see of Illiberis, to the Empress Galla Placidia, on the Trinity and Faith against the Arians*, in the second edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. IV, p. 1273. Yet in the same volume, p. 839, and indeed before this, appears *The Work of Bishop Faustinus on Faith against the Arians*. Fabricius observed [Note: [Col. 0036D] *Latin Library of the Middle and Lower Ages*, Mansi ed., vol. II, p. 146.] that in the copy published under Gregory of Baetica’s name by the first and second editions of the *Library of the Fathers*, the letter [Col. 0035D] to Flaccilla lacks its earlier part; whereas in the *Orthodoxographi* and all collections in which it was published under Faustinus’s name—and thus in these very editions of the *Library of the Fathers*—it is complete. It may therefore readily be conjectured that this defect belongs to Achilles Statius’s edition, whence it was undoubtedly brought, without any care or scrutiny, into the first editions of the Libraries as though it were a book different from Faustinus’s minor work.

### SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

**1610.** Paris, folio. *Book of Bishop Faustinus on Faith against the Arians*, in vol. IV of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 765.

[Col. 0036A]

**1618.** Cologne, folio. *Book of Deacon Faustinus on the Trinity, or on Faith against the Arians*, a book also published under the name of Gregory of Baetica; in vol. IV of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 545.

**1624.** Paris, folio. *Book of Bishop Faustinus on Faith against the Arians*, in vol. IV of the fourth edition of the *Library of the Fathers*.

**1644–1654.** Paris, at three booksellers, folio. The same book in vol. IV of the fifth edition of the *Library of the Fathers*. Here too the preface to Flaccilla appears mutilated for the greater part, as Gallandius observes; he therefore thinks that the Oxford edition was copied from it.

**1650.** Paris, at the press of Sébastien and Gabriel Cramoisy, octavo. *The Petitionary Tract of Marcellinus and Faustinus, presbyters of Ursinus’s party, against Damasus, to the Emperors [Col. 0036B] Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius*; now first brought to light through the work of Jacques Sirmond, priest of the Society of Jesus; Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, vol. I, 393, under the eighth century.

A Preface *On the Schism of Ursinus* is prefixed, and the Rescript of Theodosius in favor of the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus is appended. Sirmond’s brief and concise preface lucidly sets forth the subject of the book and of the entire cause, and has appended to it ancient testimonies concerning the controversy between Damasus and Ursinus.

**1675.** Paris, Jean-Baptiste Coignard, quarto. *Faith of the Presbyter Faustinus Sent to the Emperor Theodosius*. Edited by Paschasius Quesnel among the *Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church*, appended to the works of Leo the Great, vol. II, p. [Col. 0036C] 138.

**1677.** Lyons, at the press of the Anissons, folio. *Book of Faustinus, deacon or presbyter, on the Trinity or on Faith against the Arians*. Added was the *Petitionary Tract to the Emperors*, with Theodosius’s rescript, first edited by Sirmond, in vol. V of the *Great Library of the Fathers*, pp. 637–661.

**1678.** Oxford, from the Sheldonian Theatre, octavo. *Works of Faustinus the Presbyter, a Writer of the Fourth Century and a Most Vigorous Defender of Orthodox Faith against the Arians.*

Included are:

1. *The Faith of the Presbyter Faustinus, sent to the Emperor Theodosius and received into the Code of Canons of the Roman Church*;
2. *The Petitionary Tract of Marcellinus and Faustinus*, with the preface *On the Schism of Ursinus* and Theodosius’s Rescript, pp. 1–61;
3. the book *On the Trinity* to Flaccilla (the title at the beginning of the book itself reads “to Galla Placidia”), [Col. 0036D] pp. 65–161.

Notes elucidating historical matters were added to each tract. Besides the preface, there is prefixed a notice concerning Marcellinus from the *Fourteen Lives* by an uncertain author, attached to the Catalogue of Sts. Isidore and Ildefonsus. The preface to Flaccilla is represented here greatly abbreviated, beginning with the words: “Let us begin, therefore, obediently.”

**1696.** Paris, Royal Printing House, folio. The *Petitionary Tract*, from Sirmond’s edition, in his *Works*, vol. I, pp. 230–262. The editor of Sirmond’s works compared it with a manuscript from the Colbertine Library and supplied variant readings from it, as well as some from [Col. 0037A] the Remigian manuscript, which Mabillon had made available to him.

**1700.** Lyons, folio. *Faith of the Presbyter Faustinus Sent to the Emperor Theodosius*, in the *Code of Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church* edited by Quesnel, in the Appendix to the Works of Leo the Great, vol. II, p. 73, ch. 38.

### EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

**1757.** Venice, folio. *Faith of the Presbyter Faustinus Sent to the Emperor Theodosius*, in the *Code of Canons and Ecclesiastical Constitutions of the Apostolic See*, appended to the Works of Leo by the Ballerini brothers, vol. III, p. 278.

[Col. 0038A]

**1770.** Venice, from the press of Giovanni Battista Albrizzi, folio. *Works of Faustinus the Presbyter*. Also included is the *Petitionary Tract of Faustinus and Marcellinus to the Emperors*, edited by Andrea Gallandius, in the *Library of the Fathers, Authors, and Ancient Saints of the Church*, vol. VIII, pp. 441–474.

The books *On the Trinity* occupy first place, then follows the *Faith Sent to Theodosius*, and finally the *Petitionary Tract*. Besides variants drawn from manuscripts by various editors, there were added certain annotations of Mazocchi from the work cited above and certain conjectures of Gallandius. Most learned prolegomena concerning Marcellinus and Faustinus are also included: Prolegomena, ch. 10, pp. XIII–XV.

[Col. 0037]

# FAUSTINUS THE PRESBYTER, TO GALLA PLACIDIA [Note: [Col. 0037D] Alternatively, and more correctly with Gennadius: “to Flaccilla.”] ON THE TRINITY, OR ON FAITH AGAINST THE ARIANS. (C)

## FAUSTINUS TO THE EMPRESS FLACCILLA

[Col. 0037B]

The Roman world beholds you as its queen; and because there is now nothing remaining by which you may grow further in human affairs, not content with earthly exaltations, you desire through holy faith in God to possess heavenly things, which the true Son of God promises to those who piously believe in him. And you labor at this as one of the wisest of women, understanding that all this exaltation of royal power will profit nothing unless you strive, by knowledge and defense of the true faith, to attain heavenly glory.

Yet it is evident how pleasing you are to Christ, our God and Lord, who granted this kingdom to you; for by anxious inquiry you seek how those propositions may be resolved which the Arians, in their interpretations of sacred Scripture, set against Catholics. Possessing the disposition of true faith, [Col. 0037C] you desire, so far as possible, to understand what you faithfully believe. For the devout soul is then more richly fed, as if by divine feasts, when it understands what it believes.

And though you abhor the impious utterances of heretics, you nevertheless desire to be instructed against them by religious study, so that you may reject their reasoning also; lest what you abhor should appear to arise from presumption based on royal power, rather than from proof. But though you see me unequal to so pious, necessary, and beautiful a desire of yours, I nevertheless do not dare, in resistance, to refuse it. For I confess that on the one hand the consciousness of my unfitness and my lack of skill in unadorned speech so overwhelms me that I should be silent; on the other, the zeal of faith judges it dangerous if I should be silent. For how can it fail to seem dangerous, if, when challenged by conscience to speak against an impious enemy, [Col. 0037D] we turn our backs, as it were, through modesty? Especially since, in a matter of faith, elevation of language is not required, when the divine testimonies themselves alone suffice, and accomplish more than any more copious eloquence.

Nor ought consciousness of faults to be considered, since it is rather relieved if one does not fear first to confess God, after the example of that Gospel thief who, on the very day on which he confessed God, deserved on that same day to enter paradise with him whom he had confessed. Let us begin, therefore, obedient to your most devout commands, to engage the adversary—not relying on our own strength, but confident in the protective aid of the Savior—against whom the impiety of heretics wages war in the manner of Gentiles and with the fury of Jews.

But because in the things which you deigned to write in the person of the heretics I saw many matters confused, so that you seemed to me not fully to know what the Arians assert, I judged it better first to make plainly and clearly known how they believe, and how they ensnare simple souls by ambiguity of expression; especially when, under a shared confession, [Col. 0038C] they commend their impious words. For only then is a faithful reply evident for refutation, if the impious evasiveness of the sacrilegious sect has first been exposed.

# CHAPTER ONE. On the Impious Profession of the Arians

I. Arian impiety [Note: [Col. 0037D] “It indeed asserts many things with us in the same words,” [Col. 0038D] omitted.] asserts many things together with us in the same words, though not with the same meanings, when it is called upon to confess the divine faith. For it gives voice, in the same terms as we do, to God the Father, to God the Son, to all things made by God the Father through the Son, and to the Son begotten before the ages. Yet although it agrees with us in these words, it nevertheless departs from the pious understanding of the Catholic Church by sacrilegious interpretations of the words [Note: [Col. 0038D] Breaks off.], calling him Father in such a way [Col. 0038D] as to deny that he truly begot; and likewise pronouncing him Son in such a way that, in its view, he is Son by adoption, not by nature—that is, assumed from elsewhere into the name of Son, not truly begotten of God the Father.

For although it admits that the Son was born before the ages, it nevertheless assigns him a beginning, saying, “There was when he was not.” It also says that all things were made through him, but in such a way as to assert that he was established out of things that did not exist, because it has presumed that he was not truly begotten of God the Father. Hence it wishes men to be persuaded that Christ is indeed God, but not true God, since a beginning is ascribed to him; and that he is Son in such a way as to be understood to have been made rather than born. For if he was not truly born of the Father but established from nothing, then for this reason also it believes him [Note: [Col. 0039D] Alternatively: “changeable.”] mutable, because in its faith he is not true God and not a true Son.

To commend these impious opinions among the ignorant or simple, it also adduces, as it thinks, testimonies from the divine Scriptures, saying that this is proved from the person of Wisdom [Note: [Col. 0039D] Brought forward.]: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works” (Prov. 8:22). The Apostle also confirms that Christ is wisdom, saying: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). Therefore, it says, it is established that Christ, who according to the Apostle’s interpretation is wisdom, is a creature; and, it adds, it follows that he is not true God, since he is a creature; nor now a true Son, since he was not begotten by God [Note: [Col. 0039D] “Although he was created.”] but created. Therefore, “there was when he was not.”

II. These are the weapons of wickedness set before us, against which we are summoned [Note: [Col. 0040D] “We beseech.”] to proceed, so that the impiety of the opposing assertion may be exposed—not, as we have said, by our own ability, but by God’s grace always assisting pious endeavors. Only, I ask, do not be wearied by plain speech; rather, attentive to the force of the matters, give your judgment for truth. We do not [Note: [Col. 0040D] “We have written.”] write this as a book, but fight, as it were with the adversary present, through definite arguments.

And first, against their saying, “There was [Col. 0039C] when he was not,” we must answer that he has always existed, and set against it the testimony of the Gospel, where John says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). For just as Christ is the wisdom of God and the power of God, so too he is the Word of God. Therefore, when he says, “In the beginning was the Word,” how does Arian impiety say, “There was when he was not”? “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word”; he did not say, “In the beginning the Word was made.” And certainly that which was in the beginning must be believed always to have existed.

For if, as impiety supposes, the Son is a creature, divine Scripture would without doubt have disclosed at the beginning that very fact—that he was made—according to the pattern in which Moses also spoke [Note: [Col. 0040D] In writing.] when saying: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” For if the Son of God were also a creature, John would have said: “In the beginning the Word was made.” But the Evangelist—or rather, the Holy Spirit through the Evangelist—foresaw people of impious mind who would say concerning the Son, “There was when he was not”; and therefore he began thus: “In the beginning was the Word.” For nothing is prior to him who is found before the beginning.

The divine Scriptures were published in order that we might direct our faith according to their meaning, not that we might insert our own opinions into their sacred expressions. Let them consider whether there are certain propositions which, by their obscurity, are thought to afford occasion for ambiguity; certainly in this proposition there is no occasion for ambiguity [Col. 0040A] at all. An interpreter is not permitted to think otherwise than what is written; nor is there any need now to introduce our own opinions. For full knowledge in receiving faith, it is enough that we recite the divine words: “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word.” Is there here any notion of time, any suspicion of ages, or any interval of a point or of any moment, such that you dare to say, “There was when he was not”?

III. “In the beginning was the Word”; and lest perhaps you understand “word” as the function of one speaking, it follows: “and the Word was with God.” He did not say, “the word which God spoke,” but “and the Word was with God.” Finally, he himself explained what the Word is, saying: “and the Word was [Col. 0040B] God.” If in the beginning the Word was, and this same Word was with God, and the Word was God, the design of impiety is confounded. For this passage proves that Christ, the Son of God, both has always existed, has always been inseparable from the Father, and has always been God. For just as he is without beginning when it is said, “In the beginning was,” so also, when it is said that “he was with God,” his inseparability from the Father is declared to be without beginning. And when this Word is defined as God, there is no ambiguity that he is believed to be God without beginning. For the phrase first put forward, “In the beginning,” must be referred to everything: that is, “In the beginning was the Word”; and when it follows, “and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” “in the beginning” must undoubtedly be understood. Finally, he himself concludes in this way, saying: “This was in the beginning with God.” How then was there “when he was not,” he who always is? How is he “from things not existing” [Col. 0040C], who is always with the Father? How is he a creature, who is always God—indeed, through whom the whole creation exists? For it follows: “All things were made through him.” How was he “made from things not existing,” through whom all things were made? For if he too was made, how were all things made through him? For while being made, one who did not exist cannot be his own author. Therefore he through whom all things were made must be believed unmade; for it is vain and absurd to say that he himself, when he did not exist, was made by himself.

IV. Paul likewise teaches that Christ has always existed, is God, and is equal to the Father. For then he is truly God, when he is equal to the Father; since he would not be called equal unless he were held to be truly God. It is an injury to the true God if one equal to him is not called true God [Col. 0040D]. Accordingly, he sets forth in his Epistle: “For let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God [constituted], did not deem equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:5–7). If Christ is truly man when he takes the form of a servant, he is likewise truly God when he is declared to be in the form of God; nor would Paul call him equal for any other reason than to have it understood that in the form of God he is true God. And he who is true God surely always exists; and of him who is always God it cannot be said, “There was when he was not.”

[Col. 0041A] The Apostle Paul also says that all things were made through him, writing: “For in him were created all things, whether in heaven or on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers: all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things” (Col. 1:16–17). Therefore he always is, through whom and in whom all things were made. The Psalmist also sings: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). Yet he did not say that Wisdom itself was made, because the Apostle too, when he says, “and he is before all things,” denies that he was made. For if he had wished one who was not to be believed made, he would have written, “and he also was made before all things.” But when he says, “and he is before all things,” he gives a beginning to all things of which he is prior—indeed, their maker; but he himself is without beginning, being remembered as existing before all things, not as made before them. Again the Apostle says: “One God [Col. 0041B], the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6). Here too, when he says that all things are through Christ, he most plainly distinguishes the Maker from things made, and makes it impossible for the nature of a creature to be understood in him who made all things.

V. But let us see whether Moses too taught this same thing which the Apostles proclaimed: namely, that all things were made from God through the Son. Among other things, when he recounts the making of the world, he says: “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide water from water’; and it was so. And God made the firmament, and God divided the water in the middle” (Gen. 1:6). When he says, “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament,’” the person of the Father is to be understood in the one speaking [Col. 0041C]; but when he says, “And God made,” the person of the Son is to be understood in the one making. For unless you think this is to be understood thus, the apostolic assertion will be endangered, which says: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him.” Unless, then, you believe that the whole fabric of the world was made through the Son—indeed, all things invisible as well as visible—how can you receive in faith the Apostle’s saying, “One Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things,” and also that which we cited above, “for in him were created all things,” and likewise, “You have made all things in wisdom”?

John also pursued this point: “All things were made through him.” How can they be “all things,” if you deny that the statement, “and God made the firmament” [Col. 0041D], and “God divided the water in the middle,” was spoken of the Son of God? Therefore Moses too presents the Son as Maker, not as made. For if, by revelation of the Holy Spirit, he had learned that the Son was made, he would have mentioned, among the other things which he described as made, that he himself had first been made.

VI. But he continues more conclusively below, where the inhabitant of the now-formed world is to be made: “And God said, ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness’” (Gen. 1:26). For it is not the speech of one person to say, “Let us make according to our image and likeness”; nor is it the speech of differing divinity. For the plurality of these words—namely, “let us make” and “our”—signifies the persons of Father and Son [Col. 0042A]. But because he says “image” in the singular, the one divinity, the one power of both persons, is made manifest. If Christ is a creature, how is he employed as God’s partner in the work? For “let us make” is spoken to him. If he is not a true Son, how is there one image shared by him and the Father? An adopted son does not have the image of the adopter. He may indeed have a benefaction, but he cannot possess the nature of the image.

I know that there are distinctions among images, which it would be lengthy and unnecessary to pursue now. But I maintain what bears upon the case, saying: in this passage there is no distinction of image, where one image of Father and Son is declared. For he did not say, “Let us make according to our images,” but “according to our image.” And lest perhaps, with stupid mind, whoever you are, heretic, [Col. 0042B] you should usurp even the claim that “let us make” could have been said of one person, so that it might be an inward inclination of one thinking to himself rather than a designation of persons, it follows: “And God made man; according to the image of God he made him” (ibid., v. 27). Whoever does not see what has been set plainly in the light is blind. “God,” he says, “made; according to the image of God he made.” Is it not utterly clear that already then the Holy Spirit, through Moses, was treating of the evangelical mysteries, saying “God and God,” yet not two gods, because Father and Son have one image? And how providently all things were set forth! Holy Scripture declares “God and God” in order to exclude Sabellius, who maintained that Father and Son are one person; and lest it introduce two gods, amid the words whose plural sense signifies the persons, it inserted one image [Col. 0042C]. You will find this to be so if you attend to the testimony saying, “Let us make man according to our image.” What are you doing, Arian impiety? If Christ is a creature, how can creature and Creator have one image?

VII. [Note: This period is placed above at this point in Faustinus under “Person.”] But lest Arius again, under cover of the persons, should introduce differences of natures, diversity of nature does not admit a sharing of one form. There are many utterances in the books of Moses by which the impious may be refuted concerning the Son—indeed, concerning the Father as well. For how does this impiety not also strike at the Father, when it is exercised against the Son in a profane spirit [Note: and against the Son], since they take from the Father what truly belongs to the Father by taking from the Son what truly belongs to the Son? For how is he truly Father who, according to them, has not begotten? How is Christ truly Son [Col. 0042D], whom they deny to have been truly begotten from him?

But, as I said, there are many utterances in Moses’ books by which this impiety of theirs may be refuted. Yet because we are not pursuing these matters with the thoroughness of one writing a book, but rather, as if in a memorandum, rapidly sketching out certain fixed heads [Note: “we taste of,” or “we outline”], so that we may seem in some fashion to have obeyed your command, the other utterances must be passed over—especially because in divine utterances the number of testimonies is not what must be sought, but their authority, which is sufficient even if it is brought forward in one utterance. For the present, it is enough that in this one chapter Moses agrees with the Gospels [Col. 0043A] and the Apostles. Moses proclaims God and God. As we spoke above [Note: “Does he speak?”] concerning the testimony from Genesis, so John too proclaimed God and God, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). No one has said “two gods,” although he said “God and God”; no one has failed to proclaim one image of Father and Son, and therefore Catholic faith knows how to confess one God—yet not so that, by confession of [Note: “one God, the Son”] one God, the Son is denied to be what God is. For as the Father is God, so also the Son is God. If, however, the Son is not God in the same way as the Father is God, how is their image one according to Moses? Or how, according to Paul, is Christ, existing in the form of God, equal to God?

VIII. And when John declares that the Word, who is God, was in the beginning with God [Col. 0043B], not outside God, he seems to me by this inseparability of the Word of God from God to signify the same thing as is signified by the image and the form. For if the inseparability of Father and Son is shown by one image and the same form, why should it not be believed that, when John proclaims the inseparability of God and God by saying, “and the Word was with God,” and “this was in the beginning with God,” he signifies the one image and the same form of Father and Son?

Certainly this sense might seem ambiguous, if the same Evangelist had not pursued this very point a little further more plainly, saying: “and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (ibid., v. 14). As the image is one and the form the same, so [Col. 0043C] the Son’s glory is not different from that which belongs to the Father. Meanwhile, you who call Christ Son by adoption, how do you understand his glory as “of the only-begotten from the Father”? If you profess that there are several sons of God by adoption, and if Christ too is adopted, how is he only-begotten from the Father, when there are also other sons through adoption? But if he is truly only-begotten from the Father because he alone is truly begotten from the Father himself, how is he alleged to be adopted, when an adopted son cannot, among several adopted sons, possess the proper status of one only-begotten from the Father?

Moreover, though they are adopted, it was never said of any of them: “and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.” But it was said of Christ alone: “and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.” Therefore he is not adopted, of whom that is said which cannot be said of adopted sons [Col. 0043D]. And rightly he has one image with the Father, because he alone is only-begotten from the Father. What wonder, then, if in the Son’s image the Father’s image is marked? Thus the Savior himself said: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). I do not say this, as Sabellius does, as though he says that he himself, who is Son, is the Father. For I confess that he who begot is Father, while he who was born is Son. But when he says, “He who sees me sees the Father also,” just as he shows that Father and Son are not one person, so he shows that they are one divinity, since no diversity is found in the substance of Father and Son.

IX. Again, in this place also I ask: if the Son is a creature, how does one who sees the Son see the Father? [Col. 0044A] No one sees the Father in the vision of a creature. From the observation of a creature, the Creator may be seen; but the Father is not seen except through the observation of the Son. If, therefore, Christ is a creature and not truly Son, the Father cannot be seen in the vision of a creature. How then does he say, “He who sees me sees the Father also,” unless he is truly Son, born from God the Father? And therefore, when you see the Son, you must also see the Father. For without the Son there is no Father, just as neither is there a Son without a Father.

Hence he also added: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me” (ibid., v. 10), certainly not by some passive confusion; but because it follows that, where the Father is, the Son too is known to be there, and where the Son is, you know that the Father too is present. There is another sense of that saying, “He who has seen me has seen the Father”: it does not mean that one who saw Jesus in the body with bodily eyes saw the Father. Otherwise the Lord’s rebuke to Philip would be absurd when he says, “Have I been with you so long, and have you not known me, Philip?” (ibid., v. 9). For Philip was not the only one who saw Jesus according to the body; all the Jews who opposed him saw him as well. Yet they are not to be thought to have seen the Father merely because they saw Jesus according to the body.

What, then, is meant by “He who has seen me has seen the Father”? Direct the gaze of your heart, and see with the sight of spiritual faith that Christ, the Son of God, is not a creature but Creator. Recognize that he is truly God, eternal without beginning; and, insofar as he is God, invisible, immeasurable, incorruptible, immutable, and in every respect such as is the Father who begot him. And thus, in seeing the Son [Col. 0044C], there is no doubt that you have also seen the Father.

X. Understand in this sense also what he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me.” Since the Father is perfect, he begot a perfect Son; and since he is invisible, incomprehensible, immeasurable God and true light, the Son too was born such as is he who begot him. Therefore he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me.” For because all that belongs to the Father’s power and divinity is possessed in the Son, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Thus he first said: “If you knew me, you would know my Father also” (ibid., v. 7). Here too it is shown that the substance of Father and Son is the same, because knowledge of each is one. But the creature and the Creator do not have one knowledge, because they do not have one substance. Yet Father and Son have one knowledge; therefore the Son is not a creature [Col. 0044D], but Creator, just as the Father is Creator; and he is God, just as the Father is God. Yet by this we do not say that there are two gods.

Here, impious heretic, you blaze with diabolical rage, as though this confession were foolish, when you hear “God and God,” though we do not say “two gods.” Puffed up by secular learning, you are incurably diseased in this question; and you think you must force us to say “two gods” because we confess “God and God.” Do not, unhappy man, gather the artful arguments of Aristotle against Christ, Lord of all creation, you who in some fashion profess yourself a Christian. Do not come against the devout confession of God’s ineffable mystery as a cavilling calculator [Col. 0045A], circumscribing it as though by the rules of earthly computation [Note: “caviller”]. Rather, examine the divine books, and in matters of divine faith employ divine language. You have certainly read: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10). What distinction here is there between light and light? For he would have stated the distinction, if there were one, lest anyone should believe that no distinction exists between light and light. But if there is no distinction, then there are not two lights but one light, since in the Father’s light the Son’s light is recognized.

This is the light of which Daniel also speaks, saying: “And light is with him” (Dan. 2:22). This is not said of any creature, but of the splendor of God himself, who is eternal light. If the Father is eternal light, without doubt the Son too is eternal light. But if the Son of God is denied to be eternal light [Col. 0045B], how is the Son’s light, which is not eternal, seen in the Father’s eternal light? Yet in the praises of God this saying of the saints is not false: “In your light we shall see light.” Therefore the Son’s light too is eternal, and does not differ from the Father’s eternal light. Thus, although the Son is light and the Father is light, there is one light of Father and Son, because in Father and Son there is no distinction, no separation of light—just as, according to Moses, there is none of image, nor, according to the Apostle Paul, of form.

XI. The mystery of inseparable unity consists in this: that both, that is, Father and Son, are equally and indivisibly—not by division into portions—the one God; and the mystery of plurality consists in this: that there is one Father [Col. 0045C] and one Son. This too is made manifest by the passage which we read in the Gospel, where the Savior himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). “Are” signifies the plurality of persons, because here is Father and here is Son; but “one” establishes one and the same substance and divinity in Father and Son, so that Father and Son are truly one God, since both—that is, Father and Son—are one according to divinity, not one according to persons. “I and the Father are one”: by this one utterance both Sabellius is excluded and Arius refuted [Note: “is confounded”].

For Sabellius says that the Father himself is also the Son, as if one person possessed two names, and interprets “one” as having been said so that the singularity of one person might be believed. Arius, on the other hand, looking to the word “are,” and understanding plurality in this saying [Col. 0045D], introduced an impious plurality of gods: believing in one eternal God and another who began to be God; one almighty God and another who is not almighty. But, what blindness in both! Before their eyes lies what they might see devoutly, yet they strive impiously to contend through heedless stumbling-blocks. Let them at least apply their minds, and they will perceive the truth of devout faith.

Let Sabellius, struck by wonder at the miracles Christ performed, believe that Christ is true God—not one who at some point began, but one who has always been and can do all things. [Col. 0046A] Let Arius believe this, and not blaspheme Christ whom he confesses as Son. Likewise, Arius denies that Christ is the Father; let Sabellius deny this also, and devoutly believe that Christ is truly God, not the Father but the Son. I shall say it still more plainly. Let Sabellius overcome Arius on the point that Christ is true God; and let Arius overcome Sabellius on the point that Christ, under confession of true God, is truly Son. Then both have overcome me, a Catholic—or rather, both together with me overcome the error of impiety—when they understand with me the truth of the sacred faith, which understands both the plurality of persons and the unity of divinity in this declaration of the Lord: “I and the Father are one.”

But when Arius’ followers seek to overthrow this divine declaration and this devout understanding of it, [Col. 0046B] they interpret it differently, saying: they are one indeed, but not in substance, divinity, or power, but in will; that is, because they have one and the same will, he said, “I and the Father are one.” Tell us, most impious men [Note: “impious heretics”]: is the Word of God a substantial Word? And does he who gave speech to the tongue not know how to speak? Did he fail to express your profound meaning in words proper and suitable to it, and was he incapable of saying, “I and the Father will one thing,” if in this passage he wished unity of will rather than of substance and divinity to be understood?

XII. But now, I beg you, Queen, remember the propositions which you deigned to write down in the person of the heretics. The heretics themselves say: “The Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak” (John 12:49); and: “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6:38) [Col. 0046C]. This is the contrivance of heretics: elsewhere they deny what elsewhere they confess, so that when they see themselves tightly bound by the solutions of the questions presently at issue, they always escape by serpentine slipperiness.

Certainly, heretics, you say that the Father gave the Son a commandment concerning what he should say and speak. How then, as though he did not know how to speak, do you correct his words—or rather, now the Father’s words? For the Son says and speaks what he says and speaks according to the commandment which the Father gave him. Do you now understand that, when in a profane spirit you strive to exercise your madness against the Son’s divinity, you break out in madness even against the Father? The Son cries, “I and the Father are one”; and you, like grammarians making up for the supposed inadequacy of the Lord’s declaration by substituting a word [Col. 0046D], correct it and say: what he said, “we are,” must be understood as “we will,” so that it may mean, “I and the Father will one thing.”

But the Son protests even against you, saying what he said to the Jews, participants in your impiety: “Why do you not understand my speech?” (John 8:43). Let parables, allegories, and riddles have their place; but in this passage it is said most plainly and fully: “I and the Father are one.” Elsewhere too he declares how they are one, when he says: [Col. 0047A] “Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). And lest he seem to arrogate to himself something he was not, he first says, to show the truth of the statement: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words which I speak to you, I do not speak from myself; but the Father abiding in me himself speaks, and the works which I do, he himself does” (John 14:10).

And elsewhere: “As the Father taught me, these things I speak; and he who sent me is with me and has not left me alone, because I always do what is pleasing to him” (John 8:28–29). This is not because the Son did not know what he ought to say; for what can the Wisdom of God not know? Rather, in order to soften the hardness of your untamed faith toward a devout understanding of divine unity by the Father’s authority also, he says: “The Father abiding in me himself speaks” (John 14:10); or [Col. 0047B], “As the Father taught me, these things I speak” (John 8:28).

But just as the Son’s works are the Father’s works, because when the Son acts the Father abiding in him acts, so what the Son speaks, the Father abiding in him speaks—not something other than what the Son speaks, because neither does the Son speak something other than what the Father abiding in him speaks. Therefore the speech of Father and Son is the same, just as their operation is the same; and thus he said, “Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves” (John 14:12). He performed them in the same manner as the Father, so that at last, even by the authority of the works, it might be believed that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son.

XIII. The manner in which this saying, “I am in the Father and the Father in me,” is to be understood has already been explained above. But now I shall state it more briefly: “I am in the Father and the Father in me” must be understood according to the identity of substance [Col. 0047C]. Likewise, “I and the Father are one” means that Father and Son are one according to identity of substance. Therefore, impious heretic, I do not want you to take away the identity of the Father’s and Son’s substance and intrude, out of place, unity of will—which elsewhere you impiously deny when you say: “It is written, ‘I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me’” (John 6:38).

You who, in this passage, ignorantly deny so impiously that Father and Son have one will: how am I to believe you when you profess sincerely that the one and same will of Father and Son is signified by the Lord’s declaration, “I and the Father are one”? If you truly believe that Father and Son are one in will [Col. 0047D], I do not see how you can deny that they are also one in substance, divinity, and power. For why should those whose will is one not have one substance, one divinity, and one power? For if their will is equal, their divinity is equal. If their divinity is not equal, neither is their will equal. For the will of God and the will of one who is not God cannot be equal [Note: *pariare*, that is, “to be equal”], because the power of the will of him who is God is one thing, and the power of the will of him who is not God another [Col. 0048A].

God’s will is naturally good, perfect, immutable, ever the same, existing without beginning and enduring without end. But the will of one who is not God, because it has a beginning, can waver and change, just as he who is not God can; and therefore it is not truly good, because it is not naturally good, nor truly perfect, since it can change and diminish—so that what [Note: “what it wills today, it may not will tomorrow.” These words were imprudently omitted in the Oxford edition.] it willed today, it may not will tomorrow, and what it did not will today, it may will tomorrow.

XIV. I shall speak more plainly by an example. This angel who is now the devil had a good will before he became the devil; but when he became the devil, by the exercise of his own choice he lost his good will [Col. 0048B]—precisely because he subsists by creation [Note: “he added”] and is not naturally God. The same must be thought of every rational creature. Even if some of them have not turned aside and do not turn aside from the good will, nevertheless they have in their nature the capacity to turn aside [Note: Paris manuscript: “inborn”; perhaps, “they have it inborn”], because they are creatures and not God. For their not turning aside is obtained through the perpetual observance of discipline, not through the immutable reality of their nature [Note: “creatures”].

But God alone [Note: “as alone”] is good, perfect, and unchangeable without beginning; and he possesses a good, perfect, and unchangeable will. He does not have a good, perfect, and unchangeable will by instruction or by progress in observance, but through the immutable reality of his nature, by which he is good, perfect, and unchangeable God. Let it be seen whether [Col. 0048C] perhaps some heresy rejects this understanding. But you especially, Arian, agree with it: you call even the Son of God, whom you confess to be Lord of all creation, changeable and mutable [Note: “a changeable God”], because you proclaim that he was made by God from nothing, though not truly born from God [Note: “but perhaps”].

If this is your judgment—that every creature is changeable and mutable—and you say that Christ is a creature, then he too, according to you, being by the condition of his nature changeable and mutable [Note: “a changeable creature”], does not possess an unchangeable and immutable will. How then do you interpret that Father and Son are one in will, when, according to you, the wills of Father and Son are diverse and contrary? For one is immutable and unchangeable, but the other mutable and changeable. You are caught and exposed [Col. 0048D], deceitful heretic, in your effort to entrap and ensnare simple souls.

For, constrained and hemmed in by the testimony of the Lord’s declaration, “I and the Father are one,” in order somehow to escape from this saying [Note: “you may wish”], which in clear words shows unity of divinity in Father and Son, you have yielded to necessity, not choice, so as, at least for the moment [Note: “at the monument”; perhaps, “at the moment”], in the present passage to introduce unity of will only with the outermost lips, as it were, and only on the surface of words [Col. 0049A], in order more expressly, more forcefully, and from the heart to exclude unity of divinity. For you remove the meaning of unity of substance, which is readily believed from the very simplicity of the words, and substitute an interpretation of unity of will [Note: “or because”], so that, since the reasoning stated above is not readily understood by everyone, you may meanwhile deceive the simple hearer while seeking to prevent him from understanding unity of divinity.

For Catholic faith most sincerely and truly believes in unity of will in Father and Son—not with the lips only, but with the whole heart—while also acknowledging unity of substance and divinity. For as the Son is immutable and unchangeable in substance with the Father, so he is immutable and unchangeable in will with the Father. Therefore there is one [Col. 0049B] will of Father and Son, just as there is one power and one image; or rather [Note: “indeed”], I would say that the Son himself is the Father’s will. For just as, although Father and Son have one image according to Moses, the Apostle writes that the Son himself is “the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15), so, although Father and Son have one will, it is devoutly defined that the Son is the Father’s will. As he is the image of the invisible God, so understand likewise concerning power. For Catholic faith says that Father and Son possess one power; yet the Apostle writes that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). Therefore it is devoutly said that the Son is the Father’s will, just as he is God’s wisdom.

Yet if this point still troubles you, attend to what we say. Certainly Christ is God’s wisdom. But what is God’s will except God’s wisdom? For in God will is not one thing and wisdom another [Col. 0049C]. In human beings there can indeed be will that is not itself wisdom, because a human will reaches such wisdom as it can attain through instruction, reflection, and progress. But God’s will does not arrive at wisdom through instruction, reflection, or progress; rather, needing nothing, it is by nature substantial Wisdom [Note: “substance”]. Hence Christ, being God’s Wisdom, is also God’s will, because in God will is not one thing and wisdom another.

## CHAPTER II. On the heretics’ claim: “God made himself a Son from nothing; if he made him from nothing, he is a creature and not a Son.”

[Col. 0049D]

I. David, striking Goliath’s forehead with one blow of a stone, felled the mighty enemy of great body (1 Sam. 17:50). But it is not by our strength that we conquer with one stone, for, I think, a double reason: neither do we possess such strength as David had, and these men display a forehead excessively hardened by the impudence of their impieties [Note: “and impudence”]. Therefore, though we have now thrown many stones not [Col. 0050A] in vain, we must nevertheless repeat our attack in God’s grace, and their shameless forehead—that forehead without the Lord’s sign—must be battered with repeated stones of testimonies; so that, even if their flesh does not shed blood, yet, pierced [Note: “pierced”] and hollowed out by many wounds, they may at least blush from a flush of shame [Note: “as though by shame”], if they are overwhelmed even by the things which you had written as being theirs [Note: “and it”].

You say that these are the words of the heretics: “God made himself a Son from nothing. If he made him from nothing, he is a creature [Note: “created”] and not a Son.” What is this, that you call him Son whom you establish to be a creature when you say that he was made from nothing? Therefore you cannot call him both Son and creature: a son derives from birth, but a creature from making. Why do you profess contraries? Choose one of the two: either call him truly Son [Col. 0050B], or truly creature. If you call him Son in such a way as truly to call him Son, you have denied that he is a creature. How then do you say that he was made from nothing, when you confess him truly to be Son? But if you say that he is truly a creature, why do you call him Son, when in him you deny the truth of that name?

II. But let us strike the shamelessness of his brow with the living stones of the divine word. You say that he is a creature; I say that he is a Son. Who shall decide between us concerning the truth of this confession? I think you would gladly have him decide, from whom you say, despite our objections, that Christ was made out of nothing. Let us therefore hear what he himself pronounces from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). Did he say, “This is he whom I made out of nothing”?

[Col. 0050C] Observe that he said this for the first time when Jesus, as man, came to baptism; and, I think, for no other reason than because he who appeared bodily might be thought not to be the Son of God, and because among other human beings he too came to baptism as a sinful man, though he had no sins of his own. Therefore, lest, while Jesus completes the sacrament of baptism in the humanity he assumed, he should not be believed truly to be the Son of God, the Father cries from heaven: “This is my beloved Son.”

John indeed understood that he was his Lord when, as he came for baptism, he said: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (Matt. 3:14). But lest John’s testimony perhaps seem insufficiently weighty to others to overcome their belief in Christ’s flesh and humility, and in all that was done through his flesh, he—than whom none is greater, than whom none is a better knower—gives testimony from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

For in proportion as faith regarding the Savior’s flesh was evident, faith regarding the Savior’s deity also had to be evident. For then he is true God, if he is also true Son. No one doubted his flesh—or rather, I should say, his humanity—[Col. 0051A] because it could not be doubted. But that which was in the man and born with the man could not naturally be seen; therefore, lest it be uncertain, it is pointed out by the Father’s voice, as though by a finger, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Meanwhile, with equal authority, faith in both substances—that is, God and man—is commended in Christ.

The Son of God himself marked out in himself the evidence of his humanity: through the conception and childbirth of the Virgin; through an infant’s cry; through the cradle and swaddling clothes; through his mother’s breasts themselves and the nourishment of maternal milk; through the growth of bodily age; and through the very fact that he came to be baptized. You see how, up to baptism, he displayed in himself the reality of humanity—doing so all the more emphatically because it was more difficult to believe [Col. 0051B] that God should become man. And lest you perhaps suppose that he was compelled to this, rather than that the Son of God freely also became Son of Man, hear the Apostle speaking of him: “Though he existed in the form of God, he did not deem equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7). If, then, he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, he was not compelled, but freely became Son of Man, while existing in the form of God and equal to God. Thus you have the Son displaying in himself the evidence of humanity.

III. Likewise, let us see the evidence of deity displayed in him. Although the evidence of his deity has sufficiently been set forth above, and although there are still many further and more abundant proofs by which faith in his deity appears, I pass them over now. It is enough for me, at present, if the Father alone shows the faith of deity [Col. 0051C] in Christ, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

What do you say, heretic? You undoubtedly believe Christ when he declares that he made himself Son of Man. What do you think of the Father? Is he truthful in your eyes when he testifies that Christ is his Son? If you do not believe the Father when he testifies that Christ is his Son, then Christ has greater authority with you, since you believe him concerning faith in his humanity, while the Father is less trustworthy, since you do not believe his testimony about his Son. How, then, do you maintain that the Father is the greater God, when you despise his voice as though it were of the least account? Or how do you assert that Christ is a lesser God, when you believe him so fully that you do not even believe in the one whom you proclaim greater? This is the great honor you render to the Father: you do not believe him when he declares concerning his Son.

Yet again, elsewhere he declares that Christ is his Son. When the Lord ascended the mountain with the apostles Peter, James, and John, and his face shone like the sun (Matt. 17:2), let the divine testimony again strike the shamelessness of your brow: “And behold,” he says, “a bright cloud overshadowed them; and behold, a voice from the cloud saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; [Col. 0052A] listen to him’” (ibid., 5).

Certainly Moses and Elijah were seen speaking with him; and you cannot deny that they were made sons of God by adoption. How, then, does the divine voice testify concerning Christ alone, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him”? For if Christ too is a son by adoption, since he stood between two adoptive sons, it would surely have said, “And this too is my son,” lest Christ alone be believed to be Son. But when it said, “This is my beloved Son,” it distinguished the sons by adoption, so that the distinctive character of true birth might be believed to belong to Christ alone as Son.

But it was not enough to declare merely that Christ was his Son; he also added what was due to a true Son, saying, “Listen to him.” He showed great—indeed, equal—authority in the Son, since the Son must be heard just as the Father must be heard: “Listen to him,” he says. Whatever Christ therefore says must be heard. Let us see whether he nowhere says that he is the Son of God, whether he nowhere declares that God is his Father. His own voice says: “Every plant which my Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13). And again: “You have made my Father’s house a house of trade” (John 2:16). Elsewhere too: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” (John 9:35).

He would never have presumed to say, “My Father,” “my Father’s,” and, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” unless the confidence of nature, arising from awareness of his own birth, claimed for him the terminology that truly belongs to Father and Son. For what could he speak arrogantly, he who “humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross”?

[Col. 0052C] IV. There are very many other testimonies. But we are not now writing a book in order to pursue them all; rather, for brevity’s sake, we bring the main point to a close with a few testimonies, so that that voice which denies that Christ is the Son of God may be overwhelmed.

Christ certainly says that he is also Son of Man, when he says: “And you shall see the Son of Man” (Mark 14:62), and, “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13). For this is the mystery of faith in Christ: when you have believed him to be Son of God, you must also believe that he became Son of Man. What he is as Son of God he possesses by nature; but what he became as Son of Man he bestowed upon us by his beneficence.

> “Because he bestowed benefits upon us.” Other manuscripts read, more correctly, “because he bestowed benefits upon us”; others, “because he remained beneficent toward us.” OXON.

Therefore, whoever does not believe that Christ is Son of God is impious; but whoever disdains to confess that Christ became Son of Man is ungrateful.

Yet you, heretic, believe that Christ was also made Son of Man, and you do not deny it when the Savior himself says so. But when the Father says, “This is my Son,” and when the Son says, “My Father,” do you harden yourself like Pharaoh’s heart and refuse belief? It remains for your shamelessness, like a melancholic person who does not perceive what is true, to call Father and Son [Col. 0053A] liars.

“I do not deny that he is Son,” you say, “but I deny that he is true Son.” Then Peter earned the declaration of blessedness because he did not believe Christ to be true Son, although he confessed him to be “the Son of the living God.” Truly, a great mystery of confessed faith is present in Peter’s mind: though with his lips he says, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16), in his heart he nevertheless thinks that he is not the true Son of the living God.

I am a human being: I hear words, I understand words; I cannot hear the secret interpretation of the heart. He called Christ Son of the living God. Unless he also added “adoptive,” I understand nothing other than what he says. Christ may see otherwise, since as Lord and God he looks upon the heart; but for me, who hear only with my ears, the confession of his heart ought also to have been made manifest in speech. For Peter was questioned not for himself alone, but for all of us, so that, as he makes a right confession about Christ, we too might learn to attain blessedness through the same confession.

Meanwhile, let us see whether Peter worthily receives the proclamation of blessedness if he believes in his heart that Christ is not true Son but adoptive. Is this a worthy revelation of the Father, rather than of flesh and blood? Very many are sons of God by adoption—not only Jeremiah, who was sanctified while still in his mother’s womb (Jer. 1:5), nor John the Baptist alone, who as an infant leaped in the Spirit in his mother’s womb (Luke 1:44), nor Elijah alone, who has not yet undergone death, nor any one of the prophets, one of whom, as the Gospel relates, Christ was thought to be (Matt. [Col. 0053C] 16:14). Prostitutes and tax collectors too attain this title of adoption, provided that they reform themselves.

And lest anyone think that I speak blasphemously, let him hear the Gospel say: “Prostitutes and tax collectors shall go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 21:31), where there are only sons by adoption. Therefore, since the grace of adoption is denied neither to blasphemers nor to the immoral, if they correct themselves, was this the great mystery which the Father revealed to Peter—that he is indeed Son of the living God, but by adoption rather than by birth, and only in name, not also in the truth of the name? Indeed, whoever believes this is not blessed, but the most miserable of all people, possessing not only the understanding of flesh and blood but even the spirit of the devil.

But I ask you, Queen, to consider that many things could be said in this [Col. 0053D] place; yet, hurrying on to what follows, I pass them by, believing that when occasion is given, being as one of the wisest, you can perceive more than we say, according to Solomon’s saying: “Give occasion to the wise, and he will become wiser” (Prov. 9:9).

V. This is your doctrine, Arians; this is your distinctive interpretation; this is the secret mystery of your faith: “Christ is Son by adoption,” you say, “and not true Son.”

Let us question John as well. He too may have learned the truth, whether because he was present when Peter’s confession was praised, or because of the Savior’s special love, by which he was so close to him that he even reclined upon his breast (John 13:23). Let us see what he drank in while resting on his breast: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18).

No creature sees God according to that which God is; therefore he says, “No one has ever seen God.” But he continues and says, “except the only-begotten Son.” Therefore the only-begotten Son is not a creature, since he sees God whom no creature has seen. And lest you perhaps believe him to be one among adoptive sons, he cut off every occasion for an impious understanding when he called him not merely Son, but “only-begotten Son.” This name admits no companions. Although others are called sons, they are sons by adoption, not by nature. But Christ alone is the only-begotten [Col. 0054B] Son, because he alone is true Son—not by adoption but by nature; not merely by designation but by birth. He alone, I say, is true Son, who is also in the Father’s bosom.

Adoptive sons are in Abraham’s bosom; but he who is true Son and only-begotten Son is in the Father’s bosom. Understand also in this that the Son is inseparable from the Father’s substance, since he is said to be in the Father’s bosom.

Again we read: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). I do not see how God’s love toward the world is commended if the Son whom he gave for the world’s redemption is not true and only-begotten. The world is undoubtedly a creature. If Christ is a creature, what did he confer upon the world by giving a creature for a creature? Every creature is reckoned under the condition of servitude. If Christ is a creature, he is a servant. How did he redeem to freedom, when a servant has no right to confer freedom?

Yet Abraham, in order to commend the love which he had toward God, offered as a burnt offering his own, true, only-begotten, and most beloved son—because God himself had commanded this in order to prove to all Abraham’s love for him. And you impiously say that God, wishing to commend his love to the world, had no true Son to give, but was compelled, like the barren, since by nature he had no Son truly begotten from himself, to give one made from nothing?

VI. Say then, impious man: Abraham commended love with greater power by offering his own and only-begotten [Col. 0054D] Son than God did, who gave no Son of his own, no truly only-begotten Son. Is there anything God wishes especially to commend, yet commends less fully than a human being has commended it? And that God whom you proclaim greater is less than a human being in commending love. For he commended love less, if he did not give a true and only-begotten Son for love of the world; while Abraham commended it more by offering his own and only-begotten son.

But far be this impiety: that God, who is in every respect immeasurable, should be lesser even in commending love. Rather, loving the world, he gave his true and only-begotten Son. This is also what Paul, the vessel of election, expounds when, wishing to commend God’s love toward us, he says: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32). When he says “his own Son,” he expresses in the title the proper truth of the relationship.

Observe, however, the wording he uses: “He who did not spare his own Son.” You surely have read God saying to Abraham, when he was about to kill his son for love of God: “Do not lay your hand upon the boy, nor do anything to him; for now I know that you fear your God, and have not spared your beloved son for my sake” (Gen. 22:12). Paul also says: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” The Apostle speaks in God’s own language of how [Col. 0055B] he commended love. He would have used the divine words improperly if he were not here also speaking of a true Son.

And yet who does not know that in the father Abraham and his son Isaac there went before an image of the future reality? In God the Father and Christ his only-begotten Son, the Apostle showed the mystery of the preceding figure, confirming the reality in the very words by which the figure was first marked out: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” If, then, there was a figure in Abraham when he offered his son, but reality in God the Father when he delivered his Son, what do you say, teacher of impiety? Where ought greater force to reside—in the figure or in the reality? Undoubtedly in the reality. How, then, do you make the reality lesser but the figure fuller? For the figure is fuller where a true son is offered, while the reality is lesser where, according to you, a son who is not true is delivered up.

But plainly the reality is greater and the figure lesser. If you wish this to be proved, believe that the only-begotten Son of God is true; and you will understand that God did far more than Abraham in giving his only-begotten Son for love of the world, according to the Gospel (John 3:16), or, according to Paul, in not sparing his own Son but delivering him up for us all. Abraham indeed offered his son, but he offered him for love of God; and whatever you offer to God cannot equal what he deserves. He offered a son whom, after he could not have him by nature, he nevertheless received from God contrary to nature. He therefore offered to God what God had given him contrary to the expectation of nature: he offered his son.

[Col. 0055D] VII. It strengthens the argument if I say that Abraham’s son was lesser, and that—even apart from the present condition of mortality—he would at some time die by the law of mortality. By contrast, consider what God bestowed. He bestowed his only-begotten Son, whom he did not receive late through the favor of another, but has always possessed, without beginning, as one born from himself by the propriety of nature: such as is the Father himself who begot him—invisible, immeasurable, eternal, impassible, immortal, and omnipotent, as the Father himself [Col. 0056A] is; and finally, in every respect, according to that in which he is God, equal to him who begot him.

You see what kind of Son the Father gave. Behold, already God is found immeasurably superior in the Son. Now consider that he bestowed this such and so great only-begotten Son for love of the world; and consider what the world is: undoubtedly it is a creature. Likewise, consider what God is: undoubtedly he is Creator. Now compare whom Abraham loved and whom God loved. Abraham loved God. But recount how much God had bestowed upon Abraham, and you will find that Abraham rendered God a debt of love far smaller than he owed, although he rendered as much as he could. God, however, loves the world without having received from it any favor. You see that God’s love, which is bestowed not as a debt, is far more worthy of commendation than Abraham’s, which is bestowed as a debt.

But see still further the surpassing character of the love by which God loves the world: not merely a world to which, as its creator, he was commended by no merit of righteousness, but even a sinful and impious world opposed to him. Therefore God loved the world guilty of sins and impieties—not because he loved the world’s sins and impieties, but because he loved the world so that the world itself might be freed from sins and impieties.

Hear the Apostle wonderfully commending God’s love in these words when he writes to the Romans: “For why did Christ, while we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly? For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person; though perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. But God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, [Col. 0056C] Christ died for us. Much more, now justified in his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him” (Rom. 5:6–9).

VIII. I understand that this testimony calls for examination; but now we briefly explain what it contributes to the argument. The Apostle interpreted “world” as the inhabitants of the world and showed that Christ died for the ungodly and sinners in order to commend his love toward us who are in the world. “Christ,” he says, “dies for the ungodly and sinners, since scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person, though perhaps someone may dare to die for a good person.”

Do you now understand how inexpressibly greater is God’s love, where the reality is displayed, and how much lesser is Abraham’s love, where the figure is marked out? I do not say this as though Abraham did not love God greatly; indeed, he loved God as greatly as he could, as no one born of women can surpass. But though he loved God greatly, and loved him with all his heart and all the strength of his soul, he is surpassed without limit by the inexpressible superiority of divine love.

For who could explain the love which God bestowed upon the world, giving his only-begotten Son so that he who is God might be born a man; so that he who was born without beginning [Col. 0057A] from the Father might have, according to the flesh, a beginning of birth in the condition of human flesh; and so that he who always existed equal to God in the form of God, having received the form of a servant, might become less not only than the Father, but even than angels—indeed, perhaps much lower even than a worm by comparison? Finally, according to the nature of the human soul he assumed, he endured sorrow even unto death—he who is wholly joy, not only to Abraham, who desired to see his day, saw it, and rejoiced (John 8:56), but also to all holy people.

Therefore he bestowed upon the world his only-begotten Son, so that he who is true life, hanging upon the wood according to the flesh, might undergo the death of the cross, while his eternal and inviolable deity—one with that of his Father—remained for the time hidden. Consider this love: for the world’s salvation, the Lord of majesty is crucified on earth, while in heaven he grants eternal life to those who believe him to be the Son of God.

O most blessed patriarch Abraham, whose very great love for God is overwhelmed only by the flood of inexplicable divine love! And I do not know whether God did all this for the impious world because of his regard for your love and faith. For God had promised you and your seed that you would be heir of the world through the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:13), as the Apostle Paul teaches.

IX. But I would be excessively slow if I wished to pursue this passage more fully. I turn to you, heretic, warning you to attend to how God, loving the world, gave his only-begotten Son, or—as the Apostle says—how he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all. If you recognized the mystery of this ineffable divine love, you would never frame impious questions against the Son of God; anyone of pious mind understands them to be answered by what we have said above.

But let us consider the remaining part of the proposed testimony, so that the shamelessness of your brow may be crushed much more forcefully. For after saying, “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son,” he continues: “That everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” Again I say: he is the only-begotten Son. How can one who believes in him not perish but have eternal life, when belief in a creature is an offense against deity? Look to the Apostle Paul; consider what reproaches and abominations he reports concerning those who, as he says, “exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped [Col. 0057D] and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. 1:23).

If you believe in, worship, and serve the only-begotten Son of God in such a way as to call him a creature, unhappy man, the evils await you by which those are punished who exchanged God’s truth for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.

“Christ is Son of God by adoption,” you say, “and not true Son.” All the Gospels are read, and nowhere is it written that Christ is Son by adoption [Col. 0058A] and not true Son. It is well that John—John who reclined upon the Lord’s breast—gave the reason for writing the Gospel and said: “Jesus indeed did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have eternal life in his name” (John 20:30–31).

Is there any need to explain this more plainly? “Jesus did many other signs,” he says; and though not all are written, because the infinite abundance of deeds could not be written, nevertheless these very things were written so that we might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. To summon each person’s faith, he also displayed the reward, saying: “That, believing, you may have eternal life in his name.”

If he were, in fact, Son of God by adoption and not by nature, by designation alone and not also in the sense contained in the designation, nowhere would John have explained this more fully than at the conclusion of the work, lest faith, left in uncertainty, lose eternal life through uncertainty of belief. But the Evangelist, appointed for this purpose, who possessed the grace of the Holy Spirit so as to reveal with especial clarity those things which pertain to the rewards of eternal life, did not close the Gospel ambiguously. Rather, he stated with the utmost clarity that the Gospels were written “so that you may believe,” he says, “that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have eternal life in his name.”

Can there still be a suspicion of creaturehood in the Son of God where whoever believes that Christ is the Son of God possesses eternal life, and possesses it only in his name? He is certainly not a creature but Creator, and not Son by adoption but [Col. 0058C] the true Son of God. For in the name of a creature no one can obtain even temporal life—unless perhaps someone might be said to confer it by not taking it away.

X. “God made a Son for himself out of nothing,” you say. I pass over many testimonies. Let John speak, he whom love for Christ the Lord made clear-sighted. Writing in his Epistle, he says: “Everyone who loves the Father loves him who is born from him” (1 John 5:1). Did he say, “loves him whom God made out of nothing”? Indeed, he would not have named a Father at all unless he knew the Son to be born from him and not made.

Now suppose it is to be understood as you, heretic, interpret it—namely, that he was made out of nothing by him from whom John says he was born. I ask: according to you, was Christ alone made out of nothing? Was not even the world itself, to say nothing of other things, made out of nothing? Therefore the world too must be loved by us if the Father is to be loved. But the same John cries out: “Do not love the world” (1 John 2:15). Is John so inconsistent that he preaches contrary things to himself? Far be this impiety, that John, who spoke in the Holy Spirit, should be said to speak contradictions.

He knows the difference between what is made and what is born, already in the opening of his Gospel, as was explained above when that chapter was discussed. Therefore he does not understand as something made the one whom he says was born of the Father. Nor would he have used the singular, if he had wished “born of the Father” to be understood as “made,” since he knew that many things had been made out of nothing. But by using the singular, he spoke of the true Son alone, saying that he was born from the Father, because he alone was born from the Father, while all others were made by their Creator.

Do not, then, force the divine words. Why do you introduce what he does not say? Why do you teach what he did not teach? If you are a Christian, and if John is a true teacher in your eyes, believe what he taught. “He is born of the Father,” he says. If you believe this, you love the Father; and by loving the Father, you love the Son who is born from him. But if you do not believe that he is born from the Father, [Col. 0059B] you neither love the Father nor him who is born from him. You do not love in this way when you deny in the Father what belongs to a father—namely, begetting—and deny in the Son what belongs to a son—namely, being born.

Hear now what name blessed John gives you: “This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son” (1 John 2:22).
