You falsely give yourself the name Christian; but truthful John calls you antichrist, according to the deserts of your sect. I lie if you do not understand “Creator” under the name Father, or if you do not assert “creature” under the name Son. John calls them Father and Son, while you interpret these names as Creator and creature. You are therefore rightly called antichrist, because under an impious interpretation you deny Father and Son.

XI. But hear still further, whoever you are, insolent and [Col. 0059C] obstinate against the Son, and glorying in the person of the Father. Understand that you cannot have the Father unless you also confess the Son. John continues: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father; whoever confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father” (ibid., 23).

You see that John everywhere uses the names themselves, so that nothing other may be understood than what belongs to the nature of the names. Yet if the brow of your shamelessness can still endure the blows of stones, and if your hardness is so obstinately great that, when you hear Father and Son, you still do not believe in a true Father or a true Son, behold John himself, beloved by the Lord, repaying the Lord’s love with his own, now crushes not merely the brow but the very serpentine head of your impiety with a stronger stone. At the end of his Epistle he writes: “We know that the Son of God has come” (1 John 5:20–21), and was incarnate for us, suffered, and, rising from the dead, took us up; and “he gave us good understanding, that we might know him who is true, and might be in his true Son, Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life, and our resurrection is in him.”

It cannot be explained how many stones and rocks of argument he has piled up against you in this one testimony. “We know,” he says, “that the Son of God has come.” You have one confession concerning the Son; and a little later, after the mysteries of his incarnation, passion, and resurrection—which he surely accomplished for us—he continues: “And he gave us good understanding,” undoubtedly because he himself is the good giver, giving good understanding.

We do not understand impiously if we call this good understanding the Holy Spirit, who is also called the Spirit of understanding, in whom we know him who is true. For without the Holy Spirit truth cannot be known. You have testimony in the Gospel, where Christ himself promises the Holy Spirit as God, and says of him, “He himself will bear witness of me” (John 15:26): namely, through the apostles or through whatever preachers of the Son of God, giving them the understanding by which [Col. 0060B] the Spirit of understanding enables them to know the true one. Thus the Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might know the things given to us by God.” He therefore gave good understanding, that is, the Holy Spirit, so that we might know him who is true (1 Cor. 2:12).

XII. If you still do not understand from all the statements set forth above, observe from what follows that every suspicion of an impious interpretation is excluded. “That we may be,” he says, “in his true Son, Jesus Christ.” He further strengthens the pious faith, saying: “This is the true God.” Nor has he yet fallen silent; rather, he heaps and intensifies the terms, so that impious thought, trusting in sophistical arguments, may be overwhelmed. For he goes on to say: “And eternal life, and our resurrection in him.”

Where now are those impious sophisms of yours which you learned under the teaching of Aristotle, your bishop? You say: [Col. 0060C] “He is Son, but not true Son; he is God, but not true God.” Behold, in a single testimony the true title of Son is stated in so many ways—indeed, he is also true God. For how is he not true God who is true Son? Not only is true God proved from the title “true Son,” but also from the fact that he is eternal life. Eternal life has neither beginning nor end. Therefore Christ is true God, having neither beginning nor end, himself existing as eternal life, which is without beginning and end.

Moreover, since he is our resurrection, the power of true deity in him is recognized, since he excludes death by the power of resurrection, using as an example the humanity which he assumed. In that humanity he deigned to be born of the Virgin, and in it we too have already risen, each of us to have [Col. 0060D] a particular resurrection according to the merit of faith and life, whether unto refreshment or unto burning.

Take care, unhappy man, lest you still refuse to believe that he is true Son and begin to have a resurrection for the everlasting punishment of Gehenna, in the outer darkness, where there shall be weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8:12)—unless something still more dreadful awaits those who are impious toward the Son.

Editorial notes in the source: [Col. 0050D] “Completing”; “to one approaching.” [Col. 0051D] “Meanwhile, to the Father”; “signified”; “of the body,” and perhaps “bodily”; “displayed”; “the Father alone [shows] faith in Christ’s deity.” [Col. 0051D] “You think”; “do you believe?”; “has been honored.” [Col. 0052D] “And elsewhere”; “the death of truth and the death of the cross”; “will disdain”; “hardens.” [Col. 0053D] “Perhaps, namely, whereby”; “perhaps: but”; “Here certain material is omitted in the Paris Faust[us edition].” [Col. 0053D–0054D] “because”; “seeing”; “God”; “redeems.” [Col. 0054D] “anything”; “also”; “commended”; “who [of limits]”; “this is, if”; “that.” [Col. 0055D–0057D] “whatever”; “the condition of human flesh”; “of worms”; “of the human soul”; “you may see”; “may be stopped up”; “obscurities.” [Col. 0058D] “perhaps, in fact”; “true”; “Son, and not made: now”; “speak.” [Col. 0059D–0060D] “to truthful John”; “understanding”; “Christ”; “Lord”; “more dreadful.”

XIII. It has been sufficiently proved, I think, even by a few testimonies, that he is the true Son of God, born from the Father, not made from nothing. But I beg you still, [Col. 0061A] show tireless patience, so that we may establish this same point from the Old Scripture by even one testimony. You say, heretic, that the Son was made from nothing, though you have never read this anywhere; you deny what is written, that he was born from the Father. Tell me: whose words are these: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3)? If you doubt, look to the beginning of that Psalm and read what is written: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (ibid., v. 1). The Saviour himself used this testimony, [Note: [Col. 0061D] “So that when.” “So that” seems superfluous.] when he wished to be believed to be Lord, speaking to those who thought that he was merely a man born from David’s seed, and not also God as the Son of God. The Apostle Paul likewise believed this very thing which the Holy Spirit had formerly spoken in David and later expounded; [Col. 0061B] he says in his Epistle: “To which of the angels did he ever say, ‘Sit at my right hand’?” (Heb. 1:13). He explains by this that none of the angels is such as the Son is: for all angels were made, but the Son alone was born, to whom he also says, “Sit at my right hand,” because he alone is the only-begotten Son who is in the Father’s bosom (John 1:18).

Now an exposition of the whole Psalm is unnecessary; only this must be proved: that the Lord—the Father—says to the Son, “my Lord, Sit at my right hand,” so that what is said afterwards may also be believed to have been spoken by none other than the Father, namely: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” Is it not also most truly proved by this testimony that the impious utterance of those who say that God made the Son from nothing is buried? For how could he be [Col. 0061C] from nothing, when the Father himself cries aloud: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”?

And take care not to think that we understand God to subsist through a composition of limbs or parts. [Note: [Col. 0061D] “Subsist.”] Far be that impiety. For God, whatever he is, is simple; he is wholly the same according to substance—not part and part, not limb and limb—but, as we have said, some simple reality, whole, perfect, immeasurable, [Note: [Col. 0061D] Perhaps: “yet.”] and ineffable. Although, therefore, he is such that he does not subsist through limbs or parts, nevertheless, when divine Scripture wishes to commend to us the true understanding of the Creator, it speaks from things known to us, saying that the heavens are “the works of his hands” (Ps. 101:26), or saying the same of every creature. For among human beings a work or construction is truly and properly understood as that which is produced [Col. 0061D] by hands; indeed, when something is seen to have been fashioned by skill, it is attributed to the craftsman’s hands. Likewise, [Note: [Col. 0061D] “Among us.” I would prefer: “and among us.”] when we wish to indicate the nature of a son, we mention the womb; for no true son is born except from a womb. Thus God too, wishing to show that the Son was born from himself, said that he had begotten him from the womb, lest you, heretic, should maliciously allege that he was from nothing. But just as, when God is said to have made something with hands, it must be understood in a manner worthy of God, so also, [Col. 0062A] when he begot from the womb, we must not suppose anything contrary to what is worthy of God. [Note: [Col. 0061D] “Yet.”] This, however, must most certainly be confessed: that he is truly Creator in the expression “the work of his hands,” and truly Father in the expression of the begetting womb, although he has no limbs within himself.

XIV. But because you Arians are accustomed to say, “In God, making is identical with begetting,” I shall fittingly refute this perversity of yours on the present occasion as well. There are indeed many works [Note: [Col. 0062D] “Hands.”] of hands, but there is one only-begotten Son of the womb. Therefore making is not identical with begetting. All things were made through the Word and in wisdom; but the Word, or wisdom, was born not through someone else but from God. [Note: [Col. 0062D] “Is.”] Hence making is not identical with begetting. For if there were no difference between making and [Col. 0062B] begetting, nothing prevented him from saying, “My hands begot you,” and “the heavens are the works of my womb.” But just as the wording differs greatly, so also do the things which the wording defines.

“From the womb,” he says, “before the morning star, I begot you.” The Father says this to the Son, not because the Son [Note: [Col. 0062D] “Did not know.”] did not know it, but so that we might know the Father’s proper relation to the Son, and the Son’s to the Father. Therefore it is written thus, just as the only-begotten Son himself, who is Wisdom, says: “Before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:25). Hence he is also said here to have been begotten before the morning star. In the designation “morning star,” every especially luminous creature is signified. Thus, when it says that he was begotten from the womb before the morning star, this especially teaches that he was truly born from the Father and not made; while “before the morning star” signifies before [Col. 0062C] every creature, in accordance with what was said: “And he himself is before all things” (Col. 1:17).

## CHAPTER III. That the Son of God is almighty and unchangeable; that the omnipotence of Father and Son is one, just as their divinity is one; and concerning the mystery of the Son’s incarnation—or rather, of the man assumed by him.

I. Let us strike also at another of their blasphemies, by which, as you write, they say that the Son is not almighty. I shall do so briefly, lest by extending the discussion too far I impose labour upon the reader. [Note: [Col. 0062D] “Readers.”] Let them say when he is not almighty—the one through whom, as they themselves also confess, all things were made. Let them produce one work of the Father that the Son did not make, in order to prove that the [Col. 0062D] Son is not almighty. But since there is no work which is not both the Father’s and the Son’s, without doubt the Son is almighty, doing whatever the almighty Father does. It is sufficient if we establish this very point also by divine testimonies.

We read in the prophet Zechariah: “Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for from the four winds of heaven I shall gather you into Zion. Save yourselves, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon; for thus says the Lord Almighty: After glory he sent me against the nations [Col. 0063A] that plundered you; for whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of his eye. For behold, I bring my hand upon them, and they shall become spoil to those whom they plundered; and [Note: [Col. 0063D] “You shall know.”] you shall know that the Lord Almighty sent me” (Zech. 2:6–9).

If you attend to this passage, you will find that the almighty Son was sent by the almighty Father to aid those placed in captivity. For consider the prophet saying, “Thus says the Lord Almighty”; and let us hear, as the [Note: [Col. 0063D] “The prophet reporting.”] prophet reports, what the Lord Almighty says: “After glory,” he says, “he sent me against the nations.” Without doubt it is the Son who says that, after glory, he was sent against the nations—the one whom the prophet calls the Lord Almighty. Therefore this Son, being the Lord Almighty in the final testimony—“and you shall know that the Lord Almighty [Col. 0063B] sent me”—was, as stated above, sent by the almighty Father.

The Apostle John also says this in the Apocalypse: “Amen, the faithful witness, the beginning of God’s creation” (Rev. 3:14), “who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Lord God Almighty” (Rev. 1:4, 8; 4:8). And Solomon says, among other things, concerning Wisdom, who is surely Christ the Son of God: “For she is the brightness [Note: [Col. 0063D] “She is the brightness,” etc. This passage has been badly handled by a copyist and appears capable of restoration thus, Wisdom 7:26–27: “For she is the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness. Though she is one, she can do all things.” Also: “He who redeemed them—the Lord Almighty is his name.” Also in Maccabees: “You cannot yet escape the judgment of the almighty and all-possessing God.” “How is he not almighty,” etc., Oxford edition.—I should in fact read in the Maccabees passage: “the God who sees all things.” Vulgate, 2 Macc. 7:35: “who beholds all things.”] of eternal light, and a spotless mirror; the Lord Almighty is his name” (Wis. 7:26–27). Likewise: “He who redeemed them—the Lord Almighty is his name.” Likewise in Maccabees: “For you cannot yet escape the judgment of the almighty and all-possessing God”—“the majesty and image of his goodness; and though she is one, she can do all things.” How is he not almighty, when he can do all things? For above Solomon had said of the same Wisdom that she had [Col. 0063C] “every power” (ibid., v. 23); therefore she is almighty, possessing every power. Yet Solomon says further of the same Wisdom: “And abiding in herself, she remains” (ibid., v. 27). And elsewhere Solomon says: “For your almighty hand is not powerless” (Wis. 11:18). Likewise he says: “Your almighty Word leapt down from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18:15).

II. Recognize his omnipotence when he renews all things; meanwhile recognize also that he is unchangeable, since, abiding in herself, Wisdom renews all things. That is: although she renews all things, she herself nevertheless remains unchangeable; and this belongs to none but almighty God. But because the Son is truly unchangeable and Creator of all things, this is also established by these verses of the Psalmist: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of [Col. 0063D] your hands. They shall perish, but you shall remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment. Like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:26–28). Paul interpreted this as written of the Son of God when writing to [Col. 0064A] the Hebrews (Heb. 1:10–12).

Accordingly, through these passages you have the Son as almighty, unchangeable, Creator of all things, and maker of all things, as Solomon says: “For Wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me” (Wis. 7:21). [Note: [Col. 0064D] “Wisdom.”] But care must be taken lest you understand two almighties. For although both Father and Son are almighty, there is one Almighty, just as there is one God, because the omnipotence of Father and Son is the same, just as their divinity is the same, as has been set forth above to the extent permitted by our powers and the constraints of time. This will also be explained below by the testimony of the prophet Isaiah:

“The labour of Egypt, the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the tall men of the Sabaeans shall pass over to you; they shall be your servants, they shall follow behind you bound in chains, they shall worship you, and in you [Col. 0064B] they shall make supplication: because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, the God and Saviour of Israel. All who oppose him shall be ashamed and confounded; they shall go [Note: [Col. 0064D] “Into confusion.”] away in confusion” (Isa. 45:14).

Observe that this is said to the Son: “They shall be your servants; they shall follow behind you bound in chains; they shall worship you, and in you they shall make supplication.” Hence the Son is also shown by this to be true God, since he is worshipped. For it belongs to God to be worshipped; indeed, elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0064D] “Says.”] the Apostle teaches that it is written of the Son of God: “Let all God’s angels worship him” (Heb. 1:6), plainly because he is truly God and Lord. Yet, in this present testimony of Isaiah, just as he himself is God, so God is also in him. For it says: “Because God is in you, and there is no God besides you.” And after saying that God is in God, it continues [Col. 0064C] and says: “For you are God, and we did not know it, the God and Saviour of Israel.” Therefore, since God is in God, and there is no God besides him in whom God is, and he himself is the God and Saviour of Israel, the unity of divinity is shown in Father and Son, as also the unity of omnipotence and of everything whatsoever belonging to the divine substance. The Son differs from the Father only in this: the one is Father and the other Son—that is, the one begot and the other was born. Yet because he was born, he has nothing less than what is in God the Father, being “the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15), “the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance” (Heb. 1:3).

Those who do not believe this concerning the Son of God will bear Isaiah’s sentence: “All who oppose him shall be ashamed and confounded; they shall go [Note: [Col. 0064D] “Into confusion.”] away in confusion.” Jeremiah also—or rather Baruch [Note: [Col. 0064D] “Rather, Baruch.”]—expresses the divinity of the Son, saying: “This is our God, and no other shall [Note: [Col. 0064D] “Be reckoned.”] be accounted beside him. He found the whole way of understanding and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterwards he was seen upon earth and lived among human beings” (Bar. 3:36–38). It was surely not God the Father, but [Col. 0065A] the Son made man, who was seen upon earth and lived among human beings, exercising in himself the human nature without sin for our salvation. Of him we also read: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

III. Therefore, if the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, born from a virgin as God-with-us, where now are you going, heretic? If you object to the weaknesses of the assumed flesh, if you describe the beneficial [Note: [Col. 0065D] “Beneficial.”] affections of the human soul which he assumed together with the flesh, it is established that, inasmuch as he is God and the Son of God, he is in every respect impassible like the Father. For this reason we have first set forth those things that concern his divinity: so that, if anything of lowliness and weakness is read of Christ, [Col. 0065B] his divinity may not be thought violated, but it may be shown to belong to the nature of the man assumed and to the carrying out of the teaching which he delivered. [Note: [Col. 0065D] “May be proved.”]

For it would be pointless to have willed to be born as a man—even though from a virgin, [Note: [Col. 0065D] “Only.”] nevertheless as a man—and not to have displayed in himself the weak nature of humankind. It would be pointless to give commandments by which human beings should live, and then, since he had once deigned to become man, to have himself passed through life without observance of the commandments. If, when made man, he had not wished to experience human weakness, who would have believed that he had become man from the matrix of our origin, though without a man’s embrace? Especially since even today there are those who deny that he bore our bodily substance, even after he experienced the weakness of the flesh. If, having become man, he had not kept the discipline which he came to teach, he would not have given a good [Col. 0065C] example of teaching. For which disciple would strive to keep what the teacher himself, made man, had not kept—when now whoever keeps it is aided in keeping it by his example?

You see that he had to suffer weaknesses, in order to be proved a man born; and, having become man, he had to observe whatever he taught, in order to invite others—or rather, I should say, to sustain others. For now our flesh has learned to be sustained by his flesh. For if he had not wished to suffer human weaknesses, why was he born from a virgin [Note: [Col. 0065D] “Man in man.”] as a man? And if, because he was Lord, he did not wish to observe commandments, why had he taken the form of a servant, which is subject to commandments and obedience? [Note: [Col. 0065D] “And yet.”] Indeed, the whole mystery of the man assumed by God is this: [Note: [Col. 0065D] Perhaps “so that” is missing.] that what was not preserved in Adam through disobedience should be preserved in Christ [Col. 0065D] the man through obedience. The Apostle Paul affirms this among the other matters which he treats divinely: “For just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one man many are made righteous” (Rom. 5:19). “For just as through the contempt of one man many were made sinners, [Note: [Col. 0066D] “You have.”] so through the mystery of obedience in Christ—an obedience which he renders, not from weakness but from the goodness of [Col. 0066A] divinity, for the saving discipline of humankind—many are saved.”

IV. Let us now consider the mystery of the Passion. The whole Adam had sinned; the whole Adam had been expelled from paradise. He who came to save the whole had to assume the whole that had been expelled. But he would not appear to have assumed in himself the whole expelled humanity unless he had assumed it in the substance of flesh and soul; for this is the whole human being by nature. This could be proved only if he bore the very weaknesses of his flesh and soul, though without the defect of sins, so that he might truly not be thought to have assumed another substance of flesh and soul; and so that, when he frees humanity in himself from weaknesses and passions, we might believe that those too who follow in his footsteps have been set free.

But let the Apostle, teacher of the Gentiles, support this sense more vigorously, and as a mystic writer: “For as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:23). Yet let Isaiah describe more fully the nature of the man assumed in him:

“Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced before him as a child, like a root [Note: [Col. 0066D] “Aged.” Perhaps: “in a thirsty land.”] grown old in thirsty ground. He has neither appearance nor honour of form; we saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty. But his appearance was without honour, failing beyond other human beings: a man set in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness, because his face was turned away; he was despised and not esteemed. He bears our sins and suffers for us; and we judged him to be in pain, affliction, and evil. But he was wounded for [Col. 0066C] our iniquities and weakened for our sins; the discipline of our peace was upon him; by his wound we were healed. We all went astray like sheep; each person went astray from his own way; and the Lord delivered him up for our sins. And because he was harshly treated, he did not open his mouth. Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before the one shearing him, so he did not open his mouth. In humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who shall recount his generation? For his life shall be taken from the earth; because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death. And I shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich themselves for his death. [Note: [Col. 0066D] Perhaps: “who.”] Because he committed no iniquity, nor spoke deceit with his mouth” (Isa. 53:1–9).

V. This testimony sufficiently proves that he underwent in himself the whole of human nature, though without [Col. 0066D] sin of his own, even though he bore [Note: [Col. 0066D] Perhaps: “bore.”] our sins. But lest he be believed merely to be man, Isaiah inserted and said: “Who shall recount his generation?” Namely, that generation by which he was begotten from God the Father, which is without beginning. Therefore he says concerning it, “Who shall recount his generation?”—not as though it were unknowable, but as though it were ineffable. For all Catholics know that he was born from God the Father, but in a manner that cannot be recounted; therefore he says, “Who shall recount [Col. 0067A] his generation?”

The Gospel relates that generation by which he is born from the virgin according to the flesh, also describing its times. [Note: [Col. 0066D] “Because.” Perhaps: “by which”; for shortly afterwards: “This generation by which he is born from the Virgin.”] But the beginning of the divine generation, as we have said, cannot be investigated, any more than can the divinity which is one with the Father. Therefore he says, “Who shall recount his generation?” If, then, in the mystery of faith we have received this: that Christ is to be believed God and man—God indeed, from God and without beginning; man, because he was born from a virgin in time—let us not impugn his divinity when, for the sake of our healing, he performs the things belonging to humanity, having received in himself human nature. Nor should he be denied to be man when, having taken the form of a servant, he exercises the natural power of his own divinity.

Thus, if he prays to the Father [Col. 0067B] and says that he can do nothing of himself (John 5:19), except what he sees the Father doing: to say nothing further now, he certainly sets the measure of human humility which the teacher enjoins, so that humanity may learn all the more to defer to God because the true Son deferred, though he had no personal cause for subjection. He also gave the form of prayer, so that we should ask not so much for our own will to be done as for the will of the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 3:21). Therefore, in order to fulfil what he taught, he says: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

Likewise, that he was made lesser; that he grows, advances, hungers, thirsts, labours, weeps, suffers pain, is sorrowful, and finally dies—all this must be referred to the nature of the man assumed, which he mystically exercised for the mystery [Col. 0067C] of our salvation, according to the interpretation set out above in the testimony of Isaiah. Under this mystery of faith, not only are the passages resolved about which you deigned to inquire, but also all the questions which impious heretics assemble against the Son’s divinity.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Son’s statement: “THE FATHER IS GREATER THAN I.”

I. Receive [Note: [Col. 0067D] “They received.”] now also these questions which you had proposed as more difficult from another [Note: [Col. 0067D] “Method.”] line of argument, answered specifically. The heretics, you say, cite, to diminish the Son’s everlasting and in-all-respects perfect divinity: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:18). But we must ask when the Son said this. Was it not when that was fulfilled in him which is written: “You made him a little less [Col. 0067D] than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps. 8:6)? Let the Apostle Paul, who knows the third heaven, explain how he was made lesser: “We see Jesus,” he says, “made a little less than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all” (Heb. 2:9). “For all,” he says, not for himself. Therefore, if he tasted death for all, what wonder if he was also made lesser for all? He tasted death for all, not for himself, because, having become man for all who were held under the guilt of sin, he himself was liable to no sin of his own.

Observe how the most wise Paul interprets both his being made lesser for the suffering [Col. 0068A] of death and his tasting death for all by God’s grace as fitting the beauty of the work, when he continues: “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, to perfect the author of their salvation through sufferings” (ibid., v. 10). You see how beautiful and fitting for the mystery of our salvation it is that the Son is shown to have been made lesser. How then do you cite as a reproach, in order to obscure his divinity, that which he accomplishes for the sake of what is fitting? “The Father is greater than I”: he said this after the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

II. Take care not to believe him changeable, as if he had ceased to be the Word after becoming flesh. Rather, always remaining God the Word, he also became flesh. For although he said, “And the Word became flesh,” he wished to speak emphatically, lest anyone believe that he did not have true flesh. Indeed, even after such emphatic language there are those who say that his flesh was merely apparent. But that it may be manifest that the Word became flesh not through a change of the divine substance but through assumption of human flesh, attend to what follows: “And he dwelt among us.” The Word, which dwelt among us through the assumed flesh, was not interrupted by change; for dwelling proves the Word’s continuance. I have inserted this lest anyone believe the Son of God to be changeable when reading, “And the Word became flesh.”

Therefore the Son says, “The Father is greater than I,” after the Word became flesh and took up the office of one who ministers. For he came not to be ministered to, but to minister. “The Father is greater [Col. 0068C] than I” (Matt. 20:28). What do you say, [Note: [Col. 0068D] “Truth.”] O Divinity? How do you say that the Father is greater than you? Certainly you and the Father have one image according to Moses and the same form according to the Apostle Paul, who also taught me that you are “the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance” (Heb. 1:3). You yourself also taught this, saying: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”; “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:9); “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). And whatever the Father does, you also do similarly; for these are your words: “For whatever he does, the Son also does likewise. For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills,” and, “that they may honour the Son as they honour the Father” (John 5:19–21).

Since, therefore, you have the same image, the same form, the same substance, the same unity of nature, the same [Col. 0068D] power, the same freedom of will, the same honour, and absolutely everything that belongs to the Father is yours because what is yours is the Father’s, how do you say, “The Father is greater than I,” when in all that belongs to divinity you are such as the Father is? Let the Apostle Paul speak, in whom Christ spoke, as he himself says: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). What does the Apostle say? “[Christ Jesus], though he was in the form of God, did not regard being equal to God as robbery” (Phil. 2:6). Therefore, inasmuch as he is in the form of God and equal to God, the Father is not greater. How the Father is greater is shown by what follows: “But he emptied himself,” he says, “taking the form of a servant” (ibid., vv. 7–8).

III. Take care here too not to understand an interruption of divinity when you hear, “He emptied himself.” Attend to what follows: “taking the form of a servant.” Thus he who is said to have taken the form of a servant is shown to remain in his own state. But although the divine state remains and endures in him, he nevertheless emptied himself, namely by concealing his divinity, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.”

Such is he when he says, “The Father is greater than I.” He does not attack the equality of divinity, but indicates the mystery of humanity by his emptying himself and taking the form [Col. 0069B] of a servant. Such is he when he says: “The Father who sent me gave me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak” (John 12:49); and, “I came down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). He shows that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. Yet what diminution of his divinity is there in this, if he speaks without arrogating to himself, in order to cut off arrogance in human beings? I am mistaken if the Apostle Paul did not set down this very testimony precisely in order to summon each person to humility through the Saviour’s example. You will find it so if you read more attentively the same Epistle which he writes to the Philippians.

But the heretics do not wish “The Father is greater than I” to have been said because of the mystery of God’s emptying by taking the form of a servant. Let us also say that the Father is greater in respect of the mystery of generation alone. For some Catholics have advanced this pious interpretation, saying that Father and Son are of the same substance and that therefore, according to substance, neither is greater than the other. For as God the Father is, so also is God the Son: he begot from himself nothing less than he himself is, for being perfect he begot one who is perfect. Although, therefore, as God, the Son is equal to God, nevertheless as Son he is called lesser than the Father—that is, because the Son is from the Father, and the fullness begot fullness. But the Father begot the Son; and therefore he did not say, “God is greater than I,” but, “The Father is greater than I.”

## CHAPTER V. Concerning what is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “LET ALL THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL THEREFORE KNOW WITH CERTAINTY THAT GOD MADE THIS JESUS, WHOM YOU CRUCIFIED, BOTH LORD AND CHRIST.”

[Col. 0069D]

I. Among the other arguments of the heretics, intended to make the Son of God be believed a creature, you have also put forward, on behalf of the opposing side, [Note: [Col. 0069D] “You have put forward.” Perhaps the author wrote “you have put forward,” addressing Flaccilla, as he does frequently elsewhere. Near the end of this §1, addressing the same empress, he says: “[Col. 0070D] You see how,” etc.] what we read in the Acts of the Apostles, the blessed Peter saying: “Let all the house of Israel therefore know with certainty that God made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36).

But the solution to this question too is clear from the foregoing exposition, in which we said that the Son of God also became the Son of Man. Although he cannot suffer because he is the Son of God, being the Word and Wisdom of God—for in this respect he remains always impassible, like his Father—yet because he became man, born of the Virgin Mary, he is capable of suffering. For he endured death, even death on a cross, always remaining in himself inviolable because he is God, even when he moves among human beings and is crucified. Therefore God made this Jesus, who is according to the flesh, both Lord and Christ. For inasmuch as he is the only-begotten Son of God, the Word and Wisdom of God, he is not a creature [Col. 0070B] or one awaiting advancement, since he is perfect God in all respects, as is also his Father.

But this Jesus, according to the flesh, was made Christ when the servile form which he had assumed was first freed from Adam’s sin. For Adam fell from lordship into slavery through committing sin: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave” (John 8:34). But the Saviour renewed lordship much more firmly—indeed, incorruptibly—in the man he assumed, when in him he wiped away sin itself, which through Adam had been the cause of rejected slavery. Yet he was again truly made Lord when peoples who believed in him subjected themselves to his lordship. For, prompted by the exhortation of holy Scripture saying, “Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. 2:11), each person who now recognizes the saving lordship in Christ says: “Is not my soul subject to God?” (Ps. 61:2). To become his servant is of supreme honour and a certain nobility surpassing the world. Therefore the Apostle writes as his glory: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ” (Rom. 1:1). You see how he was made Lord when even he who had persecuted him confesses him as his own Lord, to his highest glory.

II. Jesus was made Lord [Note: [Col. 0070D] “Lord.”] according to the flesh not only as Lord but also as Christ. In the name Christ are contained the mysteries of king and priest. We read in the Old Scripture that priests and kings among the Israelites were marked by an anointing with oil, and were therefore called christs. For *Christos* (Χριστός) in Greek is rendered in Latin as “anointed” or “smeared” (*unctus* or *linitus*). But our Saviour was truly made Christ according to the flesh, being true King and true Priest—both in the same person, lest anything be lacking in the Saviour.

Hear that he was made king when he says: “But I have been established king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6). Hear that he is also priest, by the Father’s testimony saying: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4). Aaron was first made priest under the Law by anointing with chrism; and he did not say, “according to Aaron,” lest the Saviour’s priesthood [Col. 0071A] too be thought capable of existing by succession. For the priesthood which was in Aaron depended upon succession; but the Saviour’s priesthood is not transferred by succession to another, because he himself remains priest continually, according to what is written: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Therefore the Saviour according to the flesh is both King and Priest, but anointed not bodily but spiritually. For those kings and priests among the Israelites who were bodily anointed with oil were kings and priests; not both in one person, but each [Note: [Col. 0071D] Perhaps: “each one.”] of them was either king or priest. For perfection in all things and fullness are owed to Christ alone, [Note: [Col. 0071D] Perhaps: “are owed.”] who came also to fulfil the Law. Yet although they were not individually both, they were bodily anointed with royal or priestly [Col. 0071B] oil and were called christs. But the Saviour, who is truly Christ, was anointed with the Holy Spirit, so that what is written concerning him might be fulfilled: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). For in this he was anointed more than his companions in this name: he was anointed with the oil of gladness, by which nothing other than the Holy Spirit is signified.

III. We know this to be true from the Saviour himself. For when he received the book of Isaiah and read, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Luke 4:18), he said that the prophecy had then been fulfilled in the hearing of those present. Peter also, chief of the Apostles, taught that the chrism by which the Saviour is shown to be Christ is the Holy Spirit itself, and likewise the power [Col. 0071C] of God, when he was speaking in the Acts of the Apostles to the most faithful and merciful Cornelius, who was then a centurion. For among other things he says: “Beginning from Galilee after the baptism preached by John, Jesus [Note: [Col. 0071D] of Nazareth.] of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power, went about working miracles and mighty deeds, [Note: [Col. 0072D] And healing all.] and delivering all who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10:37–38).

You see that Peter too said that this Jesus, according to the flesh, was anointed with the Holy Spirit and power. Thus Jesus truly became Christ according to the flesh: through the anointing of the Holy Spirit he became both king and priest for ever. I have pursued these matters in order that it may plainly appear that Jesus, the Son of God, was not crucified, nor made Lord and Christ, according to his being the Word and Wisdom of God, but [Col. 0071D] according to that which he assumed from Mary. Nevertheless, through the passion of the assumed man, we say that the only-begotten Son of God suffered—not because the only-begotten Son himself, insofar as he is the Word and Wisdom of God, truly suffered, but because whatever outrage or suffering was inflicted upon his assumed man is, in some sense, all referred back to the impassible, only-begotten God himself.

Thus the Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “For if they had known” (1 Cor. 2:8)—that is, the rulers of this age—“they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” If these things are plain, it is now evident how it was said: “Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made him both Lord and Christ, namely this Jesus whom you crucified”; whom Peter himself above called a man, saying: “Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you through powers and wonders and signs” (Acts 2:22); namely, this Jesus Christ, whom Paul also called a man when writing to Timothy: “One God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ” (1 Tim. 2:5). He also said in the Gospel: “But now you seek to kill me, a man who have spoken the truth to you” (John 8:40).

IV. We do not say these things on behalf of the impious Photinus, who wishes Christ to be a mere man without the incarnation of the Word of God, [Col. 0072B] but we set them forth against Arius the antichrist, who wishes the only-begotten Son himself—the Word and Wisdom of God—to have been crucified as God rather than as man, and himself to have been made Lord and Christ. Yet even if, with most stubborn obstinacy, they contend that it is written of God the Word himself that God made him both Lord and Christ, we are not thereby alarmed, trusting in the truth, lest perhaps because it is written thus the Word of God be thought a creature.

Grant, then, that the Word of God was made Lord and Christ. [Note: [Col. 0072D] “What.”] What prejudice does this cause to his substance, by which he is always the Word of God? Observe that he did not say that the substance of the Word of God was made; rather, that this very Word, who is always the Son of God, was made Lord and Christ. For it is not the same thing for that which did not exist at all [Col. 0072C] to come to be, and for that which already existed to become something.

For God sometimes becomes helper and protector; yet because he has become helper and protector, one must not therefore believe that even that which he is—God—has come to be. After Moses experienced divine help and protection, he said of the God who had helped and protected him against Pharaoh: “He became my helper and protector unto salvation” (Exod. 18:4). You will find many very similar testimonies, which I pass over lest I prolong matters further. Therefore, although God is helper and protector, it is not believed that that which he is, namely God, comes to be; rather, he is designated as being helper and protector. Why then, when they say that the Word of God was made Lord and Christ, should we suppose that the substance of God’s Word was made?

Or because we read, “And the Word [Col. 0072D] was made flesh,” ought we therefore to believe that the Word itself was made? It is expressed most plainly that it was not so much the Word which was in the beginning with God that was made (John 1:3), but that the Word which always was afterward became flesh, so as to be made flesh—not that the Word which became flesh was itself made. Thus likewise, when the Word of God is said to have been made Lord and Christ, one must not understand that the substance of the Word of God was made; but that this very Word, who was always God, was made Lord and Christ. [Note: [Col. 0072D] “Made.”]

[Col. 0073A]

V. He becomes Lord of those who devote themselves to him with the purpose of serving him. And forgive me, most blessed Matthew, if I say that Christ God was not yet your Lord when you were still serving at the tax-office. Likewise, he first became Lord to all the Apostles when, leaving all things, they chose to serve him. He also became Lord of the nations when, abandoning the empty superstition of idols, the nations themselves gave themselves over to his dominion. For insofar as anyone is the slave of sin or of mammon, so far he cannot be the servant of God. But when one renounces sin and mammon, doing righteousness and rejecting the desire to possess, then Jesus becomes his Lord.

By the same reasoning he is understood also to become Christ. For, as was said above, kings and priests were designated by the title *Christs*, “anointed ones.” The Saviour therefore became king of those who are no longer held bound under the kingdom of death, in whose mortal body sin ceased to reign after they learned, through divine instruction and the teaching of the Apostles: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). [Note: [Col. 0073D] Perhaps: “through.”] And when he performs the office of priest for us, he most truly becomes Christ, especially as our defender and advocate, ever standing for us and interceding with the Father as the one most pure priest, so that, once the stain of transgression has been expiated, we may be saved through his divine propitiation.

Therefore, by Jesus’ becoming Christ and Lord, nothing is added so much to his divine substance as provision is made for those upon whom the power of his kingdom, priesthood, and lordship has been bestowed as a saving gift. It will not seem absurd if you understand similarly what he says: “But I have been established king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6). For although he is said to have been established king, yet when [Note: [Col. 0073D] “It is added.”] he adds, “upon Zion, his holy mountain,” he shows that he is not speaking of that kingdom which he possessed even before he was established king upon Zion, his holy mountain. For he is king before all ages of ages, and is proved almighty because by his power he contains every creature which he created, and is able to contain all things that have been made.

## CHAPTER VI. On Solomon’s statement: “THE LORD CREATED ME AS THE BEGINNING OF HIS WAYS FOR HIS WORKS.”

[Col. 0073D]

I. Let us touch at last upon that question which you added among the others: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works” (Prov. 8:22). The heretic says: “You see that Wisdom is a creature; and, as the Apostle Paul interprets it, Wisdom is Christ. Therefore Christ,” he says, “who is Wisdom, is not a true Son, but a creature made a son by adoption.” This is the poison of the Arians. Yet how blind is impiety to behold what is pious!

Since, as it is written, “they hated the wisdom of the Lord [Col. 0074A] and did not accept the word” (Baruch 3), they see nothing in it of most unalloyed beauty—just as inflamed eyes have no vision of truth, since their sight reports otherwise than the reality of things is. So too, if the overflowing bitterness of one’s own gall has corrupted a person’s proper taste, when he tastes sweet honey he slanders the honey’s sweetness as bitter, not recognizing the evil of his own bitterness.

But, miserable heretic, what can you see of the true light when [Note: [Col. 0074D] “You live blind.”] you are blind, or walk in paths of darkness, devising everything belonging to impiety? Let that spiritual man cry out, inviting us by the most delightful experience of the divine banquet: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9). Yet if you taste, you perceive nothing sweet in the Lord, because, as it is written, [Col. 0074B] “the poison of asps is under your lips,” because “your mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (Ps. 13:3).

Finally, although Solomon himself proclaimed countless things concerning the Wisdom of God, and spoke of it so divinely that one might believe it to be nothing other than that which belongs to the nature of God, the half-blind heretic believed that in all these matters he saw only that by which he might prove Wisdom to be a creature. “But,” he says, “it is written: ‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works.’” We shall not go further afield or produce from Solomon’s other books statements concerning the everlasting Wisdom of God. For the present it is enough that, from this very passage from which he has produced his testimony, the opposing interpretation be defeated.

II. You say, heretic, that it is written: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works.” But observe that this same Wisdom nevertheless says: “Before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:25). How, then, does this same Wisdom in the same passage say both that it was created and that it was begotten? First we must see which came first: its having been begotten, or its having been created.

Although Wisdom first said, “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works,” nevertheless, lest you should suppose it a creature, it returns to that which is prior, saying afterward: “Before all the hills he begot me.” Take care, then, not to suppose it was begotten later because it first stated that it was created. For though, in the order of the words, its being created is placed first, and its being begotten afterward, the sense determines that it was begotten before it was created. Thus the meaning is as though Wisdom said: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways [Col. 0074D] for his works. But lest anyone suppose that by this I am a creature, or that I first began to exist when he created me as the beginning of his ways for his works, I proceed and say: ‘Before all the hills he begot me,’ that you may know that I was begotten before I was created.”

For when it says, “Before all the hills he begot me,” it makes its being created later, while its being begotten comes first and is earlier. Therefore, if it was created in such a way that it had previously been begotten, the impious understanding by which it called Wisdom created is excluded: namely, that Wisdom should be thought first to have come into existence when it reported that the Lord had created it as the beginning of his ways [Col. 0075A] for his works. For behold, the meaning makes clear that Wisdom existed even before it was created, since it was begotten before it was created.

III. But this catholic interpretation will be commended even more strongly if we examine, as far as we can, the words themselves by which Wisdom reports itself either begotten or created. “The Lord,” it says, “created me as the beginning of his ways for his works.” Observe that when it said, “The Lord created me,” it did not remain silent, lest it truly be thought a creature. Rather, it goes on to explain in what respect it was created and for what reason. For it says: “He created me as the beginning of his ways”; and when it adds, “for his works,” it plainly shows the reasons why it was created as the beginning of the Lord’s ways.

Wisdom, then, was not created in order that, as something which had not existed, it might exist. Rather, although [Col. 0075B] it had always existed substantially, it was created, according to the dispensation, as the beginning of the Lord’s ways, and was created for the Lord’s works. Therefore Wisdom was created as the beginning of the Lord’s ways and was created for the Lord’s works; yet Wisdom was not created because it did not previously exist substantially.

But when it says that it was begotten before all the hills, it does not say that it was begotten for some purpose; rather, being the everlasting offspring of the Father, it says that it was created for certain purposes—as the beginning of the Lord’s ways, that is, for the Lord’s works. Thus it is evident from this also that Wisdom is not a creature: it was created for something else, namely for the Lord’s works, whereas it was begotten not for works but from the Father, as we have said, existing as his everlasting offspring.

IV. This point too must be considered: it is one thing [Col. 0075C] to say that Wisdom is created, and another to say that it is a creature. Although Wisdom is read to have been created, nowhere, however, is it read that it is a creature. For not everything which has been created is therefore to be called a creature, although every creature has been created; just as not everything which has been made is therefore to be affirmed to be a thing made, although every thing made has been made.

If this seems obscure, I shall clarify it by an example. We read that someone rejoices and says to God: “But I will sing of your power; in the morning I will exalt your mercy, because you became my protector and my refuge in the day of my tribulation” (Ps. 58:17). Behold, God became protector and refuge; nevertheless, God is not a thing made. This is what I said: not everything which has been made is therefore to be called a thing made. God, who always is and is not a thing made, [Col. 0075D] became protector and refuge for a man in the day of tribulation. Thus, by becoming protector and refuge for a man in the day of tribulation, he may be seen to have bestowed that benefit; yet because he became protector and refuge for a man, one must not believe that God himself is a creature, whose divine substance is everlasting.

Similarly, even if Wisdom is said to be created, it is not a creature, since it always is. Rather, though it always exists, it is created for some purpose, so as to benefit—not so as to be called a creature, as though it had been made when it previously did not exist. For the Wisdom of God was inseparable from God; and this same Wisdom, being God’s everlasting offspring, was created as the beginning of the Lord’s ways.

[Col. 0076A]

V. But I shall explain still more clearly. Certainly the Wisdom of God is itself that which is also written to be the Word, as has been shown above. And because it is written of the Word of God, “And the Word was made flesh,” do we therefore assert that the Word is a creature, as though it first began to exist when it was made flesh? No; for it has been demonstrated most plainly that all things were made through the Word, and that in the last times this same Word was made flesh. Therefore the Word of God is not a creature, although it is said to have been made flesh. In the same way, although Wisdom is said to have been created as the beginning of the ways and for his works, it is not a creature, since it is established to be before every creature, seeing that all things were made in Wisdom (Ps. 103:24).

I add this also: not everything which is said to be created must be understood as though it were made in substance. For example, a man, seeing his heart defiled by certain stains, pours out this prayer to the Lord: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50:12). He was certainly not praying that the substance of a heart be made within him, but that this very heart existing in him, which was defiled, might be created clean. Not everything said to be created must immediately be understood to be made according to substance, since he prayed that the heart which already existed might itself be created clean by the Lord.

Thus, when Wisdom is said to be created, its substance was not made as though it had not existed. Rather, as has often been said, it itself, already existing, was created as the beginning of the ways for his works. Therefore understand Wisdom’s being created in relation to the mystery either of things to be created or of the human dispensation, which, when the Wisdom of God graciously assumes it, is said to be created. But understand Wisdom’s statement that it is begotten as meaning that you recognize in it nothing less of divinity than he who begot it possesses. For it is exceedingly impious to believe that God was ever without his Wisdom. Hence, because Wisdom was truly begotten of God, existing in substance as the same as its begetter—and Wisdom itself is Christ (1 Cor. 1:24)—therefore Christ, who is Wisdom, is not Son by adoption but the true Son, existing as God’s offspring and not a creature.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Holy Spirit

I. I think that I have resolved all the questions you wrote concerning the Father and the Son, insofar as God’s grace has enabled me. [Col. 0076D] Whether this is true in your judgment, your religious discernment will decide. Yet I confess that, because of the constraint of time, the urgency of the matter, and the barren narrowness of my unadorned speech, I have touched upon their chief points rather than pursued them in fullness. For, as I said before, I did not begin to write a book, but to set down something like a brief outline concerning the faith, [Note: [Col. 0075D] “Lest.”] lest your remarkable kindness, having prompted me to this, should think me faithless if I were silent.

But now something must be confessed concerning the Holy Spirit, though briefly, lest, if we say nothing about him specifically, we too may be thought to blaspheme as those do who call him a creature. Yet we marvel at their madness: they think impiously concerning him whom they confess to be the Holy Spirit. For if he is the Holy Spirit, how is he a creature? He is not holy in the way that the rest are holy, who have attained the designation “holy” through faith, conduct pleasing to God, and the sealing of that same Holy Spirit. Rather, he is always holy by nature, so that he sanctifies others; he does not receive holiness from outside, as though [Note: [Col. 0077D] “As one who.”] he had not possessed it before.

The Spirit possesses the name “holy” in the same way that the Father and the Son possess it; yet he possesses it not by being the Father himself or the Son, but by being the Spirit of God. If he is called the Spirit of God, however, this is not as an angel of God or a man of God, whose nature differs immeasurably from the divine substance. Rather, he is the Spirit of God in such a way as to be of the same [Col. 0077B] substance as the Father and the Son; for there is one holiness of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is so truly and naturally holy that this designation is naturally and truly his.

Observe the Saviour’s words: “Go therefore now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Just as “Father” is a true designation and “Son” a true designation, so “Holy Spirit” is a true designation. And we shall be able to know how the designation “Father” is true if we consider how God is called true God.

II. Many are called gods, but they are not truly gods; and I now pass over Satan, demons, and their like, who are called gods by impious usurpation. Men too are called gods according to the testimony: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). But the following words show how they are not truly gods: “But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (ibid., 7). Thus, where any holy persons are called gods, this comes to them from God’s grace when they live piously and righteously, especially since the Holy Spirit dwells in them; and they fall away from that designation if they do not continue to walk in the Lord’s ways. Therefore no creature is true God, because no creature is God by nature.

But God alone is by nature the true God, existing as such without beginning and end. By this understanding of the true God, let us now understand the true designation of Father. Among human beings, someone is called father from the time he begets a son; but although he has begotten a son from himself, he is not properly a true father, since this designation came to him and was granted to him by God. [Note: [Col. 0077D] “Who.”] Indeed, he is called father only as long as his son lives. Just as he acquired the designation father when a son was born from him, so by the death of his son he loses the designation father.

But God alone is properly the true Father, who is Father without beginning and end. He did not at some point begin to be what he is as Father; rather, he is always Father, always having a Son begotten from himself, just as he is always true God, abiding without beginning and end. Therefore, just as he alone possesses the designation of true God, so he alone is called Father without beginning and end. In the same way let us understand the true designation of the Son of God.

Among human beings, one who is a son began to be what he is as son, and by the death of his father loses that designation. Moreover, he frequently passes from the designation son to that of father when he begets a son. Therefore the designation son is neither proper nor true in a creature, since the creature began to be a son and can cease to possess that designation either through the father’s death or through being himself transferred to the designation father, even before death’s condition overtakes him.

But the Son of God alone is truly Son, being this without beginning and without end, always having the Father, and never himself—being the only-begotten—begetting so as to receive the designation father. Thus the proper and true designation son belongs to the Son of God alone; he has it by nature, just as he is by nature true God. Therefore, if we have recognized how the designation father is proper and true, and how the designation son is proper and true, it follows that we should understand likewise how the designation Holy Spirit is proper and true.

III. The Holy Spirit is, by nature, Holy Spirit itself, without beginning and without end. For the designation Holy Spirit would never be joined with the true designations Father and Son with equal authority of name, unless the designation Holy Spirit were likewise proved proper and true. Therefore, if this designation belongs to him properly, truly, and naturally, without beginning and end, the Holy Spirit is not a creature, since he has the proper and true designation Holy Spirit in a way that no creature can have.

Further, when the Lord commands that the nations be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it is most clear that the Holy Spirit is not a creature, both from the association in which he is with the Father and Son, and because the Lord would never command anyone to be baptized in the name of a creature. The divine power would be greatly diminished if, together with confession of the divine name, an equal confession of a creature were also imposed. And fittingly he used one singular “name,” saying: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” so that the one supreme authority of the indivisible and perfect Trinity might be believed.

How can the Holy Spirit be believed to be distinct from supreme authority when we read concerning him in the fiftieth Psalm: “And strengthen me with a sovereign spirit” (Ps. 50:14)? [Col. 0078D] Therefore this also shows that there is one sovereignty of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, since in every act of creation the Spirit is found to share with the Father and Son. Receive for the moment even one testimony: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). Thus this too shows that the Holy Spirit is not a creature, since he is proved to be creator with the Father and the Son.

I shall declare the Holy Spirit to be fully God and Lord, taught by earlier ecclesiastical men, who themselves, first instructed in the testimonies of the divine Scriptures by apostolic men, handed them down to their successors. [Note: [Col. 0078D] “To lovers.”] I too would set out each of those testimonies, were not the divinity of the Holy Spirit evident to a faithful mind even from the points briefly indicated above—especially since what is now proposed to me is not so much a disputation concerning the Holy Spirit as the recording of a pious confession concerning his divine name.

Yet I shall add this brief proof of his divinity: the Holy Spirit is proved God by this very fact by which he is shown not to be a creature. Everything that exists is either divinity or creature; but the Holy Spirit, existing as such without beginning and end, is not a creature; therefore the Holy Spirit belongs to divinity, because he is the incorruptible, immutable, and everlasting Spirit of God. Thus the divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, just as the holiness of the same perfect and inseparable Trinity is one.

[Col. 0079B]

IV. But here let us make an end. The more attentively anyone wishes to speak concerning faith from the sacred Scriptures, the less will there be any lack of things to say. Yet I do not doubt that, if someone perhaps eloquent reads these very words, he will find faults in the unpolished style; but, if he is faithful, he will not find error in the pious confession. By God’s grace we desire to preserve this confession in ourselves until death, through the help of him who granted it, unstained by communion with heretics and transgressors; for, with God as witness, we fear being found participants in their condemnation.

Let anyone who thinks that he cannot become guilty through association with them see to it, relying upon his own conscience because he maintains the faith whole in such a way that he has never himself become a transgressor of that faith. Yet in God’s cause I am compelled to fear more cautiously. For we read this warning concerning them: “After one admonition avoid a heretical man, knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being condemned by himself” (Tit. 3:10–11).

We also read concerning the punishment of transgressors, Isaiah saying: “All flesh shall come before me to worship in Jerusalem, says the Lord God. And the saints shall go forth and see the limbs of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched; and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh” (Isa. 66:23–24). The Apostle also says: “Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers” (2 [Col. 0080B] Cor. 6:14); for elsewhere the same Apostle, after describing evils, says: “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. 1:32). There are many other divine testimonies prohibiting fellowship with those mentioned above.

But I have intimated these points, though briefly, [Note: [Col. 0079B] “At heart.”] lest anyone suppose that we refuse communion with such persons out of empty superstition, though he sees that they are rejected by the divine judgment. May the Godhead grant that you be found safe and blessed in faith in his name, together with all those dear to you, even in the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0079]

## THE CONFESSION OF FAUSTINUS THE PRESBYTER, PRESENTED TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS AND RECEIVED INTO THE CODEX OF THE CANONS AND CONSTITUTIONS OF THE ROMAN CHURCH. (C)

[Col. 0079C]

The faith written at Nicaea was sufficient against the Arian heresy. But because certain persons, with perverse ingenuity, alter impious words under the confession of that faith [Note: [Col. 0079C] Codex Thuanus: “mix”; elsewhere, “mingle.”], casting reproach upon us as though we defended the heresy of Sabellius, we set down in a few words a confession of the first faith against Sabellius also, and against those who, under the name of catholic faith, defend impious language, saying that there are three substances, whereas the catholic faith has always confessed one substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

We believe in the Father, who is not the Son but has a Son begotten from himself without beginning, not made. We believe in the Son, who is not the Father but has a Father from whom he is begotten, not made. And we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is truly the Spirit of God. Hence we confess one substance of the divine Trinity, [Col. 0080C] because, according to substance, such as the Father is, such a Son he begot. And the Holy Spirit, being not a creature but the Spirit of God, is not alien from the substance of the Father and Son; rather, he too is of the same substance with the Father and Son, just as he is of the same divinity.

Those who think us Apollinarians should know that we detest the heresy of Apollinaris no less than that of Arius. We marvel, however, that those can be judged catholic who confess three substances of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Even if they say that they do not believe the Son of God or the Holy Spirit to be a creature, nevertheless, when they say that there are three substances, they hold an impious faith [Note: [Col. 0080C] Thus the edition; but “pious” appears to be the required reading.]. For it follows that those who confess three substances confess three gods. The Catholics have always detested this expression.

[Col. 0081]

## THE PETITION OF FAUSTINUS AND MARCELLINUS, PRESBYTERS OF URSINUS’ PARTY, AGAINST DAMASUS, ADDRESSED TO THE EMPERORS VALENTINIAN, THEODOSIUS, AND ARCADIUS. (C, S)

### PREFACE. On the Schism of Ursinus

[Col. 0081A]

I. In the time of the Emperor Constantius, son of Constantine, a harsher persecution of Christians arose from the impious Arian heretics, with Constantius’ approval. He persecuted Bishop Athanasius for resisting the heretics and commanded that he be condemned by all bishops. All bishops everywhere attempted to do this out of fear of the emperor, condemning one unheard and innocent. But Liberius, bishop of Rome, Eusebius of Vercelli, Lucifer of Cagliari, and Hilary of Poitiers refused to pronounce sentence. They were therefore sent into exile for preserving the faith.

Damasus, Liberius’ deacon, pretended to set out with him; but he fled from the journey and returned to Rome, corrupted by ambition. Yet on the day on which Liberius departed for exile, all the clergy—that is, the presbyters, Felix the archdeacon, Damasus himself the deacon, and all the church officers—together, in the presence of the Roman people, confirmed under oath that, while Liberius lived, they would by no means have another bishop. But the clergy, contrary to right and to what was altogether fitting, with the gravest crime of perjury, accepted Archdeacon Felix as ordained in Liberius’ place.

This action displeased the whole people, who withdrew themselves from his procession. After two years Constantius came to Rome. The people petitioned for Liberius; immediately assenting, he said: “You have Liberius; he will return better than he departed from you.” By this he was indicating Liberius’ consent, by which he had given his hand to perfidy. In the third year Liberius returned; the Roman people went out joyfully to meet him. Felix, denounced by the senate and people, was driven from the City; but shortly afterward, at the instigation of the clergy who had perjured themselves, he forced his way into the City and presumed to hold a station in the Julian basilica across the Tiber. The whole multitude of the faithful and the nobles again drove him from the City with great disgrace.

II. Eight years later, in the consulship of Valentinian and Valens, Felix died on the tenth day before the Kalends of December. Liberius showed mercy to the clergy who had perjured themselves and restored them to their former positions. Likewise, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaisus, Liberius was removed from human affairs. Then the presbyters and deacons Ursinus, Amantius, and Lupus, with the holy people who had remained faithful to Liberius while he was in exile, began to assemble in the Julian basilica and [Col. 0082A] demanded that Ursinus, a deacon, be ordained bishop for them in Liberius’ place.

But the perjurers at Lucina’s demanded Damasus as their bishop in Felix’s place. Ursinus was consecrated by Paul, bishop of Tibur. When Damasus, who had always coveted the episcopate, learned this, he stirred up with money all the charioteers and the ignorant rabble; armed with clubs, he burst into the Julian basilica and for three days raged in a great slaughter of the faithful. Seven days later, with all the perjurers and [Note: [Col. 0081C] *Arenarii.* The term *arenarii* is commonly used for those who fight in amphitheatres, as in Law 2, §2, *On Witnesses*, Law 38, *On the Works of Freedmen*, and elsewhere. Tertullian likewise, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 22, condemns together charioteers, actors, athletes, and *arenarii*. Further, in the tenth session of the Council of Chalcedon: “having gathered an undisciplined crowd with swords and certain other arena-fighters” (*συναγαγὼν ὄχλον ἄτακτον μετὰ ξιφῶν καὶ ἄλλων τινῶν ἀραναρίων*); and below: “with swords, arena-fighters, and certain torches” (*μετὰ ξιφῶν καὶ ἀραναρίων καὶ δᾴδων τινῶν*), where the old translation renders *arenarii* as “arena-fighters.” On this term, and many other matters, see the learned Mazochius, commentary on the Marble Calendar of the Church of Naples, vol. III, p. 971.] arena-fighters, whom he had bribed at great cost, he seized the Lateran basilica. There he was ordained bishop; and, after bribing Viventius, prefect of the City, and Julianus, prefect of the grain-supply, he brought it about that Ursinus—a venerable man who had first been ordained bishop—was sent into exile with the deacons Amantius and Lupus.

[Col. 0082B]

When this was done, Damasus began to harass the Roman populace, which refused to join his procession, with clubs and various bloodshed. He also attempted, through the public authorities, to drive seven detained presbyters from the City. But the faithful people came to their aid, rescued those presbyters, and without delay brought them to the basilica of Liberius.

### III

Then Damasus, together with the faithless, summoned gladiators, charioteers, and gravediggers, and the whole clergy, armed with axes, swords, and clubs; and on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaifus, he besieged the basilica at the second hour of the day and provoked a severe battle. For, after breaking down the doors and setting fire beneath them, he sought an entrance by which he might rush in. Some also of his household, tearing apart the roof of the basilica, killed the faithful people with tiles. Then all the followers of Damasus rushed into the basilica and killed one hundred and sixty of the people, both men and women; they also wounded very many, of whom many died. But on Damasus’s side no one died.

After three days the holy people, having assembled together, began to recite against him the commandments of the Lord, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” They also sang in praise and said: “They gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth. They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them.”

Accordingly, the same people, repeatedly gathered in the Basilica of Liberius, cried out, saying: “Christian Emperor, nothing escapes you. Let all bishops come to Rome; let the case be heard. Damasus has now made a fifth war: drive murderers from the See of Peter.” And the people of God urgently begged the bishops with many prayers to condemn by a just sentence the aforesaid man, stained by such great impiety—whom matrons loved so much that he was called “the matrons’ ear-scratcher” (*auriscalpius matronarum*).

### IV

The cries of the people were therefore conveyed to the Emperor Valentinian. Moved by compassion, he granted the exiles their return. Then Ursinus returned to the City with the deacons Amantius and Lupus, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus; and the holy people joyfully came out to meet him.

But Damasus, conscious of so many crimes, shaken by no slight fear, bribed the entire palace lest his deeds be disclosed to the emperor. The emperor, not knowing what Damasus had perpetrated, prolonged the edict: Ursinus was banished into exile, so that no further impious contention among the people might clash. Then Bishop Ursinus, a holy and blameless man, taking thought for the people, gave himself into the hands of the unjust; and, by order of the emperor, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December he voluntarily hastened into exile.

But the people, fearing God and wearied by no persecutions, feared neither emperor nor judge, nor even Damasus himself, the author of crimes and murderer; rather, they held services at the cemeteries of the martyrs without clergy. Hence, when many faithful had gathered at Saint Agnes’s, Damasus rushed in armed with his attendants and struck down very many in the slaughter of his devastation. This most cruel deed greatly displeased the bishops of Italy. When he had solemnly invited them also to his birthday feast, and some of them had assembled, he attempted, by prayers and money, to induce them to pronounce sentence against holy Ursinus. They replied: “We have come to a birthday feast, not to condemn one unheard.” Thus his wicked design lacked the result at which it aimed.

Thereafter the presbyters were afflicted in various ways and dispersed through exile and foreign places. From among them the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus, concerning the confession of the true faith, the profession of sacred communion, and the persecution of those opposing the truth, presented the following petition to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius.

## THE BOOK OF PETITIONS BEGINS

### I

We beseech your clemency, most devout emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, that, in consideration of Christ the Son of God, who aids your empire, you may deign to read these matters without weariness.
