Your exalted sovereignty rises to still greater heights through the assistance of God the almighty Father and Christ his only-begotten Son when you neither despise truth even in lowly persons nor strengthen falsehood in many or powerful persons.

For this is most just and most salutary under a kingdom of justice: that persons be tested by the merit of truth, not truth presumed from the power of persons. Indeed, secular law was written for this reason: lest power or a multitude prevail against what is true and just, even if it is defended by insignificant persons. If such care must be maintained, by the provision of your serenity, even in affairs of the commonwealth, so that the right of truth may prevail against every force and power even in the smallest matters, in order that the state entrusted to your rule by God’s will may flourish—how is it that, in divine matters, the truth of the holy faith is obscured and oppressed by a crowd of impious people and their most fraudulent devices?

Especially since you, rulers of the Roman Empire, defend the devout faith and purity of the Christian religion by so many of your constitutions. Indeed, since as worshippers of Christ the Son of God you decree on behalf of the Catholic faith and exert every effort, by enactments backed by the authority of your empire, against heretics and faithless persons. You do this not as though attempting some novelty of your own opinion, as certain earlier rulers attempted to their own and others’ destruction, but in order to show that your judgments and your faith agree with the sacred teachings of the divine Scriptures and with devout confessions.

### II

Yet this, although after the most atrocious persecutions of the preceding time it ought rather to assist the holy Church, afflicts it all the more. For the same distinguished bishops who formerly persecuted it under the assertion or assent of heresy now persecute it also under the authority of the Catholic name. And the more fraudulently they act now under the counterfeit profession of devout faith, the more ruinously they rage, and the more painfully truth burns, because even under you emperors, who defend the devout faith, it is still not permitted to breathe.

But lest we seem to allege this merely to create odium without proving the matter, we explain the case as best we can. We humbly ask that you lend your imperial ears to us, the least of men, while we show that we are not heretics and yet are violently afflicted as though we were heretics—although neither those who violently afflict us nor their associates can now say or prove that we are heretics. Nor indeed can they deny of themselves that in the former period they either defended heresy most fiercely, with intolerable punishment of the faithful, or at least gave it their support, condemning the Catholic faith which they had previously defended, because they feared to suffer exile for Christ the Son of God—for whom even a faithful layperson must undergo any most atrocious death. For, as the Apostle says, “it has been granted to us not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29). Such death or suffering is an occasion of immortality.

### III

Your clemency and religion devoted to God do not fail to know how impious and deadly the Arian heresy is, against which our fathers composed the creed at Nicaea with special vigor: so that the devout confession of apostolic faith might be preserved, and, by the perpetual condemnation of that very heresy, established so firmly that no one in later times could be deceived.

But Arius, like Pharaoh in heart, refusing to believe that a divine sentence had then been given against him, by some means insinuated himself with Constantine, hoping that, if the judgment of the eminent priests were overturned through Constantine’s influence, he might be received into the Church.

> **Note: [Col. 0083D] From the Colbert manuscript:** “He insinuated himself with Constantine.”

Constantine himself had accordingly ordered that the holy and blessed bishop Alexander should communicate with him—not that Alexander who was bishop of the divine faith in Alexandria, who, filled with wisdom and fervent in the Holy Spirit, first exposed and expelled that same Arius and condemned him forever, but that Alexander who was bishop in this city of Constantinople and was himself an admirable bishop.

When he saw that Arius relied upon the ruler of this world, he cried out from the deep anguish of his heart, standing in the sanctuary, to Christ, the true and everlasting King and Lord of all kings, that he would not allow that stain to enter the Church. How steadfast and faithful his prayer was was proved by this: Arius himself, before entering the Church, paid new and most grievous penalties, unto a shameful death.

For on the day before the impious man thought that, through the emperor’s aid, he would enter the holy Church—although he suffered no sickness or bodily pain, but, what was worse, was incurably diseased by sickness of the mind alone—he sought a place of retirement according to human custom. As he sat there, suddenly tormented by a most severe pain, he discharged all his entrails, and his very heart, which was the treasury of impiety, into the filth. Thus, wonderful to say, after all his internal organs had been emptied, he was so reduced that, as if dissolved by the wasting corruption of a pallid body, in an instant he slipped entirely through the narrow opening of the latrine seat.

> **Note: [Col. 0085D] Manuscript:** “After all his internal organs had been emptied.”

This was a fitting punishment for an impious man, a fitting shameful death for a deadly heretic, and a fitting burial for the foulest limbs of the devil’s spirit. For by a new example he had to be tortured and perish, he who had invented new impieties against the only-begotten Son of God, saying that he was not truly born of the Father; that “there was when he was not”; and that he was established from nothing, lest he be believed to possess the same substance, divinity, eternity, and omnipotence as the Father.

### IV

We have related this to your august clemency so that your prudence, attentive to truth, may observe how venerable is the faith composed at Nicaea against Arius—a faith to which God bore testimony not only through the authority of the divine Scriptures but also through the most sacred prayer of holy Alexander—and how execrable is Arius’s impious doctrine, which the divine sentence condemned in Arius himself by a novel kind of punishment. It did not await the day of judgment in his case, so that others, terrified by the example of his punishment, might beware.

By that example, surely, it must not be doubted that those also are condemned before God who believed that Arius’s impious doctrine ought to be renewed or embraced. For how can perpetual punishment separate those whom impious doctrine does not separate? Even under your laws, one prison confines equally guilty persons and one sentence strikes them.

Nor can it be doubted that those are truly Catholic who, through exiles, kinds of punishments, the atrocity of death, defend without deceit that faith which was composed at Nicaea on evangelical and apostolic grounds, and which God most openly approved by the punishment of Arius when he attacked it. If these things are true before you, as they are confirmed as true by the divine Scriptures, consider, most devout and most religious emperors, in what condition those are who, under these divine rules and professions, have consecrated their faith and devotion to Christ God, setting no fear above the fear of God.

But although Arius was buried in filth, he nevertheless left some heirs of his impiety. Indeed, worms were not lacking to be born from his rotten corpse. It would take long to recount what the devil, the artificer of error, accomplished through them, even if we could recount it; for these deeds are innumerable and unbelievable, yet not false.

### V

We now set forth what bears upon the present case: those who made the Emperor Constantius a participant in Arian impiety through fraudulent disputation would themselves now have paid the penalty, had it not been necessary, according to the Apostle’s statement (1 Cor. 11:19), that heresies also should exist, so that those who are approved might become manifest.

Therefore these whom we called Arius’s worms, having royal power in agreement with them, first strove individually on behalf of Arian impiety for the overthrow of the Catholic faith and the destruction of sacred religion. Thus they attacked resisters with false accusations, or tortured and killed them by penalties or exile. Having raged still more widely in their madness and made themselves everywhere an object of terror, they were no longer content to proceed one by one.

Finally, they compelled bishops from every quarter to gather together; a place was assigned for a synod—Seleucia in Isauria for the Easterners, and the city of Ariminum for the Westerners. There the bishops who had come for the holy faith first confirmed the exposition composed at Nicaea, so that nothing should be removed from it: it had explained the evangelical faith in unassailable words and condemned Arius’s impious teaching by divine authority.

Then at last they execrated and condemned as impious the formulation of faith put forward by Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, and Gaius: a formulation which both rejected the Catholic faith and absolved Arius—indeed, introduced his deadly doctrine. They even judged those men guilty of an inexpiable crime if they violated the venerable faith of the Fathers, and if the Church tolerated those so impious persons and their impious formulation.

They also sent ten delegates to the Emperor Constantius, writing what had been done and at the same time urging him too to preserve inviolably, against heretics, the Fathers’ decrees concerning the venerable faith. The heretics likewise sent delegates, whom Constantius then received most familiarly, as his own. But he rejected the true delegates who had come on behalf of the Catholic faith against the heretics. Through his agents he now invited them with favor, now terrified them with threats, and meanwhile tormented them by delay alone, until at last, fearing the anger of the king, declining to endure exile for Christ the Son of God, and delighting in their own seats and the most ruinous possessions of churches, they overturned what they had piously defended and embraced what they had condemned as impious.

### VI

May we be permitted, before you religious emperors, to groan more sorrowfully in this cause of God: the bishops feared the anger of an earthly king more than Christ, the true God and everlasting King. They judged temporary exile more grievous than the perpetual punishment of the undying worm and unquenchable fire according to Isaiah (Isa. 66:24). They considered their own homes and possessions sweeter than a blessed and everlasting dwelling in Christ’s kingdom.

But Constantius, not content with the ruin and fall of the ten delegates, sent orders to Ariminum that all the bishops there should be similarly turned. They too, following the evil example of their delegates, rejected the devout faith of the Fathers which they had defended, subscribing to that faith of the Arians which they had condemned by uncorrupted and free judgment.

Your wisdom observes that the Synod of Ariminum was begun most devoutly but ended most impiously. The same impiety was committed by the bishops at Seleucia in Isauria. Judge, most devout and most religious emperors, what is the condition of those who refuse communion with such bishops, who, after first defending the intact faith and rejecting the impious faith, afterward—when they feared exile and delighted in their possessions and homes—changed their judgments: at the nod of a heretical emperor condemning the apostolic faith which they had defended, or embracing the impiety of Arius which they had rejected.

### VII

Should they not have thought it preferable—if indeed they believed that God’s judgment would come—to suffer every evil rather than become traitors to the venerable faith, whose truth had been approved by the prayers of holy Alexander and Arius’s punishment? Especially since an example of glorious suffering had already preceded them, though among very few bishops, who, lest they violate the evangelical and apostolic faith or yield to the impious, refused neither exile nor punishment nor any atrocity of death.

Before the Synod of Ariminum, Paulinus of Trier, a most steadfast bishop, was sent into exile, defending the devout faith and execrating communion with the Arians. Likewise the apostolic man Lucifer of Sardinia, bishop of the city of Caralis, was sent by the Roman Church as a delegate to Constantius because he had become well known through contempt for the world, zeal for sacred learning, purity of life, constancy in faith, and divine grace. Because he defended the venerable faith, exposed the heretics, and convicted them, he was led into exile amid every kind of atrocious injury.

Likewise Eusebius of Vercelli, and Dionysius of Milan—who had first been intimate with King Constantius while he did not yet know that Constantius favored heretics—afterward, when it became known and proved to him that the king defended heretics, rejected the king’s impious friendship. They preferred exile, lest they lose the friendship of Christ God and no longer have fellowship with the saints.

Rodanius too was sent into exile, as was Hilary, who published writings against heretics and apostates; although afterward he did favor apostates, not to say in the meantime that he favored the heretics against whom he had employed the strength of his eloquence.

> **Note: [Col. 0087D] “Where also [he favored] heretics.”** The text is badly corrupted at *ubi et haereticis*; it may readily be restored as *favit*, as earlier writers used *Fabit* for *favit*: “not to say in the meantime that he FAVORED heretics.” Thus Mazochius, *Commentary on the Marble Calendar of the Neapolitan Church*, vol. II, p. 576. The Oxford editor, however, would prefer: “not to say in the meantime [anything] to heretics, because where there are apostates there are also heretics,” against whom he had spoken with the power of his eloquence. This is less satisfactory.

Maximus also of Naples in Campania, because he had a weak stomach and a somewhat frail body, was first long afflicted with injuries in order that he might fall. Then, when he was not overcome by bodily weakness because of the constancy of his mind and the strength of his faith, he was led into exile; there he rested as a martyr in the Lord’s peace.

> **Note: [Col. 0088D] “Maximus also of Naples, etc.”** The cited Mazochius fully elucidates this passage, *ibid.*, p. 577.

Rufinianus too, of remarkable simplicity indeed but even more admirable in defending the faith, preceded exile by the shedding of his blood. For, when he persisted in the integrity of the faith, Epictetus—that fierce and dreadful bishop of Centumcellae—forced him to run before his carriage. After he had run for a long time, his vital organs burst on the road; pouring out blood, he expired. The people of Naples in Campania know this: there remnants of his blood afflict demons in possessed bodies, undoubtedly through the grace of the faith for which he shed his blood.

There were also other bishops from Egypt, though few: some fled, while others were sent into exile because they refused communion with impious and cruel bishops.

### VIII

How salutary, beautiful, and glorious it would surely have been if all those bishops, with equal courage and a like united resolve, had preserved to the end the faith which they had always rightly defended, fearing neither exile nor punishments, in order to attain the future and everlasting blessedness in the kingdom of Christ God. We leave unspoken that perhaps they would even have made people understand that this faith was of great value, since no bishop would refuse exile, confiscation, torments, or death for its sake.

But a great multitude of bishops, somewhat frightened, surrendered their hands to impiety in a body; and impiety, through so easy a rout of the multitude, now inclined toward greater madness. This is no lesser sacrilege, no lesser impiety, than if sacrifice had been offered to an idol under a pagan persecutor. For to subscribe to heresy through fear is to sacrifice to demons. According to the teaching of the divine Scriptures, heresy is a doctrine of demons, as is idolatry.

Meanwhile, because some people prefer a multitude to truth on the ground that truth has few followers, and because we are therefore afflicted—because we follow the inviolable faith with the few and avoid the many because of their impious heresies and the sacrilegious subscriptions of apostates—what, most just emperors and defenders of the Catholic faith, do you judge in this case? To which of these two parties do you give your vote?

One party includes many bishops. But where there are many, there the sacred faith of Christ, always previously defended, has been violated through apostasy; there, through fear of the king, the impiety of Arius, always previously condemned, has been embraced. Where there are very few, there Christ’s faith is defended through exiles, tortures, the shedding of blood, and death itself; there Arius’s impiety and every heresy are execrated as the supreme evil.

Even if there can be no doubt that the few bishops are precious because of the merit of their confession and inviolable faith, while the many are reduced to nothing because of the guilt of heresy or apostasy—for in a cause of truth, and especially in a cause of religion and sacred faith, number is not to be compared with number, but that pure apostolic faith, proved by exiles and torments even if only of one person, must be preferred to the unfaithfulness of many—nevertheless, it is necessary to produce a present divine proof of condemned apostasy. Just as Arius’s impious sect, punished by divine judgment in Arius, determines beforehand concerning his followers that the same punishment awaits them by which Arius is tormented, so regarding apostates it has been decided by divine judgment through present punishments.

### IX

Potamius, bishop of the city of Olisipo, first defended the Catholic faith; afterward, for the reward of an imperial estate which he desired to possess, he betrayed the faith. Hosius of Corduba exposed and rejected him among the churches of Spain as an impious heretic.

But Hosius himself, summoned to King Constantius at Potamius’s complaint, terrified by threats and fearing that, being old and rich, he might suffer exile or confiscation, surrendered to impiety. After so many years he betrayed the faith; and he returned to Spain with greater authority, holding the king’s terrible command that any bishop unwilling to communicate with him, now made an apostate, should be sent into exile.

But a faithful messenger brought the impious apostasy of Hosius to holy Gregory, the most steadfast bishop of the city of Eliberri. Therefore Gregory, mindful of the sacred faith and divine judgment, did not consent to Hosius’s wicked communion. Hosius was all the more tormented by this, since someone, though Hosius himself had fallen, still stood firm in defending the intact faith with unwavering constancy. He therefore had Gregory, a man of most vigorous mind, brought before the public authorities, hoping that by the same terror through which he himself had yielded, Gregory also might be made to yield. At that time Clementinus was vicarius, who, acting by agreement with Hosius and under the king’s general command, ordered holy Gregory to be brought to Corduba through the official service.

### X

Meanwhile the report of the proceeding disturbed everyone, and the people commonly asked: “Who is this Gregory who dares to resist Hosius?” For very many still did not know of Hosius’s apostasy, nor had they yet fully learned who holy Gregory was. Even among those who perhaps knew him, he was still an inexperienced bishop, though before Christ he was no inexperienced defender of the faith, by reason of his holiness.

But behold, they came before the vicarius. Many officials were present. Hosius sat as judge—indeed, above the judge—relying on imperial power; and holy Gregory, after the example of his Lord, stood as an accused man, not because of a guilty conscience but because of the circumstances of the present trial; otherwise, he was free in faith. There was great expectation among all as to which side victory would incline.

Hosius relied on the authority of his age; Gregory on the authority of truth. The former trusted in the earthly king; the latter in the everlasting King. Hosius relied on the emperor’s written order, but Gregory held fast to the writings of the divine utterance. When Hosius was refuted in every respect, so that he was overcome by his own words which he had formerly written on behalf of faith and truth, he said indignantly to Clementinus the vicarius: “A hearing has not been entrusted to you, but an execution. You see that he resists the royal commands. Carry out, therefore, what has been ordered: send him into exile.”

But Clementinus, though he was not a Christian, nevertheless reverenced the name of the episcopate, especially in a man whom he saw defending his cause rationally and faithfully. He answered Hosius: “I do not dare to send a bishop into exile so long as he remains in the rank of bishop. But you, first pronounce sentence, stripping him of the honor of the episcopate; then at last I shall execute against him, as against a private person—that is, a layman—what you desire to be done by the emperor’s order.”

> **Note: [Col. 0089D] “Private person.”** That is, a layman. In Cyril’s Glossary, *idiōtēs* (ἰδιώτης) means the same as *privatus*, “a private person.” Hence at 1 Corinthians 14:16 laypersons are called *idiōtai*, that is, private persons. Mazochius, *ibid.*, vol. III, p. 958.

When holy Gregory saw that Hosius intended to pronounce sentence so that he might appear to have been deposed, he appealed to Christ, the true and powerful Judge. With all the strength of his faith he cried aloud: “Christ God, who are to come to judge the living and the dead, do not allow a human sentence to be pronounced today against me, your least servant, who stand accused for faith in your name and provide a spectacle. But do you yourself, I beseech you, judge your cause today; deign yourself to pronounce sentence through vengeance. I ask this not because I fear exile, since no punishment for your name is not sweet to me, but so that many may be freed from the error of apostasy when they see a present and immediate vengeance.”

As he called upon God in faithful words with much force and holiness, behold, suddenly Hosius, while attempting to state his sentence, twisted his mouth and his neck together, fell from his seat to the ground, and there expired—or, as some maintain, became mute. Yet he was carried out as dead. Then, while all marveled, even that pagan Clementinus was terrified. Though he was judge, he feared that he too might be judged by a similar punishment. He threw himself at the holy man’s feet and begged him to spare him, since he had sinned against him through ignorance of the divine law, acting not so much by his own decision as by the authority of the one commanding.

All were then filled with astonishment and admiration of divine power: the whole spectacle that we have known was seen in that event.

> **Note: [Col. 0091D] “Which in that spectacle …”** A corruption wholly incurable without the aid of manuscripts. Isidore of Seville and Ildefonsus’s continuator, who copied this history together with what follows, omit this entire clause; I therefore consider it interpolated. Oxford edition.

For he who wished to pronounce a human sentence immediately suffered a graver divine one; the judge who had come to judge now stood pale and accused, fearing judgment; and he who had stood as though accused and about to be sent into exile was asked by the fallen judge to spare him as though he himself were judge. Thus Gregory alone, among those defending the intact faith, was neither driven into flight nor suffered exile; everyone thereafter feared to proceed against him.

### XI

Do you see the remarkable proofs of apostasy condemned by God? All Spain knows better that we do not invent these things. Nor did Potamius’s betrayal of the sacred faith go unpunished. As he hurried to the estate which he had obtained from the emperor as a reward for his impious subscription concerning faith, he suffered new penalties in the tongue through which he had blasphemed: he died on the road, receiving none of the estate’s fruits even by seeing it.

This was no light punishment for an avaricious man. He died who, through desire for an imperial estate, had violated the sacred faith; and as he hurried toward the estate, a punitive death overtook him lest he should possess even the consolation of seeing it. In the holy Gospel we read the words of rebuke addressed to the rich man who most vainly boasted of the stores he had laid up: “Fool,” it says, “this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20). Whoever considers that this written saying applies also to Potamius will understand that he was not lightly judged—especially since he suffered punishment in the tongue, in which that rich man too is more severely tormented among the dead.

Florentius also, knowing that Hosius and Potamius had already betrayed the faith, communicated with them at a certain place, and he too suffered new punishments. For as he sat on a throne in the congregation of the people, he was suddenly thrown down and convulsed; carried outside, he recovered his strength. Again, when he entered and sat another time, he suffered in the same way, still not understanding the punishment of his stained communion. Nevertheless, when afterward he persisted in entering, he was cast from the throne a third time, as though visibly rejected as unworthy of the throne. Thrown to the ground, he was convulsed and tortured with such rigidity and severe agonies that life was wrenched from him. He was then carried away, no longer to recover as usual, but to be buried.

The great city of Emerita knows what we report, for the people in its church saw this very thing with their own eyes. This also should be considered: Florentius suffered these things although he had not yet subscribed to impiety, but merely communicated with traitors to the faith, knowing their apostasy. We have related this so that those may see what they must do who, though they have not subscribed as apostates, have nevertheless joined themselves in communion to persons known to them as traitors. I think they will understand, from Florentius’s example, what they should fear.

### XII

But it would take long to relate the other proofs of condemned apostasy through present punishments which divine judgment has inflicted in various places. God did this so that one who does not, for some reason, heed the divine Scriptures might understand through present divine vengeance what he ought to pursue and what to avoid. Without doubt, God chose to inflict punishment even upon a few for this reason: lest the threats concerning the future punishments of apostates contained in divine Scripture be regarded as fables, if in this present age punishment were inflicted on no one.

Let all bishops who betray the faith now understand for what most grievous punishments they are reserved, when judgment has been inflicted upon their associates even in this age, to the astonishment of all. We have set forth these present punishments of apostasy so that what has been inflicted upon a few may be believed to be inflicted also upon all who are like them—especially since divine Scripture itself affirms the very point demonstrated by present examples.

And let this be considered, most devout emperors: in what condition are those who do not join themselves in divine mysteries with such persons, whose eternal punishments are read of in the sacred books and whose examples of punishment are seen in the world? Yet we beseech your wonderful benevolence to grant us, for the sake of Christ God, the untiring patience to hear us still further, while we set forth, albeit summarily, how far impiety has grown.

### XIII

For the execrable Arians in the Eastern regions, and especially in Egypt, were not content merely that bishops, after condemning the intact faith, should turn to their impious opinion. Rather, those very bishops who had first been ordained by Catholic bishops, once they had subscribed according to the Arians’ wishes, were reduced to the rank of laypersons; then the same heretics ordained them bishops again. Thus they appeared to condemn not only the Catholic faith but also the ordination performed by Catholic bishops.

Observe in this a kind of triumph by heretics over Catholics, and a wretched, as it were final and most shameful captivity. Those bishops, after condemning the devout faith and the Catholic bishops, surrendered themselves to the heretics’ dominion and mockery through fear of exile, and in order to seem to retain before human beings the episcopal title—which, after their impious subscriptions, they certainly no longer possessed before God.

The authority of that title was therefore sought even with every disgrace, lest the possessions of the Church be taken from them. Would that the Church had never possessed such things, so that, living according to apostolic custom, it might possess the intact faith inviolably. Yet now it is called the height of impiety not to communicate with such persons—and this under you emperors, who, as your constitutions declare, judge the divine holiness of the venerable Church. It is not surprising, however, if, occupied with the care of the commonwealth, you do not know of their deeds, so atrocious as these.

The bishops who execrated these impieties, whether they endured the punishment of exile for the faith or had taken themselves into flight, though separated bodily by the distances of regions, were nevertheless united in spirit. By reciprocal letters, with apostolic vigor, they decreed that communion could in no way be held with bishops of this kind, who had betrayed the faith in the manner related above, unless they sought lay communion while grieving for their impieties.

XIV. But after Constantius, the patron of the heretics, had died, Julian alone held the empire; by his command all the Catholic bishops were released from exile. Divinity is accustomed to act thus: even through opponents of its Christian religion it provides for its own, so that those who are worshippers of Christ may labour all the more for the faithful. But not long afterward Julian was slain, and Jovian became emperor. Vindicating the Catholic faith, he gave his vote to the Catholic bishops. Yet those distinguished bishops condemned by a heretical subscription the faith which under Constantius they had defended intact [Col. 0093B], seeing that at the emperor’s pleasure bishops were now made heretics from Catholics, and that the same bishops returned from heretics to the Catholic faith.

But even if certain weary confessors believed that in the end they ought to join the communion of such men—perhaps overturning those ordinances which they had previously decreed against them with prophetic and apostolic authority—can this overthrow divine truth? Can it prejudice the teachings of the Gospel? Can it undermine apostolic pronouncements, and especially that utterance of God: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22)? Moreover, the chosen vessel, the Apostle Paul, speaks through Christ the Lord [Note: [Col. 0093D] “I would prefer: ‘having pronounced.’”], and these are his words in writing to the Galatians [Col. 0093C]: “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything beyond what we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:8). Accordingly, further on in the same epistle he continues: “For if I rebuild the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor” (Gal. 2:18).

Surely one becomes a confessor through the Gospels, the utterances of the Prophets, and the doctrines of the Apostles; but it is doubtful whether a faithful man [Note: [Col. 0093D] “Perhaps: ‘the faithful man.’”] then retains the merit of confession if, overthrowing the ordinances of the divine Scriptures, he begins to build up what the Gospels destroy.

XV. Are not the divine Scriptures attacked when the peace of the Church is joined with bishops who deny the Son of God? For who, considering the force of divine religion, can trust that the peace of the faithless pleases God, unless, as the Fathers decreed, they surrender themselves to the rank of the laity [Col. 0093D], grieving for their perfidy? But let them, if you will, have peace with unbelievers. Yet how do those offend, injure, or disturb the emperors or the commonwealth, who, in contemplation of divine judgment, reject a peace of this kind—a peace which admits sacrilegious persons, honours betrayers of the faith, favours hypocrites, despises truth, sets up deniers of Christ, the true Son of God, as though they were masters of the Church, contaminates the people with the stain of perfidy, and overturns the Gospel?

For this we are accused; for this, under the authority of your name, we suffer persecutions [Col. 0094A] from those bishops who, defending heresy at the bidding of the former emperor, sinned against the Catholic faith. Alas for the grief! The same bishops set the laws of Catholic emperors against the faithful and defenders of the Catholic faith. We speak these things, weeping with pain in every inward part: not because it is not glorious for the faithful to suffer under any boy [Note: [Col. 0093D] “It certainly seems one should read ‘for the truth’ in place of ‘under any boy,’ as again below, near the end of the treatise: ‘as though we feared to be killed [Col. 0094D] for the truth.’”]; but because there is such stupor in the world that the impiety of these men, wrapped in such great perfidies, is not recognized, and that no one understands how they continually deceive even royal ears in the harassment of Christians and faithful priests.

But impiety is covered under the name of peace, and the fair-seeming name of truth is set up as a defence for the faithless. Yet it is well that the Saviour himself explained the power of his peace, lest anyone should be deceived [Col. 0094B] by the simple word “peace” and join it to the impieties of the world, saying: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as this world gives do I give to you” (John 14:27). He distinguished his own peace from the peace of the world.

For if this peace is pleasing to God, which receives unbelieving bishops into the Church, what need is there to endure distress in persecutions, to bear prison, to go to meet swords, and to endure every kind of torture and death? After denial, after the sacrileges of perfidy, on account of this peace which they think pleasing to God, every unbeliever is received securely, as though unstained, with episcopal honour unimpaired. On this argument, therefore, the martyrs must now be judged vain. To what end did they prefer to bear punishments and death [Col. 0094C]? For if those who, from fear of persecution, denied the Son of God suffer no punishment, but are rather honoured, neither ought martyrs to have hoped for the crown of suffering; rather, they ought to pay the penalties for their rashness. This consequence is unavoidable. It cannot be otherwise than that opposite judgments are made in the two cases.

Is it not evident to what conclusion they are driven by this term “peace,” or what they are compelled to pronounce: namely, that if deniers of the Son of God are rightly confirmed in honour, martyrs must be thought to be punished as though for their rashness? But far be it! Far be it that a Christian conscience should admit this. For we believe the Son of God when he declares: “Whoever denies me before men, I too will deny before my Father; and whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess [Col. 0094D] before my Father” (Matt. 10:33).

XVI. Yet in this matter also recognize divine judgment, proved by present evidence, lest anyone should suppose that the peace of such bishops should be accepted even if, after impious subscriptions or criminal communion with heretics—into which they knowingly yielded lest they lose either the possessions of the Church or their honours—they should return to confession of the true faith. [Note: [Col. 0094D] “The holy man Bishop Maximus, etc. Mazochius, as is his custom, discusses these and the following matters learnedly, *l. c.*, vol. II, p. 578 ff.”]

The holy man Bishop Maximus, whom we mentioned above, defending the right faith and rejecting fellowship [Col. 0095A] with heretics, was led into exile. In his place the betrayers ordained a man named Zosimus, who had himself formerly defended Catholic doctrine. This happened in the Campanian city of Naples. Saint Maximus learned of it and, writing from exile, pronounced sentence upon him—not merely with episcopal authority, but also, enjoying the zeal and power of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0095D] “*Fruens* [‘enjoying’]. It is more certain than certain that the authors wrote *fervens* [‘burning’] instead of *fruens*, by the addition of one letter. For ‘to burn with zeal,’ or with most ardent desire, besides being the proper sense, is confirmed by two other passages in this little work. Namely below, §23: ‘Bishop Ephesius BURNING WITH ZEAL FOR THE HOLY FAITH’; and in the following §24: ‘inflamed with divine zeal . . . .’ For even boys observe that *fervens* and *succensus* are wholly synonymous. Very many foul sores are scattered through this virulent, yet useful and most eloquent, little work, awaiting a physician’s hand. MAZOCHIUS, *l. c.*”] for the glory of God.

But after some years, when blessed Lucifer was proceeding from his fourth exile to Rome, he entered Naples in Campania. Zosimus attempted to come to him, perhaps in the confidence that he appeared to have corrected himself from impiety [Note: [Col. 0096D] “‘Corrected himself’: an intransitive use meaning ‘corrected himself’; just as *surgo* and *pergo*, contracted from *surrigo* and *perrigo*, are intransitive. MAZOCHIUS, ibid.”]. But Lucifer the confessor refused to receive him, knowing what he had done; indeed, in the ardour of the Holy Spirit he more firmly carried out the judgment of the bishop and martyr, [Col. 0095B] declaring that he would not possess that episcopate which he claimed for himself as an adulterer, by the particular judgment of God, and that in this way also he would suffer the penalty of his impiety.

Not long afterwards, when the same Zosimus wished in an assembly of the people to perform the offices of a priest, in the midst of his priestly words his tongue protruded, and he could not draw it back within the passage of his mouth. Contrary to nature it hung outside his mouth, like that of a panting ox. But when he saw that he had lost the use of his tongue, he left the basilica; and—remarkably—outside, his tongue was restored again to its function. At first it was not understood that the sentence of the martyr and confessor was being fulfilled upon him. But when he suffered this same thing repeatedly, as often as on different days he attempted to enter the basilica, he finally recognized that his tongue was denied him during the solemn words of the pontificate in order to prove the sentence rightly pronounced upon him by the holy bishops [Col. 0095C]. At last he relinquished the episcopate, so that the tongue which had withdrawn might be restored. We are not recounting ancient matters, which can usually be called into doubt for some reason. Zosimus is still alive today in the body, no longer losing the use of his tongue after choosing to live, deprived of the episcopate and grieving for his impieties.

XVII. Has it not also been prejudged in similar cases that it avails them nothing to persist as though under the rebuke of a bishop? For this is not rebuke, but mockery: according to the circumstances of the emperors’ times, they change their faith. This very thing deceived Emperor Valens when he saw steadfastness in the heretics’ defence of their doctrine, but in these distinguished Catholics an inconstancy [Col. 0095D] of faith. For it was certainly proved to him that those who asserted themselves to be Catholics had formerly subscribed with heretics, condemning the faith which they had first defended. And the heretics said: “If our faith is evil, why was it subscribed to under Constantius for its own sake by men who now call themselves Catholics, defending this faith which, when they first defended it, they condemned under Constantius after being refuted by arguments [Col. 0096A]?”

Moved by these things, Valens, ignorant of the power of the true faith and comparing steadfastness with inconstancy, defended the impiety of the heretics with a certain show of justice. And we pass over the fact that under Valens also certain persons again surrendered themselves to the heretics, whom we nevertheless now see counted among Catholics. Hence even the congregations of heretics were strengthened in their impious faith: the heretics persevere in evil, while those thought to be Catholics withdraw from good, sometimes yielding to the heretics. By what authority can bishops of this kind preach against a heresy to which they cannot deny having subscribed? And with what confidence can they endeavour to commend the Catholic faith to the people, when it is certain that they rejected it by impious subscriptions?

[Col. 0096B] XVIII. Do you see that even in your own times—though, as we believe, without your knowledge—the pious faith is defended, indeed, may it be truly defended, but even if truly, still with a certain injustice, when it is defended through unworthy bishops to the affliction of priests defending the pious faith and to the ruin of faithful laypeople? Yet it is judged criminal to depose so many betrayers, to reject a multitude united in injustice. And where is the justice of true religion if it must be surrendered to an impious multitude, and this under emperors most pious and religious?

Judgment was not thus given in the Flood, that the multitude of unbelievers should prevail. Rather, Noah, that most righteous man, pleased God all the more because in that destruction of the world he alone was found righteous. Likewise, in Sodom and Gomorrah God inflicted grievous penalties upon an impious multitude; [Col. 0096C] hence hospitable Lot alone was delivered for his righteousness, with only his two daughters. Nor was Elijah, the zealot of God, who stood alone, overcome when four hundred and fifty false priests were sent against him. Rather, that entire impious multitude of priests paid the penalty at the hand of one faithful man—and this while King Ahab hoped otherwise, he who impiously defended the false priests.

Nor did Jehu, king of Israel, yield to the impious multitude of priests. For after he had summoned all the false priests, who had flourished under King Ahab, into the house of their impious religion by a religious stratagem, as though he were about to reward them after their religious rites, he ordered them killed, so that none of them survived. And we read that this deed so pleased the Lord that the sons of that same king should sit upon the throne [Col. 0096D] of Israel unto the fourth generation.

XIX. There are many other very similar examples. We do not mention them because we wish anyone’s blood to be shed. Far be this from our desires: whoever desires it to happen departs from Christian laws. It was done then because at that time the divine law itself permitted it, when everything was still performed bodily, until spiritual instruction should grow [Col. 0097A]. But although it is now not permitted for good and faithful persons to desire the blood of false priests, faithful persons are not therefore to be surrendered to false priests so as to be afflicted by their most grievous persecutions.

Let what we say appear false if in various places the churches of faithful priests have not been invaded in some places and destroyed in others; if holy persons have not, through the accusations of those men, been seized, held long in confinement for injuries, and finally sent into exile; if certain others have not died in prison, while others, dragged away and beaten, yielded up their lives—for no other reason than that, from fear of divine judgment, they would not communicate with the faithless or with associates of the faithless.

[Col. 0097B] XX. In Spain, what atrocities did the presbyter Vincentius, a leader of the true faith, not suffer at the hands of betrayers, because he would not be a partner in their impious betrayal, because he communicated with blessed Gregory—I mean that Gregory whose faith and strength we have related above as best we could? Against him they first lodged an accusation with the consular governor of the province of Baetica. Then, under the pretext of requesting intervention, a popular crowd was gathered from other places. On Sunday they rushed into the church. They did not find Vincentius, because, having been warned, he had instructed the people beforehand not to assemble that day, when the attackers were coming with slaughter in mind. He judged that it would be better to give place to wrath.

But those who had come ready for killing, lest their fury [Col. 0097C] be thought to have come without purpose, beat with clubs certain ministers devoted to Christ God whom they found there, so that not long afterward they died. But because the holy people of the presbyter Vincentius more earnestly entreated them [Note: [Col. 0097D] “Perhaps: *imprecabantur*, ‘called down curses upon them.’ OXFORD.”] after those slaughters carried out on the Lord’s Day, the bishops went out and, to terrify the entire people, began with the leading citizens themselves. They demanded that the decurions of that city be produced, to be shut in prison. One of them, a leading man of his own country, because as a faithful man he held firmly to faith in God and abhorred the stain of betrayal, was himself chained among them and killed by hunger and cold, amid the groaning and weeping of that province which knew his honourable life very well.

The distinguished and Catholic bishops Luciosus and Hyginus were the authors of this cruelty [Col. 0097D]. Meanwhile, they did indeed seize the basilica, but they could not seize the faith of the people. Accordingly, elsewhere in a small field the same people built a basilica for themselves, where they assembled with Saint Vincentius. But Satan, who nowhere permits Christ to be worshipped devoutly, inflamed them; and again, after a petition had been submitted, a multitude of decurions and common people was gathered from various cities. At the same time Vincentius’s presbyters came to the place. They broke down the doors of that church, plundering from it everything belonging to the sacred ministries. Finally—horrible to say—to crown their accomplished sacrilege, they placed the altar of God, taken from the Lord’s house [Col. 0098A], in a temple beneath the feet of an idol.

XXI. These, surely, are the deeds of men who were received into Catholic discipline through penitence for their impious subscription, for the supposed good of peace and unity. What more grievous thing would a pagan worshipper of idols do if he had permission to persecute the Church?

But at Trier the presbyter Bonosus was imprisoned, left without a will, and as an old man endured punishments for a long time because of his observance of that undefiled faith for which the renowned Paulinus, bishop of the same city, also gave up his life as a martyr in exile. In the city of Rome itself, too, how severe were the persecutions inflicted upon the faithful, where blessed Bishop Aurelius, in communion with most blessed Gregory, was afflicted! Yet this holy man, though often afflicted, rested by his own summons [Col. 0098B].

Many impious acts were committed against the presbyter Macarius. He was a presbyter in that same city of Rome, of remarkable continence: he did not refresh his stomach with wine or sustain his body with meat, but softened harsher foods with oil alone, devoting himself to fasts and prayers. Indeed, through the merit of his faith and abstinence he possessed this grace of the Holy Spirit: that he cast demons from possessed bodies. We have mentioned his life and merit so that those who do not allow such persons to live within the Roman empire may be judged all the more impious.

XXII. At the same time a severe persecution had arisen against our people, instigated by Damasus, that distinguished archbishop, so that faithful priests were not freely permitted during the holy days [Col. 0098C] to summon assemblies of the people for the service of Christ God. But since, according to the condition of circumstances, the sacraments of our salvation must at every time be performed, even secretly, the same holy presbyter Macarius arranged for the brotherhood to assemble for vigils in a certain house, so that, even at night, the holy people might be strengthened in faith through divine readings.

But the devil, who favours the impious because the impious also favour the devil, does not permit the divine sacraments to be celebrated even in secret. So the clerics of Damasus laid snares; and when they learned that the presbyter Macarius was celebrating sacred vigils with the people, they rushed with officials into that house, dispersed the unresisting congregation, and, having seized the presbyter, did not even consider him worthy of being led away, but dragged him over stones. Thus a destructive wound was made in [Col. 0098D] his thigh. On the following day they brought him before a judge as one accused of a grave crime. The judge, as though acting under an imperial rescript and threats, sought to compel him to join Damasus. But the presbyter, mindful of divine judgment and unafraid of the judge before him, rejected communion in perfidy. Therefore he was sent into exile; and when he was at Ostia, he died from the severity of that wound.

His holiness was so great that Florentius, bishop of that place, though in communion with Damasus, received him with a certain reverence. For when the brethren had buried him in an old monument [Col. 0099A], Florentius would not allow him to lie there, where the burial seemed unworthy. Removing him thence, he buried him in the basilica of the martyr Asterius, in the place where presbyters have burial beside the tomb; by this pious service he endeavoured, insofar as he could, to dissociate himself from the crime of Damasus.

XXIII. Let Your Serenity consider whether you wish this to happen in the Roman empire against saints and faithful persons at the hands of betrayers. Is there not fear that the blood of the faithful may weigh upon the Roman empire? For Damasus himself, having received royal authority, pursued other Catholic presbyters and also laypeople, sending them into exile. He pleaded this very cause through pagan advocates, with judges favouring him, although your constitutions [Col. 0099B] were decreed against heretics, not against Catholics—and Catholics of such a kind as did not abandon the intact faith even under heretical emperors, though they endured many grievous things.

He also recently attempted severely to persecute the most blessed Bishop Ephesius, burning with zeal for the holy faith, ordained for the undefiled people of Rome by the most steadfast Bishop Taorgius—himself a man of unstained faith. Under the malicious imputation of a false designation, he brought suit against the judge Bassus through his advocates, as though against “Luciferians.” But Bassus, who had formerly revered the Catholic faith, knew that there had been no perversity of heresy in Lucifer. He knew well, indeed, that Lucifer had endured ten years of exile for the Catholic faith. Because of his own integrity and steadfastness, Bassus rejected the accusations of Damasus [Col. 0099C], declaring that he would not act so as to pursue Catholic men and men of intact faith; he said especially that the emperors’ constitutions appeared to have been promulgated only against heretics, not against those who preserve the most holy faith without worldly ambition.

XXIV. Then Damasus was for the first time put to shame, because a judge was found who alone, interpreting the imperial writings most devoutly, would protect them. For it is also necessary to examine the malicious force of the false name by which they charge that we are “Luciferians.” Who does not know that a man’s designation is given to followers of one who has transmitted some new teaching to disciples by the authority of his instruction? But Christ [Col. 0099D] is our teacher: we follow his teaching, and therefore are reckoned by the sacred designation of his name, so that we ought rightly to be called nothing other than Christians, since we follow nothing other than what Christ taught through the Apostles.

Heresies, however, have been marked by human names because they handed down human inventions. Whoever does not follow Christ’s teaching forfeits in himself the designation of the Christian name. Let them now say what Lucifer taught that was new, which was not handed down from Christ’s instruction, which was not transmitted to later generations by the Apostles, the disciples of the Saviour. And it is well that he wrote books to Constantius [Col. 0100A], not, like many, seeking the glory of literary talent, but most aptly gathering divine testimonies against the heretics and against the patron of heretics himself, inflamed with divine zeal for love of the Son of God. Let them point out what in them is contrary to the Scriptures, what novel thing he wrote as a heretic.

Athanasius himself, as a champion of truth, also approved those books, since Lucifer had treated every matter fully and soundly, and translated them into Greek so that the Greek language should not lack so great a good. Nor is that all: Athanasius himself, in his own letters, praises the same books as woven together from the doctrines and pious confession of Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles. And although he raises Lucifer with very many praises, he still does not attain to the encomium his merit deserves, even though he could praise him no more [Col. 0100B]: [Note: [Col. 0099D] Manuscript: “Thus the pre-eminence of his deeds surpasses every tongue that praises.”] thus the pre-eminence of his deeds surpasses every tongue that praises.

XXV. Although Lucifer was ignorant of artful eloquence, he nevertheless possessed, by the merit of right faith and a most sincere conscience, the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which he wrote in prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic fashion—a gift above all human eloquence. Through that Spirit he also performed divine miracles, not only in Sardinia but also in each of his four exiles. So great was this that his opponents called him a magician [Note: [Col. 0100D] Manuscript: “So that his adversaries called him a magician.”], since they could not deny that apostolic powers were worked through him.

Saint Gregory also came to him and marvelled at such learning in the divine Scriptures and at his very life, truly established as it were in heaven. How great a man Lucifer was [Col. 0100C] may be seen from the fact that even Gregory admired him—Gregory, admirable to all, not only because of that encounter with Hosius, but also because of the divine powers which, having the grace of the Holy Spirit within him, he exercised. In what, then, are these men impious here also? Since Lucifer believed, taught, and lived according to the divine Scriptures, and worked miracles in Christ’s name, they impose the name of Lucifer upon defenders of the true faith in order to oppress them. Miserable men, they do not know that they commit the highest sacrilege when they designate Christ’s teaching by the name of a human being; just as they are impious in this also, when they defend sacrilegious institutions devised by human choice under the authority of the Christian name.

Is it not the greatest impiety to defend their iniquities and sacrileges under Christ’s name? Is it not impiety [Col. 0100D] to mark with human names a pious teaching consecrated under Christ’s name? Yet this fraud, this cruelty, is practised against the faithful in Spain, at Trier, at Rome, and in various regions of Italy.

XXVI. It is now necessary to set forth what was done in these regions, where distinguished bishops, clothed not with the truth of faith but with the bare designation of the Catholic name, scatter faithful and true Catholics not only through judges or merely by military force, but also sometimes commit atrocities through their own clerics, while judges are ignorant or even connive [Col. 0101A]. What end would there be if we related all that each of the faithful has suffered and is suffering? Yet one atrocious crime of persecution must be briefly recounted: it was committed in Egypt at Oxyrhynchus, before the witness of the entire city.

At Oxyrhynchus there is a definite portion of the holy people, among whose sacred number many, the more earnestly they have applied zeal and care to divine matters, the more anxiously and carefully endeavour to preserve the Catholic faith inviolate. Thus they mingle with no heretics and no betrayers in the divine sacraments. Many of them were trained in this observance by the example and admonition [Note: [Col. 0101D] Manuscript: “of most blessed Paul.”] of blessed Paul, who lived in the same times as that most famous Antony and was inferior to Saint Antony neither in life, nor zeal, nor divine grace [Col. 0101B]. The city of Oxyrhynchus itself knows this, and still today celebrates the holy memory of Paul with the greatest devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0101D] Manuscript: “But this same portion of the people.”] But when this portion of the people saw that the bishop of that city, named Theodore, had fallen into impious betrayal—so that he not only condemned the intact faith, nor merely subscribed impiously, [Note: [Col. 0102D] Manuscript: “but also permitted himself to be made a layman.”] but permitted the impious George to reduce him to lay status and then to ordain him bishop again as a heretic—it abhorred communion with him. It retained with itself presbyters and deacons of that unstained faith, through whom [Note: [Col. 0102D] Manuscript: “was nourished with the divine sacraments.”] it enjoyed the divine sacraments, together with the above-mentioned most blessed Paul.

Afterward it also had a bishop ordained for itself by the Catholic bishops of that time: Saint Heraclidas [Col. 0101C], so much the more suitable because he had to be ordained the more firmly against heretics and betrayers. He was conspicuous in life, serving God from his earliest age, despising worldly goods, and complete in faith and teaching. Therefore, for his apostolic faith, evangelical teaching, and heavenly conduct, he is revered by all there, displeasing only heretics and betrayers. And he pleases God all the more because he displeases such men.

So great and such a man began to exercise the episcopal office in such a way that, because of the renown of his faith, teaching, and most holy conduct, many even came from the most distant regions, abhorring the criminal fellowship of betrayers and desiring his most holy communion. But that distinguished twice-made bishop would not endure this. At first he harassed him through public authorities, so that more than once he had him seized in the dead of night by lancers and carried out of the city. But when those authorities did not persist in what they had rashly begun—for what right could they have against a Catholic bishop?—they deservedly ceased their begun persecution, especially as one of them had even been warned by a divine blow.

Then this distinguished twice-made bishop, relying now upon his own forces, sent a crowd of clerics against the church of blessed Heraclidas, the Catholic bishop. He overthrew it, demolishing its walls on every side, so that [Col. 0102A] he shattered the very altar of God with axes, to the horror and lamentation of the entire city that the church should be destroyed whose bishop even people of the other party acknowledge to be of right and unstained faith.

XXVII. Consider, we beseech you, most pious emperors and defenders of the true faith: do you issue edicts on behalf of bishops so impious that those should be afflicted who, by the merit of faith and most holy life, are more precious than the world itself? Believe, most religious emperors, that blessed Heraclidas is one of that number of saints of whom divine Scripture says: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted by tribulations and pains, of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. 11:37).

For how is blessed Heraclidas not such a man? Rejecting every worldly [Col. 0102B] pleasure, through the very bitterness of this rugged life he emulates the Lord’s footsteps and, naked and unencumbered, follows the saving path of virtues. For love of the divine faith he enters into conspiracy as we read that the saints also conspired, possessing nothing from the world except tribulations and pains for the faith; he lives, walks, and conducts himself just like those saints of whom the testimony above was set forth. Rightly, therefore, blessed Gregory and the other holy bishops, in the afflicted evils of the Church, are relieved as by divine consolations through the venerable fellowship of such holiness.

Theodore did not rage only against so venerable a bishop, but also against his most holy people, instructed by the teaching and conduct of their most sincere and faithful priest. It would take long to recount [Col. 0102C] what he devised against the modesty and profession of sacred virgins, whose monasteries the city itself reveres because of their holiness. He also repeatedly afflicted the servants of God themselves with cruel injuries—the very men whom he had found to be holier. But what wonder if, like a wolf, he afflicted sheep whose good shepherd he frequently afflicted?

XXVIII. Behold the man who, under you, pious emperors and supporters of the Catholic faith, boasts that he is Catholic while overthrowing the church of Catholics, persecuting Catholic priests and servants of Christ, and impiously afflicting his sacred virgins. This is that distinguished and most holy bishop who, having first been ordained bishop by Catholic bishops, was later reduced to the rank of the laity by the impious George [Col. 0102D], yet was nevertheless ordained bishop again by that same George, for the harassment of the faithful. He sits and communicates in one and the same city with Apollonius, bishop of the Meletians, who agrees with George’s impieties; and together with that same Apollonius, Theodore persecutes blessed Heraclidas, defender of the Catholic faith.

Behold the man to whom, as though it were Catholic, the basilica of Apollonius has now been handed over by the authority of your general edict. Yet Theodore himself, who as though Catholic received the basilica of the heretic Apollonius, acted impiously in the same manner as Apollonius. Indeed, Theodore acted more atrociously: he was made [Col. 0103A] a layman from being a Catholic bishop, condemning the pious faith and subscribing to Arian impiety, in order to be ordained bishop again by a heretic. Indeed, he wishes to seem Catholic for this reason: he himself now, by a certain persuasion, makes some of Apollonius’s presbyters or deacons into laymen, and ordains them again, so that he may appear to return the disgraceful kind of ordination which he underwent. Does it not exceed every sacrilege to defend these mockeries under the Catholic name, to the affliction of faithful priests and laypeople?

XXIX. But in Palestine, at Eleutheropolis, there is also a consecrated virgin of Christ named Hermione. Though she is indeed of noble birth, she has become far nobler through faith and holiness, adorning virginity itself by contempt for worldly things and for human glory, after which most people strive, even those who boast that they have renounced the world and the lust of the flesh. To the degree that she guards bodily chastity with sacred rigor, to that degree she preserves purity of soul by the chaste observance of devout faith: she communicates neither with heretics nor with betrayers, because she understands that bodily virginity is of no avail unless she also safeguards the integrity of the soul through sacred confession, fleeing the stain of adulterous communion and pursuing the saving sacraments of faithful priests.

Accordingly, she petitioned blessed Heraclidas by a devout letter to be aided by his sacred visitations. But in place of blessed Heraclidas, holy Ephesius visited her; at that time he had come from the city of Rome to Bishop Heraclidas on ecclesiastical business. This is the Ephesius whom we said above [Col. 0103C] had been ordained bishop of the undefiled Roman people by the most steadfast Bishop Taorgius.

> [Note: [Col. 0103D] Manuscript: “bishop of the Roman people.”]

When he came to Eleutheropolis, not only was Hermione, together with her holy monastery, comforted, but also certain most faithful servants of God. Among them was the noble household of Severus, one of the tribunes, devout toward the Catholic faith, which had indeed long refrained from communion with heretics and betrayers, but had not yet found the sacred communion of Catholics.

> [Note: [Col. 0103D] Manuscript: “but had not yet found.”]

But when he saw holy Ephesius, after many examinations establishing that he was Catholic, he committed himself to him in sacred communion, judging himself blessed because divine mercy had unexpectedly visited his house. He was led to such admiration by the arrival of the holy priest—not only by the purity of his life, but also by certain heavenly [Col. 0103D] proofs. For blessed Ephesius is of such faith and holiness that, wherever he goes, divine grace accompanies him.

> [Note: [Col. 0104D] Manuscript: “Divine justice accompanies him.”]

The holy people at Oxyrhynchus, who communicate with blessed Heraclidas, also proved this. Bound to him by their devout love on account of the merit of divine grace, they escorted him as he departed with great weeping, as the Asians once escorted the Apostle Paul.

XXX. We say this not from a desire to praise, but so that you may know how holy and faithful souls are afflicted by the gravest persecutions under the authority of your name, at the hands of those who, without your knowledge, are even now either heretics, betrayers, [Col. 0104A] or accomplices of such persons.

But these men, to whom sacred truth is burdensome, made a slight attempt against holy Ephesius in Palestine and then desisted, fearing in him both freedom of faith and constancy of mind. They also considered that their heresy and impiety could more readily be exposed if, under you Catholic emperors, they had more fiercely harassed a bishop of uncorrupted and steadfast faith.

But when the same blessed Ephesius, invited by letters from the faithful, sailed to Africa, giving us, in apostolic fashion, instructions to devote ourselves to divine and ecclesiastical duties for the holy brotherhood, the distinguished Turbo, bishop of the city of Eleutheropolis, despising our lowliness, began—at the request of the holy brotherhood there—to wish to carry out against us what he had not dared to carry out against holy Ephesius. He did not know that the grace of Christ God protects even His least servants, especially those laboring for the cause of the right faith.

For this Turbo, after hearing that certain persons had joined themselves to us in the uncorrupted faith and that, by God’s grace, the cause of truth was growing, threatens us with destruction and harasses us. He has also threatened Severus’s house with fire on account of the truth—Severus, who defends the faith of God all the more because he has also served the Roman Empire faithfully.

> [Note: [Col. 0104D] Manuscript: “as much as he has also served the Roman Empire.”]

He also attempts to persecute the consecrated virgin Hermione. Whoever has come to know that woman has admired her as one of the women of the Gospel. He likewise lays snares for every person joined with us in fellowship of sacred communion, charging as though it were a crime, on the basis of that Babylonian law, that within [Col. 0104C] our homes, without the stain of heresy and without communion in perfidy, we celebrate the divine sacraments according to evangelical and apostolic traditions for faithful persons who desire them.

For the Babylonians were once driven by a similar fury to pursue holy Daniel with hostile hatred because, in his own house, he worshipped God in observance of the divine law. This is the Turbo who was deacon to the heretic Eutychius, under whom blessed Lucifer endured exile in the city of Eleutheropolis; he also grievously afflicted Lucifer himself with many atrocities while Lucifer freely defended the faith.

XXXI. There are still persons in Palestine today who, in that time, suffered the gravest punishments at their hands because they assembled with Lucifer, bishop of the Catholic faith. Let them deny, if they can, that among their other [Col. 0104D] atrocities they broke down a closed door with axes; that, rushing upon Lucifer, that most faithful priest, they also overturned the divine sacraments and slaughtered with impious violence each of the brethren assembled there. Let them deny, if they can, that even now they possess among themselves the holy mystical vessels which they then impiously plundered from Lucifer, together with the sacred books.

At that time, of course, Turbo associated with the heretic Eutychius. Since then, while calling himself Catholic, he persecutes Catholics under the authority of your name—Catholics who defend the Catholic faith in contemplation of devout hope.

Do you allow, most devout emperors, impiety to exercise dominion everywhere for so long over the faithful under the authority of your name? Is it advantageous to the Roman Empire—which we say in view of the affection and fidelity of the reverence you show to Christ God—that those who devoutly proclaim Christ suffer persecutions and death, so that nowhere may altars to God be devoutly established, or, if they are established, that they may be destroyed?

Under the impious Ahab, king of Israel, after the prophets had been killed and the altars destroyed, Elijah appealed to God against Israel, saying in the Book of Kings: “Lord, they have killed your prophets; they have destroyed your altars; and I alone am left, and they seek my life” (3 Kings 19:14). Do you permit this grievous appeal to be made to God even in your own times by each of the faithful priests? For even if they remain silent, does God not know that these very things [Col. 0105B] are being done?

What are we to think? Are these acts committed against true Catholics and against His true Church without offending God—acts which, when once committed against the servants of God, were punished most severely by divine judgments? And whence come the many scourges by which the Roman world is shaken and oppressed? There is no need now for us to enumerate each of the scourges which Your Serenity recognizes amid the turmoil and anxiety of your empire. Let us soften this common grief even by silence, lest we seem less to sympathize than to aggravate it.

XXXII.

> [Note: [Col. 0105D] Manuscript: “But this we ask.”]

This we ask, most devout emperors: deign to consider from what causes these things arise. Is it because faithful servants of Christ, fearing the divine laws, refuse to assemble with unbelievers? Or is it because true Catholics are crushed by false priests? For how are they not false priests, who must now be avoided not only for the reason of betrayal set out above, but also because very many of them still uphold their own heresies under a falsely professed Catholic name before you?

For who now fears to preach the impious doctrines of bishops, when impiety so often committed has been honored and is not in the least deprived of the priesthood? Indeed, some of them are Origenists, others Anthropomorphites, while others uphold the sect of the impious Apollinaris; and others, in a triple wedge, blaspheme against the Holy Spirit by diverse schemes. Even those among them who are thought to believe devoutly—whether maintaining or rejecting that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three substances—[Col. 0105D] nevertheless all glory in your edicts and claim churches for themselves, although our fathers have always condemned these impious sects by apostolic and evangelical authority.

It is not the task of the present little work to examine them now. We say only what may stir your mind, attentive to the true faith, to horror.

XXXIII. One heresy, as we think, was adopted at Ariminum under a heretical emperor; but now, under you devout Catholic emperors, so many heresies are maintained, no less impious than the impiety of Arius. And although they severally write books or letters [Col. 0106A] against one another, they all communicate with one another, whether directly or through an indirect chain of connection. In the vain manner of philosophers, they dispute in controversies of words alone, not—as Christians ought, out of devotion to the sacrament—avoiding one another as impious.

Thus it appears that there is among them a contest as in schools of intellectual ability, not a sacred defense of true religion; for they do not separate the sacraments from one another, although they are separated from one another by impious opinions. They do this because some of them seek human glory, while others seek greed; and hence they collude with one another under an impious pretense, so that they may lose neither ecclesiastical possessions nor honors.

Meanwhile, to conceal their many impieties and to deceive individuals, presenting themselves as tokens of a most kindly disposition, they say [Col. 0106B] that they join even those holding contrary opinions in fellowship of ecclesiastical communion, lest the good of peace perish in the Church. As though peace of this kind pleased Christ God—a peace which admits so many impieties into His Church.

But let those who think thus hear what is written concerning them:

> “And they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes” (Psalm 13:3).

And we read more plainly in Jeremiah concerning impious and unjust peace:

> [Note: [Col. 0106D] Manuscript: “Concerning that impious peace.”]

The following testimony continues:

> “From the least of them even to the greatest, all have committed iniquity; from priest even to false prophet, all have wrought falsehood. And they devised the crushing of my people, reckoning it as nothing, saying, ‘Peace, peace’; but where is peace?” (Jeremiah 6:13).

> [Note: [Col. 0106D] Perhaps *medicabantur*, “they treated/healed”; the Vulgate has *curabant*, “they healed.”]

And attention should be paid to the severity with which it proceeds against those who glory in this most empty peace. For it continues:

> “They have been put to shame because they have failed; yet they did not even submit to shame, nor did they recognize their own disgrace. Therefore they shall fall in their ruin, and in the time of visitation they shall be weakened” (ibid., 15).

XXXIV. What evil do we commit, what impiety do we perform, if, keeping faith with Christ, we reject such peace, whose great shame, disgrace, and most grievous outcome are described? Yet these distinguished lovers of peace wage war upon faithful priests. For what does the devil desire but that the impious and the betrayers may glory in the peace of the world? What does the devil desire but that those who are devout and faithful may be harassed by the persecution of their attackers?

We have set these matters forth so that, through your ignorance, the blood [Col. 0106D] of Christians defending the ancient faith may not be shed for long. What benefit is it if you are defenders of the Catholic faith, while you allow the followers of the Catholic faith everywhere to be tortured, everywhere driven away, and nowhere freely to preach devout faith?

Let them have basilicas glittering with gold, clothed in the ostentation of precious marbles, or raised by the magnificence of columns; let them also have estates extending far and wide, for the sake of which even uncorrupted faith has been endangered. Why do they also claim for their impieties cities held in common by all Romans, so as to permit no one to live devoutly in them—cities in which even vain superstition is practiced without danger by many people [Col. 0107A] and asserted without their hostility?

Let it at least be permitted to truth, even among the lowliest and most despised mangers, to worship and faithfully adore Christ God devoutly—where Christ Himself once deigned, having been born according to the flesh, to lie as an infant. We ask this not because we shrink from being killed for the truth. God, the true watcher of the heart, is our witness that, through God’s grace, it would be for us both the highest refreshment and a sure hope of future blessedness if we were slain for this faithful confession.

Therefore we have set forth these matters not as those who fear to suffer them, but lest the blood of Christians, shed through the impieties and cruelties of others, should long weigh upon the most devout empire of Your Majesty. Especially under you, most religious Emperor Theodosius, who with remarkable devotion unite against all heretics in the devout confession of the Christian religion, we believed that we should incur great punishment before God if we kept silent before so religious and devout an emperor, consecrated to Christ God in divine and complete fear, whom Christ God truly chose for empire, about matters pertaining to the true faith and the true Church.

After this, we do not doubt that you will act with a father’s concern for the empire, lest the purity of professed faith and communion be afflicted in the Roman world. Whatever holier acts you perform in the cause of sacred faith and professed truth, so much more gloriously shall you reign, both here and forever, through Christ’s favor.

I, MARCELLINUS, priest, wish for your most fortunate empire secure peace and, in the kingdom of Christ and God, everlasting blessedness, most devout emperors.

I, FAUSTINUS, who cannot be called worthy [Col. 0107C] to be a priest of God, wish that, with the aid of the most merciful divinity, you may reign happily here for many years and may attain, in the future kingdom of Christ the Son of God, perpetual blessedness with the saints, most glorious emperors.

To these petitions the imperial law replied as follows:

## RESCRIPT OF THEODOSIUS ON BEHALF OF THE PRIESTS MARCELLINUS AND FAUSTINUS

[Col. 0107D] Greetings, Cynegius, most dear to us.
