Although no reverence ought to be greater in human hearts than that owed to the divine law, nor can anything be added to the same law—whose exalted excellence, ruler of the world and the earth, keeps under the favor of almighty God everything that it has willed to be subject to us—nevertheless, when our clemency was petitioned through Faustinus and Marcellinus, priests full of faith, we feared that, if no reply were given by us to those making the petition, we might appear to assent to those who had added, contrary to our intention, something to the divine law which we serve.

Therefore we determine both matters in this way: we honor the petition that has been presented, but we do not wish or command that anything be added to the faith by our own judgment. No one has ever been of such profane mind as to decide for teachers themselves what ought to be followed, when he ought rather to follow Catholic teachers.

And certainly the commendation of the petition is sound and just, since it has embraced nearly the whole course and order of heretical superstition contrary to the Catholic faith. For it disclosed both from what source and under what author it had arisen and to what point it had advanced. Indeed, when, through the persuasion of certain persons, the antiquity of the entire age had been altered, innocents driven into exile for the faith laid down their lives with the highest praise.

Yet punishment was not delayed against those who, plotting against good morals and heavenly institutions, for a time corrupted the minds of many by detestable insinuation—not from faith, but from contentious faction. For the patience of almighty God was so moved that, by way of example, they suffered beforehand the punishment due to criminals after their deeds. Yet not even by this could they be converted and bent toward the commandment of God: by secret schemes they press upon, pursue, and attack Catholics.

So great is their persistence in error that they prefer to sin daily with adherents of diverse observances rather than to think rightly with Catholics. In this respect, the assertion of the petitioners deserves praise: communicating with Gregory of Spain [Col. 0108C] and Heraclidas of the East—truly holy and praiseworthy bishops—they desire to live in the Catholic faith without anyone’s attack or annoyance, and not to be assailed by the snares and machinations of persecutors; since they are pleased to preserve with every religious devotion the faith once received.

Let, therefore, whatever has deserved to be eternal remain inviolate. Let no agreement, no attack, no fraud attempt anything against others. Let them make use of their religious purpose wherever they wish; let them employ it, through divine love, for the Catholic faith.

Cynegius, most dear and beloved father, let Your Sublimity order the command of Our Serenity—by which we honor the Catholic faith with every favor, and without which we cannot be saved—to be observed in such a way that you protect and defend Gregory and Heraclidas, bishops of the sacred law, and the other priests like them [Col. 0108D] who have devoted themselves to equal observance, from the injuries of wicked persons and heretics. And let all know that this is our settled conviction: we believe that worshippers of almighty God are none other than Catholics.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 384. SAINT DAMASUS

## PRELIMINARIES

[Col. 0109]

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE

To Joseph Dominic von Lambergh, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Bishop and Prince of Passau, Antony M. Merenda: greetings.

[Col. 0109A]

We have learned that even the greatest men, occupied with public duties, have cherished the desire at some time to gain release and leisure, free and discharged from such cares. I cannot deny that the same thought came over me while I was occupied in judging lawsuits in the courts and in similar business.

At the time when I delighted in that most pleasant anticipation of future leisure, I also considered within myself what might be the best plan for arranging my remaining life and passing my time. Since nothing better occurred to me than to return to those studies which, though I had interrupted them under compulsion, I had nevertheless always retained in mind, I began to turn my thoughts and cares toward procuring the necessary equipment of books.

This, most eminent prince, is not unknown to you. Born to foster letters, you assisted by your liberality in furnishing, as it were, this little estate of mine, and enabled me more easily to provide for my remaining years. Therefore, if any fruit has come of it, or if, having obtained leisure, I have been able to attempt anything, it is due before all else to you by the best right. And this is especially what I now offer and inscribe to you and to your name.

For, after I had gained the free and unoccupied time which I desired, I collected certain items from ecclesiastical history which seemed either to have escaped the diligence of others or to have eluded correct interpretation. Then I turned to reviewing the works of Damasus [Col. 0109C] and explaining his deeds. Thus, narrowing my studies from that immense field to this more limited subject, a little work gradually emerged which some persons to whom I showed it judged would not be altogether useless if brought to light and into public view.

I resisted, indeed, and did not acquiesce in their judgment, both for many reasons and especially because I would have to undergo the judgment of this fastidious age. But what chiefly induced me at last to yield and publish it was that there might stand some proof of my respect for you and a lasting testimony of a grateful mind, due for the many and great benefits by which you enriched me and my relatives when, at Vienna, I was an assessor in ecclesiastical cases for the Apostolic Nunciature under Cardinal Girolamo Grimaldi, a man of immortal memory and formerly a most distinguished witness also of your virtues.

Nor do I doubt, given your kindness toward all and your exceptional and singular generosity toward me [Col. 0110A] in particular, that you will not disdain this gift, such as it is. At least, if you should at any time turn to it a mind wearied by business, you will have in it an image, as it were, of your own character to contemplate in the most holy Fathers of those times mentioned there. You will rejoice that no virtue exists which has not been expressed in you: integrity of conduct; liberality toward the poor; zeal for religion and discipline; care in restoring and enlarging the splendor of sacred buildings; magnificence in establishing and founding pious works, with such generosity and benefit to religion; the most serious labors of visiting your extensive diocese, joined with cheerfulness of spirit; and, finally, patience and constancy in teaching the peoples the faith and precepts of conduct—an abundant fruit indeed of that singular learning which you have drawn from reading the holy Fathers and interpreters of Scripture.

I could pursue these matters more fully, since I have known them not merely by hearsay but have observed many of them with my own eyes, were I not restrained by your outstanding and singular modesty. Though you deserve praise, you do not permit it to be bestowed or proclaimed upon you. Yet there is no need, since, even if I am silent, history speaks and public records have been entrusted to the memory of posterity.

There is, however, one thing which I cannot altogether pass over: that lofty greatness and constancy of mind by which, when summoned to the see of Salzburg—one of great name and dignity in Germany—you voluntarily yielded your right and, to the admiration of all, set zeal for peace and concord above your own advantage and honor. This caused profound grief to good men who regarded your administration as useful and necessary to that most distinguished Church. Yet surely there was implanted in your mind that saying of Clement, the most holy Bishop of the Roman Church: “Let him who is noble, merciful, and full of charity say: ‘If discord and schism arise because of me, I depart; I go away. Let only Christ’s one flock live in peace with its appointed presbyters; and whoever does this will gain great honor for himself in the Lord.’”

The same Clement is said to have confirmed this noble saying by his own action: he renounced the honor and dignity of the first of all sees so that another pontiff, equal in holiness, might possess it and administer it in the most desired peace. This praise is not slight, but great and splendid. When the other most holy man of Nazianzus sought to emulate it, he lamented that by no means enough persons could be found who, whenever the advantage of the Churches seemed to demand it, would leave their sees and renounce honor and dignity once acquired.

Yet in that action of yours I see divine wisdom and counsel openly displayed. For it could not be otherwise than that those over whom you had presided should grieve and complain that they were being deprived of that shepherd and prince than whom they could neither desire nor dare hope for anyone more loving or better. For, as my Damasus wrote somewhere, those who have lost a priest cannot be without grief; and those who have received the bishop of another city, even if they rejoice, understand that it will expose them to reproach to live under an alien priest.

But, to return to this work of mine: [Col. 0112A] since it is wholly owed by me to you, most eminent prince, and since your supreme kindness and generosity encourage me to hope that it will not be unwelcome to you, I gladly give, declare, and dedicate it to you and to your name. Finally, I pray God, greatest and best, that, as you most diligently imitate that most holy pontiff whose works I publish and whose deeds I relate, He may long preserve you safe, sound, and unharmed for that Church which He gave you to govern, for the people from whom He did not permit you to be torn away, and for all good and learned men, for whom He has made you a support and defense.

[Col. 0111]

## TO THE READER

[Col. 0111B] There is no reason, friendly reader, to detain you with a long preface or elaborate discourse. For what writers commonly do—first, explaining why they began to write, and then setting forth the rationale and method of the work itself—I can accomplish both briefly.

The reason for composing the work, which was at first entirely justified, failed me in the course of it through no fault of mine. Yet I wished to complete the work I had undertaken, both because I had experienced the pleasure of these studies and because I saw that this was a most beautiful and honorable way of spending the leisure into which I had not unwillingly been released, having been freed from the excessively tiresome task of deciding lawsuits in court, in which I had spent nearly all my earlier life.

Perhaps someone will think that the work I have undertaken is not important enough to deserve such attention. “Why,” he will say, “were not the *Opuscula* of Damasus collected by the learned Sarazanius and published once and again?” There is no need for me to speak of Sarazanius’s diligence and learning. I shall say only this: the idea of reviewing and publishing anew the works of Damasus issued by him has not occurred to me for the first time now. The learned men Suaresius and, almost in our own age, Pastritius contemplated doing it.

My plan, then, should not be disapproved; rather, one should wish that no care or diligence be lacking in its execution. This was the method and approach that I followed in revising the works of Damasus. First, I collated those works known to be his with manuscript copies, wherever I could obtain them. [Col. 0112B] Next, I rejected what learned men judged should be denied him; for if anyone also wants those items, Sarazanius himself and the collections of councils are available. Finally, I sought also to elucidate what I had reviewed.

Accordingly, I added annotations, mostly my own; occasionally notes by Holstenius, though these are few; and some, though rarely, drawn from Coustant. The latter are readily available to all, and, had I reproduced them all, I might seem rather to burden this little work than to adorn it. I retained everything Sarazanius added to elucidate the poems, since these materials are not so easily found. Yet I preserved the place he had given them—that is, I placed them at the end.

But if anything has been done for your benefit, friendly reader, thanks should be given to God, the giver of all good things. If there is nothing that seems able to aid sacred history, at least my effort deserves praise. If, however, the work itself should be consigned to darkness along with the other similar works by which we are overwhelmed, I do not object. I ask only that you keep in mind Pliny, Book IX, Letter 17: “How many people, do you think, are offended by the things which engross and lead you and me—some as trifling, others as most burdensome?” Let us therefore grant indulgence to the amusements of others, that we may obtain it for our own.

[Col. 0111]

# ON THE LITTLE WORKS AND DEEDS OF SAINT DAMASUS, POPE

## CHAPTER ONE

I. The family and native country of St. Damasus. Reader from boyhood in the Basilica of St. Lawrence. II. As a deacon, he follows Liberius into exile; how far? Why he later returns to the City; and whether he was the clergy’s advocate for the election of Felix. III. Ordained priest: whether by Liberius or rather by Felix; Baronius’s view. IV. The preface to the petitions of Faustinus and Marcellinus is charged with falsity, and Damasus is defended. V. What place and standing he afterwards held under Liberius after the latter’s return to his see.

[Col. 0111D]

[Col. 0112D] I. Damasus is said by Anastasius to have been Spanish by nation. Baronius, Francis Pagi, Ciacconius, and many others call him specifically a Spaniard and even dispute over the place in Spain to which he should be assigned. John Tamayo Salazar gives a detailed list of these writers in the *Spanish Martyrology*, under 11 December.

Tillemont disagrees with them if they affirm that Damasus was born in Spain, and thinks that one may doubt whether Damasus and his sister Irene were born at Rome. Nor perhaps without reason. For their father was first an *exceptor* [court secretary] and then a reader in the Basilica of St. Lawrence—offices which are the first ecclesiastical grades for boys. Thus Damasus’s father seems to have begun his probationary service in the sacred militia from his earliest years in that basilica.

Moreover, Damasus himself was also, from childhood, first a reader in the same basilica and then served in all the other sacred orders. For, as Eghinactus says:

> [Note: [Col. 0113D] *Acts of Saints Peter and Marcellinus*, June, vol. I, p. 176.]

> “While, in boyhood, he served under a teacher and grew toward the great summit of his career, he then, as a READER in the Roman Church, received from the mouth of Dorotheus the executioner the acts of the holy martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, collected them, and transmitted them to posterity.”

That boys were customarily admitted to the grade of reader is established both from the letters of Siricius and Innocent and from various examples cited by Thomassin and Bonarroti.

> [Note: [Col. 0113D] Thomassin, *On Ancient Discipline*, Part I, Book II, chapter 67; Bonarroti, *Observations on the Fragments of Victor*, p. 115.]

Damasus was therefore at least thirteen years old at that time; and since he died in 384 at nearly eighty, he must certainly have been born around 304 and must have come to Rome with his father and mother as a child of four or five years. Assume, then, that at that age he was fit for so arduous a journey. But could his father Antonius, an entirely new and unknown man, have enrolled himself in the Church immediately upon arriving in Rome and at once have been made notary and reader of that basilica? This was certainly contrary to the discipline of those times. He first had to be baptized, then, after an interval of time, to be tested as to whether he was worthy of enrollment among the clergy.

Finally, he had to spend at least either nine or seven years in performing the duties of the minor orders. When that period had elapsed, if he had proved suitable, he could be advanced to higher ranks.

> [Note: [Col. 0113D] See Siricius, Letter to Himerius, no. 14; Innocent, Letter to Felix of Nocera, chapter 5; Zosimus, Letter to Hesychius of Salona, chapter 5.]

If you add to this nine- or seven-year period, which Antonius must have spent in the exercise of minor orders, another five or six years during which his son must have been born before the journey to Rome and before his father was enrolled among the clergy, you will reach the age at which Damasus was when he heard the acts of the holy martyrs and recorded them from memory. Yet he seems already to have been a reader at that time. Were father and son, then, placed in inferior orders at almost the same time and in the same church? Let others judge.

I do not deny that I have read in the *Life of St. Damasus* from a manuscript of the Vatican Basilica, published by Sarazanius, that—as St. Lawrence was—Damasus himself was Spanish by race; and that, therefore, having been born in one homeland, advanced in one Church, honored in one basilica on earth, they were crowned by one God in heaven. Yet one may strongly doubt whether Lawrence himself was born at Rome. For in the ancient Sacramentary which the distinguished Joseph Blanchini published, and whose author he judged to be St. Leo the Great, Lawrence is called “a citizen of Rome by birth.”

> [Note: [Col. 0113D] In the Preface to Anastasius, vol. IV, p. 38: “For although, O Lord, the glory of your saints, spread abroad by you, is illustrious throughout the whole world, Rome nevertheless rejoices above all others in the feast of blessed Lawrence, whose own citizen by birth, sacred minister, and offering dedicated to your divinity he is.”]

II. After the office of reader, we know that Damasus was raised to the rank of deacon; but whether by Julius or by Liberius is uncertain. Yet if Damasus was forty-eight years old when Liberius was elected, I can scarcely bring myself to believe that his ordination was postponed for so long beyond the period fixed by the canons. It therefore seems more probable that he obtained this rank under Julius, [Col. 0114B] and took part in the great events transacted under that pontiff.

What further inclines me to believe this is the familiarity which I infer to have existed between Damasus and Athanasius from Athanasius’s Letter to the Africans and Basil’s letters to Athanasius himself. It must have begun when the Alexandrian bishop was staying at Rome under Julius and attending the ecclesiastical assemblies of that city—a circumstance which Liberius himself said, among others, had kept him there and prevented him from later subscribing to Athanasius’s condemnation.

> “Or who will accept us, if we turn away in his absence from one whom we loved when present and with whom we were in communion?”  
> —Athanasius, *Secret History to the Monks*, no. 37. [Note: Col. 0114D]

We may also infer from this what position Damasus held with Liberius at the time: he followed him as he went into exile. I think this is why he was sometimes called Liberius’s deacon—namely, because that pontiff employed especially his service and ministry, and because he was among those who attended a single pope, called in later centuries “palatine deacons.” [Note: Col. 0114D: See Mabillon, commentary on the *Roman Ordines*, ch. 3, and Bencini’s notes on the *Life of Evaristus.*]

But I must here cite the words of the Luciferians’ schismatic writer, in order to remove the accusation of ambition and perjury which was on this occasion laid against Damasus. The author—whoever he may be—of the preface to the petitions of Marcellinus and Faustinus discusses the persecution by which Liberius, Eusebius of Vercelli, Lucifer of Cagliari, and Hilary of Poitiers were forced into exile, and says:

> “These, therefore, were sent into exile to preserve the faith. Damasus, Liberius’s deacon, pretended to set out with him; but fleeing from the journey, he returned to Rome, corrupted by ambition. Yet on the day on which Liberius departed for exile, all the clergy—that is, the presbyters, the archdeacon Felix, Damasus himself the deacon, and all the offices of the Church—together, in the presence of the Roman people, bound themselves by oath that while Liberius lived they would by no means have another pontiff.”  
> —In Sirmond, Venetian edition, vol. I, p. 138. [Note: Col. 0114D]

Thus this author asserts, as you see, two things that destroy each other. First, that Damasus secretly returned to Rome, leaving his bishop on the journey, corrupted by ambition—having, that is, conceived in his mind the desire for the supreme pontificate. Secondly, that on the day when Liberius set out into exile all the clergy swore that, while Liberius himself lived, they would by no means have another pontiff, and that Damasus too was present and took this oath. But if by this oath he had cut off all hope for himself, how could he have left his bishop and returned to the city solely through ambition?

It is therefore established that Damasus, in a good and sincere spirit, made himself the companion of his bishop as he went into exile. But it is uncertain how far he accompanied him and why he afterwards returned to the City. Onuphrius Panvinius takes him as far as Milan, and in his manuscript *Ecclesiastical History* writes that Liberius kindly dismissed him from that city. Schelstrate quotes from it as follows:

> “Damasus the deacon, who later became bishop of Rome, accompanied him as he departed for a definite exile as far as Milan. When he saw him banished to Thrace, he returned to Rome; and, since there seemed to be no hope of Liberius’s restoration, he is said to have advised the clergy to elect another pontiff in Liberius’s place. Some, however, understand this as though Damasus had given the clergy this advice by Liberius’s own command.”  
> —Schelstrate, *Antiquities of the Church*, dissertation 2, ch. 9. [Note: Col. 0115D; see also Papebroch, *Conatus Historicus*, dissertation 9, no. 6.]

Others write that he remained Liberius’s companion as far as Beroea. But since all lack ancient testimony and any solid conjecture, I think that I ought to determine nothing on this matter.

Yet I shall not concede that, upon his return, Damasus advised the clergy to choose another in the place of their absent bishop. Above all, I prefer the authority of Athanasius, who writes:

> “Constantius employed the minister Epictetus; having fitted up a palace in place of a church and ordered three eunuchs to be present in the role of peoples, he finally compelled three wicked spies—for they ought not to be called bishops—to ordain a certain Felix, a man worthy of their own character, as bishop.”  
> —Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 75. [Note: Col. 0115D]

Thus Constantius the emperor alone, Epictetus alone, and—as Jerome says—Acacius of Caesarea, were the authors of this then illegitimate and adulterous election; Damasus and the Roman clergy had no part in urging or arranging it. [Note: Col. 0115D: Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 98.]

Accordingly, if Liberius entrusted anything to Damasus himself, or if Damasus did anything on Felix’s behalf, it was only to arrange that Felix should be received in the position of vicar appointed by Liberius himself, in accordance with the practice received in times of persecution, as Papebroch holds. For scarcely anyone who reads Liberius’s letters written in exile—especially those written at the time when he seemed most broken and yielding—will deny that he always retained pontifical authority. I consider it superfluous to introduce those letters here.

III. In the meantime Damasus is said to have been raised to the rank of presbyter. But whether this was by Felix, as Baronius thinks, [Note: Col. 0116D: Year 359, no. 46] or, as others suppose, by Liberius after his return, [Col. 0116A] is entirely uncertain. There is only one conjecture that makes Baronius’s opinion preferable to the other in my judgment.

For we read that Damasus was a presbyter when Liberius, to escape Constantius’s wrath, was compelled to hide in the Ostrian cemetery. It therefore seems not altogether probable that, during this intervening period—entirely turbulent and impeded by the gravest troubles, lying between Liberius’s return and his second withdrawal—Damasus could have been ordained. It may therefore easily be that he was among those promoted by Felix whom Liberius, once tranquillity had been restored, left in their own positions.

IV. As for the accusation of perjury, Jerome also proves that the Roman clergy bound their loyalty by oath to Liberius as he went into exile, writing these words in his *Chronicle*:

> “Liberius, driven into exile for the faith, all the clergy swore that they would receive no other.”

Prosper copies almost the same words. But since both are entirely silent about Damasus, I very greatly doubt whether the schismatic author did not add this too to the other falsehoods which he tells about him. What makes this easier for me to believe is the testimony of Ammianus Marcellinus, who expressly states that Liberius could only with great difficulty be carried away secretly, in the middle of the night, because of fear of the people, who burned with love for him. [Note: Col. 0116D: Book XV, ch. 7.]

For if Liberius was secretly seized and carried into exile at midnight, and with great difficulty because of fear of the people, how could an oath have been taken on the day when he departed into exile? It must, therefore, have been taken on another day than the one stated—[Col. 0116C] after Liberius had already been driven into exile, as Jerome says. If this is true, Damasus, attached as a companion to Liberius as he departed, could not have been present at the swearing of the oath. Tillemont therefore applies a remedy to this passage in vain. [Note: Col. 0116D: *On the Arians*, art. 20, p. 386.]

But grant that Damasus did take that oath: it could nevertheless have created no obstacle to the Roman clergy subsequently joining Felix, and to Damasus then being the author of that decision. We judge that this occurred—unless the darkness surrounding these matters deceives us—before the end of 358, after Liberius seemed to have been broken by exile and to have passed over to the Arians’ party and heresy; and finally after the Arian bishops assembled at Sirmium wrote to Felix and to the clergy of the same Church that they should receive Liberius himself and that both should jointly administer [Col. 0116D] the apostolic see. [Note: Col. 0116D: Sozomen, book IV, ch. 15.]

For then the same clergy, having learned what Liberius had conceived in his mind and had also openly done, and with the accusation of Liberius’s heresy afterwards increased and confirmed, perhaps withdrew from him and considered that they could no longer remain under that head, which did not appear to belong to the body of the Catholic Church. Hence, after Liberius returned to the City, the clergy themselves could with the greatest difficulty be separated from Felix, who, as regards religion, was entirely free from all reproach. [Col. 0117A] [Note: Col. 0117D: Sozomen, book IV, ch. 13.] The matter came to such a point that some sedition arose between clergy, people, and nobles, some adhering to Felix and others to Liberius. [Note: Col. 0117D: See *Disquisition on the Deeds of Liberius in Exile*, ch. 9.]

I have called the accusation of Liberius’s heresy a calumny, since he subscribed only the first Sirmian formula, which most learned persons judge could have been done without prejudice to the integrity of the faith. Those who think that he subscribed to the second Sirmian formula, or to Arian perfidy, are plainly mistaken—whether they are Catholics, though very few indeed, or persons alien from us. Their number, rather than their force, was lately increased by that anonymous man who has thrown off shame along with his cowl and published at Amsterdam, in three recently printed volumes, an unhappily patched-together history of the supreme pontiffs.

But lest I detain the reader beyond measure, let him consult, if he wishes, the special *Disquisition on the Deeds of Liberius in Exile*, [Col. 0117B] in which I have dealt with all matters relevant here.

Since Liberius, however, immediately upon his return removed every suspicion concerning himself, and since Felix, out of love for peace and lest the Church should continue any longer to be disturbed on his account, may meanwhile have appeared to resign the pontificate—[Note: Col. 0117D: Philostorgius, book IV, no. 3, “he withdrew to himself” (*εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἀπῄει*)]—Damasus could in good faith return with the remaining clergy to the man from whom he had in good faith withdrawn. And this he did without any loss of his former reputation or favour. For constant tradition, confirmed also by monuments, holds that he was appointed vicar of the Roman Church by Liberius when, after the Council of Rimini had been annulled, Liberius again withdrew from the City and took refuge in the hiding places of the cemeteries to escape Arian fury. On this matter see, if you wish, Baronius and the final chapter of the *Deeds of Liberius in Exile.*

V. What else Damasus did under Liberius, first as deacon and then as vicar, is unknown. In manuscript acts concerning him from the archive of the Vatican Church, it is written that chiefly through his efforts all bishops whom ignorance or fear had caused to stray at the Council of Rimini returned to the Catholic faith; and that he himself, with the support of Hilary of Poitiers, advised that they should be received into communion and fellowship, contrary to the opinion of Lucifer, who had separated himself.

Whatever may be true in these reports, I do not in the least doubt that Damasus was employed in every more serious ecclesiastical affair. For anyone who reads attentively the letters written by Liberius before exile and after exile, and then [Col. 0117D] compares them with those that survive from that pontiff during exile, will easily recognize how greatly they differ. The former possess great force and gravity of thought, a polished and flowing style, and a manner like that of Damasus; the latter, however, are wholly awkward and rough in expression. I think there was one reason for this: when Liberius wrote in exile, he did not have Damasus at hand, whose assistance he seems to have used both before and after exile.

## CHAPTER II. 366, YEAR 1 OF DAMASUS: GRATIAN AND DAGALAIFUS, CONSULS. 367, YEAR 2 OF DAMASUS: LUPICINUS AND JOVINUS, CONSULS.

I. Damasus is elected Roman pontiff; but Ursicinus, an antipope, is imposed by the factionalists. II. Contemporary writers are compared and assessed; from them the true sequence of events is gathered and explained; the recent anonymous author of the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* published at Amsterdam is refuted. III. The preface to the petitions of Faustinus and Marcellinus is again false. IV. Ursicinus is exiled, restored, and again expelled: for what reason? V. Baluzius is rejected.

[Col. 0118A]

I. On 24 September, Liberius having departed from human affairs, Damasus was elected Roman pontiff and consecrated on the first day of October, [Col. 0118B] which, as Blanchini and Pagi observe, was a Sunday. Yet shortly afterward Ursicinus, or Ursinus, a deacon of the Roman Church, was intruded in his place by certain factionalists.

Jerome relates the matter in his *Chronicle*, Rufinus, [Note: Col. 0118D: *History*, book II, ch. 20] Ammianus Marcellinus, [Note: Col. 0118D: Book XXVII, ch. 3] and that schismatic who wrote the preface to the petitions of Marcellinus and Faustinus published by Sirmond. [Note: Col. 0118D: Vol. III, p. 138.] Since not all pursue and clearly set forth every detail, I have thought it worthwhile to cite their words, so that the whole sequence of events may be grasped at a single glance.

II. Jerome, who perhaps was then present at Rome, writes:

> “Damasus is ordained the thirty-fifth bishop of the Roman Church. Not long afterwards Ursinus was made bishop by certain persons and, with his followers, seized the Sicinian [basilica]; when the people of Damasus’s party gathered there, most cruel slaughter of persons of both sexes was perpetrated.”

Rufinus adds matters omitted by Jerome and says:

> “Damasus, after Liberius, had received the priesthood in the city of Rome by succession. Unable to bear his being preferred to himself, a certain Ursinus, a deacon of the same Church, broke out into such madness that, having persuaded a certain ignorant and rustic bishop and gathered a band of turbulent and seditious men, he extorted his own making as bishop in the basilica called Sicininus, overturning laws, order, and tradition. From this deed such a sedition—or rather such wars—arose, with the peoples defending one side against the other, that the places of prayer were filled with human blood. Through the faction of Maximinus, a cruel man and prefect, this was turned to the prejudice of the good and innocent priest, so that the cause of the clergy was carried as far as torture. But God, the defender of innocence, was present, and punishment was turned upon the heads of those who had intended deceit.”

Rufinus here includes several things that happened at another time. What is now clear from both writers is this: Damasus’s election was superior in right because it was earlier in time. After the first there cannot be a second; and whoever has been made after one who alone ought to be such is no longer second, but nothing. [Col. 0119A] [Note: Col. 0119D: Cyprian, Letter 52, Verona edition.]

In other respects, when compared with each other, Rufinus seems to write that Ursinus was made bishop by factionalists in the Sicinian basilica and that sedition and slaughter arose from that act. Jerome, however—whose account Ammianus supports—writes that Ursinus had already been made bishop before he seized the Sicinian basilica; and that the killings occurred because he tried to keep the Damasian party, gathering at that basilica, away from it.

Now Ammianus Marcellinus, a pagan writer, must be heard. [Note: Col. 0119D: We consider him pagan with Hadrian Valesius, Johann Albert Fabricius, and critics of better standing.]

> “Damasus and Ursinus, burning beyond human measure to seize the episcopal see, were fighting with divided supporters, each side proceeding to the danger of death and wounds with its own resources. Juventius, unable to correct or soften matters, was compelled by great force to withdraw into the suburbs; and Damasus had prevailed in the contest, with the party favouring him pressing on. It is established that in the Sicinian basilica, where the Christian rite has its meeting-place, the corpses of one hundred and thirty-seven slain persons were found in a single day; and the populace, long made savage, was afterwards appeased only with difficulty.”

Ammianus therefore does not at all address who was the author of the sedition or which of the two, first desirous of occupying the see, disturbed the other’s election. Nor does he say anything about the author of the killing perpetrated in the Sicinian basilica. Nothing can therefore be inferred from this passage that weakens the testimony of Jerome and Rufinus, whatever may have seemed good to the French translator of Ambrose’s letters, who understood Ammianus to make Damasus guilty of these disturbances. [Note: Col. 0119D: Note on Letter 11.]

[Col. 0119C] The anonymous author of the *History of the Supreme Pontiffs*, whose ignorance and bad faith were noted in the preceding chapter, employs both this testimony and another famous testimony of Marcellinus, also cited by Baronius, [Note: Col. 0119D: Year 367] to reproach Damasus with pride and luxury:

> “One cannot doubt that Damasus himself was given over to luxury and the pleasures of a soft life, since Praetextatus, who later became prefect of Rome, said jokingly to him: ‘Make me bishop of Rome, and I shall at once become a Christian.’ A nobleman of such standing would not have said this if Damasus’s conduct had been a little more apostolic.”

Certainly the dignity and splendour with which God enriched the Roman Church have always offended the eyes of pagans and the envious; and I do not doubt that you are to be counted among them, to your regret. Yet I demand from you better good faith or greater force of reasoning when you say: “Was Damasus given over to luxury and pleasures merely because the Roman Church had abundant revenues? Could he not use them to feed the poor, receive bishops as guests, provide for the beauty and maintenance of churches, and promote the Christian religion, as has been the constant custom of the Roman [Col. 0119D] pontiffs?” [Note: Col. 0120D: See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, ch. 23; book VII, ch. 5.]

If anyone, especially in later centuries, did not follow the better examples of his predecessors, you could surely add your Praetextatus to their number. For if he had become pontiff of the Roman Church, I have no doubt that he would have abused both the supreme dignity he sought and abundant wealth for luxury and pride.

Moreover, the integrity of morals and modesty of life now maintained by the Roman pontiffs even amid such exaltation and royal wealth may furnish you with the clearest proof. To mention only those whom I have known and revered: Clement XI and XII, Innocent XIII, and the two Benedicts, XIII and XIV—whom we wish may long be preserved to us. I shall not dispute with you that luxury and pleasures could exist among the Roman clergy. But I shall remind you that, when you invoke Jerome and Gregory Nazianzen as witnesses for this point, you should consider how you will make good your case and with what right you may use those authors to insult Floridus and Baillet with such confidence when they attach little weight to that testimony of Marcellinus.

III. But to return to where I left off: it remains for me to introduce here the preface to the petitions of Faustinus and Marcellinus, whose writer seems to have been present at the events then occurring. He first recounts the causes of the faction and says that the Ursinians were those very distinguished men who had preserved their entire loyalty to Liberius while he was in exile. Damasus, on the other hand, he says, was elected by those perjurers who had first obeyed Felix and then, after Felix’s death or abdication of the pontificate, obeyed Liberius again. Having advanced these claims to dignify their obstinacy, he then says:

> “Likewise, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaifus, Liberius was removed from human affairs. [Col. 0120C] Then the presbyters, the deacon Ursinus, Amantius, and Lupus, together with the holy people who had preserved faithfulness to Liberius during his exile, began to proceed to the basilica of Julius and demand that Ursinus the deacon be ordained in Liberius’s place.”  
> [Note: Col. 0120D: “How then the writer who translated St Ambrose’s letters into French obtained the claim that Ursinus, established in the basilica of Julius, was ordained presbyter by Liberius, let him see to it.”]
>
> “The perjurers, however, demanded Damasus as their bishop in the Lucinae, in Felix’s place. Paul of Tibur gave Ursinus the blessing.”  
> [Note: Col. 0120D: Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 58, and *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 26, writes that the petition by which Ursacius and Valens, compelled to seek pardon from Julius, was sent to him by Paulinus, bishop of *Tiberon*. Nannius renders this “bishop of Tibur,” and the Bollandists understand it as Tibur near Rome; perhaps therefore he is the same man said to have ordained Ursicinus.]
>
> “When Damasus, who had always coveted the episcopate, learned this, he stirred up with money all the charioteers and the untrained multitude, burst armed with clubs into the basilica of Julius, and for three days raged in great slaughter of the faithful. Seven days later, with all the perjurers and arena-men whom he had corrupted at great price, he occupied the Lateran basilica, and there, having been ordained bishop and having bribed Viventius, judge of the City, [Col. 0120D] and Julian, prefect of the grain supply, he brought it about that Ursinus, a venerable man who had first been ordained pontiff, should be sent into exile with the deacons Amantius and Lupus.
>
> “When this had been done, Damasus began to beat with clubs and harass with various slaughter the Roman populace, which did not want him. He also tried, through official agents, to drive seven detained presbyters from the City; but the faithful people came to their aid, rescued the same presbyters, and immediately led them to the basilica of Liberius.
>
> “Then Damasus, with the faithless, summoned arena-men, charioteers, grave-diggers, and all the clergy armed with axes, swords, and clubs. He besieged the basilica at the second hour of the day, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaifus, and stirred up a fierce battle. For after breaking down the doors and setting fire beneath them, he sought an entrance by which to break in. Some also of his household, tearing down the roof of the basilica, killed the faithful people with roof-tiles. [Col. 0121B] Then all the Damasian party rushing into the basilica killed one hundred and sixty of the people; they wounded very many others, of whom many died. But not one person of Damasus’s party died.
>
> “After three days the holy people, assembled together, began to recite the Lord’s commandments against him, saying: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.’ They also sang in praise and said: ‘They gave the mortal remains of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth; they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them.’ Frequently, therefore, the same people, assembled in the basilica of Liberius, cried out: ‘Christian Emperor, nothing is hidden from you. Let all bishops come to Rome; let the case be tried. Damasus has now made a fifth war. Drive murderers from Peter’s see.’
>
> “The people of God begged with many prayers that the bishops should assemble, so that they might by a just judgment expel the aforementioned man, stained with such great impiety. Matrons loved him so much that he was called the matrons’ ear-scratcher [*auriscalpius matronarum*]. The voices of the people were therefore brought to the emperor Valentinian, who granted the exiles’ return. Then Ursinus returned to the City with the deacons Amantius and Lupus on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus; the holy people joyfully came to meet him.
>
> “But Damasus, conscious of so many crimes, and shaken by no small fear, bribed the whole palace so that his deeds might not be disclosed to the emperor. The emperor, unaware of what Damasus had done, extended the edict, so that, Ursinus being relegated into exile, no further impious contention of peoples might clash. [Col. 0121D] Then Ursinus, a holy and blameless man, having regard for the people, gave himself into the hands of the wicked and willingly hastened into exile on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December by the emperor’s command.
>
> “But the people, fearing God and exhausted by no persecutions, did not fear the emperor, the judge, or Damasus himself—the author of crimes and murderer—but celebrated stations without clergy in the cemeteries of the martyrs. Hence, when many faithful had assembled at St Agnes’s, Damasus burst in armed with his attendants and scattered very many in the slaughter of his devastation. This most cruel act greatly displeased the bishops of Italy. When he had solemnly invited them to his birthday feast and some had come, he tried by prayers and money to obtain from them a judgment against holy Ursinus. They answered: ‘We have assembled for a birthday feast, not to condemn an unheard man.’
>
> “Thus his wicked design fell short of the result for which he strove. Thereafter the presbyters were afflicted in different ways and scattered through exiles and foreign places. Of these, Marcellinus and Faustinus presented petitions to Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius.”

Thus far the preface of the schismatic writer. Although it teems with falsehoods, it nevertheless contains some things that provide light for discerning the truth.

First, when you hear of the Liberian basilica, [Col. 0122B] you also understand its antiquity. Although the word *basilica* denotes a place set apart even for secular assemblies, yet since this same writer declares it closed on every side and therefore besieged by the Damasians, and further asserts that its doors were broken and its roof torn down, you may readily picture a place assigned and equipped for sacred synaxes, renowned for the gathering of the Christian people like the other titular churches of the City.

Secondly, you see that this anonymous author, although he writes that Ursinus was ordained first, does not at all say which election came first. Would he have omitted this if Damasus had forestalled him not only in ordination but also in election? It is therefore most true, as Jerome and Rufinus say, that Ursinus, driven by ambition, undertook to set chair against chair.

Thirdly, you see that he was elected and then consecrated with no interval. From this very fact the defect both of the election and of the ordination is more plainly established, and Ursinus’s greater ambition becomes clear. For the lawful day of ordination fell on 1 October, which was a Sunday; [Note: Col. 0121D: Pagi, on the year 367.] nevertheless that factional deacon dared to anticipate it. In contrast, Damasus’s reverence for the sacred canons recommends itself: he was ordained seven days after his election, neither secretly nor by some rustic bishop, as the other was, but in the Lateran basilica in accordance with established custom. Here we observe the carelessness of the anonymous deserter, who writes that Damasus was elected and consecrated in the Lucinae.

[Col. 0122D] Fourthly, you may observe that only seven presbyters and three deacons are counted among Ursinus’s followers. Yet we know from Cornelius and Optatus [Note: Col. 0121D: Letter 9 to Fabius, no. 3, in Constantinus; Col. 0122D: Optatus, book II, no. 4] that there were forty titles, or churches, when Victor of Garba came to Rome on behalf of the Donatists. Their number had subsequently increased under the Roman bishops who succeeded Cornelius; for scarcely fifty years after Damasus’s election, seventy presbyters are listed as having supported Boniface alone after Eulalius’s rejection. [Note: Col. 0122D: Baronius, year 419.] What, then, are ten mad heads of clergy who stood for Ursinus, when account is taken of all the sacred ministers necessary in so many [Col. 0123A] churches and who had cast their votes for Damasus?

Now, to return to the argument: this document mentions the killings repeated on three occasions because of this schism. The first was in the basilica of Julius, and this first slaughter was perpetrated within the very seven days between the election and consecration. The question is which basilica of Julius was the one in which Ursinus was tumultuously elected and consecrated, and in which the subsequent killing occurred.

Some place it in the Lateran Patriarchate and produce several passages from Anastasius by which they think this is established. Yet I am held in doubt by the authority of the Liberian Catalogue, in which Julius is said to have built five basilicas: three outside the City and two within it. One of the latter it calls simply the Julian basilica and places in the seventh region, [Col. 0123B] near Trajan’s forum; the other in region XIV, beyond the Tiber, near Callistus. The same is also read in the breviary of the Liberian basilica.

But the Lateran Patriarchate was neither in region VII nor near Trajan’s forum. Accordingly, this basilica of Julius must be sought elsewhere, although in such obscurity of events and times it is easier to show where it was not than where it stood. I shall not, however, deny that there may have been some part of the Lateran Patriarchate called Julia. But it is uncertain whether it took its name from Julius or from Julia, since the reading varies: I have seen *Julii* written at times, but *Juliae* more frequently.

The latter reading is, I think, shown to be truer by Anastasius himself in his account of Sergius I, when he calls that part of the Lateran Patriarchate the basilica of the house of Julia. Therefore I would believe it to have been so called from some distinguished woman of that name, or from the Julian family, rather than from Pope Julius. For we learn from Capitolinus that Marcus Aurelius was born on the Caelian Hill and raised in the house of his grandfather Verus, near the Lateran buildings. It may therefore be that it had formerly belonged to Julia, daughter of Nerva, who—as Hardouin thought—married Verus; or that she had even built it. Afterwards, following other emperors, it may have passed to Julia Flavia, Constantine’s daughter, and, when joined to the Lateran buildings, retained that name. But since the question proceeds by conjectures, and uncertain ones, let each person’s opinion be law for himself.

The second slaughter, and the graver one, occurred not long after the first in the Liberian basilica. For after Ursinus had been driven into exile, complete tranquillity and peace were hindered from being restored by certain of his party and of the clergy itself, who perhaps had an interest in fomenting quarrels and prolonging the rope of contention. When they too were being led into exile on 24 October by order of Juventius, prefect of the City, the people over whom they presided forcibly snatched them from the soldiers’ hands and brought them to the Liberian basilica. It was defiled by the blood of factionalists assembling and breaking in from every side.

There is no mention in Ammianus, Rufinus, or Jerome of this killing in the Liberian basilica; conversely, the schismatic mentions no killing other than the one which they write was perpetrated in the Sicinian basilica. Hence some learned men infer that the Sicinian and Liberian basilicas were one and the same, unlike others who place the Sicinian basilica within the enclosure of St Antony’s monastery.

But anyone who notices that one slaughter occurred while Ursinus was present and leading the band of factionalists, as Rufinus and Jerome write, whereas the other occurred after Ursinus had already been removed and driven into exile, will readily understand that the killing in the Sicinian basilica differed from that in the Liberian basilica. Therefore, since two distinct killings are at issue, nothing prevents us from saying that one was perpetrated in the Sicinian basilica and the other in the nearby Liberian basilica.

Finally, the third was that which occurred at St Agnes’s outside the walls, where the schismatics were accustomed to gather. But this belongs to the following year and is the very event whose investigation Rufinus says was undertaken by Maximinus, prefect of the grain supply. The recent compiler of a history of the Roman pontiffs charges Damasus with responsibility for these killings and slaughters, relying only on the authority of Faustinus and Marcellinus, whom he values so highly that he prefers them to every testimony cited for Damasus. But what should one expect from the sort of people to whom calumny is customarily—and ought to be—more valuable than truth?

IV. To conclude the matters carried out in 366 and 367 and concerning the Ursinian schism: from these accounts it is established that Ursinus created the schism. Then, as its author and, as it were, the author of the killings that followed, he was first heard in his cause, the parties being present and disputing vigorously, as Ammianus indicates by the legal language taken from the Forum; and he was driven into exile with several associated presbyters and deacons by Juventius, prefect of the City. Since Ammianus himself calls this man upright and prudent, this false schismatic writer prates in vain that he had been corrupted by Damasus’s gold.

With Ursinus and his associates thus expelled from the City, the schism which he had stirred up could have seemed extinguished; and perhaps for this reason Prosper, in the Chronicle published by Canisius [Note: [Col. 0123D] Vol. I, Basnage edition], wrote that it had lasted six months. But when Juventius left the prefecture about May or June of 367, and Praetextatus was appointed in his place—as is clear from a law of the Theodosian Code, *On Unthankful Freedmen*, issued on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September—and when the latter, intending, as it seemed good to him, to inaugurate his magistracy auspiciously, obtained from Valentinian that Ursinus and his associates be released from exile and restored to the City, the factionalists entered Rome again on 15 September. Baronius [Note: [Col. 0124D] Year 368, no. 4] cites the edict omitted by Praetextatus, by which Valentinian grants the exiles permission to return to the City; and subsequent events prove that it was issued about July or August. For Ursinus, a man of turbulent disposition, after two months had elapsed from his return—namely, on 19 November—was compelled by another edict of Valentinian to go into exile again, as we learn from this document.

Its author passes over the real reason in silence and, after his usual fashion, [Col. 0125A] lays the blame upon Damasus, shamelessly writing that this was accomplished through Damasus’s deceit. But the true and genuine cause of this renewed exile may be gathered partly from the rescript of Valentinian cited by this author and partly from Ammianus Marcellinus [Note: [Col. 0125D] Book XXVII, chapter 3]. Valentinian had granted the exiles permission to return, rightly adding this condition: if, once restored to their former position, they again acted in a turbulent spirit so as to disturb the peace that had been restored, a most severe sentence should be pronounced against them. Conversely, in the edict by which he ordered Ursinus to be expelled again, he declares that he did so in order that, once Ursinus had been banished, no impious contention should thereafter rend the populace, as the Anonymous writer himself records. Ursinus, therefore, had behaved after his return in such a manner that he ought to be expelled again by Praetextatus; and since Ammianus writes that this was done justly, [Col. 0125B] the Anonymous writer’s calumny against Damasus is manifest. Here are Ammianus’s own words:

> By the authority of Praetextatus, and through the just support of truth, the tumult provoked by Christian disputes having been calmed and Ursinus driven out, a profound peace flourished, since the Roman citizens were now of one mind; and the glory of this distinguished governor grew as he made many useful arrangements.

And thus, so far as the years 366 and 367 are concerned, the schism of Ursinus came to an end.

## V

Baluzius assigns two councils of Damasus to these same years. One is that mentioned in the acts of Eusebius the presbyter; the other is the one which Anastasius records in his *Life of Damasus*, said to have been convened because of an accusation brought against him, in which his opponents charged him with adultery. Anastasius also writes that the Paterniani, or Venustiani, were condemned in it [Note: [Col. 0125D] Venetian edition of the Councils, vol. II, p. 1037].

[Col. 0125C] But both these councils are fictitious and fabulous. As regards the first, the acts of Eusebius the presbyter teem with and are defiled by so many lies, fables, and anachronisms that anyone who undertook to refute them severally would be doing wholly unnecessary work [Note: [Col. 0125D] See the *Dissertation on the Acts of Liberius in Exile*, chapter 9]. Hence Bossuet himself—or whoever he may be—while with one hand defending their authority in order to serve his own cause, is compelled with the other to expose their falsehood: he ascribes to Damasus as presbyter, on his own initiative, the excommunication of Liberius which these apocryphal acts say was pronounced by Damasus already pope.

We may therefore join Tillemont in laughing at Baluzius, carried away by a wholly empty opinion and applauding himself for this council, supposedly first brought to light by him, which never existed. As regards the latter council, mentioned by Anastasius [Col. 0125D], if what he narrates is true, it must be assigned to an altogether different time, since no synod was held under Damasus during this period [Note: [Col. 0126D] See the year 396]. Moreover, I would not readily admit that an accusation of adultery was instituted against this most holy pontiff; though we shall return to the matter. If Baluzius had explained more fully, from the immense store which he had collected, anything concerning the Paterniani or Venustiani, whom he says were condemned by Damasus in that synod, he would assuredly have earned great gratitude from lovers of ecclesiastical history. But something concerning them also in its proper place.

# CHAPTER III. 368, THE THIRD YEAR OF DAMASUS; VALENTINIAN AND VALENS AUGUSTI, CONSULS FOR THE SECOND TIME

I. The emperor Valentinian approves the renewed exile of Ursinus and his schismatic associates, and orders the one basilica retained by the Ursinians to be restored to Damasus. II. The slaughter committed at the shrine of St Agnes, falsely imputed to Damasus: the grave danger thereby brought upon the innocent pontiff, explained from the testimony of Rufinus and Jerome. III. Evagrius of Antioch approaches the emperor on Damasus’s behalf; Damasus is declared innocent; on this occasion Jerome is cited and elucidated. IV. Damasus fulfils a vow to St Felix, apparently of Nola, and to other martyrs.

[Col. 0126A]

## I

The emperor Valentinian, to whom Praetextatus had written that he had sentenced Ursinus anew to exile, ratified the judgment [Col. 0126B] of the Urban Prefect. This is clear from his rescript, which Baronius cites under the year 268, no. 2. Although it lacks a date, it seems that it must be referred to the beginning of the current year, because Ursinus himself had left Rome in almost the final month of the preceding year, as we have seen.

The other companions and agents of the faction followed the man whom the emperor calls the author of the dissension; the Urban Prefect likewise ordered them to depart, except for a few who had concealed themselves in hiding so as not to appear. We infer this both from the writer of the preface, who says that the schismatics held services in cemeteries without clergy, and from another rescript of Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0126D] In Baronius, year 368, no. 3], issued on the day before the Kalends of June, under the same consuls. By this, however, the factionalists themselves, having been expelled for the peace of the City, were allowed, once released from their prescribed exile, to live wherever they wished, [Col. 0126C] with Rome excepted.

Moreover, not only was Ursinus’s exile approved by Valentinian: by a most provident decision the Urban Prefect was also ordered to assign to Damasus that one church still retained by the schismatics. The emperor feared that the Church would gain no fruit from Ursinus’s exile if he permitted any further source of quarrelling to remain in the City. Valentinian writes that this was requested from him by the defender of the Church of the city of Rome. From this we gather that the office of defender of churches consisted in pleading their causes before secular judges and even approaching the emperors themselves when the circumstances required it.

This office had been established long before Valentinian’s time, contrary to the opinion of some; for Epiphanius mentions a certain Cyriacus, defender of the Church of Ancyra [Note: [Col. 0126D] *Heresies* 72, nos. 8, 11, 12]. This practice, derived from the example of cities and secular corporations, which had their own defenders, was wisely adopted for the Christian religion. They were succeeded at a later period by those called advocates; but, because they abused their power, they were subsequently removed by decrees of certain councils.

## II

These rescripts to Praetextatus, since they concern matters transacted [Col. 0127A] after Ursinus’s renewed exile, belong to the first months of this year. But the popular agitation, which in the meantime had lost little or nothing of its force, again burst out into reciprocal killings at St Agnes’s, where the factionalists had rashly assembled without any regard for the laws enacted against them. In accordance with the habitual practice of schismatics, this crime was falsely charged against the undeserving Damasus before Olybrius, who succeeded Praetextatus about June or July, as is clear from the chronology of the Theodosian Code and from Tillemont.

Olybrius, however, set aside Aginatius and employed in judicial matters Maximinus, who administered the prefecture of the annona after Julian. Reinesius [Note: [Col. 0127D] Letter LXIX, pp. 635–636] asserts that Aginatius was descended from Anicius Paulinus, formerly consul and Urban Prefect. This explains why Rufinus, after writing that the places of prayer were filled with human blood, immediately adds that the matter was turned, through Maximinus’s factional influence, into an accusation against the good and innocent priest Damasus.

[Col. 0127B] For Maximinus—whether to please the schismatics, who had drawn to their side a certain Jew named Isaac and employed him as their accuser, or to indulge his own savage disposition—resolved to prosecute Damasus before the emperor as guilty of the sedition and slaughter perpetrated in the church of St Agnes. In order to achieve this, he extracted by torture testimony against the utterly innocent pontiff from men of disreputable character and from clerics themselves.

But Aginatius, the deputy of the City, bitterly resented that Olybrius had placed Maximinus above him in the hearing of cases [Note: [Col. 0127D] Book XXVIII]. He both informed Valentinian of the proceedings against Damasus [Col. 0127C] and further reported that factionalists, with Olybrius’s connivance, were holding gatherings in the suburbs, the continuing and frequent source of quarrels and seditions. Accordingly, once the emperor had learned the truth, he prohibited those suburban meetings and decreed exile as the penalty if they met within the twentieth milestone from the City. Thus it came to pass, in Rufinus’s words: “God, the vindicator of innocence, was present, and the punishment was turned upon the heads of those who had laid their snare.”

Indeed, anyone who reads attentively the rescripts of Valentinian sent at the same time to Olybrius and Aginatius, which the great father of annalists brought to light [Note: [Col. 0127D] Year 369, nos. 3 and 4], can scarcely doubt that the matter occurred in this way. From these it is clear that both men had written to the emperor about the affair. But Olybrius reported one thing and Aginatius another. The former wrote that he had accomplished this: “that there could be no discord in the city of Rome, and that the Christian people might enjoy deep security in peace,” while deliberately overlooking what was being done by Maximinus, prefect of the annona, and by the schismatics. The latter, however, did not wish the emperor to remain ignorant that “the matters which had been somewhat quieted were still being stirred up, and disturbances were frequently raised by killings outside the walls.”

It is likely that Aginatius also added something about [Col. 0128A] Maximinus’s favour toward the factionalists and public enemies, and about his settled hatred of Pope Damasus and Damasus’s good cause. Hence Valentinian himself, who had previously entrusted the whole matter to the discretion of Praetextatus, a man attached to neither party, now gave Aginatius equal authority with Olybrius in this case, because he perceived that Olybrius had previously been prejudiced by Maximinus’s artifices; and he gave the same instructions to both.

To these two rescripts addressed to Olybrius and Aginatius, Baronius adds another addressed to Olybrius himself, in which the emperor declares his pleasure at the letter announcing that those who had disturbed the most holy law by tumult and sedition had been restrained. From this we learn that Olybrius at last complied fully with the emperor, and that this command was later than the others. Thus, after some two years, the schism of Ursinus finally came to an end.

## III

Aginatius’s letter written in Damasus’s favour may moreover have been greatly reinforced by Evagrius, presbyter of Antioch, who approached the emperor on behalf of the woman of Vercelli who had been struck seven times. Jerome narrates this as having occurred before he himself withdrew to the East [Note: [Col. 0128D] Letter I, Vallarsi edition]. Evagrius considered that he owed this service to Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, with whom he had previously come from the East into Italy and Rome.

Taking this opportunity, Jerome praises Evagrius himself for two other reasons: first, because through his efforts “Auxentius, who sat brooding over Milan, was buried before he seemed to have died”; secondly, because “the Roman bishop, almost entangled in the snares of faction, both overcame his adversaries and did not harm them once they had been overcome.” Both statements fit this year remarkably well.

For, in order that Auxentius might freely be condemned and proclaimed to the Churches as condemned—which, as I shall say, occurred in the following year—it was necessary to prevent the emperor, who had allied himself to Auxentius’s communion as though it were Catholic, from obstructing the undertaking. Thus it is not surprising if the synod in which Auxentius is said to have been condemned in the Holstenian collection is described as convened by imperial rescript. Nor was Damasus ever more entangled in the snares of faction, nor Ursinus with his associates more completely defeated and overcome, [Col. 0128C] than in this year. In the preceding year, when he returned to Rome from exile, Ursinus could have seemed victorious rather than defeated.

[Col. 0128D]

## IV

Ferrarius [Note: [Col. 0128D] *On the Cemetery of Nola*, chapter 10] writes that Damasus went to Nola to fulfil a vow at the tomb of St Felix, because under Felix’s guidance he had been saved and had broken the bonds of death; and that he built above the tomb a basilica which was narrow, later enclosed by St Paulinus within another basilica, broader and more splendid, which Paulinus built. For this claim, which many report, especially John Stephen Remondini, who recently wrote a history of Nola [Note: [Col. 0128D] Book III, chapter 4], and who rests content with the authority of Peter de Natalibus, no evidence remains except [Col. 0129A] one poem of Damasus himself, Poem XV …, which is in fact votive, as Baronius and the distinguished Muratori also observe [Note: [Col. 0129D] Notes on Poem XI, verse 11, and Dissertation 18].

But unless one wishes the vow to have been fulfilled by Damasus while absent and far away, this is sufficient, I think, to make us believe that he visited Nola. At that time, moreover, no church had yet been built in Rome which was later called St Felix’s *in Pincis*, after the Pincian residences [Note: [Col. 0129D] Donatus, Book III, chapter 8], in which Damasus could have presented himself as a suppliant and fulfilled his vow in person. Nor can this seem foreign either to the custom of that age or to the religious importance of the place, whose fame was so great that frequent crowds came to Nola from every part of the world and from Rome itself. Hence Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0129D] Poem III, distinguished Muratori edition] rightly sang on the feast-day of that saint:

> Even Rome herself, mighty in the sacred monuments  
> of the heavenly chiefs, Peter and Paul, rejoices  
> to grow thin in honour of this day; and from the mouth  
> of the Capenan Gate she sends forth twelve thousand upon twelve thousand  
> in dense procession to the friendly walls of Nola,  
> sending forth a hundred and twenty thousand in dense procession;  
> while far along the Appian Way lies hidden beneath the packed crowds.

[Col. 0129B] Since this pontiff says that, when his life was in danger, he was saved by the protection of this holy martyr, and since he had been brought into that peril through the deceit of his enemies under Maximinus, prefect of the annona, if he did go to Nola he can scarcely have gone in any other year than this or the following, when this peace and security were won for him.

# CHAPTER IV. 369, THE FOURTH YEAR OF DAMASUS; VALENTINIAN, NOBILISSIMUS PUER, AND VICTOR, CONSULS

I. The first synod under Damasus, against Auxentius, pseudo-bishop of Milan. II. Why it is assigned to this year. III. What was done and decreed in it; its synodical letter elucidated. IV. Vincent of Capua considered.

[Col. 0129C]

## I

After Damasus had thus emerged somewhat from the waves of domestic sedition, he turned his attention to the care of the Catholic Church. For in this year he convened that celebrated synod of ninety-three bishops against Auxentius, mentioned with praise by Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0129D] Book II, chapter 22], who uses a round number, and by Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0129D] Book VI, chapter 23].

A few years before, Auxentius had, as Hilary testifies, deceived even the elect by words fitted for that purpose. Having drawn Valentinian into his communion by a fraudulent confession, he obtained from the emperor an edict that no one should disturb the Church of Milan [Col. 0129D] [Note: [Col. 0130D] Hilary, *Against Auxentius*, no. 7]. Strengthened in his crime by this means, and supported in addition by the authority of a great church and by imperial protection, he began to spread the Arian poison more widely and to tear the bishops of Transpadane Italy and Venetia away from the Catholic religion.

Since Jerome writes that, after the tardy death of Auxentius and the appointment of Ambrose as bishop, all Italy was converted to the right faith, it is easy to infer that this impious zeal of the heretic caused no slight injury to the Catholic cause throughout the vicariate diocese of Italy [Col. 0130A]. In order to lead those unlearned and simple bishops into his heresy, he employed subtle and deceptive formulas of faith, which Damasus calls “perverse interpretations,” and he brandished the authority of the conciliabulum of Rimini, allegedly, though falsely, of six hundred bishops. He also employed these corrupt devices to prevent anyone from leaving him.

We learn these things from Hilary’s treatise against Auxentius himself and from the heretic’s petition to Valentinian, which sheds light upon this Roman synod and its letter. The Gallic and Venetian bishops had therefore reported these matters to Damasus. Learned men rightly count among them Hilary of Poitiers, Eusebius of Vercelli—who, returning from exile, travelled through Illyricum confirming the Nicene faith [Note: [Col. 0130D] *Life* in Ughelli, vol. IV, p. 759]—and Philastrius of Brescia; although Hilary himself establishes that there were ten bishops who met against Auxentius at Milan.

[Col. 0130B] From them, therefore, the pontiff had learned that some among the bishops of the first rank, whether from ignorance or simplicity, were tossed about by those perverse interpretations and corrupt counsels and were wavering between Catholic faith and Arian perfidy. They added that Auxentius had long before been condemned chiefly for this reason; but that Damasus above all, and the Apostolic See, ought to take care that this contagion should not spread more widely.

I believe this to be the force of these words: “Finally, they write that Auxentius of Milan was condemned chiefly for this reason,” words which appear somewhat obscure. That is, we should understand that those most vigilant bishops had reminded Damasus of the previous sentences by which Auxentius had already been censured, to the end that he might proclaim them to the churches as confirmed also by his own judgment, so that they might acquire the force of infallible and irrevocable authority and Auxentius might thereafter cease to do harm.

Thus, in the preceding century, the same Gallic bishops had asked Stephen to write letters through the provinces, so that all might know that Marcianus of Arles, already condemned and excluded from communion because of the Novatian party and heresy which he followed, had also publicly been avoided by them, lest he should continue to insult the college of bishops and scatter Christ’s flock [Note: [Col. 0130D] See Cyprian, Letter 68, Vallarsi edition]. For the same reason Basil, as we read, requested that Eustathius and Apollinaris be publicly announced as condemned by the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0130D] See Letters 262 and 263]. From this we learn both the long duration of that discipline and the meaning of the words in question.

Accordingly, Damasus convened in this year a synod of ninety-three bishops, both so that the earlier sentences against Auxentius might be held ratified by the Apostolic See, and so that the Nicene faith might be confirmed and the Council of Rimini annulled, in order that those seen to waver in faith and to think otherwise than is fitting for priests of God [Col. 0131A] might abandon their errors. That this was fully accomplished is clear from his letter to the Illyrian bishops, cited by Theodoret and Sozomen, while Holstenius published its Latin and original form [Note: [Col. 0131D] *Roman Collection*, part 1].

## II–III

Now receive the reasons why, with the great Baronius, Sigonius, Petavius, and Holstenius, I judge this synod to have been convened in this year.

1. The preface to the *Petitions* of Faustinus and Marcellinus establishes that no bishops came to the synod before Ursinus had been driven into exile. He was made an exile on 16 November 367. When Damasus, with affairs thus calmed rather than settled, called bishops from Italy for the anniversary of his ordination, which fell on the Kalends of October in the following year, [Col. 0131B] those who had assembled refused to meet in synod. It is therefore clear that no council was held under Damasus before this year. Here are the words of the schismatic writer:

> That most cruel deed—he is here speaking of the tumult at St Agnes’s—was greatly displeasing to the bishops of Italy. When he had solemnly invited them to his anniversary, and some of them had assembled, he used entreaties and money among them to procure their judgment against Ursinus. They replied: “We have gathered for the anniversary, not to condemn a man unheard.”

There is no sound reason to reject this testimony in this respect; it is further supported by the tumults, seditions, and killings by which, as is clear, both Damasus and the City itself were agitated in the preceding year.

2. The authority of Sozomen is added, for he writes that the Fathers assembled in synod after the schism of Ursinus had already been crushed through the work of the Urban Prefect; this, as we have seen, could scarcely have been achieved before the end of 367. Only then, after peace had been restored to the City, did bishops from many provinces come to Rome, and decree that Auxentius and those who shared his opinions were outside their communion [Note: [Col. 0131C] Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 23].

It is therefore established that Auxentius was condemned in the first synod assembled after the schism had been crushed; but the synod need not appear to have been convened immediately after the suppression of the schism. For after receiving the reports of the Gallic and Venetian bishops, Damasus needed some time to deliberate and determine whether a synod should be convened, then to summon it, and finally to call so many bishops from different parts of Italy and Gaul. They too had to be allowed some interval to prepare for their journey and to be present in Rome on the appointed day from distant regions. For accomplishing all this, a full year can scarcely seem an excessive time.

I know that very learned men prefer to assign the synod in which Auxentius was condemned to the year 370, or even later—to 372, as Pagius says [Note: [Col. 0132D] On the year 369, nos. 5 and 6]. They set out the matter as follows. In 367 or 368 Damasus convened a synod which confirmed the Nicene faith, restored to office priests who had fallen during the time of persecution, condemned Ursacius and Valens, the leading champions of the Western Arians, without investigating Auxentius, and wrote a synodical letter concerning these acts and decrees.

Pagius judges that the letter then written by that synod is the very one which Hilary recites in the *Fragments*, addressed in the name of the bishops of Italy to “the brethren throughout Illyricum who retain the paternal faith” [Note: [Col. 0132D] Fragment XII, Vallarsi edition]. Athanasius, having read it, then convened a synod at Alexandria. From it he wrote both to the Africans, to instruct them against Arian deceits, and to Damasus, thanking him for expelling Ursacius and Valens from the Church and further urging him to exercise the same authority against Auxentius. Stirred by the warnings of Athanasius and of the Alexandrian synod, Damasus then assembled, in 370 or later, that council of ninety-three bishops [Col. 0132B] in which Auxentius was condemned and deprived of office and rank.

They think this is established by another letter of Athanasius to Epictetus, which they consider later than the other. Writing to the Africans, Athanasius says:

> Sufficient indeed are the things written concerning sound and orthodox faith by our beloved fellow-minister Damasus, bishop of great Rome, **and by so many bishops assembled with him**, no less than those written by other synods held in Gaul and Italy.

Then, in chapter 9, he adds:

> Thus disposed, when it happened that we assembled together, we also sent a letter to our beloved Damasus, bishop of great Rome, concerning Auxentius, who has seized the Church of Milan. We reported to him his deeds: namely, that he was not only a follower of the Arian heresy but also guilty of many crimes which he had perpetrated with Gregory, his associate in impiety. **And we expressed our wonder that he had not yet been deposed and expelled from the Church**; and we gave thanks to his piety, and also to those who had assembled in the great City, because, having expelled Ursacius and Valens and others who thought with them, they had preserved the concord of the Catholic Church.

But after Auxentius had meanwhile been condemned by Damasus and the Roman synod, Athanasius wrote this to Epictetus:

> I had supposed that the empty prattle of all heretics who had ever existed had been checked by the Nicene synod; for the faith promulgated there by the Fathers is sufficient to overthrow every impiety. Therefore, since in this time various synods have been held throughout Gaul, Spain, and great Rome, all who assembled there condemned by common judgment those who even now secretly hold Arian heresy—namely, **Auxentius**, Ursacius, Valens, and Caius of Pannonia.
