[Col. 0132D] But I fear that this opinion of Pagius and other very learned men concerning two synods—the first having condemned Ursacius and Valens without touching Auxentius, the second inflicting the same penalty on Auxentius also—is more ingeniously devised than true. For, as I have said, no synod was held by Damasus before this year, nor could one easily have been held, especially with so great a number of bishops as were present at this one.

Moreover, the letter addressed “To the brethren throughout Illyricum who retain the paternal faith,” which Pagius refers to the first synod he posits under Damasus, is shown by the Benedictine editors of St Hilary’s works to belong to the pontificate of Liberius. More importantly, the very letter to the Africans whose authority is invoked destroys rather than establishes those two synods. For Athanasius there refers to one and the same synod assembled at Rome: the synod by which Damasus confirmed the Nicene faith, preserved the concord of the Catholic Church, expelled Ursacius, Valens, and others sharing their opinions from communion, and for all these things received Athanasius’s thanks.

If no one would say that Auxentius ought to be separated from the number of those who shared Ursacius’s and Valens’s views, neither can anyone rightly deny that Athanasius included his name too in the same condemnation as the rest. Accordingly, those whom Athanasius not obscurely designates under the general name of the associates of Valens and Ursacius, and says in the letter to the Africans had been expelled from communion—namely Auxentius and Caius of Pannonia—he names expressly in the letter to Epictetus, as though explaining himself. He says that they had been made partners in the same penalty as Ursacius and Valens by the very councils he mentions: those held at great Rome, throughout Gaul, and in Spain. Thus a later synod convened by Damasus at Athanasius’s urging to condemn Auxentius has been imagined in vain: Auxentius was condemned in this year and by this synod.

Finally, the same letter to the Africans asserts that the Roman [Col. 0133C] synod in which Ursacius, Valens, and their associates were condemned consisted of a great number of bishops, as we have seen. Can it, then, more plainly indicate any other than the synod composed of ninety-three bishops gathered from Gaul, Italy, and other regions, with which we are now concerned?

“But,” they say, “if Auxentius had been condemned by this synod, why does the Alexandrian bishop write to Damasus that he wonders why Auxentius had not yet been deposed and expelled from the Church?” I reply that Athanasius’s meaning and the sense of that passage are not what they suppose, but something entirely different and more consistent with the circumstances of those times. For why could he wonder that Auxentius had not hitherto been deposed, when in the very same letter to the Africans he had clearly stated that Auxentius, with Ursacius, Valens, and other associates in heresy, had been rejected from the communion of the Church? Nor could he possibly have been unaware that Auxentius had often been subjected to the same anathema in various places and by many councils [Note: [Col. 0133D] Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 6].

When, therefore, he also writes in this passage that he wonders why Auxentius “had not yet been deposed and expelled from the Church” [Note: [Col. 0133D] *Thaumazontes, pōs mechri nyn ou kathērēthē, kai ouk ekbeblētai tēs Ekklēsias*—“wondering how he has not yet been deposed and cast out of the Church”], he appears to have demanded something more from Damasus than a renewed condemnation: namely, that this man should no longer be allowed to occupy the Church of Milan, a man plainly deserving to be stripped of his throne and of the Christian name.

[Col. 0134A] For the terms *kathairō* (“depose”) and *ekballō* (“cast out”), which Athanasius uses, denote both the sentence pronounced against the accused and its actual execution, as it is called, if some circumstance or force—for example, in this case, Valentinian’s rescript—had at some time delayed it. Thus Paul of Samosata, although condemned by the synod of Antioch, is nevertheless said by Eusebius to have been driven from the Church through secular power [Note: [Col. 0133D] Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 30]. And Photinus, although he had often previously been deposed and long ago cut off from the communion of unity, could never actually be removed because of the people’s faction. Therefore Socrates and Sozomen call him deposed, and Hilary calls him cast down, when the Eastern bishops who came to Sirmium caused and obtained his expulsion from his see and place by the emperor Constantius [Note: [Col. 0133D] Socrates, Book II, chapter 21; Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 6, *katheilon*—“they deposed”; Hilary, *On Synods*, chapter 37, and Fragment XII, no. 21].

Accordingly, as it seems to me, the condemnation of Auxentius was confirmed and promulgated in encyclical letters by this first council under Damasus, in this very year. The emperor had forbidden Auxentius to be stripped of the throne and see which he had seized. Moreover, the formula of Rimini was again proscribed, and the Nicene faith strengthened, as is clear from the letter written by Damasus himself in the name of this council to the Illyrians, the sole surviving item from its acts.

Baronius believes that Ursicinus was also condemned at the same time; but the letters of Valentinian to which he appeals [Note: [Col. 0134D] Year 369, no. 72] say nothing on this subject. Yet this too seems probable to me, since from the testimony of Faustinus and Marcellinus [Col. 0134C] we know that Damasus had already contemplated it in the preceding year. It was necessary for discipline, unity, and the tranquillity of the Church that he be condemned as soon as circumstances and the times permitted, just as was done in the schism of Novatian by Cornelius [Note: [Col. 0134D] See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*].

The question is raised whether that letter which Damasus wrote in the synod’s name to the Illyrians was first composed in Greek or Latin, and whether its authentic text is that cited by Theodoret or that published by Holstenius. Labbe, Valesius, and Tillemont attribute this distinction to Holstenius’s text. Constantius denies it to that text in favour of the Greek version, but in my judgment he is led by exceedingly slight conjectures. There is no reason to say that Damasus wrote a Greek letter to the Illyrians, who were counted among the Westerners and used Latin; therefore there is no probable reason why what Holstenius found should have been taken from Greek rather than itself be the Latin and original text.

Further, neither Damasus nor other Westerners used the word *hypostasis* to express “substance,” Basil above all being witness [Note: [Col. 0134D] Letter 212]. Hence, in the letter published by Holstenius [Col. 0135A], one reads only that the Father and Son are “of one substance.” Therefore, to use the words of the very learned editor of the third volume of Basil’s works, the Westerners did not say that the Father and Son are of the same *hypostasis* and *ousia*, as the Greek texts have—*tēs autēs hypostaseōs kai ousias*—but only of the same *ousia*, omitting the word *hypostasis*. From this it follows that they did not write in Greek, and that the letter in Sozomen and Theodoret is not the principal and most authentic text, as the learned editor of the letters of the supreme pontiffs maintains against Tillemont and others. Rather, this distinction should with better right be ascribed to the letter published by Holstenius [Note: [Col. 0135D] Notes on Basil, Letter 92].

The judgment of this weighty scholar is confirmed by the variation of reading and interpretation observable in Sozomen, Theodoret, and Epiphanius, and noticed also by Valesius [Col. 0135B]. These variations, I think, clearly prove that the letter was first written in Latin and then, according to the disposition of each Greek writer and from different exemplars variously understood by each, was rendered differently into Greek.

From these letters of Damasus to the bishops of Illyricum, the most learned Joseph Augustin Orsi excellently establishes the supreme authority and irreformable judgment of the Apostolic See. For when the pontiff, expressing the mind of this Roman synod, says: “No prejudice could arise from the number of those who assembled at Rimini, since it is certain that neither the bishop of Rome, whose judgment ought above all others to have been sought, nor Vincent, nor the others, gave any assent to enactments of this kind,” he rightly concludes from this [Col. 0135C] that the force of ecclesiastical and patristic agreement, and of the unity of councils, does not rest merely in agreement as such, but must principally be derived from the fact that they are joined to the Roman pontiff as to a head—in precisely the manner in which the health, life, and motion of the body lie in its wholeness and the mutual union of its members, yet flow and take their origin from the members’ union with the head and from the head itself.

Hence, because the Roman pontiff had been present at the Nicene synod through his legates and had given his assent, Damasus calls the formula of faith then prescribed that of the Apostles, or Apostolic; but he rejects that of Rimini because it lacks that assent. For, as the distinguished writer continues, the bishops of this Roman synod compare the formula of Rimini with that of Nicaea [Col. 0135D]; and although the former had received the support of the greatest number of bishops, they principally reject it and decree it to be of no weight because it had been framed without the Roman pontiff’s assent. They determine, however, that the Nicene formula is to be retained perpetually because it had been confirmed by the judgment and authority of the Apostles—that is, of the Apostolic See or the Roman pontiff. [Note: [Col. 0135D] *On the Irreformable Judgment of the Roman Pontiff*, book I, chapter 7, article 2.]

IV. Yet it may seem strange that Vincent—the bishop of Capua, namely—is openly praised for having preserved his priesthood unstained for so many years. But can this deservedly be said of one who, in order to comply with the Arians, had abandoned communion with Athanasius? [Col. 0136A] It therefore occurs to me that Vincent never admitted anything by which it could plainly be established that he had departed either from the faith, or from the Church, or from communion with Athanasius.

Liberius laments only Vincent’s dissimulation in letters to Hosius and Eusebius of Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0135D] In Coustant, letters I and II.]; and he himself explains what he means by “dissimulation” when he says that Vincent not only obtained nothing from Constantius in the matters for which he had been sent as legate, but seemed to have accommodated his assent to the opinions of the Orientals—that is, to have adopted the counsel of those who thought that consideration of the Arian doctrine should then be set aside and that Athanasius’ condemnation alone should be urged and proposed. The same pontiff, already broken by exile, explains this in his letter to the Orientals. [Note: [Col. 0136D] In Coustant, letter XI.]

But if Vincent appeared to accommodate his assent, he had certainly not yet actually accommodated it; rather, he entertained the heretics with that false hope in order to gain time in the meantime and escape the exile which the emperor had decreed against those who resisted. This view seems confirmed both by Athanasius himself in the *Apology to Constantius*, when he says that Vincent endured no ordinary violence and grievous insults until he indicated that he was unwilling to communicate with Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0136D] Chapter 24.]; and further by Liberius in the letter sent to that same emperor through the later legates Lucifer, Pancratius, and Hilary, in these express words:

“The letters of the legates—namely Vincent and Marcellus—whom we had sent to Your Clemency remain; they arrived RECENTLY. In them they state that, because of the disturbance of all the Churches, they had indeed wished first to yield [Col. 0136C] to the opinions of the Orientals, but had proposed the condition that, if those same persons condemned the heresy of Arius, then, having been won over in this manner, they would obey their opinions.”

It is therefore clear that, when those legates wrote these things, they were close to falling but had not been altogether overcome. This was the reason why Liberius, after receiving their letters, sent other legates: the former ones were already almost broken and, because of that dissimulation, unfit for conducting the business. Yet I have not argued this in order to affirm that Vincent was entirely free from blame, but that we may understand in what sense Damasus could say that he had preserved his priesthood unstained for so many years: namely, insofar as he had done nothing openly either against the faith or against Athanasius.

# CHAPTER V. A.D. 370, THE FIFTH YEAR OF DAMASUS, UNDER THE THIRD CONSULSHIP OF THE AUGUSTI VALENTINIAN AND VALENS

I. The Illyrian synod which followed this Roman synod is discussed, together with letters written by it and by the emperor Valentinian. II. The evidence adduced is examined. III. On Zenobius, bishop of Florence. IV. On Valentinian’s law addressed to Damasus and inserted in the Theodosian Code; Baronius is defended.

[Col. 0136D]

I. The bishops of Illyricum did not disappoint Damasus’ hope. Stirred by his synodical letter, they assembled and confirmed the faith of the consubstantial Trinity, as had been done at Rome under that pontiff. They also condemned Polychronius, [Col. 0137A] Telemachus, Faustus, Asclepiades, Amantius, and Cleopater. If anyone suspects that these are the same persons who had previously been reported to the Apostolic See as innovators by the bishops of Gaul and Venetia, Socrates and Sozomen provide no slight ground for that suspicion [Note: [Col. 0137D] Socrates, book II, chapter 32; Sozomen, book VI, chapter 36.], since they place Mursa, a town of Pannonia—that is, of Illyricum—in Gaul. For “Gaul” is sometimes plainly used in a broader sense than is customary.

Then, as I think, by the command of Damasus himself and of the Roman synod, they informed the Asian bishops of all these matters through the legate Elpidius, and exhorted them likewise always to proclaim that the Trinity is consubstantial and, abandoning the error in which they had long been involved, to profess the Nicene formula of faith. Valentinian the emperor added letters of his own to the same effect to the letters of this Illyrian synod, which Elpidius was to carry; and Theodoret and Nicephorus record both sets of letters, translated, as I judge, from Latin into Greek. [Note: [Col. 0137D] Book IV, chapters 8 and 9; Nicephorus, book II, chapter 35.]

Now, since Valentinian writes openly in them that the Roman synod which the Illyrians had before their eyes had been held shortly before, Valesius rightly concludes both that the synod convened in Illyricum followed the other and that it cannot be deferred beyond this year, contrary to the view of some persons who had no solid reason. This is further confirmed by the letters of that synod itself, addressed to the bishops of the Asian diocese, Phrygia, Cataphrygia, and Pacatiana; [Col. 0137C] and especially by Valentinian himself, when he earnestly admonishes all of them not to continue abusing Valens’ authority against the right faith, nor to persecute the diligent ministers of God.

For this was done especially in the present year, when Valens spent a long time in Phrygia [Note: [Col. 0137D] Pagi, on the year 370, no. 20, and 372, no. 6.] and, elated by his successful campaigns against the barbarians, had wholly given himself over to the Arian faction. Like a pestilential whirlwind, he swept over and devastated all the provinces between Constantinople and Cappadocia, installing heretics in the churches whose lawful pastors he had deprived of office. For why would the fathers of the Illyrian synod, and why would Valentinian, write only to the bishops of the Asian diocese, Phrygia, Cataphrygia, and Pacatiana? Why would they warn them not to persecute Catholic bishops, if they were concerned with some persecution other than that raging at that time in [Col. 0137D] those regions? The subsequent persecution, by which Syria, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and other more distant provinces were later afflicted, did not concern those bishops; consequently there was no reason to seek their particular zeal above that of others on behalf of Catholics.

Moreover, I believe that the correspondence between Damasus and Ascholius began on the occasion of these most serious events and at this time, and that the apostolic vicariate of Illyricum was entrusted to the latter. For Tillemont infers from Ambrose and Basil that Ascholius administered the Church of Thessalonica about this period, [Col. 0138A] although the distinguished Gorgnaeus, canon of Soissons, dates his ordination to the time of the Council of Rimini. [Note: [Col. 0138D] Dissertation on the Council of Rimini, question 5.]

II. Thus the great Baronius made a serious mistake when, chiefly misled by these letters of Valentinian—which in the manuscript he used lacked the superscription naming Gratian and bore the name of Eustathius, whom he supposed to be the celebrated bishop of Sebaste and former legate of the Synod of Lampsacus to the Apostolic See—he assigned all these events to the year 365 and to the pontificate of Liberius, as Pagi rightly observes at that point. For the Eustathius mentioned in the letter of that synod to the Asians was not the bishop of Sebaste, but perhaps another bishop in Illyricum, the same man who is mentioned by Chrysostom. [Note: [Col. 0138D] Letter 27.]

He further thinks [Col. 0138B] that the Elpidius whose name is given in the letters of the Illyrian bishops was a presbyter of the Roman Church, indeed the very same person whom Julius had earlier sent as legate to the Orientals with Philoxenus. This opinion of the great man rests on the following Greek words of the Illyrian letter:

> Ἀνάγκην οὖν ἔχομεν πέμψαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς τὸν κύριον ὑμῶν καὶ συλλειτουργὸν Ἐλπίδιον ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλευούσης Ῥωμαίων ἀρχῆς, τοῦτο τὸ γράμμα ἔχοντα.

“We have therefore been compelled to send to you your lord and fellow-minister Elpidius from the ruling authority of the Romans, carrying this letter.”

Christophorson, Camerarius, and Langus translate this as saying that Elpidius was sent from the city of Rome, the capital of the empire. But Epiphanius Scholasticus, followed by Sirmond, understands the phrase to designate rather the Roman Empire than the city of Rome, and the emperor, whose letter Elpidius carried to the Asians, rather than the bishop of the City. [Col. 0138C]

Valesius approves Christophorson’s interpretation in part and Sirmond’s in part. He understands Elpidius to have been not a presbyter of the Roman Church, as Baronius thought, but a bishop in Illyricum, and translates the Greek words thus: “We therefore found it necessary to send to you our lord and fellow-minister Elpidius from the city that is queen of the whole empire, with these letters, so that he may learn whether your preaching is so constituted.” He thinks the reason why Elpidius may be said to have come from the city of Rome is that the bishops assembled in synod had sent him to Damasus, and that, having there received his embassy—as was necessary—by mandate of the synod itself, he had departed for Asia.

Yet, to state what I think: nowhere have I read that the supreme dignity of the priesthood was ever called ἀρχή, “authority” or “rule,” without some accompanying term distinguishing sacred from civil office. Hence Nazianzen calls the episcopate an ἀναμίακτος ἀρχή, an “unmixed authority,” and Chrysostom a πνευματικὴ ἀρχή, a “spiritual authority.” What then should one judge if, as the matter stands here, that very word is joined with another that indicates a civil rather than a sacred authority? Further, by what other example can it be established that the words ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλευούσης Ῥωμαίων ἀρχῆς mean the City? Therefore the interpretation of Christophorson, who takes it as “the city of Rome, capital of the empire,” can scarcely be tolerated; nor can that of Valesius, who understands [Col. 0139A] Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, to be designated by them.

Nor is Sirmond’s view without difficulty, since he renders the words thus: “But necessity was laid upon us to send to you our lord and fellow-minister Elpidius, carrying letters from the royal authority of the Romans.” For although I am well aware that these words often designate the Roman Empire, and other examples of this could be adduced, nevertheless, when the Illyrian bishops write that they are sending Elpidius as legate, τοῦτο τὸ γράμμα ἔχοντα, “carrying this letter,” they are speaking of the letter which they themselves wrote and handed to Elpidius for delivery. Hence Epiphanius, whose translation Sirmond follows, added the word “these,” which Sirmond omitted. Accordingly, in this place and with these words they cannot designate the emperor Valentinian himself.

Add also that, when this synodical letter was drawn up, Valentinian had not yet written; nor could those bishops then know for certain whether he would attach his own letter to that of the council. Yet this would have had to be known and certain to them if mention of that letter at this point were to be thought possible. Therefore these words must have an entirely different force from that attributed to them by these most learned men.

If, therefore, someone interprets them thus—“We considered it necessary to send to you our lord and fellow-minister Elpidius, carrying this letter, from the Latin Empire, that is, written in the Latin language”—perhaps, unless I am mistaken, he will come nearer the truth and render the passage plainer and less entangled. For it is established that Greek writers commonly used and understood the term Ῥωμαῖοι, “Romans,” to denote Latins. [Col. 0139C] Thus Sozomen says that Photinus wrote with mastery of the “Roman and Greek tongue,” Ῥωμαίων καὶ Ἑλλήνων φωνῇ, and Socrates calls him not unskilled in language. In the same sense Tertullian, Rufinus of Aquileia, Cassian of Marseilles, and other Latin Fathers were called Romans. [Note: [Col. 0139D] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, book V, chapter 38, no. 197.] Jerome himself, born in Illyricum, complains of the Orientals that they demanded from him, a Roman man, a novel name; and this could be confirmed by other examples.

III. The father of annals writes that in this year Damasus, Roman pontiff, sent to Constantinople Saint Zenobius, later bishop of Florence, to restrain the insolent violence of the Arians. This, however, had been written before Baronius by Peter Casella, following, as I think, old traditions of the Florentine Church. [Col. 0139D] [Note: [Col. 0139D] *On Tuscan Origins*, chapter 12.] The authority of the Acts that induced the great man to write this is utterly slight, as Tillemont proves [Note: [Col. 0139D] Notes on Ambrose, 50, volume IX.], and as the Bollandist editors show by judging them unworthy even of transcription. More recently, someone has vainly expended effort in defending them.

What may be observed in support of this opinion is that Valens was absent from Constantinople for almost the entire year; moreover Eudoxius the Arian had died, [Col. 0140A] and it was of the highest importance that a Catholic pastor be chosen in his place. It is therefore probable that Damasus, seizing the opportunity, sent someone there to strengthen the Catholics in his name and assist them in arranging this matter, since it is established elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0139D] See under the year 380.] that this pontiff did not lack zeal for choosing the best bishop for that Church.

Evagrius was indeed then elected by the Catholics; Socrates and Sozomen write that this occurred through the agency of Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, who was secretly in the City and exhorted the Catholics to the right faith. But since this great bishop had died long before, if Theodoret is to be believed, [Note: [Col. 0139D] Theodoret, book III, chapter 4; Tillemont, on Eustathius, note 5.] why should we not say that both authors have substituted one person for the other—Eustathius, namely, for Zenobius?

IV. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that in this year [Col. 0140B] the celebrated rescript of Valentinian was addressed to Damasus, directed against clerics and false monks who abused religion in order to obtain the inheritances of widows and other women of suspect status. Jerome [Note: [Col. 0140D] Letter 52, no. 6, Verona edition.] and Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0140D] Letter 18, no. 13.] discuss this very law; and these authors establish that it concerned ecclesiastical persons alone, and did not forbid churches to receive legacies and inheritances.

Hence Jerome says: “Let the Church, the mother of her children—that is, of her flock—which has begotten, nourished, and fed them, be heir.” Since that law was read by Damasus to the people in the churches, one may infer the zeal with which he laboured to preserve the holiness and unblemished reputation of the clergy and, moreover, to show himself free from every suspicion of avarice. For why should we say with Gothofredus [Col. 0140C] that it was published in the churches at Valentinian’s command rather than at that of the bishop of Rome himself, as something highly useful and necessary for moderating the greed of his own people? Is any trace of this imperial command present in the law itself? Moreover, was it customary for imperial laws, if they touched matters concerning the Church, to be read in churches? No one will say this, or at least prove it.

For the law concerning clerical privileges issued by Constantius, though addressed to Pope Felix, is nevertheless expressly said to have been read among the civil records, namely those of the urban prefecture. [Note: [Col. 0140D] Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 2, chapter 14, with Gothofredus’ note.] Therefore, since the law of which we speak was published in churches contrary to custom, Baronius rightly judged that this was done solely at Damasus’ command—indeed, that Damasus himself had prompted the emperor to enact the law. This adds to the praises of that pontiff; nor do I see why Constantius should reject Baronius’ opinion, which has pleased learned persons.

Moreover, I think that the conclusions which the unlearned Jannonius draws from this should be passed over, both because they are irrelevant here and because Father Antonio Blanco clearly demonstrates that he abuses this law of Valentinian to confirm his own opinions. Consult him if you wish. [Note: [Col. 0140D] Volume IV, book II, chapter 5, § 2.]

# CHAPTER VI. A.D. 371, THE SIXTH YEAR OF DAMASUS, UNDER GRATIAN AUGUSTUS’ SECOND CONSULSHIP AND THAT OF SEXTUS PETRONIUS PROBUS

I. The Ursinians, confined in exile, are recalled; the suburbicarian provinces; Rufinus’ opinion concerning the suburbicarian churches. II. Letters written this year by Saint Basil the Great to Saint Athanasius and Damasus are discussed and elucidated; the Anonymous Writer of Amsterdam is refuted. III. Other reasons are listed why Basil wrote to Damasus; on this occasion the Antiochene dissension between Meletius and Paulinus and on Marcellus of Ancyra. IV. Marcellus is defended against heresy; and Basil is shown eventually to have learned better and to have departed from his preconceived opinion against Marcellus.

[Col. 0141A]

[Col. 0141B] I. Baronius records under this year two rescripts of Valentinian: one to Ampelius, who had meanwhile succeeded Olybrius in the prefecture, the other to Maximinus, vicar of the City. By them Ursicinus and his associates Ursus, Rufus, Gaudentius, Auxanon, Auxanius, Adiedus, and Rufinus were permitted to depart from their appointed place of exile and settle wherever they wished, provided that they did not enter Rome or the suburbicarian regions. From this we learn that Ursicinus’ principal adherents were first expelled from Rome, then beyond the twentieth milestone, and finally condemned to a specified exile under the prefecture of Olybrius. Accordingly, Valentinian, as we have seen, congratulated Olybrius for having restrained the obstinate men.

[Col. 0141C] Gothofredus and Tillemont seize upon these rescripts of Valentinian, which I have mentioned and which refer to suburbicarian regions, and turn them to their own purpose. Each therefore holds that suburbicarian provinces and regions are one and the same as the suburbicarian churches, which Rufinus says were assigned by Nicene Canon 6 to the care of the bishop of Rome. [Note: [Col. 0141D] *History*, book I, chapter 6.] But the former confines the suburbicarian regions within a hundred miles of the City and encloses within the same boundaries all the jurisdiction of that Roman bishop. The latter, however, understands by “urbicarian provinces” all those subject to the vicar of the City, extending more widely: namely Campania, Tuscia and Umbria, Suburbicarian Picenum, Valeria, Samnium, Apulia and Calabria, Lucania and Bruttium, Sicily, [Col. 0141D] Sardinia, and Corsica. From this he rightly concludes that the suburbicarian churches include those located throughout all these provinces. But he denies, on an argument drawn from the rescripts themselves, that they could have extended beyond Italy and its boundaries: the rescripts permit Ursicinus, an exile, to leave Gaul and go elsewhere as he pleases, but prohibit and forbid him to approach Rome and enter the suburbicarian regions. For if by suburbicarian regions one understands the whole West, Ursicinus would have been obliged to withdraw into the East, and that emperor’s clemency would have been harsher to him than the penalty previously imposed.

Dupin had used the same line of argument before Tillemont. For, he says: “If suburbicarian regions corresponded either to the whole Roman Empire or at least to the whole West, what could be more absurd than to grant a man, as a signal favour, permission to leave Gaul on the condition that he set foot neither in the whole Roman Empire nor at least in the West? Such a favour would surely have to be regarded as the greatest punishment.” [Note: [Col. 0141D] *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, dissertation I, final section.]

Now, as regards the former opinion, scarcely anyone remains who does not acknowledge that Gothofredus and Salmasius erred in locating the suburbicarian regions within only a hundred miles, since it is entirely clear that the same expression often designated all the other [Col. 0142B] provinces governed by the vicar of the City. [Note: [Col. 0141D] See Schelstrate, dissertation 6, chapters 1 and 2; and, among non-Catholics, Bingham, book IX, chapter 1, § 9.]

But as for the view of those who would restrict the metropolitan rights of the bishop of Rome to those other ten provinces, you see that it rests upon this sole reasoning: that suburbicarian churches do not differ from suburbicarian provinces, and that the same force applies in defining the meaning of the two expressions. Hence Dupin presses the matter thus: “It remains to inquire what the suburbicarian provinces and churches were, and what their boundaries were. In the first place, however, it seems necessary to establish and take as certain in this question that suburbicarian churches correspond to suburbicarian provinces. For just as the Egyptian, Asian, and Illyrian churches are those situated in those dioceses, so the suburbicarian churches cannot be other [Col. 0142C] than those contained in the suburbicarian provinces. . . . Therefore the opinion of those who would have the name of provinces denote either the entire Empire or at least the entire West cannot be tolerated.” Thus he writes in the *Tripod*. [Note: [Col. 0142D] *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, dissertation 1, no. 14.]

I shall not now produce the arguments by which Sirmond and other most learned men have demonstrated, against this view, how futile that reasoning is, lest I repeat what has already been done. I shall add only this: the argument which Tillemont and Dupin use may have some affirmative force, but none whatever of negative force. For if you say that urbicarian churches are those contained within the four annona provinces and the other provinces also, I readily grant it—not merely because they were contained in the suburbicarian provinces, but because they had no metropolitan other than the Roman pontiff to whom they were subject.

But if, on the other hand, you contend that churches situated outside Italy in the broad sense could not have been called suburbicarian churches, although they were subject to no metropolitan, I shall exercise my right if I deny it; nor will you easily establish what you wish unless you prove in addition that there was some bishop of higher rank to whom all the churches throughout Italy and the West were subject. Indeed, anyone who surveys the ecclesiastical records of those times must concede that no bishop of this kind and rank existed throughout that whole region before the Council of Nicaea, nor even in the fourth [Col. 0143A] century—unless he wishes, with Quesnel, to speak such nonsense as rashly to assert that the Roman pontiffs had drawn to themselves all prerogatives and duties of metropolitan dignity, and that any metropolitans who existed possessed a title without reality. [Note: [Col. 0143D] On Letters 16 and 80 of Pope Leo.]

You see, then, that suburbicarian churches were not only those contained within the boundaries of Italy administered by the vicar of the City, but could have extended more widely. You therefore understand how inept and deceptive is the argument used to identify and define suburbicarian churches from suburbicarian provinces.

Or, to use the words of the very weighty Benedict Bacchini: “Could Rufinus have been ignorant of what is not hidden from us—namely, that in those times all the provinces subject to the vicar of the City were subject to the Roman metropolitan, while the remaining Italian metropolises were allowed those governed by the vicar of Italy?” It remains, therefore, that by the ambiguous expression “suburbicarian churches” he understood the churches of several provinces which, whether situated within or beyond the hundredth milestone, in Italy or elsewhere, obeyed the Roman pontiff as their metropolitan. [Note: [Col. 0143D] *On the Origin of Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, part II, section 16.]

Bacchini continues: Rufinus used the expression in order to adapt the interpretation of the Nicene canon to the circumstances of his own time. For after the Council of Nicaea, whether with the Roman bishop’s consent or without his opposition, several metropolitans had arisen throughout Italy broadly understood; apostolic vicars had moreover been instituted in certain places to supply, as Leo the Great says, the presence of an apostolic legation to provinces distant from Rome; and other changes had occurred in ecclesiastical polity. Through these changes the former authority of the bishop of Rome himself could appear diminished in the West, unlike that of the bishop of Alexandria, from whose ancient jurisdiction nothing had been taken throughout the whole diocese. Rufinus therefore thought that the old comparison, without any circumscribing boundaries, employed by the Council of Nicaea between the bishop of Rome and the bishop of Alexandria could no longer suit the circumstances. Instead, he expressed the matter as it stood in his own time, though in a more obscure manner: all the churches which he saw the Roman bishop still retaining and administering, wherever located, he called suburbicarian. By a wholly new designation, he presented to us later people, as it were, a man ancient in age and habits speaking in a youthful manner. But I now fear that I have been too diffuse in a matter unrelated to my undertaking, and I return to the road.

II. While these things were taking place in the West, the Eastern Church was being tossed in the grievous storm raised under Valens and the Arians—a storm which, to pass over others, Basil describes in many places, but especially in letters to Damasus, other Western bishops, and Athanasius. He therefore adopted the course which had often previously, and recently under Liberius, provided present relief to the Macedonians: in short, he judged that help must be sought from Damasus.

Thus he says to Athanasius: “I have long known, even from my moderate knowledge of affairs, that the one way of assistance for our Churches is if the Western bishops agree with us. For if they display the zeal which they showed when one or two [Note: [Col. 0143D] ὑπὲρ ἑνὸς ἢ δυὸ: ‘on behalf of one or two.’] persons caught holding very wrong opinions, and extend it likewise to our district, perhaps some benefit may accrue to our common affairs.” [Note: [Col. 0143D] Letter 66, Benedictine edition.]

By these words, I think, the condemnation of Auxentius is indicated. This was also noted by an old scholium which D. Maranus read written in the margin of the royal manuscript: Περὶ τῶν κατὰ Ῥώμην ἐπισκόπων Αὐξεντίου καὶ τῶν περὶ αὐτόν, “Concerning the bishops at Rome—Auxentius and those associated with him.” Basil had therefore already heard the decrees issued by the synod under Damasus against Auxentius. These decrees are consequently assigned wrongly by some to this year or even to the following year, but are most rightly assigned to the year 369 by others, whose view I have adopted.

Yet neither Basil nor Athanasius had seen its acts. For otherwise, why, after discussing matters with Athanasius, would Basil have judged that Damasus should be asked to have the legates whom he would send to inspect the East carry with them whatever documents had been issued after the Council of Rimini for the annulment of what had been done there by force? Why further, if the acts of that synod had reached Athanasius, did he not immediately send them to Basil, or even make any mention of them in the letter he wrote to him?

Basil, therefore, after discussing the whole matter with the holy Athanasius and Meletius, wrote to Damasus and entrusted the letter for delivery to the deacon Dorotheus. It is Letter 70 in the recent Benedictine edition [Note: [Col. 0144D] In the older edition, 220.], which they, as does Constantius, judge to be the first among those that we read as sent by the bishop of Caesarea to that pontiff. Maranus thinks it was written about the middle of this year. Besides the reasons advanced by that learned and diligent man [Note: [Col. 0144D] *Life of Basil*, chapters 17 and 20.], there are no slight indications of this both in the letter to Damasus itself and in others to Meletius. [Note: [Col. 0144D] Letter 68.]

Basil’s view was that Damasus should be addressed in the common name of the Orientals. He had accordingly asked Meletius both to write a letter himself and to dictate a memorandum concerning the matters and persons about whom and to whom Dorotheus ought to speak. He further asked, that those letters might carry greater authority [Col. 0144D] with Damasus, that Meletius add the names of all who were in communion with him, even if absent. For in this way Basil hoped that the Roman pontiff might more easily be persuaded to grant communion to Meletius rather than to Paulinus. Whether Meletius wrote through Dorotheus is uncertain, although the apostate Anonymous Writer whom we have mentioned—and must mention again—asserts this.

Meanwhile, from Basil’s letter may be seen his opinion of the authority and [Col. 0145A] dignity of the Apostolic See. For in judging Damasus should be asked to send legates to the East, either to reconcile those at variance, restore God’s churches to friendship, or at least indicate more plainly to him the authors of the disturbance, “so that it may be clear to you with whom communion ought to be held,” the bishop of Caesarea most clearly professed that the supreme authority of the Roman pontiff extends to all churches everywhere, and that the rights of sacred communion depend upon his judgment.

Further, lest suspicion arise that Basil did not sincerely hold these views, as the same Anonymous Writer has fancied, the following words which he had earlier written to Athanasius should also be observed: [Note: [Col. 0145D] Letter 66.] “We thought it worthwhile to write to the bishop of Rome, that he might examine our affairs and give counsel; and, since it is difficult for anything to be sent from there by a common and synodical [Col. 0145B] decree, that he himself may undertake this business on his own initiative”—or, as others translate more closely according to the force of the words, “that he himself may employ his supreme authority in this affair.”

Nor need I here reproduce what Basil wrote elsewhere, and what must be assigned to its own time, since it establishes his judgment concerning the authority of the Apostolic See and exposes the rashness of the apostate devotee of Scripture, who dared to attack Fleury when Fleury undertook, on the basis of these letters, to demonstrate with us the divinely established rights of primacy. [Note: [Col. 0145D] Book XVII, § 31.]

What Basil especially wishes to commend to Damasus is that the legates whom he would send to the East should bring with them whatever could demonstrate that the Council of Rimini had been annulled. This strongly opposes those who grant to the Roman pontiff neither supreme authority nor authority equal to that of a council, as the most learned Father Joseph Augustin Orsi observed before me. For the reader’s benefit, I shall reproduce his words here:

“Meanwhile, to the contending parties, the number of so many bishops gathered in synod could appear a great prejudice in favour of the Arian position. Therefore, if the simpler Catholics were to be protected from Arian deceptions, they were not to be fortified by arguments that would draw them into an examination of the events; rather, some simple principle, widely known among Catholics, had to be laid down—namely, that synods held without the consent of the Roman pontiff are not legitimate and are liable to the danger of error, and moreover are of no authority unless confirmed by the Apostolic See. Therefore Saint Basil the Great, although he clearly and certainly [Col. 0145D] knew that the acts performed at Rimini had been carried out under compulsion and consequently were in themselves and by law null and void, nevertheless, lest the number of bishops who had subscribed to the formula of Rimini mislead many Catholics, especially the simpler among them, judged that Damasus should be written to and asked what had been done at Rome toward annulling the acts of Rimini. For the holy Doctor knew that the final and decisive judgment in this matter belonged to the Apostolic See.” [Note: [Col. 0145D] *On the Infallibility of the Roman Pontiff*, volume I, book II, article 3, chapter 1.]

III. Moreover, Basil’s appeal to the Apostolic See was prompted, besides the distressed condition of the Eastern Church, by his great affection and zeal for Meletius, whose cause he favored over that of Paulinus. He himself admits this in writing to Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0145D] Ep. 67.], and the words which we have cited from the letter to Damasus further indicate the same. I consider it superfluous to weave the history of this Antiochene schism, since it is unknown to no student of ecclesiastical affairs. Eusebius of Vercelli, not altogether approving the course adopted by Lucifer, who had ordained Paulinus, departed from Antioch, intending to return to Italy, without, as Rufinus says, relaxing his communion with either party [Note: [Col. 0145D] Book X, ch. 30.]. Liberius does not appear to have been at all estranged from Meletius; for he expressly and by name [Col. 0146B] included him among the bishops to whom he addressed that celebrated letter which Socrates records [Note: [Col. 0146D] Book IV, ch. 12.] as having been brought to the Easterners by Silvanus, the second envoy of the Macedonians—a fact which Basil regards as evidence of communion having been granted [Note: [Col. 0146D] See also his Ep. 240, recent edition.]. Hence Basil himself, writing to Athanasius in order to draw him to the side of that same Meletius, says that this judgment had pleased your unanimous Westerners, as the letters brought to us by the blessed Silvanus show [Note: [Col. 0146D] Ep. 67.]. But Damasus approved the example of Eusebius of Vercelli and judged that a matter of such importance required longer deliberation; accordingly, he kept the question between the two parties undecided for several years—a most excellent policy, as I shall say in its proper place.

IV. Besides this, the same bishop of Caesarea writes to Athanasius that he and several others think that the pernicious heresy of Marcellus should be reported to [Col. 0146C] the bishop of Rome and that he should be asked to eradicate it:

> Arius, indeed, they strike down with an anathema. . . . But against Marcellus, who put forward an impiety diametrically opposed [to Arius’s], and was impious against the very existence of the Only-Begotten’s Godhead, they seem to have brought no censure. . . . The evidence for this is the books of that wicked writing preserved among us; yet they have nowhere appeared to condemn him, and they are censured on that account, because from the beginning, through ignorance of the truth, they even admitted him to ecclesiastical communion.

[Note: [Col. 0146D] Ep. 69.]

Yet Marcellus is not mentioned in the letter to Damasus. Therefore, matters concerning him must have been entrusted to private instructions and to a memorandum concerning the business to be conducted at Rome through Dorotheus.

[Col. 0146D] Nevertheless, I would not wish to recount all that was then argued both for and against Marcellus before Montfaucon brought out his *Analecta of the Ancient Fathers*. For that most learned man published a document adorned with a most erudite dissertation [Note: [Col. 0146D] Vol. I, *Collect. nov. vet. PP.*], and afterwards reprinted in the Venetian edition of the councils, from which it is clear that the bishop of Ancyra, his clergy, and the other Catholics who assembled separately from [Col. 0147A] those bishops appointed in Marcellus’s place, held a sound and pure faith. Yet another most learned monk from the same congregation, who had rendered excellent service to ecclesiastical history, recently objected to his companion that this document does not concern the last years of Marcellus. For, as he says [Note: [Col. 0147D] *Life of Basil*, ch. 37.], there is no indication of time in the Confession of Faith submitted to Athanasius in the name of Marcellus, his clergy, and his people; from which it follows, he maintains, that it cannot be established that Marcellus did not relapse into heresy after it.

But those who defend Basil by asserting that he is speaking of a heresy again maintained by Marcellus after Marcellus had declared it alien from himself through this solemn testimony before Athanasius and his synod, seek an escape which Basil himself blocks by his own words. For [Col. 0147B] he does not appeal to some recent document to prove that Marcellus had again fallen into heresy, but to books written by him long before; and he uses against him the very same sword which Eusebius and the other Arians had used. Moreover, he reproaches the Westerners for an ecclesiastical communion which they had granted long before, and therefore certainly for no other than that which had been decreed for Marcellus long previously by the Council of Sardica and Pope Julius of Rome.

But, what seems to me decisive is that this very Confession of Faith presented to Athanasius bears marks from which it may safely be asserted that it was submitted either a little before, or not long after, Basil wrote these things to Athanasius. For the name of Theodulus of Oxyrhynchus must be observed, which is found [Col. 0147C] subscribed to it. Montfaucon, though otherwise nothing escapes him, admits that he does not know who this man was. But I think that he was the very man whom Marcellinus and Faustinus, in their *Libellus of Petitions*, call Theodore of Oxyrhynchus: one who lapsed during the time of the Arians, was reduced by George the Arian to the rank of layman, and was again ordained bishop; who finally, after returning to the Church, subscribed with the other Egyptian bishops to the Council of Constantinople. For among Latin writers especially, one often finds Theodore or Dorotheus used for Theodulus. Thus the man called Theodulus of Trajanopolis by Athanasius, Theodoret, and Socrates is called Theodore in the letter of the Council of Sardica to all the Churches and by Hilary; Fabricius has also supplied other examples of this [Note: [Col. 0147D] See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. IX, p. 250, and vol. X, p. 546.]. This [Col. 0147D] confession, therefore, at which this Theodore or Theodulus was present, must appear to have been submitted long after the Alexandrian Council which decreed that bishops who had lapsed under persecution should be received into communion. For Theodulus is not listed among those present at that council; nor is it credible that a man guilty at that time of so great an act of betrayal could have been present.

Shortly after this Alexandrian Council, Athanasius [Col. 0148A] was compelled by the Emperor Julian to leave the country. Although, after Julian’s death, he had returned to Alexandria about the end of the year 364, he was nevertheless again compelled to hide and live in exile after four or five months by an edict of Valens [Note: [Col. 0147D] The commentary on matters concerning Athanasius, published by the learned Maffei, calls the place where he hid “Thereu.” Hence a learned man suspects forgery [Col. 0148D] because the name of that place occurs nowhere. But I think that “Chersu” should be read; there were two villages of that name, one twelve and the other eight miles from Alexandria. See the *Itinerary* published by Schelestrate, vol. II, p. 543.], and he did not return to his Church before the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaiphus. These facts are established by that ancient Life of Athanasius which the learned Maffei was the first to rescue from obscurity and publish [Note: [Col. 0148D] *Osservazioni letterarie*, vol. III.].

Since I cannot bring myself to believe either that the Ancyrene envoys wished to go to Alexandria then, or that, in those turbulent times, the Alexandrian bishop could have assembled as many bishops as took part in the proceeding, it remains that we should place this event in those final and tranquil years which he spent with his own Church. To define the time exactly [Col. 0148B] is immaterial. So far as our purpose is concerned, it makes no difference whether Marcellus submitted his confession a little before or not long afterward, since it is clear from this that he could not be said to have fallen into heresy when Basil wrote to Athanasius. If, however, there is room for conjecture, perhaps the Ancyrene envoys came to Alexandria when Theodore or Theodulus was present at the crowded synod mentioned by Athanasius in his letter to the Africans, and presented to Athanasius and the other bishops assembled in synod that most clear and excellent Confession of Faith. Perhaps also Montfaucon, who assigned it to Athanasius’s last months, came nearer the truth. For, as he rightly judges, the Alexandrian bishop ought to have sought this testimony from Marcellus [Col. 0148C] in order to counter the prejudiced opinion of Basil and others who thought with Basil. This is clear from the final chapter of the confession itself, in which the envoys of the Ancyrene clergy ask Athanasius:

> Not to believe those who accuse us, but to write to those whom he knows to be orthodox, so that, if a calumny fabricated against us should reach them, then, having seen this our Confession of Faith, they may detect the malice of those who rashly sought to stir up hostility against us.

But since death prevented Athanasius from communicating to Basil his testimony concerning the faith of the Ancyrenes, this document consequently remained unknown to Basil for a long time.

Basil nevertheless appears, before his death, to have abandoned his preconceived opinion against Marcellus and his Church [Col. 0148D] and to have admitted the Marcellians to communion as persons who had always been Catholics. I infer this from what he afterwards wrote to Eulogius, Alexander, Harpocration, and the other twelve Egyptian bishops exiled in Palestine under Valens for the faith, and to Peter of Alexandria, who had then returned. Those Egyptian bishops had admitted those Marcellians to sacramental fellowship [Col. 0149A] after they had, as Epiphanius says [Note: [Col. 0149D] *Heresies* 72, p. 843.], produced letters of communion with Athanasius and had proved themselves outstandingly Catholic. Basil was disturbed by this action, both because Marcellus and his followers were commonly considered heretics and because a few bishops, without consulting all the rest, had settled a matter which they ought not even to have undertaken by themselves. Therefore, in Letter 265, he complained sharply and asked them to inform him under what conditions they had been admitted to communion.

Accordingly, he did not yet know that excellent Confession of Faith which they had submitted to Athanasius in the name of Marcellus himself, and which had caused them to be considered Catholics by Athanasius and the other bishops then assembled and, by that testimony published by Montfaucon, to be declared such. No certain document establishes whether the exiled bishops replied to Basil, or what they replied. Yet very weighty conjecture leads me to believe that by letters sent to him they both cleared themselves and vindicated the Marcellians from the charge of heresy. For Basil, writing to Peter of Alexandria on this very matter in Letter 266, is by no means opposed to receiving them into communion; he wishes only that they be received in such a way that neither he nor the other bishops agreeing with him may seem to have gone over to the Marcellians, but rather that the Marcellians themselves may seem never to have departed from the Church. Thus, to use Zaccagni’s interpretation [Note: [Col. 0149D] Preface to *Vet. Mon.*, ch. 30.], “the malicious calumny concerning the charge of heresy, spread everywhere, may be removed through our reception of them, and we may no longer have cause for shame because we have followed their party.” If, then, [Col. 0149C] the Marcellians, as Basil says, had always been in the body of the Church, how could Basil himself, when writing this, have believed Marcellus—whom they followed and in whose name they held their assemblies—to have been cut off from the Church?

It appears, therefore, that, having then been better informed, he withdrew from his former opinion and wished only to take care that, if Marcellus’s followers were admitted to communion without inquiry, neither he nor the other Catholic bishops should lose anything of the excellent reputation which they deservedly enjoyed, on account of the widespread and established calumny against them. How wise Basil’s policy was is clear from the case of Gregory of Nyssa. Because he had joined the same Marcellians in sacramental communion, he was accused both of their heresy and of violating the canons, and had to clear himself by two apologies, [Col. 0149D] of which only the latter survives, in the letter to the Sebastenians published by Zaccagni. Regarding the canons, he says that he had not of his own accord undertaken so weighty a matter, nor done anything without inquiry and necessary deliberation; rather, at the urging of orthodox brethren and fellow ministers in the East that the affair of these men be considered, and with their approval of what he had done, he had carried everything through. Then, to remove every bad opinion concerning himself and his faith, he adds a most explicit profession of faith.

Zaccagni himself thinks that this letter of Gregory of Nyssa to the Sebastenians [Col. 0150A] was written in the year 377. At least no one will deny that it was written while Eustathius was still alive and before Peter, Basil’s brother, had been appointed bishop. For by the Sebastenians to whom it is addressed we must understand not all the inhabitants of that place, but only those Catholic clerics who, not long before, had withdrawn from communion with Eustathius when he had revealed himself to be an Arian; they are mentioned in Basil’s Letters 138 and 237 of the recent edition. Therefore, if Eustathius had departed both from life and from that see by at least the year 380, since Peter, Basil’s brother and bishop of Sebaste, was present at the Council of Constantinople convened near the beginning of the following year, the letter must have been written either while Basil himself was still alive or certainly not long after his death.

Among the bishops whom Gregory had as advisers urging him to handle the Marcellians’ case, and afterward as approvers and imitators of what he had done and determined, I for my part do not think Basil himself—Gregory’s brother and almost his teacher—should be excluded. This being so, it may readily be inferred that Basil had no right to accuse Damasus and the Roman See for never having considered or declared Marcellus expelled from the Church. It may further have happened that his great zeal for religion, characteristic of that most holy bishop, was somewhat increased by his affection for Meletius and his disposition wholly opposed to Paulinus, whose party Marcellus followed.

# CHAPTER VII. 372, THE SEVENTH YEAR OF DAMASUS; CONSULS MODESTUS AND ARINTHEUS

I. Dorotheus, deacon of Antioch, comes to Rome with letters to Damasus written by the Eastern bishops; having completed his business, he returns East with Sabinus, deacon of the Church of Milan, who brings letters in Damasus’s name to Athanasius and the Easterners. II. Sozomen is compared with these matters and examined. III. Sabinus returns to the West with Basil’s letters to Damasus and the Westerners; these are elucidated and restored to their proper time. IV. On Law 3 of the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*, and, on that occasion, on the Venustiani, who are mentioned in the *Predestined*.

[Col. 0150C]

I. Dorotheus the deacon set out for Rome with letters from Athanasius and Basil about the end of the preceding [Col. 0150D] year [Note: [Col. 0150D] See D. Maran, *Life of Basil*, ch. 17.]; consequently, he could scarcely have arrived there before the year upon which we are now entering. We have said that Basil asked three things of Damasus: first, that he send visitors into the East; second, that those whom he would send as envoys by his authority should be endowed with a gentle disposition, firmness in conducting affairs, and freedom from party spirit, so that they might more readily bring all the Antiochenes over to the one Meletius, as he desired; third, that they bring with them the decrees issued after the Council of Rimini, so that it might be publicly evident that it had been declared invalid.

Damasus, therefore, complied with Basil’s—and perhaps also Athanasius’s—[Col. 0151A] advice. He sent to the Easterners Sabinus, deacon of the Church of Milan and, as it seems, afterwards bishop of Piacenza; and he gave him to convey the proceedings of the synod held before him two years earlier, together with the letter then written to the Illyrians. Hence this synod bears, from Holstenius, the following title:

> Copy of the synod held at Rome of ninety-three bishops, by imperial rescript: Damasus, Valerianus, Vitalianus, Aufidius, Pacianus, Victor, Priscus, Innocentius, Abundius, Theodolus, and the rest who assembled in the city of Rome to hear the case of Auxentius and expound the faith, to the Catholic bishops established throughout the East: greeting in the Lord.

And at the end the following clause is found appended:

> I, Sabinus, deacon of Milan, have supplied this copy from the original, namely from the proceedings previously sent to the bishops of Illyricum.

Damasus may perhaps have known this Sabinus, deacon of the Church of Milan, well on the occasion of the synod previously convened against Auxentius. For he could have attended it either with Eusebius of Vercelli, who in the meantime was caring for the Catholics of the Church of Milan, or with Victor, whom we read in Ughelli to have presided over Piacenza at this period.

If, then, the case of Meletius be excepted, concerning which nothing is known to have been decided at that time, you see that Damasus complied with Basil in all the rest. For he sent both an envoy to the Easterners and the proceedings of the synod held by himself, by which it could be evident that the Council of Rimini had been utterly overturned and abrogated by him. Moreover, he did this by his own authority, precisely as Basil had advised ought to be done [Col. 0151C]. Hence I cannot approve those who think that Dorotheus came to Rome near the end of the preceding year, while the synod which condemned Auxentius was still assembled or had been dissolved shortly before his arrival, and then, after matters were swiftly completed, departed again with Sabinus, who delivered letters to Athanasius in Alexandria about Easter of this year.

For whatever the date when that deacon came to Rome and left it with Sabinus—which point I regard as well established—if some synod was then being held at Rome, what reason is there why Damasus gave Sabinus to carry, not a letter to the Easterners from that very synod, but merely a copy of the letter previously written to the Illyrians? Or were the affairs of the Westerners better known to Sozomen and Theodoret [Col. 0151D] than to the Easterners, so that they read the synodical letter written to the Illyrians, while the letter asserted to have been brought to the Easterners at the same time remained unknown to them? But, they say, the deacon Sabinus must have travelled through Illyricum, since he delivered to Basil letters from the bishops of those regions; Basil consequently says that he replied to them privately [Note: [Col. 0151D] “Having received the deacon Sabinus, sent by them [the Westerners], we wrote to the Illyrians and to the bishops of Italy and Gaul, and to certain others who had written to us privately.” Ep. 89, to Meletius.]. But for what other reason could he have entered those regions than to carry first to them the synodical letter of the Roman Council, and then [Col. 0152A] to go on to Athanasius and Basil in the East?

For my part, I would not readily admit that this deacon arranged his route through Illyricum. First, those travelling by land had to fear the Arians, by whom the churches were for the most part occupied. Secondly, if he travelled on foot with Dorotheus, why did he not go directly to Basil at Caesarea, the first resting place from a long journey and toil, but turn aside to Athanasius and Alexandria? Nor does Basil suggest anything else when he mentions the letters received from the Illyrian bishops. We learn clearly who they were from the following Letter 91, in which mention is made of a certain Valerian of Aquileia, whom Basil, deceived by geographical proximity, calls a bishop of Illyricum. It could therefore easily have happened that Sabinus, proceeding East by Damasus’s order, went to Aquileia to Valerian himself—who was named second after Damasus in the copy of the synodical letter being carried to the Easterners and presided over the Church of a great Western city—or for some other reason. From there, however, he could easily have sailed to Alexandria from some port of Dalmatia or Istria. Thus there is no need, for this reason, to remove from the year to which we have assigned it the first synod under Damasus, from which this letter survives.

Sabinus, then, arrived at Alexandria with the deacon Dorotheus in the first months of this year [Note: [Col. 0152D] *Life of Basil*, ch. 22, no. 3.]. He brought letters from Damasus to Athanasius, who also forwarded to Basil the items addressed to him: namely, the synodical letter of the Roman Council, which Basil calls that of the Westerners, and letters besides from certain bishops in Gaul and from Valerian of Aquileia. Whether Damasus added private letters written to Basil himself beyond that synodical letter, I would not venture to assert. Why, indeed, would Basil not have listed them among the other letters of that kind which he says he received [Note: [Col. 0152D] See Ep. 89.], when the Roman bishop ought to have been placed and mentioned first?

But a different conclusion seems necessary concerning Athanasius: either because Sabinus ought not to have been sent to him without letters, or because he seems to have been known and familiar to Damasus, or because, when Basil wrote the letters to Damasus which we have examined, Athanasius had added his own at Basil’s request, or finally because it can scarcely be otherwise than that some memorandum necessary for the affairs then being conducted was sent to him as well [Col. 0152D]. Hence this Milanese deacon remained for some time with Athanasius and then went to Caesarea to Basil. Basil accordingly says that he derived some consolation from the letters of the Westerners, as being evidence of their sound faith and their unshaken agreement in maintaining it; and he adds that this consolation was afterwards increased by the arrival of the deacon Sabinus [Note: [Col. 0152D] Ep. 90.].

II. Sozomen, I think, plainly refers to these synodical letters, first addressed and sent to the Illyrians and then to the Easterners, when he says that the controversy long under discussion—whether the Holy Spirit ought to be considered consubstantial with the Father and the Son—was brought to rest after it had been settled and determined by the judgment of the Roman Church, as soon as the Roman bishop, having been informed of it, wrote to the Churches of the East that, together with the Western priests and bishops, they should hold the Trinity to be consubstantial and equal in glory [Note: [Col. 0153D] Sozomen, Book VI, ch. 22.]. This is indeed a most weighty argument for the supreme and irreformable judgment of the Roman pontiffs in deciding matters of faith [Note: [Col. 0153D] See Orsi, vol. I, Book I, ch. 8, art. 1.].

Some attribute this action to Liberius because Sozomen subsequently relates his death and the election of Damasus in the following chapter. But in Sozomen one often seeks in vain for the order of events and dates [Col. 0153B], and it is altogether clear that it has been inverted especially in this passage. The question of the divinity of the Holy Spirit began to be debated about twelve years earlier. But when the Macedonians, harassed by the Arians and Valens, had outwardly joined themselves to the Catholics, that heresy seemed then rather to hide in darkness than to be extinguished. Thus Liberius did not demand from the three envoys of the Synod of Lampsacus that they openly profess the divinity of the Holy Spirit, but was content with the Nicene faith. It began, therefore, to raise its head again after the thirty-four bishops, by seceding from the others, had disturbed matters almost settled in the Synod of Tyana [Note: [Col. 0153D] See *Life of Basil*, ch. 18.]. It was necessary, then, that Damasus should proscribe by his judgment the heresy once more creeping forth and openly emerging, and this should accordingly be attributed to him—though Sozomen seems, as Constantius says, to have assigned it wrongly to the time of Liberius [Col. 0153C].

How certain this is will readily be perceived by one who compares Damasus’s letters with what Sozomen writes on this matter, and also with what the Emperor Valentinian replied to the Asian bishops and Basil to the Westerners after the letters had been received from Sabinus. For what Sozomen indicates was then written by the Roman bishop to the Churches of the East is found quite clearly in these letters of Damasus. After the pontiff had said that the Council of Nicaea defined that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must be believed to be of one Godhead, one power, one form, and one substance, he adds:

> Let therefore the judgment of your Charity harmonize with all the priests of God; and you ought, by reciprocal letters of your Holiness, to confirm that, as we trust you to be established and strengthened in this faith, so we also think rightly with you.

Thus Valentinian, professing to follow this Roman synod, says to the Asian bishops: “For our part, we hold the same opinion as the synods recently held both at Rome and in Gaul: that the one and same substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exists in three persons.” And the bishops of the Illyrian synod pronounce an anathema upon those who do not hold and proclaim the Trinity to be consubstantial.

[Col. 0154A] III. But to return to the road, Basil, having received the letters, thought that he should answer by three letters [Note: [Col. 0154D] See Epp. 89, 90, 91, 92.]. The first was addressed to the “Most holy brethren, the Western bishops”; the second to Valerian of Aquileia; and the third to the Italians and Gauls. But the letter addressed to the Westerners and composed in Basil’s private name belongs to the Italians and Gauls; while the one entitled “To the Italians and Gauls,” written in the common name of the other Easterners, belongs to the Westerners and to Damasus. Through error they were inscribed otherwise than they ought to have been [Note: [Col. 0154D] *Life of Basil*, ch. 22, nos. 4–5.]. All were handed over to Sabinus, who is also mentioned in them, when he was then returning to the West, for delivery.

Both commend and embrace the decisions of that Roman synod and the letter written by it. But when Basil writes to the Italians and Gauls [Col. 0154B], he asks for their prayers and aid, so that among the Easterners too “that good proclamation of the Fathers” may be freely promulgated, overthrowing Arius’s infamous heresy while building up the Churches in sound doctrine, “in which we confess the Son consubstantial with the Father, and the Holy Spirit is at once numbered and worshipped with equal honor”; and so that “the freedom which the Lord has given you for the truth, and the glorying in the confession of the divine and saving Trinity, may be granted also to us through your prayers and your assistance.”

But when, in the common name, he addresses the Westerners—that is, Damasus and the other bishops assembled under him—he asks for Damasus’s exertion and authority. He wishes that not one or two, as before, but several from the body of bishops be sent as envoys to the East without delay, because speed is required to save those who remain; and he seeks the presence of many brethren, “that they may fill out the number of a synod,” so that they may possess weight and authority for correcting affairs not only from the dignity and majesty of those who sent them but also from their own number; so that they may restore the faith written by our Fathers at Nicaea, proscribe heresy, and speak words of peace to the Churches, bringing those who think alike into concord. The last points concern the case of Meletius and the Antiochenes, which Basil once more wishes, though rather obscurely, to commend to Damasus. Finally, he concludes the letter with these words:

> For it is truly worthy of praise that the Lord has granted to your piety the ability to discern the spurious from the genuine and pure, and to proclaim without any dissimulation the faith of the Fathers—a faith which we also have received and recognized as marked with apostolic seals; and we assent to it, as also to all the other things canonically and lawfully determined in the synodical writing.

After carefully weighing these words of Basil, the most eminent Joseph Augustine Orsi rightly concludes again that, in Basil’s judgment, the Roman pontiff’s decision is supreme and irreformable. For when the letter of the Roman synod annulling Rimini had been delivered, Basil immediately received it and assented to it without hesitation; he judged that the Council of Rimini could have no force when the Roman [Col. 0155A] pontiff had determined and judged synodically, canonically, and lawfully [Note: [Col. 0155D] Vol. II, Book II, ch. 3, art. 1.].

Moreover, anyone who compares Basil’s letters with those which Athanasius wrote to the Africans and to Epictetus will readily infer that all were written at nearly one and the same time: namely, after the receipt of the letter brought by Sabinus from Damasus and the other bishops who had assembled at his council. Hence each praises the large attendance at that council and congratulates Damasus upon the harmony of the Westerners in preserving the Catholic faith. Athanasius also wrote that he wondered why Auxentius, already condemned and deposed and guilty of so many crimes, continued, as we have seen, to oppress the Church of Milan—having evidently then been informed of this matter by Sabinus, deacon of that same Church.

[Col. 0155B] The year in which this second letter to Damasus was written is readily known from two indications: it bears the name of Meletius of Antioch and that of Anthimus of Tyana. The one had not yet been driven from the see of Antioch, which happened this year after Valens came to Antioch; with the other no quarrel had yet arisen for Basil over the division of Cappadocia into two provinces, which likewise occurred in this very year, though perhaps later than some think. Sabinus therefore returned to Damasus at this same time with these letters written by Basil in the name of the other Easterners, and explained to him the state in which matters then stood both in the Eastern Church as a whole and in the Church of Antioch.

Baronius, therefore, was mistaken in thinking that the letters written by Basil to Damasus in this year [Col. 0155C] were those addressed to the Maritime bishops, and in supposing that Basil’s brother Peter brought them to Rome. For anyone who reads them attentively will readily judge that they were sent to bishops of some province not far from Basil, who, led by the calumnies of heretics, had separated themselves from his brotherly communion, and whom he desires to reconcile to himself because of his outstanding charity. The recent editor of Basil’s letters, following other careful critics, considers those Maritime bishops to have been certain bishops of the Pontic diocese [Note: [Col. 0155D] *Life of Basil*, ch. 33.]. I readily agree, because Basil addresses them in such a manner as both to show his singular affection toward them and to preserve a certain regard for his own authority and standing in relation to them—an epistolary manner which would certainly not have befitted a bishop addressing Damasus.

[Col. 0155D] IV. In this year Valentinian issued a law addressed to Ampelius, Prefect of the City, against the Manichaeans. [Note: [Col. 0155D] Cod. Theod., bk. 3, *On Heretics*.] Baronius believes that the cause of this law was the factions and disturbances which this polluted sect often stirred up and by which the City itself was afflicted; he cites the descriptions of them given by Augustine in several passages. [Col. 0156A] Gothofredus and Pagius by no means approve this statement of Baronius, though without any sound reason. For their assertion that what Augustine relates concerning the morals of the Manichaeans—long after the law was issued—has nothing in common with that law is certainly false. Augustine does not relate these things as having occurred, so to speak, in his presence, but as having occurred long before he himself came to Rome. Or did those domestic tumults, by which the peace of the City could suffer harm—having been stirred up long before and often—seem capable of being of no concern to the emperor or to the Prefect of the City, so that provision should at last be made against them? What, moreover, if we say that the law was enacted at the urging of Damasus, just as Gothofredus thinks that Law 20, [Col. 0156B] under the same title, was enacted against the same Manichaeans at the urging of Siricius? Hear then why I attribute this one to Damasus.

Praedestinatus asserts that Damasus condemned the Paternian heretics when they had been detected in their crime, and reported this to Valentinian the Elder, citing these words of his: “We wish Your Piety to know that the Venustiani, detected in a most shameful crime, have been condemned by the Apostolic See.” [Note: [Col. 0155D] *Haer.* 85.] He then adds that a law was subsequently issued against them, providing that wherever they were found they should be punished by the avenging sword; this is ordained in the same Law 3, *On Heretics*. It is established from Augustine that the Venustiani were also called Paternians; but no one, so far as I know, has explained why each of these names was applied to them. For what the Calvinist Daneus says—that they were called Paternians from Paternus—while admitting that we do not know that man’s country, age, and other matters relevant to the question—is worth nothing; and the same is true of his wish to derive Venustiani from Venus. [Note: [Col. 0155D] On ch. 85 of Augustine’s *On Heresies*.]

As the matter stands, the Venustiani must have been some sect drawn from the dregs of Manichaeism: both because they believed the lower parts of the body to have been made by the devil, and because they lived most impurely—plain marks of Manichaeism. This is clear from Augustine, [Note: [Col. 0155D] *Against Julian*, bk. V, no. 26, BB edition.] who answered Julian as follows:

> “But the Paternians, you say—”

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Marius Victorinus wrote a tract, published by Sirmond in vol. I of his works, p. 244, Venice edition, against Justin the Manichaean, whom he calls a Roman. I therefore conjecture that he was the leader of this shameful sect; for why should Victorinus attack him in particular rather than the others? [Col. 0156D] Moreover, that he was a man from these dregs of the Manichaeans is inferred from these words of Victorinus himself: “May you confess God Almighty as your Creator, so that you may truly be the temple of God . . . For if we are not the temple of God, neither is his Spirit in us; if we are his, we are his in both respects, soul and body; and that saying, uttered by a holy mouth, is true and catholic: God, all in all.” What, then, if copyists, through an easy error, turned those heretics, then called Justiniani after that man, into Venustiani? Some call that Manichaean Justus.]

> “The same Venustian heretics, akin to the Manichaeans, say that from the loins down to the feet the devil made the human body, but that God set the upper parts, as it were, upon some base. They further add that nothing is required of human effort except that the soul—which they say dwells in the stomach and head—be kept clean; but they say that the genital region, even if smeared with the filth of every shameful act, is no concern of theirs. . . . [Col. 0156D] What I set forth in my book is far removed from these Paternians, or Venustiani. In accordance with the catholic faith, I ascribe the whole human being—that is, the whole soul and the whole body—to God, the supreme and true Creator; but I say that the devil did not create human nature, or any part of it, but [Col. 0157A] corrupted it. . . .
