And if that is insufficient, behold, I condemn and anathematize the opinions which you said the Paternians and Venustiani hold; I add the Manichaeans as well.”

Thus Valentinian restrained the Venustiani condemned by Damasus through a general law enacted against the Manichaeans, a designation which embraced every pestilential shoot from that infected root. Hence Gotfridus of Viterbo [Note: [Col. 0157D] In the *Chronicle*, part XVI.] wrote that this pontiff detested the Manichaeans. Damasus’s example was afterward followed by Siricius and Leo the Great; both directly and through the emperors, they expelled this infamous kind from not merely the body of the Church but even that of the Commonwealth.

## CHAPTER VIII. 373, THE EIGHTH YEAR OF DAMASUS; VALENTINIAN AUGUSTUS IV AND VALENS AUGUSTUS IV, CONSULS

I. Damasus arranges for letters brought by Sabinus to be returned to Basil through Evagrius of Antioch, and for others to be written according to the formula prescribed at Rome: in what year Evagrius returned to the East. II. Why Basil’s letters did not please Damasus, and what he seems to have wanted in them. III. What were the views of Basil himself and of Eusebius of Samosata, whom Basil had consulted, regarding the matters then requested by Evagrius. IV. On the death of Athanasius, the election of Peter of Alexandria, and his flight to the City.

[Col. 0157B]

### I.

The letters which Sabinus had brought back to the West, written by Basil in the common name of the Easterners, did not please Damasus. This is clear from Basil’s own letter to Eusebius of Samosata, written in this year, [Col. 0157C] which says:

> “The presbyter Evagrius, son of Pompeianus of Antioch, who once went to the West with the blessed Eusebius, has now come from Rome, asking us for a letter containing word for word the very things written by them (while he brought ours back to us, since they did not please those more exacting men), and that some embassy be promptly sent through men of outstanding rank, so that they may have an honourable occasion for visiting us.” [Note: [Col. 0157D] Epistle 138, otherwise 8.]

Some infer from this passage that Evagrius visited Basil when, returning from the West and accompanying Jerome, he was travelling through Cappadocia, before he returned to Antioch, whence he had departed with Eusebius of Vercelli. But this opinion can scarcely be sustained. For if Evagrius brought back and delivered to Basil the letters Basil had sent to Rome through Sabinus, and if Sabinus, already far advanced into the preceding year, had scarcely set out from the East on his return to Damasus, it cannot be that Evagrius is said to have come from Rome only then—namely, in this year, when Basil saw him.

For Jerome, whom Evagrius is believed to have accompanied, was in the East before Rufinus, as Jerome himself proves in writing to Rufinus; [Note: [Col. 0157D] Epistle 3, Verona edition.] and Rufinus had left for the East in 371 [Note: [Col. 0157D] Fontan., *On Aquileian Writers*, bk. IV, ch. I, no. 6; the brothers Ballerini, observations on Noris, bk. I, ch. 2; the learned Vallarsi, *Life of Jerome*, ch. 29.] and reached Alexandria in the following year. I am not unaware that Syria was the final [Col. 0158A] destination of Jerome’s journey; for in that letter to Rufinus he says: “As I wandered uncertainly in my pilgrimage, after Thrace, Pontus, Bithynia, the whole journey through Galatia and Cappadocia, and the burning heat of Cilician soil had worn me down, Syria came before me like the most faithful harbour for a shipwrecked man.” [Note: [Col. 0157D] Epistle 3, Verona edition, vol. I.] But if he went east in 370 or the following year, what time are we to assign to completing that entire journey? Could he not have arrived at Antioch near the end of 371, or at least in the following year?

But Evagrius was living in that city before Jerome withdrew to his solitude. Thus Jerome himself writes to the monk Florentius concerning himself: “Evagrius the presbyter often rebuked, in my presence, the teacher of your boy, concerning whom you deigned to write, while I was still at Antioch.” [Note: [Col. 0158D] Epistle 5, Verona edition, and Preface to Obadiah.] Moreover, it must be observed [Col. 0158B] that this letter was certainly written before Rufinus reached Alexandria, as its mere reading plainly shows. Now if Melania, whose companion on the spiritual path Rufinus was, remained in Egypt only six months; [Note: [Col. 0158D] Palladius, *Lausiac History*, ch. 117.] if, further, she spent part of that time under Athanasius, from whom she received the celebrated sheepskin, [Note: [Col. 0158D] Palladius, *Paradise of the Fathers*, ch. 6.] and part under the beginning of the persecution of Peter, Athanasius’s successor, stirred up by the Arians—a persecution in which she shared [Note: [Col. 0158D] Rufinus, bk. XI, chs. 2–3; St Paulinus of Nola, Epistle 29, Verona edition.]—she could not have travelled through the monasteries of Egypt except during one or two months only of that persecution, and when that period elapsed she must have set out toward Jerusalem.

But Jerome was already enjoying his solitude, as his letter to Rufinus makes clear; [Note: [Col. 0158D] Epistle 3, Verona edition.] how, then, could he at that time have travelled through Cappadocia with Evagrius? How, further, can Evagrius—who had already established his residence at Antioch and had retained Jerome as his guest for at least some months before Jerome withdrew to the desert—be said to have come from Rome when he approached Basil, namely, in this year? It is therefore certain, fixed, and settled, unless I am mistaken, that Evagrius undertook this journey to Basil solely at the instruction and command of Damasus. When Basil wrote that he had then come from Rome, he either wrote in ignorance, or understood by “Rome” the Roman bishop Damasus, by whom Evagrius had been sent; or else τὸ νῦν (“now”) has the same force as the particle οὖν (“therefore”), as often happens, and as the proper and coherent sequence of the argument seems to require here. For Evagrius had long before established himself at Antioch, receiving letters from friends in the West and in turn distributing them.

[Col. 0158D]

### II.

But, to return to the path: why Damasus requested an embassy composed of men eminent in rank is by no means obscure. In this way the authority of the proceedings would be greater before everyone; moreover, the example of the Synod of Lampsacus, which had sent its leading bishops as envoys to Liberius, was recent. Since he wished it to be sent promptly, [Col. 0159A] this reveals his zeal for the catholic religion and for unity. Consequently, it was not the matter itself proposed by Basil that displeased him, but perhaps the manner in which Basil judged it should be carried out.

Thus Evagrius, to whom Damasus, while he remained at Antioch and was his intimate friend, had himself sent a memorandum concerning what was to be done and written, asked Basil that another letter should be prepared containing what the Roman pontiff had dictated. But what was this that displeased Damasus, and what did he wish expressed in the other letter? In my view, if conjecture is permitted, Damasus was displeased by Basil’s excessive attachment to Meletius, which Basil had openly explained to Athanasius, likewise to Dorotheus, and to Sabinus himself as he was returning to the West. For he saw that this man’s dignity and influence were so great that, unless Basil for a time withdrew from the opinion he had already adopted, he might obstruct measures which Damasus himself had perhaps devised to restore unity and peace to the Church of Antioch. Therefore he wished Basil to write again, setting out what Damasus himself had prescribed—namely, what he understood to be suited to attaining that end more readily—and that men distinguished in rank should be sent with the letters.

This, unless I am mistaken, is not obscurely gathered from what Evagrius wrote to Basil after leaving him and returning to Antioch. First, he earnestly praises peace and unity and condemns schisms and divisions; next, he urges Basil to remove them from the Church of Antioch and to establish peace among the orthodox, since Basil was especially suited to accomplish this. But because some plan for making peace had perhaps been proposed by Evagrius which neither Basil, owing to his attachment to Meletius, nor Meletius, owing to his dignity, believed that he could accept, Basil replies that he will write to Meletius on the subject, then adds:

> “Yet I expect nothing of consequence to result from letters, considering both the man’s careful manner of proceeding and the nature of letters themselves; for discourse transmitted is not ordinarily suited to persuasion with clarity. Much must be said, much heard in return, objections must be answered, and supporting points introduced; none of which can be done by lifeless, inanimate discourse thrown upon paper. Yet I shall not hesitate to write what I have already said.” [Note: [Col. 0159D] Epistle 156, otherwise 342.]

The matter therefore concerned something highly disagreeable to Meletius, and one which could scarcely be persuaded upon him except with difficulty and much effort. Since Evagrius well knew that Basil was not favourably disposed toward Paulinus, toward whom Damasus inclined, and had perhaps reproached him for this as unfitted to be a future mediator of peace, Basil adds:

> “But know, brother most truly devout and most dear to us, that by God’s grace I have no private contention with anyone. For I do not recall ever anxiously investigating the crimes to which any person is liable, or is said to be liable. You should therefore regard my opinion as that of a man who can do nothing from partiality, nor has been prejudiced by accusations against anyone.” [Col. 0160A]

Meanwhile, it may be inferred from this that Damasus had granted communion to neither Meletius nor Paulinus up to this point, but wished to keep the matter open, lest, by preferring one party of the Church of Antioch, he offend the other and thus exclude every hope of reconciliation. It is not credible that Evagrius would have wished to undertake a matter of such consequence without Damasus’s instruction and confidential commission. Add to this that Evagrius himself, who had previously promised Basil in person that he would communicate with the orthodox party of Meletius, did not keep his promise as soon as he returned to Antioch. Would he have promised communion with Meletius if Damasus had already entered into communion with Paulinus?

[Col. 0160B]

### III.

The reason, therefore, why Basil’s letters delivered through Sabinus did not please Damasus, and why Damasus requested a renewed and more honourable embassy, seems to have been no other than his ardent desire to reconcile the orthodox of the Church of Antioch, and hence to draw Basil away from every partisan attachment, so as to use him as an ally rather than an adversary. To this end he sent Evagrius to sound out Basil’s disposition.

Basil, however, deferred his answer to Evagrius until he could first consult Eusebius of Samosata in person. Prevented from doing so by a long illness, he asks, in the letter mentioned at the beginning, what Eusebius thinks should be decided concerning the matters proposed by that presbyter.

Eusebius seems to have approved Evagrius’s proposal at least in part. Basil writes to Meletius, then in exile, that he had received letters from the bishop of Samosata ordering that another letter be written to the Westerners concerning certain ecclesiastical matters and further expressing Eusebius’s wish that Basil compose a letter to be subscribed afterward by all who were in communion. [Col. 0160C] But Basil declines this responsibility and refers it back to Meletius himself. He therefore sends him, through the most holy other presbyter of the Church of Antioch belonging to Meletius’s party, an outline of the matters that Eusebius thought should be written. He promises, however, both to subscribe it himself and to ensure that the others subscribe, so that the man who was to go to the West might depart with the subscriptions of all. [Note: [Col. 0159D] Epistle 120, otherwise 58.]

He repeats the same in another letter to the same Meletius, written after [Col. 0160D] learning that this same most holy man was with him. [Note: [Col. 0160D] Epistle 129.] But while Basil, Eusebius, and Meletius deliberated over sending this embassy, the whole year elapsed, and no one was sent to Rome. Accordingly, Basil himself writes to Eusebius, who was again pressing for the embassy:

> “To send someone to the West is altogether impossible for me, since I have no one suitable for this service. But if any of the brethren who are with you should be willing to undertake labour for the Churches’ sake, he undoubtedly knows to whom he must go, for what purpose, with whose letters he must be furnished, and of what kind they must be. For, casting my eyes over the world, [Col. 0161A] I see with myself no one.” [Note: [Col. 0161D] Epistle 156.]

These statements certainly prove that no embassy from the Easterners was sent to Damasus in this year, although one was otherwise being prepared. [Note: [Col. 0161D] See Maran, *Life of Basil*, ch. 28, no. 6.]

### IV.

Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, departed to the world above in the consulship of Valentinian and Valens for the fourth time, Pachomius VIII—that is, on 3 May 373. Learned men long disputed the year of his death; but after the learned Maffei published that ancient and almost contemporary monument which recounts nearly the whole of Athanasius’s life in brief—and thereby bound scholars to him by this benefit, among others—the matter was settled. [Note: [Col. 0161D] See the learned brothers Ballerini, observations on Noris, bk. I, ch. 2.]

Peter succeeded Athanasius amid the great applause of the Church. He immediately informed Damasus, according to received custom, both of his ordination and of the calamity inflicted upon the Christian people by Palladius, [Col. 0161B] the pagan prefect. In turn, Damasus sent the customary letters of communion and also of consolation through a deacon of the city of Rome whose name Peter of Alexandria does not mention, although it was certainly most worthy of transmission to posterity. For the Alexandrian bishop writes in the encyclical letter quoted by Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0161D] Bk. IV, ch. 22.] that this blessed deacon was led away by executioners with his hands bound behind his back, like some notorious criminal; tortured with the torments inflicted on murderers; struck for a long time on the neck with stones and lead-weighted scourges; ordered to embark with very many other confessors; marked on the forehead with the sign of the divine cross; deprived of every care and consolation; and condemned to the mines.

To this dreadful persecution stirred up by Palladius against [Col. 0161C] the Church of Alexandria, the Arians added a further measure. For Euzoius, the Arian pseudo-bishop of Antioch, and the *comes sacrarum largitionum*, sent by Valens after they heard of Athanasius’s death in order to hand the churches over to Lucius, committed Peter of Alexandria to prison. Having escaped from it, however, he boarded a ship and went to the bishop of the city of Rome. [Note: [Col. 0161D] See Socrates, bk. IV, ch. 21; Sozomen, bk. VI, ch. 19.] Valesius and Pagius think that a fairly long time elapsed between Peter’s ordination and his flight, [Note: [Col. 0161D] Valesius, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. IV, ch. 22; Pagius on the year 372, no. 22.] such that he could scarcely have come to the City in that same year. Tillemont observes that this opinion of Valesius lacks the testimony of the ancients; I add that it is supported by no plausible reasoning either.

All these events could readily have been completed in three months, and Peter could have embarked in the fourth or fifth month after the persecution by the pagans and Arians, arriving at Rome in September or October. Therefore, during the first persecution stirred up by the pagan Palladius, Peter did not yield or abandon the Church. But after Euzoius, together with the *comes sacrarum [Col. 0162A] largitionum*, placed Lucius upon the throne, he then followed Athanasius’s example and took refuge at the Apostolic See. For this reason Boniface rightly counts him among those who used the protection of an appeal to the Roman pontiff in order to preserve their right intact and secure. [Note: [Col. 0161D] Boniface to Rufus of Thessalonica, Epistle 15, in Coustant. [Col. 0162D] See Lupus, *On Roman Appeals*, dissertation 1, ch. 4.] Hence the synodical catalogue writes that Lucius the robber was marked with an anathema by Damasus in the synod of which I shall speak shortly.

Moreover, though other documents are lacking to show the affection with which Damasus received Peter and kept him with himself, we may easily infer it from what Nazianzen writes: “Peter displayed before the Roman Church bloodstained garments for the dead, in order to obtain assistance—as indeed we know that he obtained it. For it often happens that one who excels in resources and power is most inclined to relieve the misery of the weak and afflicted, and in an impulse of spontaneous goodwill attaches himself to one whose dignity has been diminished.” [Note: [Col. 0162D] Oration in Praise of Hieron. (abbreviation as in the source; uncertain.)]

## CHAPTER IX. 374, THE NINTH YEAR OF DAMASUS; GRATIAN AUGUSTUS III AND FLAVIUS EQUITIUS, CONSULS

I. Basil and the other Eastern bishops send Dorotheus, presbyter of Antioch, to Damasus with letters, which are presented and explained. II. A synod convened by Damasus, and its letters to the Easterners, brought back by Dorotheus upon his return; these are explained. III. The year of this synod is established. IV. Law 20 of the Theodosian Code, book XI, title 36, is considered. V. Simplicius, deputy prefect of the City, to whom the law is addressed; Theophanes, speaking of the Sabbatians; and the tract of Faustinus and Marcellinus are reconsidered.

[Col. 0162C]

### I.

Accordingly, since the authority of Eusebius of Samosata and Meletius had moved Basil to yield to the counsel of Evagrius of Antioch and again to send persons to the Westerners to carry letters and describe orally the calamities of the Eastern Church, Dorotheus, presbyter of Antioch, undertook the Roman journey in the name of those same Easterners. [Note: [Col. 0162D] He is, I think, the same man who, as deacon, brought Basil’s earlier letters to Rome in 371 and was afterward raised to the presbyterate. Thus Possidonius, deacon under Cyril of Alexandria and afterward presbyter, often carried letters to Celestine, Sixtus, and Leo. St Leo the Great, Epistle 81, Lyons edition.] This is clear from Basil’s Epistles 242 and 243, [Note: [Col. 0162D] Otherwise 50 and 82.] of which the former is addressed to the Westerners—a designation under which we know that the Roman pontiff is principally intended—and the latter to the bishops of Italy and Gaul.

For since Evagrius’s view had been that several men, distinguished in rank, should be sent as envoys to Rome, and since Basil and the most holy bishops of his party were not unaware of this, they give the weightiest reason why they had not done so, in these words:

> “For these reasons, more of us should have hastened to your dignity, and each should have become the narrator of his own circumstances. But let this very fact now be an indication to you [Col. 0163A] of the affliction in which we live: we have not even the means to undertake a journey. For if anyone should be absent even for a very brief time, he will leave the peoples entrusted to those who lie in wait.” [Note: [Col. 0163D] Epistle 243, no. 5.]

Can there be a clearer allusion to Evagrius’s proposal? Since Evagrius had advised Basil about sending this embassy in the preceding year, are we to defer these letters, which refer to it, to 376, as has recently seemed good to a certain learned man? After Basil had explained to the Italian and Gallic bishops this very serious reason why several men of high rank had not been sent, he adds:

> “We have sent one in the stead of many, our most devout and beloved brother and fellow presbyter Dorotheus. By his own account he can supply whatever escaped our letters, since he has learned everything accurately and is a defender of the right faith. Receive him in peace, and send him back quickly, bringing us glad news of your zeal in helping the brethren.”

In the other letter—addressed to the Westerners, that is, to Damasus their leader—which was composed in a briefer and more weighty style, the Easterners again request assistance long expected from the Westerners. Having set forth the storms by which the Catholics were afflicted, they say: “We beseech you, even now at last, to stretch out your hand to the Eastern Churches, now bent to their knees, and send men to remind them of the rewards reserved for evils suffered for Christ. For customary discourse does not produce as much as the voice of a stranger usually brings in consolation, especially when it comes from men everywhere known, by God’s grace, in the most excellent light.”

But beyond this reason they add another by which the Westerners should be more strongly moved. Although it is not stated in clear words, I do not doubt that it was described in the memorandum of matters to be explained by Dorotheus:

> “Among us there are some who, out of desire for glory and through that swelling pride which especially destroys Christian souls, have uttered novel expressions of certain persons; from these the Churches have been shaken and, like dislocated vessels, have received the flowing corruption of heresy. But you, most beloved and longed-for, should be physicians of the wounded and encouragers of the sound, restoring what is sick to health and urging what is sound toward piety.”

In this passage, however, I think Apollinarius is indicated under a concealed name and depicted in these colours, because his reputation at that time, if not unimpaired, was at least not entirely bad.

[Col. 0163D]

### II.

When these letters were delivered to Damasus by Dorotheus, he convened a synod. One fragment of it survives, which Holstenius brought to light and which we have placed in its proper location. By it all the heresies then rampant in the East were proscribed: namely, Sabellianism and Photinianism, Arianism or Eunomianism, the Pneumatomachians, and the Apollinarians. The last was nevertheless attacked only lightly and, as it were, with arms directed against a fleeing enemy, because it had not yet openly emerged.

Damasus says that all these heresies fell through the united agreement of the Western bishops, just as Jericho fell when the Israelites had raised their common cry. Since Basil had first written through Sabinus that the Westerners should determine with whom they ought to hold communion, and had later judged that they should be admonished again through the presbyter Dorotheus not to receive without examination the communions of those coming from the East, [Note: [Col. 0163D] Epistle 129.] Damasus therefore adds after that confession of faith: “This, dearest brethren, is our faith; whoever follows it is our participant: with such persons we share communion.” From this it may be observed that communion granted or refused by the Roman pontiff was everywhere regarded as law.

He then warned the Easterners not to neglect the canons in clerical ordinations, nor readily grant communion to those who violated them. He concludes the letter thus:

> “Moreover, as regards removing the injuries of your charity, our brother Dorotheus the presbyter does not fail to explain everything vividly, nor have our efforts, as he himself bears witness, been lacking.” [Col. 0164B]

These words show that Damasus and the synod had attempted some means by which they might assist the Easterners.

### III.

Why we say this synod was convened in the present year is, unless I am mistaken, evident and certain. Dorotheus, who had brought the Easterners’ letters to Rome, carried back with him the synodical decree and replies to the Easterners, as is clear from the words just quoted. We have proved that the Easterners’ letters were written at the beginning of this same year: first, because they contain an explicit allusion to matters discussed not long before between Evagrius and Basil; and second, because when the Easterners wrote them, they said that it was the [Col. 0164C] thirteenth year since the heretical war against the Catholics had arisen. If this is counted from the persecution begun after the Arian Council of Constantinople, it leads us altogether to this time; furthermore, all the other matters described in Epistles 242 and 243 agree remarkably with it. [Note: [Col. 0164D] See Tillemont, on Basil, note 67.]

For although under Julian and then Jovian the Catholic bishops had returned to their sees, the former so openly favoured the Arians that the affairs of the Catholics were scarcely better than under Constantius, while the latter died after only a few months of rule. Thus the persecution could scarcely appear to have been interrupted. But if we wish to count the thirteen years from Valens’s persecution, as the writer of Basil’s *Life* preferred, then, since it did not begin before 367, as Pagius proves, [Col. 0164D] or before 365, as others think, this chronological mark would bring us to 378 or 380—which is plainly false.

### IV.

I therefore think that Law 20 of the Theodosian Code, book XI, title 36, may be referred to this synod. By it Cecropius, condemned by a council of seventy bishops, is said to have appealed from that sentence to the Prefect of the City and to have been fined a monetary penalty by Valentinian. The law was issued in the consulship of Valentinian *nobilissimus puer* and Victor, that is, in 369, on 8 July. Yet it is addressed to Claudius, Prefect of the City, and Claudius’s urban prefecture belongs to 374, [Note: [Col. 0164D] Reinesius, Epistle 19, p. 45.] the year in which we say that the synod was held under Damasus. We must therefore say that an error entered into the consular date.

But if, as others prefer, the error lies in the address and Olybrius should be substituted for Claudius, Cecropius may appear to have been condemned by the first synod under Damasus, namely in 366. The law itself, addressed to the Prefect of the City, indicates fairly clearly that the very plausible conjecture of Baronius [Note: [Col. 0165D] Year 369.] and others is correct: namely, that Cecropius was deposed from the episcopate because he adhered to Ursinus. For the obstinacy and insolence of these factious men often made it necessary for the emperors and the urban magistrates to intervene in this matter, although this always happened to the detriment of the schismatics, as I have said and shall say again.

### V.

In this year Simplicius was appointed successor to Ursicinus as deputy prefect of the City. [Note: [Col. 0165D] Gothofredus, chronology for this year; Tillemont, on Valentinian I, art. 29.] Gratian mentions this Simplicius in a rescript to Aquilinus, deputy prefect, to be considered again in its proper place. He says that he had sent Simplicius an edict ordering that all who attempted impious assemblies by profaning religion should be expelled to the hundredth milestone from the City, where their stubborn frenzy, abandoned by its followers, would collapse to the ruin of the one man who alone persisted in error.

By these words of his rescript—sent at that time to Simplicius, deputy prefect of the City, and belonging to Valentinian’s reign—we must understand that all sects of rebaptizers are designated. For Valentinian the father had earlier allowed all others freedom to practise whatever they had embraced in their minds, with the exception of the rebaptizers and the Manichaeans. [Note: [Col. 0165D] Law 9, Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*.]

Accordingly, there are learned men who refer to this year the actions which Faustinus and Marcellinus, those deranged leaders, report as having been carried out against the Luciferians at Damasus’s command. For Damasus could act through the Church’s defender under this law to prevent assemblies of Luciferians and rebaptizers; and through this law, and perhaps another constitution of Valentinian issued against rebaptizing bishops, [Note: [Col. 0165D] Theodosian Code, bk. XVI, title 6, law I.] he could arrange for Aurelius, then the Luciferian pseudo-bishop in the City, to be banished elsewhere as unworthy of the priesthood.

Theophanes appears to confirm this conjecture when he writes, under the year 377 of the divine incarnation, that Damasus expelled the Sabbatians from the Church. That year among the Alexandrians begins on 1 December 374, as Pagius also notes. [Note: [Col. 0165D] On the year 373, no. 2.] It is certain that there were no Sabbatians under Damasus. That name began to be heard after the death of Theodosius the Great, when Sabbatius withdrew from the Novatians and founded the sect named after him. From this we plainly infer that the seventh canon of the Seventh Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, in which the Sabbatians are expressly mentioned, belongs to another time and another council.

Therefore Theophanes understands all Novatians under that designation; Damasus could have proscribed them from the Church, since they could be regarded as included with the Montenses and [Col. 0166A] Luciferians under the imperial edict addressed to Simplicius. For the Novatians, no less than the Donatists, professed rebaptism; and there was a close association between them, as is clear from Innocent’s letters [Note: [Col. 0166D] In Coustant, Epistle 5, no. 2; Epistle 2, no. 11.] and from Cyprian and Ambrosiaster. [Note: [Col. 0166D] Cyprian, Letter to Jubaianus, no. 8; Ambrosiaster, on ch. I of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians.] Hilary, the deacon of the Luciferians, had in fact introduced this heresy among his own people as well, so that at Rome he might have persons with whom he could join in communion.

Damasus therefore appears to have been the author of the law which Valentinian and Gratian enacted against rebaptizers and sent to Simplicius, deputy prefect of the City, so that by their combined strength and judgments provision might be made for religion. Hence the Luciferians Faustinus and Marcellinus complain that Damasus himself, having obtained royal authority, persecuted Catholic presbyters and laymen [Col. 0166B] and sent them into exile; while they accuse the magistrates of the City of wrongly interpreting the emperors’ law and of complying too excessively with Damasus himself.

Moreover, that you may yourself recognize and decide what credence may be given to these Luciferians—schismatics though they are—these presbyters, when they assail Damasus and other distinguished Catholic bishops with calumnies, may be shown by this one example above all others. They assert that, after the Council of Rimini, Maximus was driven from his see and Zosimus was substituted by the Arians; they further say that, when Lucifer returned from the East, he did not admit Zosimus, who came to him as a mark of respect. Yet you will search in vain for this Maximus and Zosimus among the Neapolitan bishops in the Chronicle of John the Deacon or in the other chronicle published by Blanchini. Indeed, if the records of that church are to be believed, there can be no place whatever for them; for Severus—to whom Ambrose wrote Letter 59, and who is honourably mentioned by Symmachus [Note: [Col. 0166D] Letter 51, Book VII.]—held and administered that bishopric holily from at least 342 to 387. Hence the eminent Alexius Symmachus Mazochius, in his most learned notes on the ancient marble calendar of the Neapolitan Church, rightly concludes under 21 February that the alleged Neapolitan episcopate of Ursicinus must be relegated to fable—a claim which the distinguished Muratori had seemed, in notes on the same John the Deacon’s Chronicle, to place before Severus himself. Yet I do not see why, elsewhere, he could have listed this Zosimus and Maximus among the bishops of the same city and written that they administered that church from 359 to 364 [Note: [Col. 0166D] At the Nones of April, p. 188, and at 11 June, vol. II.], when Severus, then bishop of that city, excludes them no less than Ursicinus.

## CHAPTER X. 375, THE TENTH YEAR OF DAMASUS, AFTER THE THIRD CONSULSHIP OF THE AUGUSTUS GRATIAN AND EQUITIUS

I. Vitalis the Apollinarian, his journey to Rome and its reason; the profession of faith which he presented to Damasus; communion deceitfully obtained; and three letters written on that occasion by Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch. II. The last of these letters provokes disturbances among the Catholics of Antioch, reported from Basil. III. Dorotheus considers a third journey to Rome for this reason and consults Basil himself. IV. Simplicianus, later Ambrose’s successor, was a presbyter of the Roman Church; Baronius defended.

[Col. 0167A]

I. The letter of Damasus, of which only a fragment survives [Note: [Col. 0167D] See below, Letter 1, no. 1.], and the return of Dorotheus raised the spirits of the Eastern bishops, because of the aid which the Roman pontiff and the assembled bishops had promised, both in actual assistance so far as they could give it and in words and a full declaration of their will. This is gathered from what Basil then wrote to the presbyters of Antioch, to Pelagius of Laodicea, and to Vitus, bishop of the Charrans [Note: [Col. 0167D] Letters 253, 254, 255; Life of Basil, ch. 36, no. 6.].

[Col. 0167B] But shortly afterwards the situation changed because of events which had recently occurred at Antioch. Vitalis had been a presbyter among Meletius’ clergy. Resenting the preference given to Flavian over himself, and alleging that Flavian had treated him contemptuously, he went over to Apollinarius, who placed him in charge of those whom he had attached to himself in that city [Note: [Col. 0167D] Sozomen, Book VI, ch. 25.]. It is credible that Paulinus reported the whole affair to Damasus: namely, that Apollinarius’ sect was increasing at Antioch; that Vitalis, a man of considerable reputation in that city, had lately joined it; and that Apollinarius had employed him in conducting the heretics’ synaxes, thereby giving no small support to the heresy previously condemned by the Alexandrian and Roman synod, and damaging the Catholic faith. For what other cause can we assign to that great division which produced both results? [Note: [Col. 0167D] See Epiphanius, *Haereses* 77, no. 20.]

[Col. 0167C] Vitalis therefore came to Rome to clear himself; whether voluntarily or summoned is uncertain. Tillemont thinks that he came voluntarily, in order to obtain from Damasus the communion he had vainly sought from Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0167D] On Apollinarius, art. 9, vol. VII.]. But since Damasus, as Nazianzen says, required from him a profession of faith, and since in the document which he presented to the pontiff when it was demanded of him (*apaitētheis*, “being required”) he does nothing but endeavour to dissociate himself from Apollinarius’ heresy and clear himself of suspicion, we readily conclude that he undertook the journey not of his own accord but upon summons.

Cyril of Alexandria cites a profession of faith by Bishop Vitalis in these words:

> If anyone says that our Lord and Saviour, who according to the flesh was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, was deprived of soul, mind, reason, or sense, let him be anathema.  
> [Note: [Col. 0167D] To the Queens, ch. 10, vol. VI.]

Petavius hesitates whether to attribute this to our Vitalis [Note: [Col. 0167D] *Theology*, vol. IV, Book VI, ch. 1, §18.]. Yet whoever observes that it is composed in pious expressions apparently breathing the true faith, and compares it with the other statement of faith attributed to the same Vitalis by Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0167D] *Haereses* 77, from no. 20.], will scarcely doubt that, as Lequien says [Col. 0168A] [Note: [Col. 0168D] Dissertation 2, §7.], it came from his own workshop. Hence Nestorius reproaches Cyril for employing the testimony of Vitalis the Apollinarian as though he were another Vitalis: “There is a Vitalis who was an orthodox bishop, and another Vitalis who was consecrated by the impious Apollinarius” [Note: [Col. 0168D] Letter 15, in Lupus, on the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, Works, vol. VII.].

For Vitalis, like the other men of his sect, understood by the words “reason,” “mind,” and “sense”—which he seemed to allow to Christ the Lord—nothing other than the divine Word itself, which, as Epiphanius testifies, supplied the function of a mind. Therefore, since the faith which he had submitted in writing appeared sound and orthodox at first sight, Damasus admitted him to communion while he was at Rome, not at all detecting at that time the crafty wickedness and concealed, hidden fraud lying beneath those words. Yet, regarding the future and the Church of Antioch, he wrote to Paulinus that Paulinus, who ought to have been better acquainted with the matter, should settle the case; Damasus would approve whatever he judged best. He gave these letters to Vitalis when he was then departing, to deliver to Paulinus.

But shortly after Vitalis had left Rome, Damasus wrote again, sending a short letter through the presbyter Petronius, to indicate that some scruple had arisen in his mind concerning the affair. Subsequently, however, he foresaw that Paulinus, uncertain what course to take, would meanwhile do nothing and would hold the entire matter in suspense until further letters arrived from the Roman pontiff clearing up this doubt. Therefore, lest time be fruitlessly prolonged and the reception of Vitalis and others coming to the Church be delayed any longer, he wrote to the bishop of Antioch the third letter, adding conditions as a kind of memorandum for conducting the business and sending [Col. 0168C] the explicit formula of faith contained in it [Note: [Col. 0168D] See Letter 2.]: “not so much to you,” Damasus says, “who are united in the communion of the same faith, as to those who, subscribing to it, wish to be united to you—that is, to us through you.”

From this we understand that, when Damasus wrote this, he was wholly uncertain and awaiting the future outcome at Antioch. Hence that anathema by which Nazianzen says that the deceptive written profession of faith offered by Vitalis was overthrown and annulled [Note: [Col. 0168D] See Nazianzen, Letter 2, to Cledonius] is different from that expressed in this same letter and was promulgated at another time: namely, after Damasus learned that Vitalis himself and the Apollinarians persisted in their earlier formulations, and after, better informed, he saw that he had been deceived and bore it very grievously—as Nazianzen says also concerning himself.

[Col. 0168D]

II. Thus it was through this letter of Damasus to Paulinus, which I list second, that the case long contested between Paulinus and Meletius appeared at length to have been settled, as I shall immediately explain. There are many and most weighty reasons why Damasus thought communion should be maintained with Paulinus rather than Meletius.

The first is that Vitalis, a presbyter who had been treated contemptuously by Flavian, had renounced communion with Meletius; and at Antioch there remained no other Catholic bishop with whom there was hope he would be willing to communicate except Paulinus. The second is that Meletius, far removed from his flock and driven into exile, could not be present to manage this very serious affair with the diligence it required. The third is that Paulinus, on the contrary, was present at Antioch, had shown zeal for the true faith in that city, and had already commended his administration to Damasus.

Damasus, already inclined toward Paulinus for these reasons, may also have been influenced by the example of Athanasius, who while alive judged communion with Paulinus should be maintained; by the counsel of Peter of Alexandria, Athanasius’ disciple and successor, who was then at Rome; and also by Meletius’ not altogether commendable entry into the Church of Antioch [Col. 0169B] and his frequent migrations from church to church, although he subsequently effaced that reproach by holiness of life and integrity of faith. Therefore those are not far from rashness who write that Damasus wronged Meletius and that the Church of Antioch ought to have been assigned to him rather than Paulinus.

Dorotheus the presbyter, having conveniently returned from Rome about the autumn of the preceding year and remained at Antioch after completing that embassy, immediately informed Basil of what was occurring there: namely, that letters had come from the West assigning the episcopate to Paulinus, and that the Paulinians were moreover using those letters to induce the general Terentius to negotiate a union with the Meletians. Basil accordingly both reported the whole affair to Meletius and at once wrote to Terentius, urging him not to commit himself wholly to either party, but to preserve the matter intact until Meletius’ return.

From what Basil writes to both it is quite clear that the letters in question are those which Damasus had given Paulinus in the affair of Vitalis, and that before this time no others had been written to him. But let us hear Basil:

> A report has reached us that you are at Antioch and are conducting the business in hand with the highest authorities. Besides this report, we have also learned that the brethren attached to Paulinus have been discussing with you a union to be made with us—that is, with those belonging to the party of Meletius, the man of God and bishop. I also hear that they are NOW circulating letters of the Westerners which attribute the episcopate of the city of Antioch to Paulinus himself and disappoint Meletius.  
> [Note: [Col. 0169D] Letter 214, formerly 359.]

Thus before this time the Paulinians had received no letters from Damasus which they could circulate and by which they could prove that the episcopate had been assigned to Paulinus. Why Basil says that the episcopate was attributed to Paulinus by these same letters is understood from what he writes at the same time to Meletius:

> After our return, when much sickness had been contracted through rains and hardships, letters immediately reached us from the East—that is, from Antioch—reporting that certain letters had been brought from the West to Paulinus as a sort of token of primacy, and that the leaders of this party were exulting greatly and glorying in the letters; further, that they were putting forward a faith and were ready, on that condition, to unite with our Church.  
> [Note: [Col. 0169D] Letter 216, formerly 272.]

Could the letters Damasus had written to Paulinus, and the very words of those letters which we have cited, have been indicated more plainly? Did not they constitute Paulinus as a kind of sign and head of apostolic communion in the East, when Damasus put him in his own place and ordered that those who communicated with Paulinus should be regarded as joined in communion with himself?

That these letters were certainly written by Damasus in this year is proved by the most exact writer of Basil’s life [Col. 0170B], who rightly rejects his colleague Fr. Peter Constantius’ assignment of them to 378 [Note: [Col. 0169D] Vol. III, ch. 33, no. 6.]. I shall add only a few points to the arguments advanced by that most learned man, so that the matter may appear entirely certain.

First, as soon as Dorotheus returned from the West and brought letters to the Eastern bishops, Basil appeared rather to rejoice and to derive some fruit from that embassy. Could this have happened if, before this time, he had seen Meletius openly cast down from his hopes? Secondly, when Damasus wrote to Paulinus, Vitalis had not yet been ordained bishop, because Damasus treats him as a son and addresses him by that title in the letter, although Noris, pursuing a different purpose, thought otherwise [Note: [Col. 0169D] Dissertation on St. Siricius, Works, vol. IV.]. But he was wickedly raised to that rank in 376, when he held the conference with Epiphanius which the latter recounts [Note: [Col. 0170D] *Haereses* 77, ch. 20.]. This letter was therefore written during the intervening time from his return from Rome to 376.

Thirdly, when those letters were brought to Antioch and began to be circulated, General Terentius, who had withdrawn from public affairs to devote himself to his soul, was compelled to return to business; as Basil testifies, he was then administering public affairs in that city together with the highest authorities. We must therefore seek the time when he retired to leisure and quiet, and then when he returned to public business. No period occurs other than that between 373 and the middle of 375. For in 373 he is known to have been free from business from Basil’s letter written to him from Armenia [Note: [Col. 0170D] See Letter 99, in the Benedictine edition.].

Tillemont thinks that at this very time the general was sent into Iberia, placed over twelve legions, to restore Sauromatius [Col. 0170D] to his kingdom. When the undertaking had happily succeeded and any enemies had been subdued, Terentius returned from Armenia to Antioch, where Valens had established his residence, and withdrew into retirement. He thought himself slighted by the emperor, who, though Terentius had earnestly requested it, had not granted even one church to the Catholics, but instead had torn up the petition presented to him. When Terentius gathered up the fragments, he said: “I have what I asked for.” This noble action, narrated by Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0170D] Book IV, ch. 32.], is rightly placed by Pagius [Col. 0171A] in 373 [Note: [Col. 0171D] On the year 373, no. 3.]. Therefore, if the general withdrew to leisure late in that year, he could scarcely have returned to court and public affairs before the following year was drawing toward its close. Consequently, the letters that came from Damasus to Antioch, when Terentius had again and only shortly before been brought back to public business, cannot fall outside the year under discussion.

III. Dorotheus, to whom Meletius’ cause was dear no less than to Basil, accordingly wrote that he also intended to set out once more for Rome, in order to defend the cause by whatever means he could; and he asked Basil to persuade Gregory of Nyssa to undertake the journey with him. We learn this from Basil himself [Note: [Col. 0171D] Letter 215.], who replied that the journey could by no means be made in winter and that all roads leading to Constantinople were blocked by soldiers. We understand from this that the letter was written when autumn had already begun and was advancing.

If Dorotheus wished to travel by sea, however, Basil did not deny that the time was favourable and suitable for departure and that he should leave at once, provided Gregory his brother did not decline either the sea voyage or the embassy. What Basil afterwards adds concerning Western haughtiness reveals a mind wounded on Meletius’ account and shows that this otherwise most holy man experienced something merely human. For Damasus’ writings that survive to Paulinus, Jerome, and Acholius, as well as Jerome himself, who proclaims him a man of the gentlest disposition, prove that every trace of arrogance and haughtiness was absent from Damasus.

IV. The father of the *Annals*, under this year [Note: [Col. 0171D] *Annals* 375, no. 22.], writes that Simplicianus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, was sent by Damasus as teacher and guide to St Ambrose [Col. 0171C], who near the end of the preceding year had been ordained bishop of Milan from being a layman and neophyte. Tillemont seeks some stronger testimony for this claim. First, he says it is uncertain whether Simplicianus was a presbyter of the Roman Church, since it is known only that he lived at Rome under Constantius, converted Victorinus to Christian worship under Julian, was at Milan under Bishop Ambrose, and was regarded by Ambrose as a spiritual father, according to Augustine. From this, Tillemont argues, it does not follow that Simplicianus was sent there by Damasus for the purpose mentioned by Baronius [Note: [Col. 0171D] On Ambrose, art. 10, and on Simplicianus, vol. X.].

But since Simplicianus was a presbyter, and Ambrose moreover regarded him as a spiritual father—whether because he had instructed Ambrose at Rome or for another reason—he must have been a presbyter long before Ambrose’s ordination, a point Tillemont himself does not deny. At that time, however, no one could be a presbyter without being assigned to a definite place or church; he could not abandon it against his bishop’s will in order to move elsewhere. I shall not reopen a matter well known and excellently treated by Thomassin [Note: [Col. 0171D] Vol. II, Book I, with many following sections.].

Hence Jerome allowed himself to be ordained by Paulinus of Antioch only with the added condition that he should remain free to go wherever he wished [Note: [Col. 0171D] Baronius, year 378, no. 65.]. St Paulinus of Nola likewise says of himself, writing to Severus:

> I was induced to be consecrated in the Church of Barcelona on the condition that I should not be bound to that particular church; I was dedicated only to the priesthood of the Lord, not also to a particular ecclesiastical post.  
> [Note: [Col. 0172D] Letter 1, Verona edition.]

After citing this, Abbot Floridus rightly added that it should be counted among the earlier examples of free ordination [Note: [Col. 0172D] Book XIX, ch. 57.]. Therefore, since Simplicianus served as presbyter at Rome before he went to Milan, Baronius rightly called him a presbyter of the Roman Church.

There are two reasons why he should be regarded as sent to Milan by Damasus. First, presbyters could not leave their post without letters of recommendation and against their bishop’s will. [Col. 0172B] Secondly, Damasus had confirmed Ambrose’s ordination; therefore, through Simplicianus—whose holiness, learning, and familiarity with Ambrose were well known—he ought to have ensured that ecclesiastical discipline suffered no loss under a new bishop, however irreproachable, who was nevertheless not yet instructed in the sacred canons. For it was a chief concern that those newly ordained, or about to be ordained, should be instructed by those under whom they served and by their consecrators, and should often receive in writing a code of ecclesiastical rules [Note: [Col. 0172D] See Quesnel on St Leo, Letter 16.].

That Ambrose’s ordination was confirmed by Damasus after examination of the case is clear from Ambrose himself, who wrote to the Vercellians:

> The Western bishops approved my ordination by JUDGMENT, the Eastern bishops by example.  
> [Note: [Col. 0172D] Letter 63, in the Benedictine edition.]

That this then belonged to the ordinary right of the Roman bishop is gathered from the discussions of Bacchini and John Anthony Blancus, which may be consulted [Note: [Col. 0172D] *On the Origin of Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, part II, ch. 5 and following; vol. IV, Book II, ch. 1, §16.].

## CHAPTER XI. 376, THE ELEVENTH YEAR OF DAMASUS, VALENS AUGUSTUS FOR THE FIFTH TIME AND VALENTINIAN AUGUSTUS, CONSULS

I. Dorotheus journeys to Rome with another most holy presbyter of the Church of Antioch, bringing letters written to Damasus by Basil and the Easterners; these are examined, and the whole course of events between Damasus and Basil is set out. II. The same pontiff, with a synod attended by Peter of Alexandria, complies with the wishes of the Easterners and replies to them; a fragment of the synodal letter then written is cited and explained. III. In this same synod Apollinarius and Timothy are condemned. IV. The case of Meletius argued before Damasus, his standing with that pontiff, and what the pontiff thought of him; Dupin refuted. V. The remarkable thoughtlessness—or bad faith—of the anonymous writer of Amsterdam.

[Col. 0172D]

I. Gregory of Nyssa, whom Dorotheus had wished to have joined to him as companion, appears not to have considered the Roman journey, whether because he declined it or because other business and the Arian persecutions that afflicted him shortly afterwards detained him. But Dorotheus himself, to whom another most holy presbyter of the Church of Antioch had offered himself as companion, was diligently pressing forward with the journey and preparing for it about the beginning of this year.

These points are established from Basil’s letter to Eusebius of Samosata, which reads:

> As for the affairs of the West, you yourself learned of them first, when our brother Dorotheus related everything. What letters, then, should again be given to him as he departs? For perhaps the excellent most holy man, who burns with great zeal, travels throughout the East, and gathers subscriptions and letters from all those of higher distinction, will join himself to him as companion on the journey.  
> [Note: [Col. 0173D] Letter 279, formerly 10.]

The most careful editor of the last volume of Basil’s works, who reckons from this year the first journey of Dorotheus the presbyter to Rome and his first embassy to Damasus, interprets these words as though Basil were asking what letters should again be given to Dorotheus—not as he was departing for Rome, but as he was leaving Cappadocia, or another place adjoining Cappadocia, for the East; for Dorotheus might perhaps have come there on his return from Eusebius, whom he had visited [Note: [Col. 0173D] *Life of Basil*, ch. 35, no. 6.].

But anyone who reads that letter attentively will readily see that Basil is asking in that passage what should again be written through Dorotheus, who was to go to Rome with the most holy man. For he immediately continues:

> What, then, ought to be written through them, or how plans should be concerted with those who write, I do not know. But if you can quickly find persons who are setting out for us, do not hesitate to explain it to us. For I am minded to use the saying of Diomedes: “Would that you had not prayed,” since, he says, “the man is proud.” [Col. 0173C] For if the Lord is gracious to us, what other assistance do we need? But if God’s wrath continues, what defence is Western haughtiness to us?

The fresh pain of seeing Paulinus preferred to Meletius drew these harsher words from the most holy man; yet they plainly show what letters Basil was considering should be given to Dorotheus, and the nature of Dorotheus’ journey at that time. It is therefore entirely unnecessary to say that Dorotheus went to visit Eusebius, perhaps while Eusebius was exiled in Thrace, nearer Scythia, in order personally to explain the condition of Western affairs, which he could easily have done by letter. Moreover, it is wholly incredible that this presbyter intended to abandon Meletius’ cause, then in the critical position in which he wrote it was at Antioch, to undertake a journey—whether to Thrace or Cappadocia—that would be useless, especially in winter, a season usually very difficult and inconvenient in those regions, and already close at hand when Basil wrote back to him at Antioch, as we saw in the preceding chapter. It should therefore be held certain and settled that Basil here asks Eusebius what letters should again be given to Dorotheus, who was setting out once more for the West, from which he had returned not long before.

II. Dorotheus the presbyter therefore went a second time to Rome, taking with him the letter written by Basil in the name of the Easterners, Letter 74 in the old edition and 263 in the newer. It is so full of gentleness and humility [Col. 0174A], and of such splendid expressions of sincere respect toward the Roman pontiff, that the great Baronius truly says that holy men may sometimes be seized by a human disturbance of mind, but are never held captive by it [Note: [Col. 0174D] On the year 372, no. 2.].

Basil first gives Damasus thanks for the hope of some aid which he had held out earlier and for the effort he had made to ensure that the hope was not disappointed. This is the point and intention of the opening of the letter:

> May the Lord our God, in whom we have hoped, grant to each of you so great a grace that you may attain the hope set before you, inasmuch as you filled our hearts with joy both through the compassion you showed for our afflictions—clothing yourselves with bowels of mercy—as the aforementioned men announced to us: namely, Dorotheus, then returned from Rome, [Col. 0174B] and those who had been his companions. Wherefore again, through our beloved brethren, we both salute and exhort you that, if indeed the Lord grants you the opportunity of coming to us, you do not shrink from visiting us. . . . But if the good God and wise governor of our life reserves this benefit for another time, at least write to us whatever it befits you to write for the consolation of the afflicted and the raising up of the broken. . . . We expect help from no other source, unless the Lord sends healing through you, by whom He is sincerely worshipped.

He then undertakes the matter itself. Having briefly touched upon the Arian heresy, as though cut off from the body of the Church and therefore less able to harm, he goes on:

> But those who are clothed in sheep’s skin and display an attractive and gentle appearance, while within they cruelly tear apart Christ’s flock—and who, because they have arisen from among us, easily bring ruin upon the simpler sort—these are the persons who cause trouble and are difficult to avoid. We ask that your diligence make this known to all the churches of the EAST. . . . It is necessary to mention these men by name, so that you yourselves may know those who stir up disturbances among us and may make them MANIFEST to our churches.

He assigns first place among them to Eustathius of Sebaste, second to Apollinarius, and finally adds Paulinus, though he speaks of the latter less freely and seemingly with some hesitation. Thus he says that Eustathius, after receiving at Rome the faith of the Fathers and being admitted to communion, is now among those who condemn the consubstantiality and acts as a leader of the Pneumatomachian heresy. He says that Apollinarius, using an unrestrained facility in writing and relying not on proofs drawn from Scripture but on human reasoning, had fallen into various errors—especially in what he taught about the Incarnation—so that now few who had read his writings retained the ancient form of piety.

Finally, regarding Paulinus, he writes only this:

> Whether Paulinus may also be liable to censure in his ordination, you yourselves will say. We are indeed distressed that he inclines toward the doctrines of Marcellus and admits Marcellus’ followers indiscriminately to his communion.

Elsewhere we have shown that Basil himself shortly afterwards, after better consideration and fuller knowledge of the matter, did this very thing [Col. 0175A] [Note: [Col. 0175D] See ch. 6.].

> For you know that our whole hope is overthrown by Marcellus’ doctrine, which does not confess the Son to exist in his own hypostasis, but says that he was put forth and then returned again to Him from whom he had proceeded.

Having reported this to the Roman pontiff, Basil concludes the letter thus:

> We entreat you to undertake the care of these matters. You will undertake it if you do not hesitate to write to all the churches of the East that those who corrupt these doctrines, if they are corrected, are to be admitted to communion; but if they persistently wish to adhere to novelties, they are to be cut off from the churches.

This, then, is the sequence of events between Damasus and Basil and of the letters written in each direction. In 371 Basil sends Dorotheus the deacon as ambassador to the Apostolic See with Letter 70 in the newer edition. Damasus replies in the following year through Sabinus, deacon of the Church of Milan, sent to the Easterners. Basil, in that same year, writes again Letter 90 and entrusts it to Sabinus for delivery on his return to the West. Since this perhaps did not please Damasus, the bishop of Caesarea, prompted by Evagrius’ advice, writes again at the beginning of 374, Letters 242 and 243; Dorotheus the presbyter carried them to the West. In the same year Damasus replies to the Easterners through Dorotheus himself, as is clear from the first Damasian fragment and Basil’s present Letter 263 to Damasus.

This letter, written in the present year and delivered to Damasus by Dorotheus, is the latest of all; and Damasus is known to have answered it in a longer synodal letter, of which only the second fragment preserved by Holstenius remains. We distinguish it as the second fragment from the first. I infer two synods from comparison of the two fragments. In the first, Pope Damasus gives the Easterners much hope of future assistance, through which Basil’s spirit was wonderfully raised and he appeared to rejoice, as is evident from Letters 253, 254, and 255. In the second, he leaves no room for hope. For although the most wise pontiff tells the Eastern bishops to be certain that he is concerned for the members, he nevertheless openly acknowledges that no present relief can be expected from him other than that which could be derived from mutual concord in retaining the faith. Since this mutually contrary and conflicting language cannot have proceeded from one and the same synod at one and the same time, one fragment must belong to one synod and the other to another: the first, namely, to the synod assembled in 374, which was highly pleasing to Basil; the second to the synod now under discussion.

III. Damasus, therefore, upon receiving these letters from Basil, convened a synod attended by Peter of Alexandria and Dorotheus the presbyter, ambassador of the Easterners. He condemned Apollinarius together with Timothy and proscribed their senseless heresy from the Church. As for Eustathius [Col. 0176A] of Sebaste, the other Pneumatomachians, and the Marcellian doctrine of which Paulinus had been accused, he addresses them briefly by setting forth this rule of faith:

> For as we preserve the faith of the Council of Nicaea inviolate in every respect, without pretence of words or corruption of meaning, so we in no way separate the Holy Spirit, but venerate him as perfect in all things—in power, honour, majesty, and divinity—together with the Father and the Son. Thus also we believe that the fullness of the Word of God—not a Word merely uttered, but begotten; not remaining in the Father so as not to exist, but subsisting from eternity to eternity—assumed, that is, saved, a perfect, namely entire, human being.

Regarding Paulinus’ ordination, to which Basil had objected that some defect attached, Damasus had already approved it by his own judgment, and thus there was no need to add anything.

It is now not at all difficult to determine the date of this council. If the cited letter of Basil was written before this year had advanced far, then this fragment and the synod to which I assign it must certainly be referred either to the same year or to the beginning of the next. This will further be easily decided by anyone who compares that letter with the same fragment and observes that the latter accomplishes the three things Basil chiefly requested of Damasus.

Add also Socrates’ testimony that Peter of Alexandria had already returned to his church when Valens was forced to leave Antioch to march against the Goths [Note: [Col. 0175D] Book IV, ch. 37.], namely when 377 was already drawing toward its close [Note: [Col. 0175D] See Pagius on the year 378, nos. 5–6.]. But if that same Peter of Alexandria attended this synod, it must have been completed within the intervening period—and therefore either in this very year or in another not yet fully elapsed. Those who place the council in which Apollinarius and Timothy were condemned in 378 are consequently mistaken.

IV. It must indeed be admitted that this fragment cannot prove that the names of Apollinaris and Timothy were condemned in that synod, but only that his impious doctrine was proscribed; yet this is established by strong arguments drawn from elsewhere. For no one who has read the sixth letter of Damasus to the Easterners will doubt that Damasus, in the council attended by Peter of Alexandria, condemned and deposed both men. Rufinus [Note: [Col. 0176D] Book XI, ch. 20], Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0176D] Book VI, ch. 25], and several bishops in the letters to Rufus of Thessalonica inserted in the Council of Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0176D] Venetian edition of the Councils, vol. III, p. 1274] state this explicitly. But that both were condemned, deposed, and expelled from the Church at this very council of which we speak, is, I think, made plain by Basil.

For Apollinaris had not yet undergone this deserved sentence when Basil denounced him to the Apostolic See and so anxiously sought his condemnation. Hence, in a letter written about this time to Patrophilus, bishop of the Church of Aegae, he says that he does not regard Apollinaris as an enemy, though neither does he regard him as such a friend as to take upon himself Apollinaris’s accusations against him, [Col. 0177A] since, having read some of his books, he has rather matters to censure in him [Note: [Col. 0177D] Epistle 244, formerly 82]. On the contrary, Basil regarded Apollinaris as a heretic and as cast out from the body of the Church as soon as Dorotheus returned from Rome and brought that synodical letter of Damasus. For he writes to Eulogius, Alexander, and Harpocration, bishops exiled for the faith, of whom we have spoken elsewhere, praises them for rejecting the communion of Apollinaris, and urges them to try to restore him to the well-established order of the Church, and courageously to set before him the doctrines of the true faith, so that his amendment might become manifest and his repentance be made known to the brethren [Note: [Col. 0177D] Epistle 265, formerly 293].

What other reason could there have been for Basil to hold one view and adopt one course concerning Apollinaris before Dorotheus’s journey, and another after his return, except that after that [Col. 0177B] synod no ground remained for doubting Apollinaris’s condemnation?

Accordingly, besides Peter of Alexandria and Dorotheus the presbyter, acting in the name of the Eastern bishops, Timothy must have been present at this council, sent there to defend Apollinaris’s cause [Note: [Col. 0178D] See ch. 22]. But he too was condemned together with his master; and when he returned to the East, casting off every pretence, he broke forth into an open and frantic schism. He dared to anathematize that same Peter of Alexandria, as well as Basil, Epiphanius, and Paulinus—some, no doubt, as Sabellians, others as Tritheists, as I think—since the Apollinarians boasted, above all others, of their sound faith concerning the Trinity, and no other reason can be imagined why he would have dared to excommunicate men so holy and upright [Col. 0177C]. Peter himself is witness to this in his letter to bishops, presbyters, and deacons living in exile for the true faith, a fragment of which Facundus quotes [Note: [Col. 0178D] Book IV, ch. 2].

Whether Timothy dared this crime after Peter had returned to his own Church, or while Peter was still prolonging his stay at Rome, cannot be determined. What I think can be affirmed is that it occurred after Epiphanius had met Vitalis at Antioch, discovered him to be an Apollinarian, and separated himself from him; and after Basil had denounced Apollinaris to the Apostolic See and obtained his condemnation. For there was no reason why, before this time, that madman should anathematize those men. Yet it seems more likely that Timothy committed these outrages after [Col. 0177D] Peter had returned to Alexandria, confirmed this Roman synod, as Rufinus says, and announced to the bishops and churches subject to him the condemnation of those heretics. For then Apollinaris and his followers began to seek persons who would communicate with them, to sow calumnies against the chief heads of the Catholic bishops, to stir up dissensions everywhere and divisions among the churches, and, casting aside every shame, to dare every impiety. Hence it came about that Peter and Basil wrote at one and the same time to the same exiled bishops: the former to make known to them the extreme insolence of Timothy and the other Apollinarians [Col. 0178A], the latter to praise them because they had openly rejected their communion.

V. Besides the matters which he saw successfully accomplished, it is both likely that Dorotheus did not neglect the cause of his bishop Meletius, and Basil proves this in the same letter to Peter of Alexandria. Indeed, from Basil’s own words we learn that Dorotheus pursued it with a zeal perhaps more vehement than was fitting:

> Our brother Dorotheus has caused us sorrow, because, as you yourself wrote, he did not say everything gently and mildly to your dignity. On his return he told me what conversations and disputes he had held in the presence of the most reverend bishop Damasus with your excellence; and it grieved me when he said that our most religious fellow-ministers, the brethren Meletius [Col. 0178B] and Eusebius, had been counted among the Arians.

Perhaps, then, because Dorotheus was more forceful than was proper and insisted that communion with Meletius should be retained rather than that with Paulinus, Peter—who, adhering to the example of Athanasius, supported Paulinus—again objected, in order to blunt the disputant’s vehemence, first, to the communion maintained by Meletius and Eusebius with Acacius and the Arians; and secondly, that by preferring *homoiousion* (“like substance”) they seemed to depart from *homoousion* (“same substance”) and pass over to the Arians themselves.

For this suspicion, which then prevailed, continued long afterwards to cling to very many people, and led Jerome to write in his *Chronicle* that Meletius, at the Antiochene synod, rejected both *homoousion* and *anomoion* and defended the intermediate *homoiousion*, the Macedonian doctrine. It also gave occasion to the work printed among the writings of Athanasius, entitled [Col. 0178C] *Refutation of the Hypocrisy of Meletius, Eusebius of Samosata, and Their Associates against Consubstantiality*.

But Damasus, with the wisdom and firmness of mind with which he was endowed, departed in no respect from the judgment he had once formed and defined. For the requirements of ecclesiastical discipline did not permit Paulinus—who had been lawfully ordained, had never defiled himself by communion with heretics, had openly professed the Catholic faith with great courage and constancy, undeterred by the threats either of Valens or of the Arians, and whom Jerome calls a confessor and Rufinus a holy man in every respect worthy of the priesthood—to be ranked below Meletius, who had obtained the Church of Antioch, as it were, as the reward of wrongdoing, although he had renounced their communion.

On the contrary, because Meletius had anathematized Arius and was then an exile for the true faith, the old accusations perhaps then brought forward by Peter of Alexandria did not prevent Damasus from maintaining communion in sacred things with Basil and the other communicants of Meletius and Eusebius, and also communion in the sacred mysteries with Meletius himself. Hence Damasus received with great kindness Dorotheus himself and the most holy presbyters of the Meletian party, repeatedly sent to him, and admitted them to all sacred rites.

Thus Meletius was regarded as a Catholic bishop; but that close union and brotherly charity enjoyed by those who lacked no part of the full communion of the Roman bishop was neither entered into nor maintained with him. This same manner of dealing with Flavian, Meletius’s successor, was subsequently observed by the Apostolic See, until the controversy was ended—on the one side by the settlement of which there will be further discussion, and on the other by Theophilus of Alexandria and Chrysostom acting as reconcilers.

From this it is clear how deceitful and sophistical is the argument of Dupin and others of his disposition, who misuse the example of Meletius and Flavian to prove that there can sometimes be persons in the Catholic Church who are outside communion with the Roman Church. For the communion not maintained with Meletius and Flavian was not deprivation of the sacred mysteries, but separation from that close ecclesiastical fellowship and confederation which existed between [Col. 0179A] a presbyter and his bishop, a bishop and the bishops of his province, and especially with the Roman bishop. Such were reciprocal visitation, the exchange of letters of communion and recommendation, seats in councils, and other matters belonging to the Church’s external polity; to be deprived of these was regarded in those times as a most serious penalty [Note: [Col. 0179D] See Morin, *Exercitations*, book II, chs. 17, 18, 19].

This is what Sozomen aptly indicates [Note: [Col. 0179D] Sozomen, book VII, ch. 11] when he says that the Westerners, greatly offended by Flavian’s own ordination, continued to write their customary letters to Paulinus as bishop of Antioch, but wrote none to Flavian. This separation from external fellowship, sometimes extending more widely and sometimes confined within narrower limits, did not prevent those who were thus excluded from communicating, in churches where communion was permitted them, even with bishops with whom it was forbidden elsewhere. Thus Theophilus of Alexandria did not hesitate to attend a certain synod at Constantinople with Flavian himself, from whom Egypt was separated; nor is there any reason why Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0179D] On Flavian, art. 7] should profess surprise that this could have been done.

But, to return from my digression: since Damasus patiently heard Dorotheus’s arguments and even his sharper disputations, as Basil himself testifies, the otherwise most holy bishop of Caesarea showed a human weakness when he wrote that the proud man, lofty and seated on high, could not hear truth proclaimed from the ground [Note: [Col. 0180D] Epistle 215].

VI. Since these matters stand thus, the negligence—or again the bad faith—of the anonymous renegade must be exposed to the readers’ eyes [Col. 0179D]. First, he asserts that Damasus never wrote back either to Athanasius or to Basil, whether because, occupied with his own disputes, he had no need of foreign ones, or because he feared to provoke against himself the anger of Emperor Valens, which would be of no benefit to his affairs. Second, he says that the letters written by Basil were brought to Rome by Evagrius of Antioch and then returned by him to Basil. Third, he says that Basil consequently broke off all correspondence with the Roman bishop. Fourth, lest religion meanwhile suffer any harm, he says that Basil asked Athanasius [Col. 0180A] to write himself to Damasus and request that he send legates to the East. Fifth, he says that, after receiving Basil’s letters, the Western bishops preferred Meletius to Paulinus against the judgment of Damasus. Sixth, he says that the same Westerners sent a most holy presbyter as legate to the East with Sabinus and several other clerics. How false all these assertions of his are is clear both from the sequence of events reviewed by us and from what follows; and they teach us what credit can be placed in this careless, lying, and foolish writer in other matters as well.

## CHAPTER XII. 377, THE TWELFTH YEAR OF DAMASUS; GRATIAN AUGUSTUS, FOR THE FOURTH TIME, AND MEROBAUDES, CONSULS

I. Jerome’s letters to Damasus concerning the three hypostases are set forth and explained. The cause of the revival of this dispute at that time, and subsequently at the Council of Constantinople, is investigated. II. Damasus’s reply to Jerome. III. The ancient reading of Jerome’s letter is retained and defended. IV. Did Jerome regard Vitalis as a Catholic? V. Peter, restored to his see by Damasus’s letters, returns to Alexandria.

[Col. 0180B]

I. Saint Jerome, who had withdrawn to the desert of Chalcis about five years earlier, wrote this year his celebrated letters to Damasus [Note: [Col. 0180D] Epistles 15 and 16, Verona edition], asking whether three hypostases should be spoken of in God, and with whom he ought to communicate at Antioch. The reasons why, with the distinguished Vallarsi, I judge these letters to have been written in this year, or at least at the beginning of the next, are apparent from the letters themselves.

For when they were written, the Arian frenzy, supported by the resources of the world, was raging; and Jerome, uncertain with whom to communicate at Antioch, followed the Egyptian confessors exiled in Palestine, whom he knew to be in communion with Damasus, and sought from them the Body of the Lord. But in August of the following year, with the death of Valens, the Arian frenzy utterly lost its supports; and there were no longer any Egyptian confessors exiled in Syria from whom Jerome could continue to seek the Body of the Lord, since all had been released from exile.

Constantius, who republished these letters of Jerome and considers them written late in the year 380, understands by the Egyptian confessors Peter of Alexandria. But we have already seen from Basil who those persons were; and Jerome himself expressly tells us, since he had recourse to them, as nearer to himself, for the holy Body of the Lord. Therefore I scarcely think that learned men will approve Constantius’s interpretation, which departs from the genuine force of the words and from the chronology.

The reason why both the Meletians and the Vitalians said that they adhered to Damasus, no less than Paulinus, need not be sought far away, as seemed necessary to that same learned man, who thought Jerome was referring to the law issued by Theodosius concerning the restoration of basilicas, and to the dispute between Meletius, Paulinus, and Vitalis before Sapor on that occasion, which Theodoret relates [Note: [Col. 0181D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 3]. For anyone who considers that those who wish to be regarded as Catholics must be united in communion with the chair of Peter will understand Jerome’s meaning. Those who think that he indicates that dispute fail to observe that the law concerning the restoration of basilicas was promulgated on 10 January 381, while Sapor, commissioned by Theodosius to execute it at Antioch, could scarcely have arrived there before March. No one can say that Jerome left Antioch so late as to have been present at that dispute. For, to pass over other arguments that might be adduced, while he was at Constantinople, being instructed in the study of the Holy Scriptures by the most eloquent Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of that city—or administering that Church in the place of a bishop—he composed a short treatise on the Seraphim [Note: [Col. 0181D] On Isaiah, ch. VI], which, after its publication, he dedicated to Damasus.

Moreover, Jerome writes to Pammachius and Oceanus that he had composed that book twenty years earlier [Note: [Col. 0181D] Epistle 84, ch. 3, Verona edition]. Since scholars agree that the letter to Pammachius and Oceanus was written in 399 [Note: [Col. 0181D] See the distinguished Vallarsi in the preface to Jerome’s letters; Fontanini, *Sacred Antiquities*, book V, ch. 3], it follows that Jerome must have remained in the imperial city at least in the year 379.
