Besides, what Theodoret records as said and done in that dispute between Meletius, Paulinus, and Vitalis was either invented because of his partiality for Flavian, as Baronius judges [Note: [Col. 0182D] Under the year 378], or, as others think, he carelessly mingled events which occurred separately and at different times.

But, to return to my purpose: whoever reads the letter itself will readily understand what, in Saint Jerome’s judgment, is the authority of the Apostolic See, and how unfailing is its judgment in deciding questions of faith. I shall cite a few words to make this clear:

> Since the East, shattered against itself by the long-standing madness of the peoples, tears piecemeal into fragments the seamless tunic of the Lord, woven from above, I have judged that I must consult the chair of Peter and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth. I, acknowledging no first but Christ, am joined in communion with your blessedness—that is, with the chair of Peter. I know that the Church has been built upon that chair. . . .

Those, therefore, who say that Jerome consulted Damasus either because of the dignity and majesty of the Roman Church in which he had been baptized, or because the whole West followed it [Note: [Col. 0182D] Tillemont, on Jerome, art. 16], merely reveal minds wholly preoccupied with prejudice. For Christ chose Peter particularly among the rest so that the nations might not merely hear him speaking in controversies of faith but also believe him. Thus, when Peter had pronounced his judgment, the whole multitude fell silent, agreeing with Peter as he defined, as Luke relates in Acts 15 [Note: [Col. 0182D] Melchior Cano, *On the Theological Sources*, book VI, ch. 3].

Hence the holy Doctor adds: “I do not know Vitalis; I reject Meletius; I am ignorant of Paulinus.” For to no one, whoever he may be, has it been granted by God not to fail in faith except Peter and the heir of his chair. Therefore, when doctrine is in question, Jerome looks to and acknowledges him as the sole teacher of the faith. Since this is the obvious meaning of these words, Tillemont searches in vain for the reason why Jerome says that he does not know Paulinus, whom he could not have failed to know and with whom he was familiar. Jerome is ignorant of Paulinus in comparison with Damasus: that is, he disregards the bishop of Antioch in comparison with the Roman pontiff, who, he knows, cannot fail, although Paulinus may be mistaken; for Jerome immediately adds, “Whoever he may be, whoever does not gather with you scatters.”

The question concerning the three hypostases had been settled after the Alexandrian council, joined by the West through Eusebius of Vercelli and Lucifer of Cagliari, legates of the Apostolic See. For Athanasius, having summoned both parties gently and kindly and carefully and accurately weighed the meaning of their words, found them in agreement and in no way differing in doctrine. He therefore settled the matter so as to allow them the use of the terms while binding them to the realities [Note: [Col. 0182D] Nazianzen, Oration 21].

Why, then, did it seem to revive especially at this time? The reason need not be sought far away. After Damasus, in letters written to Paulinus, had chosen communion with him, we have seen that the Eustathians over whom Paulinus presided considered entering into union with the Meletians and, to that end, employed the aid of Count Terentius, then at Antioch. Basil and the other Meletians, rightly fearing that those who supported Meletius, then in exile, might readily leave him and join the present Paulinus, began again with all their strength to defend the necessity of speaking of three hypostases and vehemently to reject the term “three persons” as highly suspect of Sabellianism.

Hence that bishop of Caesarea, who had not said a word about three hypostases when he wrote to Athanasius concerning the restoration of the Paulinians to Meletius and who was consequently prepared to receive them as confessing three persons and one hypostasis, afterwards wrote to Terentius that Paulinus, in admitting one hypostasis and three perfect persons, did not depart at all from Sabellius, who likewise admitted one hypostasis and three persons. Therefore, the question of three hypostases could not be considered of slight importance; rather, if anyone who professed one hypostasis with Sabellius should obtain the primacy of the Church of Antioch in disregard of Meletius, a very wide field would be opened to heretics for reviling the Church [Note: [Col. 0182D] Epistle 214].

All this was keenly perceived by the recent most learned editor of the third volume of Basil’s works, who therefore writes:

> The purpose of that agreement was not to put an end to the Antiochene schism and bring the sheep back to the legitimate shepherd Meletius, as he himself thinks. If hope of so great an advantage had shone forth, I am certain that Basil would have subordinated everything to peace and charity and gladly received the people and clergy of Paulinus, even if they admitted one hypostasis. But all the plans of Paulinus’s friends aimed at having Paulinus rule Antioch alone, with holy Meletius excluded. Basil therefore did not without reason deny that communion should be entered into with Paulinus, since it could not be entered into without rejection of Meletius, who alone was the legitimate bishop of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0183D] Preface to vol. III, §3].

By what deference toward the Apostolic See and so many most holy bishops of the West, and by what additional weight of arguments, that distinguished author affirms and proves this, he himself will see. Now, to return to the point from which the discussion had strayed: Flavian and Diodorus, leaders of the Antiochene Church of the Meletians or Campenses, again began to employ Basil’s letters and authority in branding Paulinus’s followers with the cautery of union, accusing them of the Sabellian heresy, and thus deterring their own party from entering into union with them.

This is the reason why the controversy was renewed at the Council of Constantinople after Meletius’s death: it was devised and particularly suited to excluding Paulinus from the bishopric of Antioch. This may be inferred from Gregory’s farewell address to the 150 Fathers:

> Let those who contend with one another about these things cease their folly, as though the piety of our faith consisted in names and not in realities. . . . What, then, do hypostases mean for you, or persons for you? Surely that there are three which are distinguished not by natures but by properties. Excellent; but can persons agree more with one another, or say the same thing more completely, than when they think thus, even though they differ in syllables? [Col. 0183C]

For what purpose would Nazianzen have dealt again with this matter if there were not persons again singing the same refrain against Paulinus?

II. What Damasus answered Jerome is not certainly known, since Damasus’s letters have not reached us. Yet, since Jerome writes again to the presbyter Mark near the end of this year or the beginning of the next that he is judged a heretic although he says and believes the same things that Damasus and Peter of Alexandria both believe and profess; and since he was subsequently ordained presbyter by Paulinus of Antioch—and this occurred at precisely this time, as the distinguished Vallarsi proves conclusively [Note: [Col. 0183D] *Life of Jerome*, ch. 11]—it is apparent that Damasus then gave Jerome leave to profess one hypostasis and three persons, and instructed him to communicate with Paulinus. For one who shortly before had professed that he did not know Paulinus would not have received holy ordination from him without a rule prescribed by the Roman pontiff.

Thus the opinion of those who assert that Damasus at some time used the word *hypostasis* to denote persons is shown to be erroneous by Jerome himself. For he subsequently says to the presbyter Mark:

> Let them condemn me as a heretic with the West, as a heretic with Egypt—that is, with Damasus and Peter. Why do they accuse one man apart from his companions? If a stream flows weakly, the fault lies not in the channel but in the fountain.

Jerome is further supported by the testimony of Acacius, bishop of Beroea in Syria, from whom we know that Paulinus abstained from speaking of three hypostases in order to follow the most devout bishops of the West [Note: [Col. 0183D] In Cyril, Epistle 13]. Since Damasus abstained from speaking of three hypostases, the great Baronius [Note: [Col. 0183D] Under the year 378, no. 37] rightly rejects Theodoret’s statement that Sapor awarded the churches of the Arians to Meletius because Damasus, no less than Meletius himself, confessed one substance of the Trinity and expressly proclaimed three hypostases [Note: [Col. 0184D] Book V, ch. 3].

Accordingly, the words found in other letters of Damasus to Paulinus, “one God in three hypostases” [Note: [Col. 0184D] In Theodoret, book IV, ch. 8], have the unmistakable character of an interpolation by Theodoret himself, and are therefore absent from all Latin manuscripts. [Col. 0184B] Nor is this unusual in that writer. For, when the bishops gathered at the Illyrian synod mentioned elsewhere by us had expressly professed, with all the other bishops of the Latin Empire, that the same substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exists in three persons, Theodoret, who quotes their letter in Greek [Note: [Col. 0184D] Book IV, ch. 8], immediately adds: **τοῦτ᾽ ἔστιν ἐν τρισὶ τελείαις ὑποστάσεσιν**—“that is, in three perfect hypostases”—which is likewise an evident gloss of his own.

III. Before leaving these letters of Jerome, I shall cite a passage from them, since I have seen it frequently misunderstood. He says: “The novel term ‘three hypostases’ is demanded of me, a Roman newcomer, by the leader of the Arians and by the Campenses.” Some think that this disjunction should be omitted and understand Meletius alone by “the leader of the Arians,” since he had been raised to the episcopal chair of Antioch by the Arians’ hand. Others prefer the reading, “by the offspring of the Arians, the Campenses,” and say that Jerome could, not without plausible reason, call the Meletians the offspring of the Arians.

I think, however, that Jerome means nothing else here than that he was in fact then harassed both by the leader of the Arians—whether Euzoius or Dorotheus—and by the Campenses, that is, the Meletians, on this account. Therefore nothing should be altered in the ancient reading. For it was no less in the interest of the Arians than of the Meletians that three hypostases should be spoken of; and the cause was one and the same for all, although the end was not the same for all.

Hence in another letter he says that the Campenses were joined with the Tarsian heretics, because the leaders of the Meletian party had joined their strength and counsels with the Arian heretics in that controversy. They are mistaken, therefore, in my judgment, who suppose that Jerome here calls the citizens of Tarsus heretics and labor to discover the reason for this. Jerome joins the Campenses with the Tarsians because Flavian and Diodorus, who had been a pupil of Silvanus, bishop of Tarsus, jointly presided over the Catholics of the Meletian party. Both could appear to be joined with heretics, both because they seemed to defend with the Arians the same cause concerning three hypostases, and because, according to the testimony of Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0185D] Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, ch. 24] and Philostorgius [Note: [Col. 0185D] Book III, ch. 14], communion in prayers, hymns, consultations, and all other sacred observances—except the mystical sacrifice—was indiscriminate between the Meletians and Arians.

For what common cause could the Tarsians—if any happened to adhere to heretics—have had with the Catholics of Antioch, that Jerome should wish to specify them here before all others? Jerome himself indicates this again in his letter to the presbyter Mark, when he says:

> I am accused of Sabellian impiety for declaring subsistent, true, entire, and perfect persons. If by Arians, rightly so; if by orthodox persons who condemn such a faith, they have ceased to be orthodox.

For he marks both parties from whom he was compelled to suffer these troubles. [Col. 0185B] From this it may also plainly be inferred that these events occurred at Antioch before Meletius had returned there again; and therefore these letters must have been written in the year which I have stated.

IV. It remains to ask why Jerome regarded Vitalis as a Catholic and counted him among the bishops who said that they adhered to Damasus. Could one who obeyed Apollinaris and had been ordained by him—after Apollinaris had already been cast out of the Church—appear to Jerome to adhere to the Roman pontiff? My view is that Vitalis was ordained by Apollinaris not long after returning from Damasus with letters of communion; and that this was done deceitfully, to prevent Paulinus from being able to compel him to subscribe the formula which he knew had been sent to Paulinus by Damasus. But, lest that most cunning man incur suspicion, he then began to accuse Paulinus of Sabellianism and openly renounce communion with him.

Epiphanius relates the matter [Note: [Col. 0185D] *Heresies* 77, ch. 20]; he had come to Antioch in 376 to reconcile the two men. Meanwhile Apollinaris and Timothy were expelled from the Church, and the heresy of them and their followers was proscribed by Damasus with the Roman synod. Yet Vitalis said that he adhered to Damasus, no less than Meletius and Paulinus: either because news of this had not yet reached Antioch when Jerome wrote, or because, not having been condemned by name like the others, and being further supported by the letters of communion which he had once fraudulently obtained from Damasus, and by a pretence of virtue and religion, he passed himself off as a Catholic and deceived [Col. 0185D] the Church.

We learn from Ambrose’s letter to Emperor Theodosius and from Gregory Nazianzen’s second letter to Cledonius—examined by me in Dissertation 2, ch. 4—that he continued this deception for a long time afterwards. From them we infer, not obscurely, that this most cunning head was never openly cast out of the Church or publicly proclaimed among the heretics.

V. We have said that Peter of Alexandria returned to his Church in this year. Accordingly, the letters which he brought with him from Damasus, and which have perished, must have been written this year [Col. 0186A]. Socrates and Sozomen mention them [Note: [Col. 0185D] Socrates, book IV, ch. 37; Sozomen, book VI, ch. 39], and at the same time teach us their force: one records both the consubstantial faith and Peter’s restoration to the Alexandrian see; the other says that his ordination was confirmed by Damasus. Thus both acknowledge that Damasus gave a demonstration of the authority vested in the Roman pontiff.

This is plainly the matter to which Eutherius, bishop of Tyana, and Helladius, bishop of Tarsus, referred when they wrote to Sixtus:

> And formerly, when the tares of heretics repeatedly sprang up from Alexandria, your Apostolic See was sufficient throughout all that period to refute falsehood, repress impiety, correct what required correction, and fortify the whole world for the glory of Christ—both under that thrice-blessed bishop Damasus and under many others [Note: [Col. 0186D] Lupus, *Synodicon*, ch. 117].

Lupus had noted that this referred to the confirmation of Peter of Alexandria in his see and to the condemnation of the Arian Lucius. Baluzius, however, says that Lupus is greatly mistaken, since Damasus condemned Lucius not alone but with a council of Italy and of the entire West [Note: [Col. 0186D] *New Collection of Councils*, p. 817, note c]. How Baluzius proves that this synod was assembled from all the bishops of the West, let him see to that himself. I should believe that it consisted, apart from Peter himself, of the suburbicarian bishops and those who customarily attended upon the Roman pontiff.

Moreover, the observation is altogether foolish, although others, less favorably disposed toward the Apostolic See, commonly employ it. For the bishops themselves plainly explain what authority the bishops of Italy possessed in the Roman synod, in these words written to the Eastern clergy and monks:

> Whenever the priests of the Lord assemble within Italy for ecclesiastical causes, especially those concerning the faith, the custom is maintained that the successor of the bishops of the Apostolic See, acting in the person of all the priests of Italy and in accordance with the care of all the Churches belonging to him, determines all things, since he is the head of all [Note: [Col. 0186D] Second Roman Council under Felix, against Acacius; Councils, vol. V, Venetian edition].

For the one who determines all things has, by the judgment of those bishops, the responsibility of deciding what others must do.

## CHAPTER XIII. 378, THE THIRTEENTH YEAR OF DAMASUS; VALENS, FOR THE SIXTH TIME, AND VALENTINIAN II, AUGUSTI, CONSULS

I. Gracchus, urban prefect this year, destroys the shrine of Mithras, and the part played by Damasus in the matter. II. A certain Roman council and its extant letters to Gratian are wrongly assigned to this year.

[Col. 0186D]

I. This year is illustrious in ecclesiastical history because peace was secured for the Church by the death of Valens. But as regards the deeds of Damasus, it may chiefly be ascribed to his zeal that Gracchus, while holding the urban prefecture, overthrew, shattered, and cast down the cave-shrine of Mithras and all the monstrous images by which Corax, Gryphus, Miles, [Col. 0187A] Leo, Perses, Helios, and Father Bromius are initiated [Note: [Col. 0187D] Jerome, Epistle 107, Verona edition]. Baronius, in order to assign this act to the year 383, when Gracchus was praetorian prefect, thinks that Jerome erred and wrote “urban prefecture” in place of “praetorian prefecture.” Gothofredus, however, Pagius, and Tillemont assign the event to 376 and 377, years in which they infer that Gracchus held the same urban prefecture from two laws addressed to him in the Theodosian Code [Note: [Col. 0187D] Sole law, book I, title 2; and law 3, book IX, title 35.]. One was issued under the consulship of Valens V and Valentinian, that is, in 376; the other under that of Gratian Augustus IV and Merobaudes, namely in 377. Nor, they say, does the fact that both are addressed to Gracchus P.P. obstruct this conclusion: they consider the address corrupt and would correct it from the Justinian Code, in which the first law [Col. 0187B] is read as directed to Gracchus P.U. This is also supported by the Würzburg manuscript of the Theodosian Code, which, according to the testimony of the distinguished Ritter, reads “to Gracchus P.U.” in place of P.P.

But Philip of the Tower, bishop of Adria, whose opinion I follow, assigns both Gracchus’s urban prefecture and the destruction of Mithras to this year [Note: [Col. 0187D] Dissertation on Mithras, final chapter]. He observes that Rufinus held that office in 376, since in June law 3, *On the Office of the Urban Prefect*, was issued to him, as the Justinian Code records. In the following year, and after Rufinus, Probianus is known from Theodosian Code, book XI, title 2, law 3, to have administered the prefecture of the City; this law is recorded as issued in September. Thus only the period between January and September was available for Gracchus; and Tillemont accordingly assigns him this intervening interval [Note: [Col. 0187D] On Gratian, art. 5]. But if Probianus succeeded Gracchus in September, as Tillemont thinks, why do we again read in the Justinian Code a law addressed to the same Gracchus—“that no one shall judge in his own cause”—issued on the Kalends of December, under the consulship of Valens VI and Valentinian II, that is, in 378? It remains, then, to say that an error crept into the Justinian Code. But why could it not rather have occurred in the Theodosian Code? I am more readily persuaded of this because the Würzburg manuscript says that the law was read under the consulship of Valens and Valentinian, but suppresses the year of that consulship; it may therefore be referred to either one. Moreover, nothing prevents Gracchus from filling that year in which no prefect is recorded in Panvinius and Blanchinus [Col. 0187D].

II. I have no doubt that Damasus lent his hand to this distinguished action. For it was then the bishop’s duty both to confer baptism and, for some period or through some deed, to test those to be baptized before they were admitted to the grace of baptism [Note: [Col. 0187D] Bingham, book X, chapter I, §§3 and 5]. [Col. 0188A] Hence, since Jerome writes that Gracchus, after destroying the monstrous images, obtained Christ’s baptism “with these, as it were, sent beforehand as hostages,” we readily understand that this was the condition Damasus laid before him for obtaining it. For, since among the duties resting upon the prefect of the City were the supervision and regulation of games and spectacles—which, in Cyprian’s testimony, could scarcely be free from the guilt or danger of idolatry [Note: [Col. 0187D] Cyprian, *On Spectacles*: “For what spectacle is without an idol? What game without a sacrifice? What contest is not consecrated to a dead man?”]—he seemed, according to the Church’s accepted custom, liable to exclusion from baptism. It was therefore equitable, and conducive to the good of religion, that before admitting him to grace Damasus should require from Gracchus some greater proof of a steadfast will in his purpose.

In what part of the City the Mithraic cave-shrine destroyed by Gracchus stood I would scarcely venture to affirm, though I do not doubt that it was in a celebrated and important place. Perhaps it was on the Capitol itself, in the northern part, where the bishop of Adria reports from Gruter that an underground temple and image of Mithras were found [Note: [Col. 0187D] Chapter 5]; and Ricquius and Pignorius affirm that they saw all these things, including the inscription [Note: [Col. 0188D] Ricquius, *On the Capitol*, chapter 42; Pignorius, notes on Cartari, *On Images of the Gods*, p. 506]. In any event, Damasus was justified in demanding this act from Gracchus, and Gracchus could the more readily perform it, both because Constans had ordered altars and idols in Rome to be destroyed [Note: [Col. 0188D] Law 3, *On Pagans*, Theodosian Code], and because, according to Socrates [Note: [Col. 0188D] Book III, chapter 2], pagans misused Mithraic rites for magical arts and divination, which had been prohibited by the most severe enactments of Christian emperors [Note: [Col. 0188D] See Vulpanius, *Old Latin*, book IV, chapter 7]. Hence Nazianzen, in his poem to Nemesius, execrates the crimes and unspeakable orgies of Mithras’s shrine; and St. Paulinus, rightly censuring them, says:

> What of this—that they conceal “the Unconquered One” in caves beneath the earth,  
> And him whom they cover in darkness dare to call the sun?  
> Who would worship light and the heavenly star in secret,  
> Hide it in the underworld, unless he were the cause of evil things?  
> [Note: [Col. 0188D] Final poem, v. 112, Verona edition. See also the learned Bannier, *Mythology*, book VII, chapter 12, vol. III.]

Sirmond published letters of a Roman council addressed to Gratian and Valentinian, together with a rescript of the same Gratian and Valentinian to Aquilinus, vicar, which deals with the same matters as the council’s letters [Note: [Col. 0188D] Appendix to the Theodosian Code, vol. I, p. 422]. Pagius, Tillemont, and almost all others assign both this Roman council and its letters, as well as Gratian’s rescript, to this year, for no other reason whatsoever than that neither the council’s letter nor the emperors’ [Col. 0188D] rescript mentions either Valens or Theodosius. Thus, they suppose that these events must have occurred in the interval between the death of the one and the election of the other. This is a wholly feeble conjecture. The names of all emperors were not invariably included in letters written to them as circumstances required; nor was this necessary when it sufficed that letters or rescripts bear the names of those rulers whose authority and jurisdiction prevailed in the relevant places. This may be inferred from Symmachus, so that I need not undertake needless labour. Further, how many laws in the Theodosian Code, and edicts publicly promulgated, frequently lack the name of one or another emperor? Let anyone merely run through in Gothofredus the chronology of laws issued under Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian, and consult Reinesius’s nineteenth letter, if he wishes to see clearly how weak this kind of proof is.

There are therefore several considerations which impel me to remove this Roman council from this year and assign it to another time. First, it could scarcely have occurred that, in the very short interval between Valens’s death and Theodosius’s election, that Roman council should write to Gratian and Gratian should reply, when he was then far away and occupied with other, most serious affairs of state. The battle in which Valens perished began on 9 August, and news of the defeat was brought to Gratian by Victor, who had escaped by flight and made his way through Macedonia to Gratian, then stationed with his army in Dacia. How much time remained for news of Valens’s death to reach Rome, and for all that followed to be done, before Theodosius’s election, which was publicly announced on the 16th or 19th of January in the following year?

Secondly, after Valens’s defeat, when Gratian had halted at Sirmium, compelled by the emergency of the times, he issued a law permitting all persons of whatever religion, except Manichaeans, Eunomians, and Photinians, safely and freely to hold assemblies in their own churches. Socrates [Note: [Col. 0189D] Book V, chapter 2], Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0189D] Book VII, chapter 1], and Suidas, whose words Gothofredus quotes [Note: [Col. 0189D] On book IV, *On Heretics*], attest this law, although in the following year, while travelling, he revoked it—presumably following Ambrose’s counsel [Note: [Col. 0189D] See book V, same title]. How, then, could he at this same time have appeared to issue another law wholly contrary to it? For the one addressed to Aquilinus entirely abolishes the other.

Finally, the sequence of several events narrated in the letter of that council absolutely does not permit us to regard it as held in this year. But lest I repeat what has been said elsewhere, see, if you please, the discussion under the year 380, chapter 15.

## CHAPTER XIV. 379, THE FOURTEENTH YEAR OF DAMASUS, CONSULS AUSONIUS AND OLYBRIUS

I. The Antiochene schism ended by the parties’ mutual agreement; Theodoret criticized. II. A synod held at Antioch under Meletius: its proceedings and determinations; its acts sent to Damasus. III. The date of this synod and the year of St. Basil’s death.

[Col. 0190A]

I. Therefore, once, as we have said, Gratian’s law had made it possible for Catholic bishops to return to their churches, St. Meletius was among the first able to avail himself of it. For the place of his exile had been near Nicopolis, metropolis of Armenia, which was not far from Antioch. As soon as he returned, he pursued reconciliation and proposed, in order to repair it, that both bishops should unite their flocks and feed them jointly, or administer that church by common authority [Note: [Col. 0189D] Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 3]. Since Paulinus’s party rightly rejected this proposal, another was offered. As it pleased all, the matter was settled and the people returned to unity and communion in the sacred rites. The condition which then brought the blessing of peace was this [Note: [Col. 0190D] Socrates, book V, chapter 5; Sozomen, book VII, chapter 3]: those who seemed and were expected to be qualified to govern the episcopate were to bind themselves by oath neither to seek nor to accept an offered bishopric so long as either Paulinus or Meletius remained alive; rather, whichever of the two survived was to hold that see alone.

Theodoret, therefore, who writes that reconciliation was offered by Meletius and rejected by Paulinus, seems, as he often does, to have indulged his excessive partiality for Flavian; and Tillemont vainly seeks grounds on which to excuse him [Note: [Col. 0190D] On Meletius, note 12, vol. VIII; on Flavian, art. 3, vol. X]. For Nazianzen makes explicit mention of this agreement and oath in Oration XIV, delivered on peace in the Constantinopolitan church shortly before he took leave of that see. His words refer to it:

> Peace, delightful not only in fact but even in its very name, which I have now given to the people and received from them—I do not know whether it was a voice sincere and worthy of the Spirit from all, or rather **PUBLIC COVENANTS, VIOLATED WITH GOD AS WITNESS**, so that our condemnation may be the heavier.

Moreover, the testimony of St. Ambrose, writing in the name of the Council of Aquileia—a testimony I shall examine elsewhere—confirms the authority of Socrates and Sozomen, which is greater than that of Theodoret alone.

II. With affairs at Antioch thus settled by this agreement, Meletius convened a synod of bishops united with him in communion. Besides Eusebius of Samosata, Pelagius of Laodicea, Eulogius of Edessa, Zeno of Tyre, and Diodorus of Tarsus, whose names are expressly given in the fragment published by Holstenius and later by Constantius, another 146 bishops subscribed; their names have perished, except that of Gregory of Nyssa, who openly testifies in two passages, cited by Baronius [Note: [Col. 0190D] Under the year 379], that he attended that council.

Time has deprived the Church of the acts of this synod, to great loss. Yet it is certain that Damasus’s letters were read there: both those initially sent to the Illyrians from his first Roman synod and subsequently brought to the East through Sabinus; and those written by the second and third synods, namely in 374 and at the end of 376 or the beginning of the next year, which Dorotheus the presbyter, ambassador of the Easterners, brought with him, as we have said. After these had been read, Meletius subscribed first, then Eusebius of Samosata, and afterwards all the rest, in the following words, worthy of notice:

> I agree with all the things written above, believing and thinking thus; and if anyone thinks otherwise than these things, let him be anathema.

From this one may infer both how highly all Catholics have always regarded the judgment of the Apostolic See in defining matters of faith, and also whether Bossuet’s assertion is true: that the controversy over the divinity of the Holy Spirit, which Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0191D] Book VI, chapter 21] said had been settled by the judgment of the Roman Church, was subsequently reopened at the Council of Constantinople. For, to adopt the words of the most distinguished Fr. Orsi [Note: [Col. 0191D] Book I, chapter 8, art. 2, vol. I]:

> When the whole West, all Egypt, the entire Eastern Church, and all Catholic bishops throughout the Church embraced the judgment of Damasus and of the Roman Church concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and rejected the Macedonians from ecclesial communion as manifest heretics, devoted them to curses, and assailed them with repeatedly pronounced anathemas, who could patiently endure that so solemn a judgment should seem not yet altogether fixed and irreformable, but still liable to reconsideration?

Blondel assigns to this very council the agreement which, as we have said, was made between Paulinus and Meletius and their respective parties; yet the great Baronius had written this before Blondel [Note: [Col. 0191D] Under the year 378, no. 26], and Valesius also agrees. But Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0191D] On Meletius, art. 13, no. 8], unable to believe that a reconciliation confirmed by so numerous a body of highly eminent bishops could later be annulled and treated as of no account at the Council of Constantinople, rejects Blondel’s opinion. But Tillemont’s argument is altogether weak and of no force. First, the more eminent and senior bishops who attended the Constantinopolitan synod thought with Nazianzen that nothing should be altered, as I shall say elsewhere. Secondly, if this reconciliation had not previously been approved and confirmed by the greater number of them, why did Gregory himself lament that peace had been broken by them and that covenants publicly confirmed with God as witness had been violated?

[Col. 0191D] The acts of this synod must then have been sent to Damasus by Meletius himself, since the original documents were long preserved in the archives of the Roman Church. The synodical account also teaches us this in these words:

> Meletius, upon his throne at Antioch, convened a divine and sacred synod, which, confirming the divine Creed and marking Marcellus, Photinus, and Apollinarius with anathema, sent a divine exposition to Damasus and the bishops of the West.  
> [Note: [Col. 0191D] *Synodical Account*, chapter 74.]

Who was sent to Rome I shall state under the following year; for now, a few words on the date of this synod.

III. All learned writers assign this synod to the year 379. Certainly it could not have been held earlier, because the Edessene Chronicle, published by the most learned Joseph Assemani, establishes that Eulogius, bishop of Edessa, was ordained by Eusebius of Samosata and returned at the beginning of this year to the church from which he had been expelled under Valens [Note: [Col. 0191D] *Bibliotheca Orientalis*, vol. I]. But those who assign it to September or October seem to me to assert as certain something wholly uncertain. For although Gregory of Nyssa writes that it was convened [Note: [Col. 0192D] *Life of Macrina*, vol. III, p. 187] in the ninth or tenth month after Basil’s death, when the persecution had already subsided, yet because Basil’s day of death is still disputed, nothing certain can be extracted from this.

If we believe Nazianzen [Note: [Col. 0192D] Poem 64, no. 45], Basil lived only eight years in the episcopate; or, as Nyssen says, he began his ninth. Therefore, if we count the years from his ordination—which Petavius, Tillemont, and the recent editor of Basil’s works date to 370, though the month and day are uncertain—the most holy man must have ended his life in 378, and, in my judgment, not long after Valens’s death, while Gratian ruled alone. Jerome also places Basil’s death under Gratian [Note: [Col. 0192D] *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 116].

Another very weighty consideration, if I am not mistaken, confirms this opinion. When Basil passed to heaven, Nazianzen lamented that, because of the grave and dangerous illness from which he was suffering, he had been deprived of the opportunity to kiss the holy ashes and be present to console Nyssen, to whom he writes, and their other common friends [Note: [Col. 0192D] Nazianzen, Epistle 371]. Thus he was not far from them when he wrote this, although Tillemont, Floridus, and the author of Basil’s *Life* place him then at Seleucia in Isauria and suppose that he went directly from that city to Constantinople.

Against the judgment of these highly learned men, I give greater authority to Nazianzen himself. He writes that from Seleucia, to which he had withdrawn, he returned to Nazianzus; and he complained that he found affairs wholly unchanged from the state in which he had left them. For when he had gone to Seleucia and remained there for no short time, both to devote himself to God and in hope that in the meantime a bishop would be appointed over the church of Nazianzus—whose care he had steadfastly declined—upon his return he found none of what his mind had imagined. “I fled,” he says, “but found the very troubles I thought I had escaped rising up in a great host” [Note: [Col. 0192D] Poem *On His Own Life*]: namely ecclesiastical troubles, from which he had wished to disengage himself. Nazianzen’s words are therefore entirely plain and admit no interpretation other than that attributed to them by Gregory the presbyter in his *Life of Nazianzen* and by Billius.

Accordingly, as soon as he returned to Nazianzus, efforts were again made to induce him to assume care of that church. [Col. 0193A] Since he could not be persuaded in any way, Basil and the other bishops of the province obtained at least that he should go to instruct the Catholics of the imperial city and rekindle in that church the remaining sparks of true doctrine. This is why, in his oration in praise of Basil, he declares that he undertook that burden not contrary to Basil’s judgment and will; and Gregory the presbyter understood these words in the sense that the bishop of Caesarea added spurs to Nazianzen, already running, and anointed him for this spiritual contest. But why use unnecessary arguments when he himself declares that he came to Constantinople after leaving Cappadocia?

> “There I came, having left the Cappadocian land,  
> which seems to all a bulwark of the faith.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0193D] *Poem on Bishops*, v. 94: Ἐκεῖ δ` ἐπῆλθον Καππάδοσσαν γῆν λιπὼν ἣ πίστεως ἔρεισμα τοῖς πᾶσιν δοκεῖ.]

It is therefore constant and certain that Gregory returned from Seleucia to Nazianzus and to his own people before departing for Constantinople. It remains to prove that he had not left there before Basil’s death. But this may be demonstrated from his beautiful letter to the heretical Simplicia alone.

Several years earlier Basil had ordained bishop the slave of this woman, though she neither sought nor consented to it; later, in a grave and vehement address, he restrained the woman’s fury and insults [Note: [Col. 0193D] Epistle 115]. Yet she who had not dared say anything more while Basil lived began, scarcely after his death, to threaten secular litigation and again vehemently to press for the annulment of that ordination. Gregory, to whom the matron wrote about this matter, thought she should be soothed with the gentlest language. He first praised her for speaking most honourably of Basil, then recently deceased; then, turning to the matter itself, he begged her not to strip the Church, enriched by that excellent bishop as by a gift, of its possession. She would earn greater praise by assenting to what had been done without her counsel than if she had previously acquiesced when asked.

If she demanded that the slave who had administered her property should render accounts, Gregory says that her demand was equitable. But if she insisted that he be deposed as unworthy of the priesthood, he replied in the name of the bishops of the province:

> We do not dismiss without investigation any other person accused of some offence, nor shall we dismiss this man. But if anyone has anything with which to accuse him, then in your presence—and, if you wish, with you also acting as judge; otherwise even in your absence—after he has been examined **BY US AS JUDGES**, if he is found innocent, he shall be acquitted even though he is a slave; but if convicted, he shall be condemned.  
> [Note: [Col. 0193D] Epistle 38.]

[Col. 0193D] Nazianzen, then, had not yet moved a foot from Cappadocia when, shortly after Basil’s death, he wrote this letter to Simplicia and offered himself as judge in this matter together with the other bishops of that province. This further explains why, being nearby, he needed to justify himself to Nyssen, Basil’s brother, for not having attended Basil’s funeral. If Gregory came to Constantinople after Basil’s death, and if he administered that church for nearly a full three years [Note: [Col. 0194D] *Poem on Bishops*, v. 101, τοῦτ᾿ ἔτος τρίτον, “this is the third year”], and finally left it when the middle of 381 had scarcely passed, Basil cannot have lived until the Kalends of January 379. His day of death must accordingly be assigned to 378, and to July or August.

The arguments by which the contrary view is ordinarily defended can readily be overthrown, and other arguments might in turn be adduced which seem to establish both that Basil’s death cannot be tied to 379 and that this Antiochene council must be brought back by at least some months. But since, for present purposes, it makes no difference which opinion one chooses, I shall refrain from superfluous labour and proceed to other matters.

## CHAPTER XV. 380, THE FIFTEENTH YEAR OF DAMASUS, CONSULS GRATIAN AUGUSTUS V AND THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS

I. Law 2 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Catholic Faith*, is cited and examined. II. Acacius, bishop of Beroea in Syria, comes to Rome, apparently as Meletius’s envoy with the acts of the Antiochene synod; another reason is given for this journey of Acacius—namely, that the agreement made at Antioch between Meletius and Paulinus might be confirmed. III. A synod under Damasus, by which that agreement was ratified, Meletius received into full communion, and letters written to Theodosius that he might never permit it to be broken. IV. The other celebrated letter of Damasus to Paulinus is discussed and shown to have been written by this synod. At what earliest time did the Pneumatomachi begin to be called Macedonians? V. A passage of Pope Vigilius is examined, from which Ambrose’s presence at this council is established.

[Col. 0194B]

[Col. 0194C] I. In this year, on the third day before the Kalends of March, the famous law 2, *On the Catholic Faith*, was issued at the recommendation of Acholius, perhaps after he had required from Theodosius a testimony to his sincere faith before admitting him to the baptism which, being ill, he had requested. The reason for which Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0194D] Book VII, chapter 4] says that this law was issued also clearly shows what the emperor meant when he recalled his subjects to the religion which the divine apostle Peter had handed down to the Romans, which Pope Damasus was known to follow, and which Peter, bishop of Alexandria, also followed: namely, that his Eastern subjects, divided among diverse sects, might at last understand whither they could turn, so as no longer to waver in faith—to the Roman Church, that is, which the divine Peter had established in the faith, and to its supreme bishop Damasus, whom the Basilika books call in this passage the successor of that same apostle [Note: [Col. 0194D] Δάμασος ὁ καὶ διάδοχος αὐτοῦ δοξάσει: “Damasus, who is also reputed his successor”], and to Peter of Alexandria.

But when Peter is mentioned, why does Theodosius make no mention of the Alexandrian church? Surely not because Peter’s Alexandrian church had then departed from the faith—by no means. Rather, it was so that they might understand how great was the difference between the one church and the other, and between their respective bishops; and that this church, joined to its head, could not err, whereas the other could and did. Hence Peter of Alexandria was put before the Easterners as an example to follow for no other reason than that, since he was joined in manifest communion with Damasus and the Roman Church, there could be no doubt that he professed the true faith.

Therefore those are proved mistaken who, overwhelmed by the force of reason and Scripture, exempt the Roman Church from the danger of error, but do not think the same of the Roman bishop—as though members without a head could make a perfect body, or as though there could be principal and outstanding endowments in the body that were not the head’s and did not derive from the head. But lest I wander outside my field, consult Orsi, who treats this matter excellently [Note: [Col. 0195D] Vol. III, book XV, art. 2]; I return to my subject.

II. In the preceding chapter I said that Meletius had sent the acts of the synod held by him at Antioch. We must now inquire who carried them and in what year.

Alexander of Hierapolis writes the following to Acacius, bishop of Beroea in Syria:

> Your Holiness knows, as you once wrote to me in a letter, that at Rome, in the presence of the holy and blessed bishop Damasus, while Your Holiness was present, the question of Apollinarius’s heresy was raised. And when we confessed two natures, so as not to attribute suffering to the divinity, those who belonged to Apollinarius said that we declared two Sons.  
> [Note: [Col. 0195D] In Lupus, Epistle 57, to the Council of Ephesus, Works, vol. VII.]

After quoting these words, Pagius continues: “Lupus, in his scholia on that letter, thinks that this refers to the third Roman synod, which he believes was held in 375. But, as Baluzius notes on the same passage, Acacius was not yet then a bishop. Up to this point I have been unable to discover whether Acacius [Col. 0195C] came to the West at the end of this year 378 or in 382, when another Roman synod was held” [Note: [Col. 0195D] Under the year 378, from nos. 17–18].

I, however, think that Acacius came to Rome neither in 378 nor in 382. As to the former year, it is established that he was ordained bishop near its end by St. Eusebius of Samosata, when Eusebius returned to his church after Valens’s death [Note: [Col. 0195D] Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 3]. Thus anyone will readily affirm with Baluzius that he could not have attended the Roman synod which most people vainly maintain was convened in that year, as stated above.

What prevents us from saying that Acacius went to Rome in 382 is that Damasus and with him all the Western bishops charged Theodore of Tarsus and Acacius of Beroea with wrongdoing for ordaining Flavian while Paulinus survived, and regarded them as excommunicated [Note: [Col. 0196D] Sozomen, book VII, chapter 11]. It could scarcely have happened, therefore, that only a few months after that ordination, while matters and tempers were still inflamed, Acacius would have wished to go to a Roman synod, appear before Damasus and all the Western bishops, and have been able to take a place among them. Hence his name is not read among the three bishops whom Theodoret says the Easterners, assembled again at Constantinople in that year, [Col. 0196A] sent to Damasus [Note: [Col. 0196D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 8], nor is he mentioned in the letters then written.

But if we attend to the reasons why Acacius could and should have been sent to Rome, both the time when he went there and the year of the synod he attended can be determined without much difficulty. Two reasons may be adduced. The first was that Meletius might inform Damasus and the Western bishops concerning the agreement by which the division between himself and Paulinus, together with the Catholics of both parties, had been removed, and thereby secure full and open communion with the Apostolic See for himself and his followers; also, that this agreement might be held ratified and unshaken by the authority of the same see. For Meletius could not have been ignorant that sacred canons prohibited two bishops in one [Col. 0196B] city, and he understood well that these canons must remain in force unless, for grave reasons, the supreme head of the Church judged otherwise.

The second, and entirely just, reason was to bring the acts of the Antiochene synod to the same Apostolic See, so that Damasus might be made fully aware of Meletius’s faith and that of the Easterners in communion with him, and of their obedience to the dogmas defined by Damasus; and thereby become more favourably disposed both toward this bishop of Antioch and toward all the others whose faith had previously been viewed with suspicion. The synodical account fairly clearly indicates this reason in the words cited in the preceding chapter, when it says that Meletius sent the exposition of the same Antiochene synod to Damasus and the Westerners. This is far more probable than Valesius’s assertion [Note: [Col. 0196D] On Theodoret, book V, chapter 3] that Damasus sent delegates to Antioch to attend that synod, and that they subsequently carried the acts back to Rome for deposit in the archives.

III. Since this is so, the bishop of Beroea could have come to Rome at no more fitting time than this year, after the Antiochene synod had been completed, whose acts he brought. While he was present at Rome, the fourth synod under Damasus was held, which Alexander of Hierapolis mentions and at which he was present. The Apollinarians also attended; it is highly probable that, after the Antiochene synod which had condemned them, they left the East for Rome in order to clear themselves and, in the manner of heretics, to continue defending their bad cause.

This, indeed, is the very synod which the synodical account reports as convened by Damasus after Valens’s death, in these words:

> But when Valens had fought against the Goths in Thrace, he was consumed by fire and passed to eternal fire. After Valentinian also had died, his son Gratian recalled the pious bishops from exile, at which time blessed Damasus also convened at Rome a sacred synod against Arians, Pneumatomachi, and many other heretics.  
> [Note: [Col. 0196D] Chapter 72.]

We should not suppose either that the supreme pontiff summoned innumerable bishops from the scattered parts of Italy, or that they could have been present in those first turbulent times after Valens’s death. But once peace and security had been restored to the Church, they were all able, with greater freedom and benefit to religion, to discharge their duty.

Meletius obtained the richest fruit which he had proposed to himself from that embassy. Damasus both ratified the agreement by which the Antiochene schism had been removed and received Meletius himself into full communion no less than Paulinus. This is established both because Acacius, sent by Meletius, attended the synod under Damasus, and because the acts and subscriptions which he had brought from the Antiochene council were deposited in the archive of the Roman Church. The same points are further established by Gregory Nazianzen and by the letters of the Council of Aquileia, to which discussion will return under the following year.

Moreover, so that nothing might later disturb affairs thus settled, Ambrose, I think, and the other bishops then gathered at Rome, prudently foreseeing what later happened, wrote to Theodosius that, in accordance with the agreement of the parties, upon one’s death the church should remain with the survivor, and that no second superordination should be attempted. No one who has read the other surviving letters of the Council of Aquileia will at least deny that this letter was written before the Aquileian council. Nor can one readily devise any other or more fitting occasion, or a gathering of Italian bishops, than this one from which such a letter could have been written.

[Col. 0197C] IV. I further believe that the celebrated confession of faith addressed to Paulinus, which we print again as number four, proceeded from this fourth synod under Damasus. Theodoret, Pope Vigilius, the author of the synodical account, and other ancient writers assert that it was synodical. Hence Valesius [Note: [Col. 0197D] On Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 11] thinks it was written at the synod held by Damasus in 382 and sent to Paulinus, who, returning to the East, had stopped at Thessalonica. But there is no reason why it should have been sent to Paulinus when it could have been handed to him personally there and then.

Pagius, therefore, on the authority of the same synodical account, assigns it to the synod which he thinks was assembled after Valens’s death in 378 [Note: [Col. 0197D] Under the year 378, no. 19]; Hardouin, however, to 379. But if, as I have already observed, there is no sound reason to construe the synodical account’s words so narrowly, the person who assigns both that synod and the definition of the divine chapters to this year will come nearer the truth. Several considerations, in my view, further confirm that opinion.

First, Alexander of Hierapolis establishes that, at the synod attended by Acacius, the Apollinarians reproached the Catholics with asserting two Sons because they professed two natures in Christ the Lord. I therefore think that, in order thereafter to remove this occasion for calumny, Damasus then anathematized those who assert TWO Sons, one before the ages, [Col. 0198A] and the other after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin.

Second. Since that exposition of faith seems to have proscribed all heresies that had arisen up to that day, why is no mention made of Priscillian’s monstrous opinions? Would Damasus perhaps have passed over in silence either Priscillian himself or his notorious heresy, and failed to frame a deserved condemnation, had these matters become known to him? I shall not allow myself to be persuaded of this; rather, I shall believe that that rule of faith was written before that heretic came to Rome, and thus before the year 381, when it is established that, having been condemned by the Council of Caesaraugusta, he hastened to the City, as I shall relate.

Third. The following words of Damasus from the fourth anathema deserve notice: “We anathematize the Macedonians, [Col. 0198B] who, coming from the stock of Arius, changed not their perfidy but their name.” I think no one can be ignorant who the Macedonians are whom Damasus here identifies; but it must be investigated at what time those who attacked the divinity of the Holy Spirit first came to be called by this name, derived from Macedonius, the leader of the sect. To attain this more easily, three periods must be distinguished and observed: first, the period from the death of Constantius to the Synod of Lampsacus, assembled in 364, or before the close of the following year; second, the period from that synod to the death of the Emperor Valens; and finally, the period following Valens’ death.

After Constantius died, the Semi-Arians, defenders of *ousia* [substance], who had returned to their sees through the indulgence of the new emperor, began freely to assemble, [Col. 0198C] to bind themselves to one another in a closer alliance, once more openly to execrate and curse the Arians or Acacians. On this occasion Macedonius, who had already gone over to those same Semi-Arians, had been deposed with them in the irregular conventicle at Constantinople, and had hidden himself on an estate near that city, emerged from concealment and came forth publicly. Sending an embassy to the leaders of the Semi-Arians, he added his strength to theirs and brought it about not merely that they stubbornly retained the *homoiousion* [“like in substance”], but also that they excluded the Holy Spirit from divinity and placed him among created things. This heresy was accordingly professed by Silvanus, Eleusius, Eustathius, Sophronius, and all who had been deposed at Constantinople by the Acacians, and afterwards also by some who were otherwise sound in their doctrine concerning the Son. [Col. 0198D] These facts are established from Socrates, Sozomen, Gregory Nazianzen, and other writers of those times; it is superfluous to cite their statements here. [Note: [Col. 0198D] See Socrates, book II, ch. 45; Sozomen, book IV, ch. 27.]

That heresy, moreover, did not long remain concealed, as we infer from the Alexandrian synod which condemned it, and from Athanasius’s letters to Serapion. But Socrates says that those who professed it were THEN called Pneumatomachians [fighters against the Spirit], the designation “Macedonians” not yet having arisen. The writings of those times add no slight force to Socrates’s testimony: in them the term Pneumatomachians is continual, while Macedonians does not occur at all.

Meanwhile Jovian died; and under Valens a Synod of Lampsacus was held by the Semi-Arians. [Col. 0199A] It decreed that all acts done by the Arians at Ariminum and Constantinople should be void; that the Antiochene formula of the Dedication Synod and the *homoiousion* should be tenaciously maintained and everywhere received; and that the Acacians and Eudoxians should be granted room for repentance, or otherwise be deposed anew. Thereupon, by the command of Valens, who had attached himself to Eudoxius, arose that dreadful persecution of Catholics as well as of those same Semi-Arians. It induced them to send those three men—Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus—as envoys to Liberius and the Westerners, in order that they might profess the Nicene faith and request communion in the common name of all the rest.

Accordingly, they were received by him into the full communion of the Catholic Church, as appears from the surviving [Col. 0199B] letters of Liberius himself. Basil also frequently mentions the matter in his letters; but we read the account set out carefully in Socrates and Sozomen. [Note: [Col. 0199D] Socrates, book IV, ch. 12; Sozomen, book VI, ch. 11.] Moreover, these writers constantly call those Semi-Arians “Macedonians” by a kind of anticipation, so that we may understand the force of the term to be one and the same.

From the year 366, when these things occurred, until Valens gained control in the East, there was no distinction between Semi-Arian and Catholic bishops, and no use of that term, since all were regarded as brethren. For if any, together with Eunomius, excluded the Holy Spirit from divinity, they were still called solely Pneumatomachians, as before. At what time, then, did this term first begin to be used? At this Roman synod and by Damasus in this very year. For after Valens had died, [Col. 0199C] Gratian, compelled by the necessity of circumstances and times, enacted a law permitting everyone to profess whichever religion he wished, except Manichaeans, Photinians, and Eunomians. [Note: [Col. 0199D] Socrates, book V, ch. 24; Sozomen, book VII, ch. 2.] Those Semi-Arians began to hold separate assemblies apart from the Catholics; and, in a conventicle held at Antioch in Caria, they decreed that the word “consubstantial” must be rejected and that there must be no communion whatever with those who professed the Nicene faith.

This public and repeated profession of their old heresy, and their separation from the Catholics, must therefore be regarded as the first origin and cause of this anathema. Since that conventicle certainly cannot be dated later than the year 379, we plainly discover also that the anathema itself—in which the Pneumatomachians were first called Macedonians from Macedonius, the leader of the heresy—could have been publicly issued and proclaimed to the Catholic Church not long afterward. Hence Nazianzen, when he was administering the Church of Constantinople and delivered, in that year or the next, the discourse called the Fifth Theological Oration, calls the question concerning the Holy Spirit long since crushed and extinguished, removed and expelled from the faith; and he therefore laments and groans that it was then being revived. From that time the term “Macedonians” was used everywhere. Theodosius employs it in law 11, promulgated on 22 July 383, and afterwards in [Col. 0200A] laws 12 and 13 of the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*; and in the age of Socrates and Sozomen those heretics were called by no other name.

These facts being so, Quesnel [Note: [Col. 0199D] Dissertation 14.] and others must be mistaken in joining this letter to another which concerns Vitalis, and in considering them to be a single letter of Damasus to Paulinus, consisting of two parts. For, to omit the rest, the different causes and dates of composition prove the two letters to be separate letters of the same pope to the same Paulinus. As regards time, this one could scarcely have been written before this year, whereas the other was already known to Basil in 375. This one was sent to Thessalonica; the other, to Antioch. Further, this one is synodical, while the other is familiar or personal. Finally, since Vitalis was accused on account of the single heresy of Apollinaris, there was no reason why he should have been compelled to renounce so many heresies from which he was alien.

Thus it is not surprising that Paulinus himself did not use this letter before Epiphanius to clear himself of the charge of Sabellianism which Vitalis in turn cast against him, but proved himself Catholic by the profession of faith which he had long before presented to Athanasius. [Note: [Col. 0200D] See Epiphanius, *Heresy* 77, no. 20.] For in 376, when Epiphanius recounts the matter as having occurred in his presence, Paulinus had not yet received this full exposition from Damasus which he could profess.

Pope Celestine therefore rightly distinguishes two letters of Damasus to Paulinus when he writes: “My predecessor Damasus, writing to Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Antioch, says among other things: ‘We anathematize those who assert two sons of God, one who [Col. 0200C] was begotten of the Father before the ages, and another who was born from the Virgin by the assumption of flesh.’” These words are taken from the first letter. He then proceeds: “Likewise, the same Damasus, a man of apostolic memory, in another letter to Paulinus: ‘We anathematize those who confess two sons in the Savior, one before the Incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin, and not the same Son of God both before and after.’” The Code of Canons of the Church of Spain, recently excellently elucidated by the distinguished Joseph Cennio, likewise counts a double letter of Damasus and distinguishes one from the other.

## V.

Above I said that that celebrated exposition of faith was written in a synod of bishops by Damasus, and to prove this I cited the testimony of Pope Vigilius. But I must quote his words, since further matters relevant to illuminating the history may also be inferred from them. Here they are, from his earlier constitution: [Note: [Col. 0200D] Constitution for the condemnation of the Three Chapters, 26, Venice edition of the Councils, vol. VI.] “Having examined the synodical decrees of our predecessor Damasus of blessed memory, which were issued after the Nicene Council when the Catholic bishops assembled and conferred in the city of Rome concerning the Holy Spirit, together with Ambrose of blessed memory, bishop of the city of Milan, I found it most fully determined that those who affirm two Sons, one before the ages and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin, were struck with the punishment of anathema.” These words are taken from the sixth anathema.

First, therefore, we understand that this council, [Col. 0201A] by which that anathema was promulgated, is precisely the one in which bishops assembled after Nicaea, discussed the Holy Spirit, and also added material concerning him. The numerous chapters bearing on his divinity and worship abundantly prove this to be entirely true. Nor am I moved from this view by the fact that, at the beginning of the same exposition, it is written not “we added” but “they added,” which word indicates another council held at an earlier time. For since the beginning of the Damasian exposition is different in Theodoret, the portions which he omits show us that, according to the differing judgment of copyists, an opening was added; it must not be considered part of that same exposition.

What is more important, moreover, is that from this passage of Vigilius we learn that Ambrose was present at this council. This can be confirmed by two further arguments. First, because his letter to the Emperor Gratian, of which I shall speak in the following chapter, makes certain that very many bishops from widely dispersed parts of Italy attended this Roman council, there is no reason to exclude the bishop of Milan from their number. Second, that letter may consequently be considered the work of Ambrose himself, whatever the Benedictine editors may have thought.

Paulinus certainly records only one journey of Ambrose to Rome, placing it several years after his ordination; Tillemont and the Benedictine editors therefore assign it to 382. But if anyone attends to Paulinus’s words, he will extract nothing supporting their opinion more than ours, namely, that Ambrose came to Rome both in this year, on the occasion of the council then summoned by Damasus, [Col. 0201C] and in 382, in order to attend the other council as well. Paulinus likewise mentions only one embassy of Ambrose to Maximus. Shall we therefore say that the other embassy—of which Ambrose himself is witness in the oration delivered at Valentinian’s funeral—is false? I know that the great Baronius writes that Ambrose himself went to Sirmium in this year to ordain Avemius bishop; but whatever the truth of that may be, nothing prevents both journeys from having been conveniently accomplished.

## VI.

It remains to give the reason why this letter, according to Theodoret’s testimony, was sent to Thessalonica. Anyone will readily judge that Damasus gave it to his friend Acholius, so that it might be delivered to Paulinus, who was on his journey to Rome and would pass through that city, from which navigation to Italy was easy and readily available. [Col. 0201D]

Since Jerome came to Rome with Paulinus himself and Epiphanius, [Note: [Col. 0201D] Letter 127, no. 5, Verona edition.] he must have joined himself to both at the imperial city, to which he had gone in the preceding year after receiving holy orders at Antioch. Polybius—the author to whom Papebroch assigns the supplement to the Life of Epiphanius—writes that Epiphanius came to Constantinople at the emperor’s summons in order to sail to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0201D] Under 12 May.] I use this testimony, although he writes that Epiphanius undertook this journey on an entirely different occasion and at another time; for, since he errs in those points, the journey itself, which is confirmed from elsewhere, must not be rejected, but assigned to its proper [Col. 0202A] time and cause.

I therefore think that Paulinus of Antioch also came there, both because that city lay on the overland route from Antioch to Rome and because he wished to see his Jerome, then residing in that city. Indeed, when I read Gregory’s thirteenth oration and see him treating splendidly of the recently ended Antiochene schism, warmly praising two bishops of the same city and placing them in equal honor, I suspect that Paulinus had enjoyed familiar acquaintance with Nazianzen in that city, no less than Jerome and Meletius himself had done, before departing from it.

# CHAPTER XVI

I. The letter of the Roman council to Gratian, published by Sirmond in the appendix to the Theodosian Code, is considered, explained, and assigned to this very council. II. It is compared with the letter of the Council of Aquileia, in order to understand why the Fathers of this Roman council then wrote in Damasus’s defense against Ursicinus; why, further, this same letter should be considered written in this year and attributed to Ambrose. III. It is shown that Damasus was never accused of adultery; and the rashness and ignorance of the anonymous Amsterdam writer are noted.

[Col. 0202B]

## I.

Moreover, I think that the letter to Gratian and Valentinian which Sirmond published in the name of the Roman council [Note: [Col. 0202D] Appendix to the Theodosian Code, Works, vol. I, p. 422, Verona edition.], and which we subsequently read both in the Venetian edition of the Councils and among the letters of Damasus printed by Coustant, must be referred to this council. We have already given, in chapters 13 and 15, the reasons why it cannot be referred to [Col. 0202C] the year 378, as most suppose. It remains to say why we judge it should be attached to this year and council; and I shall more readily achieve this by explaining the letter itself.

The Fathers of this council therefore praise the piety of the emperors and their benefits conferred upon the Church and religion. They particularly commend as necessary for restoring the body of the Church, then divided into factions through Ursinus’s frenzy, the decree that, after Ursinus had been expelled and his associates separated from his communion, the Roman bishop should examine the remaining priests of the churches, so that the pontiff of religion, with his fellow-bishops, might judge concerning religion. The memory of this rescript issued by Valentinian at the beginning of the schism survives nowhere except in this passage.

Yet they lament that this benefit, which they regard as especially important, had so far lacked effect because of Ursinus. Although he had been banished beyond the suburban regions and forbidden access to the City, he nevertheless continually tried, through those whom he had sacrilegiously ordained, to stir up the people and induce the populace to abandon Damasus and their duty. Thus, they say, certain other bishops, stirred by this very bad precedent as if by a kind of authority, no longer gave any place to Damasus’s judgment or authority; and matters had reached such a point that those who either knew themselves to have been condemned by him, or justly feared that they would be condemned, purchased crowds of the populace by which they terrified and drove away judges. By this means, the more criminal any man was, the safer he seemed and the more certain of retaining a church unjustly.

They write that this is clearly observable in the bishop of Parma and Florentius of Puteoli. The bishop of Parma, though condemned by the judgment of Damasus and his synod, nevertheless shamelessly retained his church. They suppress this bishop of Parma’s name; but, if Ughelli is to be believed, he was Philip, a Roman by birth, and for that reason might have been drawn into Ursinus’s party and then deposed by Damasus. Florentius [Note: [Col. 0203D] Florentius’s name is read among those who subscribed against Athanasius at the Council of Milan, but the location of his church is not added. See Baronius under the year 355, no. 22.] of Puteoli had likewise been condemned. He afterwards fled to the emperor and was, quite rightly, expelled; but with the greatest audacity, in the sixth year after his deposition [Col. 0203B] he had crept back into the city, was pressing upon the church, and had stirred up many disturbances in that town.

From this it may be inferred without obscurity that this letter itself was written in the year to which I have assigned it. For if Florentius had crept back into the church after the sixth year from his expulsion from it, this chronological mark directs us both to the year 374 and to the synod which we said was assembled at Rome in that year, and to this very synod which we maintain was convened in the present year. Accordingly, in Gratian’s rescript, of which the discussion will return under the following year, where it was formerly read that Florentius, after the fifteenth year, was again attempting to defile the church from which he had been expelled, Blondel saw that the passage was corrupt and rightly judged that one should read not, as formerly, “after the fifteenth,” but “only after the fifth year.” Pagius and others made the same observation.

[Col. 0203C] Among those who had evaded priestly judgment in order not to be condemned, they accuse Restitutus, a bishop in Africa. Ordered by Gratian to plead his case before the synod, they say that he fled with a savage band of insolent men. Who that Restitutus was, or bishop of what church, can scarcely be conjectured amid the many bishops of this period, name, and region; among them we also know there was one who, with the other delegates of the Council of Ariminum, gave the hand of perfidy at Nice in Thrace. What may be asserted with certainty is this: either several bishops from Africa were present at this Roman synod, or a report of the matter was sent to Damasus according to custom, so that he might write back what needed to be done.

Throughout the same Africa Gratian had also ordered sacrilegious rebaptizers to be expelled. But after being expelled, they sacrilegiously ordained Claudianus and sent him to Rome to preside over the Montenses as though he were their bishop. The emperor ordered him to leave Rome and return to his homeland. But, though often placed under restraint, he still remained, contemptuous of judgments and imperial rescripts, enticing the poorer people with money and rebaptizing those whom he had bought. Optatus has transmitted to us remembrance of this Claudianus, [Col. 0204A] from whom we learn that he presided over these same Donatists at Rome after Macrobius, who was living around the year 370, at the time when Optatus was composing his work, and after Lucianus, who had succeeded Macrobius; and that he survived into the times of Siricius. [Note: [Col. 0204D] Book II, no. 4.]

Moreover, when you hear the rebaptizers in this place called “sacrilegious,” you will readily understand who those sacrilegious persons were by whom this same letter below says that Sylvester was accused, and you will recognize the reason for his accusation. They were the Donatists, whom no one will deny were rightly called sacrilegious *par excellence*, and were frequently designated by that name even by the emperors themselves. [Note: [Col. 0204D] Books II and IV, *On Not Repeating Holy Baptism*.] Therefore, when the Fathers of this Roman council write that Sylvester was accused by the sacrilegious—that is, by the Donatists—they indicate the false charge of *traditio* [handing over sacred books] and offering incense, concerning which we know from Augustine that he, together with Melchiades, Marcellus, and Marcellinus, presbyters, was accused with the utmost wickedness. [Col. 0204B] The aim was to establish that they had been condemned without right by one who could not be their judge; this is also the reason why Lupus and Noris consider the Synod of Sinuessa to have been foisted upon them. [Note: [Col. 0204D] Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, ch. 16.]

From this we further learn that that supreme head of the Church wished to clear himself before the emperor, in order to free the Church itself from the difficulties into which the sacrilegious had labored to cast it through their foul calumny. Since it is certain that Sylvester was accused by the Donatists, and since the cause of that calumnious accusation is further manifest, there is no sound reason why Floridus and Coustant should not have judged this to be the cause, seeking another with quite useless labor.

[Col. 0204C] Next, when they write in this passage that Claudianus was ordained by those who had been expelled, understand this as those expelled from the churches. Gratian had ordered the Donatists expelled throughout Africa from no place other than the churches which they occupied, so that these might be restored to the Catholics, as plainly appears from law II of the Theodosian Code, *On Not Repeating Holy Baptism*. Since this law was issued on 17 November 377 and Claudianus’s ordination was later than its promulgation, you now see that neither this letter of the Roman council nor Gratian’s rescript, which is to be considered next, can have been issued in 378, as most wrongly suppose.

For Claudianus could not have been ordained immediately after that law was promulgated, nor did he come to Rome at once. Again, he was not discovered immediately upon reaching Rome. Then a letter had to be written to the emperor and rescripts awaited ordering his expulsion. When these finally arrived, he still did not depart; but, disregarding and despising the judgments, rescripts, and chains by which he had often been restrained, he had obstinately remained before this letter was written and was still remaining. If we allow time for all this to occur, two years can scarcely seem excessive.

I do not deny [Col. 0205A] that this law, addressed to Flavianus, vicar of Africa, mentions another addressed to Nitentius, said to have been issued long before. But that issued to Nitentius, if carefully considered, concerns only the confiscation of estates and houses in which heretics held forbidden assemblies; it says absolutely nothing about expelling Donatists from the churches they occupied. Since it was customary for heretics expelled from churches and sacred places to hold profane assemblies wherever they could—as is established by several laws of the Theodosian Code [Note: [Col. 0205D] See books III, IV, and V, *On Heretics*.] and other writers—Gratian, to deprive the Donatists themselves, like other heretics, of this opportunity, employed the precedent of the law which he had earlier prescribed to Nitentius. He ordered the confiscation of large houses and estates in [Col. 0205B] which those sacrilegious men, expelled from the churches at the same time, might happen to rage in secret frenzy. But now let us return to the letter of this council.

Having therefore set before Gratian these injuries to Church and religion, the blame for which they lay upon the Ursinians, they further warn him in these words:

> “Thus at last Ursinus’s faction made such progress that, after they had suborned the Jew Isaac, the life of our holy brother Damasus was sought, the blood of innocents was shed, and plots were devised. Against these your piety’s providence, plainly by divine prompting, took action. The Church was almost stripped of all its ministries—namely through this fraud: while he who had been appointed judge over all pleaded his own case, there would be no one able to judge concerning fallen persons or certainly the factious invaders of bishoprics.”

Some writers infer and understand these words to mean that Damasus had then recently been accused by Isaac and shortly before acquitted by the emperors. They also inquire of what crime this most holy pontiff was then charged; and, moved by the flimsiest conjectures, they say that he was falsely accused of adultery. I, however, think that this passage deals not with some new accusation devised and brought against Damasus again, but only recalls those old calumnies and plots which Rufinus also indicates. The purpose was that Gratian, considering what the Ursinian faction had dared in the first storms of the controversy, might see how necessary it was for him too to beware of them in the future. For if the Ursinians devised schemes against Damasus [Col. 0205D] so that, once he had been brought among the accused, there would be no one able to judge the factious invaders of bishoprics, it necessarily follows that the matter here concerns a plot wickedly contrived before the factious invaders of bishoprics—namely Ursinus and his associates—were condemned by an assembled synod. This, we said, occurred in 369 and afterwards. It follows that all these events are recalled to Gratian for the purpose of preventing his being deceived by them and of more readily persuading him to grant the requests in this letter, as suited to destroying their future plots.

What the Fathers of this Roman council request of Gratian, in light of the circumstances of the time, consists chiefly of two things.

1. That anyone condemned by the judgment of Damasus and his synod, who unjustly wished to retain a church or, when summoned to priestly judgment, refused to appear, should be summoned to Rome by the prefects of the praetorium of Italy or by the vicar. In distant regions, he should be brought by local judges for examination before the metropolitan; but if the metropolitan himself had already been condemned or was contumacious, he should be publicly ordered to proceed to Rome or before those judges whom the bishop of Rome appointed.
