If this were done, it would necessarily follow that those deposed would be excluded from the boundaries of the city in which they had exercised the priesthood, [Col. 0206B] so that they could not again usurp what had lawfully been taken from them.

2. That Damasus should not be subject to public courts; rather, if any cases arose, they should thereafter be brought before a synod of bishops, to which he himself would voluntarily submit. For it seemed unjust that the bishop of Rome, who excelled all others by the prerogative of the Apostolic See, should be deprived of the right enjoyed by other bishops. [Note: [Col. 0205D] Ambrose again employed this same rescript of Valentinian the Elder when writing to Valentinian the son in the matter of not surrendering the basilicas, Letter 21; see that passage and compare it with this one, if you wish.]

If Gratian commanded the first, considerable authority and splendor would necessarily accrue to the Roman pontiff, and provision would be made against the audacity and rashness of the bishops of Parma and Puteoli, and of similar men who might thereafter be deposed. If he granted the second, he would close the door against future calumnies and plots of the Ursinians and other factious persons.

Nor, they say, is there any reason why Gratian should suspect that this was being requested for Damasus through some evil design, in order to withdraw him from the severity of secular courts. For they requested it after a sentence had been pronounced in his favor, and after his innocence and integrity had already been proved and proclaimed by the judgment of Valentinian his father. Therefore Gratian himself could not be unaware what might thereafter be expected of a man of recognized holiness. Damasus could not seem to be taking refuge among priests in order to evade public courts, but rather to share in the benefit conferred upon all bishops. Further, provision was made lest any calumniator who might again arise—while vainly attacking a man sufficiently protected by innocence before secular judges—should at least succeed in inflicting an injury upon religion through the tortures and vexations [Col. 0206D] of sacred ministers, as had happened on another occasion, though Damasus himself was otherwise unharmed and secure through his integrity.

Finally, lest they leave any room for that suspicion, and in order to prove that Damasus, whom they call a holy man, was willing rather to yield something of his own right than arrogate anything to himself, they ask Gratian that, if Damasus did not wish his cases to be heard by a synod of bishops, the emperor himself should take them to himself and to his consistory. They promise that Damasus would attend there, following the example of Sylvester. [Col. 0207A] They ask this only on the condition that the emperor first examine whether the case is honorable, just, and plausible; then distinguish and set out the questions to be examined—that is, specify and write out distinctly the points falling under inquiry; commit the inquiry itself to a judge, but reserve to himself the discretion of judgment. [Note: [Col. 0207D] See law XXX, *On Appeals*, Theodosian Code.]

What they hope will follow from this is that no depraved or infamous person will thereafter have unlawful opportunity either to accuse the chief priest or to give testimony against him. Such persons usually find access to the emperor more difficult and more perilous than access to ordinary judges. Indeed, this had been added to the misfortunes of the time: calumnious accusers of bishops went unpunished. To remove them from this mad license, Constantius had ordered that they should again be examined before other bishops, by the issuance of law XII of the Theodosian Code, *On Bishops*.

One might inquire here what law the Fathers of the council refer to in these words of the letter: “Certainly let your Clemency first examine the case, and, should a question arise, distinguish the matters to be investigated, so that, as YOU DEIGNED TO DECIDE LONG AGO, the account of acts performed by the judge may be sought, but the discretion of the sentence not claimed.” There can be no doubt that they refer to some law suited to the matter then under discussion; indeed, two laws are found in the Theodosian Code that are not at all unrelated to it.

One is Valentinian the Elder’s law to Praetextatus, prefect of the City, issued in 367; the other is Gratian’s law to the Senate, read under the consulship of Valens for the fifth time and Valentinian—that is, in 376. The first orders that when senators are summoned on a criminal charge and a more severe penalty is to be imposed upon them, the emperor’s decision must be sought after a preliminary report. [Col. 0207C] Theodosian Code, law X, *On Punishments*. The second establishes that ordinary judges have authority to conduct the investigation and hear the criminal cases of senators, but must decide nothing concerning punishment; preserving the person’s full legal status, they must refer the matter either to the emperor or to the illustrious authorities, namely the prefects of the City and of the praetorium. Theodosian Code, law XIII, *On Accusations*.

I would therefore think that the words cited refer to the latter rather than the former. Valentinian the father had not permitted ordinary judges even this simple inquiry, as is clear from law II of the Theodosian Code, *On Producing Accused Persons*. Accordingly, this letter must have been written no earlier than 380. For if, as others suppose, it is believed to have been written in 378, the law promulgated less than two full years earlier, which would seem rather recent, could by no possible reasoning have been called by those bishops a law enacted “long ago.”

II. But to what end did this Roman council wish to recall to Gratian those old calumnies and intrigues? Assuredly with the best and wisest purpose. For Ursinus and Valens of Petovio had at that time met at Milan in a partnership of crime, and were secretly devising plans by which the peace of the Church might be disturbed, as is plainly evident from the letter written in the following year by the Council of Aquileia to the same Gratian. [Col. 0208A] The Fathers of the Roman council, therefore—and above all Ambrose, under whose eyes these events were taking place—fearing lest from that most wicked conspiracy some injury might again be done to Damasus or harm be brought upon ecclesiastical tranquillity, judged that the emperor ought to be reminded of the former frauds of the Ursinian faction, in order thereby to rescue Damasus from the snares which perhaps they were laying for him. For this very reason, and—as Ambrose himself says—not only foreseeing the future, but also shuddering at past events perpetrated by Ursinus’s rashness, the Council of Aquileia judged that Gratian himself should again be petitioned not to allow anything from that turbulent and restless head to steal its way upon him. Since this is so, it is clear both that the same wheel was being turned in this Roman and in the Aquileian council, [Col. 0208B] and that the reason is evident why I have assigned this Roman council and its letter to Gratian to this year.

For Valens, the pseudo-bishop of Petovio, with whom Ursinus had entered into a compact to disturb the peace of the Church, could scarcely have come to Milan before the year 379. For, late in the year 378, he had joined the Goths, who, after Valens’s defeat, had broken into Illyricum and even to the very gates of Italy, and he had betrayed his native country. It is therefore manifest that this same council, if it had before its eyes, when writing, that alliance of criminal men, can scarcely be thought to have assembled at any other time than this. Further, I infer, with the most eminent men Sirmond and Hardouin, that these very letters of the Roman council ought to be attributed to Ambrose, [Col. 0208C] whatever the Benedictine editors may think, who removed them from the edition of his works prepared under their care: both because we have proved that he himself was present at this synod, and because the style and purpose of the two letters—the Roman and the Aquileian—are the same, and their sentiments are almost identical.

Moreover, the judgment of Sirmond and Hardouin is shown to be preferable by Henry the Cleric, who, in the catalogue of manuscripts of the monastery of Padolivone compiled in the eleventh century, attributes it to Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0208D] Montfaucon, *Italian Diary*, p. 93.], although he is afterwards mistaken when he asserts that it was written from the Council of Aquileia. For the other letter of that same Council of Aquileia to Gratian, which I have just indicated, proves rather that it was composed by this Roman council. Nor would I believe that, for one and the same reason, one and the same synod wrote two letters at the same time to one and the same [Col. 0208D] emperor.

III. I now return to those who think that Damasus was charged with adultery because Gratian says, in his rescript to Aquilinus the vicar, that he had been attacked by most disgraceful calumnies. As though calumnies of every kind were not always in themselves most disgraceful, and as though the infamy imposed by the laws did not attend them. Yet I do not deny that Anastasius appears to lend some weight to this opinion when he writes, concerning Damasus: “He was accused of adultery, and, after a synod had been convened, was cleared by forty-four bishops, who also condemned Concordius and Callistus, the deacons who were his accusers, [Col. 0209A] and expelled them from the Church.”

But in recounting the actions of Liberius, Felix, and Damasus, Anastasius teems with so many errors and suffers from such confusion of events that no faith at all, or very little, can be placed in him unless arguments are supplied from elsewhere. At least we have already seen, whatever Baluze may assert, that throughout the entire two-year period between the election and that celebrated synod convened in 369, there can be no place for the council at which Damasus is said to have been accused and cleared of this charge.

I am chiefly led not to adopt the opinion of those who hold this view by a twofold reason: namely, the silence of Marcellinus and Faustinus, and the very letter of this Roman council. As to the first: would these presbyters, driven by envy and hatred, who pour out every calumny against [Col. 0209B] Damasus and other bishops like him in holiness, and who further write that he was called a ladies’ ear-scraper (*auriscalpium*), have passed over this most disgraceful accusation in silence, if he had been not merely suspected of it but actually brought before judges as guilty?

Moreover, in the letter of the Roman council no charge is laid upon Damasus on the accusers’ side except that he had violated the public laws, as is clear from these words: “For as regards the public laws, what life can be more secure than that which is supported by your prudence, once it has been adjudicated?” But if no one but necessary and near relatives could accuse adulterers [Note: [Col. 0209D] *Codex Theodosianus*, book II, on the Julian law concerning adultery, and Gothofredus thereon], then there is no reason why we should think that Isaac the Jew, a man of no name or standing, was permitted to do this. Moreover, [Col. 0209C] there must have been another charge by which Damasus was alleged to have offended against the public laws, so that he could be accused under that heading. I see no other than a charge of public violence, on account of the Ursinians formerly driven from the Liberian and St Agnes’s basilicas, and of the killings committed on that occasion, as I have said. Since the penalty for that offence had been fixed as death, the assembled bishops therefore write that, at the instigation of Isaac, suborned by Ursinus’s faction, elaborate plots had long ago been prepared to seek the head of their holy brother Damasus.

I think it was for this reason that the Schismatics, in their case against Symmachus, made use of neither the example of Damasus nor that of Sixtus III to compel that pontiff to be present at the synod, although a similar accusation was at issue—namely, the same crime of adultery—and although they cited other examples for that end. For it is not credible [Col. 0209D] that Symmachus’s opponents could have been ignorant of events so important, so publicly conducted, and scarcely beyond living memory.

These matters being so, anyone may readily judge how much negligence—or rather ignorance—Jannonius reveals when he writes that Gratian was asked by the bishops of Italy to hear himself the cases of Damasus, whom they themselves had accused. But leaving aside this man, whom Father John Anthony Blancus has admirably chastised together with his master Dupin [Note: [Col. 0210D] Vol. IV, book II, ch. 3, §7], I must turn my discourse again to the anonymous writer, who is uncertain whether to absolve that most holy pontiff from this shameful charge or to condemn him. [Col. 0210A]

For if you listen to him, since that synod acquitted Damasus, the duty of Christian charity requires you to believe that he was falsely accused. But because it is scarcely credible that men could have been of a brow so brazen as to dare to bring so grave a charge against the Roman bishop and summon an innocent man to judgment, and because, further, it is not established that any capital punishment was inflicted upon those calumniators, the matter still remains in doubt, and you, anonymous judge, may lawfully choose whichever opinion you prefer. O Pope, how learned you are, how wise a theologian, when you pronounce these things! I had learned another doctrine from the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 13; but henceforth you will have precedence with me, and I shall take you at your word and risk when the honest reputation of one’s neighbour is at stake: namely, that the audacity of a few obscure, vile, and utterly worthless men may carry more weight [Col. 0210B] than a judgment confirmed by the careful deliberation of many most weighty and most holy men.

Yet I fear that, in writing this, you intend to deceive your reader. For you are by no means unaware that the one argument which you advance to establish your opinion is utterly false; and that the Church is not permitted to prosecute its calumniators in the secular forum for punishment, while, as the Fathers of this council say, the religious scruple of priests abhors tortures. In any case, I now bid you henceforth to free yourself from this anxiety. For I maintain that there was no synod in which Damasus was either accused of this crime or declared innocent, and that those who judge otherwise rest upon no grave authority or any solid conjecture.

“I do not know,” he says [Note: [Col. 0210D] *Life of Damasus*, p. 135.], “what one must believe concerning the accusation of adultery brought against Pope Damasus. Had he given occasion for this dreadful scandal? Or was it merely the malice of some partisan of Ursinus? I think that one cannot, without rashness, pronounce upon this fact, although St Jerome said of this pope that he professed a perfect continence and preserved it inviolate until death. Charity obliges us to believe that the synod which justified Damasus from this atrocious accusation acted equitably and did no more than render him justice; but will one easily persuade oneself that persons brazen enough to calumniate a pope with such insolence could have been found? And if their imposture was established, as is supposed, why were they not handed over to the secular arm [Col. 0210D] to be punished according to the full rigour of the Roman laws against public calumniators? I shall limit my reflections here: it is painful to show that one has grounds sufficient to judge unfavourably of the virtue of a prelate whose memory the Church honours.”

## CHAPTER XVII

I. Damasus declares void the ordination of Maximus the Cynic, in a letter to Acholius of Thessalonica; the letter is examined and elucidated. II. On the vicariate of Thessalonica. III. Did Damasus later change his view and defend the ordination of the same Cynic with a certain Italian council?

[Col. 0211A]

I. When St Gregory Nazianzen, whom we have said came to Constantinople at least at the beginning of the preceding year, was administering that Church as bishop to the great benefit of religion, he narrowly escaped being driven from both the Church itself and the city by the deceit of Maximus the Cynic. Since the matter is known even to those who have merely sampled ecclesiastical histories with the tips of their lips, I shall select only those points which concern Damasus.

Damasus therefore declared invalid the ambitious and illegitimate ordination of the Cynic in that most weighty and elegant letter which he sent this year to Acholius of Thessalonica, Eurydicus, Severus, Uranius, Philip, and John. Among the many letters which Nicholas I records that Damasus wrote in this affair, it was first brought out of obscurity and published by Holstenius, a man of exceptional learning and judgment, in the Roman collection; Constantius afterwards listed it eighth among Damasus’s letters, [Col. 0211B] whereas I list it fourth. No one reports of which Churches the other addressees of the letter were bishops. Yet they must have belonged to the metropolitan see of Thessalonica, since Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0211D] Epistle 15, in the Benedictine edition] calls Severus and Philip—the very men to whom it is addressed—Thessalonian priests, that is, belonging to that metropolitan see, less than three years after this letter of Damasus.

There were several reasons why Damasus annulled that ordination. First, it had been performed by outsiders, that is, by bishops who had nothing to do with that Church or province. Hence the council convened in that city in the following year judged that precautions should be taken, in canon 2, to prevent bishops from passing from one diocese to another to perform ordinations or conduct other business; and it commanded them to attend only to the affairs of their own diocese. Second, the ordination had been begun at night and secretly in a church, then hastily continued and completed in profane premises, all of which was contrary to accepted ecclesiastical discipline. Third, no request from people and clergy had preceded it. Hence Pope Julius of Rome reproaches the Arians for Gregory’s ordination—the Gregory whom they had intruded in place of Athanasius—because he was an outsider, not baptized there, unknown to many, [Col. 0211C] and neither requested by presbyters nor bishops; and he says that it is not fitting to ordain anyone thus, beyond all law and right and contrary to ecclesiastical canon [Note: [Col. 0211D] Julius, Epistle 1, no. 14]. Athanasius himself agrees [Note: [Col. 0211D] Encyclical Letter to the Bishops, no. 2].

Fourth, the dress worn by Maximus was foreign to Christian religion, and Damasus rightly calls it the dress of an idol. For the dress of philosophers of this sect, no less than that of idols, consisted only of a single little cloak worn without a tunic, together with beard and long hair, as is clear from Lucian [Note: [Col. 0212D] See note]. Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0212D] *History*, book V, ch. 8] seems to number him among the followers of Apollinarius. [Col. 0212A] Yet since no writer of that age—not even Gregory Nazianzen, who certainly knew him very well—has applied this charge to him, I fear that perhaps Theodoret, deceived by the name, took one Maximus for another: namely, that later Maximus who, after the Council of Ephesus and the agreement made with Cyril, is said to have put on the habit of a monk and, fervent in the error of Apollinarius, to have been sent by John of Antioch through the East with imperial letters and prefectural orders to spread the contagion of heresy and pronounce anathema against those who had exposed Apollinarius’s ravings and the poisons of his heresy [Note: [Col. 0212D] See the Synod against the Tragedian Irenaeus, ch. 195].

II. Gregory himself testifies that those ordaining bishops, whom Damasus says came from Egypt and had been sent by Peter of Alexandria to Constantinople to establish Maximus as bishop of that city, [Col. 0212B] were sent by Peter. Yet that Alexandrian prelate had previously been Gregory’s adviser and instigator in undertaking to administer that Church as bishop. This makes plausible to me the opinion of those who think that this Maximus was the very person whom Athanasius and Basil highly praise in letters written to him; it is therefore not surprising if Peter, Athanasius’s successor, thought him suitable to preside over the vacant Church of Constantinople.

Now, if anyone compares Damasus’s letter with those things which Nazianzen says in the poem concerning his own life, he will plainly discover that nothing which the latter reports to have happened while this drama was being enacted was unknown to the Roman pontiff. Indeed, one will marvel at how similar one is to the other, as though the very words and thoughts had been taken by one from the other. From this may be inferred the fidelity and diligence of Acholius in investigating and reporting these matters, since Damasus professes that he learned them from him.

Since the same pontiff had at the same time already been informed that Maximus’s efforts had been nullified by the Emperor Theodosius, to whom Maximus had fled for refuge while he was then residing at Thessalonica, and that what Maximus had wickedly begun had already been destroyed by public authority, we learn from this that his letters to Acholius and the other bishops must have been written in this year, which Theodosius spent almost entirely in that city, [Col. 0212C] although it is not easy to determine a precise date. Nevertheless, the sequence of events requires us to conjecture that they were sent in September or October, since they were written after Theodosius had rejected Maximus and had already summoned a council for the election of a bishop of Constantinople.

Whatever may be said of these details, what seems capable of certain assertion is that the letters were written after Damasus had confirmed the Antiochene reconciliation in the Roman synod and had granted full communion to Meletius and all in communion with him. For he says that he wishes, since a council was soon to take place at Constantinople to choose a bishop for that city, that they would take care that someone free from all reproach should be chosen, so that, God being propitious, when the complete peace of all Catholic bishops had been confirmed, no dissensions might thereafter arise in the Church; so that, by God’s gift, the perpetual peace which we have long desired might remain with the Catholic bishops. He repeats this also in a familiar letter to Acholius. [Col. 0212D] Damasus therefore feared lest anything might be done in that election which could again disturb the peace already won and confirmed. From this I infer that, when he wrote, the long-standing dissension between Westerners and Easterners had already been removed.

Some infer from the cited words of this letter that Acholius was present at the Council of Constantinople in Damasus’s name and acted as his representative. But this opinion has been rejected by the common judgment of learned men and by the weightiest additional arguments, which may be read in Baluze, Pagi, Lupus, Tillemont, and others. Yet Baluze fell into another error when he thought it could be inferred from the same passage that Acholius himself and the bishops of his district had written to Damasus after they had been summoned to that synod [Note: [Col. 0213D] *On Councils*, book V, ch. 21, no. 2]. For Gregory Nazianzen expressly asserts that the Macedonian bishops were either summoned unexpectedly by Theodosius or came unexpectedly after Meletius’s death—namely, late, and long after Damasus had been informed by them that the council had been called.

When Damasus therefore writes to Acholius that he should take care that a Catholic bishop be established in the imperial city, he means only that Acholius should pursue this matter through his services [Col. 0213A] and advice with the emperor, whom he had baptized and who was then residing at Thessalonica. For how could Damasus have asked Acholius, attached to the Western Church, to attend to the matter in person at that synod, at which only bishops of the East ought to have been present [Note: [Col. 0213D] See also the annotations to Epistle 4]?

Since, then, the bishop of Thessalonica, in accordance with his singular holiness and piety, had frequently and diligently pursued this business with the emperor himself so long as he remained in that city, and had earnestly commended it to him as he was setting out for Constantinople toward the end of that year, I think that this was why Theodosius, mindful of the matter, summoned Acholius himself and the Macedonian bishops dependent upon him so late to the council, unexpectedly, and precisely at the time when Gregory, because Flavian’s ordination had been decreed and the gravest disputes had arisen on that account, was on the point of resigning the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0213D] Poem on His Life, from line 152]: namely, so that they might labour to settle affairs and establish concord; or, failing that, ensure what Damasus had long ago commanded—that no stigma could be attached to the man who was elected.

Baluze again thinks, and Pagi copies him [Note: [Col. 0213D] On the year 379, no. 11 ff.], that Damasus did not favour Gregory, as Baronius wrote. Rather, he says, Damasus condemned the plan of those who had brought about Gregory’s translation; and to prove this he uses these words of the letter: “Moreover, I admonish your holiness: do not permit anyone, contrary to the statutes of our forefathers, to be transferred from one city to another, to abandon the people entrusted to him, and through ambition to pass to another people,” etc. [Col. 0214A] Others think that Meletius is meant in this passage.

Yet I think that neither the one nor the other is censured, but that the Roman pontiff wished to promote observance of the sacred canons, which he knew were then being violated among the Easterners both in elections and in frequent transfers, as we learn from Socrates and from Nazianzen himself, who reproaches them for this vice in his poem against bishops [Note: [Col. 0214D] Line 800, from Tollius’s edition]. At least with respect to Gregory himself, it is certain and evident that his translation could not be censured in this passage, since the letter was written long before it took place by decree of the bishops assembled at Constantinople. Thus it is by no means clear that Baronius departed from the truth in judging that Damasus favoured Gregory.

I am not unaware, however, that the Macedonian and Egyptian bishops, immediately upon reaching Constantinople—that is, after Flavian’s ordination had been decreed—disapproved of Gregory’s enthronement because the canons had been violated in the matter. But this could seem to have been done contrary to Damasus’s intention, since Gregory, who had never allowed himself to be attached to any Church, was not bound by that rule, as he says himself in the poem on his life. [Col. 0214B]

Rusticus seems to have delivered this letter addressed to Acholius. In another familiar letter, Damasus commends him to Acholius as a son, since he had himself baptized him. [Col. 0214C] He was one of the *silentiarii* of the Emperor Gratian, whose duty was to keep watch before the emperor’s bedchamber, whether he was seated in the consistory or receiving foreigners and their envoys [Note: [Col. 0214D] See Gothofredus on law IV and the title concerning Decurions and Silentiaries]. Emperors often employed them to be sent here and there as circumstances required; this perhaps happened to Rusticus, then sent to Theodosius at Thessalonica.

Both letters contain such open indications of familiarity that they clearly show an old and confirmed friendship between Damasus and Acholius. Therefore, since Ambrose says that Acholius made frequent journeys into Italy [Note: [Col. 0214D] Letter to Anysius, in the Benedictine edition], I do not at all doubt that he had even reached Rome before this time, attended councils previously held by Damasus, and was consequently well known to this pontiff. [Col. 0214D]

Meanwhile, it may be inferred quite clearly from this that Acholius had long before this time acted as the Roman pontiff’s representative throughout Illyricum, since Damasus says that he had often warned him not to act rashly. That vicarial authority conferred by Damasus upon Acholius was afterwards confirmed by Siricius, Anastasius, Innocent, and succeeding Roman pontiffs for Anysius, Rufus, and the other bishops of Thessalonica, down to the time of Justinian. From this the distinguished Joseph Cennius rightly infers that this delegation, as an attribute attached to a person, ceased upon the death of the pontiff whose place was being represented [Note: [Col. 0215D] *Antiquities of Ecclesiastical History*, disputation 3, ch. 2].

I am not surprised that Dupin and those like him, wholly intent upon diminishing the right of the Roman Church, disliked this vicariate. It may indeed seem surprising why Tillemont, who wishes to appear concerned only with truth, thought himself at liberty to reject this vicarial delegation and disparage it under the invidious name of an innovation. For this very learned man first doubts whether Damasus was permitted to establish that vicarial prefecture, and whether he adopted that policy according to the prescription of the canons, or rather merely from a desire to retain authority throughout the whole of Illyricum, recently divided by Gratian [Note: [Col. 0215D] On Damasus, art. 13]. Again, elsewhere [Col. 0215A] he openly attacks that vicariate, condemns it as established against the canons, praises Theodosius because he had revoked it by his rescript [Note: [Col. 0215D] *Codex Theodosianus*, law 45, book XVI, title 2], and dictatorially declares that there is no legally fitting reason why Damasus could originally have conferred his vicariate through the Illyrian provinces [Note: [Col. 0215D] On Boniface, art. 9, vol. XII].

But it has not yet been proved that the division of Illyricum is to be attributed to Gratian in such a way that Damasus could have been induced by it to establish a vicariate. Further, it would have to be proved that this same vicariate had not been established before the division of Illyricum effected by Gratian—something Tillemont will never demonstrate. But grant that Damasus entrusted his powers to Acholius in order to retain the whole of Illyricum, then divided, under himself and his patriarchate: what, I ask, did he violate in the canons? What did Basil do when, against Anthimus of Tyana, he claimed the whole of Cappadocia for himself with such contention, adhering—as Nazianzen says [Note: [Col. 0215D] Oration 20, *In Praise of Basil*]—to ancient custom and to the division made by the Fathers? [Col. 0215B]

Moreover, the origin, nature, and rationale of the apostolic vicariate differ from what Tillemont supposed. As Bacchini says in his dissertation on the origins of ecclesiastical hierarchy, it must be sought in the right by which the bishop of Rome, as the sole metropolitan, held the whole West under himself. He administered ecclesiastical affairs personally in neighboring provinces when he could; but in provinces far distant from him, through certain bishops to whom he judged they should be entrusted. We learn from Synesius’s letters that the bishop of Alexandria did likewise throughout his own patriarchate. This is the reason why the Nicene Synod made that celebrated comparison between them in canon 6.

This view of the most learned man seems confirmed by Innocent I in his letter to Alexander of Antioch, in which he advises him to command that bishops far distant from him be ordained through letters issued by him [Note: [Col. 0216D] In Coustant, Epistle 24]; and by Leo the Great, who professes to Anastasius of Thessalonica that he delegated his own authority “so that you might assist in the care which, by divine institution, we principally owe to all the Churches, and might extend to provinces distant from us, in some fashion, the presence of our visitation” [Note: [Col. 0216D] Epistle 12, printed by the brothers of Lyon]. [Col. 0215C]

This right of the Apostolic See over both Illyricums, which Tillemont, borrowing words from a spurious rescript of Theodosius, calls an innovation, was approved in practice and judged consonant with reason by Theodosius the Great, Gregory Nazianzen, Basil, and the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople. Boniface I, then the Emperor Honorius, and Theodosius himself, after learning the truth, praise it in an altogether different and just tone. They declare that it was established long ago by the Fathers, continually observed, confirmed by the reverence of so many ages, and obtained even under princes whom no concern for our religion constrained [Note: [Col. 0216D] In Coustant, Letters of Boniface 7, 8, 9, 10]. Let these incidental remarks suffice, since my purpose is not to assert that this right of the Apostolic See has been admirably vindicated by learned men, [Col. 0216A] but to shed light on the actions of Damasus.

III. To return, then, to the point from which the discussion departed: lastly, one might ask, since Damasus rejected the ordination of Maximus the Cynic, how an Italian council could afterwards seem to defend and approve it in a letter written to Theodosius and published by Sirmond in the appendix to the *Codex Theodosianus*. I shall set forth my view in a separate dissertation, in which I shall examine both letters, lest meanwhile I detain the reader more than is proper.

## CHAPTER XVIII. 381, THE SIXTEENTH YEAR OF DAMASUS, FLAVIUS SYAGRIUS AND FLAVIUS EUCHERIUS, CONSULS

I. The First Council of Constantinople is considered in matters concerning Damasus, and the defender of the Gallican propositions is refuted. II. Inquiry into the meaning of the “Tome of the Westerners” mentioned in canon 5, on account of which the followers of Paulinus of Antioch were received into communion; the same canon was composed and promulgated with Meletius as author, and in connection with it Gregory Nazianzen delivered Oration 13, which is explained, as also Oration 14. III. Some observations concerning canon 3 or 4, by which the ordination of Maximus the Cynic was rejected. IV. On the ordination of Flavian of Antioch and the matters then done and discussed.

[Col. 0216C]

I. This year and the next bring with them many matters of the greatest importance, in explaining which we shall linger according to the measure of our ability. I shall begin with the Council of Constantinople, which began almost at the opening of this very year and ended on 9 July.

[Col. 0216D] It has been disputed whether it was summoned at the instance of Damasus, some maintaining and others denying this; and further, whether Acholius acted there as the representative of the same pontiff. As to the first point, one can scarcely say that those are mistaken who write that it was called and assembled by order of Theodosius, with Damasus’s authority and consent also concurring. For, since the Roman pontiff was informed in good time and did not oppose the convocation—which he could lawfully have done [Note: [Col. 0216D] Socrates, book II, ch. 17; Sozomen, book III, ch. 10; Baronius, year 351, no. 20]—he could be considered and called an author of its assembly. This is surely why the Sixth Synod attributes the convocation of that council to Theodosius and Damasus [Note: [Col. 0217D] Act 18, address to the emperor].

Yet no legate of Damasus was present at all. Those, if any, who think that Acholius was honoured by him with that dignity are mistaken, since the bishop of Thessalonica was summoned only near the end of the council, and in order to be present at the election of the bishop of Constantinople after Gregory’s resignation, as I have said elsewhere. [Col. 0217A]

As to the Acts of that council, they had already perished in the age of Photius. Only a few canons remain, some concerning faith and some discipline. The first canon concerns faith: by it the Pneumatomachians and Apollinarists were condemned along with other heretics. But Damasus had already condemned these persons, and his decrees had been embraced both by all the Western bishops and by the Easterners, except for a few Macedonians. If anyone doubts this, let him consult the very learned Father Orsi, who, surveying all the Churches, places the matter in clear light [Note: [Col. 0217D] Vol. I, book I, ch. 8].

Bossuet therefore vainly misuses this canon to prove that, in settling controversies of faith, the authority of the Apostolic See must be joined by the consent of other Churches; and accordingly that this Council of Constantinople was convened in order that, by this canon, that agreement and unity might be made manifest [Note: [Col. 0217D] See part II, book XII, ch. 8]. Could the obstinacy of a few heretical bishops have made a general council necessary in order again to establish a doctrine which had been defined by the judgment of the Apostolic See [Col. 0217B] and ratified by the obedience of the whole Church? Neither pseudo-Bossuet nor anyone from the most learned and most devout body of Gallican prelates would ever say so. For by what other weapon were the Jansenist heretics, who recently clamoured vainly and deceitfully for a general council, routed and overthrown by those bishops? Or will that writer say that Gregory of both names, Meletius, Amphilochius, and the other Fathers of the Council of Constantinople held one view, while the Gallican bishops held another?

Let it therefore be certain and settled that those bishops could not have assembled, nor composed that canon, chiefly in order that agreement and unity might be established, of which there was no ground whatever for doubt. Indeed, if we read Socrates and Sozomen attentively, we openly infer that the Semi-Arians and Pneumatomachians were condemned by the Fathers at Constantinople chiefly because they had departed from the faith of the Fathers received at Rome, as Basil says [Note: [Col. 0218D] Epistle 244, according to the Benedictine edition]. For, as Socrates and Sozomen write [Note: [Col. 0218D] Socrates, book V, ch. 7; Sozomen, book VII, ch. 8], before the canon was pronounced by which the Semi-Arians, or Macedonians, were proscribed, the emperor and the bishops of his party were using every effort to bring Eleusius and his associates over to their side. They recalled to their memory the embassy which they had formerly sent through Eustathius to Liberius, [Col. 0217C] bishop of the Romans, and declared that those were not acting rightly who, after once recognizing a doctrine in agreement with the faith, now tried again to overthrow what they themselves had decreed.

From where had the bishops assembled at Constantinople learned that doctrine to be consonant with the faith, except from the former definition and judgment of the Apostolic See under Liberius, to which the Macedonians themselves had submitted? Thus, by the judgment of those same bishops, the Macedonians had been deemed alien from the faith even before the council itself, while the faith proposed by Liberius had acquired the force of an irreformable and irrevisable dogma. Will anyone then think that they assembled in synod in order to confer strength and authority upon those definitions by their assent?

“But,” says that writer, whoever he may be, “the Fathers of Constantinople, after reporting what they had decreed concerning faith and discipline, ask only that Damasus and the bishops with him should rejoice with them; and they say that it will thus come about that, when the word of God has been established by common consent and Christian charity among us confirmed, we shall cease to say what was condemned by the Apostles: ‘I indeed am of Apollo, but I of Cephas.’” The learned reader sees how he places the interpretation of Scripture and the establishment of faith in common consent. These letters do not belong to the First Council of Constantinople, but to a certain later assembly in the year following; we defer their discussion until then. But our question is not whether the Fathers of Constantinople agreed with the definitions of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0218B] as they were bound to do, but whether they could have dissented. This is precisely what they did not think permitted to them, as we have heard from Socrates and Sozomen. Therefore that same writer can draw no support for his view from this passage or from words twisted away from their proper sense.

II. Moreover, the deference and obedience shown by the Council of Constantinople toward the First See may be clearly inferred from its fifth canon. The canon says: “Concerning the Tome of the Westerners, we have also received those who confess one divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit at Antioch.” Scholars ask what the Fathers of the Council understood by “the Tome of the Westerners,” and various opinions have been advanced, which may be read in de Marca, Valesius, Lupus, Tillemont, Cave, [Col. 0218D] and others. Yet I think Baronius’s opinion comes close to the truth: he believes that these words indicate the rule or confession of faith set forth by Damasus and the Roman synod, discussed by us in the preceding year. [Note: Ann. 381, no. 28.]

For it is established that the Catholic Antiochenes were of two kinds: some confessed one divinity and three hypostases; others, rejecting the term *hypostases*, professed one divinity and three persons. The former followed Meletius as bishop; the latter, Paulinus. As regards the first kind of Antiochenes, there could be no controversy among the bishops gathered at Constantinople [Col. 0219A] that they were Catholics and were to be received into communion. That canon, therefore, concerns the Antiochenes of the second kind, whom it commands to be received into communion, although they did not profess three hypostases—a matter whose reasons we have explained elsewhere.

But why is the Tome of the Westerners mentioned here, and what Tome is this? It is as certain as anything can be that, by the term “Westerners,” the Greeks customarily designate the Roman pontiff alone as their head, writing for the most part on behalf of his synod: see chapter 20. Moreover, no one can be unaware that “Tome” denotes dogmatic definitions proposed by him. Thus Basil calls other letters of Damasus addressed to the East “the Tome of the Westerners,” and appeals to them as a rule of faith. [Note: Basil, Letter 265, no. 3.]

Thus, in this passage the question concerned some definition of the Roman bishop and his council bearing upon the case of those Antiochenes. But Damasus, in Anathemas 20 and 21, having removed the necessity of speaking of three hypostases, had declared to be perfectly Catholic those who professed one divinity, power, majesty, and glory of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and three true, equal, ever-subsisting persons. This indeed was the faith of those Antiochenes, as is clear from Jerome, [Note: Jerome, Letter 15.] Nazianzen, [Note: Nazianzen, Oration 32.] and Paulinus himself, and from the formula attached to the Antiochene synod which he professed before Athanasius.

That Tome of the Westerners, therefore, means nothing else in that Constantinopolitan canon than [Col. 0219C] that celebrated exposition (*ecthesis*) of Damasus. Since those bishops regarded it as a law, they embraced as eminently Catholic according to its standard those whom they had previously treated as strangers. This is openly asserted, besides the acts of Damasus himself published by Sarazanius, by Eutychius of Alexandria in Renaudot, [Note: Renaudot, *Historia Patriarcharum Alexandrinorum*, II, under Timothy.] and is not obscurely indicated by the synodical letter, when it says that the pontiff, having assembled a synod at Rome, issued a divine decree and sent it to the synod being convened at Constantinople. [Note: Chapter 76.]

I think, incidentally, that this canon was framed under Meletius’s influence, whose reverence toward the Apostolic See was undoubtedly great, and that on this occasion Nazianzen’s thirteenth oration, entitled *On Peace*, was delivered. Elias of Crete refers it to the same [Col. 0219D] cause for which Oration 12 had been delivered—namely, the removal of the schism of the monks who had departed from his party. Billius, rightly observing that several passages cannot be referred either to that cause or to that time, departs from Elias’s opinion but suspends judgment, nor does he himself indicate upon what occasion or at what time the oration may seem to have been delivered.

Tillemont, therefore, [Note: *On Gregory Nazianzen*, act 56 and note 30, vol. IX.] thinks that it was delivered at Constantinople after Valens’s death and the recent conferral of imperial power upon Theodosius. Certainly no one who carefully reads the oration itself near its end [Col. 0220A] will deny this. He also believes that the passage concerns the Antiochene schism, then removed and extinguished by the mutual concord of the dissentients. This is altogether certain. For Gregory, rejoicing in restored charity, turns to the Arians, who had reproached the Catholics with their former dissension:

> “Where, then, are those who observe our affairs, whether prosperous or adverse, not in order to judge but to condemn? Come, therefore . . . we summon even you who hate us to the council, so that, put to shame and overcome, you may withdraw, recognizing from the very fact that we had been ill our health . . . For we did not disagree concerning the Godhead; rather, we contended over order and discipline. Nor was there contention among us as to which impiety should be chosen—whether that which contracts God, or that which separates only the Holy Spirit, or even the Son himself, [Col. 0220B] from the divine essence . . .”

By these words he plainly refers to the Paulinians and Meletians, and says that all of them were perfectly Catholic and of sound faith, although some were slanderously charged with the Sabellian heresy because they did not mention the three hypostases, while others were charged as though Arians and Macedonians because they retained communion with them.

He then continues: “Our position is not the same. For, as regards divinity, we agree, and we were one lip and one voice . . . Yet contention existed among us over other matters. Even that, indeed, was wrong; I shall not deny it. For since, being human, we could not avoid sinning in some respect, this was our error: we were moved by an excessive love of our shepherd, and could not discover which of two good things was more to be desired, until we agreed upon this: that we should place BOTH IN EQUAL PRAISE and admiration.” Could anything be said more clearly, or more aptly, both to portray the Antiochene schism and to designate the council then being held?

Yet although that man of exact diligence came nearer the truth, he is mistaken in thinking that Gregory, in this oration, deals with a particular dissension in his own church: that one of his clergy, who believed communion should be maintained only with either Meletius or Paulinus, had seceded from Nazianzen himself—whom he identifies under the name of the sincere and upright father—and afterward returned to him; and that Gregory therefore regards him as an obedient son. For anyone who weighs the oration properly will readily judge that Tillemont’s interpretation rests on no foundation. Nazianzen had communicated with both parties. Further, that sincere and upright father stood beside Gregory as he spoke, with his obedient son. He had also spoken before Gregory concerning peace. He must therefore be someone other than Gregory himself. Finally, Gregory says that the upright and sincere father and obedient son standing beside him adorned one another mutually. In his humility and modesty, Gregory would by no means have said this of himself.

I therefore think that this passage and these words concern Meletius and Flavian, whom Meletius had not long before raised to [Col. 0221A] the rank of presbyter. He calls and identifies the latter as the upright and sincere father, the former as the obedient son. Both stood by Gregory as he spoke and adorned one another mutually, because Flavian had followed Meletius to the imperial city. Finally, Meletius—a simple man, open in manner and gentle in expression—had both laboured for peace and, shortly before, according to the custom of those times, had addressed the people on the same subject. [Note: See Gregory, poem *On His Own Life*, from line 121.] Gregory therefore publicly praises them, as authors of the peace and concord restored by that canon of the council, standing beside him as he spoke. This, if I am not mistaken, is the certain and by no means obscure subject of that oration.

This also sheds light upon the reason why Oration 14, [Col. 0221B] likewise entitled *On Peace*, was recited. For since that divine man laments that concord, scarcely restored, had again been shamefully broken, and that agreements publicly confirmed before God had been rendered void, we plainly understand that it was delivered to the bishops gathered at Constantinople after Meletius’s death, when proceedings began to install Flavian in his place contrary to the force of the agreement. It is that very oration which he mentions in his poem *On His Own Life* as delivered by him upon that occasion.

III. I now turn to Canon 3, otherwise Canon 4, by which the ordination of Maximus the Cynic was declared void. In this matter also the council followed Damasus’s judgment. Hence the Egyptian and Macedonian bishops, among whom Acholius must be counted, although they seem to have disapproved Gregory Nazianzen’s episcopate and complained that the canons had been violated by his translation, [Col. 0221C] nevertheless made no move on behalf of the Cynic or against his deposition. Indeed, they acted thus not so much out of hatred for Nazianzen or in order to place another upon his throne, as in order to inflict some pain, as he himself says, [Note: Poem *On His Own Life*, from line 155.] upon those who had made him bishop of Constantinople.

From this we learn that Maximus himself had, up to this time, neither come to Italy nor done anything before Damasus and the Western bishops to assist his cause. We omit the remaining canons of the council, both because they have no bearing upon that pontiff or the Apostolic See, and because it is still uncertain whether some of them should be assigned to this very council [Col. 0221D] or rather to some other, which appears more likely.

IV. It remains to speak of Flavian’s ordination and Nazianzen’s resignation, which form a part and appendix of the same council. Since Meletius died before its end, Paulinus alone ought, by force of the sworn agreement, to have retained the Antiochene Church. Gregory was of this opinion, and exerted all the powers of his eloquence to secure its acceptance. Among other arguments, he used especially this: it might perhaps appear pardonable that the Westerners should suffer some inconvenience from the Easterners so long as it had not yet become clear whether they would receive Meletius during his life as bishop of Antioch [Note:

> Ἕως μὲν οὖν ἦν ἐν μέσῳ θεῖος σκωπός  
> Οὐδ᾽ ἦν σαφές πω, ποθ᾽ οἱ τῆς Ἑσπέρας  
> Τὸν ἄνδρα δέξοντ᾽ ἠγριωμένοι τέως.

“That is, ‘So long as the divine watchman was still among us, and it was not yet clear whether the men of the West, still angered, would receive the man.’” Everyone knows the constant meaning of this word in ecclesiastical usage. Hence *dektoi* (δεκτοί), “those admitted to the right of communion,” are opposed to *adektoi* (ἄδεκτοι), “those not admitted.” See Apostolic Canon 13 and Suicer; see also Julius’s Letter to the Easterners, no. 13.], [Col. 0222D] but when they had received him, and peace had been obtained on both sides, and matters had already, by God’s favour, been placed in tranquillity, the Easterners should adopt other dispositions and make no innovation whatever. [Note: See Nazianzen, poem *On His Own Life*, from line 127 and following.]

But those bishops, through tumult, clamour, and even shameful intrigue, brought it about that, Gregory’s most prudent counsel and that of the other weightier Fathers being set aside, a new bishop was set against the sole existing bishop, and Flavian seemed to have been imposed upon Paulinus rather than given as successor to a vacant church. The whole matter is most elegantly described by Nazianzen himself [Col. 0222B] in his poem *On His Own Life* and elsewhere; it is also recounted by Baronius, Tillemont, and others, so that I need not rehearse it again.

Yet I cannot refrain from again maintaining that Theodoret was carried away by his excessive attachment to Flavian when he wished to defend those bishops whom Gregory calls jackdaws and wasps by means of an open calumny against Paulinus, writing as follows: [Note: Book V, chapter 23, from Valesius’s translation.]

> “Paulinus indeed claimed the episcopate of that church for himself; but the assembly of bishops objected, saying that it was unreasonable for one who had rejected Meletius’s counsels to receive his see after his death.”

For if Meletius and Paulinus had agreed by compact that whichever of them survived the other should administer the whole church, it is certainly false that Paulinus rejected Meletius’s counsels suitable for restoring concord. Hence Gregory—whose testimony no one will reject—gives another, indeed altogether ridiculous, reason why that inferior party prevailed, although the greater part of the bishops judged that Flavian should be substituted for Meletius. Therefore, if Flavian himself had bound himself by oath neither to seek that episcopate nor to accept it if freely offered, there is no reason why he should not be seen to have disregarded the sanctity of his oath, since he not only allowed himself to be chosen and ordained bishop of Antioch, but afterward strove with such contention to retain the see. Nor ought we, because the Greek Church honours his memory among the saints, to judge that he could have been guilty of no sin, one which he afterward washed away by repentance and other virtues.

Since Gregory abhorred these wicked bishops and tumultuous assemblies, he resolved to resign the episcopate of the imperial city. He carried this out after the arrival of the Egyptian and Macedonian bishops—namely, when, hands having finally been laid upon Flavian, no hope remained for the concord he had attempted. For Flavian was ordained, I think, during that interval in which Gregory, [Col. 0223A] not yet having formally resigned, withdrew from the church-house and renounced his office, lest, as he says, he should be compelled to attend evil gatherings. [Note: Poem *On His Own Life*, from line 151.]

For when he delivered his farewell address to the Fathers, he declared that he was leaving an example: if some imitated it and yielded their thrones, they would not suffer loss but would possess a heavenly seat much loftier and safer. From this it may be inferred not obscurely that Flavian himself, whom Gregory censures in this passage, had already been made bishop and placed upon the throne when Nazianzen said these things. Flavian afterward, if Sozomen is to be believed, was chiefly responsible for Nectarius succeeding Gregory himself. What Damasus thought of both these ordinations I shall state in the following year.

[Col. 0223B] I am aware that Tillemont writes [Note: On Flavian, article 3, vol. X.] that, after the bishops had returned to their sees and then assembled again at Antioch for this purpose, hands were laid upon Flavian. But he seeks support for his opinion precisely where it is overthrown, as I have shown elsewhere. Moreover, the learned man’s opinion is by no means consistent with the discipline then received. For when bishops had either died or been deposed in a full synod, a successor was appointed and consecrated in the same place and by the same full synod. Examples may be drawn from the Nicene Council, which consecrated Philogonius; the Constantinopolitan Council itself, which consecrated Nectarius; the Ephesian, which consecrated Maximian in place of Chalcedonensis [probably an OCR-corrupted reading]; the Chalcedonian, which consecrated another in Dioscorus’s place; and the Sixth Council, which consecrated Theophanes.

One argument alone seems [Col. 0223C] available in Tillemont’s defence from the acts of the same Constantinopolitan Synod, to which Flavian himself subscribes as a presbyter. But those who draw any argument from such subscriptions to confirm their opinions are, as Tillemont himself proves elsewhere, seeking light from darkness. [Note: On Nazianzen, vol. IX, note 42.] I, however, think that two councils were held and must be distinguished—an opinion of many most learned men, not obscurely confirmed by the testimony of Socrates and Sozomen. The first was not very numerous; the second much more numerous. In the first, Maximus was deposed and Gregory confirmed in the see under Meletius’s presidency. In the second, over which Gregory at some point presided, Flavian was ordained and later Nectarius; several canons besides were promulgated. The subscriptions and canons of both were afterward gathered into one, and from the two one council was made and reckoned as such.

Hence it happened that Flavian, who had subscribed to the first while Meletius lived as a presbyter, did not judge it necessary to subscribe again to that second council after he had been raised to the episcopate. [Col. 0224A] But this council and the matters pertaining to it must be discussed again in the following year.

## CHAPTER XIX

I. On the Council of Aquileia and the synodical letters written by it: the first two, addressed to Gratian, are recounted and examined to illustrate the history of those times. II. The rescript of Emperor Gratian to Aquilinus the vicar is presented and explained. Newton is criticized, and the impudence of the anonymous Amsterdam writer is rebuked. III. The third letter of the same Council of Aquileia is examined and explained. IV. Priscillian comes to Rome to clear himself. Quesnel and Dupin are refuted.

[Col. 0224B] I. Not long after the Council of Constantinople, the Council of Aquileia was assembled and concluded in September. From it—which, if not by the number of its participants, at least by the dignity and holiness of the bishops present, holds a most distinguished place among councils—I shall collect only what is not foreign to my purpose and concerns Damasus.

Besides its Acts, vainly sought by Chiffletius, three letters survive. Two are addressed to Gratian, emperor of the West, and one to Theodosius, although their superscription is common to all. The first letter mentions the matters concerning faith which had been completed in the council: namely, the deposition of Palladius and Secundianus, Arian bishops, and Attalus, a presbyter, all present at the council itself. Palladius and Secundianus are mentioned in the letters of the conventicle of Singidunum and in Germinius’s reply to them, written late in the year 366; but Secundianus had not yet been raised to the episcopate. [Note: Venetian edition of the Councils, vol. II, p. 989.]

The Fathers of Aquileia call Attalus the presbyter a disciple of Julian Valens. They write that Valens himself, though not far away, avoided the council, lest he be held there to answer for the cause of his devastated country and ruined citizens. [Note: He had seized the Church of Petovio by brigandage. Some understand this name to mean the church now called Passau, since both are in Noricum and it could easily have happened that *Petovionensis*, or *Petaviensis*, became *Petaviensis* and finally *Passaviensis*. See the author of the *Commentary on the Literati of Italy*, printed at Venice in 1749, vol. II, and Tillemont, vol. V, p. 707. In the age of Innocent III, it was certainly called *Pataviensis*, as I once read from a letter of that pontiff preserved in the Passau archive. If these things are true, then the Church of Passau may rightly claim as its own Victorinus, bishop and martyr, to whom Jerome gave a place in his catalogue. Further, the laudable piety and faith of its distinguished clergy and people will be evident, since they refused to have that brigand preside over them and expelled him after disgracefully rejecting him.]

After betraying his country to the Goths, as Ambrose says, he had withdrawn into Italy and was attempting to contaminate and infect it by establishing in various places false bishops of his sect. In this very year and at the very time when the council was assembled, he lay concealed at Milan, perhaps protected by Justina’s support. They therefore ask Gratian to order him to return home and free Italy’s most flourishing [Col. 0224D] cities from that pestilence.

The second letter of that council concerns Ursicinus. It was written at the same time as the first and given to departing legates for delivery to Gratian. [Col. 0225A] Having supposed that by their decrees they had made provision against the two men who, near the corner of Riparian Dacia, had dared attack the Nicene Council and might continue to lurk and breathe out Arian poison, they say that they ought to attend to another matter, indeed a most grave one and a source of great anxiety, since it could disturb the body of the Church spread throughout the world. I shall state in their own words what this was:

> “Although we have often learned that Ursinus has been unable to creep upon Your Piety, though he allows nothing to remain at rest and makes an importunate attempt at intrusion amid the necessities of war, nevertheless, lest your holy mind and tranquillity of spirit—which is eager to provide for all—be bent by the feigned flattery of an importunate man, we think it proper, if you deem it worthy, to entreat and beseech you, not only guarding against future events but also shuddering at past events already undertaken by his recklessness. For if he finds any path for his audacity, what will he not throw into confusion? . . . Therefore we ask and beg that you deign to deprive him of the opportunity for intrusion.”

Ursinus, then, having long since been released from a fixed and settled exile by Valentinian’s rescript, which we said had been issued in 371, had established himself at Milan and had joined in a partnership of wickedness with Julian Valens, who also afterward withdrew there. Then, compelled in the preceding year to leave at the request of the Roman council and banished to Gaul, he was able to approach Gratian, then occupied by the Alamannic war, and to use every effort of himself and his associates to bend that emperor and draw him to their side. They therefore implore him to reject that seditious man, companion of the Arians [Col. 0225C] and criminal, and thereby preserve the Church safe and tranquil.

They write that this course and method of action were all the more necessary for Gratian because Ursinus’s mind had more openly revealed itself. At the very time when he had troubled the emperor in Gaul, he was also stirring up the Roman Church and city against Damasus, sending and distributing through the City letters full of sedition by a certain Paschasius. Hence the Prefect of the City, whose duty it was to ensure that the citizens’ peace suffered no harm, had reported these matters to Gratian himself; and the Roman people, while these things were being written at Aquileia, hung in uncertainty and awaited the outcome.

Since Paschasius is mentioned only in these letters, nothing occurs to me to add concerning him. But since he is called “cut off,” I understand him to have been a eunuch—a class of men generally shameless and daring in everything. Now, if these matters are compared with the letter of the Roman council added by us in the preceding year, no one will doubt that the same matter is treated in both: namely, that Damasus should not thereafter be exposed to the frauds and calumnies of Ursinus and men like him. It is also readily understood that one letter cannot have been written long after the other.

Since Gratian, occupied with war, could then reply neither to the letter of the Roman council nor to that of the Prefect of the City, Ambrose and several others who had attended the same council and were then at Aquileia judged that they should write again and request the emperor to provide prudently as the circumstances required. Yet I would not believe that this was done apart from Damasus’s own counsel and judgment. For the opinion of some that Acholius acted as legate at the same council is overthrown by the synod’s own acts.

II. These letters prompted Gratian in this year to issue the rescript addressed to Aquilinus, apparently vicar of the City, mentioned in *Codex Theodosianus*, Book XVI, title 2, law 35. It confirmed and satisfied the requests both of the Roman and of the Aquileian councils. The great father of the *Annals* published it from a Vatican codex under the year 381; then Sirmondus published a more corrected text; finally Coustantius published it among Damasus’s letters. It is repeatedly obscure and perplexing, whether through some fault of copyists or through its very style, which perpetually rises into Gallic buskin. But its contents may be summarized as follows.

He says that he had previously sent letters to Simplicius, once vicar, commanding: first, that all who attempted impious assemblies in profanation of religion should be driven to the hundredth milestone from the City, where obstinate madness, abandoned by the obedient, might rush to the ruin only of the one who erred; second, that those condemned by the judgment of right-believing priests should not return to the churches they had defiled, nor vainly seek from the emperor a reopening of the judgment.

The first part of this rescript to Simplicius touches the Donatists, Luciferianists, and Novatians, along with the Ursinians joined with all of them in communion. I think that the second provision was occasioned by Florentius of Puteoli and the bishop of Parma, after they had been condemned by the second Roman synod assembled under Damasus. We know that Simplicius held the office of vicar of the City in the consulship of Gratian III and Equitius, namely in 374, [Note: *Codex Theodosianus*, Book IX, title 29, law 1.] while Valentinian was still alive. Valentinian, however, restrained only the Ursinians and rebaptizers by his laws: [Note: *Codex Theodosianus*, Book IX, title 5, law 5; title 16, laws 1–2.] Augustine writes to these people: “Jovian was succeeded by Valentinian: read what he commanded against you.” Thus Simplicius had been ordered by Valentinian and Gratian to expel men of this rabble and obstinacy beyond the hundredth milestone, and bishops beyond the boundaries of the churches from which they had been deposed.

Some ask why the bishop of Parma is called by Gratian nearer to the “illustrious City,” and therefore more dangerous, than Florentius. Was Puteoli not nearer to Rome? Tillemont and Coustantius therefore think that “illustrious City” denotes Milan rather than Rome; I judge this entirely true, although they do not offer an adequate reason to prove it. For it should be observed that prefects of the City and praetorian prefects were, by excellence, called “illustrious powers.” [Note: Law 13, *Codex Theodosianus*, *On Accusations*.] By the same reasoning, nothing prevents us from understanding by “illustrious cities” those [Col. 0227A] in which they habitually resided and administered justice. But to return to the matter.

We do not know, however, that the Donatists or Ursinians were driven to the hundredth milestone from the City, or that the bishops of Puteoli and Parma were thrust out from the boundaries of their churches—whether because Simplicius, occupied with other more serious matters, neglected this business, or because he left office not long after receiving this command and his successors, as happened with Aquilinus, remitted this imperial injunction as a private favour, as Gratian says.

Relying on this negligence of judges and officials, the Donatists, who should have been expelled, summoned Claudianus from Africa to the City to preside over them as bishop, and he had hitherto remained there in contempt of the emperors’ laws. The Ursinian faction, which should have been driven beyond the hundredth milestone, recovered its audacity against Damasus and stirred up the Roman people. By this example, certain bishops who had already been condemned, or who ought to have been condemned, made light of the determinations of Damasus and the Roman synod and either retained, or dared through crime, sedition, and popular favour purchased with money to reclaim, sees from which they had been deposed.

Gratian therefore indicates by this rescript that he had already partly provided against, and was now partly meeting, these most serious calamities. As regards Ursinus, who was especially the reason why the Roman and Aquileian councils had written to Gratian, he says that Ursinus was then confined by removal to Agrippina, lest he undertake restless disturbances. Since the emperor seems in some measure to excuse himself for having heard that troublesome man—who more often wearied him by unexpected appearances than admonished him—he says that he acted thus in order to draw him to sounder views and persuade him to abandon his followers. Two conclusions may be drawn from this.

First, the rescript appears to have been issued after the letters of the Council of Aquileia, in which he had been reproved on account of this very indulgence; it should therefore certainly be assigned to this year, in which Baronius places it, contrary to other opinions. Second, Ursinus himself, who had joined his forces with Julian Valens against the Church at Milan in 379, was driven out of Italy and confined within fixed limits of exile in the interval between 379 and 381.

Since Gratian writes that Ursinus and his friends came before him and were heard by him in Gaul, we readily understand that this happened late in 380, when he returned from Sirmium and went there to attend to the Alamannic war. [Note: Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 4.] This explains why Ambrose says in the name of the Council of Aquileia that an importunate intrusion was attempted amid the necessities of war. Muratori is therefore entirely correct in saying, [Note: Notes on John the Deacon, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. I.] that Ursinus went into exile in Gaul very late, although, as I have said elsewhere, he infers from this not very successfully that Ursinus could have sat in the Neapolitan see before Severus.

Since Ursinus, leader of factions, and Isaac, the old calumniator of Damasus, were far from the City and confined within a fixed exile, so that they could do nothing further by themselves to disturb the peace of the Church, it remained to determine something more severe concerning the rest. Gratian therefore orders Aquilinus to execute the laws against those expressly included in the rescript, and to drive beyond the hundredth milestone from Rome rebaptizers, Ursinians, and all others whom the judgments of bishops show to be guilty of disturbances of this kind. Deposited bishops he is to make exiles from the boundaries of those cities whose people or churches they harass, either personally or through others like themselves, binding him who refuses obedience by the penalty for neglecting the enactment.

Further, if the bishop of Parma had been condemned by decree of the Roman synod and that city was subject to the vicar of Italy, one may first infer from this [Col. 0228B] that it is vainly maintained that the suburban churches are only those included in the suburban provinces. Next, one sees how much force this fact adds to the conjectures and arguments by which Bacchini, together with some others who hold the development to be later, thought that the jurisdiction of the bishop of Milan over the remaining provinces of the Vicariate of Italy arose.

To provide more securely for Damasus’s safety and ensure that others remained in the fitting duty owed to the Apostolic See, the emperor made two further enactments. First, no one infamous either for depravity of character or for a charge of calumny was to accuse bishops or give testimony against them. Second, if anyone refused to appear for judgment before Damasus and was contumacious, then, after being condemned by him, with counsel taken from five or [Col. 0228C] seven bishops, and deposed, continued to retain the church from which he had been removed, he was to be sent to the city of Rome under prosecution—that is, under faithful and suitable guard—by the praetorian prefects of Gaul and Italy, the proconsuls, and the vicars. Likewise, if anyone contumaciously despised or fled the judgment of bishops, he was to be sent back to that episcopal judgment by the same public authority.

It is therefore established that the Roman pontiff could hear bishops’ cases even at first instance, as they say, outside the suburban provinces—through Gaul and all Italy—and that this right of his was asserted and confirmed by the emperor himself, unless such cases had previously been brought before the provincial synod of bishops. I do not deny, however, that the same rescript seems to determine that cases arising in more distant regions were to be heard by metropolitans, unless the metropolitan himself were suspect. But either no one can define with certainty what those more distant regions were, or at least it is clear that no province within the prefectures of Gaul and Italy can be called situated in more distant regions in the matter at hand. Gratian expressly commands their prefects to bring even unwillingly to Rome bishops who either had not obeyed the Roman pontiff or had fled his judgment. But since these matters lie outside my purpose, it is enough to have touched upon them.

[Col. 0229A] Newton [Note: [Col. 0229D] *On Daniel’s Prophecy*, ch. VIII, and *On the Apocalypse*, ch. III.] attributes to this rescript of Gratian the origin of the primacy of Peter’s successors throughout the whole Church; and from it he writes that the Roman pontiff is represented by the eleventh horn in Daniel chapter VIII, whose duration, having been fixed at I know not how many years, is to be followed, he says, by the Last Judgment. But if he wrote this seriously, he achieved nothing except to reveal great ignorance of both civil and ecclesiastical history, and to increase the number of prophets from the sectarians’ flock, in whose mouths God has placed a spirit of falsehood.

The anonymous compiler of a history of the Roman pontiffs, however, accuses Gratian himself of folly, because by that law he not only withdrew those same Roman pontiffs from his own and the other emperors’ jurisdiction, but even transferred to them that authority which they would afterwards abuse. For, if you trust this deserter, since the Roman bishop could then be brought before a secular tribunal, he had not yet, before this time, been the supreme judge of the Church. He thinks this proved by the example of Damasus, who, he says, first sought a synodal judgment from the emperor in order to avoid the severity and integrity of the secular magistrates, conscious of his own guilt; although afterwards, when he did not trust that he could clear himself either before a synod or before the civil magistrates themselves, he finally resolved to flee to the emperor’s own consistory as to an asylum.

Certainly, if this stinking slave of a bookseller had to be marked for each individual lie, there would be no end to the discourse. For anyone who compares the letters of the Roman Council and the Council of Aquileia, and Gratian’s own rescript to Aquilinus, with the statements of this same anonymous writer, will easily and plainly discover how many deceits he stitches together and falsehoods he entwines in this one passage. But as regards the divine exemption of Roman pontiffs, bishops, priests, and all ministers of sacred things, so many Catholic writers before me have established it by arguments so firm and unanswerable that time would be wasted by repeating what has so often been said.

III. Besides this letter, which concerns Gratian alone and was to be delivered to him, the Council of Aquileia wrote another, concerning Theodosius alone and the Eastern bishops. It was brought by envoys sent by that council and delivered to the emperor; and it contains several matters that serve to illuminate the history of that time, if they are correctly observed.

First, therefore, they praise the emperors because through their piety scarcely two heretics were to be found in the West; while in the East, after the Arians had been expelled, all the churches of God had been restored to Catholics and were attended only by Catholics. From this it is evident that, when they wrote, the bishops assembled at Aquileia had been informed of the laws enacted by Theodosius for that purpose on 10 January and 30 July. Then they lament that frequent dissensions among the Catholics themselves and an unpacified discord prevented them from enjoying these benefits in their fullness.

Since those dissensions were among the Catholics themselves, we must suppose that those intended here are the ones which, as we said, arose after Meletius’s death, and which Gregory Nazianzen says deserved tears such as no one, ancient or recent, had yet shed for any assaults of adverse fortune. For the teachers of the people, the holy bishops, bestowers of the Spirit, and those who pour forth from lofty thrones words through which salvation is obtained, assail one another with such frenzy—raising tumults, gathering forces, tearing each other with their tongues, leaping wildly, as men deprived of sound mind are wont to do, plundering whomsoever each can plunder before being plundered himself, while a rabid thirst for rule possesses their minds—that they have utterly torn the whole world apart.

All these things, therefore, which Gregory says both here and again [Col. 0230B] in his oration to the 150 Fathers occurred because of Flavian’s single ordination, were known to the Fathers of the Council of Aquileia. At the same time, understanding that no slight injury had been done to Paulinus, they say that they were deeply moved because they had learned that many things had been innovated, and because those were being oppressed who, because they had always maintained communion with the Westerners, ought rather to have been assisted: namely, Timothy of Alexandria and Paulinus of Antioch.

They complain that these men were being pressed by the dissensions of persons whose faith had wavered in earlier times: that is, those whom Gregory himself calls *amphidoxoi* (“of doubtful opinion”) and *mesoi* (“the middle party”), and who uphold the faith held by the emperor. But if Timothy, after those most disgraceful disputes had been raised and carried on, came with his bishops to Constantinople in order to assist in establishing the agreement, and was nevertheless compelled to endure the vexations and dissensions of these men, it is plain and evident that no other cause can be imagined than his maintaining communion with Paulinus and rejecting communion with Flavian, now ordained bishop.
