It is consequently manifest that the Council of Aquileia—whatever Tillemont and Floridus may have thought—was not ignorant of anything that had already been decreed and completed at Constantinople. If this is established, and if, on the other hand, they say absolutely nothing in these letters about the deposition of Maximus the Cynic, the enthronement of Gregory, or the ordination of Nectarius, you may yourself judge what Ambrose and the other Fathers of that council thought about these matters.

But, to return from my brief digression: Ambrose desires that these Eastern bishops of doubtful faith be joined to his own and the other Westerners’ communion, provided that they are of sound and sincere faith and that the same prerogative is preserved for the associates of the old communion, namely Paulinus and Timothy. They desire these men to share the same right, either because a common fellowship ought to contain no grievance, or because, since the Westerners had long ago received letters from both parties—the Meletian and the Paulinian—they had communicated with both, and there was no reason why they should choose one rather than the other.

Therefore, in order to bring about among the Catholics of both parties the peace which they themselves enjoyed with all, they add that they had long resolved to send bishop-envoys from their own body to the East. But because this plan had subsequently been delayed and impeded by hostile incursions and public disturbances, they judged that the matter should be conducted by letters. In these they requested Theodosius to regard as ratified and confirmed the agreement by which the Antiochene schism had been settled and quieted, and not to permit any “superordination” or substitutional appointment to be attempted, by which it was certainly to be feared that the schism might break out again more bitterly. But it is better to hear them:

> But because at that time our efforts could not take effect amid public disturbances, we believe that our petitions were presented to Your Piety, in which, in accordance with the AGREEMENT OF THE PARTIES, WE REQUESTED that, when one of the two should die, the churches should remain with the survivor, and that no superordination should be attempted.

Here, then, it is clear, first, that these Western petitions were presented to the emperor because hostile incursions and public disturbances had blocked the roads and prevented envoys from being sent. Secondly, after the Westerners had learned of that Antiochene agreement—which, as we said, was confirmed by an oath in that city about the middle of the year 379—it is necessary to say that the petitions themselves were presented to Theodosius in the following year, while the Gothic war was not yet finished and, as I have said, in the name of that Roman synod at which Acacius, Meletius’s envoy, was present.

But since the bishops assembled at Aquileia had subsequently learned that no regard had been paid either to that agreement or to the petitions presented to Theodosius, and that the harmony scarcely restored had again been broken and dissolved in the Council of Constantinople, they therefore set little store by its decrees and say:

> We ask you, most clement and Christian princes, also to decree that a council of all the Catholic bishops be held at Alexandria, in order that they may discuss more fully among themselves and determine to whom communion ought to be imparted and for whom it ought to be retained.

Yet the Fathers of Aquileia do not ask for a plenary Eastern council to be convened at Alexandria in order that they themselves may follow its decision in this matter. For, as regards themselves, they openly declare that they will remain in communion with Timothy and the Church of Alexandria, and that they will in no way depart from the agreement entered into at Antioch with an oath added; and therefore they will always regard Paulinus as bishop of Antioch. Here you see what the Westerners themselves thought of their own dignity and the prerogative of their vote.

Why, then, do they ask that council to be convened? The reason is stated in the same letter in these words: “lest any should seem to have been disregarded, who have requested our communion and the agreement WHICH WE DESIRE TO STAND; or lest the means of any peace and fellowship be neglected.” There were therefore two reasons for requesting this council. One was that they might appear to have taken account, through that agreement, of those who had recently joined the communion of Paulinus and the Westerners; for several who had followed Meletius’s party afterwards withdrew from Flavian because he had violated the agreement. [Note: [Col. 0231D] Sozomen, book VII, chapter 11.] The other was that blame for the dissension might not thereafter be transferred to the Westerners themselves and that they might not again be reproached for neglecting the Easterners.

Yet when they wrote, they seem to have entertained the best and most reasonable hope that affairs at Antioch would have a happier outcome in that Alexandrian council than had happened at Constantinople. Hence they say:

> We earnestly beseech that, after they have discussed matters among themselves in a fuller assembly, the assistance of Your Piety may also breathe upon their priestly decrees, and that you may decree that these be communicated to our knowledge, so that we may not waver in uncertain feeling, but, joyful and secure, may give thanks before Almighty God to Your Piety—not only because perfidy has been excluded, but because faith and concord have been restored to Catholics.

These words, however, must be understood as conditional upon the subsequent concurrence of the authority of the Roman bishop. Hence, in this case of Flavian, Ambrose writes to Theophilus of Alexandria and his bishops, judges delegated by the plenary Council of Capua: “We certainly think that the matter ought to be referred to our holy brother, the priest of the Roman Church; for we presume that you will judge nothing that could also displease him. Thus provision will be made for the decision, and thus peace and tranquillity will be secure, if your counsel determines what brings no dissension to our communion.” [Note: [Col. 0231D] In the Ballerini edition, Epistle 56.]

IV. Sulpicius Severus writes that Instantius, Salvianus, and Priscillian, having been condemned by the Council of Saragossa, set out for Rome to clear themselves before Damasus, but were not even admitted into his presence. [Note: [Col. 0231D] *History*, book II, no. 250, in Sigonius’s works, vol. IV.] No one can fail to see that this must be attributed solely to the report customarily and promptly sent by that council to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0232C] Learned men rightly refer this to the present year; for the Council of Saragossa was held in the preceding year, about the month of September. But Priscillian neither left Spain immediately nor diligently pursued the journey once begun; instead, he lingered in Aquitaine, occupied in scattering the seeds of perfidy and corrupting morals. Those who think rightly and whose minds are free from prejudice praise Damasus’s piety and religious principle in this matter. But those who either seek to defend heresy or are carried away by hatred—namely Quesnel and Dupin [Note: [Col. 0232D] Quesnel, Dissertation 5, chapter 16; Dupin, Dissertation 2, chapter 2, §2, p. 161.]—maintain that he acted thus through fear of the excommunication by which the same council had bound those who received the condemned heretics into communion.

Away with such madness! Would those two bishops really have gone directly to Rome with the purpose of clearing themselves before Damasus, unless they had been wholly certain that the Roman pontiff rightfully exercised this power as supreme judge of all in cases of faith? Or had Hosius—the chief author and promoter of the Nicene and Sardican canons—allowed his fellow Spaniards to remain ignorant that in those councils the prerogative of the divine primacy had been confirmed for them? I shall not allow myself to be persuaded of it.

Moreover, kind reader, so that you may learn not merely from conjectures but from the surviving records what observance the Spanish Church paid to the Sardican canons in this fourth century, consult the most distinguished Cajetan Cennio in his learned *Antiquities of that Church*. [Note: [Col. 0233D] Dissertation 2, chapter 4.] He has spared us this labor.

Since Sulpicius further adds that, when these heretics expelled from Rome came to Milan, they were likewise rejected by Bishop Ambrose, you may infer with that same most distinguished author that there was a great union of minds and counsels between Damasus and Ambrose himself, and that the already eminent Church of Milan was especially obedient to that of Rome. For I do not think that among Catholics—or indeed among learned persons alien from Catholic religion—there can now be anyone who would assert that the Gnostics, driven from Rome, fled to Milan because they regarded that bishop as equal or even superior to the Roman bishop.

This splendid union of the two Churches, especially conspicuous under Damasus [Col. 0233B] and Ambrose, later increased and was extended to Siricius, Anastasius, Simplicianus, and Venerius. It brought it about that African and Spanish bishops occasionally consulted the bishop of Milan, whom they knew to be bound to the Roman Church by the closest bond and to be most fully instructed in—and most steadfastly attached to—its doctrines, judgments, and counsels.

## CHAPTER XX. A.D. 382, THE SEVENTEENTH OF DAMASUS, SYAGRIUS AND ANTONIUS, CONSULS

I. Damasus thwarts the senators’ pagan plan to restore the Altar of Victory, by letters written to Ambrose. II. He holds at Rome the famous council convened by him in the preceding year. III. The principal reasons for convening it. IV. The Easterners excuse themselves for not attending it; their letter is examined according to the sequence of events then occurring, and several points are proposed for observation. V. Why they reported to Damasus concerning Cyril of Jerusalem and concerning Nectarius’s election. VI. Who attended this council? Basnage’s erroneous opinion.

[Col. 0233C]

I. In the first months of this year, through the senators of the City who worshipped idols, action was taken to restore the statue and Altar of Victory; and Symmachus was entrusted with an embassy to Gratian the emperor in order to seek this restoration. Augustus had placed that statue, long before brought from Tarentum to Rome and afterwards adorned with Egyptian spoils, in the middle breadth of the senate-house, at the point where the Fathers entered to deliberate in the senate; and he had dedicated an altar there.

When Roman generals, after successful campaigns and completed wars, sacrificed at it and referred back to it the victories received over their enemies, Symmachus derived from this a subject upon which he might pour forth more mud in his surviving letter to Valentinian. Hence senators entering the senate-house for deliberation had to sacrifice to this idol with wine and incense and pronounce an oath. Thus Ambrose writes: [Note: [Col. 0234D] Epistle 17, from the Ballerini edition.]

> Is this to be tolerated—that a pagan should sacrifice and a Christian be present? Must all, even against their will, drink the smoke with their eyes, the music with their ears, and be sprinkled upon face and mouth, however much they turn away, by the ashes stirred up from your hearths? Are baths, porticoes, and streets occupied by images not enough for them? Shall there not even be a common condition in a common council? Shall the pious portion of the senate be bound by the words of those who invoke gods and by the oaths of those who adjure?

That altar, therefore, destroyed by Constans, restored by Magnentius, again overthrown by Constantius, and once more restored to superstition under Julian, Gracchus, as is believed, had destroyed while holding the urban prefecture, supported by the authority of a law enacted by Gratian himself. Prudentius records that outstanding deed against Symmachus in these verses:

> Why should I recount in verse the Gracchi, the Publicolas,  
> Supported by the right of authority and foremost in the citadel of the senate,  
> Who ordered the images of the gods to be torn down  
> And, together with their readers, gathered themselves humbly  
> To be ruled by almighty Christ?

[Col. 0234B] But the senators who had professed the Christian faith, in order to frustrate the efforts of the other party, consulted with Damasus and composed another petition. In it they protested that Symmachus falsely put forward the name of the senate; indeed, they declared that they would no longer enter the senate-house if this measure were ordered. Damasus then sent this petition to Ambrose and charged him to use his influence with Gratian—who spent almost a whole year in Italy—that Christianity might suffer no harm in the meantime.

The names of those who assisted in drafting the petition have perished together with Damasus’s letter to Ambrose. Ambrose himself, however, says that they were countless, and Prudentius confirms this by naming several. Gratian therefore, to whom the bishop of Milan—whose zeal for religion was by no means unequal to that of Damasus—sent the petition, understood that an unjust request was being made of him, one which a not inconsiderable number of highly eminent senators opposed. He did not grant the embassy; and so, through Damasus’s foresight and Ambrose’s efforts, the undertakings of Symmachus and the others then ended badly.

What had not succeeded under Gratian was attempted again after his death before the boy Valentinian by the same Symmachus, whose memorial still survives among his letters, book X, letter 54. But Ambrose also opposed this request with great force of spirit, mindful of the embassy entrusted to him by Damasus; and by a weighty and most vehement letter and speech he brought it about that his adversaries’ hope was again frustrated.

Since Symmachus discharged this second embassy when he was already Prefect of the City, and since he began to administer the urban prefecture after the middle of 384 had passed, it is perfectly clear that the first embassy cannot be removed from the first months of this year, and that the matter was concluded before Ambrose came to Rome for the synod of which I shall shortly speak. For he writes:

> For nearly two years ago, when they attempted to seek this, Damasus, the priest of the Roman Church, chosen by God’s judgment, sent me the petition which the Christian senators had presented—indeed, they were countless—asserting that they had authorized no such thing, that it was not fitting to consent to requests of this pagan sort; they also complained publicly and privately that they would not meet in the senate-house if anything of the kind were decreed . . . . . . I sent this petition to the brother of Your Clemency.

II. It is now time to discuss the synod assembled at Rome in this year. The first question is who convened it and for what reason; then, when it was convened and also held, and what was done and determined in it.

Theodoret writes that it was convened by Damasus [Note: [Col. 0235D] Book V, chapter 8.] in these words:

> In the following summer—that is, after the summer in which the general Council of Constantinople was completed—when most of the bishops who had attended it had come to the same city, they received a letter from the WESTERN bishops, exhorting them to proceed to Rome for the great synod being prepared there.

No one is ignorant that, under the designation “Westerners,” the Roman bishop is understood above all, as their leader. Hence, from Socrates and Sozomen, we know that the letter of the Council of Lampsacus, though addressed to Liberius and the Westerners, was delivered to Liberius alone. [Note: [Col. 0235D] Book IV, chapter 12; book VI, chapter 10.] Hence also Jerome says: “Let the West and Egypt condemn me as a heretic—that is, Damasus and Peter.” [Note: [Col. 0235D] Letter 18, Ver. edition.]

Those are mistaken, therefore—to say this in passing—who think that by “Westerners” in this passage of Theodoret certain bishops of an Italian council are designated, whose letter, they say, was published by Sirmond. [Note: [Col. 0235D] Tillemont, *On Ambrose*, article 30.] For, not to repeat what has been said elsewhere, this interpretation and conjecture are clearly refuted, in addition to Theodoret, by Sozomen himself. He says that the Roman bishop and the other bishops of the Western regions, not a little angered by Flavian’s ordination, wrote to the Easterners to summon them to the West.

Since the Easterners say that they received the Roman pontiff’s letter in the summer, after they had come to Constantinople at Theodosius’s summons in accordance with the letters written in the preceding year by the Council of Aquileia, and since they complain that they were almost caught unprepared, one may rightly infer, first, that this council was convened after the Council of Aquileia had ended; and secondly, that Damasus’s letter of summons was sent in the first months of this year. The sequence of events was, I think, as follows.

For we said that in the preceding year the Council of Aquileia asked Theodosius to order a council at Alexandria, gathering bishops from all the East, in order to quiet the discord arising from Flavian’s ordination. Those letters, written near the end of September and sent through envoys, could scarcely have been delivered before the end of that year. Theodosius therefore received them after the bishops had departed, and, intending to comply with the judgment of the Aquileians, summoned the bishops of his empire again to Constantinople in order to consult with them both about the place and about the purpose of the council that had been proposed and requested.

Meanwhile the Roman pontiff judged it preferable that a council be convened at Rome rather than Alexandria, and for that purpose sent summonses. Consequently, after summer had already arrived, they were communicated to the bishops who had been summoned to Constantinople by Theodosius in accordance with the letters of the Council of Aquileia.

The Easterners explicitly mention and distinguish these two letters, one from Damasus and the other from the Fathers of Aquileia. As regards the Aquileian letter, they say that they came to the imperial city in accordance with letters sent to the Emperor Theodosius after the Council of Aquileia in the preceding year. But when they speak of the recent letter written by Damasus, they complain that its arrival took them unexpectedly and say that they were unprepared for the Roman journey.

Moreover, the summons to Rome for this council was not issued by Damasus without knowing Gratian the emperor’s judgment. From Sozomen it is clear that Gratian attached his own letters to those of Damasus. This explains why Jerome wrote that bishops of East and West were assembled at Rome by imperial letters [Note: [Col. 0236D] Letter 108, Ver. edition.], and why the Easterners themselves say that they were summoned to the Roman council by the letters of the most pious Emperor Theodosius; for the letters of one emperor had also to bear the name of the other.

III. As to the reason for convening this council, Sozomen teaches us in these words that this was its chief cause:

> Meletius received burial, but Flavian was ordained in his place contrary to the faith of the oath; from this arose a great disturbance which again seized the Church of Antioch. Very many separated themselves from Flavian’s communion and held separate assemblies under Paulinus. The bishops themselves also disagreed among themselves over this affair. But the bishop of Rome and the other bishops of the Western regions were not a little angered. They wrote their usual letters, called synodical letters, to Paulinus as bishop of Antioch, but sent no letters to Flavian. Indeed, they accused Diodorus of Tarsus and Acacius, bishop of Beroea, who had ordained him, and abstained from communion with them. Therefore, that these matters might be examined, they and the Emperor Gratian wrote to the Eastern bishops, summoning them to the West.  
> [Note: [Col. 0236D] Sozomen, book VII, chapter 11.]

What Sozomen openly asserts, Jerome indicates under a veil of words when he writes that bishops were assembled at Rome because of certain dissensions among the Churches. [Note: [Col. 0236D] Letter 127, Ver. edition.] This is why those Easterners, replying to Damasus and the bishops associated with him, declare that their disposition is ready for peace and unity.

I would not, however, assert that this was the sole reason for convening the council. But among the other alleged causes I cannot approve the one which Valesius, Baluzius, and other zealous advocates of the Italian council often press: namely, that Nectarius’s ordination was to be examined, because the Westerners seemed to reject it out of their attachment to Maximus the Cynic, who had appealed to him.

Its falsity is proved by Sozomen’s silence; by the testimonies of Boniface and Nicholas, which I have produced elsewhere; and further by the utter improbability that Damasus—who had annulled Maximus’s disorderly ordination by a solemn and public judgment—should afterwards have been so inconsistent with himself as to censure Nectarius’s ordination at the urging of that same Cynic. Therefore, if Nectarius’s ordination was discussed in this Roman synod, an altogether different reason from that alleged must have existed for discussing it.

IV. The Easterners replied to Damasus’s summons by the letter which Theodoret reproduces and highly praises [Note: [Col. 0237D] Book V, chapter 9.]. In it they give two reasons for not coming to Rome. First, although the heretics had been driven from the sheepfolds, they continued to ravage the flocks in the wilderness, hold profane assemblies, and plot everything for the ruin of religion. Therefore the Eastern bishops could not attend the council without appearing to abandon the Churches and leave them necessarily without protection.

Secondly, the time appointed was insufficient for so long a journey and for the other preparations required. For they say:

> We came together at Constantinople in accordance with the letters which Your Reverence sent in the preceding year, after the Council of Aquileia, to the most pious Emperor Theodosius. We were equipped for this one journey only and brought the agreement of the bishops who were in the province concerning this one council. We had neither suspected nor heard anything about undertaking a longer journey before we assembled at Constantinople. Furthermore, the shortness of the appointed time did not suffice either to prepare for a longer journey or to notify all the bishops in our communion who are in different provinces and obtain their consent.

I have adduced these words so that the reader may see that explicit mention is made here of the letters written first by the Council of Aquileia and afterwards by Damasus, but none at all of the letter which Sirmond published last under the name of an Italian council. From this the reader may again infer that the latter is spurious and was never written—or at least was never sent to Constantinople before the summer months of this year. Those are also mistaken who think it indicated by Theodoret under the expression “letter of the Westerners,” received by the Easterners at the time when they wrote, and answered by them.

For if Ambrose and the other bishops of the Italian vicariate alone had written it, as Tillemont and other defenders of this view maintain, there was no reason for the Easterners to reply to Damasus, Acholius, Britto, and Basil—who certainly had not attended this fictitious Italian council and knew nothing of its proceedings. But this by the way, since I have discussed the matter elsewhere at length.

After the Easterners had excused themselves on these grounds for not coming to Rome, they sent three envoys from their body—Cyriacus, Eusebius, and Priscianus—in order to repay with reciprocal charity the charity by which, as they say, they had been summoned to the synod. They instructed these men both to declare that the disposition of all the rest was peaceful and directed toward unity, and to make evident their zeal for sound faith.

That declaration indeed refutes those who falsely claim that the Easterners refused to come to Rome because they maintained that the authority of Eastern councils was supreme. Moreover, in order to show the Roman pontiff that they themselves were sound and uncorrupted, in the letter which they gave to their envoys to bring to Damasus, they condemned, first, by an open and ample exposition of faith, the heresies of Arius, Sabellius, Eunomius, Macedonius, and Apollinarius; and finally they added these words, worth citing:

> If you require anything further, you will be satisfied if you deign to read the tome composed at Antioch by the synod held there, and also the tome issued at Constantinople in the preceding year by the ecumenical council. In these tomes we have expounded our faith more fully and pronounced the sentence of anathema against the heresies recently arisen.

From this I draw especially three conclusions. First, among those who wrote this letter were some who had attended the Synod of Antioch—probably, in my judgment, Diodorus of Tarsus, Acacius of Beroea, Pelagius of Laodicea, and Gregory, bishop of Nyssa. Secondly, they were certain that the acts of the Antiochene Synod had already been brought to Damasus. For how otherwise could he read them here in order to be more fully instructed on the matter? This confirms my conjecture that in 380 those acts were brought to the City through Acacius. [Note: [Col. 0237D] See chapter 15.]

Thirdly, if you attend carefully to what the Easterners write concerning the Council of Constantinople of the preceding year, you will readily understand that nothing from the acts and decrees of that council was reported to the Apostolic See except the heresies against which they had pronounced the sentence of anathema, and certain other matters relating to discipline, of which there will now be discussion. Leo the Great therefore rightly and deservedly wrote to Anatolius, in order to curb his ambition, that the document of certain bishops—that is, the document by which the first rank of honor after Rome was assigned to the bishop of Constantinople—had never been submitted to the knowledge of the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 0238D] Letter 80, Lyons edition.] Those who appeared to doubt this inflicted a very grave injury upon that most holy man.

[Col. 0238D] The disciplinary matters concerning which the Easterners, without mentioning the remaining canons, reported to Damasus through their envoys, concern the ordinations of Nectarius and Flavian and Cyril of Jerusalem. For they write:

> Concerning the particular administration of the Churches, as you well know, the ancient ordinance and the rules of the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea have prevailed: that in each province the bishops of that province, and, if they think fit, together with the bishops of neighboring provinces themselves, should perform ordinations as may be useful. In accordance with the prescription of these laws, we ordained the most reverend and most religious Nectarius bishop of the Church of Constantinople, in a universal council, by the common consent of all, in the presence of the most religious Emperor Theodosius, with the agreement of all the clergy and the city.
>
> The bishops both of that province and of the diocese of the East, assembled together, canonically ordained the most reverend and most religious Flavian bishop of the most ancient Church of Antioch in Syria, with the consent of the whole Church, which as if with one voice highly praised the man. The whole synod accepted this ordination.
>
> And we make known to you the most reverend and most religious Cyril of the Church of Jerusalem, who was canonically ordained long ago and underwent many struggles against the Arians in various places.

Beveridge uses this passage [Note: [Col. 0239D] *Cod. Can. Vend.*, book I, chapter 51.] to establish the authority and antiquity of the Apostolic Canons, which he rightly judges to be indicated by the phrase “ancient ordinance”; and to prove that the ordinations of Nectarius and Flavian were performed not merely by bishops assembled from a single province, but by bishops from other provinces and from the whole East gathered at the Council of Constantinople.

For if it were otherwise, why would they have appealed to that ancient ordinance, namely Apostolic Canons 34 and 35? These deal only with summoning, if thought fit, bishops also from other and neighboring provinces to sacred ordinations. I wished this to be observed against those who assert that, in the meantime, Flavian was consecrated at Antioch. But let us return again to the point from which we departed.

What, then, was charged against Cyril, such that the Eastern bishops had to defend his cause before the Apostolic See and this Roman synod, is by no means clear. Some think it happened because Damasus and the Westerners knew his ordination to have been discredited. Rufinus, moreover, Socrates, and Sozomen write that he was changeable in faith, a point which certain recent Greek menaia seem to confirm. But Touttée, a man distinguished for learning and piety, carefully clears him of this charge in the Life of the same Father prefixed to his works. To the reasons adduced by him may be added what is read in the Synodical Letter: namely, that Cyril was highly praised by the synods held at Rome under Damasus and at Constantinople under Nectarius; from this one may infer that his faith was sound. Add also that, if he had at any time professed heresy, he could not have been received into communion by the Easterners unless the case had first been heard and examined by the Apostolic See. For Felix III writes that this is the rule and ancient tradition of the Church: bishops of the principal sees, when they return from heresy, are not to be received and admitted to communion until the proceedings have been reported to the first see and what had been decided has been confirmed by it. [Note: [Col. 0239D] Conc. Ven. edit., vol. V, p. 187.]

V. As regards Nectarius, there are, as we have already observed, those who think that the Easterners asserted his ordination to have been carried out according to the law prescribed by the Council of Nicaea in order to defend it against the threats of Damasus and the Westerners, who favored Maximus the Cynic. But these persons seem to me simply to be guessing, carried away by preconceived opinions. For Pope Boniface, undoubtedly a competent witness, assigns only one reason: namely, that the matter had not come to the notice of the Roman bishop and therefore lacked the firmness which could accrue to it from communion with the Apostolic See alone. Indeed, Nectarius, being a catechumen, was excluded from the episcopate by Nicene Canon 2; and this is why several of the Fathers opposed his consecration from the beginning. Therefore, since Theodosius also understood this well and feared lest some fresh proceeding might on that account be raised against Nectarius, he attached his own court officials to the three bishops who were then ambassadors sent to Rome by that synod, so that they might more easily induce Damasus [Col. 0240B] to grant letters of his communion, or a *formata*, which would validate the priesthood conferred on a neophyte. This, if I am not mistaken, is what Ambrose—not obscurely—meant when, in the words quoted by me elsewhere, he wrote that his ordination had been approved by Easterners and Westerners, assigning only an example to the former, the Easterners, but judgment to the latter, that is, to the supreme head of that Church. [Note: [Col. 0239D] See ch. 9, at the end.]

Since, then, we have a certain and necessary reason why those bishops reported Nectarius’s ordination to Damasus, there is no need whatever to have recourse to the Italian council and its letters—mere inventions. There was, moreover, another reason why a *formata* for Nectarius was sought from the Roman pontiff, though one which had to be veiled and passed over in silence. For when the bishop of Constantinople, separated from the metropolitan jurisdiction of Heraclea, had received by decree of the synod the first rank of honor after Rome, it seemed necessary, in order that he might as it were take possession of his new dignity, that, following the example of Alexandria and Antioch, he should report his ordination to the Apostolic See and receive from it letters of communion. Saint John Chrysostom and the later successors of Nectarius followed this precedent in a long succession. Thus, concluding their letter with the matters which the Easterners considered established by themselves “lawfully and canonically” (*enthésmōs kai kanonikōs*, ἐνθέσμως καὶ κανονικῶς), they ask Damasus and the other Westerners to rejoice with them. They use this ecclesiastical formula, expressing mutual charity, in order to seek confirmation of all that they had determined; for this was the end of synodical reports sent to the Roman pontiff. [Note: [Col. 0240D] *De Marc.*, bk. I, ch. 10, §9.]

VI. This letter of the Easterners is addressed to Damasus, Ambrose, Brito, Valerian, Ascholius, Anemius, and Basil, and to the others gathered in the great city of Rome. From this we infer that all were present at that council. Except for Basil and Brito, the sees of the others are sufficiently known. Yet Bollandus, whose opinion Tillemont follows, judges Brito to have presided over the Church of Trier, a church of great renown even in that age. [Note: [Col. 0240D] On St. Justus, vol. VIII.] In place of Basil, some read Bassianus; but the more numerous manuscripts have Basil, a reading that seems preferable to me. Bassianus, bishop of Lodi, had only recently been ordained; he was neither of such great standing nor dignity, nor did he administer such an illustrious church, as to deserve mention before others who are omitted. It is therefore likely that Basil, lest he should be inferior to the others addressed, was bishop of some principal church in Spain, Africa, or perhaps Gaul.

From the East Paulinus and Epiphanius were present; perhaps others too came from Egypt, owing to the close alliance with the Roman Church and the authority of the imperial letters by which all had been summoned. Basnage indeed asserts that Paulinus and Epiphanius were absent, while Maximus the Cynic was present at that council. [Note: [Col. 0241D] Under the year 382, no. 2.] From what source he infers what he writes about Paulinus and Epiphanius, he may see to himself. What he asserts concerning Maximus he may have taken from Baluze, who often delights in this tale. [Note: [Col. 0241D] See bk. V, *On Councils*, ch. 21.] Then there joined them the three bishops—Cyriacus, Eusebius, and Priscian—ambassadors from the Easterners assembled at Constantinople; perhaps the court officials sent by Theodosius attached themselves to them as companions.

Jerome also came to the City with Paulinus and Epiphanius, as he himself testifies in his letter to Principia. [Note: [Col. 0241D] Ep. 127, no. 10, Verona edition.] For if he lived at Rome for almost certainly three years, [Note: [Col. 0241D] Ep. 45, no. 2.] and if, intending to go to Jerusalem after the death of Damasus, he boarded a ship in the Roman harbor in August, [Note: [Col. 0241D] *Against Rufinus*, bk. III, no. 22.] he must have arrived in the City with those same companions in this year, about autumn, when the council was already near at hand. Accordingly, contrary to the opinion of some, he had spent a longer time at Constantinople. His name, moreover, was not unknown to Damasus, from whom he had also received letters. That he was further intimate with this pontiff may be inferred both from the letter on the three hypostases, in which he praises Damasus’s kindness, and from the friendship between Jerome himself and Evagrius, a man most necessary to Damasus. Damasus therefore retained with him a man whose learning and piety he knew, to assist him in the dispatch of ecclesiastical causes and affairs and to answer in his name the synodical inquiries of East and West. [Note: [Col. 0241D] Ep. 123, no. 20, Verona edition.] Here one may praise both the excellent judgment of Damasus and find a most certain proof of the supreme authority of the Roman pontiffs in the Church. For if you survey in thought the whole extent of the world, what other Church will occur to you whose dignity and authority, like Rome’s, were so great that the resolution of difficult and obscure questions, both in faith and discipline, should be sought from it with such constancy, duration, confidence, and humility, and received with such great and sincere obedience?

Moreover, throughout the whole time Damasus survived, he employed Jerome’s learning in elucidating the sacred Scriptures and explaining their difficulties. He urged him to do this both orally and by letters which still survive, witnesses to that pontiff’s unceasing zeal for Christian doctrine. But now to other matters.

## CHAPTER XXI

I–II. What was decided in that Roman council, and concerning the confirmation of the Council of Constantinople. III. Next, concerning the fragments published by Holstenius. IV. Baronius’s conjectures are examined and defended. V. Dandolo’s testimony concerning the same council is adduced.

I. It is indeed regrettable that the acts of this synod—which Theodoret calls the greatest—more than perhaps any others, though they seem still to have existed in the age of the writer of the synodical booklet, were later lost. For there can be no doubt that all that was done or decreed by it was wholly worthy of the learning and holiness of the Fathers who were present there in large numbers. But since the antiquity of time has robbed us of this benefit, it remains for us to attain, at least by conjecture, the little that we can.

No one, then, will doubt that matters were dealt with in it for which, as we have said, it was convened by Damasus. But meanwhile the three bishop-ambassadors from the Easterners brought the letters discussed shortly before, by which they seemed to seek confirmation of what they had decreed both concerning the faith and concerning the sees of Constantinople and Antioch. For this reason too—and it was the greatest of all, namely that of the faith—the matter must have been treated; and on that occasion what had been defined at the Council of Constantinople was again approved and confirmed at Rome. This is the opinion of Baronius and others.

It might indeed be objected that no certain evidence for this Damasian confirmation exists before the age of Photius. Rather, since the Gelasian Decree, published and reviewed from Vatican codices by Fontanini and the learned Bianchini, [Note: [Col. 0241D] Prologue to Anastasius, vol. IV, work 3.] mentions only the Nicene, Ephesian, and Chalcedonian synods—unlike the Hormisdan decree published by Chifflet, in which the Constantinopolitan council is added after Nicaea—it might seem inferable that the Apostolic See had not accepted and confirmed it before Hormisdas’s time. Yet Photius’s testimony is so open and explicit that I can scarcely doubt that he read letters written by Damasus himself on that subject, as was customary, [Note: [Col. 0242D] We learn this clearly from Emperor Marcian’s letter to Leo the Great, in which, together with the bishops present at the Council of Chalcedon, he declares his wonder that the pontiff had not in turn sent letters to be read in the holy churches, showing that the acts of that synod were approved by the Apostolic See.] or some other document from which he was informed of the matter.

For after enumerating in his book *On Synods* the bishops of the principal Eastern churches who had been present at this Council of Constantinople—Timothy of Alexandria, Meletius of Antioch, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Nectarius, whom he calls leaders of the synod—he finally joins Damasus to them, declaring him shortly afterward to have confirmed the same things and approved them by his consent. This consent, as you see, is not inferred merely from bare silence; Photius judges it to have been such as rendered those decisions valid and firm—that is, supported by some definite document and joined to authority and power:

> “Not long afterward Damasus of Rome was known to be in agreement, strengthening the same things and associating himself with those who had preceded.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0243D] Οἶς οὐ πολὺς χρόνος Δάμασος ὁ τῆς Ῥώμης τὰ αὐτὰ κρατύνων ἐγνωρίζετο σύμφωνος, τοῖς προλαβοῦσι καθιστάμενος.]

Although, therefore, this most vigilant pontiff had often previously condemned those heresies, it is credible that by some further solemn writing he wished to confer new and invincible force upon the dogmas defined at that Council of Constantinople: both because this was the wish of the Eastern bishops, and because after this peremptory judgment of the Apostolic See no hope of escape remained to the Macedonians and Apollinarians. Since, then, as I said shortly before, it is established that the Easterners sought confirmation of their acts by letters brought to Rome through bishop-ambassadors, Damasus seems to have granted it when those same men returned. For no one can say that the pontiff dismissed them on their departure without some answer and without other letters to Theodosius, by which the emperor might be assured that Nectarius’s ordination had been confirmed; Damasus is known to have been most diligent in answering synodical consultations, both from the letters that survive and from the testimony of Jerome, whose services he employed.

I think this was the reason why the same pontiff, according to Hadrian, who restored the Basilica of St. Lawrence long afterward, wished this Council of Constantinople to be represented in a painting and thus transmitted to posterity in that church. [Note: [Col. 0243D] Venetian edition of the Councils, vol. VIII, letter to Charlemagne, p. 1591.] Celestine and Sixtus later followed this example by depicting the Ephesian Council in the Liberian Basilica, and Leo the Great by depicting Chalcedon in the Vatican Basilica. [Note: [Col. 0244D] See Bianchini, notes on Sixtus III.] These are the matters concerning the faith which seem to have been transacted at this Roman council.

II. Tillemont further thinks that the reception of Apollinarians into the Church was considered. Since Jerome, by the pope’s command, had composed a formula to which those heretics were thereafter to be compelled to subscribe, the following occurred, as Rufinus’s words may best be quoted here:

> When deliberation was being held concerning the reception of the Apollinarians, Bishop Damasus commanded that a statement of the ecclesiastical faith be composed, to which they too would have to subscribe if they wished to be united with the Church. He entrusted this task, as was customary, to his friend, a most eloquent presbyter who handled such business for him. It was thought necessary in the statement itself on the Incarnation that the expression “the Lordly Man” (*homo dominicus*) should be used. The Apollinarians took offense at this phrase and began to accuse it of novelty.  
> [Note: [Col. 0244D] Jerome, *Apology* II, ch. 20.]

No one will deny that the Apollinarians may again have been discussed in this Roman council, on the occasion of the Constantinopolitan synod by which they had been condemned and whose definitions must then have been reported and read at Rome. But I scarcely think that Damasus then ordered a repeated exposition of faith to be composed against them. For what purpose would there be another formula of faith for the Apollinarians to subscribe after that which, as we have said, was sent in the year 375 to Paulinus of Antioch, and which Rufinus openly recalls in the words just quoted? Therefore this must have occurred in the year 375, as Rufinus had heard from Jerome and afterward recorded in writing. That most eloquent presbyter, whom Damasus then employed as friend and assistant, must have been someone other than Jerome himself, who, as we have seen, could not then be called a presbyter and was away from Rome, having withdrawn to the Syrian desert. Moreover, that incident was not invented by Rufinus but agrees with the truth; this may be inferred from the manuscript codices which I cited in notes to the earlier letters to Paulinus, for they include the word lacking in the printed texts.

III. Holstenius published from an ancient Vatican collection of canons a fragment entitled, “From the Council of the City of Rome under Damasus, concerning an exposition of the faith.” It consists of two parts. The first treats of the sevenfold Spirit resting upon Christ; the second explains the manifold dispensation of Christ’s names. Anyone who compares this with the sixth poem and observes that the latter repeats in more compressed verse what the fragment had here expressed in fuller prose will readily concede that both are offspring of one and the same author—Damasus, whose name appears in the title.

[Col. 0244C] Both parts, however, concern Eunomius and his followers. To begin with the latter: since those blasphemers inferred from Christ’s many names that Christ the Lord was a work and a creature, the Catholic Fathers, by contrast, employed them to show and commend especially his mercy toward us. This may clearly be inferred from Germinius’s letter to the Arians. Having passed from them to the Semi-Arians, he says:

> What they think they are bringing forth as something great from the divine Scriptures—namely, that they call Christ a work and a creature—we, on the contrary, according to the Scriptures call him Way, and Door, and Stone of stumbling, and Rock of offense, and Foundation, and Arm, and Hand, and Wisdom, and Word, and Lamb, and Sheep, and Shepherd, and Priest, and Vine, and Day, and other such names. But we understand and say all these things so as to understand the powers and operations of the Son of God, not so as to compare his divine birth from the Father.  
> [Note: [Col. 0244D] In Hilary, Fragment XI, Verona edition.]

Ambrose, Basil, and Nazianzen also often employ those diverse and manifold titles by which Christ the Lord is described. They say that these indicate the variety of his operations, his manifold beneficence, his dispensation, and the unconstrained ministry of the Savior.

As to the first part of the same fragment, everyone knows that Eunomius both denied divinity to the Holy Spirit and assigned his origin to the Son alone; both points are established by the blasphemous writings of his which survive. [Note: [Col. 0245D] See notes on Ep. 33, nos. 16 and 20.] Therefore, after Damasus had amply proved from arguments drawn from Sacred Scripture that the Holy Spirit rests in the Son—naturally and essentially—he concludes that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone or the Spirit of the Son alone, but the Spirit of Father and Son. He establishes this by the arguments which Athanasius, Basil, Ambrose, Epiphanius, Cyril, and the other Fathers used to prove that he is one, because the Father and Son have one nature, and that he cannot be relegated among created things, as being consubstantial with both. This is consequently why later Greeks of the Catholic party defended the addition of the word *Filioque* to the Creed now in use as especially well suited to overthrow Eunomius’s heresy, [Note: [Col. 0245D] See Allatius, *Greek Orthodoxy*, vol. I, pp. 72 and 460; Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology*, vol. II, bk. VII, ch. 2, no. 1.] and afterwards attributed that addition to Damasus himself.

The first to assert this was Alexius Aristenus, a writer of the twelfth century, in scholia on the *Synopsis of the Canons* published by Justellus. John, bishop of Methone, introduces him as the author of this opinion in his response to Mark of Ephesus; so does Simon of Constantinople in his letter to John Nomophylax. The relevant words of the latter, in Allatius’s translation, are these:

> It should further be known that, as the most God-loving deacon and great steward of the Great Church of God, Lord Alexius Aristenus, relates in his concise treatise on all the canons, the most holy ecumenical synods, and the matters transacted among them, after the Council of Nicaea there arose a heresy which asserted that the Son too was Father. For some said that, just as the Son is begotten of the Father, so the Spirit is begotten of the Son, and thus they declared the Holy Spirit to be the Son’s son and the Father’s grandson. Therefore, to abolish such a heresy and establish the orthodox faith, the most holy Pope Damasus, before the holy Second Council of Constantinople, gathered a council at Rome together with the Catholic bishops subject to him. They added to the holy Nicene Creed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; and they subjected to anathema those who asserted that he was begotten of the Son. In the same way they subjected to anathema those who did not freely and confidently preach that he is of one authority and essence with the Father and the Son; and they added many other anathemas against many heresies.  
> [Note: [Col. 0245D] Allatius, *Against Hottinger*, chs. 18 and 20.]

I am not unaware that Aristenus—or whoever this writer older than Aristenus may be—and other more recent Greeks are certainly mistaken in attributing to Damasus the addition to the Nicene Creed, which is of a much later age, although this is not the place to investigate when it first began. [Note: [Col. 0246D] See Allatius, ibid., ch. 20; Lequien, Dissertation I on the works of Damascene.] Yet at least this may be inferred: that the matter was considered and discussed under Damasus before the Constantinopolitan synod. Consequently, it may be asserted by me, not without some plausible conjecture, that this fragment pertains rather to another council than to this one, as Holstenius thinks—namely, to that which, as I have said, assembled in 380, and at which it is established that the heresies of Eunomius and Macedonius were chiefly treated.

IV. Besides these things, the same Holstenian codex contains a decree concerning the patriarchal sees and concerning books to be received or rejected. By the favor of Besutius—then the most learned and devout abbot, now cardinal of the Holy Roman Church—I examined a distinguished codex of the Dionysian collection in the monastery of Holy Cross, and another like it in the Vallicellian Library, made available by the celebrated and most courteous Father Joseph Bianchini. A third, from the most ancient archive of the Church of Verona, is mentioned by the ever-praiseworthy Marquis Maffei; Baluze says that he read another communicated to him by D’Achery. [Note: [Col. 0246D] On Lupus of Ferrières, Ep. 128.] All these contain the very decrees found in this Holstenian codex. Therefore the great Baronius rightly attributes this decree concerning the patriarchal sees to Damasus and this Roman synod, [Note: [Col. 0246D] Under the year 382, no. 19.] an opinion shared by the distinguished scholars Holstenius and Francis Bianchini.

They think that the occasion for enacting this decree arose when the pontiff learned that the rank of the patriarchal churches had been disturbed by the clandestine canon of Constantinople. He judged it necessary to curb by this synodical law the thoughtless ambition of that bishop and of the Easterners, especially because Paulinus was taking care that his see of Antioch and the see of Alexandria, with which he was in communion, should suffer no loss.

I am not unaware that the editor of the letters of the Roman pontiffs and others deny this very decree concerning the prerogative of the patriarchal sees to Damasus and assign it to Gelasius. Scholars agree that the canon concerning writings and books to be received or rejected, to which it is found joined, belongs to Gelasius. The principal reason for this opinion is that the Holstenian fragment, though bearing Damasus’s name and joined to this decree on the prerogative of sees, includes a list of general synods in which neither the names of Ephesus and Chalcedon nor those of Celestine, Leo, Nestorius, and Eutyches are omitted. It therefore cannot belong to Damasus. Coustant accordingly wonders how Baronius could so easily be deceived by a title and inscription whose falsity is so manifest.

But because this decree on the prerogative of sees is contained word for word in the Quesnellian Codex, this argument would not have the force Coustant supposes if that codex had already been written before the age of Leo the Great, as its editor thought. Setting aside, however, this uncertain and deceptive support, I think I can maintain the following: the order and numerical ranking of the first, second, and third sees had been established and prescribed before the age of Gelasius. Leo the Great explicitly mentions it, as does Felix, Gelasius’s predecessor, who further says in the same place that this distinction had been transmitted to him from the ancient enactments of his forefathers. [Note: [Col. 0247D] See Venetian edition of the Councils, vol. V, pp. 185 and 341.]

Indeed, those enactments of the forefathers are older even than Boniface I. For this pontiff writes to the bishops established throughout Thessaly: “Since the occasion requires it, if you please, review the provisions of the canons: you will find which is the second see after the Roman Church, and which the third.” These words are surely most explicit. I know that Coustant notes that the sixth Nicene canon is indicated by these words. But, besides what might be answered, I would only observe with Quesnel [Note: [Col. 0247D] Quesnel, Dissertation 12, ch. 4, no. 13.] that this Nicene canon does not at all determine whether the bishop of Alexandria or Antioch holds second or third place. Yet Boniface and other pontiffs expressly prescribe the order between them, assigning second place to Alexandria and third to Antioch. Baronius could therefore, with sound and correct judgment, infer from that codex that Gelasius had not so much instituted these things for the first time as set down again in writing what had previously been rightly established by his predecessors.

The same judgment should be made concerning the decree on writings and books to be received or rejected. Since a canon of sacred Scriptures and books existed in the Roman Church, it was also necessary that, according to the circumstances of affairs and times, it should be confirmed or even enlarged by the Roman pontiff. Learned men grant that this was done under Hormisdas, who enlarged Gelasius’s catalogue. [Note: [Col. 0248D] See Bianchini, notes on Clement and Gelasius.] Why, then, could Gelasius himself not have added to Damasus’s decree, so that this decree, although merely enlarged by Gelasius, might be attributed to him—as we afterwards find it sometimes attributed to Hormisdas? For in Damasus’s age there was no lack of Manichaeans, Arians, and Priscillianists, who either corrupted the sacred Scriptures or foisted apocrypha upon the Church. Their deceptions therefore had to be countered by reaffirming and publishing its canon anew, and Jerome had further to be entrusted with correcting those same Scriptures. Yet because it is not altogether certain that these fragments belong to Damasus, I have preferred to refrain from judgment and have placed them among doubtful matters as an appendix.

As for the canons enacted by the Council of Constantinople, Leo the Great, Gelasius, and Gregory the Great teach us that, except for the decree concerning Maximus the Cynic, they were held in no esteem by Damasus and the Roman See. I shall not transfer their statements here with superfluous labor. Yet Boniface I and Nicholas, wholly competent witnesses, leave us no doubt that Nectarius’s ordination was confirmed. [Note: [Col. 0248D] See Dissertation 2, §3.] On the other hand, Sozomen, Theodoret, and other monuments of the period prove that all external communion with Flavian was rejected. The Easterners vainly alleged Apostolic and Nicene canons to show that his consecration had been performed lawfully and rightly; for there was another reason why it ought not to have been performed, or, if performed, received. First, Flavian was imposed—as Nazianzen says—as a new bishop upon an old bishop, contrary to the Apostolic tradition confirmed by the Council of Nicaea. Second, the obligation of an oath rendered him incapable of attaining the episcopate of Antioch. Since the Easterners’ letters to this Roman council make no mention of these matters or of the very bitter schism arising from them, serious scholars rightly doubt whether those letters, lacking ecclesiastical simplicity and sincerity, deserve the praise attributed to them by Theodoret.

These, then, are the principal matters which seem to have been done by this last council of Damasus. Of the many other decrees circulated under his name in collections of councils, it is uncertain whether they belong to this council or another, and much more uncertain whether Damasus was their author. On this matter consult, if you wish, Tillemont and Coustant. Moreover, when I called this council his last, understand this to mean among those whose memory survives. I can readily believe that Damasus, following custom, held synods in almost every year of his episcopacy when he had summoned neighboring bishops on his anniversary; but some of these have doubtless been forgotten through the antiquity of time.

V. If one may trust a certain Landulf the Elder, bishop of Milan, while St. Ambrose occupied the see, a most serious disagreement arose before the Apostolic See in a synod between married priests and others living in continence or virginity. By order of the Apostolic See and with the consent of the other bishops, judgment was entrusted to Blessed Ambrose, so that whatever he said should be held holy and firm; and the decision was made in favor of married men. Indeed, if one listens to Pseudo-Datius, this controversy was discussed at a synod of Damasus I, held at Constantinople with 150 bishops, where Blessed Ambrose was present.

But, in the judgment of the most distinguished Muratori, to relate such trifles from those times is to refute them; although Puricelli deserves praise for the diligence with which he seriously devoted his study and labor to refuting that little fable in the dissertation published after the chronicle of the same Landulf among the Italian writers. Dandolo came nearer to the truth when he wrote that at this same council of Damasus Priscillian was condemned and that its synodical acts were communicated to the three Eastern ambassadors. [Note: [Col. 0248D] *Italian Writers*, vol. 12.] Yet from where he drew these claims is now unknown to us.

## CHAPTER XXII. 383, THE SEVENTEENTH YEAR OF DAMASUS; MEROBAUDES AND SATURNINUS, CONSULS

I. The *Book of Petitions* of Faustinus and Marcellinus, in what concerns Damasus, is subjected to examination. II. Whether these two presbyters were Luciferians or rather Ursinians; who Bassus, prefect of the City, was, and whether he was a Christian. III. On Ephesius, the pseudo-bishop of the Ursinians in Rome, and his expulsion. IV. On the tale of Liberius condemned by Damasus. V. On Hilary, Roman deacon: whether he returned to the Church, and whether he was the author of the commentaries circulated among Ambrose’s works. VI. On Arsenius, Roman deacon, tutor of Arcadius and most holy monk.

[Col. 0249A]

I. I assign to this year, while it was not yet complete, those acts (though not all of them) which, from zeal for religion and truth, we read that Damasus performed at Rome in the *Book of Petitions* of Marcellinus and Faustinus, published by Sirmond. First, then, they say that Aurelius was harshly treated by him because he communicated with Gregory of Baetica. They do not state who this Aurelius was or what sufferings he endured. I think he presided over the Luciferians at Rome [Col. 0249B]; for the Donatists, Novatians, Manichaeans themselves, and nearly all sects, persuaded—as they rightly were—that in that city lay the center of catholic communion, always took care to have bishops of their own at Rome, lest they seem to stand outside the Church.

Secondly, these schismatics mention the presbyter Macarius, whom they praise in extraordinary terms, as though Christian virtue could exist without charity. Since, contrary to imperial law, he held forbidden and clandestine assemblies, he was seized by officers and, while he was being dragged away by force in the presence of Damasus’s clergy, was severely wounded. On another day he was brought before a judge; and because neither force nor persuasion could induce him to communicate with Damasus and obey the imperial rescript, he was driven into exile [Col. 0249C]. He died at the mouth of the Tiber from the wound he had received, and was buried by Florentius, bishop of that city—of whom, however, Ughelli makes no mention—in the basilica of St. Asterius.

Such is the account in the *Book of Petitions* concerning the presbyter Macarius. But whether he was a Luciferian or an Ursinian, it does not state—by no accident, and with malicious intent. Elsewhere I have said and proved [Note: [Col. 0249D] See ch. 9.] that no imperial law forbade the Luciferians, provided they did not associate themselves with those who rebaptized, freely to practise their religion. I now add that no canon was issued against them before some council at Constantinople under Nectarius, although they were everywhere regarded as separated from the Church, especially in the West. There must therefore have been another reason why that presbyter was unable to hold assemblies, why, when arrested, he was ordered to recognize Damasus as the lawful bishop of the City, and why, after proving obstinate and unyielding, he was driven into exile—some reason other than his profession of the Luciferian name alone, a profession condemned by no public, civil, or ecclesiastical law.

What other reason can be offered than the presbyter’s settled attachment to the Ursinian schism, which the emperors had ordered to be punished by repeated enactments? This [Col. 0250A] is plainly proved by the contemporary author of the preface to Marcellinus’s *Petitions* themselves. He writes that, when Ursinus, “a holy and blameless man” (observe the insolence), had again voluntarily gone into exile by imperial command, the presbyters of his faction were afflicted in various ways and scattered into foreign places; among them he immediately places Marcellinus and Faustinus. Macarius, therefore, must have belonged to their number. Since he had secretly remained at Rome and continued to hold assemblies and foster factions, he was at last discovered and deservedly compelled to go into exile.

From this one may see how highly embellished and how artfully contrived are the *Petitions* of those presbyters. First, they indiscriminately mingle matters concerning the Luciferians, in order to lessen the odium of that sect. Then, though they were Ursinians and suffered exile for that reason, they conceal in silence the detested name of Ursinus; they wish to appear Luciferians, and assert that both their separation from Damasus’s communion and their persecution arose solely from the cause of undefiled religion—by this stratagem, plainly, in order to bend the emperors’ minds toward compassion. I think this Macarius was expelled with the rest under the prefecture of Olybrius or Ampelius. For since the *Book of Petitions* recounts these events as having occurred long before, they may be assigned to the period of those prefects, under whom the Ursinian schism appeared to have come to an end at Rome after the expulsion of its refractory leaders. I now proceed to the remaining matters which seem to belong to this year.

II. That *Book of Petitions* says that it had also recently occurred that Damasus attempted to ruin Ephesius before Bassus the judge; but that Bassus rejected Damasus’s accusations [Col. 0250C], on the ground that the imperial constitutions appeared to have been promulgated only against heretics, not against those—namely, the Luciferians—who preserved the most holy faith without worldly ambition. Damasus, they say, was then for the first time put to shame because a judge had been found who alone, by a most pious interpretation, upheld the imperial rescripts.

Before proceeding, I ask who this Bassus was, the judge or prefect of the City under whom this proceeding is said to have occurred. It is known that those alleged to have held unlawful associations were to be accused before the prefect of the City. Bassus, who was prefect of the City, had previously, before rising to that dignity, been consular governor of Campania, as we plainly learn from an inscription published in mutilated form by Sirmond and complete by Reinesius [Note: [Col. 0249D] *De Suburb.*, ch. 3; Reinesius, p. 395.]. But the man who was consular governor of Campania was called Anicius Auchenius, as Reinesius proves and as inscriptions show. One of these may be read in P. Giuseppe Volpi’s work on Antium; the other, produced by the distinguished Giuseppe Maria Pratilli, I reproduce here [Note: [Col. 0249D]

> For the safety and victory of our lords Gratian and Flavius Theodosius, most pious and fortunate Augusti: Anicius Auchenius Bassus, man of clarissimus rank, consular governor of Campania, having given games to the people and remitted the tax, set this up, under the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius.  
> [Col. 0250D]

Pratilli, *De Via Appia*, book III, ch. 4.].

Bassus, then, had not yet held the urban prefecture in 381, when Syagrius and Eucherius were consuls. Conversely, he had already discharged it in 384, when Symmachus, then prefect of the City [Col. 0251A], calls Bassus himself and Aventius his predecessors in that office. Writing to Valentinian to protect the inheritance of his father-in-law Orfitus against the treasury, he chiefly relies on the fact that, when Bassus and Aventius had most recently reported on that dispute, the heirs had been released from judgment by a recent directive [Note: [Col. 0251D] See Symmachus, *Letters*, book X, letters 33, 36, 39, and 47.]. Since, therefore, Bassus’s prefecture began after 381, and the time remaining from then to Symmachus’s prefecture must necessarily be assigned partly to Bassus and partly to Aventius, we readily understand that the case of this Ephesius, of which Bassus is said to have been the examiner, was completed in 382 or the following year.

Tillemont doubts whether he was a Christian, since the *Book of Petitions*, which calls him merely a reverer of the catholic religion, seems to determine nothing with certainty, because the expression could suit a pagan. But the most careful scholar, engaged upon another question, interpreted these words—which the Luciferians habitually employed in order to proclaim themselves alone catholic—as indicating the Christian religion. For Prudentius scarcely permits us to doubt that Bassus was a Christian, as does the monument of Junius Bassus, still surviving in the Vatican basilica and published by the authors of *Roma Sotterranea*.

III. This Ephesius had been ordained bishop of the “undefiled Roman people” by Taorgius: that is, of the people who persisted in schism against Damasus and followed the party of Ursinus, absent and banished. This passage, to note it incidentally, deserves attention, since it provides an entirely unambiguous argument that it had long been accepted practice to ordain a vicar-bishop for the Roman bishop or pontiff when he was absent or impeded [Col. 0251C].

But, not to wander too far, who Taorgius was is unknown. Perhaps he presided over the Novatians, who at that time possessed several churches in the City and with whom the Ursinians had formed an alliance and association; for we read of no action against Taorgius himself on Damasus’s side. By “the undefiled people” I understand the Ursinian laity, because the letter of the Roman council to Gratian, which we have considered above, proves that their reckless obstinacy never cooled; as also does Valentinian’s rescript to Pinianus, prefect of the City, reported by the great Baronius to confirm Siricius’s election against the repeated schemes of the Ursinian faction.

Baronius marks the name of this Ephesius [Col. 0251D] with an asterisk [Note: [Col. 0252D] Under the year 396, no. 10.], as if it lay under a textual error. Gothofredus, however, believes that our Ephesius was that Euresius whom Arcadius, in 395, ordered not to be counted among sacred bishops in *Theodosian Code*, 16.5.18, because he had already been deposed from the episcopate. Pagius and Tillemont followed Gothofredus. Their view is plausible because the letters V and F are often interchanged, and it could easily have happened that a copyist, through a slight error, wrote *Euresius* instead of *Ephesius*.

Whatever the case may be, one can scarcely doubt that Ephesius was expelled from the City, and that the *Book of Petitions*, which says that he was acquitted by judicial decision, lies on this point also [Col. 0252A], if one considers the following. First, Bassus was not appointed to the urban prefecture before 381, while some part of the following year must be allotted to Aventius, his successor. Second, the famous edict of Theodosius ordering the Arians to restore the basilicas they had occupied to the Catholics was promulgated at Constantinople on 19 July 381. Third, when this was carried into effect at Oxyrhynchus, Ephesius was present there and remained there for some time afterward. You see, therefore, what follows. If he was accused before Bassus when Bassus was already prefect of the City, and if it is established that in that same or the following year he travelled through inland Egypt and Palestine, he could not have remained long at Rome under the same prefect; he was compelled to change his residence.

For why should he either have left Rome and his adherents, for whom he had been appointed bishop, so quickly, or have had business with Heraclidas, so far removed from him, that he voluntarily went all the way to Oxyrhynchus? There is a further reason, evident from the same *Book of Petitions*, why I say Ephesius was travelling through Egypt and Palestine while Bassus held the urban prefecture. After he had seen Theodosius’s commands carried out at Oxyrhynchus, he is said to have been sent from there to Eleutheropolis by the same Heraclidas, bishop of the Luciferians, to visit Hermione, a virgin of that sect. By that occasion, perhaps, he entered into the close alliance with Faustinus and Marcellinus, who had long before withdrawn there as exiles. Having also remained for some time in that city [Col. 0252C], he sailed to Africa.

The serious and continued hardships which, after Ephesius’s departure, they say they and the other Luciferians suffered from Turbon, bishop of Eleutheropolis, were at last the reason why they wrote those petitions and presented them to Theodosius. But Damasus was still alive when that suppliant *Book of Petitions* was written and offered to the emperor. Cynegius was then administering the praetorian prefecture of the East, as we learn from the emperor’s rescript appended to the same *Book of Petitions*. Since he obtained that office in the first or second month of 384, the *Book* itself must have been presented in that same year. Let us grant, then, that it was presented and offered to Theodosius in the middle of that year. If we calculate Ephesius’s lengthy travels, his stay [Col. 0252D] in Egypt before he went to Palestine, the time he remained there, and the time that subsequently elapsed after his departure before the *Book of Petitions* was written and those presbyters approached the emperor at Constantinople, we shall readily conclude what I have said: namely, that Ephesius necessarily departed from the city of Rome during Bassus’s prefecture.

IV. What may therefore be inferred from this same pamphlet, teeming with so many falsehoods, is that the tale of Liberius condemned by Damasus—recounted in the acts of the presbyter Eusebius published by Baluze—is later than Damasus’s lifetime. For if Damasus had condemned Liberius as a betrayer at a synod, why would these same presbyters not in turn have reproached him in that pamphlet with this same betrayal, as they reproached him with Athanasius, Hilary, and other bishops of that sort and name? Why did neither they themselves nor the other obstinate clergy of the City of Rome, as their writing shows, communicate with this pontiff even for a moment? [Col. 0253A]

V. The code of canons published by Quesnel contains an exposition of faith bearing the name of the presbyter Faustinus. Quesnel conjectures that it was offered to Theodosius by that presbyter, then transmitted by Theodosius to Damasus, who was importuning the emperor against the schismatics; that it finally passed from Damasus into the archives of the Apostolic See and from them into the code which Quesnel calls peculiar to the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0253D] Quesnel, dissertation 14, no. 6.]. But the value of these claims is evident from the fact that that code was as peculiar to the Roman Church alone as it was to all the rest; as the most learned Coustant and Maffei, whom one may consult, have already shown [Col. 0253B].

VI. Before leaving the Luciferians, I shall add one final point. There are very weighty authorities who say that it was due to Damasus’s zeal for religion that Hilary, deacon of the Roman Church, returned from that schism to the Church [Note: [Col. 0253D] See Pagius under the year 362, no. 5; Natalis Alexander, century IV, ch. 6, art. 14.]. They find an illustrious testimony to this in his commentary on 1 Timothy 3, expressed in these words: “Although the whole world belongs to God, the Church is nevertheless called his house, and Damasus is its ruler” [Note: [Col. 0253D] In the Appendix to Ambrose’s works, vol. II, p. 295.].

Although these words have the very sound of truth, I am surprised that they have displeased some persons so much that, contrary to all the manuscripts [Col. 0253C], they regard them as almost spurious and interpolated. I know that there is no lack of very learned men who deny this work to the same deacon, and I have no wish to make this dispute my own. Yet I admit that these words almost compel me to think that the commentary was written at least by an author who had formerly professed the Luciferian and schismatic sect. For since they recognized neither Liberius nor Damasus as lawful bishops of the Roman Church, and Jerome had reminded them that the welfare of the Church depends upon the dignity of the high priest [Note: [Col. 0254D] *Against the Luciferians*, ch. 9.], it seemed fitting for a man then sincerely returning to the Church itself to attest publicly and openly, by arguments admitting of no doubt, his faith on that point. For the same reason he judged that he ought afterwards openly to reject rebaptism, which he had formerly upheld while a Luciferian, in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 1 [Col. 0253D].

Since these facts thus incline us to suppose that the commentary was written by a Luciferian returned to the Church, why should it not be by Hilary, to whom St. Augustine attributes it? Moreover, that the author was Roman and wrote it at Rome at about this time is clear from 1 Timothy 3, where he says:

> “Now there ought to be seven deacons and a number of presbyters, so that there may be two in each church and one bishop in the city [Col. 0254A]. For offerings must be made every week; and, if not daily for strangers, at least twice weekly for residents; and, if there are no lack of persons, the sick should also be baptized daily.”

But enough on these matters.

VII. In the earlier months, as I think, of this same year, after Arcadius, still a boy, had already been declared Augustus, Damasus sent Arsenius as his tutor, judging him equal to the office. Damasus did so at Gratian’s request, to whom Theodosius had written on the matter [Note: [Col. 0254D] Baronius under the year 380, no. 22.]. Relying on Metaphrastes, Baronius calls him a deacon of the Roman Church. But Tillemont cannot be persuaded by Metaphrastes’s authority alone that he was a deacon, and seeks some graver and more ancient testimony.

But why would that writer have invented this dignity for Arsenius? Why should he not rather have written it on the authority of some older and entirely trustworthy testimony? Nicephorus indeed, who had access to the library of Constantinople, refers the reader to books left by Arsenius and to a history written about him [Note: [Col. 0254D] Book XII, ch. 23.], which may have been read by Metaphrastes. Nor are Tillemont’s reasons weightier. It was by no means necessary for Arsenius’s dignity to be mentioned in the ancient martyrologies and Lives of the Fathers, from which only one profession of his was inferred: namely, the monastic life. That somewhat softer and more splendid manner of life to which, they say, he gave himself after entering the court was in no way consistent either with the office of deacon or with the piety he had displayed at Rome; from this one may infer that, weakened by courtly habits, he temporarily departed [Col. 0254C] from his former holiness. Is that surprising or unusual?

In any event, reader, you see how keen and mature was Damasus’s judgment in choosing men. You will also praise Theodosius because, passing over Libanius and Themistius, whom he could have made Arcadius’s teachers, he chose Arsenius. He evidently knew well that learning and other accomplishments, when separated from sincere piety and religion, more often harm than benefit those appointed to govern the commonwealth.

## CHAPTER XXIII

I. In what year, and on what occasion, Damasus’s letter to the Easterners was written; and concerning Timothy the Apollinarian. II. Concerning the creed attributed to the Council of Nicaea in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus.

[Col. 0254D]

I. I think that in this same year Damasus wrote the letter to the Easterners which Epiphanius translated into Latin from Theodoret, and which I listed last. Although the Apollinarians had once and again been condemned by that pontiff, as I have said, and afterwards by the Council of Constantinople, they nevertheless, as heretics commonly do, persisted stubbornly in their perfidy and laboured with all their strength to spread it. They shamelessly claimed that, as persons agreeing with the orthodox faith, they had been received by the Western Church, and that none of the laws promulgated against heretics prevented them from practising their religion and preaching everywhere the doctrines of their sect.

Accordingly they gathered public assemblies, held profane synaxes, and openly travelled through Egypt, Syria, Cappadocia, and the whole Eastern region to perform their rites or ordinations—actions that could not take place without the gravest inconvenience and distress to well-ordered churches and catholic bishops. Nazianzen recounts these troubles to Olympius, then governor of Cappadocia, writing [Note: [Col. 0255D] Letter 77.]:
