> “In addition to all else, they have broken out into such audacity as even to summon certain bishops whose rank had been removed by the universal synod of East and West, or to exploit those passing through; violating all imperial constitutions and all your edicts, they have imposed the title of bishop upon a certain man of their impious and adulterous flock”—that is, Nazianzus.

Though there must have been many of these wandering pseudo-bishops, Leontius has transmitted to us the names of only a few. But foremost among them, after Apollinaris had then died, was Timothy, his disciple, participant in all his secrets, and already, under the same master, a great storm for the Church. Why else would the Easterners have urgently demanded from Damasus the condemnation specifically of Timothy, unless they considered it of great importance that he, being the equal of them all in himself alone, should be condemned by name?

Leontius says that he was bishop of Berytus [Col. 0255C], but no author even a little earlier than Leontius asserts this. I therefore fear that he was misled by the subscriptions of the bishops present at the First Council of Constantinople and, having read among them “Timothy of Berytus,” mistook one man for another. It does not seem possible that a man of such disreputable character, already deposed from his rank, could have sat among catholic bishops and moreover pronounced judgment on his own Apollinaris. I therefore think that he should rather be numbered among those whom Apollinaris had impiously ordained and ordered to travel here and there to divide well-ordered churches—the persons Basil mentions and calls wanderers without people or clergy, carrying about only the bare name of bishop [Note: [Col. 0255D] Letter 265.].

This Timothy had come to Rome once and again. The first time was before the death of Athanasius. Though then guilty of simulated faith, he brought letters of recommendation from Athanasius to Damasus and carried back to the East letters attesting his communion with the Apostolic See. Besides Leontius, Facundus of Hermiane mentions this first Roman journey [Note: [Col. 0255D] Book VII, ch. 3.]. He came again after Athanasius’s death, sent by Apollinaris to manage his sect’s affairs with the Roman pontiff. But when the Apollinarians’ deceit had been exposed, at the council which, as I said, was held in 376 or at the beginning of the following year, in the presence of Peter of Alexandria, both Timothy himself [Col. 0256A], according to Leontius [Note: [Col. 0255D] *Against the Fraud of Apollinaris*, at the end.], and Apollinaris who had sent him, were condemned.

This made those wicked men far more obstinate and audacious, as we have said elsewhere. Yet Timothy continued, so far as he could, to assert that he was catholic and to deceive the simpler sort by subtle and deceptive formulas. This is clear from the pseudo-Julius letter to Prosdocium, which almost makes him appear orthodox and in agreement with Catholics. Leontius attributes it to Timothy himself; but the learned Lequien, Coustant, and Muratori reject it among the letters which Apollinarians falsely ascribed to Pope Julius. Another indication of his feigned religion is taken from Polemius’s work against him, a fragment of which survives in Photius, codex 130. There Timothy is rebuked because he wished to appear among Apollinaris’s disciples and to hold the views taught by him, although he proclaimed two natures and approached the doctrine of the Cappadocians and the arrogance of the Italians [Col. 0256B].

Gregory Nazianzen, therefore, who had not laid aside with his episcopal throne the intense zeal for religion that possessed him, wrote not only to Olympius, governor of Cappadocia, but also to Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople. He asked Nectarius to approach the emperor and remind him that his piety would bring no benefit to the Church if he allowed the Apollinarians’ license to continue any longer for the overthrow of the true faith [Note: [Col. 0256D] Nazianzen, Oration 46.]. He also wrote to Posthumianus, praetorian prefect of the East, requesting that, when bishops were about to hold a repeated synod in the imperial city, he should employ the full authority of his office to provide for the peace of the churches, especially shaken by those heretics, even if it were necessary to enact something more severe.

These letters plainly concern the synod which Socrates and Sozomen say Theodosius convened in this year [Note: [Col. 0256D] Socrates, book VII, ch. 10; Sozomen, book VII, ch. 12.], since in the preceding year Posthumianus had not yet been raised to the prefecture of the East. Nor do I doubt that Gregory wrote besides to others: to friends and worthy bishops summoned to that synod, and especially to Gregory of Nyssa, whom we know to have attended the council and to have delivered the discourse entitled *On Abraham* [Note: [Col. 0256D] Works, vol. I, p. 898.].

Nectarius and the Eastern bishops who had come to Constantinople seem, stirred by Nazianzen’s admonitions, to have sought the emperor’s help and also to have written to the Roman pontiff. For Damasus’s reply, addressed to the bishops governing the East, clearly indicates that several persons had assembled and written in a common name. So far as may be gathered from the reply, the Easterners had reported to Damasus that Timothy in particular boasted and spread abroad among the people either that he had never been condemned at Rome or that he had again been admitted to communion as a catholic. By this deception, they said, great harm was then being done, and greater danger threatened for the future, to sound doctrine and the tranquillity of the churches, unless it should be made publicly known to all churches that he had been condemned and rejected by the Apostolic See [Col. 0257A].

We learn plainly what happened in Constantinople from *Theodosian Code* 16.5.2, issued on 4 September of this year and addressed to the same Posthumianus. Along with the other heretics expressly named there, Theodosius distinctly includes the Apollinarians, who had not been mentioned in earlier constitutions. As Gregory had considered necessary, he forbids them in every way to hold assemblies, establish churches, or conduct adulterous ordinations; he orders them expelled from all gatherings and places to which they are strangers and banished to the lands from which they had originated [Col. 0257B], from which he further wills that they may never depart.

Sozomen mentions this synod and the law passed on its occasion [Note: [Col. 0257D] Book VII, ch. 12.], and says elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0257D] Book VI, ch. 26.] that it resulted in the leaders of the heretics being deported from the more pleasant parts of the Roman Empire into bleak and desert regions. I think Timothy should be counted among them, since we know that he was relegated by imperial command to Bizye, a fortress of the kings of Thrace [Note: [Col. 0257D] Addition to Augustine, *On Heresies*, at the end, vol. VIII, Venetian edition.].

But this letter of Damasus to the Easterners assures us that Damasus too did not fail in his duty. Hence the Apollinarians’ hatred against Gregory and Damasus himself—whose authority, in the manner of heretics, they treated as arrogance—was increased, as we have seen from the mentioned fragment of Polemius and as we may further infer [Col. 0257C] from writings left by Eunomius, pseudo-bishop of Beroea in Thrace [Note: [Col. 0257D] Lequien, dissertation 2, no. 21.]. In them he dares to attack Egyptians, Cappadocians, and Romans because they taught two natures, whereas that madman maintained that there was one nature composed and blended out of both, as Apollinaris had deliriously taught.

II. It should now be observed that, in the same letter of Damasus, the Easterners themselves are admonished to remain immovable in the faith handed down by the Council of Nicaea. Did the Apollinarians, perhaps, oppose the Nicene faith? Most certainly. For the Nicene Fathers affirm that the Lord Christ was incarnate in such a way that they also establish him as *inhumanatus*, “made man”: that is, as having appeared as a human being in a form and likeness like ours, not lacking soul or mind. The Council of Chalcedon explains this in its address to Emperor Marcian. Leo the Great teaches the same when he writes that what the Council of Chalcedon handed down about the incarnation of our Lord had already been defined at Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0257D] Letter 79, Lyons edition.].

This is why Damasus, in his earlier letter to Paulinus of Antioch, prescribing a formula suitable for receiving Apollinarians returning to the Church, decreed—and repeats here once and again [Col. 0258A]—that they must subscribe to the Nicene faith. From this we also understand why Vigilius of Thapsus, after writing that Macedonius had accused the Alexandrian synod of departing from the Fathers’ teaching by innovating concerning the Holy Spirit matters not handed down by the Nicene faith, immediately adds that Apollinaris used the same objection of impiety against the Church [Note: [Col. 0257D] *Against Eutyches*, book V.].

For Apollinaris could not deny that the same Nicene council had said that the Word was *inhumanatus*, “made man.” Yet the Church explained the force of this word by affirming that the Word assumed, together with flesh, a human mind and soul—a whole and perfect, sinless human being—and established two natures perfectly united in one person; thus it overthrew his heresy. He slandered this catholic and utterly true interpretation as though it introduced some addition to the Nicene creed. Eutyches, a deranged old man, later employed this argument borrowed from his master Apollinaris; Vigilius of Thapsus gives his words in the same place. For those mad heads could not, or would not, understand how the Lord Christ could be wholly in two natures and from two natures, and how one person could contain whatever belongs to each united nature, without thereby making or calling him two persons and two sons.

Thus, with the Nicene Fathers, they confessed that the Lord Christ was made man and was a perfect man; but they rejected the union of two natures without mixture as a dogma recently added to the Nicene faith. They called the Lord Christ a man perfected only by divine perfection, the Word supplying in all things the functions of a human mind, as Leo the Great says, the offices of reason [Col. 0258C; Note: [Col. 0258D] Sermon 8, *On the Nativity*.].

Since this is so, there is no sound reason why Valesius [Note: [Col. 0258D] On Eusebius, book VII, ch. 30.] and Pagius [Note: [Col. 0258D] Under the year 272.] should criticize the great Baronius. Using the old Latin translation, Baronius assigned to the Antiochene council against Paul of Samosata that exposition of faith which, in the Greek acts of the Council of Ephesus, is perhaps through a copyist’s error attributed to the Nicene Fathers [Note: [Col. 0258D] Council, Venetian edition, vol. III, p. 1502.]. He also thought that Eusebius had acted in reporting it with bad faith and zeal for the Arian dogma. Other learned writers, mentioned by Fabricius, have rightly adopted Baronius’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0258D] *Bibliotheca Graeca*, book VI, ch. 4, p. 363, vol. XI.], as has more recently the distinguished Bencini, who thinks it derived from the encyclical letters of that same ancient Antiochene synod [Col. 0258D; Note: [Col. 0258D] *De litteris encyclicis*, p. 272.].

For since that exposition of faith most openly defines the Lord Christ to be in two natures and from two natures, and proposes this as an unquestionable dogma to be believed, Apollinaris and his followers would have had no reason to accuse Catholics of adding new decrees to the Council of Nicaea if that faith had already been written and propounded by the Nicene Fathers.

[Col. 0259A] Some find it strange and unusual that Damasus addresses the bishops to whom he writes with the term “sons.” But it is not without precedent. Athanasius calls Diodorus of Tyre his son and most beloved priest. This language should accordingly be attributed both to the dignity of the See—for which reason Ambrose calls Siricius, Damasus’s successor, “father” [Note: [Col. 0259D] Letter 85.]—and to the charity with which the same pontiff wished to seem to hold them in his bosom, and also to his advanced age. Yet, if one attends to that letter, his customary vigor of intellect seems not to have diminished in the meantime.

While these events were taking place at Rome, Gratian died on 25 August and Maximus seized imperial power through tyranny. A great change in affairs occurred, which, however, for the sake of greater clarity and orderly treatment, remains to be discussed in the following and final year of Damasus’s pontificate [Col. 0259B].

## CHAPTER XXIV. 384, THE LAST YEAR OF DAMASUS’S PONTIFICATE, UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF CLEARCHUS AND RICHOMER

Damasus’s letter to Valentinian on behalf of Symmachus; concerning Priscillian and the Council of Bordeaux. This pontiff’s death, place of burial, and eulogies.

These consuls mark the final year of Damasus’s pontificate. Ambrose mentions Damasus as still alive then in his letter to Valentinian against Symmachus, whose words in chapter 20 I have cited. Symmachus himself, then prefect of the City, mentions him in letters written on his own behalf to Theodosius, Valentinian, and Arcadius [Note: [Col. 0259D] Book X, letter 34.]. For Symmachus had been accused before the emperors of having, under the pretext of investigating plunderers of public ornaments, dragged Christians from the inner sanctuaries of the Church to torture; of having brought bishops from distant and neighboring cities into chains; and of having conducted cruel interrogations of ministers of the catholic Church—ostensibly to obey the emperors’ commands, but actually to avenge the demolition and destruction of his temples against the injuries inflicted by Christian law.

To clear himself, he offered Damasus as a witness to his innocence. In a letter to Valentinian, Damasus stated that Christians had suffered no injury whatever from the prefect. Symmachus adds that, among the many accused persons of various crimes whom he held in custody, not one was found to be an adherent of the Christian religion. This testimony from a man alien to that religion greatly commends the character of those times.

[Col. 0259D] Now, to return to the year that has elapsed: scarcely anyone who reflects that Damasus regarded that excellent prince as a son could doubt that Gratian’s death brought him the deepest distress. Moreover, the hideous condition of the Church, owing to the impious crimes of the Priscillianists, increased the sum of his affliction. For, having bribed Macedonius, master of the offices, they had reoccupied the sees from which they had been expelled; and, having drawn Volventius, proconsul of the Spains, to their side, they became masters of affairs and compelled several Catholic bishops to flee. Although, therefore, while these events were taking place, Maximus had entered Gaul, overwhelmed Gratian with great speed, and added Gaul itself and the Spains to his dominion, the pontiff nevertheless wrote nothing at all to him—whether crushed by so grave a disaster, or lacking a settled course and hesitating lest he make Valentinian, then wavering in religion through the contrivances of his mother Justina, still more estranged from the Catholics and drive him wholly into the Arian camp.

From Maximus’s own letter to the successor of Damasus, written not long after he had seized imperial power, we learn that Siricius himself was the first to write, exhorting the new prince to defend the Catholic faith. But since Maximus, replying to Siricius, asserts that, immediately upon arriving in Gaul, he swiftly aided the religion which he had found polluted by the stain of criminals, learned men rightly conclude that the Council of Bordeaux must be assigned to the year 384 and to the pontificate of Damasus. For Maximus entered Trier as victor not long after Gratian’s death, Ithacius the bishop immediately approached him, and the Synod of Bordeaux then promptly applied deliberation and action to restoring the ruined affairs of the Church. It could conveniently have been convened in 383, and all could have attended it in the following year, while Damasus was not yet dead.

Hence I scarcely doubt that everything was, as usual, referred to him; but I think that strength broken by old age, grief, and illness was the reason why he left this business to be dealt with by his successor. Siricius appears to have undertaken it diligently as soon as he entered upon the pontificate, as is evident from Maximus’s aforementioned letters to him, published by Baronius.[^c0025-1] And, incidentally, if anyone reads these letters attentively, sees that the crimes of the Priscillianists were established openly not by arguments or doubtful or uncertain suspicions but by their own confessions produced in judicial proceedings, and set forth in the records transmitted to that same pontiff; and if he also consults all the histories of those times, he will surely conclude how lightly—not to say rashly—Beausobre undertook to defend that dregs of humanity and their shameful cause: truly a lid worthy of its pot.[^c0025-2] But I now proceed to the end.

[^c0025-1]: [Col. 0259D] *Ad ann.* 387, no. 65.  
[^c0025-2]: [Col. 0259D] *Dissertation sur les Préadamites*, in Lenfant, *Histoire du Concile de Bâle* [Col. 0260D].

Damasus, therefore, after completing eighteen years, two months, and ten days in the pontificate, nearly eighty years old, as Jerome says,[^c0025-3] was removed from human affairs—namely, on 10 December, the day on which the most ancient calendars place his deposition. He was buried beside his mother and sister in the basilica which he himself had built, on the Ardeatine Way in the Catacombs. Since, however, the most illustrious bishop of Aesino, lighting the way, as it were, for the distinguished Boldetti and Marangoni, has pointed out the very place almost with his finger and leads the reader thither by the hand with no little pleasure,[^c0025-4] I shall add no more.

[^c0025-3]: [Col. 0260D] Jerome, *De viris illustribus*, ch. 108.  
[^c0025-4]: [Col. 0260D] Book I, ch. 8.

[Col. 0261A] Yet, since the same distinguished Marangoni has again narrated the entire matter in his Commentaries on the Chronology of the Roman Pontiffs surviving in the paintings of the Ostian Basilica, recently published, I shall give it in his own words, as likely to be more agreeable to the reader:

> He too was buried on the Ardeatine Way, in his own basilica, beside his mother and sister. . . . We believe that we discovered the site of this basilica in the year 1736, together with the tombs of his mother and sister. For when, in that very year, the excavators of the most eminent Cardinal Vicar, under the supervision of Marco Antonio Boldetti, were engaged in work in that part of the cemetery—then situated beneath the vineyard of Margherita Bellotti, between the Appian and Ardeatine Ways—they found a marble sarcophagus of the whitest Parian stone, oval in form, nearly fourteen palms long, six high, and five broad. Its front was adorned with winding waves in relief, ending on either side in two very large lions skilfully carved. It was apparent that the body had long since been carefully removed from it; nevertheless, it was covered by a very large slab of a different kind of broken marble, upon which had been erected a brick structure extending to the upper part of the chamber. Beside the sarcophagus, in its upper portion, was a small door, through which access lay into a chamber of no great size, about fifteen paces wide, and of equal length and height. At its front was another plain marble sarcophagus, and at its side another of similar form; both likewise proved empty.
>
> A few days later, not far [Col. 0261C] from the mausoleum itself, a broad stairway or descent was found, by which that very marble vessel had formerly been brought into the cemetery. Having carefully considered these things, we resolved to investigate what building had stood above this place, supported by the wall or built column erected over that great marble tomb. We discovered the ancient plan of a church, about sixty palms in length, with three semicircular apses in its northern part. From this it was clear that it had once been a church occupying the ground above both the lower chamber and the sarcophagus. We further learned that it had once been painted, from some remaining traces of colour still extant. From these probable conjectures, therefore, we judged that this might have been the basilica [Col. 0261D] of St. Damasus, beneath which the holy pontiff buried his deceased mother and sister in the above-mentioned chamber of the cemetery; beside them he himself wished to be buried in that part of the cemetery subsequently called that of Damasus, near the Ardeatine Way.

Baronius produces an epitaph copied by Brower from a very ancient manuscript of the library at Trier, which, if the manuscript is trustworthy, Damasus had made for himself. Sirmond again printed it among the works of Theodulf of Orléans, book II, poem 14, under the title “On the Death of Damasus”; Sarazanius published it lastly. Whether, however, it was really inscribed upon the tomb is now uncertain, since the upper stone of the sarcophagus—the stone in which those distinguished men conjecture that the pontiff was buried—has been lost and broken up.

A manuscript of the Vatican Church relates that, seized by fever, desiring to be dissolved, having received the body and blood of the Lord, and praying with eyes and hands lifted to heaven, he died. This may perhaps explain why persons suffering from fever sometimes chose him as their patron.[^c0025-5]

[^c0025-5]: [Col. 0261D] Fonseca, book I, ch. 16.

The testimonies of Greek and Latin Fathers collected by Sarazanius and Father Coustant, together with his surviving writings, so commend the constancy of this most holy and wise pontiff in maintaining the Catholic faith, his integrity of character, mercy and kindness toward the poor and oppressed bishops, Christian humility, learning, care for sacred buildings, and other outstanding virtues, that all the calumnies of ancient and modern heretics against him are in vain.

## § I.—The writings of Damasus are reviewed. Why Marius Mercator said that Bonosus had been condemned beforehand by that pontiff; whether the Bonosiacs were Photinians, or merely regarded as suspected of that heresy

Jerome assigned Damasus a place among ecclesiastical writers, praising his elegant talent for composing verse and many little works in that genre.[^c0025-6] Elsewhere he mentions what Damasus had composed on Virginity in verse and prose, and advises Eustochium to read it no differently than the writings of Tertullian, Cyprian, and Ambrose.[^c0025-7] Baronius thinks that these works were dedicated by Damasus to his sister Irene; the Acts of that virgin published by Bollandus, though of no great weight, further confirm this.[^c0025-8]

[^c0025-6]: [Col. 0261D] Jerome, *De viris illustribus*, ch. 103.  
[^c0025-7]: [Col. 0261D] Epistle 22, no. 12, Verona edition.  
[^c0025-8]: [Col. 0262D] Under 28 February, vol. III.

Einhard, whose testimony I have cited elsewhere, states that the Acts of Saints Peter and Marcellinus were transmitted to us by this pontiff; but those now reported by Surius and the Bollandists under 2 June have another author. Yet, because in those Acts we read that Dorotheus, by whom the holy martyrs had been struck, after performing penance was admitted to baptism under Julius, who entered upon the pontificate in 337, it might appear that Damasus was past puberty and approximately thirty years old when he wrote them—contrary to what he himself and Einhard say of him.[^c0025-9] But since it is quite possible that this Dorotheus remained among the catechumens for many years, either under compulsion or voluntarily, credit remains due both to the Acts—which Tillemont and Baillet attack in vain and which the distinguished Mazochi illustrates with excellent notes[^c0025-10]—and to Damasus’s own statements.

[^c0025-9]: [Col. 0262D] See ch. I.  
[^c0025-10]: [Col. 0262D] On the Neapolitan Calendar, 11 June.

Oldoinus further ascribes to this pontiff one book *On Faith against Heretics* and one little book *On the Trinity*, which Verderius in manuscript and Possevinus say they saw at Constantinople. But I think that the book *On Faith against Heretics* was the very work also indicated by Trithemius: namely, the second letter to Paulinus, of which I treated in chapter 15. The little book *On the Trinity* is perhaps nothing other than the Creed often entitled with the name of Damasus, of which I shall speak shortly.

[Col. 0263A] From the surviving fragments, however, it is plain that this distinguished pontiff lacked neither talent, judgment, nor learning, and that he was not undeservedly compared with Ambrose and Cyprian by Theodoret for similarity of doctrine.[^c0025-11]

[^c0025-11]: [Col. 0263D] Epistle 146, *Works*, vol. III.

Moreover, although he was occupied with the most serious business requiring settlement throughout the universal Church and wrote little beyond necessity, it was through him that we possess several works of Jerome which we might perhaps otherwise have lacked: the treatise *On the Seraphim*, two homilies of Origen on the Song of Songs, Didymus’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, and *On the Perpetual Virginity of the Blessed Virgin Mary against Helvidius*. Jerome himself indicates in his letter to Pammachius that this latter work had first been read and approved by that pontiff.[^c0025-12]

[^c0025-12]: [Col. 0263D] Epistle 48, Verona edition.

[Col. 0263B] Helvidius himself also seems at that time to have been expelled from the Church by that pontiff, since Marius Mercator wrote that Bonosus was condemned beforehand by Damasus—in Helvidius, as I conjecture. For it is clear from the letter to Anysius of Thessalonica, formerly attributed to Ambrose but restored by Holstenius to this pontiff, that Siricius reproved Bonosus for the heresy professed by Helvidius.[^c0025-13]

[^c0025-13]: [Col. 0263D] *Collectio Romana*, part I, p. 189.

I am not unaware that Mercator himself writes that Bonosus followed the accursed doctrine of Ebion, Paul of Samosata, and Photinus; further, that Gelasius and the Fathers of the Second Council of Arles assert that the Bonosiacs were carried away by the same error as the Photinians and Paulianists. But this happened because, when they denied with Helvidius the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, they rightly came under suspicion of denying the preservation of the Mother of God’s integrity even in childbirth itself. On that account they seemed to side with Photinus and Arius and to regard God as no more than a mere human being—though only through a certain consequence of their impious doctrine.

Siricius himself implies this when he says that those who maintain this assert nothing other than the perfidy of the Jews. This is also why Ambrose, when he undertook to defend the Blessed Virgin Mary’s perpetual integrity against Bonosus himself, also undertook to defend the divinity of the Son:[^c0025-14] with excellent and wise judgment, he observed how closely connected and interlinked these two matters are. Thus too the Second Synod of Arles, which had said that Photinians and Bonosiacs proceeded from the same error, decreed in canons 17 and 18 that returning Photinians were to be baptized, whereas Bonosiacs, as legally suspect, were to be received with chrism and the laying on of hands if, when questioned, they confessed our faith with their whole heart. But to return to the matter.

[^c0025-14]: [Col. 0264D] *On the Institution of Virgins*, chs. 5–12.

As we owe these treatises of Jerome to Damasus, so we owe to Jerome two letters of Damasus, which he preserved entire among his own, as well as the part he preserved of Damasus’s letter on the prodigal and dutiful son. I have listed the surviving complete letters in their proper place. Of the last letter, which has perished, I give here the portion retained by Jerome as certainly Damasus’s own.[^c0025-15]

[^c0025-15]: [Col. 0264D] See Epistle 21, Verona edition.

“You ask: who is that father in the Gospel who divides his property between two sons? Who are the two sons, and which is the elder or the younger? How does the younger son squander the property he received with prostitutes? When famine comes, how is he set over the swine by the ruler of the country, eats husks, returns to his father, receives a ring and robe, and has the fatted calf slaughtered for him? Who is the elder brother, and how does he, returning from the field, envy the reception given to his brother? And the other matters more fully explained in the Gospel.

“You add further: ‘I know that many have offered differing interpretations of this reading and have taken the elder brother to be the Jew and the younger to be the people of the Gentiles. But I ask how this can be fitted to the Jewish people: “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command; yet you have never given me even a kid, so that I might feast with my friends”; and: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” But if, as you say, we wish the parable to concern the righteous and the sinner, it cannot suit the righteous person to be grieved at another’s salvation, especially that of a brother.’”

What Jerome replied to these proposed questions may be learned by the interested reader from the same letter.

Other letters of this Damasus to Jerome, and of Jerome to Damasus, circulate; but scarcely anyone can doubt that both sets are falsely attributed. Of the same kind are the letters issued by Sarazanius under the name of this pontiff—to Stephen, archbishop, and the councils of Africa; to Prosper, bishop of the first see of Numidia; to the bishops of Italy; and to Bishop Aurelius—numbers 8, 9, 11, and 12. Hence Peter Coustant rightly excludes all of them from the number of Damasus’s letters edited by him. Following his judgment and that of others, I have retained only those of wholly certain and entirely unquestionable authenticity.

But the principal benefit that Jerome’s study of Holy Scripture obtained through this pontiff I would readily place in his revision of the New Testament according to the Greek manuscripts, and of the Psalter according to the Septuagint. Jerome himself explains in the preface to Damasus what he achieved in revising the New Testament; from it we also learn what was the necessity and usefulness—both great—of the plan adopted by that pontiff.

The Psalter, mentioned by that holy Father in his letter to Paula and Eustochium, is believed to be the very one now used only by the Vatican Basilica. It was afterward called the Roman Psalter because it was originally proper to the Roman clergy and was given to them by Damasus. Hence Jerome says against Rufinus: “Certainly Rome has received, through our labour, a Psalter most carefully corrected according to the Seventy interpreters”—that is, at Damasus’s command. Learned men further think that, having received this occasion, Damasus arranged the divine psalmody, as Anastasius says, by establishing a proper order of psalm-singing in the churches of the City.

This was subsequently succeeded by the Psalter which the holy Father, while living at Bethlehem, translated from the Hebrew sources and which eventually prevailed everywhere except in that same Vatican Basilica. But, lest I add anything further on this subject, the distinguished Abbot Antonio Martinetti, a beneficed priest of that basilica, has done so through his singular and learned dissertation entitled *On the Roman Psalter*, which, if you wish, you will not regret consulting.

[Col. 0265A] It is now pleasing to report more fully, from the Acts of the same Damasus drawn from the archive of the Vatican Church itself, the matters I have touched on:

> Knowing that the man [Saint Jerome] was sufficiently instructed in the diversity of all languages, he began to urge him to explain the divine Scriptures and to press him with most difficult questions. Jerome willingly obeyed and dedicated to his name many works beneficial to posterity. Some are contained among his letters: namely, books resolving certain questions in Genesis; homilies on the Song of Songs; one book *On Hosanna*; one book *On the Death of Uzziah*; one book *On the Seraphim and the Coal*; and one book *On the Prodigal Son*. At his command he also restored to a straight course the sequence of the four Gospels, confused by the judgment of different persons. He also translated the Psalter from Greek into Latin according to the Seventy interpreters; afterward he rendered its pure truth not from the muddy streams of other languages, but from the very purity of the Hebrew fountain. Although that translation is not sung in the churches, because the old usage prevails, it is nevertheless very useful for avoiding Jewish mockery.
>
> The number of his letters to Damasus is uncertain and, owing to their multitude, does not lie within our knowledge. Wishing, surely, to indicate this, that most learned man says in one passage: “Blessed Damasus, of revered memory, was my companion in conversation.” And in the *Apology to Pammachius*, he thus recalls how wise and chaste blessed Damasus was: “While Saint Damasus of revered memory was alive, we wrote the book against Helvidius on the perpetual virginity of Blessed Mary. In it, since we had to give precedence to the blessedness of virginity, we were obliged to say much concerning the inconveniences of marriage. Did that distinguished man, learned in the Scriptures, the virgin teacher of the virgin Church, find anything to criticize in that discourse?”
>
> Blessed Damasus also wrote several letters in an eloquent style, some of which are contained among Jerome’s letters. He wrote as well the Passion of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, which, he asserts, was related to him in his youth by the executioner of those same saints. He also composed a book in praise of Virginity, in verse and prose, and composed in hexameter verse a summary of certain books of both the New and Old Testaments.

Sarazanius added to the works he edited the Acts of Damasus, or rather lectionaries, which Baronius frequently mentions as coming from the archives of the Vallicellian [Col. 0265D] and Vatican Churches. Yet from them—apart from a few matters which I have not neglected in their proper place—you can scarcely gather anything by which to illuminate the history of this long pontificate and of those times. I therefore conjecture that these Acts are of an age very remote from Damasus; and for that reason I judged that they could be omitted without loss.

I wished, however, to warn you only of this: the beginning is missing from the Life of Damasus which Sarazanius printed first. I have judged that it should be presented here from an ancient Vatican manuscript, formerly belonging to St. Mary of the Rotunda, as Holstenius notes, copied [Col. 0266A] into the Barberini manuscript BB, so that you may judge how much authority it too may seem to possess.

## LIFE AND DEEDS OF BLESSED DAMASUS, POPE

During the reign of Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, Liberius governed as bishop of the city of Rome. For a time he shone with extraordinary wisdom and virtues, so much so that he publicly rebuked Constantine, the enemy of the Christian name, declaring that, after accepting the Christian profession, he ought to confer benefits rather than disadvantages upon the servants of almighty God. Angered by this, Constantine ordered him to be carried, as if into exile, outside the city; and he lived three miles away in the cemetery called that of Noella on the Salarian Way.

But the enemy of the human race changed Liberius’s mind so completely [Col. 0266B] that he agreed with the heresy of Constantius. For Constantius had been rebaptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia at Aquilo, an estate belonging to the Arian doctrine; but, while the Lord provided peace for the Church, he died at Nicomedia and the persecution ceased. During the reign of Valentinian, etc.

Besides this, two Creeds bearing the name of Damasus circulate, both expressly containing the clause *Filioque* (“and the Son”). One is also attributed to Jerome by several manuscript codices. The other was produced in the debates of the Council of Florence, session 23, and by Gennadius.[^c0025-16]

[^c0025-16]: [Col. 0265D] *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, section VII.

Critics deny the first to both Jerome and Damasus, chiefly because the addition of that clause belongs to a later age. Yet this reason is certainly not decisive; for since this was also the faith of those times, as is clear from the writings of Jerome himself, Ambrose, Hilary, and other Fathers, nothing prevents Damasus, in Allatius’s judgment,[^c0025-17] from having used that formula in a private exposition (*ecthesis*) of his faith. Moreover, the formula has the character of his age and was cited by writers of the eighth century.

[^c0025-17]: [Col. 0265D] *Against Hottinger*, ch. 20.

The other, which I said was cited in the debates of the Council of Florence and is held in higher esteem by Lequien as produced from a most ancient exemplar,[^c0025-18] is nothing but part of a little book found among Augustine’s works, at the end of the Council of Toledo, chapter 40—although this manuscript lacks the clause *Filioque*. In so great a variety of manuscripts and opinions, and considering also that little praise would thereby accrue to Damasus, or be taken from him, and that no sufficiently weighty arguments can be brought on either side, but only slight conjectures, I have thought it best to determine nothing.

[^c0025-18]: [Col. 0266D] Dissertation 1, *Damasus*, ch. [incomplete citation].

There is likewise no need to speak of the *Pontifical*, which all learned men deny to Damasus, whose name it falsely bears. As for the Bucherian Catalogue, which seems to end while Liberius was still alive: although there is no reason why it could not have been written by Damasus himself while still a deacon, as some think, neither is there any certain reason why we should say that he did write it. I therefore proceed to his other writings.

## § II.—Many works written by Damasus are known to have perished; some surviving epigrams are illustrated; a few other pieces are assigned to Damasus, and others are included as an appendix

[Col. 0267A]

To say also a little concerning the poems composed by Damasus: the greater part has been lost, since the works he wrote on Virginity and on the Old and New Testaments are missing. Nor do we possess all the inscriptions with which he adorned the memorials of martyrs, as appears from this testimony of Pope Vigilius.

### ON THE HOLY MARTYRS VITALIS, MARTIALIS, AND ALEXANDER

When the doomed camps of Getae had been pitched beneath the City,

They first waged impious warfare upon the saints.

With sacrilegious heart they overthrew every tomb,

Once duly consecrated to the holy martyrs.

Damasus the pope, with God as his guide, recognized and approved them,

[Col. 0267B] And by a fixed inscription instructed that they should rightly be venerated.

But the holy inscription perished when the marble was broken,

Yet they could not again remain hidden.

Then Pope Vigilius, grieving after their destruction,

When the enemies had been expelled, renewed the entire work.

Accordingly, I do not doubt that many other inscriptions carved in stone perished for the same reason and in the same shipwreck—especially the inscription which Damasus must have placed on the tomb of Alexander, bishop and most valiant martyr. For the Martyrology of Ado, under 26 November, records that this man was transferred to Rome from the twentieth mile of the Claudian Way by that same pontiff and laid in a new crypt. Indeed, even those inscriptions which have survived and which we now possess were clearly discovered at various times and places and gradually collected from here and there.

For those first brought to light are very few: they appeared among the Christian poets published by Aldus at Venice in 1502, quarto, and again by Georg Fabricius at Basel in 1562. Subsequently, a somewhat fuller collection appeared in the corpus of ancient poets at Geneva in 1611, two quarto volumes, and at London in 1713, folio. But the diligence of Martius Milesius Sarazanius, at Rome in 1638—the edition which I use—surpassed them all. For he retained the poems already published and added many others, completing a total of forty. The earlier editions contained only these: 1. on Paul the Apostle; 2. on Agnes; 3. on the same; 4. on Andrew the Apostle; 5. on Agatha; 6. on Felix; 7. on the Name of Jesus; 8. on the same; 9. on Christ; 10. on Christ’s Ascension; [Col. 0267D] 11. on the titles of the Saviour.

Sarazanius, who received almost all these from Baronius and from the Palatine manuscripts published by Gruter, might nevertheless have added two more. Since, unless I am mistaken, Damasus is their author, I have collected them lest they remain longer separated from the rest and fatherless.

In arranging these, I have altered slightly the order followed by Sarazanius. What he did not consider important enough to do, I have done: first I have assigned a place to the verses in praise of David, because one hexameter poem may perhaps survive in them from those which Damasus composed on the Old [Col. 0268A] Testament. Then I have placed those concerning God, then those concerning the holy Apostles and Roman pontiffs. I next pass to the martyrs, first listing Lawrence, as the one whom Damasus especially honoured, then the others; lastly I place the surviving inscriptions. But first I wish to give the reader some preliminary observations, which I think may shed some light both on the poems themselves and on ecclesiastical history, so that I may not be too prolix in the notes that follow.

I. The poem on Christ the Saviour is printed among the works of the distinguished Claudian, and Barthius therefore thought Claudian a Christian. But Vossius and Colomesius, in their notes on Giraldi, assert that the name of Damasus appears in certain manuscripts; and del Rio likewise attributes it to Damasus at the end of his conjectures on Claudian.[^c0025-19] Therefore, whatever Sarazanius may doubt, I too assign it to Damasus. For the final verses make it scarcely possible that the other Claudian, namely Mamercus, should be thought its author:

[^c0025-19]: [Col. 0267D] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina*, book III, ch. 13, p. 125, vol. II, Venice edition.

> . . . . . Soon raised into the heavenly breezes,  
> Restore you, cleansed, in joyful light; may you cherish the august Father,  
> So that on festal days he may often celebrate  
> The annual fasts of the pure sacred rite.

For if you reckon the chronology, you will scarcely decide to which of the emperors who held power while Mamercus wrote and flourished these lines can appropriately be fitted. From this one may infer how ancient was the custom mentioned in the formularies of Marculf: bishops, on the more solemn festivals of the year, sent letters to kings praying for every blessing upon them.

[Col. 0268C] II. There are three poems concerning the Apostles. The first is entitled “On St. Paul,” and is perhaps one of those relating to the New Testament. The venerable Cardinal Thomasius notes in his *Hymnary* that it was customarily sung on the conversion of that apostle, with the final two verses omitted. Sarazanius doubts whether Damasus wrote the second, which concerns St. Andrew, but, in my judgment, without any reason, since it appears in every edition of his works. We also infer from the old Mozarabic liturgy, published by the most distinguished Joseph Blanchini, that it was customarily sung somewhere, with only a doxology added for choral use.

III. The last poem concerning the Apostles was read inscribed at the Catacombs of St. Sebastian, where the sacred bodies of Peter and Paul lay. This illustrious testimony of Damasus, if all else were lacking, plainly convicts those who might still be uncertain on the matter. Yet the time at which those sacred pledges were brought to the Catacombs and then taken thence and restored to their ancient and original resting-place is obscure and perplexing. Consult, if you please, the most learned Blanchini and Vignoli in their notes on Cornelius, to whom Anastasius attributes this praise, and the *Underground Rome* of the other distinguished Bottari, one of the keepers of the Vatican Library.[^c0025-20]

[^c0025-20]: [Col. 0268D] Vol. I, p. 31.

But if you ask why they remained so long in the Catacombs, Gregory the Great gave this explanation:

> What am I to say concerning the bodies of the blessed Apostles? It is established that, at the time when they suffered, faithful persons came from the East to reclaim their bodies as those of their fellow citizens. The bodies were taken as far as the second mile from the City and placed in the location called the Catacombs. When the whole multitude gathered together endeavoured to remove them thence, the power of thunder and lightning terrified and scattered them with such excessive fear that they never again presumed to attempt anything of the kind.[^c0025-21]

[^c0025-21]: [Col. 0269D] *Works*, vol. II, register 4, epistle 30, according to the Ballerini edition.

He adds that the Romans later removed those sacred pledges and laid them again in their former places, but he states neither the time nor the author of this action. Thus Damasus indicates, not obscurely, the very matter Gregory openly explains, when he says:

> [Col. 0269B] The East sent the disciples, as we willingly confess;  
> Rome deserved rather to defend them as her own citizens.

I am not unaware that this narrative also appears in the Acts of Peter, published under the name of a certain Marcellus of Florence, and later by Fabricius among the apocryphal writings of the New Testament. Those Acts further add that the sacred bodies lay in the Catacombs for nineteen months—a detail which Gregory the Great does not mention. But I shall not, because of an impostor’s audacity, be induced to relegate this plain and most ancient testimony of Damasus to uncertain traditions, or, as Pearson preferred, to fables.

First, I think that what pseudo-Marcellus recounts at the end of the Acts concerning the sacred bodies is a patch sewn onto them later. For pseudo-Abdias, another falsifier, though he writes that Peter was taken down from the cross by his disciple Marcellus and buried in the Vatican, says not a word on this subject. I suspect that this addition was taken from a history which Mabillon shows was read in Gallican churches during Charlemagne’s reign[^c0025-22] and afterward inserted into those Acts. My suspicion is justified by the same period given in both places for which the Apostles’ bodies are said to have lain in the Catacombs—namely, nineteen months.

[^c0025-22]: [Col. 0269D] In Tillemont, “Peter,” art. 3.

Moreover, no one would call that pseudo-Marcellus older than Damasus or Gregory the Great, so that those most weighty authorities could appear to have drawn from this impure source. On the contrary, that impostor betrays in his fabrication such ignorance of Roman affairs and such crudeness of style that he appears incapable not merely of equalling the age of Damasus and the other Fathers of that century but even of surpassing later times. Hence it follows that he derived something true from approved and confirmed traditions, with which to encrust his fables. But enough on these matters.

Another poem, spoken concerning his own tomb, had been inscribed in the vestibule of that same Cemetery of Praetextatus; for that reason we have joined it to this one. But it is uncertain whom Damasus means in that poem apart from Sixtus and his companions. The monk of Cinsilensis, published by Mabillon, places Fabian, Anterus, and Miltiades where Sixtus is placed; the writer of Malmesbury adds Stephen, Zephyrinus, Eusebius, Eutychian, Dionysius, Pontian, and Lucius. Some of these had been crowned with martyrdom; others died in peace, but were leading men and high priests. They may therefore seem to have been specially indicated in that place before the rest.

IV. There are four poems concerning Roman pontiffs, and they praise Stephen, Marcellus, Eusebius, and Mark. Baronius and Sarazanius had already produced those concerning Marcellus and Mark; the other two therefore now appear for the first time under Damasus’s name and among his writings. Certainly, both the style and the first verse—which Damasus often favoured and which occurs elsewhere—scarcely permit me to doubt that the first epigram has that pontiff as its author.

Anyone who compares it with the Acts produced by Baronius will readily see that it identifies Pope and martyr Stephen.[^c0025-23] For when Stephen was exhorting Christians assembled in the Cemetery of Callixtus to endure martyrdom bravely, soldiers sent there beheaded him in his seat. His followers buried him in the same place; they themselves were then dismissed unharmed, mourning their bereavement. From this it may be inferred that Stephen suffered under Valerian, who ordered bishops, priests, and deacons in particular to be put to death immediately by the sword.[^c0025-24]

[^c0025-23]: [Col. 0269D] See the Notes.  
[^c0025-24]: [Col. 0270D] Cyprian, Epistle LXXXII.

Damasus describes that seat, sprinkled with blood and long preserved in the same cemetery, which at the beginning of this century Innocent XII gave as a gift to Cosimo III, Grand Duke of Tuscany; it was taken to Pisa and placed in the church of the distinguished Order of Knights under the name of that pope and martyr, when he says:

Here, placed as ruler, I taught the heavenly commands. For, as Augustine says, the Lord teaches while seated, which pertains to the dignity of the teaching office [Note: [Col. 0270D] Book I, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*. See Bonar. Vetr., p. 102.]. From this you may infer the reliability of those *Acts*, at least regarding the kind of martyrdom—reliability rashly and vainly impugned by excessively intemperate critics. In the same Palatine codex there is an epigram concerning the martyr Nemesius, of whom those same *Acts* speak. Whether Damasus was its author, I do not assert; yet I cite it again, both that the credibility of those *Acts* may be more firmly established and, further, that you may see how little care their compiler brought to transcribing the epigrams:

> Here the shrine of the martyr Nemesius flourishes through the ages,  
> Later in adornment, nobler in merit.  
> Long doubt had formerly left it neglected,  
> But courage held firm and vindicated the faith.  
> Savage frenzy, disregarding the law of burial,  
> Made the tombs of the saints the plunder of its rage.

For these final two verses are also found in the poem in which Chrysanthus and Daria are praised.

V. From the inscription of Pope and Martyr Marcellus we learn that the controversy, begun under Cornelius, concerning the reception of the lapsed—though then settled and decided—was revived under this pontiff because of the obstinacy of those who subsequently fell away. From the following poem [Col. 0271A] we learn that it continued and widened even into the time of his successor Eusebius; for each was driven into exile by the tyrant because of apostolic steadfastness in preserving the Church’s discipline. We also understand why Anastasius says that Marcellus established twenty-five *tituli* in the city for the baptism and penitence of many people, and why he was moreover arrested and confined because he “organized the Church”: indeed, all this shows that he restored the penitential discipline that the preceding persecutions had overthrown.

Why Damasus, in the same poem, is silent about martyrdom and reports only Marcellus’s exile, I think was for this reason: namely, because the Donatists, who were present in Rome in no small number, had with the utmost criminality branded this pontiff with the charge of being a traitor [Col. 0271B]. To expose their slander openly, Damasus recalls and praises Marcellus’s lofty spirit in the face of the audacity of the lapsed, and the exile he endured with great courage because of their fault.

VI. I now turn to the funerary inscription of Eusebius, which Baronius brought forth from ancient inscriptions and referred to Eusebius the presbyter [Note: [Col. 0271D] At the year 357, no. 52.]. But since everything relating to this Eusebius the presbyter is wholly uncertain and shrouded in deep darkness [Note: [Col. 0271D] See, if you please, the dissertation on the deeds of Liberius in exile, § 1.], I follow the judgment of the most weighty scholars Tillemont, Coustant, and Father Orsi, the now most deserving master of the Apostolic Palace, whose agreement with my own view gave me pleasure: I attribute this poem to Damasus, and judge that it praises Pope Eusebius.

Anyone, I think, will judge this attribution justified who compares the poem itself [Col. 0271C] with that concerning Marcellus and sees that the two are so alike that they consist of the same ideas and almost the same words. Nor am I deterred from this view by the fact that Pope Eusebius is said in the Bucherian list to have been buried in the cemetery of Callixtus, whereas the man treated in this poem died in Sicily. Eusebius the pontiff could have been brought to Rome from Sicily, where he died, just as we read that Pontian was brought from Sardinia. Indeed, whoever held this as certain would scarcely depart from the truth. For the second Bucherian Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs records Eusebius’s death on 17 August; explain, if you can, any other reason why his burial should have been delayed until 26 September.

Hence it is clear that this pontiff is rightly and deservedly numbered among the martyrs in certain very ancient martyrologies noted by Florentinius [Col. 0271D] [Note: [Col. 0271D] At 26 September.], and that a sure argument for this must be credited especially to Damasus. If any trace of that Heraclius, who forbade the lapsed to perform penance, existed in the monuments of ecclesiastical history, or if the name of the judge under whom Eusebius was banished were stated, the matter might perhaps be set in a clearer light. We read that Heraclius Rufinus—whether he was Statius or Aradius—administered [Col. 0272A] the urban prefecture under Maxentius in 310–311 [Note: [Col. 0271D] In Sigonius, *On the Western Empire*, pp. 71 and 75, Milan edition.]; and nothing prevents his being the man mentioned in that poem, who believed that the growing fury and most serious sedition in the City could be restrained by the punishment and exile of an innocent and wholly upright pontiff.

Whatever the case, I would chiefly have attention paid to these points. First, great disturbances were then stirred up in the Church by the stubbornness of the lapsed; this is also clear from canon 3 of the Council of Arles, by which they were restrained. Secondly, that Eusebius is called *rector* by Damasus, a word by which he customarily denotes Roman pontiffs. Thirdly and finally, that this *rector* was banished for precisely the cause for which Marcellus had been banished, and that he bore exile cheerfully after Marcellus’s example. Produce, then, another Eusebius [Col. 0272B] to whom all these facts can apply, besides the one who, as supreme pontiff and the successor of that same Marcellus, had before him the recent example which he might follow.

VII. The poem inscribed upon Mark’s tomb is rendered obscure, I think, by the carelessness of the copyist, especially in these little verses:

> You, Custos, Christ’s perfect friend,  
> And Damasus, when he renders the honour of the tomb.

These yield either no sense or a sufficiently perplexed one. First, therefore, I observe that one should read *tumuli* (“of the tomb”) or *tituli* (“of the inscription”). Thus, in Gruter one may see the phrase *tituli honorem*, “the honour of the inscription,” in use [Note: [Col. 0272D] P. 954, no. 10.]. Further, if no error entered during transcription, after this *te* supply *in pace* (“in peace”): for the formulae *te in pace* and *te cum pace* were customary [Col. 0272C] and are often inscribed upon Christian tombs, as may be read in Boldetti, Marangoni, and Father Lupi [Note: [Col. 0272D] *Osservazioni*, pp. 411, 413; *Delle cose gentilesche*, p. 455; *On the Epitaph of St. Severa*, p. 171.]. Fabretti further recalls that the concluding letters *ET TV.* were carved even on pagan stones: that is, “and you, reader or traveller, who earlier bade me farewell—farewell” [Note: [Col. 0272D] *Inscriptions*, ch. 9, pp. 669–670.].

By *Custos*, moreover, unless it is a proper name, one may understand the person charged either with guarding the martyrs buried in that cemetery or with safeguarding the basilica founded there by Mark; perhaps he collaborated with Damasus in adorning that pontiff’s tomb. For both titles are often mentioned among ecclesiastical offices, even among the Greeks, for whom the *kleidouchos* (κλειδοῦκος, “key-bearer”) was the person whom we call *custos*, or guardian, and who was commonly a presbyter.

When, further, you hear that Mark prayed “that all the people might learn,” you see both that he delivered public sermons and catecheses to the people [Col. 0272D], and that Sozomen—a Greek and far removed from the City—was ignorant of that church’s custom when he seemed to write that at Rome neither the bishop nor anyone else in the Church taught the people [Note: [Col. 0272D] Book VII, ch. 19.]. For I do not think anyone would hold that fixed and customary liturgical prayers and formulae must be meant here.

[Col. 0273A] VIII. Ruinart doubts whether the poem concerning Felix refers to Felix of Nola or to another anonymous Felix, said to have been a presbyter born in Rome who, after suffering various torments for the faith, was made an exile and buried peacefully at Nola: the brother of that other Felix who suffered martyrdom with Adauctus under Diocletian and is praised in the poem following this one [Note: [Col. 0273D] See the Bollandists at 14 January.]. His basilica was not on the Pincian Hill, as the distinguished Mazzocchi thought, but on the Ostian Way, nearly opposite St. Paul’s, in the cemetery of Commodilla, discovered and identified not many years ago by the eminent Boldetti.

Damasus certainly seems to indicate that the Felix whom he praises here lay far from Rome when he says:

> Nor do you allow any traveller to return by the way he came.

Accordingly, since people came to Felix of Nola for religious reasons not merely from Rome but from [Col. 0273B] almost the whole world [Note: [Col. 0273D] Augustine, Epistle 78.], you can scarcely say that this poem identifies anyone other than him. Baronius, the Bollandists, Muratori, and other learned men therefore consider it dedicated to him. I think this explains why, when the feast day was celebrated at Rome, a basilica was built for him not long after Damasus’s death. It was afterwards called *in Pincis*, “on the Pincian [Hill],” to distinguish it from other basilicas bearing Felix’s name—for there were several Felixes in the City—and because of the nearby residences of the Pincian family. When this designation was transferred from that time to the people of Nola, who were near Rome, Felix likewise began to be called *Felix in Pincis* among them after the Roman custom. For there is no mention of this place at Nola either in Paulinus or in contemporary authors.

A recent, otherwise learned historian of the Church of Nola maintains that this poem was dedicated by Damasus to Maximus, bishop of Nola, moved solely by the authority of a certain manuscript breviary. Yet the fragment of this breviary quoted by the Bollandists at 7 February mixes in fables and has the character of a later and inferior age; these are reasons why the Bollandists themselves seem not to value it highly. But what makes it unworthy of credence is that it reports the first verse altered and proposes that *Magne* should be read where *Felix* ought to stand, as follows:

> Great one in body, mind, and spirit, and likewise in name.

For I do not think anyone will willingly allow himself to be persuaded that Damasus used *Magnus* instead of *Maximus*, as though *Magnus* and *Maximus* were one and the same name. Certainly, Maximus the bishop is very frequently mentioned by St. Paulinus; Magnus is never mentioned. Whether that verse formerly inscribed on the walls of the church at Nola had *Magne* or *Felix*, no competent witness can now tell us, since it no longer appears. Yet we may doubt the matter, since Ferrarius, a canon of the Church of Nola, both recites the verses as printed in Baronius and refers them to Felix [Note: [Col. 0273D] *On the Cemetery of Nola*, p. 34.].

But if the matter finally stood thus, and the name Magnus was at some time inscribed on the church walls in place of Felix [Col. 0274A], I would believe that the verses were altered when they were carved in stone. For this other little verse—

> With enemies destroyed, who had spoken falsely—

which neither Bollandus nor Sarazanius nor the other editions contains, and which was therefore added on that occasion, proves that the stonecutters took some liberty. For we know of none of Damasus’s adversaries having been punished with death; and no one will easily bring himself to believe that a pontiff of the gentlest disposition—whom Jerome declares not to have harmed even his defeated adversaries—paid his vows to blessed Felix because his enemies had been destroyed and put to death.

There is, moreover, a report, as I said elsewhere [Col. 0274B], that Damasus went to Nola to fulfil this vow; I shall not assail it with uncertain conjectures, as often happens. Certainly, Felix of Nola’s tomb was called “the altar of truth,” and his relics “champions of truth” [Note: [Col. 0274D] Remond., *History of Nola*, Book II, chs. 4 and 26.]. Therefore Damasus, who had escaped the calumnies of Ursicinus, Isaac the Jew, and others directed against him, could easily have made this vow and fulfilled it in person to his patron. Closely similar to it is another vow, inscribed for the return of the clergy who had separated from him.

IX. The poem which Sarazanius published as no. 17 and assigned to uncertain martyrs has been shown to concern Saints Nereus and Achilleus by the monk of Ems, first published by Mabillon and afterwards by Blanchini in the prolegomena to Anastasius, opusculum 15. The authority of this codex [Col. 0274C] is certainly not to be despised: it appears to have been written in the eighth century, and its author copied all its inscriptions from the autographs themselves and entered them in his commentary while travelling through the churches and cemeteries outside the walls.

If, therefore, this epigram concerns those martyrs, this will add to the body of conjectures for which the credibility of the *Acts* now read concerning them seems doubtful. For men who were eunuchs, dependants and guardians of the virgin Domitilla, cannot appear to have enrolled in military service, performed a beneficent duty, later abandoned the camp, and cast away shields, quivers, and weapons in order to profess themselves Christians; for persons of that condition were especially excluded from armed service at that time. Yet I preferred, with Ciampini [Col. 0274D] [Note: [Col. 0274D] *Ancient Monuments*, vol. II, ch. 20.], to follow the testimony of that same ancient writer rather than Sarazanius, and to entitle the poem as concerning these same martyrs.

The epitaph that had been carved in excellent lettering for Eutychius in the cemetery of Callixtus still survives intact in the church of St. Sebastian; but we infer nothing else from it except the extreme and repeated severity of his tortures and the martyr’s divinely granted steadfastness in enduring them. In the age of St. Gregory it had not yet been removed from that place and transferred to the basilica of St. Lawrence in Damaso; for that pontiff sent oil from his sacred body to Queen Theodelinda.

[Col. 0275A] X. The martyrdom of Tharsicius, described in Ado’s martyrology for 15 August, was taken by Damasus from the *Acts of Pope and Martyr St. Stephen* reported by Baronius [Note: [Col. 0275D] At the year 270.]; for you will seek it elsewhere in vain. Thus you see their antiquity and authority, further supported by this poem, against Pearson and several other over-fastidious and recent critics. But the Bollandists defend the *Acts* themselves against their subtleties at 2 August, as does an anonymous writer in a dissertation printed at Avignon under the title: *Papal Authority Attacked by the Well-Known Case of Cyprian, but Defended by the Theologians of France*.

From the same poem we infer several further matters. First, that the discipline of the *arcane* [*disciplina arcani*, the discipline of secrecy] was in force in that age [Note: [Col. 0275D] See Schelstrate, *On the Discipline of the Arcane*, ch. 7, § 5.]. Secondly, we understand that long before the time of Miltiades the *fermentum* was sent to the churches [Col. 0275B]. By this term it is now clear that a portion of the offerings consecrated by the bishop is denoted. Hence, when Anastasius writes that Miltiades ordered the consecrated offerings to be sent through the churches from the bishop’s consecration, he means nothing other than that, under this author and pontiff, the practice interrupted during the preceding persecutions was restored when, under Maxentius, the basilicas had already been restored to the clergy for sacred rites.

Thirdly, you see that the *fermentum* itself was brought also to basilicas outside the walls, since Tharsicius was discovered while carrying the sacraments outside the city and was crushed beneath stones. But should we say that this occurred by established custom, or because of the persecution, during which many things were permitted that were not permitted once peace had been restored to the Church? I for my part think that the *fermentum* was sent, by an established and confirmed custom, even to presbyters stationed in the cemeteries and administering suburban churches. For if, by the decree of Miltiades and Siricius, no presbyter of any place might celebrate the Eucharist during the week without first receiving the bishop’s *fermentum*, then—unless someone maintains that sacred rites could not be performed in cemeteries, which no one will say—we must admit with the most distinguished and learned Bottari that it was sent also to the presbyters of those cemeteries, whereby they were permitted to perform the sacred rites [Col. 0275C] [Note: [Col. 0275D] *Roman Subterranean Antiquities*, vol. II, p. 146.].

Add that the supreme pontiffs often held sacred synaxes in the cemeteries themselves and at the memorials of martyrs. Therefore, if at that time the *fermentum* had to be sent from suburban churches to urban ones, nothing prevents its being sent on fixed days from urban to suburban churches. What Innocent says in his letter to Decentius of Eugubium—that he does not think the *fermentum* should be sent through the parishes, because the sacraments need not be carried far—the distinguished scholar refers to some law then issued by that pontiff, ordering that this no longer be done. He further judges that Innocent established presbyters to reside in the cemeteries and first granted them authority to consecrate the sacraments.

Fourthly, you see that the *fermentum* itself was carried by an acolyte, although this formerly belonged to the office of deacons [Col. 0276A] [Note: [Col. 0275D] Justin, *First Apology*, nos. 65, 67, edition of the Bollandists.]. Perhaps necessity had first caused acolytes to perform the deacons’ office, and once this had been accepted in practice repeatedly, it finally became law in Innocent’s age. Yet someone might perhaps conjecture that this same Tharsicius was a deacon; for Damasus compares him with Stephen and assigns equal rank to the merit of each—something that surely concerns both their kind of martyrdom and their ecclesiastical rank and ministry.

XI. The following two poems concern the blessed martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, and Gorgonius. Nothing need be said about Peter and Marcellinus, since their surviving *Acts*, learnedly annotated by the distinguished Mazzocchi for 11 June [Col. 0276B], are admirably confirmed by this epigram. As for Gorgonius, Florentinius doubts at 9 September whether he is the same man as the Gorgonius whom Eusebius relates to have suffered at Nicomedia together with Dorotheus [Note: [Col. 0276D] Book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 6.]. Most think so, led by the testimony of the Roman Martyrology and Ado. But the Bollandists, at 12 March, give very weighty reasons why our Gorgonius is different from that Gorgonius.

The Fulda martyrology certainly posits two Gorgonii, one who suffered at Nicomedia and the other at Rome [Note: [Col. 0276D] See George, on Ado’s Martyrology, 9 September.]. Damasus seems to favour this view: for when he says that other blessed persons dwell in a neighbouring resting-place, he indicates that they suffered together with the same Gorgonius and were joined with him both in place and in martyrdom. Who they were is difficult to say. A *Notitia* published by Eckhard [Col. 0276C] in George reads: “There sleep those holy persons: Peter, Marcellinus, the holy thirty soldiers, Gorgonius, Geminus, etc.” Melsbury likewise mentions them and adds the Four Crowned Saints as buried not far from them. The Hieronymian Martyrology also records these thirty soldiers, crowned on one day under Diocletian on the Lavican Way at *ad duas lauros*, on 22 December; perhaps Damasus could have indicated all of them as resting in the same place.

The eminent Bottari, keeper of the Vatican Library, again published the plan of the upper and lower cemetery of Saints Peter and Marcellinus [Note: [Col. 0276D] Vol. I, plate 4.]. It depicts a chamber in which the Lord Jesus sits in the middle between the standing Apostles Peter and Paul; beneath them Gorgonius, Peter, Marcellinus, and Tiburtius are shown, identified by their written names.

[Col. 0276D] XII. Although much has perished from the cemetery of Priscilla, more poems of Damasus have survived there than from other cemeteries. There still remain those inscribed on the tombs of Marcellus, Prothus, Hyacinthus, Saturninus, Maurus, and Chrysanthus and Daria. But the inscription concerning Chrysanthus and Daria, having once been carelessly copied from an apograph, requires a healing hand, which Sarazanius applied; and, as it is now read, it must be elucidated from the *Acts* of those martyrs and from Gregory of Tours [Col. 0277A] [Note: [Col. 0277D] *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, ch. 38.]. From these sources one may understand why Damasus says that the tomb of those saints was the prey of raging idolatry: it had been wholly broken up and destroyed by the furious hand of pagans who had flocked to the cemetery against the Christians, while the crypt itself was blocked with stones and heaped-up earth.

But after peace had been restored to the Church and the site returned to its former religious use, Damasus not only inscribed these verses but also added some new work at his own expense. For this reason, I think, he quite properly described himself under the designation “poor man.”

XIII. I published the poem concerning St. Agnes after comparing and correcting it from the archetype. The stone upon which it had long ago been engraved in excellent characters had been thrown away and broken up; but not many years ago, by God’s favour, it was found near the church outside the Nomentan Gate, preserved, and, through his zeal for sacred antiquities, fixed again into the wall of the same church by the distinguished Marangonius.

From this epigram we may infer, first, that Damasus favours the view of those who believe Agnes suffered under Diocletian: for the report of the events which the virgin’s parents had formerly related had not yet perished among those then living when he wrote this poem. Secondly, that the most courageous virgin, when the herald’s voice proclaimed the judge’s sentence against her, immediately left the embrace of the nurse who had not abandoned her, in order fearlessly to undergo the punishment to which she had been condemned. For it was customary that the herald should signal silence with a trumpet [Note: [Col. 0277D] Seneca, Epistle 78.], and then read the judge’s sentence aloud. Therefore [Col. 0277C], if that custom was observed in Agnes’s martyrdom, there is no reason for us, with Tillemont, to understand Damasus’s words, “when the trumpet sounded forth mournful notes,” as referring to the then first publication of Diocletian’s edict of persecution; nor to say that the most courageous martyr voluntarily offered herself for punishment as soon as she heard the impious law against Christians proclaimed.

Thirdly, from the same poem we understand that, once Agnes had been condemned to punishment and was naked but covered by a transparent garment—when she was first, according to custom, to be taken to a brothel—God wonderfully protected her modesty from the shamelessness of men’s eyes by her hair flowing over her limbs. Therefore there is no reason not to credit the *Acts* circulated under Ambrose’s name, although neither Ambrose himself nor Prudentius mentions this matter [Col. 0277D]. Fourthly and finally, we learn that the most holy martyr was condemned to fire—something Ambrose also passes over in silence, but the commonly circulated *Acts* confirm. From this you understand how often we suspect ancient monuments on very slight grounds.

But did Agnes suffer martyrdom by fire or by the sword? Ambrose and Prudentius say by the sword; the *Acts of Western Martyrs*, with which the most distinguished Evodius Assemanus, Archbishop of Apamea, recently enriched the Church from an old Vatican Syriac codex, accompanied by excellent notes, teach that she was consumed by fire. The Latin *Acts*, however, state that the virgin was first cast into the flames [Col. 0278A], then preserved unharmed by divine power, and finally beheaded with the sword. Damasus not obscurely suggests that this latter account is truer in this verse:

> When he had wished to burn that noble body with flames.

For this makes clear that the wicked judge wished, but was by no means able, to accomplish what he wished. Thus this poem gives no small authority to the Latin *Acts* in circulation. Accordingly Agnes is represented, between the Apostles Peter and Paul, with flame rising around her, in an ancient fragment from the cemetery of Pontian, illustrated by Bonarotti [Note: [Col. 0277D] *Fragments*, p. 91.]. This is further confirmed by old paintings in her basilica, which still portray both the flames and, beneath them, the sword by which her martyrdom was completed [Note: [Col. 0278D] Ciampini, vol. II, p. 39.].

Spanish writers claim Irene, Damasus’s sister, for themselves, just as they do Damasus himself, as appears from her *Acts*, published by Bollandus at 21 February. Yet, if any credit can be assigned to those *Acts*, no one will deny that Irene must be counted among Roman virgins. For they assert that she passed to heaven in the twelfth year of Damasus’s pontificate, which falls in 378; but Damasus himself laments in this poem that she was taken from him before her twentieth year was complete. Hence you easily see that she cannot seem either to have been born or raised anywhere other than Rome. But, to tell the truth, those *Acts* have exceedingly slight authority, whichever side one wishes to take.

These are the observations I had to make here on the poems of Damasus. In addition to what I have said, from them you may see confirmed the ancient use of hymns, the cult of sacred relics [Col. 0278C], the invocation of saints, and both the making and the pious fulfilment of vows. Why I have added, as an appendix, not only those poems praising the Roman pontiffs Stephen and Eusebius which I have enumerated above, but also several others, to those published by Sarazanius, has this single reason: they too seem to me to have Damasus’s flavour and at times to reproduce his words, thought, and age. But on this matter, lest I determine anything rashly, let the reader judge.

Moreover, no one who is moderately familiar with reading inscribed verses and epitaphs will wonder that Damasus sometimes appears to offend against metre. For, to use the words of a learned man as my own, among the many epigrams found on stones you will scarcely find even a few [Col. 0278D] that do not violate metrical rules in many ways, even though otherwise they may be extremely elegant [Note: [Col. 0278D] Mazzocchi, on the Calendar for 30 June, note 18.].

## § III.—On the Works of Damasus: the site, as it appears, of the basilica built by him on the Ardeatine Way, and its cemetery. On the Basilica of St. Lawrence in Damaso; on which occasion the *tituli* are discussed, and Anastasius’s passage on Marcellus is adduced and explained.

I. It remains now to add a few words concerning the works of Damasus. The *Pontifical Book* accordingly records the following:

> He made two basilicas: one near the theatre, for St. Lawrence; and another on the Ardeatine Way, where he rests in the Catacombs. He also built the *platonium*, where the bodies of the Apostles lay, and adorned it with coverings.

By *platonium* Anastasius means precious marbles cut into slabs, with which Damasus faced the wall and pavement and so adorned the place [Note: [Col. 0279D] *Italian Museum*, vol. I, p. 89.]. The distinguished Boldetti and Marangonius—certainly competent judges—think that the basilica built on the Ardeatine Way, in which he was buried, survives for the most part even now. It was later converted to use as a wine cellar and lies between the Ardeatine and Appian Ways. First, the place extends seventy palms in length and thirty in breadth. Secondly, it has on the north a semicircular apse prepared for an altar. Thirdly, its walls retain painted colour in places: all these features certainly preserve the appearance of an ancient sacred building. Finally, beneath this very site lies a cemetery [Col. 0279B], first discovered by those most diligent men. They therefore judge it to be the basilica Damasus had built, and the cemetery beneath it to be the very one in which he lay buried. The most illustrious Bishop of Jesi has clearly set out their arguments in the place already indicated; consult him.

A poem of Damasus himself, inscribed concerning the church of St. Lawrence, manifestly proves that the other basilica, by Pompey’s Theatre, was older than his pontificate. Therefore he should seem not to have built it first, but to have restored it—though he restored, enlarged, and adorned it so extensively that he was thereafter called its sole founder. He also consecrated it after restoring, enlarging, and adorning it, as we learn from a marble monument discovered by Cardinal Farnese while again restoring that basilica. It was removed to his residence and is still preserved, inscribed with these letters.

I have transcribed the letters here as Francesco Bianchini, a man of immortal memory, reproduced them in his final revision.
