For, though he had previously reported them in the prolegomena to the first volume of Anastasius, after perhaps examining the stone more carefully he later reported in his historical notes [Col. 0279C] on the Life of our Damasus, volume III, that a single siglum *D.* should replace the *Q.* he had earlier transcribed. He explained them thus:

> Inscription in Christ’s name: I, Damasus, Bishop of the City of Rome, consecrated this building, in the ninth region, dedicated in the month of September, to St. Paul, St. Peter.

He then observes that the anniversary of this act is celebrated in that basilica on the first day of the same month. But if the sigla *N. R. S. M.* and “ninth region” do not please anyone, nor the isolated word *September*, indicating a fixed day without a date or consuls recording the year, he may perhaps read:

> I consecrated this building, renewed and restored, dedicated to the holy martyr.

For Damasus in fact did all these things at that time. Moreover, it may be observed here [Col. 0280A] that the saint’s name was indicated by the single letter *S.* already in the fourth century, and that this practice therefore did not begin after the eleventh century, as Fontanini thought [Note: [Col. 0279D] *On the Argument of the Discourse*, ch. 14.].

From this marble tablet you have, I think, the reason why they were called *tituli*, and you further understand that all the basilicas in the City could then have been, and deservedly were, called by the name of *tituli*. For just as there were more basilicas assigned for assembling ecclesiastical synaxes than twenty-five—since we know from Optatus that under Cornelius sacred buildings exceeded forty in number—so we must admit that there were also as many *tituli*. Marcellus did not take this designation away from all the other basilicas so that it should belong exclusively to the twenty-five he himself established.

Therefore this basilica, which Damasus is said to have made into a *titulus*, must necessarily have been a *titulus* before his pontificate, since it had its priests, deacons, and other orders presiding over sacred rites, as is plainly evident from poem 35 [Col. 0280B]. Thus, when Marcellus made his churches, and Damasus the church of St. Lawrence, into a *titulus*, they bestowed something more than the designation common to all the basilicas of the City. What that was, we learn from Anastasius, when he says that Marcellus established twenty-five *tituli* in the city of Rome “as dioceses” for the baptism and penitence of many who were converted from paganism. After the Decian persecution, moreover, it had become customary for bishops to appoint certain presbyters to receive the lapsed into penitence [Note: [Col. 0280D] Socrates, Book V, ch. 19.].

To provide for Christians devastated by the long and most bitter Diocletianic persecution, Marcellus may therefore seem not so much to have established places for receiving them as to have restored them. Since there were already as many *tituli* as basilicas and places assigned for sacred rites, he selected only twenty-five from them and ordered these to be, as it were, dioceses. That is, he shared with them the authority to reconcile penitents and administer baptism, which was proper to the bishop alone. By conferring this authority upon those *tituli*, he caused them to seem like dioceses, and their presbyters like bishops [Col. 0280C].

Thus both the designation *titulus* and the use of sacred rites were common also to the other basilicas of the City. But those which additionally possessed this special privilege were considered greater and more dignified than the rest; hence the name “cardinal *tituli*” afterwards attached to them. These, then, are the privileges which Damasus granted to this basilica—renewed, restored, dedicated, and increased by his estates and gifts—so that it might be raised above very many others.

Joseph Bianchini, a distinguished scholar, has shown from explicit testimony of Leo the Great, recently published by him from Leo’s own Sacramentary, that this most courageous martyr must be counted among Roman citizens, contrary to what had hitherto been believed. I think, however, that another witness may be added for this holy pontiff: namely Prudentius, who writes that the glory of the city of Rome lacked only this—that after subduing the whole world it should conquer the foul Jupiter [Col. 0281A], not by the turbulent force of Cassius, Camillus, or Caesar, but by the not bloodless battle of the martyr Lawrence. From this it evidently follows that Lawrence must by no means be separated from the illustrious sons of that City.

The *Poem on the Fountains* informs us that this pontiff also carried out some work in the Vatican basilica. What this was, Ciampini, describing as far as he could—amid so great an antiquity of time and change of circumstances—the ground plan of the old church, explained in these words:

> From the altar of the holy Three Kings there rose a structure far more elaborate and beautiful, as is apparent at no. 30, together with the most ancient altar called that of St. John at the Fonts. Not far from the steps of this altar, in the middle, a great and broad basin spread itself beneath a most precious shell of alabaster marble, distinguished alike by its smooth brilliance and by the figures upon it [Col. 0281B]. Into this, waters burst through pipes from the ground by a hidden course, and catechumens were baptized in them. Pope Liberius had formerly ordered Damasus to construct it, when he did not yet shine with pontifical majesty. Indeed, so that the memory of so conspicuous a work might reach posterity, Damasus himself, no mean devotee of the Muses, engraved certain little verses upon stone. Some fragments of these, though scarcely legible on the walls within the new Oratory of Pope St. Leo, are now seen in the Vatican crypts, restored to their original and genuine sense by learned and persistent inquiry. [Note: [Col. 0281C] *Vet. Mon.*, vol. I, p. 59.]

But since a baptistery is one thing and the font of a baptistery another, there are, in my view, two poems of Damasus *On the Vatican Fonts*: one inscribed upon the baptistery itself in its entirety, under the care of the deacon Mercurius; the other upon the water-reservoir itself, through the agency of Achatius [Col. 0281C]. For another fountain, or *cantharus*, elegantly described by Paulinus of Nola as situated in the atrium of the basilica, and taken by some for a baptistery, had been provided only for the customary washing of the people about to enter the church [Col. 0282A]. [Note: [Col. 281C] Cl. Murat. nos. 41, 42, on Paulinus, *Epistle* 13, Verona ed.]

Repeated testimonies to this work of Damasus survive, both from Paul V and from Innocent X. They state that the water of the Vatican hill—which had once wandered from an uncertain source—was discovered by Blessed Damasus, collected from its spring into a font for the washing of new birth, then lost again, sought out and rediscovered, and found remarkably serviceable. It was restored in a newly built fountain, so that, although the City abounds with waters brought from abroad, the Vatican church might possess this water of its own, to be drawn with a twofold benefit to health.

Pope Hilary relates that the very ancient basilica of St. Anastasia was adorned with paintings by Damasus, citing verses reproduced by Sarazani in his notes on poem 17. From this, perhaps some support—though in vain—may seem to accrue to the opinion of those who have written that that church was the titular church of Cardinal Jerome. [Col. 0282B] Finally, Baronius and Ciacconius, influenced by the authority of the *Acts of Damasus*, maintain that the church of SS. Rufina and Secunda in the White Wood, begun by Julius, was completed by Damasus.

There are also those who extend Damasus’s zeal to places distant from Rome. Writers on Nola attribute to Damasus the little chapel in which the tomb of St. Felix had stood—the chapel which Paulinus later says that he enclosed within his own very spacious basilica [Note: [Col. 0282C] *Ep.* 12, Verona ed.]—and offer, as especially ancient testimony to this claim, the following inscription:

> “On the seventh day, with the month of May in progress, the dedication of this Holy Church shall take place. Blessed Pope Damasus constructed and built it in honour of God and of the most blessed Felix, Confessor.”

On this matter see, if you please, the distinguished Giovanni Stefano Remondini. [Note: [Col. 0282C] *Della Nolan. Eccles. Storia*, bk. II, chs. 8–9.] Yet it may rightly seem surprising [Col. 0282C] that Paulinus himself, although he frequently discussed that little chapel, never once mentioned this pontiff.

[Col. 0281]

# TWO DISSERTATIONS ILLUSTRATING CERTAIN DEEDS OF THE POPES LIBERIUS AND DAMASUS

## FIRST DISSERTATION. On the deeds of Liberius in exile

[Col. 0281C]

### § I.—Contemporary writers on the deeds of Liberius in exile are adduced; the author proposed only these as his judges in this celebrated controversy.

[Col. 0281D]

I had resolved with myself, although an occasion presented itself, to say nothing on these matters, since they seemed to lie outside my purpose, and lest it should be said that I was turning again, with useless labour, a wheel which has been turned so often. But I afterwards changed my mind, because I saw both that the Jansenists, in years gone by, had repeated to nausea the charge of Liberius’s heresy against Catholics; that recently there had been a historian from our own side who treated it as an unquestionable fact; and, finally, that through reading and reflection I had observed that this question [Col. 0282C], owing to the deficiency of monuments, had been made not so much clearer as more entangled and obscure by men otherwise most learned, while each served a preconceived opinion.

I therefore allowed myself to be drawn along with the many [Col. 0282D] who have treated this controversy. Yet, lest I weary my readers too greatly, I have undertaken to elucidate it from contemporary writers only, whose works survive. Whether I have succeeded as I wished, let them judge.

To begin with, no one who reads Liberius’s letter to the Eastern bishops will doubt that, while in exile, Pope Liberius accepted the Sirmian faith. Nor am I one who would venture utterly to demand, against the opposition of so many centuries, that it be rejected as spurious and numbered among the inventions of the Arians. But whether in that passage Liberius declares a mere willingness expressed in words, or one already confirmed by some subscription of his own [Col. 0283A]; and also what Sirmian faith it is of which he speaks—I shall say later. For the present it is enough briefly to observe that the Sirmian faith is threefold, just as the formula or *ecthesis* issued and promulgated in that city is threefold: first, that issued when Photinus was condemned by the Eastern bishops and expelled from the bishopric of Sirmium and from the city itself; second, that composed later by Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius, and called, though wrongly, the blasphemy of Hosius and Potamius; and finally, the third, drafted by Marcus of Arethusa on 21 July in the consulship of Hypatius and Eusebius—that is, in the year 359—and for that very reason, namely because the day and consuls are appended, greeted with laughter by Athanasius in his book *On the Synods*.

When, therefore, we ask which of these three statements of faith Liberius accepted, and which he subsequently subscribed, the Fathers of that age who discuss the matter—Athanasius, Hilary, and Jerome—leave us uncertain, since none of them expressly identifies any one of the formulae. For Athanasius, in his *History of the Arians to the Monks*, or letter *To the Solitaries*, writes:

> Liberius, having been banished, was at last broken after two years; and, terrified by threats of death, he subscribed.

Then, to excuse him, he immediately adds:

> But by that very fact both their violence, and Liberius’s hatred of that heresy and his support for Athanasius, are proved—as long, that is, as he was free and able to act according to his own judgment. For things extracted contrary to a former opinion by the force of tortures are the determinations, not of those who fear, but of those who torment.  
> [Note: [Col. 0283D] No. 41.]

[Col. 0283C]

Jerome touches upon the event in two places, namely in the *Chronicle* and in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. In the former he says:

> When Liberius was driven into exile for the faith, all the Roman clergy swore that they would receive no other; but when Felix had been installed in the priesthood by the Arians, very many perjured themselves. After a year they were expelled together with Felix, because Liberius, overcome by the weariness of exile and subscribing to heretical depravity, entered Rome as though a victor.  
> [Note: [Col. 0283D] To Olympiad 282.]

In the latter place he declares that Fortunatianus of Aquileia is held detestable because he was the first to solicit and break Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, as he was going into exile for the faith, and compelled him to subscribe to heresy. [Note: [Col. 0283D] *De S. E.*, ch. 97.]

Hilary also mentions Liberius’s lapse twice. First, in his work *Against Constantius*, where he says:

> You then turned your war even upon Rome; you tore its bishop away from it. And—O wretched you!—I do not know whether you banished him or recalled him with greater impiety.  
> [Note: [Col. 0284D] Ch. 11.]

Then, in the *Fragments*, where he calls this Roman pontiff an apostate and consigns him to anathema for writing that he had accepted the Sirmian faith, I do not reproduce the words, since I must cite them below in a more suitable place.

If, therefore, Liberius is said to have subscribed to heresy, he can seem to have subscribed only to the second Sirmian formula. For the earlier formula, promulgated in the council convened against Photinus, appeared to Hilary himself Catholic [Col. 0284A] and holy in his book *On the Synods*. This is the sole reason why, to pass over the heterodox, some among our own writers have adopted this opinion.

### § II.—Hilary’s testimonies are examined at length to establish the Sirmian faith accepted by Liberius. No council of Eastern Arians could have been held in Sirmium in 349, contrary to the opinion of some.

Yet Hilary himself manifestly proves that the Sirmian faith accepted by Liberius was none other than that promulgated by the council against Photinus; and I therefore wonder that he has not hitherto been read attentively. Hilary discusses at length this Sirmian council of Arians, and the twofold reason for which the Easterners had resolved to convene it: first [Col. 0284B], so that, taking advantage of the occasion afforded by Photinus, they might overthrow the decrees of the Catholic Council of Sardica, which had pronounced Marcellus, Photinus’s teacher, and Athanasius innocent; and secondly—and more seriously—that, under the pretext of the Photinian heresy, they might promulgate a new exposition of faith by which they might undermine the Nicene doctrine through subterranean devices.

He then quotes that exposition, calls it fraudulent and heretical, pregnant with an inward poison beneath flattering words, and framed in such a way that in one and the same composition it expelled Photinus, arraigned Athanasius, and overthrew the Nicene faith. He compares it also with the Nicene faith in order thereby to demonstrate the falsity of the other, and says:

> For that which was ordained at Nicaea is full and perfect, and, with every approach by which heretics are accustomed to creep in guarded against on every side, it is joined together by the inviolable firmness of eternal unity between Father and Son. But this formula flatters by an appearance of simplicity, first asserting that we believe thus—which be far from anyone!—whereas the faith of the Westerners, established by evangelical teachings, confesses the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father: the Father unbegotten, the Son eternal by the substance of eternity; that is, that as the Father is always Father, so the Son is always in the Father, born of God and always existing in Him from whom He is. But this PERFIDY, not faith, while speaking of God from God, commending the Firstborn, and setting forth the name of the Trinity, conceals its poison beneath the modesty of religious moderation.

After this he turns to Athanasius, praises him as the author and most vigorous defender of that same Nicene faith, and demonstrates that, on that account, he was harassed by the Arians with false accusations but acquitted by the Council of Sardica. He produces letters from that council and several letters written by Liberius before his exile. [Note: [Col. 0284D] Fragments 2, 4, 5, 6.] Yet he laments that Liberius, once in exile, made void all that he had either done or promised before exile; and to prove this he cites Liberius’s letter to the Easterners and another letter written by him to Ursacius and Valens.

We must now quote Liberius’s letter to the Easterners and Hilary’s words appended to it, which decide the matter [Col. 0285A]. Liberius says:

> So that you may know that I speak the true faith: my lord and common brother Demophilus, who in his kindness has deigned to set forth for me your faith and the Catholic faith which was discussed, set forth, and accepted at Sirmium by many of our brethren and fellow bishops.

To this Hilary immediately adds the annotation:

> This is Arian perfidy.  
> [Note: [Col. 0285D] In Coustant, letter 11, and Hilary, fragment 6, nos. 4–5.]

The Sirmian faith accepted by Liberius, therefore, Hilary, as you see, calls “perfidy.” But the perfidy which is Sirmian for Hilary in this passage is, as we have seen, the one faith directed against Photinus. This is what he execrates; this he compares with the Nicene faith; this very thing he reproaches Liberius with. Therefore Liberius accepted it, Hilary being the witness.

Neither the most learned Nicolaus Faber, who first published Hilary’s fragments, nor any others who think that Hilary’s words designate the second Sirmian formula, paid sufficient attention to these points. Could Hilary have meant in this place a formula which, neither when writing this nor anywhere in the entire work of the *Fragments*, he appears ever to discuss—or even to have considered? Nor, in my opinion, do those take the best course in attempting to disentangle that pontiff from heresy who regard Hilary’s inserted annotations as interpolated, corrupt, and inserted by another hand. For, since these annotations lead us, as it were by the hand, to the Sirmian faith accepted by this pontiff, they seem rather to establish the case against him.

Why Hilary here calls Arian perfidy the Sirmian faith against Photinus, which he judged Catholic in his book *On the Synods*, I shall say elsewhere. For the present I proceed to confirm the matter by other arguments.

### § III.—Hilary’s testimonies are likewise developed to establish the Sirmian faith accepted by Liberius.

From this same letter we further understand that the faith in question had been discussed and set forth by many brethren and fellow bishops. Hilary confirms this very point by listing more than twenty bishops present for its composition. Those who composed the PERFIDY written at Sirmium, which Liberius says Demophilus expounded to him as Catholic, were: Narcissus, Theodore, Basil, Eudoxius, Demophilus, Cecropius, Silvanus, Ursacius, Valens, Evagrius, Hyrenius, Exuperantius, Terentianus, Bassus, Gaudentius, Macedonius, Marcus, Aetius, Julius, Severinus, Simplicius, and Junior—all heretics.

Manuscript codices mentioned by Baronius indicate that others also attended [Col. 0285D]. But the second Sirmian formula was composed by only three bishops—Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius. If one wishes to add Potamius and Hosius, it is certain that at most five composed it. Hilary everywhere names only these and never more. The formula itself further indicates this in the following words:

> Since some dispute concerning the faith was thought to exist, all matters were diligently treated and examined at Sirmium, in the presence of our most holy brethren and fellow bishops Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius.

Thus it is not this formula that Hilary identifies in that passage, nor could he have execrated it as accepted by Liberius; rather, he identifies the other.

Further, if you attend carefully, Hilary says that neither Hosius, Potamius, nor Germinius was present for composing the faith which Liberius accepted. Why would he have omitted them if in that place he were attacking the second Sirmian formula, which elsewhere he says they composed? He must, therefore, have indicated another formula: namely the Sirmian one issued against Photinus, at which none of them was present. Conversely, Hilary states that Theodore, Basil, and Eudoxius were present for composing the perfidy of Sirmium which Liberius accepted. But if you understand this of the second Sirmian formula, the statement is utterly false: the first had already died, while the other two were far away [Col. 0286B]. These facts are manifest from Theodoret, Sozomen, and Epiphanius, whom the reader may consult. [Note: [Col. 0285D] See Theodoret, bk. II, ch. 13; Sozomen, bk. IV, ch. 13; Epiphanius, heresy 73.] See also Petavius’s dissertations on the Sirmian synod against Photinus.

Perhaps the same might be affirmed of Narcissus and Cecropius. For we read that the latter was among those whom George of Laodicea urged by letter to come quickly to the aid of the faith, which was being ruined by the deceit of Eudoxius and Aetius. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Sozomen, bk. IV, ch. 13.] The former, meanwhile, was living quietly in his own see when he learned that, through the efforts of Basil of Ancyra and by order of the Emperor, those heretics had been expelled from Antioch. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Philostorgius, bk. VIII, ch. 10.]

Finally, the faith approved by the pontiff and called perfidy by Hilary had been composed by the Easterners, who had come to Sirmium under the pretext of deposing Photinus, but in reality in order once again to drive Athanasius from his see [Col. 0286C] and overthrow the Nicene faith. But the second Sirmian formula originated with Westerners alone. Thus, when Eudoxius learned that it had been approved by Hosius, he thanked Ursacius and Valens because through their ministry the Westerners had begun to think rightly. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Sozomen, bk. IV, ch. 12.] Therefore Hilary neither identifies it in those words nor can appear to have had it in mind.

I see one possible objection: namely, that besides the council which deposed and expelled Photinus, there was another Sirmian synod convened in 349, mentioned by Petavius and Constantius—though Petavius takes it to have been a synod of Western Catholics, while Constantius and the recent author of an *Ecclesiastical History* take it to have been a synod of Eastern Arians. Thus, it may be said, this decree concerning the faith belongs to that synod—the decree which Hilary cites in these exact words:

> For we profess thus: that there is one unbegotten God, the Father, and one only-begotten Son of His, God from God, light from light, firstborn of every creature; and, adding thirdly, the Holy Spirit.  
> [Note: [Col. 0286D] Hilary, fragment 2, no. 21.]

Accordingly, the faith accepted by Liberius was composed by this synod and by the bishops whom Hilary names.

Certainly, as concerns this Sirmian council, Petavius has weighty opponents. But whatever may be the outcome of this dispute—which I do not make my own—what I confidently maintain is this: no council of Eastern Arians can appear to have been convened at Sirmium in that year, or before the death of Constans. Could that emperor, in the capital of his empire and almost under his own eyes [Note: [Col. 0287D] Tillemont proves, from the chronology of the *Codex Theodosianus* and Libanius, *Oration* 3, art. 13, that Constans was at Sirmium and in Illyricum on 27 May, in the consulship of Limenius and Catulinus.], ever have permitted a synod to be assembled which would overthrow the Nicene faith, of which he was a steadfast adherent, and again expel Athanasius—dear to him and deservedly received under his protection—from his see? And could he have permitted this to be done by bishops subject to Constantius’s jurisdiction, whose intrigues and alienation from himself he knew? Is this consonant with the civil and ecclesiastical policy of that age?

“But,” it will be said, “the words which Hilary cites are sought in vain in the Sirmian synod by which Photinus was utterly overthrown and deposed.” I deny this. For if you attend carefully, you will say that Hilary wished to excerpt the ideas in summary rather than to report the very words, though he does retain some portion of them.

Moreover, Athanasius and Hilary prove most clearly that there could have been no council of Eastern Arians at Sirmium in that year. Athanasius relates in his *History of the Arians to the Monks* [Note: [Col. 0287D] Ch. 28 ff.] the great peace and concord that had come upon and embraced the whole Church after Athanasius had been restored to his see. He then gives the following reason why that peace was broken and why the very grave disturbances that afterwards afflicted the Church arose anew:

> When the successors of the Eusebian party and heresy—Leontius, George, Acacius, Theodore, and Narcissus—heard and saw these things, they were overwhelmed with great shame; for they had been deposed and deprived of office in the Council of Sardica. Then, seeing so great a harmony of minds and so great peace being maintained with Athanasius, they were troubled by fear and envy: because so many bishops preserved communion with Athanasius; because they feared that those whom they had deceived would desert them and join this unanimity and communion; and lest, as seemed likely, a triumph over their everywhere notorious heresy should result.

Athanasius writes that they all approached Constantius together and, while he was hastening against Magnentius, rekindled his anger against Athanasius; and this was the beginning of all the evils that followed.

Hilary, however, states that, in order to carry into effect the plans they had then devised, they met at Sirmium [Note: [Col. 0287D] Fragment 2, no. 21.]—men ardent in mind, subtle in ingenuity, persistent in intrigue—and sought an opportunity to reopen the judgment which had been settled by Athanasius’s acquittal. He writes that they raised into public remembrance, by the new case of Photinus, the question concerning Athanasius himself, a question already dead through time and buried by the judgment of truth. Hilary further says that they then produced that faith, from which I have quoted a few words, and calls it heretical and fraudulent, suffused with inward poison beneath flattering words, and finally PERFIDY; so that, once the security of readers and the simplicity of the unlearned had been ensnared by such gentle beginnings, they might be brought, by one and the same assent extorted in subscription, to the punishment of Photinus, the condemnation of Athanasius, and the condemnation of the Catholic faith [Col. 0288A].

This, then, was the purpose of this Sirmian council against Photinus. But it occurred after Athanasius had already been restored to his see and after Constans had been slain by Magnentius’s treachery. Therefore, if Athanasius could scarcely return to Alexandria before the end of 349, as eminent scholars think and as the distinguished P. Thomas Mamachi, theologian of the Casanatensian library, has recently demonstrated very fully in *On the Chronology of Athanasius*, letters 1 and 3; if the Emperor Constans died at the beginning of January in the consulship of Sergius and Nigrinianus; and if the purpose of one and the same Sirmian council was that all might, by one subscription, proceed to the punishment of Photinus, the condemnation of Athanasius, then living peacefully in his own church, and the condemnation of the Nicene faith—then one must seek another time and year suitable for carrying out these acts, rather than the one which seemed appropriate to those learned men [Col. 0288B].

### § IV.—The heresy of Demophilus, bishop of Beroea in Thrace, is discussed; he is proved always to have been a Semi-Arian and a most vigorous opponent of the Arians. Was he present at the Council of Rimini?

Finally, Liberius states that the Sirmian faith which he accepted had previously been expounded to him by Demophilus. That this may not appear surprising is explained by Hilary, who writes that, by God’s great favour, the Westerners knew no written creeds other than the one Nicene creed [Col. 0288C]. [Note: [Col. 0288D] *On the Synods*, ch. 63.] We must now inquire whether Demophilus was Arian or Semi-Arian while Liberius was an exile at Beroea, and which heresy he professed both then and thereafter.

We read that Demophilus, with Eudoxius, Martyrius, and Macedonius, brought the *Macrostich* formula to the Westerners, and that he left the Council of Milan in anger with his associates because they refused to condemn Arius’s opinion as heretical. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Liberius, letter to Constantius, in Coustant, letter 4.] Now those who brought that formula, if they sincerely professed it, could at least appear Orthodox; for they held as alien from the holy and Catholic Church those who said that the Son came from what did not exist, or from another substance rather than from God, or that there had been a time or age when He did not exist. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Socrates, bk. II, ch. 19.]

Philostorgius writes that Eudoxius at least passed, following the Arian view, to those who maintained the *homoiousion*, after reading the books of Asterius, and was finally brought back to the Anomoeans. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Bk. IV, ch. 4.] Moreover, they were all present at the Sirmian council against Photinus and all therefore professed one faith—unless they asserted one doctrine orally while retaining another opinion in mind. From the time of that council until the second Sirmian formula, we know of no other position publicly introduced, at least, among the heretics [Col. 0289A]. That blasphemy appeared, in my view, in the first months of 358 through Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius. But nowhere do we read that Demophilus ever joined them, whether when it was composed or when it was subsequently enlarged by the number and consent of certain other bishops.

Because of the disturbances that then arose, the Council of Rimini was convened in the following year. If we believe Socrates and Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0289D] Bk. II, ch. 37; bk. IV, ch. 18.], Demophilus was present there with Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, and Gaius. When they proposed the third Sirmian formula to the assembly of Fathers, he supported them, and for that reason was condemned with his associates by anathema.

Socrates and Sozomen derived this from Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0289D] *On the Synods*, ch. 9; letter to the Africans, ch. 3.]. Yet I fear that the great and most holy bishop was failed by memory [Col. 0289B] in his book *On the Synods*, just as he was in his letter to the Africans, where he also lists Eudoxius among those who attended and were deposed at the Council of Rimini. For the bishop of Beroea, who belonged to the Easterners, could neither have attended that council nor, moreover, have been deposed there. Constantius had imperiously forbidden the Westerners assembled at Rimini to decree anything whatsoever against Eastern bishops.

This is why the surviving acts of that council and its synodical letters—which ought to be held in higher esteem for their authority—mention and list among those deposed only Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, Gaius, and Auxentius, Arians then present at the synod; nowhere do they name Demophilus. For how could they mention one absent and far away from the place?

[Col. 0289C]

The authority of the same acts is reinforced by Hilary’s testimony. In his treatise *Against Auxentius*, he counts all those men among the heirs of Arius’s spirit but passes Demophilus over in silence. [Note: [Col. 0289D] *Against Auxentius*, ch. 6.] Marcellinus and Faustinus, presbyters, likewise omit him when listing other Arians who were present at that same Council of Rimini. What is more, when the ten bishops who had been sent as envoys to the Emperor after the council was concluded afterwards acted treacherously at Nicaea in Thrace, rescinded the council’s earlier acts, and expressly restored communion to Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, and Gaius, they passed over Demophilus in profound silence. Had he sinned more gravely, so that those ignorant bishops judged him wholly undeserving of every pardon [Col. 0289D]?

It must therefore be held certain and settled that Demophilus was not present at the Council of Rimini. Yet one might ask why he is mentioned nowhere in the Council of Seleucia either, which the Emperor had commanded all Easterners to attend. Did he perhaps prefer to stand aloof from those tumults? Or was he among those 105 Homoiousians mentioned by Hilary [Note: [Col. 0289D] *Against Constantius*, no. 12.], while avoiding disputes? Either could easily have occurred. For Basil the Great writes that his disposition was as follows:

> Constantinople has long had Demophilus; and, as regards him, a certain semblance of right faith and piety is loudly celebrated with the fullest agreement by all who arrive there, so much so that even the conflicting parties of the city have united into one and certain bishops from neighbouring regions have embraced communion.  
> [Note: [Col. 0289D] Vol. III, letter 48.]

But why do we use unnecessary arguments in a manifest matter? For we understand Demophilus’s opinion from a fragment which Philostorgius excerpted from his commentaries, which Suidas preserved and transmitted to us. He says:

> The Son was begotten by the will of the Father alone, without time and without intermediary, in order that He might be the minister and servant of the Father’s commands.  
> [Note: [Col. 0290D] In Valesius, *H. E.*, vol. III, p. 558.]

This ministerial service concerns, it seems, the dispensation and redemption, as he explains in the words that follow. For [Col. 0290B], if you compare these with the lengthy Antiochene formula or with the Sirmian council against Photinus [Note: [Col. 0290D] Canons 1, 3, 25, 27; Council of Ancyra, canons 17–18.], you will see one and the same doctrine expressed in both: namely, that the Son was begotten by the Father’s will alone, without time and without intermediary, in order to obey and serve the Father; and that the Father is Father not only in substance but also in authority.

Hilary further explained this authority in such a way as to detract nothing from equality, because “the subjection of piety is not a diminution of essence, nor did the duty of religion make the nature inferior.” [Note: [Col. 0290D] *On the Synods*, ch. 79.] Hence Philostorgius himself, as he is accustomed to criticize all who differ from his sect, attacks Demophilus for being muddy and confused in expression, for confusing and mixing up everything—especially ecclesiastical doctrines—and finally because, being most bitterly hostile to the Eunomians, he afflicted them with very grievous evils. [Note: [Col. 0290D] Bk. IX, ch. 9.]

Since this testimony is altogether plain and decisive, no one can rightly doubt that Demophilus was always a Semi-Arian, or that he expounded to Liberius in exile the faith which he sincerely professed.

### § V.—In what year and month can the Sirmian blasphemy appear to have been composed and sent into Gaul? Various opinions on the matter; Hilary is adduced and explained, and his testimony decides the controversy.

I have also proposed to investigate more carefully in what year and at what time this Sirmian blasphemy may appear to have been written, and what its subsequent outcome and effect were. For this too will shed some light upon the history of those times.

Most persons think it was brought forth by evil devices in 357 [Col. 0290D]. But scarcely anyone offers any reason for this opinion except Pierre Coustant, who relies on Hilary’s authority. Writing to the Gallican bishops who had condemned it, Hilary says:

> You have conquered, brethren, amid great rejoicing for the faith; and the honour of your unstained conscience has had a double glory: that of the integrity of conscience and that of the authority of example. For the fame of your undisturbed faith at length stirred certain Eastern bishops to some shame for the heresy they had fostered; and, when they heard what had been written most impiously at Sirmium, they resisted the boldness of irreligious men by certain decrees.  
> [Note: [Col. 0291D] *On the Synods*, no. 3.]

The decrees mentioned by Hilary are those promulgated by the Council of Ancyra. Hence Coustant says:

> From Hilary’s words there must have intervened between this synod—the Gallican one, that is—and the Council of Ancyra, enough time for that formula to be conveniently carried into Gaul; then for a synod of Gallican bishops to be called; for its decrees to be conveyed into Asia to Hilary, and by Hilary to the Easterners; and for the latter, stirred by the example of the Gauls, to convene the Council of Ancyra.  
> [Note: [Col. 0291D] Note on Hilary, *On the Synods*, ch. 11.]

Coustant is not alone in assigning this glory to the Gallican bishops. For Tillemont understands Hilary to mean that the Eastern bishops convened that Council of Ancyra after learning that the blasphemy had been proscribed in Gaul.

Certainly, no one will deny that the Gallican bishops of that age were most holy and learned, granted by God to defend the faith. I willingly grant also that in that same century, and even now through the benefit of God most good and great, there have been many who, as sons and heirs of such great Fathers, have increased their glory. Yet perhaps Hilary’s meaning here is not what Tillemont and Coustant suppose. For Hilary does not praise the Gallican bishops because, in recalling and condemning this Sirmian formula, they had by their example prompted the Easterners to do the same—for, as I shall shortly say, Hilary himself establishes that this is false. Rather, he praises them because the renown of their uninterrupted preservation of the right faith [Col. 0291C] had brought the Easterners at length to shame for the heresy they had fostered.

That steadfast renown could indeed easily have spread long before throughout the East and reached the bishops of those provinces, and could likewise have moved them long before to shame for the heresy they had fostered. They made this shame public only when, seizing the opportunity presented by the Eudoxian blasphemy and issuing the definitions of Ancyra, they appeared to dissociate themselves from the disgrace of heresy. Consequently, the reason for which Coustant assigned it to a date not yet advanced in 357 does not seem sufficiently sound.

Those who think that it was drawn up in the year 358 rest chiefly on this ground: Constantius, who was present when it was drafted, although he left Rome at the end of May in 357 in order to hasten [Col. 0291D] into Illyricum, nevertheless seems neither to have left Italy nor to have reached Sirmium before the final days of that year, since we possess laws issued by him at Milan on the fourth and sixth of December. [Note: [Col. 0291D] Theodosian Code, book 5, *On Sorcerers*; book 14, *On Bishops*; and book 9, *On the Public Post*.] Yet this argument too is not without difficulty. Ammianus Marcellinus writes that the emperor, having left the City reluctantly, hurried into Illyricum to quell the disturbances of the Quadi and Sarmatians. Ammianus is supported by Julian, who says that Chnodomarius, captured in the battle of Argentoratum, was immediately sent to Constantius, just as he was returning from the Quadi and Sarmatians; then he adds: “Thus it happened that, while I had fought, he had merely made a journey; and while he had spoken peacefully with the inhabitants along the Danube, not I but he celebrated the triumph.” [Note: [Col. 0292D] *Oration to the Athenians*, p. 279, Spanh. ed.] Now, since the battle of Argentoratum cannot be removed from the year 357, and Constantius travelled through Illyricum in that year, nothing prevents him from having conveniently come to Sirmium and attended the drafting of the formula.

Nor is it necessary, as some do, to bring the emperor back unwillingly and exhausted from Illyricum to Milan in December—the month in which we read that laws were issued in that city—and then place him again at leisure in Sirmium on the eighteenth of that same month for the publication of other laws. [Note: [Col. 0292D] Law 3, *On Military Distributions*, and law 27, *On Appeals*.] We can easily free him from this inconvenience if, with Reinesius, [Note: [Col. 0292D] Letter 27, p. 114.] we say that through scribes’ incompetence “Milan” was substituted for “Mediana,” either because the latter was written in abbreviated form or through copyists’ error. For Mediana was a place—or imperial retreat—three miles from Naissus, famous for the division of the Empire between Valentinian and Valens. This correction will seem still easier to approve to anyone who reflects that, given the stages and stopping-places of the journey, it could scarcely have happened that an emperor who was at Milan on the sixth and seventh of December should on the eighteenth of the same month have been free at the city of Sirmium to publish laws. But if Law 14, *On Bishops*, addressed to Felix, bishop of Rome, was issued not at Milan but at Mediana, Liberius had not yet departed from Beroea at the end of 357 or abandoned his former constancy; for we know that this pontiff, as soon as he seemed to yield, came to the emperor [Col. 0292C] and was restored by him to his see.

Why, then, do I judge more correct the opinion of those who think that the Sirmian formula was written in the first or second month of 358? The reason is a twofold testimony of Hilary: one in the book *On the Synods*, the other in the work *Against Constantius*. In the first passage, when informing the Gallic bishops concerning the definitions of the Synod of Ancyra, he says:

> And this, dearest brethren, the whole teaching of faith which was set forth by a few Easterners, in a manner proportionate to universality, emerged **at almost these very days** in which you rejected the heresy imposed upon you; and the reason for setting it forth was that silence concerning the one substance was being decreed.  
> [Note: [Col. 0292D] *On the Synods*, §28.]

From these words, which are surely decisive, it is plainly clear [Col. 0292D] that at almost one and the same time the Gallic and the Ancyrene bishops pronounced anathema upon the same thing. But if we know that this was done by the Ancyrenes at the Paschal feast, which in that year fell on 12 April, it must appear that it was done by the Gallic bishops in that same month. Sirmond uses this kind of argument in order rightly to judge that the synod at which he supposes this Sirmian blasphemy was condemned by the Gauls was assembled at nearly the same time. But how much time could have elapsed for this impious formula to be carried from the place where it was written into Gaul? For Hilary indicates that it was condemned as soon as it had been received and communicated. [Note: [Col. 0293D] *On the Synods*, §2.] Or would not one month have been entirely sufficient, especially with Ursacius and Valens exerting themselves to have it transmitted as rapidly as possible? Therefore it can scarcely be placed outside the first or second month of that year.

The other testimony of Hilary is supplied by these words addressed by him to Constantius:

> For we are tossed about by the uncertain wind of doctrines. . . . And now, what does the faith of the past year not already contain in the way of change? First, that which decrees that *homoiousion* be kept silent. Then another, which decrees and proclaims *homoiousion*. A third, which excuses *ousia*, simply assumed by the Fathers, by way of indulgence. Finally, that which does not excuse it, but condemns it.  
> [Note: [Col. 0293D] Book II *Against Constantius*, §5.]

[Col. 0293B] He wrote this while residing at Constantinople, near the end of the year 359 or at the beginning of the next. The immediately preceding year, then, is the single year nearest to it; accordingly, it gave birth to the Sirmian blasphemy and to the contrary Ancyrene exposition. These formulas were followed, not long afterwards, by the third Sirmian formula, which excuses *ousia*; then by that of the Acacians at Seleucia; and then by the same party’s addition newly appended at Constantinople, which openly condemns *ousia*.

Hilary and Phoebadius therefore leave us no room to doubt that this monstrosity was sent into Gaul as soon as it came to light. But since Hilary says that it was sent not by a synod—which had not existed—nor by bishops, but only from the town of Sirmium, he indicates not obscurely [Col. 0293C] the means by which it was sent. Ursacius and Valens, then, since they controlled affairs, employed the services of the *magistriani*, or public courier, intending both that it might be carried as swiftly as possible and that it might bear the emperor’s name and command, so that it would be received more readily. Gothofredus observes that the *magistriani* were selected for conveying the important commands of rulers; and from Theodoret we learn that Constantius was not unaccustomed to use them in disturbing ecclesiastical affairs. [Note: [Col. 0293D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 3.]

This is what Hilary himself explains more explicitly elsewhere, in these words:

> Previously, in obscurity and corners, the Lord Christ was denied to be Son of God according to nature; and it was proclaimed that, lacking the Father’s essence, he had received existence from non-existent things together with the other creatures. But now heresy, breaking forth **under a profession of public authority**, gloried openly and victoriously in what it had formerly muttered secretly.

Then, charging Ursacius and Valens as though they were authors of this impiety, he says that they deceived the ignorant emperor, so that, while occupied with wars, he might set forth the creed of such perfidy and, though not yet regenerated, might set forth a rule of belief to the Churches. From this you infer that everything was then carried out under the emperor’s name alone. They had used the same fraud, which turned out badly for them, at the robber synod assembled at Milan [Col. 0294A] in 355. For, not daring because of fear of the people to put forward their own crimes, they sent a letter under the emperor’s name, full of every perversity, intending that, if the people received it favourably, they might introduce what they desired under **public authority**; but if it were otherwise received, all the odium would fall upon the emperor, and even that would be pardonable, since, being still a catechumen, he could reasonably be thought not to have known the sacrament of faith. [Note: [Col. 0293D] Severus, *History*, book II, §460.] From this passage of Severus you also understand what Hilary means by “a profession of public authority.”

There is yet another reason why this formula ought to seem to have been sent not in the name of a synod or bishops, but in the emperor’s name alone. For, if Hosius be excepted, the other four whom Hilary declares to have been its authors were outside the communion of the Church; the Gallic bishops had determined this at least [Col. 0294B] concerning Ursacius and Valens. [Note: [Col. 0293D] Hilary, *On the Synods*, §2, and *Against Constantius*, §2.] Therefore, since all exchange of letters with orthodox bishops was forbidden to them by the canons, there was no reason for those Arians to write in the customary manner on matters pertaining to the faith. This one course remained, and they used it: they arranged for the formula to be sent by Constantius and promulgated through magistrates. We read that Constantius did this on one occasion. For when the question concerned Athanasius, he wrote to the magistrates and threatened a fine unless someone compelled the bishop of his own city to subscribe against him. [Note: [Col. 0294D] Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 829.]

This being so, the view of those who call that Sirmian blasphemy synodal and say that it was composed in a synod seems paradoxical to me; especially since neither the number of bishops necessary for defining so great a matter was present, nor were synodal letters written or sent in the customary fashion, nor were those summoned who had a right to attend. Yet if you wish to call that chance and clandestine gathering of four or five bishops a synod, and the formula issued by it synodal, I would not at all object—provided this be understood in the sense in which the Council of Sardica wrote that the Arians, while coming to Sardica, held synods among themselves in various places and made agreements with threats, so that on arriving at Sardica they might not come to judgment or assemble together with the holy synod—using that word to express their private and clandestine gatherings. [Note: [Col. 0294D] From Hilary’s translation, fragment 7; in Greek in Athanasius: “And, while coming to Sardica, they held synods among themselves in the various places.”]

But, to return to my subject, although these matters are by no means wholly irrelevant to it: as soon as this formula was reported and communicated to the Gallic bishops, it was openly rejected and openly condemned. Whether this occurred in an assembled synod, as Sirmond thinks, or by letters circulating among the bishops, as might also have happened, is of no importance to inquire. Now observe, to bring the discussion back to its point: if you assert that it was written in 357, and see that it was promulgated and supported by Constantius’s authority, why in the meantime did he do nothing against the resisting [Col. 0295A] bishops? Hilary certainly reproaches Ursacius and Valens with having compelled opposing bishops into exile after its promulgation. “For,” he says, “they forced us to the resolve to go into exile, while imposing upon us the necessity of impiety.” [Note: [Col. 0295D] *On the Synods*, chapter 78.]

But those men, prepared for every audacity and cruelty, lacked not purpose or spirit but time. For meanwhile the Synod of Ancyra was completed at the beginning of April, and it struck down the Sirmian blasphemy lurking beneath the Eudoxian heresy. The delegates sent by it to Constantius—Basil of Ancyra, Eleusius, and Eustathius—could conveniently have reached Sirmium at the beginning of May, and they turned the emperor away from his former judgment. Ursacius himself, Valens, and Germinius were compelled to obey Constantius, to abjure the Sirmian [Col. 0295B] formula, and to profess the Ancyrene exposition then promulgated. Thus all their means of doing harm were suddenly cut off, contrary to every expectation. Hilary, Socrates, and Sozomen relate the event, and may be consulted. Do you not see that all is open and plain, and that Hilary’s statement—that the Gallic and Ancyrene bishops condemned that impiety at almost one and the same time—is completely true?

But let us proceed to shed light on the matter under discussion. It may therefore be asked whether this formula was sent and promulgated in the East as it was in Gaul. Some think so; for my part, I would not readily grant that Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, and Potamius, its authors, being Westerners and lacking the consent of all the other [Col. 0295C] Churches, proposed their private creed to Easterners as one also common to them, and promulgated it to be received by all as an established and settled dogma. The following, in my judgment, further confirm this view.

First, George of Laodicea, in the letters read at the Synod of Ancyra, identifies only Aetius and Eudoxius as authors of the heresy then arising. Secondly, Basil of Ancyra, in the encyclical written from the synod which he held, touches upon them only in passing; but then he writes that he had learned from reports of the Illyrians—[Note: [Col. 0295D] “Those from the regions in Illyricum report …”]—that the destruction was spreading and propagating more widely, like leaven. The Easterners, then, had not seen it, nor had it been customarily circulated in those regions. Thirdly, I do not deny that it became known to Eudoxius, [Col. 0295D] who had recently insinuated himself into the see of Antioch; but I maintain that it was communicated to Eudoxius alone, and only in familiar letters from Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius, since they were well aware of the disposition of that thoroughly wicked man and that they had a common cause with him. Hence he alone thanked Ursacius himself, Valens, and Germinius because, through their ministry, the Westerners had begun to think rightly; in those words expressing that Hosius had been compelled to profess that blasphemy. [Note: [Col. 0295D] Sozomen, book IV, chapter 12.] And those to whom he writes back, as you see, are only three.

Fourthly, when Constantius was informed of the heresy through the delegates who had come from Ancyra, he first condemned to exile the innovators—namely Aetius, Eudoxius, and their associates—and then, in written letters, warned the Antiochenes not to abandon the faith promulgated at the Encaenia, but to abhor the Eudoxian heresy as impious, novel, and only lately emerging from the abyss of error. [Note: [Col. 0295D] Sozomen, book IV, chapter 13.] Could he have been so shameless [Col. 0296B] as to do and write these things if that formula had previously been approved by him, and had been promulgated throughout the East by his order and by circular letters of bishops for acceptance? But, you will say, it could have been circulated privately in familiar letters. What then would you infer from this? Did Demophilus therefore certainly see it? Could he have set before Liberius a creed which he had received only by rumour and uncertain report, furtively put abroad, and which he had not examined sufficiently? On the contrary, the Ancyrene definitions, which expressly confirmed the Antiochene and Sirmian exposition, were immediately promulgated by customary circular letters; Constantius moreover ordered that these alone should then prevail. [Note: [Col. 0295D] Sozomen, book IV, chapter 14.] Demophilus, therefore, could scarcely have set forth to Liberius any creed other than that which then prevailed.

[Col. 0296C] This being so, there is no need for me to linger longer in refuting Dupin and the anonymous writer who, in recent years, presented Dupin to us again in a French translation under the title *Treatise on Ecclesiastical and Temporal Power*. [Note: [Col. 0295D] *Traité de la puissance ecclésiastique et temporelle*, 1727, p. 713.] He first confidently places Demophilus among the Anomoeans; then dreams up two formulas signed by Liberius: the first at Beroea, wholly Arian and conformed to the opinion of the Anomoeans; the second at Sirmium, supposedly with the purpose and intention of clearing himself of that former subscription at Beroea and dispelling among Basil of Ancyra and the other Semi-Arians—who had been sent as delegates to Constantius at Sirmium—the report that he had professed the Son unlike the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] “This is not the place to examine what was the formula of faith to which he subscribed; it is sufficient for us that the ancients assured us that the formula of faith to which he subscribed was heretical and that he approved Arianism. . . . Besides, the formula which he had subscribed in his exile had been presented to him by Demophilus, an Arian; and it was so strongly Arian [Col. 0296D] that, on the occasion of this subscription, the Arians openly said that Liberius had acknowledged by his subscription that the Son was unlike his Father. This obliged the Semi-Arians, when Liberius had returned to Sirmium, to induce him to sign a profession of faith in which he acknowledged the Son to be like his Father. For Liberius signed twice: first, in his exile, a wholly Arian formula of faith which Demophilus presented to him; and afterwards he wrote to the Easterners. . . . Subsequently, having been recalled to Sirmium, the deputies of the Council of Ancyra . . . obliged him to sign a collection of formulas of faith and to acknowledge that the Son was like his Father. Thus Sozomen relates this history, and his account accords [Col. 0297D] with the ancient monuments in the Fragments of St Hilary. . . .” These passages are copied from Dissertation 5, §3.]

[Col. 0296D] For the matters which I have thus far stated and argued, and those which remain to be stated again, [Col. 0297A] plainly demonstrate that Dupin rashly invents events which never occurred and supports them with false testimonies, in order, as is his custom, to deceive the reader.

## § VI.—The sequence of Liberius’s whole course of action is set forth, and his letters to the Easterners and to Ursacius and Valens are explained. The account of the events then enacted is confirmed by the authority of Sozomen, and by the testimony—previously unnoticed—of Acacius and other Arians assembled at Constantinople.

What I have thus far said and argued both shows what creed Liberius accepted and now readily offers to view the whole sequence of events. Basil, then, after the Synod of Ancyra had been completed, perhaps during the Paschal days, set out for the emperor, who was staying at Sirmium; and, as I have said, he could easily have arrived there at the beginning of May. From Hilary and Sozomen we know that [Col. 0297B] he accomplished his affairs with equal speed and success. For the Sirmian blasphemy was revoked, and the Antiochene faith of the Encaenia was again confirmed. Moreover, Ursacius and Valens, authors of that same blasphemy, professed ignorance and retracted what they had done; they were compelled to subscribe to the Antiochene and Ancyrene exposition. Eudoxius, Aetius, and the other manifest followers of that impiety were made exiles. Finally, the Basilian party, now victorious, travelled through all regions to confirm *homoiousion*, or the Ancyrene faith, which is the same as the Sirmian faith. [Note: [Col. 0297D] Philostorgius, book IV, chapter 9.]

I have no doubt, therefore, that they immediately arranged for letters to be spread in all directions, so that all bishops throughout the East—and especially those who professed the Sirmian faith—might be informed of the matter. Demophilus rightly must be counted among them, because he was not far away, had attended the drafting of that Sirmian creed, and, as we have seen, openly professed it with the Semi-Arians. When he had related and explained all this to Liberius in person, he obtained from him—broken by exile and desirous of seeing the City again—that he should write to the Easterners who were at court and held influence in affairs with the emperor: Basil, that is, as Nicephorus explains, and his associates. [Note: [Col. 0297D] Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 37.]

Nor does it seem to overthrow my opinion that this pontiff wrote also to Ursacius and Valens, authors and defenders of that Sirmian blasphemy. For, after they had then retracted it and been compelled to profess the same faith as Basil and the other Semi-Arians, there was no evident reason why the same pontiff, who had written to the Easterners, should refuse communion also with those Westerners [Col. 0297D] whose influence with Constantius was great and whose faith was then the same as that of the others. From this too you understand why, in the letters written to the Easterners, Liberius says that he accepts the faith set before him by Demophilus, while in the others written to Ursacius himself, Valens, and Germinius he says not a word about the matter. Who does not see from this that, when Liberius wrote these letters, all of them had one faith, and that both letters were consequently sent after Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius had subscribed to the definitions of the Synod of Ancyra, when no outward disagreement of belief seemed to exist between them and the Easterners?

We must now see what Liberius did after he came to Sirmium. Athanasius and Hilary, as I have said, certainly state nothing that gives us clear knowledge [Col. 0298B] of the affair. Socrates says absolutely nothing about this pontiff’s lapse, since Rufinus, whom he generally follows, writes that he had discovered nothing certain on the matter. [Note: [Col. 0297D] Book I, chapter 27.] Sozomen alone remains, who transmitted the memory of the event to posterity and described it so precisely that anyone who refuses to follow his authority in this matter must have cast off every sense of shame. We should therefore hear him.

Not long afterwards, when the emperor had returned from Rome to Sirmium and the Western bishops had sent an embassy to him, he summoned Liberius from Beroea to himself. When delegates of the Eastern bishops were present, he assembled the clergy who were at court and began to urge Liberius to profess that the Son was not consubstantial with the Father. Basil, Eustathius, and Eleusius, who enjoyed the chief influence with the emperor, pressed him and drove the emperor [Col. 0298C] to this. Having gathered into one document the decrees issued at Sirmium against Paul of Samosata and against Bishop Photinus, together with the formula of faith published at the dedication of the Antiochene basilica, and alleging that some persons were attempting, under cover of the term “consubstantial,” to establish their own heresy, they secured the agreement of Liberius and of Athanasius, Alexander, Severianus, and Crescens, bishops of Africa, with that formula. Ursacius and Germinius, bishop of Sirmium, Valens of Mursa, and all bishops present from the Eastern regions likewise agreed. They also received in return from Liberius a confession in which he declared those who asserted that the Son was not like the Father in substance and in all respects to be outside the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] This passage of Sozomen was nevertheless wickedly falsified by that petty Greek writer whose rhapsodic compilation survives in various libraries under the falsely assumed name of Patriarch Photius and under this title: *Collections and Demonstrations Carefully Gathered from Synodal and Historical Writings Concerning Bishops, Metropolitans, and Other Necessary Ecclesiastical Questions.*

[Col. 0298D] **Question.** In what matters do the Romans appear to have acted irrationally?

**Answer.** Under Constantius, Liberius of Rome, after his return from exile, gave written assent to the creed promulgated at Antioch. In part, Basil of Ancyra, Eustathius of Sebasteia, and Eleusius also received from him a confession rejecting those who did **not** say that the Son was, in every respect, **unlike** (*anomoion*) the Father; nor did they withdraw from communion with them.]

. . . When these matters had been accomplished [Col. 0298D] through the advocates of the Westerners, the emperor granted him permission to return to Rome. The bishops who had assembled at Sirmium also wrote to Felix, who [Col. 0299A] was then presiding over the Roman Church, and to the clergy of that city, directing them to receive Liberius and for both to govern the Apostolic See and exercise the priesthood together without any dissension. [Note: [Col. 0299D] Book IV, chapter 15.]

Such is Sozomen’s account. But the persons whom Valesius, whose translation I use, identifies as “delegates of the Westerners,” I think did not exist. For the Greek verb *presbeuō* expresses both those who are sent as ambassadors and, at times, those who come as petitioners on another’s behalf. Langus, translator of Nicephorus, and Fronto Ducaeus understood the term in at least this sense. [Note: [Col. 0299D] Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 37.] I understand Fortunatianus of Aquileia, whom Liberius had sent with letters to the emperor, to be indicated here, as well as Ursacius and Valens themselves, whom he had bound to his interest, and the others then at court. For the short delay would not have allowed those whom the same pontiff wished to be sent from Campania through Vincentius of Capua to have been present then.

You see, then, that Liberius was recalled from exile through Basil’s agency after he had written that he accepted the Sirmian faith; and afterwards, having actually subscribed to that same creed with certain African bishops, he was granted permission to go to Rome and recover his see. Since, according to Anastasius, he entered the City on the third day before the Nones of August [3 August], he must have reached Sirmium in June and, once the business there had been completed by the close of that month, have set out on his Roman journey. If you understand it thus, all things cohere rightly. For the clandestine formula of Ursacius and Valens was revoked at Basil’s insistence, [Col. 0299C] and the Sirmian exposition against Photinus was again promulgated before May was far advanced. Liberius, not far away, accepted the faith set before him by Demophilus and notified Basil of Ancyra and the other Easterners at court in the letters I have mentioned. He was therefore summoned from exile to the emperor, and, after declaring in writing the creed which he had said he accepted, he returned to his see. No one can deny that all these things could conveniently have occurred within three months.

Moreover, Sozomen is not the sole witness to this matter; it is confirmed by the not obscure testimony of Acacius of Caesarea. He had been one of the dregs of the Arian party who had determined that *ousia* should be rejected from the faith, and had been deposed at the Synod of Seleucia by the Semi-Arians, defenders of *ousia*. [Col. 0299D] But soon the Acacians became stronger and, to retaliate in the robber gathering at Constantinople, expelled the leaders of the Semi-Arians from their sees. Seeking to appear justified in doing so, when speaking of Basil of Ancyra they alleged, among other charges, that he had been the cause of discord and disturbance among the Illyrians, Italians, and Africans, and the author of the things which had happened to the Church of Rome. [Note: [Col. 0299D] Sozomen, book IV, chapter 24: “And he became the cause of discord and faction among the Illyrians, Italians, and Africans [Col. 0300D] and of the events concerning the Church of the Romans.”]

Why Basil is said to have been the cause of discord and disturbance among Illyrians, Italians, and Africans I shall not investigate, [Col. 0300A] although I am inclined to believe that these words express his effort to secure the acceptance in those regions of the Ancyrene definitions and the condemnation of the Anomoeans. I ask rather, since this concerns our subject, what were the recent events which had happened to the Church of Rome and which Acacius charged against Basil as their principal author. Most pass over the matter, as though it lay in obscurity, without touching it. Tillemont, however, whose diligence overlooks nothing, suspects that Felix’s intrusion is indicated here and that Acacius transfers blame for it to Basil. [Note: [Col. 0300D] *On the Arians*, vol. VI, article 58.] But why could Acacius reproach Basil with Felix’s ordination, when Acacius himself, if we believe Jerome, had been its chief author and promoter at Milan, controlling Constantius along with the other Arians? [Note: [Col. 0300D] For he subscribed with the others at the robber council held then. See Baronius, year 355, no. 22.]

I am surprised, indeed, that no one has mentioned the one true explanation which presents itself of its own accord, or plainly explained the force of those words. For we understand them to refer quite plainly to the riots—and perhaps also the murders—which Socrates, Sozomen, and the petitions of Marcellinus and Faustinus report as having arisen and been perpetrated at Rome when Felix, whom Acacius had elevated, was expelled from the see upon Liberius’s return. Basil was charged with blame for them because he alone had been the principal cause of recalling that pontiff. But if Liberius was summoned from Beroea through this Basil’s agency, if he subscribed to the faith proposed by Basil, and if after these things were done he was restored to his see, I think that henceforth no one will bring against this pontiff the accusation of the Sirmian blasphemy—unless he first persuades himself that Basil defended it and, moreover, that Constantius, who presided over the transaction, who ordered the Antiochene formula to be retained, who punished Eudoxius and Aetius, its leaders in the East, for that same blasphemy, and who compelled Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius to abjure it, permitted the Roman pontiff to confirm it at the same time. I therefore cannot sufficiently wonder at the rash judgment of those who, so far removed from the age of the events, can charge Liberius—what none of the ancient writers dared to do—with having subscribed to the second Sirmian formula.

## § VII.—A question first proposed by Tillemont is examined: namely, whether Liberius not only kept silence concerning *homoousion* but also condemned it. The grounds on which that most learned writer shows himself undecided are presented. Sozomen is adduced and clarified in favour of the truer opinion: whether it should be regarded as certain that the Synod of Antioch, held against Paul of Samosata, condemned *homoousion*. Hilary and Victorinus, incorrectly understood by Tillemont, are cited and explained.

[Col. 0300D]

No one had raised this doubt before Tillemont, who first proposed it when treating of the Arians and, having considered it on both sides, finally leaves it unresolved, as he says in his singular modesty, for a more learned man. [Col. 0301A] [Note: [Col. 0301D] Tillemont, *On the Arians*, §74 and note 57.]

The reason for his doubt is found in these few words of Sozomen already quoted: “Constantius, having assembled the clergy at court, began to urge Liberius to profess that the Son was **not** consubstantial with the Father.” Tillemont interprets this to mean that Liberius was compelled by Constantius not merely to abandon the profession of *homoousion*, but openly to condemn it. There was, he supposes, a reason why the emperor wished this. For if Basil and the other Semi-Arians at the Ancyrene assembly had pronounced anathema upon this term, and if they then possessed and directed Constantius’s mind, it could readily have happened that, availing themselves of favourable circumstances and of the emperor’s authority, they drew the pontiff into this judgment.

[Col. 0301B] One fact, however, leaves Tillemont uncertain on this point: Basil and the other delegates of the Synod of Ancyra had determined that that anathema ought to be kept secret, and had deleted this decree from the definitions promulgated at Sirmium. He then offers reasons, or conjectures, why he thinks that, seizing an opportunity, they departed from their original intention and gave free rein to that anathema. First, because Hilary writes that Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius requested Basil himself that the letter concerning the exposition of *homoousion* and *homoiousion* should be read. The learned man thinks that this is the very letter written by the Synod of Ancyra and quoted by Epiphanius, [Note: [Col. 0301D] *Heresy* 73.] which, while affirming *homoiousion*, proscribed *homoousion* with an anathema. Secondly, because Victorinus [Col. 0301C] teaches us that letters were written by the Easterners to the Africans, so that, with all the Easterners and those Africans themselves who had so determined, they might expel *homoousion* from the Church; and he laments that these letters contained not arguments drawn from Holy Scripture, but commands and threats. For if all, as we have seen, subscribed with Liberius to one and the same formula, the judgment concerning them all must surely be the same; and if African bishops and Easterners are said to have proscribed *homoousion* from the Church at that time, no reason can be given why Liberius should be excepted from that charge.

These, then, are the reasons why that most exact writer appears to have left the matter uncertain. Yet, in order that it may be placed in clear light, I must first investigate what Sozomen meant by the words just quoted [Col. 0301D] and then weigh the force of the conjectures adduced. As to the first point—Sozomen’s meaning—I do not deny that Constantius and those Semi-Arian bishops urged Liberius not to profess **that the Son was not consubstantial with the Father** (*mē einai ton Huion tō Patri homoousion*). But the question is what force these words carry: whether they imply an open execration of *homoousion* or merely silence concerning it. Having rightly weighed the entire sequence of events narrated by Sozomen, I judge the latter to be entirely true [Col. 0302A] and evident.

For it is established that Basil of Ancyra proposed for subscription the decrees issued at Sirmium against Paul of Samosata and against Bishop Photinus, along with the formula of faith published at the dedication of the Church of Antioch, joined together in one document—and nothing else. What follows from this is not obscure. For since the Sirmian creed with its attached anathemas, the Philippopolitan creed, and that Antiochene creed—which is, so to speak, the source and origin of all the others—affirm only *homoiousion*, while, although they suppress *homoousion*, they do not condemn it, [Note: [Col. 0301D] See Petavius on Epiphanius, *Heresy* 73, p. 320.] Basil neither intended that Liberius should condemn that term nor can Liberius be thought to have condemned it; he merely involved it in bare silence. This alone was the force of the formula offered to and confirmed by him.

[Col. 0302B] Yet I see one point that might perhaps be objected from Sozomen himself against this view. Eudoxius, seeking supporters for the heresy then breaking out, had spread abroad the report that Liberius and the Westerners had both rejected the *homoousion* and, moreover, confessed the Son to be unlike the Father. You see, then, that the calumny has two heads. But what did Liberius do? He declared alien from the Church those who asserted that the Son is not like the Father in substance and in all respects. [Note: [Col. 0301D] Sozomen, book IV, ch. 15: “They also brought back, in part, a confession from Liberius, rejecting those who declare that the Son is not like the Father in substance and in all things.”]

Since, therefore, you see that the pontiff cleared himself by a profession of the *homoiousion* alone, he thereby lays himself open to the other branch of the calumny. But there is no necessity at all for us to say this. For Eudoxius, who rightly understood that the same faith was expressed and maintained by both terms, had proscribed the *homoousion* no less than the *homoiousion*, and had falsely implicated Liberius in that charge. Thus the sole matter then at issue was that the pontiff should assert the Catholic faith against Eudoxius’ artifices and overthrow the calumny circulated against himself. Since this was fully achieved by an explicit profession of the *homoiousion*, there was no need, either among the Eudoxians or even among the Catholics themselves—among whom at that time the two terms had one and the same force—for him to add anything concerning the *homoousion* or to declare his own opinion at that time. Moreover, when you see Liberius subscribing to the formula offered by the Semi-Arians and declaring only the Anomoeans alien from the Church, you also plainly understand that he held the Homoousians and Homoiousians in equal esteem and standing; and you may also infer without obscurity what his opinion besides was concerning that term when he was dealing with these matters. [Col. 0302C–D]

But, to return to the formula to which we have seen Liberius subscribe, scholars ask whether it was then composed afresh and produced whole, or whether the Antiochene formula of the Dedication and the Sirmian formula, already extant, were simply copied again, bound together in a single writing and a single booklet, and offered to this Pontiff. But, in order to clarify the matter, it should be observed that the Semi-Arians continually wished the Antiochene creed of the Dedication to serve as the source and pattern of all the subsequent statements composed, and as a kind of badge of their party. Hence the Pseudo-Sardican exposition was first composed and fashioned from the formulas of this Antiochene creed, and was then enlarged by the anathemas promulgated against Paul of Samosata and Photinus. [Note: [Col. 0303D] See Athanasius, *On the Councils*, p. 895, in the Benedictine edition; Hilary, *Against Constantius*, no. 23; P. Coustant, note f to Hilary’s *On the Councils*, p. 482, Verona edition.] The Sirmian formula mentioned here by Sozomen retains that Pseudo-Sardican formula and expresses it almost word for word.

If, therefore, the Sirmian creed contains the Pseudo-Sardican, if the latter contains the Antiochene, and if the former further repeats the anathemas promulgated against Samosata and Photinus, there is no need to say, according to Sozomen’s meaning, that the formula offered to Liberius by Basil was newly composed and then produced. For this one Sirmian creed contains and embraces in itself [Col. 0303A] all the items that he specifies. They therefore do violence to this writer who imagine that, by “the Antiochene creed,” he also means the formula formerly promulgated in that city against the heresy of Paul of Samosata, and who suppose that it was joined to the Antiochene creed of the Dedication and to the Sirmian formula, as something especially suitable and adapted to overthrowing the *homoousion*, which was the chief endeavor of the Semi-Arians. In fact, Sozomen names only one Antiochene creed: namely, that promulgated at the Dedication. What place, then, remains for that old Antiochene formula? And if he says that Liberius was also offered the decrees issued at Sirmium against Paul of Samosata and Bishop Photinus, since both the Antiochene formula of the Dedication and the Sirmian *ecthesis* expressly condemn those heretics by name, what need, I ask, could there have been to bring out once again the definition—if there ever was one—of that old Antiochene synod against the same Samosata? [Col. 0303B–C]

Nor would I readily concede that the *homoousion* was condemned and rejected by the Antiochene synod against Samosata. This decree, indeed—for I do not deny it—is mentioned by Basil the Great and by Hilary. But learned men oppose to Basil the authority of Athanasius and offer other reasons why we rightly doubt the matter. First, because this alleged decree of the Antiochene synod conflicts with what had occurred shortly before that synod between the two Dionysii, Roman and Alexandrian. Second, because it was utterly unknown to everyone, not even the Arians excepted, until the year [Col. 0303D] 358. A fitting witness to this is Eusebius, a man of almost boundless reading: when he presented all the arguments proposed against the *homoousion* at the Council of Nicaea, he does not even mention this one. [Note: [Col. 0303D] See his letter to Caesarea in Athanasius, *On the Councils*, vol.
