I, p. 240.] Third and finally, because it rests upon no other testimony than that of Arians then living, whose trustworthiness, as everyone knows, was highly suspect. [Note: [Col. 0304D] See the note on Basil, Epistle 52, Benedictine edition.]

As regards Hilary, he showed no concern for investigating the historical truth of this matter, but either simply believed the Semi-Arians or, as seems more likely, wished to appear to believe them. Two considerations prevent this from seeming too confident an assertion. First, he attributes that much-vaunted decree to the Samosatene synod, not the Antiochene; second, because the case he was arguing was established by other unanswerable arguments, he thought it irrelevant to inquire whether that claim was true or false. [Note: [Col. 0304D] See *On the Councils*, nos. 81 and 88.]

Moreover, if the letter inscribed with the name of Dionysius of Alexandria to Paul of Samosata is genuine and authentic, and if the exposition of faith read in the Council of Ephesus under the name of the Nicene Fathers belongs to the ancient Antiochene synod, it is certainly false that the *homoousion* was rejected by that synod, since in both places it is explicitly affirmed. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Councils, vol. I, p. 875, and vol. III, p. 1502, Venice edition.] For my part, I do not see why the judgment of those who regard these as true and authentic monuments of that Antiochene synod should not be preferred to the contrary view. The latter rests on only a few and very weak conjectures; the former agrees with the creed of the Church of Antioch and is confirmed by the testimony of authors not far removed from that age. But this is not the place to pursue those questions, which have moreover been preoccupied by the most learned Michael Angelo Jacomelli, intimate chaplain of Our Most Holy Lord, in his dissertation on the heresy of Paul of Samosata. Whoever consults it will be well rewarded.

I now come to the letter which, Hilary says, Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius demanded should be read by Basil of Ancyra. What it was, by whom it was written, and what else it contained is obscure. We learn only this from Hilary himself: that it dealt chiefly with the exposition of the *homoiousion* and the *homoousion*. “I have read,” he says, “the letter concerning the exposition of the *homoousion* and *homoiousion* at Sirmium, which Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius demanded from you; I understand that in certain respects it is no less cautious than free.” [Note: [Col. 0304D] *On the Councils*, no. 78.]

Tillemont conjectures that those Arians demanded it be read in order that the Semi-Arians, who in that same letter had proscribed the *homoousion* by an anathema and afterwards had kept this decree secret from all, might be compelled at last openly to publish it and condemn that term. But by what conjecture—let alone proof—does that learned man establish that the letter read marked the *homoousion* with an anathema? The Semi-Arians had done this in the encyclical of the Synod of Ancyra. [Col. 0304C–D] But anyone who reads Hilary and compares him with that synodical letter will easily perceive that one letter was written by the synod and another was read at that time. For in the letter of the Synod of Ancyra you will search in vain for the exposition of the *homoousion* and *homoiousion* which Hilary mentions. The reason why the letter read to Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius had to be different from the one written at Ancyra is also quite plain.

For the Ancyrene envoys had resolved among themselves that the anathema pronounced against the consubstantial should be kept secret. But Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius opposed the *homoiousion*, rightly judging that it differed in no respect from the *homoousion*: the entire matter is clear from Hilary. [Note: [Col. 0305D] *On the Councils*, ch. 79.] What, then, were those Semi-Arians to do, if they wished to draw the other Arians over to a profession of the *homoiousion*, while maintaining their policy of keeping secret from all the anathema pronounced against the *homoousion*? They had to write another letter, explaining at greater length the force of the *homoousion* and *homoiousion*, and setting forth the reasons why the latter seemed preferable to the former. This, then, was written and composed at that time; it is the letter Hilary indicates, though we now seek it in vain.

But whatever may be said about this letter read to those Arians—whether, as I think, it was different from the encyclical of the Synod of Ancyra, or whether an anathema was pronounced in it against the *homoousion*—it makes no difference as regards Liberius. For he was not present when it was read. Rather, after it had been read, after the Ancyrene definitions had already been approved and promulgated by Ursacius and Valens, he was summoned by the emperor to Sirmium through the agency of Basil, then master of affairs. Thus, as we have seen, every matter had already been concluded and arranged, and he came at a time when there was no need for that letter to be read. What I say is plainly inferred from Hilary himself, for while he writes that only those three bishops demanded its reading, he indicates that no one else was present when Basil read it. [Col. 0305A–B]

Finally, nothing is frailer or more obscure than the testimony of Victorinus, which Tillemont likewise endeavors to press into the service of his opinion. These are that writer’s words: “The Easterners write to the Africans that they should expel the HOMOUSION from the holy Church, saying that both the Africans and all the Easterners agree with them.” [Note: [Col. 0305D] Book I, *On the Faith against Arius*: “If it was necessary to write, it was necessary also to persuade them not merely by command but by arguments and Holy Scriptures.” Fathers, vol. IV, [Col. 0306D] p. 262.]

It is therefore uncertain at what time this was written by the Easterners to the Africans: whether before the Council of Rimini, or after that council and the confirmation at Constantinople of its formula. For several African bishops may seem to have rejected the *homoousion* twice: first, when Liberius professed the Sirmian *ecthesis*, as we have seen; and secondly, when the Arian formula was accepted by the delegates of the Council of Rimini. For it is established that three African bishops were numbered among those prevaricators. It is further uncertain whether the Easterners who wrote to the Africans were Arians or Semi-Arians, since it is established that both equally rejected at that time the word *homoousion*.

For my part, I judge that here “Africans” means those who had accepted the formula of Rimini, while “Easterners,” who wrote, denotes the Acacians. I think the letters mentioned by Victorinus were sent by them after they had induced even the Semi-Arians, by force and fraud alike, to profess the same formula of Rimini which the prevaricating delegates had accepted. Hilary supplies my reason for this judgment. Being then at Constantinople, he reproaches Constantius as follows: “You have subjected the Eastern bishops to your will—not only to your will, but to violence. You order the subscriptions of the Africans, by which they had condemned the blasphemy of Ursacius and Valens, to be surrendered to you; you threaten those who resist, and finally send men to plunder them.” [Note: [Col. 0306D] *Against Constantius*, no. 26.]

It is clear, therefore, that at this very period the Africans were especially solicited by the emperor through various devices to embrace the formula of Rimini and abandon the faith. It is vain to seek in accounts of the events of that time any evidence proving that Constantius could have imposed this violence on the African bishops before the formula of Rimini. Nor will anyone deny that the Acacians, who abused Constantius’ authority, at the same time sent letters to them in the common name, both informing them that the formula itself had been accepted by all and then urging them to join the rest. If we compare Victorinus’ testimony with Hilary, we readily understand that both point to those grievous times which followed the brigand synod of Constantinople, where that same formula was approved and promulgated. [Col. 0305D–0306B]

But grant that, in this passage of Victorinus, “Easterners” denotes Basil and his associates in the Ancyrene embassy, and that he then wrote letters to Africa seeking to draw the bishops of that Church to his own view by the example of those who, along with Liberius, had professed the *homoiousion*. What would you infer from this? Would you perhaps infer that, when Basil wrote that they should reject the *homoousion*, he also intended that it should be condemned by anathema? There is no need at all to say this, since to reject one thing is different from condemning it, and the one does not entail the other.

I should like to confirm a matter clear in itself by two examples, one from Hilary and the other drawn from the Arians’ own storehouse. Hilary praises the Gallican bishops because they had not merely refused to accept the impiety of an unbelieving creed sent from the town of Sirmium, but had condemned it once announced and communicated to them. [Note: [Col. 0306D] *On the Councils*, no. 2.] The Acacians, however, at the Synod of Seleucia simply reject the *homoousion* and *homoiousion* as words unknown to the Sacred Scriptures: “we cast them out” (*ekballomen*). But they explicitly condemn the *anomoion* by anathema: “we anathematize” (*anathematizomen*). [Col. 0306C]

You see, then, how weak and groundless are the arguments that appear to have made Tillemont hesitate in choosing his view. Yet I should like now to bring forward one further testimony from Hilary in Liberius’ favor. By letters from several bishops, Hilary had learned that at the Synod of Ancyra, which he had so strongly praised, an anathema had been pronounced against the Consubstantial, although those bishops afterwards sought to keep this decree hidden and secret. Having set forth all the reasons by which they could defend this rash act and vigorously refuted them, he then says:

“But perhaps someone will say to me: Some now living of those who were then present at the Synod [of Nicaea] decreed that silence should be kept concerning the *homoousion*. And I, though unwillingly, shall reply to him who says this: Do not they themselves, by keeping silence concerning the *homoiousion*, also establish that it should be silent? I beg you, let no one besides the aged Hosius be found among them who thinks that silence ought to be kept about both.” [Note: [Col. 0307D] *On the Councils*, no. 97.]

You see, therefore, that Hilary brings forward the example of Hosius alone for the Semi-Arians, although it was not sufficiently suited to support their position, because Hosius had removed the *homoousion* from the faith no less than the *homoiousion*. Why, then, does he not use the example of Liberius, so especially suitable for establishing the point in question? Did Hilary pass it over while concealing it? It is not even permissible to suspect this. Did he then not know of it? But who could bring himself to believe that the Semi-Arians could neglect the greater authority of that Pontiff, or that they wished Hilary himself and everyone else to remain silent about a fact whose widest publication was especially in their interest?

But perhaps Hilary was ignorant of it—which surely exceeds belief. Or did Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius not know it, though they had been present at the events involving Liberius? Why, when at the Council of Rimini they wished the term *ousia* to be abolished and the third Sirmian formula confirmed, and for that reason asked the Fathers, if we believe Rufinus, whether they proposed to retain with the utmost constancy the *homoousion* or the worship due to Christ the Lord, did they not say even a word about Liberius? [Note: [Col. 0307D] Book I, ch. 26.] Or was the authority and example of the bishop of the Eternal City of no value to them, though before his exile and the Council of Milan they had valued it so highly that they thought the minds of all the rest depended upon him alone? [Col. 0307A–B]

## § VIII.—It is shown that Hilary’s execrations, commonly alleged against Liberius from a famous passage of the Fragments, ought to carry no weight, since they were taken from writings rejected by him; and that those who use them do not act in good faith.

[Col. 0307C]

Since, therefore, we have established the Sirmian creed and formula which Liberius professed as an example of human frailty, the discussion ought to turn to the consequences flowing from this. But I judged that they should be omitted by me, both because I set before myself only this task—to disentangle, as far as I could, the truth of the events from the coverings by which it seemed to be obscured—and because others before me have diligently devoted their labor to treating that matter.

It remains, therefore, for us to see why Hilary, in the *Fragments*, regarded as a form of Arian perfidy the formula which he had approved as Catholic in his book *On the Councils*. For when several bishops of First and Second Germany asked him what the Easterners had done or were doing in their professions of faith, and requested him to write back what he himself thought concerning all their statements, he first praised and approved the Antiochene *ecthesis* of the Dedication and the Philippopolitan formula, which he calls Sardican on the testimony of the Easterners. Then, when he deals with the Sirmian formula against Photinus, after first citing its anathema—[Note: [Col. 0307D] “But those who say that the Son is from things not existing, or from another substance and not from God; and that there was a time or age when he was not—the holy and catholic Church knows them to be alien.”]—he says:

“What room is there here for ambiguity, or what remains wanting to a consciousness of sincere faith? There is no other substance existing as the source of his origin than that of God alone; so that nothing other can be born in him than all that belongs to God, because what does not exist from nothing cannot subsist as existing from elsewhere.” [Note: [Col. 0308D] *On the Councils*, no. 39.]

Here, therefore, you see Hilary’s open and manifest judgment. It is vain to say that he did not approve that formula as complete and perfect, but only intended to entice those who used it toward the Catholic faith. For those to whom he writes thus were Western bishops and perfectly Catholic; and, when he writes these things to them, to suspect any dissimulation in a most upright man on a matter of the highest importance is sacrilege.

Shall we then rather call him inconsistent in his opinion? The great Baronius thinks that the words we read against Liberius in these same *Fragments* had been written in the margin and were afterwards transferred into the text. Natalis Alexander both accepts Baronius’ view and adds another reason: namely, that the Sirmian *ecthesis*, though Catholic in its wording, was nevertheless rightly called perfidy by Hilary when its authors and their designs were considered. Tillemont also approved this. But I do not see why, if its authors are considered, that creed should seem perfidy in Liberius, yet sincere and Catholic when it is sent to the Gallican bishops; or why Hilary could regard the Pontiff’s subscription to it as making him a heretic, while it could not injure the faith and religion of those to whom it was sent. [Col. 0308A–B]

Peter Coustant therefore maintains that Hilary never sincerely approved that Sirmian exposition, since he consistently held whatever was outside the one Nicene faith to be perfidy rather than faith. On this ground he both clears Hilary himself of inconsistency and thinks that Hilary could not without reason pronounce an anathema against Liberius. [Note: [Col. 0308D] See the notes on Epistle XI and on Fragment 6, no. 5.] Yet, in the very book from which that learned man has drawn these words for his argument, Hilary again praises the Antiochene, Philippopolitan, and Sirmian creeds. [Note: [Col. 0308D] See *Against Constantius*, nos. 23, 24, 25.] For he says:

“You also condemn the term ‘substance,’ by which you falsely claimed before the Westerners to be pious in relation to both the Sardican and Sirmian synods; yet that term, received on prophetic authority, contained an understanding of the faith.”

If Hilary seems elsewhere in that same place not to approve those creeds entirely, he indicates that he does so because nothing was needed after the Nicene faith. For although he acknowledges no defect in them, a reason for what he calls a “religious will” was lacking: “the alteration of good things is the planning of evil, and a correction that is not necessary is an occasion of perversity.” But that Hilary could, solely for this reason, rightly call Liberius an apostate and a prevaricator and curse him with terrible imprecations, I think no one will readily grant. [Col. 0308C–D]

For my part, to state openly what I think, I do not see why such account should be taken—if I may say so without offense—of Hilary’s authority in this passage in which he expresses himself. No one, certainly, will deny that by transmitting those *Fragments* to posterity he preserved a great treasure of the Church, and that therefore great gratitude is due to him. But since no order either of time or of events has been preserved in arranging them, since matters that ought to stand first occupy the last place and those that should be last a prior one, they are regarded by learned men as a heap thrown together by chance rather than a properly ordered work. Who, then, can assure us whether the book *On the Councils* is earlier than the fragment in which Liberius’ lapse is discussed, or later, so that we may judge whether, when writing that book, he had departed—or had not departed—from his hasty judgment against Liberius after learning the facts better and more carefully? [Col. 0309A]

Furthermore, as I have already warned, that work presents a confused aggregation of materials and a monstrous appearance. Nicolaus Faber, who first published it, does not deny this; and the entire preface of the learned Peter Coustant is occupied with refining it and concealing it beneath, as it were, a coating of paint. Finally, much in it appears to have been hastily drafted and to require a final hand and critical judgment. These considerations readily lead me to believe that Hilary kept the fragments we now possess among his rejected papers and disapproved them. This, moreover, is the sole reason why we now read those imprecations: he would undoubtedly have erased them and written something wholly different, had he thought that they would someday circulate and become public. For I see no other way otherwise to defend him, since he left these unworthy words written about a Pontiff who both before the lapse and afterwards had asserted the faith with great courage, and who even in the lapse itself could not appear to have abandoned it. [Col. 0309B–C]

But what of Jerome, whose testimonies against Liberius are also commonly brought forward? The distinguished Fr. Thomas Mamachi, theologian of the Casanatense, informs us that in the Vatican manuscript of the Chronicon of Jerome belonging to the Queen of Sweden—a codex which Holstenius calls of remarkable antiquity and which learned men judge to have been written in the sixth or seventh century—there is not even a trace of Liberius’ lapse. From this he infers that the passages relating to the matter were added in later copies. [Note: [Col. 0309D] *On the Method of Chronology*, Athanasius, Epistle 4, §25.]

Another and contradictory passage of Jerome, from his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, further makes these statements suspect to me. For if Liberius, when going into exile for the faith, was broken by Fortunatianus and compelled to subscribe to heresy, [Note: [Col. 0309D] Ch. 97.] how could Jerome previously assert that he subscribed to heretical depravity not when already proceeding into exile, but after he had been overcome by the weariness of exile? From this at least one may rightly infer that Jerome himself wrote these things not from facts established by him, but rather from a false report long circulated. Since Rufinus judged that he could not safely follow so uncertain a rumor, he very wisely refrained from pronouncing a definite judgment. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Book I, ch. 27.] [Col. 0309D–0310A]

There would still be one passage commonly adduced against Liberius, from the writer of the preface to the petitions of Marcellinus and Faustinus: [Note: [Col. 0309D] “After two years he came to Rome; the people petitioned for Liberius. The emperor, soon consenting, said: ‘You have Liberius, who will return better than he left you.’ By this he indicated his consent, by which Liberius had given his hand to perfidy.”] But I pass it over, both because it is uncertain what that writer understood by the word *perfidia* and because his falsehood is otherwise manifest. For if Constantius came to Rome at the beginning of May; if he regarded Felix, whom he had intruded, as bishop; if, toward the end of that year 357, he addressed to Felix as bishop Law 14, Code 3 *On Bishops*; and if Liberius at that time had neither given his hand to perfidy nor even considered abandoning his constancy—how could that emperor have answered the people demanding back their bishop: “You have Liberius, who will return better”?

## § IX.—Liberius’ return to the City is described, together with the events that followed it. The anonymous annotator in defense of the propositions of the Gallican clergy is adduced and refuted. The Acts of Eusebius the presbyter and martyr are fictitious: under that name not Eusebius the presbyter, but Pope Eusebius, is concealed.

[Col. 0314B]

These are the matters concerning the deeds of Liberius in exile that I had to write, whether received from unquestionable ancient monuments or from probable conjectures. But I think that the events following his return to the City should not be separated from them, for they are, as it were, a part and appendage of the same exile. I do this all the more willingly because certain persons abuse them to prove that the Pontiff was not merely a heretic but even a most bitter persecutor of Catholics; such is their pleasure in disparaging Roman Pontiffs.

Liberius therefore returned to the City, according to Anastasius’ testimony, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August in the year 358, that is, in the third year after he had gone into exile, as the more common opinion of chronologists holds and as follows from the sequence of events we have narrated. Socrates and Sozomen, as we have seen, say that riots then arose in the City, but mention nothing in particular. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Socrates, book II, ch. 37; Sozomen, book IV, ch. 15.] Jerome’s *Chronicle* writes that Liberius entered Rome as a victor and that the clergy of the City who supported Felix, his substitute, were expelled along with Felix.

The author of the preface to the petitions of Marcellinus and Faustinus, however, gives some picture of what then occurred, writing:

“In the third year Liberius returned, and the Roman people went out joyfully to meet him. Felix, denounced by the senate or the people, was driven from the City; and shortly afterwards, at the instigation of the clergy who had perjured themselves, he burst into the City and presumed to establish a station in the Basilica of Julius across the Tiber. But the whole multitude of the faithful and the nobles of the City again expelled him with great disgrace.”

The sole reason why Liberius was received in the Romans’ embraces on his return and Felix expelled was the flock’s affection for its shepherd. Apart from Christian writers, there is striking evidence of this in Ammianus, which I have cited elsewhere. [Note: [Col. 0310D] See ch. 1.] This testimony is all the more weighty because the author of that same preface asserts that Liberius finally gave his hand to perfidy. From this, indeed, you understand that this malicious man had no other reason for censuring the Pontiff. [Col. 0310C–0311A]

But if you listen to Anastasius and certain others, the picture is entirely different. Liberius did not dare to enter the City when returning from exile, but lived in the monastery of Saint Agnes near Constantius’ sister, so that he might return to the city, as it were, through her intervention or at her request. When Constantius learned this, he took counsel with Ursacius, Valens, the Roman presbyters, and other Arians. Following their advice, he recalled Liberius from the cemetery of Saint Agnes; the emperor entered Rome together with the Pontiff, immediately consulted those Arians again, and expelled Felix—who was Catholic—from the episcopate. From that day persecution occurred in the clergy of the city of Rome, so that presbyters and clerics were killed within the church.

Among these, the *Acts* first published by Mombritius and afterwards issued more fully by Baluzius number Eusebius the presbyter. They state that, interrogated by Constantius and Liberius, he courageously confessed the faith and was finally, by order of both, confined in a small room and died for that same faith. [Col. 0311A–B]

But if you say that the emperor, occupied with war in Illyricum and with Arian disputations at Sirmium when Liberius entered the City and these things were occurring at Rome, could not have been present, hear how those who defend those *Acts* remove all your doubt. They say, then, that these accounts should not be understood as though Constantius were personally present at Rome; rather, you must take them to mean commands issued by him in his place and conveyed by imperial couriers. For unless you do so, the credibility both of Anastasius and of the *Acts*, which represent Liberius as openly professing heresy and moreover raging most fiercely against Catholics, will perish.

For it will avail nothing if you should then say that the *Acts* which Orosius—Eusebius’ kinsman, companion, and eyewitness—wrote are not those now found in Mombritius and Baluzius, but were interpolated and altered in later centuries before reaching us. For if anyone denies this—as he may do rightly and with good reason—by what argument or judgment will you prove the contrary? [Col. 0311C]

I am ashamed to linger any longer in refuting such trifles. Yet from this one may see how great is the power of prejudice: it presents what is plainly false as true; it esteems rancid fictions and introduces the gravest calumnies against holy and innocent men. Since there is utter silence about this persecution in every writer, both contemporaneous and near to that age, and since you see that this fabrication arose in later centuries, you will nevertheless be astonished that there could recently have been persons who, in order to establish what they wished, gathered together this filth, harassed approved authors so as to give it some value, and strove to wrench them unwillingly into their own view. They thought that they had discovered traces of this persecution in the passages cited from Sozomen and Jerome’s *Chronicle*.

Hear the anonymous annotator on the defense of the propositions of the Gallican clergy:

“As regards the persecution, besides the fact that open testimony to it is borne in the pontifical acts of Felix and Liberius, Sozomen too writes that Liberius’ adherents were so devoted to him that they caused a most grievous riot on his account and went so far as bloodshed. But Jerome most clearly of all recalls that the clergy were expelled along with Felix because Liberius, overcome by weariness of exile and subscribing to heretical depravity, entered Rome as a victor. In these words both are evidently joined together: the denial of faith, implied by subscription to heretical depravity, and victory—surely not without some force and conflict against the rivals who are said to have been expelled by that victory.

“And this is (O clever head!) the particular persecution in the city of Rome described by the Acts of Eusebius. … Our Acts wish that this local persecution, peculiar to the city of Rome, ceased either after Eusebius’ death or, as the sequence more strongly shows, after the synod assembled against Liberius by Damasus, then its author and later Pontiff; and it ceased, if not for a long time, at least until the end of the Council of Rimini. Nor is it surprising that Liberius, whom all resisted with such constancy, finally understood that he was pursuing a course that would bring his affairs into the greatest hatred and odium. Other causes also seem to have intervened shortly afterwards.

“For now, with the first and second Sirmian formulas omitted—one or the other of which Liberius had subscribed and had hitherto wished all others to subscribe—the third was being prepared in a new Synod of Sirmium. Because of the dispute concerning these matters, plans were being discussed for the greater councils to be held at Rimini in the West and Seleucia in the East; expectation of these kept all minds in suspense. Hence, during that interval, while Liberius was uncertain about future events, the Church could easily breathe again. But after the Council of Rimini, if we believe Socrates and Sozomen, the persecution was renewed, having scarcely been quiet for a full year. Thus our Acts agree with the other writers and do not exaggerate the truth when they describe either Liberius’ heresy or his persecution.” [Col. 0312A–C]

It is truly astonishing that this anonymous writer could have stitched together and published so many falsehoods with such confidence. For, to omit the rest, it is false, first, that the synod which he pretends put an end to the persecution was convened by Damasus, then a presbyter. So that the reader may judge for himself, I give the words of the Acts: “But after Liberius died, Damasus was raised up, who publicly condemned Liberius with twenty-eight bishops and twenty-five presbyters; and the persecution ceased, though not for a long time.” The defender of the Gallican propositions, who knew perfectly well that Liberius, as that man says, had long before come to his senses, interprets the Acts—which he invokes in support of his own view so as not to abandon them—as meaning that this synod was convened by Damasus, then a presbyter. [Note: Par. II, book XIV, ch. 34.] The annotator too employs this deception; but those who explain the quoted words in this manner plainly force their meaning.

Secondly, did Damasus, a presbyter, have either the right or the means to summon so many bishops to a synod? Thirdly, while the very severe persecution imagined by both writers was raging, was that additional advantage also readily available to him? Finally, fourthly, if Liberius had been condemned by Damasus the presbyter and deposed from his see by a synod, why did Damasus himself, once pope, reject the Council of Rimini principally because the judgment of the Roman bishop had not been sought? After Liberius had been condemned and deposed, was it lawful for him to exercise such a right as to direct the decrees of that council?

Yet from this passage of those Acts I seem to see whence the forger took material for weaving this fiction. He had seen the petition of Marcellinus and Faustinus and had read its preface. What we know occurred when Felix was expelled from the City and from the see, he thus understood as though it had been perpetrated against Catholics; and from schismatics adhering to Felix himself against Liberius he fabricated martyrs—being a man wholly unlearned in the character of that age. Hence he says that, after Damasus was elected, the persecution ceased for no long period, because he had seen that proceedings were often taken against the Ursinians and other schismatics, whom he likewise regarded as Catholics, under imperial laws and edicts.

Secondly, it is most false that the persecution aroused by Liberius when he returned had ceased for almost a whole year before the Council of Rimini; just as it is false that it was renewed by Liberius after the council itself. For if the Acts are to be believed, the presbyter Eusebius, after the seventh month from his confinement, received his repose on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September—that is, on 14 August. We therefore have the month and day on which Eusebius died. Now I ask you, anonymous annotator: in what year do you think he died—namely, in 358 or in the following year, 359? If you say the former, since Liberius entered the city of Rome in that year on 2 August, into what period will fall the long persecution which you imagine had previously occurred, your Eusebius’s confession, his seven-month confinement before death, and finally his martyrdom? But if you defer the matter to August of the following year, you will look in vain for that interval—almost a complete year—in which, because of expectation of the impending Council of Rimini, you say that the persecution long before aroused by Liberius had ceased. For if the Acts of Eusebius speak truth, you must confess that the anger of Liberius and of the emperor against the Catholics never cooled; rather, at the very time when bishops assembled in that city were deliberating, it flared up more fiercely, immediately after Eusebius’s death: the presbyter Gregory, who had committed him to burial, was delivered to death, and the rest of the clergy were openly butchered by the sword in streets, alleys, churches, and baths.

Thirdly, the causes for which you say that this persecution by Liberius was interrupted are falsely and foolishly invented by you. For, as I have said, either you must abandon the Acts of Eusebius the presbyter, or you must assign his death to August 359. Now you see what follows from this. For if the death of Eusebius himself and of the other presbyter Gregory was immediately followed by a graver and harsher persecution; if the third Sirmian formula had already been composed; if the Eastern bishops had long since assembled at Seleucia and the Western bishops at Rimini—then surely none of these things restrained Liberius from continuing to rage against Catholics. You are either deceived or wish to deceive us.

When, however, you assert that this pope had subscribed to the first or second Sirmian formula—or rather, that he had wished all men to subscribe to it—you act with your customary good faith and with the charity befitting a Christian: you alone and first bring into public view, as though manifest, a most serious charge that is not merely uninvestigated but certainly false. But I shall now dismiss the anonymous writer; for if I wished to pursue all his deceptions in speech, I should create disgust, joined with waste of time, for a reader occupied with weightier matters.

Yet when I reject the Acts of Eusebius the presbyter, as other very distinguished men did before me, let no one suppose that I thereby diminish the sanctity and cult of Eusebius the confessor. I transfer these, under that name, to another person concealed beneath it: namely, Pope Eusebius, who died in exile for maintaining ecclesiastical discipline and keeping it inviolate. [Note: See *On the Damasian Writings*, §2, and notes on Poem XII.] For since in later centuries there was no knowledge of matters pertaining to that pope beyond a nearly bare recollection of his name and cult, these very things were laid down as a kind of foundation upon which was built the tale, now read, concerning Eusebius the presbyter—a tale full of cracks.

Why I hold this view, hear the reasons. No one who reads the title of Eusebius expressly mentioned in the first council under Symmachus will deny that it is very ancient in Rome. But it does not seem possible to say that it was dedicated to Eusebius the presbyter, since the name of that presbyter is sought in vain in the older Martyrologies of Bede. The Gregorian Sacramentary indeed commemorates this Eusebius on 14 August; but the title *sacerdos*, “priest,” by which it honours him, according to the usage then received denotes a bishop. Moreover, in all that the venerable Cardinal Thomasius reports as collected in the Gradual Antiphonary and the Capitular of the Gospels for the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, you read material suited to a bishop who was a confessor or martyr; and it was therefore customarily sung and read in celebrating the feast-day of St Marcellus, Pope and Martyr, and of other pontiffs. [Note: See *Works*, vol. V, pp. 203, 279, and 488.]

Furthermore, the Bucherian list records the death of Pope Eusebius on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September; while those apocryphal Acts say that Eusebius the presbyter died likewise on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September. Error in expressing such numbers is easy; indeed it is so slight, if one attends carefully, that the same Eusebius may be believed to be named in both places. Finally, another Bucherian catalogue establishes that Pope Eusebius was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus; in the same fictitious Acts, Eusebius the presbyter is said to have been buried in a crypt beside the body of St Sixtus, martyr and bishop, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callixtus. You see, therefore, how similar these things are; and from this you understand how easily the impostor who wrote those Acts in later ages full of darkness might have made Eusebius the presbyter out of Pope Eusebius—whose deeds, as we know, otherwise long lay in obscurity—and imposed him upon us. [Note: Sirmond, Possinus, and Papebroch saw those Acts written under the name of Pope and Martyr Boniface; from this Papebroch himself, *Dissertation* X, draws another most obvious argument for their falsity, ignored by the anonymous annotator.]

Certainly Gregory IX, who consecrated the church of St Eusebius, by no means tells us whether he was a bishop or a presbyter. [Note: “In the year of the Lord 1237, Lord Pope Gregory IX consecrated this church in honour of St Eusebius and Vincent, with three altars, of which he consecrated the greater altar of the confessor himself with his own hands.” It is also found in Montfaucon, *Italian Diary*.] From this it may be inferred that he had nothing certain or established, and that the matter was still unsettled even then—a matter which in this century has seemed to receive light through the Damasian poem.

## § X.—Inquiry into what Liberius really proved to be after his return to the see, and thereafter, namely during the time of the Council of Rimini. Whether he ever truly withdrew from communion with Athanasius, or how long that interruption lasted. On the date of Athanasius’s letter to the bishops of Egypt, which is elucidated. A passage of Hilary from the *Fragments* explained in favour of Liberius. On Liberius’s second departure from Rome, through fear of Constantius: a passage of Lucifer is adduced and explained. The anonymous Amsterdam writer noted.

Having therefore consigned such tales to those whom they delight, let us now see what Liberius did and what opinion was held of him after Felix had been expelled and seemed voluntarily to relinquish the pontificate which perhaps he had legitimately administered for some time. Two periods must be considered: the one extending from Liberius’s return to the Synod of Rimini; the other following it.

First, it may be observed that nowhere do I read anything written or done by him in which he seems to have sought pardon from the Church, as would have been fitting. Secondly, it is not clear that he was ever regarded as a heretic either by his own people or by the bishops of Italy; and from this silence a weighty argument is drawn that he never laid aside the Catholic faith. Thirdly, Damasus writes that, while the Council of Rimini was being conducted, it was necessary to seek the judgment of the Roman bishop; and I have already said what follows from this. Finally, fourthly, when the bishops at Rimini write to the emperor that they rejected the formula proposed by Valens and Ursacius because they saw that, if it were adopted, disturbance and contention would arise both in other cities and especially in the Roman Church, [Note: Sozomen, book IV, ch. 18.] we understand that the Roman citizens and clergy with their bishop, and all the Catholic bishops who wrote, were already united with him in peaceful communion and faith.

Meanwhile the Synod of Rimini was assembled; but we know that Liberius was present neither in person nor through legates. The man who recently translated from Latin into French the published defence bearing the celebrated name of Bossuet, formerly bishop of Meaux, thinks this occurred through the deceit of Ursacius and Valens, whose interest it was to undertake their enterprise while the Roman bishop was absent, lest he impede them from conducting and bringing their affairs more easily to the end they wished. I do not deny that this may have happened. But if this explanation is true, let him see by what method and reasoning he can henceforth defend the apocryphal Acts of Eusebius the presbyter along with their author. For if Liberius was a persecutor of Catholics, as those Acts assert, why would those two leaders of the Arians have wished the Roman bishop, who agreed with them, to be absent from that council?

The opinion of those who think that he was absent lest he seem by his consent to give any force to this council—which Constantius had convened on such unjust conditions and to which he had prescribed fixed limits for action and decision—therefore appears more probable. You understand that this is the reason why the assembled bishops fell: because, with the Roman pontiff absent, who is the head of the Church, they lacked that divine gift of inerrancy which, as we know, will never fail the whole body of the Church.

But what meanwhile of Athanasius? Had Liberius retained communion with him? I indeed think so. Before Liberius was driven into exile, the Arians are known to have wanted only one thing: that the pope should condemn Athanasius. Yet not a word was said of Liberius changing his faith or abandoning the *homoousion* (“of the same substance”). Let the letters written by him then to the emperor and the conference held at Milan be read. Thus he went into exile at Beroea in Thrace solely because he retained communion with Athanasius. At last, broken, he wrote to the Easterners that he had accepted the Sirmian faith, removed Athanasius from his communion, and wished to have peace with them; he also communicated this to Valens and Ursacius, although that letter is not free from suspicion.

He therefore came to Sirmium through the agency of Basil of Ancyra, who then directed everything at his own discretion. What was then done and discussed we have already seen. One faith was the matter that occupied the minds of the Emperor Constantius, of Basil, and indeed of all; all their concern was directed to this. Nothing was said of Athanasius. Why? Because, with the situation changed, entirely different concerns were required. For the new heresy and faction of Eudoxius had broken forth into the open field; against it Basil took care either to retain or to unite with himself all who professed the *ousia* (“substance”). Hence he did not seem even to think of Athanasius, whom he knew to be joined in communion with almost the entire Church. So too Constantius, whose mind was governed by Basil, laid aside for a while his old hatred toward Athanasius.

Hence again it came about that, when Liberius saw that that matter was then wholly neglected and consigned to oblivion, and understood that nothing further was required from him, he is by no means to be judged actually to have abandoned his former communion with Athanasius, whatever he may previously have written. This, I suppose, is why Athanasius himself says that Liberius did not openly subscribe against him, but rather subscribed to heresy.

Moreover, if at any time ecclesiastical communion between them was broken, anyone who reads Athanasius’s letter to the bishops of Egypt and Libya, or the first oration against the Arians, and sees Liberius and Hosius there praised among orthodox bishops and defenders of the faith, will scarcely doubt that this bond was soon renewed. [Note: *Letter to the Bishops of Egypt*, no. 2: “If the things they write were written by orthodox men—such as the great confessor Hosius, Maximinus of Gaul or his successor, or Julius and Liberius, bishops of Rome, and others who think as they do—if, I say, those Arians were like these, there would surely be no ground for suspicion in their writings”; and no. 3.] Since, as Athanasius says, this was written in the thirty-sixth year from the Nicene Synod, it offers a most compelling argument either that affection was never broken or that it had already been renewed. For if you calculate the dates, the year then in progress was 360; but if you hold that those years had already been completed, the year is 361.

I am not unaware that some, who think this letter was composed in 356 and before Liberius’s fall, count the stated years from the Alexandrian synod that condemned Arius and first sounded the trumpet against his heresy. But those who hold this plainly force the explicit words of Athanasius, who says that by the decree of one and the same general synod—the Nicene Synod—Arians were both declared heretics and expelled from the Church. Moreover, lest there be any occasion for error or another opinion, Athanasius himself, in the place where he says that Arians were declared heretics and expelled from the Church thirty-six years earlier, says that the Meletians became schismatics fifty-five years earlier. [Note: “The Meletians became schismatics fifty-five years ago; and the Arians were declared heretics thirty-six years ago and were rejected from the Church by the judgment of the whole [ecumenical] synod.”]

Now the beginnings of the Meletian schism must be assigned to 305, or to the following year, as Baronius thought. The most learned Marquis Maffei conclusively demonstrated this by producing four previously unpublished letters of the most holy Egyptian bishops and martyrs, which they sent to Meletius. [Note: *Osservazioni letterarie*, vol. III, p. 11.] Since these letters were written while the Diocletian persecution raged and were sent from the prison in which they themselves were held; since they also report the indications and causes of the schism then breaking out, sharply rebuke Meletius himself, and urge him to return to sounder counsels—the distinguished scholar rightly concludes that those who assign the Meletian schism to 300 or the following year rest upon no solid foundation whatever and are rather in error, placing it a full three years before the persecution itself.

The time when the same letter was written is further demonstrated by the following words found in it: “While residing in these regions, I heard, as brethren who are genuine and orthodox reported, that certain followers of Arius had assembled and composed, as they wished, a statement concerning the faith; and that they wish to send letters to you so that you may subscribe either as it pleases them—or rather as the devil suggested to them—or, if anyone objects, he may be driven into exile.” [Note: No. 5.] Yet in that year or the following one no trace at all can be found in ancient monuments of any creed written and then promulgated by the Arians. On the contrary, everything remarkably agrees with the year in which we have said that this letter was written. For in these words anyone can easily see expressed the Acacian formula, confirmed by the robber-council at Constantinople, and the unrestricted authority granted by Constantius—as Socrates and Sozomen relate—for its acceptance everywhere.

At that time Eudoxius and Acacius, acting together, sent to every province of the Roman Empire the formula of faith recited at Rimini, along with the additions which they had appended as if intending to correct it; and by the emperor’s command they ordered those who refused to subscribe to this faith to be banished. [Note: Socrates, book II, ch. 43; Sozomen, book IV, ch. 26.] Then especially was introduced that state of the Church which all writers of the time describe and say endured until Constantius’s death.

Nor am I driven from this view by the fact that Athanasius in the same place mentions George as being then sent to Alexandria. For that plunderer made two incursions into the Alexandrian see: one to be assigned to 356, or, as seems to me, to the following year; the other in 361, nearly three years after he had been driven from that city by a popular uprising. Both of these violent invasions are mentioned, distinguished, and assigned to their proper time by the anonymous writer edited by Maffei. Just as Heraclius the count, Cataphronius, and Syrianus, sent by Constantius to use violence against the people, had preceded the earlier invasion, so that nothing might be lacking from the later one, Paul the Notary was sent; he published the edict in favour of George and subdued many in vengeance for him.

Who, then, can teach us with certainty whether Athanasius intended by the same letter to indicate the earlier or the later event? As for the mention there of Cecropius, bishop of Nicomedia, who perished in 358, on 24 August, when the basilica of that city was overthrown by an earthquake: I do not see what can be inferred from this if the passage is carefully considered. For just as, when Athanasius treats of Catholic bishops, he names Maximinus of Trier, Julius the Roman pontiff, and others whom he knew long since to be dead, together with Hosius and Liberius, then enjoying the light of life, and ranks them among outstanding defenders of the faith—whose writings on faith could afford no ground for suspicion—so I do not see why he could not also number Cecropius and Leontius the Eunuch among those whose writings were to be rejected and whose doctrines were to be detested, even if they had already been removed by death. For he seems in that passage to have had but one purpose: that by comparing the bishops of both parties and setting their writings alongside one another, the bishops of Egypt and Libya might understand whose opinion they ought to choose and whose avoid. [Note: See nos. 6, 7, 8, 9.]

I now return whence I departed, namely to the Synod of Rimini, concerning which the following is also read in Hilary’s *Fragments*. [Note: Fragment 4.] “But Potamius and Epictetus, while they rejoiced to condemn the bishop of Rome, as is contained in the Synod of Rimini, refused to hear these things.” No one can fail to see and acknowledge that this passage is corrupt, disordered, and awaits a healing hand, but in vain. Yet if anything can be extracted from it, it seems that the bishop of Rome, Liberius, was discussed at the Synod of Rimini. But for what reason? Surely for one that would be to that pontiff’s praise and honour.

To conjecture this, it must first be stated that Potamius was already dead and, if the presbyters Faustinus and Marcellinus are to be believed, was neither present at the council nor able to be present. It remains, therefore, that we should say that the acts committed against Liberius by Potamius and Epictetus at the Council of Milan were again brought to mind and mentioned in the Riminian assembly, on the occasion of the recent formula proposed by Ursacius and Valens. Since the Catholic bishops resisted that formula and knew that the Roman bishop would also certainly resist it, they could not but foresee that he would again be harassed and once more driven from his see.

The event proved this. Liberius annulled and rendered void, by apostolic authority, everything done at Rimini, sending encyclical letters to all bishops; Siricius mentions these in his celebrated letter to Himerius of Tarragona. Then, lest he furnish another example of human frailty, conscious of himself, he withdrew and took refuge in the hiding places of a cemetery. Sozomen expressly mentions this second withdrawal of Liberius and distinguishes it from the earlier exile. [Note: Book IV, chs. 11 and 19.] Rufinus, and Socrates, deceived by him, ignorantly confound it with the exile at Beroea. [Note: Book I, ch. 27.]

Therefore Tillemont, although he concedes that this repeated exile has some appearance of truth, says that there is no foundation upon which it can be held certain: for Sozomen, in his opinion, is doubtful, while Baronius himself gives little credence to the Acts of Liberius which confirm the matter. If this withdrawal of Liberius falls, Damasus’s vicariate also collapses. At least, this seemed so to Constantius in the preliminary warning prefixed to the same Acts of Liberius and relegated to the appendix.

But this double exile lacks neither rationale nor witnesses besides Sozomen. As regards the rationale, we know from Sozomen and Socrates that Ursacius and Valens were granted in the West the same authority which Eudoxius and Acacius had in the East. [Note: Socrates, book II, ch. 37; Sozomen, book IV, ch. 19; Nicephorus, book IX, ch. 41.] We learn both from these historians and from Jerome, Vincent of Lérins, and Augustine that those brigands abused that authority—statements which I would cite here in vain. Shall we then say that Liberius, who had annulled the Council of Rimini and frustrated one of their enterprises, was passed over by those criminals unharmed and untouched?

Prosper in the *Chronicle*, published entire by Canisius, [Note: Vol. I, Basnage edition.] and Lucifer in his work *Against Constantius* also support Sozomen. The former’s testimony is wholly unequivocal, since he mentions and distinguishes both exiles, assigning one to the ninth year of Liberius’s pontificate and the other to the consulship of Constantius VIII and Julian Caesar. What Lucifer writes, I admit, may seem somewhat obscure to us, who are far removed from those times; but carefully observed, it supplies an entirely certain argument for this repeated withdrawal of Liberius. Thus he says to the emperor:

“Will you deny that you invited us to embrace idolatry? If you think it can be denied, the expositions of the bishops of your sect—namely your blaspheming bishops—will convict you; the memorials read by you and delivered at Rome to bishops, even Catholic ones, will convict you, namely for the purpose that your blasphemy might be strengthened in every place.” [Note: Book I, p. 228, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition.]

There are, therefore, those who think these words designate the time when Constantius stayed in Rome, namely 357; and they conjecture that the memorials were then read and distributed by him to the Catholic bishops present, so that he might discover each person’s disposition toward the blasphemy already planned and to be issued from Sirmium. [Note: Tillemont, *On the Arians*, art. 67, note 6.] But since Lucifer writes that memorials were read by Constantius and handed through the bishops so that his blasphemy might be strengthened in every place, the reader easily understands that he speaks not of a merely planned but of a blasphemy already brought to light and promulgated. Moreover, no one will readily grant that the blasphemy which all know was later composed at that clandestine and accidental meeting at Sirmium could already have been formulated, read to Catholic bishops, and handed through them at the time Constantius stayed in Rome.

If, therefore, anyone judges that Lucifer denotes and indicates the impious Riminian—or rather Acacian—formula which I have mentioned, I believe he will scarcely depart from Lucifer’s true meaning. For this is the formula which, after a lengthy disputation before the emperor himself, had been received by the prevaricating bishops, then set forth and publicly read at Constantinople. [Note: See Socrates, book II, ch. 41; Sozomen, book IV, ch. 23.] Because it could not be read at Rome, where it had meanwhile been conveyed by imperial order, while Bishop Liberius and the whole Church resisted, we read that it was merely handed through the bishops’ hands, yet with absolutely no success. Although Lucifer does not state there whether Liberius was absent or present when these things occurred at Rome, it is nevertheless credible that he was absent, in order that, free from the power of those to whom Constantius had decreed that all things were lawful against bishops opposing this formula, he might continue by his own flight and withdrawal to safeguard the integrity of the Catholic faith.

Moreover, the following words of Anastasius concerning Julius are the chief reason why I do not doubt a second departure of Liberius from Rome: “He lived in the times of Constantius, the heretical son of Constantine. Under him he was in great tribulation and exile for ten months; and after the death of this Constantius he returned with glory to the see of the blessed Peter.” The old martyrology of the Queen of Sweden, cited by Georgius, contains the same statement. [Note: *Martyrology of Ado*, 2 April, p. 662.] You see, therefore, Julius driven from his see under Constantius; you further see him returning with glory to his own see after a ten-month exile following Constantius’s death.

Now if you attribute these things to that pontiff, they are utterly false. But if you remove them from the Acts of Julius and restore them, with Baronius and other men of exceptional judgment, to the genuine Acts of Liberius—from which they were mistakenly taken—then you have his second exile, and all becomes clear and coherent. For the robber-synod at Constantinople was completed in February. It is certain that Valens and Ursacius, to whom at that time power had been given to harass the Western churches at their pleasure, did not immediately leave that city; for, if we believe Fortunatus, they persuaded Constantius to order Hilary to return to Gaul. [Note: Fortunatus, *Life of Hilary*, no. 8.] But from the letter of the Gallican bishops to the Easterners preserved in the same author, we learn that Hilary had not yet left Constantinople in the first months of that year. [Note: Fragment 11.]

It is likely that these criminal disturbers did not set out for Italy before the emperor himself began his journey against the Persians, when spring was already advanced, as Ammianus says. If you grant this, you will easily grant also that they could scarcely have exercised, before the middle of that year had passed, the tyrannical power over the Western churches which the emperor had given them. If you assign some further time for carrying out these measures in churches more remote from Rome, and add besides the ten months during which Julius is falsely said to have lain hidden, you easily reach the death of Constantius and the time when, as Jerome says: “The bishops who had been driven from their own sees returned to their own churches through the indulgence of the new prince.” [Note: *Against the Luciferians*, ch. 19.] Thus both those statements foreign to Julius pertain to Liberius, and his second exile cannot be called into doubt on any solid ground.

These, then, are the things which I have thought can be gathered and asserted with certainty, from a careful reading of contemporary witnesses, concerning the deeds of Liberius while in exile. I know that there are men eminent in learning who think that this pontiff never lapsed in any way, that what has been published against him rests only on uncertain rumour, and that all writings said to be his are false inventions of the Arians, whose tricks and deceptions are otherwise well known. They hold this opinion not without some plausible reason. But even if we treat these documents as true and genuine, I think it is now clear that nothing can be produced or forced from them that could benefit the desperate cause of those cast out from the Church. There is therefore no solid reason why that anonymous patcher-together of the Lives of Roman Pontiffs should continue, as he has done, to insult Catholic writers with boastful arrogance and reproach us, in captious and convoluted language, with that pontiff’s lapse. [Note: “One must be horribly prejudiced in favour of infallibility to maintain that Liberius did not wound the faith by adhering to the perfidy of Sirmium. We also see that those who speak in this way are obscure persons who do not dare make themselves known, though they are protected by powerful persons; but the fall of Liberius is too odious in all its circumstances. On this subject I content myself with referring to the excellent dissertation of M. Larroque.”]

For if there was any fault in him, it was not loss of faith but the laying aside of his former, more rigorous steadfastness; and it was not so grave that it cannot be, if not wholly removed, at least mitigated by some explanation. For in the state of affairs then existing, the force of *homoousion* and *homoiousion* (“of the same substance” and “of like substance”) was considered—and in fact was—the same both among Catholics and among Anomoeans, as Touttée and the distinguished Gorgneus, canon of Soissons, have very thoroughly demonstrated. [Note: Touttée, on St Cyril, Dissertation 1, chs. 7 and 16; Gorgneus, dissertation on the Synod of Rimini, question 3.] Liberius perhaps subscribed to the Sirmian creed because he trusted that he could attain these two aims: retain the faith intact, and form a closer alliance between Catholics and the Semi-Arian bishops who upheld *homoiousion*, so that their forces might be enlarged against the then openly emerging enterprises of Aëtius, Eudoxius, and the Anomoeans—an alliance especially useful and necessary.

# DIATRIBE II. Whether Damasus at any time favoured Maximus the Cynic against Gregory of Nazianzus; and concerning two letters issued in the name of an Italian council and published by Sirmond.

## § I.—Basnage refuted. Writers are cited: some say that Maximus the Cynic’s appeal to Damasus and the Westerners was invalid and held of no account by the Easterners; others judge that it was not without effect and that he was received into Western communion. Both sides rest upon one letter of a certain Italian council, which is produced. Those who have doubted its authenticity.

If those letters still existed which Nicholas I says Damasus wrote in order that Maximus might be expelled from the episcopate, there would be no place for this controversy, and no one would have dared, even on this account, to attack the reputation of a most holy pontiff and one most observant of the sacred canons. But through the injury of time all have perished, except two which Holstenius published and which I listed in fourth and fifth place. Arguments must therefore be drawn from elsewhere to vindicate the name of Damasus from calumny.

Moreover, since Basnage had the opportunity of seeing the two letters which survive, he made himself ridiculous when he dared accuse Nicholas himself of falsehood because no letter of Damasus survives to support Nicholas’s statements. [Note: On the year 381, no. 5.] Would that the registers of the Roman pontiffs still existed! For from them, I do not doubt, the greatest support and honour would shine upon us, while upon heretics and other assailants of the Apostolic See there would shine a light for recognizing the truth. But now to my purpose.

Those, therefore, who think that Damasus supported Maximus the Cynic against Gregory of Nazianzus fall into two classes of writers: some intent on diminishing the rights of the Apostolic See and of the Roman Pontiffs, others intent on vindicating them. Yet all employ one and the same support, [Col. 0323B] namely a single Italian council and a single letter of that council; and all, proceeding by one and the same road, set before themselves contrary destinations. The first to publish this Letter was James Sirmond, a man of the highest judgment and boundless learning, who placed it last in the appendix to the Theodosian Code [Note: [Col. 0323D] *Works*, vol. I, p. 429, Verona edition.]. Thereafter all embraced it as especially well suited to prove what they had proposed; and the latest editors of Ambrose’s works allowed it to be printed among his other letters, as though it were an offspring worthy of so great a father. For from it Baluzius [Note: [Col. 0323D] *Councils*, book VII, ch. 4.], and several others, infer that the Sardican canons concerning appeals then had no force or authority; for, if they had already been accepted, why were they not brought forward by the Italian bishops in this very [Col. 0323C] letter, in order that they might uphold Maximus’s appeal by them? Dupin [Note: [Col. 0323D] *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, dissertation 2, §2.] and Quesnel, however, according to their custom venture upon every assertion, and rashly maintain, first, with the Eusebians assembled at Philippopolis, that the synod of the Westerners could determine nothing against the Easterners; secondly, that their efforts came to nothing, since Maximus the Cynic remained permanently deposed; and, thirdly, that the Westerners themselves openly acknowledge this when they claim for themselves not a prerogative of examination but seek a share in a common judgment. By those words they plainly mean only that they would judge with the Easterners, not concerning the Easterners.

On the other hand, Lupus [Note: [Col. 0323D] *On Roman Appeals*, ch. 31.] and Schelstrate [Note: [Col. 0324D] *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, dissertation 6, ch. 4, art. 2.] attribute this very letter to the Roman synod and to Damasus. From it they conclude that both Maximus made use of the benefit of appeal and Damasus exercised his right [Col. 0323D] when he received him into communion and restored him to the rank of bishop, from which he had been cast down by the synod of Constantinople. This also appears recently to have been the opinion of the distinguished Fr. John Anthony Blanc, of the Observant Franciscan family [Note: [Col. 0324D] Vol. III, book II, ch. 3, §11.], and of Fr. John Chrysostom of St. Joseph, one of the Clerics Regular of the Pious Schools [Note: [Col. 0324D] *Dissertation on the Appeal of St. Athanasius*, ch. 4.], whom I should wish to name with due honour. But whether the argument which those most learned men draw from this letter is sufficiently firm and properly suited to asserting the rights of the Apostolic See, let those judge who consider with themselves what issue that case eventually had. Accordingly, since the letter seemed of doubtful authenticity to John David [Note: [Col. 0324D] *On the Judicial Force of Canonical Letters*, p. 196.] and Natalis Alexander [Note: [Col. 0324D] Fourth Century, dissertation 28, proposition 3.], and since those eminent men seem to have touched the matter only with the tips of their lips rather than completed it, I thought I should do worthwhile work if I examined it more carefully and submitted to the judgment of readers several weightier arguments by which both the reputation of Damasus might be placed beyond danger and the falsity of the letter—because of which he is here charged, as it were, with a certain prevarication—might be more clearly established. But so that readers may themselves decide the matter with less inconvenience, I have thought it proper first of all to transcribe here again the letter of the Italian council itself.

**The Council of Italy to the Emperor Theodosius, [Col. 0324B] concerning the bishop substituted at Antioch after the death of Meletius; and requesting that Nectarius, ordained at Constantinople after Maximus, yield his place, or that a council be held at Rome concerning the ordination of both. Ambrose and the other bishops of Italy to the most blessed emperor and most merciful prince Theodosius.**

We knew that your holy mind was devoted to Almighty God with a pure and sincere faith; but, Emperor Augustus, you have heaped fresh benefits upon us by restoring the Catholics to the churches. Would that you had restored the Catholics themselves to their ancient reverence, so that they might introduce no innovations contrary to the ordinances of the elders, nor rashly either annul what ought to be preserved or preserve what ought to be annulled. Therefore, Emperor, we perhaps groan more sorrowfully than imprudently that heretics could more easily be expelled than agreement achieved among [Col. 0324C] Catholics. For the extent of the recent confusion cannot be explained.

Long ago we had written that, since the city of Antioch had two bishops, Paulinus and Meletius, whom we thought to be in harmony in faith, either peace and concord should be established between them while ecclesiastical order remained intact, or at least, if one of them should die while the other survived, no one should be substituted in the dead man’s place while the other remained alive. But now, Meletius having died while Paulinus survives—Paulinus with whom the fellowship which has endured unbroken from our forefathers testifies that we have remained in communion—another, contrary to divine and ecclesiastical order, is said to have been placed in Meletius’s place, not so much as substituted as superimposed. And this action is alleged to have been carried out with the agreement and counsel of Nectarius, though we do not see what order his own ordination possessed.

For recently, at a council, [Col. 0324D] when Bishop Maximus had shown, by reading letters of Peter, a man of holy memory, that communion with the Church of Alexandria remained with him; and had established by clear testimony that he had been concealed in a private house because the Arians still held the basilicas, and that bishops acting under mandate had ordained him, we had nothing, most blessed prince, by which we could doubt his episcopacy, since he testified that force had been inflicted upon him against his will by many persons, even among the people and clergy. Yet, lest we should seem rashly to have determined anything [Col. 0325A] while the parties were absent, we thought your Clemency should be informed by letter, so that provision might be made for him in the interest of public peace and concord. For we truly perceived that Gregory was by no means claiming the priesthood of the Church of Constantinople for himself according to the tradition of the Fathers.

Therefore, in that synod which seemed to have been prescribed for the bishops of the whole world, we judged that nothing ought rashly to be determined. But at that very time, what is it said that those who avoided the general council did at Constantinople? For when they learned that Maximus had come from those regions for this purpose, to plead his own cause in a synod—although, even if no council had been summoned, he ought by right and the custom of the ancestors, as both Athanasius of holy memory and, formerly, Peter, bishops of the Church of Alexandria, and most [Col. 0325B] Easterners had done, to be regarded as having fled for judgment to the Church of Italy and of the whole West—when, as we have said, they learned that he wished to seek redress against those who had denied his episcopacy, they certainly ought also to have awaited our judgment concerning him. We do not claim the prerogative of examination; but there ought to have been a sharing in a common judgment. Finally, it was first necessary to establish whether the priesthood should be taken from this man before it was conferred on another, especially by those of whom Maximus complained that he had been either unjustly abandoned or unjustly attacked.

Accordingly, since our fellowship has received Bishop Maximus into communion, because it is established that he was ordained by Catholic bishops, we did not think him to be excluded from seeking the episcopate of Constantinople. We judged that his plea should be weighed in the presence of the parties. [Col. 0325C] But since our modesty recently learned that Nectarius had been ordained at Constantinople, we do not see how our communion can remain united with the Eastern parties—especially since Nectarius is said immediately to have been deprived, without the fellowship of communion, by those very persons who had ordained him. This is therefore no slight scruple. Nor does some private partisan contest or ambition trouble us; it is communion, broken and divided, that disturbs us. Nor do we see how it can otherwise be restored, unless either he who was ordained first is reinstated at Constantinople, or a council of ourselves and the Easterners is held in the city of Rome concerning the ordination of the two men.

For it does not seem unworthy, Augustus, that those who thought the judgment of the one bishop Acholius ought so to be awaited [Col. 0325D] that they considered bishops of the Western regions should be summoned to Constantinople, ought to submit to the deliberation of the bishop of the Roman Church, of the neighbouring bishops, and of the bishops of Italy. If anything was reserved to this one man, how much more ought it to be reserved to many? But we, having been instructed by the most blessed prince, the brother of your Piety, to write at the command of your Clemency, request that where communion is one, judgment too may be one, with concordant agreement.

### § II.—The sequence of events devised by those who regard that letter as genuine is set forth: In what year did Maximus the Cynic come to Milan? To what council besides did he attend, in order to defend his ordination there? The opinion of Peter de Marca, Valesius, and others on this subject is shown, by arguments and by Tillemont’s authority, to be erroneous.

Those, therefore, who regard this Italian council and its letter as true and certain say that this was the sequence of events [Note: [Col. 0326D] See Pagi at the year 379, no. 12, and 381, no. 6; Tillemont, *On Ambrose*, art. 33; Fleury, book XVI, no. 17.]. Maximus the Cynic, who had meanwhile come to Italy, attended the same council—according to some, in 381 after the Council of Aquileia had been held; according to others, about the middle of 382—and, producing letters of Peter of Alexandria, who had already died, proved himself Catholic and, moreover, by presenting false testimony, to have been duly and rightly ordained. Tillemont’s reason for thinking that Maximus came to Italy about this time is that he hoped to restore his affairs, ruined by the judgment of the Synod of Constantinople, through the ecumenical council summoned at Rome by Damasus. The Italian bishops, however, judged that nothing should rashly be determined by themselves, so that this case might be considered by the general council soon to be held. [Col. 0326B] But lest meanwhile they themselves should seem lacking in their duty, they both received Maximus into communion and wrote to Theodosius, asking him to take account of his rights and make provision for him in the interest of public peace and tranquillity.

This first letter, as these writers think, has perished. For they say that three letters were written to Theodosius by the same council, of which the one transcribed above occupies second place, while another, concerning which I shall speak hereafter in § IV, occupies the last. They infer from this second letter the substance of the first letter which has perished, and therefore say that the second was sent not long after the first, namely when those Italian bishops learned for certain that the general council called by Damasus in that year was being avoided by the Easterners [Col. 0326C] and that another was being held by them in the imperial city.

Having received these letters from the Italian council, now hear, if you please, what—according to the imagination of these authors—Theodosius replied. They say that the emperor replied that the reasons for which the bishops of Italy had requested a council in the West did not seem at all suitable or weighty. The causes alleged concerning the ordinations of Flavian and Nectarius had arisen in the East and concerned the Eastern Church; they ought to be examined and determined in the East and could not be transferred to the judgment of the West, lest the boundaries established by the Fathers be disturbed. The request was therefore unjust and likely to provoke resentment among the Easterners themselves, since the latter were being summoned to assemble at a council in Rome over such matters. Thus, if anything were determined in the West while they were absent, [Col. 0326D] it would be invalid and would create a greater cause of quarrels between the two Churches. Further, the Italian bishops had either shown themselves too ready, contrary to all considerations of fairness and propriety, to trust the lying Cynic, or had allowed themselves to be carried away by excessive zeal against the Easterners. The only reason they offer for thinking that Theodosius wrote these very things to those Italian bishops is that, in their final letter, the bishops excuse themselves before the emperor and offer, in their defence, reasons why they judged a general council necessary—or, as these writers think, reasons for which they admit that they had been at fault.

[Col. 0327A] But these matters, in my view, are easier to invent from one’s imagination than to demonstrate as true. Certainly no one doubts that Maximus came to Italy. It is also possible that he came to Italy in 382, as Tillemont thinks, although the conjecture by which that learned man is moved to think so is indeed exceedingly slight. For Maximus, long before rejected by Damasus, could expect no good from a synod in which what had pleased that most wise pontiff was bound to be ratified. Moreover, to pass over other considerations, the examples of Athanasius and Peter of Alexandria could have made him more certain that recourse and the way of appeal to the Roman Pontiffs were open and readily available at every time, and that no summoning of a council was needed for that purpose.

The testimony of Jerome, writing as follows, makes me more readily believe that the Cynic came among us in that year: “Maximus the philosopher, born at Alexandria, was ordained bishop at Constantinople and expelled; he wrote a notable book on the faith against the Arians, which he presented at Milan to the emperor Gratian” [Note: [Col. 0327D] *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 117.]. It must indeed be noted that he did not come to Italy immediately upon being expelled from Constantinople, but went to Emperor Theodosius, who was residing at Thessalonica when the year 380 was already half over; then, driven again from that place like a dog, he departed for Alexandria. There, after causing trouble to Peter, bishop of that city, he was compelled by the prefect’s action to go into exile from there also. Finally, as Nazianzenus elegantly says: “He seemed to be at rest, like a cloud pregnant with heavy hail, awaiting a wind by which, driven onward, [Col. 0327C] it may pour out its hail upon those who do not expect it” [Note: [Col. 0327D] Poem on His Own Life.]. In carrying out these matters, he must have consumed what remained of that year and the greater part of the next. Hence we infer that the philosopher could not have appeared at Milan and brought that book to Gratian in March 381, when the emperor spent only a few days at Milan, if indeed he spent any there; whereas it is clear from the Theodosian Code that in the following year he remained in that city for almost the whole year. But the question is not whether the Cynic came to Milan—for that cannot be doubted—but at what council he was to plead his case, and, further, from what bishops that council was assembled.

Peter de Marca thinks that these events occurred at the Council of Aquileia [Col. 0327D]:
