> Nectarius having been ordained in Gregory’s place, Maximus, disappointed of his hope, withdrew to Italy, so that, supported by the favour of the Italian pontiffs, but especially of Damasus of Rome and Ambrose of Milan, whose authority at that time was supreme, he might retain the Church of Constantinople after Nectarius had been rejected. But it is established that the ordination of Nectarius did not please Damasus. We may therefore affirm that Damasus and the Western council approved this recourse of Maximus and eagerly seized that opportunity to exercise the authority [Col. 0328A] of the Roman and Western Church over the see of Constantinople. Hence, at the Council of Aquileia under Ambrose—which was general as regards the West, and in which, among other things, Damasus’s authority is inferred to have intervened because Gratian wrote to him concerning its assembly, as the authority of the *Synodical* attests in ch. 74—in that Council of Aquileia, I say, Nectarius’s ordination having been condemned, Maximus was approved to such a degree that the bishops wrote back from that council to Theodosius that they had nothing by which they could doubt his episcopacy.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] Book V, ch. 21; book VII, ch. 4.]

Basnage eagerly embraced this opinion too [Note: [Col. 0327D] At the year 380, no. 4, and 381, no. 5.], and Valesius agrees with it, although he recognized it as poorly grounded when he wrote:

> Therefore the bishops of Italy, who had assembled in council at Aquileia, after reading Maximus’s letters received him into [Col. 0328B] communion . . . and afterwards, when Nectarius had been ordained bishop of the same city in the Council of Constantinople, they refused communion with him and wrote to Emperor Theodosius that a council should be held at Rome in which the case of Nectarius and Maximus might be debated. . . . At first Damasus disapproved Maximus’s ordination; afterwards, however, he seems to have favoured Maximus. For the council of the bishops of Italy would not have received Maximus into communion, nor would it ever have asked the emperor that a synod be held at Rome concerning his ordination, unless with Damasus’s consent. But whether Maximus was received into communion by Damasus is obscure.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] Notes on Sozomen, book VII, ch. 9.]

But the acts of the Council of Aquileia itself and what followed it overthrow this opinion, which Baluzius also, Valesius, Dupin, Coustant, and others have embraced. [Col. 0328C] For if the Fathers of that council had examined Maximus’s case and judged it consonant with law, why does none of this appear in the acts themselves which still survive? Further, if they had asked Theodosius to make provision for that philosopher in the interest of public peace and concord, why, in their letters sent to that same Theodosius, do they treat only of the Antiochene schism because of Flavian’s ordination and of the troubles inflicted upon Timothy of Alexandria, while passing Maximus’s affair over in silence? Those letters survive as witnesses to the same matter [Note: [Col. 0328D] Venetian edition of the Councils, vol. II.]. Likewise there survive in Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0328D] Book V, ch. 9.] other letters which the Eastern bishops wrote in reply to the Westerners when the year 382 was already advanced; elsewhere I have already examined why, although they mention having received those letters of the Aquileian [Col. 0328D] council, there is no word whatever about Maximus or at all about his recourse to that council.

Valesius, therefore, who clearly perceived the difficulty, advances two inventions in order to escape it: first, that Maximus was not present at the council but pleaded his case only by letters written to Aquileia; second, that it was not the entire Council of Aquileia itself, already concluded and dissolved, but those Italian bishops who had, if you believe Valesius, most opportunely [Col. 0329A] remained at Aquileia, who heard Maximus’s case as presented in writing and wrote the letter under discussion to Theodosius. But the very words of that same letter, if they are merely read, plainly demonstrate how absurd and falsely devised these assertions are. Add that the genuine letters of Aquileia and the fictitious letter of the Italian council conflict and disagree with one another: the Aquileian Fathers request that a council be convened at Alexandria, to which all the Easterners may gather; the Italian bishops summon those same persons to Rome. Who, then, could believe that both letters proceeded from bishops of one and the same council? Tillemont therefore rightly rejects this opinion; Pagi, Fleury, and other learned writers agree with him.

### § III.—Tillemont’s own opinion is presented, examined, and rejected. Arguments are adduced from that very letter and from other contemporary documents, by which it is established that the letter could neither belong to any Italian council nor be genuine, nor moreover could ever have been written by Ambrose, but must be regarded as fabricated. A brief digression into the investigation of its author.

[Col. 0329B]

It remains now to inquire whether the opinion is preferable of those who, setting aside the Council of Aquileia, think that Maximus fled to, and attended, this Italian council, assembled from those bishops who were subject to Ambrose. After some difficulties have been proposed by me, the reader may judge this for himself.

First, the superscription of this council, which is called Italian, gives me serious concern, since no definite and known place in Italy is designated [Col. 0329C] where it can be said to have been held and celebrated. This is unusual and foreign to accepted ecclesiastical practice, according to which all councils down to that time, and those also celebrated afterward, took their name from some definite and specified place. Hence Jerome asks Rufinus, who asserted that he had been approved by the judgment of a synod: “In what city was the synod held? Give the names of the bishops; produce the judgments of those who subscribed; show who were consuls at the time; what emperor ordered this synod to be assembled; and certainly for what cause the synod was assembled” [Note: [Col. 0329D] Book II against Rufinus, no. 19, Verona edition.].

Second, scarcely any council may be produced about these times which was called Italian rather than Roman. For the whole of Italy still obeyed the bishop of Rome as its metropolitan; [Col. 0329D] and the bishops of Milan and Aquileia had scarcely begun, because of the prerogative of their sees, to be distinguished from the other bishops and to exercise that right which they later exercised. Bacchini learnedly proves this in his dissertation *On the Origins of Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* [Note: [Col. 0329D] Part II, from §7.], citing the explicit testimony of Eusebius, who calls Roman the council assembled by Cornelius in the case of Novatian from all the breadth of Italy. But, not to go far from the age of Damasus, Julius, writing from his synod to the Eusebians, says: “You must be informed that, although I wrote alone, that judgment is not mine alone, but belongs to all those who are in ITALY and who dwell in these regions” [Note: [Col. 0329D] In Coustant, letter I, no. 81.]. Further, Liberius, in letters written to the Easterners which Socrates records [Note: [Col. 0329D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, ch. 12.], calls himself bishop of Italy and speaks with one voice for the Italians and Westerners; and Theodoret says that the first Roman synod under Damasus was assembled from Italy and Gaul [Note: [Col. 0330D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, ch. 22.]. Consult also Fr. Anthony Blanc, a learned Observant Franciscan, who admirably confirms this conclusion against the absurdities of Giannone [Note: [Col. 0330D] Vol. IV, book II, §16.].

From these things, therefore, it follows that there was then only one council in Italy, namely the Roman council assembled from all Italy; and consequently another Italian council, separate and distinct from the Roman one, either did not exist or belongs to a later age. Hence, when Jerome [Note: [Col. 0330D] *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 76.], from a passage of Eusebius misunderstood, seems to have recognized an Italian synod distinct from the Roman synod when speaking of Cornelius, Pearson rightly observes that the matter is unclear concerning this Italian synod and says that he doubts whether that Italian council was correctly constructed by Jerome [Note: [Col. 0330D] *Annals of Cyprian*, at the year 251, no. 13.].

Third, if this letter is to be trusted, the council at which Maximus was present was assembled while Gregory of Nazianzus was bishop. I shall give the words which establish this. “For recently, at a council, [Col. 0330C] when Bishop Maximus had shown, by reading letters of Peter, a man of holy memory, that communion with the Church of Alexandria remained with him; because the Arians still held the basilicas, he had established by clear testimony that he had been concealed in a private house and ordained by bishops acting under mandate, we had nothing by which we could doubt his episcopacy. Yet lest we should seem rashly to have determined anything while the parties were absent, we thought your Clemency should be informed by letters, so that provision might be made for him in the interest of public peace and concord, because we truly perceived that GREGORY was by no means claiming for himself the priesthood of the Church of Constantinople according to the tradition of the Fathers.”

The consequences that follow of themselves are these. First, if Maximus was present at this council while Nazianzenus was confirmed as bishop of Constantinople, his arrival and recourse to Italy would necessarily have to be assigned to the first months of 381, since Gregory ceased to be bishop in May or June. But that this is false is proved both by the chronology and sequence of events [Col. 0330D] that we have examined above, by Nazianzenus himself in the poem on his life, and by the Council of Aquileia, since nothing at all is read either in the Synod of Aquileia or in Nazianzenus himself about Maximus’s flight to the Italian bishops or letters written to Theodosius on his behalf. Secondly, it is evident that those err who transfer this matter and the Italian council to the year 382, since no controversy against Gregory—who had already voluntarily withdrawn from the episcopate—could then exist for which those Italian bishops might write these things to Theodosius.

Crushed by this difficulty, Valesius and Tillemont cut the knot with the sword. In the words of the letter which we have quoted, they say that there is an error and that *Nectarius* ought to be read in place of *Gregory* [Note: [Col. 0331D] Tillemont on Gregory Nazianzenus, note 43.]. But this reading rests upon and is confirmed by the authority of no manuscript whatever. Further, whoever properly observes the sequence of events laid out in this letter will find that there is no room for error, but that all things hang together correctly; he will admit that both the name Gregory and the name Nectarius are correctly placed where each stands. For, as we have said, three letters are alleged to have been written concerning the same case of Maximus. Hence, when he first came to the Italian bishops assembled in council and the first letter was written, Gregory Nazianzenus [Col. 0331B] was bishop; but when this second and later letter was written, Nectarius was already presiding over the Church of Constantinople, and consequently they seem also to disapprove his episcopate.

That being so, either this Italian council must be placed outside the year 382 and assigned to a point in 381 not yet far advanced, when Gregory really was bishop; or, if you think it should not be removed from that year and wish to retain Nectarius’s episcopate, you must admit that the council, once begun, was never afterward dissolved but was extended for several months beyond the whole course of a year—something no one, surely, will say.

Fourth, in the council at which that philosopher was present and submitted his case for decision, we ought to find three things: first, that it was at least general in its summons; second, that it was held about the time of the Synod of Constantinople, by which Maximus was deposed and Nectarius ordained; and third, that it was avoided by the Easterners. You have these three points from these words of the letter: “We judged that nothing should rashly be determined in that synod which seemed to have been prescribed for the bishops of the whole world; but what did those who avoided the general council do at Constantinople at that very time? For when they learned that Maximus had come from those regions to plead his own case in a synod, when they learned that he wished to seek redress against those who had denied his episcopate, they certainly ought also to have awaited our judgment concerning him.” Now each of these points [Col. 0331D] must be weighed, and inquiry made whether they can be fitted to this Italian council.

To begin with the first point: did Ambrose ever write that his Italian synod of a few bishops had been prescribed for the bishops of the whole world? Let no one even imagine it. Fleury therefore ignores the difficulty. Tillemont, however, in order to remove it, thinks that “we [judged that nothing ought to be determined] except in that synod” ought to be read; through this single addition, made in order to serve the hypothesis, he says that the Italian bishops judged that nothing ought to be determined in the synod which they themselves were holding, so that Maximus’s case might be heard in the general council already summoned and soon to be held by Damasus [Note: [Col. 0331D] *On Gregory Nazianzenus*, ch. 81.]. Pagi too says that this is the council designated here; but, without using the addition employed by Tillemont, he is compelled to do violence to the most plain words and deceive the reader.

But on what manuscript or printed copy, or what printed books, does this reading rest, that it may be forced upon us by Tillemont? Moreover, do not the quoted words of the letter and the sequence of events expounded reject his correction and addition? For the words immediately added, “but those who avoided the general council,” plainly explain what is the synod prescribed for the bishops of the whole world which is being discussed here and which judged that nothing should rashly be determined. They express and represent a synod already held in Maximus’s case, not one to be held in the future, and indicate a matter not yet to be conducted but already done and past. Further, if this Italian council, by which Maximus’s case was deferred to that council already summoned by Damasus, was held at the very time at which the Synod of Constantinople had assembled, then either you must, just as with Maximus’s recourse, draw it back to the first months of 381, when the Synod of Constantinople had already met and ordained Nectarius, whereas Damasus’s general Roman council had not yet been summoned; or, if you maintain that it was assembled in 382, you must necessarily assign Nectarius’s very ordination to the same year and to that assembly which the Easterners then held at Constantinople.

The first alternative is precluded by the silence of Gregory Nazianzenus, by the acts of the Council of Aquileia, and by Tillemont himself. The second, though it pleased John David [Note: [Col. 0332D] *On the Judicial Force of Canonical Letters*, p. 203.], is nevertheless demonstrably entirely false from *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 1, law 3, which is recorded as promulgated on 28 July 381 and proves that Nectarius was already presiding over the Church of Constantinople. There remains, therefore, either to reject this letter among the fabrications, or to admit at last with Tillemont himself that whoever wrote it was so senseless and dull that he did not know or pay attention to what he was writing [Note: [Col. 0332D] Note 45 on Gregory Nazianzenus.]. But can such great carelessness be believed in so recent and evident a matter, and moreover in Ambrose, whom they think wrote the letter itself? Let whoever wishes believe it; I certainly will not allow myself to be persuaded.

Finally, as to the third point I proposed: if the council at which Maximus was present was avoided by the Eastern bishops, and the Italian bishops are said to have reproached them for this, it must be understood either of the Council of Aquileia, or of that Italian council, or of the Roman council convoked by Damasus; and one of these three must be chosen. If the first, this may perhaps seem to have been said with justice, since the Easterners, though afforded an opportunity to attend, preferred to be absent, as the acts show. But, as we have often said, Maximus neither attended nor could have attended it, nor was his cause handled there. If, however, you choose the Italian council—that which, Tillemont says, was assembled from the bishops of the Vicariate of Italy—this assertion must appear rash and false [Col. 0333A]. For by what right could Ambrose reproach the Easterners with having avoided that council of his, on which they in no way depended? Or were the Eastern bishops themselves even summoned to it? It remains, then, that you choose the third, and refer this to the council which Damasus had called at Rome, to be assembled from bishops of West and East, and which was subsequently convened toward the end of the year 382.

But if you maintain this, you must necessarily admit that Ambrose and the other Italian bishops already knew, when they wrote, that this council had certainly been, or would be, refused by the Easterners. Now observe the following. Before midsummer of that year they knew nothing of this Roman council; and when, summoned by Theodosius, they had come to Constantinople in accordance with the letters of the Council of Aquileia, they acknowledge that they were then informed both that it had been convoked by Damasus and that they themselves had been summoned, and, struck by the novelty of the matter, they sent legates with letters explaining why they could not all be present [Note: See chap. 20.]. It is certain that these letters were written after midsummer—thus when July was already declining or had passed—and that they were carried by those bishops whom they had sent as legates. I now ask you: in what month of that year do you think they reached Rome, so that Ambrose and the other Italian bishops could know with certainty that the Roman council had been avoided by the Easterners? It seems to me that their arrival at the City can scarcely be placed before October.

Either, therefore, Ambrose and the other Italian bishops had already come to Rome, as I think [Col. 0333C], or they had not. If we say the former, did Damasus, Acholius, or the Eastern legates allow Ambrose himself to remain ignorant of Maximus’s frauds and intrigues? Not even Tillemont could digest that. Or, moreover, could the bishop of Milan, present at the council, undertake so great a business alone with his own associates, without consulting Damasus, Acholius, and the other bishops already assembled? Far be it from me to cast this calumny upon a man most holy and most prudent! For all who were in the same communion ought to have been satisfied, so that the acts done might be strengthened by the agreement of many and peace not be broken, while some were cut off as others were admitted. Thus deliberation concerning matters affecting the churches of the whole world ought to be undertaken gravely and gently [Note: Basil, Epistle 265, in the Benedictine edition].

But if you say that Ambrose wrote these things with his Italian council [Col. 0333D] before setting out for Rome, you will scarcely persuade me either that time could have sufficed him or that, already on the point of departure and with a general synod soon to be held at Rome in view, he undertook matters of such consequence. Moreover, how did he learn that the Easterners had declined that general synod, so as to impute this to them as a fault? “But,” says Tillemont, “he had already learned that those who ought to have undertaken the Roman journey had halted at Constantinople and had established their own synod there by midsummer” [Col. 0334A]. Thus this author speaks by divination, in order to serve his hypothesis. But I ask again: who informed Ambrose that the Easterners had established their synod for the purpose of avoiding the Roman one? Could they not, after completing that synod, conveniently afterward proceed to the West? Thus the matter always returns to this: he could not have been certain about it before the letters of those Easterners, in which they excused themselves, had been brought to Rome; and consequently the same difficulty constantly remains.

Fifth. Maximus is said to have been received into communion by the Italian bishops because it was established that he had been ordained by Catholic bishops. But this contains a double fault. First, it is against Nicene Canon 5, which decrees that one who has been expelled is not to be received by others. The African bishops, though most absurdly, used this safeguard to prevent Celestine from granting communion to those whom they themselves had condemned [Note: Epistle 2, in Coustant, no. 2]. Secondly, how did those Italian prelates think themselves permitted to do this without consulting Damasus, bishop of Rome, who had rejected Maximus? For if Apostolic Canon 34 had determined, and the constant discipline of the Church had everywhere accepted, that the bishops of each nation should know the one who was first among them, should regard him as their head, and should do nothing of great importance apart from his judgment, this was surely owed with greater right to the Roman pontiff, to whom all Italy had from the very origin of the nascent Church been wholly attached and, as Bacchini says [Note: *On the Origin of Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, part II, §13, with [Col. 0334D] following], as it were cemented together. Since this fact is very well known and confirmed by the testimony of the sixth Nicene canon [Col. 0334C], I think it superfluous to support it with examples and other unnecessary arguments.

Yet I cannot omit what is especially suited to demonstrate the matter under discussion: namely, that none of the Western bishops believed himself permitted to receive Athanasius into communion after his expulsion by the pseudo-synods of Tyre and Antioch, before Julius had pronounced judgment. Hence it came about that Julius himself was condemned in the Arian assembly at Philippopolis because he had been the first to open the door of communion to wicked and condemned persons, and had made a way for others to dissolve the divine laws. Let me therefore here marvel with Jerome: how did **ITALY** approve what **ROME** despised? How did bishops receive what the Apostolic See condemned? [Note: *Apology against Rufinus*, book III, no. 15.] But the authority of Ambrose himself prevents me from bringing myself to believe this of Ambrose. For from the Council of Aquileia he had already taught us that from the venerable Roman Church flow all the rights of communion [Note: Epistle 12, in the Benedictine edition].

Sixth. In the same way, because Maximus was rejected and Nectarius ordained bishop, the Italian bishops declare communion between themselves and the Easterners broken:

> Since our modesty has recently learned at Constantinople that Nectarius has been ordained, we do not see our communion cohering with the Easterners . . . nor do we see that it can otherwise be brought together [Col. 0335A], unless either he who was first ordained be restored to Constantinople, or at least there be at Rome a council of ours and of the Easterners concerning the ordination of the two.

First, I shall scarcely ever grant that this could have been written by bishops of the Vicariate of Italy without consulting, and against the opposition of, the Roman bishop to whom they were subject. Secondly, I assert that communion between Westerners and Easterners was never broken on account of Nectarius’s ordination against Maximus. The testimonies, I think, of Sozomen and Pope Boniface make this clear. The former gives only one cause of the dissension that arose between the two parties—namely, the episcopate of Flavian—and teaches that the Easterners were summoned to the Roman council solely for that reason [Note: *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 11]. The latter writes:

> Theodosius, judging that Nectarius’s ordination lacked firmness because it had not occurred with our knowledge, regularly requested, by court officials sent from his side together with bishops, that a *formata* [official letter of communion] be sent him from the Roman See, to confirm his priesthood. [Note: In Coustant, Epistle 15, no. 6.]

Thus there was no controversy or dissension with the Easterners because Maximus had been rejected, nor could there have been any ground on that account for breaking communion. Hence communion with Nectarius himself was immediately accepted in the Roman council, whereas we know that Flavian was rejected by all. Accordingly, when Emperor Michael defended the election of Photius by the example of Nectarius, Nicholas I replied with perfect justice that Nectarius had truly assumed the government of the Church of Constantinople without scandal, **WITHOUT FORCE, WITHOUT ANY SCHISM**; and that, consequently, the holy Second Synod, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, had decided well and most excellently concerning Nectarius [Note: Epistle 8, Venetian edition of the Councils]. How far this is from what is stated in this letter is evident to everyone.

Seventh. Moreover, after Meletius had died while Paulinus survived, the Italian bishops assert that Flavian was not so much substituted as imposed contrary to divine and ecclesiastical law, by the consent and counsel of Nectarius. Here you see that Flavian is said to have been substituted contrary to divine and ecclesiastical law, not contrary to the pact confirmed with God as witness. But since explicit mention of this pact occurs in the letters of the Council of Aquileia, why is it omitted here, if Ambrose was author of both letters and if it added great weight to the cause he was defending?

Furthermore, Flavian had already been ordained bishop of Antioch when Nectarius had not even been thought of. Sozomen relates the matter in these words [Note: Sozomen, book VII, chap. 8]:

> By chance Diodorus . . . seeing Nectarius, judged him worthy of the episcopate, and immediately gave him his vote in the secret recess of his mind, considering the man’s gray hair, his countenance worthy of the priesthood, and the gentleness of his character. Thus, as though on another matter, he brought him to the bishop of Antioch, and, after lavishing many praises upon him, asked the bishop to support him with his vote.

Was Flavian, then, already presiding over the Church of Antioch [Col. 0336A] when Diodorus of Tarsus approached to solicit him for Nectarius? For, according to Sozomen’s testimony, Flavian the bishop draws up the list of candidates, presents it to Emperor Theodosius, and plays the leading role in Nectarius’s election. Or could he be called bishop before the laying on of hands? Or was episcopal power then divided in two—jurisdiction and order—so that these things might be permitted to one not yet ordained? Therefore it was not, as the writer of this letter says, Flavian who was made bishop through Nectarius’s aid and counsel, but Nectarius through Flavian’s.

I am not unaware that Tillemont, who thinks Flavian was designated at Constantinople but ordained at Antioch, impugns Sozomen’s credibility [Note: *On Flavian*, article 3, vol. X]. But his opinion rests upon absolutely no witness. The credibility of Sozomen’s statement is established by the letter which the Easterners wrote in 382 to Damasus, Ambrose, and the other bishops assembled in the Roman synod, in order to give account of what they had done in the preceding Council of Constantinople. These are its words:

> The bishops of the province and of the Eastern diocese, gathered together as one, ordained Flavian—the most reverend and devout bishop of the most ancient Church of Antioch in Syria—while the whole Church consented and praised the man, as it were, with one voice; and the whole SYNOD ALSO ACCEPTED that lawful ordination.

We do not deny, then, that the bishops of the Antiochene province and the Eastern diocese—namely Diodorus of Tarsus and Acacius of Beroea—could have ordained Flavian, as they say [Col. 0336C]. But when they add that his ordination was accepted by the whole synod, they additionally prove plainly that it was celebrated at Constantinople, where the synod was assembled. In vain does Baluzius twist these words toward a synod of the Antiochene province [Note: *On Councils*, book VIII, chap. 3, no. 9]. For if the bishops of the Antiochene province and Eastern diocese, gathered together, had canonically ordained him, they had undoubtedly already considered whether he was barred from the episcopate on any ground, as discipline and the canons required. Therefore, when it is added that the ordination was accepted by the whole synod, an altogether different and more weighty synod is indicated—namely the Council of Constantinople then in session—as Socrates expressly explains [Note: Socrates, book V, chap. 8].

Moreover, Gregory Nazianzen says that friends begged him, and even sought to influence him by shameful artifice, to vote with the others for Flavian, before he had relinquished the episcopate and before the council over which he presided had been dissolved. Let the entire course of the affair, most elegantly described by him in the poem *On His Own Life*, be read. What business, then, had the bishop of Constantinople with the bishops of Syria and the Eastern diocese, that the influence of himself and of the others—who in no way depended on the See of Antioch—should have been sought with such ardor? And is it credible that a matter pursued with such contention of minds [Col. 0337A], and pressed so urgently that they wished to complete it in a single hour, should afterward have been delayed so long as to be accomplished only after several months?

Finally, it is established that Gregory himself resigned the episcopate after the arrival of the Egyptian and Macedonian bishops. Why? Because they, in order to avenge affronts—both ancient and recent—received from the Easterners and to inflict some pain upon them in return, alleged that the canons had been violated in his own translation, as Gregory himself says. But what just cause—if I may use the term—for requiting ancient and recent affronts could there have been if Flavian had not yet been ordained and that affair had been completed and settled?

Add, finally, that under the ecclesiastical discipline then received, election or designation and ordination were customarily so connected [Col. 0337B] that they seem scarcely ever to have been separate [Note: *On the Council of Marcian*, book VIII, chap. 3, no. 2; Thomassin, vol. II, book II, chap. 8, no. 2; see also, if desired, chap. 18]. Therefore there can scarcely be anyone who may rightly think that Flavian himself was elected and designated at Constantinople long beforehand, but could afterward have been consecrated at Antioch.

Such being the case, I shall never be brought to believe that that letter was written by Damasus, or that Ambrose was its author, or that it proceeded from any other bishop of those times who was informed about the events being carried out. I am confirmed more and more in this opinion when I attend to its barbarous, rough, obscure style, alien to the polish and clarity of Damasus and Ambrose. For what can those words mean: *dolentius forte, quam inconsultius ingemiscimus*—“perhaps we groan more sorrowfully than imprudently”? Was pain perhaps a greater cause for grieving [Col. 0337C]? Who, indeed, could endure someone speaking and thinking in this manner? Again, why should I mention the often awkward repetition of the same words: “with ecclesiastical order preserved,” “contrary to divine and ecclesiastical order”; “as to what order the ordination of Nectarius had, we do not see”?

By contrast, what abundance of matter, what elegance of words joined with seriousness of thought, occurs in the letter which Ambrose truly wrote to Theodosius in the name of the Council of Aquileia upon this very matter! Let the reader compare the two himself and determine by his own judgment whether both can appear to have proceeded from the same hand. Finally, what of the fact that the author of this Italian letter seems ignorant of the compact sworn between Meletius and Paulinus, which had restored concord to the Church of Antioch, although Ambrose knew it perfectly well? Hence, writing to Theodosius, he says:

> We think that we have presented to Your Piety our petitions, in which, according to the COMPACT of the parties, we requested that, when one should die, the Church should remain with the survivor, and that no superimposition should be attempted.

But the writer of the other letter, of which we are speaking, says that he had requested what had already been done and established—that is, that some concord should be entered upon:

> We wrote some time ago that, since the city of Antioch had two bishops [Col. 0338A], Paulinus and Meletius, whom we believed to agree in faith, either peace and concord should be established between them, with ecclesiastical order preserved, or at least, if either should die while the other survived, no substitution should arise in the place of the deceased while the other survived.

In another place I have said in what year and on what occasion the petitions mentioned by Ambrose were presented to Theodosius [Note: See chap. 15]. For the present matter, first observe how far bronze differs from lupins; then you will readily judge whether Ambrose ought rightly to be considered author of both letters.

But who patched this letter together, and for what reason thrust it upon us as belonging to this Italian council? I confess that I do not know. Yet, if conjecture is permitted, the wretched Latin style, which at times savors of Greek [Col. 0338B], together with a certain knowledge of ecclesiastical history joined to ignorance of it, causes me to suspect that it issued from a Photian workshop. It is beyond doubt that Photius, a crafty man, fabricated many things. Learned men have already observed that the forgeries he produced often reflect Greek diction and depart from the idiom of Latin [Note: Allatius, *On the Photian Synod*, chaps. 3 and 12]. Moreover, we know that he repeatedly, indeed nauseatingly, invoked Nectarius’s example in support of his own ordination. Why, then, should he not also have fabricated this letter, especially apt and suited to confirm his obstinacy against the Apostolic See?

Add that Pope Hadrian, in a letter written to Emperor Basil, had rightly compared Photius with Maximus the Cynic. His words are:

> For we judge that there is no distinction between Photius the adulterer and Maximus the Cynic, condemned by the Second Synod, nor between the ordination of the former and of the latter; and therefore he who is proved in every way to have had the same beginning as the other seems bound to the same end. [Note: In Baronius, under the year 869, no. 5.]

For this very reason the Eighth Synod pronounced anathema upon Photius, the fabricator of lies, Photius the new Maximus the Cynic. From these facts it is clear how important it was to Photius to give the cause of that same Maximus the Cynic a different appearance from what it really had.

Whatever may be the case in these matters, what can henceforth be asserted with certainty is, first, that after the Council of Aquileia no other Italian council can be shown to have assembled during this intervening period; secondly, that this letter contains several things wholly alien to truth and is for this reason unworthy of the bishop of Milan [Col. 0338D]. Therefore, if—as the sole remaining possibility—you say that by the name of an Italian council some bishops, perhaps of one province, are denoted, who wrote it in a common name though outside a synod, you must produce men wholly ignorant of the events then occurring, who dared to write it without consulting either the Roman pontiff or Ambrose himself. You may hold that opinion, if you wish.

§ IV.—The discussion concerns another letter published by Sirmond under the name of the Italian council. This letter is genuine and was written by Ambrose, or perhaps also by Siricius. The question is on what occasion and at what time it was written; it is referred to the Council of Capua as an appendix to it. The reasons for this opinion are presented. On this occasion, the time of the letters written by Gregory Nazianzen to Cledonius is discussed. A passage of Chrysostom is also adduced and explained; and Paulinus of Antioch is defended against the forced and unfair interpretation of the latest editor of that Father’s works.

[Col. 0339A]

It remains only to say something about the other letter of the Italian council to Theodosius, which begins *Fidei tuae* (“Of your faith”). Critics have hitherto thought it written on the same matter, that of Maximus; in the Benedictine edition it occupies place 14 among Ambrose’s letters. I judge it genuine no less than the others, and wholly worthy to be attributed to Ambrose, whether one considers its flowing style, its polished expression, its gravity of thought, or the truly apostolic spirit joined with equal deference with which he writes back to the emperor.

Moreover, I think that Flavian’s affair moved Ambrose to write it. This is not obscure from these same words of his: “For it was grievous that the exchanges of sacred communion between Easterners and Westerners had been interrupted.” It is established, indeed, that this occurred because of Flavian’s ordination alone. Since, therefore, after Paulinus’s death, the long-standing division of the Church of Antioch was by no means extinguished, but still kept the churches of both empires divided in the person of Evagrius, his successor; and since the Easterners attributed the blame for this division to the Westerners, who, as it seemed, had preferred Evagrius, unlawfully ordained, to Flavian [Note: Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 23], Ambrose—possessed by the single desire of restoring peace to the Church and seeking means suited to that end—neither favors either party nor openly condemns either, both in this letter and in another which he addressed, I think, on the same occasion to Theophilus of Alexandria [Col. 0339C]. Nor does he enter into the controversy to inquire by whose error or fault this had happened, lest he seem to “sow fables and idle words.”

It is therefore established that this letter was written in the cause of Flavian and refers to it. But on what occasion and at what time? Certainly not long after the Council of Capua. Both Ambrose and Theodoret indicate this to us, although Theodoret mingles falsehood with truth because of his manifest zeal for Flavian’s party. For after Paulinus died, the protracted division in the Church of Antioch was not at all extinguished; rather, in Evagrius, his successor, it still divided the churches of both empires. Not without the counsel of Theodosius, then resident at Rome, it was decided to convoke in Italy a general synod to investigate that case and at last put an end to the schism.

Theodosius himself had given the Western bishops hope that he would take care for Flavian and other bishops from the East to be present at that synod. Therefore, after he had left Italy once affairs there had been settled, that synod was convened at Capua, and Flavian was summoned by Theodosius to Constantinople in order to sail thence to Rome. But he pleaded that winter had already arrived and promised to do as commanded at the beginning of spring, then returned home. When he was vainly awaited and did not appear at the appointed time, the synod was meanwhile held as convened. Communion was granted to all who professed the Catholic faith in the East, whether they followed Evagrius or Flavian [Col. 0340A]; but the judgment of the case of the two men competing afresh for the episcopate was entrusted to Theophilus of Alexandria, while remaining subject to confirmation by the supreme judgment of the Apostolic See.

Ambrose had hoped that by these most equitable decisions of the synod a remedy had now been provided and that the discord would end. But when he learned that Flavian had again resorted to the aid of petitions and the support of imperial rescripts, he wrote, apparently in the name of that same synod, another letter to Theodosius, in which, according to Theodoret’s testimony, Flavian was sharply censured. For it was through the emperor’s indulgence that the labor expended in vain by so many bishops, undertaken for attending the Council of Capua, had been wasted:

> Again must there be recourse to the judgments of this world; again to rescripts; again must aged bishops be harassed; seas crossed; again must those infirm in body exchange their homeland for foreign soil; again must altars be abandoned so that they may set out for distant lands. Meanwhile Flavian alone is exempt from law: he had neither come to Capua nor presented himself before the judges appointed by the synod. [Col. 0340B]

Since Ambrose wrote these things at that time to Theophilus of Alexandria [Note: Epistle 56], we can scarcely think that he did not write the same things, and others of a similar but more forceful nature, to Theodosius, through whose fault especially these events had occurred. Consequently, when the emperor, more sharply censured, had written back, he gave Ambrose occasion finally to write that letter which Sirmond published under the name of the Italian council, as one that was a part and appendix of the Council of Capua [Col. 0340C].

It is plainly established that this letter was composed solely to soothe the emperor’s mind. Moved by the single desire for peace, the bishops of Italy wrote to Theodosius and exhorted him, already hastening, to win for himself alone the glory of restored public peace. They grieved that this had proved fruitless, and did not wish to inquire through whose fault it had happened. Yet since it had not been their fault that this great and desired good had not come about, they were free from blame; and they had at least achieved this: that they might not thereafter seem to have neglected fellowship with the Easterners or to have held it cheap. The Western bishops had imposed upon themselves the labor of coming to Capua, not for the benefit of Italy, Gaul, or Africa, which flourished in harmonious religion, but so that at that synod the matters which had disturbed communion on the Eastern side might be examined and every scruple finally removed.

But because Ambrose had censured the emperor on the ground that it was through his indulgence that Flavian had evaded the Council of Capua and moreover refused to obey its decisions, the emperor perhaps replied that Flavian had rightly avoided it, both because the Westerners favored Evagrius and because they had no jurisdiction over the Easterners. Ambrose therefore replied in this very letter that the Westerners had requested a council to be assembled also from the Easterners themselves, and that accordingly no suspicion of excessive indulgence or partisan favor could fall upon them [Col. 0341A]. Further, they had committed the examination of this case to Theophilus of Alexandria, not in order to decide it but in order to investigate it; Flavian ought to have presented himself before him. Thus, those who had entrusted themselves to another’s arbitration—while preserving the supreme authority of the Roman bishop, by whom the judgment was to be confirmed—had sought a just judgment rather than imposed a prejudgment.

Nor could it be thought that the Westerners had offered any insult to the Easterners when a council had been requested to which the latter also were summoned: first, because the more numerous the bishops, the better and more prudent the deliberation; secondly, because the Easterners themselves had set the Westerners an example, when Paul, presbyter of Constantinople, had requested in Achaia a synod of Easterners and Westerners alike [Col. 0341B]. The Westerners had thought that it should be convened at Capua so that all might more easily and safely come by sea, whereas the land route was full of danger because a threatening disturbance was then stirring in Illyricum, through which they would have had to pass.

Finally, when the synod was convened at Capua and was also to be attended by Easterners, the Westerners had not torn up the boundaries fixed by the Fathers or violated Eastern rights. Rather, they had observed the decisions of Athanasius of holy memory and of the same Fathers. When Ambrose appealed to Theodosius to this example, perhaps also to the Sardican canons, and to Eastern cases judged by Julius, Liberius, and other earlier bishops in Roman synods, he says that he had detracted nothing from the reverence due to him.

I therefore recognize this letter as a genuine offspring of Ambrose and worthy of that bishop. Yet if anyone wishes to attribute it to Siricius, I do not at all oppose this: both because Siricius’s style resembles Ambrose’s, because it treats matters in which Siricius had a large share, and because Theodoret seems to number Siricius himself among the Roman bishops who had sharply censured Theodosius in this affair [Note: Book V, chap. 23].

What further moves me to think that this letter was written not long after the Council of Capua, and after Flavian had evaded its most prudent decision, is what is written in it: that a council had been requested both to extinguish the Antiochene schism and to investigate those attempting to introduce into the Church the dogma attributed to Apollinaris; and that this council had been requested in Italy because, as a disturbance was threatening in Illyricum, sea routes, being safer, had to be sought [Col. 0341D]. These things lead us to the time when Theodosius, after pacifying Italy, had returned to Constantinople.

For then we know that the heresy of Apollinaris was openly spreading in the East and that various disturbances had arisen in Illyricum, which he suppressed. The first point is established from Nazianzen, Socrates, Sozomen, and others whom it is unnecessary to transcribe here, and from Law 14, book XVI, title 5, of the Theodosian Code, issued at Thessalonica toward the end of 388. The second follows from Zosimus and Sigonius, whose words are these:

> Theodosius returns to Greece. [Col. 0342A] Having proceeded, however, to Thessalonica, he encountered a great disturbance in Macedonia. For all the barbarians who had survived among the marshes and neighboring woods after the earlier Roman expedition, stirred up by Theodosius’s occupations in Italy, were ravaging Macedonia and Thessaly without restraint and with no one resisting. But when Theodosius returned to Thessalonica, they withdrew into hidden places and, breaking forth at daybreak, rendered all the neighboring regions unsafe. [Note: *On the Western Empire*, book IX, no. 392, vol. I of the Works.]

Those are therefore mistaken who refer the disturbances in Illyricum mentioned in that letter to the Gothic war and who wish the council said to have been convoked in Italy because of those disturbances to be the council celebrated by Damasus at Rome toward the end of 382. Since the Gothic war had been wholly concluded and entirely extinguished in 380 [Col. 0342B], this excuse drawn from disturbances in Illyricum would appear utterly senseless and ridiculous—not to say false—if understood of that Roman council; whereas, conversely, it is wholly just and true if referred to Capua.

Add that the letter seems capable of having been written at no other time more suitable than that which I have stated. First, so far were the Easterners from regarding themselves as insulted in 382, when they were summoned to that council, that in their letter to the Westerners they instead praised their charity on that account. Secondly, they say that they were summoned to the Roman council not only by Damasus’s letters but also by those of Theodosius, as Jerome likewise asserted [Note: See above, chaps. 20, 21]. How, then, could Theodosius at that time have written to Ambrose the things which Tillemont [Col. 0342C], Fleury, Cellerius, and others suppose and invent? Finally, Theodosius himself could not have written these things to Ambrose before the year 382 was already declining. You must therefore admit that this very letter of Ambrose, of which we are speaking, was issued toward the end of that year, at the very time when the Roman council was being held. Those who concede this should say why it was not inscribed in the name of that same Roman council. Moreover, let those who say this consider whether they are properly consulting the reputation of the most holy bishop of Milan.

These, then, are the considerations that move me to think that this letter—whether it is Siricius’s or Ambrose’s—was written not long after the Synod of Capua, after the rejection of the judgment of that synod and of Theophilus of Alexandria. [Col. 0342D] Some greater light would be shed upon this question if we could know with certainty from the records of history who that man was, and bishop of what Church, who had been reported to the Roman pontiff on account of the heresy of Apollinaris; and likewise who that presbyter Paul of Constantinople was, said to have requested a council in Achaia composed of Western and Eastern bishops. As regards the latter, I have nothing certain to offer. This alone is established: since Paul, the great bishop of the Church of Constantinople, who died a martyr under Constantius, had been a presbyter of that Church, he cannot have been designated by that name, whatever Labbe and Sirmond may have thought. It must therefore have been some presbyter indeed from the Constantinopolitan clergy; and that several ministers in that Church were addressed by this title is clear from Palladius’s *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*. Nor will I readily concede to Tillemont and the other defenders of the Italian council that this council in Achaia could have been requested by that presbyter in the year which this author supposes—381 or 382—namely, at the time when we know that councils were numerous both at Rome and in the imperial city, and when the Easterners themselves, summoned by the emperors’ letters, gave reasons besides this one for not going to Rome and sent delegates. The letter, therefore, must have been written in one year, and Paul must have requested in another year this council in Achaia drawn from both Churches. [Col. 0343B] No time more suitable for this affair can be devised than that which began to pass after Flavian’s obstinacy had rendered the Synod of Capua fruitless, and after Theodosius’s return to the imperial city. For when Flavian had been summoned there by the emperor and was seeking a synod in the East and among his own people, this presbyter of Constantinople, led by zeal for public concord, could have proposed Achaia as more convenient for the Westerners.

> [Note: Col. 0343D: Baronius, year 389, no. 67.]

Accordingly, Ambrose, writing to Theophilus, complains that after that unsuccessful Synod of Capua, aged bishops were again to be harassed, seas again to be crossed, and holy altars abandoned, so that they might set out for distant places. Yet that very council in Achaia was rejected by the Westerners because a gathering in Illyricum, of which Achaia was a part, was then regarded with suspicion. [Col. 0343C]

Under the name of that bishop who had been reported to the Apostolic See because of the heresy of Apollinaris, one can scarcely understand either Apollinaris himself or Timothy, as very many suppose; both because each had long since been deposed by Western and Eastern synods, and because one was already dead while the other had been punished with exile.

> [Note: Col. 0343D: See chapter 22.]

It is difficult, indeed, to assert anything certain, since pseudo-bishops were numerous in the East and were destroying the Lord’s vineyard. Yet, if conjecture has any place, Vitalis seems to be indicated here. He presided over the Apollinarians at Antioch, whose number was by no means small. For since the Synod of Capua was chiefly to deal with extinguishing the Antiochene schism and at last restoring entire peace to that Church, [Col. 0343D] it can scarcely be that, at the same time, no action or deliberation was taken concerning Vitalis himself, from whom the greatest obstacle to this good arose.

Moreover, these words of this letter seem to designate him: “that, having been convicted of a new doctrine, he should by no means lie concealed beneath the general name of the faith, but should immediately, since he did not maintain the teaching office, lay aside both his function and the title of priest; and that no remnants might thereafter remain for those wishing to deceive, nor contrivances of imposture.” For these words portray for us a man who feigned his faith among Catholics and was a wolf under the appearance of a lamb: precisely a man like Vitalis, whom Epiphanius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret describe as crafty, and full of fraud and deceits. [Col. 0344A]

> [Note: Col. 0343D: See chapter 10.]

My conjecture seems confirmed by Gregory of Nazianzus’s letters to Cledonius, especially by the other letter in which he mentions both Vitalis himself and Damasus. Tillemont and several others think that it was written not long after Gregory had resigned the Church of Constantinople and had withdrawn to Arianzus, although they offer no adequate reason to prove this. What plainly destroys that opinion is that Gregory says Vitalis was then alive and calls him a man most dear to himself, [Col. 0344B] whereas he indicates that Damasus—whom he addresses with the title “blessed”—was already dead when he wrote. That letter was therefore written after 384, the year in which Damasus died. But in precisely what year? I would not venture to offer a time wholly fixed and certain; nevertheless, I think it may safely be asserted that it was written after 388 and around the time of the Synod of Capua.

For first, from law 14 of the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*, which was issued against the same persons, it is clear that the Apollinarians were then raging and especially troubling the Catholic Church. Next, Gregory himself indicates this very period when he says that they had arisen thirty years earlier—thus, around the year 358 or the following year. In 356, indeed, as Basil testifies, this plague had not yet broken out.

> [Note: Col. 0343D: Epistle 73, no. 4, new edition.]

Hence Nicephorus says that there were writers who maintained that Apollinaris had separated himself [Col. 0344C] from George of Laodicea because George had assented to the decrees of the Synod of Seleucia.

> [Note: Col. 0344D: Book IX, chapter 17.]

But by 362, when the Alexandrian Synod proscribed it, the heresy had already infected the Church with its poison. If, then, Vitalis had not yet died at this time; if, while feigning himself a Catholic in faith—as we observe from the same passage of Nazianzus—

> [Note: Col. 0344D: Chapter 12.]

he presided over the Apollinarians established at Antioch and was a great increase and support to this heresy; and if, finally, the Synod of Capua considered and deliberated upon securing peace at last for that city, scarcely any other person can seem to have been indicated and portrayed by him in this letter itself, or in that of Siricius to Theodosius.

From this we understand approximately in what year Chrysostom’s homily entitled *On the Anathema* was delivered, [Col. 0344D]

> [Note: Col. 0344D: Works, vol. I, p. 692, edition of the Benedictines.]

and to whom these words of his refer: “But what do those men, bold in every wickedness, say?”—that is, his own Flavian partisans, whom he addresses. “‘He has become a heretic,’ they say; ‘he has the devil dwelling within him; he speaks wickedness against God; and by deceit, cunning and vain, he leads many down into the abyss of destruction. Therefore he has been expelled by the Fathers—especially his teacher, who cut off a portion of the Church.’” Thus they designate either Paulinus or Apollinaris.

Montfaucon, whose edition I use, after quoting these words says: “At first glance they plainly indicate Paulinus as living and teaching. For he who speaks wickedness against God and leads many astray seems to be Paulinus; nor do we think these words can be applied to anyone else. But his teacher, who had been expelled by the Fathers, is Apollinaris, mentioned second, who, after he had been admitted to communion in a synod with Paulinus subscribing, was later expelled by Athanasius and the other Fathers when they discovered his heresy. Certainly, these sayings of the crowd attack only two men, namely Paulinus and Apollinaris, as Chrysostom explains. For if such words had been uttered after Paulinus’s death, they would undoubtedly have attacked Evagrius, his successor, who is nevertheless not mentioned here.”

I, however, think that Evagrius and Vitalis are designated under the names of Paulinus and Apollinaris, [Col. 0345B] and that this homily was consequently delivered after the death of Paulinus, who had chosen Evagrius as his successor—namely, after the close of 388—and not far from the time of the Synod of Capua. For surely no one who has properly understood how continually Paulinus himself contended with Apollinaris and his disciples for the Catholic faith will ever assert that Apollinaris could have seemed or been called Paulinus’s teacher by Chrysostom.

> [Note: Col. 0345D: See chapters 10 and 11.]

Nor can I sufficiently wonder that such a statement against an outstandingly Catholic bishop escaped so learned a man. Vitalis alone, therefore, is designated by those words; and that Apollinaris was indeed his teacher was openly known to all, as Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret testify. Chrysostom almost points at Vitalis with his finger, I might say, when he speaks of one leading many into the abyss of destruction by deceit, cunning and vain. [Col. 0345C]

Furthermore, the teacher of the man whom Chrysostom indicates had cut off a part of the Church and for that reason had been cast out by the Fathers. As this is rightly said of Apollinaris, who had drawn many Catholic Antiochenes after Vitalis—whom he had impiously ordained bishop—and after his own heresy, and was afterward placed outside the Church by the Fathers, so it could not even be imagined of Paulinus except through open and manifest calumny. The Catholic Eustathians had followed Paulinus voluntarily, and they were certainly the older and purer part of the Church of Antioch.

Therefore Chrysostom, addressing his own party, so as not explicitly to name Evagrius and Vitalis—both then alive, the latter hitherto of doubtful faith and communion—indicated both them and their followers under the persons of Paulinus [Col. 0345D] and Apollinaris, who had long been dead. From this very homily of Chrysostom, then, it may certainly be inferred that great disturbances were stirred up in the Church of Antioch at this time on account of that heretic; and, for that reason, it may rightly be maintained that he is designated by me in this same letter and that the letter belongs, finally, to the Synod of Capua and its proceedings, contrary to the opinion hitherto held by learned men. But I have judged that this letter itself should here be submitted once more to the eyes and mature judgment of readers, as a second document.

## Letter of the Council of Italy to Emperor Theodosius

It writes that, among other persons condemned in the synod, were those who were attempting to introduce [Col. 0346A] the doctrine of Apollinaris.

To the most blessed Emperor and most clement Prince Theodosius: Ambrose and the other bishops of Italy.

The knowledge of your faith, spread throughout the whole world, has deeply gladdened the affection of our hearts. And because we judged that this glory also should be added to your rule—that you might seem to have restored unity to the Churches of the West as well as of the East—we considered that your clemency should at once be entreated and instructed by our letter concerning ecclesiastical affairs, most tranquil and faithful Emperor.

For it was a source of grief that the bonds of sacred communion had been interrupted between Easterners and Westerners. We are silent now about through whose error or fault this occurred, lest we seem to spin tales and empty talk. Nor do we regret having made the attempt, since leaving it unattempted would have resulted in blame. For we were often reproached [Col. 0346B] on this account, as though we seemed to set aside fellowship with the Easterners and reject their goodwill.

Indeed, we thought that labour ought to be undertaken—not for Italy, which has long been quiet and secure from Arians and is troubled by no disturbance of heretics; not, I say, for ourselves, because we seek not what is our own but what belongs to all; not for Gaul and Africa, which enjoy the harmonious fellowship of all their bishops—but so that those matters which had disturbed our communion on the Eastern side might be examined in a synod and every scruple removed.

For we were moved by many considerations, not only concerning those matters about which your clemency deigned to write, but also concerning those who are said to be trying to introduce into the Church some doctrine of Apollinaris; these matters had to be cut off in the presence of the parties, so that one convicted [Col. 0346C] of a new doctrine and refuted in error might by no means hide beneath the general name of faith, but might immediately lay aside both his office and the title of priest, since he did not uphold the teaching ministry; and so that no remnants might thereafter remain for those wishing to deceive, nor contrivances of imposture.

For anyone not convicted in the presence of the parties will always seize upon a loophole for reopening the question—something which your clemency, in a truly august and imperial ruling, determined should be referred back. Therefore we requested a council of bishops, so that no one might be permitted to fabricate a lie against an absent person, and so that the truth might be examined in council. Thus no suspicion of hostility or undue readiness attaches to those who observed everything in the presence of the parties. Certainly, we have set out the allegations not in order to pronounce judgment but to provide information; and, although we have requested judgment, we do not offer a prejudgment. [Col. 0346D]

Nor should any summons to a council be regarded as an insult to those bishops whose absence was often more present when they deliberated for the common good. For neither did we consider it an insult when one presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, named Paul, requested within Achaia a synod of Easterners as well as Westerners. Your clemency has observed that the request was not unreasonable, since it was sought even by the Easterners; but because a gathering in Illyricum was regarded with suspicion, coastal and safer places were sought.

Nor indeed have we innovated anything as though without precedent. Rather, preserving the decisions made in councils by Athanasius of holy memory, who [Col. 0347A] was as it were a pillar of the faith, and by the Fathers of old holiness, we neither remove the boundaries set by our Fathers nor violate the rights of inherited communion. But, reserving the honour due to your imperial majesty, [Col. 0348A] we show ourselves zealous for peace and tranquility.

# Short Works of Saint Damasus

[Col. 0347]

## Letters. (C, S)*

## First Letter. Copy of a Synod Held at Rome by Ninety-Three Bishops, from an Imperial Rescript

### Notice

[Col. 0347B]

Sarazanius received this from Theodoret and furnished it with his own translation; but I use the Latin edition of Holstenius, as though it were the original offspring of Damasus, as I said in chapter 5. Why it is addressed in Sozomen and Theodoret to the Illyrians, but in Holstenius to bishops established throughout the East, see chapter 7. Moreover, the manuscript codex from which it was taken had been transferred from Bobbio to the Vatican Library by Scipione, Cardinal of Santa Susanna and librarian; long before Holstenius, Fr. Louis Capellus had inspected it and promised to publish it in his second dissertation *On the Succession of the Bishops of Rome*, chapter 5. It also exists in the Vallicellian codex 23, p. 107, copied from an old Tridentine book—that is, a book brought to that city at the time of the council.

## Letter

[Col. 0347C]

Damasus, Valerianus—

> [Note: Col. 0347C: That is, the celebrated bishop of Aquileia, whose ordination Dandulus places in his *Chronicle* in the year 368; for Fortunatianus died in the waning year 366 or in the following year (Fontanini, *Writers of Aquileia*, chapter 2, at the end). Basil the Great replies to him in Epistle 91, Works, vol. III.]

—Vitalianus—

> [Note: Col. 0347C: We read in Baronius, year 155, no. 22, that Vitalianus and Victor were numbered among those bishops who subscribed against Athanasius at the robber-synod of Milan [Col. 0347D]; but the Churches over which they presided are not specified. Ughelli says that Victor governed the Church of Piacenza around this time. Moreover, Peter Casella, *On the Origins of the Tuscans*, chapter 12, identifies for us a Bishop Victor of Florence, whom he says was succeeded by Zenobius. Priscus is read in Hilary, Fragment 8, with the delegates of the Council of Rimini, who in the end betrayed the faith. It can therefore easily be that, once they had all repented, they were present at this synod under Damasus. Nothing occurs to me concerning the others.]

—Aufidius, Pacianus, Victor, Priscus, Innocentius, Abundius, Theodulus, and the rest who assembled in the city of Rome to hear the case of Auxentius and to set forth the faith: greetings in the Lord to the Catholic bishops established throughout the East.

We are confident, indeed, that your Holiness, founded upon the teaching of the Apostles, [Col. 0348A] holds and makes known to the people that faith which in no respect departs from the institutions of the elders. For it does not befit bishops to think otherwise concerning God, since it is their role to instruct others. Yet from the report of our brothers in Gaul and Venetia, we have learned that some persons, not through devotion to heresy—for surely [Col. 0348B]

> [Note: Col. 0347D: The distinguished editor of the letters of the Roman pontiffs thinks that this could scarcely have been written at a time when so many Arian bishops were before everyone’s eyes; from this he concludes that the Holstenian copy was taken not from an authentic Latin original but from Greek through an unskilled translator, or from a corrupt copy. But this observation of the learned man is frivolous. Damasus declares heresy to be so great an evil that it can scarcely seem to fall upon God’s bishops; thus he instills horror of it in those to whom he writes, so that they may more readily return to their duty and guard against it.]

such an evil cannot fall upon bishops of God—but agitated by perverse interpretations through ignorance or a certain simplicity, do not sufficiently discern which judgment of our Fathers ought especially to be maintained, when divergent counsels are pressed upon their ears.

> [Note: Col. 0348C: So also Sozomen and Theodoret. The bishops of Gaul and Venetia had therefore reported Auxentius as a chief source of that heresy and as the author of counsels injurious to simpler bishops; and they had written that for this reason he had been condemned by them. [Col. 0348D] Why? Namely, so that this judgment might be confirmed by the Apostolic See—from which the fountain of communion arises—and promulgated everywhere. Such was the force of the ruling which Roman pontiffs appended to synodal definitions: that no enemy of truth might presume to excuse himself by their silence from obedience, as Leo the Great says, Epistle 107, no. 1. It is probable that this occurred after Hilary and Eusebius of Vercelli had confronted that heretic at Milan and Hilary’s encyclical tract against him had been published. All admit that he was condemned; but this is by no means plainly established from these letters, since they were written only to bishops who appeared to be wavering, in order to keep them in their duty. The acts of the synod, from which this could have been demonstrated, have perished.]

Finally, they state that Auxentius of Milan was condemned chiefly for this reason. It is fitting, therefore, that all [Col. 0348D]

> [Note: Col. 0348D: That is, bishops; so Paul I, to Timothy, chapter XIII, and to Titus, chapter I.]

teachers of the law throughout the Roman world should think alike concerning the law, and should not violate the Lord’s faith by diverse teachings. For when the poison of heretics had long ago begun, as it now begins again, to creep in, and especially when the blasphemy of the Arians began to spread, our elders, three hundred and eighteen bishops, together with bishops sent from the holy city of Rome, assembled at Nicaea and set up this wall against the weapons of the devil. By this antidote they drove away deadly draughts, establishing that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit must be believed to be of one Godhead, one form, and one substance; anyone holding the contrary they judged alien to our communion.

Later, certain persons tried by other arguments to overturn and [Col. 0349A] violate this saving definition. Yet even at the outset it was so amended by those very persons who were compelled to reconsider it at Rimini that they admitted that they had been deceived by a different argument, because they had not understood that the Fathers’ judgment formed at Nicaea was contrary.

> [Note: Col. 0349C: Valesius: “contrary.” Vallicellian codex: “because they had not understood that the Fathers’ judgment formed at Nicaea was contrary.”]

> [Note: Col. 0349C: This celebrated passage has recently also been used by the distinguished Giovanni Battista Bartolus, educated at the University of Padua, formerly chief professor of canon law and now bishop of Feltre, in his apology for Honorius. Having established by weighty arguments that one of Honorius’s letters to Sergius had been falsified and corrupted, and that the other was wholly fabricated, he finally establishes by this testimony of Damasus and other pontiffs that those letters can derive no authority from the Sixth Synod. For he says that the definitions of a synod are one thing, and the judgment of bishops assembled in a synod another: namely, a judgment pronounced either against or apart from the commands of the Apostolic See. But it will be better to consult him, chapter 23 and following. [Col. 0349D]]

For no prejudice could arise from the number of those who gathered at Rimini, since it is established that neither the bishop of Rome, whose judgment was to be sought before all others, nor Vincent, who had preserved his priesthood unstained for so many years, nor other such persons, gave any assent to its decrees; especially since, as we have said, those very persons who seemed to have yielded under pressure later declared, upon better counsel, that the decrees displeased them.

[Col. 0349B] Hence your sincerity recognizes that this faith alone, founded at Nicaea upon Apostolic authority, must be retained with perpetual firmness; in it the Easterners who acknowledge themselves Catholic, together with us, and the Westerners glory. Nor do we think it far off that those who think otherwise—

> [Note: Col. 0349D: Theodoret has *alla nosountas* (“holding other diseased opinions”), which departs far from the Latin sense, though even this may be tolerated. So Photius, *Bibliotheca*, p. 552, Heschel edition: *ta Apollinariou nosountas* (“those holding the diseased opinions of Apollinaris”). Moreover, all acknowledge the passage to be corrupt and defective. Valesius therefore supplies it in Theodoret, book II, chapter 22: “that those who think otherwise, although by this very attempt they are alienated from our communion, may be stripped of the name of bishops, and that their peoples…”]

although by this very attempt they may be stripped of communion with us, their peoples, freed from errors, may breathe again. For how will they be able to correct the errors of peoples if error itself has besieged them?

> [Note: Col. 0349D: Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*: “Since a bishop is appointed in the Church for the purpose of restraining the people from error, how great will error be among the people when the one who teaches is himself in error?”]

Therefore let the judgment of your charity accord with that of all God’s bishops. As we believe you to be fixed and strengthened in it, so we too must think rightly with you—

> [Note: Col. 0349D: Read “must,” on the authority of Valesius. Synodal letters were sent for the purpose of seeking the consent of bishops throughout the world, so that, once that consent had been determined, the defined doctrine might acquire unshakable force. This consent was usually requested in explicit words; but the manner of requesting it which Damasus uses here is more in keeping with Christian humility. Thus the Synod of Ancyra, assembled in 358, says: “Therefore we pray again and again, venerable lords and colleagues, that after reading this letter you signify both that the faith handed down to us by our elders is dear to your hearts and that you think and profess the same with us.” Coustantius’s emendation and interpretation therefore do not please me. The recent biographer of Jerome, printed at Ancona, asserts that Damasus sent these letters to the Illyrians in 382 for no other reason, evidently, than to attribute them to his Jerome. [Col. 0350C]]

—and approve it by reciprocal letters from your Holiness.

I, Sabinus—

> [Note: Col. 0350C: Since Sabinus, a deacon of the Church of Milan, brought to the Easterners only this letter, which was otherwise sent to the Illyrians, it is clear that the fragments that follow are later than this embassy of his. Quesnellus, note on Leo, Epistle 14: he says it was most customary that when Roman pontiffs wrote to a synod or to certain bishops concerning a matter of some importance, they did so through one of their own persons especially appointed for this purpose, and not through another cleric. This single example at least refutes that assertion. [Col. 0350D]]

—deacon of Milan, delegate, have supplied this from the authentic copy. [Col. 0349C]

## Fragments of Letter II, or an Exposition of the Faith Published in a Roman Synod under Pope Damasus and Sent to the East

[Col. 0350A]

### Notice

These two fragments belong to other synods held under Damasus, as I have already said. Coustantius also saw this, as did the distinguished Fr. Joseph Mansi, *Supplement to the Councils*, vol. I, p. 234; but we do not calculate the dates of those synods in the same way. For the synod which I judge to be the first of all, and believe assembled in 369, he, along with Pagi, thinks was gathered in 372. Then, whereas I establish two synods from these two fragments—the one in 374 and the other in 376 or the following year—he considers there was only one, and says that these fragments belong to it, it having assembled in 377.

But although the authority of this most learned man is, as it ought to be, very great with me, [Col. 0350B] I nevertheless judged that nothing in what I had already written should be altered. For since the Easterners, to whom the letters written by those Roman councils had already been brought, could not convene their own synods amid those dreadful and turbulent times under Valens, as soon as his death made it possible they assembled in 379. In a numerous gathering they read all those synodal letters, embraced the doctrines defined in them, and inserted into the acts of that council the excerpts from them which appeared necessary (see chapter 14). This is why I have not thought that these fragments should be separated, even though they were written at different times.

## First Fragment

### Likewise, from Part of the Decree

[Col. 0350C]

I. By that grace, brothers, that Jericho—

> [Note: Col. 0350D: Ambrose imitates this in *On the Faith*, book V, chapter 4: “He did not lead mailed ranks into battle, nor with a battering-ram and the other engines of war, but by the sound of the trumpets of seven priests he cast down the enclosing walls of the enemy.” Likewise Sixtus III represented in pictures, which still survive, in the Liberian basilica the Nestorian heresy overthrown by the Council of Ephesus as the city of Jericho collapsing when the Ark was carried around it and priestly trumpets sounded. Ciampini, *Ancient Monuments*, p. 75, plate 43, p. 223.]

—which is a figure of worldly pleasures, has fallen with a shout and does not [Col. 0351A] rise again, because with one mouth we speak of the Godhead as of one power, one majesty, one divinity, one *ousia* [essence]; so that, while asserting an inseparable power, we nevertheless affirm three persons—not returning into itself or diminished, as many blaspheme, but always remaining.

> [Note: Col. 0351C: In this passage and these very words you read the heresy attributed to Marcellus of Ancyra expressly stated and condemned, but his name left untouched, contrary to Basil’s request. For Basil had reported him to Damasus, charging that he wrongly understood the appellation “Word,” and admitted that the Only-Begotten was indeed called the Word, proceeding for use and for a time, but returning again to him from whom he had proceeded. And, again, at another time Basil accused Paulinus of Antioch of leaning toward the doctrines of Marcellus: “You know,” he says, “that our hope is overthrown by the doctrine of Marcellus, who does not confess the Son in a proper hypostasis, but says that he flowed forth and returned again to him from whom he had proceeded.” But see chapter 7.]

Nor do we affirm certain grades of power or unequal periods of origin; nor a “prolated” Son, so as to take generation from him; nor an imperfect Son, as though the Father’s nature or the fullness of divinity might be lacking to him in respect of his person; nor a Son unlike in works, unlike in power, or unlike in every respect. He does not subsist from another source, but is born of God; he is not false from the true God, but true God begotten from true God, true light from true light, lest he be thought diminished or different. The Only-Begotten possesses the radiance of the eternal light [Col. 0351B] because, by the order of nature, light cannot exist without radiance, nor can radiance exist without light; and he is the image of the Father, so that whoever sees him sees the Father also.

For the sake of our redemption, that same one came forth from the Virgin, so that a perfect man might be born for the perfect man who had sinned. Therefore, brothers, let us affirm that the Son of God assumed a perfect man—
