> [Note: Col. 0351C: The Apollinarians afterward admitted this; but, being consummate deceivers, by “man” they meant the man they had imagined for themselves, made perfect by divine perfection, the Word performing the function of a soul. This is clear from the faith which Vitalis professed in Epiphanius, *Heresy* 77, no. 23. When Damasus wrote this, therefore, this fraud of the heretics had not yet been discovered; but the deceit had become plain when the same pontiff wrote the letters to Paulinus concerning that same Vitalis. You see, then, that this fragment is earlier than those letters.]

—and let us confess that the Holy Spirit also is uncreated—

> [Note: Col. 0351D: Compare this with Basil’s Epistles 242 and 243, written at one and the same time and brought into the West through Dorotheus, and you will readily recognize that this very fragment replies to them and that Damasus and that synod directed their attention to the matters reported in them.]

—and of one majesty, one *ousia*, and one power with God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. For he who was sent forth to create is not deserving of the affront of being called a creature, as the holy prophet affirmed, saying: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created”; and another likewise says: “The divine Spirit who made me.” He is joined in the work and in the remission of sins.

This, most beloved brothers, [Col. 0352A] is our faith; whoever follows it shares with us. A mottled body disfigures its members. We grant communion to those—

> [Note: Col. 0351D: What is the point of this? We understand its purpose from Basil himself, Epistle 129. “It seemed to me,” he says, “that the subject was, as it were, untouched and offered occasion for a letter: that we should urge them—the Westerners, that is—not to receive into communion without judgment persons coming from the East; but that, after choosing one side once for all, they should admit the rest upon the testimony of those in communion, and should not assent to anyone drawing up a formula under the pretext of orthodox doctrine.” [Col. 0352C] He wrote this in 373, when the matter under discussion was sending Dorotheus to Rome again.]

—because (perhaps: “who approve our judgment,” or “who approve that judgment”) in all things approve the judgment. Far be it that pure faith should be patched together with diverse colours.

Furthermore, we warn that care must be taken lest canonical order be neglected in the ordination of priests or clerics, or communion too readily granted to those who transgress it, so that encouragement may be given to sin in other matters.

> [Note: Col. 0352C: What the Easterners had brought forward is rightly returned to them by the Westerners. For the violation of the canons in the East in this affair was such that bishops in those regions could in turn be justly and properly reproved by the Westerners.]

These, therefore, were the matters to be communicated from our judgment. But as concerns removing the wrongs suffered by your belovedness, neither our brother Dorotheus the presbyter can explain everything, passing over many matters in silence, nor have our efforts (read: *nisus*, “endeavours”), as he himself testifies, been lacking.

> [Note: Col. 0352C: See, if you please, chapter 9. What plan the Westerners adopted to assist the Easterners is obscure. Tillemont thinks that they resolved to send some leading bishops from among themselves into the East, and reasonably infers this from the second letter of the Council of Aquileia, in which the Westerners say that public disturbances prevented them from carrying out their contemplated journey (*Life of Ambrose*, article 11). But since these final words plainly prove, unless I am mistaken, that if any scheme for bringing aid to the Easterners’ affairs was devised, it must chiefly be credited to Damasus’s counsel, there is likewise no reason why the learned man should attribute this praise to Ambrose alone and rashly declare that the Roman pontiff seems to have had no part in that deliberation. [Col. 0352D]]

## Fragment II

### Likewise, from Part of the Decree

[Col. 0352B]

We are indeed astonished that some among our own [Note: [Col. 0352D] Basil, on Apollinaris, Epistle 265: “What afflicted us most was that he seemed from the beginning to be one of us.” Nazianzen also, in an iambic poem against the same man: “What say you, most vehement champion of the Word, to whom those who divide the Godhead are grievous?” The Apollinarians loved to make much display of their orthodox faith concerning the Trinity, although, as Nyssenus reproaches them in the *Antirrheticus*, they surpassed even the Arians in impiety in this respect also.] are said to be persons who, although they seem to hold a pious understanding concerning the Trinity, nevertheless, being ignorant of the powers and Scriptures of the mystery of our salvation, do not think rightly. For they maintain that our Lord and Savior assumed from the Virgin Mary an incomplete human being—that is, one without a mind. Alas! How close, under such an opinion, will they be to the Arians! The Arians assert incomplete divinity in the Son of God; these persons falsely assert incomplete humanity in the Son of Man. But if an incomplete human being was indeed assumed, then God’s gift is incomplete [Note: [Col. 0352D] All the Fathers afterward employed this argument; but Ambrose seems to imitate this passage of Damasus in his work to Sabinus: “Let them confess that, as in the form of God nothing was lacking to him of the divine nature and fullness, so in that form of man nothing was lacking to him by which he might be judged an incomplete man—he who came in order to save the whole human being. For it was not fitting that he who had completed a perfect work in others should allow it to be incomplete in himself. For if anything was lacking to him, he did not redeem the whole; if he did not redeem the whole, then he deceived when he said that he came in order to save the whole human being.” Epistle 46, in the Benedictine edition.]; our salvation is incomplete, because [Col. 0353A] the whole human being has not been saved. And where then will be that saying of the Lord: “The Son of Man came to save that which had wholly perished”? That is, in soul and body, in mind, and in the entire substance of his nature. Therefore, if the whole human being had perished, it was necessary that that which had perished should be saved. But if he was saved without a mind, then, contrary to the faith of the Gospel, that which had perished will be found not to have been wholly saved, since the Savior himself says elsewhere: “You are angry with me because I have made the whole human being whole” [Note: [Col. 0353D] See the preceding note.].

Moreover, the chief offense itself and the whole sum of ruin consist in the human mind [Note: [Col. 0353D] The Apollinarians first denied a soul to Christ; then they conceded a soul, but one such as belongs to brute animals—namely, without reason and mind; finally, they seemed even to concede a mind, but by that term they understood nothing other than the divinity itself [Col. 0354D] performing the office of mind. This Damasian fragment therefore belongs to the year 376 or the following year; for this absurd and latest invention of Apollinaris, which is refuted here, had scarcely begun to be heard and spread abroad in 375. See what I have said in chapters 10 and 11.]. For unless the human mind’s capacity for choosing good and evil had first perished, the human being would not have died. How, then, could it be supposed that at the end that which is known to have sinned before all else ought by no means to be saved? But we, who know that we have been saved whole and [Col. 0353B] complete, profess, according to the confession of the Catholic Church, that the perfect God assumed the perfect human being. Therefore take care that, through the understanding of sound doctrine, the minds also of those who do not yet believe that the mind has been saved may be saved.

## ALSO FROM THE DECREE

No ability is available to us by which our labor could bring you even slight refreshment. Yet, most blessed brothers, you may derive great consolation from this: that, knowing the integrity of our faith, you may glory that you agree in one mind, and may sufficiently and abundantly—as is fitting—be assured that we are solicitous for the members.

For, preserving in every respect inviolate the faith of the Nicene Council [Col. 0353C], without feigned words or a corrupted meaning, we by no means separate the Holy Spirit; rather, we confess him to be perfect in every respect—in power, honor, majesty, and Godhead—with the Father and the Son. Thus we also confidently hold that the fullness of God the Word—not uttered forth, but begotten, nor remaining in the Father so as not to exist, but subsisting from eternity unto eternity—assumed and saved a perfect, that is, whole, human being.

Here ends this letter, or exposition, of the Roman synod held under Pope Damasus and sent to the East; in which the whole Eastern Church, having held a synod at Antioch, believing in harmonious faith and all assenting thus to the faith set forth above, each confirms it by his own subscription.

[Note: [Col. 0354D] Why, however, do they subscribe “having determined” (*horisantes*) rather than in the manner customary in councils? Was it because matters already defined by the Apostolic See were under consideration? This indeed seems to me entirely so.]

Meletius, bishop of Antioch: I assent to everything written above, believing and thinking thus; and if anyone thinks otherwise than these things, let him be anathema.

Eusebius, bishop of Samosata: I assent to everything written above, believing and thinking thus; and if anyone thinks otherwise than these things, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0354A] Pelagius, bishop of Laodicea: I assent to everything written above, thinking and believing thus; and if anyone thinks otherwise than these things, let him be anathema.

Zeno, bishop of Tyre: I believe and have subscribed as above.

Eulogius, bishop of Edessa: Likewise I believe and have subscribed.

Bematius, of the city of Mallo: Likewise I believe and have subscribed.

Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus: As above, and I have subscribed.

Likewise, another 146 Eastern bishops subscribed, whose subscription is today preserved as an authentic document in the archives of the Roman Church.

Here ends the Roman and Antiochene Synod.

# LETTER III. OF DAMASUS, POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME, TO PAULINUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ANTIOCH

[Col. 0354B]

## NOTICE

Why I have separated this from the other letter of Damasus to Paulinus, unlike Holstenius, Quesnellus, and Coustantius, I shall not repeat, since I have already said so. Holstenius, however, made no decision on this question, but published it as he found it copied in his manuscript. Quesnellus, on the other hand, treated Holstenius’s manuscript, though disordered and confused, as authoritative; and he was the first to judge that both should be printed together as if one letter joined to the other.

Besides the authority of Holstenius’s manuscript and his own, he adduces this as his chief reason: since Damasus writes to Paulinus that he has sent him a confession of faith, he must mean one wholly other than that contained in the same letter—namely, a confession separate from that letter. But what other confession can we understand here except that which is immediately appended to the same letter?

Yet how weak this argument is, the very reading of the letter clearly proves. For since it expresses the doctrines to which it orders Vitalis and his party to subscribe, and consequently lacks nothing whatever for the complete overthrow of the Apollinarian heresy—the only matter then under consideration—there is no need to say that another formula was appended to it, one wholly unnecessary and, besides, apparently entirely irrelevant to that question. Nor shall I seek any other witness to this judgment than Damasus himself. After setting forth in this same letter all the conditions by which Vitalis [Col. 0354D] and others could be received into communion, he finally says that those who subscribe to this letter without any ambiguity are to be received. From this it is most plainly clear, unless I am mistaken, that no other conditions were either appended by him or required, besides those which he stated in that same letter.

[Col. 0355A] I also compared manuscripts for the sake of this question, including two older than the rest. One is from the Dionysian collection, supplied by the then most devout and learned abbot Besozzi—now cardinal penitentiary of the Holy Roman Church—from the monastery of Holy Cross in the Sessorian district, no. 225. The other, in the Vallicellian library, was written in the age of Nicholas I, shelf-mark A. V. From them I discovered two things.

First, this letter concerning Vitalis stands entirely alone, that is, separated from the other called the Confession of Damasus. The former manuscript contains it as the only one of all Damasus’s letters, after which follows the decretal of Siricius to Himerius. The Vallicellian manuscript first gives the same pope’s anathemas under this title: “Confession of the Catholic Faith, which Pope Damasus sent to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch”; then, in another and later place, it recites this letter, which concerns Vitalis, under this heading: “Here begins the reply of Pope Damasus to Jerome’s request, to Bishop Paulinus.” Other manuscripts of similar character could be produced.

The second observation is that each manuscript is fuller than the printed books, by an entire passage in which the “Lordly man” (*homo dominicus*), mentioned by Rufinus, is set forth and which is absent from the editions. I have therefore followed these manuscripts, as well as Isidore Mercator, Baronius, and Sarazanius, and have published this letter separately from that called Damasus’s Confession, or Rule of Faith. Other reasons also moved me to do this; since I have given them in chapters 10 and 15, where there was occasion to discuss the circumstances and time of composition, I shall not repeat them here, though I shall add some further points in the notes.

## LETTER

Damasus to his most beloved brother Paulinus.

[Col. 0356A]

Through my son Vitalis [Note: [Col. 0355C] Vitalis therefore does not yet seem to have been elevated to the episcopate when Damasus wrote these things.] I had sent writings to you [Note: [Col. 0355C] Quesnellus notes this in Dissertation 14, no. 10, and draws from it I know not what conclusion, whatever it may be, of no weight. For in one and the same letter Damasus often refers to himself both in the plural and in the singular. See the letter to Acholius and the letter to the Easterners.], leaving all things to your will and judgment. Through the presbyter Petronius I had also briefly indicated that, at the very point of his departure, I had been moved to some extent.

Therefore, lest either a scruple should remain with you, or your prudence should defer approving those who perhaps wish to be joined to the Church, we have sent a confession of faith—not so much to you, who share fellowship in the same faith, as to those who, subscribing to it, may wish to be joined to you—that is, through you to us—most beloved brother [Note: [Col. 0355C] The Council of Chalcedon, Part III, chapter 1: “Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome and ornament of justice, in letters sent to Paulinus, disclosed the mysteries of the dispensation, warning that those who wished to participate in his communion should assent to the matters well decreed.”].

Accordingly, if my aforesaid son Vitalis, and [Note: [Col. 0355C] Namely, those Antiochenes placed under his direction by Apollinaris. See Sozomen, book VI, chapter 25. This was always the spirit of the Church: to embrace again the leaders of heretics and schismatics if they restored to unity and faith the brothers and children torn away from them. See Tertullian, *On Prescription*, chapter 30; Cyprian, Epistle 64, to Antonianus.] those who are with him, wish to be united with you, they must first subscribe to that exposition of faith which was established [Col. 0356B] at Nicaea by the pious will of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0355D] Perhaps the Eastern synod under John of Antioch referred to this in these words: “We understand the exposition of the Nicene faith as did the bishops before us—Damasus, Innocent, Ambrose, and others in the West.” See the Synodical Letter against the Tragedy of Irenaeus, chapter 197. Thus both parties—the Catholics and the Apollinarians—appealed to the Nicene Creed: the Catholics, to show that God was like us, namely endowed with mind and soul. See Leo the Great, Epistle 134, Lyons edition. Apollinaris, however, did so in order to establish his heavenly man who descended from heaven and was composed of flesh as well as of the Word. See Ambrose among the testimonies of the Fathers cited by Leo the Great, Epistle 134, Lyons edition; Nyssenus, *Antirrheticus*, chapters 9–10; Nazianzen, Letter to Cledonius, §§8 and 23.].

Then, because no one can apply a remedy to wounds still to come, the heresy that is said afterward to have sprung up in the East must be uprooted: that is, it must be confessed that Wisdom itself, the Word, the Son of God, assumed a human body, soul, mind—that is [Note: [Col. 0355D] Eusebius of Vercelli, in his letter to the Antiochenes from the Alexandrian synod: “Having assumed everything without sin, such as our old human being is constituted.” Athanasius, *On Salvation against Christ*, book II, chapter 10: “We have learned that the second Adam possessed both soul and body, and the whole first Adam.” So too the other Greek and Latin Fathers, whom it would take too long to cite.], the whole Adam—and, to say it more explicitly, our whole old human being without sin.

For just as, when we confess that he assumed a human body, we do not thereby also attach to him the passions of human vices [Note: [Col. 0356C] This chief argument of Apollinaris is reported by Fabricius from an English Greek manuscript containing the pseudo-questions of Apollinaris and Basil’s responses: “If Christ had a human mind, he also suffered from forgetfulness and ignorance and could commit sin.” Basil: “Certainly, unless he was united to divinity.” *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. VIII, p. 101. Athanasius himself sets before himself this objection received from the heretics: “For if he assumed this mind, he will also be subject to the prince of wickedness and will not be free from sin.” *On Salvation against Christ*, II, chapter 3. But these words are found in Dialogue 6 against the Apollinarians, among the works attributed to Theodoret, vol. V, p. 388.], so also, when we say that he assumed both a human soul and a human mind, we do not thereby say that he was subject to the sin of human thoughts [Note: [Col. 0356C] Athanasius again, chapter 6: “But you object: ‘If he assumed everything, then surely he had human thoughts; but it is impossible for human thoughts not to contain sin.’” See also Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, book V, chapters 11–12. Yet, as Nyssenus elegantly answered, in taking our filth upon himself he was not polluted by its defilements, but purified filth in himself. “For the light shone in darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.” *Antirrheticus*, chapter 26. At this place Vallicellian manuscript no. 18 and the manuscript of Holy Cross contain after the word *sin* the words which I have said are lacking in the printed editions: “Whatever it is that our Savior feared to assume from humanity, he will not save; or, if it was so insuperable an evil that he feared to assume it, why did he place it in the human being whom he himself created, and avoid it in the human being he assumed? Therefore the Lordly human being was rational and intelligible—what the Greeks call *noeros* (νοερός).” This reasoning is familiar to the Fathers. See John of Damascus, works, vol. I, pp. 228 and 240.].

But if anyone says that the Word functioned in the Lord’s flesh in place of a human mind, that person the Catholic Church anathematizes. [Col. 0357A] Likewise [Note: [Col. 0357C] Arnobius, drawing this from the earlier letter to Paulinus, recites it thus: “We anathematize those who confess two sons in the Savior, one before the Incarnation and another after the flesh was assumed from the Virgin; and who do not confess that the same Son of God is both before and after, the true Son of God, Christ himself, who was born from the Virgin.” Ambrose, *On the Incarnation*, chapter 6, also refers to this, unless I am mistaken: “We must condemn those who say that the Son of God is not one and the same, but that one was born from God and another was begotten from the Virgin.” Compare these words with anathema 6 of the other letter to the same Paulinus, and consider whether it can be that in one and the same writing Damasus repeats the very matter in the same words—which those who posit only one letter to Paulinus must nevertheless concede. For this reason, according to Coustantius, the Corbie manuscript omitted the second anathema to avoid that faulty repetition, unlike the Holstenian and Quesnellian manuscripts.] we anathematize those who confess two sons in the Savior—that is, one before the Incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin—and who do not confess the same Son of God both before and afterward.

Whoever wishes to subscribe to this letter, provided that he has first subscribed to the ecclesiastical canons, which you know very well, and to the Nicene faith, you must receive without any ambiguity. Not because you could not set before converts, for their reception, these very things which we write; but because our agreement grants you a free precedent in receiving them [Note: [Col. 0357D] Vallicellian manuscript: “authority.”].

# LETTER IV. CONFESSION OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH WHICH POPE DAMASUS SENT TO PAULINUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

## NOTICE

[Col. 0357B]

This is the other of the extant letters of Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch, and I have already given the reasons why it must be separated from the former. Yet I again wish to note that Theodoret attached it in Greek translation to his *History*, and presented it separately from the former, book V, chapter 11. Why, then, did he not recite it in full, if Damasus had joined both in such a way that one was an inseparable part of the other? Did he perhaps judge that what was written concerning Vitalis could in no way pertain to ecclesiastical history? Who would even suspect this? Or did he rather think Vitalis should be spared? Yet in book V, chapter 4, he by no means conceals that man’s heresy.

It remains, therefore, that the letter had already come to Theodoret mutilated and divided. But what benefit was there in this tearing apart and corruption of an entire letter, especially when the time was so close and copies so plentiful? It should therefore be held established and certain that Damasus sent not one letter divided into two parts, but two separate letters to Paulinus.

Moreover, that this letter of which we speak was continuously celebrated and received with highest approval is clear from the writers who mention it and treat it as authoritative: Celestine [Col. 0358A] and Vigilius, Ambrose, the ancient author of Sermon 129 *On the Seasons*, formerly attributed to Augustine and now relegated to the appendix, volume V, Sermon 233, where several of its anathemas are cited; Arnobius the Younger, Isidore in the Code of Canons of the Spanish Church, Paulinus of Aquileia, the Council of Troyes, and others thereafter. Among Greeks, omitting the more recent writers, there are Theodoret, as well as—so I think—the Council of Constantinople and Nazianzen.

Since, therefore, it was often copied for this reason, the reading of the manuscripts could not fail now to vary, whether by accident, rashness, or each copyist’s inclination. Besides the examples I have observed, Peter Coustantius has given more than one from the manuscripts he examined with his exceptional diligence. In this edition [Col. 0358B] I have therefore followed his exemplar, both because it more closely approaches the Greek transmitted to us by Theodoret and because it more closely approaches Quesnellus’s text. In my judgment these are the two streams nearest to the source and for that reason more easily the purer. For anyone wishing to consult and report all the manuscripts, since their number is immense, must either undertake an excessive and unnecessary labor or be uncertain in judgment which of them to choose—although I have sometimes used the Vallicellian manuscript because it was at hand.

## CONFESSION OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 73, calls this a book *On Faith*, against heretics.]

After the Council of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0357D] In Trithemius the beginning of this dogmatic statement is: “Because after the Council of Nicaea”; and [Col. 0358C] so we also read in Theodoret. This reading seems truer to me, for the words prefixed in other printed and manuscript copies have more the appearance of an opening added by copyists. Indeed, the Roman synod itself, which I said was convened in 380, is the very synod which, according to Vigilius, added to the Nicene Council those things which, as Nazianzen says in his second letter to Cledonius, had been stated less fully and which concern the Holy Spirit. For in the earlier councils under Damasus, the statements concerning the same Holy Spirit [Col. 0358D] are neither as precise nor as complete as these, nor do they have added anathemas against every individual blasphemy of the Pneumatomachians.], when a council had assembled in the city of Rome from Catholic bishops, they added something concerning the Holy Spirit. And because afterward an error grew up, such that some persons with sacrilegious mouth dared to say [Col. 0358C] that the Holy Spirit was made through the Son [Note: [Col. 0358D] These are the words of Eunomius in the *Apology*, first published by Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. VIII, p. 297: “Made indeed by the command of the Father, but by the operation of the Son.” To this belongs the passage of Simon of Constantinople in Allatius, *Against Hottinger*, p. 503: “In letters sent to Paulinus of Antioch, Damasus writes that an addition was made to the synodal decree in the holy Nicene Creed to overthrow the blasphemy of those who maintained that the Son was also the Father.”]:

I. We anathematize those who do not proclaim with complete freedom that the Holy Spirit is of one power and substance with the Father and the Son.

II. We also anathematize those who follow Sabellius’s error [Note: [Col. 0358D] We read that there were in fact no Sabellians at that time, but we know that many were called so by the Easterners through calumny and suspicion. On this point the presbyter Faustinus complained in the *Memorial of Faith*, which we read in Quesnellus’s Code of Canons, chapter 38, as did that Gregory whose Oration 49 is among the works of Nazianzen [Col. 0359B]. For this reason Paulinus of Antioch, his adherents, and almost all Westerners were commonly attacked because they did not speak of three hypostases. Damasus perhaps intended by this promulgated anathema to destroy that calumny. It was also the reason why Athanasius and the other Fathers of the Alexandrian synod decreed that Sabellius’s foolishness should be branded with anathema: “if this is done, every suspicion among all people will cease.”], saying that the Father is the same as the Son.

[Col. 0359A] III. We anathematize Arius and Eunomius, who, with equal impiety though in different language, maintain that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures.

IV. We anathematize the Macedonians [Note: [Col. 0359B] Before the year 380, when this dogmatic statement was promulgated, you will nowhere find the name “Macedonians” used. For they had not yet again withdrawn from the Church—to which they seemed to have returned under Liberius—by an open schism, nor had they again repudiated the Nicene Council, which, as I have said in chapter 15, happened only in 379. They were of two kinds: some thought rightly concerning the Son but wrongly concerning the Holy Spirit; others professed both forms of Arian heresy. Damasus therefore refers here [Col. 0359C] to the latter, who, coming from the Arian stock, had changed not their perfidy but their name, as Epiphanius also calls them. But let us hear Epiphanius himself, *Heresy* 74, §1: “From these Semi-Arians and Orthodox arose a certain monster of two-formed and half-wild men. Some, indeed, proceeding from the Arian stock, determine that the Son is not absolutely a creature but was begotten without time . . . Yet they in no way depart from that former opinion which Arius vomited forth . . . and then they speak blasphemously concerning the Holy Spirit.” The author of the Dialogues republished by Garnerius in the supplement to Theodoret’s works also distinguishes both Macedonian parties, speaking differently against the former and against the others.], who come from the stock of Arius and have changed not their perfidy but their name.

V. We anathematize Photinus, who, restoring the heresy of Ebion [Note: [Col. 0359C] Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapters 3 and 7: “Ebion—that is Photinus.”], confesses the Lord Jesus Christ only as being from Mary.

VI. We anathematize those who assert two Sons [Note: [Col. 0359C] Celestine recites this anathema as follows: “We anathematize those who assert two Sons of God, one begotten of the Father before the ages, [Col. 0359D] and the other born from the assumption of flesh from the Virgin.” Apollinaris had, by gross calumny, charged the Catholics with this doctrine because they asserted two perfectly united natures in Christ Jesus. Under this pretext he tried to bolster his own heresy by the appearance of so absurd an opinion. This is clear from passages cited by Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, book VII, chapter 2; and Damasus himself heard this calumny being circulated, with Acacius, bishop of Beroea, present. Apollinaris said: “If perfect God is united to perfect man, they would surely be two, not one.” Nyssenus, *Antirrheticus*, chapters 35, 39, and 42: “If perfect God is joined to a human being—perfect, of course, to perfect—they would surely be two: one Son of God by nature, the other by adoption.” By this promulgated anathema the same pope judged that the calumny must be removed from the Catholics. Nazianzen afterward plainly imitated its pattern in his first letter to Cledonius, writing: “If anyone introduces two Sons, one from [Col. 0360A] God and the Father and the other from the Mother, rather than one and the same, let him also fall away from that adoption as sons [Col. 0360B] promised to those who believe rightly.” Again, in his second letter to Cledonius: “Affirm this also to everyone concerning us: we unite the Son of God, first begotten from the Father and then from the holy Virgin Mary, and do not call him two sons but one and the same, whom we worship in his invisible divinity,” etc. Athanasius, Epiphanius, Ambrose, and the other Fathers of those times also repudiate this slander against the Catholic Church; and from this we understand with what zeal it had been spread abroad and repeated by the Apollinarians. Eutyches, a deranged old man, took this calumny along with the heresy from Apollinaris and again brought it forward against Catholics; and after him the Monophysites, Monothelites, and whatever other shoot from that virulent root infected the Church. Therefore the Emperor Marcian, writing to the Alexandrian monks, professes: “The same one is truly both God and man—not one and another, far be it, but one and the same. We too abhor and anathematize as God-fighters those who say or have said that there are two Sons or two persons.” I shall publish below in full, from Ottobonian manuscript 29, folio 415, recently transferred with the rest to the Vatican through the favor of the most holy Pope Benedict XIV—born to advance and illuminate sacred learning—that Greek letter, most of which had escaped the diligence of the very great men to whom we owe the collection of councils. From the same manuscript is copied the beginning of another letter as well, namely to Macarius the bishop and the monks of Sinai, which is absent from that collection. See vol. IV, Venetian edition, pp. 1792–1793.]: one before the ages and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin.

[Col. 0360A] VII. We anathematize those who say that the Word, the Son of God, functioned in human flesh in place of a rational and intelligent human soul [Note: [Col. 0360C] Nazianzen writes in his second letter to Cledonius that the crafty profession of faith offered at Rome by Vitalis was annulled and pierced through by Damasus’s anathema, and that all who persisted in the deceitful exposition were at the same time excluded from the Church. But whether he indicates this passage or the similar passage stated in the earlier letter to Paulinus, see under the year 375.], although the Son himself is the Word of God and was not in his body in place of a rational and intelligent soul, but assumed and saved our soul—that is, an intelligent soul—without sin.

VIII. We anathematize those who contend that the Word, the Son of God, is separate from the Father by extension or contraction, is without substance, and will have an end.

IX. We likewise hold as separated from our communion those who have migrated from churches to churches [Note: [Col. 0360D] Quesnellus thinks this anathema and the next were falsely and fraudulently attached to Damasus by Paulinus of Antioch, so that he might overcome Meletius, his rival in the episcopate. But what a reckless judgment, wholly unworthy of a man who claimed to champion stricter discipline! Theodoret, certainly, did not detect that alleged fraud when he retained the same anathemas, although he so valued Meletius himself and his successor that he pursued every opportunity, certain or uncertain, to praise them. Theodoret was not so far removed from the time when the events occurred that he could not easily have seen, detected, and exposed the trick, had he wished—as Quesnellus, so many centuries later, enjoys this glory unimpaired. Moreover, if this dogmatic statement was written and promulgated by the Roman synod which had already confirmed the concord made between Meletius and Paulinus, as seemed to me in chapter 15, you now see what becomes of Quesnellus’s fantasies. For these anathemas can neither seem false nor suspect; rather, Damasus added them out of his constant concern for ecclesiastical order, that he might restore discipline in this matter which, according to Athanasius and others, had fallen apart throughout the East. Finally, from this you may readily conclude how unfair and embittered was that writer of condemned memory toward a bishop who had deserved extremely well of religion and was most observant of the Apostolic See.], until they return to those cities in which they were first established. But if, when one has moved elsewhere, another has been ordained in his place during his lifetime, the one who abandoned his own city shall remain deprived of priestly rank until his successor rests in peace.

X. If anyone does not say that the Son always exists and that the Holy Spirit always exists, let him be anathema.

XI. If anyone does not say that the Son was begotten of the Father—that is, of his very divine substance—let him be anathema.

XII. If anyone does not say that the Word of the Lord, the Son of God, is God as his Father is God, and is able to do all things, knows all things, and is equal to the Father, let him be anathema.

XIII. If anyone says that, when the Son of God was present in the flesh [Col. 0362A] and was on earth, he was not in heaven with the Father, let him be anathema.

XIV. If anyone says that in the passion of the cross [Note: [Col. 0361B] Gelasius recites this chapter among the testimonies of the Fathers concerning the two natures in these words: “If anyone says that in the passion of the cross God the Son of God suffered pain, and not the flesh with its soul, which he put on in the form of a servant and assumed for himself, as Scripture says, let him be anathema.” Theodoret repeats the same chapter in Dialogue 3; Valesius observes that the wording there more nearly approaches Damasus’s Latin exemplar than the wording he cites in the *History*. He also cites it a third time in Letter 144 to Militias: “Let them also hear the much-discussed Damasus, bishop of Rome, crying aloud: ‘If anyone says that in the cross the Godhead endured pain, and not the body with its soul—the form of a servant which he assumed complete—let him be anathema.’” Vallicellian manuscript no. 18 seems to correct the text thus: “If anyone says that in the passion of the cross God the Son of God endured pain, and not the flesh with its soul, which he had put on in the form of a servant and had taken to himself.” Yet this had been the ancient Christian way of speaking, confirmed even by the Nicene Creed: that God for our sake suffered, was crucified, and died. All the Fathers, both during Damasus’s life and afterward, used it; Petavius collects them in *On the Incarnation*, book IV, chapters 15–16. If that class of people who recently harassed and still secretly harass the Church had lived in Damasus’s age, they would have gathered their incoherent cries from every side and shouted that the Roman pontiff was destroying the faith, asserting the impiety of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, and paving the way for the Nestorian heresy. Yet Damasus did not regard those Fathers as heretics, nor did they call Damasus a heretic; on the contrary, they praised him precisely for this reason. From this you understand that statements which are true in a Catholic sense, yet in view of the circumstances of the times and of those by whom they are uttered, may not merely be capable of prohibition by the Church but ought to be prohibited, lest error—which, as Irenaeus says in book I, preface, does not show itself according to its own nature but, craftily adorned, makes itself appear truer—deceive the inexperienced by its outward appearance. For Arius and Apollinaris abused that expression and blasphemed that divinity itself was subject to suffering: the former, in order to prove that the Son was less than the Father and a creature (Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book X, chapter 9); the latter, in order to establish his mixture of Flesh and Word, as is clear from Nyssenus in the *Antirrheticus* and others too numerous to cite in vain.] God the Son endured pain, and not the flesh with its soul, in which he had put on the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0361D] This seems not to have been said by chance. For Apollinaris could not endure the claim that our Lord Jesus undertook servitude for us by assuming that body, since he maintained that the Word and the Flesh were of one substance. Ambrose, Epistle 46 to Sabinus.], which he had taken to himself, as Scripture says, let him be anathema.

XV. If anyone does not say that he sits at the right hand of the Father in the flesh which he assumed, and in which he will come to judge the living and the dead, let him be anathema.

> **[Note: Col. 0362B]** Nazianzen repeats this anathema in different words in his First Letter to Cledonius: “If anyone should suppose that the holy Flesh has now been laid aside, and that the Divinity is bare and devoid of body, rather than that it both is and will come with the part which it assumed, let him not behold its glory when it is revealed.” He gives two reasons for promulgating this: first, to remove suspicion; secondly, to refute error. For there were some among Catholics who spoke so magnificently of the transformation of human nature for the better that they seemed to think that, once mortality had been laid aside, the human being was in some way absorbed into God, and that the distinction of the natures was removed after the Ascension. Among them were Nazianzen himself and Nyssen, whose statements may be read in Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, book III, chapter 4, and book X, chapter 1, and in Zaccagni’s preface to the *Antirrheticus*, chapter 21. Zaccagni excellently clears Nyssen of this stain in chapter 24. Nazianzen, however, frees himself from this suspicion; but the error at which he aims and which he refutes there was proper to Apollinarius and a necessary consequence of his heresy, which continually denied the two natures in Christ. Thus Apollinarius first said that the Flesh of Christ the Lord had been brought from heaven; afterward he sometimes admitted that it was consubstantial with ours, but brute and devoid of sensation. When he maintained the first opinion, he taught that, after the mystery of the dispensation had been accomplished, that flesh fell back into the divine nature from which it had been taken. When he admitted the second, he said either that the flesh had been laid aside or converted into God’s substance, and that no form of it remained. Eutyches, in the later century, also received this invention together with the entire heresy from his master Apollinarius. See Hardouin, *Selected Works on the Sacrament of the Altar*, chapters 6 and 7, where this is admirably explained.]

XVI. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly from the Father, as the Son is from the divine substance, and is true God, let him be anathema.

> **[Note: Col. 0362C]** Bryennius, in Allatius, *Against Hottinger*, p. 316, recites it thus: “If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly from the Father, as also the Son of God is from the divine substance, and God the Word, let him be anathema.” He took this from Theodoret, for the Latin copies have “true God” in place of “God the Word.” This and the following three anathemas concerning the Holy Spirit are directed against the impious theses of the Pneumatomachians, who denied that he is from the divine substance, that he can do all things or is everywhere present, or that he made all things together with the Son. Thus Eunomius, in his *Apology*, chapter 25, in Fabricius, *Greek Library*, vol. VIII: “He is worshipped in the third place because he surpasses the other works of the Only-Begotten in rank and dignity, lacking divinity and creative power but richly possessing the power of sanctifying and teaching.” See Athanasius, vol. I, pp. 794 and 881, edition of the *Greek Fathers*; Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 16 and following; and also Theodoret—or whoever he may be—in the *Dialogues against the Macedonians*, refuting each of these blasphemies in the *Supplement*.

XVII. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit can do all things, knows all things, and is everywhere, as are the Son and the Father, let him be anathema.

XVIII. If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a creature, or was made through the Son, let him be anathema.

XIX. If anyone does not say that the Father made all things through the Son and the Holy Spirit—that is, things visible and invisible—let him be anathema.

XX. If anyone does not say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity, power, majesty, might, one glory, dominion, kingdom, and one will and truth, let him be anathema.

> **[Note: Col. 0363B]** Aristenus mentions this anathema in Allatius, *Against Hottinger*, p. 504: “Likewise he anathematized those who do not proclaim with complete frankness that he is, together with the Father and the Son, of one authority and substance.” Eunomius blasphemously maintained that there could be no comparison of power, rule, and essence between the Son and the Holy Spirit on the one hand and the Father on the other; therefore he ascribed to the Father an incomparable preeminence of essence, power, and authority. As for whom this chapter and the following one additionally concern, I have stated this in chapter 18.

XXI. If anyone does not say that the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are true, equal, ever-living, containing all visible and invisible things, able to do all things, judging all things, giving life to all things, making all things, and saving all things that are to be saved, let him be anathema.

XXII. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped by every creature, as are the Son and the Father, let him be anathema.

> **[Note: Col. 0363C]** This and the following anathema strike at that other group of Macedonians who thought rightly concerning the Father and the Son but departed from the faith concerning the Holy Spirit. Their number was by no means small, as we learn from Epiphanius, Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen, and from Athanasius, *Works*, vol. I, p. 649. Nazianzen too addresses them, as though distinct and separate from another body of Macedonians, and not wholly dead and extinct, in gentle terms, *Oration* 37, §28. But here Damasus finally decrees that they must be anathematized and regarded as heretics, separating them from the Catholics, with whom they had been allied and mingled so long as Valens held power throughout the East; see chapter 15. Basil, Letter 128, may also be consulted on this matter. Hence we read in Socrates, book VII, chapter 7, that in the following year, when they were summoned to the First Council of Constantinople, they were already regarded as heretics.

XXIII. If anyone thinks rightly concerning the Father and the Son, but does not hold rightly concerning the Holy Spirit, he is a heretic; for all heretics who think wrongly concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are found in the unbelief of Jews and Gentiles.

> **[Note: Col. 0363D]** Other manuscripts read “because,” which is preferable. For whether one thinks wrongly of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, the result is the same: in either case one is a pagan and a Jew, because one denies the Trinity.

XXIV. If anyone permits God the Father, God his Son, and God the Holy Spirit to be called “gods,” and not “God,” despite the one divinity and power which we believe and know to belong to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; or if, by excluding the Son or the Holy Spirit, he so supposes that the Father alone is God as to call or believe him the one God: let him be anathema. For the name “gods” has been assigned and bestowed by God upon angels and all saints; but concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their one equal divinity, the name shown and declared to us is not “gods” but “God.” Thus we believe that we are baptized in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alone, and not in the names of archangels or angels, as heretics, Jews, and even mad Gentiles do. This, therefore, is the salvation of Christians: that, believing in the Trinity—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—we should without doubt believe that in it there is one true and only divinity, power, majesty, and the same substance, so that we may deserve to attain eternal life.

> **[Note: Col. 0363D]** This final chapter is obscure and confused through the carelessness or ingenuity of copyists. I therefore set before you the clearer and better reading which I copied from the Vallicellian manuscript, unless it bears the marks of a corrector’s hand:
>
> “If anyone permits God the Father, God his Son, and God the Holy Spirit to be called ‘gods,’ and not ‘God,’ because of the one divinity and power which we believe and know to belong to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; or if anyone, by excluding the Son or the Holy Spirit, so supposes that the Father alone is God as to call or believe him such: let him be anathema. For we read that the name ‘gods,’ in the plural, has been assigned and bestowed by God upon angels and holy human beings; but concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their one and equal divinity, the name shown and declared to us is not ‘gods’ but ‘God.’ Therefore we are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alone, and not in the names of archangels and angels, as heretics, Jews, and even mad Gentiles do. This, therefore, is the salvation of Christians: that, believing in the Trinity—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—we should without doubt believe in that true and only one divinity, power, majesty, and substance.”
>
> Moreover, it is clear from Basil, Letters 131 and 169, and Nazianzen, *Orations* 29 and 37, that Catholics were accused by Arians of being tritheists because they professed one divinity in the Trinity. Socrates relates, *Tripartite History*, book X, chapter 8, that, to revile the orthodox, Arians used to sing and resound at the gates, through the streets and porticoes, and in the midst of the city: “Where are those who say, ‘One by triple power’?” Modern Arians and Unitarians use this same calumny against Catholics of sound belief. See Crellius among the Lacroze letters, vol. I, p. 94.
>
> **Fragments of the Greek letter missing from the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon.**
>
> “And it cut off also the impiety of Nestorius.” Thus far the Greek copy; what now follows is missing.
>
> “It has preserved intact in every respect the venerable Creed of the 318 holy Fathers, neither harmed by diminution nor by addition. Our Serenity considers that our divine letters, and likewise the decrees already published in the great city of Alexandria, suffice to persuade those who, I know not how, even now remain doubtful that nothing novel has been introduced by the most holy and Catholic Synod, and that no one ought any longer to remain in doubt on this account. For we do not suppose that anyone could be so obstinate as, after encountering so many decrees which thus clearly proclaim the orthodox faith, still to persist in the same error.
>
> “But if there should be any such persons—which we do not think, in view of the benevolence innate in us—we wish them once again to be fully persuaded by our divine letters that the most holy and Catholic Synod has decreed everything in accordance with the teachings of the holy Fathers. It has destroyed the impiety of Eutyches, which Dioscorus and certain others followed—persons who did not hesitate to disseminate among the populace the books of Apollinarius under the names of most holy orthodox Fathers, so as completely to enslave the minds of the more simple to falsehood. It has confirmed the venerable Creed of the 318 holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, neither taking anything away from it nor adding anything, which our Serenity, having been baptized into it and having believed it from youth, holds and prays to remain in.
>
> “For we believe that our Master and Savior Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father, for us and for our salvation became human, being born of the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin, Mother of God; that he is truly both God and man, the same one, not one person and another—far be it—but one and the same, in no way divided, separated, or changed. Those who say or have said that there are two Sons or two persons, we too abhor and anathematize as fighters against God.
>
> “Having therefore learned these things yourselves, if any among you still persist in falsehood, make haste to return to truth, withdrawing yourselves from unlawful assemblies, lest you bring about the destruction of your souls and become subject to the penalties prescribed by the laws. But all of you unite yourselves with the orthodox of the most holy and Catholic Church, which is one, as the godly definitions of the holy Fathers teach us. By doing this, you will grant salvation to your own souls, do what pleases God the Master of all, and, by entrusting yourselves to our Serenity, enjoy its protection.
>
> “For this reason we have selected and sent John, the most illustrious decurion, who can accurately set forth the matters concerning the holy faith. He was present at the ecumenical and Catholic Synod of the holy bishops and clearly knows all that occurred there. Thus, having been fully informed in every respect, those who still hesitate—something we do not suppose—may at last return to the true and blameless faith.
>
> “Copy of the divine letters sent by the same person to Macarius, bishop and archimandrite, and to the other most devout monks on the holy mountain of Sinai.
>
> “No one at all, including your devoutness, is unaware how dangerously Theodosius innovates against the godly religion and the Roman commonwealth; if anyone finds punishment for his deeds, he is convicted. For he has come in advance, as the divine Scriptures foretell, of the expected coming of Antichrist—or, to speak more truly, has been sent by him to wage war upon the holy and orthodox faith,” etc.

## LETTER V. OF POPE DAMASUS TO ACHOLIUS AND THE OTHER BISHOPS OF MACEDONIA

**[Col. 0365A]**

After condemning the ordination of Maximus the Cynic, Damasus urges the Macedonians to ensure that a bishop worthy of that city be appointed at the synod soon to be held at Constantinople; he also urges observance of the enactments of the Fathers against the transfer of bishops.

To the most beloved brothers Acholius, Eurydicus, Severus, Uranius, Philip, and John: Damasus.

> **[Note: Col. 0366B]** Basnage thought these bishops Egyptian, in the year 380, §4; this is wholly absurd, for what had Acholius to do with Egyptians? Ambrose, I think, mentions several of them in his letter to Anysius, Acholius’s successor. See chapter 17.
>
> **[Note: Col. 0366B]** This and the following letter appear to belong to the number of the many letters which, according to Nicholas I, Letter 8, Damasus wrote to various persons in order to expel Maximus from Constantinople. Baronius regretted the loss of these letters under the year 380, §5 (Holstenius). Who, then, would not be astonished at Basnage’s rashness in accusing Nicholas of falsehood?

Having read the letter of your affection, dearest brothers, I was deeply grieved that, at the very time when, by God’s favor, heretics had been cast down, certain men coming from Egypt wished, upon a petition contrary to the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, to call to the priesthood in the city of Constantinople a Cynic foreign to our profession. What heat of mind, therefore, or what foul presumption this was, we cannot know.

> **[Note: Col. 0366C]** From this one may readily infer the time at which Maximus was unlawfully ordained and this letter written. It cannot have been before March in the consulship of Gratian and Theodosius, when the law *Cunctos populos, on the Catholic faith*, was promulgated and heretics could be called and regarded as dishonored and rejected.
>
> **[Note: Col. 0366C]** Nazianzen says that they had been sent by Peter of Alexandria, whom Damasus spares here. The Alexandrian prelate seems to have believed that the consecration of the bishop of Constantinople belonged to him. Theophilus certainly claimed it for himself, and Dioscorus once obtained it when Anatolius was consecrated.
>
> **[Note: Col. 0366C]** Constantius conjecturally emends: “without a petition.” Nazianzen supports this, saying that they placed the captive dog in the see before informing the flock and the leaders of the Church.

From this it appears that restless people, while presuming much, do not know what they ought to do. They had not read the Apostle writing, “If a man wears his hair long, it is a disgrace to him.” They did not know that the habit of philosophers was unsuited to Christian conduct. They had not heard the Apostle warning them lest, through philosophy and empty deception, they should be stripped of the garment of sound faith in which they had long believed.

> **[Note: Col. 0366D]** Socrates, book III, chapter 23, writes that, when Jovian assumed the imperial power, the philosophers laid aside the cloak and took up ordinary dress.

How great, then, was this haste, that, although this dress displeased Christians, the entire unseemly business was conducted so insolently? But what else could the recklessness of utterly frivolous men do, except, after they had been expelled from the Church, ordain this restless man, so far as may be understood, within other people’s walls?

> **[Note: Col. 0366D]** Nazianzen: “Immediately a crowd, many strangers and also bastards, flock together to the magistrate.
>
> “For all were there because of this crime. Why say more? They at once withdraw their feet from the church, grieving greatly that their undertaking had come to nothing.”
>
> **[Note: Col. 0366D]** Nazianzen: “Having entered the filthy house of the flute-player, and with some of the dregs of the lowest populace present, they mark the dog, his hair cut, as bishop.” The letter of the pseudo-Italian council says that Maximus was taken aside into a private house by his ordainers because the Arians possessed the basilicas.
>
> **[Note: Col. 0366D]** Nazianzen: “Not by force, nor while bound; for the dog was eager and ardent for the highest things.”

But these are understood to have been contrivances of enemies, supplying the heretics with material for reproach. What the Gospel saying declared has been fulfilled: “Every plant,” it says, “which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up.” This is what I have often urged upon your affection: that nothing be done rashly. Does not your sincerity know that in earthly wars the soldiers keep more vigilant watch where the enemy presses hardest? Therefore, if we must always resist with episcopal arms, we ought carefully to act lest, God forbid, we leave Christ’s flock to ravening wolves. Philosophy, the friend of worldly wisdom, is the enemy of faith, a kind of poison to hope, and a most grievous war against charity. What agreement, then, has the temple of God with idols? What fellowship has Christ with Belial?

**[Col. 0367A]**

But perhaps some will say: “He was a Christian.” The name Christian must never be assigned to a man who walks in the dress of an idol; for one who wishes in this way to please the Gentiles cannot have any fellowship with us in the integral faith.

> **[Note: Col. 0367A]** He means Maximus, the Cynic philosopher wearing a cloak, and calls the cloak “the dress of an idol,” perhaps because the gods of the Gentiles were painted in that dress (Holstenius). The sole reason why Damasus says that Maximus walked in an idol’s dress is that he was a Cynic. That class of people wore nothing except the *tribonion*, or worn little cloak, and an under-tunic, and were consequently almost half-naked; moreover, they wore long hair and a beard. Hercules was depicted in this dress; the Cynics had chosen him as their patron and model. We learn this from Lucian’s Cynic, defending his own cause:
>
> “But, to learn how much this dress becomes not merely good men but even the gods themselves, look at images of the gods and consider whether they seem more like you or like me. Examine not only Greek but barbarian temples: are the gods long-haired and bearded, as I am, or are they depicted and painted shorn, as you are? Indeed, you will see that most of them, like me, wear no tunic.”
>
> Chapter 20, vol. III, Amsterdam edition. Hence Ausonius on Diogenes:
>
> > I am the first inventor of Cynicism. What is the reason  
> > That Alcaeus is said to be much earlier?  
> > Once I was second to Alcides as my teacher;  
> > Now I am first among Cynics, and he is a god.
>
> Why Nazianzen praises him, *Oration* 23, §3, for professing our faith in an alien dress, is explained by this.

Nor without reason were those who had come from Egypt marked by all as they departed, condemning their own error: so that, after his hair had afterward been cut off, he who had been improperly ordained might suffer the loss of his head of hair and be unable to become what he had sought.

> **[Note: Col. 0367C]** Coustantius thinks that Damasus here speaks of their departure from the Church, where the first act of the comedy was performed, and of their arrival at the flute-player’s house, where the second act was completed by Maximus’s ordination. He says that the ordaining bishops condemned their own error because they had left him unshorn in the Church and had not carried their begun crime through to the end. But what error was theirs if the gathering of the people prevented them from finishing what they had begun? Therefore the error displeasing to them must be located in the fact that the Egyptians, by their rash undertaking, had accomplished nothing except that the Cynic remained, as Damasus says, long-haired and disappointed in his hope, and that they departed the imperial city marked by all. For, because of the crime committed, such grief seized the city that there was then no one who did not rage. Gregory uses the same sarcasm as Damasus:
>
> > And a long-tended section came upon the Cynic’s hair,  
> > Paying off in a moment the labor of many hands;  
> > But when the shameless dog had become a shepherd,  
> > From a wealthy dog he became again a dog  
> > (O grievous disgrace), a dog alone and now  
> > Lacking his fine hair, yet not governing the sacred flock.

It was therefore rightly done that what had been badly begun should be destroyed by public authority.

> **[Note: Col. 0367D]** That is, by authority of the Emperor, who was then at Thessalonica, by whom he was “driven out again, like a disgraceful dog.”

For the future I admonish your holiness: since I have learned that it has been decided that a council must be held at Constantinople, let your sincerity take care that a bishop is chosen for the aforesaid city who is beyond reproach, so that, by God’s favor, once the entire peace of the Catholic priests has been secured, no dissensions may henceforth arise in the Church and, by God’s grace, the perpetual peace which we have long desired may endure with the Catholic priests.

> **[Note: Col. 0367D]** Socrates, book V, chapter 8, and Sozomen, book VII, write that this council was convened by Theodosius after Victor entered the imperial city, namely toward the end of 380; but Theodoret, book V, chapter 6, says that it was convened immediately after he assumed the empire. The latter seems much more consistent with the truth. So many bishops summoned at the beginning of that year could not have been in Constantinople in March; nor would Damasus have written this if he had not been informed long beforehand about the coming council.
>
> **[Note: Col. 0368B]** Theodoret, book V, chapters 6 and 7, says that Theodosius summoned only Eastern bishops to this council. Since Acholius and the other bishops under him were counted among the Westerners, how could Damasus so admonish men who, on that reading, seemed to have no part in it? I have stated my view in chapter 17. But since Acholius and the other Macedonian bishops were present, I do not reject the opinion of Pagi, who holds that, because of his singular holiness, Acholius was informed prematurely by Theodosius so that he might attend with his clergy; yet came late because he waited for Damasus’s instructions. Baronius, on the contrary, thinks he was summoned after Meletius’s death, when the dispute over the bishopric of Antioch divided the Easterners among themselves; Tillemont inclines to the same view in his note 43 on Gregory Nazianzen, as confirmed by Gregory’s own testimony:
>
> > “They came, suddenly called,  
> > As though they were to contribute something to peace’s purpose—  
> > Egyptians and Macedonians.”
>
> Yet it is unclear whether Nazianzen means that the Macedonian bishops were summoned unexpectedly, or that they came unexpectedly and beyond expectation; the latter is more likely. For the chronology does not permit Macedonian and Egyptian bishops, if they were summoned after Meletius’s death and during the heated dispute between Paulinus and Flavian, to have arrived before Gregory himself resigned.
>
> **[Note: Col. 0368C]** I have said in chapter 17 what this is intended to achieve.

I further admonish your affection that you do not permit anyone, contrary to the ordinances of our Fathers, to be transferred from one city to another, abandoning the people committed to him and passing through ambition to another people. Then disputes arise; then schisms take on a more grievous character. For those who have lost their priest cannot be without grief of heart, while those who have received a bishop from another city, even if they rejoice, understand that it will bring them reproach to live under another city’s priest.

> **[Note: Col. 0368C]** The transfer of bishops was forbidden by a canon of the Council of Nicaea, and the Roman Church also strongly disapproved of it unless necessity compelled or a great and most evident benefit recommended it. Hence Nicephorus Callistus and others who anxiously collected examples find in the West only one transfer, that of Perigenes, approved by the Roman bishop. In the East as well, Roman pontiffs permitted it only with the gravest reasons. The Greeks were less scrupulous in this matter, as the examples collected by Nicephorus show (Holstenius). This passage was therefore not written against Gregory, as Baluze and others suppose, but against arbitrary migrations from church to church throughout the East, and to promote observance of that canon. Moreover, if Gregory, as he often says of himself, had never been assigned or bound to any church, Damasus could not have been criticizing him. Nevertheless, when they came to the council, the Macedonian and Egyptian bishops used this admonition to oppose Gregory’s enthronement; but, as he says: “It was not so much from hatred of me, nor to put another upon the throne, as to inflict some pain upon those who had placed me upon the episcopal throne; at least, sometimes when arbiters were removed, they themselves asserted this.” *On His Life*, v. 155 ff.

## LETTER VI. OF DAMASUS TO ACHOLIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA

Rusticus, the *Silentiarius* of Gratian, is commended; and the instructions of the preceding letter concerning Maximus’s ordination and the election of another bishop are confirmed.

To the most beloved brother Acholius, Damasus.

Nothing further can be added to the merits of my son Rusticus, honorable lord and brother. For, besides enjoying the prerogative of his office as *Silentiarius* of our son Gratian Augustus, he has also received the grace of God at Rome and desired to come, strengthened by it, when sent into those regions. I ask your honor to receive him in every way as a personal pledge, so that, by God’s favor, while living abroad he may know that he is loved and honored by God’s fellow priests.

> **[Note: Col. 0369C]** That is, baptism. Holstenius discusses this more fully in his notes, and the very learned P. Edward Corsini illustrates it from ancient inscriptions in his second dissertation on the inscriptions of learned Greeks.
>
> **[Note: Col. 0369D]** As we have seen, Damasus had also written to other bishops; but here he says that he wrote to Acholius alone because he was their head throughout Illyricum.

I replied fully to the letters of your holiness that I did not approve the attempt by certain men coming from Egypt to ordain at Constantinople as bishop a certain long-haired Maximus, especially since, according to the Apostle, his dress was disgraceful. Your holiness will therefore do better if it takes care that henceforth a Catholic is appointed with whom, by God’s favor, perpetual peace may endure for us.

## LETTER VII. OF DAMASUS TO THE BISHOPS GOVERNING THE EAST

> **[Note: Col. 0369]** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

**[Col. 0369]**

That your love renders due reverence to the Apostolic See, most honored sons, brings the greatest honor also to yourselves. For although the foremost place belongs to us in the holy Church, in which the holy Apostle, sitting, taught us how we ought to guide the helm entrusted to us, nevertheless we confess ourselves far inferior to that dignity. Yet for this reason we strive by whatever means we can, if perhaps we may at last attain the glory of his blessedness.

Know, therefore, that we have long ago deposed that profane Timothy, disciple of the heretic Apollinarius, together with his impious doctrine; and for that reason we believe that his relics will have no force in the future. But if that ancient serpent, struck once and twice, has revived to increase his own punishment and, being outside the Church, does not cease to attempt to corrupt certain faithful people with his deadly poisons, avoid this deceit of his as though it were a pestilence. Yet remember the apostolic faith, especially that which was committed to writing by the Fathers at Nicaea; stand firm upon it with a secure step, remaining immovable in the faith; and do not hereafter tolerate your clergy or laity listening to vain talk and obscure questions.

For we have already more than once issued a formula that whoever knows himself to be a Christian should preserve what was handed down by the Apostles, as holy Paul says: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema.” Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, through his own passion bestowed the fullest salvation upon humankind, in order to free the whole human being, held in the bonds of sins, from every sin. If anyone says that he possessed either an imperfect humanity or an imperfect divinity, being filled with a devilish spirit, he shows himself to be a son of Gehenna.

Why then do you seek again from me the deposition of Timothy, who here also, by the judgment of the Apostolic See, in the presence of Peter, bishop of Alexandria, was deposed together with his teacher Apollinarius, and on the day of judgment will endure the penalties and torments due to him? If he persuades certain more frivolous persons, as though retaining some hope, though he has altered, together with his confession of faith, the true hope in Christ, whoever chooses to fight against the canon of the Church will perish with him in like manner. May God preserve you in health, most honored sons.

> **[Note: Col. 0369D]** Whoever translated this synodical letter of Damasus into Greek seems to me to have erred here because he encountered a corrupt manuscript. Damasus undoubtedly wrote, “You confer the greatest honor upon us,” as the sense and sequence require; but the translator read “upon yourselves,” without any sense (Valesius). What follows strongly approves and supports his emendation. Pseudo-Anacletus, Letter 2, appropriated this statement of Damasus and transferred it to his own property, from the translation of the *Tripartite History*, book IX, chapter 15.
>
> **[Note: Col. 0369D]** Sigonius, *On the Western Empire*, under the year 382, §112, Milan edition, translates the phrase *ta malista* felicitously and, as it seems to me, correctly. Epiphanius and Christophorson omit its rendering, as if the expression had no force here. Sirmond renders: “For indeed, even if especially in the holy Church, in which the holy Apostle sitting taught how we should handle the helm entrusted to us…” Finally Valesius, whose version Coustantius follows, has: “And although especially in the holy Church in which the holy Apostle sitting taught, it is fitting in some way that we hold the helm which we have undertaken to govern,” etc.; but both are inelegant, I think, and far from the true sense. What then if, after *ta malista*, one understands *esti*—“there is”? If this is done, *ta malista* expresses nothing other, I think, than “what is greatest and most authoritative of all.” Then one may say that Sigonius and Sarazanius have expressed Damasus’s true meaning and thought, which the Venetian collection of councils retains. See an example in Plutarch, *On the Education of Children*, part II, §15: “Above all, cultivate and train children’s memory.” Likewise in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*: “the emperors who chiefly rule the whole world.” Thus, with Sarazanius, I have retained Sigonius’s rendering. On the rest, see chapter 23.

## LETTER VIII. OF DAMASUS TO JEROME

He asks Jerome clearly to explain the meaning of *Hosanna* among the Hebrews.

**[Col. 0371C]**

To his beloved son Jerome, Damasus, bishop, greeting in the Lord.

As I was reading commentaries written in Greek and Latin on the interpretation of the Gospels by our own—that is, orthodox—writers, both ancient and recent, concerning the passage, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” I found that they advance not merely different but even mutually contradictory explanations. It belongs to your affection, with that ardent vigor of talent, to cut away those opinions and subtle ambiguities and write clearly what the word means among the Hebrews, so that, in this matter as in many others, those entrusted to our care may give thanks to you in Christ Jesus.

> **[Note: Col. 0371D]** In Damasus’s time writings of heretics were not lacking, men who had abused learning and talent; but he preferred to beware of reading them. We, far removed from his holiness, act otherwise: not only the writings of heretics, but even those of utterly depraved people who make Christian religion a mockery, wonderfully please us, and we seek a small glory of learning in reading and praising them, although joined with the loss of piety and faith.

## LETTER IX. OF DAMASUS TO JEROME

With what eagerness he reads Jerome’s writings; why he does not read Lactantius’s books with equal interest; and his request that Jerome briefly resolve the questions appended below.

To his beloved son Jerome, Damasus.

I have decided to rouse you—sleeping, and for a long time now reading rather than writing—by sending you a few questions. This is not because you ought not to read, for speech is nourished and enriched by reading as by daily food; rather, the fruit of reading is that you write. Since, when yesterday the messenger returned to me, you said that you now possessed no letters except those which you had once dictated in the desert—and which I read and copied with the greatest eagerness—and voluntarily promised that you could dictate some writings by stealthy nocturnal labor if I wished, I gladly accept from one offering what I would have asked even had you refused.

Nor do I think there will be any conversation more worthy of our discussion than if we speak with one another about the Scriptures: that is, I ask and you answer. I think there is nothing more pleasant than such a life in this world; all honeys are surpassed by this food of the soul. “How sweet,” says the Prophet, “are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth.” For since, as the foremost orator says, human beings differ from beasts because we can speak, how worthy of praise is one who surpasses others in that very thing in which humans surpass beasts?

> **[Note: Col. 0372D]** Baronius, having persuaded himself that this letter had been received from Jerome at Jerusalem, thought that the text should read, “since Etherius the courier,” which Marimus also adopted. But the true reading, received by the agreement of the ancient manuscripts, ought not to be altered; this is shown both by what we asserted in the preceding note and by Jerome’s own words at the beginning of the following letter (Coustantius, notes on Letters 16 and 17). The distinguished Vallarsi likewise adduces the agreement of all manuscripts.

Therefore prepare yourself and explain to me the matters set below, observing moderation in both directions: so that neither the questions require an answer nor the letter brevity. For I confess to you that I do not read with pleasure the books of Lactantius which you gave me long ago, because many of his letters extend to the length of a thousand verses and rarely discuss our doctrine. Thus their length produces weariness in the reader; and any portions that are brief are more suited to schoolmen than to us, discussing metres, the location of regions, and philosophers.

I. What does it mean that it is written in Genesis: “Whoever kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance”?

II. If God made all things very good, why did he give Noah commands concerning clean and unclean animals, since nothing unclean can be good? And why, in the New Testament, after the vision shown to Peter, when he said, “Far be it from me, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth,” did the voice from heaven answer: “What God has cleansed, do not call common”?  

III. Why does God say to Abraham that the children of Israel would return from Egypt in the fourth generation, whereas Moses subsequently writes: “But in the fifth generation the children of Israel departed from the land of Egypt”? Unless this is explained, it certainly appears contradictory.

IV. Why did Abraham receive the sign of his faith in circumcision?

V. Why did Isaac, a just man and dear to God, deceived by error, bless not the one whom he wished, but the one whom he did not wish?

## ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE FAITH

[Note: Vallicellian manuscript A. V, p. 234: “Here begins the council of the city of Rome under Pope Damasus, on the explanation of the faith.”] From the council of the city of Rome under Pope Damasus.

It was said: First we must deal with the sevenfold Spirit, [Col. 0373C] who rests in Christ. The Spirit of wisdom: Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God. The Spirit of understanding: “I will give you understanding and instruct you in the way in which you shall walk.” The Spirit of counsel: “And his name shall be called Angel of Great Counsel.” The Spirit of power, as was said above: Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God. The Spirit of knowledge, on account of the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Jesus Christ, as the Apostle says. The Spirit of truth: “I am life and truth.” The Spirit of fear: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

The dispensation of Christ’s names is manifold. He is Lord, because he is Christ; Word, because he is the Son of God, because he is the Only-begotten from the Father; man, because he was born from a Virgin; priest, because he offered himself as a burnt offering; shepherd, because he is guardian; worm, because he rose again; mountain, because he is [Col. 0373D] strong; way, because through him there is a straight entrance into life; [Col. 0374A] lamb, because he suffered; cornerstone, because he is the foundation; teacher, because he shows the way of life; sun, because he enlightens; true, because he is from the Father; life, because he is Creator; bread, because he is flesh; Samaritan, because he is guardian and merciful; Christ, because he is anointed; Jesus, because he is Savior; God, because he is from God; angel, because he is messenger; bridegroom, because he is mediator; vine, because we have been redeemed by his blood; lion, because he is king; rock, because he is a firm foundation; flower, because he is chosen; prophet, because he reveals things to come.

For the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone or of the Son alone, but the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. For it is written: “If anyone loves the world, the Spirit of the Father is not in him.” Likewise it is written: “But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.” Therefore, when the Father and Son are named, the Holy Spirit is understood, concerning whom [Col. 0374B] the Son himself says in the Gospel that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, and “will take from what is mine and declare it to you.”

[Note: After this, the same Vallicellian manuscript continues as follows: “Likewise it was said: Now we must truly deal with the divine Scriptures: what the universal Catholic Church receives, and what it ought to avoid.
