The order of the Old Testament begins: one book of Genesis; one book of Exodus,” etc. Baronius mentions this manuscript along with the chapter on the canon of the Scriptures under the year 69.]

From Baronius, under the year 382, no. 19.

After all these prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures which we have set forth above, upon which the Catholic Church is founded through the grace of God, we have also thought it necessary to declare that, although the Catholic Churches spread throughout the world are, as it were, one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church has been set before the other Churches by certain [Note: The Quesnellian manuscript reads in the preface, “not by any synodical decrees, but by the evangelical word,” which is preferable; this is also the wording in Gelasius’s decree on apocryphal Scriptures.] synodical enactments, and has also obtained primacy by the evangelical word of our Lord and Savior, [Note: Quesnell adds: “where he said to blessed Peter.”] “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell [Col. 0374C] shall not prevail against it; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

There was added also the fellowship of the most blessed Apostle Paul, the vessel of election, who, not at a different [Note: The Quesnellian manuscript omits these words and writes: “who on one day and at one time, by a glorious death,” etc. Gelasius, however, has them as here.] time, as heretics babble, but at one time, on one and the same day, contending in the city of Rome under Caesar Nero and crowned by a glorious death with Peter, consecrated together with him the aforesaid Roman Church to Christ the Lord; and by their presence and venerable triumph set it before all the other [Note: Quesnell adds “cities,” which is quite unnecessary.] places in the whole world.

Therefore the first see of the Apostle Peter is the Roman Church, [Note: The Quesnellian manuscript: “Therefore the first see is the Roman Church by heavenly favor, which the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul dedicated by their martyrdom.” Gelasius, however, reads as here.] having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the sort.

[Col. 0374D] The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed [Col. 0375A] Peter by Mark, his disciple and Evangelist. [Note: Quesnell: “Because, sent by Peter, he was the first to preach the word of truth in Egypt.”] Sent by the Apostle Peter into Egypt, he preached the word of truth and completed a glorious martyrdom.

The third see is at Antioch, [Note: Quesnell: “Likewise venerable through the dwelling of blessed Peter.” [Col. 0376A] Gelasius: “It is held honorable in the name of Peter.”] that of its most blessed Apostle Peter, which is held honorable because he lived there before he came to Rome, and there the name “Christians” first arose for the new people. [Note: Quesnell more correctly reads *exortum*, “arose.”]

Thus far Gelasius also. The Quesnellian manuscript has something further concerning the sees of Jerusalem and Ephesus.

[Col. 0375]

## POEMS

[Note: Here, as there is a double series of annotations, so there is a double method of directing the reader: Sarazanius’s notes are marked by numbers, Mereuda’s by small letters.] (C, G, S)*

### POEM I. In praise of David

[Note: Baronius prefaces these verses as follows: “Having received these learned labors of St. Jerome on the Psalter of David, Damasus sang the praise of so great a king and prophet in these verses, which we found in the library of the Basilica of St. Peter, in manuscript 1 of St. Jerome, containing his exposition of the Psalms. The same verses are contained in a manuscript of the Vatican Library, although they are read in a highly corrupt form in both places.” Thus he. But the things Damasus sings concerning David are found in the sacred books of I Kings. The same Baronius says: “The manuscripts contain Jerome’s verses, which he sent to St. Damasus as a recitation, with such a heading.”]

### VERSES OF LORD JEROME THE PRIEST

He who taught the saints to sing in sweet melody  
knew the ten words of the Law which he had given;  
as many strings as the lyre has under the fingers, so many  
names—or the Cross itself might indicate the number by its sign.

[Col. 0375D] Why should you hesitate to believe? The power of Christ governs all things,  
he who joined diverse languages beneath one song,  
so that cattle and birds may be able to know God.  
For them sound is faith, soothing bitter minds;  
thus the earlier creation rejoices in so great a gift,  
[Col. 0376C] that it may offer to the Lord those whom the grace of speech saves.  
Whoever thirsts, let him come, desiring to draw from the streams;  
he shall find waters that preserve sweet honey.

May Your Blessedness pray for us, most blessed Pope. I saw the penultimate verse, “Whoever thirsts,” etc., engraved in an ancient marble basin for fountains before the Church of St. Bartholomew on the Island, in an ancient script, so that it appears to have been written in the time of Damasus. There are also several letters of St. Damasus to St. Jerome, and of Jerome to him, which you have here in this collection of letters of St. Damasus.][Col. 0375B]

Now lend kindly ears to Damasus’s admonitions;  
with filth cast off, they cleanse the innermost chambers of the heart,  
when they renew their court, ready to serve Christ.

[Note: I suspect that the beginning of this poem should be taken from here, and that the preceding three little verses do not belong here, but rather to those found in various manuscript codices, from Jerome to Damasus, along with his labors on the Psalter. First, they can be separated from the rest without inconvenience, since the remaining verses were written in praise of David; indeed, the elegance of the composition seems to require it. Further, in Vatican manuscript 4226, immediately after the earlier line, “Now lend kindly ears to Damasus’s admonitions,” etc., the following occur in one continuous sequence, taken from the same verses of Jerome:

[Col. 0376D] “Whoever thirsts, let him come, desiring to draw from the streams;  
he shall find waters that preserve sweet honey;  
with filth cast off, they cleanse the innermost chambers of the heart,  
and renew the heart as well, ready to serve Christ.”

For this reason all these verses formerly occupied one and the same place, but were afterwards confused and separated.]

You ought to recognize Christ’s holy prophet:

A shepherd-boy, one among many brothers,  
an angel took him from the sheep and consecrated him king,  
he alone knowing how to arrange instruments with his hands,  
[Note: The same manuscript: “to sing through the lyre of the people.”] to sing by the lyre of the heavenly kingdoms to the people.

The giant, threatening vainly with heavy shield,  
[Note: The same manuscript has *impia*, “impious.” It should be written *impius*, “impious.”] impious and blaspheming, bearing trappings and weapons,  
who, madman that he was, worshipped the temples of deaf gods,  
he struck down with a smooth stone and left a corpse;  
and, when the great slaughter was soon accomplished by God’s judgment,  
he showed the peoples what trophies he had taken from the enemy.

[Col. 0375C] For Damasus knows, O Holy One, [Note: The same manuscript:

“. . . . . knows, O Holy One, to display your triumphs.”] God himself knows your triumphs.

### POEM II. On Christ

[Col. 0376B]

Christ, mighty ruler of all things, maker of the returning age,  
voice and intelligence of the highest God, whom the Father pours forth from his lofty  
mind and grants a share in so great a kingdom;  
you subdued the impious crimes of our life,  
suffering to clothe the world in bodily form  
and openly address peoples and confess yourself man.

Whom, enclosed by the Word, Mary’s virgin bosom  
soon swelled at the divine visitation, and the unwedded Mother  
was awestruck that her womb should be filled by a hidden birth,  
about to bear her own Creator, the maker of heaven and earth, beneath her deep  
breast—he who encompasses the whole world far and wide.

And he who is contained neither by the expanses of earth nor by the waves of sea,  
nor by heaven, [Note: Formerly *confluxit* was read; perhaps *confulsit*, “shone forth,” should be read, from *confulgeo*. If not, *confluxit* may be from *confluo*, as in Lucretius, Book I:

“From every side it flowed together with solid weights to the bottom.”

Yet I found the poems among Claudian’s works with this title, “On Christ the Savior,” where that word is read as *confuxit*, “molded”; this confirmed my conjecture. But if perhaps the verses are not all Damasus’s, they certainly will not be Claudian’s, since, according to St. Augustine, *City of God*, V.26, he was estranged from the name of Christ; Orosius, VII.37, and Paul the Deacon, XIII, in his additions to Eutropius, call him a pagan poet. They are rather the work of Mamertus Claudianus the priest, a Christian poet, on whom see Sidonius Apollinaris, *Letters*, IV.3 and 11, V.2, and Gennadius and Honorius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Certainly this poem is far more elegant than the rest.] flowed together into small limbs,

[Col. 0376C] and indeed underwent the name and binding of punishment,  
that you might snatch us from death and banish death  
[Col. 0377A] by your own death; soon raised into the heavenly airs,  
restoring the Father, joyful in purified light, to yourself.

May you protect Augustus, so that on feast days  
he may often celebrate the annual fasts of the pure Sacrament.

### POEM III. On Christ’s Ascension

God rises to his own seat, death having been exiled,

[Note: We have emended this, since it was formerly read: “May he teach believers that life is to come.” In Acts 1 the angels are said to have spoken: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will so come as you saw him going into heaven.”]

that he may teach believers that life is to come.  
The angel sang these words, bearing back that each [of them],  
“Thus he will come”; thus it is right to believe concerning Christ.

### POEM IV. On the Name of Jesus

[Note: This and the following epigram have the name JESUS written in the sequence of the first letters of the verses, called an acrostic, [Col. 0377C] and also in that of the final letters, called a telestich—such as occur in the Greek verses of the Erythraean Sibyl in Emperor Constantine’s oration to the assembly of saints, in Eusebius after his *Life*; translated into Latin in St. Augustine, *City of God*, XVIII.23, and by the translators of Eusebius, Portesius and Christophorsonus, and by Gyraldus, *On Poets*. The version Panvinius has in his little book *On the Sibyls* is the former version of the aforementioned Portesius, the latter that of Gyraldus. In their acrostic one reads, as St. Augustine writes: **ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΥΙΟΣ ΣΩΤΗΡ**, that is in Latin, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” In the same oration the translators mentioned above add “Cross”; Gyraldus, “Crucified.” Eusebius reports that Cicero, having chanced to read that poem, translated it into Latin prose and attached it to his own writings. Cicero himself, in *On Divination* II, says of the Sibyl’s verses: “There is that which is called an *acrostic*, when something is connected in sequence from the initial letters of verses, as in certain verses of Ennius and of the Sibyl: from the first letters of the first verse of each sentence the whole poem is woven before that sentence.” Thus Cicero; but Ennius’s examples have perished.

The plot summaries of Plautus’s comedies also display the title of the play in the first letters of their verses. Porphyry used this same form in his *Panegyric* addressed to Emperor Constantine: acrostics, telestichs, and even letters in the middle of verses—works worthy of reading, which you have among the epigrams and poems of ancient poets. Hrabanus Maurus also used it in the second figure of *The Praises of the Holy Cross*; later writers used it as well, as on the tomb of Peter Leo, a most noble Roman citizen, in the Basilica of St. Paul, [Col. 0378B] where the initials of the verses form the name “Peter Leo,” who lived five hundred years ago. For he was the father of the pseudo-pontiff Anacletus II. Baronius printed the complete epigram, vol. XII, under the year 1144.

Indeed, on the tomb of Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, there is an ancient inscription in which “Eusebius bishop and martyr” is written by the first letters of the verses; John Stephen Ferrerius published it in full in his book *On the Bishops of Vercelli*. The same device occurs in the monument of St. Eugenia, martyr of Córdoba, in Ambrosius Morales’s Appendix to Eulogius; in the epitaph of Duke Hugh, which Baronius gives in vol. II of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 1002, in the beginnings, middles, and endings of the verses; and in the epitaph of Blessed Eugenius the Younger, bishop of Toledo, in which “Eusebius” is expressed from the beginning and “Misellus” at the end. There is another epitaph of Eventius, in which “Nicholas” is formed from the initial letters and “Eventius” from the final ones. Likewise, in the opening of a letter of St. Columbanus the abbot, published by Sirmond together with other little works.

Baronius, vol. VIII, also published the epitaph of Blessed Eugenius; and in the epitaph of St. Florentinus the abbot, which Baronius likewise reports in the Appendix to vol. XII under the year 553, the beginning of the verses reads: “Florentinus, abbot, rests in peace. Amen.” There is also at Naples, in the church of St. Januarius, the epitaph of Duke Stephen, in which both the first and final letters of the verses read “Stephen consul twice”; Caesar Caracciolus reports it in full in his *Sacred Naples*, as does Julius Caesar Cappaccius in his *History of Naples*.]

In affairs so great, the threefold union of the world  
[Col. 0377B] raises the human mind to fitting praise:

The sole salvation for us, and the supreme power of the world,  
came to dissolve the knot of sin by its fruit;  
supreme salvation has shone upon all lands through the ages.

### POEM V. On the same subject

[Col. 0378A]

With equal right the common maker of the age reigns,  
and reigns with the Father, exalted in the holy citadel;  
in heavenly majesty he sits upon the kingdoms of the saints.

From there, by a nod alone, he sees all sea and lands;  
he supplies human affairs and gives gifts to created things.

### POEM VI. On the Titles of the Savior

[Note: In Book I of the Greek Epigrams are two poems, one in praise of Bacchus and the other of Apollo, setting forth the diverse names of false gods. Both are composed with great care, in accordance with the number of the twenty-four Greek letters: each poem has the same number of verses, and every word in each verse begins with the same letter. St. Damasus successfully imitated, or even surpassed, this Greek artifice. In these seven verses he embraced almost all the names given to Christ the Savior by prophets and apostles, so artfully and concisely that not a syllable is superfluous. But since St. Dionysius the Areopagite wrote a separate work on divine names, and some modern writers have written brilliantly on them as well, and since there is no difficulty in these verses, we shall not waste time by heaping up many words in vain. In verse 1 a syllable is lacking.]

[Note: Orientius, a Christian poet of the fifth century, likewise embraced all these and other titles of the Savior in a similar poem and explains their force; see *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Martenianus*, vol. V, p. 43.]

Hope, Life, Salvation, Reason, Wisdom, Light,  
Judge, Door, Giant, King, Jewel, Prophet, Priest;  
Messiah, Sabaoth, Rabbi, Bridegroom, Mediator;  
Rod, Pillar, Hand, Rock, Son, and Emmanuel;  
[Col. 0378B] Vineyard, Shepherd, Sheep, Peace, Root, Vine, Olive;  
Fountain, Wall, Lamb, Calf, Lion, Propitiator;  
Word, Man, Net, Stone, House, All Things, Christ, Jesus.

### POEM VII. On St. Paul the Apostle

[Note: Baronius calls this “a distinguished poem of St. Damasus on Paul’s conversion” in his notes on the Martyrology for 25 January; it is a summary of Paul’s deeds.]

[Note: But Vatican manuscript 5104 reads: “Pope Damasus, as a preface to Paul’s Epistles, on his wondrous praises.” Venerable Cardinal Thomasius: “On the Conversion of St. Paul the Apostle.”]

[Col. 0379A]

Long ago Saul, [Note: Another Vatican manuscript, 1598: “in the manner of.”] following the commands of the leaders,  
when he wished to set ancestral laws before the Lord,  
refused to praise Christ, whom the holy prophets proclaimed, [Note: The same: “having praised.”]  
and desired by continual killings to tear apart the people,  
[Note: This name for the people is frequent in the sacred Scriptures and means the same as *populus*, “people.” Paul, Romans 9: “As he says in Hosea: ‘I shall call not-my-people, my people.’” Hosea’s passage, at the end of chapter 2, reads: “And I shall say to not-my-people: ‘You are my people.’”]  
when, blind, he tore apart the holy Mother’s sacred bonds,  
after darkness he deserved to know the true Light.

Having been tested, he perceived what the glory of Christ could do;  
with his ears he received the Lord’s voice and the light,  
and reformed his conduct, following Christ’s commands.

[Note: Thus Walafrid Strabo also writes of St. Paul the Apostle:

> Saul, who punished holy crowds with imprisonment,  
> becomes a believer, changed in name to Paul, etc.

In the Acts of the Apostles, from the killing of St. Stephen narrated in chapter 7 onward, the name Saul is always read. Christ the Lord likewise calls him Saul at his conversion; in the vision the Lord uses the same name to Ananias; Ananias himself calls him Saul; and the Holy Spirit also calls him thus in Acts 13: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” Soon afterwards in the same chapter it is written: “But Saul, who is also Paul,” [Col. 0379C] etc.; thereafter he is always called Paul in the same Acts, and is always named Paul both by himself and by everyone else.

Various opinions of learned men are found on this matter. Chrysostom, in his homily on the conversion of St. Paul, vol. III, and Oecumenius, on the Acts of the Apostles, maintain that God gave him the name Paul. St. Ambrose, however, writes in Sermon 31 of the Roman edition that Ananias called him by this name at his baptism. St. Jerome, in his letter to Philemon, holds that he was named Paul after Sergius Paulus, converted to the faith, on account of his victory over him; but Baronius, vol. I of the *Annals*, thinks that Sergius Paulus himself gave him the name from attachment and affection for him, supported by many examples from that age. Sedulius, in his commentary on Paul’s Epistles, considers that he had two names, Saul and Paul, based on the Acts’ words: “But Saul, who is also Paul,” etc. Origen likewise, in the preface to the Epistle to the Romans: “That is, called Saul among the Hebrews and Paul among the Romans.” St. Augustine, in Tractate 2 on the Psalms, and St. Ambrose, on Paul’s Epistles, say that he did not change his name, but became Paul from Saul, humble from proud.]

After the change of name, he was pleased to be Paul.

[Col. 0380A] [Note: Learned writers also disagree concerning the time when Paul was caught up to the third heaven. Some think he was caught up at the time when he remained for three days and three nights without seeing, eating, or [Col. 0380A] drinking; Baronius does not approve this opinion in the aforementioned vol. I of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 36. For since Paul himself says in 2 Corinthians 12 that he was taken up to the third heaven fourteen years before he wrote that same epistle, it must certainly be affirmed that this happened not in the year in which he was converted and baptized, but eight years later.] [Note: This recurs concerning St. Saturninus and Saints Nereus and Achilleus.]

Wonderful faith in events: suddenly [Note: The earlier manuscript reads “raised high into the aether”; the other, “borne beyond the aether.”] beyond the heaven’s aether  
he deserved to know what the rewards of life could accomplish.  
Caught up, the martyr ascended to the inner courts of Christ;  
the third light of heaven, paradise, held him as he went.  
He enjoys the Lord’s conversations and preserves the secrets.

Commanded to preach truth to nations and peoples,  
to penetrate the depths of the sea, and night and day  
[Note: This entire verse has disappeared in the Fulda manuscript in the Venetian 1533 edition of the Epistles of St. Paul, as has nearly the whole poem. The verse is also given differently:

> He lived; yet it is wonderful that he surpassed so great a labor.

Both readings are obscure. Perhaps light may be shed on the former by this line of Horace:

> Nor did he live badly who, born and dying, passed unnoticed.

Thus it would be an allusion to Neocles’s saying, **λάθε βιώσας**, “live unnoticed.”]  
to behold [Note: The earlier manuscript has “with great,” but that reading is still more obscure.], for whom [Note: So also in Venerable Thomasius, *Works*, vol. II, p. 382. Perhaps Damasus alludes to the words of this same Apostle in 2 Corinthians 11 and 12.] it is a great enough thing to have lived in obscurity,

[Note: Concerning the rage of beasts, Paul admits in 1 Corinthians 15 that he fought with beasts at Ephesus; but Tertullian, Chrysostom, and others think that by “beasts” he meant fierce and wicked people. Thus we read in 2 Timothy 4 that he was delivered from the mouth of the lion; interpreters teach that “the mouth of the lion” there signifies Nero’s cruelty. Baronius treats this more fully, vol. I, under the year of Christ 55, chapter 5. St. [Col. 0380C] Ignatius also writes to the Romans: “From Syria as far as Rome I fight with beasts, by land and sea, night and day, bound with ten leopards—that is, with a military guard—who become worse from acts of kindness.”]

beatings, chains, hunger, stones, and the rage of beasts;  
the filth of prison, rods, tortures, and fetters;  
[Note: These matters are found in Acts 27 and 28, and were expressed in heroic verse by Arator the subdeacon in his work addressed to Pope Vigilius. Prudentius also splendidly describes the shipwreck, serpent, and so forth in the preface to Book I *Against Symmachus*, beginning, “Paul, herald of God,” etc. In the preface to Book II against the same Symmachus, he elegantly sang of Peter shipwrecked amid the waves and raised by the Lord’s right hand lest he sink:

> Simon, whom they call Peter, etc.

Juvencus the priest also rendered this in hexameter verse from the Gospels, Book III.]

shipwreck, tears, and the dreadful venom of a serpent.

[Note: The same Paul says: “I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.” I would, however, warn the reader that this poem was taken from two editions. One is that of Aldus Manutius of 1501; the other, highly valued by us, is that of Christopher Broverius of the Society of Jesus, who took these verses of St. Damasus from a most ancient manuscript in the treasury of the Church of Fulda, as he himself testifies in these words: “Verses of Pope St. Damasus, copied from the book which the glorious St. Boniface, apostle of the German nation, carried about with him, whose subject was a HARMONY [Col. 0381B] OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.” The book itself bore this inscription: “St. Boniface used this book while he lived.” St. Boniface flourished under the Roman pontiffs Gregory and Zachary, in the year of human salvation 750.

The heading prefixed in that same manuscript is: “Here begin verses of St. Damasus on St. Paul the Apostle.” Near the end, some verses have been consumed by the injury of time; some occur differently than in Aldus’s edition. For where Aldus has, “The teacher, worthy of God’s love, lives through the ages,” Broverius printed from the cited manuscript: “Worthy of love, given . . . . . teacher through the ages.” Whoever should supply *populis*, “to the peoples,” would do so not inappropriately, since St. Paul is called the teacher of the nations.

In Aldus’s edition the penultimate verse reads: “In these verses, I confess briefly, most holy teacher.” But in the manuscript: “In these verses, patron . . . . . our thrice most just one.” I would prefer this reading; the missing syllable can readily be restored thus: “In these verses, Father, our most just patron.” It is not at odds with the meaning or style of the holy [Col. 0381C] pontiff. In Aldus’s edition the last verse is: “Damasus himself wished to display your triumphs.” In Broverius: “O holy one, Damasus wished to display your triumphs.”]

He did not fear to bear [Note: This recurs concerning Saints Nereus and Achilleus, and in the poem on St. Eutychius.] the marks of Christ in his body.

[Col. 0381A] He taught believers how they could conquer death.  
The teacher, worthy of God’s love, [Note: We understand that Paul the Apostle is customarily so called above the others from Paulinus, Letter 23, no. 11; Letter 30, no. 5; Letter 32, no. 23; Letter 37, no. 3; Poem 16, line 260; and Poem 34, line 555:

> Yet he preferred to cultivate the word of the Teacher.  
> All things are permitted, but not all things are beneficial;  
> for that Teacher teaches this in the Lord’s Word,  
> under whose star as guide we strive to go by heavenly paths.] lives through the ages.

In these verses I briefly confess, most holy teacher  
Paul, Damasus wished to display your triumphs.

### POEM VIII. On St. Andrew, Apostle

[Note: Venerable Cardinal Thomasius does not have it; but it is read in the Mozarabic text published by the distinguished Blanchinus from the archive of the Church of Verona, Thomasius, *Works*, vol. I, p. CXLI. A doxology is added.]

[Note: Baronius, in the Martyrology for the last day of November, calls this an elegant poem of Pope St. Damasus on Andrew suffering the cross. Yet it does not seem to me to be by Damasus, but by someone more recent. At the beginning Damasus says:

> The glory of a sacred name,  
> expressing life by its name, etc.  
> Andrew, apostle of Christ,  
> by this very title  
> you are marked by this name.

He alludes to Andrew’s name, since **ἀνδρεῖος** means “manly, brave.” St. Paulinus, in a natal poem for St. Felix, says concerning St. Andrew:

> Here is Father Andrew, here he who, a fisherman sent to the fields,  
> taught babbling tongues to fall silent;  
> after he freed peoples from the torn nets  
> [Col. 0381D] of wicked error and drew them into Christ’s nets,  
> he condemned Thessalian Patras by shedding his blood.]

The glory of a sacred name,  
expressing life by its name, [Note: From Blanchinus: “and expressing life by the name.” But he corrects it to “life and name.”]  
proclaims you beautiful through this [Note: In the same source: “Hence you,” but he corrects it to “you by this very [thing] now.”]  
glory of the blessed Cross.

Andrew, apostle of Christ,  
by this very [Note: There: “by this very himself,” but he corrects it.] title  
you are marked with that name,  
beautiful in the same mystical sense.

Whom the Cross brings to heights,  
whom the blessed Cross loves,  
for whom the bitter Cross prepares  
the joys of the life to come.

In you the mystery grew great;  
you are renowned by a double mark,  
when you conquer disgrace through the Cross  
and reveal [Note: There: “hang,” but he corrects it to “and reveal the Cross’s.”] the blood of the Cross.

Now cherish us in our weakness,  
and undertake care for us,  
so that through the Cross’s victory  
we may seek the homeland of heaven.

### POEM IX. In the Catacombs of the Holy Apostles

[Note: These verses formerly stood at the Basilica of St. Sebastian, at the place where the bodies of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul lay; it was called the *Platonia*. Thus Bede writes: “In that place, he adorned with verses the Platonia itself where the holy bodies lay.” Anastasius says: “He built the Platonia where the bodies of the Apostles Peter and Paul lay, and adorned it with verses.” Ado says the same as Bede; the Roman Breviary: “He also built the Platonia where the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul lay for some time, and adorned it with elegant verses”; and others mention these poems as well. Baronius also affirms this in the appendix after vol. XII, p. 911, where he gives the verses from this edition as follows: “As to the epitaph inscribed there at the Catacombs, preserved hitherto in documents, we here reproduce it in full for you.”

I think it was called *Platonia* from the breadth of its construction and vaulted roof; Plato likewise, according to Laertius, was so called from the breadth of his forehead, and, according to Suidas, from the breadth of his chest or amplitude of expression. The Librarian writes of Sixtus III: “He made a Platonia in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Appian Way,” etc.—perhaps he restored or adorned it. Yet see Baronius, vol. IV, who interprets *Platonia* otherwise.

For an understanding of this epigram, it is useful to cite here the words of the letter of Pope St. Gregory, *Register*, III.30, to the Empress Constantina: “What am I to say about the bodies of the blessed Apostles, when it is agreed that, at the time when they suffered, faithful men came from the East to reclaim their bodies as those of their fellow citizens? The bodies were brought as far as the second milestone from the City, to the place called the Catacombs, and placed there. But when all their multitude assembled and tried to move them from there, such force of thunder and lightning terrified and scattered them by its overwhelming violence that they did not dare to attempt anything further. Then the Romans came forth and, having deserved this by the Lord’s mercy, took up their bodies and laid them in the places where they are now buried.”

On this matter hear Anastasius the Librarian, whose book on the Roman pontiffs is believed to derive from Damasus himself. Speaking thus of Pope St. Cornelius: “In his time, at the request of a certain matron Lucina, he removed by night the bodies of the Apostles Peter and Paul from the Catacombs. First, blessed Lucina placed the body [Col. 0383B] of blessed Paul on her estate on the Ostian Way, beside the place where he was beheaded. But Bishop Cornelius took the body of the Apostle Peter and placed it near the place where he was crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops, in the Temple of Apollo on Mount Aureus in the Vatican of Nero’s Palace, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.”

The same Anastasius writes, from the same Damasian source, concerning what Emperor Constantine later did to these holy bodies of the Apostles at St. Sylvester’s request: “Likewise, in these times Emperor Constantine, at the request of Bishop Sylvester, made a basilica for the blessed Apostle Peter in the Temple of Apollo. He enclosed Peter’s coffin containing the body of St. Peter on every side with Cyprian bronze, so that it was immovable: five feet at the head, five feet at the feet, and five feet on the right side. Thus he enclosed and laid up the body of the blessed Apostle Peter, and adorned it above with porphyry columns and other vine-shaped columns brought from Greece.” And below: “At the same time Emperor Constantine made a basilica for the blessed Apostle Paul at the suggestion of Bishop Sylvester, and laid up and enclosed his holy body in bronze, as Constantine Augustus did that of blessed Peter.”

[Note: See what I have observed concerning this poem in *On the Poems of Damasus*, ch. 25, §2, no. 3, and Sarazanius (in this very column, no. 3).]

You should know that the saints formerly dwelt here,  
you who seek alike the names of Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0383A] The East sent forth the disciples, as we freely acknowledge;

by the merit of their blood, and following Christ through the stars,

they sought the heavenly bosom and the kingdoms of the blessed.

Rome deserved rather to defend her own citizens.

Let Damasus proclaim these new stars as your praises.

### POEM X. On St Stephen, Pope and Martyr

At the time when the sword cut the Mother’s holy entrails,

this ruler, set here, was teaching the commands of heaven;

but suddenly there came men who seized him as he happened to be teaching.

When soldiers had been sent, then the people offered their necks.

As soon as the Elder perceived that someone wished to take

the palm, he himself first offered both himself and his own head,

lest impatient savagery be able to harm anyone.

He showed that Christ renders the rewards of life:

he himself preserves the shepherd’s merit, the number of the flock.

[Note: Baronius had read: “Christ through the stars.”]

[Note: In Appendix no. 2:

> They sought the ethereal dwelling and the kingdom of the blessed.]

[Note: This little verse of Damasus is read again in the poem on St Saturninus and in Appendix no. 2.]

[Note: Venerable Cardinal Thomasius, *Works*, vol. II, p. 506. Fourth day before the Nones of August: the feast of St Stephen, Pope and Martyr, in Callixtus’ cemetery.]

[Note: By this word Damasus usually designates the Roman pontiffs, as in poems 8 and 9 and in Sarazanius’s note on this very page. Damasus here calls Pope Marcellus “ruler,” and also applies this name to himself above, concerning the martyr Maurus:

> “Which Damasus, ruler of the people, after a long time …”

And in the next epitaph:

> “Damasus adorned the tomb; recognize the ruler.”

And concerning St Felix and Adauctus:

> “That true priest, at the command of Damasus the ruler …”

And below, concerning St Tarsicius:

> “Damasus the ruler renders these inscriptions after the rewards.”]

[Note: *Acts*, in Baronius under the year 259, no. 22: “On the following day he assembled in the same crypt; and, seated, taught all concerning the kingdom of God and eternal life.” It should be observed here that the crypt, or cemetery, of Lucina, where Stephen is said to have assembled, is almost connected with the Catacombs. See Boldetti, book III, ch. 18.]

[Note: “When Valerian heard this, he sent soldiers to seize him.” Appendix, poem 2:

> “Straightway, when leaders had been sent, they offered their necks.”]

[Note: *Acts*: “We too desire to pour out our blood for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”]

[Note: *Acts*: “who, fearless and steadfast, was beheaded there upon his own seat.”]

[Note: “There arose the greatest mourning among the Christians, who had sent before them such a shepherd with the glory of martyrdom. They buried his body together with the very chair, sprinkled with blood.”]

### POEM XI. On St Marcellus, Martyr

The truthful ruler, because he had declared that the fallen must bewail

their sins, became a bitter enemy to all the wretched.

Hence followed fury, hatred, discord, quarrels,

sedition, slaughter; the bonds of peace were dissolved.

He who, because of another’s crime, denied Christ in peace

was driven from the borders of his homeland by the savagery of the tyrant.

Damasus wished briefly to record these established facts,

that the people might be able to recognize the merit of Marcellus.

[Note: Baronius, p. 904, under the year of Christ 309: “There exists an epitaph of Pope Damasus on St Marcellus, brought to light together with others, in which another history of St Marcellus hitherto unknown is reported; it runs as follows,” etc. “At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the feast of St Marcellus, pope and martyr,” etc. It is found in the Roman Martyrology and in Usuard, on the old Salarian Way, 16 January. But in the old Roman Martyrology, and in Bede, Ado, Rabanus, Notker, the Roman Breviary, and Anastasius: “On the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla.” In the acts of St Marcellus, believed to have been written by notaries of the Roman Church, in Surius: “In the cemetery of Priscilla, on the Salarian Way, not far from Rome, at the third mile, where St Marcellus rests in peace.” Concerning this cemetery and St Marcellus Anastasius writes: “He asked a certain matron named Priscilla, and made a cemetery on the Salarian Way,” etc. Concerning Pope Vigilius, the same writer states: “His body was brought to Rome and buried near St Marcellus, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla.”]

[Note: Cyprian, epistle 22, Verona edition: “Finally, the beginning of this sedition has already arisen. In several cities of our province an assault was made by the multitude upon the leaders, and they compelled them to grant and publicly restore to them the peace which had been conceded,” etc.]

[Note: Papebroch thinks that this verse identifies Licinius, who, he observes, first appeared at least outwardly Christian, then became an open idolater, caused civil war, and finally, defeated by Constantine, was exiled to Gaul. Therefore, instead of *tyranni*, which he says was introduced by a copyist’s ignorance, he thinks *tyrannus* should be written. His sole reason is that this exile of Marcellus is mentioned nowhere but in this poem. But this reasoning is wholly unworthy of so learned a man: for what had the Licinian war to do with Marcellus himself, who had died before it arose or was even contemplated? Moreover, in the genuine Martyrology of Bede, under 16 January, we read of Marcellus: “By command of Emperor Maximinus, he was beaten with rods and expelled from the presence of the man whom he had rebuked.” If, therefore, in place of Maximinus—who was neither in Rome nor capable of being rebuked by Marcellus, and who was introduced by an ignorant copyist—you read Maxentius, then this man, who at one time wished to seem Christian, could and ought to have been rebuked by that pontiff; and we have another testimony to this exile of Marcellus.]

[Note: From this passage we learn either that the Roman Church’s discipline toward those who had fallen into idolatry outside a time of persecution and during peace was always milder, or that, if it had been harsher, it had already been moderated in Marcellus’s age. For scarcely anyone was granted a place in canonical penitence to expiate a voluntary crime. See Council of Elvira, canon 1, and Cyprian, epistle 52.]

[Col. 0385A] [Note: Do you see why Damasus observes the discipline maintained by that pontiff, but says nothing of martyrdom endured for the faith? The latter was public and manifest to all; the former had been obscure and unknown.]

### POEM XII. On St Eusebius, Pope

Heraclius forbade the fallen to bewail their sins;

Eusebius taught the wretched to weep for their own offences.

The populace was divided into factions as fury grew;

sedition, slaughter, war, discord, quarrels.

Likewise driven out by the savagery of the tyrant,

while the Ruler preserved intact the bonds of peace,

he cheerfully endured complete exile under the judge;

on the Sicilian shore he left behind the world and life.

[Note: Boldetti, book I, ch. 19, from the cemetery of Praetextatus:

> “Equitius Heraclius, who lived 19 years, 7 months, 20 days; reader of the Roman Church. They made [this tomb] for themselves and their well-deserving son. He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of …, in the consulship of Steb[anus] Ursus and Polemius, A.D. 338 …”

Is this Heraclius the Reader’s father, then, indicated in the poem? The dates certainly agree well enough; and the man who had undertaken to defend an unjust cause for the fallen against the bishop must have been some Christian, and an eminent member of that man’s party. Yet the best Christians now lament that such unjust times are renewed somewhere.]

[Note: Namely, some were striving to burst into the Church by force, with no penance imposed, while others adhered to discipline and repelled them. We learn that this occurred under Cornelius and Cyprian from epistles 22 and 55 of the Verona edition.]

[Note: That is, Pope Marcellus. Thus Tillemont and Coustanti, with whom I agree. Compare the preceding passage.]

[Note: Namely, Maxentius. Prudentius, book I *Against Symmachus*:

> “The Milvian [bridge], hurling the tyrant received into the Tiber’s pools …”

The Bucherian calendar also belongs here, fifth day before the Kalends of November:

> “Defeat of the tyrant.”]

[Note: Namely, the fallen were rejecting those conditions which previous Roman bishops had ordered to be observed in order to obtain peace. Cyprian to Stephen, epistle 67: “The glorious honor of our predecessors, the blessed martyrs Cornelius and Lucius, must be preserved. For they, filled with God’s Spirit, judged that peace should be granted, and in their letters indicated that, when penitence had been completed, the fruit of communion and peace ought not to be refused.”]

[Note: I have already offered several reasons why I think Pope Eusebius is praised in this poem, in *On the Poems of Damasus*, ch. 25, § 2, no. 6, and in *On the Acts of Liberius in Exile*, § 9. Now I must examine the martyrologies which deal with Eusebius on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September and the sixth day before the Kalends of October.

The Hieronymian Martyrology, the source and origin of all the rest, has the following on 14 August: “At Venbera in Syria, the feast of the saints Eusebius, Titulus, founder, Prospolinus,” etc. Florentinius takes all these for martyrs, but struggles in vain to find Venbera in Syria. The Corbie manuscript writes, in place of *Venbera Syriae*, “Vinda Syri: feast of St Eusebius, Sicilian founder,” in place of Titulus. So also does another copy published by D’Achéry at the beginning of volume II; Basnage absurdly thinks that *Vinda Siri* there is the name of a martyr. The Antwerp manuscript has: “Vinderia Siri, Eusebius, Titulus, founder.” Bede calls Eusebius a presbyter, but prudently passes over the place and companions in silence, although the Bollandists cite only one among so many manuscript codices—the Barberini manuscript—in which the place is given as in the Hieronymian: *Viridena Siri*. Usuard and Notker likewise omit the place; but, significantly, Notker calls this Eusebius a bishop. The old calendar of the Vatican church, published by Venerable Cardinal Thomasius in volume IV of his works, and the Gellone Martyrology mention Eusebius, but add nothing further—whether he was bishop, presbyter, or martyr.

No one, I think, will deny that the Martyrology of Jerome itself and works copied from it describe an Eusebius other than the Roman presbyter. But because the place is manifestly corrupt, we are forced to remain ignorant who that Eusebius was and where the place of his feast lay; nor do the more recent hagiologies which celebrate the Roman presbyter Eusebius merit confidence, since they depart from their source. Yet this verse of Damasus provides a light by which, unless I am mistaken, we may recover the true and genuine reading of the Hieronymian Martyrology.

I therefore suspect that, from *Bidi Siciliae*, or Bidenum of Syracuse, copyists’ incompetence has produced the present monstrosities *Vindera Syriae*, *Vinderia Syri*, *Vinda Syri*, and *Viridena Syri*. Who does not know how frequent the interchange of B and V was? And who does not see how easily the word *Siciliae* or *Syracusanorum*, perhaps abbreviated or written in shorthand by notaries, could afterwards be changed by unlearned scribes into *Syriae* or *Syri*? Clerc, *Art of Criticism*, vol. II, part III, section I, ch. 12, has produced many similar examples, together with the errors and corrupt interpretations that resulted.

Bidinum was once a fairly notable town, now largely ruined, fifteen Roman miles from Syracuse; in the local language it is now called Abidino. Cicero, however, calls it Bidi in the second book *Against Verres*, and calls its citizens Bideni and Bidini. Moreover, Cluverius, *Sicilian Antiquities*, book II, ch. 4, mentions another fortress and town, namely Bidium or Bidinum, located in the territory of Tauromenium. Therefore, since Pope Eusebius died in exile in Sicily, he must have ended his life in one of these two places, though I would more readily suppose it happened at Bidinum near Syracuse, as nearer the sea and more convenient for letters going and returning.

From this we understand: first, the meaning of the words *Tituli Conditoris* (“founder of the title-church”), which in the most ancient martyrologies some have read as commemorating and identifying unknown martyrs of that name; they express nothing other than that this one Eusebius, whose feast is celebrated on this day, was the Roman pontiff and founder of the title-church which still exists. Secondly, we understand why his feast—that is, the day of his death—is recorded on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, while his burial on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Callixtus is recorded on the sixth day before the Kalends of October: he could not have been buried before that day, since he had not yet been brought to Rome. Thus there is no need, with Papebroch and others, to say that Eusebius himself held the see until the day of that burial. Thirdly, we have a most just reason why this Roman pontiff Eusebius, whose burial is commemorated on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, is called a confessor in the Vatican, Barberini, St Cyriaca’s, and Ado’s martyrologies, and in others indicated by Florentinius and Sollerius: he had surely deserved that title by exile endured for discipline.]

### POEM XIII. On St Mark, Pope

The life of Mark is known to us all:

by the word of God he was able to despise the world.

The people prayed that everyone might learn

the great honor of counting life as contemptible.

Virtue possessed the innermost chambers of his heart:

you, Christ’s guardian, perfect friend.

And Damasus pays honor to the tomb:

here is Mark, companion to Mark in life, faith, name,

and merits.

[Note: Nothing has ever occurred by which this poem, apparently corrupt, can be restored to its integrity. Besides what I observed in *On the Poems of Damasus*, ch. 25, § 2, no. 7, Sarazanius may also be consulted, on this very page, note 1.]

[Note: Concerning the tomb of Pope St Mark, Baronius likewise, p. 909: “There exists an epitaph of the same St Mark, composed by Pope Damasus, which we have recently caused to be published and, so far as possible, rescued from the injuries of time.” Thus he writes. It must be said to have been placed in the cemetery of Balbina on the Ardeatine Way, since, according to Anastasius, he was buried there. Anastasius says: “He built two basilicas, one on the Ardeatine Way, where he rests, and another in the city of Rome near the Palatine”; and at the end: “He was also buried in the cemetery of Balbina, on the Ardeatine Way.” The Breviary says: “He was buried in the cemetery of Balbina.” The Roman Martyrology has, under 7 October: “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the burial of St Mark, pope and confessor.” Bede, however: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of St Mark, bishop and confessor, who sat in the episcopate for … years … and was also buried in the cemetery of Balbina on the Ardeatine Way.” The same words occur in Ado’s Martyrology, adding: “in the cemetery of Balbina on the Ardeatine Way, which he himself, while bishop, made.” So also Usuard and Notker: “At Rome, on the Appian Way,” etc. The Appian and Ardeatine Ways, as I have said elsewhere, were adjacent. At present St Mark’s body lies in the church of St Mark the Evangelist, built by that holy pontiff himself. I have not found when it was transferred there, but we know that this was very ancient, perhaps under Gregory IV, who adorned the apse of that church with mosaic work; he had undertaken its administration during his priesthood and bestowed many gifts upon it, as Anastasius reports.]

[Note: It seems that *tumuli* (“of the tomb”) should be read, as I have already noted; or, if you retain *tumulum* (“the tomb”), read *honorat* (“honors”). The tomb of St Mark, with its inscription, remained until the time of Gregory VII. While he sat as pope, it was discovered with the sacred remains, which were transferred elsewhere, as the distinguished Marangoni recounts in the Appendix to the *Chronology of the Roman Pontiffs*, § 28:

> “Ambrose rendered the last brotherly honor to his brother Uranius, at the martyr’s left hand.”]

### POEM XIV. On St Lawrence

Blows, executioners, flames, tortures, chains—

faith alone enabled Lawrence to conquer them.

Damasus, in supplication, heaps gifts upon these altars,

looking up to the martyr’s outstanding merit.

[Note: Baronius, in the said volume XII, Appendix, along with three others from p. 1164, as given above, prints these from the church of St Lawrence bearing the title of Damasus. The following inscription was also found there, and there can be no doubt that it belongs to our Damasus. Sirmond published it in his notes on the Synod in these words: “Relevant here is an ancient epigram of the city, which may be added to the others published from the Palatine library, from a manuscript of St Mary of Verdun.”

Attica was the wife of Felix Magnus, a man of clarissimus rank, to whom Sidonius Apollinaris wrote an apologetic poem, no. 9, beginning:

> “Tell me, Magnus, tell me what I ask—tell me, I beg you:
> Felix in name, mind, honor, fame,
> in children, wife, brothers, parent,” etc.

At the end he calls himself his fellow student:

> “Therefore protect my wrongdoing,
> and, I pray, defend the heedless modesty
> of your obedient fellow student,” etc.

He also mentions him at the end of the *Propempticon*:

> “Hence, to the spacious house of the consul Magnus,
> and, more truly, to your fortunate books,” etc.

Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 85, reports that Bishop Faustus wrote a letter to the same Felix, in the following words: “He afterwards wrote to Felix, praetorian prefect and a man of ancestral rank, son of a great consul and now religious, a letter exhorting him to the fear of the Lord, appropriate to persons intending with full purpose to undertake penitence” [perhaps *disponentibus*, “to those so intending”].]

[Note: Sarazanius supplied another poem on the same St Lawrence, namely poem XIX, of which it may very much be doubted whether it is Damasus’s. Nevertheless, lest the reader be without it, I give it here:

> It is not surprising that the deceitful flame threatens greatly  
> and burns the martyr’s body with no power to harm it.  
> For the great punishment of faith teaches, without an avenger,  
> that amid the flames there is a path to heaven.  
> The martyr Lawrence therefore enjoys this fire,  
> and by highest merits achieves that he does not die.

He further added a third poem, though by an uncertain author, in which Attica, wife of Felix Magnus, is praised for restoring the same martyr’s basilica; he appended notes to it, no. 14. Both, I think, appear to have come from the same hand; and it is likely that, according to the custom of that age, they were then inscribed upon the walls of the restored basilica and copied from there—unless they came from another basilica in the Veranus district.]

### POEM XV. On St Felix

Blessed in body, mind, spirit, and equally in name, Felix;

consecrated among the number of the saints by Christ’s triumphs;

you grant everything to those who come anxiously to you,

and permit no traveller to depart sorrowful.

Under your guidance, having been saved because I broke death’s bonds,

Damasus in supplication pays you his vows in these verses.

[Note: Vatican Latin manuscript 5087 reads this inscription: “Verses of Pope Damasus in honor of St Felix, pope, concerning his cleansing from a false accusation and the restoration of his health, represented in remarkable mosaic work in the basilica of the same Felix.”]

[Note: The Roman Martyrology places the feast of St Felix the presbyter on 14 January; there Baronius notes that the poem written by Damasus in fulfilment of vows concerns him. There was a celebrated solemnity at Rome for St Felix the confessor. St Gregory preached homily 13 on the Gospels in his basilica on his feast day; from this it is inferred that the basilica formerly had a station, as Panvinio attests in his little book on the stations of the city of Rome.

Anastasius the librarian mentions the church of St Felix *in Pincis* under Pope Hadrian: “The basilica of Blessed Felix situated *in Pincis*, which was in ruins and whose roof had collapsed, he renewed, having newly made the roof, and he offered a covering for the altar of the same church made of fourfold cloth.” Under Benedict III: “Likewise in the church of Blessed Felix the martyr, which is situated *in Pincis*, he made a textile of patterned fabric, with griffins.” Cencius the chamberlain, who became Pope Honorius III, mentions it in his *Ritual*; Martin of Poland in his *Chronicle*; Nicolaus Signorilis, who dedicated his work on the churches of Rome to Pope Martin V; Andreas Fulvius in his *Antiquities of the City* addressed to Clement VII; Lucius Faunus under Paul III; and Marlianus, who also identifies the place. Martin of Poland is clearer: speaking of Rome’s gates, he says, “The Pincian Gate, which is near the church of St Felix *in Pincis*.” An old manuscript *Book of the Antiquities of the City* in our library, written about 250 years ago, enumerates the Pincian Gate near the church of St Felix *in Pincis* under Pope Urban VI. An older marble tablet at St Mary in Cosmedin speaks, among other gifts donated by the most glorious George, of “vineyards which are *in Pincis*.” From this I infer that the gate and the Pincian hill took their name from this church, rather than, as antiquaries following Blondus wish, from the houses of the Pincii, mentioned in Cassiodorus, epistle 10, book III: “marbles from the Pincian house,” etc.

Anastasius the librarian says, in his Life of St Sylvester, “the palace *in Pincis*,” or “of Pincis,” or “of Pincius,” where Belisarius lived; it may have received the name from this church, although the Pincian family is also mentioned in the ancient inscription: “Proba Faltonia Anicia Faltonia adorned the Annii Pincii and the Anicii.” For St Felix himself is called “Felix *in Pincis*” by St Gregory in the Antiphonary, under the title “Feast of St Felix *in Pincis*”; and in ancient manuscript and printed missals and breviaries he is commonly called “St Felix the presbyter and martyr *in Pincis*,” I believe in order to distinguish him from others. For we read of more than sixty Felixes in the martyrologies; and three of these were connected with Nola: one a bishop, another a martyr with companions, and this Felix, our presbyter. According to the Roman lesson, St Felix was buried near Nola, in the place called *in Pincis*; and Ado says of him in the Martyrology: “he was buried beside the city”—that is, Nola—“in a place called *in Pincis*,” etc. The old Roman Martyrology has the same, and Ado at the beginning of his work: “At Nola, Felix the presbyter, buried *in Pincis*.” Bede also writes in the Martyrology: “He was buried near the city by the holy presbyter Elpidius, in a place called *in Pincis*”; and Notker’s Martyrology: “He was buried not far from the city of Nola, in a place called *in Pincis*.”

St Augustine mentions St Felix’s tomb in epistle 187, volume I, to the people of Hippo: “The holiness of the place where the body of blessed Felix of Nola was laid is very well known to many,” etc. Procopius himself teaches in book I of the *Gothic War* that the Pincian Gate was so called from his time; before that it was called the Collatine Gate, and we know that the mountain or hill was called the Hill of the Gardens. St Paulinus, bishop of Nola, wrote St Felix’s life in verse in ten *Natalicia*. The first begins almost like our Damasus:

> “Illustrious confessor Felix in merits and in name.”

And the second *Natalicium*:

> “Felix by that merit which he possesses in his name as well,” etc.

These are among the works of St Paulinus and in Lippomano, vol. II. From Paulinus, Bede composed the life in prose, as he himself declares at the end of the Life and at the end of his *History of the English*: “I translated the book of the life and passion of St Felix the confessor from Paulinus’s metrical work into prose.” That history of the life is also found in Surius. Gregory of Tours gives more in ch. 104 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, also borrowed from Paulinus, as he affirms; he calls Felix a martyr, whom St Paulinus more than once calls a martyr without blood. St Augustine too, in *On Care for the Dead*, ch. 16, mentions St Felix’s appearance when Nola was being besieged by barbarians. St Gregory’s Book of Sacraments contains prayers and a Mass preface under the title: “Eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, feast of St Felix.” Peter de Natalibus in the *Catalogue of Saints* turns one Felix into three, writes confusedly about them, and reports some things wrongly. Mombritius, vol. I of the *Lives of the Saints*, has: “On St Felix, presbyter of Nola,” etc. Ancient coins and inscriptions teach that *Felix* must be written without a diphthong.]

[Note: The same manuscript, and likewise from the name.]

[Note: There: “associated.”]

[Note: Immediately after, or rather attached to, this verse is the following little verse:

> “Once their enemies had been destroyed, who had spoken falsehoods.”

On this see *On the Poems of Damasus*, ch. 25, § 2, no. 8.]

[Note: *Repedare* means “to go back, depart,” says Festus. Pacuvius: “to step back from the threshold.” Nonius Marcellus: “*Repedare*”; Lucilius, book XXVI: “To have returned and gone back, in order that Rome may avoid gladiators. … I too was returning to Rome from the service of Metellus.”]

[Note: Solinus also uses this word, ch. 32 or 42; Apuleius, book VI and at the beginning of the *Florida*; Sidonius, book IV, epistle 3, at the beginning; and Symmachus, book I, epistle 74.]

[Note: Prudentius, returning to Spain, on St Lawrence:

> “And no one returns sorrowful.”

And again concerning St Hippolytus, Hymn XI.]

[Note: Pope Hilary, in the Lateran Baptistery built by him: “Hilary the bishop, servant of Christ, [dedicated this] to his deliverer, blessed John the Evangelist.”

Moreover, in the same manuscript the following verses immediately follow this poem, as though an inseparable part of it:

> “The place was small and narrow for sacred rites,  
> and refused to open wide its doors to suppliant hands.”

Since we read these and other connected verses among the works of Paulinus of Nola, epistle 32, and again on p. 568, one may suspect that they were truly inscribed on the walls of the basilica of St Felix built at Nola, and that a foolish copyist attributed them all to Damasus.]

### POEM XVI. Vow of St Damasus

All who read this, venerate the tomb of the saints.

Antiquity could preserve neither their names nor their number.

Damasus adorned the tomb; recognize the Ruler,

triumphing, Christ granting it, at the return of the clergy.

The priest renders his own vows to the holy martyrs.

[Note: Baronius, p. 909, under the year of Christ 362: “It is found in ancient inscriptions that Damasus made vows to the martyrs for the union of the holy Church, and fulfilled them when the Roman clergy, abandoning the schismatic Ursicinus, joined Damasus. An ancient inscription concerning these matters exists in the following words,” etc.

In the Palatine manuscript this poem follows:

### On the Holy Martyrs Vitalis, Martialis, and Alexander

> When the doomed Getae had pitched their camp beneath the City,  
> they first stirred up impious wars against the saints.  
> And with sacrilegious mind they overturned those tombs,  
> once duly consecrated to the blessed martyrs.  
> When God showed them, Pope Damasus declared, by an inscription fixed up,  
> that they were rightly to be venerated.  
> The holy inscription perished when the marble was broken,  
> yet it was not possible for them to remain hidden again.  
> Pope Vigilius, grieving that these things had been destroyed,  
> soon, when the enemies had been expelled, renewed the entire work.

This is not by Damasus, but I have placed it among Damasus’s poems because it was erected by Pope Vigilius concerning Damasus and his poems. Baronius also has it and believed it to be by Damasus, writing: “There also exist verses of the same Damasus, by which he adorned other churches of holy martyrs, destroyed by barbarian fury, which he himself restored.” In the margin of the book he notes that they concern memorials of martyrs in the suburbs.

The martyrs whose names are read in the inscription appear to be among the seven sons of St Felicitas; of them these three were punished by capital sentence, as we read in the martyrologies on the fourth day before the Ides of July. The cemetery of Felicitas stood on the Salarian Way. Anastasius, in his Life of St Boniface: “Boniface lived in the cemetery of St Felicitas the martyr on the Salarian Way.” And below: “He made an oratory in the cemetery of St Felicitas, near her body, and adorned the tomb of the holy martyr Felicitas and of St Sylvester; there he also placed a silver paten,” etc.; and again at the end: “He too was buried in the cemetery of St Felicitas the martyr on the Salarian Way.” Under St Hadrian: “The cemetery of St Felicitas on the Salarian Way, together with the churches of St Silvanus the martyr and St Boniface the confessor and pontiff, all adjoining on one site, he restored on a marvelous scale.” And there: “Indeed he also restored anew the cemetery of the Jordani, namely of the holy martyrs Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis, and of the holy seven virgins.” Under St Symmachus: “He repaired the basilica of St Felicitas, which was threatened with ruin.” A little below: “He improved the cemetery of the Jordani for the body of St Alexander.”

Concerning another St Alexander, bishop and martyr, the Roman Martyrology states on 21 September: “At Rome, on the Claudian Way, twenty miles from the City, the passion of St Alexander, bishop,” etc.; “his body was later transferred into the City by Blessed Pope Damasus on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, on which day he instituted the celebration of his feast.” The old Roman Martyrology in Ado, under 26 November: “Blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, suffered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October and was transferred by Pope Damasus on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, when he dedicated a feast to him.” Peter de Natalibus, *Catalogue of Saints*, book VIII, ch. 101, says of him: “The holy martyr was carried to the Claudian Way, twenty miles from the City,” etc.; “but afterwards Pope Damasus built a crypt and laid him there.”]

[Note: “Names, nor number.” Paulinus, *Natalicium* XIII:

> “Here the great circuit of the City contains all the martyrs,  
> innumerable together.”

See also Prudentius, Hymn XI; the credibility of these eyewitnesses refutes Dodwell’s ingenious invention concerning the small number of martyrs.]

[Note: Cornelius likewise rejoiced at the return of confessors who had adhered to Novatian, in Cyprian, epistle 46, Pamel edition.]

[Note: A Christian stone recently excavated at St Mary of the Angels and inscribed on both sides. On the first side:

> “To the holy martyrs Paprus and Mauroleon, the lords: Camasius, also called Asclepius, and Victorina, fulfilled a vow on their feast day, the tenth day before the Kalends of October. The boys who made the vow: Vitalis, Maranus, Abundantius, Telesphorus.”

On the other side:

> “To the holy lords Paprus and Maurelon, martyrs: Camasius, also called Asclepius, and Victorina, [made] a vow on the feast day, 513, the day before the Kalends of October … Arane, Vitalis … nti, Telespos.”

The author of the Venetian *Commentary on Italian Literature*, vol. II, pp. 532–533, informs us that both inscriptions were recently published by the distinguished A. F. Gori.]

### POEM XVII. On St Eutychius

Eutychius the martyr, able to conquer the cruel commands of the tyrant

and likewise a thousand ways of harm by executioners,

showed forth the glory of Christ.

The filth of prison was followed by a new punishment: through his limbs

they arranged fragments of potsherds, lest sleep should come to him.

Twice six days passed; food was denied him.

He was cast into a pit. Holy blood washes away every wound

which the dreadful power of death had inflicted.

In the sleep-bringing night, sleeplessness troubled his mind.

The hiding-place revealed where it held the innocent man’s limbs.

He is sought, the young men worship, cherish, supply everything.

Damasus has expressed his merit: venerate the tomb.

[Note: The Roman Martyrology, 10 February: “At Rome, St Eutychius the martyr, who completed an illustrious martyrdom and was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus; Pope St Damasus adorned his tomb with verses.” This epigram for that day exists engraved on a marble tablet in the basilica of St Sebastian, published more accurately and faithfully—as it appears on the stone—by Panvinio in his book on the seven churches of Rome and by Baronius in the Martyrology; also in volume XII, the Appendices, from this book of inscriptions, though according to its reading. We compared it with the original and transcribed it as above. In verse 3 Panvinio writes *monstrante*; Baronius in the Martyrology, *monstrantis*. In verse 8 the Book of Inscriptions has *tulerat*; the stone has *intulerat*. Then follows a verse and the beginning of another, as given above, which are absent from that book; for it transcribed the halves of two verses as one and made one verse from portions of two.

The body of St Eutychius, transferred from this place, lies in the basilica of St Lawrence bearing the title of Damasus, beneath the high altar, where remains of Damasus’s own body also exist. The inscription reads: “Under this altar are laid the bodies of St Damasus, pope and confessor, and St Eutychius, martyr of Christ.”]

[Note: Venerable Cardinal Thomasius, *Works*, vol. V, p. 465, tenth day before the Kalends of June: “The feast of St Eutychius.” For the rest, see Sarazanius’s note.]

[Note: Thus in the poem on St Paul: “he perceived what the glory of Christ could do”; on SS Nereus and Achilleus: “what the glory of Christ can do”; on St Lawrence: “faith alone was able to conquer.”]

### POEM XVIII. On St Tarsicius

[Note: See what I have observed on this in *On the Poems of Damasus*, ch. 25, § 2, no. 10.]

> [Note: [Col. 0392C] Receive also Damasus’s epigram on the martyr Tarsicius, who was carrying the sacred Eucharist. The same Baronius believes that, in the penultimate verse, where *pulgare* is incorrectly read from the Palatine manuscripts, one should read *peteret vulgare* (“should seek to divulge”), a form of expression which Ovid also uses in *The Art of Love*, II:
>
> “Who dares divulge the rites of Ceres to the profane?”
>
> Moreover, *tropaeum* (“trophy”) is written here without aspiration, in the ancient fashion. Cicero, in the *Orator* addressed to Brutus: “Since I knew that our forefathers had spoken so as to employ aspiration nowhere except with a vowel, I spoke thus: *pulcros*, *Cetegos*, *triumpos*, *Cartaginem*, etc.” In ancient inscriptions *tropaeum* is commonly found; the Greeks have τροπαῖον (*tropaion*, “trophy”); see Nonius. For understanding the epigram, see the Martyrology for 15 August, where he is said to have been buried on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Callixtus; this is also stated in the martyrdom of St Stephen, pope, in Metaphrastes for 2 August, found in Lipomanus, vol. VII, and in Surius, vol. IV; see also Peter in the *Catalogue*, book VII, ch. 66. See likewise Baronius’s note on the Martyrology; and do not be surprised that an acolyte carried Christ’s Body. An old marble inscription teaches that this saint’s body rests in the church of St Sylvester in the Campus Martius; its heading is:
>
> +. In the name of the Lord, this is the record of the feast-days of the Saints resting here.
>
> Then follows: “In the month of July, on the twenty-sixth day, feast of Pope Zephyrinus and of the martyr Tarsicius.” There is variation in the day of his feast: the Martyrology has 15 August; the martyrdom of Pope St Stephen, 2 August; and the marble calendar of St Sylvester, 26 July. This may have arisen from the date of his martyrdom and from translations of his relics. There is also another martyr Tarsicius, who suffered at Alexandria with Zoticus and Cyriacus, in the Martyrologies for 31 January.]

Whoever you are who read this, learn the equal merit of the two,

whom Bishop Damasus, their governor, commemorates with inscriptions after their rewards.

The Jewish people had struck down Stephen, counselling better things,

with stones—he who had borne away the trophy from the enemy.

The faithful Levite was the first to seize martyrdom.

When an impious band sought to divulge to the profane

the sacraments of Christ which holy Tarsicius was carrying,

he himself, struck down, preferred to yield up his life

rather than betray the heavenly members to rabid dogs.

> [Note: [Col. 0392D] Perhaps *Queis* (“to whom”).]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0392D] Thus sepulchral inscriptions are called; very frequent examples may be found in Gruter and Muratori.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0392D] In the poem on St Paul: “who had borne trophies from the enemy”; in the poem on his own tomb: “who bear trophies from the enemy”; and in the Appendix, no. 4: “who took trophies from the enemy.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0392D] Let heterodox persons observe the faith of those times.]

### POEM XIX. On St Gorgonius

> [Note: [Col. 0393C] Who is this Gorgonius? See the discussion of the poems of Damasus, ch. 25, §2, no. 11.]
>
> [Col. 0393A]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0393B] From another marble tablet, formerly over the tomb of the holy martyr Gorgonius and now fixed into the wall by the principal door of the basilica, as also from the other tablet transcribed above. Baronius published it in vol. IV of the *Annals*, under the year of the Lord 384, and in vol. VIII of the appendices; Gruter published it in the appendix to his *Roman Inscriptions*.
>
> This Gorgonius appears to be the one who suffered with Dorotheus at Nicomedia under the Emperor Diocletian, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 6; Nicephorus, book VII, ch. 2; the Roman Breviary and Martyrology; and the Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Notker, for 9 September; and Peter de Natalibus, *Catalogue*, book VIII, ch. 55. They affirm that his body was later brought to Rome: the Roman Breviary and Martyrology, as also Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Peter in the *Catalogue*, say that it was placed on the Latin Way. The Martyrology writes that it was transferred from there to the basilica of St Peter by Pope Gregory IV; so do the Breviary and Anastasius in his account of Gregory.
>
> Ado adds “on the Latin Way between the two laurels”; hence I had thought that the Martyrologies should be corrected and that “Lavican Way” should replace “Latin Way,” since the site *inter duas lauros* (“between the two laurels”) was on the Lavican Way: the place of St Tiburtius, of SS Marcellinus and Peter, and of Helena, once very famous for churches and relics, and for the feast of the Thirty Martyrs on 22 December. The reading in the Roman Breviary published under the authority of Pius V confirmed this view: there St Gorgonius is said to have been buried between the two laurels on the Lavican Way; nor did I find the Latin Way described elsewhere as “between the two laurels,” although in more recent Breviaries “Latin Way” has been restored. See what we have noted above on the Lavican Way at the Two Laurels.
>
> Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 764, writes concerning the later translation of Gorgonius’s and other martyrs’ bodies into Gaul:
>
> > “Bishop Chrodegang transferred the bodies of the martyrs Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius from Rome to Gaul; he placed Gorgonius in the monastery of Gorze, Nabor at Hilliariacum, etc.”
>
> Bede, followed by Rabanus, writes in the Martyrologies:
>
> > “On the second day before the Ides of June, Chrodegang [Rabanus has Hruodgang], bishop of Metz, with the permission of Paul, pope of Rome, transferred Nazarius together with the martyr Gorgonius from Rome to Gaul in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 765, and the aforesaid bishop placed St Gorgonius in the monastery called Gorze.”
>
> Notker says nearly the same in his Martyrology for that day; Peter likewise says in the *Catalogue:*
>
> > “In the year of the Lord 764, the bishop of Metz, nephew of King Pippin, transferred him to the monastery of Gorze.”
>
> Understand this, however, as referring to a portion of the bodily relics, since relics of this saint still remain in the Vatican basilica, where they are shown to the people on the solemn Monday of Easter; it is also maintained there that his body is preserved. Yet in the church of St Sylvester in the Campus Martius, on the marble tablet listing the feasts of saints resting there, one reads: “In the month of September, on the 10th day, feast of St Gorgonius and of others whose names the Lord knows.” In the Acts of this same St Gorgonius, preserved in manuscript in the library of the Congregation of the Oratory, codex no. 7, it is stated that his relics were transferred to Gaul after his body had been carried from Nicomedia to Rome, and that some of those relics were later sent on to Saxony.]

This tomb of the martyr, beneath the great summit of the hill,

holds Gorgonius, who guards Christ’s altars.

Whoever comes here, let him seek the thresholds of the saints;

he will find the blessed dwelling nearby in their abode,

whom devotion bore together to heaven as they went.

> [Note: [Col. 0393C] Thus again in the poem on his own tomb, concerning an unidentified Greek martyr, and elsewhere Damasus uses this expression. Muratori therefore thinks that many altars were placed in cemeteries and over martyrs; Aringhi also thinks so. See the note on Paulinus, poem XIX, v. 398, Verona edition.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0393D] The monk of Einsiedeln reads *ovantes* (“rejoicing”).]

### POEM XX. On St Saturninus, Martyr

> [Note: [Col. 0394C] Baronius says that Damasus also caused these verses to be inscribed on the tomb of St Saturninus, martyr, on the Salerian Way. These are Baronius’s words as he transcribes the verses from that book after the preceding poems. In the Palatine codex and Gruter’s edition, the beginning of this poem is read thus:
>
> > “Damasus, bishop, servant of God, worshipper of these martyrs:
> >
> > Now may Christ’s … be … ashes …” (thus).
>
> ]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0393D] Tillemont rightly complains that copyists’ errors have caused this poem, as well as others, often now to be scarcely intelligible; my efforts to restore it to its integrity were in vain. See also Sarazanius’s note.]

At the time when the sword cut the devout entrails of the Mother—

Rome, that is—by blood he changed both country, life, and lineage:

his origin made him a Roman citizen of the Saints.

A wondrous steadfastness in suffering taught greatly after his death.

When Gratian rages like an enemy and mangles his holy limbs,

after he had vomited forth the venom conceived from gall,

he could not compel you, holy one, to deny Christ;

confessing him, he himself earned departure through your prayers.

This is the voice of the suppliant Damasus: venerate the tomb;

it is permitted to fulfil vows and pour forth chaste prayers,

because here is the tomb of the martyr, holy Saturninus.

> [Note: [Col. 0393D] This verse is repeated in the poem on St Stephen and in Appendix no. 2.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0393D] Rome, of course. For Saturninus: “His origin made him a Roman citizen, but the wondrous faith of the Saints made him a citizen [of the saints].” The sense is nevertheless somewhat obscure.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0394C] The codex reads *namque genusque* (“indeed, and lineage”); with Baronius we have restored *vitamque genusque* (“both life and lineage”). Saturninus’s feast day is 29 November in the Roman and Usuardian Martyrologies, and more fully in Bede’s Martyrologies.
>
> Concerning the basilica where St Saturninus’s relics were, Anastasius the Librarian—who also records these verses under Felix IV—says: “In his times the basilica of the martyr St Saturninus on the Salerian Way was consumed by fire; he rebuilt it from the ground.” Under St Hadrian: “He also renewed the basilica of Saturninus situated on the aforesaid Salerian Way, together with the cemetery of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria, and restored the cemetery of St Hilaria.” Under Gregory IV: “For at that time he caused the church of the blessed martyr Saturninus, built outside the Salerian Gate, which through excessive age and long decay had fallen from its foundations, to be rebuilt with new construction and adorned with varied paintings; there he also offered one garment from an endowment.” Baronius also discusses this basilica in the Martyrology.
>
> The walls of the shrine still remain outside the Salerian Gate, and the place retains the name of St Saturninus; there was also the cemetery named after Thrason, concerning which see Cencius the chamberlain in the *Book of Revenues of the Roman Church*, Volaterranus, Albertini, Panvinio, etc. The body of St Saturninus, however, was transferred to the church of SS John and Paul, the title of Pammachius.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0393D] Is he the one who suffered with the deacon Sisinnius and gave his name to the cemetery on the Salerian Way, also called that of Thrason? So it is believed. For a celebrated commemoration of this Saturninus was held in that place, as is clear from the Calendar of Bucherius and other ancient monuments for 29 November. I consider this altogether true, since I see that the tombs of the other martyrs placed in the same location—namely Chrysanthus, Daria, Maurus, Hilarus, and perhaps others—were repaired and adorned with verses by Damasus. The Gelasian Order indeed has a Mass for Saturninus, Chrysanthus, Maurus, and Daria, in one and the same place and on the same day. See the distinguished Blanchini, *Works of Thomasius*, p. 140.
>
> Why then do the statements written by Damasus in this poem not altogether agree with what we read in the Acts of Marcellus concerning St Saturninus? In those Acts, the man who ordered the martyr to be tortured and killed is Laodicius; here Gratian is named. Moreover, those Acts contain no mention of the confession of Christian faith by that judge, whoever he may have been, which Damasus recounts. But, as Baronius and Bollandus observe, those Acts are not wholly free from difficulties.]

### POEM XXI. On St Maurus

> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Son of Claudius the tribune and of Hilaria, martyrs, and brother of Jason, as in the Acts of St Chrysanthus and Daria. See Sarazanius’s note.]
>
> [Col. 0395A]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395B] Baronius has the following from this place, p. 912, with these added words: “There are in the cited codex other epitaphs assigned to memorials of other holy martyrs, which he either adorned or restored, all included in the same volume; among them is one on the boy Maurus.” This boy Maurus is apparently Jason’s brother, son of Claudius the tribune and Hilaria; concerning them all the Martyrologies speak on 3 December, as does the History of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria, which Metaphrastes has for 19 March in Lipomanus, vol. VII, and Surius, vol. V:
>
> > “This holy boy was killed for Christ’s confession together with his brother Jason under the Emperor Numerian. In the place where they were killed there is an ancient monument; after Christians had cleared it out, they laid within it at night all the bodies of the holy martyrs, not far from the City, beside the road now called the Mauran Way.”
>
