> These are the words of that history. The bodies of these holy brothers were transferred from the cemeteries to St Praxedes under Pope Paschal, as is recorded on a marble tablet in that church. They were later carried to Lucca by Pope Alexander II, as Baronius reports from ancient records of the church of Lucca, vol. II, under the year of the Lord 1070.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395C] Similarly above, concerning St Gorgonius:
>
> > “This tomb of the martyr, beneath the great summit of the hill,
> >
> > holds Gorgonius.”]

This tomb of the martyr Maurus holds his holy limbs,

which Damasus, governor of the people long afterward,

humbly adorned, embellishing them with a better cult:

an innocent boy, whom no punishment cast down.

> [Note: [Col. 0395D] This popular term was likewise used by other ancient Roman supreme pontiffs. At St Mary Major, at the summit of the arch in mosaic: “Bishop Sixtus to the people of God”—this Sixtus being the third of that name. At the Lateran, on the marble door of the chapel of St John the Baptist: “+ Bishop Hilarus + to the holy people of God.” And in the church of St Andrew on the Esquiline, which Anastasius calls Catabarbara, St Simplicius, successor of St Hilarus, wrote these verses in mosaic: “Devout people, come, and through these exchanges learn,” etc. We still see them entire; Platina also records them.
>
> Felix III, successor of John, wrote at St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, where there was a mosaic inscription recovered from the Palatine manuscripts and published by Gruter; Baronius reproduced it in the Appendices to vol. XII under the year of Christ 530. It concludes: “Pope Felix, adding the splendour of mosaic, completed [this work] for the holy people of God.” Our Damasus likewise says above concerning St Paul: “He desired to tear apart the people,” etc.
>
> Leo IV also uses the title in verses which stood at the gate of the Aelian citadel, as did Pope John VIII in an epigram formerly found on the gate of the suburb of St Paul, as is evident from an old manuscript codex entitled *Description of the City of Rome*. The book was written under Pope Urban VI, and we possess it. I append the verses here as they are, so that they may live again, since I have not read them elsewhere:
>
> **OF LEO IV: At the entrance to the City of Rome through the gate of the Aelian citadel**
>
> “Roman, Frank, and Lombard traveller, and everyone  
> who turns his attention to this work, sing worthy songs.  
> What the good bishop Leo IV duly renewed,  
> behold, for the safety of his native land and his people.  
> Rejoicing with the supreme prince, John completed  
> all these things; his high honour shines forth.  
> May almighty God bring to the citadel of heaven  
> those whom reverend faith has bound in exceeding love.”
>
> *Called the Leonine City.*
>
> **OF JOHN VIII: At the gate of the suburb of St Paul**
>
> “Here stands the saving wall and unconquered gate,  
> which bars the reprobate and receives the devout.  
> Enter it, nobles, elders, and youths in the toga,  
> and consecrated people seeking God’s holy thresholds.  
> The bishop of the Lord, John, duly accomplished it,  
> he who excelled in radiant character and merits.  
> Behold, the venerable city is renowned as Johannepolis,  
> made from the name of Bishop John the Eighth.  
> May the holy angel of the Lord, with Paul the prince,  
> always guard this gate from the wicked enemy—  
> this signal monument, which rejoicing Pope John  
> of the Apostolic See built with a great wall—  
> so that after his death the gate of the heavenly kingdom  
> may be opened to him, through the abundant mercy of Christ God.”
>
> ]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Thus Baronius, followed by Sarazanius; Gruter, p. 1171, reads *delicti* (“of sin”).]

### POEM XXII. On an Unidentified Greek Martyr

> [Note: [Col. 0396C] In the second verse I have restored *fratremque* (“and brother”) from the requirements of the metre; the exemplar has only *fratrem*, or perhaps rather *civem quoque fratrem* (“both fellow citizen and brother”). This epigram, like the others, was not copied by Baronius, I believe because the martyr’s name was uncertain, although he was Greek.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Thus of St Saturninus: “By blood you changed your country.”]

Long ago, as report relates, Greece sent you forth.

By blood you changed your country; love made you both fellow citizen and brother,

having suffered for the holy name of the law.

Now a dweller with the Lord, you guard Christ’s altars;

that you may favour Damasus’s prayers, I pray, illustrious martyr.

> [Note: [Col. 0395D] See Sarazanius’s note.]

### POEM XXIII. On SS Marcellinus and Peter

> [Note: [Col. 0396D] This is a poem on Saints Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs—the one a presbyter, the other an exorcist. Bishop Rabanus Maurus also wrote a hymn about them nearly eight hundred years ago; it begins, “Brothers, I ask you to utter clear and saving praises.” It is no. 23, and other verses follow the hymn as the next no. 24.
>
> To explain the poem and indicate the place where this epigram stood, it is useful to cite the words found in the martyrdom of the aforesaid holy Marcellinus and Peter:
>
> > “In a vision St Tiburtius appeared to Lucilla and Firmina with these two martyrs, Marcellinus and Peter, and instructed them how their bodies, carried from the dark wood, should be buried beside him in the lower part of the crypt. Two acolytes of the Roman Church assisted them. Damasus, while still a little boy and a reader, learned all this from the man who had beheaded them; afterward, having become bishop, he adorned their tomb with these verses: ‘Marcellinus, and you, Peter, learn alike of your triumphs,’ etc.”
>
> All this is also related in the history of the Martyrs, written in iambic verse, found in vol. VII of Surius after the account of the translation of the bodies. The Roman Martyrology says of these saints on the same day, 2 June: “Their bodies were buried in a crypt beside St Tiburtius; Pope St Damasus afterward adorned their tomb with verses.” Ado says in his Martyrology:
>
> > “Afterward, at the martyrs’ own revelation, Lucilla and Firmina, most Christian women, carried away their bodies and buried them beside St Tiburtius in the lower part of the crypt.”
>
> Nearly all the Roman Martyrologies—Bede’s, Usuard’s, Ado’s, and Notker’s—state that this tomb of Tiburtius was on the Lavican Way, three miles from the City, between the two laurels. At that spot Emperor Constantine built a basilica, as Damasus—or Anastasius the Librarian—in the *Life of St Sylvester* relates:
>
> > “At the same time Augustus Constantine built a basilica for the blessed martyrs Marcellinus the presbyter and Peter the exorcist, between the two laurels; and a mausoleum in which his most blessed mother Helena was buried, in a porphyry sarcophagus, on the Lavican Way, the third mile from the city of Rome. There, for love of his mother and reverence for the saints, he placed offerings from his vow: a paten of purest gold weighing thirty-five pounds.”
>
> He goes on to list many other offerings of great value, estates, and so forth. Bede, in *On the Reckoning of Time*, says nearly the same:
>
> > “Likewise, a basilica on the Lavican Way between the two laurels for the blessed martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, and a mausoleum in which he placed his mother in a purple sarcophagus.”
>
> Ado says the same in his *Chronicle*. Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 31, writes concerning Helena’s death, in Langius’s translation:
>
> > “Outside the city of Rome she was placed in a marble urn in a round shrine, and two years later was carried with the urn to Constantinople.”
>
> Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 849: “The holy Empress Helena was buried at Rome in the church of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, in a purple mausoleum,” etc. Peter de Natalibus, book VII, ch. 73, says the same.
>
> Anastasius the Librarian reports concerning Pope Honorius I: “He renewed the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter on the Lavican Way.” And concerning Hadrian I: “He renewed the cemetery of the blessed Peter and Marcellinus on the Lavican Way, beside the basilica of Blessed Helena; and he newly made its roof—that is, of St Tiburtius and the same saints Peter and Marcellinus—because there was no longer any descent to the bodies of the saints.”
>
> The martyrs’ bodies were later translated to Gaul. Einhard, or Eginhard, wrote the history of this event; Surius has it in vol. VIII, where he says of the place:
>
> > “First they came to the basilica of St Tiburtius, martyr, on the Lavican Way, three thousand paces from the city; then they descended into the crypt adjoining that basilica, in which the bodies of the blessed martyrs of Christ, Marcellinus and Peter, had been buried,” etc.
>
> Sigebert in the *Chronicle* for 826, Annon—or Amon—in *Deeds of the Franks*, book IV, ch. 114, at the end, who states that it occurred under Gregory IV, and others also recount the translation. Rabanus Maurus writes in verses on the same martyrs:
>
> > “The upright Einhard summoned these witnesses of Christ from the Roman city  
> > and established a place for them,” etc.
>
> And in Einhard’s epitaph, the same author says:
>
> > “For having performed worthy honour to these saints,  
> > he sought their bodies at Rome and brought them here,” etc.
>
> Panvinio reports in his booklet *On the Stations of the City* that a station was held in this basilica: “On the fourth day before the Nones of June, station at SS Marcellinus and Peter on the Lavican Way.” For St Gregory carefully distributed the stations among basilicas and cemeteries of holy martyrs, a custom which the Roman people zealously retained, as though he were still living, even as times declined. Pope Gregory himself visited those basilicas in reverence and delivered twenty homilies on the Gospels before the congregation at different times, as John the Deacon writes in the *Life of St Gregory*, book II, no. 18.
>
> Cencius Sabellus, who was Pope Honorius III, later mentioned this place in the *Book of Revenues of the Roman Church*: on their feast day he had one [station] at the basilica of SS Marcellinus and Peter, “the cemetery between the two laurels at St Helena.” Nicolaus Signorilis, who lived under Pope Martin V, also mentions it while listing all the churches of the City then extant:
>
> > “Outside the City: the church of St Paul; St Anastasius at the Waters of Salvation; St Mary of the Annunciation; St Sebastian at the Catacombs; St Helena,” etc.
>
> At that time, and still, traces remained of this church and Helena’s mausoleum. We ourselves saw them long ago; Bosius reports in his notes on the *Life of St Cecilia* that he was the first to uncover and survey them. We have treated these matters at length because this basilica was known to few; indeed, the church dedicated to these martyrs near the Lateran was commonly believed to be it, although the foregoing makes clear that that church was not built by Constantine, as Ugonius likewise affirmed in *On the Stations*. Nevertheless, since in our own time, while Urban VIII sat as supreme pontiff, that church has been restored and renovated, what we have said will be clear and evident to everyone.
>
> Incidentally, one should note that *ad duas lauros* (“at the two laurels”) may perhaps be the correct reading rather than *inter duas lauros* (“between the two laurels”), because, as Arnobius says in book III, the Greeks call streets *laurae*. Tertullian in the *Apology* writes: “Whence came Cassius, Niger, and Albinus? Whence those who besieged Caesar between the two laurels?” He means the Emperor Commodus, who withdrew to a laurel grove in order to avoid the plague, since that region was cooler and shaded by very many laurel woods—whence the district received its name—and was there besieged by the Romans demanding Cleander’s death; concerning these matters see Herodian, *History*, book I.]

Marcellinus, and you, Peter, learn alike of your triumphs.

The executioner related to me, Damasus, when I was a boy,

that the frenzied butcher had given orders concerning you:

that at that time he should cut off your necks amid thorns,

and that no one might be able to discover your tomb;

that you, cheerful, had cleared your graves with your own hands

before you lay hidden in a spotless cavern;

that afterward, Lucilla, instructed by your devotion,

had thought it better to lay your most holy bodies here.

> [Note: [Col. 0395D] In ancient martyrologies and monuments Marcellinus is placed before Peter, and Peter before Marcellinus, with no distinction between them. See the Gradual Antiphonary and Lectionary of St Gregory published in the learned Father Vezzosi’s editions of the works of Cardinal Thomasius, vols. II and V.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0396D] The Palatine codex, cited by Gruter, has *nosse* (“to know”): that is, the executioner said that he knew [this]; the distinguished Mazochius judges that it should be written so in his commentary on the old marble Neapolitan Calendar for 2 June.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0396D] From this you understand that no consular Acts of the Martyrs could then have been recorded by Christians, or, if any had been written, that they had been torn up, lest learned ages, instructed by enduring documents, might pass on to posterity through their listening ears the date and manner of the Passion, disclosed by sweet tongues—as Prudentius says in his hymn on Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius. See the Acts of St Vincent in Ruinart.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0397D] Sarazanius and Henschenius read thus; but the sense requires that we read *haec sibi* (“these things to himself”), as the most distinguished Mazochius also observes.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0398D] Here is a full stop, correctly supplied by Mazochius, though omitted by Sarazanius and Henschenius. The martyrs did not themselves clear the place of their grave with their own hands after they had lain there; they did so before they died.]

### POEM XXIV. On SS Felix and Adauctus, Martyrs

> [Note: [Col. 0399B] Baronius, p. 912, further reports an epigram of the same Damasus on the holy martyrs Felix and Adauctus in the same place. The Martyrologies give their feast as the third day before the Kalends of September. Their cemetery was renewed by Pope St John, according to Anastasius the Librarian, who writes concerning St Leo III: “He renewed the roofs of the blessed martyrs Felix and Adauctus beside St Paul the Apostle.”
>
> The name Adauctus is not this saint’s proper name: since Christians did not know his name, they called him Adauctus (“Added”), because he had been added to St Felix for the crown, as is written in the Roman Martyrology and those of Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Notker, which report that they suffered on the Ostian Way. Baronius further reports in his note on the Roman Martyrology for 22 September that the Acts testify that the holy women Digna and Emerita, who suffered in the persecution of Emperor Valerian under the judge Gaius, were buried in the cemetery of Comedilla on the Ostian Way near Saints Felix and Adauctus. It may be believed that this epigram stood in that place. St Gregory has an antiphon for the feast of these saints.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0399C] In the same manner above, concerning St Felix the presbyter:
>
> > “Felix in body, mind, and soul alike, as in name.”]

O Felix, truly Felix in name once and again,

who, in unstained faith, despising the Prince of the world,

confessed Christ and sought the heavenly kingdoms.

O faith truly precious! Know, brothers,

that Adauctus likewise hastened victoriously to heaven.

A true priest, by the command of Bishop Damasus,

prepared the tomb of the Saints, worshipping at their thresholds.

> [Note: [Col. 0399C] Concerning this Felix, whom Marbod says was born, reared, and ordained priest at Rome, it is clear from Papebroch, *Paralipomena to Conatus*, p. 42, that his basilica on the Ostian Way near St Paul was formerly called “in the Pine Groves.” This perhaps caused the distinguished Mazochius to read *in Pincis* (“on the Pincian [Hill]”) and to conjecture, in his note on 14 January, that this Felix, not Felix of Nola, was called “of the Pincian.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0399D] In Appendix no. 2: “having overcome the Prince of the world.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0399D] In the poem on Nereus and Achilleus: “having confessed, they rejoice”; on St Saturninus: “confessing, he earned departure”; and in Appendix no. 2: “having confessed Christ the martyr,” and no. 3: “having confessed Christ the martyr.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0399D] The name of this blessed martyr is proper to him, contrary to what some formerly supposed. The Acts of these martyrs, written in Italian and annotated through the work of the learned and devout Francis Valesius, who died in recent years, are extant.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0399D] I therefore do not doubt that this epitaph was composed by Damasus himself and given by him to be inscribed.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0400C] The monk of Einsiedeln appears to have read *adornans* (“adorning”), which is not objectionable. Besides, the other reading also has nothing objectionable if it is rightly understood; compare Paulinus, poem XIX, v. 305, Verona edition:
>
> > “And he worships the seat of the great Confessor.”]

### POEM XXV. On SS Nereus and Achilleus, Martyrs

> [Note: [Col. 0399C] Baronius, p. 909, thought this epigram composed when the enraged part of the Roman people, abandoning the armed Ursicinus, turned to Damasus as their lawful bishop. I would rather believe, however, that it could be applied to holy martyrs, specifically soldiers, who despised the triumphal glory of pagan warfare and, having professed the Christian name and cast aside military arms, gained more glorious triumphs of Christ by following Christ as commander.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0400D] The monk of Einsiedeln testifies that this was inscribed on the martyrs’ tomb; Cardinal Thomasius agrees with Ciampini. See *On the Poems of Damasus*.]

They had entered military service and jointly bore

the honourable duty of observing the tyrant’s commands,

ready to serve under the pressure of fear and orders.

Wondrous steadfastness! Suddenly they laid aside their fury;

converted, they flee and abandon their leader’s impious camp.

They cast away shields, trappings, and blood-stained weapons;

having confessed, they rejoice to bear Christ’s triumphs.

Believe through Damasus what Christ’s glory is able to do.

> [Note: [Col. 0400D] Mabillon, *Ancient Analects*, p. 363, reads “and savage.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0400D] The Palatine codex in Gruter reads “their.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0400D] Mabillon reads “and blood-stained weapons.”]

### POEM XXVI. On SS Protus and Hyacinthus, Martyrs

> [Note: [Col. 0399C] Baronius, p. 913D of the Appendix: “And likewise Damasus on the martyrs Protus and Hyacinthus,” etc. Another epigram on the same saints appears at p. 1173, no. 11, which we shall place below because Baronius joined it to the preceding one. There was a notable Roman memorial of these martyrs, whose confessio Pope Symmachus adorned, as we read in Anastasius.
>
> It probably stood on the old Salerian Way, in the cemetery of Basilla, where the Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Notker place the feast of these saints on 2 September: “On the Salerian Way, in the cemetery of Basilla.” Usuard simply says, “On the Salerian Way.” Under Pope Clement VIII their sacred relics were solemnly transferred on 21 June 1592 from the church of St Saviour near the bridge of St Mary across the Tiber to the church of St John the Baptist of the Florentine nation, as Baronius reports in the Martyrology and as we ourselves witnessed. In the former church, called St Saviour at the foot of the bridge, there was the following monument:
>
> > “Beneath this stone rest the bodies of the most glorious Saints Protus and Hyacinthus.”
>
> The front portion of the marble bearing Damasus’s preceding inscription still survives in the church of the Four Crowned Saints, the remaining portion having recently been supplied, with this heading prefixed: “Fragment of the Poems of Pope St Damasus, taken from the pavement of the church, placed here and completed.” This was plainly done from the Palatine manuscripts.
>
> More concerning the deeds of these holy martyrs is found in the martyrdom of St Eugenia in Metaphrastes, also in Lipomanus, vol. V, Surius, vol. VI; St Gregory too has an antiphon and Mass for these holy martyrs in his Antiphonary and Book of Sacraments.]

The tomb lay hidden beneath the far slope of the hill;

Damasus points out this tomb, which preserves the limbs of the devout.

A better palace of heaven keeps you for itself, Protus.

You follow, Hyacinthus, proved by purple blood.

Brothers, both of mighty spirits:

here one victor earned the palm, the former the crown.

> [Note: [Col. 0400D] One sometimes sees on sarcophagi a palm carved on one side and a crown on the other. Examples occur in Boldetti, book II, ch. 9, and Muratori, vol. IV, *Inscriptions*. Did Damasus therefore intend, by this little verse, to indicate the position in which each of the holy brothers had been placed? It seems so. The monk of Einsiedeln adds to this poem: “The priest Leopardus adorned [it].”]

### POEM XXVII. On the Same Saints

> [Note: [Col. 0400C] From p. 1172, no. 9, to be placed after the other poem above, since Baronius also joined it to that one as Damasus’s; both epigrams concern SS Protus and Hyacinthus and this one likewise has Damasus’s character.]

Look at the descent: you will see a marvellous deed;

you see the monuments of the Saints uncovered from their tombs.

Here lies the tomb of the martyrs Protus and Hyacinthus,

which, though hill, earth, and darkness had long covered it,

the earnest priest Theodore built this work,

so that the greater works might contain the people of the Lord.

> [Note: [Col. 0401C] The style proves that this too is a poem of Damasus. I therefore think that one was inscribed on the tomb of these holy martyrs, the other in their cemetery, enlarged through the care of the priest Theodore. Boldetti describes the site of the cemetery, book II, ch. 18.]

### POEM XXVIII. On SS Chrysanthus and Daria, Martyrs

> [Note: [Col. 0401D] See *On the Poems of Damasus*, lest I repeat here what I have observed at that place.]

> **[Note: Col. 0401A]** These are verses by Damasus, as Gregory of Tours testifies at the end of chapter 38 of his *Book of Miracles, on the Glory of the Martyrs*, when he speaks of the basilica of the Saints Chrysanthus and Daria in these words: “Damasus, bishop [Col. 0401B] of the holy Apostolic See, ordered the window to be more carefully covered, and adorned the place with verses,” etc. Baronius did not copy it out as he did the others; nevertheless, he mentions it in the *Martyrology*, drawing on Gregory, when he says: “Concerning the discovery of their bodies, and the epitaph written by Pope St. Damasus at their tomb,” etc.  
>   
> We infer that this basilica or crypt stood on the Via Salaria; for the ancient manuscript codices, quoted by Surius under 17 January in the account of the discovery of St. Diodorus and others, read as follows: “Blessed Chrysanthus and the virgin Daria, etc., by the emperor’s fury, were placed outside the gate of the city of Rome on the Via Salaria in a sand-pit, and were ordered to be buried alive beneath earth and stones.” The lesson of the Roman Breviary for 25 October says: “Then both were led to the sand-pit on the Via Salaria; the ground having been dug out, they were covered with stones and obtained an equal crown of martyrdom.” And the Roman Martyrology on that same 25th says: “By command of the Emperor Numerian they were placed in a sand-pit on the Via Salaria and there buried alive beneath earth and stones.” Usuard says the same, on the same day [Col. 0401C]. Bede and Ado, however, place them on 1 December; the Greeks too, in the *Menologion*, and in the Life in Metaphrastes, on 19 March. This diversity of feast-days may have arisen from the day of martyrdom, discovery, or translation.  
>   
> Gregory of Tours says further: “A crypt also was built above them in wonderful workmanship, which afterwards rose in a vaulted arch and stood with the firmest stability.” Anastasius, writing of Hadrian, says: “He also restored the basilica of St. Saturninus situated on the aforesaid Via Salaria, together with the cemetery of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria.”  
>   
> You have these verses written in another order in the same book, p. 1171, but of the eight verses only the latter four, and there it reads:
>
> *From slender means these things now rise better.*
>
> Therefore, from this book we add the word *better* (*melius*) [Col. 0402A], so that the verse may be complete. There it reads *excessu* (“from an outlay”); here, however, *ex censu* (“from resources”). No. 14 on the same leaf contains only the first two verses, and the second verse reads:
>
> *Of Chrysanthus and Daria: now their honour is revered;*
>
> while the next two occur together with another epigram also on p. 1171, no. 15. The bodies of these saints [Col. 0402B], Chrysanthus and Daria, were discovered together with other relics by Pope Stephen VI in the first year of his pontificate, A.D. 886, removed from that place, and deposited or distributed in the Lateran palace, the basilica of the Twelve Holy Apostles, and elsewhere, as appears in the history of the discovery of Saints Diodorus and others in Surius, vol. I, 17 January; Peter also discusses it in his *Catalogue*, book I, chapter 12.  
>   
> An altar of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria also stood in the Lateran basilica beneath the apse, and their bodies had once been laid there. But when, at the time when the church collapsed under Stephen VI, it had been desecrated and ruined, they were transferred to the oratory of St Mary and St Pancras the Martyr, which stood on the right side of the basilica, where the sacristy now is, and there were deposited beneath the altar of that oratory, as Panvinio writes in *On the Seven Churches*, concerning the church of St John. Sigonius, however, reports in book VI of *The Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 947, that Adelandrus, bishop of Reggio, obtained the holy bodies of the martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria from Berengar and carried them to Reggio [Col. 0402C], where the people of Reggio venerate them with special devotion to this day. In the liturgical offices of the city of Reggio there are also lessons concerning the translation of those saints; there it is said that in A.D. 915 Pope John X obtained the bodies of these saints from Berengar and granted them in response to the prayers of Bishop Adelard.

Here two names, joined in equal vows, keep watch over the tomb:

Chrysanthus and Daria, now an honour to be revered.

[Col. 0402A] **[Note: Col. 0401D]** Thus it is now read, *lapidari* (“to be stoned”), whether through a copyist’s error; perhaps it should have been written: “What savage madness!”

What savage frenzy [the transmitted *quem*, “whom,” is grammatically uncertain]—disregarding the law of burial—

made the tombs of the saints the spoil of raging violence?

**[Note: Col. 0401D]** Read *tumulus*, “tomb.” For on inscriptions *o* is not infrequently used for *u*: thus *oxori* for *uxori*, “for his wife”; *avonclo* for *avunculo*, “for his maternal uncle”; *secos* for *secus*, “otherwise.”

**[Note: Col. 0401D]** That is, from Damasus’s own resources; for we read that he adorned the tomb of Maurus, situated in the same place as that of Chrysanthus and Daria. William of Malmesbury, in Blanchini’s notes to Anastasius, opusculum 14: “On the Via Salaria, in the other church, are Chrysanthus and Daria, Saturninus and Maurus, Jason, and Mother Hilaria.” Cardinal Thomas, *Works*, vol. II, p. 518: “The third day before the Kalends of December: the feast of the holy martyrs Saturninus, Chrysanthus, Maurus, Daria, and others, on the Via Salaria in Thrason’s [cemetery].”

From the poor man’s means these things now rise better,

yet, through a generous intention, will please God more.

Mourn your crime, savage race: your frenzies have perished;

through your losses, honour has increased in these shrines.

## POEM XXIX. On St Agnes the Martyr

**[Note: Col. 0401D]** In Vatican codex 3860, the verses once inscribed in the apse of the basilica are given first, under this title: “Verses of Constantina, daughter of Constantine, written in the apse of the basilica which she founded in honour of St Agnes,” as also in Gruter:

[Col. 0402D]

Constantina, reverencing God and consecrated to Christ,

having provided all expenses with a devoted mind,

greatly aided by divine power and by Christ,

dedicated the temple of Agnes, the victorious virgin—

a work surpassing temples, where earthly things are joined

to heaven, for the golden pinnacles of the lofty roof gleam;

**[Note: Col. 0402D]** The codex reads *quae* (“which”) for *nam* (“for”).

for the name of Christ is celebrated in these seats—

he alone who was able to conquer death of Tartarus,

borne into heaven, and he alone to bring in triumph,

still bearing the name, the body, and all the limbs

raised from death’s shadows and blind night.

**[Note: Col. 0402D]** The codex reads *igitur* (“therefore”).

A worthy gift, Agnes, martyr and devoted to Christ,

you shall possess from our resources through long ages,

O blessed virgin Agnes, of a name to be remembered!

Immediately thereafter is read the poem of St Damasus, in almost the same words as it still appears engraved on stone in that same basilica, where I compared it once again. [Col. 0403D] Muratori likewise reported it from the eminent Marangoni in vol. IV of the *Inscriptions*. Marangoni himself repeated it in *On Gentile Matters*, p. 405, from the stone still extant.

.

**[Note: Col. 0402C]** Baronius says in the *Martyrology* for 21 January that these two following epigrams are by Damasus; they have also been published under Damasus’s name in the collection of ancient poets. The first concerns the martyrdom of St Agnes, whose suffering Prudentius also celebrated in this most elegant hymn:

Agnes’s tomb is in Romulus’ city,

renowned martyr’s tomb of a brave young girl.

[Col. 0403A] St Ambrose also composed a hymn about her, which in the edition of his works published at Rome is hymn 33, beginning:

*Agnes, the blessed Virgin’s*

*feast-day is that on which she gave up her spirit,* etc.

The same St Ambrose wrote her praises in book I of *On Virgins*, more fully in his sermon on her Passion, and in book I, chapter 4, of *On Duties*. St Maximus, bishop of Turin, likewise delivered a homily on the feast of St Agnes; Lippomano printed it among the *Lives of the Saints*, vol. I, and it treats fully of her life and suffering. Hildebert of Le Mans described the martyrdom of St Agnes in elegiac verse: it is a rather long poem divided into eleven chapters, published by Gaspar Barth in *Adversaria*, book XXXI, chapter 13.

Tradition reports that the holy parents long ago brought Agnes,

[Col. 0403A] when the trumpet had sounded its mournful summons—

**[Note: Col. 0403D]** The eminent Mazocchi, on 21 January, discusses whether the name *Agnes* should be aspirated, as in better ages. Yet the surviving stone has it thus.

**[Note: Col. 0403D]** Basil, *Works*, vol. I, Oration 5: “When the day for deciding the case arrived, behold, the herald called each person by name.” Heralds used a kind of silver or bronze tube, like a trumpet, so that the voice might be heard louder and more distinctly, as the annotator to Lucian’s *On the Death of Peregrinus*, chapter 32, infers from Hesychius.

the girl suddenly left her nurse’s embrace;

**[Note: Col. 0403D]** We learn also from Chrysostom, vol. I, Homily 51, that nurses attended girls even at a more advanced age. So too Ambrose says of St Agnes:

*Faith, knowing not how to be held in youth,*

*breaks the bounds of custody.*

of her own accord she trampled the threats and fury of the cruel tyrant;

though he wished to burn her noble body in flames,

she overcame boundless terror with her slight strength;

**[Note: Col. 0403B]** St Ambrose in the sermon cited: “At this the mad judge ordered her to be stripped and taken to a brothel, while the herald cried: ‘Agnes, a sacrilegious virgin, who utters blasphemies against the gods, is given as a prostitute to brothels.’ But as soon as she was stripped, divine grace bestowed such abundance upon her loosened hair [Col. 0403C] that she seemed more adequately covered by its fringes than by clothing,” etc. St Maximus similarly says in his homily on her: “For the virgin, though stripped, is covered by her hair; though made naked by evil men, she is clothed by good angels; and though condemned in the shameful brothel, she appeared in the lap of chastity,” etc.

and naked gave up hair and limbs exposed to sight,

lest a dying face should behold the temple of the Lord.

**[Note: Col. 0403C]**

O Agnes, true glory, gracious image of chastity. St Jerome, Letter 8 to Demetrias: “In the writings and languages of all nations, but especially in the Church, the life of Agnes has been praised: she conquered both her age and the tyrant, and consecrated the title of chastity by martyrdom.” St Jerome’s words are also cited in the Roman Martyrology on the feast of St Agnes.

O venerable Agnes, gracious glory of holy chastity to me,

**[Note: Col. 0404D]** Vatican codex, but incorrectly:

*O venerable Agnes, gracious glory of chastity to me.*

grant, I pray, that you may favour Damasus’s prayers, glorious Virgin.

**[Note: Col. 0404D]** Prudentius: “Agnes, of the brave young girl, the renowned martyr.”

## POEM XXX. On St Agatha the Martyr

**[Note: Col. 0403C]** St Damasus the pope wrote a sacred hymn on her feast-day. Thus Baronius in the *Martyrology* for 5 February, where he recorded very much concerning her.

**[Note: Col. 0404D]** Venerable Cardinal Thomasius, *Works*, vol. II, p. 384, from ancient monuments: “On the feast of St Agatha, virgin and martyr; by Pope St Damasus.”

Behold, the day of the martyr Agatha,

an outstanding virgin, shines forth.

[Col. 0404A] Christ joins her to himself—

**[Note: Col. 0404D]** Others: “because Christ joins her to himself”—

and adorns her with a double diadem.

**[Note: Col. 0403C]** The diadems are those of virginity and martyrdom: white for virginity and purple for martyrdom. She is represented as a virgin whitened and purpled by a double martyrdom, either because she was healed after her wounds [Col. 0404A] and then killed by further tortures. Thus Prudentius says of St Agnes:

*A twofold crown is bestowed on the martyr:*

*virginal, untouched by every fault,*

*then the unfettered glory of death.*

And at the end:

*Turn your countenance upon our defilements,*

*you who wear the twofold diadem.*

St Cyprian says in Letter 9 to the Martyrs: “O blessed is our Church, which the honour of divine dignity so illuminates, which in our own times the glorious blood of martyrs has made illustrious. Formerly she was white in the deeds of the brethren; now she has become purple in the blood of martyrs. Among her flowers neither lilies nor roses are lacking. Let each now strive for the highest dignity of either honour, to receive crowns white from good works or purple from suffering. In the heavenly camp both peace and battle have their flowers, by which Christ’s soldier is crowned for glory.”

Noble in birth, fair in appearance—

**[Note: Col. 0404D]** Another reading: “in face”—

yet more so in deeds and faith,

counting earthly prosperity as nothing,

binding God’s commands to her heart.

**[Note: Col. 0404B]** Born of most noble parentage. Ado, in the *Martyrology on the Feasts of the Apostles*. Metaphrastes, in her Life: “I am freeborn and sprung from an eminent family, as all my kindred attest.”

**[Note: Col. 0404C]** In St Gregory’s *Book of Sacramentaries*, in the Preface for the Mass of St Agatha, we read: “Through Christ our Lord: for whose name you have granted contempt for punishments and death to the faithful of both sexes and every age, so that among the palms of the blessed martyrs you have crowned also Agatha, most blessed virgin, with victorious endurance. She was neither frightened by threats nor overcome by tortures; she triumphed over the devil’s cruelty because she remained steadfast in the confession of your Godhead. And therefore,” etc.

Stronger than savage men,

she exposed her limbs to their scourges;

how stout was her heart

her torn breast declares openly.

**[Note: Col. 0404C]** Ado in the *Martyrology*, etc.: “Agatha went most joyfully and gloriously to prison; as though invited to a banquet, she gladly commended her contest to the Lord in prayer.”

For her, prison was a delight;

**[Note: Col. 0404C]** St Peter healed the virgin, wounded in prison, and said: “I am an apostle of Christ; do not doubt me in anything, daughter.” “A boy bearing light went before him,” says Ado, “and the virgin’s breast was restored,” etc.; [Col. 0404D] likewise Metaphrastes.

the shepherd Peter restored this sheep.

More joyful then, and more ardently aflame,

[Col. 0405A] **[Note: Col. 0405C]** Thus Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, chapter 5: “Others most patiently walked among the thongs of hunters.” The hunters stood in a long row with whips arranged before them, and naked Christian martyrs were compelled to walk before them so as to receive the harshly inflicted thongs of each in turn. See Eusebius, book V, chapter 1, with the notes of Valesius and others there, and book VII, chapter 2. Holstenius therefore thinks that Damasus referred to this kind of punishment in this verse, in his notes on the Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas, verse 33. Yet, while the Latin Acts describe this most courageous [Col. 0405D] virgin as struck with fists, and the Greek Acts as scourged, Tillemont would prefer *ῥαπίζεσθαι* (“to be struck”) to *ῥαβδίζεσθαι* (“to be beaten with rods”). But since *ῥαπίζω* can mean both to strike with fists and to strike with a rod or staff, Damasus himself proves here that the Latin translator of the same authors rendered one for the other.

she joyfully ran through every scourging.

**[Note: Col. 0405B]** When Mount Etna spewed fire, pagans fled to the virgin’s shrine; they applied her veil, taken from her tomb, against the onrush of fire, and by God’s favour the fire immediately receded. Metaphrastes.

The pagan crowd fleeing the pyre

even earns her aid;

may she more forcefully subdue Venus

in those whom the title of Faith adorns.

**[Note: Col. 0405B]** Hence Agatha’s aid is sought by Christ’s faithful against the fires of Venus: as she extinguished Etna’s fire for pagans, so may she repress for believers the flames and impulses of Venus.

Now shining like a bride in heaven,

**[Note: Col. 0405B]** This verse was adapted for ecclesiastical use as follows: “Pray to the Lord for the wretched.” So it is read in Clichtoveus’s *Ecclesiastical Elucidarium*, which gives and interprets this hymn.

pray for wretched Damasus.

**[Note: Col. 0405D]** For choir use: “Pray to the Lord for the wretched.” But which Damasus is this? Ours? Tillemont finds it hard to persuade himself of this, for he judges the use of the rhythms of which this hymn consists to be much later than the age of this Roman pontiff. I would not readily concede, however, that rhythms are later than Damasus’s age, since the distinguished Marquis Maffei proves in *Historia diplomatica*, p. 187, that they are rather far more ancient. Meanwhile, whoever reads that the same metrical form was used by Hilary, Ambrose, Paulinus, Prudentius, and others will scarcely deny that it was at least in use in that period [Col. 0406C].

May she make your feast thus observed,

and favour those who celebrate her.

## POEM XXXI. Epitaph of His Sister Irene

**[Note: Col. 0405B]** Baronius, p. 910 of the Appendix, under A.D. 584: “Moreover, we think that those golden reflections upon Virginity were written by Damasus to his holy virgin sister, named Irene; when she died, he also honoured her with an epitaph, which, long hidden, has by God’s favour come to light in these days. It runs as follows.” Thus far he. I would suppose that this epitaph was in the basilica of St Sebastian at the Catacombs, since Anastasius the Librarian says of Damasus: “He made two basilicas, one near the theatre for St Lawrence, and the other on the Via Ardeatina, where he rests in the Catacombs,” etc.; and at the end: “He was buried on the Via Ardeatina in his own basilica, on the third day before the Ides of December, beside his mother and sister.” The Via Ardeatina is often confused with the Appian Way because of their proximity, or because the latter extended there. Thus in the *Acts of St Sebastian* we read that Saints Mark and Marcellian were [Col. 0406B] buried on the Appian Way, at the second mile from the City, in the place called *ad Arenas*, because there were sand-pits there from which the walls of the City were built. The Martyrology and Breviary say: “on the Via Ardeatina.”

Here now rest limbs consecrated to God amid this tumult.

Here is Damasus’s sister, Irene, if you ask her name.

**[Note: Col. 0406C]** Paulinus, poem 21:

*… the heroine, now betrothed to eternal*

*marriage-chambers in heaven, whom Christ, snatched from her mother’s breast,*

*consecrated to himself in swift and pleasing love.*

Let those see this who either disapprove such vows or suppose that they may be broken with impunity.

While life remained, she had vowed herself to Christ,

that holy modesty itself might attest a virgin’s merit.

[Col. 0406A] Her age had not yet completed twice ten winters;

her age had outstripped the excellent qualities of her life.

The venerable devotion of the girl’s purpose

had borne splendid fruits in her earlier years.

You, sister born with me, pledge of our love—

when she fled the world, she had given you to me,

whom, when heaven’s better kingdom seized her for itself—

**[Note: Col. 0406C]** In the poem on Protus and Hyacinthus: “heaven’s better kingdom keeps her for itself”; concerning his own tomb: “heaven’s kingdom seized the exalted souls for itself” [Col. 0406D]; and in Appendix II.4: “heaven’s kingdom seized her for itself.”

I did not fear death, because she went free to heaven;

but I grieved—I confess it—to lose life’s companionship.

**[Note: Col. 0406D]** She was therefore among those consecrated virgins who professed the religious life at home and among their own family, such as Marcellina, Eustochium, Principia, and others.

Now, when God comes, remember us, virgin,

**[Note: Col. 0406B]** Baronius published *per extenso*, “at length,” for his manuscripts of D. M. read thus.

that through the Lord your lamp may grant me light.

## POEM XXXII. Epitaph of Projecta

**[Note: Col. 0406B]** There is a marble tablet in the basilica of Saints Martin and Sylvester, at the title of Equitius, from which I copied this; Baronius also published it among the appendices to volume VIII of the *Annals*. It is for the tomb of Projecta, daughter of Florus the consul recorded there; according to Panvinio, the year was A.D. 383, as in the *Fasti* and the *Chronicle*, and Baronius, vol. IV of the *Annals*. Damasus ruled from A.D. 366 to 384, so this was the seventeenth year of his pontificate. The final inscription, *DEP.*—“laid to rest”—means *depositio* here; such abbreviations, *depos.* and *deposit.*, are common in ancient Christian inscriptions, and the Martyrologies sometimes read *depositio sancti*, “the resting of a saint.” The Church says in the prayer for the dead: “whose day of resting we commemorate.” Prudentius, in his hymn for the funeral rites of the dead: “Now receive and cherish [Col. 0406C] her, earth”; and below: “Cover the body entrusted to you.” Indeed St Paul, 2 Timothy 1, says: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit until that day”; and St Peter, Second Letter, chapter 1: “I know that the laying aside of my tent will be swift.” A *deposit* means something entrusted only for a time, not for ever, in view of the hope of resurrection; hence “to sleep” for “to die,” and “those asleep” for “the dead,” are extremely common in sacred Scripture [Col. 0407A], because, as Augustine says on Psalm 87, it intends them to be understood as those who will wake, that is, rise again. Hence too a tomb is called a *coemeterium*, as if a dormitory.  
>   
> I would suppose this inscription was transferred here from the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, since Pope Sergius II transferred many bodies of saints from that cemetery to this basilica, as an ancient marble tablet at this place teaches. Sergius may therefore also have transferred monuments; he restored this church of Saints Sylvester and Martin from its foundations to a better and more beautiful condition, as Anastasius writes.

**[Note: Col. 0406D]** Projecta, or Prejecta? From the most distinguished Marangoni:

`MAR PREJECTO IN REFRICER`

And again:

`PREJECTE QUAE VIXIT ANNO UNO MENSES X. DIES VIIII. QUIESCET IN PACE`

“Prejecta, who lived one year, ten months, nine days. She shall rest in peace.”

What shall I say, or keep silent? Grief itself forbids expression.

This tomb holds tears; know the parent

[Col. 0407A] of Projecta, who had first been joined to a husband,

lovely in her beauty, content with modesty alone;

alas, beloved enough by her unhappy mother’s love!

Learn how, after the first bonds of marriage, from the sight

of her father Florus she was taken away and departed—

**[Note: Col. 0407D]** The stone reads: *abiit*, “she departed.”

desiring to ascend to heaven’s ethereal light.

This Damasus offers as solace for every tear.

**[Note: Col. 0407D]** Muratori read, in papers sent to him: “she survives, crying aloud, after the fates to which she recently yielded,” *Thesaurus Inscriptionum*, vol. IV, fol. 1999; but that has no sense and conflicts with the original.

## POEM XXXIII. On His Own Tomb

**[Note: Col. 0407B]** Baronius saw this and copied it from this place, p. 913, saying: “Again, concerning the placing of the place of his burial among the holy martyrs—unless reverence had deterred him—there is an inscription of the same Damasus of this kind,” etc. In the third verse from the end, he prints *queis* for *quis*, that is, “whom.” There is also another epitaph of his, given above from Baronius, vol. VIII. Understand here the cemetery of Callistus near St Sebastian, and it must be said that it was situated there; for the preceding and following two monuments were copied from the same place [Col. 0407C], making this probable as well.  
>   
> Yet Xystus II, the pontiff’s companions mentioned in the epigram, are said in the Roman and Usuardian Martyrologies and in Anastasius the Librarian to have been buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the same Appian Way. Bede also names Felicissimus and Agapitus, deacons, and Vincent and Stephen, subdeacons. Likewise blessed Quartus, on the testimony of St Cyprian, in the Martyrology; and Xystus himself in the cemetery of Callistus, according to the same Anastasius the Librarian and the Roman, Bedan, and Adonian Martyrologies. The cemetery of Praetextatus was contiguous with and equivalent to that of Callistus, as Bosius—well informed about them—rightly affirms in his notes on the Passion of St Cecilia. Panvinio says in his work on cemeteries: “The cemetery of Pope St Damasus lies between the Via Ardeatina and the Appian Way.” Concerning this cemetery of Damasus, Anastasius writes under Pope John VII: “He also laboured in the cemeteries of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Mark, and of holy Damasus the Pontiff.” If it is not the same as the cemetery of Callistus, it will be adjacent to it and even a part of it; for Athanasius also writes of Damasus, as cited above: “He made two basilicas, one,” etc., “and another on the Via Ardeatina, where he rests in the Catacombs.” And a little below: “He was buried on the Via Ardeatina in his own basilica, on the third day before the Ides of December, beside his mother and sister.” Bede [Col. 0408B], in *On Times*, says in the same words: “Damasus, bishop of Rome, made a basilica near the theatre for St Lawrence and another in the Catacombs, where the holy bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul had lain,” etc. Ado in the *Chronicle* has Bede’s words verbatim, as do others.  
>   
> Relevant to what Damasus says at the end of the epigram is Law 2, *Code on the Most Holy Churches*: “Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augusti, to Pancratius, Praetorian Prefect: Let no one suppose that the seat of apostles or martyrs has been granted to human bodies.” Later Emperor Charlemagne, in the *Capitularies of France*, book I, no. 159, “On Where Burial Shall Not Take Place,” decreed that no one thereafter should bury a dead person in a church. Certainly this was out of reverence for the Church; for canon 17 of the Council of Tibur says: “No layman is buried in a church, except in the common cemetery. Yet bodies buried in church in ancient times must by no means be thrown out; but, after a pavement has been laid over them, with no trace of tombs visible, reverence for the church shall be preserved.”

`VIXIT. AN. XVI. M. X. DIES. XXV. DEP. III KAL. JAN. FL. MEROBAUDE ET. FL. SATURNIN. CONSS.`

“She lived sixteen years, ten months, twenty-five days; laid to rest on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Flavius Merobaudes and Flavius Saturninus.”

If you ask what throng of the devout lies gathered here,

revered tombs hold the bodies of saints;

[Col. 0408A] heaven’s kingdom has taken their exalted souls to itself.

**[Note: Col. 0407D]** You see, therefore, that Sixtus had other companions in martyrdom—namely, those whom the *Pontifical* mentions; Ruinart was wrong to doubt this in his notice on the martyrdom of St Lawrence.

Here lie Xystus’s companions, bearing trophies from the enemy;

**[Note: Col. 0408C]** Thus above:

*Gorgonius keeps watch, he who guards Christ’s altars.*

Here the company of nobles guards Christ’s altars;

**[Note: Col. 0407D]** “I have said who they are,” in the poems of Damasus.

here lies one who, placed here, lived long as a priest in peace;

here are holy confessors whom Greece sent;

here are youths, boys, old men, and chaste descendants,

who especially delighted to preserve virginal chastity.

Here, I confess, Damasus wished to lay down his own body,

**[Note: Col. 0408D]** This was anciently included in Christian vows. See Boldetti, book I, chapter 14, note 339, on Paulinus, Verona edition.

but he feared to disturb the holy ashes of the devout.

**[Note: Col. 0408D]** From this it may be seen that this poem was composed by Damasus when he was already nearly eighty, after the publication of Law 2, *Code on the Holy Churches*, by the Augusti Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius. See Sarazanius’s note.

## POEM XXXIV. Epitaph of Pope Damasus, which he composed for himself

**[Note: Col. 0408C]** Baronius says: “Finally, we add for you here the epitaph of the same Damasus, which he wrote for himself while alive, a very devout work. It was taken from a very ancient codex of the library of the church of St Peter at Trier; Christopher Brover, professor of the Society of Jesus, copied it, and Nicolaus Serrarius, likewise a professor of that Society, sent it to us at Rome. See below Damasus’s epigram on the placing of his tomb, from the book of ancient inscriptions and p. 1172, no. 11, noted also by Baronius in Appendix XII of the volume of *Annals*. This epigram may be believed to have been copied from the basilica of St Sebastian, where, as Bede, Anastasius, and others say below, St Damasus was buried.  
>   
> The relics of this most blessed pontiff’s body were later transferred, even in ancient times, to the basilica of St Lawrence built by him. Anastasius the Librarian writes of Pope St Hadrian I: ‘He restored the roof of the basilica of St Lawrence, called that of Damasus, and made a cloth of *stauracim* [so written] over its altar, and another cloth behind the altar, where the body of St Damasus rests.’ Thus Anastasius. Therefore it was found there from the time of Hadrian, who reigned from A.D. 772, or from Anastasius’s own time. His head, however, is preserved in the Vatican basilica. Panvinio, Serranus, Ugonius, and before them Signorilis bear witness; the latter recorded the sacred relics of the City already two hundred years ago, and his manuscript book is held in the Vatican Library. This venerable head is solemnly shown to the people on Easter Monday with other relics [Col. 0409B]. An ancient marble tablet also teaches that his arm has been kept at St Thomas in Parione since A.D. 1130, under Pope Innocent II: ‘These are the relics: the arm of Pope St Damasus,’ etc. His relics are also found in the basilica of St Mary in Trastevere, St Mary of the Martyrs, and other churches of the City.”

He who, walking, stilled the bitter waves of the sea;

he who grants the earth’s dying seeds to live;

[Col. 0409A] he who was able to loose Lazarus from his bonds of death—

**[Note: Col. 0409C]** Vatican codex 1578: “He who was able to loose the bonds of the Law.”

**[Note: Col. 0409C]** Tertullian also uses this word in *On the Resurrection*, chapter 54, to describe the swathing bands wound around Lazarus.

after darkness, after the sun’s third light,

and restore the brother again to his sister Mary among the living—

**[Note: Col. 0409C]** Vatican codex: “to Martha,” as also in Sirmond, *Works*, vol. II, p. 786. Moreover, ancient Christians frequently represented Lazarus bound in swathing bands and presented to Christ the Saviour by his sisters Martha and Mary, on sarcophagi or in cemetery paintings, as a sure proof of the future resurrection; see Aringhi, Bosius, Boldetti, and, more recently, the eminent Father Thomas Mamachi, *Christian Antiquities*, vol. I, pp. 272, 273, and 282.

will cause Damasus, after his ashes, to rise, I believe.

## POEM XXXV. On the Church of St Lawrence Restored by St Damasus

**[Note: Col. 0409B]** Concerning this poem and the following two, Baronius writes on p. 911 of the Appendix to the aforementioned volume XII, under A.D. 384: “There still survive from that same basilica notable memorials of the same Damasus—ancient inscriptions placed there by him at that time, which, long buried in oblivion, have as it were returned from exile to recover their place.”

Here my father—as clerk of shorthand, reader, deacon, priest—

**[Note: Col. 0409C]** Eunodius describes the office of ecclesiastical shorthand clerk in his *Life of Epiphanius of Pavia*: “At about eight years old he undertook the office of reader … Having quickly mastered shorthand notation in writing and the various symbols that convey a multitude of words in brief, he distinguished himself as enrolled among the *exceptores* [shorthand clerks], and began to take down dictation such as he could compose without the disparagement of good men.” Sirmond, *Works*, vol. I, p. 996, Venetian edition. From this you may readily discover the causes of errors often occurring in manuscript codices. You also see that from the rank of reader one was appointed to the office of *exceptor*. But were there shorthand clerks at every title church of the City, or only seven—the number of notaries whom we read were established by Clement to write the Acts of the martyrs? I would think the latter: for what need would there be for individual notaries and shorthand clerks in every title church? Although the father of our Damasus was enrolled at the title of St Lawrence, nothing prevents his having served as notary and *exceptor* for the seventh ecclesiastical district to which that basilica belonged. After persecutions had ceased [Col. 0410C] and peace had been secured for the Church, we read that they were employed to record disputations and speeches delivered in synods and other ecclesiastical assemblies. Bingham, book III, chapter 13, §5; Valesius on Socrates, book V, chapter 22. They were further bound to record all proceedings in cases which in any way concerned the Church or its affairs and to report them to the chief of the notaries, to whom they were subordinate. See Anastasius and the notes of Altaserra and others.

grew here in merit, because of better deeds;

from here, when I had advanced, Christ, whose power is supreme,

willed to grant me the honour of the Apostolic See.

**[Note: Col. 0409B]** *Archibis* stands for *archivis*, “archives,” since *v* and *b* are frequently interchanged. *Archium* derives from the Greek *ἀρχεῖον* (*archeion*), meaning a palace, royal residence, official buildings, or judicial court; from this it also came to mean a records office (*chartophylacium*), because archives are adjacent to records offices and are their parts. Ulpian, Law 9, § *On Punishments*: “Let them not sit in the place where public instruments are deposited—perhaps an archive or records office.” The *Decretals* frequently mention the archives of churches, and Burchard, under *By What Means Natural Children Are Made Legitimate*, § *that point at the end*, reads: “the archives of churches,” that is, where sacred vessels are kept.  
>   
> Besides this and the two following epigrams on the basilica of St Lawrence, another by the same Damasus appears below. Anastasius the Librarian says: “He made two basilicas, one near the theatre for St Lawrence, and another on the Via Ardeatina, where he rests in the Catacombs,” etc.; and further: “He established a title in the city of Rome, namely the basilica which he himself built, where he also donated a silver paten weighing [a stated number of] pounds,” etc.; the rest of his gifts you may read in Anastasius himself [Col. 0410B]. Bede, *On the Six Ages*, or *On Times*: “Bishop Damasus made a basilica near the theatre for St Lawrence and another in the Catacombs,” etc. Ado says the same in the *Chronicle*.  
>   
> Pope St Hadrian I, in his letter to King Charles *On Images*, found after the Seventh Synod, says: “Likewise, in the holy Second Council, St Damasus, the most elegant pope, made his own church, which Pope St Gregory mentions in the *Dialogues* as called after its founder Damasus; likewise, from then until now we have it painted with sacred histories and images.” St Gregory’s words in the *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 31, are: “At the church of St Lawrence the martyr, which is called after its founder Damasus,” etc. Anastasius the Librarian writes of Pope Hadrian: “He also restored the roof of the basilica of St Lawrence, which they call that of Damasus; there he made a cloth of *stauracim* [so written] over the altar, and likewise another cloth behind the altar, where the body of St Damasus rests.”  
>   
> This epigram implies that this church had been a title before Damasus’s pontificate, and that Damasus himself had been a cleric, deacon, and priest there, when he writes:
>
> *Here my father—as clerk of shorthand, reader, deacon, priest—*  
> *grew here in merit, because of better deeds;*  
> *from here, when I had advanced, Christ,* etc.
>
> [Col. 0411A] And, once made pontiff, he built a new church there:

I confess that I wished to build new roofs with “Archibis” [reading uncertain],

and moreover to add, etc. For many years previously it had been customary in this church to give cups to the people in honor of St. Damasus on his feast day, and for the health of the sick and fever-stricken, as is read in an old booklet on the wonders of the city of Rome, and as Novidius writes in the *Sacred Fasti* under Pope Paul III in these verses:

> That cups may restore bodies weakened by panting illness,  
> he gives drink to the people, and the sick man receives relief.

The most ancient seal of the chapter of this church, which I once discovered and which remained for many years in our Museum, I gave as a gift to the chapter and canons of the same basilica so that it might not perish; and I have had it reproduced here [Col. 0411B]. Its letters signify: “THE CHAPTER SEAL OF ST. LAWRENCE IN DAMASUS” (the Sarazanian edition here has “Seal”). The figures engraved upon it are St. Damasus, seated upon a throne, wearing, I think, a cope and a mitre or crown, and holding a church or basilica in his hands, according to the ancient ecclesiastical manner in which, in many old paintings and mosaics, we see pontiffs bearing in their hands the very church which they either built or adorned; and presenting it to St. Lawrence, who stands clothed in a dalmatic and receives it as entrusted to him.

Among pontiffs whom we see holding a church in their hands is Honorius I, in the mosaic apse of St. Agnes on the Via Nomentana; the verses inscribed there declare:

> Bishop Honorius offered these dedicated vows.  
> His countenance is marked by garments and deeds.

Anastasius also mentions him. In the Church of St. Vincent at the Lateran, Pope John IV is seen in the same manner with a church, where the epigram begins:

[Col. 0411C]

> John the bishop rendered pious vows  
> to the martyrs of Christ the Lord, through the life-giving God, etc.

Anastasius also speaks of this church. At St. Praxedes and at St. Cecilia across the Tiber, we see Pope Paschal with a church. The verses still extant in those places indicate this; [Col. 0412A] and likewise Gregory IV at St. Mark’s, where his name also is read, “THE MOST HOLY LORD OUR GREGORY, POPE,” and in the six-line poem occurs:

> For you and for your honor the bishop completed this,  
> Mark: Gregory the Fourth, eminent in name.

After them, Innocent II appears at St. Mary across the Tiber, where at the end of the epigram we read:

> When the old structure was about to collapse,  
> Innocent the Second, a pope born here, renewed it.

[Note: [Col. 0410C] If we believe the distinguished Facciolati, who calls Vossius as witness, since *archium* is sometimes understood to mean a temple, or the inner sanctuary of a temple, the word could be accepted in that sense. But what if we read: “Beneath the arches I wished to build these new roofs”? [Col. 0410D] I therefore suspect that the lateral aisles of the basilica—arched aisles—were built by Damasus; for the columns seem to indicate this, which he says that he further added on the right and left. Above the arched aisles, supported by those columns, were built chambers and dwellings from which widows and virgins could look into the church. For Sarazanius’s remarks about royal buildings, a palace, and a judicial forum are trifles.]

I confess that I wished to build new roofs with “Archibis” [reading uncertain],

to add besides columns on the right and left,

[Note: [Col. 0410D] Namely, those very columns which now adorn the courtyard of the magnificent Palazzo della Cancelleria. They are said to have been transferred there by command of Cardinal Riario, when he demolished the old decaying basilica from its foundations and caused a new and larger one—the present building—to be erected on a site not greatly changed, with stone piers set underneath in place of the columns. See the distinguished Marangoni, *Delle Cose gentilesche*, ch. 64. To the poem on the Temple of St. Lawrence should be joined the poem on the Fountains of St. Lawrence, if it were a product of Damasus, [Col. 0411C] as Sarazanius thought. But since I hold a different opinion, I shall print it here so that the reader may judge freely:

> This famous life-giving fountain contains waters,  
> and is accustomed to cleanse human defilement.  
> Do you wish to know what gifts the consecrated liquid possesses?  
> The holy streams bestow sovereign faith.  
> Wash away in the sacred fountain the contagions of the old life;  
> O exceedingly blessed one, live reborn through water.  
> Whoever seeks this fountain leaves earthly things behind  
> and treads underfoot blind servitudes.

Moreover, this fountain is mentioned in the *Life of Damasus* written by Benedict the priest. From it I judged the following worth transcribing and introducing here:

“This event occurred recently, and we saw it take place in his church at the sacred [Col. 0411D] font which the venerable Damasus himself built. On the Saturday of the Paschal festival, while crowds pressed toward baptism, a little boy slipped from the priest’s hand and was submerged in one font. After almost an hour had passed, while everyone believed him already dead, a certain attendant of that church, entrusting himself to St. Damasus, threw himself into the font, drew the boy out, and brought him back safe and unharmed with him. Seeing this, none of us doubted that it was due to the merits of St. Damasus.”

Where that font stood is now unknown. Water was commonly brought to the courtyards and vestibules of churches for baptismal use and for the washing of clergy and people. See notes 41 and 169 to the Verona edition of Paulinus’s works.]

which may preserve Damasus’s own name through the ages.

## POEM XXXVI. On the Vatican fountains

[Col. 0411A]

[Note: [Col. 0412A] From a marble tablet surviving in the underground crypts of St. Peter’s Basilica in the Vatican. It is a monument concerning the former Vatican fountains of St. Peter’s, which had collapsed: Pope Damasus, lest they undermine the memorials of the bodies of those resting in Christ, had the hill cut away, the waters drained, and a spring discovered for use in saving baptism, under the supervision of the deacon Mercurius. [Col. 0412B] Baronius published it in vol. IV of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 384, the eighteenth of Damasus; but in the first line he wrongly reads *lacus* (“lakes”) instead of *latices* (“waters”), for it had been copied from manuscripts of that basilica. On the same baptismal font of St. Peter, see also Damasus’s poem below from the Book of Inscriptions, and p. 1163, no. 10. Prudentius also speaks of these fountains in the *Peristephanon*, in his poem on the Passion of the Apostles Peter and Paul:

> The right-hand region holds Peter, received beneath brazen roofs,  
> singing with olive trees and murmuring with a stream;  
> for liquid, issuing from the brow of the rock, produced  
> an ever-flowing spring fruitful in chrism.  
> Now its precious flow rushes in murmurs and glides down the slope,  
> until, with its green wave and pool,  
> there within, where the tomb lies,  
> a lake rolls with sounding falls in snowy depth, etc.

St. Paulinus too, in Letter 31 to Bishop Aletius, describes the fountains in the courtyard of St. Peter’s while most elegantly describing the basilica itself and the aforesaid fountains. To these poems of Damasus was recently added there a memorial of this kind:

“Paul V, Supreme Pontiff, ordered that the verses composed by St. Damasus, Pope I, twelve hundred and fifty years ago, after he had dried the dampness in the pavement of this old basilica that was undermining the memorials of many who rested in Christ, and which had been devoutly preserved as a monument of venerable antiquity, be placed here after being engraved on this marble from the ruins of the same church, in the year 1607.”

From Baronius, vol. VIII, in the additions to vol. IV, p. 789 of the Appendix, together with what follows; and vol. IV, second edition, p. 449.]

Waters surrounded the hill and, in a gentle course,

[Col. 0412A]

watered the bodies, ashes, and bones of many.

[Note: [Col. 0411D] See whether I am repeating matters which I noted beforehand from Ciampini in the final chapter, §3 [Col. 0412C]. Damasus, the first author of the work, seems to have collected the waters and led them into a fountain. But from this other poem, which Sarazanius placed last in his collection, we infer that the work itself was later enlarged through the zeal and expenditures of Macrobius Longinianus, *praefectus urbi*:

> You who wish to abolish the filth of former sins  
> and free your life from earthly stains,  
> come here to Christ’s fountain and sacred water,  
> where body, mind, and senses alike are washed.  
> And through pure baptism an eternal gift is given.  
> This seat of faith he built from its foundations—  
> Longinianus, illustrious in offices of service  
> and faithful to the imperial court, prefect of the city of Rome.

On this matter another inscription survives, copied by Suaresius [Col. 0412D] outside the Porta Portuensis and reported by Muratori, *Thesaurus Inscriptionum*, vol. IV, p. 1984:

> THIS IS LONGINIANUS, WHO BUILT THE BAPTISMAL FOUNTAINS,  
> MADE FAMOUS BY THE VERSES OF HOLY POPE DAMASUS.

Longinianus held the urban prefecture, as Muratori likewise observes, in 394, that is, ten years after Damasus’s death. He is the same man under whose supervision statues of Arcadius and Honorius were set up, as we read in an inscription reported by Donatus, book I, ch. 15. Therefore Prudentius’s verses cited by Baronius describe fountains not merely formerly gathered and built by Damasus, but afterward renewed and more elegantly adorned by Longinianus.]

Damasus could not endure that those buried according to the common lot,

after their rest, should again pay the sad penalties.

[Col. 0413A]

At once undertaking to overcome a great labor,

he cast down the summits of the immense mound of earth.

Carefully searching the deepest recesses of the ground,

he dried up all the moisture that had made it wet.

He discovered a spring that offers the gifts of salvation.

These things were attended to by Mercurius, the faithful levite.

## POEM XXXVII. At the fountains

[Col. 0414A]

[Note: [Col. 0413A] The following poems were published at the end of Gruter’s book of ancient inscriptions. He copied them from an ancient parchment manuscript in the Palatine Library, later brought to Rome and now preserved in the Vatican Apostolic Library, no. 532. [Col. 0413B] From that Book of Inscriptions Baronius published this as poem 17, vol. XII, Appendix, p. 913, under the year of Christ 384; in the final line he read *tenent* (“hold”), whereas *teneat* (“may hold”) is wrongly read there. The first verse is from Virgil’s *Aeneid*. Above we had another epigram on these fountains from St. Peter’s Basilica in the Vatican; the title appended to the first epigram of the said Palatine manuscript shows that these poems too stood there.

Pope St. Sixtus III also adorned the Lateran baptistery with verses, as Anastasius writes: “He made in the Constantinian basilica an ornament above the font, which had not been there before; likewise he erected marble architraves and porphyry columns which Emperor Constantine had left gathered together, and ordered them erected; and he adorned them with verses,” etc. The verses still appear, arranged in pairs around the frieze. Panvinius first printed them in his booklet on the Seven Churches; but because their order is altered in his edition, we give them restored to their proper order. Since they begin on the side where one enters the baptistery from the portico of St. Venantius, they must then be followed around in a circuit to the end. The verses are as follows:

> Here the nation to be consecrated for heaven is born from a life-giving seed,  
> which the Spirit brings forth from waters made fruitful.  
> Plunge in, sinner, to be cleansed by the sacred stream;  
> the water receives the old person and brings forth the new.  
> There is no distinction among those reborn, whom  
> one font, one Spirit, one faith make one.  
>
> [Col. 0414A] Mother Church, by a virginal birth, bears in the stream  
> the children whom she conceives by God’s breathing.  
> Whoever wishes to be innocent, let him be cleansed in this bath,  
> whether oppressed by ancestral sin or by his own.  
> This is the fountain of life, which washes the whole world,  
> taking its beginning from Christ’s wound.  
> Hope for the kingdom of heaven, you who are reborn in this fountain;  
> the blessed life does not receive those born only once.  
> Let neither the number of anyone’s crimes nor the nature of his sins  
> frighten him: whoever is born in this stream will be holy.

We also have verses of St. Ambrose on fountains, [Col. 0414B] which we insert here. They were published with some other poems of the same saint from the same Palatine manuscript in Gruter under this title:

### Verses of Ambrose for the Fountain of St. Thecla

> The temple rose in an octagonal form for sacred purposes;  
> the octagonal font is worthy of that gift.  
> It was fitting that the hall of sacred baptism  
> should rise in this number, by which true salvation returned to peoples  
> in the light of Christ’s resurrection—he who opened  
> the bars of death and raised the lifeless from their tombs.  
> Loosing confessed offenders from their stained guilt,  
> he washes them in the flowing water of the pure fountain.  
> Whoever wishes here to lay aside the crimes of a shameful life,  
> let them wash their hearts and bear clean breasts.  
> Let them come here joyfully; though someone darkened by sin  
> dares to approach, he will depart whiter than snow.  
> Let the holy bring forth here [perhaps “hasten here”; reading uncertain]; none is without the waters.  
> In these are the kingdom and counsel of God,  
> the glory of righteousness. For what is more divine than this—  
> that by a tiny drop the people’s guilt should fall away?

After these verses of Ambrose, the Palatine manuscript follows with others concerning the church of St. Anastasia, once [Col. 0414C] adorned by Damasus, and therefore we judged that they should be published here:

### On St. Anastasia

> Bishop Damasus adorned the roof with the honor of painting,  
> and now splendid metals give it beauty.  
> The hall, more precious for its rich splendor, bears witness  
> to what effects faith in these matters can achieve.  
> The devout mind of Pope Hilary, once dedicated to Severus,  
> and likewise that of Cassia, gave these things to God.]

Not through human resources, nor through skilled art,

but with Peter’s assistance—to whom the gate of heaven was entrusted—

Damasus, bishop of Christ, arranged these things.

One is Peter’s See, one the true baptismal bath.

No bonds hold him; Acbathius fulfills his vow.

# UNPUBLISHED POEMS  
*(From D. de Levis, *Sacred Anecdota*, pp. 17, 20.)*

## OBSERVATION

[Col. 0415]

[Col. 0415B] It is certain and beyond doubt that the first of all writers to observe that several—and indeed the more important—poems of Damasus had perished was the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, under the year 384, §§21 and 31. Although Martius Milezius Sarazanius collected the works from the Palatine parchments published by Gruter and was the first to elucidate them, and although Federicus Ubaldinus published them in print when completed in 1638, nevertheless Baronius, in his latest enlarged edition of the works of St. Damasus, published at Rome in 1754 with writings falsely attributed to that most blessed pope appended, reached the same conclusion; so did the most distinguished Antonius Maria Merenda, when discussing the poems, following St. Jerome, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, ch. 3.

For from St. Jerome we learn that Damasus possessed talent in composing verses and produced many brief works; yet they confess that they do not possess them all. Since, therefore, a parchment manuscript of the Novalesa Library, marked A.B., perhaps written in the ninth or tenth century, came into my hands, containing the Epistles of the Blessed Apostle Paul with the prefaces of Blessed Jerome, I found at its beginning several poems ascribed to Lord Damasus. Among them were these. Lest these poems, which have been carefully compared with the edition of St. Damasus’s works, with Merenda, and with vol. VI of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* new edition of the most distinguished Gallandius, should perish unpublished though highly similar in style, I arranged for their publication, in order to oblige lovers of ecclesiastical learning, so that each might compare these verses, which we bring to light, with those already published. We have been content to add a few notes.

Although these poems teem with many errors in the old manuscripts, [Col. 0415D] I did not judge it right to emend them, in order that their genuine antiquity might be apparent.

[Col. 0416B]

> From these, if any poems please you, take them and read.  
> You see meadows full of thorns and an abundance of flowers:  
> if you wish to take thorns, take roses.  
> Here the venerable volumes of the twofold Law shine forth;  
> here the new things have been set together with the old.

# ADDITIONS

## NOTICE

After the printing had already been completed, several annotations and observations were communicated to me through the learning and kindness of the distinguished Abbot Terribilini. I judged that they should be added here, lest readers be deprived of their benefit.

First, then, that learned man judges that Damasus was born in Rome, and employs in confirmation of this opinion those arguments which I have mentioned. He also observes that Sarazanius and [Col. 0417C] Coustant mention several ancient writers who deal with and praise that pontiff; yet among them there is not even one who calls him Spanish before the Catalogue of Roman Pontiffs, said to have been compiled under Felix IV, or before Anastasius, from whom that Catalogue is thought to have been copied. Yet he judges the authority of both these writers to be slight.

He then brings forward more recent authors from that illustrious nation, saying that they rest on no firm foundation and that they further dispute with one another about the place. Finally, from the Évora Breviary printed in 1548 he copies the prayer and lessons assigned for the Feast of St. Damasus. Here, then, are all the materials collected.

From the Breviary of the Church of Évora in Portugal, printed in 1548, p. 837:

## ON THE FEAST OF ST. DAMASUS, POPE AND CONFESSOR

[Col. 0417D]

**Prayer.**—Through the intercession of your blessed confessor and pontiff Damasus, we beseech you, Lord, mercifully grant us your mercy; and by his intercessions be gracious toward our sins. P.

**Lesson I.**—Blessed Damasus, the first of this name, a Spaniard by nation and a native of Guimarães in the province of Braga, son of Antonius, according to Jerome in the *Ecclesiastical History* succeeded Liberius, but according to others Felix II, in the pontificate, in the year of the Lord 369, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens. He sat eighteen years, two months, and ten days. T.

**Lesson II.**—But Ursicinus—or Ursinus, as others read it—[Col. 0418B] deacon of the Roman Church, unable to bear Damasus’s being preferred to him, burst into such fury that, having persuaded a certain unlearned and rustic bishop and gathered a band of turbulent and seditious men, he forcibly had himself made bishop in the basilica called Sicininus, overturning laws, order, and tradition. And so, since the matter was conducted not only by votes but also by force and weapons, many fell on both sides. Ammianus Marcellinus, a historian of that period, reports that the corpses of one hundred and thirty-seven persons slain in one day were found in the Basilica of Sicininus [Col. 0418C]. At last, with the agreement of clergy and people, Damasus was confirmed; Ursicinus was expelled from the City and transferred to the Church of Naples. T.

**Lesson III.**—Damasus, however, having been maliciously accused of adultery, cleared himself at a synod held before forty-four bishops. By them he was acquitted as innocent, while his accusers, the deacons Concordius and Callixtus, were condemned and expelled from the Church. Certainly Blessed Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius, calls him not merely an outstanding man and learned in the Scriptures, but also “the virgin teacher of the virgin Church.” T.
