**Lesson IV.**—At last, when the Church was at peace, Damasus delighted in literary leisure. He wrote the Lives of all the Pontiffs [Col. 0418D] who had preceded him and sent them to Jerome. Having searched for and discovered many bodies of saints, he adorned their tombs with poems. For he had elegant talent in composing verses. He composed many brief works in heroic verse, and likewise many letters. T.

**Lesson V.**—He greatly increased the churches and divine worship. For he built two basilicas, one beside the theatre, the other on the Via Ardeatina at the catacombs, and dedicated them. He adorned with verses, for the remembrance of posterity, the Platonia, where the bodies of the Apostles Peter and Paul had at one time lain, and the bodies of saints buried in that place. T.

**Lesson VI.**—The basilica which he founded in honor of St. Lawrence not far from the Theatre of Pompey [Col. 0419A] he adorned with very great gifts: a silver paten weighing twenty pounds; a silver *hama* weighing fifteen pounds; an embossed silver cup weighing ten pounds; five silver chalices; and five silver crowns. He also gave as a gift houses situated around the basilica, the Papirian estate in the territory of Ferentinum, the Antonian estate, and baths situated not far from the church. T.

**Lesson VII.**—After holding a council at Rome, he condemned Apollinaris of Laodicea and his disciple Timothy for heresy, as we read in the letter sent by him to the Eastern bishops. We also read other synodal letters of his: for example, to bishops throughout Illyricum and to Paulinus, bishop of Thessalonica, against various heresies. He established that psalms should be sung in church by day and night in alternating fashion, with the choir divided into two parts, [Col. 0419B] and that at the end of psalms there should be sung, “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.” He also ordered that the confession be said at the beginning of the celebration of Mass. T.

**Lesson VIII.**—At his urging Jerome also corrected the Psalter according to the Seventy translators and divided it according to the vigils; Damasus was the first to give authority to Jerome’s writings. For Jerome’s Bibles began then to be read, whereas previously the writings of the Seventy translators alone had been held in esteem. Tu.

**Lesson IX.**—He held ordinations five times, in which he created thirty-one priests, eleven deacons, and sixty-two bishops in various places. He died an octogenarian on the third day before the Ides of December, in the second year of Emperor Arcadius. He was buried in his own basilica on the Via Ardeatina beside his mother and sister, and the pontificate was vacant for thirty-one days. Tu.

At the end of this Breviary are read the following words:

“TO THE PRAISE OF ALMIGHTY GOD AND OF MARY, THE EVER-UNDEFILED VIRGIN. HERE ENDS

the Breviary of the divine offices according to the rite of the holy Church of Évora, newly emended, corrected, revised, and made far more orderly and elegant, by the command and authority of the most reverend Father in Christ, the most illustrious prince and lord, Lord Henry, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of the Four Holy Crowned Ones, Infante of Portugal, [Col. 0419D] and first archbishop of the same Church.

LISBON, at the shop of LUDOVICUS ROTORIGIUS, bookseller and royal printer, in the year from the birth of Christ 1548, in the month of April.”

## VARIOUS TESTIMONIES CONCERNING THE HOMELAND OF ST. DAMASUS

Lucius Marineus Siculus, *On the Affairs of Spain*, book II, p. 309, Frankfurt edition of 1603 (the second edition, since the first appeared in 1552), says this of the town of Madrid:

> It is called *Madritum* by some and *Majoritum* by others. In its circuit we counted one hundred and twenty-eight towers. Moreover, it is singularly blessed by the merits of St. Damasus, supreme pontiff, who is reported by many to have been a native of Majoritum [Col. 0420A]. It also now possesses as its son a most holy man named Isidore, who was a farmer.

From the *Chronicle of Spain* by John Vasaeus of Bruges, printed with Marineus at Frankfurt, I copied the following from p. 653:

> St. Damasus is ordained Roman pontiff, etc. He was born in the town of GUIMARÃES in Portugal, between the Douro and the Minho, three leagues from Braga Augusta, as the Church of Braga sings. See the Évora BREVIARY restored to its former splendor by RESENDE.

There, p. 656:

> Pope Damasus, etc. Petrus Antonius Beuter says that he was a native of TARRAGONA; Marineus Siculus enrolls him as a citizen of MADRID. But many churches of Spain, as we have said, affirm that he was a native of GUIMARÃES.

In vol. II of *Illustrated Spain*, cited Frankfurt edition of 1603, there is an apologetic account of the academies and learned men of Spain, by Alfonso Garzia Matamoros of Seville, who first published this little work in 1553. There, p. 809, we read:

> They were preceded in age by Hosius of Córdoba, and by that unique light of Jerome, Damasus of MADRID—if, indeed, any faith can without shame be placed in Lucius Siculus, who calls him from MANTUA CARPETANA.

In the same vol. II of *Illustrated Spain* is sold the First Reply of Andreas Resende (the author of the lessons in the Évora Breviary) to Bartholomaeus Kebedius, priest of the Church of Toledo. There I read, p. 1004:

> The river Viscella, called in Portuguese VIZELLA, enters the greater and more famous river Ave [Col. 0420C] a little below the memorial of the Emperor Nerva Trajan, which still remains upon the very bank of the Ave. Between the confluences of these rivers lies the city of GUIMARÃES, once the native city of the holy pontiff Damasus, if it were permitted by your people. Yet less than ten years ago appeared the book *On the Roman Pontiffs* by the most diligent Onuphrius Veronensis, compiled with the greatest accuracy after searching all the churches, archives, and libraries of the City. He makes Damasus wholly Portuguese and a native of IDANHA. “ST. DAMASUS,” he says, “SON OF ANTONIUS, OF EGAITANIA, A PORTUGUESE SPANIARD.” But I followed an ancient manuscript of the Church of ÉVORA when I inserted his life into the BREVIARY.

Petrus Antonius Beuter, a native of Valencia, published a *Chronicle of Spain* composed in the Valencian language, [Col. 0420D] which I have not yet seen. But in 1604 he reprinted his *Chronicle*, translated from Valencian into Castilian, under this title: *First Part of the General Chronicle of All Spain and Especially of the Kingdom of Valencia*, etc., printed in Valencia, 1604. There, book I, ch. 25, p. 146, we read:

> Afterward Julian the Apostate was the thirty-sixth emperor, in the year three hundred and sixty-five, and he stirred up persecution against the Church; but when he died, it quickly ceased. POPE DAMASUS, A NATIVE OF TARRAGONA, was then pope. Valentinian and Valens followed, then Gratian and Valens. Then the great Theodosius followed, born and raised in Spain.

Henricus Flórez, a Spaniard, [Col. 0421A] member and master of the Augustinian order, in vol. IV of his work entitled *España Sagrada*, treatise 6, final chapter, fol. 308, Madrid edition of 1751, writing on the saints of Toledo, says:

> XII. ST. DAMASUS, whom some make a native of Madrid, and therefore of the diocese of Toledo; but we reserve him for another place which we judge more proper, since we do not depend on any particular opinion. Then it will be seen whether he was SPANISH.

From the *Life of Blessed Gonzalo of Amarante of the Order of Preachers*, written by Fr. Didacus de Rosario by command of Fr. Bartholomaeus of the Martyrs, Archbishop of Braga, in the Bollandists, for 10 January, no. 3, p. 641, Venetian edition:

> Within the district of this metropolitan see—that of Braga—. . . . . in which holy Damasus too was once born from the town of GUIMARÃES, etc.

## ANALYSIS OF CERTAIN OPINIONS OF ABBOT TERRIBILINI

[Col. 0421B]

On poem IX, concerning the Catacombs of the Holy Apostles, he does not doubt that the blessed Apostles at one time “dwelt” there, as Damasus says—that is, were deposited there. But he conjectures that they were carried there immediately after their martyrdom and buried there, unlike others who write that Blessed Peter was buried at the foot of the Vatican and Blessed Paul on the Ostian Way. He thinks that they were transferred from the Catacombs to the site of their martyrdom long before the pontificates of Cornelius and Sixtus, because Gaius, a Roman priest, writing before the completion of the second century, says that the memorials of the Apostles were to be found for Christian devotion at the Vatican and on the Ostian Way.

For my part, I shall not address this question, which men far more learned than I have scarcely yet disentangled. I shall add only this: I can perceive no reason why that Damasian little verse, of which I gave notice in the notes, should not express that remarkable event [Col. 0421C] which Gregory the Great recounts. If, therefore, anyone does not think so, I ask that he assign another interpretation to the passage equally suitable. Let him also state for what purpose Damasus first warned us with the other verse:

> The East sent the disciples, as we freely confess.

Could this perhaps ever have been unknown? But if Easterners did not endeavor to claim and appropriate for themselves the memorials of the blessed Apostles, let him offer some reason why

> Rome deserved rather to defend her own citizens,

and show also what other force the same word *defendere* (“to defend, claim”) could bear. I know that Pearson, under the year 258, no. 2, rashly wrote that the story told by Gregory deserved no credit. Let that be permitted to him alone, and to those like him.

On poem X: the poem which I published from the Palatine manuscript of Gruter in that place, and which I judged capable of application to St. Stephen, pope and martyr, the learned man also considers a product of Damasus. But he conjectures that it praises Sixtus, pope and martyr, [Col. 0421D] whom we know from Cyprian to have been seized in the cemetery. Yet the poem itself opposes this conjecture, since it establishes that Stephen alone then fell as a martyr, while all the others who were apprehended with him in the cemetery were released unharmed. On the contrary, four deacons, and perhaps others, were killed with Sixtus, as that learned man himself observes regarding Poem XXXIII. Therefore the poem in question suits the former, rather than the latter, most holy martyr and pontiff.

Carmen XIII, on Saint Mark, pope, he thus completes by conjecture:

> Mark’s life was blameless, as we all know;  
> Gentle in God’s love, he could despise the world.  
> By his example the whole people prayed, that all might learn.  
> Life’s honor was small; great was his contempt for possessions.  
>   
> And diligent Virtue held the inner chambers of his heart,  
> Guardian of Justice. A perfect friend of Christ,  
> Damasus adorned the tomb while rendering honor, etc.

Thus also in the epitaph of Sisinnius the presbyter, which he judges, not without probable reason, to have been composed by the same Damasus, in Gruter, p. 1173, no. 9:

> Here the presbyter Sisinnius wished to lay his limbs.  
> [Note: Thus in Poem XXIII: “to bury his limbs.”]  
>   
> Accepted by all peoples, and a worthy priest,  
> Who knew how to preserve the covenants of his holy mother.  
> [Note: Thus Poem XII: “he preserved the covenants of peace.” He therefore lived in the age of Marcellus, Eusebius, and Mark, under whom disputes concerning the lapsed were debated.]  
>   
> Gentle in God’s love, who always knew how to live,  
> And content with his own lot, knew nothing of a rich man’s hall.

On Poem XX, concerning Saint Saturninus. At the beginning of this poem the Palatine manuscript in Gruter, p. 1171, reads thus: “Damasus, bishop, servant of God, worshipper of these martyrs. OLA NUNC FUERAT CRARTA . . . . . CINIS AN . . .”

Likewise Sarazanius, see col. 394 of this edition, note [2], note 20. Then, from the same manuscript, p. 1176, he adduces this: “NUNC XPI FUERAT CHARTAGINIS ANUS.”

He therefore supplies and reads:

> Damasus, worshipper of these martyrs:  
> A resident now of Christ, formerly you were of Carthage.

Thus the same Damasus, Poem XX:

> By your blood you changed your native country, etc.  
> Now a resident of the Lord.

This conjecture and reading are plausible. If retained, Saturninus, of whom this poem speaks, will be the same man who was detained at Rome under Decius, praised in Cyprian, Epistles 20 and 21, and subsequently a martyr. He further observes that in the Hieronymian Martyrology and in the Gelasian Sacramentary, under the third day before the Kalends of December, one reads at Rome, in the cemetery of Thrason: Saturninus, Chrysanthus and Daria, Maurus, and seventy-two others. Since Damasus had praised them all as blessed martyrs, would he have passed over those seventy-two without praise? But since error in copying numbers is easy, the distinguished scholar rightly conjectures that the verses which I reported in the Appendix, no. 2, concern them, and that Damasus himself was their author.

For the same reason he judges Poem XXII, concerning an unidentified Greek martyr, to concern Saint Hermes. It is certain that this martyr was buried in the cemetery of Basilla, also called that of Hermes, and apparently in nearly the same place as Protus and Hyacinthus. Thus the Mabillonian Anonymous: “On the Pincian Way: Pamphilus, Basilla, Protus, Hyacinthus, Hermes”; and likewise the Gelasian Sacramentary under the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

On Poem XXXIII, concerning his tomb. Cyprian wrote in Epistle 82 of the Verona edition that Xystus was seized in the cemetery, and four deacons with him. Thus Baluzius and Vignolius read from manuscript codices. By contrast, Fell reads, “and Quartus with him”; and he cites the Martyrologies, because they assign several companions to the same Sixtus—namely Felix or Felicissimus, Agapitus, Donatianus, Faustinus, Praetextatus, and others. This reading was also favored by Ruinart and Castellan. [Note: Cf. the marginal reference to Cyprian, *Epistle* 82, and the cited editions.] The careful scholar therefore observes that the earlier reading is confirmed by Damasus’s testimony, which attributes several companions to Sixtus; the Bollandists likewise used this argument after Baronius under 6 August. Indeed, further force is added to this view by the fact that Florentinius and Sollerius observed yesterday that this Quartus is nowhere mentioned before Ado and Usuard. Whatever may be said of him, what may certainly be maintained is that the blessed pontiff cannot without injury be deprived of the long-established possession of his companions; for, as the so-called Leonine Sacramentary says in his Mass, he urged “the sons of his teaching” to win the same glory. Yet, with the same eminent scholar, I would exclude Praetextatus from their number, since, upon examining the other Martyrologies and Sacramentaries, he is mentioned in Florentinius’s Martyrology not to designate any martyr, but the famous cemetery named after him, where the commemoration of those martyrs was celebrated. As for who and how many Sixtus’s companions in martyrdom were, the Bollandist associates investigate this carefully; anyone who consults them will do well.

The most distinguished scholar also labors to identify by conjecture the rest whom Damasus says were buried in the same place, but seemingly in vain. For my part, if anyone wished to learn the same from me, I should answer with Prudentius, Hymn XI, *On the Crowns*:

> . . . . . . . . . . Do you ask for each name?  
> It is difficult for me to repeat them:  
> So great a multitude of righteous persons did impious fury devour!

On Poem XXXII, the epitaph of Proiecta. Sarazanius gives no reason in his notes for calling Florus, Proiecta’s father, a consul. Perhaps he made “Florus” from *Fl.*—that is, *Flavius*—on that inscription, as the learned scholar says. He suspects this Florus to be the person whose poem for the tomb of Saint Liberalis the martyr survives in Gruter, p. 1171, no. 9, and which he adduces:

> Here rest the limbs of the holy martyr Liberalis,  
> Who was once a consul in honor on earth.  
> Florus, arranging these chambers, offered them to the Lord,  
> That, venerating the saints, he might receive his just reward.

## APOCRYPHAL WORKS OF SAINT DAMASUS. (G, S)*

### TO THE READER

I had decided to dismiss the apocryphal writings. But since some profit and use may sometimes be derived from the Letters, and since the printer requested it of me, I allowed them to be appended to the genuine minor works of Damasus. For, to omit others, Labbe in his *Collection of Councils*, and Coustant in his Preface to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 145, have already shown that those addressed to Stephen and the bishops of Mauretania, to Prosper and the bishops of Numidia, to Aurelius of Carthage, and to the bishops of Italy issued from the workshop of Isidore Mercator. Erasmus rightly complains that someone could have been so shameless as to dare attribute to Damasus those writings addressed to Jerome; on this point Schelstrate may be consulted, Dissertation 2, chapter 3.

Yet I could not bring myself to retain the decrees circulated under his name. For after Sarazanius and Crabbe, Coustant carefully collected them all again in the work he entitled *A Critique of the Decrees Ascribed to Damasus*, and furnished very weighty reasons why they falsely claim this pontiff’s name and authority. The reader, therefore, will best employ his effort by consulting that learned man rather than trifling with me.

[Note: Nevertheless, lest anything be lacking from our edition, we shall supply in an appendix at the end of this volume what Merenda omitted.]

## LETTER I

[Note: In Isidore’s Collection: “To his most blessed brother.”]

Damasus to his most reverend brother and fellow bishop Aurelius.

We have received the writings of Your Holiness with due veneration, and from them have learned that your reverence and prudence thirst for apostolic institutions, as was fitting. For this reason, we have sent some of the things you requested; and when you send again, we desire to send certain further matters. Yet, from the time of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have omitted none of our predecessors whose ordinances we did not send you, under specified seals, through Ammonius the presbyter and Felix the deacon. We desire that you preserve these; and we command that they be proclaimed and published to others, so that they may be kept by all with due veneration, inviolate, and so preserved; and that they may be carefully revered by all in times to come. For voluntary violators of the canons are judged severely by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose prompting and gift the canons were dictated. For those who, not compelled by necessity but willingly—as has been stated—either act or presume to speak arrogantly against these holy canons, or voluntarily consent to those wishing to do so, seem not inappropriately to blaspheme the Holy Spirit. Such presumption is plainly one kind of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, because it acts against him by whose impulse and grace those holy canons were issued.

But diabolical malice often cunningly deceives many people, and frequently mocks the imprudence of some by a semblance of piety, so that it persuades them that harmful things are beneficial. Therefore the rule of the holy canons, which were composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, must be faithfully known and carefully observed by us, lest in any way—God forbid—we transgress the enactments of the holy Fathers without unavoidable necessity. Rather, by walking most faithfully according to them, may we deserve, through their merits and with the Lord’s assistance, to share with those who framed them by divine inspiration the glory of reward and the full recompense of labor.

These matters having therefore been duly considered and communicated by deliberation to the knowledge of your Churches, it is altogether fitting that you obey the rules of those holy canons, lest the sloth of certain persons cause you to oppose them in anything. Rather, may your wise and sound teaching, which desires that you please God in all things, show you to be co-heirs and fellow-partakers of the heavenly kingdom, faithful fellow-workers in their seats.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Gratian and Cyricius, most distinguished men.

[Note: These consuls are not in the Fasti.]

## LETTER II

Damasus, servant of the servants of God, and by his grace bishop of the holy catholic Church of the city of Rome, to Stephen, archbishop of the council of Mauretania, and to all the bishops of the African province.

Having read the letter of your brotherhood, I first give thanks that I have deserved to enjoy the blessing of so many brethren; then, because I find you solicitous for the brethren and bearing the cross of the Lord with them, he who says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,” and the other passages relevant to this purpose.

Therefore, since in your consultation concerning matters opportunely transacted your blessedness, stirred by apostolic compassion, has exhorted us to extend the protection of apostolic authority to the brethren and to aid them in their injuries—since it is clear that you say with the Apostle in compassionate sympathy: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I do not burn?”—and since you are laboring lest any of those entrusted to you be torn apart or captured by savage beasts, it is fitting, in accordance with your prudent admonition, or rather with the Lord’s divine command, that we, who have received episcopal ministry over his household—that is, the universal catholic Church—watch carefully, lest, while we sleep, anyone may prevail to suppress or unjustly condemn, without consulting us, any of his sacred gifts: that is, apostolic men, successors of the apostles, and ministers.

I. You know, dearest brethren, that the apostolic see has been established as the firm and immovable foundation fixed by God, and as the most radiant title of his priests—that is, of all bishops—and the summit of the Churches. For “You are Peter,” as the divine Word truly declares, “and upon your foundation the pillars of the Church”—understood as the bishops—“have been established”; and “I have entrusted to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and proclaimed to you the power to bind and loose things in heaven and on earth.” You are acknowledged as prince and teacher of orthodox and immaculate faith among profane men and my members, especially my disciples; in whose stead today, by the grace of God, we discharge an embassy for Christ, and all the prelates of this holy see have discharged, do discharge, and will discharge his office.

For this reason, I would command that none of the matters you have made known be permitted, unless I knew you to be so fully instructed that you do not doubt that everything about which you inquire is unlawful.

II. Bishops may indeed be examined, and the principal causes of ecclesiastical affairs, by the metropolitan together with all his fellow-provincial bishops, so that none of them is absent and all agree in the affairs of each individual. But it is by no means permitted to determine their principal complaints and ecclesiastical causes, or to condemn bishops, without the authority of this holy see, to which all must appeal if need be and whose assistance they must invoke. For, as you know, it is not catholic for a synod to be held without its authority; nor can a bishop be definitively condemned unless in a lawful synod, assembled at the proper time by an apostolic summons. Nor are any councils ever deemed valid unless supported by apostolic authority.

III. The accusers and witnesses of bishops, concerning whom you have asked, must be free from every infamy, suspicion, or manifest stain, fully instructed in the true faith, and such as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood. For priests, as ancient authority teaches, cannot be accused or testified against by persons who ought not, and cannot, be advanced to the same rank of honor.

IV. The summons to a synod, according to the decrees of the Fathers, must be made canonically to the person accused, through his own presence as well as through letters and apocrisiaries, and over an appropriate canonical interval. For unless he has been summoned canonically at the proper time and in canonical order, even if he comes to the assembly because of some necessity, he shall in no way answer his accusers unless he wishes to do so voluntarily. For not even secular laws permit this, much less divine laws.

V. Concerning those expelled and stripped of their possessions, I can communicate nothing truer to you than what the holy Fathers determined and our predecessors confirmed by apostolic authority. The matter stands thus: the holy canons decree that expelled bishops who have been despoiled of their property shall first be restored to their own Churches and that all their possessions shall be lawfully returned to them. Afterwards, if anyone wishes to accuse them, he must do so at equal risk. They decree that the judges of bishops are to be bishops who think rightly and desire justice; and that, after sufficient time, when their strength has been regained, when they enjoy their possessions by full right, and when they have consulted friends and wise men who are servants of God, they are to meet in the Church where there are witnesses for each of those who appear to have been oppressed. And the remaining matters pertinent to this order we have not inserted here, to avoid prolixity, since we believe these sufficient. If anyone is not content with them, let him read those materials and he will be satisfied.

For we know that unarmed men cannot properly fight armed men. Likewise, those who have been expelled or stripped of their goods cannot properly litigate with persons who remain in their own rank and enjoy their friends and property. Nor do secular laws permit such treatment even for laypersons; instead, they command that those expelled, oppressed, or despoiled be restored first with all that is theirs, and afterward, at the proper time, as their law provides, be summoned to plead their cases. They do not permit an appellant to be barred by any prison custody. For earthly things, as you know, teach in part the heavenly.

VI. Accusers and accusations not admitted by secular laws must by no means be admitted in these cases, because the catholic Church defends everything that is beyond reproach. And there is no doubt that this was determined by the elders because of the snares of wicked people. For it is fitting that the Lord’s priests handle the causes of brethren piously and attend to them reverently, ordering their judgments above sacrifices; and that they conduct all things not arrogantly or with tyrannical domination, as is reported of some, but charitably for God and fraternal love. No one should presume to inflict on another what, according to the Lord’s saying, he does not wish inflicted on himself; and “with the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured to you.” We must always hold fast to what we have received through the preaching of the Apostles and the instruction of the Fathers, lest we appear to forge some novelty or to aim at the harm of brethren. Rather, let us bear one another’s burdens, so that, according to the Apostle, we may fulfill the law of the Lord.

VII. A suitable time must be foreseen when the case of each accused person may be most properly brought forward publicly, so that it may by no means be discovered that its gravity and tenor run contrary to the decrees of the Fathers or to the confession of synods. Let all attend to it in an orderly manner, so that they may answer it reasonably in every respect and plainly show their desire to act justly. No one, however, is to be introduced personally; rather, accusers and accused are to be heard with equal reason, as the order of proceedings requires. Accusers and judges must not be the same persons: accusers separately, judges separately, witnesses separately, accused separately—each in his own proper order.

For the formal accusation must always first be entered, so that the false accuser may incur the penalty of retaliation. Before a formal accusation, no one ought to be judged or condemned, since secular laws preserve these same rules. True equity must always govern all these matters, so that through the truth of the proceedings they may obtain the due recompense of accusation, judgment, and testimony. For it is written: “The Lord will abominate lying lips, and a false witness uttering lies, and one sowing scandals and quarrels among brethren”; and he himself admonishes and says: “You shall not bring false accusation against your neighbor, nor oppress him by force. You shall not do what is iniquitous, nor judge unjustly. You shall not regard the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful. Judge your neighbor justly.” And, “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another,” and the rest.

Above all, we must heed the apostolic command to attend to ourselves and to the flock in which the Holy Spirit placed us as bishops, to govern God’s Church, which he acquired through his own blood. And again: be on guard against wolves; be on guard against evil workers, who do perverse things and speak contrary things, so that they may always slander and defame the disciples of the Lord. You and all the Lord’s priests must correct them with the greatest diligence, because there is no worse evil than citizens envying citizens, and priests or clerics laying snares for priests or pontiffs. The voice of Truth itself testifies: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye”; and “whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung about his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea.” And likewise: “Blessed is he who is not offended in me.” Without doubt, whoever scandalizes God’s bishop or priest is offended in God.

There are many similar passages which are not inserted here, lest the Letter become too long. You must also admonish and instruct your aforesaid neighbors to withdraw from such people, promptly correct what they have unlawfully done against the brethren specified above, heal by full satisfaction those whom they injured without consulting us, and quickly be reconciled to them, unless they wish to incur the censure of the apostolic see. For if anything perhaps had arisen concerning or against them, our examination should have been awaited, so that they might be condemned by our authority or supported by our help, as the privilege has always been granted to this see. They ought not, according to their own pleasure, to invade our rights without a decree of the apostolic see.

Henceforth, let all priests abstain from such conduct if they do not wish to be excluded from the censure of the Apostolic Rock—upon which Christ, as stated above, built the universal Church, and to which, as was mentioned a little earlier, the supreme judgments of bishops and greater causes are reserved and secured—and from priestly honor.

VII. A respite of six months, or longer if necessary, must be granted to bishops accused in criminal cases. No one acquainted with secular legal discipline is ignorant that this is permitted even to laypersons, much more to priests, who are unquestionably their superiors. The decrees of the holy Fathers likewise ordain that it is not canonical to judge or condemn any priest before the canonically examined accusers are present and he has received the opportunity to defend himself—that is, ecclesiastical time to clear away charges and crimes.

IX. No accusation for an initial examination is to be brought outside the person’s own province without an apostolic command, to which reverence must be preserved in all cases; for the ancient rule of the Fathers teaches this, and imperial enactments concur with it. “The examination of crimes,” they say, “must be conducted where the crime was committed. For an accused person is forbidden to be heard elsewhere.” Elsewhere it is commanded in the canons: “Whatever business arises in its own locality must be concluded there”; and other such and similar provisions—while apostolic authority is preserved in all things, so that nothing in these matters may be decided before it is known to please that see, by whose support all ought to be sustained. And if anything grave and intolerable should happen to them, its censure must always be awaited.

No one should presumptuously, or driven by the spur of his own thought, dare to slander or accuse any priest, as we have often known to happen. For injury done to them pertains to Christ, in whose stead they perform an embassy for the people redeemed by Christ’s blood. Their cause, because it is God’s cause, we know must be reserved for the judgment of him who can kill the body and cast the soul into Gehenna, who says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.” Before him conscience lies bare; hidden things are not concealed from him.

All must also be instructed that Christ has declared through us that it is not for sheep to foresee the snares of wolves, but for the shepherd. Therefore the blessed Apostle Paul warns that judgment should not be rashly and lightly presumed concerning matters of which no one can judge more truly or better than God: “Why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise him? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to the Lord.’ Therefore each of us shall render an account of himself to God.”

Accordingly, no one should arrogate such rash undertakings to himself as to do, beyond what pertains to concord, something from which the Church’s unity may be broken apart. No one, therefore, should lightly assent to the detraction, judgment, or condemnation of brethren, especially priests, who are nearer to God and who consecrate Christ’s body with their own mouths. For this reason God’s wrath comes upon the children of dissension, who persecute Christ in his members.

Do not, brethren, do not become partners in such persons; do not share their sins or their unfruitful words. Instead, rebuke the assemblies of those who seek to stretch their tongues against the brethren like a bow. Defend the brethren, therefore, and warn all to arm themselves against the persecutors of brethren. Yet we are confident of better things in you, things nearer to salvation: for neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, neither present things nor future things, neither strength nor height nor depth nor any other creature, as the teacher of the Gentiles teaches, can separate us from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is especially fulfilled in priests and his remaining members.

Do not, therefore, lose your confidence, which has great recompense. For behold, the judge stands before the door, cheerfully promising crowns to those who for his sake bring assistance to brethren, help the oppressed, and labor together in charity. But if anyone draws back, he will not please God; rather, he falls because he did not raise up the fallen person but withered away. Yet let us not be of those who draw back unto oppression, but of those who give help toward the gaining and support of brethren.

Therefore take up the armor of God, that you may withstand all who presume in this manner; put on the breastplate of righteousness, with your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace; and in all things take up the shield of faith, by which you may quench all the fiery darts of the evil one. Take also the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God; through every prayer and supplication, being rooted and grounded, so that you may all say the same thing and there may be no schisms among you, dividing the good and whole body of the Church into twisted novelties.

The Apostle therefore warns us no longer to judge one another rashly. For whoever condemns a bishop without the authority of the apostolic see judges rashly, since this privilege, as noted a little above, is specially reserved to it. “Judge this rather,” he says, “that you put no stumbling block or occasion of offense before a brother.” For it is manifest from these and innumerable other testimonies of decrees that a bishop must not be condemned, even though his reputation is investigated, until the judgment concerning him of our apostolic authority—that is, of Peter, prince of the apostles—is known. For he alone, before all others, was entrusted with and deserved to receive from Christ God, King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven, to open it to faithful persons well disposed toward our same Lord and to close it against unbelieving and ill-disposed persons, and against those who assail or harm his priests and the holy Church redeemed by his precious blood.

This is what he also required us to do. Not because anything new is now commanded, but so that what through some persons’ indolence, whether knowingly or negligently, is transgressed may henceforth be observed by all: namely, that those things established by apostolic and patristic tradition always be maintained under the fear of unassailable authority. For in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians and to Timothy it is written, as the Apostle admonishes: “Stand firm and hold to your traditions which you have learned, whether by word or by letter.” Likewise elsewhere through the prophet: “I waited also, as blessed Isaiah proclaimed, that they should do judgment; but they did iniquity—not justice, but a cry”—troubling all pious people.

They should also know that God’s judgment is according to truth upon those who do such things, even though they despise the riches of God’s goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads them to repentance. But according to their hardness and unrepentant heart, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will render to each according to his works. And elsewhere it is written: “I am the Lord your God. You shall not commit iniquity in judgment. You shall not show partiality to a person, nor be awed by the face of the powerful. You shall depart from every unjust word. You shall not attack or kill the innocent and righteous.”

Without doubt, the person who claims for himself things which he is not permitted to claim commits iniquity in judgment. Therefore no one should presume, without consultation with this holy see, to usurp what has been granted to it, if he does not wish, as a contemner, to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor. The negligent must therefore be repelled, but in such a way that the guilty are not strengthened; and the good must resist the wicked or those who lay snares for brethren, lest, oppressed by the torpor of sloth, they become liable for silence.

For whoever is able to oppose and confound the perverse but does not do so does nothing other than favor their impiety. Nor is anyone free from the taint of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime. But be perfect and whole, established in the same mind and the same knowledge, so that, directing your ways unwaveringly toward him through this knowledge, you may come to the aid of all the oppressed, because the Lord is entrusted to you. Coming to him, the living stone—rejected by men because of the impiety of such persons, but chosen and honored by God—you yourselves, as living stones, are built up in the Lord into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices to him as an odor of sweetness.

For it is an exceedingly pleasing sacrifice to the Lord to aid all the oppressed—how much more those of whom he says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me,” and so forth. The person who removes adversities from the afflicted and oppressed indeed offers prosperous things to the Lord. But now, brethren, we commend you to God and to the word of his grace, who is able to perfect you and give you an inheritance among all the sanctified. May the God of peace and consolation grant you to think the same toward one another, and always in him and in all things, that with one mind, one mouth, and one heart you may honor him for the concord and assistance of the brethren. He is able to strengthen all and console them according to his Gospel and according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages but now disclosed through the holy Scriptures and the teachings of the orthodox Fathers, according to the command of the eternal God, for obedience to the faith, in all things made known to us—to the only wise God, our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory, honor, dominion, and power to the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

May the Lord keep you always safe, most beloved brethren.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Flavianus and Stilicho, most distinguished men.

[Note: These consuls are not in the Fasti.]

[Note: Quesnel, Dissertation 11, observes that this is taken from canon 7 of the Second Council of Seville, as is also Leo’s Letter 88 in the older edition.]

## LETTER III. On Chorepiscopi: Who They Are, Whether They Are Anything at All, or Nothing

To the venerable lords and brethren: Prosper, bishop of the first see of Numidia; Leo, Reparatus, Alexander, Benedict, Rufus; and all other orthodox bishops, wherever they stand firm in the right, holy, and apostolic faith: Damasus, bishop.

[Note: This Letter too is false, in Petavius’s judgment, in Epiphanius, p. 278. It is in Isidore’s collection.]

[Col. 0431D] Although, dearest brothers, the decrees of the Fathers are known to you, we nevertheless cannot but admire your diligence concerning the institutions of the ancients [Note: [Col. 0432D] Innocent I, Epistle 4.], in that you do not cease to refer to us, as to the head—as has always been the custom—all matters that may admit of any doubt, so that you may receive answers from the source from which you received instruction and the rule for right living. Therefore we recall that you are not unmindful of the canons, [Col. 0432A] which themselves command that this be done—not because you lack anything in the rules of ecclesiastical knowledge, but so that, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, you may in no respect depart from its rules.

Accordingly, concerning the chorepiscopi, about whom you wished to consult us—what their ministry is, what they may lawfully do, what authority they possess, whether they may be appointed at all, since we have heard that they have already been forbidden, and what is to be done with those who are found already ordained—we think that no answer can be given you more certain than the decree which we find was issued long ago by our predecessors: namely, that nothing whatever is reserved for their indulgence except deprivation of the sacred ministry which they unlawfully assumed, because they had been forbidden both by this holy See and by the bishops of the whole world.

Their institution, therefore, is exceedingly blameworthy, [Col. 0432B] exceedingly perverse. For their presuming anything from the highest ministry of the priesthood lacks every authority, is found contrary to the sacred canons, and through its proud and superfluous elevation tends toward disturbance of the whole [Note: [Col. 0432D] Leo, Epistle 33.] Church. Whatever they have done in the aforesaid highest priestly ministry is void and empty.

That they are the same as presbyters is sufficiently established [Note: [Col. 0432D] In the Council of Neocaesarea.], because they were originally instituted after the pattern and example of the Seventy. But since, thanks be to God, they are not now necessary, as they were in the primitive Church on account of the care required for the poor; and because they presumed unlawful things; and because what they did was not validly done; and because many thereby fell into a false security and were deprived and defrauded of ecclesiastical ministry: therefore [Col. 0432C] they have been removed from pontifical offices both by this holy See, as we have mentioned above, and by all the bishops of the whole world.

For, as has been reported to us, certain bishops, for the sake of their own ease, did not fear to entrust their peoples to them. Thus these men usurp for themselves things owed only to pontiffs, in order to perform unlawful and forbidden acts; while the bishops themselves lie idle in their ease and neglect the care entrusted to them by God. Yet the Lord says: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep; he calls them by name, and knows his own, and his own know him.” And again: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep.” You know well what he says concerning the hireling: he sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep and flees; and the wolf [Col. 0432D] seizes and scatters the sheep; and so forth.

Through such men the care of the Church is neglected and her condition disturbed. Therefore they have been prohibited, so strictly that, if any such persons are found, they are to fall from their own rank. Those bishops who presume such things seem to me like prostitutes, who, as soon as they give birth, hand their infants over to other nurses to rear, so that they may sooner satisfy their lust [Col. 0433A]. So too these men hand over their infants—that is, the peoples entrusted to them—to others to rear, that they may gratify their desires: that is, that according to their own inclination they may devote themselves to secular affairs and more freely do whatever each of them pleases.

For this reason souls are neglected, sheep perish, diseases increase, heresies and schisms arise, churches are destroyed, priests are corrupted, and other evils ensue. The Lord did not teach thus, nor did the Apostles establish it. Rather, those who undertake the care must themselves carry it out, and themselves present their own sheaves to the Lord. For he himself diligently sought the lost sheep, himself found it, himself carried it back upon his own shoulders, and taught us to do the same.

If he himself had such care for the sheep—if he himself taught, cared for, healed, carried them on his own [Col. 0433B] shoulders, and loved them so greatly that he even gave up his life for us, enduring many injuries, many reproaches, and many sufferings—what shall we, wretched and indolent men, say, who neglect to expend care even upon the sheep entrusted to us and hand them over to others to rear? These things must be corrected, brothers, because whoever labours more will receive a greater reward [Note: [Col. 0433D] Distinction 86, chapter 5, “Chorepiscopi tam ab hac.”].

For we know that there are no more than two orders among the disciples of the Lord: that is, the Twelve Apostles and the Seventy Disciples. We are wholly ignorant whence this third order has arisen. What lacks rational basis must be uprooted. It is plain to everyone that those ordained by fewer than three bishops are not bishops, since, as you well know, [Col. 0433C] the holy Fathers forbade that persons ordained by one or two bishops should even be called bishops. If they do not possess the name, how shall they possess the office? Whatever they may have done among bishops, or concerning matters belonging solely to bishops, must, as was stated above, be void, because they cannot give what they do not possess.

Especially since none of the Seventy Disciples—whose figure these men bore in the Church before they were forbidden, as mentioned above—is read to have assumed anything of what was specially owed to the Apostles and their successors. [Note: [Col. 0433D] Second Council of Seville.] Nor, in the law of the Lord, which is said to have been dictated to Moses by the Lord himself, did the sons of Aaron presume anything concerning those matters specially granted to the high priests, that is, Moses and Aaron.

[Col. 0433D] For no one doubts that Moses and Aaron alone, by the Lord’s command, erected the altar in the tabernacle of God; alone anointed; alone instituted priests by sacred anointing; and performed the other acts belonging to the highest priesthood, of which sufficient account is read in the divine Scriptures. For they were priests of the Most High Lord, as it is written of them: “Moses and Aaron among his priests.”

So too now, since the shadow of the Law has passed away and, by God’s grace, the light of the Gospel [Col. 0434A] shines manifestly upon us, those who bear the form of the Seventy Disciples—in whose type, indeed, the sons of Aaron stood—must presume nothing concerning those things that belong to the high priests, that is, bishops, whose figure Moses and Aaron bore; just as the sons of Aaron did not touch anything of the ministry of the highest priesthood.

For the canon sufficiently makes clear that chorepiscopi, before they were forbidden by the tenor aforesaid, were instituted after the pattern of the Seventy, when it says: “The chorepiscopi also appear to be after the example and pattern of the Seventy” [Note: [Col. 0433D] Council of Neocaesarea, canon 13, from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus.]; and so forth. Nor does it seem to us that we should pass over what is elsewhere expressly stated in the canons: [Note: [Col. 0433D] Council of Antioch, canon 10, from the same translator.] “Those who are called chorepiscopi in villages and estates, although they have received the laying on of hands of bishops and have been consecrated [Col. 0434B] as bishops,” and so forth.

I consider the expression, “although they have received the laying on of hands of bishops,” not without significance. Since the word *episcoporum* (“of bishops”) contains a plural number and is, according to grammarians, a plural genitive, it appears to me that they were then ordained not by one but by several. For the canon would by no means have said “of bishops” if the ordination of such men were performed by one bishop, since *episcoporum* is said in the plural. But when it says *chorepiscopus*, it undoubtedly means a rural bishop; and if he is rural, what is he doing in a city, when two bishops are altogether forbidden in one city?

And if he is in a village, and in a place where bishops had not previously existed—when a bishop is forbidden to be made even in a small city, [Note: [Col. 0434D] Council of Laodicea, canon 57.] village, or fortress, and in absolutely all places where bishops had not previously existed, [Col. 0434C] lest the authority [Note: [Col. 0434D] Carthage II, canon 2; Toledo XII, canon 4.] and title of bishop be cheapened—what, I ask, will they be? Behold: neither the place agrees with the ordination nor the ordination with the place. For if they received the laying on of hands of bishops and were consecrated as bishops, where were they consecrated? In a village, because *χώρα* (*chōra*) means “village” among the Greeks. But how in a village, when, I ask you to explain, it is not even lawful for one to be appointed in a fortress or a small city? And if you cannot explain it—as I know you cannot by reason or by full authority—put your finger to your mouth, and do not doubt that they lack all authority.

For there are three obstacles which invalidate their action or institution. First, they are accustomed to be ordained by one bishop, in which their ordination conflicts with the canons that command them to be instituted by the laying on of the hands of bishops [Col. 0434D]. Secondly, if they are ordained by several bishops, they are either in a village, fortress, or small city, or altogether in a place not appointed for the lawful creation of bishops, or in a place where bishops had not formerly existed, [Note: [Col. 0434D] Council of Sardica, canon 6.] lest the authority and title of bishop be cheapened; or else they are in a city together with another bishop, whereas, as stated above, two bishops ought not [Note: [Col. 0434D] Council of Nicaea, canon 8.] to exist in one city. Thirdly, they may have been instituted without a definite assignment [Note: [Col. 0434D] Council of Chalcedon, canon 6.], as we have heard concerning some persons. All these things [Col. 0435A] wholly lack episcopal authority.

There also remains this: their order has no authority in the divine Scriptures, because, as stated above, the only two primary orders in the Church are those of the Apostles and the Seventy Disciples. Certainly, if they are not bishops, since for the aforesaid reasons they cannot be bishops; and if they refuse to be called presbyters because they aspire to be more; and if they attempt to presume more than the Seventy Disciples would have done—after whose pattern, as we noted a little above, these men were instituted before being forbidden by certain foolish persons who sought their own interests and not those of Christ Jesus—and presume to do unlawful and forbidden things, while refusing to be called what they are: I ask that you plainly declare what they are. For either they are something [Col. 0435B] or they are nothing.

It is plainly evident that they are not bishops. If they are not bishops and disdain to be presbyters, what are they? They must either be something at all or nothing; for nothing can exist unless it has a basis from which it exists. If it has no basis of existence or source from which it derives its origin, it has neither authority nor a lawful standing; for it is empty, and necessarily must be destroyed and fall, because it is nothing and will be reckoned as nothing.

But if they are none of the things mentioned above, then they must possess none of the things owed to priests. Therefore they are not to be included in the priestly register, except only—as we stated at the outset—that, out of mercy, this alone may be granted to those who humbly consent to bear it, seek no higher position, and confirm this same point in writing signed beneath by their own hand: namely, that [Col. 0435C] they may have a place among priests, be content with the ministry of presbyters, and be participants only in the Lord’s table. But those who seek higher things are not even to retain this, namely to be priests, but are to be wholly deprived of every ecclesiastical honour.

That they may not consecrate priests, deacons, subdeacons, or virgins; erect an altar; anoint or consecrate; dedicate churches; prepare chrism [Note: [Col. 0435D] Second Council of Seville, canon 7.]; mark with chrism the foreheads of the baptized; reconcile anyone publicly in the Mass as a penitent; send letters of commendation; bless the people; enter before the bishop into the baptistery or sanctuary; baptize or sign an infant in the bishop’s presence [Col. 0435D]; reconcile a penitent without the command of their bishop; prepare the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood in his presence unless he commands it [Note: [Col. 0435D] Gelasius, Epistle 9, canon 7.]; teach or greet the people before him; or exhort the congregation [Note: [Col. 0435D] In St Leo, Epistle 88.]—all these things, as you have learned both from the foregoing and from other enactments of the Fathers and sacred canons, belong to pontiffs alone.

If some persons are insufficiently informed, they may be fully taught and instructed, [Col. 0436A] so that both the distinction of ranks [Note: [Col. 0435D] Seville II, 7.] and the height of dignity of the highest pontiffs may thereby be shown. The same is to be held concerning presbyters: without the command [Note: [Col. 0435D] Laodicea 57; Toledo I, 28.] of their own bishop, they are to do nothing, because what is rare is also seen to be more beautiful. If the title of pontiffs is cheapened, the whole condition of the Church is disturbed. Thus there is a threefold offence in this matter: forbidden acts are performed; the sacred ministry is defiled by the cheapness of such association; and the rights of bishops are undermined, so far as concerns the rashness of unlawful usurpation.

That it belongs to the Apostles alone [Note: [Col. 0436D] Innocent I, Epistle 1, canon 3; Acts VIII; Paris VI, A.D. 839.] and to their successors, by virtue of their own office, to confer the Holy Spirit, the book of the Acts of the Apostles teaches. Above all, none of the Seventy Disciples, whose figure these men bear in the Church, [Col. 0436B] is read to have bestowed the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, as has been said. Therefore no priest who does not wish to be separated from our priestly fellowship may henceforth usurp or consent to these things, since they lack every rational basis.

Nor may that which is extinguished by us, and was already extinguished by our predecessors and, as stated, by the bishops of the whole world, be sown among anyone with dark [Note: [Col. 0436D] St Leo, Epistles 2 and 1, canon 2.] roots. Rather, things known to have sprouted wickedly must be pulled up by the roots, lest any tares corrupt the Lord’s harvest. For the priests of the Lord will yield an abundant crop if the things accustomed to destroy the growing field are cut away by the roots.

Let the presumption so often forbidden and condemned therefore cease, cease. Let not the high priests imitate [Col. 0436C] prostitute women, who, for the aforesaid pleasure, hand their infants over to others to nurse. Rather, let them themselves nurse them, themselves render fruit to their Lord with increase, and present fruitful sheaves to him with glory.

For if the Lord, amid his other cares for his sheep, touched and cleansed lepers, why do we disdain to do the same? Or why do we ourselves, who have undertaken the pastoral office, hand over our sheep to others to rear? Especially when the Lord said to Peter, our leader: “If you love me, feed my sheep”; and many other similar things. For the blessing which the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0436D] Capitularies, book VII, canon 187.] chorepiscopi gave through the laying on of hands before their prohibition seems to us to inflict a wound rather than health. How could men who did not possess the summit of the pontificate give what they did not have? [Col. 0436D] For there was nothing in the giver [Note: [Col. 0436D] Innocent, Epistle 22, canon 3.] that the recipient could receive. Or what human being, even speaking in ordinary human terms, can give what he does not possess? Especially since they were not pontiffs, they could not give things owed to pontiffs alone.

Thus they injured rather than healed the heads which they touched by the laying on of hands, when by some blessing they purported to confer things never bestowed upon themselves. Therefore whatever they presumed from the aforesaid pontifical ministries [Col. 0437A] was void and gave no benefit to those touched; rather, in the prophet’s phrase, they conferred a curse instead of a blessing, if it is proper to say so.

Consequently, through that unlawful laying on of hands [Note: [Col. 0437D] 25, I, question 7; and 3, IX, question 1, “Per illicitam manus.”], as we noted a little above, those who appeared to have received something had a wounded [Note: [Col. 0437D] The same Innocent, in the cited passage.] head. Where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied to heal the affixed blemish. That is, what is not approved as having been lawfully performed or conferred must necessarily be repeated, if it is to be complete. For I cannot see how a person can retain an honour received from one who had no lawful power to confer it. A man who lacked pontifical rank cannot grant pontifical rights, nor could they claim for themselves that of which, through the impediment confronting them, [Col. 0437B] they were not capable.

Claiming for ourselves a special responsibility for examining this question [Note: [Col. 0437D] St Leo, Epistle 1, canon 2.], we exercise mercy in such a manner that, if any such acts have perhaps been committed, they are corrected, so that they may not be committed hereafter and that no excuse of ignorance may arise. For as the condition of churches, granted or ordered through wholesome arrangement, gives us cause for rejoicing, so we are saddened by no slight grief whenever we learn that anything has been presumed or committed contrary to the institutions of the canons or to ecclesiastical discipline.

If we do not cut off such things with the vigilance owed by us, we cannot excuse ourselves before him who willed us to be watchmen, should we fail, so far as we are able, to keep his Church, which has been generally entrusted to us, pure from such unlawful superstitions. For we are not otherwise [Col. 0437C] one flock and one shepherd unless, as the Apostle teaches, “we all say the same thing” and “are perfected in the same mind and in the same understanding.” Nor shall we otherwise be true disciples of the Lord unless each one, according to his strength, hastens to eradicate the root [Note: [Col. 0437D] Pope Martin, Consultation 1, Lateran Council.] of bitterness springing up—as you assert that it is now doing—lest it be able to cause harm or make the episcopal ministry cheap through the negligence of those who have been set over by him to uproot evils and plant better things, that is, all priests. Let each man who must render an account to the eternal Judge for his own sheep strive to cherish and rear them.

If we desire to be the Lord’s disciples, let us imitate his footsteps, so that it may be said of us: “I am the good Shepherd; I know my sheep, call them by name, and my own know me”; and so forth. And again, by the authority of the Lord’s voice, through which the most blessed apostle Peter is imbued by a threefold repetition of mystical sanctification [Col. 0437D], let him who loves Christ diligently and with great care feed Christ’s sheep. For we are constrained by love and reverence for that holy See over which, through the abundance of divine grace, we preside, to avert, as far as we can, the danger of so great a superstition, supported by the authority of no one, as has often been said. Otherwise the love of our blessed teacher Peter [Col. 0438A], chief of the Apostles, by which he professed himself a lover of God, may be found vain in us. For everyone who negligently feeds the Lord’s flock, so often entrusted to him, is proved not to love the supreme Shepherd nor to wish to become a disciple of him whose examples he neglects to imitate.

For a far greater grace is acquired if a shepherd’s care offers to the Lord a gain from the sheep committed to it [Note: [Col. 0438D] St Gregory, Epistle 43, book VIII.]. We remember also that blessed Jacob [Note: [Col. 0438D] The same, Epistle 48, book VII.], who had served long for his wives, said: “For twenty years I was with you. Your ewes and she-goats were not barren; I did not eat the rams of your flock, nor did I bring to you an animal seized by a beast. I made good every loss; whatever was stolen, you required from me. By day and night I was burned by heat and frost; sleep fled from my eyes.” If then one who feeds [Col. 0438B] Laban’s sheep labours and watches thus, with how much labour and with how many vigils ought one to attend who feeds God’s sheep?

But in all these matters may he himself instruct us, who gave his life for his own sheep; and may he help us, so that from those entrusted to us [Note: [Col. 0438D] The same Gregory, ibid.] he may grant us to bring a manifold harvest and an overflowing measure into eternal joys. May so great a love for blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0438D] The same, Epistle 97 of the same book VII.], inflame you that, within his sheepfold—to which all creatures have been entrusted—you may hasten, with holy zeal and supreme desire, to restore all who thus go astray and presume unlawful and forbidden things, so that souls redeemed by Christ’s precious blood may not perish through their deception.

There remains also this: these men have not entered through the door, because they had no door through which to enter. For, as stated, [Col. 0438C] if they are not bishops and seek to be more than presbyters, through what door shall they enter, when only these two orders are read of in the Church and no further door is open to any pastoral office through which a shepherd may enter? Hear, brothers, not me but Truth herself speaking: “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in another way, is a thief and a robber”; and so forth.

The eminent preacher also says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid.” Since only the aforesaid two foundations are found laid in the Church, whatever is found to be laid in addition to them cannot stand at all. Therefore it must be uprooted together with all its foundations, acts, and roots, so that it can no longer sprout or germinate [Col. 0438D].

Let not this often-repeated discourse, then, beget weariness in you, brothers. It is a most urgent necessity that what is, as we have learned from you, so frequently usurped unlawfully, should be forbidden again and again. For truth, [Note: [Col. 0438D] Zosimus, Epistle 1, canon 2.] when repeatedly assailed, shines more brightly into the light; and what is repeatedly enjoined is less often usurped. Much has already been said concerning these matters by our predecessors, by whom these men were condemned and forbidden in former times, as they are now by us.

Therefore, repeating these things often, [Col. 0439A] we admonish everyone to avoid such persons and abstain from them, unless they wish, together with them as rebels, to be excluded from the priestly ministry. We shall at last be able to prove this if you strive to root out such men and not favour them. Thereafter complaint about this matter will cease, because whatever is repeatedly prohibited yet usurped is done out of a desire for insult [Note: [Col. 0439D] St Leo, Epistle 1, canon 5.].

We command that all these decretals and enactments of all our predecessors concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons [Note: [Col. 0439D] St Celestine, Epistle 1, canon 1.] be observed by you, by all bishops, and generally by all priests in such a way that anyone who violates them is to know that pardon will henceforth be denied him. For truth would prevail if falsehood were displeasing. It is right that the matter concerns us who ought to hold the highest [Col. 0439B] helm of the Church, should we favour error by silence.

Given on the Kalends of June, under the consulship of Libio and Theodosius, most illustrious men. [Note: [Col. 0439D] These consuls are not in the Fasti.]

## EPISTLE IV. It commands that henceforth no one be judged on the basis of writings, but through a lawful accuser; and that all cases to be judged be referred to the Apostolic See.

Damasus, bishop, to all bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy: greeting in the Lord.

I had wished, most beloved brethren, [Note: [Col. 0439D] St Leo, Epistle 47.] in the love of our fellowship, that all the Lord’s priests—as in the primitive Church—should be one heart and one soul, persevere in one devotion, and that no priest should be corrupted by favour or fear of secular persons, or [Col. 0439C] depart in any way from the path of truth. But many things that can be corrected occur, and the mercy of God exceeds the fault of sinners; therefore punishment is deferred so that correction may have an opportunity.

For it has been reported to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0439D] Question 2, cause 5, “Relatum est ad sedem.”] that you receive accusations against brothers in writing without a lawful accuser. By Apostolic authority we forbid this henceforth throughout the whole world, and we ask that what has recently been done be corrected without any delay. Nor may the case of persons accused [Note: [Col. 0439D] Question 3, cause 76, “Eorum qui accusantur.”] ever first be investigated from writings before they are canonically summoned to a synod through the formal charges of the complainants [Note: [Col. 0439D] Manuscript: *querelantium*; elsewhere, *querelarum* (“of complaints”).] [Note: [Col. 0439D] Pope Martin I, Consultation 2, Lateran Council.], so that one present may truly know and understand from a present person what is alleged against him.

This is well stated also by the wisdom of Solomon: “Before you investigate, do not rebuke; understand first, and then reprove. Before you have heard, do not answer.” [Col. 0439D] Even if the accusation of opponents is most manifest, nevertheless those appointed to examine it must preserve the procedure established by those [Note: [Col. 0439D] Question 3, cause 5, “Relatum est ad sedem.”] who are charged with examining matters according to God, [Col. 0440A] so that, with action cooperating, we may find God also affirming it, who says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst.”

Our Lord Jesus Christ knew that Judas [Note: [Col. 0439D] Ambrosiaster on 1 Corinthians V.] was a thief; but because he was not accused in person, he was not cast out. Nor ought you in any way to do what he refused to do. The laws of the world require accusers to be present, not absent by means of writings. Hence the canonical enactments of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0440D] Question 1, cause 5, “Relatum est ad sedem.”] cry out not once but very often that no accusations or testimony may be presented by anyone in writing; nor may anyone testify concerning other matters except those known to have been done in their presence.

Likewise, whoever chooses to accuse another [Note: [Col. 0440D] Question 6, cause 3, “Qui accusare alium.”] must accuse in person, [Note: [Col. 0440D] “This very ruling,” says Hincmar against his nephew, chapter 43, “was taken from the ancient Roman laws,” from Anianus.] on his own behalf and not through another, with a formal written charge first submitted. [Col. 0440B] No one is ever to be judged before lawful accusers are present and he is granted an opportunity of defence to clear away the accusations. Care must be taken lest anger overtake anyone and make him hastily do everything that is unlawful.

May almighty God protect you, as you observe these things and all divine commands and apostolic precepts, by the outstretched arm of heaven in all your actions, and bring you, with an abundant harvest of souls, to the reward of the heavenly homeland. Amen.

Given on the third day before the Ides of April, under the consulship of Siricius and Ardabur, most illustrious men. [Note: [Col. 0440D] These consuls are not in the Fasti.] [Note: [Col. 0440D] Gratian further adduces these two decrees under the name of Pope Damasus: 2, question 3, *Calumniator*; 15, question 1, *Hanc consuetudinem*.]

## EPISTLE V. TO JEROME THE PRESBYTER.

[Col. 0440C] Damasus, bishop, to Jerome, brother and fellow-presbyter: greeting in the Lord.

When many volumes of books had been brought for my consideration, it happened that I was eagerly drawn in mind to the book of Psalms and to imbue the memory of my capacity with it. I thought, most loving brother and ever priest in Christ, that, according to the Seventy interpreters and presbyters—that is, Matthias and Ptolemy, Muchius, Sacreus, Hydronius, Pamphilus, Zoastites, Didymus, Sanius, Epiphanius, Ciater, Simon, and the rest—I might, so far as my awareness allows, discover traces of the Seventy.

I also ask your charity that, as you learned from your teacher Alexander, bishop of our church, your brotherhood may be pleased to send us the Greek manner of psalmody [Col. 0440D]. For the simplicity among us is so great that on the Lord’s Day only one Apostolic Epistle is read and one chapter of the Gospel is recited; neither the custom of psalm-singing is observed nor the beauty of hymnody known in our mouths. I therefore ask through our brother and fellow-presbyter Boniface that your Brotherhood may be willing to disclose to us the outlines of this matter.

Sent on the fifth day before the Kalends of November to Jerusalem through Boniface the presbyter.

## EPISTLE VI. Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, to Jerome the presbyter.

The Church rejoices, now satisfied from your fountain, and the curiosity concerning the times of priests thirsts still more, so that what is worthy may be known and what is unworthy rejected. But we have gladly sent to your charity the records of the pontiffs which we were able to discover through the diligence [Col. 0442A] of our See. Pray for us at the holy Resurrection, brother and fellow-presbyter. Farewell in Christ, God and our Lord.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, and received on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, sent from Rome to Jerusalem.

In the name of the Lord begins the series of Roman pontiffs who sat in the See of the blessed apostle Peter, from Peter himself down to the present time.

Blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles, a Galilean by birth, from the village of Bethsaida, son of Jobius, brother of Andrew, etc.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 258. CATALOGUE OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS COMPILED UNDER LIBERIUS; TO WHICH ARE ADDED, AS CONFIRMATION, TWO MARTYROLOGIES OF THE ROMAN CHURCH AND ALSO THE MOST ANCIENT CALENDAR OF THE CHURCH OF CARTHAGE.

(From a work published a few years ago, entitled *Origins of the Roman Church*, by members of the community of Solesmes.)

[Col. 0441]

## PREFACE

Extracted from the fourth chapter of the work cited, and presenting preliminary observations composed in French.

[Col. 0441B]

Having examined the earlier monuments concerning the succession of the Roman pontiffs, the most learned authors proceed to elucidate the catalogue in question in the following manner.

Until now we have not been able to consult the archives of the Roman Church itself concerning the succession of the pontiffs. The ravages of persecutions, and still more the injury wrought by time, have deprived us of all documents earlier than the fourth century—but not without a profound design of divine Providence. It was fitting that the first page of the annals of the Apostolic See, absent from its own archives, should be [Col. 0441C] found again in the traditions of all the Churches; and that, even before Christian Rome had found leisure to compose its domestic chronicles, ecclesiastical histories should bear witness to its great activity during three centuries among the churches.

The peace granted to Christianity by Constantine brought, among other advantages, that of a tranquil stability by whose help it became possible to compile memorial records and collect a thousand traditions. The persecution of Diocletian had destroyed the documentary titles of these traditions; or, at least, because they were not recorded in the more general chronicles, they risked disappearing together with the isolated monuments upon which they rested. The existence of Christians was no longer furtive and hurried. They now lived [Col. 0441D] at peace in a world which, until then, they had merely traversed in great haste. The Church had a place—and the first place—in the annals of humanity.

This was [Col. 0442B] the idea which Eusebius wished to express in his *Chronicle*, where he groups around sacred and ecclesiastical history the eras, Olympiads, kingdoms, and dynasties, so that it is remarkable to see all the records of the earth exhaust themselves one after another, while the Jewish Church and then the Christian Church pass majestically through the ages.

On every side people devoted themselves to the search for origins and antiquities; and, as we have seen above, the West wished to have its Latin version of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, pending its own large-scale exploration of the science of chronology. A reason no less powerfully impelling Christians toward this kind of work was the computation of the feast of Easter, a question of the highest [Col. 0442C] religious interest at all times, but especially then, when it had been the subject of lively controversies. Its solution required profound chronological investigations as well as learned astronomical observations.

Thus, in the preceding century, Saint Hippolytus, in composing his Paschal Cycle, had been led to record his research in a true chronicle. Everything at that time therefore combined to prompt Christians to gather their earliest monuments; and this is likewise the period in which the chronicle that is the subject of this chapter was compiled.

In 1634 Fr. Gilles Boucher, a learned Jesuit, published at Antwerp a celebrated commentary on the Paschal Cycle of Victorius of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0441] *Aegidii Bucherii Atrebatis e Societate Jesu de doctrina temporum commentarius in Victorium Aquitanum* [Commentary of Aegidius Bucherius of Arras, of the Society of Jesus, on the Doctrine of Times, upon Victorius of Aquitaine]. Antwerp, 1634.]. Among the monuments which he inserted in that work, five chronological treatises of the highest interest are especially noteworthy; Fr. Boucher stated that he had extracted them [Col. 0443A] from one and the same manuscript. The first was a sequence of Consular Fasti from the second consulship of Antoninus and Geta to the seventh consulship of Constantius Augustus and the third of Constantius Caesar. The second was a list of the Prefects of Rome from Lollianus, in office under the second consulship of Valerian and Gallienus, to Vitrasius Orfitus under that of the two Constantii just named; that is, down to the year 354. The third was an ancient ecclesiastical calendar containing the feast-days and death-days of several holy martyrs and bishops of Rome, the last being Pope St. Julius, who died in 352. The fourth is the Chronicle of the Popes which is the subject of this chapter: it reaches Liberius, whose accession it records under the consuls Constantius for the fifth time and Constantius [Col. 0443B] Caesar, without recording his death, which occurred in 366, doubtless because he was still alive. Finally, the fifth is an ancient civil calendar recording the births of the principal Caesars, and ending with Constantius, who is styled not *Divus*, “Deified,” as the others are, but *Dominus*, “Lord,” as still living when this calendar was compiled. Constantius is known to have died in 361. Thus these five monuments must have been written within a period of about ten years, namely from 354 to 364. It is clear that they mutually support one another; and, although the author who composed them cannot be identified, one must at least acknowledge, with Fr. Boucher and the entire body of learned scholars, that their date is indisputably fixed in the middle of the fourth century.

[Col. 0443C] Of these five monuments, the fourth alone is to occupy us particularly. It contains the names of the Popes from St. Peter to Liberius, with their years distinguished by the consuls and certain other particulars whose authenticity we shall discuss later. In short, this monument is of truly great importance and deserves our fullest attention; for, in Pearson’s words, “if any certainty concerning these times seems capable of being found among Latin chronologists, it must be sought from no other source than this more ancient catalogue” [Note: [Col. 0443D] *De successione primorum Romae Episcoporum*, ch.
