XII, p. 133. *Si qua apud latinos chronologos certitudo istorum temporum haberi posse videatur, non aliunde quam ex isto vetustiori catalogo petenda erit.*].

Before examining, however, what degree of confidence should be accorded to this celebrated chronicle—which we shall henceforth call the Catalogue of Liberius, because it ends with that Pope—we shall [Col. 0443D] devote a few pages to the history of its discovery and publication.

This precious monument, which remained in manuscript until Fr. Boucher first published it in 1634, had already before that date attracted the [Col. 0444A] attention of scholars who had had the opportunity to consult it. The first known to have used it was Spiesshammer, better known in the learned world under the name Cuspinianus. In his commentary upon the Chronicle of Cassiodorus, he used it because of the consular fasti which it contains, and inserted it almost entire, but in sections, into his commentary as he needed it. He calls it a very ancient treatise [Note: [Col. 0443D] “Moreover, there was presented to me a very ancient little work by an anonymous author, in which the chief pontiffs are enumerated together with the consuls under whom they held office. In it the following is written: ‘In the reign of Tiberius,’ etc.” (*Joannis Cuspiniani de Consulibus Romanorum Commentarii, ex optimis vetustissimisque authoribus collecti. In Chronica magni Aurelii* [Col. 0444D] *Cassiodori Commentarius* [Commentaries of Johannes Cuspinianus on the Roman Consuls, collected from the best and most ancient authors. Commentary on the Chronicle of the great Aurelius Cassiodorus], Basel, 1553, at the year from the foundation of the city 781, p. 369.)]. In several places he also speaks of the four other works joined to it, likewise published by Fr. Boucher. Cuspinianus’s manuscript, which seems to have been the original of the various copies to be mentioned, appears originally to have been in the hands of a privy councillor of the Catholic King, whom Fr. Boucher [Col. 0444B] names in Latin Assonvillius. He had received it from Jean Brenner, secretary to the same prince and member of the Senate of Luxembourg [Note: [Col. 0444D] Bucherius, *De doctrina temporum*, p. 243.]. Be that as it may, this original manuscript has long since ceased to exist [Note: [Col. 0444D] Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, Bologna, 1673, p. 7.—Pagi, *Critica Baronii*, at the year of Christ 67.].

Henschenius [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I.—*Diatriba in catalog. Rom. Pont.*] claimed that Onofrio Panvinio had likewise had the Catalogue of Liberius in his hands while working in Rome on the consular fasti, around the middle of the sixteenth century. Pagi thought the same, as he explains in his *Critique of Baronius* [Note: [Col. 0444D] Pagi, at the year of Christ 67.]; but both were mistaken. In his major work on ecclesiastical antiquity, Emmanuel de Schelstrate attests that he found, in the Vatican Library—of which he was in charge toward the end of the seventeenth century—an index of the books and manuscripts used by [Col. 0444C] Panvinio in his work on the consular fasti; he declares that it mentions no catalogue of Popes other than the *Liber pontificalis* [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Antiquitas Ecclesiae illustrata*, vol. I, dissertation 3, ch. II.].

Here, however, is something more certain. Around 1620, Nicolas Fabry de Peiresc, councillor of the Parliament of Aix and a man of genuine learning, received from a magistrate of Arras access to a precious manuscript containing the Catalogue of Liberius together with the four other treatises. Peiresc extols the importance of these monuments in a letter which Pagi inserted in substance in the passage of his *Critique* already cited. Peiresc, who, according to the express intention of his correspondent at Arras, was only to copy the manuscript and then return it, faithfully [Col. 0444D] fulfilled these two conditions, but did not permit the public to benefit from the fruit of the discovery.

Pagi also speaks of two other manuscript copies of the Catalogue of Liberius which are said to have existed at Paris during the seventeenth century: one [Col. 0445A] in the library of the Regular Canons of Saint-Victor, entered in the catalogue under the title *Chronica Damasi*; but it had subsequently disappeared, and no one knew what had become of it. The other was in the Jesuit library of the Collège Louis-le-Grand, where it had been deposited by Fr. Sirmond. Moreover, it agreed in every respect with the copy published by the Bollandists, according to the attestation made by Fr. Hardouin himself to Fr. Pagi.

Fr. Boucher was therefore the first who, not content with using the precious monument that concerns us, thought to admit the public to his confidence by publishing separately and in full the celebrated catalogue, of which Cuspinianus had inserted only detached fragments in the work already cited. [Col. 0445B] In October 1632, having come from Liège to Antwerp to arrange with the Plantin house for printing his treatise *De doctrina temporum*, he naturally came into contact with Fr. Bollandus. Intending to assist his confrère in explaining the cycle of Victorius, which was the object of that publication, Bollandus supplied him with a copy formerly made by Fr. Rosweid from the manuscript which Cuspinianus had had in his hands. This copy contained precisely the five chronological treatises that concern us [Note: [Col. 0445D] *De Doctrina temporum*, p. 243.]. The original had by then been lost; nevertheless Fr. Boucher judged that he should publish these various items entire in his work on Victorius, and through him the learned world truly came into possession of them.

[Col. 0445C] In 1675 a new edition of the Catalogue of Liberius appeared at Antwerp through the care of Fr. Henschenius, at the head of the first April volume of the *Acta Sanctorum*. In this new edition—which Fr. Papebroch repeated word for word in his *Conatus chronologico-historicus ad catalogum Pontificum Romanorum*—some fairly serious variants were noticed in comparison with the text published by Fr. Boucher. Pagi seems inclined to attribute them to corrections which Henschenius may have allowed himself to make to the manuscript reading. But this conjecture appears to lose much of its force if it is demonstrated that Fr. Boucher established his text not only from the Bollandists’ manuscript but also from another preserved in the Imperial [Col. 0445D] Library of Vienna. In that case Henschenius and Papebroch, by accurately publishing their Antwerp manuscript, would necessarily present certain differences from a reading established from two manuscripts rather than one.

As for the manuscript of the Catalogue of Liberius preserved in the Vienna Library, among the Latin manuscripts, no. 56, it was published by Schelstrate in his [Col. 0446A] *Antiquitas illustrata*; one cannot fail to be struck by the identity between its text and that of Fr. Boucher. They have this further feature in common: both supply in the same way several lacunae found in Henschenius’s edition. It is therefore impossible that Fr. Boucher, whose scholarly connections were very extensive, did not have access to the Vienna manuscript: otherwise, how could his divergences from the Antwerp text reproduce the very words of the former? Lambecius had maintained that the Vienna manuscript was the oldest of all, and that the one used by Cuspinianus was merely a copy of it [Note: [Col. 0445D] *Commentar. de Augustissima Bibliotheca Vindobonensi*, [Col. 0446D] bk. IV.]. Schelstrate, assisted by Fr. Conrad Janning, one of the Bollandists, overthrew the assertion of the distinguished [Col. 0446B] bibliographer. These two scholars proved that the Vienna manuscript was not, in 1688, more than three or four hundred years old, and that it was, like that of Antwerp, a copy of a more ancient original [Note: [Col. 0446D] *Antiquit. illustrat.*, dissertation III, ch. II, no. 2.]. Now, was this original manuscript, the source of the Antwerp and Vienna copies, indeed the one which Cuspinianus and Peiresc had in their hands? We can scarcely doubt it. Did Fr. Boucher himself have it available, rather than the Vienna Library’s copy? We do not know how to answer that question. What is certain is that these various copies—divergent, it is true, in some non-essential details, but in agreement in almost the whole body of the work—while demonstrating the existence [Col. 0446C] of a common original, clearly show that they ought not to be regarded as the work of a forger. Indeed, it has never occurred to anyone to suppose that the Chronicle of Liberius had been fabricated at will.

Apart from Schelstrate, who reproduced the text of this treatise according to the Vienna manuscript in the first volume of his *Antiquitas illustrata*, and Henschenius, at the head of the first April volume of the *Acta Sanctorum*, we know only Du Cange, in the documentary appendices to the *Chronicon Paschale*, and Bianchini, at the head of the second volume of the edition of Anastasius, to have acted as editors of the Catalogue of Liberius. The latter two, moreover, merely reproduced the text as it [Col. 0446D] was given by Fr. Boucher.

We therefore reduce the proper editions to three: that of Fr. Boucher, that of Fr. Henschenius, and that of Schelstrate. In order that the reader may be able to weigh their authority, we set out below all three at one view, together with the notes with which the three learned editors to whom we owe them enriched them.

[Col. 0447]

# CATALOGUE OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS

[Note: [Col. 0447] The following versions of the *Catalogus* (the reading of Aegidius Boucher, the reading of Fr. Godfrey Henschenius, and the reading of Emmanuel Schelstrate) are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## READING OF AEGIDIUS BOUCHER

*Commentary on the Paschal Canon of Victorius of Aquitaine*, p. 269, Antwerp: Plantin, 1634.

This catalogue is rather confused and corrupt down to Callistus; after him it is somewhat clearer, especially after Lucius.

IN THE REIGN OF TIBERIUS CAESAR our Lord Jesus Christ suffered, when the two Gemini were consuls, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March]; and after his ascension the most blessed Peter assumed the episcopate. From that time onward, the succession is set out: which bishop presided, for how many years, and under which emperor.

PETER: twenty-five years, one month, nine days. He lived in the times of Tiberius Caesar, Gaius, Tiberius Claudius, and Nero, from the consulship of Vinicius and Longinus to that of Nero and Veterus [Note: [Col. 0447] “My manuscript has: ‘of Nerva and Verus.’”]. He suffered, moreover, with Paul on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June], when the aforesaid were consuls, in Nero’s reign.

LINUS: twelve years, four months, twelve days. He lived in Nero’s time, from the consulship of Saturninus and Scipio to that of Capito and Rufus.

CLEMENT: nine years, eleven months, twelve days. He lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus to that of Vespasian for the sixth time and Titus.

(Eusebius and Baronius place Clement after Cletus.)

CLETUS: six years, two months, ten days. He lived in the times of Vespasian and Titus, and at the beginning of Domitian’s reign, from the consuls Vespasian for the eighth time and Domitian for the fifth time to Domitian for the ninth time and Rufus.

ANACLETUS: twelve years, ten months, three days. He lived in Domitian’s time, from the consuls Domitian for the tenth time and Sabinus to Domitian for the seventeenth time and Clement.

EVARISTUS [Note: [Col. 0447] The manuscript has *Aristus*.]: thirteen years, seven months, two days. He lived in the last years of Domitian, and in the reigns of Nerva and Trajan, from the consulship of Valens and Verus to that of Gallus and Bradua.

ALEXANDER: seven years, two months, one day. He lived in Trajan’s time, from the consulship of Palma and Tullus to that of Velianus [Note: [Col. 0447] Perhaps *Aelianus*.] and Veterus.

SIXTUS: ten years, three months, twenty-one days. He lived in Hadrian’s time, from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus to that of Verus for the third time and Ambibulus.

TELESPHORUS: eleven years, [Col. 0449] three months, three days. He lived in the time of Antoninus Macrinus, from the consulship of Titianus and Gallicanus to that of Caesar and Balbinus.

HYGINUS: twelve years, three months, six days. He lived in the time of Verus, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Veterus to that of Praesens and Rufinus.

(Anicetus, to whom they assign nearly eight years, is missing here.)

PIUS: twenty years, four months, twenty-one days. He lived in the time of Antoninus Pius, from the consulship of Clarus and Severus to that of the two Augusti. During his episcopate his brother Hermes wrote a book in which is enjoined and contained what the Angel commanded him when he came to him in the guise of a shepherd.

SOTER: nine years, three months, two days. He lived in the times of Antoninus and Commodus, from the consulship of Verus and Erennianus to that of Paternus and Bradua.

(Eleutherius, whom they maintain held office for fifteen years, is again missing.)

VICTOR: nine years, two months, ten days. From the consulship of Saturninus and Gallus to that of Praescatus and Extricatus.

(Zephyrinus, to whom they assign eighteen years, is likewise missing.)

CALLISTUS: five years, two months, ten days. He lived in the times of Macrinus and Elagabalus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Adventus to that of Antoninus for the third time and Alexander.

URBANUS: eight years, eleven months, twelve days. He lived in Alexander’s time, from the consulship of Maximus and Aelianus to that of Agricola and Clementinus.

PONTIANUS: five years, two months, seven days. He lived in Alexander’s time, from the consulship of Pompeianus and Pelignianus. In that time Nepotianus [Note: [Col. 0449] Cuspinianus reads: “Pontianus”; I believe this is better.] the bishop and Hippolytus the presbyter, as exiles, were deported to the harmful island of Sardinia, when Severus and Quintianus were consuls. On that same island he was stripped [of office?] on the fourth day before the Kalends of December [28 November], when the aforesaid were consuls.

ANTEROS: one month, ten days. He died on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January], when Maximus and Africanus were consuls.

FABIANUS: fourteen years, one month, ten days. He lived in the times of Maximinus, Gordian, and Philip, from the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus to that of Decius for the second time and Gratus. He suffered on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January]. [Col. 0451] He divided the districts among the deacons and ordered many structures to be made throughout the cemeteries. After his martyrdom, Moses and Maximus, presbyters, and Nicostratus, a deacon, were seized and sent to prison. At that time Novatus arrived from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church, after Moses died in prison, where he had been eleven months and eleven days.

CORNELIUS: two years, three months, ten days. From the consulships of Decius for the fourth time and Decius for the second time to that of Gallus and Volusianus. During his episcopate Novatus, outside the Church, ordained Novatian in the city of Rome and Nicostratus in Africa. Once this had been done, the confessors who had separated themselves from Cornelius, together with Maximus the presbyter, who had been with Moses, returned to the Church; after this he was banished to Centumcellae. There he received death in glory.

LUCIUS: three years, eight months, ten days. He lived in the times of Gallus and Volusianus to the consulship of Valerian for the third time and Gallienus for the second time. He was an exile and afterward, by God’s will, returned unharmed to the Church [Note: [Col. 0451] “It seems that *he died* is missing here.”], on the third day before the Nones of March [5 March], when the aforesaid were consuls.

STEPHEN: four years, two months, twenty-one days. He lived in the times of Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Volusianus and Maximinus to that of Valerian for the third time and Gallienus for the second time.

SIXTUS: two years, eleven months, six days. He began with the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio, continuing to that of Tuscus and Bassus; and he suffered on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August], from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus until the twelfth day before the Kalends of August [21 July], when Aemilianus and Bassus were consuls.

DIONYSIUS: eight years, two months, four days. He lived in Gallienus’s time, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August [22 July], when Aemilianus and Bassus were consuls, to the seventh day before the Kalends of January [26 December], when Claudius and Paternus were consuls.

FELIX: five years, eleven months, twenty-five days. He lived in the times of Claudius and Aurelian, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus to the consulship of Aurelian for the second time and Capitolinus.

EUTYCHIANUS: eight years, eleven months, three days. He lived in Aurelian’s time, from the consulship of Aurelian for the third time and Marcellinus to the seventh day before the Ides of December [7 December], when Carus for the second time and Carinus were consuls.

CAIUS: twelve years, four months, seven days. He lived in the times of Carus and Carinus, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January [17 December], when Carus for the second time and Carinus were consuls, to the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April], when Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius for the second time were consuls.

MARCELLINUS: eight years, [Col. 0453] three months, twenty-five days. He lived in the times of Diocletian and Maximian, from the day before the Kalends of July [30 June], from the consulship of Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius for the second time to the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth time. At that time there was persecution and the episcopate was vacant for seven years [Note: [Col. 0453] “It seems that *three* should be read here, from the sequence of consuls, which is nevertheless confused here.”], six months, twenty-five days.

MARCELLUS: one year, seven months, twenty days. He lived in Maxentius’s time, from the consulship of the tenth time and Maximian [Note: [Col. 0453] “It seems that *seven* is missing here. Others read: ‘the ninth time and Maximian.’”] to after the tenth and seventh consulship.

EUSEBIUS: four months, sixteen days, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May [18 April] to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [17 August].

MILTIADES: three years, six months, nine days, from the sixth day before the Nones of July [2 July], from the sole eighth consulship of Maximian—which was in the month of September, when Volusianus and Rufinus were consuls—to the third day before the Ides of January [11 January], when Volusianus and Annianus were consuls.

SYLVESTER: twenty-one years, eleven months. He lived in Constantine’s time, from the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, from the day before the Kalends of February [31 January], to the day of the Kalends of January [1 January], when Constantius and Albinus were consuls.

MARCUS: eight months, twenty days. He too lived in Constantine’s time, when Nepotianus and Facundus were consuls, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January] to the day of the Nones of October [7 October], when the aforesaid were consuls.

JULIUS: fifteen years, one month, eleven days. He lived in Constantine’s time, from the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, from the eighth day before the Ides of February [6 February], to the day before the Ides of April [12 April], when Constantius for the fifth time and Constantius Caesar were consuls. He built many structures: a basilica on the Portuensian Way, at the third milestone; a basilica on the Flaminian Way, at the second milestone, called that of Valentinus; the Julian Basilica, in Region VII, near the Forum of the Deified Trajan; a basilica across the Tiber, in Region XIV, near Callistus; and a basilica on the Aurelian Way, at the third milestone, at Callistus.

LIBERIUS lived in the time of Constantius, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of June [22 May], until . . . . . ., under the consuls Constantius for the fifth time and Constantius Caesar.

(Almost all these little works end with these consuls; from which it appears that they were written in this year, A.D. 354, or thereabouts.)

## READING OF FR. GODFREY HENSCHENIUS

*Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I.—Preliminary Dissertation on the Ancient Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs, received from the most ancient manuscript codices, p. 4.

From that time onward, the succession is set out: which bishop presided, for how many years, and under which emperor.

PETER: twenty-five years, one month, nine days. He suffered, moreover, with Paul on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June], when the aforesaid were consuls, in Nero’s reign.

CLEMENT: nine years, eleven months, twelve days. He lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus to that of Vespasian for the seventh time and Titus.

ANACLETUS: twelve years, ten months, three days. He lived in Domitian’s time, from the consuls Domitian for the tenth time and Sabinus to Domitian for the seventeenth time and Clement.

ALEXANDER: eight years, two months, one day. He lived in Trajan’s time, from the consulship of Palma and Tullus to that of Aelianus and Veterus.

SIXTUS: ten years, three months, twenty-one days. He lived in Hadrian’s time, from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus to that of Verus for the third time and Ambibulus.

TELESPHORUS: eleven years, [Col. 0449] three months, three days. He lived in Hadrian’s time, from the consulship of Titianus and Gallicanus to that of Caesar and Balbinus.

HYGINUS: twelve years, three months, six days. He lived in the time of . . . . . . . . .

ANICETUS: . . . . years, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Veterus to that of Praesens and Rufinus.

PIUS: fifteen years, four months, twenty days. He lived in the time of Antoninus Pius, from the consulship of Clarus and Severus to that of the two Augusti. During his episcopate his brother Hermes wrote a book in which is enjoined and contained what the Angel commanded him when he came to him in the guise of a shepherd.

ELEUTHERIUS: . . . years. He lived in the times of Antoninus and Commodus, from the consulship of Verus and Erennianus to that of Paternus and Bradua.

ZEPHYRINUS: . . . years. From the consulship of Saturninus and Gallus to that of Praesens and Extricatus.

URBANUS: eight years, eleven months, twelve days. He lived in Alexander’s time, from the consulship of Maximus and Aelianus to that of Agricola and Clementinus.

On that same island he was *discinctus* [perhaps “deposed” or “died”?] on the fourth day before the Kalends of October [28 September], and Anteros was ordained in his place on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December [21 November], when the aforementioned were consuls. He lived in the times of Maximinus, Gordian, and Philip, from the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus to that of Decius for the second time and Gratus. After his martyrdom, Moses and Maximus, presbyters, and Nicostratus, a deacon, were seized and sent to prison. At that time Novatus arrived from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church, after Moses died in prison, where he had been eleven months and eleven days.

CORNELIUS: two years, three months, ten days, from the consuls Decius for the second time and Decius to Gallus and Volusianus. He was an exile and afterward, by God’s will, returned to the Church. (*He died*) on the third day before the Nones of March [5 March], when the aforementioned were consuls.

STEPHEN: four years, two months, twenty-one days. He lived in the times of Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Volusianus and Maximinus to that of Valerian for the third time and Gallienus for the second time.

SIXTUS: two years, eleven months, six days. He began with the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio, continuing to that of Tuscus and Bassus; and he suffered on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August]. (And the presbyters presided) from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus to the twelfth day before the Kalends of August [21 July], when Aemilianus and Bassus were consuls.

DIONYSIUS: eight years, two months, four days. He lived in Gallienus’s time, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August [22 July], when Aemilianus and Bassus were consuls, to the seventh day before the Kalends of January [26 December], when Claudius and Paternus were consuls.

FELIX: five years, eleven months, twenty-five days. He lived in the times of Claudius and Aurelian, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus to the consulship of Aurelian for the second time and Capitolinus.

EUTYCHIANUS: eight years, eleven months, three days. He lived in Aurelian’s time, from the consulship of Aurelian for the third time and Marcellinus to the seventh day before the Ides of December [7 December], when Carus for the second time and Carinus were consuls.

CAIUS: twelve years, four months, seven days. He lived in the times of Carus and Carinus, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January [17 December], when Carus for the second time and Carinus were consuls, to the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April], when Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius for the second time were consuls.

MARCELLINUS: eight years, [Col. 0453] three months, twenty-five days. He lived in the times of Diocletian and Maximian, from the day before the Kalends of July [30 June], from the consulship of Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius for the second time to the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth time. At that time there was persecution and the episcopate was vacant for four years, six months, twenty-five days.

MARCELLUS: one year, seven months, twenty days. He lived in Maxentius’s time, from the consulship of (Maximian Herculius for the tenth time) and (Maximian Galerius for the seventh time) to after the tenth and seventh consulship.

EUSEBIUS: four months, sixteen days, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May [18 April] to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [17 August].

MILTIADES: three years, six months, nine days [Note: [Col. 0454] “Others: eight; but the Caesarean codex has the reading which we have published.”], and from the sixth day before the Nones of July [2 July], from the sole eighth consulship of Maximian—which was in September, when Volusianus and Rufinus were consuls—to the third day before the Ides of January [11 January], when Volusianus and Anianus were consuls.

SILVESTER: twenty-one years, eleven months. He lived in Constantine’s time, from the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, from the day before the Kalends of February [31 January], to the day (*before*) the Kalends of January [31 December], when Constantine and Albinus were consuls.

MARCUS: eight months, twenty days. He lived in Constantine’s time, when Nepotianus and Facundus were consuls, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January] to the day of the Nones of October [7 October], when the aforementioned were consuls.

JULIANUS: fifteen years, two months, six days. He lived in the time of Constans, from the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, from the eighth day before the Ides of February [6 February], to the day before the Ides of April [12 April], when Constantius for the fifth time and Constantius Caesar were consuls. He built many structures: a basilica on the Portuensian Way, at the third milestone; a basilica on the Flaminian Way, at the second milestone, called that of Valentinus; the Julian Basilica, in Region VII, near the Forum of the Deified Trajan; a basilica across the Tiber, in Region XIV, near Callistus; and a basilica on the Aurelian Way, at the third milestone, at Callistus.

LIBERIUS lived in the time of Constantius, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of June [22 May], until . . . . . ., under the consuls Constantius for the fifth time and Constantius Caesar.

## READING OF EMMANUEL SCHELSTRATE

*Antiquitas Ecclesiae illustrata*, vol. I, p. 402.

[Col. 0448]

According to the older catalogue of the Imperial Library, compared with the manuscript exemplar and Cuspinianus’s edition.

In the reign of Tiberius Caesar our Lord Jesus Christ suffered, when the two Gemini were consuls, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March]; and after his ascension the most blessed Peter assumes the episcopate. From that time onward, the succession is set out: which bishop presided, for how many years, and under which emperor.

PETER: 25 years, 1 month, 9 days. He lived in the times of Tiberius Caesar, Gaius, Tiberius Claudius, and Nero, from the consulship of Vinicius and Longinus to that of Nero and Veterus. He suffered, moreover, with Paul on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June], when the aforesaid were consuls, in Nero’s reign.

LINUS: twelve years, 4 months, 12 days. He lived in Nero’s time, from the consulship of Saturninus and Scipio to that of Capito and Rufus.

CLEMENT: 9 years, 11 months, 12 days. He lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus to that of Vespasian for the seventh time and Titus.

(Clement is placed third and Cletus fourth; for what reason is unknown, since the Canon of the Mass presents the tradition of the Roman Church in these words: “Linus, Cletus, Clement.”)

CLETUS: 6 years, 2 months, 10 days. He lived in the times of Vespasian and Titus, and at the beginning of Domitian’s reign, from the consuls Vespasian for the eighth time and Domitian for the fifth time to Domitian for the ninth time and Rufus.

ANACLETUS: 12 years, 10 months, 3 days. He lived in Domitian’s time, from the consuls Domitian for the tenth time and Sabinus to Domitian for the seventeenth time and Clement.

EVARISTUS: 13 years, 7 months, 2 days. He lived in the last years of Domitian, and in the reigns of Nerva and Trajan, from the consulship of Valens and Verus to that of Gallus and Bradua.

ALEXANDER: seven years, two months, one day. He lived in Trajan’s time, from the consulship of Palma and Tullus to that of Aelianus and Veterus.

SIXTUS: ten years, three months, twenty-one days. He lived in Hadrian’s time, from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus to that of Veronius and Ambibulus.

TELESPHORUS: eleven years, [Col. 0450] three months, three days. He lived in the time of Antoninus Macrinus [Note: [Col. 0449] “Henschenius and Papebroch read ‘Hadrian’ in place of ‘Antoninus Macrinus’; nevertheless the manuscript codex has the reading which we print here.”], from the consulship of Titianus and Gallicanus to that of Caesar and Albinus.

HYGINUS: twelve years, three months, six days. He lived in the time of [Note: [Col. 0449] “Lacunae occur in Hyginus and Anicetus in the Caesarean manuscript, but they can be supplied from the second catalogue, since they existed in the manuscript codex in the author’s time; from it the notices of emperors and consulships may be gathered.”]. . . . . . . . .

ANICETUS: . . . . years, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Veterus to that of Praesens and Rufinus.

Pius: twenty years, four months, twenty-one days. He lived in the times of Antoninus Pius, from the consulship of Clarus and Severus to that of the two Augusti. During his episcopate his brother Hermas wrote a book, in which is contained the command enjoined upon him by the Angel when he came to him in the guise of a shepherd.

Soter: nine years, three months. He lived in the times of [Note: [Col. 0450] The lacuna in the Catalogue under Soter could be supplied from the Caesarean manuscript, where it reads: “In the times of Antoninus and Commodus, from the consulship of Verus and Herennianus to that of Paternus and Bradua.” But through a copyist’s error this consulship has intruded into the manuscript from another source.] . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Eleutherius: [number of] years . . . . He lived in the times of Antoninus Commodus, from the consulship of Verus and Herennianus to that of Paternus and Bradua.

Victor: ten years, two months, ten days. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Zephyrinus: [number of] years . . . . from the consulship of Saturninus and Gallus to that of Praesens and Extricatus.

Callistus: five years, two months, ten days. He lived in the times of Macrinus and Heliogabalus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Adventus to that of Antoninus III and Alexander.

Urban: eight years, eleven months, twelve days. He lived in the time of Alexander, from the consulship of Maximus and Aelianus to that of Agricola and Clementinus.

Pontianus: five years, two months, seven days. He lived in the time of Alexander, from the consulship of Pompeianus and Pelignianus. At that time Pontianus the bishop and Hippolytus the presbyter were deported into exile to the unhealthy island of Sardinia, Severus and Quintinus being consuls. On that same island he was deposed on 28 September [IV Kalends of October], and Anteros was ordained in his place on 21 November [XI Kalends of December], in the consulship mentioned above.

Anteros: one month, ten days. He fell asleep on 3 January [III Nones of January], in the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus.

Fabianus: fourteen years, one month, ten days. He lived in the times of Maximinus, Gordian, and Philip, from the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus to that of Decius II and Gratus. He suffered martyrdom on 20 January [XIII Kalends of February]. He [Col. 0452] divided the districts among the deacons and ordered many structures to be made through the cemeteries. After his martyrdom Moses and Maximus, presbyters, and Nicostratus, a deacon, were arrested and sent to prison. At that time Novatus came from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church, after Moses had died; Moses had been there eleven months and eleven days.

Cornelius: two years, three months, ten days, from the consulship of Decius IV and Decius II to that of Gallus and Volusianus. During his episcopate Novatus, outside the Church, ordained Novatian in the city of Rome and Nicostratus in Africa. This done, the confessors who had separated themselves from Cornelius, together with Maximus the presbyter, who had been with Moses, returned to the Church. Afterwards he was expelled to Centumcellae, where he received death in glory.

Lucius: three years, eight months, ten days. He lived in the times of Gallus and Volusianus, until the consulship of Valerian III and Gallienus II. He was in exile, and afterwards, by God’s will, returned unharmed to the Church. He died on 5 March [III Nones of March], in the consulship mentioned above.

Stephen: four years, two months, twenty-one days. He lived in the times of Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Volusianus and Maximinus to that of Valerian III and Gallienus II.

Sixtus: two years, eleven months, six days. He began with the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio and continued to that of Tuscus and Bassus; and he suffered martyrdom on 6 August [VIII Ides of August]. . . . . . . . . . from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus until the twelfth day before the Kalends of August [21 July], in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus.

Dionysius: eight years, two months, four days. He lived in the time of Gallienus, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August [22 July], in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, to the seventh day before the Kalends of January [26 December], in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus.

Felix: five years, eleven months, twenty-five days. He lived in the times of Claudius and Aurelian, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus to the consulship of Aurelian II and Capitolinus.

Eutychianus: eight years, eleven months, three days. He lived in the time of Aurelian III and Marcellinus, until 10 December [IV Ides of December], in the consulship of Carus II and Carinus.

Gaius: twelve years, four months, seven days. He lived in the times of Carus and Carinus, from 17 December [XVI Kalends of January], in the consulship of Carus II and Carinus, until 22 April [X Kalends of May], in the consulship of Diocletian VI and Constantius II.

Marcellinus: eight years, [Col. 0454] three months, twenty-five days. He lived in the times of Diocletian and Maximian, from 30 June [the day before the Kalends of July], in the consulship of Diocletian VI and Constantius II, to the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII. At that time there was a persecution, and the episcopate ceased for seven years [Note: [Col. 0454] Papebroch reads: “four years, six months, twenty-five days”], six months, twenty-five days.

Marcellus: one year, six months, twenty days. He lived in the time of Maxentius, from the consulship of Maximian Herculius X and Maximian Galerius VII until after their tenth and seventh consulships.

Eusebius: four months, sixteen days, from 18 April [XIV Kalends of May] until 17 August [XVI Kalends of September].

Miltiades: three years, six months, eight days, from 2 July [the sixth day before the Nones of July], from the sole eighth consulship of Maximian—which was in September—in that of Volusianus and Rufinus, until 11 January [III Ides of January], in the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus.

Sylvester: twenty-one years, eleven months. He lived in the time of Constantine, from the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus, from 31 January [the day before the Kalends of February], until 31 December [the day before the Kalends of January], in the consulship of Constantine and Albinus.

Marcus: eight months, twenty days. He lived in the time of Constantine, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus, from 18 January [XV Kalends of February] until 7 October [the Nones of October], in the consulship mentioned above.

Julius: fifteen years, one month, eleven days. He lived in the time of Constantine, from 6 February [VIII Ides of February], in the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, until 12 April [the day before the Ides of April], in the consulship of Constantius V and Constantius Caesar. He constructed many buildings: a basilica on the Portuensian Way at the third milestone; a basilica on the Flaminian Way at the second milestone, called that of Valentinus; the Julian Basilica, in Region VII beside the Forum of the Deified Trajan; a basilica across the Tiber, in Region XIV, beside Callistus; and a basilica on the Aurelian Way, at the third milestone, at Galistus.

Liberius lived in the time of Constantius, from 22 May [XI Kalends of June] until . . . , in the consulship of Constantius V and Constantius Caesar.

[Col. 0453]

## FRENCH DISSERTATION: ON THE DATE, AUTHOR, AND AUTHORITY OF THE PRECEDING CATALOGUE

[Col. 0453] Having set this catalogue before the reader, the learned Benedictines add the following:

[Col. 0454] Such is the Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs known by the name of the Catalogue of Liberius. Before establishing its authority, we must first examine the period at which it was composed and the author to whom it may be possible to attribute it.

Of all the scholars who have concerned themselves with this monument, we know only Dodwell who wished to make it later than the time of Liberius; and he was refuted by Tillemont himself. Without speaking of the argument naturally furnished by the coincidence in date between this monument and the four other small works that accompany it in the various manuscripts—a circumstance which by itself is sufficient to determine its date—since there is nothing in the text of the catalogue that contradicts this antiquity, does not this chronicle indisputably bear the date of its composition in these final lines: “Liberius [Col. 0455B] lived in the time of Constantius, from 22 May [XI Kalends of June] until . . . , in the consulship of Constantius V and Caesar”?

“This ending,” as Tillemont says, “is much less suitable to a copyist interrupted by some accident than to an author who knew the beginning of Liberius’s pontificate but did not know its end because it had not yet occurred.” [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Memoirs on Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, Notes on St Clement, p. 551.]

But there is another argument still more irresistible. Besides the catalogue of the Popes called that of Liberius, there is another, composed in the sixth century and ending with Felix IV. Now this second catalogue, which Dodwell would have us regard as the older one, while that of Liberius would merely be its abridgement [Note: [Col. 0455D] *On the Primitive Succession of the Roman Pontiffs*, ch. XV, p. 224], itself inserts word for word the consular lists established in the first for the years [Col. 0455C] of each Pope; and, when it reaches the time of Liberius, it ceases to give them, supplies nothing in their place, and resumes them only more than a century after the point at which the Liberian Chronicle ends. Why, unless because the monument it was transcribing went no further than the fifth consulship of Constantius and the consulship of Constantius Caesar? What can this monument be, then, if not the one under present discussion? It is therefore earlier than the Chronicle of Felix IV, and it alone can explain that chronicle’s strange gap. Pearson did not hesitate to make this observation [Note: [Col. 0455D] *On the Succession of the First Bishops of Rome*, ch. XII, p. 130]; and Tillemont, almost as severe in his examination of Catholic traditions, judiciously observes that Dodwell’s conjectures, which make [Col. 0455D] the Catalogue of Liberius a mere abridgement of sixth-century monuments, are overturned by the experience of critics, who, he says, have always observed that works of this kind tend rather to increase [Col. 0456A] than to diminish, as experience shows. [Note: [Col. 0455D] Tillemont, *ibid.*, vol. II, p. 551.]

The question of the author of the Catalogue of Liberius is far less easy to clarify. Henschenius claimed that the first part of the Chronicle, extending from Saint Peter to Saint Urban, had been written by Saint Anteros, and the rest as far as Liberius by Saint Damasus. Papebroch, in his *Chronico-Historical Essay on the Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs*, went even further, seeking to prove that the second part of this Catalogue bears traces of four different hands. Schelstrate vigorously attacks this system [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Ecclesiastical Antiquities Illustrated*, vol. I, dissertation 3, ch. 2, nos. 6, 7, 8, 9], which also seems to us to give far too much to conjecture. Yet, although we are inclined to follow this author when he shows that the compilers of this Catalogue cannot precisely be named [Col. 0456B] or arbitrarily multiplied without the risk of proceeding somewhat at random, his arguments for proving unity of style in every part of this Chronicle seem far from conclusive. On close inspection, it is difficult not to perceive great diversity of form in its several parts; but might this not be explained by regarding the monument as an assemblage, a compilation, of notes or memoranda written at various times? Nothing resembles a series of inscriptions recorded one after another more closely than this Catalogue, which possesses unity only in the idea governing its arrangement as a chronicle.

[Col. 0456C] Who, then, was the editor or compiler of this whole? Tillemont and Pagi would readily attribute the honour to Saint Damasus, and we ourselves are strongly inclined to take that position. Yet we do not rest our opinion upon the two famous letters, one attributed to this holy Pope and the other to Saint Jerome, which have divided scholars who judged them. Today they seem abandoned by everyone; nevertheless, in our judgment, the arguments adduced in their favour by Ciampini in his *Examination of the Liber Pontificalis* are far from negligible. Be that as it may, we refrain from citing them in this discussion, contenting ourselves [Col. 0456D] with placing them in a note before the reader so as to omit nothing that may make our work on the origins of the Papacy more complete. [Note: [Col. 0455D] **Jerome to the Most Blessed Pope Damasus.** Our humility entreats the glory of Your Holiness that, in accordance with the authority of the Apostolic See, which we know to be governed through Your Holiness, you may deign briefly to set forth for us in sequence the acts and deeds from the primacy of the blessed Apostle Peter down to your own times—that is, those performed in your See—so that our humility, being informed, may recognize which bishops of the aforesaid See deserved to be crowned by martyrdom, or whether any may be known to have transgressed against the canons of the Apostles. Pray for us, Most Blessed Pope. (See above, col. 441, the reply of Saint Damasus.)]

[Col. 0457A] If, therefore, we attribute the composition of the Catalogue of Liberius to Saint Damasus, it is not on the faith of these two letters, but on the testimony of numerous authors who, from approximately the seventh or eighth century onward, have never ceased to regard this Pope as the author of a Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs. Since we cannot make Saint Damasus the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, or even of the Catalogue of Felix IV—monuments whose style is too different from his—we are essentially led to assign the Chronicle of Liberius to him. Here again, though by a wholly different route, we meet Tillemont, who says in the passage cited above: “I do not see why it is said that this catalogue is falsely attributed to Saint Damasus, or why he could not have compiled it, being a deacon in 353, when [Col. 0457B] Pope Liberius was banished; and the catalogue appears to have been made in the year 354, under Pope Liberius.” [Note: [Col. 0457D] P. 550.]

In vain does Dom Ceillier object that, in Saint Jerome’s notice of Saint Damasus’s writings, he does not name this Catalogue [Note: [Col. 0458D] *History of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. VI, p. 477]. For this Catalogue, which moreover appears to have been composed only for a local purpose, is not properly a book; and it is natural to suppose that it did not reach the East, where Saint Jerome wrote, when one sees that even in the West it did not begin to receive attention until the sixteenth century. Dom Ceillier’s other difficulty—that Saint Damasus did not place his name upon this small work, as he placed it on almost all his epigrams and inscriptions—is no more serious. First, that is already to admit that he did not affix it [Col. 0457C] to everything that came from his pen. Further, how could Saint Damasus have thought of placing his name at the head of a Chronicle which is nothing more than the compilation, in two pages, of a sequence of notes and inscriptions? We may conclude, therefore, that the opinion which makes this holy Pope the author of the Chronicle of Liberius rests on solid foundations. A far more serious question—the truth of the facts contained in this catalogue—now demands our entire attention.

The facts contained in the Catalogue of Liberius are simply the consular lists corresponding to the accession and death of each Pope; the reckoning of the years, months, and days of his [Col. 0457D] pontificate; and finally a few historical particulars, small in number and very succinct, as has been noted above. We shall examine in succession the degree of authority to be accorded to these various details. Let us begin with the consular lists.

Once the antiquity of the Catalogue of Liberius has been established, it seems evident to us that genuine authority must be recognized in the indications of consuls that it contains, unless two things can be demonstrated: first, that the Christians of Rome—who, as cannot be doubted from [Col. 0458A] all that we have established in preceding chapters, preserved the names of their bishops—did not use consular lists to mark the years of their episcopates; and secondly, that, if they did so, it would have been impossible in 354 to collect the records of this sort compiled by them during the first three centuries. We defy anyone whatsoever to offer the slightest proof in support of these two assertions; yet they would have to be demonstrated before the authority of the Catalogue of Liberius could be attacked with regard to the truth of its consular calculations. Meanwhile, we hope to prove that the two contrary propositions are certain.

First, the Christians of Rome used consular lists to count the years of the Popes. Our readers cannot be unaware that throughout [Col. 0458B] the Roman Empire, the most customary and most national manner of measuring time and classifying historical events was by the consuls. This practice was not only employed for matters concerning public order; circumstances of private life were also subject to it. Contracts between private persons—everything, even the most familiar details of household life—received this authentication just as much as the acts of governing authority themselves. Laws and custom jointly established this practice; and perhaps it was observed all the more willingly because, while it offered a means of recalling facts less abstract than calculation by numbers, it gratified private pride by associating, in some fashion, the events of one’s existence with the destinies of the Empire.

Christianity found this practice established when it appeared in the world. Since it contained nothing contrary to its dogmas or its morality, the first believers, accustomed to use it in civil life to give authority to their acts, naturally had to transfer it, with all its advantages, to religious calculations. What, indeed, could have been more important or more worthy of remembrance for them than the succession and years of Saint Peter’s successors, in whom that apostle continued always to teach and govern the Church? Was there a subject [Col. 0458D] more capable of stirring that sense of national identity which a society experiences ever more strongly in proportion to the degree of spiritualism it professes, than the desire to preserve pure and certain annals of those Pontiffs—so humble, so obscure, yet guardians of an authority whose effects, as several examples in Eusebius show, resounded to the farthest ends of the East, and whose power, though buried beneath the vaults of subterranean Rome, rose in the third century sufficiently as a rival to the Caesars that a Decius feared it equally with [Col. 0459A] a competitor for the Empire? [Note: [Col. 0459D] “That Cornelius sat fearless at Rome in the priestly chair, at a time when the tyrant, hostile to God’s priests, uttered threats lawful and unlawful; when he would have heard far more patiently and tolerably that a rival emperor was being raised against him than that God’s priest was being appointed at Rome.” (Cyprian, *Letter to Antonianus*, Rigalt edition, 1666, p. 68.)] Let us not doubt it: Christians did for the preservation of the memory of the Church’s leaders what they did every day in their domestic affairs; and even if the last traces of it had now been erased, let us not be so ignorant of human nature as to believe that the first Christians allowed so much glory—glory so pure—to pass without doing anything to preserve its remembrance.

Will it be said that this way of reckoning by consuls seemed to them too profane, too secular, even contrary to the austere dignity of a religion which took notice of the particulars of present life only to despise them? To this we reply [Col. 0459B] that, far from being so, Christianity made it almost a duty for them to employ this mode of calculation. No one, surely, is ignorant of the supreme reverence which the first believers had for Holy Scripture, or of the zeal with which they reproduced its spirit and circumstances in their habits and language. Not only did the ceremonies of worship take their origin from it, but the usages of private life were, as it were, permeated by it: they thought and expressed themselves only through these divine books. Its style and images adorned the writings of Tertullian and Origen, while its sayings strengthened the already sublime replies of the martyrs. Yet these books themselves, wholly heavenly and supernatural, [Col. 0459C] did not disdain to use, in reckoning divine events, the mode employed for earthly calculations. They proceeded with the aid of the annals of humankind as by the light of a torch; and the word of God, in a sense, borrowed factual certainty from the events of this mortal abode.

To recall only a few examples: open first the Old Testament at the prophecies—those wholly spiritual phenomena of the first infusion of the divine Word by the Holy Spirit into humanity—and you will find the fleeting years of earthly kings attached, as a necessary seal, to the oracles of eternal Wisdom. Let us select from a thousand examples: “The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.” [Note: [Col. 0459D] Isaiah 1:1.] Further on: “In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated upon a throne,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0459D] *Ibid.*, 6:1.] “The words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth, in the [Col. 0460A] land of Benjamin. The word of the Lord came to him in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.” [Note: [Col. 0459D] Jeremiah 1:1.] “The word which came to Jeremiah concerning the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, which was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.” [Note: [Col. 0460D] *Ibid.*, 25:1.] “In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0460D] Daniel 7:1.] “In the third year of the reign of Belshazzar.” [Note: [Col. 0460D] *Ibid.*, 8:1.] “In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, of the race of the Medes, who ruled over the empire of the Chaldeans,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0460D] *Ibid.*, 9:1.] “In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, the word was revealed to Daniel,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0460D] *Ibid.*, 10:1.] This is surely enough; we may dispense with citing the Minor Prophets, who furnish a much greater number of examples [Col. 0460B] of this feature. Let us pass to the New Testament.

“In the days of Herod, king of Judaea, there was a priest named Zachariah,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0460D] Luke 1:5.] Thus Saint Luke begins the account of Gospel history. In the following chapter: “In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus for a census of the whole world. This census was made while Quirinius was governor of Syria.” [Note: [Col. 0460D] *Ibid.*, 2:1.] Saint Matthew, speaking of the arrival of the Magi: “When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 0460D] Matthew 2:1.] Saint Luke, wishing to announce the preaching of Saint John, the solemn prelude to Christ’s, likewise fixes its date by that of the rulers of the time: “In the fifteenth year of the reign [Col. 0460C] of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, Philip his brother tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John son of Zachariah in the wilderness,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0460D] Luke 3:1.]

This is certainly more than was needed to justify the first Christians in their own eyes when they used consular lists to establish the years of the Roman Pontiffs. And lest these observations be thought the fruit of systematic research, more ingenious than conclusive, we cannot resist the desire to cite here the following passage of Saint Ambrose, who saw the matter from the same point of view and comments as follows on one of the texts just cited: “The census of which Saint Luke speaks took place while Quirinius was governor of Syria, as though the Evangelist intended to place upon his book, [Col. 0461A] like a seal, a kind of consular indication. For if consuls are entered upon deeds of purchase, how much more ought a date to be entered for the redemption of all? Here you have everything customarily included in contracts: ordinarily one puts in them the name of the person exercising supreme authority, the day, the place, the cause, and witnesses. Christ likewise employed these marks to authenticate his nativity and generation according to the flesh—he who said to his apostles: ‘You shall be witnesses to me in Jerusalem.’” [Note: [Col. 0461D] “This first registration was made under the presidency of Quirinius, so that the Evangelist seems to have inscribed him in this book, as it were, as a consul for the sake of an identifying sign. For if consuls are entered upon deeds of purchase, how much more ought a date to have been entered for the redemption of all? You have, therefore, everything customarily found in contracts: the designation of the one exercising supreme authority; the day, place, cause, and witnesses, whom people are also accustomed to employ. Christ also employed these to attest his nativity and generation according to the flesh, saying: [Col. 0462D] ‘You shall be witnesses to me in Jerusalem.’” (Ambrose, *On Luke*, ch. 2.)]

There is, therefore, no reason to be surprised that the first believers transferred to religious facts a mode of calculation which the genius of the [Col. 0461B] sacred books rendered holy for them, while the customs of the time left no other at their disposal. Thus is explained this passage of Tertullian, in *On the Soldier’s Crown*: “The populace also is crowned, now in exultation over the prosperity of rulers, now by reason of the particular observances of municipal festivals; and luxury is the seducer of every public rejoicing. But you are a stranger in this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. ‘Our commonwealth,’ he says, ‘is in heaven.’ You have your own registers, your own annals.” [Note: [Col. 0462D] “The populace also receives crowns, now in rejoicing over the prosperity of rulers, now because of the special character of municipal solemnities; and luxury is the ensnaring attraction of every public joy. But you are a stranger to this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. ‘Our commonwealth,’ he says, ‘is in heaven.’ You have your own registers, your own annals.” (Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, Rigalt edition, p. 109.)]

Having shown that the existence of Christian annals during the first three centuries is entirely natural, we shall have no difficulty [Col. 0461C] in showing that, in 354, one could still read those which the Christians of Rome had composed concerning the years of the Popes. Only one reason could have made this impossible: all such records would have had to perish before that time. But this supposition is inadmissible. Undoubtedly, the persecutions—especially the last—destroyed a great number of monuments. Yet the small number remaining to us, which must necessarily have been still larger in the fourth century, suffices to prove that not all had perished. We shall strengthen these otherwise unassailable conjectures by facts.

Let us take, for example, the Acts of the Martyrs, monuments so important in the practices of the primitive Church, on which Christians would naturally inscribe the consuls in order to establish the date of the glorious confession. Everyone knows that the greater part of these precious Acts has been lost. Yet our assertion is so certain that [Col. 0462A] a single glance at the remnants that remain will suffice to show even the least discerning that, in the age of Liberius, it was possible far more readily to determine, by the light of the consular record, the ecclesiastical acts of the preceding three centuries. We shall not cite here the Acts of Martyrs judged authentic by the Bollandists in their immense compilation, nor those in the various collections later than Dom Ruinart’s. Let us simply pause at his collection, as the most widely circulated, and read there what, in the fourth century, could have been read even more readily in so many monuments which time, the negligence of those who ought better to have preserved them, and the ravages of the barbarians have caused to disappear from the earth. Let us take at random from the *Acta sincera* of that learned and highly impartial Benedictine.

In the year of Jesus Christ 107, the Acts of Saint Ignatius of Antioch: “These things occurred on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [20 December], Syrius and Senecio II presiding at Rome.” In the year 200, the proconsular Acts of the Scillitan martyrs: “In those days, under the twice-consul Claudianus, on 17 July [XVI Kalends of August].” In the year 250, the martyrdom of Saint Pionius: “These things took place under the proconsul Julius Proclus and Quintilianus the consul, under the Emperor Gaius Messius Quintus Trajan Decius and Vettius Gratus; and, as the Romans say, on 12 March [IIII Ides of March], and, as the Asians say, in the sixth month, on the Sabbath day, at the tenth hour.” In the year 258, the proconsular Acts of Saint Cyprian: “In the fourth consulship of the Emperor Valerian and the [Col. 0462C] third of Gallienus, on the third day before the Kalends of September [30 August],” etc. In the year 259, the Acts of the holy martyrs Fructuosus, Augurius, and Eulogius: “Under the Emperors Valerian and Gallienus, Aemilianus and Bassus being consuls, on 16 January [XVII Kalends of February], the Lord’s Day,” etc. In the year 285, the Acts of the holy martyrs Claudius and Asterius: “This martyrdom took place in the city of Aegaea, under Lysias the governor, on 23 August [X Kalends of September], Augustus and Aristobulus being consuls,” etc. In the year 295, the Acts of Saint Maximilian: “Tuscus and Anulinus being consuls, on 12 March [IV Ides of March], at Theveste,” etc. In the year 303, the Acts of Saint Felix, bishop: “Diocletian eight times and Maximian seven times consuls, being Augusti,” etc. In the year 304, the Acts of Saints Agape, Chionia, Irene, etc.: “In the ninth consulship of Diocletian Augustus and the [Col. 0462D] eighth of Maximian Augustus, on the Kalends of April,” etc. In the same year, the Acts of Saint Euplus, deacon: “Diocletian nine times and Maximian eight times being consuls, on the day before the Ides of August, in the city of the Catanenses,” etc.

We shall stop here. But we wished [Col. 0463A] to put the reader in a position to judge for himself that the most exacting criticism cannot reject the consular chronology of the Catalogue of Liberius merely because this little work was composed only in the fourth century. Now, the Catalogue of Liberius does not confine itself to indicating the consuls corresponding to the accession and death of the Roman Pontiffs; it also gives the years, months, and days of their episcopates. Let us now examine the certainty of these particulars.

Having observed to the reader that these assignments of years, months, and days must have been more exposed to scribal errors through the centuries than the consular lists themselves—and that we consequently do not mean to vouch for every figure with which the Catalogue of Liberius is filled—we say that there is nothing less surprising in itself than the preservation at Rome, in the fourth century, of these chronological details. Have not historical monuments, as Dodwell himself admitted [Note: [Col. 0463D] *On the Primitive Succession of the Roman Pontiffs*, ch. XV, p. 225], preserved, despite the distance of time, the years, months, and days of emperors? To do the same in a chronicle of the Popes, whose years were already fixed by the consuls, did such great efforts need to be made? And when the voluminous writings of Clement of Alexandria and Origen passed safe and sound through such disastrous storms, was it so impracticable to preserve the page on which had been written the years, days, and months during which approximately thirty [Col. 0463C] bishops held office—especially when the contents of that page were so widely familiar that, for that very reason, they could not be lost?

For the facts here again support what might be called our conjectures, and this is how. Is it not true that, if we can prove that Christians naturally knew the day of death of most of the early Popes, they could thereby readily calculate not only the years of their pontificates, already indicated by the consuls, but even, in a certain way, the months and days, independently of the records which the Church must have preserved concerning all these matters? Now this is something no one with the slightest acquaintance with ecclesiastical antiquity can doubt. [Col. 0463D] From the beginning of Christianity, the day of saints’ death was consecrated by a feast in their honour under the beautiful name of birth, *natalis*, retained in the Roman liturgy. Thus, as early as the year 107, the circular letter sent from Rome to announce the confession of Saint Ignatius of Antioch said to the Churches: “We have informed you of the day and the time, so that, gathering at the anniversary of his martyrdom, we [Col. 0464A] may share in the commemoration of this noble athlete and martyr of Christ.” [Note: “And we have indicated to you the day and the time, that, assembling at the time of his martyrdom, we may share in the commemoration of the athlete and noble martyr of Christ.”]

Such was the apostolic tradition. When the Roman Church sent a message to the other Churches to notify them of the sublime death of its Pontiff [Note: “Already news had come from the city concerning the good and peaceable shepherd, and therefore most blessed martyr” (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, no. XIV).], it never forgot at the same time to transmit, for registration, the day on which the sacrifice had been offered. “You shall know,” Saint Cyprian writes to Successus, one of the bishops of his province, “you shall know that Sixtus was put to death in the cemetery, on the eighth day before the Ides of August.” [Note: “Know that Xystus was executed in the cemetery, on the eighth day before the Ides of August” (Cyprian, *To Successus*, ed. Rigalt, p. 160).]

At Rome, therefore, by means of the records and commemorations of the martyrs, the precise day on which each Pope ended his course was preserved. Here it is appropriate to place before the reader [Col. 0464B] the famous ecclesiastical calendar of the Roman Church. Also drawn up about the year 354, it formed part of the four short works which Cuspinian and Father Boucher found in the same manuscript beside the Catalogue of Liberius. There one may see the anniversaries of the various martyrs whose feasts Christian Rome celebrated in the fourth century; inspection of this monument will do much to demonstrate the truth of our assertions. We give this calendar not from Dom Ruinart, who merely reproduced Father Boucher’s reading, but from Father Conrad Janning, who published it in 1717 [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. VII for June, p. 185.] without altering the original reading, as Father Boucher had done in some places.

## DEPOSITION OF BISHOPS

[Col. 0464C] Sixth day before the Kalends of January: Dionysius, in Callistus. Third day before the Kalends of January: Felix, in Callistus. The day before the Kalends of January: Silvester, in Priscilla. Fourth day before the Ides of January: Miltiades, in Callistus. Eighteenth day before the Kalends of February: Marcellinus, in Priscilla. [Note: One must read: “Seventeenth day before the Kalends of February: Marcellus, in Priscilla.”] Third day before the Nones of March: Lucius, in Callistus. Tenth day before the Kalends of May: Gaius, in Callistus. Fourth day before the Nones of August: Stephen, in Callistus. Sixth day before the Kalends of October: Eusebius, in Callistus. Sixth day before the Ides of December: Eutychianus, in Callistus. Nones of October: Marcus, in Balbina. The day before the Ides of April: Julius, on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, in Callistus.

## DEPOSITION OF MARTYRS

[Col. 0464D] Eighth day before the Kalends of January: Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judaea.

### IN THE MONTH OF JANUARY

Thirteenth day before the Kalends of February: Fabian, in Callistus; and Sebastian, in the Catacombs. Twelfth day before the Kalends of February: Agnes, on the Nomentan Way.

### IN THE MONTH OF FEBRUARY

Eighth day before the Kalends of March: the birthday feast of Peter’s Chair.

### IN THE MONTH OF MARCH

[Col. 0465A] Nones of March: Perpetua and Felicitas, in Africa.

### IN THE MONTH OF MAY

Fourteenth day before the Kalends of June: Parthenius and Calocerus, in Callistus, in the eighth consulships of Diocletian and Maximian.

### IN THE MONTH OF JUNE

Third day before the Kalends of July: Peter, in the Catacombs; and Paul, on the Ostian Way; in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.

### IN THE MONTH OF JULY

Sixth day before the Ides: Felix and Philip, in Priscilla; and, in the cemetery of the Jordani, Martialis, Vitalis, and Alexander; and, in that of Maximus, Silanus. This Silanus the martyr was stolen by the followers of Novatus [Note: Read: “Novatian.”]; and, in Praetextatus, Januarius. Third day before the Kalends of August: Abdon and Sennes, in Pontianus, which is at the Bear of Pilate.

### IN THE MONTH OF AUGUST

[Col. 0465B] Eighth day before the Ides of August: Xystus, in Callistus; and, in Praetextatus, Agapitus and Felicissimus. Seventh day before the Ides of August: Secundus, Carpoferus, Victorinus, and Severianus, at the Alban and Ostian [cemeteries]. Sixth [on the] *Ballistaria* [Note: Read: “Via Salaria.”]: Cyriacus, Largus, Crescentianus, Memmia, Julianetis, and Ixmaracdus. Fourth day before the Ides of August: Lawrence, on the Tiburtine Way. Ides of August: Hippolytus, on the Tiburtine Way; and Pontianus, in Callistus. [Col. 0466A] Eleventh day before the Kalends of September: Timothy, on the Ostian Way. Fifth day before the Kalends of September: Hermes, in Basilla, on the Old Salaria.

### IN THE MONTH OF SEPTEMBER

Nones of September: Acontius, at Porto, and Nonnius, Herculanus, and Taurinus. Fifth day before the Ides of September: Gorgonius, on the Labican Way. Third day before the Ides of September: Protus and Hyacinthus, in Basilla. Eighteenth day before the Kalends of October: Cyprian, in Africa; at Rome he is celebrated in Callistus. Tenth day before the Kalends of October: Basilla, on the Old Salaria; in the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian.

### IN THE MONTH OF OCTOBER

The day before the Ides of October: Callistus, on the Via Aurelia at the third milestone.

### IN THE MONTH OF NOVEMBER

Sixth day before the Ides of November: Clement, Sempronianus, Clavius [Note: Read: “Claudius.”], [Col. 0466B] Nitratus, in the retinue. Third day before the Kalends of December: Saturninus, in Traso.

### IN THE MONTH OF DECEMBER

Ides of December: Aristo, in Pontus.

The reader will thereby [Col. 0467A] be able to judge how, through comparing the calendars of the various Churches, it became easy to compile that famous martyrology of the Roman Church of which Saint Gregory the Great speaks to Eulogius, and in which he expressly says that the precise day upon which every martyr suffered was recorded. [Note: “We have in one codex the names of almost all the martyrs, their passions being distinguished according to their individual days . . . Yet the same volume does not state how each suffered, but only gives the name, place, and day of suffering” (*Register*, book VII, epistle 29).] Finally, all these details which we have been pleased to accumulate will have served abundantly to prove that one cannot, without rashness, claim that it was impossible in the fourth century to determine in detail the minor chronological circumstances of each pontificate. We shall now answer our Protestant adversaries.

The first objection, common to Dodwell [Note: Dodwell, *De Romanorum Pontificum primaeva successione*, ch. XV, p. 225.] and Pearson [Note: Pearson, *De successione primorum Romae episcoporum*, ch. IV, p. 17.], is that Saint Irenaeus and Saint [Col. 0467B] Epiphanius, who cited the succession of the Roman Pontiffs in their treatises against heretics, and Eusebius, Rufinus, Saint Prosper, and the other historians and chroniclers who included it in their narratives, did not specify the years, months, and days of the tenure of these bishops of Rome with the same detail as the Catalogue of Liberius. Nothing is easier to resolve than this difficulty. Why should the holy doctors Irenaeus and Epiphanius—along with whom one might also name Saint Optatus and Saint Augustine—have minutely cited to heretics the months and days of the Roman Pontiffs, when they needed only to show their succession in order to silence every innovator? As for the chroniclers, [Col. 0467C] who does not see that this multitude of details regarding months and days would have drawn them beyond the proper genre of their work, which consists solely in tracing the principal chronological outlines, not in probing such irrelevant particulars? Finally, even if the nature of the historical work undertaken by Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret had required them to enter into the minutiae which chronicle ought to neglect, what is surprising in their having been ignorant of them in the East, where they wrote, while Rome retained these domestic traditions with full certainty?

Pearson, who, like ourselves, has been struck by the argument that may be constructed in favour of the calculations of months and days in the Catalogue of Liberius from [Col. 0467D] consideration of the practices of the ancient Church, which carefully preserved the anniversary records [Col. 0468A] of martyrs, exerts every effort to escape the consequences that we draw from it. [Note: *Ibid.*, pp. 18, 19, and 20.] He regards, as we do, the Roman calendar we have just cited as a highly respectable and very important monument for the chronology of the Popes, since it contains the days of their depositions. But he makes an entirely gratuitous assertion when he claims that the author of the Catalogue of Liberius possessed no other records from which to draw up the count of the months and days assigned to the different Popes; and that, because this calendar, according to Pearson, contains the depositions of only twelve Popes, from Saint Lucius to Saint Julius, the compiler of the Catalogue must necessarily have drawn from his imagination the chronological circumstances which he attributed to the preceding pontificates [Col. 0468B].

We reply first that it is inaccurate to count only twelve depositions of bishops in the calendar, since, upon closer examination, it is easy to find four more under the heading “Deposition of Martyrs”: Saint Fabian, thirteenth day before the Kalends of February; Saint Sixtus, eighth day before the Ides of August; Saint Callistus, the day before the Ides of November; and Saint Clement, fifth day before the Ides of November. Thus there are sixteen in all, to which we should be entitled to add Saint Peter, whose day of martyrdom is marked on the third day before the Kalends of July. Now, because this precious calendar has come down to us, is it sensible to conclude that it was the sole indication which could have been found in the third century concerning the days of death of the thirty Popes who had sat [Col. 0468C] up to that time? And can that utterly gratuitous negative conjecture prevail over the weighty reasons by which we have sought to demonstrate to the reader’s common sense that a religious institution as strong and powerful as the Roman Church must, after three centuries of existence, have had documents somewhat more extensive and detailed than those which we are now able to register in two pages?

The author of the Catalogue of Liberius had the calendar in hand and used it to compose his chronicle, Pearson tells us. We might just as readily say that these two short works were composed simultaneously from earlier records; for the author of the Catalogue of Liberius could not have taken from the calendar the consular fasti [Col. 0468D] that he uses, since they were not in it; but, conversely, the author of the calendar might well [Col. 0469A] have compiled from the catalogue the death-dates of the sovereign Pontiffs. We do not, however, claim this as fact, but merely set one probability against an assertion lacking every shadow of plausibility.

But, Pearson further says, one may derive from the annals of the Roman See itself certain proof that all that is authentic in the papal fasti of the first three centuries is found in Father Boucher’s *Calendarium*. For the twelve bishops whose certain dates of deposition are given are later than Fabian, who established the notaries and founded, in the middle of the third century, the archives of the Roman Church, which it did not possess earlier. Since we shall establish in the following volume that the institution [Col. 0469B] of the notaries of the Apostolic See dates from the first century, not the third, and since we cannot enter upon that interesting discussion here, we shall confine ourselves to repeating what we have already had occasion to observe several times: namely, that notes concerning the names, years, months, and days of the bishops of Rome were not a work so considerable that one must imagine an official body of notaries occupied in producing it; that one cannot without absurdity suppose that the Roman Church, which even then played so great a role, as is evident from the Easter controversy, and which from the time of Saint Clement addressed such powerful letters to the other Churches, had passed through more than two centuries without even thinking of creating any kind of archive for [Col. 0469C] its own needs. On that supposition Saint Fabian, when called to govern it, would have found it silent concerning all its fruitful and yet glorious past—without recollections, writings, or monuments; in short, known to all the Churches, according to Saint Irenaeus, yet not knowing itself. Truly, the learned Anglican counts altogether too much upon his readers’ simplicity; and we cannot sufficiently wonder that the paradoxes of his work were not earlier refuted by Catholic authors.

Nevertheless, since no error lacks some pretext more or less well founded, we readily acknowledge that, from about the period of Saint Fabian—that is, from the middle of the [Col. 0469D] third century onward—the Catalogue of Liberius contains more definite detail, and dates less uncertain but more precise and circumstantial. It is apparent that greater care was taken from that period in compiling the records, and that the holy Pope’s improvements bore fruit in the archives of the Apostolic See. For his part, the author of the catalogue recorded the documents as he found them, in their more or less disparate form, without attempting to give his work that unity of tone which a forger would not have failed to seek. This brings us once again to our conclusion: [Col. 0470A] in assigning the years, months, and days of each Pope, his authority cannot but be very great, while his good faith remains fully beyond suspicion.

We have only a few words to say concerning the authenticity of the facts included, apart from chronological information, in the Catalogue of Liberius. First, they are very few.
