Under the pontificate of Saint Pius there is a notice concerning Hermas, the author of the book called the *Shepherd*, said to have been this Pope’s brother. This book is certainly by Hermas and still exists. The relationship of its author to Saint Pius is a question debated among scholars. Under Saint Pontian there are several lines stating that he was relegated to Sardinia and there martyred. [Col. 0470B] Nothing is less suspicious than this tradition, so simple and related with so little pretension. Of Saint Fabian it is said that he divided the regions among the deacons and had structures made in the cemeteries. We shall later prove the certainty of this information. What is said concerning Moses, Maximus, and Nicostratus, as well as Novatus and Novatian, is amply supported by Saint Cyprian’s letters. The facts alleged under Saint Cornelius may be verified from the same source. The notice of Saint Lucius’s exile and return likewise offers no matter for dispute. No one doubts the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian mentioned under Saint Marcellinus. Finally, nothing is easier to justify than the details included under [Col. 0470C] Saint Julius’s pontificate concerning construction of the basilicas which recognize him as their founder.

Here we conclude what we had to say concerning the Catalogue of Liberius. At the same time, we feel obliged to repeat that, though we present this monument as ancient and venerable, we are far from concealing its imperfections. Some must be attributed to copyists, others to the ravages of time; perhaps several arose from the inadequacy of the records, which in one circumstance or another the compiler sought to supplement with conjectures more or less successful. The assignment of consuls to certain pontificates is obviously faulty and several times introduces confusion [Col. 0470D] into the years. Besides the general explanations just given, we are rather drawn to Father Henschenius’s system. He conjectures that, because persons raised to the Papacy had sometimes been vicars of their predecessors for several years, as Saint Clement was of Saint Linus and Saint Cletus, the year of their episcopal ordination was confused with that of their accession to the Holy See; and no more than this was needed to generate a confusion rendered almost irremediable by the lapse of time. [Note: *Diatriba in Catalogum Romanorum Pontificum*, *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I.]

Likewise, by adopting moderately another idea of the learned [Col. 0471A] Jesuit—strongly contested by Father Pagi [Note: *Critica Annalium*, vol. I.] because false in its general application—we might explain some errors regarding days and months through a common mistake that would have taken the day of a particular Pope’s burial, entered in the calendar for one reason or another, for the day of his death. We otherwise leave these hypotheses [Col. 0472A] for what they are. But since we shall sometimes have to challenge and correct the Catalogue of Liberius in certain details, we owed the public this frank explanation. In our judgment it in no way diminishes the importance of this monument, one of the most authentic in all Christian antiquity.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 380–394. THEODOSIUS THE GREAT AND PACATUS

[Col. 0471]

Part One. CONTAINING PACATUS’S PANEGYRIC DELIVERED TO THEODOSIUS THE GREAT, IN PLACE OF A PREFACE TO THE WORKS OF THAT EMPEROR.

(From the *Panegyrici Veteres* of Jacques de la Baume.)

## INTRODUCTION TO THE PANEGYRIC

[Col. 0471B]

### § I. Chronological Index of the Deeds of Theodosius

**Year of the City 1098, of Christ 345; ninth year of Constantine’s reign.**

Flavius Theodosius the Elder, or the Great, was born in Spain—not of Theodore, as Aurelius Victor says, but of Theodosius as his father, and Thermantia as his mother. He was educated in the city of Cauca in the province of Gallaecia, according to Zosimus; or, according to Marcellinus, at Italica, the homeland of Trajan, from whom he traced his descent.

**Year of the City 1119, of Christ 366; third year of the reign of the Augusti Valentinian and Valens; Theodosius aged 21.**

While still a young man, he had in his father illustrious examples of military valour. For that father crushed the Franks and Saxons along the Rhine and Waal in Batavia, and at [Col. 0471C] Boulogne.

**Year of the City 1120, of Christ 367; fourth year of the reign of the Augusti Valentinian and Valens; first of Gratian; Theodosius aged 22.**

Theodosius’s father, sent with an army to Britain, pacified the whole island over four years and suppressed the tyrant Valentinus. Ammianus indicates that Theodosius served under his father in both wars, when he says that Maximus, before he suppressed the tyranny in Britain, had been a fellow-soldier in Britain of the Emperor Theodosius.

**Year of the City 1123, of Christ 370; seventh year of the reign of the Augusti Valentinian and Valens; fourth of Gratian; Theodosius aged 25.**

After pacifying Britain, Theodosius’s father returned to Constantinople.

**Year of the City 1125, of Christ 372; ninth year of the reign of the Augusti Valentinian and Valens; sixth of Gratian; Theodosius aged 27.**

[Col. 0471D] While his father, then Master of the Horse, attacked the Alamanni, scattered in fear, through Raetia, killing some and carrying others off into Italy, he himself, being commander of Moesia, renewed the war against the Quadi which had been undertaken with an unfortunate outcome, [Col. 0472B] and checked the Sarmatians (*Ammianus*, book XXVIII).

**Year of the City 1126, of Christ 373; tenth year of Valentinian and Valens; seventh of Gratian; Theodosius aged 28.**

Theodosius’s father compelled Firmus, tyrant of Africa, to surrender, and drove him, when he rebelled again, to the noose (*Ammianus*). The same man was put to a most unjust death at Carthage in Africa by Valens after receiving baptism, because, when Valens was investigating by magical arts who would succeed him, the first letters of that person’s name had been disclosed: THEOD. Theodore, indeed, because he presumed upon the empire on account of the similarity of his name, paid the just penalty of criminal ambition. Theodosius’s son, already highly renowned for military valour, was sought out to suffer the same fate, but secured his safety by flight.

**Year of the City 1132, of Christ 379; thirteenth year of Gratian; fifth of the younger Valentinian; Theodosius aged 34.**

[Col. 0472C] Seeing that the Empire was being most grievously harassed by Germans and Goths, Gratian summoned Theodosius from his native Italica, where, after his father’s death, he had withdrawn to escape Valens’s ferocity, and made him his partner in the Empire at Sirmium (a city of Illyricum), on the fourteenth—or, according to Socrates, the seventeenth—day before the Kalends of February. Gratian immediately departed for the West and defeated the Alamanni. Charge of the East was entrusted to Theodosius. He drove from Thrace, with great slaughter, the Goths, Scythians, Taifali, and Huns, who had joined forces against him; after taking hostages from them, he secured peace and returned to Gratian. (Sozomen, Hydatius, Prosper, Theodoret.)

**Year of the City 1133, of Christ 380; fourteenth year of Gratian; sixth of the younger Valentinian; second year of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 35.**

[Col. 0472D] Theodosius, consul for the first time, was seized at Thessalonica with a severe illness; he was baptized by Acholius, the most holy bishop of that city, and immediately recovered. He decreed, on the third day before the Kalends of March, that no one should profess any faith [Col. 0473A] except that which Damasus, Bishop of Rome, and Peter of Alexandria had prescribed to the faithful as received from Saint Peter. Through Gratian’s agency—because, as Socrates says, Theodosius was ill—peace with the Goths was established on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. Theodosius expelled the Cynic philosopher Maximus—who presided over the church of Constantinople—from that church; much has been said of him in the Life of Julian (Gregory Nazianzen). Entering Constantinople on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, he took the churches from the Arians. He installed Gregory Nazianzen in the church on the sixth day before the Kalends of December. (Socrates, Hydatius, Count Marcellinus.)

**Year of the City 1134, of Christ 381; fifteenth year of Gratian; seventh of the younger Valentinian; third year of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 36.**

Theodosius received Athanaric, king of the Goths, driven out by his own people and imploring his aid at Constantinople, with great honour on the third day before the Ides of January; when he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, he honoured him with wholly royal funeral rites. Won over by this magnificence of Theodosius, the Goths refrained from incursions. (Hydatius, Zosimus, Prosper, Count Marcellinus.) In the same year the second ecumenical synod was held at Constantinople, where 150 bishops issued a decree against Macedonius concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, together with the Creed.

Theodosius received with royal magnificence, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, the body of Valentinian the Great, who had died of apoplexy in Gaul near Bergentio while answering the envoys of the Quadi in the year of Christ 375. Meanwhile, [Col. 0473C] Clemens Maximus (for Severus calls him thus), a Briton by origin, seized tyranny in Britain; he established the imperial seat at Trier and made Victor, his son, partner in the Empire. (Zosimus, Socrates, Aurelius Victor.)

**Year of the City 1136, of Christ 383; seventeenth year of Gratian; ninth of Valentinian; fifth year of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 38.**

Theodosius made his son Arcadius Augustus on the seventeenth—or, as Socrates says, the fourteenth—day before the Kalends of February. Arsenius, a man distinguished no less by uprightness of character than by learning, was sent by Pope Damasus to Constantinople to direct him. When the tyrant Maximus attacked Gratian, weakened by German wars, and deceitfully put him to death at Lyons through Andragathius on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, Maximus was admitted by [Col. 0473D] Valentinian into partnership in the Empire, though from necessity. Theodosius gave no definite answer to Maximus’s envoys seeking the same from him, lest that same Maximus should also plot against the younger Valentinian before he could, having gathered troops, defend the boy emperor’s youth by arms. The tyrant, suspecting this, prepared a numerous army, although he had made a treaty with Valentinian, and was coming to Milan, where Valentinian was residing. Valentinian fled with his mother Justina and the prefect Probus to Thessalonica, intending to seek Theodosius’s aid. Martinus had foretold Maximus that, if he came into Italy against Valentinian, he would indeed be victorious in the first onset, but would perish shortly afterward—as in fact occurred.

**Year of the City 1137, of Christ 384; tenth year of Valentinian; sixth of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 39.**

[Col. 0474A] Theodosius willingly granted peace to the Persian envoys sent to him at Constantinople to request it, all the more because he was considering war against Maximus. Therefore, leaving his son Arcadius at Constantinople with the title Augustus, he met Valentinian at Thessalonica. Meanwhile Honorius was born to him by his wife Placilla, as Hydatius and Marcellinus say, on the fifth day before the Ides of September. Themistius delivered his sixth panegyric oration to Theodosius. Ambrose was again sent as envoy to Maximus to reclaim Gratian’s body.

**Year of the City 1138, of Christ 385; second consulship of Valentinian; seventh year of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 40.**

Theodosius granted the consulship to Arcadius Augustus.

**Year of the City 1139, of Christ 386; twelfth year of Valentinian; eighth of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 41.**

[Col. 0474B] He made Honorius both Caesar and consul; he himself, triumphing together with Arcadius, entered Constantinople on the fourth day before the Ides of October, as Hydatius, Marcellinus, and Zosimus report. There, after the death of his former wife Placilla, he married Galla Placidia, daughter of the elder Valentinian and Justina, on the condition, Zosimus says, that he should promptly carry out the expedition against Maximus which he had already planned and often promised. He kept his promises; and immediately sent Justina with her son Valentinian and her daughter Galla by ship to Rome.

**Year of the City 1140, of Christ 387; thirteenth year of Valentinian; ninth of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 42.**

Theodosius, together with his son Arcadius, as Hydatius says, celebrated his fifth-anniversary festivities [Col. 0474C] with indictions and games. About this time, Maximus, according to Marcellinus, suddenly invaded Italy, where he had heard that Valentinian had arrived with his mother and sister. Struck by fear, Valentinian again fled to Theodosius at Thessalonica. Maximus vainly attempted to lay ambushes for him on the way there.

**Year of the City 1141, of Christ 388; fourteenth year of Valentinian; tenth of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 43.**

When Theodosius, consul for the second time, was preparing for war against Maximus, he imposed upon the Antiochenes a new kind of tax. Enraged, they pulled down Placilla’s statue and dragged it about in mockery. Deeply moved by this outrage, Theodosius had already sent soldiers to exact punishment, but was appeased by the embassy of Flavian, the holy and prudent bishop of the Antiochenes. [Col. 0474D] Meanwhile Maximus, after devastating all Italy except the city of Milan—which the holiness and exertions of its bishop Ambrose preserved—was planning to advance on Rome. Therefore Theodosius, moved by the prayers of the saints, especially John the Anchorite and Senuphius, marched to Aquileia. There, as Socrates says, he utterly destroyed Maximus’s army on the sixth day before the Kalends of September. Maximus was captured and led away from Theodosius’s sight; enraged soldiers stripped him of the royal insignia and killed him at the third milestone from Aquileia, on the Kalends of August. Victor, Maximus’s son, was killed not long afterward in Gaul by Count Arbogastes (Zosimus). Andragathius, his commander, who held the Ionian Strait with a great fleet, on hearing of Maximus’s death threw himself headlong into the sea.

**Year of the City 1142, of Christ 389; fifteenth year of Valentinian; eleventh of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 44.**

[Col. 0475A] Leaving Milan, Theodosius entered as victor with Valentinian and his own very young son Honorius, whom for this purpose he had summoned to himself from Constantinople, on the Ides of June. Of his own accord he restored to Valentinian not only Italy, which the latter had held, but also all the Gauls, Spains, and Britains, which Valentinian himself had never held, but only his father and grandfather. Here Latinus Pacatus delivered his panegyric to the victorious Theodosius. But Justina, Valentinian’s mother, was forestalled by death, so that she did not recover the kingdom with her son. (Prosper of Pithou, Sozomen.)

**Year of the City 1143, of Christ 390; sixteenth year of Valentinian; twelfth of Theodosius’s reign; Theodosius aged 45.**
[Col. 0475B] The Thessalonians kill Botheric, commander of the troops in Illyricum. The emperor was so inflamed by this that he ordered the populace, having been invited to the circus games, to be slaughtered indiscriminately—some seven thousand persons—by soldiers admitted for that purpose into the theatre. Sozomen alone says that this occurred after Eugenius had been slain. However that may be, Theodosius expiated the public penalty imposed by him in a remarkable example of piety (Rufinus, Theodoret, Paulinus in the *Life of St Ambrose*, Prosper). Galla, Theodosius’ wife, is driven out by her stepson Arcadius (Marcellinus).

Year of the City 1144, of Christ 391; Valentinian’s 17th, Theodosius’ 13th year as emperor, age 46.

Theodosius, having excellently arranged all other matters, left the government of the city to Valentinian. Then he set out with his son [Col. 0475C] Honorius for Constantinople, and arrived there in the consulship of the same men, Tatianus and Symmachus, on the fourth day before the Ides of November [10 November] (Socrates).

Year of the City 1145, of Christ 392; Valentinian’s 18th, Theodosius’ 14th year as emperor, age 47.

When Valentinian had been killed at Vienne in Gaul by Count Arbogast: Arbogast, a man of Frankish descent, had been ordered by the Emperor Gratian to occupy the position next below that of the general Bauto, the most powerful man of his time. After Bauto’s removal from human affairs, relying on his own ability, Arbogast had, without the emperor’s authority, claimed military command for himself. In his court he had Eugenius, the master of a school of letters, commended and entrusted to him by Richomer. Eugenius’ supreme learning, joined with equal uprightness of life and elegance of character, had won him great authority [Col. 0475D] in Gaul. Therefore, wishing to remove from himself the odium of his usurped tyranny, and at the same time to administer the empire himself under Eugenius’ name, Arbogast proclaims this man Augustus in the West.

Year of the City 1146, of Christ 393; Theodosius’ 15th year as emperor, age 48.

Theodosius, consul for the third time, set out against the tyrant Eugenius. Having first reconciled the divine power to himself by prayers and fasts, and having left Arcadius at Constantinople—and also, if we believe Socrates, Honorius, whom, as Socrates himself says, he had declared Augustus in the Hebdomon on the fourth day before the Ides of January [10 January], or, as all others maintain, on the second day before the Kalends of December [30 November]—he enters the Alps with a very numerous army from beyond the Danube, [Col. 0476A] over whom he had set Gainas and Saul.

Year of the City 1147, of Christ 394; Theodosius’ 16th year as emperor, age 49.

In the first battle, fought at the beginning of September, Theodosius lost ten thousand of his men. Thus, says Rufinus, God permitted it, not that Theodosius might be defeated, but lest he should seem to conquer through barbarians. But during the night, while Theodosius lay prostrate at prayer, two Apostles assured him of the victory which John the Anchorite and Theodosius had previously foretold to him. Accordingly, battle being joined on the following morning on the bank of the river called the Frigidus, near Aquileia, a sudden and unusually violent wind arose. It shook shields from the hands of the enemy, snatched away their bucklers, and drove their missiles back into their own faces. [Col. 0476B] Then came the incredible terror and slaughter of Eugenius’ party, who pierced themselves with their own arrows. Eugenius was captured; stripped of the imperial insignia, and though he begged most humbly for his life, he was put to death. Arbogast, despairing of his cause, fled and two days after the battle struck himself down with his own hand (Orosius).

Year of the City 1148, of Christ 395; Theodosius’ 17th year as emperor, age 50.

Theodosius returned from Aquileia, where he had remained for some time after Eugenius’ death, to Milan. There he received Arcadius and Honorius, summoned to him from Constantinople, in the church, and commended them, having entrusted them, to Ambrose. Some maintain that Honorius alone was summoned, that he was brought to Theodosius by Serena, Stilicho’s wife and Theodosius’ niece through his brother, and that he was entrusted to Stilicho’s guardianship. When these arrangements had been made, Theodosius died during the night of the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February [16 January], from dropsy, after having himself attended the circus games that morning. He was not, as Socrates maintains, in the sixtieth year of his age, but in his fiftieth, and in the seventeenth year of his reign (Victor, Prosper, Marcellinus). [Col. 0476C] His body was carried to Constantinople with great pomp and buried there.

No other emperor undertook more wars, or more difficult ones, more bravely; none completed them more swiftly or more gloriously. One may therefore doubt whether he was braver or more fortunate. He conquered not for himself but for others: both the defender of oppressed kings and most energetic and upright. He was a man whose mind could encompass all things, and who, as his very name indicated, seemed to have been granted by some divine gift for the good and peace of the whole world. Moreover, he was conspicuous for the piety of [Col. 0476D] Christian religion; never brutalized by his continual experience of war; obliging toward all; inferior to no emperor, had moderation in anger been added to his other virtues.

## § II. On the author and year of this panegyric

The author of this speech is Latinus Pacatus Drepanius—not an Italian or a Sicilian, as some foolishly suppose, but a Gaul by nationality, as is clear from panegyric §24: “Whence, then, shall I begin,” says Pacatus, “unless from your misfortunes, my Gaul?” His native place was Bordeaux, as Elias Vinetus observes in his notes on Ausonius, from panegyric §2, where Pacatus calls himself Transalpine and says that he comes “from Gaul’s furthest retreat, where the shore receives the setting [Col. 0477A] sun into Ocean, and, where lands fail, mingles with its companion element.” Furthermore, he had an intimate friendship with Ausonius of Bordeaux, who calls him proconsul in more than one place and dedicates to him several small works: the *Epigrams*, the *Game of the Wise*, the *Technopaegnion*, and the *Grammaticomastix*. In *Idyll* 7 he calls him an outstanding poet. Nevertheless, the same Elias Vinetus doubts, in his edition of Ausonius, whether he was the same man as the author of extant psalms, several hymns, and other poems, including an elegiac letter to the bishop of Autun.

Our own Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, however, in his illustrated edition of Paulinus, denies that this Pacatus was the same as the man who, writing to Uranius, promised to compose the *Life of St Paulinus* in verse-bound prose. He says that the latter Pacatus was forty-three [Col. 0477B] years younger than ours, and is the man to whom Symmachus sends Letter 12 of Book VIII and Letters 58 and 69 of Book IX.

This panegyric was delivered in the year of Christ 391, according to Haloander’s calculations, on the Kalends of September [1 September], as Count Marcellinus records; at Rome, to which Pacatus had been sent from Gaul to offer congratulations on the victory over the tyrant Maximus; in the presence of the emperor, whom he seems to address face to face; and before the Senate, as he himself says at the opening of this panegyric.

## § III. Synopsis of the panegyric

**Exordium.**—Though many things give him apprehension as he is about to speak, Pacatus says that he is especially troubled because he, a Gaul, must speak at Rome before the emperor and before the Senate. Nevertheless, he approaches the praise of Theodosius: both because he has come to Rome for this purpose across a great distance, and because no necessity compels him to praise the prince.

**Division.**—The arrangement appears to be this: I. The private life of Theodosius; II. his public life is praised.

**First part.**—Theodosius is associated by Gratian with the imperial power in the most difficult times, so that he may support the state as it falls headlong toward ruin (§2). That no one else ought to have been chosen is shown by his country (§4), his father’s victories and the splendour of his house (§5), the excellence of his appearance (§6), and an age sound and ripe for empire (§7). From the gifts of fortune Pacatus passes to the endowments of the mind: military experience, by which Theodosius was already as a boy being formed for empire (§8); his splendid achievements in war (§10); his modesty in declining the imperial office (§11); [Col. 0477D] his economy in administering it and reducing palace expenses; his foresight in enacting laws (§13); his discernment in selecting those to whom he entrusted secrets and whom he advanced to magistracies (§15); his outstanding fidelity to friends (§16); his conscientiousness in fulfilling promises (§17); and his exceptional kindness toward those whose ambition he could not satisfy because of the limited number of offices (§20).

**Second part.**—On his public virtues. How good and civil he is in admitting all persons to his presence and hearing their complaints (§21). His face is no less familiar to enemies than to citizens. His victories over Goths, Huns, Saracens, Scythians, Albanians, and Persians are mentioned (§22). He advances with his army into the farthest part of Gaul against Maximus, the tyrant of Gaul, swollen by the defection of many legions (§23) and by five years’ impunity; after murdering Gratian, Maximus rages in Gaul through slaughter, plunder, and every kind of cruelty (§24). It was not without divine assistance that this tyrant violated the treaty, however concluded, with Theodosius (§30); that he could not withstand Theodosius’ arrival (§31); that he was routed and utterly destroyed at the river Ascia (§32); and that Marcellinus’ army was likewise overthrown (§35). Theodosius spares the life of a man throwing down his arms (§36). He enters Emona as victor, amid what a concourse of peoples (§37). Maximus, uncertain where to flee, shuts himself up in Aquileia (§38). Theodosius rushes there with his army at astonishing speed (§39). Every virtue of the emperor contributes to this triumph; above all, his good fortune, by which Maximus did not escape the shameful death deserved by his crime through voluntary death [Col. 0478C]; by which, stripped of royal insignia, he was led captive to Theodosius’ feet (§43); and by which he was immediately removed from the emperor’s sight and killed without his knowledge (§44), to stand for posterity as an example of tyranny avenged. The victor’s supreme clemency is praised (§45), unlike that of Cinna, Sulla, Marius, and Caesar (§46). Theodosius’ entrance into the City follows. The laws wisely restored by him are discussed (§47).

**Conclusion.**—Finally, Pacatus congratulates himself that he has come from Gaul to Rome and will be a witness of such great events: with what eagerness he is to be welcomed by his fellow citizens when he recounts what he has seen there; with what a crowd of listeners he is to be surrounded; and how many subjects for writing he will supply to poets and orators.

# THE PANEGYRIC OF PACATUS BEGINS

[Col. 0477]

[Col. 0477D] **I.** If ever there has been anyone, most august Emperor, who would rightly have trembled before speaking in your presence—

> **Note: [Col. 0477D] “Would have trembled before.”** In the Pithoean manuscript it reads *iure trepidaverit*, “would rightly have trembled”; in the Bertinian, *in re trepidaverit*, “would have trembled in the matter”; in others, *ore trepidaverit*, “would have trembled in speech.”

—I surely feel that I am that man; and I see that this may appear so to those who share your counsels.

> **Note: [Col. 0477D] “Those who share your counsels.”**

For although you have always had to be praised above all former princes, now indeed, praised beyond the measure in which you have formerly been celebrated, you must be honoured by speech in that City whose liberty you have defended under arms and whose dignity you have increased in the gown.

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] “Now, since in addition to the praises by which you were formerly celebrated, you must be praised in that City,” etc.**

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] “Under arms.”** That is, after the tyrant Maximus had been defeated and killed. “In the gown,” that is, by most wise laws.

How, then, can my speech attain to the majesty of you both, especially at this moment, when you have mutually grown so greatly that you have never yet been greater, nor Rome happier?

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] “Both.”** Rome and Theodosius.

To this is added the Senate as my audience. Since, because of the love with which it is endowed toward you, it is difficult for it to hear enough concerning you, it is still more difficult, because of its native and inherited power of speech, for this rough and uncultivated harshness of Transalpine language not to be tiresome—

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] Because of the inborn eloquence received from their ancestors, it is more difficult for the unpolished and imperfect speech of a man born beyond the Alps not to be tedious, and indeed to seem harsh.**

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] “And inherited.”** In some copies: “and indeed inherited.”

—particularly when it may seem absurd and ill-judged boastfulness to display eloquence before men from whose fountain a late transmission has carried it down even to our use.

[Col. 0479B] 

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] “This indeed torments me so much that,” etc.**

As I reflect on these things, I am so troubled that I think not only those whom I see are present today, but that Catos themselves, Ciceros, Hortensii, and all those orators stand beside and before me as I speak—those who hear me in their descendants.

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] “In their descendants.”** As though, reviving today in their descendants, they were personally present before this speech of mine. [Col. 0479D]

Thus surrounded by manifold fear, as though what I see were not enough to make me afraid, I see what I have to fear.

> **Note: [Col. 0479D] “I see what I have to fear.”** The words “I see,” absent from the Putean edition, were judged necessary from Livineius and Balduin. The sense is: as though the things before his eyes—the Senate and the emperor—did not inspire enough fear, other causes of fear also occur to him, namely his thought of the ancient orators, whom he thinks he sees before him.

**II.** What then? Has a new terror and unforeseen trembling seized me at the very moment of speaking?

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] “A sudden fear has seized me.”**

But all these agitations, which toss me from both sides, have long been considered and foreseen.

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] “From both sides.”**

Yet when, in admiration of your virtues, I had hastened from Gaul’s furthest retreat—

> **Note: [Col. 0479D] “From Gaul’s furthest retreat.”** From Aquitaine, where we have said Pacatus was born and from which he was sent to Rome.

—where the shore of Ocean receives the setting sun, and where lands fail the companion element mingles with them—

> **Note: [Col. 0480C] “And Ocean encircles the extremities of the lands, to see you,” etc.**

—to behold and reverence you, so that I might enjoy with my eyes the blessings which I had received through my ears, I feared, I confess, that I might spoil by silence the service owed for so great a journey. [Col. 0480A]

> **Note: [Col. 0480C] Thus, while I excuse my boldness in the name of duty.**

Thus, while I interpret boldness as obedience, while I think that joy and silence do not suit the same man, I have joined two utterly different things: fear and rashness. Moreover, this too urged me to speak: no one compelled me to speak.

> **Note: [Col. 0479D] “For not.”** He refers to Pliny, *Panegyric* §2: “Therefore let those utterances depart which fear extorted,” etc.

For no longer does compulsory praise, nor words squeezed out by fear, redeem the danger of silence.

> **Note: [Col. 0480C] “Which lies in silence.”**

Let that sad necessity of servile eloquence have existed and passed away—

> **Note: [Col. 0479D] “Of enslaved eloquence.”** Eloquence flattering in a slavish fashion.

—when deceitful flattery tickled a savage master, greedily seeking every breath of public applause with windy popularity;

> **Note: [Col. 0480C] When wicked flatterers fawned upon a fierce emperor hunting public applause through empty ambition.

> **Note: [Col. 0479D] “A savage master.”** He alludes to the times of the Neros and Domitians.

—when men gave thanks in sorrow, and an accusation against tyranny was called failure to praise the tyrant. Now there is equal freedom to speak and to be silent; and, as it is easy to praise the prince, so it is safe to have kept silent concerning the prince. [Col. 0480B] Therefore I delight in testing by speech the security restored to us by right of return; I delight, I say, because no emperor is more fittingly praised than he whom it is least necessary to praise.

> **Note: [Col. 0480C] “Than him whom no necessity of praise presses upon.”**

**III.** Therefore, let that day—the herald of public happiness—which first inaugurated you into empire, be the beginning of this discourse concerning you.

> **Note: [Col. 0480C] “Therefore, concerning you.”** Pulmannus reads: “Let him therefore give me the beginning of this speech,” etc. Antonius Sconhovius likewise reads this from an old manuscript.

> **Note: [Col. 0480C] “The day which first…”** The day on which Theodosius was first associated by Gratian with the imperial power was the fourteenth, or according to Socrates the seventeenth, day before the Kalends of February [19 or 16 January] in the year of Christ 379. [Col. 0480D]

For as, when engaged in divine rites, we turn our faces toward that region of heaven from which light begins, so, as I am about to fulfil vows of words formerly pronounced, I shall seize in my speech that moment at which Roman light began.

> **Note: [Col. 0480D] “We turn our faces.”** It was formerly the custom alike of pagans and Christians to offer prayers while turned toward the rising sun. Tertullian, in his *Apology to the Nations*, says of Christians: “There is a suspicion that we worship the sun, because it has become known that we pray toward the eastern region; but many also, out of an inclination to worship heavenly things, move their lips toward sunrise.”

The commonwealth lay sick from innumerable evils—or rather, I should say, lifeless—while barbarian nations had poured over the Roman name like a flood.

> **Note: [Col. 0480D] “The lifeless commonwealth.”** It had been most grievously afflicted by Germans, Goths, and Scythians.

But I shall refrain from unfolding the causes and wounding a people now at peace.

> **Note: [Col. 0480D] “But I shall refrain.”** That is, I shall abstain from investigating the causes of so many evils. Below, §6: “I shall refrain from probing the heavenly mystery.”

> **Note: [Col. 0480D] “A people now at peace.”** Others read *placatum ulcus*, “a wound now healed,” so that he says he does not wish to reopen that wound of empire now healed.

For remembrance of calamities is in itself enduring, and I fear to darken this present brightness of joy by recalling sorrowful things. [Col. 0480C–0481A]

> **Note: [Col. 0480C] I fear that by remembering unhappy events I may diminish the sense of this present joy.

I shall therefore do what I have often seen physicians distinguished in knowledge do: after the scars of deep wounds have closed by sound healing, I shall touch them with a hesitant hand, content to ask whether they still feel pain; and I shall ask all individually and collectively whether, since it was clear to everyone that our exhausted affairs needed healing by placing at the public helm some such man as would protect the youth of one emperor and assist the labour of another, we could have wished for a prince of this kind.

> **Note: [Col. 0481C] “Of one emperor.”** Valentinian the Younger, who, after his father died at Brigetio in Gaul, was himself created emperor there while still only four years old. Epitome of Victor.

> **Note: [Col. 0481C] “Of another.”** Gratian, who, being unable by himself to drive the Goths, Taifali, the most savage of all the Huns, and the Alans from Thrace and Dacia, summoned Theodosius from Spain as his colleague in empire.

Let us therefore suppose the entire matter still undecided, and imagine that in some assembly of the world the question is being asked who ought to undertake so great a burden and assume the tottering destinies of the Roman state. Would not that man be chosen by the votes of all humankind, tribe by tribe and century by century,

> **Note: [Col. 0481C] “Tribe by tribe and century by century.”** Hence some assemblies were called centuriate, others tribal, others curiate.

—whose country was prosperous, whose house illustrious, whose appearance godlike, whose age sound, and who had acquired experience in military and civil affairs?

> **Note: [Col. 0481C] “Whose country was prosperous.”** Here you have the summary of the entire speech.

**IV.** Let us therefore pursue all these points in the order proposed from the beginning. It will surely then be established that the man declared prince was one who both ought to have been chosen by all and from among all. For first, Spain is your mother-country—

> **Note: [Col. 0481C] “Spain is your mother-country.”** In his Life we have said that Theodosius was Spanish by descent.

—a land more fortunate than every other land, upon whose cultivation—indeed, whose enrichment—the supreme Maker of all things has bestowed more generously than upon other nations. It is exposed neither to southern heats nor subjected to northern frosts, but is cherished by the temperate mean of both poles. Bounded on this side by the Pyrenees, on that by the tides of Ocean, and elsewhere by the shores of the Tyrrhenian Sea, it is enclosed, as though another world, by the contrivance of provident nature.

> **Note: [Col. 0481C] “The Pyrenean mountains.”** These are the boundaries of Spain. Spain is divided from Gaul by the Pyrenees; by Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea it is surrounded on three sides like a peninsula.

Add its many outstanding cities; add all its cultivated and uncultivated places, full either of crops or flocks; [Col. 0482A] add the riches of its gold-bearing rivers; add its mines of glittering gems. I know that poets’ fables, devised to charm the ears, have assigned certain marvels to various nations; even if these be true, they are each single marvels.

> **Note: [Col. 0481C] “Even if they be true.”** That is, even if they were true; as in Horace, *Epodes*, Book I, Ode 1: “Not, though she be present, to bring more aid to those who are present.” I refrain from citing further examples of this kind lest I become endless. [Col. 0481D]

Nor do I now examine their truth. Let Gargara, as it is written, rejoice in its abundant wheat harvest:

> **Note: [Col. 0481D] “Gargara.”** A summit of Mount Ida; also a town at the foot of the same mountain, near Ilium and close to Pergamum, where there is a plain of extraordinary fertility.  
> “Gargara themselves marvel at their own harvests.” Virgil, *Georgics* I.103.

let Mevania be famed for its cattle;

> **Note: [Col. 0481D] “Mevania.”** A city of Umbria on the river Clitumnus and the Flaminian Way, the native place of Propertius, rich in pasture; Lucan therefore calls it “bull-bearing” in Book I:  
> “There is one who, where Mevania spreads across her bull-bearing plains,” etc.

let Campania be valued for Mount Gaurus;

> **Note: [Col. 0481D] “Campania.”** A region of Italy extending between the river Anio and the Tiber, beside the Mediterranean Sea; part of ancient Latium.

> **Note: [Col. 0481D] “Mount Gaurus.”** A mountain of Campania near Puteoli.

let Lydia be praised for the river Pactolus—

> **Note: [Col. 0482C] “Lydia.”** A region of Asia Minor, bounded by Ionia to the west, Greater Phrygia to east and north, and Lycia to the south.

> **Note: [Col. 0482C] “Pactolus.”** A river of Lydia, famous for its golden sands.

—provided that whatever is praised anywhere may rise up in Spain alone. This country produces the toughest soldiers, the most experienced commanders, the most eloquent orators, and the most illustrious poets; it is mother of judges and of emperors.

> **Note: [Col. 0482C] “The most experienced commanders.”** For example Viriathus, a most energetic commander, who defeated in various battles C. Laelius the praetor, Q. Fabius Maximus Aemilianus the proconsul, and his brother Servilianus the consul, sent against him; at last, however, he was treacherously killed in the year of the City 614 by Q. Servilius Caepio, after the latter had bribed Viriathus’ envoys.

> **Note: [Col. 0482C] “Orators.”** Quintilian and both Senecas.

> **Note: [Col. 0482C] “The most illustrious poets.”** Lucan of Corduba; Martial, born at Bilbilis, a not undistinguished town of Celtiberia; and Seneca, author of the tragedies.

It sent into empire that Trajan, and afterwards Hadrian; to it the empire owes you. Let the Cretan land yield, proud of the cradle of its lesser Jupiter;

> **Note: [Col. 0482C] “The Cretan land.”** An island not far from the Peloponnese, renowned for the birth of Jupiter—today Candia.

let Delos yield, crept upon by two divinities;

> **Note: [Col. 0482D] “Delos.”** An island in the Aegean Sea, to which Latona came with her children Diana and Apollo.

and let Thebes, famous for its foster-child Hercules, yield.

> **Note: [Col. 0482D] “Thebes.”** The chief city of Boeotia on the river Ismenus, the native place of Pindar.

We do not know whether faith should be placed in what we have heard; Spain has given us a god whom we see. [Col. 0482B]

**V.** It would have been a fitting compensation if, having said little in praise of your country, I might linger more fully in praising at least your father’s virtues.

> **Note: [Col. 0482D] “Your father.”** This was Theodosius, not Theodorus, as Victor thinks.

But what shall I do? Abundance brings me a new kind of difficulty. What, I ask, shall I do? Shall I begin with what the Rhine or the Waal saw? At once the Danube, bloodied by the slaughter of Sarmatians, will place itself before me.

> **Note: [Col. 0482D] “The Rhine or the Waal.”** This touches on Zosimus, Book IV: the barbarians beyond the Rhine, while Julian was alive, were content if no one troubled them; when Julian’s death was announced, they immediately left their settlements and made war. Against them Theodosius was sent by Valentinian in the year 366; he freed Batavia from Franks and Saxon pirates. Ammianus, Books XXVII–XXIX.

> **Note: [Col. 0482D] “By Sarmatian slaughter.”** The same Theodosius crushed the Sarmatians on the Danube; scattered the Scots laying Britain waste, entering London as victor; and overcame the Moors. Ammianus, Book XXVII.

Shall I recount Batavia worn down in infantry battles? The Saxon, exhausted by naval wars, will come forward. Shall I speak of the Scot driven back to his marshes? Every Alamannian thrust into trackless wilderness, and each of the two Moorish peoples, will meet me. Since this crowd obstructs selection, it is better, in the case of so great a man, [Col. 0483A] to state his deeds in summary than diminish them by enumeration.

Let it suffice to say that he alone was divinely raised up as a man in whom all the virtues flourished together which are praised separately in all others. Or if, in his age, that custom had survived by which Roman commanders took an adopted title from the names of conquered peoples—the Macedonian, the Cretan, the Numantine—

> **Note: [Col. 0483C] “Macedonian.”** Philip, father of Alexander the Great, king of the Macedonians.

> **Note: [Col. 0483C] “Cretan.”** For example Metellus, called Creticus after conquering Crete in the year of the City 687. See Florus, Book III, chapter 7, on the Cretan war.

> **Note: [Col. 0483C] “Numantine.”** Namely Scipio, called Aemilianus or the Younger Africanus, son of Paullus Aemilius and adopted by Scipio Africanus, who was called Numantinus after destroying Numantia in the year of the City 621.

—would not fewer surnames now be read in the archives of annals than in the titles of your house? For he himself would be called Saxonicus, Sarmaticus, and Alamannicus; and one family would display as many triumphs as the entire commonwealth possesses enemies.

**VI.** But why is it necessary to send careful curiosity into the past?

> **Note: [Col. 0483C] But why is there any need to investigate more carefully and curiously what is past?

Let us judge your father, Emperor, by you. Nor is the inference difficult. For since two things make illustrious commanders—supreme virtue and supreme good fortune—it is obvious what virtue belonged to the man who taught you, and what fortune belonged to the man who begot you. [Col. 0483B]

> **Note: [Col. 0483C] “Who taught you.”** That is, the father who trained you in the art of war. [Col. 0483D]

O nobility worthy of an emperor: that a prince should be the son of one who ought himself to have been prince, who could have matched this summit of Roman greatness not merely in courage and wisdom but also in beauty of body and dignity! Like this venerable appearance of yours, equal to your fortune—how far and wide it is seen, how it commends your empire! So that it is wholly uncertain whether your virtue more deeply commends you to our minds or your face to our eyes.

Nor is it without reason, according to the opinion of philosophers who have more subtly examined the forces of natural causes and devoted noble inquiry to the secrets of heaven, that every most august appearance is believed [Col. 0484A] to derive very much from heaven.

> **Note: [Col. 0483C] It is not rashly believed, according to the opinion of philosophers who investigate the causes of natural things more carefully and explore heavenly mysteries with great care, that every most excellent form derives its origin from heaven.

Whether that divine soul, destined to enter a body, first measures out a lodging worthy of itself;

> **Note: [Col. 0483D] “Measures out a lodging.”** He refers to a very similar passage of Eumenius, *Thanksgiving Speech*, §17: “Nature herself measures out dwellings of bodies worthy of great minds.” It is known, moreover, that Ethiopians and Indians, when choosing a king, were accustomed first to observe that the man placed above others in governing them should excel in distinguished and lofty bodily stature. Aristotle, *Politics* VII.

or whether, once it has entered, it shapes its dwelling in accordance with its own character; or whether each grows out of the other, and, when they have joined as equals, both become greater—I shall refrain from probing the heavenly mystery. Let that secret, Emperor, lie open to you alone, with God as your companion.

> **Note: [Col. 0483D] “With God as your companion.”** With that genius who presides over your counsels. The ancients believed that each person—and especially emperors—had his own attendant genius.

I shall say what it is lawful for a human being to understand and say: such ought to be the man whom nations worship, to whom private and public vows are paid throughout the world, from whom the sailor asks fair weather, the traveller a return, and the soldier an auspice.

**VII.** For some time now, as I see, you have disdained this praise; but allow me to place among the parts of your praise those things which used to be praised as the sole merits of others.

> **Note: [Col. 0483D] “Allow me to place these among the parts of your praise.”** I follow Fr. Balduin’s correction, since the Putean edition reads: “but allow it to be placed among the parts of your praises which used to be praised alone in others.” This cannot be accepted unless *solebat* is read for *solebant*.

Your virtue deserved empire, but your appearance added its vote to virtue. The former ensured that you ought to become prince; the latter, that it was fitting for you to become one. Do we really suppose that anything was overlooked when your imperial appointment was made, when we see that account was taken even of your years?

> **Note: [Col. 0484C] “Years.”** Theodosius was in his thirty-fifth year when he was made Augustus.

Our ancestors took such care in this matter that, not only in attaining the highest magistracies, but also in seeking praetorships or aedileships, the age of candidates was considered; and no man, however powerful through birth, influence, or money, occupied offices prematurely before the years prescribed by the electoral law.

> **Note: [Col. 0484C] “In the highest magistracies.”** In the consulship.

> **Note: [Col. 0484C] “By the electoral law.”** He means the *lex annalis*, by which L. Villius, tribune of the plebs, fixed the ages at which each magistracy might be sought and held. From it the family received the surname Annales, as they were called. Livy, Book XL, chapter 43. Although this had in fact been determined long before, as may easily be inferred from Livy himself and other writers, Villius may be said either to have renewed the law or established it by a new edict so that it might be observed more strictly. Cicero often boasts that he attained every magistracy *suo anno*, that is, at the age fixed by law. He went to Sicily as quaestor at age thirty-one, was curule aedile at thirty-seven, praetor at forty, and finally consul at forty-three. The same Cicero, *Philippics* V.48, says that Alexander died at thirty-three, “an age,” he says, “which is ten years below the consular age under our laws.” [Col. 0484D]

And rightly so. For even those who are to be adopted into virtue still stagger, though they do not fall, upon that slippery ground of youth.

> **Note: [Col. 0484C] “Those whom virtue is to make her own.”

> **Note: [Col. 0484C] “Although they do not fall into crime.”

Did not luxury claim for herself, for some while, the most famous men of the Roman name—I mean Sullas, Catuli, [Col. 0485A] Scipios?

> **Note: [Col. 0484D] “Sullas, Catos, Scipios.”** Cicero refers to these in his speech *For Caelius*, §28: “Indeed, I have both seen and heard of many men in this state who not merely tasted this manner of life with the tips of their lips, or touched it, as the saying is, with their fingertips, but devoted their whole youth to pleasures, yet afterwards emerged and, as the saying goes, returned to sound fruitfulness, becoming serious and illustrious men.” Valerius Maximus discusses them more fully in Book VI, chapter 9.

Though changed winds carried them back, bettered, to harbour, still the storm of vices tossed them for a long time, and age only with difficulty recovered them, shipwrecked and drifting, from the errors in which they were being sunk. Therefore all things fitted well, and, besides the innumerable other qualifications which suited you, your years too added their vote—years which alone, as a perfected good in a human being, possess the advantages of two ages: the vigour of the young and the maturity of the old.

> **Note: [Col. 0485C] “Age too was suitable: it alone is perfected in a human being.”

Perhaps you ought to have entered upon empire earlier, so that you might rule longer; but provision will be made, without setting a precedent, that you lose nothing.

> **Note: [Col. 0485C] “Without danger of precedent.”** Without allowing anyone to hope for the same.

What you lost in the past must be made good by a longer life. It matters little when that begins which will have no end.

VIII. Thus far, Emperor, let the gifts of fate be celebrated in you; now let us proceed to those which you owe to yourself. For that former glory of yours in warfare, won through so many trials of hardship, is not to be ascribed to Fortune. Indeed, one may even be angry with her on this account: that she never treated indulgently the man whom she had destined for sceptre and throne.

> [Note: Never indulgently. After his father had been executed by order of the emperor, Theodosius was compelled to flee to Spain in order to escape danger; there he lay concealed until he was recalled to imperial power. He was also tested by other adverse turns of fortune, so that Ambrose could rightly say of him in his funeral oration: “Theodosius bore a heavy yoke from youth, when those who had killed his father, though a triumphant general, plotted against his safety.”]

But as stern fathers are harsher toward those sons whom they love more, so she trained you through very many wars and through the Republic’s most difficult times, while preparing you for empire. Yet before I come to those deeds which you performed when mature in years,

> [Note: Mature in years. *Aeneid* V.73: “Acestes, mature in years”; and IX.246: “Alethes, mature in spirit.”]

I shall briefly touch upon that fellowship in the camp which you shared with your divine father: winters passed beneath hides, summers sweated out amid wars, days and nights consumed in fighting or watchfulness, and the hardest battles fought by land and sea.

> [Note: Harsher.]

Scipio Africanus did not endure the first elements of military service under his father Paulus with such patience; nor did Hannibal, as a boy, enter the Spanish tents with an equal natural disposition; nor did Alexander, not yet “the Great,” fill the Macedonian camp with a surer hope of future virtues.

> [Note: Africanus. Scipio the younger, Aemilianus, son of Paulus, campaigned under his father in Spain in the year 603 A.U.C.]

> [Note: Hannibal. Son of Hamilcar, when nine years old was brought by his father to the altars and swore perpetual hatred toward the Romans. Thereafter he was a companion and soldier in the camp. See A. Victor for further details.]

Though antiquity, that magnifier of truth, may have endowed them with abundant praise, it has bestowed no greater flattery upon them than to proclaim that at such an age they followed the camps of kings or commanders—the camps in which you performed so many brave deeds that not only Alexander, Scipio, or Hannibal would have wished to see them while learning, but their parents and instructors would have wished to perform them while teaching.

IX. How hidden have Fortune’s counsels always been!

> [Note: How concealed!]

Who, I ask, would then not have thought that your withdrawal from military service into retirement was hostile to the public interest?

> [Note: Your withdrawal. I understand this of the time when Theodosius, immediately after his parent’s death, withdrew to Spain, where he lived privately for almost a full year, until Gratian recalled him from there to partnership in the empire.]

Yet she, carefully adorning the future emperor, wished you for a little while to be a private man, so that, since you already possessed military accomplishments in full measure, you might acquire experience of civil life during leisure.

> [Note: Carefully adorning the future emperor.]

> [Note: *Comens.* Or perhaps *conans* (“endeavouring”), as Barthius wishes in *Adversaria*, book XXIV, chapter 2.]

But I put your leisure before other men’s business. For pleasant shores and retreats arranged according to the changing seasons did not possess you; rather, whether you gave your time to estates or towns, you increased alike your substance and your reputation.

> [Note: According to varying seasons.]

In towns, indeed, you won men of every age and rank by one benefit or another; you aided the advantages of friends and the affairs of absentees by diligence, counsel, and material assistance.

> [Note: You bound them to yourself.]

And if it pleased you to exchange towns for the countryside, how, forgetful of urban life, did you play the farmer!

> [Note: To exchange towns for the countryside. Horace, book I, ode 17: “Swift Faunus often exchanges pleasant Lucretilis for Lycaeus,” etc.]

I hear also, Emperor—and believe—that you often imposed tasks of labour upon yourself and, lest you contract bodily torpor, scrubbed away through work of this kind the rust of idleness, which always lies in wait.

> [Note: To have undertaken some labour.]

Thus the rustic Curiuses, thus the ancient Coruncaniuses, thus the venerable names of the Fabricii, when truces had suspended wars, lived among their ploughs; and lest virtue grow weak through rest, these triumphant men, having laid their laurels in the lap of Capitoline Jupiter, farmed their land.

> [Note: Curiuses. Understand Marcus Curius Dentatus, who, after subduing the Samnites, Sabines, and Lucanians in various wars, retired to the country to live as a private citizen.]

> [Note: Coruncaniuses. He was the first man of plebeian origin made pontiff by the Romans. Sent as ambassador to Teuta, queen of the Illyrians, he was killed contrary to all law and right. Pliny, book XXXIV, chapter 6, reports that the Roman people dedicated a statue to him. Cicero, *For the House*, and Livy praise his self-restraint.]

> [Note: Fabricii. The abstinence of the Fabricii has been mentioned above. See also Cicero, *Cato* and *For Roscius of Ameria*; Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 8; Columella, book I, preface; Seneca, *Consolation to Helvia*; Valerius.]

> [Note: That virtue might not be weakened by inactivity.]

Hence we have received the tradition that the fasces were given to men while sowing, and that palm-decorated robes were sent out into the countryside along with their curule chairs: that consular farmers, shepherds in the trabea (official robe), and dictators among their herds were arrayed in the insignia of office.

> [Note: Palm-decorated robes. The *vestis palmata*, or triumphal robe, was so called because triumphant generals—or at least those who had won the palm—customarily wore it. Hence Sidonius in his panegyric: “After the palm comes the palm-decorated robe.” It seems also to have belonged to the consul; for Ausonius in a panegyric says: “The palm-decorated garment belongs in peace to the consul, as in victory to the triumphant general.”]

> [Note: Arrayed. Clothed in the insignia of consuls. Perhaps one should read *quaesitos*, as Claudian, *On the Consulship of Mallius Theodorus*, verse 9:
>
> “A consul sought amid the ploughs.”]

But narrow family means drove those men to labour: their suburban gardens, the steep Janiculum, and acres restricted by the city boundary had to be turned with ploughshare or hoe. Nor was it unjust that the work should return to the masters, since there was no one to whom they could give orders.

> [Note: Janiculum. A hill overlooking the region beyond the Tiber, named from Janus. Ancus Martius added it to Rome and decided that it should be joined to the city not only by a wall but also by the pile bridge, then for the first time laid across the Tiber.]

> [Note: Nor without reason. Since they lacked persons to whom they could entrust the care of cultivating their fields, they themselves necessarily had to undertake this labour.]

Need detracts from the praise of endurance; labour without necessity is a greater example.

X. The divine powers assuredly delight in perpetual motion; eternity is sustained by constant activity; and whatever we human beings call labour is your nature. As the tireless revolution turns the sky, as the seas are restless with tides, as the sun does not know how to stand still, so you, Emperor, are always active amid uninterrupted tasks returning upon themselves in a kind of circuit.

> [Note: By continuous activity.]

> [Note: And always exercising yourself through tasks that succeed one another in a kind of cycle.]

You had scarcely entered beneath Spanish roofs when you were already sheltered by Sarmatian tents. You had scarcely hung up your earned weapons when, armed again, you pressed upon the enemy. You had scarcely seen your own Ebro when you were already stretching yourself along the Danube.

> [Note: You had scarcely arrived in Spain, and already you were pitching camp in Sarmatia; you had scarcely laid aside victorious arms, and already, etc.]

> [Note: Spanish roofs. This refers to the period when Theodosius withdrew to Spain, about A.D. 370, to escape the rage of Valens.]

Nor, when you had advanced to a higher rank, did you relax your efforts so as merely to command, divide leisure with business, and enjoy glory already won as though military service were a burden laid aside. Rather, you performed first—or among the foremost—every kind and duty of camp service: you stood before the standards, took your turn at sentry duty, carried earth for the rampart, seized ground in advance for battle, went out to reconnoitre, laid out camps, entered battle first, left it last; you were a commander in counsel, a soldier in example. Thus even then it could be understood that others fought for an emperor, but you fought for yourself.

> [Note: When you had advanced to a higher grade: when you became emperor.]

> [Note: To divide leisure with duties. Compare Pliny, book VIII, to Arrianus: “I distinguish more serious work by games and jokes.” Velleius, book I: “No one more gracefully than Scipio punctuated the intervals of business with leisure.”]

> [Note: As though the burden of military service had been laid aside.]

> [Note: Restored honour. As though dignity had temporarily been laid aside. Others read *onere*, “burden,” rather than *honore*, “honour,” as in Catullus.]

> [Note: The whole range of military duties—that is, their parts and offices. Compare Pliny: “You performed every branch of attendance.”]

> [Note: To carry the rampart: to carry earth for constructing the rampart.]

Yet most remarkable of all is this: though you did everything that should make you fit to command, you did nothing in order to command.

XI. The proof is that day—the originator of the common good—on which, when you were summoned to undertake the Republic, you declined the empire offered to you. And this was not merely for appearance, that you might seem to be compelled; rather, you resisted earnestly, long, and as though you expected to prevail.

For there was no reason for pretence. The emperor did not court you alone and at home, as though he were testing you; he did so publicly, in the assembly, and in such a way that he could no longer act otherwise.

> [Note: In the assembly. *Comitium* may mean either the gathering itself or the place in which people assembled to elect magistrates.]

Indeed, unless you had sincerely and wholeheartedly refused empire, you could safely have wished for it.

> [Note: That is: unless you had truly and from the heart rejected imperial dignity, you could safely have accepted it.]

It is necessary here to address you in the words of the Republic herself. Having fallen back from the midst of hope into the extremity of fear because of your hesitation, she undoubtedly confronted you with some such speech—though one heard by you alone:

> [Note: She indeed addressed you in words such as these, but words which you alone heard.]

“Have the Fates delayed me, Theodosius, so little until now that you also attempt to increase their delays? Do you not know that your state is being consumed moment by moment? Do you not know that I am diminished for you and for your children? Whatever the Goth wears away, whatever the Hun snatches, whatever the Alan takes away—Arcadius will one day miss it.

> [Note: And for yours: your children.]

> [Note: Goth. The Goths, a people originating in Scandinavia, crossed thence into Scythia and soon overflowed into all Europe.]

> [Note: Hun. The Huns were a people of European Sarmatia, formerly dwelling near the Maeotian marsh; departing from there, they first migrated into Pannonia and then into Gaul, where they were defeated in A.D. 451 on the Catalaunian Fields by Aetius and Meroveus, together with Visigothic and Burgundian leaders. Jordanes, *Getic Affairs*, chapter 24; Ammianus, volume III.]

> [Note: Alan. The Alans, peoples of European Scythia near the Maeotian marshes, took their name from the river of the same name.]

> [Note: Arcadius will one day miss this. Compare Aeneas concerning his son Ascanius, *Aeneid* IV.354:
>
> “My boy Ascanius, and the wrong done to my dear head,
>
> whom I deprive of the realm of Hesperia and of fated arms.”
>
> Arcadius was the eldest of the children of Theodosius the Great.]

“I have lost unhappy Pannonias; I mourn the funeral of Illyricum; I watch the destruction of Gaul.

> [Note: I have lost the unfortunate Pannonias. Rhenanus says that Lower Pannonia, now called Hungary, evidently was occupied by the Huns at this time. Or should we understand it of the disturbances of the Quadi in Pannonia after their king Gabinius was killed by the Romans? They became so inflamed that, having crossed the Danube, they slaughtered the rural population during harvest and nearly carried off the daughter of Constantius, soon to be married to Emperor Gratian. Ammianus, book XXIX, chapter 35.]

> [Note: I mourn the funeral of Illyricum. This refers to the disastrous defeat which occurred under Valentinian in A.D. 374. Ammianus, volume III, book 8.]

> [Note: I watch the destruction of Gaul. Trans-Rhenish peoples were invading Gaul. Ammianus.]

“The elder of the emperors is not sufficient for such great wars; the other, though he may someday become most brave, is still a child. Do you hesitate to receive me in my collapse, and to restore me—too late even if you make no delay?

> [Note: Elder of the emperors. Gratian was then twenty years old.]

> [Note: He is still a child. Valentinian the Younger was only in his ninth year, according to Ammianus, Hydatius, the Alexandrian Chronicle, etc.]

> [Note: To be restored too late, even if you introduce no delay.]

“Is this the gratitude you return to me because, even while prosperous, I longed for you? Because, when tranquil Nerva, Titus—beloved of the human race—and Antoninus, memorable for piety, possessed me; when Augustus adorned me with walls, Hadrian instructed me with laws, and Trajan enlarged me with territories, I did not think myself sufficiently fortunate because I was not yours?

> [Note: “Adorned with walls.” Balduin restores *moribus*, “with morals,” in place of *moenibus*, “with walls,” following Horace, *Epistles* II.1:
>
> “May you protect Italy’s affairs with arms, adorn them with morals.”]

“What would you do for me if I were yours by right? Look: my lord entreats you; he who is still your lord entreats you, and though he could compel you, prefers to obtain your consent. An empire offered by an emperor you are no longer permitted to refuse, just as you were not permitted to desire it.”

> [Note: My lord: Gratian.]

XII. Therefore, Augustus, you alone—yes, alone—of all who have hitherto ruled, obtained the position of prince by refusing it.

> [Note: “You obtained the position of prince.” Perhaps, as Acidalus thinks, one should add *restitisti*, “by resisting.”]

Others were imposed upon the Republic by the purchased votes of legions, others by a vacant court, others by royal kinship. Neither canvassing, opportunity, nor relationship made you prince. For you were outside the imperial family, were admitted as a third ruler, and were compelled unwillingly—unwillingly, I say.

> [Note: You were admitted as a third. Gratian and Valentinian then held imperial power.]

Hear this, you public parricides who, forgetful of loyalty, seized your masters’ sceptres and, at a risk no less great than your crime, bartered your lives for empire and bought the royal title at the price of blood. Sovereignty suffers rejection; and this is the sole canvassing of a candidate: that he should not be declared emperor.

> [Note: Public parricides. Although this can apply to many, it seems especially to allude to the tyrant Maximus, Gratian’s murderer; for the deed was recent.]

> [Note: Forgetful of loyalty. *Oblita* is used passively, as in Virgil, *Eclogues* IX.53: “Now so many songs have escaped my memory.” Others read *obliti caede*, “stained by slaughter.”]

Will future posterity ever believe this, and grant us so glorious a credit as to acknowledge that in our age at last there occurred what in so many ages before and after has found neither equal nor precedent? Yet whoever has known the course and principles of your life will readily believe it, and will not doubt that one who was to rule in this fashion refused empire.

> [Note: The course of your life. This looks back to Pliny, *Panegyric*, section 84: “But whoever has known the institutions and principles of your life will easily discover the source of this abundance.”]

> [Note: One who was to rule: that is, one who was to administer the empire with such great praise.]

For let those men greedily desire kingdoms whose life, freed from laws, delights them; whose cruelty seeks the right and impunity to kill the uncondemned; whose greed seeks to plunder private property; whose lust seeks to defile honourable things. What did it matter to you to become prince, who would remain a private man even as emperor?

> [Note: A private man in the emperor: one who would preserve the moderation of a private individual while in power.]

Unless, perhaps, in you today devotion to chastity is more lax, fear of human blood less, or desire for another’s property greater.

> [Note: I understand this ironically.]

You are the same man you were, and through yourself you have only as much power as you formerly had through the laws. You experience supreme authority as the capacity and abundance to benefit others, not as security in wrongdoing. The principate has conferred one thing upon you: it has made us certain that, even under other emperors, you lived by your own laws. For one who does nothing lawlessly when able to do so never wished to do it.

XIII. Indeed, as soon as you had shown yourself worthy of empire, not content with having yourself withdrawn beyond vices, you added concern for correcting the vices of others; and you did so moderately, so as to seem rather to recommend honourable conduct than compel it.

> [Note: You had shown yourself free from every vice.]

And because, either through long familiarity with the East or through the laxity of many preceding emperors, such extravagance had infected some people that a fully grown habit of excess seemed by no means likely easily to obey medicine, you wished censorship to begin with yourself, lest anyone should think that he suffered an injury. By reducing palace expenditure, rejecting not merely excessive cost but using scarcely even the necessary allowance, you reformed men with their willing consent—a thing which nature finds most difficult.

> [Note: Long familiarity with the East: because of the wars waged in Syria.]

> [Note: By reducing palace expenditure. What other writers of Theodosius’s life say, Zosimus, *History* IV, denies. On the contrary, he says that Theodosius brought such expenditure upon the royal table that, because of the multitude and luxury of dishes, populous companies of cooks and cupbearers were established. But what credit should be given to this writer in matters concerning Christian emperors?]

> [Note: Allowance. Properly, *demensum* was the monthly provision given to individual slaves for food. Terence, *Phormio*, act I, scene 1: “Scarcely, penny by penny, cheating his own appetite out of his allowance, he saved miserably.” Here the term is used more broadly for any necessary food.]

Would anyone take it ill to be restrained to the standard of his prince? Or regret that something had been taken from his private extravagance when he saw the emperor, master of affairs and lord of lands and peoples, living sparingly and contentedly, consoling long fasts with modest soldier’s food?

> [Note: Soldier’s food—that is, bacon, cheese, and *posca*, according to Spartianus in his *Hadrian*. This passage on Theodosius’s frugality and self-restraint appears to be taken from Mamertinus’s panegyric on Julian, section 11.]

And would he see the entire court harder than Spartan gymnasia, abounding in examples of labour, endurance, and frugality? Would a single person be found who dared demand for the imperial larder fish from remote shores, a bird from foreign skies, or a flower out of season?

> [Note: Harder than Spartan gymnasia. Spartan boys, as everyone knows, were customarily scourged with thongs at Diana’s altar until blood flowed.]

XIV. For those delicate and self-indulgent men, such as the Republic has often produced, did not think themselves sufficiently luxurious unless extravagance reversed the order of the seasons: unless winter roses floated on their drinking-cups, unless in summer they broke Falernian wine with ice in capacious gem-studded vessels.

> [Note: Self-indulgent: dissolving in luxury. Velleius calls Sardanapalus “flowing with softness”; likewise, “flowing with leisure and softness almost beyond womanhood.” Quintilian calls soft and delicate boys lax and self-indulgent. For further examples of intemperance see Capitolinus on Aelius Verus, whose banquet is said to have been valued at sixty million sesterces; and Vitellius, who spent nine hundred million sesterces on feasts, *Tacitus, Histories* II. The latter sum amounts to 39,375,000 French pounds.]

> [Note: Unless it reversed the order of the seasons.]

> [Note: In capacious vessels of large gems.]

Our world was too small for their appetite. They valued dishes set before them not by flavour but by cost, and took satisfaction only in foods sent by the farthest East, by Colchis beyond Roman dominion, or by seas notorious for shipwrecks—foods which human dangers had snatched, as it were, from an unwilling and resisting Nature.

Not to mention fowlers often enlisted in the provinces by disgraceful selection, and companies of hunters led beneath military standards to serve banquets: have we not known of a former emperor whose meals—indeed, not merely meals but individual courses—were valued at a thousand million sesterces and thus attained the price of equestrian estates?

> [Note: A thousand million sesterces. A manifest error has entered this passage, since Horace, Juvenal, Pliny, and others establish that the equestrian census was only 400,000 sesterces. Therefore one should read “four hundred thousand sesterces”; and I think this the more readily because, if ancient manuscripts perhaps contained “CD. LL.” for “four hundred thousand sesterces,” copyists could very easily, owing to the resemblance of the symbols, write “CIC LL.”—“a thousand million sesterces.” That sum of 400,000 sesterces comes to 17,500 of our pounds, whereas a thousand million sesterces rises to 4,375,000 French pounds. Note also that *fercula*, though usually meaning food-courses, sometimes means certain contrivances on which several dishes were placed upon a table, as may be seen in Petronius.]

Your banquets, Emperor, more restrained than ordinary tables, are supplied with the produce of place and season. From this there has sprung up everywhere, in mutual emulation, shame at luxury and esteem for frugality; and, though the threats of laws lay dormant, each person privately began to repent of himself.

> [Note: Hatred of luxury and love of frugality gained strength among all.]

For it is so, it is so: correction imposed by command exasperates people; by example, command is most gently given.

> [Note: Correction joined with authority.]

XV. But although these measures, and others of this kind, have shaped human manners and institutions, I think nothing has contributed more to casting off vices and adopting virtues than your having always devoted yourself to men whom public imitation ought to set before itself as models—men who, as easily as they were compliant and obedient pupils to you, were as desirable teachers to all others.

> [Note: Those whom the people ought to set before themselves for imitation.]

> [Note: Obedient.]

Not to speak of those whom that first day of your rising empire presented to you, endowed with such great virtues that they seemed chosen not from the resources available, but because of the abundance of them: how many men, and of what quality, did you later select, to entrust some with the guardianship of provinces, others with supreme military command, others with the secrets of your counsels?

> [Note: Those who held magistracies when you attained empire.]

Therefore, since this selection was twofold, one by judgment and the other by fate, it is uncertain whether your wisdom or Fortune found the better men, since you possess men either received from fate or discovered by your own industry, such that the former deserved to be retained and the latter ought to have been enrolled.

> [Note: Received: that is, from fate. Then “discovered”: that is, by your own industry.]

XVI. Which emperor ever thought that the cultivation of friendship ought to be counted among royal praises? This was regarded as a humble virtue, and it was doubtful whether it was a virtue at all; it was thought unworthy of palaces, but dangerous. It would therefore be easier to find men who lavished money from the treasury than men who offered fidelity from their hearts.

> [Note: Hence it is easier to find examples of liberality than of loyalty and friendship among princes.]

That excellent man enriched others, but did not also love them; he knew how to benefit them, but did not know how to love.

> [Note: “That excellent man”: perhaps *optimus*, “the best men.” Then “that man”: Gratian.]

You brought friendship—a name formerly private—not merely into the court, but, clothed in purple and crowned with gold and gems, received it upon the throne. You asserted in deed, not words, that a prince’s mind ought to be more kind toward his own people in proportion as his fortune is more eminent: for you act with fidelity equal to your generosity, and as emperor grant your intimates what, as a private man, you had wished for.

> [Note: “You [brought] friendship.” This is taken from Julian’s panegyric, section 23.]

> [Note: What wishes could ever attain what most persons have obtained under your rule?]

And yet what prayers could embrace what very many have obtained under you as prince? I do not now speak of those honours which an emperor must confer upon one person or another. Is a general elevated? Military discipline demands it. Is a prefect raised? A head must be imposed upon the province. Is a consul created? The year will take its name from him.

> [Note: The year must receive its name from him.]

Thus, even in those greatest and most splendid benefits, there is some advantage for the giver. But through your novel generosity an honour has been bestowed upon friends which belonged wholly to those on whom it was conferred, and from which nothing returned to you except the pleasure of giving.

> [Note: Some benefit returns to the person who grants it.]

Although you had at home your sons, those twin hopes and eyes of the Republic, you delayed their magistracies and adorned friends with the consulship.

> [Note: Sons: Arcadius and Honorius.]

> [Note: Friends: namely Mamertinus and Nevitta.]

By Hercules, if that divine man, the author of public prosperity—your father—were alive, what else would he have expected from his son than that he should be preferred to his grandsons? You therefore bestowed on friends what you could not have bestowed more greatly even upon your father.

> [Note: Your father: Theodosius.]

O singular plan of your benevolence! You increase by time a dignity which could not be increased by greatness. Your friends are proclaimed consuls before your sons, because they could not be more than consuls.

> [Note: Because they could not. You made the benefit of the consulship—the greatest you could confer on friends, if one considers the dignity of that supreme magistracy—greater still by preferring them even to your sons in order to confer it sooner.]

XVII. Let antiquity now go, that exhibitor of itself, and boast of those examples published abroad in innumerable literary memorials. Let it proclaim the loyalty of Pirithous and praise the devotion of the Phocaean youth sung on every stage; let it also speak, if it wishes, of Pythias and Damon, one of whom offered himself as surety in his friend’s death, while the other came on the appointed day to meet the death for which he had given surety.
