> [Note: The loyalty of Pirithous. I say nothing of the friendship of Pirithous and Theseus, Pylades and Orestes, Damon and Pythias or Phintias, since the matter is well known.]

Let us believe these things true: tales fashioned out of poets’ falsehoods for the applause of theatres owe their credibility to their age.

> [Note: The theatres. Properly, the *cavea* is the central area in a theatre, where the seats of the equestrian order customarily stood, because the awnings resembled a cave. Yet it is often used, as here, for the whole theatre, as in *Aeneid* V.340:
>
> “Here the whole seated assembly of the great theatre, etc.”]

> [Note: They owe their credibility to antiquity.]

Can we grant more in believing than to judge that those whom fame counts among the renowned examples of friendship were more attentive to their friends than to themselves? But since Nature, in her instruction, generally causes us to love our children more than ourselves, he surpassed every example who preferred friends to those whom he preferred to himself.

> [Note: “But you indeed.” Perhaps “and you indeed,” as Acidalus notes; for the repeated particle *sed* has something awkward about it.]

But you, in order to relieve the embarrassment of those indebted to you, do not wish what you confer upon your own people to appear a gift but a repayment. Let us follow your custom; and, reckoning the total of your benefits according to your own desire, let us suppose that whatever you grant your intimates is not expenditure but repayment. Indeed, when you enrich persons slightly known to you, or even seen only once, with honours of which friends might be content, do you not wish to prove to everyone that any good man is your friend?

> [Note: That you may spare the modesty of those whom you bind to yourself.]

To whomever some public duty has been assigned, a reward is promised and paid. Let virtue lying low impute to itself its obscurity and neglect, if it has not presented itself for proof. So far as your conscience is concerned, the person approved has been honoured.

> [Note: “So far as your conscience is concerned.” This looks back to Eumenius, *Thanksgiving*, section 20: “Let anyone who did not wish to use your benefit, and did not judge himself worthy of life when through you he was permitted to live, blame himself; you, so far as suffices for your conscience, spared even those who did not deserve it.”]

XVIII. Yet I should like you to say whence it comes that, while you discharge what has been promised to so many people, you know what you have promised to each; and that neither concern for the Republic nor the very multitude of your benefits confuses you, so that you become sparing or tardy, deceiving anyone as to the time or manner of your gift.

> [Note: “So many”: for “so great a number.”]

> [Note: So that you might be more sparing: that is, either fail to give someone what you promised, or fail to give it at the time when you promised to give it.]

What scrupulous debtor repays a loan on its due date as exactly as you weigh out what you promise? Nor do you think that negligent people can be imposed upon.

> [Note: You deal with those to whom you have made promises as though you thought they observed so carefully the measure and time of promises that they could not easily be deceived.]

Every day we examine your benefits and consult our memories; and, lest forgetfulness ensnare any single one of us, each compares them with another.

> [Note: We calculate your benefits in our minds and recall them in memory; and lest any one of them be forgotten, we converse among ourselves about them, comparing them as though they were present.]

We cannot find a single person whose hope and expectation you have disappointed—or even delayed, which is the more delicate complaint.

> [Note: More delicate. He calls the complaint of a benefit delayed, rather than wholly denied, “more delicate”; for to deny what has been promised belongs to a man of no fidelity, while delay seems a kind of negligence which might befall any person.]

> [Note: Far smaller.]

Do you think, Emperor, that I admire only your benevolence? I also admire your memory. For did Hortensius, Lucullus, or Caesar ever have recollection so ready as your sacred mind, which at the place and moment you command restores every deposit?

> [Note: Hortensius, Lucullus, or Caesar. Cicero commends Hortensius’s outstanding memory in *Tusculan Disputations* I and near the end of *On the Orator* III, where he also mentions Hortensius; likewise in the *Brutus*, section 301. Pliny, book VII, chapter 25, reports that Caesar used to write and read simultaneously, dictate and listen, and dictate four letters concerning very important matters to secretaries at once—or, if engaged in nothing else, seven. We have spoken above of other examples of outstanding memory.]

Do you yourself nevertheless remind yourself? Or, as the Fates are said to stand beside the god who shares your majesty with tablets—as they attend Jupiter—does some divine power serve you, writing down and suggesting what you have said?

> [Note: “Do you yourself nevertheless?” Others read: “Or do you yourself?”]

> [Note: God. Whether this means God or Jupiter is uncertain; for whether Pacatus was a Christian is uncertain. Martianus Capella, book I, says that the Fates stand beside Jupiter as celestial secretaries and record his judgments. Lucian relates this cleverly in his own manner, section 366. Greek poets and mythographers say that the Fates are Jupiter’s scribes.]

You promise nothing merely with the first touch of your lips without adding fulfilment to the promise and ratifying words by deed. No one now thinks that benefits which you have given should be counted from the time when you gave them, because what you promise is so certain that it appears received at the moment when you promise it.

> [Note: “So certain.” Perhaps read *tam sunt certa* (“they are so certain”), as Livineius notes in the margin of his edition from the Viennese codex.]

XIX. Does not the very fact that you promise beforehand [Note: [Col. 0494D] Before you promise. You promise before conferring any benefit.] proceed from the highest radiance of a most unclouded mind? For whose disposition is it neither to weary men’s wishes [Note: [Col. 0495C] Nor to weary men’s wishes. That is, to grant men’s wishes quickly, or even to forestall their wishes by beneficence and liberality.] nor to introduce into gifts the artifice of difficulty, but to announce beforehand what will be granted—so that the perception of blessings may be more prolonged, sudden good fortune may not leave men stunned, and they may become like the ungrateful? For joy and sorrow alike bewilder our minds, unequal as they are to sudden emotions, if they take them by surprise. [Note: [Col. 0495D] Bewilders. “Stuns.” Catullus, in the *Argonautica*: “Ah! how wretched Erycina, sowing thorny cares in her breast, bewildered her with unceasing griefs!”] Did not that Roman mother, renowned for her devotion, [Note: [Col. 0495D] A mother most famous for devotion. Pliny, VII.53; Aulus Gellius, III.15; Valerius Maximus, IX.12, relate this.] terrified by news of the disaster at Cannae, freeze to death when the son whom she mourned returned; [Note: [Col. 0495C] She was frozen by the chill of death.] nor could she who had survived bereavement be equal to joy? Thus, knowing the heavenly mystery and the natural deposits entrusted to you [Note: [Col. 0495D] Deposits. Secrets entrusted to the fidelity of a few and, so to speak, placed in their hands as a deposit. Gruter prefers “things laid up,” as below, section 21: “unless, shut up within the recess,” etc. See this passage.], you prefer benefits hoped for to advance toward men rather than benefits unhoped for to come upon them. And rightly so. For as fleeting pleasure from sudden success seizes us, so it leaves us; [Note: [Col. 0495D] As it seizes. As suddenly as it seizes, so quickly it leaves.] but a more lasting happiness is the secure expectation [Note: [Col. 0495D] To expect securely. To expect something certain.]. Accordingly, whereas nature had hitherto ordained that men should not know their own blessings, and should only then begin to rejoice in happiness when they had begun to be happy, by promising what you would grant you discovered for us the time which nature had withheld: so that blessings which helped us only when obtained might delight us even while they were being obtained.

XX. With equal kindness, when you wished to honor more persons than the places of honor could admit, [Note: [Col. 0495D] Of honors. This, rather than “of goods,” seems to me required by the sense. Puteanus therefore conjectures it, as he noted in the margin of Livineius’s edition after Rittershusius.] and the available scope was narrower than your goodwill, and an empire, however extensive, could not contain your mind, you nevertheless consoled with your gracious notice the man whom you had not yet advanced to some rank. [Note: [Col. 0495C] You deigned to console him.] And I do not know whether this consolation was not enough for some. One was honored by your address, another made blessed by your table, another consecrated by your kiss. Thus, for all who could rightfully trust in you as their prince, either dignity advanced or humanity satisfied—humanity, I say, which is as illustrious in an emperor as it is rare.

[Note: [Col. 0495C] For pride is an inseparable companion of those who are fortunate.] For since pride is the undiscriminating attendant of the fortunate, scarcely anyone has been granted both abundance of fortune [Note: [Col. 0495C] And freedom from pride.] and freedom from arrogance. Indeed, our ancestors so utterly detested this that they always judged contempt more grievous than slavery; and, driven by impatience with it, after the warlike Tulli, [Note: [Col. 0496C] The warlike Tulli. The well-known courage of Tullus Hostilius in subduing the Sabines and Albans.] the priestly Numas, [Note: [Col. 0496C] The priestly Numas. The conspicuous piety and religious devotion of Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, in establishing rites was celebrated.] and the founding Romuluses, [Note: [Col. 0496D] The founding Romuluses. Who does not know Romulus, founder of the city of Rome?] they came to hate kingship even in its name. Finally, they condemned Tarquinius himself by the final curse of this reproach: they called a man headlong in lust, blind through greed, savage in cruelty, and mad in frenzy, “the Proud”; and thought the insult sufficient.

If it were permitted by the nature of things that Brutus, that champion of Roman liberty and hater of the royal name, [Note: [Col. 0496D] Brutus. He has in view Martial, II.5, on Trajan: “If the mighty names of the ancient fathers return, if it is permitted to empty the Elysian grove, Brutus will rejoice under your leadership … Even Cato himself, recalled from the infernal shades of Dis, if restored, will become a partisan of Caesar.”] restored to life at the prayer of others, [Note: [Col. 0496C] Restored to life at the entreaty of prayers.] could behold your age imbued and filled with devotion to virtue, frugality, and humanity; could see no trace remaining anywhere in the whole world of pride, lust, or cruelty; could see you yourself living, in public and private, with the sternness of ancient commanders, the chastity of pontiffs, the moderation of consuls, and the affability of candidates, [Note: [Col. 0496D] The affability of candidates. Should we read “the affability of praetors,” as Balduin prefers? It suits well Pliny’s *Panegyric*, section 9: “For me, in your tribunate, you were an example of tranquillity; in your praetorship, of moderation,” etc. Perhaps *petitores* also means candidates.] then, surely, after so long an interval, he would change his judgment; and, while approving Roman dignity and liberty, he would necessarily confess that, in a better condition under you as emperor than he himself had enjoyed as consul, Tarquinius ought to have been removed—not kingship.

XXI. But as, when we enter great cities, we customarily first visit their sacred buildings and shrines dedicated to the highest deity, then admire their forums, gymnasia, and promenades extended beneath their porticoes, so, having reverenced in your praises the holy observances of the palace and institutions to be compared with ancient ceremonies, we proceed to matters situated in the midst and serving public uses: things which benefit not a part but the community, [Note: [Col. 0496D] Not in part. That is, not privately, says Puteanus. Some read “open,” others “powerful,” others “a part.”] which are bounded not by walls but by the world, and covered not by a roof but by heaven.

Foremost among these—lest we immediately seize upon the highest—is that, by your frequent appearances in public, [Note: [Col. 0496C] You appear frequently in public.] you offer yourself to the peoples awaiting you, to be seen and recognized; [Note: [Col. 0496C] You offer yourself to be looked upon and recognized.] and you not only tolerate being seen but are easy of access, [Note: [Col. 0496D] Easy to approach. For “easy in access.”] receiving at close quarters the petitions of your people: so that whoever comes to you to make a request [Note: [Col. 0496C] So that anyone who brings some business before you.], even if he receives—what is rare—a refusal, [Note: [Col. 0497C] At least he may be conscious that he has seen the divinity.] may nonetheless carry away the consciousness of having seen the divinity.

How unlike this was the practice of those former princes whom I need not name, who believed that royal majesty was diminished and made common unless, shut up in the inner recess of the palace, [Note: [Col. 0497C] Within the sanctuary of the sacred house.] they were sought out by secret reverence as though they were some Vestal mystery; [Note: [Col. 0497C] A Vestal secret. He alludes to the fire which the Vestal Virgins guarded with the greatest religious reverence in the innermost sanctuary of Vesta.] unless, lying hidden in domestic shade, they were protected by a solitude deliberately arranged and by silences broadly secured. [Note: [Col. 0497C] Unless solitude were sought within domestic walls, etc.] Indeed, if they could ever come into the light and endure the day, they were carried in litters [Note: [Col. 0497C] Litters. Lipsius observes that before Cicero’s time litters were customarily used in the countryside, not in the city; for travel only, not for urban idleness. Later they became so common that their use had to be restricted to certain persons, ages, and days. See Lipsius, *Electa*, I.19, for more on their varying forms.] and ceremonial carriages, [Note: [Col. 0497C] *Tensae*. *Tensae*, or *thensae* as others write, were sacred carriages in which images of gods were carried in circus games.] enclosed around and above by a most dense tortoise-shell formation of men and arms; they moved slowly and in measured order. Then the people were driven far away, and the hand of no idle passerby [Note: [Col. 0497C] Passerby. See Pliny’s *Panegyric* to Trajan, section 76, note 8.] cleared the crowd with a lash—so that there might be privacy in public. [Note: [Col. 0497D] There might be privacy in public. That is, even when they were in public, they might appear to be in private.]

But this emperor of ours is presented for all to behold; and we are permitted to see our emperor no less commonly than this day and sun that belong to us all. Indeed, though ready access commonly breeds contempt, he never satisfies the eyes that marvel at him. He is sought more and more eagerly by sight; and, strange to say, though present, he is missed.

XXII. Shall we marvel that in your cities and among your peoples you are seen, when scarcely any foreign nation upon its own soil has not seen you—and so often that this face is almost as familiar to barbarians as to ourselves? Nor without reason. For, spending all summers abroad and winters at home, you have divided the seasons of the year equally between citizens and enemies; and if there are any barbarians who have not received the thunderbolt of your valor, they rest, struck by terror at your name and, as it were, blasted.

For your auspices, Emperor, are feared not only by those nations which woods, rivers, or mountains separate from our world, but also by those whom nature marks off as inaccessible through everlasting heat, severed by continuous winter, or divided by intervening seas. No Indian is secure because of the ocean, no Bosporan because of the cold, [Note: [Col. 0497D] The Bosporan because of the cold. A people of European Sarmatia near the Cimmerian Bosporus, where part of Perekop Tartary now lies. All geographers speak of that region’s cold, but Ovid especially treats it extensively in the *Pontic Epistles*.] no Arab beneath the midday sun; [Note: [Col. 0497D] Nor the Arab because of the sun. The Arabs’ dark complexion, for which in Holy Scripture they are called Ethiopians, sufficiently shows how intensely that region burns beneath the sun.] and where the Roman name had scarcely reached, Roman power now arrives.

Shall I speak of the Goths [Note: [Col. 0497D] The Goths. After the death of their king Athanaric, they surrendered themselves to the Roman Empire. Marcellinus, *Chronicle*; Orosius, VII.34.] received into service, supplying your camps with soldiers and your lands with cultivators? Shall I speak of punishment exacted from the rebellious Saracens [Note: [Col. 0497D] Saracens. Peoples of Arabia Felix.] for their violated treaty? Shall I speak of the Tanais forbidden to the Scythians, [Note: [Col. 0497D] The Tanais forbidden to the Scythians. Orosius, VII.34, and Zonaras, *Annals*, vol. III, report this. There are two rivers called Tanais: one in Muscovy, which divides Asia from Europe and empties into Lake Maeotis; the other in eastern Scythia, which flows from Mount Parapamisus into the Caspian Sea. The latter is properly called the Jaxartes, but was named Tanais by the Macedonians.] and of the unwarlike bows even of the fleeing Albanians? [Note: [Col. 0498C] The Albanians. An eastern people between Iberia and the Caspian Sea, whom Strabo says were skilled in archery, II.] Every barbarian nation that has ever been burdensome to us through strength, ferocity, or numbers either accepts its lot graciously [Note: [Col. 0498C] Or accepts it graciously. A frequent manner of speaking in Cicero. *Boni consulere*, or *aequi bonique consulere*, means to take in good part.] or rests, or rejoices, as though it were friendly, if it serves. Persia itself, once the rival of our commonwealth and made famous by the many funerals of Roman commanders, excuses by obedience whatever it ever did more harshly against our emperors.

Finally, that very king of Persia, [Note: [Col. 0498C] That very king. Artaxerxes, or another king, who, in the consulship of Richomer and Clearchus, sought peace from Theodosius through envoys sent with gifts, as Socrates, V; Count Marcellinus; and Claudian, *On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius*, say: “The Persian nobles were sent to request a treaty,” etc.] who once disdained to acknowledge that you were a man, now confesses fear and worships you in the temples in which he himself is worshipped—by sending an embassy, supplying gems and silk, and even furnishing triumphal beasts for your chariots. Though he is not yet allied by treaty, he is already tributary to your worship. [Note: [Col. 0498D] He is not allied by treaty. But later he was, as Puteanus observes from Aurelius Victor, who says that the Persians made peace with Theodosius. Orosius confirms this.]

XXIII. Yet do not suppose, Emperor, that I shall say everything merely to please your ears. [Note: [Col. 0498D] To please the ears. Compare Trebonius to Cicero: “Do not suppose, my Cicero, that I say this to please your ears,” Cicero, *Letters*, XII.16; that is, do not think I said it in order to flatter you.] You may be amazed at your Gallic triumphs; [Note: [Col. 0498D] Your Gallic triumphs. For Maximus had seized Gaul.] we are angry at them. While you advance in conquest through remote regions of the earth, while you extend the kingdoms of the East beyond the limits of things and the boundaries of nature, [Note: [Col. 0498D] The kingdoms of the East. The rule of the East had fallen to Theodosius alone after Gratian was killed by Maximus.] while you hasten toward the natives of first light and toward the very resting-place of the sun, if such a place exists, the tyrant found privacy for his crimes. [Note: [Col. 0499C] Privacy for crimes. A place suited to the wicked seizure of tyranny.]

How great evils come from such small beginnings! Thus, toward the final destruction, almost, of the Italian race, a band of *mirmillones* burst forth after the gladiatorial school of Gnaeus Lentulus had been broken open. [Note: [Col. 0499C] After the school of Gnaeus Lentulus was broken open. He refers to the Servile War, called the Spartacan War, raised in Italy in the year of Rome 681 by Spartacus, Oenomaus, and Crixus. Having broken open Lentulus’s school at Capua, where they were kept with seventy-four gladiators, called *mirmillones*, and summoned slaves to arms, they seized Mount Vesuvius and defeated in war the legate Claudius Pulcher and the praetor Publius Vatinius. Florus, III.20; Eutropius; epitome of Victor.] Thus the Cilician pirate kindled wars fought by consuls with uncertain fortune. [Note: [Col. 0499C] The Cilician pirate. He means the pirate wars concluded by Pompey; Florus. The Cilicians inhabited the coast bounded by Mount Amanus, Mount Taurus, Pamphylia, and the sea.] Thus, while runaway slaves bore arms, Roman javelins long yielded to the iron of the slave-prisons. [Note: [Col. 0499D] While runaway slaves bore arms. Understand the Servile Wars, undertaken in A.U.C. 681 and 683, which Florus records.]

Who did not laugh at the first report of this unprecedented crime? The affair seemed beneath the dignity of anger: a few men, and islanders at that, were setting fire to the whole continent; and those exiles of the world were clothing their own exile [Note: [Col. 0499D] Their own. Maximus, a Briton by origin.] in royal dress. [Note: [Col. 0499D] Exiles of the world. Virgil, *Eclogues*, I.67: “Britons divided from the whole world”; and Horace, I.35: “The farthest Britons of the world.”] Yet what disturbances Fortune was bringing to birth, what calamity for the commonwealth this growing plague held in store, and what glory for you in extinguishing it! Especially since, through the treachery of commanders and the defection of legions, whatever had been armed for the commonwealth had been turned against the commonwealth. [Note: [Col. 0499D] Through the treachery of commanders. Namely Merobaudes, says the common recension of Prosper’s *Chronicle*.]

XXIV. Yet I do not wish utterly to burden either the deed [Note: [Col. 0499C] To aggravate.] or the fate of the wretched men, who, because they unhappily trusted a purple-clad executioner boasting of kinship with you and of your favor, committed the gravest of all crimes through affection for innocent men. I understand into how difficult and rocky a place I have come. For while your ears reject the recollection [Note: [Col. 0499C] To be recalled.] of that five-year cessation of justice, [Note: [Col. 0499D] The five-year cessation of justice. He means the five years in which Maximus seized tyranny by force and without any exercise of law or equity.] and seek praise; while, for the commendation of present blessings, it contributes to glory that past evils should be remembered, but supreme clemency, on the contrary, prefers that its benefit be diminished rather than increased by the enumeration of sorrows, [Note: [Col. 0499C] Rather than be sullied by the added narration of sad events.] I must necessarily, whether I keep silent about public misfortunes or speak of them, appear either ungrateful to valor or burdensome to piety.

Yet, Emperor, impose a small measure of patience upon your feelings. For if, amid prosperity, the memory of miseries is sweet; if sailors take pleasure in remembering storms and physicians in remembering diseases, why should you not also hear of our evils, so that you may recognize your benefits? From where, then, should I begin, if not from the evils of my Gaul?—Gaul, which, of all the lands occupied by that pest, you may rightly claim as having the special privilege of greatest suffering: [Note: [Col. 0499C] You may rightly say that, of all the lands ravaged by that tyrant, this land was most grievously afflicted.] compelled to endure before her very eyes, not merely through the ears, whose perception is weaker, [Note: [Col. 0499D] The perception is weaker. For Horace says in the *Art of Poetry*: “Things conveyed through the ears affect minds more slowly than those placed before faithful eyes.”] the victory of Maximus and the death of Gratian. [Note: [Col. 0499D] The death of Gratian. As Pacatus says here, and likewise Zosimus and Prosper in the *Chronicle*, Gratian was defeated by Maximus; according to some, betrayed by his army and overcome by Maximus through deceit; according to others, fleeing from Paris toward the Alps and Italy with three hundred horsemen to his brother Valentinian, he was killed at Lyon by Andragathius, sent by Maximus.]

Though our neighboring Italian and adjacent Spaniard may display wounds as deep as ours—this must be confessed—each has his consolation amid utmost grief. [Note: [Col. 0500C] Although deep wounds. Though the fame of Maximus spread from Gaul into neighboring Italy and Spain, each is nevertheless consoled in one respect: Spain did not see Maximus’s frenzy, while Italy saw his death. Maximus was killed at Aquileia, which Pliny places in the tenth region of Italy. Note that the pronoun “this” refers, contrary to the usual pattern, to the more remote noun, and “that” to the nearer.] Spain did not see tyranny; Italy saw the killing of the tyrant. We were the first to receive the onset of the raging beast; with innocent blood we satisfied his savagery, with public poverty his greed. Among us cruelty, now secure, exercised itself, and greed, still unsated. Elsewhere the public evil either began [Note: [Col. 0500C] Began. In Britain; it ended in Italy.] or ended; in Gaul it settled.

XXV. [Note: [Col. 0500C] What land’s calamity can be compared with ours?] Who can compare himself with us in calamity? We endured the tyrant both with others and alone. Why should I recount cities emptied of their citizens, wildernesses filled with noble fugitives? Why recount the property of men who had discharged the highest offices being confiscated, their civil status diminished, [Note: [Col. 0500D] Civil status diminished. In the jurists, diminution of status is a change from one’s former condition, when one loses liberty, citizenship, or family. Hence there are three kinds of diminution of status: greatest, intermediate, and least. See the jurists on these.] their lives assessed in money? We saw dignities reduced to the ranks, [Note: [Col. 0500D] Reduced into the ranks. Or “into an order”: both are frequently used in the same sense by Cicero and other writers, says Lipsius, the metaphor being taken either from military service or magistracies. Since among soldiers legates, tribunes, and the like stand outside or above the ranks, they seem to be forced into the ranks when deprived of their office and treated as equals of common soldiers. Likewise, a magistrate of distinction who is not in the common class or rank is said to be reduced to the ranks when his authority is disregarded or violated.] consulars stripped of their purple-striped robes, [Note: [Col. 0501C] Stripped of their *trabeae*. That is, deprived of the insignia of the consulship.] old men surviving their fortunes, [Note: [Col. 0501C] Survivors of their fortunes. That is, old men bereft of their fortunes before their lives.] and the pitiable security of children playing beneath the very auctioneer. Yet we miserable people were forbidden to behave as miserable; [Note: [Col. 0501C] To behave as miserable men.] indeed, we were compelled to pretend happiness. [Note: [Col. 0501C] Happy.] After we had entrusted our stolen grief at home and in secret only to wives and children—[Note: [Col. 0501C] We had entrusted. We had secretly complained of our misfortunes.] we went out in public wearing faces unsuited to our fortunes. [Note: [Col. 0501D] Not with a face suited to our fortune. With an expression not corresponding to our condition.]

For you might hear an informer say: “Why does that man walk so sadly? Is it because he has become poor after being rich? Does he not rejoice that he is alive? Why does this man parade about in public in black? [Note: [Col. 0501D] Clad in black. A dark garment was proper to men in mourning. Among women, however, the custom varied by period: sometimes black, sometimes white.] He is mourning his brother, I suppose. But he has a son.” Thus we were forbidden to weep for what was lost, through fear for what remained. We therefore put on cheerful faces over clouded minds and, like those who, after tasting the juice of Sardinian herbs, [Note: [Col. 0501D] Sardinian juice. It is well known what is said of the Sardinian herb: it contracts the faces of those who taste it so that they die as though laughing. Hence the proverbial Sardonic laugh, for a feigned or bitter laugh. Yet there are some who give another origin for this account. The Sardi were the people of the island of Sardinia.] are said to laugh in death, we imitated joy while grieving.

There is some alleviation of calamities in giving tears to evils and relieving the breast through sighs. No punishment is greater than to be miserable and not seem so. Meanwhile there was no hope that the plunderer could be satisfied. For abundance was not followed, as nature ordinarily has it, by satiety; day by day the hunger for possessing increased, and possessions acquired inflamed the madness of acquisition. As drink kindles the thirst of the sick, as fire is not smothered by dry materials but increased, so riches amassed through public destitution sharpened the greed of a starving mind.

XXVI. [Note: [Col. 0501D] He himself stood there. A vivid depiction (*hypotyposis*) of a man wickedly intent upon selling the goods of men who had discharged the highest offices, of matrons, wards, and whole provinces, after stripping them.] He himself stood there, robed in purple, beside the scales, watching anxiously and greedily the slightest movements of the weights and balances; [Note: [Col. 0501C] And he anxiously and greedily observed the inclinations of the weights and the slightest movements of the scales.] pale and gaping, he demanded the signals of the scales. [Note: [Col. 0502C] The nods of the balances. He calls them the “nods” of the balances when one pan inclines downward and outweighs the other.] Meanwhile the spoils of provinces, the possessions of exiles, and the property of the slain were brought together. Here was gold torn from women’s hands; there, golden bullae snatched from the necks of wards; [Note: [Col. 0502C] Bullae from necks. Asconius says that a golden *bulla* was customarily hung around the necks of freeborn children, a leather one around those of freedmen. The custom is said to have been introduced by Tarquinius Priscus, when he conferred this honor upon his fourteen-year-old son after a victory over the Sabines.] elsewhere, silver stained with the blood of its owners was weighed out. Everywhere money was counted, treasuries filled, bronze heaped up, vessels cut to pieces: so that anyone looking on would have thought it not an emperor’s residence but a robber’s den.

Yet a robber uses what he steals and makes what is taken from others his own. He does not therefore lie in wait on roads and mountain passes in order to pile up and bury treasure, making himself miserable through crime; rather, he does so to supply his appetite and belly, so that expenditure may not lack resources. For he squanders and neglects alike, with equal ease in seeking and in wasting. But that pirate of ours heaped into that Charybdis of his cave everything he had swept together from every source, [Note: [Col. 0502D] He had swept together. Balduin, after several others, reads *converrerat* rather than *convenerat*, as in other editions.] to perish for us and for himself. Charybdis, do I say? Charybdis, after swallowing full ships, is nevertheless said to cast up wreckage and throw twisted hulls from the deep upon the shores of Taurominium. [Note: [Col. 0502D] Charybdis. The strait between Italy and Sicily, which, by the collision of opposing waves, swallows and disgorges whatever is caught up. Poets say that Charybdis was a most rapacious woman who, after stealing Hercules’ cattle, was struck by Jupiter’s thunderbolt and transformed into a monster.] [Note: [Col. 0502D] On the shores of Taurominium. Taurominium is a city of Sicily with a harbor on the eastern coast between Messana and Catana, today Taormina.] Our property went to his treasury by one continuous route; that common maw cast up no remnants and no fragments, even when at last conquered by disgust.

XXVII. The last defense of wicked rulers is to take away in order to give, and to avert the odium of plunder by the magnitude of their gifts. [Note: [Col. 0502C] To excuse.] What a miserable argument: to have taken from everyone what no one is to possess! The greed of private persons, though evil, has at least some defense: poverty is feared, provision is laid up for old age, [Note: [Col. 0502D] It is laid up for old age. Thus Horace, *Satires*, I.1: “Old men, they say, endure labor in this spirit, that they may withdraw into secure leisure … just as the little ant is an example of great industry.”] and thought is taken for an heir. What reason for coveting can one offer who possesses whatever exists everywhere?

Indeed, if it is right and reverent for mortals to form judgments of heavenly things, I should believe that no greater happiness exists for rulers than to have made someone happy, to have intervened against want, [Note: [Col. 0502C] To remove want.] to have conquered fortune, and to have given a human being a new destiny. [Note: [Col. 0502C] A new lot.] Therefore, to an emperor who properly values his own majesty, what he has given ought to seem more his own than what he has taken. For since all things circulate within himself, and just as the ocean, which surrounds all things, receives back from the land the waters it supplies to the land, so whatever flows from a prince to his citizens flows back to the prince; and a generous emperor serves both his resources and his reputation well. For he gains glory when he gives money that will return.

XXVIII. But to that man every plan for gaining praise seemed foolish. Besides the hatred of a good example innate in every worst person, [Note: [Col. 0503B] Thinking that he would be the happier the more he possessed and harmed.] he defined the height of happiness in terms of possessing and harming; and he labored not only to acquire and seize as much as possible, [Note: [Col. 0503B] To seize.] but to leave nothing remaining to anyone. He did not, as kings commonly do, devote vigilance to working metals [Note: [Col. 0503C] Working metals. Either mining them, smelting them, or coining them.] so as to call forth nature’s hidden goods for use and create harmless riches that made no one poorer. He thought gold too little precious when it had been extracted from veins in the mountains or gravel in rivers [Note: [Col. 0503C] From mountain veins. Gold is found: first, in river gravel, as in the Tagus of Spain, the Po of Italy, the Hebrus of Thrace, the Pactolus of Asia, and the Ganges of India; secondly, in mine shafts; thirdly, in collapsed mountains and the bowels of the earth. Puteanus notes this from Pliny, XXXIII.4.] by a Bessian prospector or a Callaician searcher. [Note: [Col. 0503C] A Bessian prospector. The Bessi were a Thracian people dwelling near Mount Haemus, described by Vegetius, III.11, and Claudian, *On the Consulship of Mallius*, 39, as exceptionally skilled at searching for gold through tunnels: “Whatever gold is rolled down by rivers; whatever hidden pale vein, traced from afar by its following light, the industry of the Bessi digs out.”] [Note: [Col. 0503C] A Callaician searcher. A people of Spain inhabiting the region now called Galicia, where Pliny, XIII.4, says there was a great abundance of gold.] He believed purer and more splendid that which had been given in pain, which human tears rather than river waters had washed, which had not been dug from earthly caverns but excavated from the necks and throats of slaughtered men.

Thus, when both the pen—meaning proscriptions—and the sword of the cruel tyrant were feared, [Note: [Col. 0503C] And the pen. That is, proscriptions. It is a legal term: Cicero, *For Cluentius*, calls it “the censorial pen and the dictatorial sword.”] poverty had become an object of prayer, and in order that we might escape the executioner we wished to submit to the auctioneer. [Note: [Col. 0503D] To submit to the auctioneer. Budé says that those were properly called *sectores* who, by bringing accusations, obtained confiscations from rulers, sometimes ruining innocent persons of all their property. Asconius and nearly all jurists after him hold this view. Above there is mention of children playing beneath the auctioneer.] If anyone thinks that he was less cruel than usual in these crimes, let him remember the death of the triumphal Vallio [Note: [Col. 0503D] The triumphal Vallio. Balduin and Puteanus, from Ambrose, Letter 27, restore Balio for Vallio. There Ambrose says that Balio, a distinguished soldier, when Maximus ordered him killed, laid hands upon himself. Some think this Vallio or Balio was none other than Saturninus, consul with Merobaudes when Gratian was killed. But those who understand him as the consul Bauto are mistaken; Ambrose plainly contradicts them, adding in the same passage that Maximus wished to decide concerning Bauto as though he were another Balio.] and of Merobaudes in the consular robe. [Note: [Col. 0504C] Merobaudes in the *trabea*. That is, consul when Gratian was slain. Idatius reports in his *Chronicle* that Merobaudes was Spanish by birth and distinguished in eloquence, especially poetry. When he joined the fleeing Gratian in order to escort him into Italy to his brother Valentinian, both were overtaken at Lyon by Andragathius. Therefore Prosper’s common recension gravely errs in saying that Gratian fled after being defeated at Paris by the treachery of Merobaudes, master of soldiers.]

After the highest magistracies, consular purple, and a kind of senate of offices gathered into one household, [Note: [Col. 0504C] And gathered together. After he had brought every magistracy and senatorial dignity into his own household.] the former was compelled to renounce life; the latter had his throat broken at home by the hands of British guards [Note: [Col. 0504C] British guards. Maximus had first seized tyranny in Britain.] and was branded with the disgrace of a woman’s death [Note: [Col. 0504C] A woman’s death. A cowardly death.]—as though a man especially fond of the sword had preferred to die by a noose rather than by the sword. [Note: [Col. 0504B] With the reproach of an ignoble death imposed, as though, etc.] But perhaps the tyrant might be thought to have had special grounds of hatred against them: each had stood in Gratian’s battle line, and Gratian had loved them both. What shall we say of those who, knowing nothing of honors or the friendship of emperors, [Note: [Col. 0504B] Those inexperienced in honors and in the friendship of emperors.] distinguished only among their own people, poured out noble lives beneath the executioner?

XXIX. I speak of the deaths of men—when I recall the descent to the blood of women, and the merciless savagery inflicted even upon the sex which wars spare. Yet, of course, there were grave and odious grounds for dragging to punishment with the hook the wife of a famous poet.

> **[Note: Col. 0504C] “With the hook to punishment.”** We have said above, in the notes on Pliny’s *Panegyric*, ch. 33, note 11, that the condemned were customarily dragged to death with the hook.

> **[Note: Col. 0504D] “The wife of a famous poet.”** Euchrocia, wife of the poet Delphidius, concerning whom Ausonius, *On the Professors of Bordeaux*, poem 6. She was condemned to death at Trier, together with many others implicated in the same offence, on account of Priscillian’s errors. (Prosper, *Chronicle*.)

For excessive devotion and too scrupulous a worship of the divinity were alleged—indeed, cast reproachfully in the teeth—of the widow.

> **[Note: Col. 0504D] “Widow.”** Delphidius having died.

What graver charge could a priestly accuser bring?

> **[Note: Col. 0504D] “A priestly accuser.”** He means Bishop Hydatius; for he immediately adds, “bishops in name, but in truth henchmen.” Ambrose relates that Hydatius was excommunicated because, not content with proscribing Priscillian’s errors, he demanded Priscillian’s blood before the royal consistory and accused many holy men—above all St Martin—before the emperor as guilty of the same error. Since several bishops among those at Maximus’ court followed this precedent of cruelty, St Ambrose refused communion with them.

For there was—there was also this breed of informers: men who were bishops in name, but in truth henchmen, indeed executioners; not content with stripping wretches of their ancestral estates, they levelled calumnious accusations aimed at bloodshed and oppressed the lives of defendants already impoverished.

> **[Note: Col. 0504B] “Stripping.”** *Evertisse*, “to have overthrown” or “stripped.”

Indeed, when they had stood beside capital trials—

> **[Note: Col. 0504D] “Capital.”** That is, trials in which the life of the accused was at issue.

—when they had drunk in with eyes and ears the groans and tortures of the wretched; when they had handled the weapons of the lictors and the restraints—

> **[Note: Col. 0505C] “Restraints.”** *Vincula*.

> **[Note: Col. 0505C] “Bridles.”** *Fraena*. Or perhaps *funera*, “funerals,” as Livineius emends.

—of the condemned, they brought hands polluted by contact with punishment back to sacred rites, and defiled in body as well the ceremonies which they had already violated in spirit.

> **[Note: Col. 0505C] “They defiled.”** *Polluebant*.

That Phalaris kept such men among his friends.

> **[Note: Col. 0505C] “Phalaris.”** The cruelty of Phalaris, tyrant of the Agrigentines, is proverbial; when one seeks an example of a ferocious tyrant, he immediately comes to mind.

They were in his eyes—

> **[Note: Col. 0505C] “In his eyes.”** *Esse alicui in oculis*, “to be in someone’s eyes,” is a Ciceronian and Terentian expression for being exceptionally loved. As for *esse in osculis*, “to be in kisses,” I do not know where else it is found.

—and even in his kisses; nor without reason, since from them came at once all that he desired: for the greedy man, the goods of the rich; for the bloodthirsty man, punishment of the innocent; for the impious man, injury to religion.

> **[Note: Col. 0505C] “Violation.”** *Violatio*.

XXX. At last God turned His eyes toward us; intent upon the blessings of the East, He looked back upon our miseries and set madness before this most accursed head.

> **[Note: Col. 0505C] “He cast [madness] upon a most wicked man.”** *Homini improbissimo injecit.*

> **[Note: Col. 0505C–0505D] “He set madness before him.”** The ancients thought that evil counsels were sent into human minds by angry gods. Pacatus therefore here attributes Maximus’ madness to God, patron of the whole East. Thus Homer, *Iliad* I.8:  
> “Which of the gods set these two at strife, to fight?”  
> Cicero, *For Milo*, 88: “The immortal gods, as I said above, gave that ruined and frenzied man the thought to lay an ambush for this man; otherwise that pest could not have perished.” Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* X.72:  
> “What god drove us into treachery—what harsh power of ours?”

He did so that he might not fear to break the treaty—

> **[Note: Col. 0505D] “To break the treaty.”** Maximus, having formed the design of invading Italy, feared that he might be overwhelmed while crossing the Alps. Accordingly, when Domninus, whom Valentinian had sent as envoy from Aquileia, whither he had withdrawn, ostensibly requested peace, Maximus assented; but secretly followed him back with his army and suddenly occupied Italy. (Prosper Pithaeus.)

—to violate the law of the fetiales—

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “To violate the law of the fetiales.”** That is, to wage war before the fetiales had been sent. War could not lawfully be undertaken unless they had declared both that it was undertaken for a just cause and that it had first been formally proclaimed. (Varro.)

—and to declare war. Am I to think that this occurred without divine agency: that the man who, under the name of peace, could have played false and, by remaining quiet, escaped the penalties of his first crime—

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “His first crime.”** The penalty for having seized the imperial power.

—should raise a second and third standard of civil brigandage; that, after crossing the Cottian Alps, he should also force open the Julian barriers and lay upon you, Emperor, the necessity of conquering, though the assurance of pardon was still preserved?

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “The Cottian Alps.”** The Alps are partly Cottian and partly Julian, etc.

The commonwealth, I suppose, was driving him headlong toward the avenger now close at hand; and the lord whom he had extinguished by open parricide—

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “The lord.”** Gratian.

—was demanding from him the punishment due. It was not confidence, but madness; not recklessness, but necessity. Nor was he of his own accord provoking you to war; rather, he could no longer withdraw himself further from death.

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “To withdraw himself from death.”** *Se subducere morti.*

For otherwise how could one so cowardly and so afraid of death have conceived such audacity as to dare rush upon the sword and meet death face to face—he who later, even when defeated, was unable to kill himself?

And for you indeed, most august Emperor, merely to come into the war would have sufficed to restore the commonwealth and claim the victory. For if in former times masters, about to fight rebellious slaves, brought whips into battle-line, and the force of conscience was so great that armed men turned from the unarmed, and those who had offered their breasts to death gave their backs to the lash, would you not likewise, with your legions idle, have seemed to accomplish the whole affair?

> **[Note: Col. 0506C–0506D] “They brought whips into battle-line.”** Herodotus at the beginning of *Melpomene*, Justin, book II, and Claudian, *Against Eutropius* I.508, relate this of the Scythians: “When, after many years of campaigns, the fierce Scythian returned and a youth of servile stock came against him upon his own borders, keeping the masters from their recovered land, they routed the armed line by displaying whips.”

XXXI. Could that most negligent little house-born slave of your household—

> **[Note: Col. 0506D] “A most negligent little house-born slave.”** Namely Maximus, whom Ausonius soon calls a “stationary camp-follower”; Pacatus calls him an “armour-bearing camp-follower.” Yet Zosimus, book IV, says that Maximus was Theodosius’ fellow soldier. But what trust, as I have often said, is to be placed in that author? Unless perhaps he calls him Theodosius’ fellow soldier because he waited on him while fighting like a servant or house-slave. A *vernula* is one born of a female slave; so the gloss of the Basel edition.

—and a stationary camp-follower at slaves’ tables, have endured your presence and borne the mere glance of your eyes? Would not the recollection of his own past and yours have immediately overwhelmed the whole man? Would he not have set before himself that you were the son of a triumphal man—

> **[Note: Col. 0506D] “The son of a triumphal man.”** Theodosius’ father had earned triumphal honours after conquering the Goths.

—but that he was of uncertain fatherhood?

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “Himself of uncertain fatherhood.”** *Se incerti patris.*

That you were heir to a most noble family, but he its client?

> **[Note: Col. 0506D] “A client.”** Of your family.

That you had, throughout all preceding time, been commander of the Roman army and champion of liberty; but that he was an exile from the world and a fugitive from his fatherland?

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “Driven out by all and expelled from his country.”** *Se ejectum ab omnibus et patria pulsum.*

> **[Note: Col. 0506D] “An exile from the world.”** Because he was born in Britain, which lies separated from the whole world.

That you had been desired as prince in the very bosom of the commonwealth, by the vote of all the soldiers, the agreement of the provinces, and finally the eager desire of the emperor himself; while he, in the remotest recess of the earth, with legions unaware, the inclinations of the provinces hostile—

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “Hostile.”** *Adversantibus.*

—and with no auspices whatever, had aspired to the theft of that tyrannical title? Finally: that with you were fidelity, right, justice, clemency, chastity, and religion; with him, perfidy, wrong, injustice, impiety, lust, cruelty, and the entire fellowship of every crime and every ultimate vice?

Let us ask the facts themselves; and, by the surest inference, let us gather what was to be done from what has been done.

> **[Note: Col. 0506C] “Let us judge actions still to be performed from actions performed.”** *Ex gestis rebus gerendas aestimemus.*

Can there at last be any doubt what he would have done in your presence, when he fled from you whom he never saw?

XXXII. Although, therefore, Emperor, you had before you such an enemy to misuse, and came not so much to join battle as to exact punishment from that impious head, still you conducted the war with counsels so great and calculations so weighty that you appeared to be about to contend with some Perseus, or Pyrrhus, or Hannibal himself.

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “As with Perseus.”** Perseus, the last king of Macedonia, whom Aemilius defeated. See Livy, book XL, Justin, book XXXIII; and concerning Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, see Plutarch.

First, you secured by pledged and received right hands the loyalty of the kings around whom the eastern frontier is bounded, so that you might act securely abroad, having left nothing troublesome or suspect at home. Then you divided your forces three ways—

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “Into three parts.”** *Trifariam.*

—so as both to strike down the enemy’s audacity with multiplied terror and to surround him, cutting off every avenue of flight.

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “Enclosing and blocking his path of escape on every side.”** *Fugiendi viam undequaque involvens praecluderes.*

Finally, you granted the title of fellow soldiers to barbarian peoples—

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “Barbarian peoples.”** The Scythian nations, as he says shortly afterward.

—who voluntarily promised you their service, so that a suspect force might leave the frontier—

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “The frontier.”** The Danubian frontier.

—and auxiliaries might join your army.

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “You grant this so that suspect men may depart from the frontier and join your forces as auxiliaries.”**

Drawn by your generosity, all the Scythian nations flocked together in such vast hosts that you seemed, having released men from your own army, to have imposed a levy upon the barbarians. O deed worthy of remembrance! The enemy, once Roman, marched beneath Roman commanders and standards; he followed standards against which he had stood, and filled as a soldier the cities of Pannonia which he had long ago emptied by hostile devastation.

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “The cities of Pannonia.”** On Pannonia see the notes on Pliny’s *Panegyric*, ch. 8, note 5.

The Goth, the Hun, and the Alan answered to the roll-call, took turns in guard duty, and feared being marked absent.

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “And he feared being accused of having failed in his duty.”** *Et metuebat ne officio defuisse accusaretur.*

There was none of the tumult, confusion, or plunder customary with a barbarian.

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “As barbarians are accustomed [to do].”** *Ut barbari solent.*

Indeed, whenever the supply of grain became more difficult, he bore scarcity patiently; and by sparing provisions he enlarged the ration which his numbers had restricted.

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “And the grain supply which, because of the multitude, etc.”** *Et quam annonam ob multitudinem, etc.*

For every reward and every payment, he asked only this: that he might be called yours. How great is the ambition for excellence! You received a favour for which you might claim credit.

> **[Note: Col. 0507D] “You received a favour.”** They conferred a favour upon you in such a way that they thought you were incurring a great obligation to them.

XXXIII. Antiquity thought it memorable that in the Actian war foreign Egypt once mingled its arms with Roman commanders and Roman movements.

> **[Note: Col. 0507D] “In the Actian war.”** Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.685:  
> “Here Antony, victorious with barbarian aid and varied arms, brings with him Egypt, the strength of the East, and remotest Bactra, from the peoples of Dawn and the Red Shore.”

And the event was thought so extraordinary that, had it not repeatedly entered written record, belief in the deed would have seemed likely to fail among posterity.

> **[Note: Col. 0507C] “Unless this deed had often been transmitted in writing, it would scarcely have found credence among later generations.”**

What writer of annals or poetry, Cleopatra, has passed over those fleets of yours—

> **[Note: Col. 0507D] “Cleopatra.”** Concerning Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, and her magnificent fleet, Roman historians everywhere provide accounts.

—those ivory-decorated ships—

> **[Note: Col. 0508C] “Adorned with ivory.”** *Ebore ornata.*

—and purple sails with gilded ropes? Indeed, history has rehearsed the matter so constantly that it seems rather to have been often told by the same writers than ever omitted by any one of them.

I shall not compare the commanders. For I would not say that defeated Antony—or victorious Augustus—equalled our prince. But what comparable feature do we discover, at least in all else—especially if we set the circumstances and times on each side against one another and bring those peoples, here and there, before the eyes of our minds?

> **[Note: Col. 0507D] “Those peoples and these.”** An elegant contrast between Antony and Theodosius.

A fleet, entrusted to the winds, had brought the former as they set sail.

> **[Note: Col. 0508C] “Entrusted to the winds.”** *Ventis permissa.*

These men were making their long march beneath the burden of arms.

> **[Note: Col. 0507D] “Beneath the burden of arms.”** Compare Virgil, *Georgics* III.346: “Just so the keen Roman, under the burden of his native arms, makes his way, etc.”

> **[Note: Col. 0508C] “Burden.”** *Onere.*

A queen, sighing with foreign passion—Antony’s mistress—had enticed the former.

> **[Note: Col. 0508C] “With foreign fire.”** Inflamed by love for Antony.

Love of glory and concern to share in renown carried off the latter. The sluggish Pharos, soft Canopus, and the Nile, nourisher of effeminate peoples, had sent out the former.

> **[Note: Col. 0508C] “Pharos.”** Once an island opposite the mouth of the Nile and a day’s sail from the mainland, it is now joined to Alexandria by a bridge. There stood a huge tower, in which lights kindled at night guided sailors’ course; hence watchtowers built for a similar purpose were called *phari*.

> **[Note: Col. 0508C] “Soft Canopus.”** A city of Egypt at the mouth of the Nile; the Canopic region is called “soft” because the Egyptians were effeminate.

> **[Note: Col. 0508D] “The nourishing Nile.”** On the Nile, nourisher of Egypt because it fertilizes that land with its floods, see the notes on Pliny’s *Panegyric*, ch. 30.

Threatening Caucasus, freezing Taurus, and the Danube, hardener of mighty bodies, had poured forth the latter.

> **[Note: Col. 0508D] “Threatening Caucasus.”** A part of the Taurus range, between the Euxine and Caspian seas. It is called threatening because it is high, precipitous, and like something falling.

> **[Note: Col. 0508D] “Freezing Taurus.”** Because of the snows with which that mountain is mostly covered.

> **[Note: Col. 0508D] “The Danube, hardener of mighty bodies.”** That is, the hardener of the Germans, a people of tall stature.

The former, shining through delicate garments and scarcely able to bear even light linen against the sun, were led by rattling sistrums shaken in alternating rhythm.

> **[Note: Col. 0508C] “To ward off the sun.”** *Ad arcendum solem.*

> **[Note: Col. 0508D] “Sistrums led them.”** Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.696, concerning Queen Cleopatra: “In their midst she calls her troops with her native sistrum.” On the shape and form of the sistrum, see our Ruaeus on this passage of Virgil.

The latter, burdened with cuirasses and enclosed in iron, were sharpened by the harsh blasts of trumpets and the clamour of enormous horns.

> **[Note: Col. 0508C] “Cuirasses.”** *Cataphractis.*

> **[Note: Col. 0509C] “Harsh sounds of trumpets.”** Unmelodious sounds. Virgil, *Georgics* IV.72: “And a voice is heard imitating the broken sounds of trumpets.”

What comparison of peoples could there ultimately be, even if the causes driving them to war had not been so different: that those men sought the enslavement of the Roman Empire, while these sought the recovery of liberty?

> **[Note: Col. 0509C] “Even if the causes that impelled them to war had not been so different: those attacked the liberty of the Roman Empire, while these defended their own.”**

How much more shameful did it seem to you, Emperor, that anyone could have been found to share in that crime, for which even the barbarian did not refuse to act as avenger?

> **[Note: Col. 0509C] “That any accomplice in that crime could have been found, when even the barbarians did not refuse to be its avengers.”**

XXXIV. But those men, who steeped the first-fruits of battle in impious blood, furnished proof that guilt and punishment were equal. Siscia bears witness.

> **[Note: Col. 0509C] “Siscia.”** Or Sisak: a famous city of Pannonia on the Save or Sava River and its island Segestica, by which one goes from Pannonia into Italy. Strabo, book V, and Pliny, book III, ch. 25, discuss it. Here Maximus was first defeated.

The glorious conflict on the Sava bears witness—

> **[Note: Col. 0509D] “The glorious conflict on the Sava.”** I depart from Puteanus, whose text reads “the conflict on the most beautiful river,” and follow Cuspinianus’ manuscript. For the Savus or Sava is the river at Siscia at which the battle was fought and Maximus defeated by Theodosius.

—if it should be called a conflict at all: in it the army, full of wrath against public traitors, charged with such force that neither the number of those resisting nor the depth of that great river delayed it. Panting and dusty as it was from its very long journey, it spurred the horses on, crossed the river by swimming, leapt upon the bank, and at last caught its enemy ready and waiting.

> **[Note: Col. 0509C] “It charged.”** *Irruit.*

This account is longer than the event itself. Hardly had the unconquered force crossed the river when it held the field of battle. Hardly had it found the enemy when it pressed him. Hardly had it seen their breasts when it was cutting down their backs. The rebel battle-line is given over to its deserved destruction; impious crowds roll in their own blood; one slaughter covers whole fields, and all things far and wide are buried beneath unbroken heaps of corpses.

Already those who had hurried toward the walls in order to defer death were either filling the ditches level with corpses—

> **[Note: Col. 0509C] “To defer death.”** *Ad differendam necem.*

—or were impaled upon the points of stakes opposed to them—

> **[Note: Col. 0509C] “They were driven upon the opposing points of stakes.”** *Impingebant in adversos sudium mucrones.*

—or were closing by their deaths the gates which they had opened in their sortie. But those before whom the river, impassable in flight, had thrown up its banks, gathered in panic and embraced one another, every man clutching another, and were rolled together down the precipices. The river foamed discoloured with blood and, scarcely struggling free of corpses, forced onward its obstructed channels.

> **[Note: Col. 0509C] “And it moves its waters only with difficulty.”** *Et fluctus aegre agit.*

And so that it might claim for itself a distinctive military service on your behalf—

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “That it might in its own manner be able to serve and favour you.”** *Ut suo modo tibi militare posset ac favere.*

—it swallowed in its greedy whirlpools the very standard-bearer of that sacrilegious faction—

> **[Note: Col. 0509D] “The standard-bearer of the sacrilegious faction.”** He means Andragathius.

—and, lest burial should accompany death, concealed his corpse. Must we not believe that the river laboured for your vengeance in both ways: by assisting the victory and by forestalling clemency?

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “In both respects.”** *Utraque re.*

> **[Note: Col. 0509D] “By forestalling clemency.”** By leaving no place for clemency.

XXXV. Behold for you a second battle and a second victory. Marcellinus was leading chosen cohorts into battle, together with the very strength of the impious faction; that Megaera of civil war carried them forward.

> **[Note: Col. 0509D] “The Megaera of civil war.”** Marcellinus, brother of the tyrant Maximus. The other defeat of Maximus occurred at Poetovio, when Marcellinus was slain, as Ambrose seems to indicate in Epistle 29.

He was bolder than all the other henchmen by as much as a tyrant’s brother gave more strenuous service to the tyrant.

> **[Note: Col. 0509D] “More strenuous.”** Statius uses *exertum bellum* for open war. Here it means more intense or vehement. For he “exerts himself” who puts every sinew to work and leaves nothing untried.

Your army was especially delighted at this, when it saw itself voluntarily challenged—an army which had feared nothing more than being feared.

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “Than being feared.”** Compare Claudian, lines 235 and 240: “A wondrous thing to tell: you fear being feared.”

Thus, when the camps had been set opposite camps and the steeply declining day did not permit them to join battle, it spent the night sleepless in expectation of the victory that daylight would bring.

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “Declining.”** *Inclinante.*

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “It spent the night.”** *Noctem ageret.*

It accused the slow sun, the deserting day, and the year-long duration of a summer night, as though it were longer than a year.

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “It accused the summer night as though it were longer than a year.”** *Aestivam noctem accusaret, quasi anno longiorem.*

At last dawn came, and now the whole plain bristled with armed forces: cavalry divided into wings; light-armed skirmishers before the standards; cohorts arrayed by maniples; and square legions advancing in full step occupied the whole expanse as far as sight could reach.

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “Divided into wings.”** In an army, “wings” are the parts of the battle-line projecting on either side. One is the right wing, the other the left; the space between them is called the centre.

> **[Note: Col. 0510C–0510D] “Light-armed skirmishers.”** Soldiers of light equipment and more swift in running because they did not use heavier armour. Some think they were called *velites* as though *velati*, “clothed,” because they were dressed rather than armed; others derive the name from swiftness, as though *volites*, with *o* changed into *e*; others again derive it from Greek *βάλλειν*, “to throw,” because they fought chiefly with javelins and slings. (Livy, book VI of the Punic War.)

> **[Note: Col. 0510D] “By maniples.”** That is, in maniples. According to Livy, a maniple contained twenty light-armed soldiers and another group of shield-bearers. Vegetius, however, writes in book II of *Military Affairs* that a maniple is a tent-group of only ten soldiers living beneath one and the same roof. See Lipsius, *On the Roman Military System*, book II.

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “And, driving their columns in close ranks, they had filled from afar the spaces which the eye could reach.”**

> **[Note: Col. 0510D] “Square legions.”** A legion was called square from the form and order which it held in battle, not because it consisted of four thousand soldiers, as some wrongly suppose. But on this matter, see above.

Courage had not yet made trial of itself; already discipline was victorious. But after each line advanced within missile-range, and showers of javelins and arrows were poured out on either side, the matter came to the sword-hilts.

> **[Note: Col. 0510D] “The matter came to the hilts.”** That is, close fighting began with swords drawn.

> **[Note: Col. 0510C] “To swords.”** *Ad gladios.*

The soldiers, mindful of their former valour, of the Roman name, and finally of their emperors, fought for the public cause with their hands. The enemy, thinking of their purchased service, Italy torn apart, and their sole remaining hope in the sword, fought with a gladiator’s desperation; they did not give ground but stood or fell where they stood.

XXXVI. But when the battle-line had been driven back, its front loosened, and confidence turned to flight—

> **[Note: Col. 0511C] “Confidence turned to flight.”** That is, hope began to be placed in flight. The phrase is taken from Nazarius’ panegyric of Constantine, ch. 28: “when the line has loosened or the front, struck back, has begun to stagger, confidence in hands has turned to feet.”

—they rushed headlong away, or fled in groups, and by hurrying delayed one another. Armed and unarmed, sound and wounded, first and last, were mingled. The soldiers pressed them from afar and near at hand, striking with swords and spears, thrusting and cutting.

> **[Note: Col. 0511C] “To strike by thrusting and cutting.”** Sometimes they directed the point; sometimes they swung the whole mass of the sword. Livy and Vegetius use this mode of expression; it itself became proverbial for doing something with all one’s strength and effort.

Some struck at hamstrings; others pierced backs; or, when they could not overtake men by running, they reached them with missiles.

> **[Note: Col. 0511D] “To press upon the hamstrings.”** Compare Horace, *Odes* III.4: “Death pursues even the fleeing man, and spares neither the hamstrings of unwarlike youth nor the cowardly back.”

> **[Note: Col. 0511D] “Reach.”** I restore *contingere* with Gruter in place of *continere*.

> **[Note: Col. 0511C] “To overtake.”** *Assequi.*

Weapons, missiles, horses, men—living and slain bodies, bodies face down and face up—lay scattered everywhere or heaped together. Some, with limbs mutilated or cut off, fled in what remained of themselves; others followed the pain of their wounds; still others carried received mortal blows into woods and rivers.

> **[Note: Col. 0511C] “Mortal blows received.”** *Acceptas lethales plagas.*

There they breathed out their last breath in admiration of your name and hatred of their own commander. There was no end to killing and pursuit until death at last took the enemy away from the victors, and night took away the day.

But how much better did that body of men decide, which, lowering its standards in supplication, sought pardon for necessity—

> **[Note: Col. 0511D] “Pardon for necessity.”** It asked to be forgiven for having fought against you under compulsion of necessity.

—and, pressing the earth with kisses, cast down bodies and weapons to be trodden beneath your feet.

> **[Note: Col. 0511C] “By your footsteps.”** *Gressibus tuis.*

You did not pass them by proudly, as conquered men; not angrily, as guilty men; not negligently, as men of little use; but ordered that they be treated with kindness and generosity as Romans. Allied battle-lines were joined, and the distinct limbs of the commonwealth grew together under one head. Both armies were borne forward with equal joy: one rejoiced in its service, the other in its pardon, and both in victory.

XXXVII. Nor did loyal Haemona delay too long.

> **[Note: Col. 0511D–0512C] “Haemona.”** A city on the route from Siscia to Aquileia, today Laibach [Ljubljana]. Rhenanus errs, as Livineius rightly observes, in substituting Narona for Haemona. For how could Theodosius lead an army hurrying “to join Illyricum to Aquileia in the space of a single day,” as Pacatus says, back by a very long route into the deepest part of Illyricum, where Narona lies? Baldwin thinks the passage refers to Aquileia itself, where Maximus was finally defeated; but, in my opinion, incorrectly.

Once it was announced that you were coming, it burst through its opened gates and rushed forth to meet you. As every longing, after hope has arisen, is more impatient, it scarcely believed the way open enough for one who was arriving and hurried to meet one who was coming.

Fear, as we know, can counterfeit joy; yet the face, betrayer of the mind’s deepest feelings, so reveals them that the image of souls appears in the mirror of brows.

> **[Note: Col. 0511C] “It can counterfeit joy.”** *Laetitiam simulare potest.*

> **[Note: Col. 0512C] “It indicates.”** *Indicat.*

Like a city recovering breath after a long siege—for the tyrant, occupying the Alpine approaches, had worn it down as though it were the threshold of war—it displayed itself with such great and unfeigned exultation that, if its joy had not been real, it would have seemed excessive.

> **[Note: Col. 0512C] “So unfeigned.”** *Tam non fucata.*

Bands of dancers came streaming out to meet you. Everything rang with song and rattles.

> **[Note: Col. 0512C] “Rattles.”** A *crotalum* was a noisemaker of wood, bronze, or other material so fashioned that, struck by the hand, it could make a sound. *Crotala* are named from Greek *κρούειν*, “to strike.”

One chorus sang your triumph; another sang before the tyrant funeral dirges and a burial song.

> **[Note: Col. 0512C–0512D] “Dirges.”** Quintilian, book VIII, ch. 2: “A funeral song is properly called a *naenia*, from *νειάτον*, ‘last’; for it was the last thing sung over the dead, to the flute, before the corpse was buried.” Horace, *Odes* II.20: “Let dirges be absent from my empty funeral, and shameful mourning and lamentation, etc.”

One desired perpetual departure for the defeated; the other frequent arrival for the victors. Wherever you turned your step, people followed, ran around you, and hurried ahead; indeed, they blocked the roads on which you were carried. No regard for themselves or for you restrained anyone: the stubborn extravagance of their joys committed a pleasant injury against you.

> **[Note: Col. 0512C] “An excessively obstinate expression of joy.”** *Significatio laetitiae nimis obstinata.*

Why should I recount the festive procession of free-born nobility before their walls: senators conspicuous in white dress; priests venerable in municipal purple; priests distinguished by their pointed caps?

> **[Note: Col. 0512C] “Before their walls.”** *Ad moenia.*

> **[Note: Col. 0512D] “Priests in municipal purple.”** This passage seems to show that priests in certain cities possessed the right to wear purple.

> **[Note: Col. 0512D] “Distinguished by pointed caps.”** That is, marked by caps tapering to a point. Because they could not wear them in summer without discomfort, and because it was unlawful to go wholly bareheaded, they bound them with a thread; hence they were called *flamines*, as though *filamines*.

Why recount the gates crowned with green garlands; the streets waving with hangings; the day prolonged by lighted torches?

> **[Note: Col. 0512C] “Adorned with waving tapestries.”** *Ornatas undantibus tapetis.*

Why recount the crowd pouring out from their homes; old men congratulating you upon their years; boys vowing you a long freedom from servitude; happy mothers and secure maidens?

> **[Note: Col. 0512D] “Of homes.”** That is, a multitude poured out of houses. Some read *bonorum*, “of the good”; in other editions the word is entirely deleted.

> **[Note: Col. 0512D] “Old men congratulating [you] upon their years.”** Compare Pliny, *Panegyric*, ch. 22: “Little children know you, young men point you out, old men marvel at you, etc.”

You had not yet finished the whole war; already you were celebrating a triumph.

XXXVIII. Meanwhile Maximus went on; looking back over his shoulder at you, he fled in the stunned manner of a madman. He pursued no counsel, no plan, nor even that hope which is last to desert humankind.

> **[Note: Col. 0513D] “Which is last to desert humankind.”** That well-known little verse of Tibullus, book II, elegy 6: “Hope sustains us and always says that tomorrow will be better.” Aldus Manutius gathered many further passages from the best authors into one collection in his notes on Catiline.

> **[Note: Col. 0513C] “He retained [nothing] remaining.”** *Reliquam habebat.*

Rather, he entangled even the errors of his route; now turning right or left, now meeting his own tracks, he wove an uncertain course in a double winding.

> **[Note: Col. 0513C] “At one moment he was carried this way, at another that way; at one moment he retraced his footsteps.”**

How often, do we suppose, did he say to himself: “Where am I fleeing? Shall I attempt war? Shall I withstand in part the man whom I could not endure with all my strength? Shall I block the Cottian Alps?

> **[Note: Col. 0513C] “I shall block them.”** *Praecludam.*

The Julian Alps helped me so well!

> **[Note: Col. 0513D] “Because the Julian Alps helped.”** Ironically; for the Julian Alps had been of no help at all, and Theodosius had burst through them.

“Shall I seek Africa? I have exhausted it. Shall I return to Britain? I have left it. Shall I entrust myself to Gaul? But I am hated there.”

> **[Note: Col. 0513D] “I am hated.”** Because of Gratian’s murder.

“Shall I commit myself to Spain? But I am known there. What then shall I do, caught between arms and hatreds? Enemies press me from behind, crimes face me from before. If only I died, I should escape!”

> **[Note: Col. 0513D] “I should escape.”** “I should have escaped these evils.”

But look: neither hand follows his will, nor sword his hand; the steel slips, his right hand trembles, and his mind fails.

> **[Note: Col. 0513C] “Nor does his hand obey his will.”** *Nec voluntati manus paret.*

> **[Note: Col. 0513C] “His spirit fails.”** *Animus deficit.*

O how difficult it is even for wretches to die! Therefore, as a beast caught in nets, after long seeking an exit and despairing of one, comes to a standstill and does not flee because of fear, so he, bound by the very fear which drove him, cast himself into the town of Aquileia—not to defend his life by resistance, but to delay punishment by evasion. Yet what further delay was possible, when the ardent soldier pressed so closely upon his tracks and back that swift vengeance had nearly anticipated the whole procession which followed?

> **[Note: Col. 0513D] “It anticipated.”** Read, with Acidalus and Livineius, *praeceperit*, “had anticipated.”

XXXIX. Rightly indeed that shared fiction of painters and poets—

> **[Note: Col. 0513C] “Common fictions of painters and poets.”** *Pictoribus et poetis communia figmenta.*

> **[Note: Col. 0513D] “Of painters and poets.”** There is a great affinity between painters and poets. Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 361:

As in painting, so in poetry, etc.] Painters’ and poets’ inventions have represented Victory as winged. [Note: What Fortune favours do not so much go as fly.] For the movement of men advancing with Fortune is not a course but a flight. That army, snatched up from the remotest gulf of the East [Col. 0513C] by hurried marches, exhausted by leaving behind so many nations, swimming so many rivers, and climbing so many mountains, stationed in another world and beneath another—almost, I would say—sun, traversed the distance from Illyricum to Aquileia within the span of a single day’s light. [Note: It came from Illyricum and reached Aquileia.] Yet your soldiers claim no credit for this. [Note: They do not wish any praise to be attributed to them on that account.] Whenever they gather circles of admiring hearers, [Note: When they draw around themselves circles of people wondering at them and eagerly clustering in assemblies and gatherings to hear them recount their achievements, as in Horace, *Odes* II.13, where, while Alcaeus sings, “The dense crowd drinks in battles and expelled tyrants with shoulder and ear.”] or prolong our banquets with their conversation, they set the whole measure of their exertion at the boundary of the Alps, and deny that the speed belongs to them, since they found themselves arriving, without having experienced the exertions, at a place to which they had not felt themselves going. Indeed, they deny that they were borne by their own bodies, but say that, as though carried through some images of dreams, they were conveyed absent, offering to the winds that bore them the services of idle limbs. [Note: “Absent”: perhaps “compliant,” as Livincius and Acidalius conjecture.]

Nor is the evidence doubtful. For if the stern men of old believed that the twin Castors—Castor and Pollux, twin brothers born of Leda and Jupiter—distinguished by white horses and starry crests, washed Thessalian dust and blood in the waters of the Tiber, announced victory, and rendered military service to the Romans in that battle, why should we not suppose that some acknowledged care of the immortal God laboured for your vengeance and that of the state? Unless perhaps the Roman state required a greater work of divine favour in order to enlarge the Macedonian kingdom than to release itself from tyrannical servitude. [Note: The reference is to the aid they rendered the Romans in that battle.]

But I, if heavenly concern is to be assessed according to the worthiness of causes, would rightly maintain that your cavalry were carried by Pegasi, [Note: “Pegasian”: it is unnecessary to say anything about Pegasus, who is very well known from the poets’ fables.] and your infantry borne aloft and suspended by winged sandals. [Note: “By winged sandals”: by *talaria* he means the wings which Pegasus is said to have had on his feet.] For because divine powers disdain to disclose themselves to mortal eyes, we should not for that reason doubt that things which were not seen have been done, when we see accomplished the very things whose accomplishment we had doubted. [Note: Since divine things withdraw themselves from mortal eyes, we ought not to doubt that what was not seen occurred, when we see the thing accomplished—namely, the defeat of Maximus—which we had thought scarcely capable of occurring.]

### XL.

[Note: Whoever thinks so sparingly of your good fortune.] He thinks too narrowly of your fortune, Emperor, whoever believes of you only what can happen.
