When, from the Julian Alps onward, I see not a battle but a triumph, with the sword idle and kept holiday, should I doubt that I have called this some special military service of your good fortune? [Note: The obedience of Fortune, as though serving you.] We know indeed, Emperor, that you have administered everything in such a way that successes cannot claim credit with you, [Note: So that you owe nothing to accidents.] yet you must admit that Fortune did as much for you after the war as you yourself did in the war.

If we give her a voice and a judge, would she not recount her service at length and, while conceding much to your virtues, claim some share for herself? [Note: She would claim something for herself. The reference is to the passage in Cicero’s speech *Pro Marcello*, no. 6.] And why, I ask, should we not grant this, so that we may receive the assertions of both parties, when what you have conquered belongs to you? [Note: We should accept what each side claims for itself: whether something is attributed to Fortune or to courage, it is yours.]

I hear Constancy say: “I undertook a fierce and dangerous war.” I hear Endurance recall: “I endured an immense journey, through a season always harsh, armed throughout and often fasting.” I hear Prudence insist: “I divided the army and, by strategy, multiplied terror.” [Note: “I divided the army”: into three parts, as he said above in section 32, both to strike the enemy’s boldness with multiplied terror and to surround their flight.] I hear Courage assert: “Twice I fought the enemy; twice I conquered.” [Note: “Twice I fought the enemy”: at Siscia and Aquileia.] Finally, I hear them all cry: “What do we owe you, Fortune, whom we have made?”

But if she says: “I aided the soldiers’ haste, I impeded the enemy’s flight, I drove Maximus into the walls, and him whom you were forcing to die I preserved alive for his master,” I do not see what judgment could be rendered except that, while one party claims credit for the tyrant’s flight and the other for his preservation, the commonwealth, equally indebted to each, should reconcile both by confessing that it owes victory to the one and vengeance to the other. [Note: What judgment could be rendered concerning that dispute, unless, since one party attributes to itself the tyrant’s flight and the other his preservation alive, the commonwealth—which owes much to both—reconciles them by admitting, and so forth.]

### XLI.

Nor do you, for your part, disown or reject the gratitude due for this benefit. For although through yourself you accomplished what you wished, through Fortune nevertheless you obtained more than you wished. Come then, if you please: consult your former thoughts and consider your prayers. [Note: And see what you most earnestly desired.] Did you hope for anything further than that Maximus might be reported to you slain; that his half-living head, his eyes not yet wholly closed in death, might be brought back from the battlefield; or, at most, that he might be captured while fleeing or resisting? But when did you wish, or could you have wished, what actually happened: that he should preserve himself for you, that he should neither wish nor be able to bring about his own death?

Life is indeed, I admit, a great—indeed the greatest—object of love to human hearts, and death an object of horror, [Note: Life.] but only insofar as the former may be hoped for or the latter avoided. But if the final hour stands over one’s head, if the day that will never return has come, and death has declared itself, [Note: And the danger of death has become manifest,] the end is not feared when it is certain.

Hence criminals fear until condemnation; afterwards comes a stunned torpor, security born of despair, and a voluntary haste to the place of punishment, with no executioner dragging them. Not to mention those who, making a braver compact with fate, forestalled an uncertain end by a certain one; [Note: They anticipated it.] not to speak of slaves who escaped lashes by hanging, [Note: And, to escape their masters’ hands, rushed over precipices.] and fled their masters’ anger by rushing over precipices; who has ever feared beyond hope? [Note: Having lost hope.] Who, for that very reason, refused to kill himself in order that he might be killed?

[Note: “Beyond hope”: although nothing is so opposed to hope as fear, the wisest men have observed that, once every hope has been entirely removed, fear itself cannot remain. For the mind of one who fears must be suspended; if nothing at all remains of hope on which it may rest, it wholly collapses. The young Terence seems to have expressed this most elegantly, *Andria* II.1: “Alas for unhappy me! As my mind until now was intent alike upon hope and fear, so, once hope has been removed, exhausted and worn out by care, it is stunned.” Muretus, *Variae lectiones* XII.8.]

Unless another’s hand is less to be feared than one’s own, or a private death more shameful than a public one, or it is longer to submit oneself to the sword, burden the body with a wound, and receive death all at once, than to endure punishment in portions—to bend the knee, stretch out one’s neck for perhaps more than one blow.

[Note: Since these things are so, when Maximus resolved to lay hands upon himself, should he not be judged to have feared this kind of death no less than the others?]

### XLII.

And yet, when he judged that he must settle the matter with the sword, was he not rather afraid of fire, plates of heated metal, the cross, the *culeus*, and whatever else he deserved? [Note: The *culeus* was a sack made of linen, hemp, or leather, its name deriving from concealing or enclosing; offenders shut inside it were cast into running water. It was the punishment of parricides.] Surely he never thought so well of his own crimes as to hope for the death by which he perished. [Note: His own crimes were always better known to him than that, and so forth.]

Therefore, if the accused man could neither presume pardon, nor hope for escape while shut in, nor fear death when about to die, [Note: Since he could not avoid the final outcome,] and if, among certain extremities, a voluntary death must appear lighter than a compelled one, a private death more honourable than a public one, and a death anticipated shorter than one awaited, [Note: Who can doubt that, where reason had no place, everything must be attributed to Fortune?] who can doubt that, where reason had no place, Fortune was at work?

She, she blinded the tyrant’s counsels; she dulled both his spirit and his sword; she struck down—or restrained—the hand ready for the wound. [Note: Whether she struck it down, as some wish, or restrained it, is uncertain.]

Unless you, venerable Gratian, surrounded your own executioner with avenging Furies, and, an angry and threatening shade, shook before his face and smoking eyes torches blazing with infernal fire and crackling whips of twisted serpents, so that he might not attend to an honourable death; so that he might not pollute with impious blood that royal and sacrosanct dress; so that the attire once yours and thereafter to be your brothers’—Valentinian’s, Gratian’s brother—might not receive, even while vengeance was being exacted, the fatal stain of blood; and finally, so that the tyrant’s hand might not avenge you, and you might not owe Maximus even his own death. [Note: It was not fitting for your majesty that you should owe Maximus even his own death.]

The threatening shade reflects the ancient belief that the spirits of murdered persons were hostile to their murderers. Plato likewise reports this in Book IX of the *Laws*: thus a mother pursues Orestes in the tragedies; thus Virgil’s Dido threatens Aeneas (*Aeneid* IV.386):

> “In every place my shade shall be present:  
> You, wicked man, shall pay the penalty.”

### XLIII.

And indeed everything fell out so that vengeance appears not merely to have been preserved, but to have been ordered. [Note: What happened appears not merely to have involved vengeance, but to have involved vengeance taken in due order.] For whence, I ask, came so sudden a reversal, that he who had feared to meet death no longer feared to seek it, and courage brought forth the man whom fear had enclosed? [Note: He no longer hesitated.] Now no delay remained for hurrying matters on. Immediately the bravest commanders set about preparing the triumph: the diadem is struck from his head, the ornaments are removed from his shoulders, the adornment is torn from his feet, and, in short, the whole man is fitted for destruction. [Note: For the punishment of death.]

The public plunderer is publicly stripped; his rapacious hands are bound; the fugitive’s legs are bared; and he is offered to your eyes such as it was fitting that a captive be offered to a victor, a slave to his master, a tyrant to an emperor.

Nor would you, in your clemency, have wished him to come into your sight, lest a man destined for death should profane eyes that bring salvation to all, except that you wished to refute the report of a lie and clear yourself by the testimony of the very man who had accused you. [Note: He had been your accuser.]

A guilty mind has strength; it has, I know not what inward executioners; either conscience itself is its own executioner, or—as I rather believe—it is harsher than every torture to be questioned by you. [Note: More dreadful than any torture.] At your first word confession was shaken out of that impious breast; nor could he even hesitate or mutter without laying bare his whole plan: namely, that he had put forward the pretext of your favour because he could not otherwise entice the soldiers into partnership, unless he had pretended that you were the author of his enlistment. [Note: “Auctoramenti sui”: this reading is restored from the Viennese edition and the emendation of all interpreters; other editions read, “unless he had pretended that he was the author of your enlistment.”]

[Note: “Auctoramenti sui”: unless he had pretended that you were the author of his enlistment.]

### XLIV.

And after this statement, you did not order him raised upon a cross, sewn into a sack, torn limb from limb, or finally that tongue guilty of so great a lie be torn out by the roots, together with that portion of his vital organs which had uttered the invention? [Note: The part of the inner organs from which his lie had proceeded.]

Rather, you had already begun to hesitate concerning his death; you cast down your eyes, your face was suffused with blushes, and you spoke with pity. But it is well that you cannot do everything: the gods avenge you even against your will. [Note: This is taken from the panegyric in which Eumenius says to Constantine, concerning Maximian, likewise killed by soldiers: “The gods avenge you even against your will.”]

Thus he is snatched from your sight—as Socrates relates—and, lest clemency should have any opportunity, is carried through countless hands to death. Look away again, Emperor, and shrink from the account of the tyrant’s end. Now, now be at ease: I shall comply with the custom of your clemency; you shall not hear what you did not wish to see.

Come here, come here, all you inspired prophets of learned nights; devote your entire care to this subject and celebrate it in every language and form of literature. Do not be anxious about the permanence of your works. The immortality which you have usually supplied to histories will come from History herself. [Note: From history itself, from the dignity of history.]

You too, artists, to whom belongs the second lot—the hope of immortal glory placed after poets and writers, in giving renown to deeds—despise those hackneyed subjects of ancient fables: the labours of Hercules, the Indian triumphs of Liber, and the wars of snake-footed monsters. [Note: On the labours of Hercules, see, if desired, Mamertinus’ *Panegyric to Constantine*, no. 4, note 3.]

Rather let skilful hands represent these deeds; [Note: Let them reproduce them.] let forums and temples be adorned with them; let them be rendered in ivory, in marble, live in colours, be set in motion in bronze, and let gems increase their value. [Note: Gems have greater value when their workmanship represents some noble deed or the face of a ruler.]

### XLV.

It concerns the security of every age that what has been done should be seen by posterity, [Note: That what has been accomplished may be seen by those who come after,] so that, if anyone should ever conceive wicked designs, he may read the memorials of our time and, through his eyes, imbibe innocence. [Note: By reading them.]

Whoever may at any time think of clothing his shoulders in royal purple—let Maximus, stripped, confront him. Whoever may desire gold and jewels upon private feet—let Maximus appear to him with bare soles. Whoever may plan to place a diadem on his head—let him behold Maximus’ head torn from its shoulders and a body without a name:

> “A mighty trunk lies upon the shore,  
> A head torn from the shoulders, and a body without a name.”  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* II.557

We know indeed that nothing will ever require alteration, since the Roman Empire will always belong either to you or to your descendants. [Note: No one will ever attempt a revolution.] Yet it pertains to the double security of the commonwealth that even what cannot occur should be feared.

But however the hands of artists may present the works of your courage to the curious eyes of posterity, whether they depict you surmounting the ridges of the Alps, swimming through obstructing rivers, or crushing the hostile column beneath triumphant steps, by what sky, what pigment, what bronze or gold will your clemency be represented, Emperor? How will you, yourself the victor over Victory, be depicted? [Note: This is taken from Cicero’s *Pro Marcello*, no. 12: “You seem to have conquered Victory herself, since you restored to the defeated the very things which she had won,” and so forth.] You laid aside every anger along with arms: no one fell after the war—certainly no one after Maximus.

A few Moorish enemies, whom, about to die, he had shut up with himself in Aquileia as though they were an infernal column, and two or three trainers of the mad gladiator, were killed as an expiation for the crimes of war. [Note: *Lanistae* were the overseers and instructors of gladiatorial schools, who trained gladiators for mutual slaughter.] [Note: To atone for the crimes of the war.] All the rest, enclosed in pardon as in a motherly bosom, were spared. No one’s property was confiscated; no one’s liberty was fined; no one’s former rank was diminished. No one was branded, [Note: With disgrace,] assailed with reproach, or even touched by punishment; no one who ought to have paid for his fault with his life paid it even with the affliction of hearing a rebuke. [Note: No one paid with the annoyance of hearing a reprimand for a fault which he ought to have paid for with his life.]

All were restored to their homes, all to their wives and children, all—what is sweeter still—to the reputation and honour of innocence. [Note: They recovered the reputation and honour of innocence.] See, Emperor, what you achieved by this clemency: you made it so that no defeated person thinks himself defeated while you are victor.

You, Rome, watched this from your hills and, exalted upon your sevenfold citadel, were borne aloft still higher by joy. [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.783, concerning the city of Rome:

> “And with one wall she shall encompass herself with seven citadels.”]

### XLVI.

You, who had experienced Cinna’s fury, Marius cruel after exile, Sulla fortunate through your ruin, and Caesar merciful toward the dead, trembled at every trumpet-call of civil disturbance. [Note: On Cinna, Marius, and Sulla, compare, if desired, the anonymous *Panegyric to Constantine*, no. 20, notes 1 and 4, and the anonymous *Panegyric to Maximian and Constantine*, no. 13, note 91 (La Baune, *Paneg. vett.*).]

Beyond the slaughter of soldiers perishing on either side, you had mourned the extinguished lights of your senate at home, consuls’ heads fixed upon spears, Catos driven to death, Ciceros mutilated, and Pompeys left unburied. [Note: “Catos”: he alludes to Cato of Utica, who, after Pompey’s defeat, laid violent hands on himself at Utica rather than be compelled to look upon the face of the victorious Caesar. “Ciceros”: Augustus and Antony, fighting one another with bitter hatred, were reconciled by an agreement for Cicero’s death. “Pompeys”: Pompey, murdered by agents sent by Ptolemy, was thrown into the Nile.]

To you the madness of citizens, divided into factions, had brought losses graver than the Carthaginian threatening your gates, [Note: The Carthaginian Hannibal threatening the gates—“Hannibal at the gates.”] or the Gaul received within your walls. [Note: This touches upon the invasion of the city by the Senonian Gauls, who, after ravaging Italy, climbed the Capitol, until Marcus Manlius Capitolinus, awakened by the cry of a goose, repelled them.]

A civil war more disastrous than the day at the Allia, more fatal than Emathia, more deadly than Cannae, than the Colline Gate, had once left scars so deep that, having always experienced your own valour as more burdensome than that of outsiders, you feared nothing more than yourself.

[Note: “The day at the Allia”: when the Romans were routed and put to flight by the Gauls at the Allia. The Allia is a river flowing from the Crustumine hills, forty miles from Rome, into the eastern side of the Tiber. “Emathia”: the famous battle between Pompey and Caesar in the Emathian fields. Emathia was properly a region bordering Thrace; the name was first applied to part of Macedonia, then to the whole of Macedonia, and even by poets to Thessaly itself. “Cannae”: the battle in which Hannibal killed forty thousand Romans; Cannae was a village in Apulia beside the river Aufidus. “The Colline Gate”: the Colline Gate stood on the Quirinal Hill, from which it received its name; the famous battle between Sulla and Marius was fought there.]

You saw civil war ended by the slaughter of enemies, the peace of soldiers, the recovery of Italy, and your own liberty. You saw, I say, a civil war ended for which you could decree a triumph.

### XLVII.

Thus far, most august Emperor, I may be permitted to have touched upon your past deeds. But since the time reminds us to remember present events, I would rather end my speech than intrude upon the task of that most illustrious order, the Senate. [Note: From this passage it may be inferred that this speech was delivered at Rome in the Senate.]

Some pardon will nevertheless be granted to pious boldness if we appear to have made use of what is common, not to have appropriated what belongs to others. I have been permitted to speak of what, for the supreme cause—the recovery of Italy, Gaul, and Britain—you have done bravely and successfully among barbarian peoples and distant provinces, with your divine power assenting and the Senate favouring. [Note: “For the supreme cause”: for recovering Italy, Gaul, and Britain.]

But what has been done and is being done at Rome must be entrusted to Roman talents: how the first day brought you into the City in triumph after Maximus’ death; [Note: The triumphal entry of Theodosius into the City after Maximus had been killed.] what you were in the senate-house, [Note: For the meaning of *curia*, see Pliny’s *Panegyric*, no. 66, note 2, and no. 65, note 1 (La Baune, *Paneg. vett.*).] what you were on the rostra; how you followed the procession of the preceding platforms, [Note: Concerning the ceremonial platforms, see above in Pliny’s *Panegyric*, no. 17, note 5,] now in a chariot and now on foot, distinguished by alternating manner of progress, triumphing now over wars and now over arrogance; how you showed yourself a ruler to all and a senator to each individual, [Note: Protecting all by your majesty and addressing each person individually with exceptional courtesy;] how, in frequent and civic progress, you not only inspected public works but consecrated private dwellings too with your divine footsteps, military guards withdrawn, safer under the watch of public affection.

Let these things be praised by their tongues—by their voices, I say—who can speak both more worthily of joys shared by all, especially the greatest ones, and more justly of what is their own. O my happy journey abroad! O labours well undertaken and exhausted! Among what blessings am I present! For what joys am I being prepared! [Note: What joys are being prepared for me.] What marvels shall I recount on my return to the cities of Gaul! Before how many astonished peoples, surrounded by what a great audience, shall I say: “I saw Rome; I saw Theodosius; and I saw both together. I saw the father of an emperor”—that is, of Honorius, whom Pacatus saw present; [Note: “The father of an emperor”: namely, Honorius, whom Pacatus saw in person.] “I saw the avenger of an emperor”—Gratian, slain by Maximus; [Note: “The avenger of an emperor”: Gratian, killed by Maximus;] “I saw the restorer of an emperor”—the younger Valentinian. [Note: “The restorer of an emperor”: the younger Valentinian.]

Distant communities will assemble before me; every pen will receive from me the order of these accomplished events; poetry its subject from me; history its authority from me. I shall compensate you, Emperor, for this injury: if I myself have said nothing about you that should be read by posterity, I shall instruct those whose works will endure what they are to write about those who will be read. [Note: Since I have said nothing that will reach posterity to be read by it, I shall teach others—whose writings will endure—what they ought to write.]

[Col. 0521]

# THEODOSIUS THE GREAT AND PACATUS

Part Two, comprising selected decrees of Theodosius concerning religion.

## BOOK I. TITLE X. ON THE OFFICE OF THE COUNT OF THE SACRED LARGESSES

[Col. 0521C]

### 1

The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Syagrius, Praetorian Prefect.

We order that energetic palace officials assigned to the several regions shall exercise in all matters such diligence that not only may no person be permitted to leave a province unless he can demonstrate by the most certain records that he has collected the assessment belonging to his administration, but also that, once our clemency has been fully informed, it may judge him to require correction by a heavier punishment.

Given on the third day before the Nones of July, at Viminacium, in the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius (381).

### 2

The Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Trifolius, Count of the Sacred Largesses.

Very numerous palace inspectors shall always assist the ordinary judges in bringing fiscal assessments to completion. Further, if anyone’s diligence in this matter is found too lax, every judge, after completing his office, shall be detained by palace officials within the province which he administered until the amount due through him has been exacted.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April, at Constantinople, in the first consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Bauto (385).

[Col. 0522C]

### 3

The same Augusti to Florianus, Count of the Sacred Largesses.

In every case you shall devote such care to the hearing of disputes that, reviewing matters extraordinarily and without fixed time-limits, you shall know that a final judgment must be pronounced promptly when reason requires, and more sternly when justice persuades.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the first consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Bauto (385).

### 4

The same Augusti to Severinus, Count of the Sacred Largesses.

We have learned that merchants were, without consultation with and in complete ignorance of the Urban Prefect, seized for punishment, subjected to bodily injuries, and additionally stripped by the harshness of a heavy fine. Since you recognize that every class of corporate body active in the city of Constantinople, together with all citizens and inhabitants, is governed by the authority of the urban prefecture: if the treasury’s inquiry should perhaps require examination of any person, or if hereafter a similar accusation should fall upon any of these persons, he shall be brought—not through the palace office but through the staff of the urban authority, after the case has been prepared for examination—to the judge under whose jurisdiction the whole city lies, so that he may be heard by him or, if necessity advises, transmitted at your request to your court.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, at Milan, in the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus (391).

### 8

The Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, Augusti, to Volusianus, Praetorian Prefect.

A palace official shall perform no public duty more than once in the same province; but the assistant’s written report, entered in the official record, shall explicitly state both the palace official’s name and that nothing has previously been entrusted to the person to be sent into that same province. If, with this formality neglected, or after a repeated appointment, a palace official is sent into a province, a penalty of thirty pounds of gold shall strike the assistant of the office, the chief clerk, and the second clerk. Nor may they employ this evasion: that different duties, though not the same duty, may be entrusted to the same man. For the same palace official may not again administer any public duty within the same province.

Palace officials shall understand that they have nothing in common with provincials. Judges, however, must be vigilant; and if any discrepancy arises between the lists which the officials bring to the province and those produced by provincial record-keepers, the provincial governor, having summoned five honourable men of the province to his council, shall hear the dispute between the palace official and the provincial record-keeper. Having examined the authenticity of the lists, he shall order collection expedited, or shall be subject to the sanctions of the former laws.

Provincial governors must know that no part whatever of collection belongs to the palace office, nor are any supports ever to be supplied to it. Nor shall a palace official press either the provincial collector or record-keeper, nor demand from the collector the total of sums paid in, nor from the record-keeper the lists of names, since all this responsibility belongs to the judge.

Likewise, if necessity should require that Counts of Titles be sent into a province, we order that no assistance from the palace office be supplied to them; the provincial staff alone shall obey them. A penalty of twenty pounds of gold shall strike the Count of Titles and the palace office if any palace official is attached to any Count of Titles.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of March, at Ravenna, in the consulship of Felix and Taurus (428).

## BOOK II. TITLE VIII. ON HOLIDAYS

### 18

The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Principius, Praetorian Prefect.

On the day of the Sun, which our forefathers rightly called the Lord’s Day, let all proceedings in lawsuits, business, and formal meetings entirely cease. Let no one demand either public or private debt; nor, even before arbitrators either required by courts or freely chosen, shall there be any hearing of disputes. And whoever departs from the prompting or observance of holy religion shall be judged not merely blameworthy but sacrilegious.

Published on the third day before the Nones of November at Aquileia; received on the eighth day before the Kalends of December at Rome, in the consulship of our lord Honorius and Evodius (386).

### 19

The Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Albinus, Urban Prefect.

We order all days to be judicial days. Only those days shall remain holidays which the more indulgent year has assigned in two months for rest from labour: to moderate summer heat and to gather autumn fruits.

#### § 1

We also devote the customary days of the Kalends of January to leisure.

#### § 2

To these we add the birthday festivals of the greatest cities, Rome and Constantinople, to which laws ought to yield, since they too were born from them.

#### § 3

We likewise count among the same observances the holy days of Easter, whether they precede or follow it in a number of seven, and also the days of the Sun which recur in their repeated cycle.

#### § 4

Equal reverence must also be observed for our own days, which have brought forth either the first light of life or the beginning of our reign.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of August, at Rome, in the consulship of Timasius and Promotus (389).

**Interpretation.** We order that cases be heard according to the laws on all days throughout the year. Although the law has granted four months for gathering crops, we have nevertheless judged that, according to the character of the provinces and the presence of the lords, the following arrangement should be made: harvest holidays shall be granted from the eighth day before the Kalends of July until the Kalends of August; from the Kalends of August until the tenth day before the Kalends of September, permission shall be granted to conduct cases; from the tenth day before the Kalends of September until the Ides of October, vintage holidays shall be granted.

We exempt Sundays, which are holidays, from the hearing of cases and the collection of debts. We also exempt the holy days of Easter—that is, the seven days preceding and the seven days following it. We further wish the birthday of our Lord and Epiphany to be celebrated without the clamour of the courts. The emperor’s birthday and the beginning of his reign should likewise be observed with equal reverence.

### 20

The same Augusti to Proculus, Urban Prefect.

On festive Sundays, contests of the Circus are to be prohibited, so that no gathering for spectacles may distract from the venerable mysteries of the Christian law, except on the birthday festivals of our clemency.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, at Constantinople, in the second consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Rufinus (392).

### 21

The same Augusti to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect.

All acts, whether public or private, shall be suspended during the fifteen Paschal days.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, at Constantinople, in the second consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Rufinus (392).

### 25

The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Jovius, Praetorian Prefect.

After other provisions: On the Lord’s Day, commonly called the day of the Sun, we permit absolutely no entertainments to be given, even if by chance the anniversary of the beginning of our reign should fall on that day as the yearly cycle returns, or if the solemn observances due on a birthday should be performed.

Given on the Kalends of April, at Ravenna, in the eighth consulship of Honorius Augustus and the third consulship of Theodosius Augustus (409).

[Col. 0524D]

### 26

The same Augusti to John, Praetorian Prefect.

After other provisions: On the Sabbath day and on the remaining days during the period in which the Jews observe the reverence due to their worship, we order that no one be compelled either to do anything or to appear in any capacity, since the remaining days are clearly sufficient for fiscal interests and private litigation, etc.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, at Ravenna, in the eighth consulship of our lords Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti (409).

**Interpretation.** On the Sabbath day we do not wish any Jew to be summoned, either for the advantage of the treasury or concerning any matter whatever, because the day of their religion ought not to be disturbed by any legal proceeding.

## BOOK III. TITLE VII. ON MARRIAGES

[Additional apparatus notes: “Having traversed so many regions.” “The labours undertaken by them.” The passage is a full prosopopoeia, especially suited to running through the virtues of Theodosius. “Whom we have made”: “What you owe us, whatever you are, whether because …” (the source note breaks off).

2. Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Cynegius, Praetorian Prefect. Let no Jew take a Christian woman in marriage, nor let a Christian contract marriage with a Jewish woman. For if anyone commits anything of this kind, the offense so committed shall carry the status of adultery, with freedom to bring accusation relaxed even to public voices. Given on the day before the Ides of March at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the second time and Cynegius, *vir clarissimus* (388).

**INTERPRETATION.** By the severity of this law it is forbidden both that a Jew should enter into marriage with a Christian woman and that a Christian man should take a Jewish woman as his wife. If any persons, contrary to the prohibition, join themselves in such a union, they shall know that they are to be prosecuted with the penalty by which adulterers are condemned, and that accusation of this crime is permitted not only to relatives but to everyone for purposes of prosecution.

## BOOK V. TITLE III. CONCERNING THE PROPERTY OF CLERICS AND MONKS

1. Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, Augusti, to Taurus, Praetorian Prefect, and Patricius. If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, deaconess, subdeacon, cleric of any other rank, monk, or woman devoted to a solitary life dies without having made a will, and has neither parents of either sex nor children, nor any persons joined to him or her by the right of agnation or cognation, nor a wife, the property belonging to that person shall in every respect be united to the most holy church or monastery to which he or she had been assigned—excepting such estates as clerics or monks of either sex, perhaps enrolled in the tax-registers, subject to the right of patronage, or liable to the status of curials, leave behind. For it is not just that property or peculia which by law are owed either to a patron, to the owner of the estate to which one of them was enrolled, or to municipal councils under a fixed rule of a constitution issued long ago, should be retained by churches; while, of course, the proper actions are reserved to the most holy churches if anyone liable to the aforesaid conditions dies bound either by transactions entered into or by any other ecclesiastical acts. Thus, if any lawsuits arising from claims of this kind are pending in the courts, they shall be wholly extinguished; nor after publication of this law shall it be lawful for a claimant to enter judgment or to trouble stewards, monks, or agents. The claim itself being annulled, and the property left behind being consecrated to the most religious churches or monasteries to which the deceased had been dedicated. Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Ariovindus and Aspar (434).

**INTERPRETATION.** If any bishop, or any of those whom the law itself mentions, or any religious man or woman dies intestate without children, relatives, or a spouse, provided that they owe nothing to a curia or patron, whatever they leave shall belong to the churches or monasteries which they served. If they wish to make a will, they shall have full power to do so.

## BOOK V. TITLE V. CONCERNING POSTLIMINIUM

2. Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Theodorus, Praetorian Prefect. No one shall retain against their will persons of whatever sex, status, or age, from different provinces, whom barbarian savagery had carried away under the necessity of captivity; rather, those wishing to return to their own homes shall have free opportunity to do so.

§ 1. If anything has been expended upon them for clothing or sustenance, it shall be regarded as given in humanity, and no claim for the cost of provisions shall remain. Excepted are those whom it is shown were purchased from barbarians selling them: in their case, it is equitable, for the public benefit, that the price of their status be restored to the purchasers. For lest consideration of loss should cause purchase to be refused to persons placed in such necessity, it is fitting that those redeemed should either repay purchasers the price given for them or, by five years’ labor, service, or work, render the equivalent of the benefit, while retaining unimpaired the freedom into which they were born, if born free.

§ 2. Therefore let them be restored to their own homes under the moderation which we have prescribed, since by the right of postliminium, according also to the opinions of the ancients, all things have been preserved intact for them.

§ 3. If any actor, tenant, or procurator attempts to oppose this command, let him know without doubt that he shall be sent to the mines, with the penalty of deportation. But if he is the owner of the estate, let him know that his property shall be claimed by the fisc and that he himself shall be deported.

§ 4. And in order that execution may be easy, we desire Christians of the neighboring places to undertake care in this matter. It has also seemed proper to admonish the curials of neighboring cities that, when such cases arise, they should know that the aid of our law must be supplied; and all governors shall know that ten pounds of gold shall be exacted from themselves and an equal amount from their official staffs if they neglect this command. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of December at Ravenna, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the eighth time and Theodosius Augustus for the third time (409).

**INTERPRETATION.** Those who have been carried off by enemies in time of captivity, if they have received anything from anyone either for sustenance or clothing, shall in no way be required to pay anything for those expenses when they wish to return to their own homes. Yet if a raider has received a price for his captive which the purchaser proves that he paid, the purchaser shall without doubt receive it back. If the captive lacks the price, he shall serve the purchaser for five years and, after the five years, shall be restored without payment to freeborn status; when he returns home, he shall receive all his possessions whole and unharmed. If anyone attempts to resist this most just command, let him know that he is to be assigned to exile; but if he is a possessor, his property shall be adjudged to the resources of the fisc. Certainly, we desire Christians, who ought to labor for redemption, to be solicitous for captives. This care shall also belong to curials, so that all judges shall know that they will pay ten pounds of gold to the fisc if they neglect the commands of this law.

## BOOK IX. TITLE VII. UNDER THE JULIAN LAW, CONCERNING ADULTERIES

5. Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Cynegius, Praetorian Prefect. Let no Jew take a Christian woman in marriage, nor let a Christian contract marriage with a Jewish woman. For if anyone commits anything of this kind, the offense so committed shall carry the status of adultery, with freedom to bring accusation relaxed even to public voices. Given on the third day before the Ides of March at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the second time and Cynegius (388).

**INTERPRETATION.** Let neither a Jew take a Christian woman nor a Christian a Jewish woman as wife. If he does so, let him be punished as an adulterer upon the accusation of anyone whatever.

## BOOK IX. TITLE XXV. CONCERNING THE ABDUCTION OR MARRIAGE OF VIRGINS OR WIDOWS CONSECRATED TO RELIGION

3. Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Palladius, Praetorian Prefect. After other matters: If anyone, reckless of himself, as an abductor seeks a virgin dedicated to God, he shall be punished by deportation after confiscation of his goods; and permission to bring this accusation is granted to all without fear of being charged as informers. For it is not fitting that a prosecutor be demanded where humanity invites action for the chastity of religion. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May at Ravenna, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the ninth time and Constantius, *vir clarissimus*, for the third time (420).

## BOOK IX. TITLE XXXV. CONCERNING INTERROGATIONS

4. Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Albucianus, Vicar of Macedonia. During the forty days which, under the auspices of the ceremonies, precede the Paschal season, every investigation involving criminal interrogations shall be prohibited. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of April at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Gratian Augustus for the fifth time and Theodosius Augustus for the first time (380).

**INTERPRETATION.** During the days of Lent, in reverence for religion, every criminal proceeding shall cease.

5. Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. During the sacred days of Lent there shall be no corporal punishments, by which absolution of souls is awaited. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of September at Forum Flaminii, in the consulship of Timasius and Promotus (389).

## BOOK IX. TITLE XXXVIII. CONCERNING PARDONS FOR CRIMES

6. Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Antidius, *vir clarissimus*, Vicar. The days of Paschal joy do not permit even those minds to remain confined which have committed crimes; let the grim prison, unaccustomed to light, be opened at last. Yet we judge alien from pardon anyone who has proudly directed his guilty consciousness of crimes against majesty; anyone seized by parricidal frenzy who has stained his hand with his own blood; anyone further defiled by the murder of any person; anyone who invaded another’s marriage-bed and couch; anyone who has been the ravisher of virginal modesty; anyone who, blind with profane incest, violated the venerable bond of kindred blood; anyone who prepared poisons for mind and body from harmful herbs sought out and muttered over in dreadful secret rites; or anyone who, an imitator of sacred utterance and seeker of divine manifestations, having learned sacrilege, fashioned venerable forms. Therefore, while these persons remain condemned even under such an absolution, we limit the indulgence of our Serenity by this provision: crimes shall not receive remission of pardon unless committed only once, lest imperial generosity be applied to those who have counted impunity for an old offense not as an occasion for amendment but as a habit. Read aloud on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August at Rome, in the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius (381).

7. The same Augusti, to Marcianus, Vicar. Religion at the annual season of supplication urges that we command all persons charged with a lighter crime to be removed from the danger of prison and fear of penalties. It is consequently clear that those are excepted whom fierce desire has driven into graver crimes: first and greatest among these is the crime of majesty; then homicide, poisoning, and sorcery; sexual violation and adultery; and, of equal enormity, sacrilege, violation of tombs, abduction, and the falsification of coinage. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April at Milan, in the consulship of Richomer and Clearchus (384).

8. The same Augusti, to Neoterius, Praetorian Prefect. Henceforth let no one perhaps await slower pronouncements from our Eternity: judges shall execute what we customarily grant. As soon as the Paschal day has arrived, let no prison hold anyone enclosed; let everyone’s chains be loosed. But from these we separate those whose release, we perceive, would rather pollute the common festivities and joy. For who would pardon a sacrilegious person on holy days? Who would forgive an adulterer or one guilty of incest during a season of chastity? Who would not more urgently prosecute an abductor amid the greatest peace and common rejoicing? Let no one receive relief from chains who, in a certain enormity of crime, did not know how to let the buried rest. Let the poisoner, sorcerer, and counterfeiter of coin suffer torments; let the murderer always await what he has done; and one guilty of majesty ought not to hope for pardon from the sovereign against whom he plotted such things. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March at Milan, in the consulship of Arcadius Augustus for the first time and Bauto (385).

**INTERPRETATION.** A sacrilegious person, adulterer, person guilty of incest, abductor, violator of tombs, poisoner, sorcerer, counterfeiter of coin, and murderer shall by no means be released during the days of Easter. All others, whom guilt in lesser cases binds, shall especially be released on the venerable days of Easter.

## BOOK IX. TITLE XLV. CONCERNING THOSE WHO TAKE REFUGE IN CHURCHES

1. Emperors Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius, Augusti, to Romulus, Count of the Sacred Largesses. If public debtors believe that they must take refuge in churches, they must either immediately be drawn out of their hiding places, or the bishops themselves, if proved to conceal them, must be called upon in their stead. Therefore let Your Eminent Authority know that henceforth no debtor is to be defended by clerics, nor is the debt of one whom they believe should be defended to be paid by them. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November at Constantinople, in the consulship of Arcadius Augustus for the second time and Rufinus (392).

## BOOK XV. TITLE VII. CONCERNING STAGE PERFORMERS

4. Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Paulinus, Prefect of the City. Women born from a humbler condition who are obliged to the services of spectacles, if they decline stage duties, shall be assigned to theatrical services—provided that the consideration of most sacred religion and reverence for Christian law has not yet claimed them for its faith. For we forbid the recall of those whom a better mode of life has released from the bond of their natural condition. We also command that those free women who, by the benefit of our Clemency, have deserved exemption from the more shameful duty shall remain free from the taint of association with stage performers. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of May at Milan, in the consulship of Gratian Augustus for the fifth time and Theodosius Augustus for the first time (380).

5. The same Augusti, to Paulinus, Prefect of the City. Whoever, forgetful of propriety, removes a *thymelica* [a female theatrical performer] from the venerable City and transfers her to a distant place, or keeps her even within his own house so that she does not serve public entertainments, shall be fined five pounds of gold. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of May at Milan, in the consulship of Gratian Augustus for the fifth time and Theodosius Augustus for the first time (380).

6. The same Augusti, to Valerianus, Prefect of the City. As to horses which either the bounty of our Clemency supplies for the customary contest, or which our Serenity has hitherto decreed to be provided in abundance by various magistrates of the most distinguished order: whatever is gathered in this way, glorious in the number of palms and renowned for victories celebrated on both sides, shall serve the spectacles of the urban populace rather than be allotted to plunder and profit. Therefore, whoever judges that anything which our Serenity, the ordinary consuls, or praetors provide for entertainments of this kind should be diverted to private advantage and profit, having been punished by a fine of one pound of gold, shall be compelled to be generous toward our largesses. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of May at Trier, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

7. The same Augusti, to Valerianus, Prefect of the City. Let Your Illustrious Authority know that those who perform the function of charioteer ought to be subjected to no punishments except the circus contest. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

8. The same Augusti, to Valerianus, Prefect of the City. If a woman of the stage seeks exemption in the name of religion, leniency shall not be lacking on the pretext of her petition. But if afterwards, having wallowed in shameful embraces, she is shown both to have betrayed the religion she sought and still in intention to pursue what she had ceased to perform as a stage performer, she shall be brought back to the stage, and shall remain there without hope of any release until she is a ridiculous old woman, deformed by age; nor even then shall she obtain release, when she can be nothing other than chaste. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May at Aquileia, in the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius (381).

9. The same Augusti, to Herasius, Proconsul of Africa. Whatever women born from such dregs decline stage duties shall be assigned to theatrical services, provided that the reverence for most holy religion and the mysteries of Christian law, to be observed perpetually, has not yet claimed them for its faith. We also command that those women freed from the taint of association with stage performers who, by the benefit of our Clemency, have deserved exemption from a more shameful duty shall remain free. Posted at Carthage, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

10. The same Augusti, to Cynegius, Praetorian Prefect. Let no one be permitted to buy, teach, sell, or employ at banquets or spectacles a female lyre-player. Nor shall anyone be permitted, for the desire of pleasure, to possess female slaves trained in the study of the musical art. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of July at Constantinople, in the consulship of Arcadius Augustus for the first time and Bauto (385).

11. Emperors Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius, Augusti, to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect. No mime actress shall use gems, sealed silks, or gold-woven fabrics. Let them also know that they must abstain from those garments which, by a Greek name, are called *crustae* in Latin, in which the pure red glow of purple burns when mixed with another color. We do not, however, forbid their use of the same checked and multicolored silks, nor the use of gold without gems upon neck, arms, or girdle. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October at Constantinople, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the third time and Abundantius (393).

12. The same Augusti, to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect. If, in public porticoes or in those places of cities where our images are customarily consecrated, any painting depicts a pantomime in humble dress, a charioteer in wrinkled folds, or a low actor, it shall immediately be torn down; and henceforth it shall never be permitted to portray dishonorable persons in an honorable place. We do not, however, forbid their placement at the entrance to the circus or upon the fronts of theatres.

§ 1. To these provisions we add that mime actresses, and women who earn a livelihood by the degradation of their bodies, shall not use the public dress of those virgins who are dedicated to God; and that no woman or boy shall be trained in association with *thymelici* [theatrical performers] if known to belong to the Christian religion. Given on the third day before the Kalends of July at Heraclea, in the consulship of Arcadius Augustus for the third time and Honorius Augustus for the second time (394).

## BOOK XVI. TITLE I. CONCERNING THE CATHOLIC FAITH

2. Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti. Edict to the people of the city of Constantinople. We desire all peoples ruled by the moderation of our Clemency to adhere to that religion which the religion introduced to the Romans by the divine Apostle Peter, and maintained from him down to the present, declares that he delivered, and which it is clear that Pope Damasus follows, together with Peter, bishop of Alexandria, a man of apostolic holiness. That is, in accordance with apostolic discipline and evangelical teaching, we should believe in the one deity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, under equal majesty and under a devout Trinity.

§ 1. Those who follow this law we command to embrace the name of Catholic Christians; but the rest, whom we judge demented and insane, shall bear the infamy of heretical doctrine. Their assemblies shall not receive the name of churches, and they shall be punished first by divine vengeance and afterwards by the retribution of our own action, which we shall assume in accordance with heavenly judgment. Given on the third day before the Kalends of March at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Gratian Augustus for the fifth time and Theodosius Augustus for the first time (380).

3. The same Augusti, to Auxonius, Proconsul of Asia. We command that all churches be handed over without delay to bishops who confess Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as of one majesty and power, of the same glory, one radiance, making nothing discordant by profane division, but affirming the order of the Trinity, the distinction of persons, and the unity of divinity; and who are known to be joined in communion with Nectarius, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, and Timothy, bishop of the city of Alexandria in Egypt; and who are known, in the regions of the East, to communicate with Pelagius, bishop of Laodicea, and Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus; in Asia, both in the Proconsular and Asian diocese, with Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, and Optimus, bishop of Antioch; and in the Pontic diocese with Helladius, bishop of Caesarea, Otreius of Melitene, Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, Terentius, bishop of Scythia, and Marmarius, bishop of Marcianopolis. These men must be admitted to possess the Catholic churches by virtue of communion and association with approved priests. But all who dissent from the communion of faith of those specifically named shall be expelled from the churches as manifest heretics; henceforth they shall not be permitted in any way the episcopal office or authority to possess churches, so that the priesthoods of the true and Nicene faith may remain pure and no place be given to malicious cunning after the evident form of our command. Given on the third day before the Kalends of August at Heraclea, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

## BOOK XVI. TITLE II. CONCERNING BISHOPS, CHURCHES, AND CLERICS

25. Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti. . . . . . Those who, whether through ignorance, confuse the sanctity of divine law, or through neglect violate and offend it, commit sacrilege. Given on the third day before the Kalends of March at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Gratian Augustus for the fifth time and Theodosius Augustus for the first time (380).

26. The same Augusti, to Tuscianus, Count of the East. We decree that all who are known to be guardians of churches or holy places and to serve in religious duties shall endure harassment from no attempted interference. For who could permit persons to be bound by a head-tax whom he necessarily understands to be devoted to the aforesaid service? Given on the day before the Kalends of April at Constantinople, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

27. Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. No woman, unless she has completed sixty years and has children at home, shall be admitted to the association of deaconesses, in accordance with the precept of the Apostle. Then, having sought a guardian for her children if their age requires it, she shall entrust her property to suitable persons for diligent religious administration, while herself receiving only the revenues of her estates; and she shall retain full power, both while she survives and, when she departs to her fate, while her will remains free, to preserve, alienate, give, sell, or bequeath them. She shall consume none of her jewelry or household goods, none of her gold, silver, or other ornaments of an illustrious house, under the protection of religion; rather, she shall transfer the whole intact to her children, relatives, or whomever else she chooses at her discretion. And when she dies, let her name no church, cleric, or poor person as heir. For any instrument made by one dying contrary to this prohibition concerning persons specifically included shall necessarily lack force. Indeed, if anything has been extorted from a dying woman by such persons, nor by a concealed trust shall anything be conveyed to clerics, by cunning artifice or the shameful connivance of anyone, in fraud of the venerable enactment; let them be excluded from all property for which they had grasped. And if anything is discovered written for the benefit of those excluded by this enactment, whether by letter, codicil, gift, will, or any kind of instrument whatever, it shall not even be brought into court; instead, the person who understands that the right belongs to him shall succeed under the definition of this statute as in intestacy—if anyone acknowledges himself a son, if anyone proves himself a relative, or finally, whether by chance or judicial determination, is discovered by open codicils to be heir, legatee, or beneficiary of a trust, in whole or in part. Let him enjoy the gift of fortune as the fruit of his own right, and, after these persons have been excluded and cast down, let him exercise the authority of heir in the hereditary estate.

§ 1. Women who, prompted by a misguided profession, have cut off their hair contrary to divine and human laws shall be barred from the doors of the church. It shall not be lawful for them to approach the sacred mysteries, nor shall they deserve by any supplications to frequent the altars venerable to all; so strictly that, if a bishop allows a woman with shorn head to enter, he too shall be deposed from his office and barred together with such associations. And he shall understand that nothing assists him not only if he advised it to be done, but even if he learns by any means that it was demanded by others or actually done. This shall undoubtedly be corrected as a law for those requiring correction, and as custom for those corrected: so that the former may have a warning, and the latter may begin to fear judgment. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July at Milan, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the fourth time and Neoterius, *vir clarissimus* (390).

28. The same Augusti, to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. Let no one fail to recognize that the law recently promulgated concerning deaconesses and widows—that no cleric, nor anyone under the name of the church, should invade slaves, household goods, or plunder as a despoiler of the weaker sex, and, after removing relatives and kinsmen, should himself act as heir of a living woman under the pretext of Catholic discipline—has been revoked to such an extent that it shall be removed from all records if it is already entered there, and no litigant may use it nor any judge know that he must enforce it. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of September at Verona, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the fourth time and Neoterius (390).

## BOOK XVI. TITLE III. CONCERNING MONKS

1. Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. All who are found under the profession of monk shall be ordered to pursue and inhabit deserted places and vast solitudes. Given on the third day before the Nones of September at Verona, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the fourth time and Neoterius (390).

2. The same Augusti, to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. We command that monks, to whom cities had been forbidden while judicial wrongs were being committed, be restored to their former position by removal of this law. For, the command of our Clemency having annulled it, we grant them free entrance into towns. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May at Constantinople, in the consulship of Arcadius Augustus for the second time and Rufinus (392).

## BOOK XVI. TITLE IV. CONCERNING THOSE WHO CONTEND ABOUT RELIGION

1. Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Eusignius, Praetorian Prefect. Those who believe that permission to assemble has been granted only to themselves, if they attempt to do anything turbulent contrary to the command of our Tranquillity, shall, as authors of sedition and disturbers of the Church’s peace, pay the penalties of treason with their lives and blood. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of February at Constantinople, in the consulship of Honorius, *nobilissimus puer*, and Evodius (386).

2. The same Augusti, to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. Let no opportunity be open to anyone going out in public either to dispute about religion, to discuss it, or to offer any counsel. And if anyone hereafter, with grave and condemnable audacity, thinks that he must act contrary to a law of this kind, or dares to persist in a movement of destructive obstinacy, let him be restrained by an appropriate penalty and fitting punishment. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July at Stobi, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the second time and Cynegius (388).

3. The same Augusti, to Potamius, Augustal Prefect. Deportation is deserved by anyone who, neither warned by the general law nor corrected by an appropriate judgment, disturbs both the Catholic faith and the people. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August at Constantinople, in the consulship of Arcadius Augustus for the second time and Rufinus (392).

## BOOK XVI. TITLE V. CONCERNING HERETICS

5. Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Hesperius, Praetorian Prefect. Let all heresies forbidden by divine and imperial laws cease forever. Whoever, being profane, diminishes God by punishable opinions, let him know that he harms only himself and not disclose what will harm others. Whoever corrupts bodies redeemed by the venerable laver and restored from death, by taking away that which makes them twice-born, let him know that such acts concern himself alone and not destroy others by a wicked teaching. Let all teachers and ministers of that perverse superstition alike—whether they disgrace the name of bishops by assuming priestly office, falsely claim religion under the designation of presbyters, or call themselves deacons when they are not even regarded as Christians—abstain from assemblies of an opinion long condemned. Finally, the rescript recently issued at Sirmium having been annulled, let only those provisions concerning Catholic observance remain which our father of everlasting memory and we ourselves have commanded in ordinances, equally numerous and destined to live forever. Given on the third day before the Nones of August at Milan; received on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius (379).

6. The same Augusti, to Eutropius, Praetorian Prefect. Let there be no place for the mysteries of heretics, no opportunity open for practicing the madness of a too-obstinate mind. Let all know that even if anything has been obtained by this class of persons through fraudulently procured special rescripts, it has no force.

§ 1. Let the crowds of all heretics be excluded from unlawful assemblies. Let the name of the one and highest God be celebrated everywhere; let observance of the Nicene faith, handed down long ago by our forefathers and established by the testimony and affirmation of divine religion, be maintained forever. Let the contamination of Photinian taint, the poison of Arian sacrilege, the crime of Eunomian perfidy, and the wicked monstrosities of sects named after their authors be abolished even from hearing.

§ 2. But he shall be regarded as an adherent of the Nicene faith and a true worshipper of the Catholic religion who confesses the almighty God and Christ, the Son of God, as one in name: God from God, light from light; who does not violate the Holy Spirit by denying him—the Spirit through whom we receive what we hope for from the highest Father of all things. In him, by the understanding of undefiled faith, there flourishes the undivided substance of the incorrupt Trinity, which, in the Greek expression, is called *ousia* (οὐσία) by those who believe rightly. This assuredly is what is more approved by us; this is what must be revered.

§ 3. But those who do not adhere to these doctrines shall cease, by affected artifices, to assume the alien name of true religion and shall be marked by their openly acknowledged crimes. Let them be removed from and wholly barred at the threshold of all churches, since we forbid all heretics to hold unlawful assemblies within towns; and if factious outburst attempts anything, we command that its fury be expelled even beyond the walls of cities, so that Catholic churches throughout the world may be restored to all orthodox bishops who hold the Nicene faith. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of January at Constantinople, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

7. The same Augusti, to Eutropius, Praetorian Prefect. If any Manichaean, male or female, from the day of the law issued long ago, first by our parents, has transferred his or her property to any person by a will made under any designation of liberality or appearance of gift; or if any person among them has been enriched by receiving an inheritance under any form of succession: since we immediately take from such persons, under the perpetual mark of just infamy, every capacity to make a will and to live under Roman law, and permit them to have no power either to leave or acquire any inheritance, the whole shall be joined to the resources of our fisc after searching investigation. Whether the unlawful gift has accrued for the benefit of a husband, relative, anyone deserving well, or even children—provided, however, that the acts of that person’s life and crime join them to him—or by means of any interposed person, and is found to benefit the same person belonging to this class and flock of men, it shall be claimed under the title of escheat.

§ 1. Nor shall the form of this law issued by our Clemency prevail only for the future; rather, fiscal acquisition shall pursue also in the past whatever property such persons left or whatever succession they possessed. For although the order of heavenly enactments points to observance for those who follow after the sacred constitution, and has not customarily harmed completed acts, nevertheless, because we recognize what persistent nature of obstinacy deserves, in this enactment alone—which we particularly desire to remain in force—we hold as liable for sacrilege, as though for injury to the law itself plainly set forth, those who, even after the law was first given, could not be restrained from unlawful and profane gatherings even by divine warning. We have enacted the severity of the present statutes as a model not so much for establishing as for avenging the law, so that no defense based on time may avail.

§ 2. Succession to paternal or maternal goods shall be granted only to those children who, though born from Manichaeans, have nevertheless, admonished by concern and affection for their own salvation, withdrawn themselves from the associations of that life and profession and devoted themselves with pure religion, being free from such crime.

§ 3. We add also to this enactment that they shall not establish in the meeting places of towns or in famous cities the customary tombs of their deadly mysteries; they shall be wholly restrained from the sight of the public city. Nor shall they protect themselves by the deceitful pretense of those names by which, as we have learned, many wish to be called and designated as persons of approved faith and purer profession. In particular, some of them wish to call themselves Encratites, Apotactites, Hydroparastatae, or Saccophori, and by the variety of differing names falsely represent the duties of a religious profession. All of them, therefore, ought not to be protected by the profession of their names, but should be held notorious and accursed by the crime of their sects. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May at Constantinople, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

8. The same Augusti, to Clicherius, Count of the East. We command that no Eunomians, Arians, or followers of the doctrine of Aëtius have opportunity to construct churches in cities or in the countryside. If anyone has rashly presumed to do this, the house in which such prohibited structures have been erected, together with the landholding or private estate, shall immediately be claimed by the resources of our fisc; and every place that has received either a seat or ministers of this sacrilegious doctrine shall at once become fiscal property. Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August at Constantinople, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

9. The same Augusti, to Florus, Praetorian Prefect. Whoever among the Manichaeans, by the false pretense of solitary life, avoids the association of good people and chooses the secret cities of the worst, shall, as a profaner and corrupter of the Catholic discipline which we all reverence, be subjected to the law: he shall live incapable of making a valid will, spend nothing while alive on unlawful persons, and leave nothing at death to the unworthy; he shall restore everything not according to his habits but according to nature, or leave it to relatives, if lawful succession is lacking, for better administration; or, if agnation fails, he shall understand it to be bound to the dominion of the fisc, without fraudulent contrivance. These provisions concern solitaries.

§ 1. Moreover, those whom they call Encratites by a portentous designation, together with Saccophori or Hydroparastatae, once refuted by judicial judgment, exposed by accusation, or found in even a slight trace of this crime, we command to be afflicted with the highest punishment and an inexpiable penalty; while the condition concerning their property which we imposed upon this entire workshop of error from the beginning of the law issued long ago shall remain in force. Therefore let Your Sublimity appoint investigators, open the tribunal, and receive accusers and informers without the odium of denunciation. Let no one obstruct the commencement of this accusation by an ordinary prescription. Let no one force such persons into hidden and concealed gatherings: let it be forbidden in rural districts, prohibited within city walls, and condemned in public and private places.

§ 2. Let the most searching inquiry be made, so that whoever gathers on the one day of Easter in a manner not conforming to religion shall without doubt be regarded as one of those condemned by this law. Given on the day before the Kalends of April at Constantinople, in the consulship of Antonius and Syagrius (382).

10. The same Augusti, to Constantinianus, Vicar of the Pontic Diocese. The Tascodrogites shall by no means be driven from their own dwellings; nevertheless, no crowd of heretical superstition shall gather at any church, or, if it does gather, it shall be driven from its assemblies without delay. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July at Constantinople, in the consulship of Merobaudes for the second time and Saturninus (383).

11. The same Augusti to Postumianus, Praetorian Prefect. Let absolutely all whom the error of different heresies agitates—that is, Eunomians, Arians, Macedonians, Pneumatomachi, Manichaeans, Encratites, Apotactites, Saccophori, and Hydroparastatae—hold no assemblies, gather no multitude, draw no people to themselves, nor display private walls in the likeness of churches; nor are they to practise, publicly or privately, anything that may offend Catholic sanctity. And if anyone should appear who so openly transgresses the prohibitions, let him be expelled, with all being granted leave to do so, by the united action of all good men who delight in the worship and beauty of right observance. Given at Constantinople, the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Merobaudes for the second time and Saturninus (383).

12. The same Augusti to Postumianus, Praetorian Prefect. Let the institution of vices, hateful to God and humankind—namely, the Eunomian, Arian, Macedonian, and Apollinarian, and those of the other sects which the sincere faith of Catholic observance condemns by the venerable worship of the true religion—presume neither by public nor private approaches, within the bounds of cities, estates, and villages, to have opportunity either to assemble congregations or to establish churches; nor let it carry on the public celebration of its perfidy or the solemnity of its accursed communion, nor usurp or possess any ordinations for creating priests. Likewise, those houses, whether in cities or in whatever places crowds of such professors and ministers are gathered indiscriminately, shall be made subject to the ownership and jurisdiction of our fisc; so that those accustomed to practise either the teaching or the mysteries of such assemblies, having been sought out from all cities and places, shall, constrained by the force of the promulgated law, be expelled from their gatherings and ordered to return to the lands from which they originate, lest any of them have power either to travel to any other places or to wander into cities. But if the measures established by Our Serenity are carried out too negligently, both the staffs of the provincial judges and the chief men of the cities in which a prohibited gathering [Col. 0536C] of a congregation is found shall be subjected to sentence and condemnation. Given at Constantinople, the third day before the Nones of September, in the consulship of Merobaudes for the second time and Saturninus (383).

13. The same Augusti to Cynegius, Praetorian Prefect. Eunomians, Macedonians, Arians, and likewise Apollinarians are names notorious among the offices of the sacred religion because of their errors. Therefore, all who have claimed for themselves either the priesthood or ministry of these professions, who assert themselves to be priests of a proscribed name, and who in a criminal religion assume for themselves the title of ministers—who say that they teach what it is shameful either not to know or to learn—shall, after a more searching investigation of all the hiding places of this city, be expelled without any intervention of favour; they shall live elsewhere and be wholly separated from the company of respectable people. Given at Constantinople, the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Richomeres and Clearchus (384).

14. The same Augusti to Cynegius, Praetorian Prefect. We order that the Apollinarians and the adherents of the other various heresies be excluded from all places: from the walls of cities, from the society of honourable persons, and from communion with the saints. Let them have no authority to appoint clerics; let them lack the capacity to gather congregations either in public or private churches. Let no authority be granted them for making bishops; the bishops themselves also, deprived of the name, shall lose the designation of that rank. Let them go to places that may especially, as it were by a rampart, exclude them from human society. To all those mentioned above we further add this: access for approaching and petitioning Our Serenity [Col. 0537A] shall be denied them. Given at Thessalonica, the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the second consulship of the Augustus Theodosius and the consulship of Cynegius (388).

15. The same Augusti to Trifolius, Praetorian Prefect. Let all persons of the various perfidious sects, whom the wretched madness of conspiracy drives against God, nowhere be permitted to hold an assembly, enter into discussions, conduct secret meetings, or with impious hands shamelessly raise altars of nefarious transgression for their rites, and adapt a simulation of mysteries to the injury of the true religion. In order that this may attain its proper effect, let Your Sublimity place the most trustworthy persons on watch, who may both restrain them and bring those apprehended before the courts, where, in accordance with the preceding enactments, they shall suffer the most severe punishment at the hands of God and the laws. [Col. 0537B] Given at Stobi, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of our Lord Theodosius Augustus for the second time and Cynegius, *vir clarissimus* (388).

16. The same Augusti to Cynegius, Praetorian Prefect. We have learned that certain Arians produce a purported order of Ours in such form as to allow them to claim what appears suited to their own advantage. Since that document has been annulled, let them know that no such order issued from Our sacred chancery. Therefore, whatever they have produced for their own convenience, whoever henceforth circulates it shall be held liable for forgery. Given at Constantinople, the fifth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the second time and Cynegius (388).

17. The Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius Augusti to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. Eunomian eunuchs shall have no permission either to make or to acquire a will. We wish this to be observed with respect to all whom the law finds alive, [Col. 0537C] and that no one be defended by the privilege of anyone’s earlier will. For, whether wills are shown to have been made previously or not made, after the promulgation of this oracle of Ours they shall have no capacity to possess, to claim, or even to leave an heir by direct institution, by fideicommissum, by legacy, by tacit fideicommissum, or by whatever designation the order of law has established in affairs of this kind. Rather, everything proved to be, or to be destined to become, theirs shall be claimed as lapsed property by the resources of Our fisc. Let them have nothing whatsoever in common with the rest. Given at Milan, the third day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of Timasius and Promotus (389).

18. The same Augusti to Albinus, Urban Prefect. Whoever disturb the world under the name of Manichaeans shall be expelled from the whole world indeed, but especially from this city, under threat of judicial punishment. § 1. Their wills, or rather even their property itself, having been declared public property, shall neither retain the force of wills nor be lawfully left by them or to them. Let them have nothing whatsoever in common with the world. Given at Rome, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Timasius and Promotus (389).

19. The same Augusti to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. Those who hold the leadership of a baleful doctrine—that is, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and readers—and those who, under the covering of clerical rank, attempt to bring a stain upon religion, being constituted under the name of any heresy or error, shall in every way be driven out from their deadly conventicles, whether these are found within the city or in the suburbs. [Col. 0538A] Given at Milan, the sixth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Timasius and Promotus (389).

20. Copy of the sacred letters. We order that the polluted contagions of heretics be driven from cities, expelled from villages, and that no assemblies whatsoever be open to them, lest in any place a sacrilegious band of such persons be gathered.
