Let neither public meeting places nor more hidden retreats for their errors be granted to their perversity. Given at Rome, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus, *viri clarissimi* (391).

21. The same Augusti to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. With respect to heretical errors, we decree that all persons proved either to have ordained clerics or to have undertaken clerical office shall individually be fined ten pounds of gold; moreover, the place in which the prohibited acts are attempted, if it has been available through the connivance of its owner, shall be added to the resources of Our fisc. But if it is established that the owner was unaware of the matter, since it was done secretly, We command the lessee of that estate, if freeborn, to pay ten pounds of gold into Our fisc; if, descended from servile dregs, he despises the penalty for loss because of his poverty and low condition, he shall be beaten with rods and sentenced to deportation. We especially provide further that, if the property belongs to the imperial domain or is of any public right, and both the lessee and the procurator have given permission for persons to assemble, they shall be fined under the stated penalty of ten pounds of gold each. But if any persons are henceforth found to be participating in such mysteries and usurping for themselves the names of clerics, We order that ten pounds of gold be exacted and paid by each individual. Given at Constantinople, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the second consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Rufinus [Col. 0538C] (392).

22. The Emperors Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius Augusti to Victorius, Proconsul of Asia. Heretics shall have neither the authority to make bishops nor lawful confirmations of bishops. Given at Constantinople, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the third consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the second consulship of Honorius Augustus (394).

23. The same Augusti to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect. We had formerly thought fit to promulgate a law preventing Eunomians from receiving anything or leaving anything by will; but we now revoke it after fuller deliberation. Let them live under the common law and alike write and be written as heirs. Given at Hadrianopolis, the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the third consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the second consulship of Honorius Augustus (394).

24. The same Augusti to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect. Let the madness of heretics no longer attempt to perpetuate what it has discovered, nor hold unlawful councils; nowhere are profane teachings either to be taught or learned. Let their leaders not dare to inculcate a faith which they do not possess, nor create ministers, which they are not. Let such audacity not be neglected and grow through the connivance of judges and of all those to whom care for this matter has been entrusted by the constitutions of Our fathers. Given at Constantinople, the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the third consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the second consulship of Honorius Augustus (394).

## BOOK XVI, TITLE VII. CONCERNING APOSTATES

1. The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augusti to Eutropius, Praetorian Prefect. From those who have become pagans after being Christians, let the capacity and right to make a will be taken away, [Col. 0539A] and any will of the deceased, if there is one, shall be rescinded without exception. Given at Constantinople, the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius (381).

2. The same Augusti to Postumianus, Praetorian Prefect. We prohibit Christians and believers who have passed over to pagan rites and cults from having any capacity to make a will in favour of any person whatsoever, so that they may be without Roman legal status.

§ 1. But from those who, although Christians and only catechumens, have neglected the venerable religion and passed over to altars and temples, if they have children or full brothers—that is, their own or lawful succession—the right to make a will, at their own discretion, in favour of any other persons shall be taken away.

§ 2. The same rule is to be observed in respect to their capacity to receive: apart from their own and lawful successions which may come to them from the property of parents or full brothers, they shall claim no rights at all in receiving inheritances by a will, even one made by judicial decision if circumstances so require; and they must unquestionably be excluded from every power connected with wills, not only that of making them, but also that of using them for the acquisition of a pontifical inheritance. Given at Constantinople, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Merobaudes for the second time and Saturninus [Col. 0539B] (383).

3. The same Augusti to Hypatius, Praetorian Prefect. We affirm the established denial of testamentary capacity to Christians who pass over to altars and temples. Let the offences also of those be punished who, having disregarded the dignity of the Christian religion and name, defile themselves with Jewish contaminations. But those who have preferred at any time to follow the nefarious secrets and criminal retreats of the Manichaeans shall constantly [Col. 0539C] and perpetually be accompanied by the punishment which the father Valentinian prescribed by imperial decision, and which Our enactments likewise have repeatedly commanded. The instigators of this persuasion, who have turned unstable minds toward their own fellowship, shall be accompanied by the same punishment as those guilty of this sort of error; indeed, according to the circumstances and the nature of the offence, we decree that still graver extraordinary punishments shall often be imposed upon the nefarious artificers of this crime.

§ 1. But lest the injury of an everlasting accusation afflict even the dead, or hereditary disputes, wholly extinguished by the passage of long periods, be continually stirred again into renewed conflicts, We set a time-limit for inquiries of this sort: if anyone accuses a deceased person of violating and abandoning the Christian religion, and alleges that he passed over to the sacrileges of temples, to Jewish rites, or to the disgrace of Manichaeism, and for that reason could not make a will, he shall bring his own action within the continuous five-year period established for actions concerning undutiful wills. The beginning of a future trial of this kind shall be such that, while the person whose defection is to be charged is still alive, the accuser, having publicly testified, shall show that he was a participant in this offence and crime; nor shall one who, acquiescing in crimes, silently displayed perfidy toward the heavenly Name thereafter accuse that defection as though unaware of it. Given at Patavium, the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Merobaudes for the second time and Saturninus [Col. 0539D] (383).

4. The Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius [Col. 0540A] Augusti to Flavianus, Praetorian Prefect. Those who have betrayed the holy faith and profaned holy baptism shall be separated from association with all persons; they shall be incapable of giving testimony; as We have already decreed, they shall have no capacity to make a will; they shall succeed to no inheritance, and no one shall write them as heirs. We would even have ordered them cast far away and banished more distantly, had it not seemed a greater punishment to live among men and to lack the support of men.

§ 1. But they shall never return to their former status; their moral offence shall not be erased by repentance, nor shall any shadow of a contrived defence or protection be extended over them. For those who have defiled the faith which they had dedicated to God and, betraying the divine mystery, have passed over to profane things cannot be defended by what is fabricated and [Col. 0540B] concocted. Aid is indeed given to those who have fallen and gone astray; but to those who are lost—that is, those who profane holy baptism—no remedy of repentance, which usually benefits other offences, is afforded. Given at Concordia, the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus (391).

5. The same Augusti to Flavianus, Praetorian Prefect. If any splendour of rank has been conferred upon, or is innate in, those who, straying in faith and blinded in mind, have revolted from the worship and reverence of the most holy religion and devoted themselves to sacrifices, let them lose it; cast down from their position and rank, let them burn under perpetual infamy, and let them not be counted even in the lowest part of the ignoble populace. For what can they have in common with human beings, since, with unspeakable and death-dealing minds, hating the grace of communion, they have withdrawn from humankind? Given at Concordia, the fifth day before the Ides of May, [Col. 0540C] in the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus (391).

## BOOK XVI, TITLE VIII. CONCERNING JEWS, COELICOLAE, AND SAMARITANS

8. The Emperors Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius Augusti to Tatianus, Praetorian Prefect. Complaints of Jews assert that certain persons are received into their sect by authority of judges, although the leaders of their law object, whereas the Jews themselves expel those persons by their own judgment and will. We order this injury to be wholly removed. Nor shall the diligent assembly in that superstition of those persons obtain the undeserved aid of reconciliation, against the wishes of their own leaders, either through the coercion of judges or by the surreptitious procurement of a rescript; for it is evident that those leaders, at the discretion of the most distinguished men and illustrious patriarchs, have their own judgment concerning their religion. Given at Constantinople, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the second consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Rufinus [Col. 0540D] (392).

9. The same Augusti to Addeus, Count and Master of Both Services in the East. It is well established that the Jewish sect is prohibited by no law. We are therefore greatly disturbed that their assemblies have been forbidden in certain places. Accordingly, when you receive this order, Your Sublime Magnitude shall restrain with suitable severity the excess of those who, under the name of the Christian religion, presume unlawful acts and attempt to destroy and plunder synagogues. Given at Constantinople, the third day before the Kalends of October, in the third consulship of Theodosius Augustus and the consulship of Abundantius (393).

## BOOK XVI, TITLE X. CONCERNING PAGANS, SACRIFICES, AND TEMPLES

7. The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius [Col. 0541A] Augusti to Florus, Praetorian Prefect. If anyone, by forbidden sacrifices, whether by day or night, as a madman and sacrilegious person, immerses himself in consultations with the uncertain, and thinks himself bound to acquire a shrine or temple as an excuse for this sort of crime, or thinks that he should visit one, let him know that he is liable to confiscation. For by a just ordinance We admonish that God must be worshipped with pure prayers, not profaned by dreadful incantations. Given at Constantinople, the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius (381).

8. The same Augusti to Palladius, Duke of Osroene. We decree by authority of public counsel that a building formerly dedicated to public gathering, now common to an assembly and indeed to the people as well, in which statues are said to have been placed—objects to be valued for the worth of their art rather than for divinity—shall remain continually open. Nor do We permit a surreptitiously obtained imperial rescript to impede this, so that it may be seen by the city’s assembly and its frequent gathering. Let your Experience, while preserving every celebration of vows, permit the temple to remain open by authority of Our rescript, [Col. 0541B] lest it be thought that, under this pretext, access has been permitted for the use of prohibited sacrifices there. Given at Constantinople, the day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Antonius and Syagrius (382).

9. The same Augusti to Cynegius, Praetorian Prefect. Let no mortal presume to perform a sacrifice so as to receive, from inspection of the liver and the omens of the entrails, the hope of a vain prediction, or—what is worse—to learn the future through an execrable consultation. For the torture of a harsher punishment shall threaten those who, contrary to the prohibition, attempt to investigate the truth of present or future events. Given at Constantinople, the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the first consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Bauto, *vir clarissimus* (385).

10. The same Augusti to Albinus, Praetorian Prefect. Let no one defile himself with victims; let no one slaughter an innocent sacrificial animal; let no one visit shrines, inspect temples, or gaze upon statues formed by mortal labour, lest he become liable under divine and human enactments. Judges too shall observe this rule: if anyone devoted to a profane rite enters a temple anywhere, whether on a journey or in a city, in order to worship, he shall immediately be compelled to pay fifteen pounds of gold; and his staff shall pay an equal sum with like promptness, unless it has both opposed the judge and immediately reported the matter by public attestation. Consular governors shall pay six pounds, and their staffs in the same manner; correctors and provincial governors, four pounds, and their staffs shall pay the same amount by an equal allotment. Given at Milan, the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus (391).

11. The same Augusti to Evagrius, Prefect of Egypt, and Romanus, Count of Egypt. Let authority to sacrifice be granted to no one; let no one go about temples; let no one gaze upon shrines. Let them recognize that Our law has barred them from these profane approaches, so completely that anyone who undertakes anything concerning the gods or sacred rites contrary to the prohibition must recognize that he is to be deprived of every indulgence. Moreover, if any judge, during his administration, relying on the privilege of his authority, enters polluted places as a sacrilegious violator, [Col. 0542A] he shall be compelled to pay fifteen pounds of gold; and his staff likewise shall pay an equal sum into Our treasury unless it has joined forces to prevent him. Given at Aquileia, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus (391).

12. The Emperors Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius Augusti to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect. No one at all, of whatever class, order of persons, or rank, whether invested with power or having held office, whether powerful by birth or humble in birth, condition, or fortune, shall in any place or city whatsoever slaughter an innocent victim before senseless images; nor, in a more secret expiatory rite, shall anyone worship a household god (*lar*) with fire, a genius with unmixed wine, or the Penates with fragrance, light lamps, offer incense, [Col. 0542B] or hang garlands.

§ 1. If anyone dares to sacrifice a victim or consult living entrails, he shall, as one guilty under the precedent of treason, be subject to a proper sentence upon accusation by anyone whatsoever, even if he has asked nothing against the safety of the emperors or concerning their safety. For it suffices for the gravity of the crime that one should wish to overthrow the laws of nature, investigate unlawful things, uncover secrets, attempt forbidden acts, seek the end of another’s safety, or promise the hope of another’s death.

§ 2. But if anyone venerates statues made by mortal labour and destined to endure only for an age by offering incense, and, fearing in ridiculous fashion what he himself has fashioned, or attempts, whether before a tree bound with fillets or an altar raised from dug-up sods, to honour vain images—even with a more humble offering, yet one full of injury to religion—he, as guilty of violating religion, shall forfeit the house or estate in which he is proved to have served the superstition of the Gentiles. For We decree that every place proved to have smoked with the vapour of incense shall be added to Our fisc, provided that it is proved to have been under the legal ownership of those burning the incense.

§ 3. But if anyone attempts such a kind of sacrifice in public temples or shrines, or in another’s buildings or lands, and it is established that he acted without the owner’s knowledge, he shall be compelled to pay twenty-five pounds of gold as a fine; but one who connives at this crime shall be held under the same punishment as the sacrificer.

§ 4. We wish this to be observed through the judges, defenders, and councillors of each city, so that matters discovered by the defenders and councillors shall immediately be brought before the court and, once reported, be punished by the judges. But if they think, through favour or negligence, that anything should be concealed or left unaddressed, they shall be liable to judicial inquiry. And if the latter, once warned, delay punishment through dissimulation, they shall be fined thirty pounds of gold, with their staffs likewise subjected to an equal penalty. Given at Constantinople, the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the second consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Rufinus [Col. 0542D] (392).

## APPENDIX

[Col. 0543]

## LETTER OF THE ECUMENICAL COUNCIL OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS

(Labbe, *Councils*, vol. II, cols. 945–946.)  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0543A] To the most observant of religion and piety, and most devoted to God, the Emperor Theodosius: the holy council of bishops who have assembled at Constantinople from various provinces.

At the beginning of our letter to Your Piety, we give thanks to God, who has established the rule of Your Piety for the common peace of the Churches and the confirmation of sound faith. While rendering to God the thanks due to him, we also necessarily report to Your Piety what has been accomplished in the holy council: namely, that, since we assembled at Constantinople in accordance with the letter of Your Piety, we first renewed mutual concord among ourselves; then we also pronounced concise definitions, by which we confirmed the faith of the Fathers assembled at Nicaea and, [Col. 0543B] with the utmost execration and detestation, rejected the perverse heresies and wicked opinions that had arisen against it. Further, for the proper establishment and ordering of the condition and discipline of the Churches, we set down definite canons. We have appended all these matters to this letter of ours. [Note: [Col. 0543] If desired, see these decrees of the Council of Constantinople in Labbe, vol. II, col. 946.] We therefore entreat Your Clemency that the decree of the council may likewise be ratified by a letter of Your Piety, so that, as you honoured the Church by the letters with which you summoned us, you may also set your seal upon the conclusion of what has been decreed. May the Lord establish your rule in peace and justice, prolong it through many ages and generations, and add to your earthly empire the joy and fruition of the heavenly [Col. 0543C] kingdom as well. May God graciously grant to the world that it may see you strong, flourishing, and eminent in every excellent quality—you who are truly an emperor most devoted to piety and most beloved of God—as the saints too ask and pray for this from him in their prayers and vows.

To the most pious Emperor Theodosius, the holy council of bishops who assembled at Constantinople from various provinces.

[Col. 0544A]

The beginning of our letter to Your Piety is thanksgiving to God, who has established the sovereignty of Your Piety for the common peace of the churches and the strengthening of the sound faith. Rendering to God the thanksgiving that is due, we also necessarily report to Your Piety the things accomplished in the holy council: that, having assembled at Constantinople according to the letter of Your Piety, we first renewed concord with one another; then we pronounced concise definitions, confirming the faith of the fathers at Nicaea and anathematizing the heresies that had sprung up [Col. 0544B] against it. In addition, for the good order of the churches, we established explicit canons; all of which we have appended to this letter of ours. We therefore entreat Your Piety that the council’s resolution may be ratified, so that, just as you have honoured the Church by the letters of convocation, you may likewise seal the conclusion of the determinations. May the Lord establish your sovereignty in peace and justice, prolong it for generations of generations, and add to your earthly power the enjoyment of the heavenly kingdom. By the prayers of the saints, may God grant to the inhabited world that it may see you strong and distinguished in every good thing, you who are truly the most pious and God-beloved emperor.

(See other letters written to the same Emperor Theodosius by Bishop Ambrose among the works of this holy bishop.)

## A.D. 381–398. SAINT VIGILIUS, BISHOP OF TRENT AND MARTYR

[Col. 0543]

## PROLEGOMENA. HISTORICAL NOTICE

From Gallandius’s *Library*, vol. VIII, pp. X–XII.

[Col. 0543D]

I. Very few facts concerning the deeds of Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr of Trent, are readily available, and they are not wholly beyond doubt. His *Acts* survive; if they are not entirely original, in Papebroch’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0545D] Papebroch, on the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. V for June, p. 163, no. 1.], [Col. 0545A] they are at least close to the original. The Bollandists published them from a manuscript codex of Saint Maximinus at Trier. [Note: [Col. 0545D] Ibid., pp. 165 ff.] Nor, indeed, is any monument older or more reliable than Acts of this kind to be found, from which we might make any safer determination about our bishop. From these Acts, therefore, we learn [Note: [Col. 0545D] Ibid., § 1.] that Vigilius was Roman by origin, a citizen of Trent, and educated at Athens in liberal learning. After returning to Trent, he is reported to have been ordained bishop of that city, third from the first: namely, successor of Abundantius, who is known to have attended the Council of Aquileia in 381, convened against Palladius and Secundianus. The same Acts maintain that Vigilius was twenty years old when he was raised to the episcopal chair; nevertheless, Tillemont denies their authority credit on this matter. [Note: [Col. 0545D] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. X, p. 812, note 1, on St Vigilius.] But the learned men Galeardus [Note: [Col. 0545D] Galeardus, on St Gaudentius’s *Sermon*, p. 332 of the new edition, note f.] and Tartarottus [Note: [Col. 0545D] Tartarottus, *On the Origin of the Church of Trent*, § 43, p. 79.] remove this scruple from his mind. For in antiquity it was not unusual that, on occasion and contrary to the established custom of the Church, some persons outstanding for remarkable piety and learning should be promoted to the episcopate even at an immature age. Many examples of this occur among ancient writers. Eusebius relates concerning Gregory Thaumaturgus and his brother Athenodorus [Note: [Col. 0545D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 30.] that they made such progress in divine learning that, while both still young, they were judged worthy of episcopal office in the churches of Pontus: “they advanced so greatly in matters of the divine words that, while still young, both were deemed worthy of the episcopate of the churches in Pontus” (*τοσαύτην ἀπηνέγκαντο περὶ τὰ θεῖα λόγια βελτίωσιν, ὡς ἔτι νέους ἄμφω ἐπισκοπῆς τῶν κατὰ Πόντον ἐκκλησιῶν ἀξιωθῆναι*). Moreover, Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, who flourished in the same period as our Vigilius, begins his treatise on his own ordination [Col. 0545C] as follows: [Note: [Col. 0545D] Gaudentius, *Sermons*, p. 332, new edition.] “Conscious of my own incompetence, and deterred by shame at the very immaturity of my age for the dignity of the priesthood, I properly sought from the chief priests permission to remain silent.” Finally, to pass over the remaining examples, when Remigius reached his twenty-second year, in the city of Rheims he was not so much elected as carried off to the summit of the episcopate by the general wishes of all, as we learn from Flodoard. [Note: [Col. 0545D] Flodoard, *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, book I, ch. 11.]

II. The above-mentioned Acts testify that Vigilius was ordained by the bishop of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0545D] *Acts of the Saints*, cited place, § 2.]; this was certainly Valerianus, appointed in place of Fortunatus in 368. Valerianus is reported to have governed the Church of Aquileia for twenty years, dying in 388, as the distinguished Bernard de Rubeis demonstrates at length. [Note: [Col. 0546D] Bernard de Rubeis, *Ecclesiastical Monuments of Aquileia*, chs. 7 and 10, pp. 64, 89.] Since Vigilius is known to have succeeded Abundantius after 381, when the latter subscribed at the Council of Aquileia, [Col. 0545D] as noted above, [Col. 0546A] Vigilius’s ordination must consequently be dated before Valerianus’s death in 388—contrary to Tartarottus’s conjecture. [Note: [Col. 0546D] Tartarottus, *On the Origin of the Church of Trent*, § 44, p. 81; and *Apology for the Memoirs of Rovereto*, p. 288, note 2.]

This appears capable of confirmation from a letter of Saint Ambrose of Milan addressed to Vigilius when he had recently been admitted to the episcopate, as is clear from the beginning of the letter itself. The holy Doctor says: [Note: [Col. 0546D] Ambrose, Letter 19, *Works*, vol. II, p. 842, no. 1.] “You have asked from me the distinctive marks of your instruction, because you have been newly called to the priesthood. And since you have built up yourself, as was fitting, you who have been accounted worthy of so great an office, it seems necessary to indicate how you may build up others.” Now in this letter the bishop of Milan first of all urges the new bishop of Trent [Note: [Col. 0546D] Ibid., no. 2, p. 843.] to teach the people entrusted to him that the bond of marriage must be sought not from foreigners but from Christian households; yet he nowhere mentions the law of Theodosius issued at the beginning of 388, which forbade marriages between Jews and Christians. Ambrose surely ought to have brought it forward to reinforce his exhortation, since that law could not have been unknown to him. It therefore follows properly that Ambrose’s letter was written before 388, perhaps in 385, as will become clear from what follows. This is the opinion of the most learned men Nourry [Note: [Col. 0546D] Nourry, in his recension of Ambrose’s letters, under the year 385.] and Bernard de Rubeis [Note: [Col. 0546D] Bernard de Rubeis, cited place, p. 87.] just mentioned. Nor are the conjectures by which Tartarottus seeks to weaken it conclusive. [Note: [Col. 0546D] Tartarottus, *On the Origin of the Church of Trent*, § 44, p. 83.]

III. It remains to determine how many years Vigilius governed the Church of Trent from the date on which he was taken by martyrdom. The Acts cited above report [Note: [Col. 0546D] *Acts of the Saints*, cited place, § 13, p. 167.] that blessed Vigilius suffered in the reign of the Augusti Theodosius and Honorius, when Stilicho was consul of the city of Rome. Bartholomew of Trent, whom we know to have flourished around the middle of the thirteenth century, reads it no differently. [Note: [Col. 0546D] Bartholomew of Trent, in Tartarottus, *Apology for the Memoirs of Rovereto*, p. 310.] From the consular fasti, however, we learn that Stilicho held the consulship twice: first in 400, then in 405. But Theodosius the Younger, mentioned in the Acts, was created Augustus on 10 or 11 January 402 [Note: [Col. 0546D] See Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, vol. V, p. 470.], while not yet one year old, having been born on 10 or 11 April of the preceding year, 401. Thus, if the Acts are true, Saint Vigilius’s passion falls in 405, when Stilicho held his second consulship.

Nor, with Papebroch, must the reading of the Acts be altered. [Note: [Col. 0546D] *Acts of the Saints*, cited place, p. 168, note m.] He thinks that Arcadius should be read in place of Theodosius [Col. 0547A] in order to establish his view that Vigilius suffered when Stilicho was first consul, namely in the secular year 400. His chief reason, he says, is that because the Acts do not read “Stilicho II,” there is no reason to defer that death to 405. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Ibid., p. 163, preliminary commentary, no. 2.] Tartarottus adopted the same view. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Tartarottus, *On the Origin of the Church of Trent*, p. 81; and *Apology for the Memoirs of Rovereto*, p. 313, note 15.] We do not approve it. Although the Acts do not read “Stilicho II,” the mention of the imperial rank of Theodosius the Younger sufficiently proves Stilicho’s second consulship, since Stilicho is understood to have entered upon it during Theodosius’s reign. Since, therefore, Vigilius was crowned by martyrdom in 405, after having spent twenty years in the episcopate, as his Acts published by Donatus Faetius state above all others, and since, further, he was appointed to govern the Church of Trent at the age of twenty, according to what has been said above, it follows that he was born in 365, that his ordination occurred in 385, and that he departed this life as a martyr in the fortieth year of his age.

I am not unaware that the most learned Mabillon saw a manuscript copy of the Acts of this same Vigilius [Note: [Col. 0547D] Mabillon, preface to the fifth century, Benedictine edition, § 93, p. 46.], near the end of which it is stated that the blessed martyr exercised the episcopate in the city of Trent for twelve years. Yet, apart from the fact that an error can easily have slipped into the number of years, the considerations set forth thus far especially prevent us from finally giving credence to these Acts.

IV. It now remains for us to speak of the literary monuments of our bishop of Trent. Gennadius writes of these as follows:

> Vigilius the bishop wrote to a certain Simplicianus a little book, and a letter containing the deeds of the martyrs among the barbarians in his own time.

[Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 37; Col. 0547D.]

By these words this priest of Marseilles plainly seems to indicate the two letters of Vigilius concerning the martyrdom of Saints Sisinnius and his companions. One is addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan; the other to John, bishop of Constantinople, who, given the period, was Chrysostom. Lipomanus first published the former letter [Note: Lippomano, vol. II, *Lives of the Saints of the Early Fathers*, p. 151, first Venetian edition, 1553; Col. 0547D.]; it was subsequently printed by Surius [Note: Surius, *Lives of the Saints*, 29 May, vol. III, p. 319; Col. 0547D.] and, in a more corrected form from various manuscripts, by Baronius [Note: Baronius, under the year 400, §§ 7 ff.; Col. 0547D.]. The latter, which Baronius himself thought lost [Note: Ibid., §§ 7, 11; Col. 0547D.], was published by Papebroch from a manuscript codex in the Vatican Library [Note: *Acts of the Saints*, May, vol. VII, pp. 42 ff.; Col. 0547D.], appended to the other letter, which had already appeared long before. Ruinart in turn had both reprinted among the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*. [Note: Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs*, pp. 334 ff., Verona edition; Col. 0548D.]

V. Nor should this point be passed over: although nearly all learned men, following the great Baronius [Note: Baronius, cited place, § 2; Col. 0548D.], have rightly believed that Gennadius’s words, “to a certain Simplicianus,” refer to the one Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, Labbe, in criticizing Miraeus [Note: Labbe, *Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 475; Col. 0548D.], and then Natalis Alexander, attacking the very father of ecclesiastical annals [Note: Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. III, p. 1, in the synopsis of the fifth century, ch. 1, near the beginning; Col. 0548D.], opposed this view. Their reasoning was that, by saying “to a certain Simplicianus,” Gennadius meant a man other than Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, whom he had honorably mentioned in the immediately preceding chapter.

The learned Tartarotti, however, ably defends the great man. [Note: Tartarotti, *On the Origin of the Church of Trent*, § 36, pp. 66 ff.; Col. 0548D.] His words deserve transcription here:

> “This sort of argumentation, that of Natalis Alexander, is exceedingly weak. Gennadius, it seems, had not read Vigilius’s letters. Let us grant even that he had read them: nevertheless he did not know that the former had been sent to the Simplicianus whom he had mentioned in the immediately preceding chapter; therefore he said ‘to a certain [Simplicianus].’ There is consequently no reason why we should depart from the earlier opinion on this account. And Baronius at least ought to have been spared, since he says this on the matter: ‘But since, when Gennadius mentions Simplicianus, he does not say that he was bishop of the Church of Milan, but says A CERTAIN [Simplicianus], as though he were a man of uncertain identity, it may seem possible to question whether this is that bishop Simplicianus, successor of Saint Ambrose; especially since, in the preceding chapter, the same author treats of that same bishop of Milan, enumerating the writings published by him.’
>
> “Behold: the most learned father of ecclesiastical annals had foreseen the French critic’s attack. Yet he did not judge it so unanswerable that he ought, for that reason, to abandon his earlier conjecture; rather, supported by these arguments, he establishes it in the same place. First, Vigilius’s letter is entitled in every codex ‘To Simplicianus, Bishop.’ Second, although it does not at all state over what church he was bishop, yet because it calls him ‘Father,’ while bishops ordinarily call their fellow bishops ‘brothers,’ it is reasonable to suppose that this was none other than Simplicianus, venerable for his great age. This is especially so since Saint Augustine himself, already a bishop, calls the same Simplicianus ‘Father’ in writing to him the books of *Questions*, although he was then only a priest. Finally, it is established on Paulinus’s authority that the relics of these martyrs were shortly transferred to Milan. [Note: Paulinus, *Life of St Ambrose*, near the end; Col. 0548D.]
>
> “One may add that it is acknowledged by all that reciprocal correspondence passed between Ambrose—the teacher and episcopal predecessor of the Simplicianus of whom we speak—and Vigilius. Labbe perhaps first kindled Alexander’s error, for which he charges not Baronius, but Miraeus, with rashness; as if Miraeus had been the first of all to introduce that opinion, or had committed some unprecedented offence merely by touching upon it.”

Thus far the distinguished Tartarotti.

VI. One further question remains: namely, at what time Saint Vigilius wrote these two letters. From their context we sufficiently understand that both—or at least the first—were written in the same year in which the martyrs suffered. This is especially confirmed by Paulinus, who reports that about two months after the death of Saint Ambrose, while Simplicianus was already presiding over the Church of Milan, the relics of these martyrs were brought there. His words are:

> “When we received at Milan, with the greatest devotion, the relics also of the martyrs Sisinnius and Alexander, who in our times—that is, after the death of Saint Ambrose—won the crown of martyrdom in the region of Anaunia while pagan men were persecuting them,” etc.

[Note: Paulinus, *Life of St Ambrose*, § 52, in the Appendix to vol. II of Ambrose, p. XIII; Col. 0549C.]

Moreover, Saint Vigilius gives this chronological note in Letter I on the martyrdom of Sisinnius and his companions:

> “The day of the saints’ suffering was the fourth day before the Kalends of June, Friday, at daybreak.”

[Note: Vigilius, Letter I, § 3, at the end; Col. 0549C.]

In Letter II he says only:

> “The gracious light of Friday had gone forth.”

[Note: Ibid., Letter II, § 11; Col. 0549C.]

These chronological marks indicate the year 397, in which the fourth day before the Kalends of June fell on a Friday, as Pagi and others observed after Papebroch. [Note: *Acts of the Saints*, May, vol. VII, p. 39, preliminary commentary, no. 4; Pagi, under the year 400, § 2; Col. 0549C.] But Tillemont saw what escaped the notice of others: the same chronological indication occurs also in the year 403. [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. X, p. 812, note 3 on St Vigilius; Col. 0550C.]

Accordingly Scaliger, correcting Baronius—who believed that the martyrdom of the Anaunian saints occurred in 400, and therefore that Vigilius’s letter to Simplicianus was written in that same year—argues from Vigilius’s words just quoted:

> “Therefore they suffered in the year 403, in the twentieth solar cycle, when 29 May was Friday. Yet the *Annals* say that Vigilius’s letter was written in the year 400 of Christ. It would therefore have been written three years before the slaughter of those martyrs. I know for certain that he [Baronius] will not ascribe this absurdity to himself.”

[Note: Scaliger, *On the Correction of Chronology*, in the prolegomena, p. 19; Col. 0550C.]

Very neat, indeed. Baronius erred because he was misled by the Mombritian edition, in which he found the Acts of the holy Anaunian martyrs dated by Stilicho’s consulship. But Scaliger, Baronius’s critic, erred far more disgracefully. First, this most critical man (*κριτικώτατος*) failed to notice that Vigilius’s chronological indication also fits the year 397, when the lunar cycle was XVIII, the solar cycle XIV, the dominical letter D, and Easter was 5 April; consequently the fourth day before the Kalends of June—that is, 29 May—fell on Friday.

Further, and this is the main point, he failed to notice that Vigilius’s letter was addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, who died during the course of the year 400, as learned men know. [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. X, p. 797, note 3 on St Simplicianus; Col. 0550C.] Therefore Vigilius’s letter would have been written, to return Scaliger’s own words against him, three years after Simplicianus’s death. I know for certain that he himself will not ascribe this absurdity to himself. I have wished to discuss these matters at greater length because, so far as I know, Scaliger’s intemperate criticism and gross error have hitherto escaped the notice of others.

[Col. 0549]

# TWO LETTERS OF SAINT VIGILIUS

(From Gallandi, *Library*, vol. VIII, pp. 203–206.) (C)

## FIRST LETTER. TO SIMPLICIANUS, BISHOP OF MILAN. On the martyrdom of Saints Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander

[Col. 0549C]

### I.

To the holy and venerable lord and Father Simplicianus, to be preferred above all good things: Vigilius, bishop of the Church of Trent, sends greetings.

Although, when the martyrs are mentioned, merits are commended not by words but words by merits, and although it is more fitting for constancy to pass in silence over those whose virtue has been proved: nevertheless, because piety prompted me to set forth the causes, places, and conflicts of their martyrdom, obligation reminded me and duty compelled me, I did not deny my grieving tongue to the page. For a lamp could not be hidden under a bushel, nor could the voice of pious blood be silenced.

After many stages of endurance and unremitting struggles, a fresh injustice of faithlessness was added. Ministers in churches newly founded were assailed and gained the titles of martyrdom. Ready for everything, gladly suffering everything, giving occasion to none, they merited glory through the occasion of glory.

To summarize the highest points of their lives: through their knowledge of sacred learning, their manner of life was singular both in diligence and in purpose. All free from the bond of marriage, they offered to God spotless souls as holy victims. First, Sisinnius by name brought the new peace of the Christian name to a barbarian people. Through a succession of years he preserved it continually, so far as lay in him, acknowledging no fellowship in polluted hospitality. Like Lot in Sodom, he preserved religion in awesome fear. Yet, though a safe sheep placed among wolves, he sought a fold; and, generously expending the vows of his small faith, he was the first to establish one in that region. If you deign to review this with me, its minister thereby earned, as though by right, that he should take precedence—old in years as in merit.

### II.

The reader Martyrius, joined to him as his helper and now commended by the pledge of his name, after temporal military service put on the beginnings of a religious profession as a catechumen. Casting away his military belt and rejecting the company of parents and brothers according to the flesh, he understood that he had received grace from God, the author of the true light. Joined to the readers in office, he was the first to make the song of divine praise sound in the ears of that deaf region. Constantly intent upon spiritual works, worn by continual fasts, himself the tutor of his reading, anxious to win souls, he sent so great an investment ahead in so brief a time that the crown was rightly believed to be his.

Why should I recount souls delivered and gone in full light to Abraham’s bosom—souls whom the faithless observance of superstitious days, alienating nature’s rightful claim, condemned to a cruel death? But he, taken from his mother’s milk-swollen breasts and reared abroad, always sought an affection worthy of his mother, intending to proclaim the resurrection, preached by examples visible to the eyes. These are a few things out of many.

### III.

Alexander likewise, Martyrius’s brother by blood, completing the third victim of the Trinity, opened an equal gateway of confession. For God’s sake he became a stranger from his country and left his parents: faithful as a companion in trials, great-souled in faith, inclined to compassion. And if my testimony is believed in any degree, no one is to be preferred to them except themselves; nor did they need commendation except, perhaps, such as was fitting.

But enough has been said to relieve weariness, if you still willingly admit these things into your ears. For smoky paganism grew hot with the flame of rage against the vapor of faith, through the devil’s jealousy. From this point the serpent was already kindling a lingering tinder, because the first deacon of that place, devoutly poor in worldly resources but rich, as I said, in faith, had set up the tabernacle of a church. Another just cause contributing to their titles was that the faithful ministry of the deacon forbade victims to be offered from a Christian household to the devil, and forbade the banner of a funeral purification rite to be set before the banner of the Passion.

For a crowd summoned by a single reward rushed upon blood. In the morning hours it found him exhausted by the many wounds of the preceding day, and, discovering him in bed, buried him in the rest he had earned. The reader too, never slack in service, was serving at the pre-dawn ministry, while the deacon ministered in the sacrifice; and the said Martyrius was administering medicine to his wounds—a ministry which they completed by the deed for which they were found. For the reader withdrew to the garden adjoining the church; there he was captured and planted the tree of his life from the root. The doorkeeper too was joined to the Passion. Found in the lodging, he neither offered his life nor denied it.

All were gathered together and, dragged for some distance, breathed out their souls to God. The lifeless bodies of two were carried away; but the third, as his life clung more tenaciously, so his punishment was more acutely felt: alive, he watched his own funeral. A pyre was prepared from the sacred roof-timbers or beams of the church. This flame veiled the martyrs. With reverent intention, we consider among ourselves building a basilica in that place, where they first merited the glorious testimony of faith.

Now console me, though unworthy, as a companion in both respects, with fatherly love; and with them approach those saints as an intercessor, that on that day, setting all else aside, I, a sinner, may be able to touch the hem either of priests or of martyrs. We greet your holiness with special devotion. I beg you to deign to commend my grief to the Lord.

Likewise, in another hand:

I could not refuse what was yours in us, so that it might become more glorious through the merit of the recipient, not through the favor of the giver. The day of the saints’ suffering was the fourth day before the Kalends of June, Friday, at daybreak.

## SECOND LETTER. TO SAINT JOHN CHRYSOSTOM. On the same martyrs

The letter of Saint Vigilius begins, concerning the praises of the most blessed martyrs Sisinnius, Alexander, and Martyrius, whose relics reached John, bishop of the city of Constantinople, through the illustrious man Jacob.

### I.

A new guest of charity would not otherwise have addressed holy ears; nor would an unprompted man have pressed upon the reserve of a first approach; nor would an unknown man have begun discourse, unless both request and reward urged him on. Therefore, dearest brother, the tenor and full substance of this present letter will begin from an apostolic man, so that from the easy connection you may understand that the praises of the martyrs are to follow.

For Jacob, a faithful man of heavenly longings, intending to lay aside the dignity of the *comitiva* among Christ’s companions, asked for the relics of the saints, recent and still steaming with their warmth. I said “lay aside,” because a dignity that is accumulated with the Lord cannot be put off. I, sufficiently timid and not a little aware of the matter, struggled with myself in the dispensation: almost, while fearing that I was not a suitable distributor, I refused what I had caused to be expended so that someone might always lend it out and remain in debt.

I confess: I feared with a private fear the great loss of many persons, unless I looked to Jacob, who was to deliver these things as certain offerings of reverence to holy John. Thus, through the sacred names of the martyrs, brotherhood not foreign to them might be conveyed by delegated love and joined again by blood. Gladly accepting this view of faith among other considerations—which rightly smiled upon my grief—I delayed only; I did not refuse. I delayed in order that my slowness might again be openly revealed: I who had not deserved to follow my companions. I confess: I wished it; but the crown of righteousness does not lie in desire alone.

But now, if the fitting order of a weighty account will not be burdensome to thirsty ears, I shall begin with the situation of the region and the route, following without weariness the principal traces of the matter, so that the flood of merits may flow more easily if with capacious love you reach the source of the spring.

### II.

The place called Anaunia, lying twenty-five stadia from the city, is shut in by narrow passes both through its faithlessness and by nature; it is opened by almost one approach only—one might call it the route of the three martyrs. Lying back on a gentle ridge, with a descending rampart on every side and fortresses placed all around in a crown, its neighboring peoples conspiring together in faithlessness, it presents a spectacle, a stage of nature.

The place lacked a cause; but Christ supplied a sufficient cause, so that the devil’s sport might furnish a procession for martyrdom. Let the description of the places not be unwelcome to the hearer’s ears. The place was always its own evil companion, echoing hollowly among the mountains. When Christ’s army first ascended there, savage paganism—often aroused by trumpets—was inflamed with hostile frenzy and the clamors of war.

But the saints had one perfect kind of combat: to endure everything, to yield when attacked, to bear patiently, and, destined to suffer, to restrain public rage by private gentleness; to conquer by refusing. Yet the destined glory pressed toward the titles of a timely end, which the proper sequence of events had produced. For, omitting digressions and cutting off lengthy windings, I shall not pass over the things by which the martyrs’ virtue was nourished, lest brevity take away the due honor of praise.

### III.

While the Lord’s name was still foreign in the aforesaid region and there was no sign displaying the seal of faith, these men came there—then few in number, now singular in merit—strangers alike in religion and nation. Through them God, not without cause, was proclaimed unknown. Their peaceful life had been composed through a long period, while no advantage of faith provoked them.

But if the cause of the hatred rising against the Lord is sought, it was the title of violated peace. For one of them, Sisinnius by name, older than the other two, venerable even by age alone, raised a church at his own expense. Richer in faith than in wealth, affluent in spirit and poor in property, he entrusted the fold to the shepherd. Its founder became its guardian. But the fold was hostile to wolves. The devil envied the height raised up from ruin. This was the first lot of martyrdom: that the sheep, while pursuing the Lamb, should be slain.

There was added, as a sacrifice more just before God, this cause: when they wished to lead the evil of lustration around the boundaries of the fields in a funeral pageant, trampling and defiling the growing crops; when, about to trample Christ’s shoots also, crowned in mournful ornaments, chanting the devil’s howling song, and raising standards bearing processions of diverse animals toward the Lord’s house, they compelled one recently converted from their own people to offer victims to the works of darkness. The ministers of the Lord could scarcely see this done without their own guilt, since by standing by they seemed also to share in these shameful deeds. Thus, on that day, the bodies of the saints were pledged to a deadly slaughter, though the palm of victory was deferred.

### IV.

Here, brother, I wish briefly to compare with you the distinctions of these events, lest anyone think martyrdom lowly because it was accepted in humility. Every present good is judged cheap, although it is new and marvelous, raised up without the envy of time and so completed that nothing came before it and nothing follows; it is singular, concluded solely by its granted consummation.

The man who guards a sheep from a robber is, I think, shown to be not a hireling but Christ’s disciple. He who flees is a hired servant; he who does not abandon it is a shepherd. He who lays down his life lives; he who preserves it loses it. For what else did the Master and Lord do, except refuse to abandon those who abandoned him? Or what did the Lamb do except defend the sheep, so that the devout victim might be consummated for the sheep?

But as I enter the gate of their sufferings, having set forth the manifold cause, I shall not gather or steal a foreign praise. For it is not the martyrs’ way to desire what belongs to another, nor priests’ to deceive—unless it be that I confess myself incapable of following these things even by recounting them, and least of all in this respect, since I am about to speak of lesser things.

### V.

After the standard of the devilish lustrations, which, as we have related, was the sign of glory soon to come, in one night they ascended to their delayed crown. At the morning hours, as the darkness of heaven suddenly yielded to dawn, an unexpected but concerted band gathered, armed with fire-hardened stakes and axes, and with whatever weapon the devil’s rage had fashioned for those who searched for arms. Finding several Levites in the church singing the morning hymn, they carried out a vast devastation and savage plundering. Everything, both the hidden things and the divine mysteries, was profaned; finally, religion became spoil.

Let no one think this conflict ordinary, when either senseless idols are overthrown by sentient beings, or masses of stone are moved together with those who worship them, so that one cannot tell, between worshipper and object worshipped, whom to judge the harder. Christ the Rock was afflicted in all of them; the cornerstone was rejected by the nations, to be proved again, and by pure blood was to build up a world rising from ruin.

Amid these things faith had its spectacle. The body of Sisinnius the deacon was held in his bed, pierced and wounded also by earlier injuries. He was ordered either to call back a sheep for sacrifice or himself to become a victim, unless he agreed to the deadly sacrifices. He was struck with the trumpet by which they made the devil’s song resound—he who had deservedly first brought in the sound of faith; he was cut with axes—he who had guarded the axe from the fruitless tree of paganism. And, lest I prolong confirmed facts further: he was found, as we said, in the rest he had earned in bed, having confessed, I believe, that by a private mystery he might more quickly reach the cross and free the paralytic people.

### VI.

The reader Martyrius too was bound to a piece of wood with ropes: alike a confessor and defender of his own name. He had sung the new song, then first and now alone, in a foreign land; amid the noisy, harsh pastoral cries, he had already rendered sweet-voiced praises to God, as I mentioned above. He had also brought medicine and fomentations to the deacon Sisinnius, to heal pains although he himself was to receive wounds, recalling the fleeing soul by choice draughts—not for the body, but for martyrdom.

But the saint, already appointed to the journey of martyrdom toward Christ, refused a drink of water because the wine of suffering had come; he had mingled it with the offered cup from the stream of truer life. While attending to this service, he withdrew into the secluded part of the adjoining garden—that is, he did not depart from the Church. For, as you know better, the Church is a garden planted with the hedges of living commandments.

He did not force forward the body that he was unwilling to deny; nor did he assume the boldness of rashness in confidence of piety. As it is said in African regions, those who arm themselves for a voluntary death seek, through pride, what they do without fear. Yet the future martyr stood: captured, he was free; fearless, he confessed; wounded, he gave thanks; his body torn, his mind secure; his head cut off, he was washed in blood by a private baptism.

No one deserved to follow him who was thought to be fleeing. Therefore the charge that he withdrew is vain and akin to fear; but the righteous confession of one taken prisoner showed that he stood only in order to conquer, whereas he withdrew so that the persecutor might perish in his glory as well. Martyrius was brought from the garden to which he had fled. This was a withdrawal of mystery: that, like a purple flower dwelling in springing places, he might deservedly be dyed as a rose, preceding the new martyr; or, amid the whitening tresses of lilies, all watered by baptism and replanted through recurring death, the silent will of life might be declared. He too was transfixed with stakes and dragged toward an idol; but he merited to become a victim before reaching the devil’s altar.

### VII.

The third crown of the Lord, which was to honor Alexander, was also completed. He found an entrance close at hand, he who stood watch at Christ’s gates; with him as guardian, the veil of the temple had torn open the covered hearts of the pagans. Diligently sought by the crowd, because he was sufficiently known to all for zeal of faith, he was captured but not made captive; fear seized him, but he did not fear.

The disciple of Christ was often mocked, and in this case the greater labor of martyrial torments produced a more intense punishment. Thus, to compensate for his dignity by the excess of suffering, he merited by lot that in nothing should he be inferior to the three. For in the others rage did not delay its torments; for him a slow punishment against the Lord was reserved. He knew what he endured, a spectator of his own body. And although the wounds inflicted had brought the aforesaid deacon to martyrdom, the tortures made Alexander guardian of himself.

With their bodies joined and bound together, dragged in public like dogs, though not to return to their vomit, Alexander was drawn alive among them, his feet tied, destined to leave portions of his quivering limbs upon the rocks until he was brought to the end of the place—that is, of life. After this they went up to the religious heights, that is, the lofty temple of God. After the bodies came the beams laid upon the ground; a pyre was made from consecrated timbers, in the sight of Saturn, an ancient idol long-standing through time.

After the bodies of the two brothers had been sent first into the fire, wounded Alexander stood to confess again. The reward of life was offered him on condition that he lose life: if he wished to escape the present flame, he was to say that he had agreed with their darkness. But as he looked aside and rejected the offerings of the impious, light stood before his eyes against the light; fear of punishment prevented punishment; the heat of faith repelled the flame. The sequence of suffering also maintained the reverence due to rank. He was received last, but he was not crowned least among his brothers.

Brothers, in the three ministers the mystery of the Trinity was fulfilled, now indeed in the banquet of heavenly joy. Others too might have suffered as living sacrifices by a similar lot, had not all things been reckoned complete in the threefold number. For amid these things we ourselves were perhaps no small part, and because of them we were reproached by the pagans. We did not abandon our companions; but rank has its election.

### VIII.

Moreover, many things were shown in the days approaching the martyrdom—not so much displayed as painted by truth—which we omit in summary, so that through these few deeds which occurred we may teach the mysteries more fully. Yet if you deign patiently to reread with me what has been related: from the very cradle of that region, Sisinnius was a Cappadocian by nation, or a Greek, formerly of foremost blood among you; swift in faith, great-souled in spirit, lavish in labor, persevering in everything, closing his course with a palm not late, [Note: Perhaps “best”; Col. 0555D.] destined to come by the seventh lot of promise; always joined in the bond of charity, harmonious in peace, holding the reins of divine discipline, tamer of the yoke of so great a people, herald of Christ.

Finally, as common usage—the teacher of things—speaks, he is recognized as holding the leadership of the way for the future flock or blood-brothers: a bold trampler-down and vanquisher of danger, so that the ranks may safely follow behind him. Thus, in our dawn herald of faith there was primacy both of blood and leadership: he who, after showing the way, led to life or brought into glory, the guide of salvation and knower of truth. As the Prophet bears witness:

> “And my herald in the morning.”

[Note: One must consult the Old Latin version of Scripture to find this passage. Papebroch; Cols. 0555D–0556D.]

And, in order that the events might increase the mysteries still further and that the herald should not lack a sign appropriate to himself: when they dragged the lifeless body of Saint Sisinnius like an animal, they fastened around his neck the hollow ringing of a bronze witness, which the common people call a little bell (*tintinnabulum*). Insulting the body, reproaching death, casting in Christ’s teeth that he was no avenger, and mocking the Lord’s disciple, they fulfilled a saving mystery.

For what did that ringing mean—the sound useful to animals that follow and appropriate also to their adornment, suspended from the neck? Surely that a voice might belch forth Christ’s name, hoarse with shouting to the deaf, and that it might confirm him as leader alike of flock and people. For he first uttered the word of the religious voice; he first resounded through hollow valleys. Among animals still nearly brute—or at least among sheep of an untouched pasture—he was the new bell-ringer heard, the chewer-over of the flowering law among the nations.

### IX.

Following the order laid down, Martyrius likewise fulfilled by his own name the prophecy which he held. He unfolded the parable of his designation, a true revealer in all things. The name he bore smiled upon him and increased his merits. He established the name given at birth, destined to attain its meaning in suffering as in origin.

Why should I unfold the mysteries of the garden’s secret places, conscious of punishment? He first betook himself to the place into which the martyr entered again: the gate of paradise. He contemplated its pure delight and the venerable delights properly his own, planting in verdant places the living flower, still ill-attached to the thorn of the world; he was shown by the Virgin whose garden it was.

Why do you draw me back again to mysteries enacted? That Virgin gave him up—the Virgin who had always desired to keep her own. She wished to release him whom she had received; she chose the cultivator whom she had approved. Already, in the affection of familiar love, she held God himself as an invited guest. Solomon says in the *Song of Songs*:

> “Let my brother come down into his garden” (Song 5:1).

He came down—and certainly came down. For he whom rich desire loved, even at the time of suffering, was unwilling to go out, to express a familiar event in terms of our own times. Judas Iscariot seized the Lord in a garden, together with the Jews. Let no one object to such a withdrawal by the disciple: the Master and Lord too is found so. He was thought to be a gardener, one who waters living things and plants souls. Therefore the garden is an asylum not for one fleeing, but for one seeking refuge; those who understand the garden will see that they have merited paradise.

### X.

But what mystery of death could Alexander contribute, who fulfilled the whole mystery while alive, except that his name suited the vice of the people? Thus Anaunia might be thought Alexandria: religious in its private monstrosities, teeming with demons, with two-formed Anubises, with idols of many shapes, half-human beings—such as belong to mockers of the law—full of Isis’s madness and Serapis’s flight; finally, the alluring mother of crimes to its inhabitants, or rather their stepmother; nurse of a brood of vipers, through the offspring of a venomous race. It knows not how to conceive unless it rejoices in the father’s bereavement; it knows not how to grow unless it is born through death; it knows not how to live unless it does not know its mother.

Thus, in conversion to the faith, the offspring of an evil progeny—conceived through the loss of God the Father, born with its head denied, brought forth by piercing the womb of Mother Church—may take the beginning of life through the death of the saints; yet now it grows more fruitful through loss, more alive through death, more joyful after grief. For it is plain and fully evident, disclosed by the Scriptures speaking in Romans 11:32, that all were enclosed under one sin [Note: “Enclosed.” Thus we correct the corrupt reading of the editions, *shaken*. Saint Vigilius refers to Romans 11:32; Col. 0557.] so that all might obtain mercy.

These are the hundredfold returns of suffering, by which that people now absolves its own guilt. Captivity made people free; pardon released those in bonds. Then heaven consented to darkness; the light shuddered at the Passion, I think confused by the blindness of faithless minds.

### XI.

Believe, brother, the eyes of your brother. A certain shadow of black cloud covered—or enveloped—the whole region. Thunderbolts crashed close to the earth; terrible thunder repeatedly resounded; a flashing red fire shone forth in abundance. You would have said that heaven knew of the blood. After the shadow of that foreign night, as I may call it, it is no longer possible to conceal manifest truth under a cloud.

The day itself also revealed the horror of the suffering, not merely by retreating but by being taken away. For the gracious light of Friday had gone forth, always, after God, friendly to martyrs. Reverently holding still a part of the Lord’s body, it rendered service through the holy disciples to the servants of God, though the envy of religion rivaled the lot that was to come. Thus the Lord makes himself known by his works; thus he shows himself a companion in all things, joined by equality of time as well.

I confess that I was a witness among these mysteries and guardian at the saints’ ashes. Though I did not deserve to be a participant, I felt that to which I could not attain. I saw—scarcely even now do I believe myself. The deeds reported exceed the reverence of the words spoken. It will therefore be God’s task, brother, to uphold what he has chosen and to bear witness to the witness.

Receive now, brother, the gifts of the three youths—or the three youths from the furnace—still almost walking amid the blazing fires of panting flame. Had not the envious rage of flame received them half-dead, the example of the history would have come to life again. Thus almost everything portrayed itself in a similar honor: Voice, Dew, Number, Furnace. Voice signifies harmonious faith; Dew, rain; Furnace, the pyre; Number, the Trinity.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 336. ANCIENT DOCUMENTS RELATING TO THE DOCTRINE OF THE ARIANS

[Col. 0557]

## [LETTERS AND DECREES. (S)]

### FIRST LETTER OF CONSTANTIUS TO ATHANASIUS

[Note: These and the following letters through the Constitution of Valens, col. 575, are taken from Labbe, vol. II, cols. 519–541; Col. 0557D.]

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne; Col. 0557.]

Constantius, victorious Augustus, to Athanasius.

[Col. 0557D]

The humanity of our clemency has not permitted you long to be tossed and distressed by the enormous storms of the waves. Indeed, our untiring piety has not abandoned you, stripped of your ancestral home and despoiled of your possessions, wandering in pathless and desolate places. For although I had long postponed my purpose of writing to you, because I expected that you would come of your own accord [Col. 0559A] and seek a remedy for your troubles, nevertheless, since perhaps fear hindered the resolve of your purpose, we have sent to your steadfastness letters most full of our generosity, so that you may safely present yourself before us as soon as possible, and, having attained your desire and experienced our benevolence, may be restored to what is yours. For this reason I have approached with entreaties on your behalf my lord and brother Constans, victorious Augustus, that he grant you leave to come, so that, with the assent of us both, you may be restored to your native country and may hold this as a pledge of our favor.

Constantius, victorious Augustus, to Athanasius the bishop. [Col. 0558D]

The humanity of our clemency has not permitted you long to be tossed and distressed by the monstrous storms of the waves of the sea. Our untiring piety has not abandoned you, stripped of your ancestral home and deprived of your possessions, wandering in pathless and desolate places. Although I had long postponed my intention of writing to you, expecting that you would of your own accord come [Col. 0560A] to us and seek a remedy for your troubles, yet, since perhaps fear hindered the resolve of your purpose, we have therefore sent most ample letters of generosity to your steadfastness, so that you may hasten fearlessly to present yourself before us. Thus, having obtained what you desire and experienced our benevolence, you may be restored to your own possessions. For this reason I have also entreated on your behalf my lord and brother Constans, victorious Augustus, that he grant you permission to come, so that, with the assent of us both, you may be restored to your native country, holding this as a pledge of our favor.

## Second Letter of the Emperor Constantius to Athanasius

[Note: [Col. 0559] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0559]

[Col. 0559B] Although in our earlier letters we declared that you should come without anxiety to our court, because we particularly desire to send you back to your own people, nevertheless we have now sent these letters also to your steadfastness. We exhort you, therefore, to board the public conveyances without any distrust or fear, and hasten to us, so that you may attain what you desire.

[Col. 0560B] Although we had already made known by earlier letters that you should come without concern to our court, since we particularly wish to send you back to your own people, nevertheless we have now also communicated these letters to your steadfastness. Therefore we exhort you to board the public conveyances without any distrust or fear, and to hasten to us, so that you may be able to obtain the things you desire.

## Third Letter of the Emperor Constantius to Athanasius

[Col. 0559]

[Col. 0559B] When we were staying at Edessa, in the presence of your presbyters, it seemed good that a presbyter should be sent to you, and that you should hasten to come to our court; so that, once you had seen us, you might immediately proceed to Alexandria. [Col. 0559C] But because much time has elapsed since you received our letters and did not come, we now [Col. 0560B] wish to admonish you again: at least now, come to us as swiftly as possible, so that you may thus be restored to your native country and we may enjoy your prayers. Moreover, for fuller information we have sent to [Col. 0560C] you the deacon Achitas, from whom you may learn both the intention of our mind and that you are able to obtain what you seek in your desires.

## First Letter of Constantius to the Alexandrian Clergy

[Note: [Col. 0559] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0559]

Constantius, victorious, greatest Augustus, to the bishops and presbyters of the catholic Church: greetings.

[Col. 0559C]

The most reverend Athanasius has not been abandoned by the grace of God, although for a brief time he was subjected to human trial. For he has now received the just and due verdict of the Providence that bears and sustains all things, since, by the will of the Supreme Being and by our judgment, he receives back his native country and the Church over which he had formerly presided by divine appointment. Accordingly, what is fitting must be granted him by our benevolence: namely, I wish all decrees formerly issued against those who communicated with him [Col. 0559D] to be consigned to oblivion; that henceforth every suspicion against them be abolished; and that the immunity formerly possessed by his clergy be preserved for them, firm and valid, as is proper.

Indeed, we have also judged it right that this further favor be added for his sake: that it be publicly proclaimed among all members of the sacred order that security has been granted to all who adhered to Athanasius, whether bishops or clergy. For it will be sufficient evidence of each person’s upright intention that he was united with Athanasius. For all who, having adopted the better judgment and lot, chose communion with him, we have commanded—after the pattern of the preceding Providence and according to our will—to enjoy securely the favor granted by the Supreme God. May God preserve you.

Constantius, victorious, greatest Augustus, to the bishops and presbyters of the catholic Church. [Col. 0560C]

The most reverend bishop Athanasius has not been deprived of the grace of Christ. Although for a short time he was subjected to the trial that belongs to human beings, he nevertheless received the due judgment from all-sustaining Providence, recovering, by the will of the Higher One and by our judgment, both his native land and the Church of which, by a divine nod, he had been the presiding guardian. It was necessary that the consequent measures should come from our clemency: that all measures previously determined against those who had communicated with him [Col. 0560D] should now be handed over to amnesty; that every suspicion of henceforth being angry with him should be removed; and that the exemption from public service formerly enjoyed by the clergy with him should fittingly be confirmed for them.

Moreover, we have judged this also to be added to the favor shown him: that all who belong to the sacred register should know that freedom from fear has been granted to all attached to him, whether bishops or clergy. Their union with him will be a sufficient indication of each person’s sound intention. For all who, having embraced the better judgment and lot, choose communion with him, we have commanded to enjoy the favor granted by the Higher One, in accordance with the earlier providence and with the decision now made by us.

## Second Letter of the Same Emperor to the Same Recipients

[Col. 0561]

Constantius, victorious, greatest Augustus, to the people of the catholic Church at Alexandria: greetings.

[Col. 0561A]

Since we have before our eyes your good order in all things, and since we know well that you have for a long time been deprived of episcopal care, we have resolved to send back to you Bishop Athanasius, a man renowned among all for uprightness and excellence of character. If, therefore, you receive him gladly and fittingly, and appoint him as your helper in prayers poured out to God, you will preserve both concord worthy of you and peace most pleasing to us, perpetual in accordance with the ordinance of the Church. For it is unreasonable that any discord or sedition should be stirred up among you; indeed, this is foreign to the sound condition of our times. We therefore wish this evil wholly to depart from you, and exhort you to continue, as I have said, steadfastly in your prayers with him as your presiding protector and helper before God, according to your accustomed practice. Thus, when your such disposition is celebrated by the mouths of all, even the Gentiles, who still cling to the error of idols, may hasten most eagerly to knowledge of sacred religion, most beloved Alexandrians.

We therefore exhort you again to abide by what has been said before. Receive gladly the bishop sent to you by the judgment of the Higher One and by our decision; regard him as welcome with the judgment of your whole soul. This is fitting for you and accords with our clemency. For, in order that every pretext for disturbance and sedition may be removed from those who willingly practice evil, we have ordered your judges by letter to subject to the penalties of the laws all whom [Col. 0562C] they discover to be seditious. Therefore, keeping in view both our judgment together with the Higher One, our concern for you and for concord, and the punishment decreed against the disorderly; preserving what is proper and fitting to the ordinance of sacred religion; and treating the aforesaid Athanasius with every reverence and honor, make haste to offer, together with him, prayers to God, the Father of all, both for yourselves and for the well-being of your life.

## Letter of the Same Emperor to Nestorius

[Col. 0561]

Constantius, victorious Augustus, to Nestorius; and in the same form to the governors of Augustamnica, Thebaid, and Libya.

[Col. 0561D]

If anything previously done against those in communion with Bishop Athanasius is found to have caused them injury or insult, we wish it now to be removed. We also wish his clergy to have again the exemption from public service which they formerly possessed. We command that this our order be observed: when Bishop Athanasius has been restored to his Church, those in communion with him are to possess the exemption from public service which they have always had and which the other clergy also possess, so that in this condition they too may rejoice.

## Fourth Letter of the Same Emperor to Athanasius

[Note: [Col. 0561] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0561]

Constantius, victorious Augustus, to Athanasius: greetings.

[Col. 0561D]

You are not unaware that it was always my wish that everything should turn out according to the desire of my brother Constans. [Col. 0563A] Your prudence can also readily infer how great was my grief when I learned that he had been murdered by certain most impious persons. But because there are some in this present and deeply mournful time who endeavor to frighten you, we have judged that these letters should be delivered to your steadfastness. I exhort you to teach the people, as befits a bishop, those things which pertain to sacred religion; to devote yourself, as usual, to prayers with them; and not to believe empty rumors, whoever may spread them. For this is fixed in our mind: in accordance with our intention, we wish you to remain bishop in your own see forever. May divine Providence preserve you for many years, dearest father.

Constantius, victorious Augustus, to Athanasius. [Col. 0562D]

It was always my wish that all things should turn out according to the desire of my late brother Constans; nor has this escaped your understanding. Your good sense can again conjecture how great was my grief when I learned that he had been killed by certain most impious persons. Since, then, there are some who in the present time, so full of mourning, attempt to frighten you, I have judged these letters to be given to your steadfastness, exhorting you, as is fitting for a bishop, to teach the peoples what is due to divine worship, to occupy yourself with prayers together with them according to custom, and not to believe vain rumors, whoever may spread them. For this is fixed in our soul: consistently with our purpose, we wish you always to be bishop in your own place. May divine Providence preserve you for many years, most beloved father.

## A.D. 337. Letter of the Emperor Constantine the Younger to the Alexandrians

[Note: [Col. 0563] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Constantine Caesar to the people of the catholic Church of the city of Alexandria.

[Col. 0563B]

I think that it has not escaped the knowledge of your sacred mind that Athanasius, the interpreter of the venerable law, was sent for a time into Gaul, lest, when the savagery of his bloodthirsty and hostile enemies threatened his sacred head with danger, he might suffer some irremediable harm through the perversion of the wicked. Therefore, to evade this savagery, he was removed from the jaws of the men lying in wait for him and commanded to live under my protection. Thus, in the city in which he resided, he possessed an abundance of all necessities, although his renowned virtue, trusting in divine assistance, despised even the burdens of harsher fortune.
