Now although my lord Constantine Augustus, my father, had especially intended, for the sake of your most beloved godliness, [Col. 0564C] to restore this bishop to his own place, yet, overtaken by the human lot before fulfilling his wish, he rested. I thought it fitting, therefore, having inherited the intention of the emperor of sacred memory, to fulfill what he could not. When Athanasius has come into your presence, you will then know how great was the honor in which he was held by us. Nor should it seem strange if I have done anything of this kind on his behalf, for both the image of your longing and the appearance of so great a man moved and urged my soul to this. May divine Providence preserve you, beloved brothers. Given at Trier, fifteen days before the Kalends of July.

## A.D. 349. Letter of Ursacius and Valens to Athanasius (C)

[Note: [Col. 0563D] Extant in Athanasius, *Apology* II; Baronius, year 350, no. 22.]

[Col. 0563D]

To Lord and brother Athanasius the bishop, Ursacius and Valens, bishops: greetings.

Taking the opportunity offered by our brother and fellow-presbyter Musaeus, who is going there to your belovedness, dear brother, we wished especially, through his service, to send you greetings from Aquileia. We pray that you may read our letter in good health. You will give us assurance of this if you too observe the reciprocal duty of writing. For we wish you to know that peace exists between you and us, and that ecclesiastical communion is maintained. We wish our greeting inscribed in this letter to be proof of this. [Col. 0564C–D] May divine Providence preserve you, beloved brother.

## A.D. 355. Letter of Constantius to Eusebius (C)

[Note: [Col. 0564D] Found in the Acts of Eusebius.]

[Col. 0564]

Constantius, victorious and triumphant, ever Augustus, to Eusebius the bishop.

The magnitude of the matter itself, I am confident, easily enables your seriousness to judge that, among all concerns belonging to my diligence, I set before all else reverence for the heavenly religion; and that it holds the foremost place in my mind. Yet your prudence has also learned this from the documents frequently sent out, since you perceive that by night [Col. 0565A] and day I pursue what I believe can advance the venerable worship. For what could be more pleasing or useful to me than to dedicate my mind to God, so fully that I feel every resource is bound to this pursuit?

Accordingly, I always look upon the venerable churches with the deepest affection of my heart, and I desire that their unity, salutary for all, be recovered and firmly maintained. For this reason it was decided that an assembly of holy bishops should be held in the city of Milan—especially those capable of readily disclosing, or perhaps refuting, what had been done elsewhere. Councils of bishops had indeed been convened in different provinces; but what the most prudent bishops had decreed unanimously in each case was clearly declared in the synod of Milan. Finally, the few who came from each province [Col. 0565B] expressed their unanimous common will and confirmed it with the reverence due to the law.

Therefore, what was consistent with religion—or, perhaps, with religious persons—was strengthened by their decision: they judged that four of their company should be sent to your holiness, jointly advising your seriousness to follow what is not at variance with the benefit of the Church. We certainly, who glory in being servants of God, likewise exhort and admonish you not to delay in adhering to the agreement of your brothers. For we trust that, when this has been done, the churches will be able to rejoice in a most firm unity. May God always protect you for many years, dearest and most beloved brother.

## A.D. 359 or 360. Letter of Constantius to the Synod of Rimini

[Col. 0565C] Constantius warned them not to presume to make any determination concerning the Eastern bishops, who were meeting separately at Seleucia.

Constantius, victorious, greatest, triumphant, ever Augustus, to the bishops.

The earlier enactments, venerable fathers, contain the principle that the holiness of the law rests upon ecclesiastical affairs. In letters given to our—perhaps your—prudence, we have more than sufficiently made clear that diligence must be given to these matters, since this surely accords with the office of bishops and the salvation of peoples far and wide is strengthened by this foundation. But the matter has prompted us to reiterate these injunctions. For no one will judge it superfluous to repeat settled matters, since frequent admonition is accustomed to increase the fullness of diligence.

This being so, let your sincerity recognize that the faith and unity must be considered, and that care must be taken for a fitting order to be provided in ecclesiastical affairs. For the posterity of all peoples everywhere will spread abroad, and reliable concord will be preserved, when all such questions have been completely cut off and have ceased to stir everyone in their pursuit. [Col. 0566B] This matter ought not to extend the mind’s attention any farther. For reason does not permit anything concerning the Eastern bishops to be determined in your council. Accordingly, your seriousness must deliberate only about those matters which it knows belong to you; and, once all things have been swiftly completed, send ten men with common agreement to my court, as we informed your prudence in earlier letters. These men will be able to answer all matters which the Eastern bishops may raise, or to discuss the faith, so that every question may be brought to a fitting conclusion and uncertainty put to rest.

This being so, you ought to establish nothing against the Eastern bishops; or, if you should wish to decide anything against them while the aforesaid persons are absent, what has been presumed will vanish without effect. For [Col. 0566C] that decision can have no force to which our enactments already testify that strength—and perhaps opportunity—is now denied. Therefore you must, with the moderation appropriate to religion, accomplish what is fitting for venerable bishops, so that what religion requires may be completed and no one may presume what reason forbids to be heard. May the Divinity preserve you for many years, dearest fathers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius.

## First Letter of the Synod of Rimini to Constantius

[Note: [Col. 0565D] Extant in Athanasius, *On the Synods*.]

[Note: [Col. 0565] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565C] Obeying God’s command and your pious edict, we judged that the doctrines formerly handed down should be confirmed as having been transmitted, by our votes. For we bishops assembled at Rimini from all cities situated toward the west, [Col. 0565D] in order that the faith of the catholic Church might be recognized and those of another opinion made manifest. After long deliberation there appeared good to us the faith that has endured from ancient times until now, which prophets, evangelists, and apostles preached through our Lord Jesus Christ, the guardian of your empire and defender of your welfare. It was therefore determined that, holding this faith, we should preserve it, and preserving it should keep it until the end.

For it is improper and unlawful to wish to alter anything of what was rightly and justly decreed, and of what was established at Nicaea after careful deliberation jointly with your most illustrious father, Emperor Constantine. Its teaching and understanding have gone abroad and been proclaimed into the ears and minds of all people. It alone has been the adversary and destroyer of the Arian heresy; through it not only that heresy but the remaining heresies have been overthrown. In it, indeed, both to add anything is hazardous and to subtract is dangerous; if either should occur, the enemies will have free license to do whatever they wish.

### On the Condemnation of Ursacius and Valens

For this reason Ursacius and Valens, who had long been associates and adherents of the Arian doctrine, were by a formal judgment separated from our communion. In order to recover it, they sought repentance and forgiveness for the offenses of which they acknowledged themselves guilty, as their written instruments testify; and because of this they received pardon and remission of their offenses. These things occurred when the synod was assembling at Milan, with the presbyters of the Roman Church also present. We were therefore fully persuaded that it was unjust, once the Emperor Constans—worthy of all remembrance after his death—had promulgated this faith, written with every care and diligence, and once he had been baptized and departed from humankind to the rest due to him, to attempt any innovation in that faith and to disregard so many holy confessors and martyrs, its writers and authors. They remained in that conviction according to the ancient law and custom of the Church; and God has transmitted their faith, through our Lord Jesus Christ, into the times of your empire, through whom you reign so extensively as to rule even our inhabited world.

### On the Inconstancy of Ursacius and Valens

But these pitiable men, lamentable in their disposition, have again, with unlawful audacity, proclaimed themselves heralds of an impious opinion and are attempting to overthrow every ordinance of truth. For at the time when the synod was assembled by your edict, they exposed the design of their own deceit. With the associates of that faction—Germinius, Auxentius, and Gaius, sowers of strife and division—they attempted through trickery and disturbance to introduce innovations. Their one and identical teaching surpasses every multitude of blasphemies. But when they saw that the men there were not of the same intention and did not agree with their perverse opinions, they joined our council, appearing to write something different; yet shortly afterward they showed their true mind.

Therefore, lest ecclesiastical affairs should continually fall into the same troubles, and disturbance and tumult, rolling on, should throw everything into confusion, it seemed firm to preserve the decrees made long ago as permanent and unshaken, and to exclude these men [Col. 0568D] from our communion.

### On the Embassy Sent to Constantius

For this reason we have sent envoys to your clemency, to communicate by letter the judgment of the council. We instructed the envoys above all to establish the truth from ancient, just, and well-founded considerations, and to show your holiness that peace will not come about, as Ursacius and Valens say, if anything just is overthrown. For how can those who destroy peace conduct themselves peaceably? Rather, from this will arise contention and disturbance, both in the other cities and in the Roman Church.

We therefore entreat your clemency to receive the concerns of our embassy with kindly ears and a serene countenance. Do not allow any innovation to be introduced to the dishonor of the dead, but permit us to remain in what our forebears determined and enacted, whom we affirm to have done everything with discernment, prudence, and the Holy Spirit. For the innovations now being produced by them cause unbelief in those who believe, and hardness—or, perhaps, credulity—in those who do not believe.

### The Bishops Request Dismissal

We further entreat you to command that bishops residing in foreign places, worn down both by the burden of age and by lack of means, be enabled to return easily to their homes, lest the churches remain bereft of bishops separated from them. We ask in addition that nothing of the former settlement be diminished and nothing increased, but that everything remain inviolable, as observed from the piety of your father until the present time. Do not permit us henceforth to suffer hardship or to become strangers outside our own dioceses; rather, let bishops, with their own peoples, live peacefully in leisure for prayers and worship, entreating God for your safety, empire, and peace, which the Divinity will grant you perpetually. Our envoys bring the subscriptions and greetings of the bishops, and from the sacred Scriptures themselves they will instruct your divinity in this matter.

## Letter of Constantius to the Same Synod

[Note: [Col. 0569D] Extant in Socrates, book II, chapter 29.]

[Note: [Col. 0569] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

The emperor commands the bishops at Rimini to await his return from the barbarian campaign.

[Col. 0569]

Constantius, victorious and triumphant Augustus, to all bishops assembled at Rimini: greetings.

[Col. 0569C]

Although your holiness is by no means unaware that we have always had the greatest concern for the divine and venerable religion of Christ, nevertheless this is not a suitable time for us to admit into our presence the twenty bishops whom your prudence sent to discharge your embassy. For the expedition which we are presently undertaking against the barbarians keeps us occupied; and it is fitting, as you know, that the mind of one who is to handle the business of the most holy religion should be free from every care and disturbance.

Accordingly, we have commanded the bishops to await our return at Hadrianopolis, so that, once the affairs of state have been duly administered, we may then carefully hear and examine [Col. 0569D] the matters which they intend to lay before us. Meanwhile, let it not be burdensome to your seriousness to await their return, so that, when they have returned and reported our answers to you, you may carry through to completion those matters which will serve the benefit of the catholic Church.

Constantius, victorious and triumphant Augustus, to all bishops assembled at Rimini. [Col. 0570C]

Your goodness is not unaware that we always make foremost our concern for the divine and venerable law. Yet at present we have not been able to see the twenty bishops sent from your prudence to undertake the embassy before us, for our journey against the barbarians is necessary. And, as you know, it is fitting that a soul free from every care should occupy itself with matters concerning the divine law. We have therefore commanded the bishops to await our return in the city of Hadrian. When all public matters have been properly arranged, we shall then be able to hear and examine what they submit. Let it not, however, seem burdensome to your steadfastness to await their return, so that when they return bringing you our answers [Col. 0570D] you may bring to completion what pertains to the advantage of the catholic Church.

## Second Letter of the Synod of Rimini to Constantius

The synod requests permission to leave Rimini before the severity of winter.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0569]

[Col. 0569D] Most holy emperor, we have received the letters of your clemency, from which we learned that, because of necessary affairs of state, you did not at that time have sufficient leisure to admit our envoys to your presence; and that you command us to await their return until your prudence has learned from them what has been determined and decreed by us in accordance with the institutions of our forebears. [Col. 0571A] Yet through these letters we now confess and assure you that we will by no means depart from our purpose and judgment; and we have given the same command to our envoys.

We therefore ask you to ensure that these letters, written to you by our moderation, are read with a gracious countenance; and also to receive favorably what we have entrusted to our envoys to perform. Your kindness also recognizes with us how sorrowful and grievous it is that, in these most blessed times of yours, so many churches are deprived of their bishops. We therefore once more entreat your clemency, most august emperor, that before the severity of winter—if it so please your piety—you command that we be permitted to return to our churches, [Col. 0571B] in order that, together with the people, we may offer our customary prayers for your reign to God the Father almighty and to our Lord and Savior Christ, his only-begotten Son, as we have always done before and do not cease to do even now.

[Col. 0570D] We have received the letters of your benevolence, lord emperor most beloved of God, which state that, because of the necessities of public affairs, you have not yet been able to see our envoys; and you command us to await their return until your reverence learns from them what has been determined by us in accordance with our forefathers. [Col. 0572A] But even now, through these letters, we confess and confirm that we shall in no way withdraw from our purpose; for we gave this command also to our envoys.

We therefore ask that you command the present letters of our moderation to be read with a serene countenance, and that you also receive gladly the matters which we committed to our envoys. Your gentleness sees with us how great is now the sorrow and dejection, because in these most blessed times so many churches are without bishops. Therefore we again ask your benevolence, lord emperor most beloved of God, that before the harshness of winter, if it please your piety, you command us to return to our churches, so that we may be able, together with the peoples, to offer our customary prayers for your reign to almighty God and to our Lord and Savior [Col. 0572B] Christ, his only-begotten Son—as we have always performed them and continue to do now.

## A.D. 365. Letter of the Bishops of Italy and Illyricum, Rejoicing That the Nicene Faith Has Been Accepted

[Note: Extant in Hilary, *Fragments*, book I, p. 38; Baronius, year 365, nos. 26–27.]

[Col. 0571]

To the most beloved brothers throughout Illyricum who retain the faith of the fathers: the bishops of Italy, eternal salvation in the Lord.

[Col. 0571B]

It is the grace of a divine gift that, according to the Apostle, we have all begun to think one thing and all to confess one thing. So far as Italy is concerned, it has returned to the faith of the fathers—that is, to the faith written at Nicaea—[Note: formerly] recognizing the deception it suffered at Rimini. [Col. 0571C] We rejoice that God has also looked upon Illyricum with a merciful nod, and that, having cast off the fellowship of unbelief by which it was burdened, it has begun to approve what belongs to sound judgment.

Receive, therefore, most beloved brothers, our one and identical firm judgment, confirmed by subscription. We preserve the determinations of the Nicene deliberation against Arius and Sabellius, in whose shared inheritance Photinus is condemned. By the agreement of all provinces, we rightly annul the decrees of the Council of Rimini, corrupted by the evasions of certain persons. We have also judged that copies should be sent, so that no concession might appear to exist either in retaining the faith or in refuting the Council of Rimini.

Whoever, therefore, desires fellowship in our unanimity, whoever desires indivisible peace with us, should hasten to approve our judgment [Col. 0572C] and send us, without ambiguity, his subscription to the faith mentioned and to the annulment of the Council of Rimini. We ask, certainly, for what we ourselves offer: the agreement of many of these provinces. It is manifest that Valens and Ursacius, authors of the Arian or Aetian heresy, along with their other associates, were condemned not merely now, because they have begun to be exposed in Illyricum, but long ago.

## Letter of the Synod of Singidunum to the Semi-Arian Germinius (C)*

[Note: [Col. 0571D] Hilary, *Fragments*, book I, p. 40; Baronius, year 366, no. 26.]

[Col. 0571]

To the most religious lord and brother Germinius: Valens, Ursacius, Gaius, and Paulus, greetings.

[Col. 0571D]

When concern for hope and salvation presses upon us, those who are concerned should be praised rather than bear any reproach. Salvation and hope principally consist in the catholic faith. Therefore, although at every meeting our lords, brothers, and fellow-bishops Valens and Paulus have not wished to respond to the report [Note: “is circulated”] that is being spread concerning you, most religious lord, yet because in your letter you have testified that you persevere in the same charity and are ready to show an undiminished love toward us, we have assembled at [Note: Singidunum] and again admonish your holiness by this letter.

Exclude every occasion for ambiguity and deign to write back to us again, clearly stating whether, as you have already professed, you will not depart from the catholic faith that was set forth and confirmed at Rimini by the holy council, and to which all the bishops of the East also consented. This faith states, as it was safeguarded there: “We say that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures,” not “according to substance,” nor “in every respect,” but absolutely. For if this exposition is altered, the formerly treacherous assertion of Basil—on account of which the council was held and by which he was deservedly condemned—will plainly be restored.

Deign, therefore, to declare clearly in your letter what is required: that you have not said, do not say, and will not say that the Son is like the Father in every respect except unbegottenness. Otherwise, what the bearers of this letter, the deacon Jovianus and the subdeacon Martyrius, asserted in their plea before our aforesaid lords, brothers, and fellow-bishops Valens and Paulus may seem more credible: namely, that you profess the Son to be like the Father in every respect.

If in your written reply you make clear that your opinion is as we desire, then the complaint of injury made by certain of your clergy against our brothers and fellow-bishops Palladius and Gaius—although, despite your being admonished at the first meeting, you were unwilling to investigate it—concerns [Col. 0573A] your reputation, those men being answerable for their rashness. We have sent these matters to your charity through the presbyter Secundianus, the reader Pullentius, and the exorcist Candidianus, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of the most noble Gratian and Dagalaifus, retaining a copy with us.

## Letter of the Semi-Arian Germinius against the Arians (C)

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Hilary, *Fragments*, book I, p. 41; Baronius, ibid., no. 27.]

[Col. 0573]

To the most religious lords and brothers Rufianus, Palladius, [Col. 0573B] Severinus, Nica, Heliodorus, Romulus, Mucianus, and Stercorius: Germinius, greetings in the Lord.

Through a report of Vitalis, now serving in the office of the exalted prefecture, we have learned that your Holiness desires to have plainly set before you what it is in our faith that displeases Valens, Ursacius, Gaius, and Paul. I have judged it necessary to disclose this in writing to your Holiness, and to affirm that which [Note: “in us.”] I trust has been in yourselves from the beginning: namely, that we hold what we received handed down from the Fathers and what we have learned once for all from the divine Scriptures and teach daily—that Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, is like the Father in all respects, except in being unbegotten: God from God, light from light, power from power, whole from whole, perfect from perfect; begotten before the ages and before all things that can be understood or spoken [Col. 0573C]; whose generation no one knows except the Father alone, as the Son himself declares: “For no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11); through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1), according to the divine utterances of our Savior himself, the Son, saying: “My Father is working until now, and I too am working” (John 5). And again: “Whatever the Father does, these things the Son likewise does” (ibid.). And again: “I and the Father are one.” And again: “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” And again: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 14). And again: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son [Note: “Whom.”] gives life to whom he wills.” And again: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 5). And again: [Col. 0573D] “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father.” And again, to whom the Father said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). He did not say, “according to your image,” or “according to my image,” lest he indicate some dissimilarity in the divinity of his Son; rather, he joined the words “according to our image and likeness” in order to show that his Son is God like himself in all respects. Again, the Evangelist says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1). And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “In whom [Col. 0574B] the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that they should not shine with the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Cor. 4). And the same Apostle again: “And he transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love [Note: “His.”], in whom we have redemption and remission of sins; who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature” (1 Thess. 1). And again the same Apostle: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not deem it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men” (Phil. 4). Who does not understand that, just as according to the form of a servant our flesh in Christ was real, so also, in the form of God, the divinity of the Father is real in the Son? And again: “See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and [Col. 0574C] empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ; for in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:8). If, therefore, all the fullness of divinity dwells in Christ, he is no longer like in part and unlike in part, as those now maintain who, turning backward because of the contention of their own desire, turn themselves [Note: “They turned away.”] away from us.

For what they think a great point to bring forward from the divine Scriptures—when they call Christ a product and a creature—we, on the contrary, according to the Scriptures, call him also the way, the door, the stone of stumbling, the rock of offense, the foundation, the arm, the hand, wisdom, the Word, the lamb, the sheep, the shepherd, the priest, life, the day, and other such things. But [Col. 0574D] we understand and speak all these things in such a way as to understand the powers and operations of the Son of God, not as to compare his divine birth from the Father with names of this sort. For all things were made from nothing through the Son; but the Son was not made from nothing: he was begotten from God the Father.

**The craftiness of Valens noted.**—Yet I wonder whether the aforesaid Valens has forgotten, or at least is craftily pretending not to remember, what was done and settled in the past. For under the Emperor Constantius of blessed memory, when a disagreement concerning the faith had arisen among certain persons, in the presence of that emperor, with George, bishop of the church of Alexandria, the bishop of the Pelusians, [Col. 0575A] Basil, then bishop of Ancyra, and Valens and Ursacius themselves present, and also my own insignificance [Note: “by my insignificance.”] in that perversity, after a discussion concerning the faith lasting until night and brought to a definite rule, Mark, rejected by all of us [Note: “chosen.”], set forth the faith, in which it was written thus: “The Son is like the Father in all respects, as the holy Scriptures say and teach.” We all assented to this entire confession and subscribed it with our own hands. But if some spirit of this world now suggests anything else, we cannot yet know it openly. For as we have confessed from the Scriptures that the Son is like the Father in all respects except in being unbegotten, let them too expound from the Scriptures how he is like in part [Col. 0576A] and unlike in part. Therefore, beloved brethren, I have sent this confession without fear and without delay to the knowledge of your love, through Cyriacus, an official—the first opportunity found after the deacon Carinus, whom I sent to you—so that through your most watchful devotion before God it may be made known to the whole brotherhood, lest anyone, unaware, be entangled in the snares of the deceitful [Note: “of the deceitful.”] devil. It now belongs to your unanimity to write back to me what the Holy Spirit suggests to you. I further inform your charity that I could not subscribe this letter because my hand was in pain; I ordered our brethren and fellow-presbyters Innocentius, Octavius, and Catulus to subscribe it.

## A.D. 370. Constitution of the Emperor Valentinian to Pope Damasus

(From Coustant, p. 473.)

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575B] **That ecclesiastics and persons professing continence may receive nothing from the property of widows, whether by will or by gift.**

The Emperors Valentinian, [Note: The name of Valens is lacking in the Coislin manuscript.] Valens, and Gratian, Augusti, to Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome.

Ecclesiastics, or those belonging to ecclesiastical circles, or those who wish to be called by the name of persons professing continence [Note: Here Jerome, *Epistle* 2 to Nepotian, understands “persons professing continence” to mean monks, where he says: “The priests of idols, actors, charioteers, and prostitutes receive inheritances; only clerics and monks are prohibited by this law.”], shall not visit the houses of widows and orphans. Rather, if hereafter their relatives or kinsfolk think they ought to be denounced, they shall be excluded by public [Note: That is, secular courts, as is clear from the Code of Canons of the African Church: first, chapter 15, where, according to the Third Council of Carthage, canon 9, it is prescribed that any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric against whom an accusation has been brought in the Church, or against whom a civil suit has been initiated, shall lose his position if, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, he wishes to clear himself in public courts, even if a verdict is rendered in his favor; then chapter 104, where it is enacted: “It has seemed good that whoever seeks from the emperor a hearing in public courts shall be deprived of his own rank; but if he requests episcopal judgment from the emperor, let this not prejudice him.”] courts.

We also decree that the persons mentioned may obtain nothing, whether from any liberality or [Note: Here and below, *nothing ... or by last judgment* appears to mean no more than what is shortly expressed as “or by will”; a will is indeed called a “last judgment,” because it is valid only upon a final act of will and the intervention of death.] final disposition, from that woman to whom they have privately attached themselves under the pretext of religion. And whatever [Col. 0576B] any of these persons may have been left by such women shall be entirely ineffective, so that they may not receive anything either by gift or by will through an intermediary [Note: Here fideicommissa, or testamentary trusts, are prohibited. Jerome complains that this law was later evaded by them, as observed above.] person. Indeed, should those women perhaps think that they ought to leave anything to these same persons by gift or final disposition after the warning of our law, the treasury shall appropriate it.

But if any [Note: That is, if any of those women. Here and throughout the rest of this constitution, clerics and persons professing continence are prohibited from receiving gifts from unmarried widows. Hence, where Ambrose and Jerome, in the passages cited, seemed to speak generally of every gift left by the will of anyone, they must be understood to mean a gift from unmarried widows. Ambrose himself indicates this more plainly in the cited letter: “What a Christian widow has bequeathed to a priest of a shrine is valid; what she has bequeathed to ministers of God is not valid.” Indeed, Baronius considers that this law barred only ecclesiastical persons, not churches likewise, from accepting widows’ legacies; and Jerome’s *Epistle* 2 to Nepotian supports him: “Let the Church—the mother of her children, that is, of her flock, which bore, nourished, and fed them—be heir; why do we insert ourselves between mother and children?”] of them receive by the will of women to whose succession or property they are assisted by civil law or by the benefits of an edict, let them take it as kinsmen.

[Note: In the Coislin manuscript: “Read in the Roman church, III Kalends,” etc.] Read in the churches of Rome on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the third consulship of the Augusti Valentinian and Valens.

## A.D. 378 or 381. Letter of the Roman Council Held under Damasus to the Emperors Gratian and Valentinian

[Note: This letter was published by Jacques Sirmond in the appendix to the *Codex Theodosianus*, p. 78. It is therefore, apparently, entitled in the name of the Roman Council rather than Damasus, because, although he attended this council, he did not sit in it as judge, but in order that the innocence already attested by the emperor’s judgment might also be established by the judgments of the priests. Nevertheless, he may rightly be regarded as its principal author. Certainly no one will deny that whatever is requested in it was sought at least at his prompting and with his assent. It therefore rightly has a place among Damasus’s letters. Some date it to the year 381, others to the end of 378. Labbe briefly reviews the arguments opposed to the first view and favoring the latter, *Councils*, vol. II, p. 1005: “Baronius, Sirmond, and others taught that the Roman council from which the preceding letter was sent met in the year 381. But the following arguments refute them. The first is drawn from the heading of that letter: since it contains no mention whatever of Valens or Theodosius, it is evident that it was written after the death of the former and before the accession of the latter. Valens died on 9 August 378; Theodosius was hailed Augustus on 19 January immediately following. Hence it is inferred that the letter was written either at the end of 378 or at the beginning of 379. Secondly, the Fathers of the Council of Aquileia teach, in their first letter, published shortly below, col. 998 E, that in 381 Ursicinus at Milan was allied with the Arians and joined his counsels with Valens of Mursa, their standard-bearer. But when the Roman synod wrote to the emperors, the withdrawal of Agrippina, far distant from the city of Milan, restrained and confined this same Ursicinus in Gaul, as is clear from the emperors’ rescript itself to Aquilinus, vicar of the City, above, col. 1004. Thirdly, in 381 Antidius, to whom the law of the *Codex Theodosianus*, book IX, title 38, law 7, was addressed on 21 July, and Potens, to whom *Codex Theodosianus*, book IV, title 22, law 2, was directed on 14 October, administered the vicariate of the City—not Aquilinus, whom Baronius mistakenly called vicar of the ordinary judges, though he was vicar of the City, as Sirmond correctly observed according to his custom. Fourthly, because the basis of the contrary opinion collapses of itself. Florentius of Puteoli was not condemned in A.D. 367 but in 372; and in the emperors’ rescript, above, col. 1004, one should not read, as the manuscript used by Baronius and Sirmond had it, ‘after the fifteenth year,’ but ‘only after the fifth year.’ Condemned by the judgment of a synod in that year, 372, expelled from Puteoli by the emperor’s order in the following year, 373, he began again to stir up disturbances at the end of 378—the sixth year after the synod’s sentence (above, same col., in the letter of the Roman Council), and the fifth after his expulsion. Add that the year of Christ 381, beginning the fifteenth year from Ursicinus’s condemnation, cannot be called ‘after the fifteenth year,’ as Blondel also observed.” Of these, the principal and chief point is that in the heading of this letter, just as in the superscription of the following rescript, the names of Gratian and Valentinian alone are recorded, not those of Valens or Theodosius. They therefore infer that this letter was composed within the period between Valens’s death and Theodosius’s acclamation as emperor—that is, between 9 August 378 and 19 January 379.] (Coustant, p. 523.)

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575D] **That they ensure enforcement of the law whereby they had enacted that, concerning religion, the pontiff of religion should judge together with his colleagues, and that a priest should not readily be subjected anywhere to the sentence of a profane judge.**

1. **That what the emperors had already granted voluntarily may not lack effect.**—This too, most merciful princes, is an illustrious proof of your glory and piety: when almost innumerable persons from the widespread regions of Italy had assembled [Col. 0576D] at the exalted sanctuary of the apostolic see, and we considered what ought to be requested of you for the condition of the churches, we could discover nothing better than what your providence had voluntarily bestowed. We see that there ought now to be no shame in asking, [Col. 0577A] nor [Note: That is, there is no longer any need for us to obtain them by entreaty.] need we now obtain benefits which are already yours, and the series of imperial decrees itself surrounds us in our favor. For as regards the justice of the petition, we have long since deserved to obtain what we ask; but as regards the need to make request, we lack the effect of what has been granted to such an extent that we wish to obtain it again. This, indeed, most merciful princes, displays the madness of ruined men, but increases the service of your justice, so that benefits may be bestowed more often in your Church.

2. **The law granting the Roman pontiff authority to judge cases concerning religion.**—For from the beginning, filled with the divine Spirit and observing in the Lord’s religion the command of the holy Apostles—whose support you possess in your honor—you decreed, for the restoration of the body of the Church, which the frenzy of Ursinus, who had attempted to seize an unlawful honor, had cut into different parts, that, after its author had been condemned [Note: Baronius reports different imperial rescripts in the case of Ursinus: the first under the year 368, by which Ursinus, with his associates and agents, was expelled from the City, though they were allowed to live wherever they chose without injury to religion, exercising their own legal rights, so that they might seem to be travelling rather than exiled; the second in the same year, by which the Emperor Valentinian permitted Ursinus and his associates, who had been expelled, to return to the City, but to be punished more severely if they should thereafter stir up disturbances; the third under 369, by which their gatherings outside the city walls, from which frequent commotion arose, were prohibited, and it was enacted that those who took pleasure in turbulent separation should hold no meeting within the twentieth milestone. Moreover, a fourth, before 371, was issued—unmentioned by Baronius, but sufficiently known from the one he places last—by which Ursinus and his companions, namely Gaudentius, Ursus, Rufus, Auxano, Auxanius, Adiedus, and Rufus, were ordered to remain in one place within Gaul. Finally, the distinguished Cardinal places a fifth under 371, by which the preceding command was relaxed so that they were permitted to leave Gaul on condition that they could not reside in the city of Rome or the suburban regions. Yet in none of these orders were Ursinus’s companions separated from him or forbidden to reside with him. In each, either a common punishment or a common indulgence is decreed for the author and his associates. But the edict issued to Simplicius, mentioned at the beginning of the following letter and almost certainly noted here, separates Ursinus from his associates: the withdrawal of Agrippina confines him in Gaul, while the others are expelled only to the hundredth milestone from the City. Simplicius held the office of vicar of the City at the beginning of 374.], and the others whom he had associated with himself as incentives to disturbances had, as was proper, been separated from association with that ruined man, [Col. 0577B] the bishop of Rome should examine the remaining bishops of the churches; so that in matters of religion the pontiff of religion might judge together with his colleagues, and no injury might seem to be done to the priesthood if a priest should not readily be subject anywhere to the discretion of a profane [Col. 0578A] judge—which could often happen.

3. **Praise of this law.**—This is plainly a splendid decision, worthy of religious princes: it gives the greatest deference to divine ministry and is not open to error. For what is more fitting than that the one who judges a priest’s fault should be one who knows that he cannot yield to the favor of inward conscience without danger to himself, and who incurs guilt if he acquits the unworthy or condemns the innocent; one who, finally, in avenging an injury to religion, seeks that injury not in the sides [Note: This refers to tortures by which it was customary for either accused persons or others to have their sides racked; ecclesiastical courts are said, in the final words of this letter, to abhor this practice.] of innocents but in the conduct of the accused? For how often has it been evident that persons whom courts have acquitted have been condemned by bishops, and that persons whom courts have condemned have been acquitted? Thus the cause of those who, considering not secular but divine judgments, have withheld their punishment lest the innocent be tortured is better than that of those who proved their own lives by the tortures of innocents. We might add many examples, most tranquil princes, if it were not an injury to assert imperial decrees rather than to uphold them.

4. **That the same law be confirmed. Ursinus secretly stirs disturbances.**—But since Ursinus, although long ago relegated by the judgment of your Clemency [Note: Ursinus had been relegated to Gaul at least from the year 370, as is clear from the edicts just recounted.], tries through those whom [Col. 0579A] that sacrilegious man unlawfully ordained to solicit, though secretly, every most contemptible person; and since, following his example, certain bishops who improperly prey upon churches, by habitual recklessness and a profane conspiracy of contempt, strive not to submit to the judgment of the Roman priest; so that even those who understand themselves to deserve condemnation according to their merits, or have seen themselves condemned, having bought the multitude of the populace, harass their judges with fear of death and, scorning or driving away the examiners, obtain an unlawful priesthood: therefore we request not novelty, but firmness, for the imperial ordinance. It is unworthy that any assembly which brings armed force with it should be so much the more secure the more criminal it is.

5. **Deposed bishops retain churches.**—Thus [Col. 0579B] the bishop of Parma [Note: Tillemont conjectures that “bishop of Portus” ought to be read here, especially for this reason: Gratian, in the following rescript, addressing Simplicius—whom he takes certainly to have been prefect at Rome—complains that Florentius retains the church of Parma through the negligence of Simplicius’s predecessor. But Parma, he says, was a city of Aemilia, and Aemilia was subject to the prefect of Italy, not to the prefect of Rome. He adds that in the same rescript Florentius is called more pernicious because he is nearer to the illustrious City, whereas this is not said of the bishop of Puteoli, who was much closer. But the chief obstacle to accepting this learned man’s conjecture is that, although this letter and the following rescript are known to have come from different manuscripts, “of Parma” is read in both places. It is scarcely possible that different copyists, in different writings, should err in precisely the same manner in giving one name. Moreover, we observe that Florentius is not called simply near the illustrious City, but nearer—namely, in comparison with Ursinus and Isaac. Since one was held in Gaul and the other in Spain, both were farther from the City than Florentius. The bishop of Puteoli was indeed nearer than Florentius; but perhaps he was not considered more pernicious because he confined himself to Puteoli. Perhaps this concern also belonged to Simplicius: that he should not allow the judgment of the Roman Council to be violated; that he should drive Florentius, stirring disturbances in the suburban regions, beyond their boundaries; and that he should punish this adherent of Ursinus with the penalty decreed by the emperors against Ursinus’s associates.]—deposed by our judgment—nevertheless shamelessly retains his church. Florentius of Puteoli was likewise condemned; after he had been deposed, he troubled the ears of your Serenity and obtained a rescript of this kind [Note: If the very rescript mentioned here is the one issued to Simplicius in the following letter, §1, then, since Simplicius is known to have been vicar of the City at the beginning of 374, there will be no slight basis for conjecturing that Florentius was deposed from his church around 373 and began to creep back into it toward the end of 378.]: that, if he had been deposed by the judgment of priests in the city of Rome, he should not even be permitted to speak in the courts. Yet after the sixth year he crept back into the city, occupied the church, and by his insolence stirred up many seditions in the town of Puteoli, from which he had been deposed.

6. **Restitutus, ordered to plead his case, evades the command.**—Your Clemency likewise ordered a man named Restitutus in Africa to plead his case before the bishops. [Col. 0580A] He ought to have submitted; but with a savage band of insolent men he fled from the obligation of pleading his case.

7. **Claudianus, a Donatist pseudo-bishop, commits abominations at Rome.**—Again, in Africa you ordered, by God’s prompting, sacrilegious re-baptizers to be expelled [Note: There survives a law of Gratian, *Codex Theodosianus*, book XVI, title VI, law 11, issued in October 377 to the Vicar of Africa. It orders those who, having received the sacraments of the Christian name, do not purify but defile them with another baptism to abstain from churches which they hold against the faith, once these have been restored to the Catholics. In the text of this constitution Gratian says that he follows the decrees of his forebears, especially Valentinian, and immediately adds: “But many, though expelled from the churches, nevertheless continue their ravages in hidden frenzy.” Hence either this command of Gratian or another of Valentinian is suitably understood to be the one mentioned here.]; but Claudianus was ordained by those expelled and sent, as though a bishop, to disturb the city of Rome. Contrary to the precepts of divine Scripture and contrary to evangelical law, he calls all bishops devoid of the mysteries and—using his own term—pagans, whether in the past or present tense [Note: This was not the practice of Claudianus alone but also of others of the same sect: they called pagans those baptized anywhere but among themselves. Optatus addresses them generally in this way, *Against the Donatists*, book III, after the middle: “What sort of thing is this, that you say even to Christian men, even clerics: ‘Go away, Christians’; and, with a certain astonishment, say to each person: ‘Gaius Seius, or Gaia Seia, are you still a pagan man or a pagan woman? …’ If any Christian should commit some offense—which God forbid—he may be called a sinner; he cannot become a pagan again.”]. Your Serenity ordered him expelled from Rome and sent back to his native country. But, despising judgments, though repeatedly arrested, he nevertheless remains, frequently soliciting poorer people by payment and daring to rebaptize those who have been redeemed. He takes away more what they had received than he gives what it is evident cannot be conferred twice [Col. 0580B].

8. **Ursinus suborns Isaac as accuser of Damasus.**—Thus, finally, Ursinus’s faction advanced so far that, after suborning Isaac [Note: This Isaac is thought to be none other than the person listed by Gennadius among ecclesiastical writers, chapter 26, and whose book *On the Trinity and the Incarnation* Jacques Sirmond published in 1630.], a Jew who, by returning to the synagogue, profaned the heavenly mysteries, the head of our holy brother Damasus was sought, innocent blood was to be shed, and plots were contrived. By a clearly divine prompting, the providence of your Piety met these designs. The Church was almost stripped of all its ministries, by this fraud, namely: while the man appointed judge over all was pleading his own case, there would be no one able to judge the fallen—or rather the factional—invaders of bishoprics.

[Col. 0581A] 9. **Damasus is shown innocent; Isaac suffers the penalty for his calumny. How one who resists ecclesiastical judgment should be restrained.**—Since, therefore, the innocence of our aforesaid brother Damasus has been established by the judgment of your Serenity and his integrity proclaimed, Isaac himself too, when he could not prove the charges he had brought, received the lot due to his merits [Note: That is, he was deported to a remote corner of Spain, as Gratian says in the following letter, §2, under the force of those laws issued by his predecessors which Gratian confirmed in 385 by the constitution found in *Codex Theodosianus*, book IX, title XXXIX, law 2, in these words: “It has been provided in the constitutions of ourselves and our forebears,” etc. Therefore deportation follows a most calumnious head and a person rendered infamous by a judgment for a baseless accusation, so that thereafter all, individually and collectively, may know that they are not permitted to agitate the minds of princes concerning what cannot be demonstrated.]. We beg your Clemency that we may not again seem burdensome in very many cases: may your Piety deign to command that whoever has been condemned either by his judgment or by ours, who are Catholics, and unjustly wishes to retain a church, or who, summoned to priestly judgment, contumaciously refuses to appear, shall be summoned by the illustrious men, the prefects of the praetory of your Italy, or by the Vicar, to come to the city of Rome. Or, if a question of this kind arises in more distant [Col. 0581B] regions, let him be brought to examination before the metropolitan by the local courts; or, if he himself is metropolitan, let him be ordered without delay necessarily to proceed to Rome or to those judges whom the bishop of Rome has appointed. Thus those who have been deposed shall be separated only from the boundaries of that city in which they exercised the priesthood, lest they again shamelessly usurp what has been lawfully taken away. Certainly, if favoritism or injustice is suspected in the case either of a metropolitan or of any other priest, it shall be permissible to appeal either to the bishop of Rome or at least to a council of fifteen neighboring bishops [Note: Canon 10 of the Second Council of Carthage, incorporated as chapter 12 of the Code of Canons of the African Church, decrees even for the first hearing of any bishop’s case, in accordance with the statutes of earlier councils, that, if a bishop incurs an accusation and there is urgent necessity such that many cannot be assembled, he shall be heard by twelve bishops, lest he remain under accusation. Nicholas I, in a letter to King Solomon, confirms with the testimony of his predecessors Leo II and Benedict III that the Roman Church also customarily observed this practice. One might have added Gregory I, book V, indiction 13, letter 53, and others.]. Whoever has deserved to be excluded in this manner should keep silence and remain at rest; and if he does not fear God’s judgment, let him at least be compelled by necessity to sin less, so that thereafter we may at least be able, peaceful and concordant, to return to your Serenity fitting thanks before our Lord.

10. **Damasus was entitled to avail himself of the law assigning priests’ cases to the judgment of priests.**—Our aforesaid brother Damasus, since in his own case he possesses the distinguished proof of your judgment, must not be placed beneath those to whom he is equal in office but surpasses in the prerogative of the apostolic see; so that he may appear subject to public courts [Note: We would prefer the reading: “may appear to be subject.” In *Epistle* 21 to Valentinian the Younger, §2, Ambrose praises a law of Valentinian the Elder whereby that emperor enacted that in a matter of faith or of some ecclesiastical order the judge ought to be one “who is neither unequal in office nor unlike in right”—these are the words of the rescript—that is, he wished priests to judge priests. Moreover, if a bishop were accused in another matter and a case concerning conduct had to be examined, he wished this too to belong to episcopal judgment. That this law is indicated here by the Roman Council seems all the more probable because the Council’s words, “equal in office, but surpasses in the prerogative of the apostolic see,” in some measure correspond to the words of the law itself, “neither unequal in office nor unlike in right.” Nor is it inconsistent that Ambrose praises a law which he attributes to Valentinian while the Council here indicates a law which it attributes to Gratian. Nothing prevents the same law, which bore the name of both, from being attributed separately to Valentinian by Ambrose when he addressed Valentinian’s son, and separately to Gratian by the Council in the petition offered to him. Yet in the collections preserved by the Coislin manuscript, written in the ninth century, I have found another law on this subject cited in this form: “Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius decreed that no one should dare to accuse a bishop before public judges, but should not delay in bringing before a hearing of bishops whatever he thinks he may claim according to the nature of the affair, so that what he alleges against a bishop may be decided by the judgment of other bishops.” But if this law were judged to be recalled here by the Roman Council, the basis of the position held by those who think this letter written before Theodosius entered upon the empire would collapse. Moreover, Valentinian III, in Novel 12, issued in 452, derogated from the law just cited.] from which your law has exempted the priestly head. In this he does not seem, after judgment has been rendered, to decline judgment, but to demand the honor conferred by you. For as regards public laws, [Col. 0582B] what life can be safer than one that rests upon the judgment of your Clemency? [Note: That is, than the life of one who has been judged and acquitted by the emperor himself. After such a judgment public judges can do nothing against it.] But as regards the proclamation of the bishop’s conscience [Note: The same phrase “as regards” is to be supplied in the latter words, “but as regards the public attestation of the bishop’s conscience.” We therefore alter the former punctuation, by which the Council’s meaning was altogether confused. If we correctly grasp the Council’s words here, it does not deny that Damasus, acquitted by Gratian’s judgment, submitted examination of the same case to ecclesiastical judgment; but, lest he seem by that course to have diminished the emperor’s authority at all, it now excuses his action to the emperor.], he submitted himself to the stricter judgments of priests, by whom an account is weighed not merely of reputation but also of conduct; lest, should another calumniator arise and seek to attack the aforesaid man, he might indeed be unable to harm the man himself, protected as he is by his innocence, but an injury might nevertheless be done to religion through harassment of its ministers.

### 11. That the Roman bishop should defend himself either before his own council or before an imperial council. The judge may investigate acts, but may not pass sentence concerning them. Priestly religion recoils from torture.

Receive also this further request, which the holy man desires rather to contribute to your piety than to secure for himself—not to derogate from anyone, but to ascribe authority to princes. For he asks nothing new, but follows the examples of the ancients: that, if the case of the Roman bishop is not entrusted to his own council, he may defend himself before an imperial council. For Pope Sylvester also, when accused by sacrilegious persons, pleaded his own cause before your ancestor Constantine. Similar examples are supplied by Scripture [Note: That is, they are available.]: when the holy Apostle suffered violence from the governor, he appealed to Caesar and was sent to Caesar (Acts 25:11–12).

Certainly, let Your Clemency first examine the case, and, if any question arises, distinguish it by inquiry: so that, as you formerly deemed proper, an account of the acts may be required from the judge, but the discretionary power of his sentence may not be challenged. Thus no abandoned or infamous person will have unlawful opportunity either to accuse the chief priest or to bear testimony against him; since holy Scripture prescribes that no accusation against even a presbyter, much less a bishop, is readily to be received except upon competent witnesses (1 Tim. 5:19). For mercy is not to be granted either to an enemy, a calumniator, or men of the sort lately shown to have been accusers; their life does not deserve credit, and the religion of a priest recoils from tortures.

**In the Year of the Lord 380.**  
[Note: Baronius found this rescript in a Vatican manuscript and, after collating it with another copy, inserted it in his Ecclesiastical Annals under the year 381. The preceding letter of the Roman council gave occasion to it. Whether Gratian wrote the rescript to the council itself is unknown. The same argument drawn from the superscription—in which neither Valens nor Theodosius appears, whence scholars infer that the immediately preceding letter of the synod was written between August 378 and January 379—also applies here, so that this rescript may be conjectured to have been issued within the same interval.]

## Rescript of Gratian Augustus to Aquilinus, Vicar of the City

By this, nearly everything requested in the preceding letter is granted.

(Coust. p. 530.) (C)

[Col. 0583]

Gratian and Valentinian Augusti to Aquilinus, vicar.

[Col. 0583B]

### 1. Gratian complains of neglected commands. Edicts against Ursinus had already been issued to Simplicius.

The decisions of regular judges—whether established by the limitation of time, by a ruling upon contumacy, or by an examination held before the fathers [Note: F.: *partibus*, “parties.”]—do not fear to be weakened and overturned by persons of inferior authority, nor by the powerful, nor by the shameless. What decision, then, can make firm our commands, abandoned through your negligence? Yet, while you disregard them, do not provoke them to bring the effect of long patience upon desperate men, so that compulsion of fear may oblige them to recognize their duty.

Or is what the madness of Ursinus commanded not more absurd than what our Serenity has persuaded by mild edicts: namely, that all who should attempt impious gatherings by profaning religion should be expelled to the hundredth milestone from the City, where persistent madness, deserted by its adherents, might rush only to the destruction of the one person who alone had gone astray; and that those condemned by the judgment of right-thinking priests should thereafter have no return either to the churches they had polluted, nor vainly beg from us, with shameless obstinacy, a reopening of the judgment?

[Note: These edicts, and perhaps this rescript itself, are cited by Honorius in *Codex Theodosianus*, book XVI, title II, law 33, as follows: “Whoever, while priests are established in office, has been cast down from the episcopal rank and title, if he is discovered plotting anything against custody or against the public peace, and again seeks the priesthood from which he appears to have been expelled, shall live a hundred miles away from the city which he polluted, according to the law of divine-memory Gratian. Let him be separated from the assemblies of those from whose communion he has been cut off; and by the tenor of this law it shall be unlawful for persons of this kind to approach our sacred private presence and obtain rescripts.” Nor does Godfrey seem to be right in thinking that Honorius here recalls a law issued by Gratian after the Council of Caesaraugusta in the case of the Priscillianists. It is much more probable that Honorius cites Gratian’s law, enacted in the case of those concerning whom the preceding Roman synod complains. To make this clearer, we should add what Honorius, in Sirmond, appendix to the *Codex Theodosianus*, p. 6, prefaces immediately before the words just quoted, where his constitution is read more fully: “On the representations of bishops, we have learned that certain priests of the Christian law, whose offences have both been discovered in an episcopal assembly and punished by its judgment, remain in the bosom of the cities in which such things were committed; that they seek to convene crowds of the people, become disturbers of peace and authors of popular tumult, call themselves innocent after judgment, gather the populace, are greeted as though still bishops, seek the sacred imperial court, and gain oracles and surreptitious rescripts by falsehoods.” Certainly nothing could be imagined more fitting to this preface than the matters set forth by the Roman council in the preceding letter. Moreover, it is certain that, on the occasion of Ursinus and his associates, Gratian ordered bishops deposed by priestly judgment to be compelled to live a hundred miles away from the city they had polluted.]

Let your praiseworthy and proven integrity recall what letters our Clemency formerly sent to the most distinguished man Simplicius, then vicar, and cease to expect a reiteration of the command; for it is a shameful burden upon our gentleness to renew an order.

[Note: It is evident from *Codex Theodosianus*, book IX, title XXIX, law 1, that he held this office in March 374. By the year 376 he had already suffered capital punishment.]

### 2. Ursinus, the bishop of Parma, and Florentius of Puteoli disturb the Church.

Ursinus indeed is restrained by Gaul, and his withdrawal to Agrippina prevents him from stirring up restless commotions.

[Note: Labbe notes in the margin that this occurred in 378—that is, in the very year in which he considers this rescript to have been issued. But from the words of the preceding letter, both in no. 2, where Ursinus is said to have been condemned and separated from those whom he had associated with himself, and in no. 4, where, although already long banished, he is nevertheless said to be attempting through his adherents to stir up disturbances, it may be inferred that the banishment mentioned here is rather that by which Ursinus was punished in 374 through letters addressed to Simplicius.]

Yet we have heard that he himself, more often browbeating than warning those he encountered, acted in order to cast off his followers.

[Note: We would prefer *obtendentem* or *obtinentem*—“opposing” or “holding forth”—rather than *moventem*, “stirring”; so clearly do the emperors mark Ursinus’s restless schemes, concerning which they had been warned in no. 4 of the preceding letter: “Though banished, through those whom the sacrilegious man unlawfully ordained, he attempts, even if secretly, to solicit every most worthless person.”]

[Col. 0585A]

The remote corner of Spain has confined Isaac under the designation of condemnation; a measure not ill-advised, should he in madness stir up any tumults.

[Note: Perhaps “likely to be salutary.”]

The bishop of Parma is all the more destructive because he is nearer to the illustrious city, more vehemently agitates the multitude of the unskilled, and disturbs the Church from which he was deposed by the judgment of holy bishops, evidently expecting the empty glory of a more severe sentence. Had your predecessor possessed any devoted vigor, he ought immediately to have driven him beyond the borders.

[Note: Can Milan, because the emperors of the West commonly maintained their residence there, be understood by “the illustrious city”? But if usage requires that Rome be understood, Florentius was nearer to that city than Isaac and Ursinus, as we have already observed. The terms “more severe sentence” suggest that the imperial judgment—or the decision of judges appointed by the emperors—is meant; compare no. 1: “those condemned by the judgment of right-thinking priests … vainly beg from us a reopening of the judgment.”]

Florentius of Puteoli, after receiving condemnation upon conviction by a right judgment, attempted to disturb our gentleness and received an appropriate answer while on his journey. After the fifteenth year, he attempts again to pollute the Church from which he had been expelled; he endeavors to hold unlawful assemblies and, by the persuasion of a ruined mind, corrupts a multitude lacking counsel.

[Note: In the preceding letter, no. 5, we read: “After the sixth year he crept back to the city.” Blondel rightly observed that “after the fifteenth year” must be restored here. Thus what had been somewhat exaggerated in the preceding letter—as often happens in such cases—is now corrected and more precisely stated by the emperors.]

He plainly relies upon the indolence of our judges, who surrender imperial commands to private favor and patiently allow the disturbance of a religion which we rightly venerate, though they perhaps neglect it themselves.

### 3. Claudian the Donatist.

Claudian too, summoned by those who renew the corruptions of religion contrary to divine commands—by those, I say, whom we had ordered expelled—has, it is said, introduced himself at Rome, as though he had undertaken too little wickedness if he had remained in Africa. As a false teacher, he endeavors either to profane those still without baptism by a wandering mystery, or to corrupt those already initiated anew by a greater crime; whereas repetition does not add to, but overthrows, the discipline of the most holy religion.

[Note: We have scarcely any doubt that the reading here should be *mysteria religionis*, “the mysteries of religion,” namely those performed especially in the administration of baptism. Hence the Roman council, in the following letter, no. 7, reproaches Claudian himself for saying that Catholic bishops are all devoid of the mysteries. He is therefore marked as one summoned by Donatists, who do not fear to renew and repeat baptism.]

[Note: Perhaps “made his way in.”]

[Note: Supply: “of baptism.”]

[Col. 0585C]

We, pursuing this Claudian with a punishment unlike that which he deserved, have so far ordered, tempering severity, merely that he return to his native country. Yet he is said still to remain, soliciting the unlearned and seeking a wholly empty reward; he destroys the souls of bodies that have been redeemed.

### 4. The innocence of Damasus was proved to Valentinian I.

Therefore those persecutors of the most holy see, not fearing to harass Bishop Damasus with most disgraceful calumnies—a man whose most holy mind had been tested not only by the divine power, which was enough, but also by judicial examination, as it had likewise been proved to your deified father Valentinian—after despairing of being able to strike him down, disturb the people for whom he is a pledge before the Godhead. But thus far the inert dissimulation of the judges snores on; and there is no need to remind you to what end a despised enactment may proceed. Thus far, I say, the supine negligence of the officials snores on.

### 5. Authors of disturbances are to be expelled one hundred miles from the City.

After this, unless you expel beyond the hundredth milestone from the City all whom the wording of our command expressly includes, or those whom councils of holy bishops have shown by common agreement to be contriving disturbances of this kind; and unless you order them to live banished from the territories of those cities whose people or churches they harass, either personally or through a mob like themselves—you will incur, besides injury to your reputation, whose loss among good men is no slight matter, the guilt of neglecting the enactment.

### 6. The order of ecclesiastical judgments by which the contumacious are restrained.

We further desire that whoever has been condemned by the judgment of Damasus—which he has rendered with the counsel of five or seven bishops—or by the judgment or council of those who are Catholic, if he seeks unjustly to retain a church, just as one summoned to priestly judgment who had not appeared through contumacy: he is to be remitted, with authority employed, to episcopal judgment by the illustrious men, the praetorian prefects of Gaul and Italy, or by proconsuls or vicars; or he is to arrive at the city of Rome under prosecution. But if such audacity should arise in more distant regions, the whole pleading of his cause is to be brought before the examination of the metropolitan bishop in that province; or, if he himself is metropolitan, he shall proceed without delay to Rome, as necessity requires, or to those judges whom the Roman bishop has appointed.

[Note: In Baronius: *si juste*, “if justly”: wrongly, as is evident from the preceding letter, no. 9. Shortly afterward, instead of *ut qui*, “that whoever,” *vel qui*, “or whoever,” would be preferable.]

[Note: In the same author: *ut ab*, and shortly afterward, *vel vicariis ut ad urbem Romam sub prosecutione perveniat*: “or by vicars, so that he may arrive at the city of Rome under prosecution.”]

Provided, however, that all who have been deposed shall be separated only from the boundaries of that city in which they had been priests. For we restrain those who have deserved less severe treatment, and punish sacrilegious obstinacy more mildly than it deserves.

[Note: Sirmond and Labbe read, with Baronius, *detecti*, “discovered”; and Labbe alone reads *orbis finibus*, “the boundaries of the world.” The preceding letter, no. 9—“that those who have been deposed be separated only from the boundaries of that city”—does not permit doubt that *dejecti*, “deposed,” must be restored. Thus *dejecti* here has the same meaning as *depositi* there; and it no less certainly proves that the word *orbis*, “world,” has mistakenly entered in place of *urbis*, “city,” in Labbe.]

But if the injustice or favor of a metropolitan bishop or of any priest is suspected, it shall be permitted to appeal to the Roman bishop or to a council of fifteen neighboring bishops summoned for that purpose—provided only that, after the hearing has taken place, what has been decided is not reopened.

### 7. Those who bring charges against a bishop are not readily to be heard.

Moreover, what natural justice has implanted in our minds even in affairs of lesser importance and in minor pleadings, we desire to have force with much greater care in the most weighty cases: namely, that no one marked by notable depravity of character, or branded with infamous calumny, may readily assume the role of accuser or undertake to give testimony in an accusation against a bishop.

[Note: That is, one upon whom the mark of the infamous calumniator has been stamped. Gratian indeed declares a calumniator infamous in *Codex Theodosianus*, book IX, title XXXIX, law 2.]

[Note: We may rightly suspect that this rescript is incomplete. For the emperors review and confirm, in the order in which they were requested, everything sought by the Roman council. But when they come to the case of Damasus, for whose benefit above all the council had written to them, they suddenly fall silent. The concessions so religiously granted do not permit us to believe that bishops suffered rejection in this one matter, or that emperors so pious gave no reason for that rejection.]

**In the Year of the Lord 381. Letter of the Council of Aquileia to the Emperor Gratian.**

[Note: In the appendix to the *Codex Theodosianus*, published by Jacques Sirmond in 1631, this letter appears; yet, contrary to Labbe’s opinion, it was not first published by him, since it had earlier appeared in the Roman edition of the works of St Ambrose. We do not think it unworthy of a place among the letters of Damasus, since it was written in his favor against Ursinus. It is issued in a more corrected form after comparison of the editions of Ambrose and Sirmond.]

(D. Coust. col. 551.)

[Col. 0587]

[Col. 0587B]

That he should not permit Ursinus to insinuate himself into his favor, but should provide for the peace of the Church by the removal of this most troublesome man.

To the most clement emperors and Christian princes, the most glorious and blessed Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius: the holy council assembled at Aquileia.

[Note: Namely, on the third day before the Nones of September, in the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius—that is, on 3 September 381, as is read in the heading of the Acts in Ambrose. It had assembled by authority of the imperial rescript prefixed to the same Acts.]

### I. The Arian plague has been checked by the imperial decree.

Your Serenity has indeed provided, most clement princes, by your enactments, that Arian perfidy can no longer conceal itself or creep abroad. For we think that the decrees of the council will not lack effect. So far as the western regions are concerned, only two men have been found who dared to oppose the council with profane and impious voices, accustomed scarcely to disturb the corner of Riparian Dacia.

[Note: We possess an edict bearing the names of these same emperors, given on 27 February 380, in *Codex Theodosianus*, book XVI, title I, law 2: “We desire all peoples whom the moderation of our Clemency rules to practice that religion which the religion introduced to the Romans by the divine apostle Peter declares that he delivered and which it is clear that Pope Damasus and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, follow,” etc. In the same work, title V, law 6, another constitution of the same emperors is recorded, dated 9 January 381. It commands that heretics have no place for mysteries and no opportunity to exercise the madness of a more obstinate mind, and that Catholic churches be restored to all orthodox bishops who hold the Nicene faith. Hence the Fathers of this Council of Aquileia thank the emperors in Ambrose, Epistle XII, no. 1, because all the Churches of God, especially those in the East, had been restored to Catholics.]

[Note: In the old Roman edition of Ambrose there is added here, “and not without reason,” which in the newest edition was deleted on the authority of the royal manuscript. Sirmond, however, reads “but nevertheless, insofar as,” in place of “for insofar as.”]

[Note: In Ambrose, Epistle X to Gratian, no. 2, the same council calls them “Palladius and Secundianus, names of ancient perfidy,” and writes concerning them: “They indeed received the sentence due to them in their presence, having been convicted of impiety.”]

[Note: Sirmond reads “beside the corner.” The Ambrosian edition more aptly reads “scarcely a corner.” In the letter to Theodosius among the Ambrosian letters, XII, no. 1, one reads: “In the western regions, only two heretics have been found who could oppose the holy council”; and in no. 3: “Throughout the western regions it seemed that the faith was opposed in only two corners, that is, along the side of Riparian Dacia and Moesia.”]

### II. That the emperor should not allow Ursinus to insinuate himself into his favor.

There is another matter by which we are more troubled, and which, because we had assembled, had properly to be discussed, lest it might disturb the whole body of the Church spread throughout the whole world, and everything besides. For although we have often learned that Ursinus has not been able to insinuate himself into your Piety—though he allows nothing to remain quiet and attempts troublesome intrusion amid so many necessities of war—nevertheless, lest your holy mind and the tranquillity of your spirit, eager to provide for all, be bent by the feigned flattery of a troublesome man, we judge it proper, if you deem it worthy, to entreat and beseech you: not merely guarding against the future, but also shuddering at what has already been done by his recklessness. For if he finds any opening for audacity, what will he not throw into confusion?

[Note: The particle is rightly absent in Sirmond.]

[Note: Ambrose reads *convenerimus*, “we have assembled.” We prefer with Sirmond *compererimus*, “we have learned.” They had learned this through the various exiles by which Ursinus had been punished—eventually banished into Gaul at Agrippina, as we read elsewhere in the preceding Rescript—and through Gratian’s own judgment, by which, once the innocence and integrity of Damasus had been proved, he sent Damasus’s accuser Isaac into Spain, as is shown in the letter of the Roman council to Gratian and Valentinian, no. 8, and in the rescript cited above, no. 2.]

But if compassion for one man can bend you, much more should the petition of all the priests move you.

[Note: Namely, compassion for Ursinus, whose prayers they fear may move the emperors’ pity, having repeatedly experienced his obtaining from them a relaxation or remission of exile.]

For which of us will be joined to him in communion, when he has attempted to usurp for himself a rank not due to him and could not lawfully attain it, and endeavors most importunately to recover what he importunately sought?

### III. Ursinus joined with Arians.

Though so often condemned for disturbances, he still proceeds as though the examples of the past were not to be feared.

[Note: Sirmond reads: “yet he proceeds as though.”]

What then of this: as many of us learned and saw in this council, he was associated and joined with the Arians at the time when, along with Valens—now before the doors of the synagogue, now in the houses of the Arians—mingling secret counsels and joining his own followers to them, they were attempting by their detestable assembly to disturb the Church of Milan; and, since he himself could not appear openly in their congregation, instructing and directing them how the peace of the Church might be disturbed? By this frenzy he hoped to win their favor and fellowship.

[Note: The Ambrosian edition has “who for the most part, just as,” and below *moliebatur*, “was attempting,” for *moliebantur*, “were attempting.” When the things narrated here occurred can be determined only by conjecture.
