Baronius assigns to the year 371 the rescript of Valentinian by which Ursinus’s exile in Gaul was so mitigated that he received freedom to depart wherever he wished, provided that he set foot neither in Rome nor at least in the suburban regions and did not attempt to spread the contagion of his wickedness. In 374, however, as we observed in the cited letter of the Roman council, no. 2, note b, Ursinus was sent by Gratian’s rescript to Agrippina in Gaul. Hence it is conjectured that, in the interval between the two rescripts, and especially after Valentinian’s death, Ursinus withdrew to Milan, and that the events now narrated occurred then. If this is so, Valens, bishop of Petavium, must have begun to disturb Italy in 375 and not ceased until this year, 381. Certainly the Council of Aquileia asks Gratian in Ambrose, Epistle X, no. 10, that that pseudo-bishop return home and not pollute the cities of flourishing Italy—he who now joins to himself men like himself by unlawful ordinations and seeks to leave behind among all manner of ruined persons a seed-bed of his impiety and perfidy, though he never even began to be a bishop. If Auxentius the younger is understood in Jerome’s words above, Epistle X, no. 4, “Auxentius is joined with Ambrose,” we may rightly conjecture that this spurious bishop was ordained by that same Valens.]

[Note: In Ambrose, Epistle X, no. 9, this heretic is called Julian Valens; and in no. 10 it is said that he was first placed over the holy man Marcus at Petavium, but was deposed by the people and then troubled Milan. There also see more concerning his corrupt morals.]

[Note: In the Ambrosian edition: “by whose frenzy he hoped.”]

### IV. He must be avoided.

Therefore, since it is written, “Avoid a heretic after one correction” (Titus 3:11), and since another holy man, speaking by the Holy Spirit, said that beasts of this kind must be avoided (2 John 10), neither received with greeting nor with intercourse: how can it be that we do not judge him, whom we have seen inserted into their society, also to be a defender of their perfidy? Even if this were absent, your Clemency ought to have been entreated not to permit the Roman Church, the head of the whole Roman world, and that most sacred faith of the Apostles to be disturbed; for from it the rights of venerable communion flow forth into all.

[Note: Sirmond reads “of admonition.” The Ambrosian edition more rightly reads “of communion.” This is said in the sense in which Cyprian, in Pamel’s edition, Epistle LV, after the middle, calls the Roman Church “the principal Church, from which priestly unity arose”; and observes in *On the Unity of the Church* that Christ, in order to manifest unity, established one chair and established the origin of that same unity beginning from one man, Peter. Accordingly, the Roman Church was always believed to be the center of ecclesiastical unity and the source and origin of Catholic communion.]

And therefore we ask and beseech you to deem it worthy to remove from him the opportunity of insinuating himself into your favor.

[Note: Another reading: “of being insinuated.”]

### V. That by the removal of this most troublesome man provision may be made for the peace of the Church.

We know the holy modesty of your Clemency. Let him not thrust before your hearing things unworthy of it; let him not make noisy interruptions with matters alien to the office and name of a priest; let him not speak shamelessly to you. Since he ought to have a good testimony even from those outside (1 Tim. 3:7), may your Clemency deign to remember with what testimony his own fellow-citizens have pursued him. For it is shameful to speak of it, shameless to recount how disgraceful a reputation wounded him with reproach.

[Note: *Turpi*, “disgraceful,” would be preferable—namely, “with disgraceful reproach.”]

At least, pierced by such shame, he should have kept silent; and, if he had any conscience of a priest, he would have preferred the peace and concord of the Church to his ambition and pursuit. But, far removed from every sense of shame, through the mutilated man Paschasius, the standard-bearer of his fury, he sends letters, strikes up disturbances, and endeavors to rouse every pagan and ruined person.

We pray, therefore, that now, by the removal of this most troublesome man, you grant security both to the Roman people, who remain uncertain after the report of the prefect of the City, and to us priests, to whom security has been denied. Once this is obtained, may we celebrate thanksgivings in unceasing continuance before God the almighty Father and Christ, his Son and Lord.

[Note: Valerianus is recorded as prefect of the City in 381 in *Codex Theodosianus*, book VI, title 10, law 2, and title 26, law 2.]

[Note: The Ambrosian edition reads: “the Lord God.”]

**In the Year of the Lord 385. Letter of the Emperor Maximus to Pope Siricius.**

[Note: This was first published at Rome among pontifical letters from an old manuscript of the Vatican Library, and from there Baronius assigned it to the end of 387. Tillemont considers that it belongs rather to 385. It appears that Maximus wrote it in response to a letter in which Siricius, shortly after beginning his governance of the Church, had urged Maximus to defend the Catholic faith. Further, Maximus’s statement about gathering a council of all bishops from Gaul or from the Five Provinces indicates that he had not yet suspected anything of the war threatened against him by Theodosius, in which he was defeated and killed in August 388. Baronius himself notes that what is reported in no. 4 as having recently been discovered concerning the Manichaeans must be understood of the Priscillianists, and no one can rightly oppose that interpretation. Yet Priscillian and his companions were convicted and punished in 385. The writing in which Maximus announces what has lately been discovered concerning them, and indicates what has been done on this occasion as recent and not yet known at Rome, may therefore rightly be referred to that same year.]

(D. Coust., col. 640.)

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589D]

Maximus promises concern for the Catholic faith. He also promises that the case of Agricii, whom Siricius had written to have been improperly advanced to the rank of presbyter, will be examined in a synod. He again professes his zeal for the Catholic faith and sends the proceedings by which the crimes of the Manichaeans, or Priscillianists, have recently been disclosed.

Victor Maximus, perpetual triumpher Augustus, to Siricius, bishop, lord and truly holy apostolic man: greeting.

[Note: That is, to the successor of the apostle Peter, whose see and successors deserved to be called apostolic.]

### I. Siricius’s letter was worthy of his dignity.

We have received the letters of Your Holiness, most pleasing to us and entirely fitting both to the name of a priest and to the dignity of the most splendid City. As for the Catholic faith, concerning which you wished to consult our Clemency: the greater and more special a judgment of the Godhead I experience concerning myself, the more I confess that I have care for it. For I ascended to imperial power directly from the saving font itself, and in all my endeavors and successes God has always been my helper; may he deign today, and, as I hope, forever to be my protector and guardian, most dear Father.

### II. The case of Agricii is to be judged in a Gallican assembly.

But concerning Agricii, whom you mention as having improperly ascended to the rank of presbyter, what can I offer more reverently to our Catholic religion than that Catholic priests judge this very question—what kind of person he appears to be? At a suitable time I shall convene them all, whether resident within Gaul or within the Five Provinces, in whatever city they choose; so that, as they sit and investigate, it may be judged what custom requires and what the law requires. For they themselves can better establish those things that must be supported by books and by the most religious ordinances of our forefathers, since they know them.

[Note: That is, the Narbonensian provinces, as Tillemont interprets.]

### III.

Moreover, we profess this to be our disposition and will: that the Catholic faith, with every dissension removed far away, may remain uninjured and inviolable, all priests agreeing and serving God with one mind. For our arrival found and discovered some things so defiled and polluted by the stain of wicked persons that, unless our provision and remedy, proceeding from fear of the highest God, had quickly brought aid to these matters, a vast division and destruction would certainly have arisen, and evils scarcely curable afterward would have grown strong.

### IV. The unspeakable crimes of the Manichaeans.

But as for what crime the Manichaeans have only recently been discovered to have committed—not by arguments or doubtful and uncertain suspicions, but by their own confessions produced in judicial proceedings—I prefer that Your Holiness learn from the proceedings themselves rather than from our mouth, because we cannot utter without blushing deeds of this sort, not merely shameful in fact but foul even to speak of.

[Note: That is, as we have already observed after Baronius, the Priscillianists; they were called thus because they renewed the mad inventions of Mani. There seems no difficulty if we understand Maximus’s earlier remarks concerning the defilements of certain wicked persons, to whom he hastened to bring aid, and his present remarks concerning Manichaean crimes recently discovered, of these same Priscillianists—first condemned at Bordeaux in the council held by this emperor’s order about 384, and then at Trier by Maximus himself, to whom they had appealed. The word *adhuc*, “still,” indicates that at Trier some new crime was disclosed beyond those already detected and proved at Bordeaux.]

By the Emperor’s own hand: “May the Divinity preserve you for many years.”

## Letter of the Emperor Maximus to Valentinian Augustus

(Labbe, *Councils*, vol. II, col. 1031.) (C)

[Col. 0591]

[Col. 0591C]

The younger Emperor Valentinian, prompted by his mother Justina, who was devoted to the Arian heresy, was vigorously persecuting St Ambrose and the other Catholics at Milan. On learning this, Maximus exhorts Valentinian, by imitation of his father’s religion, to refrain from inflicting violence upon churches and priests.

Unless our straightforward faith in Your Serenity and our grace, full of concord, prevailed in this matter, I should even be confident that these things now said to be happening in the regions of Your Tranquillity—the disturbance and overthrow of the Catholic law—could serve my own interests. For what could be more desirable to anyone, if he were an enemy, than to devise something against the churches of God—that is, against God himself—and, where error is not excusable, to choose to sin?

But because our reverence toward God is greater than that we should judge it desirable for him to be violated even by the bitterest enemy, and because our concern for your most serene youth is so close and so attentive that your good actions delight us more than your errors, we have therefore thought Your Eternity should be admonished: having examined the significance of the supreme Name and considered the power of that Majesty itself, weigh with a settled mind what you ought to do.

For I have heard—for report does not allow what is done among peoples to remain hidden—that by new edicts of Your Clemency violence has been inflicted upon the Catholic churches; that priests are besieged in basilicas; that a fine has been announced, a capital penalty added, and the most holy law overthrown under the name of I know not what law. How grave this is you may perceive if you are willing to consider the greatness of God. I should be ashamed if I wished to construct any argument which Your Serenity might suppose supports this, and to plead God’s cause.

What if this alone were at issue? If you saw fit to alter something now grown together and established through so many ages, would you not stir up no slight discord? Even in this mortal life custom has our reverence under human laws; and in a matter already old and customary, to introduce something new is blameworthy. All Italy and Africa believe in this sacrament; Gaul, Aquitaine, and all Spain glory in this faith; Rome herself, venerable Rome, has even in this respect a primacy, because she acknowledged God as she wished to follow him.

I shall confess what is said not without sorrow: Illyricum alone dissented. Would that its error had not remained as an example! Would that the town of Mursa, unhurt by that Arian law, had endured, and that they had not formerly fallen in judgment for their wretched error, because it had instructed its very authors not to collapse beneath the special vengeance of an angered deity. Believe me: divine things are dangerously assailed.

The lord Valentinian, of venerable memory, father of Your Clemency, ruled faithfully in this faith. He wished to touch nothing which he saw well established. Under him these very bishops already held office. What a great change it is, that those who were formerly priests are now judged sacrilegious persons! Consecrated by the same ordinances, the same sacraments, they believe with the same faith as those who believed before. Does Your Serenity, venerable to me, suppose that a religion once conceived in human minds, and established by God himself, can be uprooted?

What discords will be raised from this! What conflicts will arise! How frequent and destructive the seditions! How many prayers of the righteous, and what prayers, will reach God, when among Christians—an abomination even to say—a kind of persecution comes into being. You will see in what sense you interpret this earnest concern of ours. Certainly I could show you my concern for Your Clemency in no greater way than by urging you to desist. For I think you will recognize that no enemy would give this counsel.

I desire that you understand that these words are spoken lovingly by us; I hope that you will believe it. It is therefore altogether fitting that you do not overthrow things consecrated to the holy divine power. Restore all Italy, venerable Rome, and the remaining provinces to their churches and their priests. Do not insert yourself as an intermediary, when it is more just that those who have departed from the Catholic Church through an Arian interpretation should exchange their error for true religion than that they should impose their perversity upon those who think rightly.

[Note: This rescript, extracted from a Vatican manuscript, was published by Baronius under the year 385, no. 6. Pinianus, to whom it is addressed, is well known from Augustine’s Letters 124, 125, and 126. Imperial constitutions establish that he was prefect of the City in July 386 and in June 387. But laws addressed to Salustius, prefect of the City, dated June 386, show that Pinianus had not yet been invested with this dignity before July of that year. Therefore Tillemont, vol. X, p. 788, conjectures that, when Valentinian gave him this rescript, Pinianus was acting rather as vicar than as prefect, or held another related office. Nor is there lacking a suitable reason why this affair was entrusted to someone other than the prefect, especially if Symmachus had not yet laid down the prefecture which he is known to have held in 384. For it is manifest that Valentinian, as soon as he learned of Siricius’s election, hastened to approve it by his own vote; accordingly this rescript must be assigned to February 385. The emperor prudently did not wish to entrust such a task to Symmachus, the prefect, since he was both a pagan and had recently been denounced to the emperors, as hostile to Christians, as we explained under the name of Damasus in the *Notice of the Letters*, §19. Ursinus’s renewed intrigues made it necessary to obtain this rescript, so that the seeds of a new schism might be crushed more quickly.]

# LETTER OF THE EMPEROR VALENTINIAN TO PINIANUS

(D. Coustant, *Epistles of the Popes*, col. 639.) By which he approves the election of Siricius, bishop of Rome.

[Note: Hail.]

Greetings, Pinianus, most dear to us.

We believe it to be the established practice of the people of the eternal City to rejoice in concord and to choose an excellent priest, and we are glad that this has occurred in our time. Therefore, since they have wished the religious Siricius, a bishop of holiness, to preside thus over the priesthood, while rejecting by their acclamations the wicked Ursinus [Note: Perhaps: “while they refused Ursinus the wicked one.”], let the aforesaid bishop himself remain, Pinianus most dear and most pleasing to us. For it is a great example of innocence and integrity that, by one acclamation, he himself should be chosen and the others rejected.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of March [23 February].

# MOST ANCIENT FRAGMENTS OF ARIAN DISCOURSES, DISCOVERED IN RESCRIPT PALIMPSEST LEAVES AND NOW PUBLISHED FOR THE FIRST TIME WITH SUITABLE REFUTATIONS

[Note: As I said in the prologue, these fragments are produced partly from an Ambrosian palimpsest manuscript and partly from a Vatican palimpsest manuscript. The Ambrosian manuscript comprises pages 17, 18, 19, 20, 23, 24, 25, 26, 29, 30, 31, 32, 115, and 116. The rest are Vatican leaves. No one should be surprised that these Arian fragments survived, at least in palimpsests, since Hilary says in Book 7 against Constantius: “All the sheets of the churches and now all the books are full of the most impious blasphemies of the Arians.”]

(Mai, *Collection*, vol. III, part II, p. 208.) (C, G)*

# FIRST FRAGMENT

Recently, dearest brother, you judged that I should be warned concerning those slanderers against our faith, which is true, who say: “How do you say that God is one, and yet assert that Christ is his Son? If God has a son, he must have a wife, or at least be female, and have conceived and begotten a son from elsewhere. Behold, you now speak of several gods; how do you reproach us for saying that there are gods?” [Note: This is known to be an objection of pagans. Yet the same objection was sometimes raised even by Anomoean heretics, whose silly—or rather *aischra* (shameful)—words St Hilary reports in Book 13 against Constantius. Hilary also discusses at length, *On the Trinity* III.17 ff., the ineffable and eternal divinity of the Son of God, which is unlike human generation. In the *Summary of Faith against the Arians*: “If you ask the Church what the Father is, it says, God; but it also calls the Son and the Holy Spirit God. Yet it does not say three gods, lest it be compared with the Gentiles, who combine many gods. Let us believe Scripture when it says that God is one. If, as the Arians say, one is greater and the other less, he cannot be called one; inequality excludes unity. Equality of powers makes unity; the distinctiveness of persons makes Trinity.” See also Arnobius, *On the Triune and One God*; Ferrandus, *Ep. Casin.*, fol. 2; and Fulgentius, *On the Trinity*, ch. 2.]

We learned from you that sacrilegious people make these objections against us [Note: Manuscript: “against you.”]. Therefore we judged it necessary both to meet their error and to instruct your holiness concerning the hope which we hold. Nor could we any longer refuse, since your holiness desired to receive a written instruction in the true faith—not from ourselves, however, but according to the tradition of the divine Scriptures, through the grace of almighty God, with the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, and through the ministry of the Holy Spirit, who distributes [Note: Manuscript has *dividet* for *dividit*, as below *loquetur* for *loquitur*. Thus *e* for *i* occurs often in fourth-century writings.] graces to those who believe in God through Christ without hesitation. [Note: A short space is left here.]

Therefore, trusting in your prayers and approving also the good desire of Your Holiness, we hastened, with the Lord’s assent, to satisfy you, dearest brother. For, since you had urged us repeatedly and with ever more importunate persistence, we could no longer defer. We do not rely upon loftiness of language or elaborately composed speech, for we have pursued no such study [Note: This Arian says that he is uneloquent and unlearned; he must doubtless be considered a bishop. Readers of the fragments will judge, as seems appropriate, how far to credit this claim. Jerome, speaking specifically of Arian bishops in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, fol. 11, makes a remarkable observation about the learning of ancient bishops: “Truly they are called to the episcopate from the bosom of Plato and Aristophanes. For how few are there who have not been thoroughly educated in these disciplines? Finally, all literate men ordained today take care not to drink in the marrow of the Scriptures, but to delight the ears of the people with the little flowers of declaimers.” Moreover, the Arian heresy accords more closely with worldly wisdom and borrows the streams of its argumentation from Aristotelian springs. Compare Ambrose, *On Faith* I.5 and 13, who says that Arians derive every colouring of their impiety from philosophy and habitually place the force of their poison in dialectic.]; but, fleeing to the mercy of the Lord, for whose glory we have undertaken to speak, we believe him who said: “Open your mouth wide, and I shall fill it.” [Note: Thus the manuscript: *eum*, “it.”] And again the prophet says: “The Lord gave [Note: Manuscript: *davit*, as elsewhere.] the word to those who proclaim the good news with great power.” And again: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father.”

Thus the insult of sacrilegious persons [Note: Manuscript: *sacrilegum*, singular.] moved us also to speak; and the insistence of your charity compelled us. But he who gave the mouth for speaking is able also, through your prayers, to supply us with speech, so that, strengthened at the fitting time by his grace [Note: Manuscript: *canfoti*, with one *p*, as in other ancient manuscripts.], we may speak for the common benefit and for the glory of the same maker of our nature.

For the holy and divine Scriptures, having deep and infinite treasures within themselves, do not need persons to make them shine. The Lord says: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life. And they are those which bear witness concerning me. Yet you do not wish to come to me, that you may have eternal life.” Again: “He who believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” [Note: This manuscript has *flumina*; elsewhere the same manuscript has *fluenta*.] Our Lord Jesus Christ also says: “I am the light of this world; whoever follows me does not remain in darkness, but shall have the light of life.”

The holy prophets proclaimed him the sun of righteousness. Therefore Christ, the Son of God, is this sun of righteousness. He [Note: Thus the manuscript.] is the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world, and which the darkness did not overcome. He shines in pure hearts and is seen by the clear eye of the mind in the unique and incorruptible proper nature of the Only-Begotten [Note: Thus the manuscript.]; he most plainly shows to all who desire it the knowledge of the one true God, saying to the Jews: “How can you believe, receiving glory from one another and not seeking glory from the one God?” Again he says to the Father: “The hour has come; glorify your Son, that the Son also may glorify you, as you gave him authority over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” [Note: Augustine elegantly interprets this Gospel passage in *Against an Arian Sermon*, fol. 1: “What is written in the Gospel, ‘that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent,’ must be understood as though he had said: ‘that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent as the one true God.’ For John also said of Christ: ‘He is the true God and eternal life.’ But against the Arians, whose chief error was that the Father alone is the one true God, it is especially useful to quote the principal and classic passage of the ancient writer Tertullian—who wrote long before the Council of Nicaea, indeed before Arius was born—on the Son’s true divinity and his *homoousia* with God the Father. Thus, *Apology*, ch. 21: “We have learned that this Logos was brought forth from God, generated by being brought forth, and therefore called Son of God and God by unity of substance. For God too is spirit; and when a ray extends from the sun, it is a portion of the whole; yet the sun will be in the ray, because the ray is the sun’s, and the substance is not divided but extended. Thus spirit from spirit, and God from God, as light kindled from light. The source-matter remains whole and undiminished, however many offshoots of qualities you borrow from it. So that which has gone forth from God is God and Son of God, and both are one. Thus also spirit from spirit and God from God: he made another by measure, not by number; by rank, not by state; and it did not depart from the source, but proceeded from it. This ray of God, therefore, as had always been foretold, descended into a certain virgin; formed as flesh in her womb, it is born as a human being mingled with God. Flesh instructed by spirit is nourished, grows, speaks, teaches, acts—and is Christ.” We have another equally classic passage of Tertullian in *Against Praxeas*, ch. 2, a book which students of theology ought to know well.]

It is therefore necessary for those who wish to be Christians to know the one true God, who alone is unbegotten and without beginning; and his only-begotten Son, true God in his own proper and uniquely begotten nature, obedient [Note: Thus the manuscript.] and subject [Note: Hilary explains in a Catholic sense how the Son is said to be subject to God the Father, *On the Trinity* XI.30, 43. See also Cyril, *Treasury*, assertion 29. Ambrose then expounds the same doctrine, *On Faith* V.13–15, plainly showing that Christ is called subject to the Father only according to the flesh. In ch. 14 he says: “Therefore let there be no prejudice because he is called subject; nor is there prejudice because he is read to be a servant, declared to be crucified, proclaimed dead. For when he died, he lived; when he was subjected, he reigned; when he was buried, he raised [the dead].” St Zeno, Tractate 6, fol. 4, against the Arians: “The Son is subject to the Father not by a diminishing but by a religious subjection; with him he has one substance and one equality of co-eternity and omnipotence,” etc. Finally, the aforesaid Hilary, Book XI, fol. 6, complains of Arians who abused Scriptural expressions concerning Christ’s humanity in order to weaken his divinity: “They seize the economy of the assumed body as an insult to divinity, and take occasions for impiety from the sacrament of our salvation. If they held fast to apostolic faith, they would understand that he who was in the form of God assumed the form of a servant,” etc.] by will and nature to the unbegotten God, his Father.

Since, therefore, according to the tradition of the Scriptures, we have spoken of one true God—as indeed there is according to true reason one true God, one king, one lord, one creator and maker of the universe [Note: Hilary refutes and exposes at length in the whole of Book V of *On the Trinity* the following blasphemies, whose substance is that the Son differs from the Father’s substance and that the Father alone is true God. Compare also Alcuin, *Confession of Faith*, III.2.]—he alone possesses supreme power without beginning; he alone needs nothing [Note: Thus the manuscript.]; he alone is not under another’s law or awaiting a command; he alone has no superior [Note: Thus the manuscript.], since he made no one equal to himself. Being wholly unbegotten God, he made a wholly begotten Son; through him he created all things, as it is written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”: the Creator [made] a creator, God [made] a God subject to the whole creation and obedient in all his commands.

He made him not to develop later, but perfect at once, as we have said: such as he could make him, committing all power and all wisdom to the establishing of the Son, as it is written: “God the Father sealed him.” Thus also the Apostle proclaims him the image of the invisible God, displaying God—his invisible power or wisdom—in the substance of the Son. Therefore God displayed in the Son as much power and wisdom as he could; hence the Apostle teaches that the Son is God’s power and God’s wisdom—not that power or wisdom which is in the invisible God, without beginning [Note: Arian doctrine similar to this appears in Hilary, *Against Auxentius*, fol. 6, and is intimated in many places also by Eusebius of Caesarea. But let us set against the impious Arian our orthodox Augustine, who says in *On the Trinity* VII.12: “Let him believe in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one God, alone, great, almighty, good, just, merciful, creator of all visible and invisible things. And when he hears that the Father alone is God, let him not thereby separate the Son or the Holy Spirit; for he is alone God with whom he is also one God. Likewise, when we hear that the Son alone is God, we must understand this without any separation of the Father or the Holy Spirit. Thus let him affirm one essence, so that he does not suppose one thing different from another, greater or better, or in any respect unlike.” Compare Alcuin, *Confession of Faith*, I.15.]—but [the Son] seated at God’s right hand, receiving from the Father, the Son of God’s love, whom God loves.

He defrauded him of nothing, to whom he handed over all things, as the Gospel proclaims: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.” The Son also, receiving all things from the Father, is above all things, before all things, and with all things worships the Father. Thus through the Scriptures we acknowledge him to be God of the whole creation: begotten and subject to the unbegotten God [Note: Augustine, *Debate with Maximinus the Arian*, fol. 14: “I profess, as you say, that the Father is unbegotten; but their natures and substances are not therefore different because the one is unbegotten and the other begotten.”]; the begotten lord of the whole creation, but minister of the unbegotten Lord [Note: The manuscript lacks *non*, “unbegotten.”]; the begotten king of the whole creation under the power of the unbegotten king [Note: Manuscript: *regi*, “to the king.”]; begotten true light, subject to the unbegotten inaccessible light; begotten wisdom, obeying in all things the one wise unbegotten God [Note: Thus the manuscript here and below: *solo* for *soli*.]; begotten creator under the unbegotten Creator; good shepherd of the whole creation, begotten lamb of the unbegotten God; begotten life, giving life to the whole creation at the Father’s will, subject [Note: Manuscript: *subjacente.*] to the one living God without beginning.

As the Son says: “Just as the Father has life”—he has it in himself and has not received it—“so he gave the Son also to have life” [Note: Manuscript: *vita*, “life.”] “in himself” [Note: Thus the manuscript.] incomparable in his own proper begotten substance, just as the Father is known to be incomparable in his unbegotten substance.

Therefore we confess one God and one [Note: Thus the manuscript; likewise in Fragment IV.], not two gods [Note: The Arian responds to the Catholics’ justified accusation, known from Ambrose, *On Faith* I.1: “Therefore we say one God, not two or three gods, as the impious Arian heresy, while accusing us, itself incurs the charge. For he speaks of three gods who separates the divinity of the Trinity, whereas the Lord, in saying, ‘Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,’ showed the Trinity to be of one power.” Ambrose presses the same charge, I.13: “Let us now see how Arians differ from pagans. The latter name gods unlike in sex and dissimilar in power; the former assert a Trinity of differing divinity and dissimilar power,” etc. Finally, V.3: “Arians, in saying that the substance of Father and Son is distinct and different, plainly assert two gods.” Eusebius evaded the Catholics’ objection by a very poor escape in *Against Marcellus* II, p. 109, defining two substances unequal in honour—as if this did not make two gods, one greater and the other lesser.]; for we do not speak of two unbegotten beings or two fathers . . . .

# SECOND FRAGMENT

. . . assisting the prayer of believers through the benefits of Christ, interceding for them with inexpressible groanings, and bringing the saints [Note: Manuscript: *sanctum*, singular.] to the Son, that through the Son they may be brought to the Father. As the holy apostle Paul says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” And the Son declares: “No one can come to the Father except through me.”

It is therefore necessary that we confess this Trinity. The Holy Spirit magnifies the Son, as the Son says: “He honoured me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” And the Son glorifies the Father, as he says: “I glorified you upon earth; I made known your name to the people whom you gave me.” This Spirit therefore remains in all the saints, as the Son said: “I shall ask my Father, and he will give you another advocate, that he may be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, because he remains with you and is in you.”

He remains, therefore, as we have said, in all the saints—not divided, but whole. For that nature cannot be divided: what is not composed of members cannot be divided, but remains whole in all. Yet we do not call the Holy Spirit God [Note: Nicetas of Aquileia, a fifth-century writer whom I recently published from a Vatican manuscript, replies to this Arian in his treatise *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*—that is, the person, as Victorinus says in his commentary on Galatians IV.6 and in *Against Arius* III.17. In that excellent and golden little work, after listing from the sacred Scriptures the divine attributes of the Holy Spirit, Nicetas concludes decisively, p. 26: “I shall now make a recapitulation. If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; if he liberates; if he sanctifies; if he is Lord, as the Apostle said; if he creates with the Father and Son; if he gives life; if he has foreknowledge, as the Father and Son have it; if he reveals; if he is everywhere; if he fills the world; if he dwells in the elect; if he will convict the world; if he judges; if he is good; if he is upright; if it is proclaimed concerning him, ‘Thus says the Holy Spirit’; if he appoints prophets; if he is the Comforter; if he washes and justifies; if he kills those who tempt him; if one who blasphemes against him has forgiveness neither in this age nor in the future—which is certainly proper to God—if these things are so, indeed because they are true, why is it asked of me that I say what the Holy Spirit is, when by the greatness of his works he himself makes known what he is? He is certainly not alien from the holiness of the Father and Son, since he is not alien from the power of their works. In vain is the name of divinity denied him whose power cannot be denied. In vain am I forbidden to worship him with the Father and Son, when truth itself compels me to confess him with the Father and Son.” You may read another recapitulation concerning the Holy Spirit in Fulgentius, *To Trasimund* III.35. Compare Didymus, *On the Trinity* II.6; Augustine, *On the Trinity* I.13; Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit* III.18–19; Hilary, *On the Trinity* I.29 and XII.55 ff.; Leo the Great, Sermons 75 and 76. Indeed, the baptismal formula prescribed by Christ shows especially clearly that the Holy Spirit is God, as the Fathers commonly observe, among them the great Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 10.], because Scripture does not say so; but [we call him] subject to God the Son [Note: Augustine skilfully denies and refutes this in *Against an Arian Sermon*, ch. 20 ff.; I refrain from quoting the passage both because of its length and because the Arian here offers no support for his assertion.], and in all things obedient to the commands of that Son, just as the Son is to the Father.

And as the Father committed all power, all wisdom, and goodness to the establishing of the Son, so also the Son, at the Father’s command, displayed all power and all wisdom in the Holy Spirit. In that Holy Spirit, therefore, archangels [Note: Thus the manuscript, without aspiration.] and angels, all spiritual powers, and all saints worship the Son, and through the Son the Father.

For after the resurrection, while handing over to his disciples the saving mystery of the Trinity, the Son says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe all that I commanded you. And behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.” [Note: The treatise ends. In the manuscript a blank space remains before the page is filled, with asterisks, which are two indications of the end.]

# THIRD FRAGMENT
. . . . the Father is unique, a simple Spirit, alone good, [Col. 0600B] alone possessing immortality [Note: [Col. 0600D] Thus a certain Arian speaks in Hilary, *On the Trinity* VI.4: “We know one God, alone uncreated, alone everlasting, alone without beginning, alone true, alone possessing immortality, alone best, alone powerful.” Arius uses the very same words in Ambrose, *Letter* 10, class 1. This was the foundation of the Arian heresy, which excluded the Son from these attributes.], and dwelling in inaccessible light [Note: [Col. 0600B] The manuscript has *inaccessibilem* (“inaccessible,” accusative).]; so also the Son, in his own only-begotten nature which he received from the Father, is unique. He is better by incomparable preeminence than all things made after him and through him by God’s providence [Note: [Col. 0600B] Thus the manuscript.], so that none of those things made through him can be compared with him; because he is God of all things, giving life to all things by the Father’s will. He is not compared with his Father [Note: [Col. 0600D] This is the customary blasphemy of the Arians, from which even Eusebius—alas, too devoted to the Arians—is not free, *Commentary on Psalm* LXXXVIII, p. 560. But let us hear our pope Leo the Great, saying in Sermon 75: “We detest the Arians, who would have some distance between Father and Son.”], from whom he received that he might be the life of all things. Nor, as we have said, could anything be compared with him, since all things received through him, by God’s will, both their being and their life. Foremost among these is the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete [Note: [Col. 0600D] Rather, Didymus, *On the Trinity* II.6, fol. 1, shows from Job that it is not the Holy Spirit who is the first creature, but Satan.], made through [Col. 0601A] Christ by God’s providence [Note: [Col. 0601B] Didymus extensively demonstrates that the Holy Spirit is not a creature, *On the Trinity* II.6. See also Fulgentius, *Against Fabian*, fragment XXXIV. Hilary states briefly, *On the Trinity* XII.55: “I shall never call the Holy Spirit created.” Didymus, *On the Holy Spirit*, translated by Jerome, fol. 4: “The very name Holy Spirit manifests the underlying essence; [Col. 0601C] he is associated with the Father and Son and utterly alien from creatures.” Then, fol. 8: “If the Holy Spirit is of a nature other than creatures and subsists in his own essence, he is shown to be uncreated and unmade.” Finally, fol. 13: “These matters having thus been set forth, the Holy Spirit is shown to be of another substance than visible and invisible creatures. But if this is true, certain persons most impiously count the Holy Spirit among all things, saying that, in the statement that all things were made through the Word, the making of the Holy Spirit is also signified.” See also fol. 14.], better and greater than all the rest; in the holy Scriptures he is proclaimed in third place after the Father and the Son. This Spirit is recognized as unique and alone in his uniqueness, in third place. Such a one could not be compared with Christ, the Son of God and maker of his nature [Note: [Col. 0601C] The Arian blasphemies against the Holy Spirit continue; to refute them Nicetas of Aquileia, recently published by me, as I said, is sufficient.]; nor can anything else among the remaining beings, which received existence through him by God’s providence, be compared with him [Note: [Col. 0601B] Thus the manuscript.]; for he is the unique sanctifying power.

This Spirit is not God [Note: [Col. 0601C] Thus the Arians deny that the Holy Spirit is God in Augustine, *Against Maximinus* II.12. Augustine further says, *On the Trinity* I.13: “Testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit have been gathered, which those before us who discussed these matters used more abundantly, because he too is God and not a creature. If he is not a creature, he is not merely God but [Col. 0601D] also true God. Therefore he is wholly equal to the Father and the Son, and consubstantial and coeternal in the unity of the Trinity.” Ambrose demonstrates that the Holy Spirit is called Lord in Scripture, *On the Holy Spirit* II.1; III.14–15. On the divinity of the Holy Spirit he argues more closely in the cited work, chapters 18–19. Then Didymus, fols. 18 ff., and Fulgentius, *Against Fabian*, fragment XXIX, should be read.], nor Lord, since he is not a creator. For he neither made, nor can make, things which were not, so that they might be; because he is not God, but the minister of Christ, the Son of his God [Note: [Col. 0601D] This Arian doctrine is succinctly stated in Jerome’s *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, fol. 9: “The Arian believes nothing else—close your ears, I beg you who are about to hear, lest you be polluted by the words of so great an impiety—than that the Father alone is true God, that Jesus Christ the Savior is a creature, and that the Holy Spirit is servant of both.” Fulgentius, *To Thrasamund* III.34: “God will hand over to endless torments those who distinguish the nature of the Holy Spirit from the substance of Father and Son, so that they either suppose that he has no personal existence at all [Col. 0602B] or regard him as a minister of wholly inferior rank.” Read also Fulgentius, *Against Fabian*, fragment III, where he distinguishes service-rendering (*subministratio*) from ministry (*ministerium*).]. In this capacity he ministers, sanctifying, enlightening, and teaching the rational beings made through Christ by God’s will; reminding them to keep Christ’s commands [Col. 0601B]; distributing grace to all believers; helping the weakness of our prayer; interceding for us with unutterable groanings [Note: [Col. 0602B] That is, he causes us to groan and to intercede, as Augustine interprets against the Arians, *Against Maximinus* I.9; II.19; likewise Fulgentius, *Against Fabian*, fragment V.]; by Christ’s nod forgiving sins to penitents [Note: [Col. 0601B] The manuscript has *remit* (“he forgives”).]; and leading them to true and certain knowledge of Christ. He does not speak from himself, but [Note: [Col. 0601B] The manuscript has *saed*.] whatever he hears he will speak [Note: [Col. 0602B] Thus the manuscript instead of *loquitur* (“he speaks”), as *talis* occurs for *tales*.], and he teaches and announces future things to believers.

[Col. 0602A] This Spirit declares Christ to be his Lord and God, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord [Note: [Col. 0602C] This is a perverse interpretation by an Arian. The Holy Spirit does not here speak in his own person concerning Christ; rather, he makes David speak. The prophet introduces the Father as speaking with the Son, as the ecclesiastical Fathers commonly understand these words of Psalm 109.], ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.’” And again the same Spirit says to Christ, his God: “Your throne [Note: [Col. 0602B] Thus the manuscript.], O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom; you loved righteousness . . .”

## FRAGMENT IV

. . . . “that the world may know that I love the Father [Note: [Col. 0602B] The manuscript has *Patre*.], and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do.” Therefore, the saying so often repeated, “I am in the Father and the Father in me,” signifies not one substance but two: the unbegotten nature of the Father and the only-begotten nature of the Son [Note: [Col. 0602C] What a ridiculous subtlety of this Arian! Yet it again shows how necessary it is to interpret the divine Scriptures in accordance with the consensus of the Church and the Fathers. But let us hear Hilary, *On the Trinity* III.23: “You hear, ‘I and the Father are one.’ Why do you sever and divide the Son from the Father? They are one: namely, he who is has nothing that is not also in him from whom he is. When you hear the Son saying, ‘I and the Father are one,’ apply the statement to the persons; allow its meaning to the begetter and the begotten in their confession. Let them be one, as are he who begot and he who was begotten. Why do you exclude nature? Why do you destroy truth?” etc. See the same author, III.1; VII.40; IX.52.]. Thus the Son is understood to be in the Father’s bosom, as he is perceived in love [Note: [Col. 0602C] This concerns the same Arian heresy: that the Son is Son not by nature but by adoption and love. [Col. 0602D] The Fathers repeatedly refute it, especially Hilary, *Against Constantius*, fol. 9. Faustinus, however, says in *The Book of Faith* II.5: “This is your doctrine, Arians; this is your peculiar interpretation, this your secret, this the mystery of your faith: ‘Christ is Son by adoption,’ you say, ‘and not a true Son.’” Faustinus then proceeds to refute this and says, among other noteworthy matters: “And lest you should perhaps believe him one of the adopted sons, John the Evangelist cut off the impious mind’s occasion when he called him not only Son but also only-begotten Son. This name admits of no associates; though others are called sons, they are sons by adoption, not by nature. But Christ alone is the only-begotten Son, because he alone is Son—not by adoption but by nature, not merely by designation but by generation.”] and in the power of him who contains all things; but he himself is infinite, and he too contains the other. The latter [Note: [Col. 0602B] The manuscript has *illius*.], receiving from the Father power over all things made after him and through him [Note: [Col. 0602B] The manuscript has *potestate*.], encompasses the universe.

Therefore Father and Son are not one and the same: he who encompasses and he who is encompassed [Note: [Col. 0602D] Hilary, *Against Constantius* 13, reports nearly this objection of a certain Anomoean heretic: “To the extent that the Son stretches himself out to know the Father, to that extent the Father extends himself beyond, lest he be known by the Son.” When these words were read, an uproar arose. Vigilius of Thapsus, *On the Trinity* VI, Chifflet edition, p. 284, says: “The Arians say that the entire Father cannot be comprehended or beheld by the Son. I believe that, just as the Son is in the Father and is wholly seen by the Father, so also the Father is wholly seen by the Son and is wholly in the Son.” Augustine, *Against Maximinus* II.9, fully refutes and sharply ridicules the same Arian objection. Finally Isaac says of the Son in *The Book of Faith*: “How is he believed to be lesser who is beyond estimation, immeasurable, and infinite?”]; the unbegotten and the only-begotten; the begetter and the one begotten; he who commands and [Col. 0603A] he who receives and obeys a command; he who gives and he who receives what is given; he who orders and he who obeys the order [Note: [Col. 0603B] Thus the manuscript.]; he who sends and he who is sent; he who was seen and he whom no human being has seen or can see; he who is impassible and he who suffered for us; the Son who rose from the dead and the Father who raised him; the Son who ascended above the heavens and the Father who never descended; he who sits at God’s right hand and the Father who ordered him to sit at his own right hand; the Son who denied knowing that day [Note: [Col. 0603C] A famous Arian argument, extensively and excellently refuted by Hilary, *On the Trinity* IX.56 ff. At fol. 71 he concludes: “Knowledge in God is not understanding of something he did not know, but speech. By the fact that the Father alone knows, the Son is not understood not to know; for the Son says that he does not know precisely so that others may not know, and says that the Father alone knows precisely so that he himself may not be said not to know. For if God is said then to have known that Abraham loved him, when he did not conceal this from Abraham, it follows that the Father is said to know the day because he did not conceal it from the Son: God’s knowledge being understood not as sudden discovery, but as timely declaration. Therefore if the Son, according to the mystery, does not know the day in order to remain silent, conversely the Father alone is necessarily shown to know the day because he does not remain silent.” See also Ambrose, *On Faith* V.16.], and the Father who placed it in his own authority; the Son who will judge, and the Father who judges no one but gave all [Note: [Col. 0603B] The manuscript has *omnem*.] judgment to the Son [Note: [Col. 0603D] This heretic plainly fails to recognize the attributes and distinctions of the divine persons. Moreover, he confuses what is predicated of Christ as man with his divine predicates. Augustine explains these matters admirably in *Against an Arian Sermon*, fol. 4.].

Do not therefore err: Father and Son are not one and the same, nor are they two equals, according to another assertion of error [Note: [Col. 0603B] Thus the manuscript.], but one is one [Note: [Col. 0603B] Thus the manuscript, as at the end of Fragment I.] Father. For he alone is unbegotten [Col. 0603B] and without beginning [Note: [Col. 0604B] The manuscript has *initium* (“beginning”).], and there are not two gods without beginning, or two equals, or two fathers, or two brothers, or two sons. Rather, there is one unbegotten God, almighty God, who alone is and is called true, alone [Col. 0604A] good, alone possessing immortality [Note: [Col. 0603D] Recall p. 213, note 2. Augustine, *Against Maximinus the Arian* I.3: “You wish the words ‘He alone possesses immortality’ to be understood of the Father alone; yet both Father and Son possess immortality. Otherwise, if the Son does not possess it, the Father did not give it to the Son,” etc.], and dwelling in inaccessible light [Note: [Col. 0604B] The manuscript has *inaccessibilem*.]. Therefore alone in his uniqueness he is such [Note: [Col. 0604B] Thus the manuscript for *talis*.], and there is no other such God without beginning [Note: [Col. 0604B] The manuscript has *initium*, as above.] [Note: [Col. 0603D] Augustine, *Against an Arian Sermon*, fol. 1: “When the Arians confess our Lord Jesus Christ indeed to be God, but refuse to confess him true God and one God with the Father, they introduce for us two gods of distinct and unequal nature: one true, the other not true.” Fulgentius says the same, *Against Fabian*, fragments XI and XXXIII; likewise the aforementioned Augustine, *Against Maximinus* I.1; II [Col. 0604B].13; and finally Boethius, *On the Trinity*, at the beginning.], all-containing, and sole author of all things.

The only-begotten Son of God also is God by nature, truly unchangeable by the will of God and his Father; but, as only-begotten, he was created, made, and begotten [Note: [Col. 0604B] Ambrose, *On Faith* I.16: “I now ask the Arians themselves whether they think ‘begotten’ and ‘created’ mean the same. If they say that they do, there is plainly no difference between begetting and creating. Therefore, since we too are created, there is no difference between ourselves, Christ, and the elements. [Col. 0604C] —But if, as I judge, there is a difference between created and begotten, when we read ‘begotten’ we certainly do not understand ‘begotten’ and ‘created’ as the same.” Ambrose demonstrates the same in the cited work I.13, fol. 85, and V.3. See also Cyril, *Treasury*, assertion 28.] by the unbegotten God: God of all things made after him and through Jesus, by the providence of God and his Father. The Father is God even to the Son, of whom he is the author, as he is of all things; and therefore he alone is true God [Note: [Col. 0604C] Against this blasphemy, the Nicene Creed says of the Son: “God from God, true God from true God.”], because he is God of God [Note: [Col. 0604C] This most pernicious and already-mentioned Arian doctrine—that the Father alone is properly God, for they called the Son “god” in some different sense—is extensively and conclusively refuted by Hilary, *On the Trinity* V. Then, *Against Auxentius*, fol. 6: “They wish this their Christ not to possess the same divinity as the Father,” etc. (the passage there should be read for a clear understanding of the error), “so that the oneness which the Son and Father are proclaimed in the Gospels to have may consist only in a fellowship of will and love, not in truth of divinity,” etc. “If the Arians proclaim Christ true God, they have confessed God without deceit. But if they call him God and deny that he is true, they confer the name and remove the reality.” Although by their most impious [Col. 0604D] blasphemies, etc. Hilary again presents the Arian blasphemous creed in V.4–5, whose foundation was that the Father alone is true God. Finally Ambrose, *On Faith* III.4: “It is sufficiently clear that the Father is not ‘God alone’ without the Son, nor is the Son understood as ‘God alone’ without the Father.”], holds the Son in his power, has subjected all things beneath his feet according to the Apostle, and gave him the name above every name.

Therefore the Father is one God, who neither received authority nor received existence from another [Col. 0604B], but is what he was: unbegotten without beginning [Note: [Col. 0604D] Listen, Arian, to Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation*, fol. 4: “The Father’s eternal generation is without beginning; the Son’s eternal birth is without beginning; the Holy Spirit’s eternal procession is without beginning. For from the eternity of God the Father, which remains without beginning, there is likewise such a birth of the Son and procession of the Holy Spirit that both that birth and that procession are coeternal with that origin in which no beginning could possibly be found.” And in *On Faith to Peter*, fol. 10: “The Father begot the Son from his own nature without beginning.” Read also Victorinus, *Commentary on Philippians*, p. 63.], all-containing God. The holy Scriptures therefore declare him one God and Lord, one good [Note: [Col. 0604D] Ambrose refutes the Arian argument in *On Faith* II.1 ff.: “‘No one is good except the one God,’ they, the Arians, say. I acknowledge the text, but the letter contains no error; would that the Arian interpretation did not! The written characters are blameless; the meaning is culpable.” The sum of Ambrose’s answer is that Christ said this to the scribe, by whom he was believed to be not God but a man. He continues: “Thus goodness is not denied of the Lord, but such a disciple is corrected. For when the scribe had said, ‘Good teacher,’ the Lord replied, ‘Why do you call me good?’ That is, he whom you do not believe to be God, it is not enough merely to call good.” Cyril, *Treasury*, assertion X, and Paulinus of Aquileia, *Against Felix* III.10–11, say likewise. Augustine refutes the argument at greater length in *Against Maximinus* II.23, a passage well worth reading.], alone possessing immortality [Col. 0605A] [Note: [Col. 0605D] The *Compendium of Faith* says: “The Arians say that the Father is greater because he is immortal. They must be asked whether they admit that the Son is mortal in the substance of his divinity. If they say so, every person can recognize how contrary to reason they speak, since no one doubts that even the human soul is immortal.”], and dwelling in inaccessible light [Note: [Col. 0605C] The manuscript has *inaccessibilem*.]. This is not because the Son is not God or Lord, but because the Father is God even to the Son [Note: [Col. 0605C] The manuscript has *Filius*, but it is corrected below.] and to all things. But the Son is the only-begotten God and Lord of all things made through him; he too is good and gracious, immortal and unchangeable by nature. Yet he received all these things from the Father and is found obedient in all things to God and to his Father [Note: [Col. 0605C] The manuscript has *Patreque*.].

Thus Father and Son are not called one God [Note: [Col. 0606D] But, O Arian, the whole Catholic Church affirms this, as Ferrandus says in *Letter to Cassian*, fol. 2.]; rather, the Father alone is called one God, who, as stated, is God even to the Son and to all things. The Son, however, is not God to the Father; but the Son is Lord and God to every creature. He adores, entreats [Note: [Col. 0605C] *Petet* for *petit*, “entreats,” as above *tales* for *talis*.], worships, and gives thanks to the Father; and he is indebted, because he declares that he lives through the Father and glories that he received all authority from him in heaven and on earth, according to [Col. 0605B] the evangelical tradition, where Jesus is reported as saying to the Samaritan woman: “We worship what we know, but you worship what you do not know” [Note: [Col. 0606D] Ambrose refutes this entire objection, based upon Christ’s worship of the Father and his conversation with the Samaritan woman, in *On Faith* V.4. He says that Christ speaks there as man; just as, as man, he had grown weary from the journey, asked to quench his thirst, and acted as a devout Jew.].

The Gospel tradition frequently shows Christ praying to his Father, giving thanks to his Father, and declaring: “I give you thanks, Father, because you have heard me; and I know that you always hear me.” Therefore he always worships, because he always declares that the Father hears him. Attend, therefore, to the Gospel’s meaning: Jesus gives thanks openly [Note: [Col. 0605C] Thus the manuscript, evidently *e* for *i*.] because of those standing by, as he himself declares, saying to his Father: “Indeed, I know that you always hear me; but I say this because of those standing by, that they may recognize that you sent me.” Attend diligently and see the saving teaching: Christ wishes to be known as what he is, and not to be called what he is not [Col. 0605C]; for whoever calls Christ what he is not falsifies the knowledge of him who is.

Do not therefore err. Those who declare the Father to be one and the same person, and greater than Jesus Christ, do not know his Father, according to the judgment of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who says: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice that I am going to the Father, because my Father is greater than I” [Note: [Col. 0606D] I shall discuss this celebrated saying at Fragment XVI.].

With this knowledge of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we must diligently seek the dwelling in the Lord’s tabernacle and the rest on his holy mountain, which are promised in the present psalm [Note: [Col. 0606D] I would have thought that a commentary on the Psalms was being made here, or a homily recited, had the connection of the leaves not clearly shown me that this part too, like the others, belongs to the Arian treatise. Tertullian speaks similarly of another psalm in *Against Praxeas* 27.]. For the soul that is without stain can walk the way which leads on high [Note: [Col. 0605C] Thus the manuscript.], as we have explained above; and with a clear and simple eye it can complete that journey and continually behold the good things prepared, according to the saying: “Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” It also continually sees God, the giver of good things, as it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” This, therefore, is the meaning of the words: “He who walks without stain and works righteousness.”

He has taught what kind of person [Note: [Col. 0606C] Thus the manuscript for *qualis*.] one must be who hastens to possess the good things prepared in heaven. He then sets forth the commandments as though they were steps [Note: [Col. 0606C] Thus the manuscript, here and below.], since those who ascend on high appear to ascend by steps: first rising upon the nearest step, one advances to the next, then to the third and fourth, until one reaches the appointed place—which cannot be done without labor. Therefore those who desire to attain the dwelling on high must apply themselves with every diligence to the labors and sweat of piety, so that they may reach their destination.

Once the soul has been made unstained by the knowledge of piety [Note: [Col. 0606C] So the passage stands in the manuscript.], those who desire to travel the way that leads on high must adorn and train it in good works, according to the saying: “So let your light shine before people, [Col. 0606C] that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” In accordance with this sequence, the Lord explains what sort of person one who desires to dwell on high must be, and what he must do [Note: [Col. 0606D] Thus the manuscript.], saying: “He who walks without stain and works righteousness, speaking truth in his heart.”

Further, in this he teaches in due order that one should first establish truth within oneself and in one’s heart, and prove it as though sending down a root, so that one may be found righteous according to the apostolic teaching which says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Therefore he says: “Speaking truth in his heart, who has not practiced deceit with his tongue.” For one who desires heavenly goods ought not to speak deceit, nor recount whatever he pleases, but should bring forth through his lips truth examined and tested in his heart, for the salvation both of himself and of his hearers.

The Apostle also teaches this, saying: “Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but whatever is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear.” For one who speaks carelessly and without concern can harm a neighbor’s soul [Note: [Col. 0607D] I would prefer *quis* (“someone”).]. Therefore one who wishes to dwell in heaven must guard and measure his words, as is said in Psalm 111: “Blessed is the person who has mercy and lends; he will order his words in judgment.” And the Lord Jesus teaches in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0607D] Thus the manuscript.], saying: “By your word it is evident that you will be justified as righteous [Note: [Col. 0607D] Thus the manuscript.] without deceit and hypocrisy; and by your word it is evident that you will be condemned as deceitful and wicked” [Note: [Col. 0607D] Thus the manuscript: *v* for *b*, here and below.]. For this reason we are taught to guard and measure our words, so that we may instruct our neighbor.

Desiring to enter the Lord’s tabernacle, we shall do no harm to our neighbor, neither in word nor in pretence, according to the saying: “And he has not done evil to his neighbor.” But one who desires to attain that blessed life must have those around him trained [Col. 0607C] in the Lord’s discipline, lest reproach concerning them come upon him from anyone. For people are accustomed, when they see some persons uneducated and undisciplined, to reproach those who have them about them or under their authority. It is indeed a just reproach against those who ought to train them if those under their control are found unruly or undisciplined, because they have not been sufficiently constrained to discipline; as it is said: “An untrained son is a reproach to his father.” This saying therefore teaches those who desire . . . . . . . .

[Col. 0607D] confirms this saying: “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” [Col. 0608A], according to that . . . therefore err . . . . if anyone has seen the Son in a human body, he judges the Father also to be bodily; which is a horrible impiety. But if they are willing to receive the true meaning, he who has seen the Son sent by the Father and carrying out the Father’s commands has seen the Father—that is, has known . . . they are light . . . . not . . . . . For if anyone acknowledges the Son of God—that is, Jesus—in his own unique nature and dignity, which he received from the Father in being begotten, and . . . . the Jews . . . asserting . . . . the Father and Son, named by their names, from the things stated above; but here in God’s light . . . . to the Jews, as has often been said, according to . . . . the prophet . . . “Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock [Note: [Col. 0607D] The manuscript has *Patram*.] of offense, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame.”

[Col. 0608B] And again: “Whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it shall crush him.” And again: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising again of many.” It is therefore clear that he is set for the rising of believers, who shall not be put to shame; but for the fall of those who do not believe, who take offense at his teaching with the Jews and do not interpret rightly: they themselves shall be shattered [Note: [Col. 0608D] Thus the manuscript.].

Therefore those who saw the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, saw him in two ways. With bodily [Note: [Col. 0608D] The manuscript has *Carnalis*.] eyes they saw the human body; but with the eye of the mind, through his works, they knew God—the Son of God. Therefore when he says, “He who has seen me has seen also the Father who sent me,” the meaning is this: whoever has seen the Son’s works and through the works has known the power of deity, has seen—that is, known—him who sent me and commanded me [Col. 0608C] to perform these works, or who works through me [Note: [Col. 0608D] The manuscript has *operantem*.] [Note: [Col. 0607D] The heretic explains it thus in order to exclude the Catholic meaning of the words, “I and the Father are one.” Faustinus, *On Faith* 1, fol. 12 ff., vigorously demonstrates against the Arians that these words refer to sameness of nature, not unity of will. His notable words are: “I do not want you, impious heretic, to take away the sameness of the Father’s and Son’s substance and improperly introduce unity of will.” Likewise Tertullian, *Against Praxeas* 25: “‘I and [Col. 0608D] the Father are one’ was said with respect to unity of substance, not numerical singularity.”]. Those, therefore, who see become seeing; enlightened and instructed by the Son, they knew and saw him who sent him—the Father—according to the assertion of the Son himself, who says . . . . .

. . . . . . or have had the desire to make a vow, cannot be advanced [Note: [Col. 0608D] The manuscript seems to read *promovi*, or *pro me ut*.] by God. “For just as the Father has life in himself” [Note: [Col. 0609C] Thus the manuscript.], “so he gave the Son to have life in himself; and he gave him authority to execute judgment.” As though he had said: God, unbegotten, my begetting Father, who is and was God without beginning—living, powerful, good, wise, perfect, everlasting, without beginning and without end—willed that I should be before all things living, powerful, good, wise, perfect, everlasting [Col. 0609B] (we call the Son everlasting in this sense: though the Son has a beginning, yet he will have no end, but will remain forever [Note: [Col. 0609C] “Not” is absent.][Note: [Col. 0609D] Observe how the Arians denied eternal generation, which the orthodox Fathers most splendidly establish: Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, ch. 5; Hilary, *On the Trinity* I.24; II.20; III.3; IV.6; XII.21 ff., 51; Ambrose, *On Faith* I.8; Cyril, *On the Trinity*, dialogue 2; Fulgentius, *To Trasimund* II.7, and *Against Fabianus*, fragments XIX–XX; and many others throughout their works.], and would give everlastingness to all the other good things).

“And he granted such capability in me, in whom he willed me to be, that I could fulfill all his wills, arrangements, and commands; and so I have fulfilled them and always fulfill them. Likewise, all the other things which were afterward done—whether the flood, the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all things that are always done and governed—are always done and governed at the Father’s command, because he is the Son of Man. “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good will come forth unto the resurrection of judgment.”

As though he had said [Note: [Col. 0610C] The manuscript has *dixisse*, “to have said.”]: Do not be unbelieving because you see that I am flesh and think that I am merely a human being. For they agree concerning the Father and the Son but disagree concerning the Holy Spirit: these people make the Holy Spirit equal in every respect and in all things to the Father and Son, while the Macedonians maintain that the Holy Spirit was created by the Father’s command through the Son, and proclaim that he is the Father’s messenger and minister [Note: [Col. 0611C] The orthodox Didymus says, *On the Holy Spirit*, fol. 30: “The Holy Spirit, sent by the Father, must be understood not as a servant, not as another, nor as separated from the Son.”], as do we [Note: [Col. 0611C] On the contrary, it is established that the Macedonian heresy sprang from Arianism, as Damasus says in his letter to Paulinus. (The treatise ends, as the blank space on the page demonstrates.)

. . . they slander us. Paulinus of Aquileia, *Against Felix* III.7 agrees with Augustine’s former view but differs from the latter.]: “And this is his will: that of all which the Father has given me I should lose none of it, but raise it up [Note: [Col. 0614C] The manuscript has *resuscitet*, “he may raise.”] on the last day.” Likewise in the Gospel: “For this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life; and I will raise him . . . . . . .

## FRAGMENT XIII

[Col. 0617B] . . . . . most especially he who, at the beginning of the Gospel, is proclaimed to be the Word, God with God. Because of the matters stated above, and when he had given the devout a devout understanding concerning him, then proceeding a little further he says: “And the Word was made flesh [Note: [Col. 0617C] The loose sheets have *factus*, “made [masculine]”; below, however, *factum*.], and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only [Son] from the Father, full of glory and truth.”

Thus the Holy Spirit through most blessed John has most certainly and plainly shown that the Word himself is God, so that you may not suppose that this only-begotten Son of God is unbegotten; at the same time he most plainly announces the manner of his humanity, and stops the mouths of those who say that he did not assume a soul together with a body [the negation appears to be lost in the Latin] [Note: [Col. 0617C] Augustine refutes this very error of the Ariomanites in *Against an Arian Sermon*, fol. 7: “See in what words they make wholly clear that they deny that a human soul also belongs to the unity [Col. 0617D] of Christ’s person; instead, in Christ they confess only flesh and divinity. For when he hung upon the wood and said, ‘Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,’ they wish him to be understood to have commended divinity itself to the Father, not the human spirit which is the soul,” etc. “Let them acknowledge that Christ joined not merely flesh but a human soul also to the Only-begotten,” etc. Read also Ambrose, *On the Incarnation*, ch. 7; Fulgentius, *To Trasimund* I.18; III.18, 19, 21, 24; and *Against Fastidiosus*, ch. 22; likewise Ferrandus, *Letter to the Monks of Cassino*, fol. 9. Theodoret teaches us in his dialogue against them that the Macedonians too held this error, than which nothing could be more absurd. For since Jesus was subject to sorrow and fear in the Passion, and these affections cannot occur in a body, it would follow that divinity was sorrowful, fearful, and in pain, if Jesus lacked a soul and divinity occupied its place.].

He says: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us [Note: [Col. 0617C] Thus the manuscript.],” that is, he put on flesh—not because God the Word himself changed into the nature [Col. 0617C] [Note: [Col. 0617C] The manuscript has *in natura*.] of flesh, but because he took flesh and dwelt among us, that is, in our flesh. In that flesh, God the Word, who is impassible, suffered; and the incorruptible God endured corruption, in order to change us to incorruptibility.

But the divinity of the Word himself [Col. 0618A] did not die or endure corruption. Rather, the temporary separation of the divinity from the body is understood to be the corruption of that body. Yet God the Word suffered nothing except insult alone for our sake. For if, when we die, our souls do not die, but the departure of the soul from the body constitutes the corruption of our human being [Note: [Col. 0617C] The loose sheets have *homini*, “of/to a human being.”], much more does the divinity of the only-begotten God not die. But when he willed, at the Father’s nod, he died voluntarily—that is, he departed from the body, and that separation is called his death [Note: [Col. 0618C] On the contrary, Christian doctrine teaches that, in Christ’s death, divinity did not abandon either his lifeless body or the soul separated from it. Read also Fulgentius, *To Trasimund* III.25, 31.][Note: [Col. 0617C] In the loose sheets approximately four letters have been obliterated. Yet there seems to be no lacuna.].

But after the third day, by the Father’s will, he again took up the body and raised it [Note: [Col. 0618C] Thus the loose sheets, for *id*, “it.”] to incorruption; he ascended with it above the heavens; he possesses it as a glorious, holy, living temple; and in the very body in which he saved the human race, in that very body he is worshiped at the right hand of God’s power [Col. 0618B] by [Note: [Col. 0618C] The loose sheets have *ad*, “to.”] all.

Learn certain knowledge of these things, therefore, from the most blessed Stephen, the first martyr of Christ’s divinity, who says: “I see,” he says [Note: [Col. 0618C] The loose sheets have *inquid*.], “the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power.” The Son of Man—the body which . . . . .

Those, however, who say that whenever divine Scripture mentions Jesus Christ it signifies only a human being—body and soul, not God—and that he is Jesus Christ because he was born of Mary and did not exist before, as Photinus and his predecessors maintained, we regard as excluded from our communion.

For although in it there is brightness, the nature of light; heat, the power of burning; and mobility, the capacity for glowing—yet the whole is fire, and all these are one nature.” Likewise Hilary: “Therefore let the Father be the one who is all his own.” Likewise Hilary: “I ask whether God is of another kind, who remains God in the form of God; and whether, according to impressions that seal and are sealed, we see in seals iron with stamped lead and a gem with wax, an image impressed in the form either of a convex or of a concave [seal].” Likewise Hilary: “I ask, therefore, whether there is division and separation when fire is from fire. Is the nature cut off? Or does not nature follow, so that it is present with light kindled from light?”

We thought it useful to set forth these comparative examples in support of the Father, so that he might not be thought to lie concerning his profession, since the understanding of the divine confession and certain natural examples from creatures supplied [support]: “But because heretical fury disturbed the faith of the simpler people, so that they might not suppose one ought to believe of God what can scarcely be understood except through a bodily comparison, therefore, according to that saying of the Lord, ‘What is born of flesh is flesh, but what is born of Spirit is spirit’; because God is spirit, and he was born from God.”

[Note: [Col. 0622C] Thus the manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0623B] Manuscript: *prestarent*. Rather, in the preceding passage read *ne mentiri*, and *ex aliquo*.]

[Note: [Col. 0623B] *Fidem* is absent from the manuscript. Likewise, shortly afterward, *credi*.]

[Note: [Col. 0623B] Manuscript: *oportere*.]
