[Note: [Col. 0623C] Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit* III.10, uses this passage to demonstrate the divinity of the Holy Spirit. He says that the Arians understood these words to concern the Spirit so thoroughly that they fraudulently removed them from their codices.]

Most vain Hilary deceives innocent minds; and what the Lord said concerning the baptized and those who are spiritually born, he asserted had been written concerning the birth of the Son of God. But the very reading destroys Hilary, for divine Scripture says: “Do not marvel that I said to you: You must be born again.” Let them therefore see and understand.

[Note: [Col. 0623C] John 3:6 is indeed cited by Hilary, *On the Trinity* VII.30; yet it is not used of the Son’s divine birth except in VII.14. In truth, in John the Lord Christ speaks of those reborn and of baptism; Ambrose too acknowledges this, *On the Holy Spirit* III.10, fol. 63. Nevertheless Hilary uses the words quite aptly to show that the Son possesses the Father’s substance—that he is God because begotten from God, not created [Col. 0623D] as other worldly things were. Indeed, if those reborn in baptism are spirit because they are reborn of spirit, much more will the Son, naturally born from God the Spirit, be spirit. Perhaps this consequence was what Hilary had in view, together with Tertullian in the passage cited among us at p. 210, n. 1, and Phoebadius, ch. 11.]

## FIRST CHAPTER OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH

[Note: [Col. 0623C] Note *capitulus* for *capitulum*.]

[Note: [Col. 0623D] One may marvel at the shameless Arian who calls his own church catholic—presumably, I suspect, after the Council of Rimini, concerning which the Arian Maximinus boasts in St Augustine, *Conference with Maximinus*, fol. 2. Jerome complains of it with excessive rhetorical emphasis, *Against the Luciferians*, fol. 19: “The whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian.” Not, of course, because correct faith then failed; rather, as Jerome says in the same place, the orthodox bishops were deceived by the Arians’ crafty creed-formula and other artifices. St Hilary, at the beginning of Book VI, likewise laments the disastrous disease of Arianism, infecting churches in almost every province of the Roman Empire, so that the heresy presumed authority for itself from the immense number of its followers. Moreover, there are various Arian creedal formulas, which St Hilary recounts in *On the Trinity* IV.12 and VI.5; *Against Auxentius*, fol. 13; and *On the Synods*, chs. 11, 28, 35, 38. Hilary himself complains of the multiplicity of these formulas in Book II *To Constantius* and *Against Constantius*.]

[Col. 0623B] We confess, believe, and maintain that God the Father almighty is without beginning, unbegotten, indivisible, unchangeable, and immutable; supreme, most high, incomparable, and God of all. And because God the Father almighty willed, determined, and commanded it, God the Holy Spirit and all other heavenly and earthly things, visible and invisible—created, made, born, founded, established, fashioned, and brought into being—received their subsistence through the only-begotten Son. And because God the Father almighty arranged and determined it, all the prophets spoke through the Son by inspiration, declaring that the Son himself would come, sent by God the Father as the enlightener and savior of the human race; and that he would take a temple—that is, flesh—from a Virgin, so that the Son of God almighty, because of his assumption of flesh, should be called the Son of Man and man, that is, Son of David, because he received flesh from David’s seed. ## FRAGMENT XVIII

“. . . His birth is before eternal times. If there is anything in reality that precedes eternity, there will certainly be something that exceeds the concept of eternity. For he is yours, and your only-begotten one; not a portion, not an extension, not some empty name according to a theory of effects, but Son—Son from you, God the Father—true God, and begotten from you in the unity of your nature. After you he must be confessed, yet with you; because you, the author of his eternal origin, are eternal. Since he is from you, he is second from you; but since he is yours, he must not be separated from you, because you must never be confessed without your Son, lest you be charged either with being imperfect without generation or superfluous after generation.”

[Note: [Col. 0626D] Up to this point I supplied the lacuna in the manuscript from Hilary, *On the Trinity* XII.54.]

[Note: [Col. 0626C] Namely, the Son.]

[Note: [Col. 0626C] The loose sheets read *generatione*.]

Likewise Phoebadius, the Aquitanian associate of Hilary: “Whoever, therefore, proves that the Father was at some time without Word, without Reason, without Wisdom, [Col. 0627A] without Power, and without Spirit, has thereby proved that the Son was not with and in the Father before every beginning. Yet I do not know whether, deprived of these powers, he can be called God. For not only could God, who is perfect in his eternity, not so exist; even a creature, incomplete according to its kind, does not subsist. Nothing can be if it is not; but it will not be if it lacks what it must have in order to be. Therefore the Father lacked everything if he lacked anything. But he lacked everything if his Son—that is, the fullness of his powers—did not lack a beginning. And this opinion must by a profane and sacrilegious definition pass into one or the other branch of blasphemy. Either the Father must be believed to have received a beginning together with his Son, since he could not be without his Son, that is, without his powers; for, if this is so, I do not know what third god exists before their beginning. Or, if the Father alone is said to be without beginning, then he must be said to have been imperfect before the generation of the Son. For he is imperfect if he began to have what he did not have before and nevertheless ought to have had. Finally, he always wished to have what he ought always to have had in order to be perfect, because whatever has occupied the whole receives no increase.”

[Note: [Col. 0626D] Thus the manuscript.]

This divine law, these holy Scriptures, Constantius defended in writing to the holy . . . [Note: [Col. 0627D] A gap in the manuscript prevents us from learning more precisely about these letters of Constantius. Otherwise, it is well established that this emperor, ensnared by Arian bishops and heresy, enacted many erroneous measures and condemned orthodox bishops by edicts. (It is well known [Col. 0628D] that by edict he even prohibited the term *homoousion*.) Such letters are mentioned by St Hilary, *To Constantius*, book II, §2, and by Lucifer of Cagliari, Colet edition, p. 17. Indeed, Sulpicius Severus, *History*, book II, expressly relates that a heretical letter was composed and circulated at Milan in Constantius’ name by Arian bishops. St Hilary mentions Arian confessions of faith framed by Constantius in his book against that emperor, fol. 7, and in *On the Synods*, fol. 78. Finally Pope Liberius (*Works of St Hilary*, fragment V) complains of a speech of the Emperor Constantius sent to the people, in which Liberius himself was attacked.] . . . . . . . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0629D] Note.—Since in my scholia on the Arian Fragments I made extensive use of Hilary of Poitiers, I was reminded of another Hilary, of Arles, whose lost verses on the burning spring are mentioned by his ancient biographer (in Quesnel, *Works of St Leo*, vol. I, p. 367). I myself recently read them in a fairly ancient Vatican manuscript, in which a certain little work *On the Wonders of the World* is written. Indeed, before Hilary’s verses, there is a fragment from the likewise lost *Chorography* of Julius Titianus (who lived under Commodus), which Servius cites on *Aeneid* IV.43. In the same little work Lactantius’ *Phoenix* is also cited, as well as Berosus in his *Babylonian History*. But leaving these matters aside, I shall reproduce the passage which provides us with the fragments of Julius Titianus and Hilary.

“The fourth wonder is Aetna. Julius Titianus also mentions this mountain in the following words: ‘There are four greatest mountains in Sicily: Eryx, Nebrodes, [Col. 0631A] Neptune, and Aetna. Seeing it frequently roll flames from its summit, the world feels near the faith of believers [ [Col. 0631A] The passage is corrupt.]; although, when it was first reported at Rome that it had burned, this too had already been dealt with among portents.’

“The fifth concerns the spring near Grenoble, from which both water and fire flow together. For you see flames flying over the nymphs; you draw water from the middle of the spring; you run, drink, and are not burned; you carry it away, and are not caught by the fire. But if you bring wax or torches near, as soon as they touch the flames, [Col. 0632A] they catch fire. If you put in your hand, it too is not burned. Hence Hilary says:

> If the fires truly burn, why do you, waters, live?  
> If the waters truly extinguish, why do you, fires, live?  
> Hostile fire lies hidden in the bosom of the streams;  
> And the high hand commands their common origins, etc.

“The author of the little work did not report the remaining verses. Its date—the sixth century—may be inferred from its mention of the death of King Sigebert I as an event of its own time.”]

[Col. 0631]

# REMAINS OF ANCIENT SERMONS FROM ANOTHER PALIMPSEST OF THE AMBROSIAN LIBRARY. (C, G)*

## FRAGMENT I. SERMON III BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0631D] Thus I read in the manuscript, unless perhaps there was a C before III, making this Sermon CIII, which I scarcely believe. Moreover, before this sermon another ends on the same page in these words: “For this is the true knowledge of God: the working [Col. 0632D] of the Holy Spirit. Amen. The discourse on the substantial Word ends.”]

[Col. 0631B]

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself is the foundation, himself the perfection, himself the cornerstone. He is from earth and from heaven: for God descended from heaven, assumed a human being from earth, and was joined to humanity. Behold, from heaven; behold, the foundation; behold, the cornerstone. In him there was good pleasure among human beings; and to those who are from the earth he gave the Holy Spirit from heaven, in order to make the higher and lower realms one Church—that is, mingling humanity with divinity and divinity with humanity. [Note: [Col. 0632D] The author speaks in a free and, as it were, popular sense. Christ, however, is one, not by confusion of substance but by unity of person.]

But when you hear “foundation,” understand the Lord: for he himself [Note: [Col. 0631D] I would prefer *ipse*, so that it may refer to “has measured.”] measured out the foundation. The stones built upon it must have a measure equal to the foundation, so that it may become suitable for the purposes of building [Note: [Col. 0631D] The manuscript: *aedificanti*.] [Col. 0631C] . . . . .

## FRAGMENT II. FROM SERMON V

. . . . . . . . which we behold through a mirror, transformed into the same image from glory to glory. For just as someone examines royal garments—purple, a diadem, and other such things—and marvels at their variety, fineness, charm, and the beauty of precious [Note: [Col. 0631D] Thus the manuscript.] stones, and gazes with inexhaustible delight; or just as [Note: [Col. 0631D] The manuscript: *quemammodum*. Elsewhere, however, sometimes *quemadmod.* Indeed also *quaemamm.*—exactly as in the manuscript of Cicero’s *Verrines*.] . . . . [Note: [Col. 0631D] Space for one word.] looks upon . . . . . uo [Note: [Col. 0632D] Space for several letters.] the remote and heavenly image of Christ, burning [Note: [Col. 0632D] Perhaps *habitantem*, “dwelling,” for *ferventem*, “burning”?] within us, and beholds the beauty of the ineffable light: so they are transformed from glory to glory, beholding varieties and diverse beauties which cannot be related by bodily speech, indeed cannot even be comprehended by the intellect—how great are the things accomplished in this world among the saints.

For the parables themselves are certain images: divine things are recognised by those who have experienced them and are beheld in truth by those in whom they ought to be beheld. Thus you must understand or hear beyond your knowledge, beyond perception, until the reality itself pours the grace of the mystery into your mind. For purple and royal clothing bestow neither profit nor life upon those who see them, except only the pleasure of the sight; but divine glory and the beauty of the heavenly image bestow eternal life, true love, purity of heart, and heavenly food. Therefore those who behold this divine light shining in their hearts are occupied by no earthly things, but are wholly united with that beauty.

For just as a little child, looking at its mother while being carried in her arms, rejoices and is glad because [Col. 0632C] it receives from her the life of milk and looks upon her, so those who have the true light within themselves, attending to it, rest and rejoice with joy that cannot be described. From it they learn [Note: [Col. 0632D] Thus the manuscript.] immortal food, and in it they live the true life in the age. Sermon V ends.

Therefore he granted a great benefit to the human race: redeeming us from the prison of darkness, showing the way of life, and teaching the door [Note: [Col. 0632D] The manuscript: *dicendo*, “saying.”] by which one might escape from bonds, when he says: “Ask, and it shall be given you; knock, and it shall be opened to you.” For through this door those willing to seek and knock are set free; and in it they will attain a twofold grace: both that the soul may be freed from the most grievous bonds of death and sin, and that it may recover itself and its thoughts, with Christ the heavenly king dwelling with it as a bridegroom. [Note: [Col. 0633D] I omitted page 30 and the two remaining pages of the palimpsest, namely 31 and 32, because when I was leaving Milan I lacked time to copy them.] . . . . . . . .

## FRAGMENT V. FROM HOMILY XXXIII

. . . . . . . . . just as if a city is deserted or ruined, and someone wishes to restore it: first he will completely demolish what remains or has fallen down; [Col. 0633C] and then he begins to lay foundations and raise the structure, though the house is not yet complete. Likewise, one who wishes to make a paradise in desolate and remote places first begins to clear them, enclose them with a hedge, and mark out watercourses; then he plants, so that after a long time the paradise may produce fruit.

So too the human will has become embittered, desolate, and thorny through transgression. For God said to it: “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you.” Therefore one must labour, seek with much effort, and lay a foundation, until heavenly fire comes into one’s heart and cleanses all the thorns. Only then will one begin to be sanctified. Homily XXXIII ends.

## FRAGMENT VIII

. . . . . . . . For the Law commanded that animals having a cloven hoof and chewing the cud [Note: [Col. 0634D] Thus the manuscript. The word is otherwise attested only on the authority of Apuleius.] were to be eaten [Leviticus 11]. This means that a person must understand himself to be twofold, opposed and not in agreement with the sin dwelling within. But the soul, together with its thoughts, must be separated, judged through the Word, and set apart from fellowship with sin. [Col. 0635A] Then God discerns you when reversed [Note: [Col. 0635D] Thus I read it.] and separates the soul from evil spirits, which are the roots of thoughts.

For just as a farmer who carefully tends land first renews it and clears it of thorns and thistles, and then sows seed so that it may yield fruit in due season, so one who wishes to please God and hopes to receive the seed of grace must cleanse, renew, and adorn with every virtue the very soil of one’s heart, so that the seed of the Spirit, falling in the heart’s good soil, may render the manifold fruit of the Holy Spirit.

Or, just as a craftsman who carefully prepares the skins of animals called parchment cannot have the Lord’s law written on them unless he first removes their hair, the superfluous fat of the flesh, the blackness of blood, and the remaining impurity, and makes them diligently clean and clear: [Col. 0635B] so the wise craftsman removes everything superfluous, cleansing and imparting brightness; then God’s laws are written there, and then there will be spiritual writings. By the same analogy, those who wish and hope that the laws of the Holy Spirit may be written in their mind or soul, and that they may put on the heavenly image of Christ’s life, should, with every care and diligence, present their hearts pure as craftsmen do: cleansing themselves from all the gross fat of this age, from the care of flesh and blood, and, separated from every earthly bond and from the distraction of earthly things—which is like the blackness of blood—cleansing this [Note: [Col. 0635D] The manuscript: *hunc*. I have written *hoc*, referring it to the heart.], so that, when they have thus cleansed and prepared their own mind and heart, holy God may write there his own laws, according to his promise, giving laws in their heart and [Col. 0635C] writing them in their minds, and they shall be his people. As the Apostle also says: “Having these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from every flesh . . . . . . . . .”

## FRAGMENT IX

. . . . . . . . Therefore now let each person demand an account from his own soul, judging his thoughts by the divine commandments; let him test to what things he is devoted and by what he is held, and see whether his heart or thoughts agree with the laws of God. If not, let each hasten to turn with every power of soul and body, so that, just as he preserves the outward body [Note: [Col. 0635D] The manuscript: *exteriorem*.] from fornication, malice, and corruption as though it were God’s temple, so inwardly he may guard the soul and thoughts against the corruption of evil spirits; so that he may not share their thoughts [Col. 0635D] nor defile himself, because she is Christ’s bride.

For just as the body commits fornication, so the soul, secretly communing in its thoughts with evil powers and invisible sins, is corrupted and commits fornication . . . . . . . . in desires . . . . . . . . in empty glory, in envy, in robbery. For where the soul has fellowship, there also it ministers and serves: if it has fellowship with the divine Spirit, it ministers to him; but if [Col. 0636A] with dark and evil spirits, it likewise ministers and serves them. As it says: “Their mind is corrupted.” And again: “Their mind and conscience have been defiled.” And again: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds should be corrupted.”

There is therefore visible fornication; there is also invisible fornication through wicked thoughts. For in the Law the Holy Spirit, revealing a certain mystery to the soul, separated unclean four-footed animals from clean ones; for clean things must produce clean fruits. Thus the thoughts of souls, through knowledge of the Word, ought to be clean in their own nature, apart from the sin dwelling within and from unclean thoughts, so that the soul, by knowledge of the Word, may produce clean thoughts proper to its own nature, neither consenting to nor sharing the unclean fruits of wickedness; through that knowledge [Col. 0636B] which is natural . . . . . . . . . it will produce ignorance, nor does it hear or speak or immerse itself in the darkness of sin, because it has been rescued from vices.

For the mind which lived in darkness and was not born for death . . . . . . . . is not of Christ’s body, is not of the body of light, but is a companion and portion of darkness. And again, those whose souls have been enlightened by heavenly [Note: [Col. 0635D] Thus the manuscript.] light have become [Note: [Col. 0635D] Thus the manuscript.] a portion of light. But someone will say: “How is a soul that is not the devil’s creature the devil’s body of darkness?” Consider this and understand rightly. Just as the garment which you use was made or woven by another, and you put it on; likewise another built and established the house in which you live: so, by the same analogy, Adam, transgressing the command, [Col. 0636C] obeying the evil serpent, and despising God’s holy commandments, was sold away, selling himself to the powers [Note: [Col. 0636D] That is, the principalities or powers.] of wickedness. He subjected to the enemy [Note: [Col. 0636D] The manuscript: *sibi nicos*.] the soul which God had made good, the proper dwelling-place of his image. Therefore the soul becomes the body of the darkness of wickedness as long as it remains in sins, etc.

## FRAGMENT XIII
[Col. 0637D] . . . . . . they filled the souls of many as though with unclean spirits. As the psalm says: “for they have been filled with the darkened dwellings of iniquities.” And he set up a covenant against the true king—the law of sin—and stamped shadowy images full of pains, and a debased coin [Col. 0638A] to be rejected; he taught habits of wickedness, brought in legions—spirits of perversity—which hold the soul in solid fetters and iron chains, keeping watch lest it escape. And he compelled it to perform their works according to their will; they corrupted it and committed fornication with it; they covered its eyes with darkness lest it see its Lord; and they compelled it to grind in the mill of darkness, so that it might think carnally and worldly, perceive earthly and muddy things. And he stirred up within it a muddy fountain, bubbling with iniquity; they scattered within it the counsels of malicious spirits and led its people—that is, the multitude of its thoughts—into captivity. They stripped it of garments of glory and put upon it rags of shame and uncleanness, full of bitterness and gall; and [Col. 0638B] filled it with every impurity.

Then, after much time had passed, they themselves, by the fitting power of habitual darkness, had no memory of their king or of their own freedom; rather, they were as though they had been created such from the beginning. Therefore Christ, the heavenly and true King, first sent word through the holy prophets, admonishing the human being and recalling him to the memory of his own noble dignity; also reminding him how bitterly [Note: The manuscript reads *acervo*, “heap,” here and below.] and deceitfully he was held in error, announcing that he himself would come and free him by himself from those who held him captive. . . . . . . that he would erase the coinage of adultery and destroy all the enemies by whom he is held. He promised to renew him according to his own will and to give the peaceful and divine law of the Spirit, so that at the same time he might change the old [Col. 0638C] habits of wickedness that were in him—provided only that the soul, mindful of itself, should flee to its own Lord, surrender itself to him, and lend him its will; that it should believe that he would do all that he promised; and should entreat him, crying out day and night that he might rescue it from evil captivity and bitter slavery.

But when the saving goodness of our Jesus Christ shone forth [Note: The manuscript has *illustravit*, “made bright,” for *illuxit*, “shone forth.”], the times of promise were fulfilled, and Christ the King came to redeem and reclaim his human being, whom cruel bondage had held for many ages, all who believed in him and fled to him were redeemed. And he prayed, confessing his captivity, that he could not free himself or be delivered from slavery by himself, [Note: There appears to be a lacuna.] that is, to the higher world; and from this age he flies more readily, with great rest, to the blessed and everlasting age [Col. 0638D]. For now they become sons of God, higher and exalted, without any fear of unclean spirits or their savagery, just as birds no longer fear the snares of wild beasts.

But just as no human being understands the speech [Note: The manuscript reads *loquellam*.] of cattle, so no person full of worldly spirits recognizes the language of the Holy Spirit; only the children of grace recognize the words of their mother. As it is said: “comparing spiritual things with spiritual”; but “the natural person does not receive the things that are of the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him.” For as the voice of swallows is unknown to human beings, so carnal persons are barbarians to spiritual persons.

We speak, however, by a certain shadowy likeness concerning birds and such things, which are true; taking examples and gathering material from visible things, because spiritual things admit of no interpretation. Thus too the Lord spoke [Col. 0640A] in parables, for he said: “I will open my mouth in parables.” Spiritual things are invisible and cannot be expounded in human speech unless the Spirit himself is entreated to teach. For we cannot know spiritual rebirth, growth, and perfection, but can only believe that it works thus in those human beings who have been able to please it by their manner of life. Thus spiritual speech too is barbarous to worldly persons. For all the fish of the sea know its paths and depths, whereas human beings, wild animals, and cattle cannot recognize . . . .

[Col. 0639]

## FRAGMENT AGAINST THE ARIANS. (C,G)*

[Col. 0639B]

In the miscellaneous Vatican Regius manuscript DLVII, pp. 6–7, there survive two parchment leaves written approximately in the eleventh century. On the first of them I discovered part of a sermon on the Creed against pagans and Arians, which the Maurist editors place among the spurious works attributed to Augustine, in the appendix to volume VIII, p. 11 ff. On the second leaf, copied in the same hand, I also read a fragment against the Arians. On considering it, I suspected that it belonged to those treatises of Augustine against the aforesaid heresy which we know to have been lost.

I certainly feel that I am speaking very rashly on this matter. For it may be either a known fragment of Augustine—though, owing to lack of time, I cannot investigate the matter more deeply—or the work of some other Father. Very many writings against the Arians survive, and I have read most of them; yet I do not now remember having read this particular passage in them, although I seem almost to recall having seen something somehow similar somewhere. But what prevents me from presenting this aforesaid leaf here to my readers after the Arian fragments? Whether it has been published elsewhere or not, it admirably defends Catholic truth.

Certainly Basil, *Oration against the Arians*, ed. Garnier, vol. II, p. 194, and Ambrose, *On the Sacrament of the Incarnation*, chs. 8–9, wisely propose and refute this very Arian objection concerning “begotten” and “unbegotten”; likewise Augustine, *On the Trinity* V.4, who introduces it thus: “Among the many things which the Arians habitually argue against the Catholic faith, this seems to be the most cunning device which they set before themselves [Col. 0639D] when they say,” etc. At the end of the leaf is written the quire-mark of the seventh quaternion; hence we know that this fragment is the remainder of some larger codex.

. . . . not taught in the words of human wisdom, but taught by the Spirit. Give back, therefore, heretic, what the Spirit taught; give it back, so that faith may not rest in human wisdom, and there will be no heresy. And, not to linger longer, let us come to those things which they are accustomed to set against us like an iron wall, saying: “Are unbegotten and begotten the same, or not?” By the dissimilar sound of the name, they seek to make it appear that the Father, the Son, and [Col. 0640B] the Holy Spirit are not of the same substance.

By the same method I too ask: if the name “begotten” differs from “unbegotten,” so that the substance may seem not to be the same, then whatever is called unbegotten will be of the same substance, if the name “begotten” differs from “unbegotten.” Therefore the Father is called unbegotten and unmade; the Son is called begotten and unmade. If, then, they differ in being unbegotten and begotten, they will be of the same substance in that both are called unmade.

What, then, is to be said of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is written that he is neither the Father nor the Son, nor something made? He will be unbegotten; but if unbegotten, he will be of the same substance as the world, or as those things which are from nothing. Yet the world, although made, is unbegotten: for it is not the Son, because it was made. Therefore it will be what the Father is, who is unbegotten. By this mode of reasoning, if the Holy Spirit too was made, he also, like the world, will be unbegotten.

But we have said that the Son is unmade, for he was not made; therefore whatever has not been made will be of the same substance. The Father was not made; the Holy Spirit was not made; the Son was not made: therefore the Holy Spirit and the Son will be of the same substance as the Father. The Father is unbegotten, the Holy Spirit is unbegotten, and the world is unbegotten—for they were not born—therefore they will be of the same substance as the Father. But the world was made, whereas the Father was not made, nor was the Son, nor the Holy Spirit; therefore the world alone will not be of the same substance as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Why, then, do we linger over names and over the wisdom [Col. 0640D] of human beings, which merely agree with one another, rather than over those things which Scripture has marked out, declaring that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are to be believed in? But if faith is to be put in names, then whatever sounds either “unbegotten” or “unmade” must necessarily be of the same [Note: The manuscript reads *esse*, “to be.”] substance as whatever is unbegotten or unmade. By this reasoning, whatever is called immortal, incorruptible, incorporeal, or unmade must seem to be of the same substance.

The world and the things in the world were made: are the things that were made—[Col. 0641A] heaven, earth, air, water—therefore of the same substance? If things made are not of the same substance because they were not born, then the unbegotten and the begotten, which were not made, will be of the same substance, because being born is one thing and being made another. Things made by the will of their maker subsist in diversity of substance; but things born, even from made things, always possess the reality of the same nature.

Consider the natures of trees, seeds, cattle, wild beasts, birds, and human beings; consider also their works: human dwellings, dens of wild beasts, nests of birds, chambers of bees, storehouses of ants, dens of spiders, and the hiding places of every kind. Consider in these things which I have named their works. Are they of similar [Note: The manuscript reads *similia*, “similar things.”] substance? The things which they either generate or that are generated are works far removed from the nature of their generators [Note: Thus the manuscript.]. Birth alone is an indication of the substance that generates itself.

Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Thrones, and Principalities were also made: are they called begotten because they were made? But if they are not called begotten because they were made, they will certainly be unbegotten; and if they are unbegotten, will they be of the same substance as the Father, who is unbegotten? Thrones, Powers, Principalities, Dominions, and Virtues are so called: will they be of the same substance merely because there seems to be diversity of names? [Col. 0642A] For diversity of names signifies rank, not their substance. For their being called Virtues, Dominions, Thrones, and Powers expresses honors, not an indication of what their substance is or what sort of substance it ought to be understood as.

Certainly all these are called incorporeal, incorruptible, immortal, and unbegotten; for they are not sons, because the only Son is he who has revealed the Father’s bosom [Note: Thus the manuscript.]. Finally, what does the Apostle say concerning angels? “For to which of the angels did the Lord ever say, ‘You are my Son’?” (Heb. 1:5). Thus, by denying that they are sons, he denied their birth, not their creation. So the Apostle says: “Whether Dominions, or Principalities, or Virtues, or Powers: all things were made through him” (Col. 1:16). He said that all things were made, but not that they were born.

Then, because they are called incorporeal, incorruptible, or immortal, is this a confession of what their substance is or of what sort it is? Is it not rather a denial of their passibility? For when we call something incorporeal, we deny body; we do not thereby affirm its substance. Or when we call something incorruptible and immortal, we state not what it is but what it does not suffer: for that which is called immortal or incorruptible does not suffer death or corruption. Hence, lest anyone, from so many and such great names, say either that all are of the same substance, or again compo . . . . . .

[Col. 0641]

## SUNDAY SERMONS IV [Note: From the same very ancient codex from which I took the epitomes of Paris and Augustine.]. (C,G)*

### SERMON I. FOR SEPTUAGESIMA

1. Stirred by today’s reading to run the course of the spiritual stadium, most beloved brothers, we must consider with anxious minds how we are to run and from what we must abstain. Literally, a stadium is called the fourth part of a mile. Hercules, it is said, first ran this distance in one breath. In former times, a pole was set at its finish, with a crown woven from flowers placed upon it. For the sake of winning this, a swift company of young men used to run there, so that whoever among them could run most quickly and arrive first might seize the prize—which we call a crown—and thus receive the praise of the king and spectators, and thereafter especially many gifts.

Many strove toward this with a common purpose, but all were defeated by one; he who was swifter in running seemed more worthy than the rest of the collection of rewards. And as greatly as the victor rejoiced, enriched with royal gifts, so greatly did the defeated grieve, not only deprived of gifts but also dishonored by the shame of their slowness. They abstained indeed from foods that hindered running, but not equally: the abstinence of the one who was swifter than the others in the race had been greater.

Do not be surprised, brothers, that the Apostle drew an example fit for imitation from pagan observance for the safeguarding of souls, lest any of you suppose that in no respect are the practices of the Gentiles to be followed, from whom the Christian religion, at Christ’s command, has made us strangers. First, then, let your charity understand that the Church has appropriated as sacred certain things from their custom, which are to be followed not carnally but spiritually. Among these is the very useful example set forth for us by today’s reading.

The finish of the stadium, which was fixed for their running, signifies the limit of this present life, given to us for the race of [Col. 0642D] our salvation, as the Lord says and exhorts: “Run, wretch, run; hasten while you have time, lest you fall into death.” They ran in order to win a temporal and perishable prize, that they might receive earthly gifts from a mortal king. Let us run better, to receive after the end of the flesh a spiritual and imperishable prize, that we may receive eternal and unfailing gifts from the King of kings, who is eternal and immortal, hearing his desired voice say: “Come, you who labor,” etc.

They abstained from rich foods so as to be made readier for running; let us abstain better, not so much from foods as from vices, that we may be swift in running. But the fact that one man from among the great multitude of youths won the prize while the others ran in vain is, as far as we are concerned, dearest brothers, greatly to be feared: namely, lest we all be defeated by one, though we have resolved to run for the crown. Therefore the Apostle exhorts: “So run that you may obtain it.” And how shall we obtain it, since we refuse to run? Or if we sometimes begin to run, alas, exhausted by the grossness of vices, we shamefully fail in the race!

For although the whole Church is divided into clerical and lay orders, no one among them runs for the crown of glory. Some are anxiously occupied by insatiable greed, some defiled by unbridled pleasure, and some swollen with the pride of worldly pomp. They not only refuse to run but do not even know how to open their eyes to seize the crown. Thus the Psalmist says: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless.” And the Prophet: “As the people, so the priest.” So blinded and cast down into a certain pit of forgetfulness have we become that, thinking nothing of the future, we suppose that beyond this life—in which we pursue our pleasures—there is no other.

Indeed, to say more, in their madness, while they feed covetous souls with sensual desires and rage like wolves against those subject to them, they say that they wish to possess another glory and renown. Such persons lose human nature and acquire the nature of four-footed beasts, as they irrationally and shamelessly devote themselves continually to the belly and to lust. For the Creator of all things set humankind over earthly creatures on this condition: that, using temporal things rightly, they might enjoy eternal things after death.

What, then, must be done, dearest brothers? We are all lost unless we are quickly raised up by divine mercy. This mercy itself calls us to run, saying: “Walk, lest darkness overtake you.” If, at its call, we wish to resume our course, it will be lawful not merely for one but for very many to attain the crown. And just as the same person did not always win every race, but one who was defeated at one time became a victor at another after renewing his strength, so let us, if we have hitherto been defeated, take care henceforth to be victors. For the way of running has been placed before our eyes; and the slower we have been, the swifter we can be, if we wish.

2. How can we remain sluggish and lazy, ceasing from the race, when we have not only the Apostle as an exhorter toward the crown, but even our Savior himself as an exhorter to receive the denarius? For he, the supreme householder, who planted the vineyard—that is, the holy Church—promises to give the denarius of heavenly reward to us who entered the vineyard to labor late, that is, at the end of the world. He makes us equal to the first laborers, who bore the burden and heat of the day from morning until evening.

You have heard him, in the true and fitting parable of the Gospel, inviting laborers to cultivate his vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, and, once their work was completed, giving an equal denarius to all. If you desire the meaning of the hours you have heard: learn that the morning was from Adam to Noah; the third hour, from Noah to Abraham; the sixth, from Abraham to Moses; the ninth, from Moses to the coming of our Lord and Savior; [Col. 0644A] and the eleventh was from the Lord’s coming until the end of the world. In this hour we, the last laborers, entered the vineyard. But because we are lazy and slow at work, we cannot be certain of the denarius.

Let us therefore strive to work more swiftly, that we may be secure concerning the denarius; and since today we are called by the supreme householder, let us not despise his call but strive to enter the vineyard to labor. For he established the present fast for this purpose: that we may strive during this season, by repentance and the mortification of the flesh, to wipe away the countless sins committed on other days of the year through delight in the flesh.

3. Moreover, this day, which is like the doorway of the fasts and withdraws from us the song of joy, that is, *alleluia*, expresses throughout the whole sequence of its office the voice of a penitent in lamentation. It teaches us that we must cease from immoderate joy and remain in weeping and tears of repentance. Therefore on this night we addressed *alleluia* itself, often repeating its name and desiring in some fashion to keep it as a guest, saying to it: “Remain with us today,” and so forth. We also bade it a final farewell, saying: “May a good angel accompany you, that you may return to us again with joy,” so that we may know that we shall not rejoice perfectly before we have been renewed by the body and blood of our Redeemer and received that song joyfully.

The antiphon of the Mass, commonly called the Introit, laments with penitents, saying: “The sorrows of death surrounded me, and in my tribulation.” The collect together with the response likewise sounds the affliction [Col. 0644C] of repentance. Finally, that chant which we have substituted for *alleluia*—called the *tract* because it has long chants—teaches penitents to cry out to God with deep groaning. And thus the remaining words of the office, arranged in order, seem to express not the joy of those rejoicing but the mourning and sorrow of sinners.

4. If you ask concerning the name of the day, which is called Septuagesima, know that it received its name not from the number of days—as those suppose who count so many days from it to the Paschal feast—but from the perfection of the number from which that number took its beginning. This number consists of ten multiplied seven times. The seven pertains to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, while the ten pertains to the Ten Commandments of the Law. They are joined to one another in such a way that neither can the gifts of the Holy Spirit be kept by anyone without the commandment of the Law, nor the commandments of the Law without the gift of the Holy Spirit; and whoever keeps one will undoubtedly have the other.

This number rightly suits penitents, so that, by especially keeping the Ten Commandments of the Law during this season, they may be able to recover the grace of the Holy Spirit which they lost by sinning. Alternatively, according to some, Septuagesima is called this literally because the Israelite people was held captive in Babylon for so many years; when it returned from there long afterwards, it consecrated to God a fast of the same number in commemoration of that liberation. But since this suits penitents both according to history and according to allegory, let us strive [Col. 0645A] in this season to bewail our sins, so that, after this life which revolves through seven days, our souls may be delivered from Babylon—that is, infernal captivity—and enriched with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and may joyfully receive from the King of kings both the unfading crown for their race and the denarius for the day’s labor in the vineyard. Amen.

### SERMON II. FOR LENT

1. Beloved, you who desire to cleanse your souls from sin, take care not to depart through any detour of baseness from this path of fasting and amendment which you have undertaken to keep. For, through the deceits of the ancient enemy, some of you have adopted on this day a custom which ought not merely to be avoided but despised. Because bodily food alone is not taken away from us today, you think that you may freely indulge every bodily pleasure and every shameful act; you have found in yourselves this pretext: that because it is permitted to eat meat, it is also permitted to use the pleasures of the flesh.

Such works belong not to Christians but to pagans. The pagans, also called Gentiles, observing the feast of their gods—that is, Jupiter, Saturn, Minerva, and Venus—after boundless gluttony in food and drink and shameful banquets, gathered outside the city at the theatre, which is also called a brothel. There they first exhausted themselves with games of various sorts, and finally with prostitutes who hid in the caverns of that theatre. To this filthy shamefulness, as Paulus Orosius recounts, the same devil whom they worshipped incited them, so that, to him to whom they offered sacrifice from animal victims, they might also offer sacrifice from the strength of their own bodies.

For the devil is defiled and unclean, and he demands a defiled and unclean sacrifice. Hence he is interpreted as *pelliceus*, “for the sake of skin,” because he delights greatly in lust, which is aroused by the beauty of skin. But as far as God’s service differs from the devil’s slavery, so far differs the life of those who are called Christians from Christ from that of those who, subject to the devil, serve him in all things.

Therefore, brothers, we must cease on this present day from this and every evil custom, because this day is not only the beginning of fasts but also of the ages. It must therefore be honored with great reverence and devotion, not defiled with lustful pleasures, because it appears consecrated above the rest both by its name and by its mystery. It is called the Lord’s Day because he placed it first in the order of days, and because, having overcome death—which he underwent for us unworthy persons—and conquered the enemy, from whose power he snatched us, he rose powerfully from the dead on it and appointed that we should observe it in honor of his resurrection.

How, then, do we wish to rise from the death of the soul if we refuse to honor the day of the Lord’s resurrection? And on what grounds do we suppose that we can cleanse our minds through fasts if we wish to enter polluted through the gate of fasting?

2. Perhaps some unbridled person, more obedient to bodily pleasures than to God’s laws, may answer me as I rebuke such conduct and censure my own sins together with the iniquities of others: “You preach that the natural union of male and female and the bond of love established from the beginning must be separated. You ask altogether impossible and useless things: that during some fast I should abstain from the woman who is my flesh as though from foods.”

To him I, although a sinner, will answer easily: God gave the good things of the world not that we might abuse them, but that we might use them rightly. Marriage, like the other riches of the world, is good when it is rightly maintained; when wrongly so maintained, it turns into sin. Hence Gregory says: “Whatever we receive for the use of life, we turn back to the use of vices.” Nor do I preach the separation of so sacred a fellowship; rather, I prescribe abstinence for the brief period of thirty-six days. [Note: It is well known that conjugal abstinence during Lent is strongly commended in the homilies of various Fathers and in several sacramentaries of ancient bishops, although the universal Church never strictly commanded it.]

For what profit is there in abstaining from meats while not laying aside carnal works? You who have lived throughout the year amid these and other delights must, at least in this small space of time, cease for God’s sake. Why, indeed, are you called *vir*, “man,” from the strength of the body, if you do not possess this strength in the mind, so that you cannot fast for God, who gave you all things and from whom you daily ask greater things, for a tenth part of the year?

3. For whoever looks closely finds no more than thirty-six days—the tithe of the year—in this abstinence. Since the complete year consists of three hundred sixty-six days, if three hundred thirty are subtracted, the remaining days, namely the number I have stated, are consecrated to fasting. Of the six days left over, which with their nights amount to one hundred fifty hours, a tenth part is fifteen hours. But because we cannot make up from these a whole day with the following night to add to the aforesaid number and devote to fasting, ecclesiastical usage has established that what is not rendered in that respect should be completed on the Sundays of the same season by fasting from meat and from carnal pleasures. For on these days, because they are consecrated in the very name of God, refreshment of food is granted and permission to sin is removed. What brings life and is better is given to us; what brings death and is worse is taken away.

If we do not defile these days with vices and carnal pollution, we shall indeed restore from them the full tithes of the whole year. But because to us, regenerated by the sacred font and tasting not the flesh of the figurative lamb but that of the true Lamb, the Lord himself said: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven,” Christian religion ordained that the fast should comprise not only these thirty-six days for the tithes of the year, but also the four beginning from the head of the fast, making forty days for the perfection of so great a mystery.

For this forty-day fast possesses great authority from the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. Moses the lawgiver fasted forty days in order to receive the Law. Likewise Elijah, greatest of the Prophets, who deserved to be borne into heaven in a fiery chariot, when he was persecuted by Jezebel, first fed with angelic food and afterwards abstained from all food for the same number of days. [Note: Something is missing at the close of the sermon, certainly including the example of Christ the Lord fasting forty days.]

### SERMON III. FOR PASSION SUNDAY

1. As the time of Lent now declines and the joys of the most sacred Resurrection draw near, the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, beloved brothers, annually confronts us and today strikes the universal Church with its tearful recital. Although many days still remain from this day until that which especially deserved to see its Creator crucified, the holy Fathers have directed that the same Passion be recited to us during the days that follow—especially blessed Gregory, who in all the ecclesiastical offices, namely the daily and nightly ones, introduces from this point until the Paschal feast both the words and the mourning of the Passion. He thereby teaches that we ought to weep for him, without whom we can possess no joy perfectly.

Therefore, whoever trusts that he or she is to be a member of our Redeemer should feel the grief and injury of so great a head. Hence the prophet says: “The whole head is sick and the whole heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it.” And the Apostle: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer together.” Since we know that Christ himself—our head and crown—is the higher and more honorable member that suffered, let us, the lower members, suffer with him, especially because he chose to suffer not for any fault of his own but for our redemption, that he might redeem us from the ancient slavery of the devil and make us perpetual inhabitants of the heavenly homeland, from which we were excluded as captives.

For he, ineffably merciful, chose to cleanse our sins and ancient iniquities not with gold or any kind of metal, or with garments of beautiful variety, nor even with sacrifices of other animals, but by offering his own body upon the altar of the cross to God the Father and pouring out his most precious blood. Hence the prophet says: “Surely he bore our sicknesses; he carried our infirmities.” And he himself, our mediator with the Father, said: “You did not require burnt offering and sin offering; then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’” And the sense is: “O God the Father, because I saw that you did not demand animal burnt offerings for the redemption of the human race, I immediately said, ‘Behold, I come, that I may be offered [Col. 0647D] for the salvation of my people.’”

Behold, dearest brothers, we have heard that Christ was sacrificed for us. Therefore we may both rejoice greatly and grieve: rejoice, because blessed is the fault that had so great and such a Redeemer; grieve, because we see no imitator of so great a Passion. Having died bodily, he demands a sacrifice from us not only of our bodily death, should it be necessary, but also of amendment of life and humiliation of spirit: namely, that our spirit, amazed and trembling at so great and ineffable a humility of its Creator, may overcome the enticements of the flesh and have a certain compassion with him who suffered.

[Col. 0648A] Hence: “A broken spirit is a sacrifice to God.” And although it is impossible for our bodily frailty to follow his immeasurable divinity, nevertheless we follow him well according to the measure of our humanity if we put to death the vices of the body through fasting, prayers, and vigils; if we rejoice to remain clean and pure before his eyes. Hence the prophet says: “Wash yourselves; be clean,” and the rest.

2. But how, when the persecutor’s rage threatens, shall we lay down our lives for him, for whose love we cannot even fast, for a short time at least, from vices and from every kind of food? In what respect, then, do we imitate his Passion, when we do not restrain our bodies from any defilements? Indeed, what is worse, vigorously resisting his commandments, we are opposed to him as though to an enemy. For when he cries out in the Old Testament [Col. 0648B]: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit theft,” and the other commandments of the Law, we—almost as though provoking his wrath against ourselves—madly and insanely commit adultery, kill, and steal; moreover, the more all vices are forbidden us, the more eagerly we seek and love to follow them. Likewise, when in the new Testament of the Gospel he threatens: “Everyone who says to his brother, *Racha*, and whoever says, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna,” we, on the contrary, touched by the zeal of envy, proudly and stubbornly heap every insulting reproach upon our brethren. Therefore we must restrain our minds from such things and from all like them, if we hope to be made participants in his redemption.

For he is the true priest and high priest of good things to come, who offered to God his Father not the blood of goats and bulls, but himself—[Col. 0648C] that is, the spotless lamb—cleansing our conscience from dead works, that is, from sins; and thereby entered once into the holy places, that he might now appear before the face of God the Father on our behalf. Other priests, after slaughtering the flesh of animals according to the custom of the old Law, entered the holy places once every year. But this priest forever, who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it, entered the holy places once—not every year, but in the last year of his life—having sacrificed himself upon the altar of the cross; that is, he entered heaven, in order to disclose the Father’s mysteries to servants who follow him by faith, mysteries which he will grant them to possess after the end. Other priests, when the time of sacrifice was completed, took care to return home, intending to return to the temple the following year. But he, having accomplished the mystery of his Passion and Resurrection, [Col. 0648D] returned to his own heavenly palace, to come again not in the following year but at the end of the age, so that by a righteous judgment he may examine the deserts of good and evil persons, rendering rewards to the good and punishments to the evil.

What shall we do on that day, brethren, when we must give an account not only of evil deeds, but also even of idle words? And if we shall suffer punishment for all the sins of the tongue, which we count as nothing, what must be feared concerning the other members—namely hands and feet and the rest—which we know without doubt have committed many unlawful acts? For if we pay the penalties for all the faults we have committed, [Col. 0649A] we are damned and lost eternally. Therefore, the more each one of us loves his own soul, the more he should erase past sins through repentance; let him beware of repeating them, and let him not rekindle what he has once extinguished through God’s grace. For whoever repeats the sin for which he has already groaned provokes God’s wrath against himself, so that, when called, he may not be heard. Hence he says through Solomon: “I called, and you refused; you despised all my counsel and neglected my reproofs. I too will laugh at your destruction and mock when that which you feared has come upon you.”

How dreadful is that voice, dearest brethren, by which our Redeemer threatens that he will laugh at our destruction! Therefore let us continually open the ears of our mind to his commandments, that in judgment we may see him not terrible but gracious. [Col. 0649B] And how shall we be able to endure him terrible and angry against us, when in this present life we can scarcely bear his lightning or thunder for fear? And if the movement of one creature terrifies us for a time, with what courage shall we be able to await the Creator coming with fire to judge, shaking not only the earth but also the heavens? For, as the Psalmist says: “Fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him.” And the Judge himself says through the prophet: “Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.” Fear greatly, brethren, the coming of that Judge, in whose determined judgment there will be no opportunity for redemption. Cease from depraved morals and from the evil habit of a shameful life, and strive to suffer with your Redeemer, [Col. 0649C] so that you may both rise with him from the tombs of vices and happily ascend after judgment to the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON PALM SUNDAY

1. Rejoicing, dearest brethren, in the delightfulness of the present day, you ought diligently to recognize the mysteries with which it shines, so that an instructed mind may inwardly examine whence arise the joyful delights which we celebrate outwardly. But lest an excess of words breed weariness in your minds—especially since the office of this day is prolonged in very lengthy chants and most delightful rejoicings concerning our God—I shall first endeavor briefly to set before you something concerning its name, which is distinguished by various titles.

For it is called the Day of Palms, [Col. 0649D] or of Flowers, and of Branches; also Hosanna; the Pascha of the Applicants or Competents; and the Day of Head-Washing. Although these are so named by popular custom, all nevertheless retain a certain fitting meaning. It is called the Day of Palms because on it our Lord, seated upon a little ass and about to suffer for the salvation of humankind, went to Jerusalem; and a very great multitude of joyful people met him with branches of palms and of various trees, crying: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” It is also called the Day of Flowers because holy mother Church, in commemoration of so great a joy, has wished on this day, above other annual observances, to carry flowers blessed and consecrated with chant, [Col. 0650A] so that she may joyfully go to meet her Redeemer. It is also called the Day of Branches because, for the same reason, not only palms but also green branches are today carried by the children of the Church.

It is called Hosanna because the Hebrew people, going before and following the Lord, seemed to sing to him: “Hosanna,” which in Latin is interpreted, “Save.” It is called the Pascha of the Applicants or Competents because on this day the Creed—that is, the confession of holy faith—was delivered to the catechumens who were preparing for baptism, so that those hastening to receive God’s grace in the Paschal solemnity might know the faith which they ought to profess. They are called *competentes*, as though “seeking together,” that is, seeking God’s grace. The common people call this day the Day of Head-Washing because on that day [Col. 0650B] it was customary to wash the heads of infants who were to be anointed on Holy Saturday, lest perhaps, made unclean by the observance of Lent, they should approach the anointing. This week, moreover, is called the Greater Week, either because greater sobriety is observed in it, or because a greater office than in other weeks is celebrated in it.

2. Let these brief remarks on the names of this day suffice. Some of them remain as they are understood literally; others signify something else allegorically. For throughout all Scripture, Old and New Testament alike, the palm always signifies victory. Thus, by palm branches is denoted that victory by which our Lord, through his death, destroyed our death and, by the trophy of the cross, overcame the devil, prince of death. By flowers is expressed the fragrance of virtue, [Col. 0650C] by which faithful souls, captured by it, accompany their king as he goes toward Jerusalem—that is, toward the holy Church—so that, celebrating with him Pascha, that is, the passage, they may deserve to rise with him to heavenly things.

By the branches of trees are signified the sayings of the ancient prophets. He who strews them in the way instructs the simple and less learned hearts of the brethren by examples, lest they stray from the path of truth. But the *hosanna* so often repeated and doubled by the people signifies the unity of faith by which we ought to live. For though among the faithful people there is diversity of rank, sex, and age, yet with one voice and one praise of confession we ought to cry out to our Savior, saying: “Hosanna,” that is, “Save,” or “Make safe.” It is a Hebrew word which, expressed in Latin, [Col. 0650D] means: “Save,” or “Make your people safe,” or “Make the whole world safe.”

3. Since, then, such names are assigned to this day from fitting significations of mysteries, it must be shown you, beloved, in however brief an account, by what works of our Savior it is made illustrious. For, as the holy Evangelist relates, six days before the old Passover—counted from yesterday—Jesus came to Bethany, to the house of Simon the leper, where he had raised Lazarus; and they made him supper there. Mary too, taking a pound of ointment, anointed the Lord’s feet and wiped them with her hair. When Judas the traitor was indignant at this, Jesus answered in praise of the woman: “She has done a good work upon me,” and the rest [Col. 0651A] which is related in the Passion concerning this matter.

Following the custom of that good work, the holy man Gregory, on this very day—that is, yesterday—devoted himself wholly to giving alms and washing the feet of the poor, so that what the most devout woman had done to the head, that is, to Christ, he might do to Christ’s members, that is, to the poor. Hence the same day, having no proper office, is entitled in the Sacramentary: “Saturday is free from the public station, when the lord pope gives alms.” If you wish to pluck the allegorical flower from this deed, know that the ointment signifies righteousness, and for that reason is said to have been measured by the pound. Whoever perfectly observes righteousness undoubtedly washes the Lord’s feet; whoever, by living well, loves mercy anoints his feet with ointment; and whoever [Col. 0651B] gives abundantly to the poor wipes the Lord’s feet with his hair. The house, therefore, was filled with the fragrance of the ointment—that is, the whole world—with the fame of that most devout woman and the virtue of faithful persons who imitate her in such things.

For the fact that the Son of God, who was to suffer, went to Bethany six days before Passover signifies that he was hastening, on the same sixth day, to redeem with his own blood the human being whom, created on the sixth day, he had lost through the serpent’s deceit, passing through Bethany—that is, through the house of obedience. Leaving the aforesaid city of Bethany on the following day, namely the fifth day before Passover, which is today, he sent his two disciples to Jerusalem, saying to them: “Go into the village opposite you, and you will find an ass and a colt; untie them and bring them to me.” Having untied them, they brought them to Jesus and laid [Col. 0651C] their garments upon them, and made him sit above them. When the crowd which had come for the feast heard that Jesus was going to Jerusalem, they took palm branches, came out to meet him, and cried: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

4. But because these deeds of the Lord, recalled in the Evangelist’s words, are sufficiently clear in their literal sense, since they occurred as they sound, their mystical meaning must briefly be disclosed to us, though it is hidden from all except the wise. The two disciples signify the two orders of preachers, [Col. 0652A] one among the circumcised and the other among the Gentiles; or Peter and Philip, whom Christ sent to Jerusalem—that is, to the holy Church. One of these, Philip, brought Samaria, as though an ass; the other, Peter, brought Cornelius from among the Gentiles, as though a colt, to faith in Christ.

Again, by the two animals are figured the two peoples, namely Jewish and Gentile. At the coming of the disciples they were bound, because each people was constrained by the chains of its sins. The Apostles’ garments are either the teachings of virtues or works of righteousness. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.” The very great crowd which spread its garments in the way signifies the innumerable multitude of martyrs, who, stripping themselves of their own garment, [Col. 0652B] make a way for the simpler, by which they may be able to attain the vision of peace.

For by the little ass upon which he sat are figured the simple hearts of the Gentiles, which remained as it were untamed, bound by no reins of discipline, proceeding toward dumb idols wherever they were led. The Lord, presiding over and governing it, led it to the vision of eternal peace. Finally, it is believed not to have been without the cause of a great sacrament that the Lord, specially proceeding toward Jerusalem on this day, employed the service of beasts of burden, and wished that the varied adornments of palms, branches, and flowers should be borne about him, and that he should be called king and Lord—all things which, though he had often previously come to Jerusalem, he had refused to have done. For this reason he entered with so great glory: because he knew that the time of his Passion was now at hand, he compelled the minds of the Jews to be stirred against him, so that through the death of his body he might destroy the death of our souls.

Therefore, thrice-blessed ones, we who commemorate his Passion, although we cannot all die for him, and, the calumniators of the Church having been pacified, have no war with them, should nevertheless take care to mortify the vices of our members, so that, receiving the joys of the Resurrection after the mourning of the Passion, we may be able to rise with him from vices to the heights of virtues. Amen.

[Col. 0651]

## EXPOSITION OF THE FAITH

> **Note:** [Col. 0651D] From an ancient Vatican manuscript, formerly from Bobbio, after the books of St Augustine *On the Trinity*. (C)*

[Col. 0651D] We profess that we believe in the indivisible and inseparable holy Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God, so one and three, and so three and one: the Trinity in distinct and discrete persons; that is, the Father, from whom are all things; the Son, through whom are all things; and the Holy Spirit, in whom are all things. Yet they are of one Godhead, one essence, and one substance, in three subsistences or persons: so that the Father may be Father, the Son Son, and the Holy Spirit Holy Spirit; while in one nature and one substance God is believed to be one, alone, and supreme.

We do not introduce three [Col. 0652D] natures, as Arius blasphemes, who proclaimed three gods: a more excellent, a lesser, and an inferior. Rather, we confess the holy Trinity in unity, and unity in the holy Trinity. For when we say “almighty Father,” the designation of this paternal name refers to the person of the Son. And when we say “eternal Son,” it refers to the person of the eternal Father. And when we name the Holy Spirit, we show that we believe him to be from the person of the eternal Father.

> **Note:** [Col. 0652D] Manuscript: “from the person of the eternal Father and believe.”

But when we say “God the almighty Father,” the mystery of this name cannot be emptied [Col. 0653A] of its meaning. For when we say “Father,” we show the Son; when we say “Son,” we declare the Father; and when we say “eternal Father,” we show the eternal Son. For if we cannot find the beginning of this paternal name—that is, when he began to be called Father—it consequently follows that neither shall we find a beginning of the Begotten One.

We ask that an explanation be given us: when did the Father receive this designation, so as to be called Father? If in time, or outside time, let someone tell us when he first began to be called so. If this can be proved, there will be no doubt that from that beginning of the paternal name the Son received his beginning, at which the Father was named. But if he fails—and indeed he does fail—and no beginning of the paternal name can be proved or given, as to when he began to be Father, then let him confess to us the holy [Col. 0653B] Trinity to be coessential and consubstantial: neither the Father before the Son, nor the Son after the Father, nor the Holy Spirit inferior. For, since the beginning of the paternal name cannot be found, we do not know on what ground a beginning can be ascribed to the Son; because when we call God the Father everlasting, we show the Son of God to be everlasting. [Col. 0654A]

Therefore we profess the holy Trinity in one nature and one essence and substance, in three subsistences or persons. We believe that the very Word of God—that is, the Son of the Father—begotten without beginning, the same eternal Son, one of the three subsistences of the holy Trinity, descended through the dispensation made for us and for our salvation, the incarnate Word of God, and became human. Entering the Virgin’s womb, he assumed to himself the power of our nature from the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God: perfect God and perfect human, in two natures, namely divinity and humanity; likewise consubstantial with us according to his humanity. He is not divided into two sons, but is one and the same Son of God and of humankind, in the reality of two natures, with [Col. 0654B] the union of divinity and humanity accomplished in one subsistence or person. Thus, from two perfect natures, not two sons but one Son, the same Son of God and of humankind—remaining what he was—began to be what he was not, when the Son of the eternal Father, without beginning, became the son of a human being. Therefore there is also one Lord.

[Col. 0653]

## COMPENDIUM OF THE FAITH AGAINST THE ARIAN HERETICS, IN WHICH THE EQUALITY OF THE THREE DIVINE PERSONS IS CLEARLY PROVED BY VERY MANY PASSAGES AND ARGUMENTS FROM HOLY SCRIPTURE. BY AN UNKNOWN, BUT VERY ANCIENT, AUTHOR. (C, G)*
[Col. 0653C] The chief cause that makes heretics err is that they either do not know, or refuse to observe, that in the Lord Jesus Christ, just as there is one person, so there are two substances: God from God the Father, and man from a human mother. And the things which the Lord himself says of himself according to the dispensation of the flesh assumed are attributed by them to his divinity—for example: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); or: “Jesus, wearied from the journey” (John 4:6); or: “He wept for Lazarus” (John 11:35); and other such passages that are read.

If they wished to consider the Apostle’s statement, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19), or the Gospel’s statement, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), they would not hesitate, as was said above, to confess that there are two substances in one person. Thus, when they hear it said, [Col. 0653D] “The Father is greater than I,” they would understand it according to the humanity; but when they hear, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), they would not doubt that it was said according to the divinity, as may be understood from his works.

For according to his humanity he hungered, in order to show that he possessed true flesh; but according to his divinity he satisfied five thousand people from five loaves, in order to prove himself God by his mighty works. According to his humanity he thirsted, but according to his divinity he refreshed the Samaritan woman with living water. According to his humanity he entered a boat, but according to his divinity he walked over the sea with dry feet. According to his humanity he slept in the boat; according to his divinity he commanded the winds and waves. According to his humanity he wept for Lazarus; according to his divinity he raised him dead from the tomb after four days. [Col. 0654C] According to his humanity he hung upon the cross; according to his divinity he granted Paradise from the cross to the thief. According to his humanity he suffered and tasted death; according to his divinity he raised himself from the dead.

If they wished wisely to distinguish these things and others like them, and to attribute to each substance what belongs to it, they could easily keep the course of right faith. They would not heap insults upon his divinity because of the benefits which he undertook or suffered for our redemption in the form of a servant; and wherever they read in the Scriptures something in which the divinity seems to speak in a lesser way according to the humanity, they would understand that the humanity declares this on account of the dispensation of the flesh assumed. For we, just as we read that he is God, nowhere read that he is either a greater or a lesser God; nor ought we to believe this with a devout mind.

But he still persists and says: “It cannot be otherwise than that the Son should be believed lesser than the Father, because he is known to be from the Father.” Human generation misleads him, so that, because he is called Son, he is believed lesser than the Father. Among men a father begets a son who is lesser because he himself was begotten lesser by a father. Accordingly, as the son grows, the father grows old; when the father dies, the son is shown to succeed him; and the son sometimes becomes better and more powerful than his father. But with God it is not so. For where divinity has neither growth nor old age, it is fitting that love should have an equal Son, because fullness cannot have one greater than itself. Therefore the Perfect One begot the perfect, the Almighty the almighty, the full the full. And because he had no increase of age, [Col. 0655A] he could not beget one lesser. Rather, I know that the Son is altogether such as the Father is, as he himself says: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9); and elsewhere: “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John 5:23).

But perhaps, because you hear that he was sent, you therefore think him lesser. I ask you: do you believe the Son to be God, or not? Without doubt you will answer, “God”; for even if you wished to deny it, you would be convicted by the holy Scriptures, with the Apostle saying: “From whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9:5). And John says in his Epistle: “That we may be in his true Son, who is true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). And Thomas says: “My God and my Lord” (John 20:28). And Melchizedek, [Col. 0655B] the high priest, says: “Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, who created heaven and earth” (Gen. 14:19).

You see that Melchizedek’s words establish not merely that he is God, but that he is God Most High. The prophet Hosea also bears witness, saying: “I, the Lord your God, establish heaven and create earth; my hands created all the host of heaven” (Isa. 41:18; 42:5). If, therefore, the Son is God—indeed, because he is God, because all things were made through him, and because he is not merely not lesser but is God Most High—I ask you whether God is everywhere, or perhaps confined to a place. Since it is impious to deny that God is everywhere, I ask: where was he sent? Understand the sending of the Son, however, as his incarnation, as the Apostle himself explains: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4).

Finally, concerning him [Col. 0655C] we read in the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord” (Jer. 23:24). And the Evangelist says of the same: “Of his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). If he himself fills all things, where was he sent, whose majesty fills all things? Yet perhaps you still say, according to a carnal understanding, that between the Father who begets and the Son who is begotten there could not but have been some interval. An interval makes an hour; hours indicate time. Thus, if you place time before the Son, you do not confess that all things were made through him. And where is that saying: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3)?

Certainly I answer according to your proposition, you who say that the Father was at some time without the Son. We read together in the Apostle that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), and the Lord himself says of himself: “I [Col. 0655D] am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). If, then, as you say, the Father was without the Son, he was without power, without wisdom, without life, and without truth. But because the Father must be believed never to have been without these, it accords with your salvation that, according to the Catholic faith, you confess the Son coeternal and equal with the Father. For his power is also read to be eternal, the Apostle saying: “His eternal power also, and divinity” (Rom. 1:20). Likewise concerning truth the Psalmist says: “The truth of the Lord remains for ever” (Ps. 116:1).

They also commonly raise these matters as if they were an objection, generating accusation: “The Father is so much greater that he is always named first.” Even if he were always named first, this would seem wholly fitting, because the Son is from him, not he from the Son. Yet, that you may recognize equality, hear from the Scriptures where the Son too is named first. John the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:2). By “the Word” he plainly indicated the Son. And the Apostle writes to the Ephesians: “Do you not know that every fornicator and unclean person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God?” (Eph. 5:5). Behold, here too the Son is named first. And to the Galatians: “Paul, an Apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Gal. 1:1). And to the Thessalonians: “But our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God and our Father, who loved us” (2 Thess. 2:15). To the Corinthians: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all [Col. 0656B] of you” (2 Cor. 13:13).

And the Lord himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He does not say, “The Father and I.” And elsewhere: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). And again: “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John 5:23). See how often the Son is named first. But because there is equality in Father and Son, whether one is named before or after cannot produce any disadvantage for the other; for there is no difference where divinity is equal in both. We read it this way because human speech cannot otherwise express itself: when it has named one, it must name the other thus.

See, therefore, that you may recognize that there is nothing greater or lesser there: let the objection concerning the Father’s being named first cease.
