For where there is one substance, one divinity, and incorporeal immensity, no inequality or difference should be thought to exist. For where one God is believed, lesser and greater are excluded. Unity does not know number, and equality admits no rank, as it is written: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar” (Exod. 20:26). Therefore let him put away contention and, with the Catholic faith, hold the inseparable Trinity: united without confusion, distinct without separation; because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one full God.

Reason itself teaches that one admits neither one later nor one earlier. He who is alone knows neither comparison nor separation. He who is full cannot be lesser: nothing can be added to perfection or taken from it. Therefore let three persons be believed, but not three substances; three properties, but not three powers. Thus there is one eternity without beginning, just as there is one majesty without end: the Father without an author, the Son without time, the Holy Spirit without one greater than himself.

[Col. 0656D] For we Catholics say that our Lord God Jesus Christ is both lesser than the Father and equal to him: lesser on account of the humanity assumed, because, though he was in the form of God, he deigned to put on the form of a servant; equal on account of the everlasting divinity by which, existing as Son from the Father, he is also coeternal with the Father. Why, then, do they not confess him equal with us, when we do not deny with them that he is lesser? Especially since we read both in the holy Scriptures. For the Evangelist says: “For this reason the Jews sought to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

[Col. 0657A] Behold, the impiety of the Jews says “equal,” while the Christian is not ashamed to say “lesser.” Elsewhere the same Evangelist says: “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (ibid. 23). Equal honor is given only to equals. And in another place he says: “As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (ibid. 21). Hear him saying, “As the Father, so the Son.” Hear him saying, “Whom he wills,” and recognize that he is equal to the Father and possesses authority of his own. Do not call God lesser, because nowhere in the holy Scriptures do we read of either a greater God or a lesser God.

As he himself says to Philip: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). And: “All things whatsoever the Father does, these the Son likewise does” (John 5:19). Or: “The Word was God” (John 1:1). And the Apostle, as we have recalled: “Who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9:5). And the Apostle: “Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. 2:6). Why? Because no one seizes except what he does not possess. Therefore he who possessed equality did not deem it to be by robbery. But what the rebellious angel wished to assume by seizure, Christ possessed by nature.

And that he is true God, hear blessed John saying in his Epistle: “That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ: this is true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). You hear “true God,” and yet dare to call him lesser and do not confess him equal? The blessed Apostle also says to Titus: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” (Titus 2:13). [Col. 0657C] I do not know with what face one can call lesser him whom the Apostle professes to be great God.

This faithless error also commonly says that where we read in the Scriptures either “God alone,” or “the Most High alone,” or “wise alone,” this is not said of the Trinity but should be understood of the Father alone. How absurd it is to think so may be demonstrated from this one testimony. For the Apostle says: “Made known to God alone wise” (Rom. 16:26). They do not understand that he did not say, “To the Father alone wise,” but “To God alone wise,” which is the Trinity. For while they attribute this to the Father alone, they blaspheme the Son as unwise. And how does the Apostle call him the wisdom of God, if the Father alone is wise, when no one can be wise except through his own wisdom? And where is the statement which the same Apostle makes concerning Christ Jesus to the Colossians: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 1:3)?

Thus let them recognize how foolish is what they put forth; and wherever they read something similar, let them not attribute it to one person but to the blessed Trinity, which alone is the highest and true God. For the Apostle also says of the Holy Spirit: “To one indeed is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, and to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:8). If, therefore, as is true, both the word of wisdom and of knowledge are bestowed through the Holy Spirit, how can it be ascribed to the person of the Father alone that he alone is wise, unless, as has been said, these things belong to the coeternal Trinity?

[Col. 0658A] They also commonly say that the Son is lesser because he is visible, while the Father is invisible. They do not understand that the Son too is not visible in the substance of his divinity, except in the man whom he assumed, who is also called Christ. For the Son of God—that is, the Word, who in the beginning was God with God, through whom all things were made—could not be seen in his own substance, just as neither could the Father in his substance.

But I ask, without offense to him who says that the Son of God was seen, whether he confesses his own soul to be visible or invisible. When he has said “invisible,” as is true, let it be said to him: if a creature—that is, your soul—is invisible, though assuredly it is a creature of God, how could the Creator of the universe be visible? But he put on flesh that could be seen because divinity could not be seen by man.

In respect of this flesh the Father is greater; he is equal in respect of the Word, greater in respect of the flesh: equal to him through whom he made us, greater than him who was made for our sake. Although the many testimonies set out above clearly teach that the Son is God, I have nevertheless judged that a few more should be added.

It is written in Genesis: “God created heaven” (Gen. 1:1), and the Evangelist surely confirms that all things were created by the Son (John 1:3). Again there follows: “God created man in his own image and likeness” (Gen. 1:27). Behold, recognize God here, because he himself created man. And Isaiah says concerning John, the forerunner of the Lord: “Make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40:3). Of which God, unless surely of the Son, whom we do not doubt came in the flesh? And shortly afterward: “Strengthen the feeble hands, and make firm the weak knees. [Col. 0658C] Say to the fainthearted: Behold, your God will come in strength, and he will save you; and then the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isa. 35:3). We know that this was fulfilled at the coming of Christ.

The Psalmist also says: “All the nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you; you are wonderful and work wonders; you alone are God” (Ps. 85:9). I do not think anyone is so impious as to deny that the Son of God both worked wonders and created all nations—unless perhaps the Jews. And elsewhere Isaiah, when he announces Christ’s coming through a virgin, says among other things: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God” (Isa. 9:6).

The blessed Apostle also says: “For we must all be made manifest before the judgment-seat of Christ” (2 Cor. 5:10). And that you may recognize Christ as God, he says elsewhere: “We shall all [Col. 0658D] stand before the judgment-seat of God” (Rom. 14:10). “As I live,” says the Lord, “every knee shall bow to me.” He plainly speaks of Christ, whom we believe will come to judge the living and the dead.

The Psalmist, speaking in the voices of the angels when Christ had ascended into heaven, says: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:7). When they ask who this King of glory is, he answers: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord of hosts: he is the King of glory” (ibid. 8, 10). And lest they perhaps think this said of the Father, as they understand many things absurdly, let them hear the Apostle agreeing with this verse: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

[Col. 0659A] Since both these present and the foregoing testimonies, drawn from the holy Scriptures, demonstrate that the Son is God, I wonder why some are not afraid, perhaps, to blaspheme him by calling him lesser. For nowhere at all do we read that God is lesser, except, as was said, on account of the dispensation of the flesh assumed, in which he was not only made lower than angels, but is even found younger than his mother, as we have already said.

Accordingly, by this rule believe that there are two substances in Christ: true God and true man. According to the humanity he is subject to death; according to the divinity he is known as the author of life, as blessed Peter says: “You asked that a murderer be granted to you, but you killed the author of life” (Acts 3:14). According to the humanity: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38); [Col. 0659B] according to the divinity: “I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again; and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself” (John 10:18).

They also commonly take occasion for accusation from the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “The Son cannot do anything else except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). A carnal mind, not understanding this, thinks it said in order to show that he is from the Father, being both God and Son, in the way things commonly occur among men: for example, an artisan father teaches his craft to his son, so that the son may especially imitate what he sees his father working.

How absurd it is to believe this of God the almighty Father, who is incorporeal, invisible, inestimable, and immense, can plainly be recognized by one who has sound eyes of the heart. For those who think this way must be asked: by whom was this world that we see made? Certainly they will not deny that it was made by the Son, since the Evangelist testifies and says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). Let them say, then, where the Son saw the Father first making another world, so that he might afterward create this one in the same way—especially since, in God’s power, to have willed is to have created, as we read: “He speaks, and they are made” (Ps. 32:9).

But, with the veil removed from their heart, let them learn to believe that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. For the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is everywhere whole and present and can nowhere be without itself, as he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). Let them recognize what the Son’s “seeing” is: there is one substance, one will, one power, one glory. [Col. 0659D] Let nothing there be believed greater or lesser.

For if we earthly human beings accomplish through bodily action, wisdom putting into effect, what we wish to do after the intention of deliberation has first been set forth in our mind—if, in a manner of speaking, with the counsel born in our mind we first perform inwardly in the heart what we intend to do, while nevertheless one mind accomplishes this inseparably and without any division of its faculties—how much more does God the Father, with God the Son, who is his wisdom and remains in him, since, as we have often said, he himself is the Father’s wisdom and power, accomplish all things in one will and one operation?

Nor does the Father do some things and the Son others; rather, the Son does the very things that the Father does, as he himself testifies: “Whatever the Father does, these same things the Son likewise [Col. 0660A] does” (John 5:19). But he said, “The Son cannot do anything of himself except what he sees the Father doing” (ibid.), so that we might recognize and believe that the Son is from the Father and not from himself or from elsewhere, but is coeternal with the Father. For the Father always exists perfect in himself; nothing was ever lacking to him or added to him.

For if, as the Arians blaspheme, the Father was at some time without the Son, then the Father was imperfect; then he was without the Word; and, as we have already noted, without wisdom, power, life, righteousness, and truth. For all these forms of divinity are known from the Scriptures to be the Son. But because it is blasphemous to say that the Father was ever without these powers, this is right and fitting: that you confess the Son coeternal and coequal with the Father.

If God, when he speaks in our hearts, speaks wonderfully without sound, do you suppose how he can speak to his Son, who is his Word? Think therefore that he spoke to the Son incorporeally, because he also begot the Son incorporeally. Nor did he teach him as though he had begotten him untaught. Rather, to have taught him is to have begotten him learned and knowing. And “The Father taught me” (John 8:28) means: “The Father begot me knowing.”

But how can the Son, concerning whom the Prophet testifies and says, “God in heaven above, and on earth, did all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113:11), be unable to do anything of himself? Perhaps you will say this was said of the Father. Return to the Evangelist, who says of the Son that all things were made through him and without him nothing was made [Col. 0660C] (John 1:3). He also speaks to Moses: “Go, tell the children of Israel: the God of your fathers sent me to you” (Exod. 3:12). When Moses answered, saying, “Tell me your name, for they will not believe me,” God afterward said to him: “Go, say to the children of Israel: I am who I am, and he who is has sent me to you” (ibid. 14).

And lest you understand this as said of the Father, hear the blessed Apostle agreeing with this passage and, as it were, explaining the testimony itself to the Corinthians: “The Son of God, who was preached among you by me, Silvanus, and Timothy, was not ‘yes and no’; rather, in him was ‘yes.’ For however many promises of God there are, in him is ‘yes’” (2 Cor. 1:19). Hear Paul agreeing with Moses, and do not disagree with the Catholic faith.

For if you ask the Catholic Church what the Father is, it says “God”; but it also says that the Son is God, and that the Holy Spirit is God. Yet it does not say “three gods,” lest it be likened to the nations who, deceived by their error, invent many gods. But let us believe Scripture, both New and Old Testament, when it says that God is one. If one is greater and another lesser, as the Arians say, they cannot be called one: inequality excludes unity.

But observe how we are to believe three and one. Equality of powers makes unity; the distinct property of persons makes Trinity. You have heard how he himself taught his equality with the Father to be understood: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). “One” is different from “are.” For when he says “are,” he signifies persons. [Col. 0661A] “We are one,” that is, we are one justice, the same wisdom, undivided power, equal glory. Since this is so, let dissension be removed and the faith kept whole.

They also say: “The Father is greater because he is immortal.” They must be asked whether they confess the Son, in the substance of his divinity, to be mortal. If they say so, every person can recognize how contrary to reason they speak, since no one doubts even the human soul to be immortal. Rather, it must be said to them that he is said to have suffered and died according to the flesh. For according to the divinity by which he has always existed and created all things, he remains immortal.

They also call him visible. Let those who say this recognize how absurd it is, since even the human soul cannot be visible—how much less God in his own substance? But he assumed flesh which could be seen because divinity could not be perceived by bodily eyes.

Let these remarks for the present suffice concerning the equality of the Father and Son. Later, if the Lord grants it, we shall demonstrate from the holy Scriptures the equality of the works of the Trinity—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Now, however, a few testimonies from among many must be set forth concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, whom heretics are said not only to assert to be lesser, but even wholly to deny to be God.

Hear a few testimonies concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit. In Genesis the divine word says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2): this denotes the eminence of power, not the poverty of necessity. And in the Gospel: “God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). And lest you perhaps understand this as said of [Col. 0661C] the Father and not of the Holy Spirit, hear what follows: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8). Hear “where he wills,” so that you do not doubt that he possesses authority of his own.

And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:4). That you may recognize the Spirit himself to be called Lord and God, hear how he concludes below: “To one indeed is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit” (ibid. 8), and the rest. Thus he concludes: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (ibid. 11). He who dispenses divine gifts as he wills knows no law of one above him.

Recognize at last that he who distributes as he wills is proved subject to no one, but is known to possess authority of his own. For will proceeds from supreme authority, against which no authority contends. Similarly, in Hebrews he speaks of distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will. And who this distributor and divider is, he plainly shows in Romans, saying: “To each one as God has apportioned the measure of faith” (Rom. 12:3).

And to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:16–17). And who is this God whose temple he forbids to be violated? Hear in what follows: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy [Col. 0662A] Spirit?” (2 Cor. 6:19). And who this Holy Spirit is, whose temple we are, he shows in concluding thus: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (ibid. 20). Recognize plainly that the Holy Spirit is God, and cease blaspheming.

In the Acts of the Apostles, blessed Peter says to Ananias, who had vowed an offering to God and afterward proved faithless concerning it: “Who compelled you to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men but to God” (Acts 5:3). Here too blessed Peter’s testimony most plainly shows him to be God. Again, in the same book: “The Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them” (Acts 13:2). And blessed Paul says there: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you Apostles to govern the Church of God, which he acquired by his own blood” (Acts 20:28).

And who it is that sets apart and sends Apostles, the same Paul declares to the Corinthians, saying: “God has appointed some in the Church, first Apostles, second Prophets, third Teachers” (1 Cor. 12:28), and the rest. Behold how he showed more clearly than light that the Holy Spirit is God: the one whom he calls Holy Spirit in the Acts of the Apostles, he openly confesses to be God in Corinthians.

The same chosen vessel says to the Jews: “The Holy Spirit rightly prophesied concerning you through the mouth of Isaiah the Prophet” (Acts 28:25). And blessed David states who this Holy Spirit is, who spoke in the Prophets: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9). And in Acts: “That the Scripture might be fulfilled which God had spoken beforehand through the mouth of his prophets” [Col. 0662C] (Acts 3:18). Here again recognize that he plainly declares to be God the one who spoke through the mouth of the prophets, just as Zechariah says in the Gospel: “Blessed be the God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people” (Luke 1:68); and shortly afterward: “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets” (ibid. 70).

You recognize the Holy Spirit to be the Lord God who spoke through the mouth of the prophets, a fact which even impious Jews do not deny. If he were not God, he would not be joined with Father and Son in one name of divinity in baptism, as it is written where the Lord himself established the rule of baptism: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). This testimony alone ought to suffice for heretics concerning the faith of the inseparable Trinity, because they themselves do not dare to baptize otherwise, lest they seem to corrupt the Lord’s rule. And where one name is spoken, greater and lesser are excluded.

And in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (1 Cor. 13:13). That you may recognize the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to have one substance and divinity, hear Isaiah the prophet say: “Who measured the mass of the earth with three fingers?” (Isa. 40:12). For in Scripture we find the Holy Spirit called, in the singular, “the finger,” as in the Gospel where he says: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:[Col. 0663A] 20), which another Evangelist explains, saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28). And Pharaoh’s magicians, overcome by divine signs, say: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8:19).

At Pentecost, which the Jews also celebrated before Christ’s coming, Moses received tablets inscribed by the finger of God, that is, by the Spirit. What was then prefigured in tablets of stone—the most hardened hearts of the Jews—he deigned after the Lord’s Ascension visibly to appear in tablets of flesh, that is, in the disciples’ hearts, in the very form of fire in which he appeared to Moses in the wilderness. Concerning him we believe Isaiah says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29).

And since, as we read, no one knows human thoughts except God, how is the Holy Spirit not God, who is known to know not only what is in man, but also what is in God? For the Apostle says: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2:10); and shortly afterward: “Thus no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (ibid. 11).

But perhaps someone says that he is lesser because he is read to have been sent. What then will he say when he reads in Isaiah the prophet Christ speaking in his own person: “The Lord sent me and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:16)? And elsewhere: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me to proclaim remission to the poor and sight to the blind, to announce the acceptable year of the Lord” (Isa. 61:1), and the rest. And that you may know it is plainly said of the Lord, the Evangelist says: when the Lord Jesus came into the synagogue, the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him, and opening it he found written: “The Spirit [Col. 0663C] of the Lord is upon me” (Luke 4:17), and the rest we mentioned above. After this, he says, “He closed the book, gave it to the attendant, and said: Today this Scripture has been fulfilled among you” (ibid. 20).

Should one who is known to be everywhere be believed to be sent? As the Psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 138:7). But just as the Son’s sending signifies his incarnation, so the Spirit’s sending is declared when he deigned to make himself known in the form of a dove, or in fire, or through diverse such assumed signs.

How, then, is he to be believed lesser, who is proved also to have sent God—who, like himself, is equal to the Father—for our forgiveness? And not only to have sent him, as we have recalled was said through Isaiah, but also to have created him according to the flesh, as you have in the Gospel when the angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35), and the rest. For Christ was conceived not by generation but by the command and blessing of the Holy Spirit, as another Evangelist says: “She was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:18; OCR reads 1:28).

But the Prophets frequently say, as we have already noted, “Thus says the Lord.” And Micah the prophet plainly shows who this Lord is when he speaks to Ahab: “If you return safe from the battle, God has not spoken in me” (3 Kings 22:28). And the Apostle Paul demonstrates who this God is, who spoke in the Prophets, when he says to the Jews: “The Holy Spirit rightly prophesied concerning you through the mouth [Col. 0664A] of Isaiah the prophet” (Acts 28:25): “Go, blind the heart of this people” (Isa. 6:10), and the rest.

Yet heretics should be asked whose offense is greater: that of one who sins against the Father, or that of one who sins against the Holy Spirit, whom they say is not God. When they say that the offense is greater for one who sins against the Father, they should again be asked whether the children of Israel sinned against the Father or against another. When they answer that they sinned against the Father, they should again be asked whether their sins were forgiven them. They will certainly not deny it, since we read that they were converted to God and their sins were forgiven.

Then they should be asked to explain how they understand the Lord’s saying: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32). If he is not God, why does the Lord say that offense against him is so grave? Again they should be asked whether the children of Israel were rebellious against God or not. Since they will not deny it—for they cannot—it must be said to them how they understand what blessed Stephen reproaches the Jews with, saying: “You have always resisted the Holy Spirit and have always been rebellious against him.”
likewise as your fathers did” (Acts 7:51). Hear also in the Epistle to the Thessalonians, where he puts the Holy Spirit first and calls him Lord, saying: “May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and the patience of Christ” (2 Thess. 3:5). Observe carefully that here the Holy Spirit is prayed to, that he may direct the hearts of believers into the love of God and the patience of Christ.

They must also be asked which is greater: heaven [Col. 0664C] or the powers of heaven? And when they undoubtedly say, “the powers of heaven,” they must be told: The Holy Spirit is not in the least inferior, but is supreme, since the heavens are said to have been created by the word of the Lord, and the powers of heaven by the Holy Spirit. Receive further evidence that the Holy Spirit is explicitly described as Creator. Job says: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4). In a single verse he certainly shows the divine Creator: by calling him divine, he shows him to be both God and Creator. So too David says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created; and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:30).

They must further be asked whether a creature can be everywhere or not. When they answer that it cannot be everywhere—as indeed is true—they must be told without doubt that the Holy Spirit is God and not a creature, since he is described as being everywhere [Col. 0664D]. Concerning him, as has already been said, the Prophet, in awe of his omnipotence, says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 138:7). Recognize, therefore, that there is no place where the presence of the Holy Spirit’s omnipotence is not proved.

Again, they must be asked whether anyone besides God can forgive sins. When they answer that none can do so except God—for it is written, “No one can forgive sins except God alone” (Luke 5:26)—they must be told that beyond doubt the Holy Spirit is God, since he is recognized as granting forgiveness of sins. As the Lord said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20:22). In baptism also, together with the Father and the Son, he grants those baptized forgiveness [Col. 0665A] of sins.

Hear also that the Holy Spirit is God, since he is frequently joined with the Father and the Son. To the Corinthians, as has already been said: “The grace,” he says, “of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Cor. 13:13). If he were not God but a creature, as the heretic blasphemously claims, he would never be joined with the Father and the Son in baptism, where the salvation of the human race is accomplished.

For Isaiah the prophet says that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance, as we have already recalled: “Who has measured the mass of the earth with three fingers?” (Isa. 40:12). In this passage he indicates, by the three fingers, that there is one substance in three persons. The Apostle, understanding this to be said of the Trinity, says: “For all things are from him, and through him, and in him” (Rom. 11:36); that is, all things are contained through the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Again, the same Apostle says to the Corinthians: “God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, who has shone in our hearts unto the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 4:6). In this passage the Trinity is understood most clearly. In “God, who said that light should shine out of darkness,” the Holy Spirit is recognized; where he says, “unto the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God,” the Father is understood; while where he says, “in the face of Jesus Christ,” the Son is designated.

Hear further that the Trinity remains in unity and unity in the Trinity, as the voices of angels and archangels declare in Isaiah, where the Seraphim are written to sing the hymn: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isa. 6:3). They did not conclude by saying three holy ones, but “holy” three times, saying, “Lord God of Sabaoth”: that is, that you may understand three persons and one God. They do not say it once, lest you believe in singularity; nor twice, lest you exclude the Holy Spirit; nor “holy are the Lords of Sabaoth,” lest you confess three gods in the manner of the Gentiles. But they say, “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” and there is the Trinity. God is praised, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

That he too is God, one who has sound eyes of the heart can readily prove from the equality of their operations, as we shall demonstrate in what follows. As the Father saves, so also does the Son, and so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “Save us, our God, and gather us from among the nations” (Ps. 105:47). Of the Son: “The Son of Man came to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10) [Col. 0665D]; and elsewhere: “For he himself shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:25). Of the Holy Spirit, to Titus: “He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).

As the Father strengthens, so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Esther says of the Father: “Strengthen me, O King and God of gods” (Esther 14:12). Of the Son, the Apostle says: “I give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ, who strengthened me and judged me faithful” (1 Tim. 1:12). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Gospel: “But the child grew and was strengthened by the Holy Spirit” (Luke 1:80).

The Father gives life; so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Epistle of the Apostle Peter [Col. 0666A]: “Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit” (1 Pet. 3:18). And the Apostle Paul says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). And in the Gospel: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64).

As the Father delivers, so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “God Most High, their deliverer” (Ps. 77:3, 5). Of the Son, in the Gospel: “If he sets you free, you shall truly be free,” and, “the truth shall set you free” (John 8:36, 32). Of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8:2).

The Father chooses; so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, the Apostle says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:3). Of the Son: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). Of the Holy Spirit, in Acts [Col. 0666B]: “When they had fasted and prayed, the Holy Spirit said to them: Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have chosen them” (Acts 13:2).

The Father is called Creator; so is the Son, and so is the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, the Apostle says: “What is the dispensation of the mystery hidden in God, who created all things” (Eph. 3:9). Of the Son, to the Colossians: “For all things were created by him, and all things subsist in him” (Col. 1:17); and in the Gospel: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: “He saw, numbered, and measured all things; he created them through the Holy Spirit” (Ecclus. 1:9); and in the Psalm: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created” (Ps. 103:30); and elsewhere: “By the Spirit of his mouth is all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

As the Father foretold, so did the Son, and so did the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “But God, who foretold that his Christ would suffer, fulfilled it” (Acts 3:18). So of the Son, in the Gospel the angel said to the women: “Go and announce to the brethren that he goes before you into Galilee; there you shall see him, as he foretold you” (Mark 16:17). Of the Holy Spirit, Peter says in Acts [Col. 0666C]: “The Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David” (Acts 1:16).

Great is the Father; so is the Son, and so is the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “Our God is great and worthy of praise” (Ps. 47:2). Of the Son, to Titus: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). Of the Holy Spirit, in Kings, the Lord says to Elijah: “Behold, the Lord passed by, and the Holy Spirit, strong and mighty” (3 Kings 19:11).

As there is the love of the Father, so there is that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “But the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of our God abounded exceedingly” (1 Tim. 1:14). Of the Son: “For the love of Christ urges us” (2 Cor. 5:14). Of the Holy Spirit: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in the love of the Spirit?” (1 Cor. 4:21); and elsewhere: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

The Father gives eternal life; so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, in the Epistle of John: “Because God will give us eternal life” (1 John 5:11). Of the Son, in the Gospel: “My sheep hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life” (John 10:27). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Galatians [Col. 0667A]: “He who sows in the Spirit shall reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. 6:8).

As the Father gives peace, so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7). Of the Son, in the Gospel: “I leave my peace to you” (John 14:27). Of the Holy Spirit: “The prudence of the Spirit is life and peace” (Rom. 8:6).

The Father reveals; so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, to the Galatians: “That he might reveal his Son in me” (Gal. 1:16). Of the Son, in the same place: “For neither did I receive it from man, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (ibid. 1:12). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Ephesians: “Which was not made known to other generations, as it has now been revealed to his saints through his Holy Spirit” (Eph. 3:5); and elsewhere: “For God revealed it to us through the Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:10).

As the Father enlightens [Col. 0667B], so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “You will enlighten my lamp, O Lord” (Ps. 17:29). Of the Son, in the Apostle: “Awake, you who sleep, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). Of the Holy Spirit, the same Apostle says: “For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts unto the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 4:6).

As it is called the Gospel of the Father, so also that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, to Titus: “Which is according to the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God” (1 Tim. 1:11). Of the Son, to the Romans: “Whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son” (Rom. 1:9). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Epistle of blessed Peter: “These things were ministered to you by those who preached the Gospel to you in the Holy Spirit” (1 Pet. 1:12).

As the Father has shone forth, so has the Son and so has the Holy Spirit [Col. 0667C]. Of the Father: “My God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 17:29). Of the Son, in the Psalm: “God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. 117:27). Of the Holy Spirit, the Prophet says: “I shall no longer hide my face from them, because my Spirit has shone upon the whole house of Israel” (Ezek. 39:29 [printed “VXXIX”]). And the Apostle: “For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts unto the illumination of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus” (2 Cor. 4:6).

The Father has foreknowledge; so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “God, knower of hidden things” (Dan. 13:42). Of the Son: “From the beginning Jesus knew who would betray him” (John 6:65). Of the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete Spirit comes, he will teach you all truth and will announce to you the things to come” (John 16:13) [Col. 0667D].

As the Father is said to be everywhere, so also the Son and the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord” (Jer. 23:24). Of the Son: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. 18:20); and the Apostle: “He ascended above the heavens that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4:10). Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7), and he who is over the world filled the Lord himself, the Creator of the whole world, as we read: “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1). And David says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Ps. 138:7).

The Father rebukes; so does the Son, and so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger” (Ps. 6:2) [Col. 0668A]. Of the Son: “I will rebuke you and set these things before your face” (Ps. 49:2). Of the Spirit: “When the Paraclete Spirit comes, he will rebuke the world concerning sin” (John 16:8), and the rest.

Good is the Father, good the Son, and good also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “Good Father” (John 17:11). Of the Son: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:14). Of the Holy Spirit: “Your good Spirit will lead me in the straight way” (Ps. 142:11).

The Father sanctifies and justifies; so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Apostle says: “But you have been sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6:11).

The Father is called holy, the Son is called holy, and the Holy Spirit is holy. Of the Father, in Leviticus: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11:44). Of the Son, in the Gospel [Col. 0668B]: “That which shall be born from you, holy, shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Again, in the same place: “We know who you are, the Holy One of God” (Luke 4:34). Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: “For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. 1:5).

Strong is the Father, strong the Son, and strong also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “God, strong and patient” (Ps. 7:12). Of the Son, in Isaiah: “And his name shall be called Mighty God” (Isa. 9:6). Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: “The spirit of strength is in his ways.”

The Father works, the Son works, and the Holy Spirit does so as well. Of the Father, to the Philippians: “For God is he who works in you both to will” (Phil. 2:13). Of the Son, in the Gospel: “I must work the works of him who sent me” (John 9:4). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Corinthians: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually [Col. 0668C] as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11).

The Father is power, the Son is power, and the Holy Spirit is power. Of the Father, the Apostle says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes” (Rom. 1:16). Of the Son, the Apostle says: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Thessalonians: “Our Gospel did not come to you in word only, but in the power of the Holy Spirit” (1 Thess. 1:5).

The Father is a fountain, the Son a fountain, and the Holy Spirit a fountain. Of the Father, Jeremiah says: “They have forsaken the fountain of living water” (Jer. 2:13). Of the Son, in Solomon: “The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God” (Ecclus. 1:5). Of the Holy Spirit, Isaiah says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar, burning in the wrath of indignation; he will devour the nations, and his Spirit is like a torrent of water drawing a valley along” (Isa. 30:27–28) [Col. 0668D].

The Father is love, the Son is love, and the Holy Spirit is love. Of the Father, in the Epistle of John: “God is love” (1 John 4:16). Of the Son, the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “For the love of Christ urges us” (2 Cor. 5:14). Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says: “I beseech you, brethren, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit” (Rom. 15:30).

The Father regenerates, the Son regenerates, and the Holy Spirit regenerates. Of the Father, Peter says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us unto the hope of eternal life” (1 Pet. 1:3). Of the Son, in the same place: “Loving one another from the heart, as though reborn through the word of the living God” (ibid. 1:23). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Gospel: “Unless anyone has been born again [Col. 0669A] of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

The Father raises up, the Son raises up, and the Holy Spirit raises up. Of the Father, in Acts: “The God of our fathers, who raised Jesus, will also raise us through his power” (Acts 5:30). Of the Son, in the Gospel: “The Jews came not only because of Jesus, but also that they might see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead” (John 12:9). Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:11).

There is the grace of God the Father, the grace of the Son, and the grace of the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: “Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 7:24). Of the Son, to the Corinthians [Col. 0669B]: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that for your sakes he became poor though he was rich” (2 Cor. 8:9). Of the Holy Spirit, in Acts: “And those who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon the Gentiles” (Acts 10:45).

The Father seals, the Son seals, and the Holy Spirit seals. Of the Father, to the Corinthians: “He who sealed you with us in Christ, and who anointed us, is God” (2 Cor. 1:21). Of the Son, to the Ephesians: “Having heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation, in whom you were sealed” (Eph. 1:13). Of the Holy Spirit, as cited above: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30).

The Father dwells in believers, the Son dwells, and the Holy Spirit dwells. Of the Father, in Isaiah: “Keep the Sabbath day and sanctify it, that I may dwell in your midst” (Jer. 17:22) [Col. 0669C]. Of the Son, to the Ephesians: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. 3:17). Of the Holy Spirit: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).

The Father searches, the Son searches, and the Holy Spirit searches. Of the Father, in the Psalm: “God searches hearts and reins” (Ps. 7:10). Of the Son, in Revelation: “And all the churches shall know that I am the searcher of heart and reins” (Rev. 2:23). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Apostle: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2:10).

The Father bears witness, the Son bears witness, and the Holy Spirit bears witness. Of the Father, in the Psalm: “The testimony of God is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones” (Ps. 18:8). Of the Son, to Timothy: “I command you before God, who gives life to all things [Col. 0669D], and Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate” (1 Tim. 6:13). Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says: “He bears witness to our spirit” (Rom. 8:16).

The Father shows, the Son shows, and the Holy Spirit shows. Of the Father, to Timothy: “Whom the blessed and only mighty one will show in his own times” (1 Tim. 6:15). Of the Son, in the Gospel, the Son himself says: “But I will show you whom you should fear” (Luke 12:5); and, “I have shown you many good works from my Father” (John 10:32). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Corinthians: “My preaching was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a manifestation of the Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:4).

The Father fills, the Son fills, and the Holy Spirit fills. Of the Father, Jeremiah says: “I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord” [Col. 0670A] (Jer. 23:24). Of the Son, in the Apostle: “May the Lord fill your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word” (1 Thess. 2:16). And in the Gospel: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). Of the Holy Spirit, in Acts: “He filled the whole place where the disciples were gathered” (Acts 2:2). And: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1).

The Father speaks, the Son speaks, and the Holy Spirit speaks. Of the Father: “God has spoken in his holy place” (Ps. 59:8). Of the Son: “While Jesus was speaking to the crowds” (Matt. 12:46). Of the Holy Spirit: “It is he who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

The Father appeared, the Son appeared, and the Holy Spirit appeared. Of the Father, in Acts: “The God of glory appeared to our fathers” (Acts 7:2). Of the Son, in the Epistle of John: “For this purpose the Son appeared, that the works of the devil might be destroyed” (1 John 3:8) [Col. 0670B]. Of the Holy Spirit, in Job: “And a spirit appeared before my eyes, and terror rushed upon me” (Job 4:15).

The Father is truth, the Son is truth, and the Holy Spirit is truth. Of the Father, in the Psalm: “You have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth” (Ps. 30:6). Of the Son: “Truth sprang up from the earth” (Ps. 84:12). And in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:16). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Gospel: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13).

Behold the unity of operation; do not doubt the unity of the Trinity. They are also accustomed to say concerning baptism that their baptism is better than ours, because when persons from among them convert to us, we do not rebaptize them but reconcile them through the laying on of hands [Col. 0670C]. Yet if they can seduce any from among ours, they recklessly rebaptize them. They must be asked: Do they call the baptism which they administer theirs or ours? If it is ours, why do they presume to administer it, baptizing in the same way as we do? If it is theirs, why do they violate it by repeating it?

But we have reverence for the Lord’s words; and just as he commanded, so we baptize: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. It is certain that they too baptize in this manner. For if they baptized as they believe—in the name of a greater Father, and in the name of a lesser Son, and in the name of a much lesser Holy Spirit—then we would not repeat baptism; rather, we would confer it, because they would not have baptized according to the rule which the Lord handed down. But what do we do? They baptize rightly, but believe wrongly; they baptize rightly, but it is wrong that they rebaptize. They baptize according to the rule, but inculcate faith wrongly. And while they carnally establish degrees within the Godhead, they incur offense against the Godhead, not fearing what the Lord said: “He who has been washed once does not need to be washed again” (John 13:10) [Col. 0670D].

For the Lord said in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5:13); and whoever is wise understands that this was not said without purpose. Salt is made from water; but if it is thrown back into water, it dissolves and perishes. Thus one who has once been baptized from water has been made salt; but if he permits himself to be baptized again, he is reduced to nothing, like salt thrown into water, and his soul is punished with everlasting death.

For the Apostle says concerning the Church [Col. 0671A]: “Because we, though many, are one bread, one body” (1 Cor. 10:17): because, just as one loaf is made from many grains, so one Church is gathered from many peoples. And bread, as everyone knows, is made with water and baked by fire; and every Christian, through the water of baptism and the fire of the Holy Spirit, has been made an offering to God, as the Lord says: “Unless anyone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

But just as, if someone puts bread already baked once back into water and wishes to mix and bake it again, he loses its former quality and it turns into blackness [Col. 0672A] and earth; so does anyone become who permits baptism to be repeated in himself. Therefore everyone ought, with God’s help, to preserve his baptism until death, if he wishes faithfully to attain the kingdom of heaven. For whoever permits himself to be rebaptized thereby blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, denying that he is a Christian and that he was born again through water and the Holy Spirit. And he must receive that threatening sentence of the Lord which we have mentioned: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32).

KALENDARS OF TWO ANCIENT AUTHORS, COMPOSED BY FURIUS DIONYSIUS PHILOCALUS IN A.D. 354 AND BY POLEMIUS SILVIUS IN A.D. 403, AND TAKEN FROM THE MANUSCRIPT CODEX OF JOHANNES CUSPINIANUS.

*(Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, June, vol. VII.)*

[Col. 0671]

## EDITOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0671B] **1. Bolland’s promise to publish Polemius Silvius.**—At last, by God’s favor, we have reached the end of the first sacred half-year of the *Acts of the Saints*. Before finally bringing it wholly to a close, I return to the beginning of the entire work, remembering that Bolland, in the General Preface, as he promised in §7 that he would publish Usuard’s Martyrology in its native simplicity, so in §3 he expressed the hope that he would someday publish the *laterculus* of Polemius Silvius from a manuscript codex. He fulfilled neither promise, because he found no leisure after he had seriously undertaken the great work which he had conceived; and this gave that excellent man so much business that, laying aside concerns foreign to his proposed undertaking, he was soon compelled even to enlist an assistant for advancing another work.

Our colleague John Baptist Sollerius, distinguished by diligent study and accuracy, has recently fulfilled Bolland’s pledge in its first part: he published the genuine Martyrology of Usuard, restored to its original simplicity after the removal of many additions, which he nevertheless appended separately, lest they escape the readers’ notice. The entire work is divided into two parts, to be attached to the two June supplements—that is, volumes VI and VII—although it has also been printed separately. For that Martyrology very closely concerns the *Acts of the Saints*, since from it the ancient and lawful cult in the Church of almost all those who flourished in holiness during the first eight and a half centuries of the Christian era is firmly established.

[Col. 0671D] **2. The promise is here fulfilled.**—We here fulfill Bolland’s other promise concerning the *laterculus* of Polemius. Our codex, in which the *laterculus* is contained, is parchment and thick, numbering 231 leaves; it is written, from beginning to end, in a small but upright hand by the same copyist, and not without errors. It includes various short works by writers on diverse subjects, the greater part of whom flourished in earlier centuries, at least before the year 1000. Among them the present little work of Silvius occurs on page 94.

Bolland printed its beginning in the place cited, together with the month of January from the Calendar and some other items; and he rightly noted that the author should rather be called P. Anneius Silvius than Polemius Silvius. The author wrote, as he himself states in the other little works attached to and interwoven with the Calendar, in A.D. 403 and at the beginning of the following year. For under the heading, “Names of all Roman rulers,” he has the following at the end:

> Our Lords Placidius Valentinianus, under whom the tyrant John was destroyed, and by whom, together with the Lady mother Placidia and the Lady wife Eudoxia, the Augusti now possess the empire. I recorded this under the consulship of the most illustrious men Postumianus and Zeno.

It is certain that the consuls named here held office in the year of Christ 403.

[Col. 0672C] **3. The writer’s date. Another Calendar is added.**—Likewise, under the heading “Summary of Times,” which is inserted into the Calendar after the month of August, the following words are also read at the end:

> Of this kingdom of the Romans—for it treats of their kings, consuls, and emperors—when 1,200 years from the foundation of the City have been completed, under the consuls Postumianus and Zeno, the year of Asterius begins as the first.

Postumianus and Zeno were consuls, as we have already said, in the year 403; Asterius held office in the following year. Therefore Silvius wrote these things, to use Bolland’s words, in 403 [Col. 0672D] and at the beginning of the following year, when it was not yet known at Rome who was consul at Constantinople; he was Protogenes.

Having stated this in order to establish the date of our writer, I proceed to the Calendar itself, which we have long been requested by the letters of many persons to publish. I shall reproduce it from the cited codex as it stands there; and in parallel columns I shall set beside it another Calendar of nearly the same form, but published almost a hundred years earlier by Furius Dionysius Philocalus and dedicated to a certain Valentinus, I know not who. Giles Bucherius formerly published it from our manuscript likewise, but lacking four months, in his commentary on the Paschal Canon of Victorius of Aquitaine. That Calendar was composed in the common year of Christ 354.

**4. Bucherius’s preface concerning the aforesaid Calendar.**—Bucherius prefaces that Calendar as follows:

> If any doubt remained concerning the date of these little works—which he had already printed from our same manuscript in his commentary—it could be removed by this Calendar alone. For it displays the principal victories of Constantine the Great and of his son Constantius over tyrants and barbarians, as though still fresh, and assigns them to their dates. Moreover, in the birthdays of the Caesars it calls this same Constantius not, as it does the other dead emperors, *DIVUS* (“deified”), but, as still living, *DOMINUS* (“lord”). The value of the little work is enhanced by not a few matters here published, both for sacred and for civil history, untouched elsewhere, as you, reader, will immediately recognize. It is regrettable that it has reached us mutilated by the loss of four months—March, April, May, and June. . . . It is dedicated to a certain Valentinus, hitherto unknown to me; unless I should note that a little earlier, in the *Catalogue of Roman Pontiffs*, it calls the basilica built by Pope Julius on the Via Flaminia, at the second milestone, “of Valentinus.” Whether he is the same man I leave for consideration. I do not think so.

[Col. 0673B] **5. The church of St. Valentinus was named after the saint himself.**—Because at that spot on the Via Flaminia, not far from the Milvian Bridge, there formerly stood a church called after St. Valentinus, not after some founder Valentinus—for Julius himself is said above to have founded it. Anastasius also affirms this, saying that Julius built one basilica near the forum and another on the Via Flaminia, where he also made a cemetery and placed the body of St. Valentinus, who had been beheaded on the same road under the emperor Claudius.

The same church is subsequently said by Anastasius to have been of great renown, restored, adorned, and enriched with honors by various pontiffs: namely Theodore, about 745; Benedict II, in 685; Adrian I, in 772; Leo III; and Gregory IV. Although it long ago fell into ruin through the changing fortunes of time, memory of its location did not entirely perish. Panvinio, Bosio, and Floravante write that it stood in the vineyard at that place which is now owned by the friars of St. Augustine.

[Col. 0673D] And recently Augustine Lubin, in his *Notice of the Abbeys of Italy*, p. 346, thus reports concerning the church and cemetery of St. Valentinus, built by Julius:

> At this very moment when we write these words—namely, in the middle of January 1693—some traces have appeared to us. For while the wall of a new building was being constructed, many indications of the ancient church were found: tombs, inscriptions on tombs, very many bones of the dead, and an incontrovertible proof of a Christian cemetery—a sepulchral shell of Parian stone, admirably carved with wavy meanders, with a cross-sign a cubit high carved above it, together with three skulls and many bones of the dead; likewise a marble stone with a cross two cubits high carved upon it; a marble lectern, projecting by the width of two fingers, for Masses; and a bronze little bell for the elevation of the Host—all of which I myself, a most exact investigator and eyewitness, saw.

This is Lubin, who has detained us here too long.

[Col. 0674A] **6. . . . it was named after the saint, not after another Valentinus, who therefore cannot be called a Christian.**—That basilica of St. Valentinus, then, was so named after the saint himself, not after a former founder Valentinus, for there was no such person here. Nor can he on that ground be called a Christian.

If any indication of a Christian man is sought, either in the writer or in the person to whom the little work is dedicated, it should be drawn either from the painted panel prefixed to it or from the seven dominical letters which, in Christian fashion, are appended in their sequence to the individual days together with the eight nundinal letters. [Col. 0674B] Everything else appears profane.

**7. . . . he was a Christian: perhaps this may be inferred from elsewhere.**—The panel placed at the front represents a doorway before which a curtain is drawn. At its top is written: “Valentinus, may you flourish in God.” In the middle is seen a monogram enclosed in a circle, with these letters variously intertwined: I. R. A. F. V. T. Let Oedipus explain it, not I.

Below, two genii, one on either side, hold an oblong tablet; on its two handles are these words: “Furius Dionysius Philocalus inscribed it.” On the tablet itself, in the middle and in large letters, is written: “Valentinus, read happily”; on the right: “Valentinus, may you live, may you flourish”; and on the left: “Valentinus, may you live, may you rejoice.”

The genii who carry it are winged. If one looks at their projecting breasts, they may seem a pagan painting; if at their private parts carefully covered by a robe, one would call them angels. Certainly this covering, unusual among pagans, has something of Christian modesty and propriety. Nor does the inscription “may you flourish in God” smell of paganism; nor can one easily believe that a pagan would have placed Christian dominical letters in his Calendar. It is easier to believe that a Christian added nundinal letters to his dominical letters, according to ancient practice, for the understanding of pagans, who were still then too numerous.

**8. Let each decide as he wishes concerning the foregoing. I shall offer a few remarks on the following Calendars.**—I do not reproduce here directly the first Calendar, which I said was published by Bucherius, because, besides other inaccuracies, it lacks four months: March, April, May, and June. In 1688 we inspected the Imperial Library at Vienna in Austria, and there found a codex of Cuspinianus similar to that from which Bucherius’s copy was taken. We copied afresh from it everything printed by him, including the Calendar under discussion, adding the four months missing in Bucherius.

Peter Lambecius likewise published it complete from the same codex, in volume IV of the *Imperial Library*, p. 277. We therefore reprint it here in the first column of the pages; in the second, opposite it, we shall present from our manuscript codex the Calendar of Polemius Silvius, so that they may be compared more closely day by day and it may more readily be noted what is lacking in one and what has been added to the other.

## ANCIENT CALENDAR OF POLEMIUS SILVIUS, COMPOSED IN THE YEAR 403

### JANUARY

31 days. Among the Hebrews it is called Sebit; among the Egyptians, Tibi; among the Athenians, Pusidicon; among other Greeks, Edinen.

Kalends: called ἀπὸ τοῦ καλεῖν, that is, “from calling,” because at that time the people were summoned at Rome in the Rostra for contention—or rather, perhaps, for an assembly.  
IV Nones. Private circus games. South wind, sometimes with rain.  
III. Day of auspices. Birthday of Cicero. Games.  
II. Games. Assembly-day.  
Nones: so called because the ninth day distinguishes them from the Ides. It indicates stormy weather.  
VIII Ides. Epiphany: the day on which, after intervals of time, the star again announced the Lord’s birth, and water was made wine, or the Savior was baptized in the river Jordan. South wind sometimes, or west wind.  
VII. The consul’s first napkin, so called because King Tarquinius at Rome, while dining in the circus on the day of the Circus Games, threw a napkin from his table outside, to give the charioteers the signal to race after dinner.  
VI. South wind and rain sometimes.  
V. Lawful meeting of the Senate. Substitute consuls or praetors are appointed.  
IV.  
III. Carmentalia, from the name of Evander’s mother.  
II, or the day before.  
Ides. Called ἀπὸ τοῦ εἰδεῖν, “from seeing,” because before this present year existed, at mid-month the full moon, which began the Kalends and from which we understand the months to have received their name, was seen. The second napkin. Wind or storm sometimes.  
XIX Kalends of February.  
XVIII. Birthday of Honorius. Circus games. South wind and rain sometimes.  
XVII.  
XVI. Palatine Games.  
XV. Games.  
XIV. Games.

Here, reader, you have two ancient Calendars with their errors, as they were read in the manuscript codices. I did not think that anything should be annotated in them. Do this yourself wherever there is need. Bucherius added a few notes in the margin of his edition; whoever wishes may consult him.

[Col. 0687]

## SOME BIRTHDAYS OF SAINTS EXCERPTED FROM THE CONSULAR FASTI

We found in the same manuscript codex of Cuspinianus two fairly ancient catalogues of Roman consuls, one ending around A.D. 493 and the other around 536. Both begin with Gaius Julius Caesar. The names of the consuls are written very badly in both places, and not infrequently wrongly arranged, with pairs of consuls sometimes joined who were never colleagues. We therefore did not consider it worthwhile to transcribe all the consuls.

Nevertheless, various events of various kinds and the martyrdoms of saints also were inserted under various consulships, usually with the Kalends, Nones, and Ides on which they suffered. I thought these should be transcribed, both because they may be useful for our purposes and because they may be useful for those of others; not because I wish all that I have excerpted to be accepted as established, but so that at least they may be consulted in doubtful matters.

I give everything as I received it, omitting the consuls except those under whose consulship the events are recorded as having happened, and those said to have succeeded in the following year. Thus, by comparing the two consulships with better lists of consuls, the time at which the reported events occurred may be established more easily and more certainly.

Receive, therefore, the older catalogue here, which I said ends before the close of the fifth century. At the same time, note from this specimen the unreliable writing of the catalogue. In the first consulship Gaius Julius Caesar is given Marcus Antoninus as colleague instead of Antonius; in the second, Chrysauricus is entered, although no Roman consul of that name ever existed, and it should be written Isauricus. Examine the rest similarly. Finally, know that what is written here in Roman letters is written in red in the codex; the rest, written in the ordinary black color, is here represented in italic letters—namely the names of the consuls. The catalogue begins as follows:

There were altogether, from the creation of the earth until Gaius Julius Caesar, 5,044 years.

The first emperor: Gaius Julius Caesar.

Gaius Julius Caesar and Marcus Antoninus. Chrysauricus and Antoninus.

Under these consuls Caesar was killed—he who discovered the leap-year and the course of the moon—on 10 Kalends of January, on the first day of the moon; and Octavian received the empire, a boy eighteen years old.

Lentulus and Orestes. Lepidus and Plancus.

Under these consuls three suns appeared in the sky.

Censorinus and Salvinus. Cicero and Antoninus.

[Col. 0688] Under these consuls Augustus received his name.

Augustus and Tullius. Augustus VI and Agrippa.

Under these consuls Carthage was restored on the Ides of July.

Augustus VII and Agrippa. Saturninus and Cinna.

Under these consuls Virgil died, aged sixty.

The two Lentuli. Domitius and Ahenobarbus.

Under these consuls the Aqua Virgo was brought into Rome.

Libo and Piso. Augustus XII and Silanus.

Under these consuls Christ was born on 8 Kalends of January, on the fourteenth day of the moon.

Lentulus and Piso. **A.D. 14.** Pompeius and Aquileius.

Under these consuls Augustus died, aged seventy-seven.

**15.** Drusus and Flaccus. **27.** Bassus [read Crassus] and Piso.

Under these consuls John the Baptist suffered.

**29.** The two Gemini.

Under these consuls Christ suffered on 8 Kalends of April.

**30.** Tiberius III and Silius [read Sejanus]. **31.** Tiberius IV and Gallus.

Under these consuls the apostle Peter came to Rome.

**44.** Crispinus and Taurus. **48.** Vitellius II and Publicola.

Under these consuls the phoenix appeared for the first time.

**49.** Veranus and Gallus. **57.** Nero II and Piso.

Under these consuls Peter and Paul suffered at Rome on 3 Kalends of July.

**58.** Nero III and Messala. **62.** Marius and Gallus.

**63.** Rufus and Regulus. **67.** Capito and Rufus.

Vespasian VIII and Titus VII. **118.** Hadrian and Salinator.

Under this consul Glycerius was elevated emperor at Ravenna on the third day before the Nones of March.

474. Under the lord Leo the Younger Augustus.

Under these consuls . . . . . . from imperial power Glycerius in the harbour of the city of Rome. In that year the lord Julius Nepos was elevated on the eighth day before the Kalends of July.

475. After the consulship of Leo the Younger Augustus.

Under these consuls the Patrician Orestes entered Ravenna with an army and drove the emperor Nepos into Dalmatia on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. In that year the emperor Augustulus was elevated at Ravenna by his father, the Patrician Orestes, on the day before the Kalends of November.

476. Under Basiliscus II and Armatus.

Under these consuls Odoacer was elevated king on the tenth day before the Kalends of September. In that year the Patrician Orestes was killed at Piacenza on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. In that year Paul, his brother, was killed at Ravenna in the Pineta on the day before the Nones of September.

476. After the consulship of Basiliscus and Armatus.

Under these consuls Branila was killed at Ravenna by King Odoacer, on the fifth day before the Ides of July.

478. Under Hel(l)o as sole consul. [Col. 0691] 480. Under the younger Basilius as consul for the sixth time.

Under these consuls the emperor Nepos was killed on the seventh day before the Ides of May.

481. Under Placidius as sole consul.

Under these consuls . . . . was killed on the seventh day before the Ides of October.

482. Under Severinus as sole consul.

Under these consuls . . . . was killed in Dalmatia on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

483. Under Faustus as sole consul. 487. Under Vettius as sole consul.

Under this consul a battle was fought between King Odoacer and Feunanus, king of the Rugians; Odoacer prevailed and brought King Feunanus captive on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December.

488. Under Dinamius and Sifidius.

Under these consuls the bridge of Apollinaris burned by night at Easter, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

489. Under Probinus and Eusebius. 490. Under Faustus as sole consul.

Under these consuls King Theodoric entered the ditch at the bridge of the Sontius on the fifth day before the Kalends of September; and King Odoacer fled from the ditch and went to Verona. In that year King Odoacer entered the ditch of the Heruli in the Pineta; Libila, master of the soldiers (*magister militum*), was killed; people fell on both sides; and King Odoacer shut himself up in Ravenna on the sixth day before the Ides of July, while King Theodoric returned to Ticinum on the twentieth day before the Kalends of September.

492. Under the lord Anastasius Augustus and Rufus.

Under these consuls an earthquake occurred by night, before the cockcrow, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

493. Under Albinus as sole consul.

Under this consul King Theodoric returned to Rimini and came with “dramonis” [uncertain] to the ditch of Palatiolus on the fourth day before the Kalends of September. In that year a battle was fought between Theodoric and Eufanes, master of the soldiers (*magister militum*), between Trent and Verona.

Under this consul peace was made between the lord King Theodoric and Odoacer on the third day before the Kalends of March. And the lord Theodoric entered the fleet . . .

Under this consul King Theodoric entered Ravenna on the third day before the Nones of March, and King Odoacer was killed by King Theodoric in the palace, together with his fellow-soldiers.

These matters, then, have been excerpted from the first catalogue. We judged that nothing should be added by us except the years of the common era in which the consuls named held office, both to assist the reader’s memory and to make it easier to correct the number of consulships which is wrongly [Col. 0692A] assigned to many consuls, perhaps through copyists’ carelessness. The other catalogue which we mentioned is far more confused and faulty, and contains more matters relevant to secular than to sacred history. It states that Christ suffered under the consuls known as the Two Gemini—who were consuls in the twenty-ninth year of the common era—on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, a Friday, the third day of the moon, in the thirty-first year of His advent. I should suppose that the author wrote, as he ought to have written, the twenty-ninth year, because immediately after the consulship of the Gemini he records Unicius and Longinus, who were consuls in the thirtieth year of the common era. It also has certain chronological notices: for example, that from the Passion of the Lord to the consulship of Niger and Apronianus there were eighty-four years; likewise, that from the Lord’s advent to the consulship of Viator there were five hundred years. Niger and Apronianus were consuls in the 117th year of the common era, while Viator was consul in 394. Let the reader see whether he can derive any benefit from this, and let him correct for himself whatever errors he notices in the catalogue. I shall pursue the matter no further.

There also remains for us another ancient manuscript work, completed under Pope Liberius, who was created pope in the year 352. It enumerates the Roman pontiffs down to that point, indicating who presided over the Church, and for how long; under which Roman consuls each began and under which each ended. But since Bucherius long ago published this very work from our same manuscript in his commentary on the Paschal Canon of Victorius of Aquitaine, p. 269, and especially since our Henschenius reprinted it before the first volume of the *Acts of the Saints* for April and carefully elucidated it at length, we refer the reader desirous of such knowledge to them. Here, then, we conclude the acts of the saints of the first half-year, or first six months of the year, begun by Fr. Jean Bolland, shaped by Fr. Godfrey Henschenius, and wonderfully advanced by Fr. Daniel Papebroch. We shall now proceed, with God and the saints assisting us, to the second half-year. When it has been completed, those who then labour on the work will finally reprint and double in size the months of January and February, which, as the beginning of the work, are more imperfect and need much addition of the acts collected later—especially in the year 1660 by Henschenius and Papebroch, who travelled for that purpose through Germany, Italy, and France. The remaining months, which were published after that year, do not need this so greatly.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 371. LUCIFER, BISHOP OF CALARIS

*(Venetian edition printed by the Coleti brothers.)*

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691]

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE

To the Most Holy Lord, Pius VI, Supreme Pontiff, John Dominic and James Coleti, sons of Sebastian, send greetings.

What the Apostle Paul wrote by the prompting and inspiration of the heavenly Spirit—that neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but rather He who gives the increase—we, Most Blessed Father, ought to keep before our eyes and fully recognize in preparing and completing this new edition of the works of Lucifer, Bishop of Calaris. Let us therefore be permitted to transfer this divine saying, by which that great Doctor of the Gentiles intended to designate God as the giver of all good things, from its proper meaning to him who holds on earth the place and authority of Almighty God. For it is especially through your protection, next after God, that this labour of ours now finds itself so far advanced that [Col. 0693] we, formerly hesitant and distrustful of the slenderness of our talents, are encouraged to a sure hope: namely, that a work approved by you and commended also by the judgment of others may safely stand before the vast assembly of learned men.

For before our efforts to complete this work had been received into the fidelity and patronage of the Apostolic See, they were confined within those hiding places and narrow limits in which private persons are usually contained. They dared neither to emerge nor to behold, much less endure, the public light, so that they seemed perhaps destined to remain, as it were, in our own bosom. But after we had reverently and humbly approached the Roman Pontiff, requesting that they be shielded and cherished under his patronage, and had found that they were received by him with the utmost kindness and judged worthy of papal favour, only then did we seem to raise our spirits, to congratulate ourselves as it were, and to think of one thing alone: how we might answer the Supreme Hierarch’s favourable disposition toward us and his weighty and truly great judgment.

Although that majesty by which you stand nearest to God might have deterred us from seeking what we have obtained chiefly through your beneficence, yet we were not free, even for the sake of modesty, to seek from elsewhere the inauguration and patronage of this work. For to alienate, so to speak, from the Roman Pontiff and turn elsewhere the admirable writings of so great a man—in which shone forth his unconquered strength of soul, marvellous power of speech, and supreme knowledge of sacred literature, in defence of religion and innocence, in exposing the snares of heretics, in recalling the wicked to the straight path of eternal life, in sustaining all good people in the endurance of hardships and firmness of faith, and finally in vindicating Apostolic authority on numerous embassies—we should have regarded as a kind of sacrilege.

Especially so, since we had observed that by Lucifer’s singularly happy fortune, when his books were first brought forth from darkness into light, they themselves, devoted and consecrated uniquely to this Holy See even then, considered that their own distinction and protection, and fame for their author, were to be obtained from it. Thus it has plainly come about by divine providence that the same works which first safely appeared in public under the pontificate, patronage, and auspices of Pius V should now be published anew in print under the most gracious commendation of your auspices—you who truly bear the name of that most holy predecessor of yours and follow in his footsteps.

This being so, surely no one will charge us with presumption because we have not hesitated to offer to you, Most Blessed Father, the works of Lucifer published through our efforts. Yet there is also, indeed, ample cause why we should congratulate ourselves that you have of your own accord and with such kindness assented to the inscription of our labours with your name. For to whom is not well known that singular zeal and exceptional piety with which, from your earliest years, you devoted yourself to reading and meditating upon the books of the ancient Fathers, the Councils, and the monuments of all ecclesiastical antiquity, so that you most eagerly acquired for yourself the immense inheritance of heavenly wisdom and most beautiful virtues which they left behind?
