Would that your modesty, Most Blessed Father, allowed us here to comply with the praise of your fame, stirred everywhere by the applause of all, and to celebrate in our humble and however inadequate speech what is on everyone’s lips. Yet the discourse itself slides down to this point of its own impulse, not so much by our will as by a certain force of its own; it can neither be restrained altogether nor recalled. For though we are compelled to pass over in a silence almost neglectful so many and such conspicuous matters as would declare that no day of your life has been empty of piety, religion, the study of sacred literature, and the vigilant practice of every virtue, nevertheless, Most Holy Father, we cannot but remember that day at whose recollection all good people still rejoice and exult; nor can we avoid recalling that time which God from all eternity willed to be most fortunate and salutary for the Catholic Church—that time, that day, when you, thinking of nothing less, or rather fearing nothing of the kind, were proclaimed Pontiff by so sudden a unanimous consent of the entire Apostolic Senate.

For neither the nobility of your birth, in which you otherwise greatly excelled, nor flattering recommendations, nor splendid displays and adornments—from which, through zeal for Christian humility, you utterly recoiled—opened the way to the pontificate for you. That same virtue which, from your very cradle, received you and nurtured you in its bosom, and brought you up to this eminence, itself placed you with its own hands in this highest seat of honour and dignity, close to heaven.

There is indeed nothing here for you to fear—that we shall advance too far in recounting your praises. For we have now come to the point at which we must rather fear lest, if we attempt anything further, we seem to have undertaken more than the weakness of our talents can accomplish. Let us leave this immense harvest to posterity, in which they may freely and confidently labour without any offence to you and with greater praise. They will admire and celebrate with just praise your unblemished innocence of character and life; they will marvel at your composed and gracious disposition amid so great a dignity; at a mind and spirit constantly intent on matters both greatest and least; at the almost complete absence of time granted for restoring strength and caring for health; and at days and nights uninterruptedly devoted to sacred occupations and the continual duties of religion and piety. And as often as your image comes before their minds, so often will they think that they behold a true example of the supreme priesthood.

But, to return to the point from which we did not unwillingly depart, no one should wonder that we rejoice so greatly for these writings of ours to appear inscribed with your name and to glory in your patronage. For we see that, though you are occupied with such great cares, you persist in the same zeal of studying the most excellent volumes of the ancient Fathers and writers, whence you derive counsel, a rule, and courage for successfully dispatching all the most difficult affairs of the universal Church. Nor should it be doubted that our studies will always find open access to your favour and clemency—the access which you recently opened in your kindly disposition, when, by the most upright judgment of yours, you graciously approved our effort, however slight it may be, in publishing Lucifer’s books.

And these indeed are the reasons, [Col. 0695] Most Blessed Father, why this volume is owed to you above all, and by the fullest right. If in discharging this task we have achieved anything by our watchfulness and labour, we understand that we have advanced no more than one who plants or waters, whose efforts the Apostle declares useless and vain unless there is added the kindness and beneficence of another, who both presses the work forward and supplies its increase. Therefore, moved both by the consideration of our due obligation and by a certain impulse and inward feeling of the soul, we dedicate and consecrate the work itself to you, Most Holy and Supreme Pontiff. It remains only that, by that same clemency with which you are accustomed to foster the diligent industry of others in cultivating studies of this kind, you may be pleased to receive this modest gift, whatever it is, and protect it with your patronage, so that it may be both a witness of your singular kindness toward us and an enduring memorial of our reverence for you.

Venice, from the ancestral house, on the third day before the Kalends of March, 1778.

[Col. 0695]

# PREFACE

[Note: [Col. 0695] Since in this preface the reader is very frequently referred to various places in the Veronese edition, we have, in order to facilitate reading, supplied in parentheses the column of our edition corresponding to each cited page. **EDS.**]

## To a New Edition of the Works of Lucifer

[Col. 0695A]

The first editor to publish the works of Lucifer, Bishop of Calaris, transcribed from ancient codices, was John Tilius, Bishop of Meaux, at Paris in 1568; he dedicated them to Pope Pius V. He certainly expended some effort and labour in correcting them, and, by notes appended below, attempted to explain certain difficult and obscure expressions and statements in each book. But he left much more—especially matters concerning the testimonies of Holy Scripture—to be gathered and corrected by a reader less occupied than he was, as he himself acknowledges in his letter to the Pontiff.

Accordingly, when the authors of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, published in 1687 in seventeen volumes, had also inserted the Luciferian works in Volume IV, [Col. 0695B] they undertook to produce them in a more corrected form. But with rash judgment and wholly at their own discretion they dared to lay hands upon them in such a way that, relying on no authority of ancient codices or learned men, they altered words, sentences, and even punctuation. What is more blameworthy, they forced the scriptural testimonies—which abound in Lucifer’s books—into conformity with the text of the Vulgate edition of the Bible, and in many places corrupted rather than corrected them at their own pleasure, though they sometimes employed the observations and corrections of Latinus Latinius and appended Tilius’s notes at the end.

Those who published the same works of Lucifer in the earlier libraries of the Fathers, before the Lyons editors, laboured no more diligently or painstakingly to [Col. 0695C] correct them. Since, therefore, very corrupt copies of Lucifer were still being circulated, the exceedingly learned John Baptist Cotelerius undertook with the greatest zeal the task of publicly presenting Lucifer’s books cleansed of every error and restored entire, insofar as this might finally be possible, in a form approved by learned men. He himself testified to this in Volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, and in the note appended to chapter 56 of Book II of the *Apostolic Constitutions*:

> Here, where I have attempted to elucidate a passage of Lucifer—an author, as everyone knows, utterly corrupt, but extremely useful for the knowledge of the Scriptures—I would have you know, candid reader, that I have expended very great [Col. 0696A] labour in cleansing this Augean stable, and that I am ready to undertake an edition if I should obtain some manuscript book. Thus, if one should happen to come into your hands or knowledge, do not disdain to share it with me, thereby binding to yourself by a singular benefit a man who will not be ungrateful.

“But it is indeed regrettable,” says Cave in his *Historia Literaria*, under the year 354, in the Arian age, “that this new edition of Lucifer of Calaris, which the distinguished John Baptist Cotelerius had planned—as he himself attests in his notes on the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 177—perished with the death of that very learned man, to the great loss of ecclesiastical antiquity.” Fabricius, however, discussing Lucifer and his books in the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, assigns another reason why Cotelerius did not complete the work he had undertaken: that he did not wish to offend the king of France, who was then especially hostile to the Calvinists. Let others judge the reason for this unfinished [Col. 0696B] work.

Meanwhile, people were not lacking who gave some thought to correcting Lucifer’s books. Besides certain corrections of Cotelerius, scattered either through his notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions* or inserted in the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Latinus Latinius carefully recorded in his *Sacred and Profane Library*, p. 157, numerous corrections of every book of Lucifer, some his own and some those of Gonsalvus Ponce. Ludovicus de la Cerda undertook the same labour in his *Sacred Adversaria*. “For there are many things,” he says in chapter 37, “that require consideration; John Tilius, Bishop of Meaux, expended no useless labour in elucidating this author, that is, Lucifer.” “But,” he adds in chapter 38, “we have added and removed many things”—that is, from Tilius’s notes; and, he adds in chapter 47, “I long lingered over [Col. 0696C] Lucifer, making use of Tilius’s work and of my own.”” In these chapters he includes all the observations on Lucifer which he had himself planned, apart from his other observations on certain passages of Holy Scripture, of which more will be said below.

But all these materials, scattered through several books and not easy to find, were of no service whatsoever in enabling everyone to behold at a single glance Lucifer’s whole and authentic countenance. Indeed, very many things were still lacking which might fully represent the man’s native colour and features. Therefore Andrew Gallandius, a priest of the Venetian Congregation of the Oratory, a man distinguished alike for learning and erudition, when he had resolved to publish [Col. 0697A] at Venice a library of the ancient Fathers, embellished and enlarged by renewed effort and study, judged that he should omit nothing that might restore the Luciferian works to their original integrity and illuminate them more fully than anyone before him, using every resource of textual criticism that he could collect.

On this matter it is better to set out his opinion in his own words, from the prolegomena to p. 6 of Volume VI of his work, in which Lucifer’s books are included:

> Concerning the work which we applied to publishing these books, receive briefly the following account. We resolved to print Tilius’s first edition, which the Parisian editors followed in 1644. But since it had been grievously corrupted through the fault of copyists and was covered with foul errors, we took care, to the best of our ability, to cleanse it of these stains. The corrections and conjectures of learned men—especially Latinus and Cotelerius—furnished assistance; there were also added others which we discovered, when occasion [Col. 0697B] presented itself, in the writings of other authors.”

And a little further below:

> Yet we do not claim to have rendered Lucifer’s books completely clean. On the contrary, in revising them we ourselves found some matters which we proposed perhaps to correct still further in the *Emendations*. Thus we freely acknowledge that many things still remain in Lucifer which await a healing hand, especially one aided by manuscript codices. Moreover, in order that the subsequent reading of Lucifer’s works may proceed more readily and easily, we divided all the books into sections. We also added certain letters, whether of Lucifer himself or of others addressed to him, revised and elucidated.

Having observed these matters, we conceived and have now carried out a new plan for publishing Lucifer’s books. It is altogether necessary to preface an account of it, so that those who judge it useful to engage in reading them, whether for instruction and learning or for worthy curiosity, may clearly see [Col. 0697C] what we have accomplished, what aids have been obtained for us, and what in Lucifer himself and in his books seemed deserving of critical investigation.

First, we resolved to follow Tilius’s edition itself, because it is a genuine representative of the ancient codices from which he first brought forth Lucifer’s books. For the errors found in it should be attributed less to the printer than to the ignorance or negligence of ancient copyists, as we shall note below. The other editions, excepting Gallandius’s, do not carry such authority that we could safely follow them, since editorial caprice rather than [Col. 0697D] impartial examination may have removed a few errors but certainly introduced no small number into the same texts, as has been said a little above.

But, since we saw that the assistance of some codex was necessary in order to compare it with Tilius’s edition, we fortunately found one in the Vatican Library, written, as they say, in the ninth century and marked in the library cases with the number 75 and the letters N. P. Its readings differing from Tilius’s were copied out and most kindly sent to us. Yet they are not of such a kind as to alter the sense, and for the most part they merely offer different words and names different from those published from Tilius’s codex. From this one may infer that the many errors found in Lucifer’s books should be attributed rather to the author’s uncultivated and almost [Col. 0698A] barbarous style than to copyists’ fault.

Moreover, the most gracious and highly learned priest Matteo Luigi Canonici, a Venetian citizen, supplied us from his own library—richest in extremely ancient codices, especially biblical ones—with another codex for use. This codex, which we call the Venetian codex, was written nearly eight hundred years ago. It contains works of Athanasius and certain works attributed to Athanasius, and among them the longer of Athanasius’s letters to Lucifer; we compared its manuscript copy with the text already published by Tilius.

Accordingly, on the authority of these codices, and from the notes of Tilius, Latinius, Ponce, La Cerda, and Gallandius himself, and from other notes on the Luciferian letters collected from Baronius, Coustant, Chifflet, Papebroch, and [Col. 0698B] Montfaucon, we prepared the annotations appended below. Our own observations are intermingled with them, especially those that concern ecclesiastical history. I am surprised that Gallandius passed these over, since many things written by Lucifer very greatly elucidate the acts of the Council of Milan of 355 and the life of Athanasius, and expose the deceptions and cruelties of the Arians toward Catholics. We shall speak later of the notes appended to individual testimonies of Holy Scripture.

We have not, however, copied the critical observations of these authors in such a way as immediately to approve them. We have inserted all of them in their respective places, but have not approved all. Nor did we judge that we might lay hands upon Lucifer’s text so as to be permitted, even when relying on the testimony and opinion of others, to [Col. 0698C] reverse, alter, or even delete words and meanings. This would not have been just, nor consistent with sound principles of textual criticism. It was enough to correct those things which could in no way be left untouched, and to leave the rest to the judgment of readers through the notes.

Besides this, we arranged the individual books in an order different from that in which they were published, since we do not think that Lucifer composed them all in one uninterrupted course of writing or at one time. Tilius, indeed, held in his letter to Pope Pius that the whole volume was one work continuously addressed to the emperor Constantius, though divided into treatises by the author himself. But Baronius, under the year 356, no. 65; Papebroch, Volume IV for May of the *Bollandists*, in the historical commentary on St. Lucifer, chapter 4; and Gallandius, in the prolegomena to Volume VI of the *Library of the Fathers*, judged otherwise—and we agree with them. [Col. 0698D] Lucifer himself confirms this in his book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, distinguishing and separating his book *On Apostate Kings* from the others: “Since I have already made clear that these things are so in the book entitled *On Apostate Kings*,” etc.

Yet we hold a different opinion from the authors cited concerning the time at which each book was written by Lucifer; we shall discuss this in its proper place in relation to each individual work.

To Tilius’s edition we have added matters which certainly could not be omitted and which are printed before Lucifer’s books: first, Lucifer’s letter, written with his fellow-envoys Pancratius and Hilary, to Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli; then another letter of Pope Liberius to Lucifer, already condemned to exile. These letters [Col. 0699A] are followed by Lucifer’s books: first, *On Not Associating with Heretics*; then *On Apostate Kings*; and two books *For St. Athanasius*. To these we have added the letters of Florentius to Lucifer and Lucifer to Florentius; below them is placed the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, followed by the last book, which Lucifer entitles, *That One Must Die for the Son of God*. Finally, two letters of Athanasius to Lucifer close the volume.

Tilius had added to these a letter of Liberius to Constantius and another of Athanasius to the Solitaries; but these could have no place here, since they are not necessary for elucidating the affairs of Lucifer. Among his spurious works, however, we have relegated to the end of the volume the *Formula of Faith* attributed to Lucifer; a particular critical discussion is placed before it.

Having thus prefaced [Col. 0699B] these remarks concerning this new edition, it remains necessary to discuss, in several sections, Lucifer himself in relation to his writings, and then each of his books individually.

## § I.—On Lucifer’s Interpretation of Holy Scripture
No one, certainly, who has read Lucifer’s books can fail greatly to admire both the man’s ready ingenuity in adducing, and his acuteness in applying to each of his propositions, the testimonies of the divine books, together with his singular eloquence. Athanasius was the first to observe this, writing in his second letter to him: “Whence comes this great memory of the Scriptures? Whence their sound sense and understanding?” And the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus, in their Petition-book to the emperors, especially praise Lucifer because he had become well known through his study of sacred letters, and because he wrote books to Constantius, most aptly assembling divine testimonies against the heretics and against the very patron of heretics. Thus Gallandius rightly affirms that Lucifer’s writings are composed almost exclusively of passages from both Covenants.

Hence Cotelerius, in the testimony quoted above, calls Lucifer an author most useful for the knowledge of Sacred Scripture; and Mill, in the *Prolegomena* to the New Testament, no. 772, writes of Lucifer as follows: “From Hilary we proceed to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, whose little works display a great abundance of testimonies from Sacred Scripture, everywhere cited accurately according to the text of the codex itself.” Yet since the edition of these works, prepared from only one manuscript copy—and that incorrectly transcribed—abounds miserably in faults, neither have the passages of the sacred text escaped uninjured.

But whatever codex or codices Tilius used in publishing Lucifer’s books, our Vatican manuscript differs scarcely at all from the Tilian edition in the transcribed biblical testimonies. We must therefore seek some other reason why readings occur in Lucifer which differ from the Vulgate and are not altogether free and purged of errors.

Ludovicus la Cerda, in *Adversaria Sacra*, chapter 163, undertook a difficult task indeed: to compare the sacred testimonies cited by Lucifer in Book I *For St. Athanasius* with the new Vulgate edition of the Bible. But almost at the beginning of the chapter he regretted the task he had undertaken. “Wonderful,” he says, “is Lucifer’s freedom in his use of Scripture; yet it makes the matter so difficult that one must generally divine the passage of Scripture.” And concerning the testimony from Proverbs 19:28, “Mercy and truth are a safeguard to a king,” p. 89 (col. 855) of this edition, he adds: “I do not find it in the Vulgate. There are many such passages in Lucifer unless one tracks them down elsewhere. I pass over the rest, which are hard to find.” For this reason he also made the mistake of assigning to verse 15 of the same chapter in the Vulgate the testimony cited by Lucifer from 1 Kings 7:16, p. 69 (col. 833).

[Col. 0700A] We ourselves experienced this difficulty so fully when we had only the Tilian edition that, at p. 51 (col. 816), concerning the passage, “when you have turned and groaned,” etc., we said in the note below that it was perhaps composed from the sense of the preceding words of Joel, whereas afterward it became possible to find the same passage in Isaiah 30:15.

Thus, examining Deuteronomy 1:29, “Do not speak, nor …,” p. 59 here (col. 824), by comparison with the Vulgate, la Cerda himself, astonished at so different a translation, added: “When I see these things, I do not know what else I can say except that this man either rendered these passages by some sort of accommodation, or used some translation—of which there were many before Jerome—that we do not possess.” And on Malachi 3:13, p. 105 (col. 872), he adds: “Do not be surprised at Lucifer’s version, which is so unusual that we must suppose he possessed some peculiar codex.”

But what he conjectured had already been noticed by others, including Tilius in his letter to the Pope: “The translation of passages from the sacred volume,” he says, “shows that it was certainly the common version, and had not, as it later was, been revised and corrected.” Papebrochius too, chapter 3 of the *Life of St. Lucifer*, says: “In citing passages of Scripture there appears a very notable discrepancy between the ancient version and that corrected version which we use today, as Tilius observes.” Above all, this was observed by Peter Sabatier in the most learned work which he completed through immense diligence and labor, entitled *Ancient Latin Versions of the Sacred Bible, or the Old Italic*, etc.

For in Part II, §3 of the Preface to Volume I, Part I, discussing in order the individual Fathers and the Fathers’ writings from which he had extracted fragments or verses of Scripture, and testifying how much Lucifer’s books had contributed to the preparation of his work, he says in no. 101:

> “But Lucifer of Cagliari supplied us with by far the more numerous fragments of the ancient translation in the several books which he wrote: *For St. Athanasius*; *On Apostate Kings*; *On Not Associating with Heretics*; *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*; *That One Must Die for the Son of God*. Lucifer flourished about the year 354. In quoting words of Scripture he is sufficiently consistent with himself; he scarcely differs from the present Greek text. Sometimes he agrees with Tertullian, sometimes with Augustine and Ambrose. But what above all deserves to be observed is that, in the books of Tobit and Judith, which we have recovered with the aid of various manuscripts, and indeed manuscripts of the best quality, there is such agreement and such similarity in the scriptural statements occurring in Lucifer’s books that one finds scarcely any discrepancy and can no more distinguish them than one egg from another.

> “From this it follows that Lucifer did not himself translate the sense of the sacred books from Greek codices into Latin, but used those Latin versions which at that time were very widely circulated.”

Nor did Nobilius think otherwise in the Preface to the Roman Latin edition of the Septuagint: “So ancient is the Italic translation that not only St. Augustine in the *Mirror*, but also Lucifer of Cagliari, St. Ambrose, St. Cyprian, and other ancient writers use it.” La Cerda therefore wrote incorrectly in chapter 163 of the *Adversaria Sacra* that Lucifer translated Greek testimonies into Latin at his own discretion as occasion required.

Thus, on Deuteronomy 17, p. 60 here (col. 825), he says: “He translates almost the entire chapter in such a way that one marvels at the man’s license in translating—now subtracting, now adding, now altering”; whereas this text corresponds exactly to the old Italic translation. Likewise, the text from 1 Kings 4 cited here at p. 68 (col. 834) agrees with it, concerning which la Cerda says: “Lucifer renders it in such a way that neither foot nor head corresponds to a single form, provided only that he preserves the sense.” So too concerning the other passage from 1 Kings 19, p. 70 (col. 836): “Lucifer twists it around so that it is difficult to say what part corresponds to what part.” Yet this testimony is expressed in no other manner in the Italic translation; likewise the passage from 1 Kings 26, p. 73 here (col. 839), which he supposes Lucifer had translated paraphrastically into Latin.

It may indeed sometimes have happened that Lucifer, writing these books amid the gravest hardships of exile, lacked Latin codices and either drew many biblical testimonies from memory or copied them from Greek books and translated them into Latin. Nor were sacred codices entirely lacking to Lucifer, as these words of Marcellinus and Faustinus concerning Eutychius, bishop of Eleutheropolis, and his followers, in the *Petition-book*, indicate:

[Col. 0701C] “Let them deny, if today they do not possess among themselves the holy mystical vessels which they then impiously plundered from Lucifer, together with the sacred codices.”

But the great agreement of Lucifer’s translation with the old Italic version, preserved partly in manuscript biblical codices and partly in the books of Latin Fathers down to our own time, is evidence for us that Lucifer generally—if not always—followed it.

Moreover, it is certain that there were once very many ancient Latin translations of the sacred books. For, as St. Augustine writes in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, according to the degree of competence each person thought he possessed in Greek and Latin, as soon as he had obtained a Greek codex, he dared to undertake a translation. Morinus, however, rightly observes in the Preface *On the Greek and Hebrew Text of Sacred Scripture*, prefixed to the Paris Greco-Latin edition of the Septuagint reproduced from the Roman edition, that for four hundred years—that is, until St. Jerome—no Catholic had dared to translate otherwise than as the Septuagint had prescribed. All the Catholic translations, however many there were—and Augustine testifies that they were almost innumerable—were made from the Septuagint edition.

Among the other translations, one always stood out. Augustine called it the Italic; Jerome, the Vulgate; Gregory the Great, the Old; and other writers commonly call it the Common version. Sabatier proves in the Preface cited, Part I, §3, that it was more like the Greek Septuagint translation, from which it had been rendered into Latin, than the others were. For, as Augustine testifies in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, it adhered more closely to the words while preserving clarity of sense.

That Lucifer used this version and had it before him is confirmed all the more certainly by Sabatier’s statement that the sacred testimonies copied by him scarcely differ from the present Greek text. La Cerda had already seen this in the passage from Lucifer concerning 1 Kings 26: “Although he may have translated it from some other source or rendered it through an innate freedom, for the most part he has it from the Septuagint version.” And concerning Malachi 3: “He clings to the translation of the Septuagint interpreters and adds much which requires divination to understand, although he says it is from Scripture.” Then on 3 Kings 18, p. 75 here (col. 841): “Lucifer adhered to the Septuagint version, adding, subtracting, and altering much, as is his custom.”

But in truth Lucifer neither adds nor subtracts nor alters through an innate freedom.

[Col. 0702B] The old Latin version was originally one. “Although,” says Sabatier, Part I, §2, “the readings of the original text sometimes differ among themselves and disagree in various words and senses; although various discrepancies occur in manuscripts which seem to indicate various translations made by different translators”—yet these discrepancies, as he says a little earlier, generally point not so much to different translators as to different copyists, either careless or overbold, who altered many details according to their own judgment or through negligence. It is certain from the scholia appended by Nobilius to the Roman edition of the Septuagint that this also occurred in the Greek Septuagint translation. We find the same in the New Testament, especially from the various readings in Mill’s Greek edition.

Accordingly, there is no need to fear that, in maintaining that the original text has various and sometimes discrepant readings, the authority of Sacred Scripture may be impaired and our faith shaken. Sabatier adds this in the same place and proves it at greater length.

Therefore, when in Lucifer a discrepancy of this kind occurs, whether from Greek Bibles on occasion or from Latin Bibles already published, we hesitated considerably, uncertain and doubtful what we ought to do in the edition of these books which we had undertaken. We could not approve the rashness of the authors of the Lyons Library and other Libraries of the Fathers, who sought to correct Lucifer’s testimonies into the form of our Vulgate. On the other hand, it would have been useless labor to pursue what la Cerda had begun, comparing them with the Vulgate itself. Nor was it our purpose to play the part of a translator or to undertake questions from which we could not have refrained, had we chosen to examine and correct Lucifer’s Latin translation by a Greek exemplar. Besides, this would have caused an excessive addition of many discussions in the notes below and produced annotations longer than was appropriate, almost to the weariness of readers.

Gallandius perhaps noticed this too late, and consequently did not complete the work he had undertaken and proposed to himself. “Since,” he says, “Lucifer, in composing his books, runs through nearly entire volumes of the sacred books in order and uses a version older than the Vulgate, we have chiefly applied ourselves to comparing the passages of both Covenants—of which Lucifer’s writings are composed almost exclusively—either with the Septuagint translation or with the text of the New Testament. This was particularly appropriate because that ancient Latin version, as regards the books of the Old Covenant, is known to have been made from the edition of the seventy interpreters.”

But he did not fulfill his promises. The passages which he compared with the Greek translation are few, though adorned with learned observations; the rest he left to themselves, wholly passing them over bare of Greek comparison and critical judgment. Nor did Flaminius Nobilius in the Roman edition of the Septuagint contribute much to correcting Lucifer’s testimonies, although he frequently used him as an authority in the scholia and notes appended to that edition. For, as Sabatier correctly argues in Part III, Preface, §1, though Nobilius had set before himself the aim of restoring the old Vulgate there, he instead rendered the Greek exemplar word for word, acting as a faithful translator. Of the passages praised by the holy Fathers, he copied only those agreeing with the Greek exemplar, neglecting those which disagreed and differed from the Greek codex itself. Indeed, the passages which he excerpted from the Latin Fathers are fewer; and in the New Testament he presents nothing but the text.

We therefore judged that a matter beset by so many difficulties should finally be resolved by one plan: namely, to compare every passage of Sacred Scripture transcribed by Lucifer with the old Italic translation, such as Sabatier has presented to us completed in his most finished work; to relegate to the notes below whatever differs in that version from Lucifer’s testimonies; and, where readings taken from Greek or Latin codices, or from Latin Fathers cited by Sabatier, agree with Lucifer’s readings in passages where Lucifer differs from the text of the old version, to transcribe them, so that Lucifer’s version might be confirmed by some testimony. We also judged it better not to omit the various readings from the Tilian edition which Sabatier himself gives in Lucifer, when importing Lucifer’s testimonies into his work.

Thus it seemed much more convenient and useful to offer readers, in Lucifer alone, a truly illustrious exemplar of the Old Latin Version, corrected with the aid of Cotelerius, Mill, and Sabatier himself, as derived from their observations, and cleansed of those errors which could more readily present themselves to anyone’s eyes.

[Col. 0703D] Yet Lucifer’s books contain certain things which it would be a fault to correct, and which would oppose the writer’s meaning, even though an error be detected in them. An example is the testimony from St. Paul, Galatians 5:7, p. 26 here (col. 790): “You who have consented to no one, your persuasion is from God,” etc. This agrees excellently with Lucifer’s meaning. For he writes: “Knowing that you are enemies of the Son of the one God, we flee your wicked counsels, observing the Apostle’s word: ‘You who have consented to no one, your persuasion is from God.’” By this testimony Lucifer proves that his decision not to associate with Arian heretics proceeded from divine inspiration.

But in Greek books the Apostle’s words had been incorrectly transcribed, whence the error also entered the Latin translation. “The phrase *nemini consenseritis* [‘you have consented to no one’],” Mill says in the *Prolegomena*, no. 773, “arose from incorrectly transcribed Greek: *τίς ἀνέκοψεν ὑμᾶς ἀληθείᾳ; μὴ πείθεσθε*—‘Who cut you off, or removed you, from truth? Do not consent.’ Later the improved text produced, ‘Who hindered you from obeying?’ and the appendix of the former reading, ‘do not consent,’ was added to the rest by some unskilled copyist.”

He confirms the same in his notes on this apostolic passage, since a copyist had written *πείθεσθε* (“obey”) for *πείθεσθαι* (“to obey”), as the corrected Greek text reads: *τίς ὑμᾶς ἀνέκοψεν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι;*—“Who hindered you from obeying the truth?” Zegerus, cited by Mill, had indeed suspected that this clause, “do not consent,” had been erased from Greek codices by heretics long before Jerome’s time. But it contained no ground for fostering or defending heretical error, and Jerome adds on this Pauline testimony that he thought it should be passed over because he had found it written neither in Greek books nor in those who had commented on the Apostle.

Mill adds that Lucifer, who thought “You have consented to no one” pertained to what follows, inserted on his own authority the relative pronoun *qui* (“since” or “who”), which nevertheless is read in the Codex Boernerianus cited by Sabatier.

The same judgment should be made concerning the following clause, “your persuasion is from God,” which lacks the negative particle *non*, Greek *οὐκ*—that is, “is not.” It was indeed absent from several Greek codices which Jerome read. But Jerome, Mill testifies in the passages cited, believed it had been omitted by certain simpler persons who, thinking that they were honoring God by making even our persuasion subject to his power, removed the word “not” and gave the Apostle a meaning contrary to his own. Mill therefore most rightly judged that it should be restored to the Greek and Latin text.

And here Mill may be criticized. In no. 648 of the *Prolegomena*, citing from Clement of Alexandria these words of Jude 6—*Δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις ὑπὸ ζόφον ἀγρίων ἀγγέλων τετήρηκεν*, “He has kept wild angels in everlasting bonds under darkness”—he adds: “The copyist represented this in a disordered arrangement; *ἀγρίων* [‘wild’] incorrectly for *ἁγίων* [‘holy’]. But *ἁγίων ἀγγέλων* [‘of holy angels’] should be placed after *ἀϊδίοις* [‘everlasting’], as we learn in full from Lucifer of Cagliari.”

Then, in his notes on that testimony from Jude, he disagrees with himself, writing that Lucifer read the corrupt word *ἁγίων* for *ἀγρίων*. For Lucifer’s reading is sound and correct at p. 28 here (col. 792): namely, that evil angels are kept in bonds of holy angels under darkness. This would indeed be quite different if he stated that evil angels were held bound by other evil angels. For Revelation 20:1 says that an angel came down from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years.

It must further be admitted that other readings also occur in Lucifer’s version which, even though some believe that an error lies beneath them, should nevertheless not be changed according to their own opinion, since it is clear that neither is the meaning of the expression weakened nor are examples lacking upon whose testimony and authority they rest. We have therefore collected some of them here, so that, when approved by the judgment of readers, they may demonstrate that the integrity of Lucifer’s version is greater than those who accuse it of a fault in the codices or of an injury or carelessness on the part of the Latin translator are willing to allow.

In the book *On Apostate Kings*, p. 33 here (col. 798): “Sin is an abomination,” from 1 Kings 15:23. Cotelerius, on Book II, chapter 62 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, thinks that copyists foolishly wrote *abominatio* (“abomination”) for *ominatio* (“divination”), since the Septuagint reads: *ἁμαρτία οἰώνισμά ἐστιν*—“sin is divination.” But Aquila in the Hexapla translates from the Hebrew: *ἁμαρτία μαντείας παραπικρασμός*, “the sin of divination is provocation”; and Symmachus: *ἁμαρτία τῆς μαντείας τὸ προσερίζειν*, “sin of divination is to contend.” In the Hebrew text we read, “rebellion is the sin of divination.”

And if it does not express the words, the Complutensian Greek edition expresses the meaning of Lucifer’s version: *ἔστι παραπικρασμὸς ἀδικία*, “provocation is injustice.” It will agree with the Hebrew, Aquila, and Symmachus if one adds the word “divination,” which could easily have slipped from a copyist’s pen.

In the same place, p. 34: “Rehoboam reigned twenty years in Jerusalem,” 3 Kings 11:43. The Septuagint does not give this number of years, but 3 Kings 11 says: *Δώδεκα ἔτη ἐβασίλευσεν*, “he reigned twelve years”; while chapter 14:21 says: *ἑπτακαίδεκα ἔτη ἐβασίλευσεν*, “he reigned seventeen years”; likewise 2 Chronicles 12:14 and Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 10. “All books agree in this number of years of the reign,” Nobilius adds on chapter 14 of 3 Kings. Yet this very variation in the reckoning of the years in some measure supports Lucifer’s version.

In the same place, p. 40 (col. 805): “It is also written concerning Jambre the king,” etc. Latinius, in the note below, corrects this to “Zambri.” But Zambri was the commander of cavalry who killed Elah, king of Israel; Omri succeeded him, as he is called in the Septuagint at 3 Kings 16:16 and in our Vulgate. He is the Jambres whom Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 12, calls *Ἀμαρῖνος*, “Amarinus,” and whom the Vatican codex at this passage of Josephus calls *Ζαμβρίας*, “Zambrias.”

Moreover, Sulpicius Severus, in Book I of the *Sacred History*, calls this king both Zambri and Jambri. Jerome a Prato notes that all printed and manuscript books prefer the former name in both passages of Sulpicius; but Vorstius substituted Jambri for Zambri. For although the man concerning whom Sulpicius writes in the first passage was in fact Zamri or Zimri, the other was Omri, whom he calls Zambri and Jambri. It is clear, however, that Sulpicius mistakenly confused Zambri, the commander of cavalry, with Jambri, the king and father of Ahab, because he says: “But Zambri before him—that is, before Thamni—reigned seven years and twelve years with him.” He should therefore have said either Zambri throughout or Jambri throughout.

Vorstius further defends his correction by the authority of the old Cologne edition and the Drusian manuscript. Pratensis, on the contrary, thinks that King Jambri was originally called Zambri, and that Jambri subsequently arose either from the pronunciation customary in earlier times or from the similarity of the letters Z and J in manuscripts. He is confirmed in this opinion by the testimony of the Alexandrian manuscript of the Septuagint, in which *Ζαμβρί*, “Zambri,” always appears in place of *Ἀμβρί*, “Ambri.” He then refutes Drusius, whom he believes to have read Jambri in the former passage of Sulpicius not from a manuscript of Severus but either from the Cologne edition itself or from some printed book, when he says: “Besides, I found Jambri in one manuscript.”

Moreover, Pratensis adds, because our Sulpicius inserts the letter *b* in this name, he followed the Greek reading, in which not only Zambri is written for Zamri and Ambri for Amri, but also Mambre and Nembrod for Mamre and Nemrod. The Vulgate also retains Zambri. The same may be asserted of Lucifer’s Jambre.

In the same place, p. 41 (col. 806): “Jezebel, daughter of Basan and Hela, king of the Sidonians,” from 3 Kings 16. Latinius corrects this passage from the Vulgate, substituting Ethbaal for Basan and Hela. Nor can it be denied that this is indeed the reading in Greek also, and that Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 3, calls Jezebel the daughter of Ithobal, *Ἰθοβάλου*; he also distinguishes this king by that name in Book I *Against Apion*.

The *Sacred Critics* on 1 Kings—which is the third book in the Vulgate—chapter 16, note that Menander of Ephesus, in his Phoenician history, writes the name thus, according to Grotius, and likewise in the records of Tyre: *Εἰθώβαλον*, “Eithobal”; while Diodorus Siculus calls him Ithobalus, according to Junius. For just as the Jews incorporated God’s name in their own names, idolaters incorporated the name of Baal. Bochart confirms this in Book I, chapter 24 of *Sacred Geography*: “Ethbaal or Ithobalus, Ahab’s father-in-law.”

Yet Lucifer’s version is not without precedent. Sulpicius Severus, in Book I of the *Sacred History*, calls Jezebel the daughter of Basa, king of Sidon. Jerome a Prato defends Sulpicius’s reading by the example of Lucifer’s version, in this note: “Sigonius, Hornius, and Vorstius assert that *Basae* was either wrongly written by Severus or corrupted by copyists, and advise that Ethbaal be restored in its place, or, following the Greeks, *Ἰεθεβαάλ*, Jethebaal. But if there is an error in this, it should not be ascribed to Severus or his copyists, since Lucifer of Cagliari likewise reads in the book *On Apostate Kings*: ‘Jezebel, daughter of Basan and Hela, king of the Sidonians.’”

In the same place, p. 45 (col. 810): “His mother’s name was Ebsibas,” from 4 Kings 21:1. Clericus, cited by Cotelerius on Book II, chapter 22 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, thinks that Epsiba or Ephsibas should be read here. But who can maintain a certain meaning for this name, when he himself adds that Syncellus reads *ἐψιβαάλ*, that two manuscripts of Kings read Haphsiba, that Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book X, chapter 3—not 4—has *Ἀχιβάς*, “Achibas,” and Rufinus, Echib? In Hebrew she is indeed called Hephzibah; but the Septuagint wrote *Ἀψιβά*, as in the Roman edition, though Havercamp in his notes on the cited passage of Josephus reads *Ἀψιβᾶς*.

In Book I *For St. Athanasius*, p. 55 (col. 820): “Why have you not offered rightly? You have sinned; be still,” Genesis 4:8. We made certain observations on this testimony in the notes. But Gallandius’s opinion is not to be approved when he supposes it contracted from the words of the Septuagint. At least the sense of the complete expression would have to agree with them, whereas it differs from them entirely. This is clear from the very words of the Septuagint: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still.”

At p. 65 (col. 831) here, we observed that Gallandius, together with Latinius, erred in thinking that Lucifer’s memory had failed because he wrote: “It is written in the first book of Kingdoms: ‘Let him not boast,’ etc.” For this testimony is truly found there in the Septuagint, chapter 2, verse 10.

In the same place, p. 68 (col. 834): “He himself judged for twenty years,” 1 Kings 4:18. Thus the Septuagint also wrote concerning Eli: *Καὶ αὐτὸς ἔκρινε τὸν Ἰσραὴλ εἴκοσιν ἔτη*—“And he judged Israel for twenty years.” Eusebius testifies in the *Chronicle* that he read this reckoning of years in the same text, and Chrysostom copies its very words in Book III *Against the Opponents of the Monastic Life*. Sulpicius Severus agrees in Book VII of the *Sacred History*, affirming that Eli administered the priesthood for twenty years.

Jerome a Prato adds there: “Sulpicius followed the Greek codices, or rather the old Latin Vulgate, which was made from them. Thus the frequently cited Hilarion: ‘Eli the priest judged for twenty years.’ The Hebrew codices, however, followed by Eusebius in the *Chronicle* and in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book X, chapter 14, assign Eli forty years, as our Vulgate also has, and likewise some Greek codices, though these are corrupt. For the Roman edition—that is, the Septuagint—and the Alexandrian manuscript retain the ancient and genuine reading of the Septuagint interpreters.” Josephus too, in *Antiquities*, Book V, chapter 11, gives forty years.

In the same place, p. 69 (col. 835), on 1 Kings 5:6, Gallandius notes: “With Latinius, a learned man, the words ‘mice swarmed forth for them,’ improperly introduced here from what precedes, should be expunged, and the reading should be, ‘and he struck them in their seats,’ as in the Septuagint.” But this ought not be asserted so readily.

Montfaucon warns in his notes on the Hexapla at this passage that these matters are confused in the edition of the Septuagint. For the Hebrew at verse 6 has “and he struck them in the high places”; Aquila, “and he struck them in the seats”; Symmachus, “and he struck them in the hidden places”; the Vulgate, “and he struck them in the more secret part of the buttocks.” The Septuagint does not have these words at verse 6. Then follow the Septuagint’s words: “and he brought upon them, and it boiled forth for them in their ships, and mice sprang up in the middle of their territory,” where Lucifer has, “he brought mice upon them.”

But at verse 9 the Septuagint has: “and he struck them in their seats”; the Hebrew: “hidden high places were upon them”; Aquila: “their seats were swollen round about”; Symmachus: “he struck them in the hidden parts”; the Vulgate: “their projecting intestines were decaying.” Here, however, Lucifer has: “and mice swarmed forth for them in their seats, and the Gittites made themselves leathern seats.” These words seem to hang together better. The Septuagint, however, has merely “seats,” and Theodotion, “golden seats.” These readings certainly indicate that an error could have entered the other versions no less than Lucifer’s.

In the same place, p. 71: “And on that day he killed three hundred and five men,” from 1 Kings 22:18. “I am astonished that Lucifer wrote this,” says la Cerda, “when the Vulgate says, ‘and on that day he slaughtered eighty-five men.’ Perhaps he took it from Josephus, who nevertheless says that three hundred and eighty-five were killed. I suspect that they spoke of all Abimelech’s kindred.”

In fact, Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book VI, chapter 12, reports: “Saul orders Doeg the Syrian to slaughter them; and he, having taken with himself several villainous men like himself, kills Ahimelech and all his kindred; there were altogether about three hundred and eighty-five.” But some manuscripts present this number differently in Havercamp’s notes on Josephus: Vatican manuscript: *ἦσαν δ᾽ οἱ πάντες πέντε καὶ ὀγδοήκοντα*, “they were all eighty-five.” Busbecq manuscript: *ὡς πεντακόσιοι καὶ τριάκοντα*, “about five hundred and thirty.” Henneberg manuscript: *ὡς πέντε καὶ τριακόσιοι, πεντήκοντα καὶ τριάκοντα*, “about five over three hundred, fifty and thirty”—perhaps *πεντακόσιοι*, “five hundred,” and thirty.

Theodoret counts them as *πεντήκοντα καὶ τριακοσίους*, “three hundred and fifty”; Epiphanius and Zonaras have *ὡς πέντε καὶ τριακόσιοι*, “about three hundred and five”; and the Septuagint itself agrees with Lucifer in saying that *τριακοσίους καὶ πέντε*, “three hundred and five,” were killed. These facts sufficiently support Lucifer’s translation.

In the same place, p. 72 (col. 837): “Saul entered to the seat,” 1 Kings 24:4. On this passage la Cerda observes: “The Vulgate says ‘to relieve his bowels,’ an expression used by Cornelius Celsus. Vatablus has ‘to cover his feet’; to cover the feet is the same as to relieve the bowels, concerning which expression Drusius writes. Further, see how varied are the expressions for one meaning. Hebrew: ‘Saul entered to cover his feet.’ Septuagint: *καὶ εἰσῆλθε παρασκευάσασθαι*, ‘and he entered to make preparation,’ where Theodoret reads *ἀποσκευάσασθαι*, ‘to put off,’ and adds: ‘The Septuagint interpreted decorously; Aquila, however, expressed it more openly, for he says *εἰσῆλθε ἀποκενῶσαι*, “he entered to empty himself.”’”

Henri Estienne, in the *Treasury of the Greek Language*, suspects that the Septuagint interpreters originally wrote *ἀποσκευάσασθαι*; but the Royal manuscript reads *κενῶσαι*, “to empty,” from Aquila, as Procopius also had read it. Another translator in the Royal manuscript has *σεμνῶς ἄγειν*, “to act decently”; and the Coislin manuscript: *διευθύναι, ἀποκενῶσαι τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ, ἀποπατῆσαι*, “to set right, to evacuate his feet, to defecate.” This interpretation seems to have coalesced from several into one, Montfaucon says in the Hexapla. Yet all add Josephus’s interpretation, which Nobilius reported in these words: *τὰς φυσικὰς ἐκκρίσεις ποιήσασθαι*, “to perform the natural excretions.”

But in Havercamp’s edition, *Antiquities*, Book VI, chapter 12, we read: *ἐπειγόμενος οὖν ὑπὸ τῶν κατὰ φύσιν, εἴσεισιν εἰς αὐτὸ μόνος*—“therefore, impelled by the demands of nature, he entered it [the cave] alone.”

Jerome a Prato is mistaken when, in his notes on Sulpicius Severus, Book I of the *Sacred History*, he writes that Severus—or rather the very ancient Latin translator—translated the Greek word *παρασκευάσασθαι* as “to refresh the body,” from the Septuagint. Sabatier does not cite this translation in the Italic Version. Sulpicius follows not the words of Sacred Scripture but its sense, and narrates the events in an entirely personal Latin style and with his own expressions. For concerning Saul he says: “Saul, unaware, had gone aside at the entrance of the cave to refresh his body.”

In the same place: “He came to the flocks of sheep, which,” etc. Tilius notes that *qui* should be corrected—that is, “the flocks.” But this relative pronoun may refer to either antecedent; and, besides Lucifer’s exemplar, the Latin translation of the Septuagint retains the same wording in the Roman edition: “He came to the flocks of cattle, which,” etc.

IB. p. 75 (col. 841): “You limp in your judgment.” Cotelerius also calls this interpretation, from III Kings XVIII.21, into doubt in his note on Apostolic Constitutions VII.1 [Col. 0709A], suspecting that the translator had read in Greek ἐννοίαις, “thoughts,” instead of ἰγνύαις, “hams” or “knees.” But he read neither: for the singular Latin word *sensu*, “judgment,” corresponds to the singular ἐννοίᾳ. Nor did Cotelerius observe that the Greek noun ἰγνύα, used by the Septuagint, is said by Hesychius in his Lexicon to mean “mind,” or “the back part of the knee”: ἰγνύα, ψυχή, ἢ τὸ τοῦ γόνατος ὄπισθεν μέρος, “*ignya*: soul, or the part behind the knee.”

Heinsius aptly adds, in support of our view, the following on Hesychius’s testimony: “What have these two things in common, ἡ ψυχή καὶ τὸ γόνυ, ‘the soul and the knee’? Or who could understand this, unless he knew that there is an allusion, proverbially, to the celebrated passage III Kings XVIII.21: ἕως πότε ὑμεῖς χωλανεῖτε ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέραις ταῖς ἰγνύαις, ‘How long will you limp upon both ἰγνύαι?’” Since the Hebrew word in this passage signifies “thoughts,” some translators rendered it, ἕως [Col. 0709B] πότε χωλανεῖτε τῇ ψυχῇ, “How long do you limp in your soul?” The Chaldee renders it “sects,” “pursuits,” or “parties,” as do the Syriac and Arabic.

Some read Ψύα, “ham,” in Hesychius; Albert cites them in his notes on this passage of Hesychius, adding: “But Heinsius’s elegant interpretation pleases me.” Lucifer of Cagliari comes closer: “How long do you limp in your judgment?” Hence the most learned L. Bos conjectures that he read ἐννοίαις instead of ἰγνύαις; but Hesychius supports that interpretation.

Julius Pollux, in *Onomasticon* V.3, writes ἰγνύαν, meaning “the ham,” and various manuscripts give both ἰγνίαν and ἰγνύαν. But in Book II, chapter 4, one reads ἰγνύα and ἰγνύς, and then ἰγνύη, which he states is the hollow opposite the ham, that is, the hock. Hence the ancient translator of Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 6: “How long will you limp upon both hocks?” And the Septuagint: “How long will you limp [Col. 0709C] upon both hams?” Yet Lucifer’s translator correctly understood the Greek noun ἰγνύα as “mind” or “the judgment of the mind,” and, as we said, came closer to the Hebrew text. For it is of this kind: “How long are you limping over two thoughts?” Symmachus likewise gives its sense: ἕως πότε χωλανεῖτε ἐπὶ δύσιν ἀμφιβόλως, “How long do you limp ambiguously over two alternatives?” Then our Vulgate: “How long do you limp between two parties?” From this, I think, it is evident that Cotelerius’s criticism of Lucifer—and that of Nobilius before him—is to be regarded as worthless.

Ibid., p. 82 (col. 847): “In the first ways of his father,” from II Chronicles XVII.3. Latinius corrects this passage in a note, substituting “David” for “first,” as it stands in the Vulgate. But Lucifer’s translator correctly wrote, “in the first ways of his father.” For in II Chronicles XIV.2 Asa, Jehoshaphat’s [Col. 0709D] father, is said to have done what was good and right before the Lord his God at the beginning of his reign; and afterward he is said to have departed from the straight path of virtue in chapter XVI. Hence the Septuagint also: “He walked in the first ways of his father.” Theodoret appears to have followed them when, instead of “first,” he wrote κατ’ ἀρχάς, “from the beginning.”

Nevertheless, Nobilius affirms that in most books the reading is ἐν ὁδοῖς Δαβίδ, “in the ways of David.” In the *Sacred Critics*, vol. I, *Synopsis*, both readings are retained: “in the first ways of David his father”—that is, before David sinned; or “in the ways of David, the first [ways] of his father,” namely, those which were the first ways of Asa his father.

Ibid., finally, p. 103 (col. 869): for the word *defendam*, “I shall defend,” read in Zephaniah I.12—“I shall defend against the men” [Col. 0710A]—Latinius substituted *ulciscar*, “I shall avenge,” from the Vulgate. Learned critics nevertheless observe that Latin writers very properly use *defendere* in the sense of repelling or warding off harmful things. Caesar, in *The Civil War* I.7, having said that he complained of the injuries and violence inflicted both upon himself and upon the tribunes’ authority, adds that the soldiers cried out that they were ready “to defend the wrongs of their commander and of the tribunes of the people”—that is, to repel them, which in Passeratius has the same sense as “to avenge.” Heinsius defends this meaning at greater length in his notes on Ovid’s *Heroides* V.16, and Oudendorp in his note on Caesar’s *Gallic War* VIII.9.

Therefore Lucifer’s translator used the Latin word *defendere* in its proper sense, although the expression consequently becomes obscure, since it ought to have added that for which God was to exact vengeance—namely, the contempt shown to Him and the injury inflicted upon Him. [Col. 0710B] Enough thus far concerning the Luciferian translation.

§ II.—Theological Observation upon Certain Expressions of Lucifer

The plan of our work requires that we by no means pass over this discussion as well, since it is especially necessary for elucidating Lucifer’s works and explaining the purpose which he pursued in them. The titles of his books are indeed various; yet in them he strives exclusively to defend the actions performed by himself and the Catholic bishops at the Council of Milan in the year 355; then to reproach the emperor Constantius for the crimes which he had unjustly ordered to be committed against Catholics, so that the Arian heresy, widely spread by its contagion, might rage unpunished throughout the whole world; and finally openly to declare to all, even in written books, his abhorrence of this sect’s errors [Col. 0710C].

Yet he does not pursue this last object by constructing the disputations which were then extensively treated both in councils and by the other Fathers. Lucifer confesses the Catholic doctrine concerning the Trinity; he defends each point which the Arians had brought into controversy; he denounces the errors opposed to each; and he frequently and forcefully exhorts Constantius, to whom he addressed these books, to renounce them and embrace the Catholic Faith.

But we observe that Lucifer attacks especially the Arian doctrine as devised and put forward by its impious author. Of the many very different sects into which the Arian heresy was almost immediately divided from its beginning—such as the Eusebians, Eunomians, [Col. 0710D] Acacians, and above all the Semi-Arians—he seems to say scarcely anything, except of the Pneumatomachians, who will be discussed later.

Petavius briefly summarizes Arius’s impious doctrine in *On the Trinity* I.8, drawing it from Arius’s own words as set out in his *Thalia* in Athanasius’s *On the Synods*, and in his letters to Alexander of Alexandria and Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia. To make Lucifer’s expressions more plainly and deeply understood as directed wholly against Arian heresy, the following points concerning Arius’s doctrine must be set down.

Arius taught that God the Father had been God from eternity, but had not been Father from eternity; that He afterward produced the Son from nothing; that the Son was Son not by nature but by grace and adoption; and therefore was neither true Son nor true God except in title and by participation, but was a creature, though superior to the rest, whom God employed as a sort of minister for creating all other things. This is Arius’s impious and genuine profession of faith. Accordingly, Lucifer often sets against it such expressions as that the Father is truly Father from eternity and has a true Son; that the Son is true Son and true God [Col. 0711A]; that the Father and Son possess one eternity; and similar assertions concerning the identical goodness, power, and majesty of Father and Son. He very frequently reproaches Constantius with, and vigorously condemns, the common Arian formulas: “The Son is from nothing”; “there was a time when He was not”; “He was made from non-existent things”; and “the Son is adoptive.” These occur in the other books, but most frequently in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God* [Col. 0711B], in which he also copied out the Nicene Creed in full.

Furthermore, Arius openly taught that the Son was mutable by nature and naturally inclined toward evil, but exempted from among all creatures because God foresaw that He would possess steadfastness and constancy in the good. Athanasius states this from Arius’s writings near the beginning of his *Second Oration against the Arians*: that, as all things are subject to mutability by their nature, so the Word Himself was subject to mutability; that it was within His free choice to remain good as long as He wished; that His will could have changed after our manner because His nature was mutable; and that, since God foreknew that He would be good, He granted Him in advance the glory which a human being would later earn through virtue. As though His works, foreseen by God, already existed, God willed Him immediately to be such in the present [Col. 0711C].

Alexander the bishop bears the same witness in his letter to the Catholics, where he writes that Arius and his followers, convicted of impiety, were further asked: εἰ δύναται ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τραπῆναι ὡς ὁ διάβολος ἐτράπη· καὶ οὐκ ἐφοβήθησαν εἰπεῖν· Ναὶ δύναται, τρεπτὸς γὰρ φύσεώς ἐστι, γενητὸς καὶ τρεπτὸς ὑπάρχων· “Can the Word of God be changed, as the devil was changed? And they did not fear to say: ‘Yes, He can; for His nature is mutable, being created and changeable.’”

In this passage Valesius rightly judges that γενητὸς, “created,” ought to be read instead of γεννητὸς, “begotten,” as we too have written, and as, he says, it is read in Gelasius of Cyzicus. Nor does Epiphanius read otherwise, for he translates: “They say that He is made and changeable.” But γεννητὸς has a Catholic sense, concerning which see Petavius, Book V, chapter 1 [Col. 0711D]. “What follows,” Valesius adds, “καὶ τρεπτὸς, is better read in Gelasius as καὶ κτιστός, ‘and created,’ than in the reading which I followed in my translation.”

We have dwelt upon these matters in order to note Theophilus Alethinus’s criticism of Petavius at Book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8, no. 1. He says that Arius denied the mutability of the Word in his letter to Bishop Alexander, found in Epiphanius, *Heresy* LXIX, where he expressly calls the Son ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον, such that He can neither be converted nor changed. The same may also be read in the letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, which occurs in Theodoret’s *Ecclesiastical History* I.5.

But there was no reason for this Theophilus to defend Arius on this point [Col. 0712A]. For as many words as Arius uttered or wrote, so many evasions were there by which he fraudulently concealed his opinion, now denying, now affirming, now feigning and disguising it under a specious appearance of words, as is clearly evident from ecclesiastical history.

Lucifer, however, to whom Arian impiety was entirely plain, openly professes the Catholic truth against the heretic in *For St. Athanasius* I, p. 98 (col. 864): “For it was not possible for the only Son of God, God from God, because the Apostle said, ‘He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,’ to become other than what He is—incorruptible, ineffable, immutable—since He always remains in that state of eternal greatness in which His Father likewise remains.” He calls the Son “ineffable” in order to condemn another blasphemy of Arius, who in the *Thalia*, cited by Athanasius in *On the Synods*, taught that God the Father alone is ineffable and indescribable [Col. 0712B]: “God is ineffable to the Son, for He is to Himself what He is—that is, indescribable. For it is impossible for Him to investigate the Father as He is in Himself, since the Son Himself does not know His own substance.”

Lucifer repeats the same teaching, p. 108 (col. 875), in these words: “What else does the faith of the glorious Church maintain except that the only Son of God is immutable, unchangeable, beyond estimation, immeasurable, eternal, just as He is whose Son He is?”

But the chief point of Arian heresy consisted in denying, in one word, that the Son is consubstantial with the Father. Arius had openly written this in his *Thalia*, as though he foresaw how great would later be the force, effective meaning, and firm authority of this term for defending the divinity of the Word: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔστιν ἴσος, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ὁμοούσιος αὐτῷ, “For the Son is neither equal nor consubstantial with Him” [Col. 0712C], that is, with the Father. Therefore Lucifer, both in *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God* and in the other work entitled *That One Must Die, etc.*, defends the word ὁμοούσιος, “consubstantial,” and the Son’s perfect equality with the Father. He does this occasionally in the other books also, affirming that the divine properties belonging to God the Father, insofar as He is God, must likewise be attributed to the Son.

In *For St. Athanasius* I, we observe that Lucifer also employs the term ὁμοιούσιος, which signifies similarity of substance in the Son to the Father. Catholics sometimes used it in a Catholic sense, when by that term they understood the Son’s perfect similarity and equality to the Father. Thus Lucifer says that the Son is like and equal to the Father [Col. 0712D].

But Hilary of Poitiers, in his apologetic replies on behalf of his book *On the Synods*, testifies that he mentioned *homoiousion* unwillingly, and that he had to explain the force of this word because Lucifer proclaimed the Son’s similarity to the Father. These words require a somewhat fuller explanation than we provided in the note appended to Lucifer’s testimony.

Hilary wrote *On the Synods* approximately in the period between August 358 and May 359, as the Maurist monks observed in the preface to that work, no. 1. He undertook the work in order to explain to the bishops of Gaul, at whose request he wrote, his opinion concerning the creeds issued in the East, and concerning the words and phrases over whose interpretation the eastern bishops disagreed, so that the Catholic doctrine against Arian heresy might be clearly and safely expounded to them. Accordingly, he especially examines in that work the terms ὁμοούσιον and ὁμοιούσιον, showing at length what is the proper meaning of each and what is their true and Catholic interpretation [Col. 0713A].

Yet this work had brought Hilary into odium and suspicion with some, especially Lucifer, to whom these words of Hilary seem to have been less acceptable: “Having set forth a faithful and pious understanding of one substance, which in Greek is called *homoousion*, and of like substance, which is termed *homoiousion*, etc.” Lucifer seems to have maintained that the meaning of *homoiousion* which Hilary set forth was not merely pious but truly Catholic; nor could anyone be like another by nature without also being equal to him, as Hilary himself acknowledged that he understood in the same work: “I call God of heaven and earth to witness that, though I had heard neither term, I nevertheless always understood both in the sense in which *homoiousion* ought to be understood through *homoousion*.” That is, nothing can be like another according to nature unless it is from the same nature [Col. 0713B].

Thus Hilary writes to Lucifer in his apologetic reply to the critics of *On the Synods*: “I do not think anyone needs to be reminded here to consider why I spoke of a pious understanding of like substance, except because I understood that there was also an impious one. Therefore I said ‘like,’ not only ‘equal,’ but also ‘the same,’ so that I might neither disapprove the similarity which you, brother Lucifer, wished to be proclaimed, nor fail to remind readers that the only pious understanding of similarity is that which proclaims unity of substance” [Col. 0713C].

For Hilary knew the ambiguities to which the term *homoiousion* was liable; he said it should not be approved unless “similarity” signified perfect equality of substance. Lucifer nevertheless used it more confidently, so that those who had begun to recognize the impiety of the Arian error and wished to separate themselves from heretical communion might, attracted by the shared term, more willingly unite with Catholics—unless they had become entangled in the obscure and confused ambiguity of terms which they heard commonly used concerning the nature and substance of the divine Word according to each person’s private opinion and free interpretation.

Hilary further said that *homoiousion* should not be rejected merely because many abused its meaning. For not a few also interpreted *homoousion* wrongly, although the authority of the Nicene Council had approved both its sense and use. Nor could the decree of silence concerning *homoiousion* harm the Catholic interpretation of the term, since the Synod of Sirmium in 357 had also decreed silence concerning *homoousion* [Col. 0713D].

“But perhaps,” says Hilary, “someone will tell me: Some today of those who were then present at the Synod”—that is, at Nicaea; he plainly means Hosius, who approved silence concerning the term *homoousion* at the Council of Sirmium—“have decreed that *homoousion* should be kept silent. And I, though unwillingly, shall reply to him: Did they not likewise determine that *homoiousion* should be kept silent? I pray that no one besides the aged [Col. 0714A] Hosius, who loves his own tomb too much, may be found to think that silence should be kept about both. And to what refuge shall we turn amid such great frenzies of heretics, if we do not now receive both terms and retain both? For it cannot appear impious to say that, because neither is found written, either neither ought to be confessed, or both.”

But perhaps Lucifer did not approve the comparison drawn between the two terms. Their standing was very different. *Homoousion* rested upon the testimony of a most holy ecumenical council; *homoiousion* possessed no such authority. The former was the certain watchword of Catholics, although some distorted its explanation toward a corrupt sense; the latter was the mark of heretical men, who, after separating from the Arians, were called Semi-Arians because they rejected *homoousion* and taught *homoiousion* with the sense of imperfect similarity to the Father [Col. 0714B].

Hilary therefore replies in his *Apology*: “It can be known quite plainly, lord brother Lucifer, that I mentioned *homoiousion* unwillingly. But because you proclaimed the similarity of the Son to the Father, its demonstration had to be set forth by me without error.” It is clear from this that Lucifer allowed the term *homoiousion* to be admitted provided that it was understood in a Catholic sense. Hilary, however, in order to remove every ambiguity of language and ensure that communion in the same term might produce communion in the same faith and concord among minds at variance, demonstrates in a longer discussion what was the erroneous and what the correct signification of each term. Although unwillingly, he confirms by his own assent and testimony the use of *homoiousion* too, lest anything might hinder the establishment of the true Faith and the restoration of peace to the Church. Thus what Lucifer approved in a certain straightforward confidence of mind, Hilary supported with learned arguments and reasons [Col. 0714C].

Nor is the following inference slight: Lucifer composed his own works *For St. Athanasius* after Hilary’s *On the Synods*; prompted by its teaching and counsels, he joined “like” with “equal” in the testimony quoted above, so that both his meaning and the signification of the term might be clearer.

Moreover, Lucifer has other—and very weighty—expressions that plainly oppose the Arian error. Among them, the confession of one Godhead has the greatest force. He uses it very frequently in order to attack the impious heresy from every side [Col. 0714D]. For since Arius taught that, as regards substance, the Father was alien and external to the Son, it followed that their natures were entirely dissimilar and mutually separated. Yet, with his exceedingly crafty talent for deception, in the letter written to Bishop Alexander—which is found both in Athanasius’s *On the Synods* and Hilary’s *On the Trinity* IV—he says that he had not thereby divided the μονάδα, the “monad,” in the Godhead, as Sabellius had divided it, although Sabellius had asserted that Father and Son were one and the same.

But the heretic used this term in the sense of singularity, assigning a perfect and singular Godhead to the Father alone [Col. 0715A]. Hence the notion of “union”—for Hilary translates μονάδα in that way—denotes that union which rejects every communion of one with another. Arius, says Petavius, *On the Trinity* VIII.8.7, accused Sabellius of having divided the μονάς insofar as Sabellius believed that the same hypostasis assumed different persons—that is, qualities and functions—so that one and the same [God] acted now as Father, now as Son [Col. 0715B].

Here it should be observed that the editors of Hilary’s works did not grasp the meaning of the Arian expression. In their note on this passage in Hilary, vol. I, *On the Trinity* IV.12, they say that Sabellius divided the union in the Incarnation—that is, introduced into Christ a duality of persons. But later, in Book VI.11, they interpreted that passage about Sabellius differently in connection with Hilary’s words, “the division of that union divided the same God in the Virgin,” namely Sabellius. They add: “Since union is customarily referred to persons, this in itself means that the person in Christ was not singular, as we explained on p. 80, namely concerning Book IV, no. 12. Yet it seems preferable to understand it thus: Sabellius divided the union in the Virgin insofar as, after assuming flesh in her, he began to attribute the names Father and Son to the same God, increasing the number of names, not of persons.”

This agrees in some measure with Petavius, although Sabellius did not first distinguish these names of Father and Son in the Incarnation. Rather, the Son’s offices and actions, distinct from the Father’s, themselves distinguished them. Nor can the term “union” here be referred to persons, because in the Arian sense, as we have observed, it properly means singularity. The Greek μονάδα, which Hilary translates “union,” has rightly and truly been translated [Col. 0715C] by others as “unity,” or, to express its force more clearly, “oneness.” For what Latin calls *unio*, Greek calls ἕνωσις.

Furthermore, the assertion that Sabellius introduced a duality of persons in Christ is not to be approved. For, as Epiphanius reports in *Heresy* 62, that heretic said that the Son was sent forth from the Father into a human being as a ray of divinity, and that He accomplished all things pertaining to the redemption of humankind. But he did not acknowledge a true ἐνανθρώπησις, or Incarnation, only a mere ἐνέργεια, an operation of divinity in the human being Christ, as Petavius says in *On the Incarnation* I.3.7. For the notion that the person of the Father assumed a human being and that the Father suffered in the human being—whence arose the Patripassians—was the distinctive heresy of Noetus and the Noetians, concerning which see Epiphanius, *Heresy* 57.

Indeed, in the slightly earlier note on Hilary’s words in *On the Trinity* VI.11 [Col. 0715D]—“The Arians, wishing there to be nothing one between Father and Son, charge Sabellius with the crime of having divided the union”—the same editors wrote wrongly that it was Sabellius’s distinctive and universally recognized heresy to proclaim union in God, while it was less well known that he divided union in Christ. They say that Arius deceitfully expressed the latter, not the former, in order that he might condemn Catholics together with Sabellius as persons who abhorred union in God and professed equality in nature of distinct persons.

For Arius defended himself solely by craftiness and verbal disguise. By advancing the doctrine of Sabellian heresy as an accusation, he aimed only to make it appear that he himself affirmed unity of the Godhead by the deceptive word μονάς [Col. 0716A], which he boasted Sabellius had divided. For Sabellius attributed, in an undivided substance, the same Godhead of the Father to Him who in the sacred books is called the Son; this Arius wholly denied.

Therefore the meaning of the Arian monad was that the Father alone is God by nature and essence, while the Son, alien to the Father, obtained divinity only in name and by a certain participation of rank. Thus the double-faced heretic did not deny one God, having separated the Son from the Father’s Godhead; and he denied one God when he advanced, in some fashion, two gods—one by essence and the other by grace.

To this, then, belong Lucifer’s expressions in which he repeatedly affirms throughout his books that the Father and His only Son have one Godhead; that Catholics claim one Godhead for the Father and His only Son; that they defend the proposition that the Godhead of the Father and His only Son is one; and that the Father and Son possess one Godhead [Col. 0716B]. Those repeated formulations declare that the Godhead which Arius called one, but in the Father alone, is one and the same in Father and Son; and hence that the nature of each is one and the same.

Petavius also used these testimonies of Lucifer in *On the Trinity* IV.14 to establish from the Latin Fathers the singularity of the divine essence: “Lucifer of Cagliari, Hilary’s equal, more than once affirms one Godhead of Father and Son, and that the divine Trinity is perfect and possesses one substance,” in *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God* and *That One Must Die for the Son of God*.

The force of the term *Deitas*, “Godhead,” is indeed so great that, as Petavius observes in *On the Trinity* VIII.8.7, several Fathers maintain that Godhead or divinity is μονάς—that is, unity—and the most perfect unity, namely numerical unity. He presents their testimonies in Book XIV, chapter 13, no. 5 [Col. 0716C]. Thus “one Godhead” means the same as “unity of divinity”; and since this belongs properly to nature, it signifies unity of essence. Lucifer expressed this more forcefully, ἐνεργικῶς, “with operative force,” in *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, when he writes that Christians believe that the Father and Son have one eternity because they have one Godhead.

Nor should it be passed over in silence here that something escaped us when, in *On Not Associating with Heretics*, p. 16 (here col. 780), we noted concerning Lucifer’s words “concerning God’s counsel”—which had formerly been read in Tilius’s edition—that according to Latinius and the Vatican manuscript, “concerning God’s Son,” or, as the same manuscript has it, “concerning the only Son of God,” should be read [Col. 0716D]. For the expression “concerning God’s counsel” is correct and true, and exceptionally effective for defending Catholic doctrine against Arian deceptions.

For Arius had taught in his *Thalia* that the Son, since He is Son, truly came to exist by the Father’s will. He therefore argued that the Son was later than the Father, since He had a beginning. He confirmed this in his letter to Bishop Alexander, writing that God begot the Son . . . “born not merely in appearance but truly, obedient to His will,” as it is read in Hilary, *On the Trinity* IV. In Athanasius, *On the Synods*, the Latin translator expresses the thought thus: “God, who begot the Son . . . did not make Him or conceive Him merely in opinion, but caused Him truly to subsist by His own will.” The Greek is [Col. 0717A]: οὐ δοκήσει, ἀλλὰ ἀληθείᾳ ὑποστήσαντα ἰδίῳ θελήματι, “not in appearance, but truly subsisting by His own will.”

On this point the ancient Fathers sometimes disputed among themselves. Some taught that the Son was begotten naturally and without will; others, that He was begotten not by necessity but by will.
