Petavius excellently explains and reconciles their views in *On the Trinity* VI.8.22: both in fact admit a will which is necessary, and exclude from the generation of the Son that will which is free, joined with deliberation and the power of either alternative. Arius’s teaching principally aimed at this latter point, most impiously asserting that in the Father there was a free will for generating the Son [Col. 0717B].

“Therefore,” to use Petavius’s words in no. 21, “some of the ancients defended themselves against the Arian evasion by this argument: they said that the Son is the Father’s very will and His very counsel [Col. 0717C]; from this they inferred that the Father was not prior to Him, because He could not exist without will and counsel.” A number of Fathers used this argument, whom Petavius there enumerates, especially Cyril of Alexandria in *Thesaurus* VII: “The Son,” he says, “is the living counsel of the Father, through whom He made all things. Therefore, if He is the Father’s counsel and will, how can will precede His generation?”

Augustine praises this way of speaking in *On the Trinity* XV.20, though he judges it more correct to say “counsel from counsel, will from will.” “Some,” he says, “lest they should call the only-begotten Word the Son of God’s counsel or will, said that the Word Himself is the Father’s counsel or will. But, in my judgment, it is better to say counsel from counsel and will from will, just as substance from substance and wisdom from wisdom.”

From these points it is evident how correct Lucifer’s expression is, how well suited to frustrating and repelling Arius’s snares and deceptions, and why it ought therefore to be restored to its proper place.

A second original and equally impious doctrine of the Arian heresy, which its author wickedly disseminated, was this: that the Holy Spirit is a creature created by the Son, as Petavius reports in book I, chapter 14, no. 13, on the authority of Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 69, and Augustine, *On Heresies* 69. Arius indeed had written in the *Thalia* that the Trinity is not of like majesty, [Col. 0717D] and that their hypostases are mutually unmixed; or, as Athanasius interprets the heretic’s meaning in *Oration 2 against the Arians*, that the substances of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are reciprocally alien and incommunicable. Hence the Arians were called “Triusians” by Fulgentius in his *Reply to the Seventh Arian Objection*, because they boasted that there are three distinct essences in the Trinity and that one is more perfect than another.

Petavius rightly conjectures, moreover, that Arius did not openly teach his blasphemy against the Holy Spirit from the beginning. No mention of it occurs either in his letters and pamphlets or in Alexander’s letter against Arius; and the Nicene Council made no particular decree concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, because this question had not yet then been raised, as Basil says in Epistle 78, otherwise 125. But as the seeds of impiety gradually grew—seeds first cast by Arius, the author of the heresy, and afterward nurtured to the destruction of the Churches by those who wickedly adopted his errors—the very course of that impiety burst forth into blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly Lucifer, pursuing in Emperor Constantius the impiety of this most unjust doctrine, as in the most powerful patron of Arian heresy, reproaches Constantius with this in the book *On Not Meeting with Heretics*: “As soon as you occupied Italy, you attempted to overthrow its Church. You said that God the Father was not the true God the Father, denying His only Son and asserting that He was not the true Son; you further maintained that the Holy Paraclete Spirit had been made from nothing, that He came down from nothing.” But in his other books he maintains that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son in eternity, power, greatness, and dominion. Thus, in book I *For St. Athanasius*, he says that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess one power; and in book II, that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess one eternity, as the sacred Scriptures proclaim. And in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*: “When you begin to recognize that we rightly confess one eternity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; when you begin to see that there is one greatness and one power in the Father, in His only Son, and in the Holy Paraclete Spirit,” etc. These statements have the greatest force for signifying that the Holy Spirit has the same nature and divinity as the Father and the Son, especially in view of the accompanying titles “Holy” and “Paraclete,” as Petavius demonstrates on the authority of the ancient Fathers in book II, chapter 13.

[Col. 0718C] Above all, however, Lucifer deserves praise because he was one of the few who, while Arian heresy raged under Constantius, openly and expressly bore witness to the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Petavius also used his authority in book III, chapter 7, no. 14, when rejecting John Crellius’s argument against the Holy Spirit, drawn from ancient Fathers whom that new Arian claimed had never called the Holy Spirit by the name of God down to the age of Hilary of Poitiers. Petavius gathers numerous testimonies from the writings of the ancient Fathers which clearly attest the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and defends Hilary himself against the calumnies heaped upon him and his books *On the Trinity* by Erasmus and Crellius himself. He then adds: “Lucifer of Cagliari, Hilary’s contemporary, says: ‘One is the divine sublimity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.’”

But this testimony is of no use to Petavius, for there is an error of punctuation here, as the passage is read in the Tilian edition: “unless there is one sublimity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, remaining in the blessed Apostle,” etc. This error has been removed in the present new edition on the authority of Latinius, who judges that a full stop should be placed after the word “Son,” and rightly so. For Lucifer, p. 25 (here col. 1025), introduces the following in the form of questions: “What is meant by: ‘Who, being in the form of God’? Unless the Son inhabits the same inaccessible light as the Father; unless there is one divine sublimity of Father and Son. The Holy Spirit, remaining in the blessed Apostle,” etc.

There are, however, other expressions of Lucifer [Col. 0719A] which more clearly indicate the divinity of the Holy Spirit and expressly call Him truly God. In *On Not Meeting with Heretics* he writes: “The apostolic faith confesses a perfect Trinity and acknowledges one divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit”; and again, “one divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” In book I *For St. Athanasius* he likewise calls it one divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and in book II he says that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess one divinity.

We say that Lucifer was one of the few who in those times openly and plainly professed the divinity of the Holy Spirit. This is confirmed by Petavius and by the Maurist monks in the Preface to volume III of the Works of St. Basil. “Some,” he says, “otherwise Catholics, at the same period did not permit the Holy Spirit to be openly and plainly called God; and they protested against those who dared to call Him so as though they were enemies of the Catholic faith. Others, although they did not doubt that He was God, yet from zeal for peace and concord, and lest they offend these ill-disposed persons, did not publicly profess it at all.” Basil refutes the former in *On the Holy Spirit* and in Epistle VIII, otherwise 141, written in A.D. 360. The latter, however, Basil himself sometimes imitated, chiefly for two reasons. The first was to have regard for the weak; the second, to deprive the raging heretics of an opportunity to disturb and devastate Cappadocia, as the Maurist editors state in the cited Preface, no. 3, where they defend Basil’s policy at length and with learning.

But Lucifer, fervent in spirit as he was and endowed with remarkable freedom of speech, had regard solely for the cause of faith. By every means in his power—by deed, word, or writing—he strove with all the force of his talent to testify publicly to it without any ambiguity of expression, in order to compel the Arians to renounce the impious doctrines of their heresy. Therefore Athanasius deservedly wrote the following of Lucifer’s faith and teaching in his second letter to him: “Who, except the Arians, does not clearly see in your teaching the true faith, and the stain of the Arians? Very greatly and admirably, as light is separated from darkness, so have you separated truth from the cunning and hypocrisy of the heretics; you have defended the Catholic Church and proved that Arian words are nothing but a phantom.” Ambrose also praises the integrity of Lucifer’s faith in *On the Death of His Brother Satyrus*, declaring that he left behind him heirs of that faith; and Faustinus and Marcellinus warmly commend it in the *Book of Petitions*, etc.

## § III.—A Critical Question concerning Certain Passages of Lucifer

As regards this part of the Preface, the matters which we said ought to be examined here concerning the number of bishops present at the Council of Milan in A.D. 355, in the note appended to p. 11 (here col. 777, note a), may now be seen treated in Lucifer’s *Life* itself, as a more suitable place; likewise the matters which Lucifer writes so frequently concerning the edict of Emperor Constantius, especially at the beginning of the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*.

The first place in this question belongs, then, to Lucifer’s judgment concerning Emperor Constantine, whom he taints with the stain of Arian error in *On Apostate Kings*, p. 39 (here col. 804). There he makes Constantius say: “Unless my father had done well to join himself to the Arians, we his sons would not reign.” Lucifer offers no reply in defense of Constantine’s cause. Then, in book I *For St. Athanasius*, p. 91 (here col. 857), he says to Constantius: “For you yourself are witness that Athanasius was sent into exile because of the faith which the Church has always held and still holds, because he refused to condemn it, because indeed he refused to be an Arian. It has not escaped you that Athanasius was held in hatred by your father for that reason, since you too deign to persecute him for the same cause for which your father persecuted him.” And in book II he declares that he would unjustly have condemned Athanasius had he obeyed the will of Constantius and his father.

Hence Baronius, under A.D. 336, no. 14, deservedly rebukes Lucifer, since he wrote things utterly at variance with truth. But under A.D. 324, where he discusses Constantine’s Roman baptism, no. 51, he says: “We know that Emperor Constantine suffered the reproach of heresy in Lucifer of Cagliari because he had ordered St. Athanasius into exile. But we give more credit to Athanasius himself, who frequently excuses him and, after his death, calls Constantine pious, of blessed memory, and most religious, in *Oration I against the Arians* and the *Apology to Constantius*, and then in the Letter to the Solitaries, in which he attributes the cause of his exile to the fraud and snares of the Arians.”

Indeed, many ancient Fathers praise Constantine’s Catholic sentiments and their conformity with the true faith. Hilary, in book I *Against Constantius*, calls this rebel the heir of his father’s piety; and Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69, likewise reproaches Constantius for not proceeding according to his father’s faith. Yet there were some who, from the events then taking place, readily formed suspicions concerning the integrity of Constantine’s faith, being insufficiently informed about affairs. Athanasius’s exile, and Constantine’s approval—through Eusebian deceit—of Arius’s restoration to Catholic communion, quite understandably kept everyone’s minds doubtful in so grave a matter. Therefore, as he approached death, Constantine is said by Eusebius in his *Life of Constantine*, book IV, chapter 62, to have uttered these words: “Μὴ δὴ οὖν ἀμφιβολία τις γίγνηται”—“Let there therefore be no further doubt.”

The sense of these words is sufficiently obscure. Valesius adds in his notes: did Constantius mean to say, “Let all now cease to doubt me, whether I am truly a Christian; let no one henceforth suspect that I embraced the faith of Christ only in words and not with the affection of my inmost heart”? Although the Greek word *amphibolia* (ἀμφιβολία) may here be taken for *anabolē* (ἀναβολή), that is, “all delay, all postponement, is removed”; and this interpretation better coheres with the preceding discussion of baptism delayed until death.

Thus Baronius excuses Lucifer under A.D. 336: “Moreover, being wholly ignorant of the events then occurring, because he knew that Constantine, persuaded by the Eusebians and likewise by the Arians, had banished Athanasius into Gaul, he fully believed this had happened because Constantine had adopted the Arian heresy; and he did not cease too heedlessly to declaim against him.” Furthermore, reports then circulating publicly increased suspicion against Constantine: that he had received Arian baptism from Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, a man of suspect religion who attended the dying emperor; and that he had entrusted his will to a certain presbyter who praised Arius, whom his sister Constantia, when dying, had commended to him as a good man, as Sozomen writes in book II, chapter 34. We should therefore not wonder that Lucifer fell into an opinion which, as commonly happens, he heard spread by the words and general agreement of others in private conversations.

Jerome indeed wrote the following concerning Constantine in his *Chronicle*: “At the end of his life Constantine, baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, inclines toward the Arian doctrine.” These words occur in all published copies of this *Chronicle* and in seven Vatican manuscripts, as Pontacus observed in notes on this passage. One Lodonian manuscript, however, records the same words thus: “At the end of his life Constantine was baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia; Eusebius inclines toward the Arian doctrine.” The Alcobacian manuscript and one Vatican manuscript name Constantius instead of Constantine; but Constantius was baptized far from Nicomedia by Euzoius, an Arian bishop, according to Athanasius in *On the Synods*.

Baronius, under A.D. 324, believes that these words of the Hieronymian *Chronicle* should be expunged as falsely attributed to Jerome. Pontacus, however, did not dare do this against the evidence of the manuscript codices, although he follows Baronius’s view that Constantine received only one baptism, at Rome, through the ministry of Pope Sylvester. It is certainly not our task to enter upon this controversy, pursued with great partisan zeal on both sides among ecclesiastical writers—whether Constantine received baptism at Nicomedia or at Rome. Daniel Papebroch, however, in the Historical Commentary on St. Constantine the Great, Emperor, for 21 May in the *Bollandists*, chapter 2, defends the Nicomedian baptism against Baronius and gives Jerome’s words this interpretation: “That is, Constantine appeared to incline toward the opinion of those who held that the word *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος, ‘of one substance’) should be avoided, not because it was heretical but because it was novel and therefore gave offense to those who professed complete adherence to the Nicene faith, and who persuaded the emperor that those called Arians would return to concord if that word were suppressed.” And similarly Jerome elsewhere wrote, concerning the confession of Valens and Ursacius which was Catholic in appearance: “The whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian.”

This is Papebroch’s defense of Jerome; it cannot be applied to Lucifer, nor to Isidore’s testimony in his *Chronicle*, which runs as follows: “At the end of his life Constantine, baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, converted to the Arian doctrine. Alas and woe! good in his beginning, evil in his end”; or, according to another reading, “good in his beginning and evil in his end.” Jacobus Breulius adds in his notes: “Cedrenus learnedly refutes this opinion in the *Compendium of History*, in the life of Constantine.” Yet although these writers erred, an error arising solely from common popular report greatly lessens the blame of those who erred; and we think this happened to Lucifer and Isidore. On the veneration of St. Constantine the Great among the Greeks, see Papebroch in the cited place.

It is much more difficult to explain Lucifer’s meaning in the passage of *On Apostate Kings*, p. 40 (here col. 805), where in plain words he compares Jehoshaphat, the most holy king of Judah, with Constantius and manifestly calls each sacrilegious: “When you consider also that the son of Baasha reigned among the Jews for thirty-five years, though he was sacrilegious like you.”

There is indeed an error in the name Baasha, whether through the translator’s or copyist’s fault, since in the sacred books Jehoshaphat’s father is everywhere called Asa, and by Josephus in book VIII, chapter 2 and following of the *Jewish Antiquities*, Asanus and Assanus, without any variation in the ancient manuscripts. Lucifer also erred in recording the years assigned to Jehoshaphat’s reign. The thirty-five years which he counts in his reign are years of age, which Jehoshaphat had attained when he came to the throne, as is clear from 2 Chronicles 20 in the Septuagint: “Καὶ ἐβασίλευσεν Ἰωσαφὰτ ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰουδὰν, ὢν ἐτῶν τριακοντάπεντε ἐν τῷ βασιλεῦσαι αὐτόν”—“And Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah, being thirty-five years old when he began to reign.” The Vulgate confirms this in the same place. But that he reigned twenty-five years is likewise attested by the Septuagint, both in the same chapter of 2 Chronicles—“καὶ εἴκοσι καὶ πέντε ἔτη ἐβασίλευσεν,” “and he reigned twenty-five years”—and in 1 Kings, chapter 16; the Vulgate agrees, as does Josephus in book IX, chapter 3, who writes that this king died at the age of sixty, having reigned twenty-five years. Hence Latinius rightly conjectures that Lucifer did not grasp the meaning of this testimony, so clear in the sacred books.

There is no doubt, moreover, that Lucifer meant Jehoshaphat in the words which he transcribes from the sacred text and which concern this king, 1 Kings 16 in the Septuagint: “And in the eleventh year of Omri Jehoshaphat son of Asa reigned … and he walked in the way of Asa his father, and did not depart from it, doing what was right in the sight of the Lord. Only he did not remove the high places. They sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.” These words are repeated in chapter 22: “And he walked in all the way of Asa his father; he did not depart from it, doing what was right in the eyes of the Lord. Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places. The people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.”

These things are surely said in praise of this most pious king, except that he allowed the Hebrew people to frequent the impious rites of the gods and did not utterly destroy the profane groves and the shrines of deities erected in them. Lucifer therefore seems to have thought that he had found a reason to compare Jehoshaphat with Constantius: namely, so that Constantius should not find it strange, if, while persecuting the Catholic faith in support of the Arian heresy, he nevertheless enjoyed a tranquil and long-lasting reign, since King Jehoshaphat too, by permitting the worship of idols through excessive indulgence toward the people, provoked against himself the avenging wrath of God, yet still obtained long-lasting prosperity in his kingdom.

Nor is a comparison actually made between the guilt of the two men, but between the prosperous course of life enjoyed by each. Constantius, indeed, was truly sacrilegious and had already deserved from God the punishments due to him; and Jehoshaphat, who tolerated the people’s sacrileges, would have deserved punishment by a just chastisement for his fault. In the Book of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 49, verse 5, we read: “Except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all the kings of Judah committed sin.” Lucifer, observing this and carried away by the force of vehement passion, called Jehoshaphat sacrilegious in order to rebuff Constantius’s empty boastfulness, which trusted in the example even of a pious king. He ascribes to Jehoshaphat the sin of allowing the people’s sacrilege, in these words: “Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places.” Yet elsewhere, in book I *For St. Athanasius*, p. 81 (here col. 847), he praises Jehoshaphat as a king of Judah devoted to God and expounds at length his praises as a man devoted to God. Thus we have thought Lucifer’s meaning in this passage should be explained, so that every doubt about his reverence toward the sacred books, which celebrate this king’s piety in many places, and every contradiction with those books may be removed.

It is worth adding here another passage of Lucifer in which, comparing King Manasseh of Judah also with Constantius, he threatens the emperor in *On Apostate Kings*, p. 46 (here col. 811): “Do not spare yourself so as to turn yourself toward God; do not correct your wicked deeds, and you will find yourself tortured with Manasseh.” If we wish to understand this as referring to Manasseh’s eternal punishment, it surely does not accord with what the sacred writings testify concerning this king’s repentance in 2 Chronicles 33: “After he was distressed, he prayed to the Lord his God and repented greatly before the God of his fathers. He entreated Him and earnestly implored Him; and He heard his prayer, restored him to Jerusalem and to his kingdom, and Manasseh knew that the Lord Himself was God.”

The same passage narrates with praise the pious and holy deeds he performed in his kingdom. From this one may see that Manasseh’s repentance was sincere and that the forgiveness granted him by God was approved, as Calmet also observes on 2 Kings, chapter 21. Indeed, after undertaking a religious way of life, we do not read that he ever again departed from it. Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book X, chapter 3, records the following concerning Manasseh: “But having in these matters changed for the better, he spent the rest of his life in such a way that from that time he was considered most blessed and worthy of imitation, since he began to cultivate piety toward God.”

It is true that when Manasseh reigned after his captivity, the people sacrificed on high places to the Lord their God in an unlawful worship. But, Calmet adds at verse 17, this misfortune befell that king: he possessed less authority than was needed to abolish the abuse, although he commanded Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel, as the sacred writer testifies at verse 16. It certainly does not follow from this that God imposed eternal punishment upon Manasseh. Since nothing may be affirmed on that subject, the divine books being wholly silent, it is more fitting, in our judgment, to interpret Lucifer’s passage as threatening Constantius with temporal punishment, just as Manasseh, deposed from his kingdom, underwent a long and most grievous captivity among the Babylonians.

The final passage of Lucifer requiring particular notice concerns Elijah. In book I *For St. Athanasius*, p. 80 (here col. 845), he writes: “Behold Elijah, translated to enjoy the eternal friendships of God; and now Ahab is tormented in the outer darkness. Elijah is rejoicing in God’s friendships, and Ahab is paying everlasting penalties. Athanasius will without doubt be at the banquet where Elijah is, and you will be in that place of torments,” etc. “Is this wisdom: that you chose the eternal misery of King Ahab rather than enjoy the perpetual happiness which Elijah has attained?”

These words certainly appear to indicate that Elijah has already attained the eternal happiness of heavenly glory. Many opinions indeed are reported among sacred interpreters and theologians concerning the place to which Elijah was translated. But the Church has never designated a definite abode in which Elijah and Enoch dwell, as Calmet says on 2 Kings 11. And St. Augustine, book II *On Original Sin*, chapter 3; St. Chrysostom, Homily 21 on Genesis and Homily 22 on the Epistle to the Hebrews; and Theodoret, Question 45 on Genesis, disapprove the license of those who, amid such silence of the Scriptures on this matter, boldly pronounce an opinion in the manner of teachers.

Some Hebrews, whose views Munster and Vatablus report, believed that Elijah had truly been caught up into heaven itself, namely Paradise, and that his garments and body had been consumed in the sphere of fire. Yet the authority of Josephus alone can refute them. “At about the same time,” he says in *Jewish Antiquities*, book IX, chapter 2, “Elijah was removed from human sight; and to this day no one knows what became of him.”

Nevertheless, among Christian writers there were some persuaded that Enoch and Elijah are blessed with complete glory of soul and body. Procopius of Gaza thus holds that in his Commentary on Genesis, affirming that both behold the divine essence and reign with Christ in glorified bodies. Procopius was followed by Augustine of Eugubium in the *Recognition of the Old Testament* on Genesis 2, and Catharinus in the treatise *On the Consummation of Christ’s Glory*. Against them Francisco Suárez argues most fully in section 1, disputation 55, on the Third Part of St. Thomas, question 19, article 3, volume XVII of the Works.

Perhaps they were led to this opinion both by the testimony of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 44, where it is read, “Enoch was translated into Paradise,” and by expressions of certain Fathers not unlike Lucifer’s. Jerome, for example, in his letter to Pammachius calls Enoch and Elijah inhabitants of Paradise, enjoying divine fellowship and heavenly bread, nourished by every word of God, having the same Lord as both Lord and food. Ambrose, in book *On Naboth*, chapter 15, likewise writes, as Lucifer does, that Elijah was crowned with an eternal reward.

But as regards the place in which both dwell, Suárez excellently proves from the authority of the Fathers that it is some hidden region of the earth, yet a most excellent and blessed one, suited to their condition—whether finally it be the earthly Paradise or a region like it. As to the life they live, it must altogether be held that, their bodies being incorrupt by divine power and free from concupiscence and human miseries, they enjoy by faith and an abstract knowledge of God the contemplation and love of God. Many Fathers assert this when they deny that the two have attained the eternal blessedness of the heavenly kingdom.

The same Suárez teaches in volume I of his Works, book II, chapter 30, that it is not absolutely impossible for a person in a mortal body to be raised in mind to see God, although under the common law and power the clear vision of the divine essence is not granted to mortal persons. If it seems to have been granted to anyone, such as Moses and St. Paul, they deserved to receive it only for a brief time and, as it were, in passing; for that any person, throughout the whole time of mortal life or for any considerable part of it, should have possessed that vision permanently and immutably—in this sense it is certain that no dispensation has been made.

Therefore, to return from this to Lucifer, his words must be understood as signifying a certain extraordinary perfection of divine contemplation, just as Suárez explains Jerome’s testimony. Lucifer, like Ambrose, wrote by a kind of prolepsis that Elijah is already united to the truly eternal friendship of God at that banquet where Athanasius will without doubt be, because in his translation he was confirmed in grace and goodness and, according to Suárez, lives secure in the future possession of blessed eternity.

Moreover, the following four arguments readily persuade us that these two men have not obtained eternal glory: first, bodies do not enter there except after being glorified; second, the entrance into heaven had not yet been opened; third, Christ alone is the firstfruits of those who rise; and lastly, each of them, shortly before the world’s end and consummation, will foretell the coming of the divine Judge—a view that is either an article of faith or very close to the faith—and will suffer death in a glorious contest against Antichrist. On this, see especially Suárez cited above, section 2 of the said disputation 55.

Having disposed of these matters, it remains finally for us to inquire:

## § IV.—On the Time at Which Lucifer’s Several Books Were Written

Accordingly, with regard to the letter which Lucifer wrote to Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, urging him to attend the Council already assembled at Milan, we readily conjecture that it was sent about April of the year 355. For Pagius, in his *Critique of Baronius* for that year, observes from book of Theophilus, patriarch of Alexandria, *On the Conduct and Particular Life of the Saints Pachomius and Theodore*, chapter 4, that Athanasius was condemned before 25 May at that council, which must therefore already have been convened in April. Eusebius, after all, still remained at Vercelli when he received letters from the Arian bishops in the name of the entire Council and then from Lucifer; finally moved by Constantius’s letter, and after replying to it, he set out conveniently for Milan. There he remained for ten days before being summoned into the council to subscribe Athanasius’s condemnation.

Baronius, under that year, judges that Lucifer’s letter to Eusebius was written after Constantius’s letter. But Eusebius himself replied to Constantius that he had also received letters from his brethren and fellow bishops, “who have thought fit to communicate this to me, so that,” he adds, “after receiving a full report through those whom I judged it necessary to obey your command in this matter, I might hasten to Milan.” Yet he arrived there compelled by Constantius’s command, as Hilary indicates in book I *To Constantius*, and was called into the Council ten days after his arrival:

“Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, is a man serving God throughout his whole life. After the Synod of Arles, when Bishop Paulinus had opposed such great crimes of these men, he was ordered to come to Milan. When the synagogue of the wicked had already assembled there, he was forbidden for ten days to approach the church, while perverse malice spent itself against so holy a man. Then, when all their plans had come to a head, he was summoned when they pleased.”

If one compares together these chronological indications and the intervals necessarily occurring between the first letter of the Arians to Eusebius in the Council’s name, the second from Lucifer, and the third from Constantius, together with Eusebius’s delay and journey and Athanasius’s condemnation itself, one will surely recognize that Lucifer’s letter to Eusebius must be assigned to April. It follows that the Council of Milan did not begin precisely at the very opening of 355, as Constantius states, following what he calls the opinion of learned men, in the note appended to Liberius’s letter to Lucifer; rather, it must have begun either toward the end of March or at the beginning of April. This is also how we understand Pagius’s words in the cited passage, where he writes that the Council of Milan was held at the beginning of the current year 355.

After the Council of Milan had ended about May, and Lucifer and the other Catholic bishops had been condemned to exile, Pope Liberius of Rome wrote his letter to them, which in our edition immediately follows the Luciferian letter. Baronius, under A.D. 355, believes that when Liberius learned what had been done to them, he promptly sent these letters to each of them from Rome, before he himself was taken to Milan to the emperor. Constantius, in the appended note, places their composition about the middle of 355.

We can establish nothing certain in this matter, since the very wording of the letter seems to contain some ambiguity. It calls them martyrs destined for future glory, then adds: “I know that I offer you more probable consolations if you believe that I have been cast into exile together with you. Finally, I am greatly grieved that I still hang in anxious expectation, because a harsher necessity meanwhile separates me from your fellowship. For I had wished to be expended before all of you,” etc. And: “Because you have been made nearer to God, raise me up by your prayers … so that we may be able to bear tolerably the assaults that come upon us, which, as they are announced day by day, inflict more grievous wounds.”

Thus Liberius had heard, when he wrote this, that exile had been decreed for Lucifer and the other bishops. He affirms that in inward disposition he is in exile together with them, which he had wished to undergo before them himself; but he remains suspended in uncertain expectation, foreseeing storms and assaults threatening him and preparing his mind to endure increasingly serious evils. All this may rightly be assigned to the time when, immediately after the Council, the eunuch Eusebius was sent by Constantius to Rome to compel Liberius, at the emperor’s order, into communion with the Arians and to force him to condemn Athanasius. A fierce storm then arose against the Catholic Romans. Shortly afterward Liberius, with great difficulty and in the middle of the night, could be conveyed to Milan about June, against the will of the people, who burned with love for him and made his removal difficult through fear; he had been ordered by Constantius to be sent there, as Marcellinus says in book XV, chapter 7.

Therefore we agree with Baronius concerning the place and with both him and Coustant concerning the time at which the letter was written. Hilary, in his *Fragments*, volume II of the Maurist edition of his Works, placed the following before Liberius’s letter in Fragment VI: “Before Liberius went into exile, he wrote this identical letter to the confessors, that is, to Eusebius, Dionysius, and Lucifer, who were in exile.” But the words “before he went into exile” cannot be understood to mean that Liberius wrote the letter after his journey to Milan and after he had already been condemned to exile. In it he declares his desire that the Lord may deem him worthy to be made equal to them, namely in the merit and honor of martyrdom. Nor is it likely that Lucifer, like the others, had by then reached Cappadocia, the first place of his exile and very far from Milan, while Liberius was still living at Rome.

Thus, by the phrase “who were in exile,” Hilary indicates that the penalty of exile had been decreed against them; or else, being himself an exile and little informed concerning the events in Italy, he thought that Liberius’s letters had been written when the holy confessors had taken up their places in the several destinations of exile. Whether Lucifer and the other bishops were still at Milan, or were being led on their journey to the places of exile assigned to each, when Liberius wrote; and whether each of them received Liberius’s letters—nothing whatever can be determined even by conjecture. This, however, is certain on the authority of Ammianus Marcellinus, Baronius, Petavius, and Pagius: Liberius was driven into exile at Beroea in the same year, 355, not in 356, as Henry Valesius supposed in his notes on Socrates, book II, chapter 37.

After these events Lucifer, now an exile, unconquered in spirit amid the most grievous hardships of banishment and inflamed with a vehement zeal for defending the Catholic religion, first wrote a book to Constantius entitled *On Not Associating with Heretics*. In it he devotes himself wholly to proving, in a weighty style of speech and by accumulated examples, testimonies, and authorities from the sacred Scriptures, that it had been sinful for himself and the Catholic bishops to agree with the Arians [Col. 0727D] at the Council of Milan. He knew their deceptions and unjust schemes, and that it had been wrong for himself and the Catholic bishops to be authors of the peace which the Emperor, with wicked and feigned intent, was striving to bring about between the two parties. Read especially the words and arguments which, in the book *On Not Associating with Heretics*, he forcefully hurls against Constantius and the Arians. Thus the whole book includes a kind of defence of himself, who had presided over the council in the Pope’s name, and of his associates. This, consequently, was the reason that led us to assign this book the first place before the others: since Constantius’s first concern had been that, in that council, the Catholic bishops should come together with the Arians into one understanding of faith and into a fellowship of minds and opinions; and certainly nothing ought to have been more important to Lucifer [Col. 0728A] than that the rationale of his own policy and of his conduct at that same council should be evident to everyone, and that he should defend the justice of his cause.

Tillemont, in volume VII, note 1, and Montfaucon, in the Life of St Athanasius, hold a different view. They maintain that all Lucifer’s books were composed by him in the year 360. We too affirm this concerning the two books for St Athanasius, but not concerning the rest. Nor do we follow the opinion of Gallandius, who chooses to hold that, after the two books on Athanasius were written, as he says, in 360, the others were written shortly afterwards and successively within the year 361. These authors offer no argument for their view.

Baronius, under the year 356, assigns to about this year the first four books of Lucifer in the old edition, in which, after the Council of Milan, he defends the cause of Athanasius and of the faith:

> Those bishops who had already previously been proscribed for preserving Athanasius’s innocence—those, I say, who, lest they subscribe to the sentence issued against him by the Arians, had been carried from the Milanese conventicle into exile in various places—did not cease, however much among enemies, to proclaim that same Athanasius’s innocence, and, when allowed, to testify to it also by letters. Among the first to do this splendidly was Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari. For while living in exile he wrote, principally for Athanasius and against Constantius, two books; a third against the same emperor, *On Not Communicating with Heretics*; and again another, *On Apostate Kings*. Yet he did not keep these studies of his for publication after the death of the Emperor whom he had vehemently attacked in them, but entrusted them to a reliable man to carry them to the Emperor himself. [Col. 0728C]

But the books for Athanasius must certainly be placed around the year 360; and whether the other two books were carried to the Emperor with them will be investigated in its proper place. Papebroch, agreeing with Baronius, likewise assigns first place to the books written for Athanasius in chapter 11 of the *Life of St Lucifer*, volume IV of the May Bollandists. In chapter 4, he denies that the whole volume was delivered to Emperor Constantius in one continuous sequence, as Tilius thought, since the four other books were written neither all at one place nor at one time, but successively. He does not, however, specify the year in which they were composed.

But we conjecture that Lucifer wrote this book, *On Not Associating with Heretics*, while exiled at Germanicia, where he endured the cruelty and savagery of Eudoxius, the Arian bishop of the people of Germanicia. For Eudoxius was a most implacable enemy of Catholics. Accordingly, as Peter Bosch says in the *History of the Patriarchs of Antioch*, in volume IV for July of the Bollandists, Constantius, the chief heretic, sent Lucifer to Germanicia as though into the safest custody, to Eudoxius. Lucifer indicates this place of his exile in Book I for St Athanasius, p. 65 (here col. 830). In this book he himself describes, p. 11 (here col. 775), how cruelly the Arians dealt with him, in these words addressed to Constantius:

> Therefore you hate us because we abominate your council of evil men; therefore we are in exile; therefore we are killed in prison; therefore the sight of others is forbidden to us alone; for this reason we are shut up in darkness and guarded under heavy custody.

The precise year in which Lucifer composed this book cannot be established. After his first exile in Cappadocia—which was very brief, as Papebroch observes in chapter 1 of his *Life*—he was taken to Germanicia in 356, after George the Cappadocian had seized the church of Alexandria, as has been said both in the *Life of Lucifer* and at p. 66, note 1 (here col. 831, note c). Eudoxius had already seized the episcopal see of Antioch around the beginning of 358, according to Peter Bosch; while Valesius, in his notes on Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 1, places this crime of Eudoxius in the latter half of 357. Therefore, within the period extending from some months after the beginning of 356 to the incomplete year 357, or the beginning of 358, Lucifer seems to us to have written his first book; and on this chronology we agree, to some extent, with Baronius.

[Col. 0729B]

Lucifer subsequently wrote another book, *On Apostate Kings*, separate from the others, as he himself testifies in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, p. 261 (here col. 1031). Its subject and substance are this: by setting forth the example of impious kings, who, although they had led very wicked lives and approved the worship of idols, nevertheless flourished for a very long time in their kingdoms, he shows Constantius that the opinion in which he inferred from the flourishing state of his own reign that he was right to uphold the Arian faith and persecute the Nicene faith was false. He repeatedly rehearses certain things which Constantius cast against Lucifer and which appear to be referable to the proceedings of the Council of Milan. Thus, at p. 33 (here col. 796):

> If I had acted badly, if, as Lucifer says, I were a heretic, God would already have taken the kingdom from me.

And at p. 38 (here col. 803):

> If I were a heretic, if, as Lucifer, Pancratius, and Hilary say, I attacked the religion of God, vengeance would already have been inflicted upon me. [Col. 0729C]

This book was written after the slaughter of the Alexandrians perpetrated in 356 by George the Cappadocian and Syrianus, Constantius’s commander, and after the most disgraceful storm stirred up against the Catholic bishops throughout Egypt, which Lucifer mentions at p. 43 (here col. 808). A chronological indication in the same book permits it to be assigned to 358. In that year Constantius first wholly subdued the Sarmatians and Quadi, and then drove the Limigant Sarmatians from their settlements with a great victory; hence, from the name of the subjugated people, he was called Sarmaticus, says Marcellinus, Book XVII, chapters 12 and 13. Lucifer himself seems to allude to this victory at p. 42 (here col. 807):

> Therefore, just as God delivered him [Ahab] from the son of Jader, king of Syria, so he delivered—and delivers—you from all who desire to destroy you … so that you may infer that victory was not granted you for the merits of your faith and life.

Unless he instead means to recall for Constantius the victory won over the tyrant Magnentius in Pannonia near Mursa in 351. In this year, 358, Lucifer was bearing his third exile at Eleutheropolis with the utmost steadfastness.

In the same place he published two books for St Athanasius. By the strongest arguments and testimonies from the sacred books he so defends Athanasius’s cause that, with remarkable force of intellect, he readily proves that Athanasius could not have been condemned without being seen or heard in judgment, nor removed from his see by the authority and sentence of the Council of Milan and the Emperor. Marcellinus indicates the same in Book XV, chapter 8, where he says this of Pope Liberius:

> Liberius, warned by the Emperor to reject Athanasius from the priestly see by subscription, though sharing the views of the others who refused, resisted steadfastly, often crying out that to condemn a man neither seen nor heard was the utmost impiety; plainly resisting the Emperor’s will. [Col. 0730A]

On this passage Lindebrogius comments: “The very words of Bishop Liberius to Emperor Constantius.” Theodoret adds, *History*, Book II, chapter 16: “For it is not possible to condemn a man whom we have not tried” (*οὐδὲ γὰρ οἷόν τε καταψηφίζεσθαι ἀνδρὸς ὃν οὐκ ἐκρίναμεν*). To the same effect belong what Lucifer of Cagliari wrote for Athanasius. They knew that not only divine law but also the Twelve Tables forbade putting anyone to death before the case had been heard. Salvian of Marseilles, Book VIII; Basil the Great, Epistle LXX, p. 318: “No wrongdoer is condemned without proofs” (*Κακοῦργος μὲν οὐδεὶς ἄνευ ἐλέγχων καταδικάζεται*). “Even sacrilegious persons, traitors, and poisoners are granted the opportunity to defend themselves, nor is it lawful for anyone to be condemned beforehand when the case is unknown.” Lactantius, Book V, chapter 1. [Col. 0730B]

Papebroch carefully set out the substance of these books in chapter 3 of the *Life of Lucifer*. In chapter 4 he states that they appear to have been written, probably presented, and returned again through Florentius while the saint was still exiled at Germanicia under Eudoxius, the Arian bishop. He was led to this view by Lucifer’s own words in Book I, p. 65 (here col. 830): “Or to whom you sent me among the people of Germanicia—Adoxius.” This indeed indicates the Germanician exile which he had endured earlier, not one which he was then enduring when he wrote these words. For at p. 91 (here col. 857) he plainly signifies that war between the Romans and Persians had then broken out again: “Saporinus, king of the Persians, is now waging war against you.”

But after the Council of Milan in 355, affairs with the Persians appear to have been peaceful under a truce. Indeed, in 356 Constantius negotiated a peace to be firmly established with them. In the East, they were pursuing plunder of persons and cattle “by stealth and brigandage rather than, as formerly, by their customary pitched battles,” says Marcellinus, Book XVI, chapter 9. Toward the end of 357 and the beginning of 358, letters and envoys were sent by both sides to establish a lasting treaty, as the same author testifies, Book XVII, chapter 5. But the Romans returned from Persia without accomplishing their business, he adds in chapter 14. Then Sapor, king of the Persians, having concluded peace with the Chionites and Gelani, against whom he had waged war for nearly two years earlier, attacked the Romans in 359 with all the forces of his empire and, as autumn advanced, surrounded Amida with a siege. The author just cited narrates this at length throughout Book XVIII. From this, therefore, one may infer that Lucifer wrote both books for Athanasius about the end of 359 and the beginning of 360, as Tillemont, Montfaucon, and Gallandius rightly affirm.

A little above, we observed that Baronius was of the opinion that the books for Athanasius, together with the other two, *On Not Communicating with Heretics* and *On Apostate Kings*, were presented to the Emperor at the same time. Papebroch, chapter IV, says more plausibly that, once Constantius had received the earlier books—namely, those for St Athanasius—together with the author’s confession, he repeatedly ordered him to be transferred farther away. [Col. 0731A] But in this matter Florentius’s letter to Lucifer seems to indicate nothing certain. For the “codex” which it mentions could include either one book or several, if one considers the genuine meaning of that term.

Yet our judgment—or, if you prefer, our conjecture—is that the books were carried separately to Constantius, one by one, as in the new edition; and that, inflamed to fiercer anger against Lucifer by reading the earlier ones, he ordered the most holy bishop to be transferred from Germanicia to Eleutheropolis, a more grievous place of exile; and then, after receiving the books written for Athanasius, to the fourth place of exile in Egypt. We have discussed these matters more carefully in the *Life of Lucifer*.

Francis Pagius, in his *Critique of Baronius* under the year 354, adduces a passage from Book I of Lucifer’s work for St Athanasius to prove [Col. 0731B] that George the Cappadocian received episcopal consecration before the Council of Milan of 355:

> Lucifer of Cagliari, who attended the Council of Milan, testifies in the *Apology for Athanasius*, Book I, that George was ordained before the Council of Milan, addressing Constantius in these words: “You persecute him through whom the Lord commanded you to be heard, while he was still engaged in human affairs; in whose place you send your heretic George as successor, although, even if Athanasius had been released from the body, you would not have been permitted to send him.” A little later: “Can God be with George, the enemy? Can He be gracious to one whom He has not ordained, whom He has not chosen?” etc.

But who could infer anything certain from this in support of Pagius’s opinion? Lucifer’s language is entirely general [Col. 0731C] and tied to no particular time or place; and in those words he reproves only the fact that George, a heretical man, was appointed to the Alexandrian episcopate while Athanasius was alive. Moreover, the testimony of Lucifer as Pagius presents it contains several errors of words and punctuation which obscure the writer’s meaning. Therefore compare it with what is printed here at p. 64 (here col. 829).

Around the same year, 360, the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God* was written. The meaning of its title is that bishops must not, through a base kind of timidity and a silence injurious to God, conceal the errors and unjust acts of men—especially heretics. For it belongs to their office openly to uphold the Catholic faith and freely [Col. 0731D] and courageously rebuke the crimes of the impious. Constantius, of course, was raging against Lucifer; after reading his books, he alleged that Lucifer and the Catholic bishops were arrogant, insolent, and insulting toward the imperial majesty. Therefore Lucifer gives Constantius an account of himself. He explains why he had composed the earlier books in so sharp a style. Then, with such force of intellect and eloquence of speech, he defends himself, the cause of religion, Athanasius, and the Catholic bishops, as well as his own books, that, except for his unpolished manner of expression, he seems to come very near Ciceronian eloquence.

Papebroch gives a synopsis of the whole book in chapter 4 of the *Life of Lucifer*:

> The whole book tends to prove that the Emperor himself and the other bishops, when they resist him, show him what he is in relation to the peoples entrusted to him, and explain to him the enormity and gravity of his sins, are performing their duty and doing nothing other than what the prophets and apostles did on such an occasion. Finally, they are not insulting, but truthful; they fear no one but God and are concerned for the salvation of his soul. The book ends with the example of the seven Maccabees, who freely reproached Antiochus, whom Constantius was imitating. [Col. 0732A]

Baronius writes this concerning the same book under the year 356, no. 68:

> Moreover, Lucifer himself shows, in that treatise which he later wrote against Constantius with repeated force, *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, that Constantius complained against Lucifer, his critic, after reading those books … In that book he assails him with more weighty invectives.

Baronius agrees with us about the date at which this book was written, since he judges it to have been completed after the Constantinopolitan conventicle of that year, 360. Gallandius, however, thinks that Lucifer composed this distinguished work in 361—but much too late. For after the books for St Athanasius had been delivered to Constantius near the beginning of 360, not enough time could have elapsed for Lucifer to learn, around the end of that same year, the Emperor’s thoughts, feelings, and fury aroused against him by reading them, and then to write this new book against him only in 361. This is especially so because the final book, entitled *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, was published at the beginning of 361, and in that same year Athanasius wrote the letter in which he testifies to Lucifer that he had received all his books against Constantius. [Col. 0732C]

The final book composed by Lucifer against Constantius is that in which he shows, says Papebroch shortly after the passage quoted above, that one must die for the Son of God. Papebroch demonstrates that it was written after the beginning of 360 from its mention (here col. 1028) of Eudoxius—whom it again calls Adoxius—having been elevated to the see of Constantinople, which happened on 17 January. In November of the following year, when Constantius died, he began to experience the truth of what Lucifer, wholly aflame with desire for martyrdom, threatened him with both in his other books and especially in this one.

Indeed, while Lucifer was enduring with the greatest constancy the grievous calamities of his exile in Egypt, “because he supposed,” Baronius adds under the same year 356, no. 69, “that Constantius and his ministers would conspire for his death, he added another treatise, whose title and subject are *That One Must Die for the Son of God*.” One may see the man ever rising against Constantius with greater freedom and steadfastness of spirit, as is evident from one or two statements in the same volume. In this book you have the form of a just and perfect discourse, worthy of a Catholic bishop, in its variety of arguments, weightiness of thought, force of sacred testimonies, and easy eloquence of utterance; it can rightly be compared with Cicero’s *Philippics*. It powerfully defends the Nicene faith, the actions of his embassy, and Athanasius’s cause; it pursues the crimes of Constantius and the Arians; and it extols the nobility, honour, and praises of a glorious death for Christ, [Col. 0733A] which Lucifer testifies that he ardently desires. Yet it is wholly certain, says Baronius, no. 80, that Constantius himself and all the other Arians begrudged him this glory of martyrdom, for which he professed himself so eager in so many and such great published writings.

But the same author writes, no. 73:

> From what he says later in the same book about Eudoxius, appointed by Constantius to take Macedonius’s place in the see of Constantinople, it appears that this treatise was written two years afterward. It is consequently clear that the things which he has just said were done by Constantius’s rescript to the church of Alexandria are different from those recounted above from Athanasius.

Concerning these cruelties inflicted upon the Alexandrians, see what we ourselves conjecture in the notes on this book of Lucifer. With Baronius, we judge that the slaughter of the Alexandrians which Lucifer mentions at p. 252 (here [Col. 0733B] col. 1022) is different from that impiously perpetrated in 356 after Athanasius had been expelled from his see, which Athanasius himself describes in his *Apology concerning His Flight* and in his Letter to the Solitaries.

But we do not approve Baronius’s opinion when he maintains that this treatise was written two years after Eudoxius occupied the see of Constantinople. If Eudoxius was appointed bishop of Constantinople in Macedonius’s place in January 360, it follows that Lucifer composed this book in 362. But Constantius had already died in the preceding year, and Julian, as Ammianus indicates, Book XXII, chapter 5, permitted the exiled bishops to return to their churches in 361. Moreover, George the Cappadocian was torn to pieces by the Alexandrians at the beginning of 362, and Athanasius was restored to his see shortly afterward. Yet Athanasius had received all Lucifer’s books while still in exile, as his own letter to Lucifer testifies.

Nor do we agree with Papebroch, who prefers to hold that this final work of Lucifer was composed after approximately the beginning of 360. It is later than the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, written in 360 itself, when Lucifer had not yet heard of Eudoxius’s episcopate at Constantinople. Therefore we decide this matter as follows: the book entitled *That One Must Die for the Son of God* was written and published by Lucifer before Constantius’s death, which occurred on the third day before the Nones of October—or November, as others prefer—in 361; either toward the end of 360, although Tillemont and [Col. 0733D] Montfaucon assign the year 360 absolutely, or at the very beginning of 361, which with Gallandius may be affirmed much more probably.

“These,” Baronius continues, no. 73, “and many other things like them were weapons which Lucifer, legate of the Apostolic See, with an apostolic heart hurled from exile against Constantius.” When these had been conveyed to Athanasius, hiding in the desert, he rejoiced somewhat; and, sending his deacon Eutychetes to Lucifer, he gave him letters, which you have printed here after Lucifer’s books.

Montfaucon published them among Athanasius’s works, writing that it was uncertain whether they were written in Latin and later translated into Greek by someone. But no Greek exemplar of them survives, and the second letter seems to have been written in Latin, as we observe with Montfaucon himself in the note appended to it, p. 270 (here col. 1040, note q). Montfaucon further mistakenly supposes that the first letter was perhaps sent by Athanasius to Lucifer shortly after Lucifer’s exile, and therefore about 356, when Lucifer may not even have published his first book, *On Not Associating with Heretics*.

Papebroch assigns both letters to 360, for, he says in chapter 4, “I am persuaded that Athanasius received all these things”—namely the Luciferian books—“while Lucifer was living, in his fourth exile, nearer to the regions of Egypt, in 360, because I observe in the second letter of Athanasius himself the title of the final book, the trampling of diabolical gnashings, and other phrases occurring here.” But while the first letter can conveniently be assigned to 360, the second cannot. Papebroch himself, in volume I of the May Bollandists, in the *Life of St Athanasius*, chapter 24, more clearly writes that it was given about the year 360.

In that year, indeed, Lucifer had sent persons to visit Athanasius and through whom he might communicate concerning their shared concerns. But Athanasius could neither see nor speak with them, because he had fled into more secret hiding-places, fearing the plots of the Arians. They watched the roads and, as he himself says in the same letter, “concern themselves with those departing and leaving the city of Alexandria; they seek ships, range through deserts, disturb houses, shake down the brothers, and fabricate charges against individuals.” Shortly before this, they had been ravaging monks with impunity through the deserts of Egypt. Athanasius indicates this storm at the beginning of the second letter. These events seem to have occurred in that same year, 360, after the first letter was written. Since, in the second, Athanasius says that he had received Lucifer’s final book also—and that book was written at the end of 360, or rather at the beginning of 361—the second letter must certainly be assigned to that very year.

Baronius writes the following concerning both letters, under the year 356, no. 75:

> Having received these first letters, Lucifer gladly shared with Athanasius a copy of all the writings which he had given to Constantius. When Athanasius had read them with great wonder and joy of heart, he sent other letters to the same man, making him aware of the state of his affairs: namely, of the raid upon the holy monks out of hatred for Athanasius, as though they had received and hidden him; and of Athanasius’s renewed flight and search for refuge in more hidden retreats (about 361). [Col. 0734D]

Antonius Felix Matthaeius, in *Sacred Sardinia*, p. 72, seems to hold that Athanasius’s letters to Lucifer were written immediately after Lucifer had published the books for Athanasius, and he maintains that those books were composed at Germanicia:

> While at Germanicia, he wrote two books for Athanasius and presented them to Emperor Constantius, whom he rebuked in them with the sharpest words. When Athanasius himself learned this, he wrote to Lucifer, earnestly asking him in several ways to send a copy of them. Lucifer complied, and by this means attained Athanasius’s friendship.

But it is readily clear from what has been said that neither claim is true, especially since Lucifer sent Athanasius not only the two books for Athanasius but all the books he had written; and all were translated into Greek. Nor are we concerned with the testimony of Ambrose Machin, archbishop of Cagliari. In his *Defence of the Holiness of Blessed Lucifer*, chapters 7, 8, 9, 10, and 12, where he discusses Lucifer’s books, he copies Baronius and follows his opinion. Yet he disagrees both with Baronius and with us when, in chapter 12, he says that the book *On Not Associating with Heretics* was written about the year 360. For then the Arians held supreme power and nearly all Catholics, under the name of peace, were defiled by communion with Arians—something Lucifer grieves intensely in this book. Yet Lucifer’s arguments can much more conveniently be referred to the proceedings of the Council of Milan, as we have observed. [Col. 0735B] We have sufficiently discussed both what he understands there by “peace” and by “edict,” in the *Life of Lucifer* and in our notes.

Machin also places among Lucifer’s final works the book entitled *That One Must Die for the Son of God* and the other, *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*. He places the latter after the former in order, which is false. He assigns both to 360 in chapters 10 and 12, which is wholly true of the latter, but more nearly true of the former. How highly Athanasius valued Lucifer’s books is evident from the same letter. He also translated them into Greek so that they might be more widely accessible to all Easterners, as Marcellinus and Faustinus testify in their *Book of Petitions to the Emperors*. Here it is useful to transcribe their testimony about Lucifer’s books in full:

> Let them now say what new doctrine Lucifer taught which was not handed down from Christ’s teaching, which was not transmitted to posterity by the apostles, the disciples of the Saviour. And it was good that he wrote books to Constantius—not, as most do, seeking glory for his talent, but most aptly gathering divine testimonies against the heretics and against the very patron of heretics, aflame with divine zeal for love of the Son of God. Let them point out what he wrote there that is contrary to the Scriptures, or what novelty he wrote as though a heretic. When Athanasius was considering all these things afresh, he admired these books as true defenders and translated them into Greek style, lest the Greek language lack so great a good. Nor is this all: Athanasius himself, in his own letters, praises the same books as woven from the doctrines of prophets, evangelists, and apostles, and from a devout confession. And although he exalts him with very many praises, he does not attain an encomium proportionate to his merit; indeed, when he could praise him no further, the excellence of his deeds surpassed every tongue that praised him. But Lucifer, though ignorant of artificial eloquence, nevertheless had, by merit of right faith and a most sincere conscience, the grace of the Holy Spirit to write in prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic fashion—which surpasses all human eloquence. [Greek translation of Lucifer’s books.] [Col. 0735D]

Papebroch adds, in chapter 2 of the *Life of Lucifer*, that although these authors are by no means to be approved elsewhere, in that in which they praise Lucifer they are not at all to be despised, since Athanasius himself—and indeed the whole Church of Christ—supports them. The loss of Athanasius’s translation must be deeply lamented. Since it has unhappily perished, or perhaps still lies hidden in obscurity, we rightly grieve that a most ready aid for correcting Lucifer’s works has been taken away from us.

Lucifer wrote some other things which have been consumed by antiquity itself. In chapter 1, Papebroch indicates a letter sent by Lucifer to the Catholics assembled in the church at Milan, mentioned in the *Life of St Dionysius, Bishop of Milan*:

> A letter was sent by Lucifer, a Catholic bishop and president of the Council of Milan in the Pope’s name, from the palace where he was held by the Emperor; it was delivered to Dionysius and Eusebius, and the people began to request that it be read to them.

In chapter 4 he also suggests that Lucifer published a Profession of Faith together with the books [Col. 0736B] for St Athanasius and sent it to Constantius. He affirms this without any authority, and we find nothing in Lucifer’s books or in the letter to Florentius to support Papebroch’s opinion. Lucifer certainly would not have been silent about this, nor would it have been necessary for him to present the Nicene Faith to Constantius as a confession of his own faith in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, p. 204 (here col. 973).

Lucifer himself mentions having written several letters in the same book, p. 212 (here col. 981):

> The letters of my humble self, and my books, though written in rustic speech, prove that I have often said that our sins indeed have caused us to fall into your hands, you precursor of Antichrist.

And Athanasius, in his second letter to Lucifer, writes that he received Lucifer’s letters along with the codex of his books. Beyond this, nothing is known concerning Lucifer’s writings.

[Col. 0736C]

His style in writing is plainly crude and almost barbarous, as anyone reading him can see. He freely admits this in the words quoted a little above, and in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, p. 247 (here col. 1017): “Meanwhile, you must see that readers will pardon the fact that the eloquence of my modest talent … has been unable to set [these matters] forth.” Then, at p. 258 (here col. 1028):

> But we, for whom nature suffices in speaking, strangers to all learning and therefore strangers to letters, are able to destroy every heresy because the matter itself and truth speak.

And again in the same place:

> We know only the sacred writings; our speech is ordinary. Yours, by contrast, is polished and ornate, and may even be called eloquent.

Thus in the *Book of Petitions* he is said to be ignorant of artificial eloquence. Yet Tilius says in his Preface to Pope Pius V:

> His language seems to me common to himself [Col. 0736D] and to his age, so crude and unpolished that he himself even calls it rustic. But anyone who considers it carefully will find it weighty and full of thoughts, and the work of a man of vigorous intellect.

And La Cerda, chapter 37, excuses Lucifer: carried away by zeal for religion and dwelling among Greeks when he wrote his books, he was almost unwillingly led to express many things with a negligent pen and followed Greek diction, as we have noted in places with Tilius: “He seems in many respects to have neglected Latinity and followed the Greeks; he boiled over with such zeal that many things flowed out as though against his will.”

[Col. 0737]

# LIFE OF LUCIFER, BISHOP OF CAGLIARI

## § I

[Col. 0737A]

Methodius wrote in the preceding century that Lucifer had Calaris [Note: [Col. 0737C] Καράλις; in Ptolemy, *Carallis*. In many manuscripts: *Caralis*, *Caralitanus*; Sophronius, in *On Illustrious Men*, has Καρακαλέως, *Caracalis*, *Caracalitanus*, Καρακαλίνων, “of the Caracalini.” Gerardus Casteel, in *Ecclesiastical Historical Controversies*, controversy 19, p. 343, col. 1, called Lucifer Bishop of Calagurris. This is the city of Calagurris in Tarraconensian Spain mentioned by Livy, now Calahorra in Old Castile. But what could be further from the truth?]—the chief city of Sardinia—as his native city, and that his parents were of Roman descent, from the family of the Lucifers [Note: [Col. 0737C] From fabricated Calaritan inscriptions: *T. AELIUS LUCIFER*, *L. AELIUS LUCIFER*, *IV. AEMILIA LUCIFERA*; and from a certain forged Sicilian stone: *L. CAESIUS LUCIFER*. See Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. IV, 20 May, Venetian ed., p. 660, no. 2.], a family most distinguished for virtue and for blood shed for the Christian religion [Note: [Col. 0737C] Fr. Ambrosius Methodius of Taranto, Order of Hermits of St Augustine, in his manuscript *Life*, from the Bollandists at the place cited.].

He further recorded that, after Lucifer had been orphaned as a boy, St Juvenal, Bishop of Calaris [Note: [Col. 0737C] Bollandists, ibid., preliminary matter for 28 May. Whether he was Bishop of Calaris in the fourth Christian century, or at its beginning—namely, in A.D. 303, as Ferrarius, Arca, Bonfantes, Fara, Machinus, and Papebrochius contend—is doubted by the distinguished Matthaeius, *Sardinian Sacred History*, p. 70.], took him in for education; that, having thereafter gone to Rome at a more mature age, he had St Eusebius of Vercelli, later bishop, as his teacher; that he was regenerated to Christ in the sacred font by him; that Pope St Sylvester of Rome honoured him with the office of Reader; that the task of interpreting the sacred Scriptures in both Greek and Latin was entrusted to him, as one fully approved; and that at last, after the death of Protogenes, Bishop of Calaris [Note: [Col. 0737D] He attended the Councils of Nicaea and Sardica. He was bishop not of Sardinia but of Sardica in Moesia, as is clear from Andronicus Palaeologus the Elder in Goar, at the end of Codinus, p. 405, and from Le Quien, vol. II, *Oriens Christianus*, col. 301 ff. Machinus nevertheless argues with all his strength, throughout chapter 17 of book II of his *Defence of Holy Blessed Lucifer*, that this Protogenes was Bishop of Calaris.], he was appointed to that see by Pope Julius of Rome after A.D. 347. But Methodius, excessively indulgent toward conjectures, handed down such matters about Lucifer as ought, if weighed on the fair scales of criticism, to be accounted of no value [Note: [Col. 0737D] The distinguished Matthaeius, in the place cited above, p. 72, says: “Methodius indeed recounts these things concerning Lucifer, but all are uncertain—to say nothing more serious.” See Papebrochius, place cited, nos. 2 and 3.].

The same judgment is due to what Machinus, Archbishop of Calaris, drew from Bonfante and wrote concerning Lucifer’s year of birth, lineage, and episcopal ordination [Note: [Col. 0737D] *Defence of Holy Blessed Lucifer*, part 1, ch. 1.]. Thus Lucifer’s birthplace is uncertain, his lineage and chronology uncertain, and uncertain everything which the dreaming Methodius asserted, down to the year 354. For in that year Lucifer’s name and office first occur in the letter of Pope Liberius to the Emperor Constantius, who at that time was stationed at Arles in Gaul after the defeat of Magnentius, attended and manipulated by Valens and other Arian bishops.

In the preceding year Liberius had sent an embassy, through the bishops Vincent and Marcellus, hoping to persuade the Emperor that a council should be freely convened at Aquileia, both for the cause of Athanasius and to refute and condemn the errors of the Arians. But since the affair had not succeeded as he wished, and all was daily going to ruin through the lapse of Vincent, Bishop of Capua [Note: [Col. 0738C] See the letter of Pope Liberius to Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli, vol. II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 803, and Binius’s note there, p. 800.], Liberius sent another envoy to Constantius: Lucifer, Bishop of Calaris, who at that time, by the providence of God so arranging things, was staying in Rome in order more easily to settle some pressing business of the church entrusted to him. He sent him with the presbyter Pancratius [Note: [Col. 0738C] Cave calls him Eutropius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers of the Arian Age*. See “Lucifer”; but incorrectly.] and the deacon Hilary [Note: [Col. 0738C] This Hilary, deacon of the Roman Church, joined the Luciferians and, having become their leader, added heresy to schism. St Jerome calls him “a new Deucalion of the world” in his book *Against the Luciferians*, because he rebaptized Arians returning to Catholic communion. Yet the distinguished Sarazanius, in his notes on the acts and minor works of St Damasus, ch. 22, no. 6, holds with Pagi in his annotations on Baronius for A.D. 362, no. 25, and Natalis Alexander, fourth century, ch. 6, art. 14, that through the work and zeal of Pope St Damasus Hilary at last returned to a sound mind and adhered to the Catholics; and we too, supported by the same arguments, subscribe to this view.].

The same Methodius maintains that Lucifer came to Rome and left his flock at God’s summons, in order to bring aid to the Catholic Church as it struggled against the Arians [Note: [Col. 0738C] At the place cited above. See Bollandists, cited place, no. 3.], perhaps from these words of Liberius: “By God’s cooperation, our brother and fellow-bishop Lucifer of Sardinia has arrived” [Note: [Col. 0738C] In the letter to Eusebius of Vercelli, vol. II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 803, from the *Acts of the Life of St Eusebius*.].

Those who called Lucifer not a Sardinian but a Sirmian bishop [Note: [Col. 0738D] “The Luciferians derive their name from Lucifer, Bishop of Sirmium, who opposed Catholic bishops who, during the persecution of Constantius, had consented to the Arian perfidy and afterwards, corrected, returned to the Catholic Church,” etc. St Isidore, *Origins*, book VIII, p. 105, Paris ed. 1601; Honorius of Autun, *On Heresies*, in *Bibliotheca Patrum*. So also Erasmus in his notes on St Jerome’s *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, Nauclerus in his *Chronicle*, vol. II, and Montholonius in *Promptuarium*, vol. II, p. 28.], or even a Sardian one [Note: [Col. 0738D] See Cornelius a Lapide on Revelation 3:1: “Write to the angel of the church in Sardis,” etc.], have strayed most disgracefully from historical truth—established by the votes of nearly all learned men and critics and by the authority of councils.

Quite distinct from our Lucifer is that Lucifer of Sardis who attended the Council of Caesarea in Cappadocia, at which St Basil was elected to occupy that see, in A.D. 370 [Note: [Col. 0738D] “And, having summoned those recalled from exile—Eusebius of Samosata and Lucifer of Sardis.” Vol. II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1039.]. By the end of that year, or at least at the beginning of the next, our Lucifer, as we shall say in § VIII, had closed his last day.

## § II

Therefore, since Liberius knew Lucifer to be especially fitted, by learning and piety, for carrying out a weighty charge [Note: [Col. 0739D] “Because he was well known through contempt for the world, zeal for the sacred Scriptures, purity of life, constancy of faith, divine grace,” etc. In the *Book of Petitions* of Marcellinus and Faustinus, in Sirmond, vol. I, ed. 1696, col. 234.], when he sent him as ambassador to the Emperor, he gave him a letter to carry to the same Emperor, in order to obtain from him a council for restoring the Church’s peace [Note: [Col. 0739D] “To entreat your Clemency to deign to hear our representations with a favourable disposition, I have resolved that my brother and fellow-bishop, the holy man Lucifer, should set out with Pancratius, my fellow-presbyter, and Hilary, deacon; through your Clemency we believe that they can without difficulty obtain a council for the peace of all the churches.” From the letters of Liberius in Baronius, at A.D. 354, no. 5.]. At the same time he sent other, commendatory letters to Eusebius, asking him to assist Lucifer and his companions in undertaking this most difficult mission [Note: [Col. 0739D] “That you may undertake the task with them, so that the Faith handed down by the Apostles to the Catholic Church may in no way be attacked . . . that your faith may join itself to their fellowship and, wherever there is need, your like holiness may be present; that in one conference and with one counsel you may do what pleases God and his angels and benefits the Catholic Church.” From the same letters in Baronius, ibid., no. 6.].

Having set out from Rome for Vercelli with Pancratius and Hilary, Lucifer was received with great kindness by Eusebius. To prove himself ever more fully to Liberius as a vigorous defender of the Catholic Faith and one ready to carry out commands, Eusebius immediately joined the envoys as their companion, in order to meet the Emperor, who was staying at Arles. There the envoys pressed their case before him so earnestly that they successfully obtained all that Liberius had desired and requested of Constantius: both that Athanasius’s case be heard, and especially that a council be convened for the tranquillity of the Church.

Yet Constantius, being hindered by a barbarian war [Note: [Col. 0740D] Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV; and Baronius from him, cited place, no. 9.], deferred the council’s celebration at Milan until the following year. Eusebius returned to his church, and Lucifer withdrew to Dionysius, Bishop of Milan, while awaiting the time for the council already proclaimed. Accordingly, early in the spring of the year 355 of Christ—the fourth of Pope Liberius and the nineteenth of Emperor Constantius, in the consulship of Arbitio and Mavortius Lollianus—a few bishops from the East and a larger number from the West assembled at Milan, where the Emperor himself was stationed with the army, and began the Synod, the fourth held in that city.

Socrates wrote that a few bishops from the East, but more than three hundred from the West, attended this council [Note: [Col. 0740D] “At that time bishops assembled in Italy. Not very many of the eastern bishops were present, since old age and the distance of the journey prevented most of them from attending; but more than three hundred of the western bishops came.” Book II, ch. 36.]; Sozomen agrees [Note: [Col. 0740D] “When, at the Emperor’s urgent instance, a synod was held at Milan, few came from the East . . . but more than three hundred gathered from the West.” Book IV, ch. 9.]. Nearly all modern writers—Baronius [Note: [Col. 0740D] At A.D. 355, no. 3.], Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0740D] In the notes to the *Life of St Eusebius*.], Calmet [Note: [Col. 0740D] *Universal History*, vol. V.], and others of high repute—have adopted this opinion and stated that more than three hundred Latin Fathers filled the Council of Milan.

Valesius, however, scarcely able to persuade himself that so many bishops had gathered there, suspected an error in the Greek text of both historians. For τριακόσιοι in Sozomen and τριακοσίους in Socrates, he thought one should read τριάκοντα—that is, thirty [Note: [Col. 0740D] In his notes on Socrates, p. 25.]. Jerome a Prato, applying a stricter judgment, rejects the testimonies of the Greek historians and contends that the number of Fathers, counting both Catholic and Arian bishops, scarcely reached sixty [Note: [Col. 0740D] In his notes on Sulpicius Severus, no. 7, pp. 207–208.].
