But, upon closer consideration, the two opinions seem reconcilable. If the words of Athanasius, Constantius, and the authors of the *Lives* of Saints Eusebius and Dionysius are weighed, both the Greek historians and Valesius and Prato will retain their respective truth. For the intention of the Emperor, manipulated by Valens and Ursacius when he convened that council, was that Athanasius should be condemned by the whole Western Church and that Arian doctrines should be approved. But since most Catholic bishops, having perceived the deception of Constantius and the Arians, refused to come to Milan for the synod, court officials were dispatched through every province of the West to declare to the bishops that they must either subscribe to Athanasius’s condemnation or go into exile.

Here are Athanasius’s very words in his *Letter to the Solitaries*, which we quote in Peter Nannius’s translation:

> “How many bishops, therefore, as it is written in the sacred Scriptures, were brought before governors and kings and heard this sentence from the judges: ‘Either subscribe, or withdraw from your churches; for the Emperor has commanded that you be removed from the churches.’ For orders were sent also to the magistrates, and heavy financial penalties were announced unless each compelled the bishop of his own city to subscribe.”

As a result, many bishops, overcome now by threats, now by force and deceit, subscribed against Athanasius. They thought that, without injury to the Nicene Faith, the condemnation of one man would restore peace and tranquillity to the troubled affairs of the Catholic Church; this was what Constantius himself had also deceitfully promised. “We,” he says in his letter to Eusebius, “who glory in being servants of God, jointly exhort and admonish you not to delay in adhering to the agreement of your brethren”—meaning the thirty Arian bishops who had already subscribed against Athanasius at Milan. “For we are confident that, once this has been done, the churches may rejoice in a most firmly established unity.”

Thus, by forcibly obtaining from a great many absent Western bishops subscriptions against Athanasius, Constantius imagined that he could impose the appearance of an ecumenical council, Athanasius having been condemned by so great a number of Fathers. Athanasius himself speaks thus in the same letter:

> “For in this way the Emperor gathered so great a number of bishops, intimidating some by threats and enticing others by promises, so that they might declare that they no longer held communion with Athanasius.”

I judge that our Lucifer also referred to this when he said to Constantius: “You invite the entire choir of bishops to the murder of an innocent man” [Note: [Col. 0741D] Book II, *For St Athanasius*, p. 132 (here col. 898).].

In truth, however, only a few Western bishops came to the Synod of Milan: namely, those who were nearer to Milan, or who, though far away, considered their presence necessary at that council to defend Athanasius and uphold the Nicene Faith. Thus, in Constantius’s very letter to Eusebius, it is said that few bishops came to Milan from each province: “Finally, the few who came from each of the provinces, unanimously and by common will, issued their decision and confirmed it with the reverence due to the law.” Thus in the *Life of St Dionysius, Bishop of Milan*, from Mombritius and the Milanese and Blaudurian manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0741D] Ch. 2, in the Bollandists, vol. V of May, 25 May, no. 9, p. 512, Venetian ed.], we read that bishops neighbouring Milan attended the council: “For bishops arrived from neighbouring cities, and, gathered together, took their seats within the church.” Finally, the author of the *Life of St Eusebius of Vercelli*, from the Nonantolan codex, settles the matter thus [Note: [Col. 0741D] Vol. II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, pp. 840–841.]:

> “While the Emperor waited and expected the arrival of Liberius and the other bishops who had not yet come, Constantius meanwhile negotiated with the Arian bishops that their faith should be subscribed and Athanasius condemned. Dionysius, bishop of the city of Milan itself, and after him twenty-nine other bishops subscribed; for the Catholic bishops had not yet arrived.”

It then happened that Pope Liberius and the other Catholic bishops designated among themselves by letters a day on which they would come unanimously to Milan. Therefore, after the thirty who first subscribed against Athanasius, other bishops subsequently arrived and made up the number of the council. How many these were appears later in the same source: “The other holy Fathers, forty in number, also subscribed”—that is, to the formula of the Nicene Faith. If we add these to the first twenty-nine, we have approximately seventy Fathers assembled at the Council of Milan.

[Note: [Col. 0741D] The names of the bishops who first subscribed against Athanasius are given by Baronius, vol. III of the *Annals*, at A.D. 355, no. 22, p. 813, Venetian ed., from a document in the Vercelli archives following the letter of the Council of Milan to Eusebius; and by Hardouin in his notes on that letter, who reads *Marinianus*, rather than *Matinianus*, as the eighth name, in vol. II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 830.]

This being so, it is clearly evident that the total of three hundred bishops did indeed consist of subscriptions forcibly and deceitfully extorted by Constantius from bishops of the Western provinces. The Emperor himself displayed this number as that of an ecumenical council, in order to proclaim Athanasius condemned by the common vote of the Western Church, and Arian doctrine ratified by an ecumenical council. “This,” Athanasius continues, “was why he compelled so many to join the few, striving eagerly to collect the names of many, both to bring odium upon the bishop”—Athanasius—“and to win for the Arian heresy, of which he himself was the champion, some appearance and image of authority.”

In this way, in our judgment, the testimonies of Socrates and Sozomen may be accepted, inasmuch as they report that, from all those subscriptions deceitfully gathered by Constantius, more than three hundred bishops gave their names to the Council of Milan; and historical truth is preserved together with Valesius and Prato, who maintain that about sixty bishops attended that council. We determine nothing certain in this matter, although we think the two opinions can easily be reconciled from the testimonies cited. Let the learned render their judgment and vote. But now, from this byway back to the road.

Therefore Lucifer, in the name of Pope Liberius, presided with his companions over the Council of Milan. Although he had fully recognized the intention of the Arians and the Emperor’s spirit, most ready to employ violence against the Catholic bishops, he nevertheless did not wholly despair of a favourable outcome in defending Catholic truth and Athanasius.

Meanwhile Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli, having thoroughly perceived the schemes of the Arian party and foreseen that the Milanese assembly, though bearing the name of a Catholic council, would prove rather a tyrannical consultation and an Arian conspiracy, refused to go there. Yet the apostolic envoys and Constantius himself, though with differing aims, urged the Bishop of Vercelli toward the council with the same endeavour: the latter, that he might at last draw the holy man to his side by fear or deceit; the former, that in so great a crisis they might have the staunchest defender of Catholic truth. Therefore supporters of the Arians, through the bishops Eudoxius and Germinius, and also Constantius and Lucifer himself with his companions, sent letters to Eusebius, earnestly summoning him to the synod already assembled [Note: [Col. 0742D] From the *Acts of the Life of St Eusebius* in the Vercelli archives, Baronius gives those letters and Eusebius’s reply to Constantius, cited place, nos. 6–7.].

At length, though unwillingly, Eusebius yielded to their joint requests; coming to Milan, he joined Lucifer and the Catholic Fathers. I gladly pass over the tumults then raised by Ursacius and Valens, the threats they made against the orthodox bishops, and the impious and grievous acts which they committed against them with Constantius’s support. For the records of every ecclesiastical historian everywhere clearly recount not the proceedings of this brigand council but its crimes.

As for our Lucifer, he fought bravely for Athanasius against the Arians; he vigorously defended the Nicene Faith, constantly adhered to the Catholic bishops, above all Eusebius and Dionysius, and kept the people of Milan, harassed by the deceits and threats of heretics, in the orthodox Faith. Yet, through the cunning of the Arians—who held their own assemblies in the palace with Constantius, separated from the Catholics—Lucifer was seized and detained in the Emperor’s very court. The Arians had been carried to such madness that they hoped, by tearing Lucifer away from the rest, to undermine the constancy of the Catholic Fathers in the Nicene Faith.

Although the Bishop of Calaris was shut up, his spirit was free; and he found a means and method of writing and sending a letter to his fellow bishops assembled in the church. When it was delivered to Eusebius and Dionysius, the Arians tumultuously opposed its being read to the people. But after they had been forcibly expelled from the church, Lucifer’s letter was freely read to the sacred assembly at nightfall [Note: [Col. 0743C] From the *Life of St Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli*, in the Bollandists, 25 May, no. 14.]. It is deeply regrettable that it has perished—unless perhaps someone examining the archives of Vercelli or Milan may someday hope to bring it into public light.

After being held for several days in the palace, Lucifer was at last restored to his own party. But afterwards, through the treachery of the Arian bishops, he was dragged with Eusebius and Florentius before Constantius. Eusebius and Florentius were immediately released and returned to the church; Lucifer remained with the Emperor. While held there for several days, he fought vigorously with the Arian bishops in disputation over the Nicene Faith. Constantius himself, though hidden behind a drawn curtain, was present and admired the strength of his spirit and force of eloquence [Note: [Col. 0743C] “But you see that, though standing within a curtain in your palace, you received from me this answer for the preservation of salvation: that all God’s servants, trampling underfoot your frivolous authority, agree in mind, will, zeal, courage, and voice.” *On Dying for the Son of God*, p. 239 (here col. 1009); and below, p. 244 (here col. 1014): “Do you not remember, Constantius, that I said to the judges, while you listened behind a drawn curtain, that although you had determined to hurl upon us all the weapons of your sovereignty—upon us, the detesters of your blasphemy, as despisers of your sacrilegious decree—and that all their weapons should be shattered against us, still we could not depart from our resolve?” And ibid., p. 245 (here col. 1015): “It is not new that we ambassadors declared in your palace, and do not cease always to affirm, that Christians have so believed and do believe, as the sacred Faith appears to have been written at Nicaea against your Arian heresy and every error.”].

But after an assault upon the church by the eunuch Eusebius, when most of the Catholic bishops had been seized and imprisoned in the Baths of Hercules [Note: [Col. 0743D] Baths near the temple of Hercules, close also to the residence of Maximian Herculius. The church of St Lawrence now stands there; some ruins and enormous columns still survive nearby. See Castiglioni, *Milanese Antiquities*, pp. 7, 124, 126; Torre, *Portrait of Milan*, p. 112; Galeazzo Gualdo Priorato, *Account of Milan*, part 1, p. 42.], Lucifer too was imprisoned with Florentius under Caius, tribune of the soldiers [Note: [Col. 0743D] From the *Life of St Eusebius* in the Bollandists, cited place, no. 6, and from another *Life of St Dionysius*, ch. 3, vol. V of May, p. 513, no. 29: “After the assault by the eunuch Eusebius, one hundred and forty-seven faithful men were seized; with them certain priests and clerics, bound in chains, were shut up within the Baths of Hercules. Florentius and Bishop Lucifer were committed to the custody of the tribune Caius; Eusebius to that of the tribune Galbio.”].

## § III

Meanwhile Lucifer, utterly steadfast in the Faith amid the plots and afflictions of the Arians, did not yield although he was kept in a harsh prison. Rather, he resisted them invincibly for the Catholic religion and Athanasius’s innocence, so that the raging enemies, by Constantius’s command, compelled him to leave Milan and Italy as an exile.

When Pope Liberius learned this, he sent Lucifer and the other exiles for Orthodox truth a letter full of consolation and apostolic strength [Note: [Col. 0744D] See this letter at the beginning of this edition.]. When they received it is uncertain. Lucifer was therefore first relegated to Cappadocia, as Papebrochius [Note: [Col. 0744D] In the *Life of St Lucifer*, vol. IV of May, ch. 1, no. 8.] and Matthaeius think [Note: [Col. 0744D] At the place above in *Churches of Calaris*, p. 73.]. But his stay there was brief; and I believe this is why no sufficiently clear and certain record survives of that first exile.

Transferred from there to Germanicia [Note: [Col. 0744D] Germanicia, an episcopal city in the province of Euphratensis, or Coele-Syria, also called Commagene.], he had this as a second and more prolonged place of exile. He himself plainly testifies to it in the first book *For St Athanasius*, p. 65 (here col. 830), where he mentions Eudoxius, the pseudo-bishop of the Germanicians, whom by antiphrasis he calls *Adoxius* [Note: [Col. 0744D] “Such is George as Arius was, and such are Ursacius and Valens, or Adoxius of the Germanicians, to whom you sent me.” Book I *For St Athanasius*, p. 65 (here col. 830).]. He sufficiently indicates that he suffered this man, as one of the Arian dregs, as a most bitter enemy.

Jerome attests that Lucifer changed this place of exile for a third [Note: [Col. 0744D] “Because he refused, under the name of Athanasius, to condemn the Nicene Faith, he was relegated to Palestine. With remarkable constancy and a mind prepared for martyrdom, he wrote a book against Emperor Constantius and sent it to him to read.” *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Lucifer.”] and was transported to Palestine, namely to Salutaris, in which lay Eleutheropolis. There Eutychius, an Arian fiercely hostile to Catholics, acted as bishop. Lucifer was maltreated by him and by Turbo [Note: [Col. 0744D] Baronius, at A.D. 356, no. 80.], Eutychius’s successor, a man of the same bran, because he freely defended Catholic doctrine and Athanasius’s teaching and holiness [Note: [Col. 0744D] Baronius, at A.D. 355, no. 17; Sirmond, cited place, col. 256.].

While Lucifer was staying in that city, he had Hermione, a virgin of great renown, utterly devoted to him and his helper in bearing the hardships and troubles daily inflicted on him by the Arians [Note: [Col. 0744D] Baronius, at A.D. 362, no. 119.]. We also know that Turbo, that pseudo-bishop of Eleutheropolis, together with his Arians, burst in upon Lucifer while he was conducting the sacred rites; they broke down the doors of the church, plundered the sacred vessels and holy books, and impiously put some of Lucifer’s companions to death. “There are still today in Palestine,” say Faustinus and Marcellinus [Note: [Col. 0744D] In the *Supplementary Book of Petitions to the Emperors*, in Sirmond, cited place.], “men who at that time suffered the severest punishments at their hands because they met with Lucifer, bishop of the Catholic Faith. Let them deny, if they can, that among their other atrocities they broke down a locked door with axes; that, rushing upon the most faithful priest Lucifer, they even overturned the divine sacraments and punished by impious slaughter every one of the brethren gathered there. Let them deny, if they can, that they still possess among themselves the holy mystical vessels which they then impiously seized from Lucifer, together with the sacred books.”

Not content with this, the Arians, in order to harass the most steadfast athlete of Christ more harshly, punished him with a fourth exile in Upper Thebes, or the Second Thebaid, as Socrates [Note: [Col. 0745C] Book III, ch. 5.], Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0745C] Book III, ch. 4.], Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0745C] Book V, ch. 12.], and Cassiodorus [Note: [Col. 0745C] *Tripartite History*, book VI, ch. 19: “For both of them—Lucifer and Eusebius—returned from exile beyond the borders of the Thebaid,” etc.] report; or in parts adjoining Egypt, as Rufinus preferred [Note: [Col. 0745D] Book I, ch. 17; Baronius, cited place, no. 80; Papebrochius, cited place, no. 8; Matthaeius, cited place.].

The distinguished Richard, of the most learned Dominican family, believes that Lucifer changed even this exile and was transferred elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0745D] “Constantius sent him into exile at Germanicia, a city of Syria, from which he was transferred to Eleutheropolis in Palestine, then into the Thebaid, and to another place whose name is unknown.” *Universal Ecclesiastical Dictionary*, vol. III, letter L, p. 712, col. 2, under “Lucifer.”]. But since he does not name the location and enumerates only three previous deportations of Lucifer, I would suppose that Richard referred to the exile in Cappadocia, which was the first, and reversed the order.

During this period of seven years, though not a full seven [Note: [Col. 0745D] Marcellinus and Faustinus are to be charged with error, since in the cited *Book of Petitions* they assign ten years to Lucifer’s exile.], from the year 355, in which he was driven into exile from the Milanese assembly, until the declining part of 361, in which he was released from exile, it is easy to infer from the very character of the heretics and their unrestrained determination to rage against the Orthodox what and how much Lucifer suffered from the Arians, even though writers of that age did not record it. And if Faustinus and Marcellinus are to be believed, we know that Lucifer was led into exile amid every kind of atrocious injury [Note: [Col. 0745D] In the *Book of Petitions*, in Sirmond, cited place; and from Lucifer himself, *On Not Consorting with Heretics* (in this *Patrology*, col. 775), where he says: “For this reason you hate us: because we execrate your council of the wicked; for this reason we are in exile; for this reason we are killed in prison; for this reason sight of us alone is forbidden; thus, shut up in darkness, we are guarded with a great guard. For this reason no human being is admitted to visit us.”], so that it seems miraculous that this most devout man prolonged his life for many years.

Moreover, from the history of Sulpicius Severus we have this testimony concerning these most courageous exiles—Lucifer, Eusebius, Dionysius, and the other Catholic Fathers of the Council of Milan: “It is sufficiently established,” says the historian, “that the exiles were celebrated by the devotion of the whole world; money in abundance was collected for their expenses; and they were frequently visited by embassies of the Catholic laity from almost every province” [Note: [Col. 0746C] Book II, no. 40.]. This is also admirably confirmed by many passages of Hilary, by the testimony of Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0746C] *Heresies*, 30.], and by the remarkable letter of Eusebius reported by Baronius [Note: [Col. 0746C] At A.D. 356, no. 92.], from which it is likewise clear how shamefully those most holy confessors were harassed by the Arians.

The reason the Arians spared Lucifer and did not put him to death was fear of the odium of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0746C] Baronius, ibid., no. 80.]. Constantius had ordered and directed that Lucifer be preserved altogether, led on by the impious or empty hope that he would someday yield to his will and give his hand to Athanasius’s condemnation—the one thing he especially desired.

Here it is worth noting that Photius left it written in his *Library* that after the Council of Milan our Lucifer went into exile at Rimini with the bishops Dionysius, Eusebius, Rhodanus, and Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0746D] “For this reason he convenes a synod at Milan, a city of Italy; and he perverts some to his own will. But Dionysius, Eusebius, Rhodanus, Paulinus, and Lucifer, having not dishonoured their own conviction and that of piety, nor endured to condemn Athanasius—for they knew that Athanasius’s condemnation was the prelude to the overthrow of the Faith—were exiled at Rimini.” *Library*, Rouen ed. 1653, p. 1444.]. That city, however, was not suited for exile, being situated in a most flourishing region of Italy; nor is any mention of this place found in other contemporary authors. On the contrary, all unanimously affirm that the holy bishops were compelled by Emperor Constantius to live in exile in the eastern provinces, exceedingly remote and difficult because of the harshness of their places and the perfidy and power of the Arians.

Finally, and incidentally, one should note the glaring error of Philippo Ferrari, who wrote that Lucifer was sent into exile by Emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0746D] “He was driven into exile with St Eusebius of Vercelli by Constantine.” In the *Catalogue of Saints*, 18 January, p. 45.], unless, by a more charitable judgment, we wish to suppose that *Constantine* crept in through a printer’s error in place of *Constantius*.

## § IV
While Lucifer, an exile, was confounding the perfidy of the Arians by his endurance, he also overthrew their errors by writing. We possess four earlier books, excellently written by our Lucifer and addressed to the Emperor Constantius, in defence and protection of Catholic truth against the impious doctrines of Arius and his followers, and against the Emperor’s own violent efforts to uphold them. Lucifer therefore sent these writings to Constantius [Note: [Col. 0746D] St Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Lucifer”]; Constantius received and read them, was astonished, and, scarcely able to persuade himself that there could be a man of such confidence and freedom as to dare accuse him so frankly and openly of impiety, ordered Florentius, Master of the Offices, to write in his name to Lucifer [Col. 0746C], asking whether he was the author of those volumes, and also to send the books themselves to Lucifer for his recognition [Note: [Col. 0746D] See Baronius, under A.D. 356, no. 73, and Tilius at the end of Lucifer’s Works, Paris edition of 1568.]. When Lucifer received the books together with Florentius’s letter, he frankly acknowledged that he was their father and author, and, replying to Florentius himself, returned the manuscript [Note: [Col. 0746D] Baronius, ibid., and Tilius, ibid.].

The distinguished Matthaeus supposes that the two books *For Athanasius* were written at Germanicia and sent thence to Constantius [Note: [Col. 0746D] *Sardinia Sacra*, under the Church of Cagliari, p. 73.], being led to this conclusion because Lucifer in them calls Eudoxius “the Germanician,” an Arian bishop. Cave, however, disagrees with Matthaeus, maintaining that these books were both composed at Eleutheropolis [Col. 0747A] and sent to Constantius from there [Note: [Col. 0747D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers of the Arian Age*, p. 136.]. But reasons that are not slight, together with conjecture, suggest that they were written partly at Germanicia and partly at Eleutheropolis, as was said in § IV of the Preface. This one point I hold certain and established: these books were begun by Lucifer during his exile after A.D. 356 and completed about the beginning of A.D. 360.

As soon as Athanasius, himself then in exile, received news of this excellent work, he immediately sent a letter to Lucifer through the deacon Eutyches, earnestly requesting him to send the books presented to Constantius also to him for careful reading [Note: [Col. 0747D] See at the end of Tilius’s edition, and Baronius, cited above.]. Lucifer did this without delay; and from Athanasius he thereby earned an honourable testimony to his holiness and learning, as is apparent even to one merely reading Athanasius’s letter to Lucifer [Note: [Col. 0747D] Baronius, ibid.].

Marcellinus and Faustinus, authors of the *Pleading Petition* [Col. 0747B], report that Athanasius translated Lucifer’s books into Greek, so that they might be a consolation and example to the Eastern Catholics amid that disturbance of the universal Church; yet we regret that Athanasius’s translation, along with other letters to Lucifer [Note: [Col. 0747D] We infer that Athanasius at other times sent letters to Lucifer from the words, “We have now also sent,” etc., in the surviving letter of which we are speaking; but they have perished.], has been lost. Here are the words of Marcellinus and Faustinus:

> When he had examined these books throughout anew, Athanasius also esteemed them as true champions and translated them into the Greek style, lest the Greek language should lack so great a good.

But what the Emperor did after receiving these books, we do not know. That he took badly Lucifer’s free address to him, and was especially indignant with him, may nevertheless be inferred from these words of Lucifer: “You say that we have behaved insolently toward you, whom it was proper to honour. If any worshipper of God has spared apostates, then what you say of us is true” [Col. 0747C; Note: [Col. 0747D] In the book *On Not Sparing*, etc., p. 169 (col. 937).].

Not content with these works, Lucifer afterwards issued another treatise, which his own words show was written after the completion of the Council of Sirmium and that of Constantinople. For he mentions Eudoxius as substituted for Macedonius in the see of Constantinople; Eudoxius was certainly transferred from the episcopal chair of Antioch and installed there after those pseudo-councils [Note: [Col. 0747D] Baronius, under A.D. 356, no. 69.]. He entitled this work *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*. And because he burned wholly with desire for martyrdom, and judged that what he had published was not enough to crush the Arians, he next produced a final work, entitled *That One Must Die for the Son of God*. Although some have judged these books to be comprised in one volume [Note: [Col. 0747D] Tilius, in the Preface to Pius V in his edition of Lucifer’s works, [Col. 0748D]], and presented together to Constantius, it is nevertheless certain that they were written with the same firmness of spirit and composed by Lucifer after the earlier books [Col. 0747D] which we have mentioned, as Papebroch says [Note: [Col. 0748D] Vol. 3, May 20, ch. 4, no. 23.], perhaps in the final place of his exile.

In these labours of Lucifer there appears a great power of expression, and a fiery sword issuing from his mouth, as though to destroy the enemies of the Church with a single stroke. Hence the Fathers bestowed so many encomia [Col. 0748A] upon him and did not hesitate to call him the Elijah of their age [Note: [Col. 0748D] St Athanasius, cited by Cornelius a Lapide on 2 Timothy 1; and St Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 95.].

Here it may be permitted to bring forward the judgment of the distinguished Bishop of Meaux concerning Lucifer’s style, since he was the first to apply himself most diligently to publishing his works:

> His language—that is, Lucifer’s—is so rough and unpolished that he himself even calls it rustic. Yet one who weighs it carefully will find it weighty, full of thought, and the work of a man of vigorous intellect, etc.

Then:

> The entire work would be exceedingly small if the divine Scripture—which he could not have had more readily at hand—were cut away and removed from it [Note: [Col. 0748D] In the cited Preface.].

So he says, and rightly. The version of Holy Scripture used by Lucifer is wholly ancient and differs noticeably from the Vulgate now in use, as is clear from the notes appended to this edition [Col. 0748B]. He also very frequently inserts Sardinian and Greek words adopted into Latin, and employs phrases of an entirely barbarous and Greek-influenced syntax, certainly novel; every reader will find these illustrated in this edition by notes of learned men [Note: [Col. 0748D] Cotelerius, Tilius, Sabatier, Latinius, La Cerda.].

## § V

Before proceeding to other matters concerning Lucifer’s deeds, we consider it worthwhile, in order that the facts may be set in a clearer light, to investigate carefully that celebrated Edict which Lucifer himself mentions so often and indignantly in nearly all the books listed in the preceding paragraph. It seems to require fuller treatment from us, both in order to ascertain Lucifer’s meaning and so that matters pertaining to the history [Col. 0748C] of that time may be established by Lucifer’s own testimony.

On this point we hold the following certain from Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0748D] Book 4, ch. 8, Valesius edition.]: Constantius summoned the Council of Milan with the intention that the divided minds of the bishops might agree upon one statement of faith, which would nevertheless oppose the Nicene decrees. “Constantius,” says Sozomen, “who now alone held the Roman Empire, endeavoured with every effort to bring it about that the Western bishops should agree with those who asserted that the Son was like the Father in substance”: **Τοὺς ἀνὰ τὴν δύσιν ἐπισκόπους τοῖς ὁμοούσιον πατρὶ τὸν υἱὸν δοξάζουσι συνεῖναι**, “that the bishops in the West should join with those who held the Son to be consubstantial with the Father.” Yet here there is a typographical error: *homoousiou* has been printed in place of *homoiousiou*, “of like substance”; for Sozomen himself writes elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0748D] The same, book 3, ch. 18.] that Constantius had not entirely ceased to confess the Son **κατ᾽ οὐσίαν ὅμοιον**, “like in substance.”

But when the heretical bishops continually attending Constantius—the crafty promoters of peace—perceived that they could not obtain this, they first suggested to the Emperor a plan for proscribing Athanasius. Once he had been condemned by Western bishops as well, the Nicene faith could thereafter easily be overthrown. For thus, says the same Sozomen, he reasoned: [Col. 0749A] if Athanasius were removed by the common vote of all, he could thereafter easily determine religious matters as he pleased. That this was the true cause of the Council of Milan is confirmed by Sozomen himself in chapter 9.

Accordingly, the things which Lucifer repeatedly throws in Constantius’s teeth must be referred to this council: he calls him a deceitful promoter of peace, when in truth he was peace’s enemy [Note: [Col. 0749D] *On Not Associating with Heretics*, pp. 9 and 12 (cols. 773 and 775).]: “You said, ‘I desire peace to be established in my empire,’ while desiring to violate the Lord’s peace in us”; and, “If you are not Constantius the Emperor, who pretended to make peace”; and, “You said to us, ‘I desire peace to be made.’” Thus in the book *On Not Associating with Heretics*; and in Book I *For St Athanasius*, p. 54 (col. 819): “You asserted that you were acting for the sake of peace”—that Athanasius, namely, might be condemned. Then in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, p. 223 (col. 992): “Pretending to establish peace, you had attempted to destroy the whole Church of God.” All these statements undoubtedly concern the Council of Milan, whose wicked acts Lucifer frequently attacks in all his books.

Nor can they be referred to the Council of Rimini, although Constantius likewise later summoned that council under the pretext of peace, as Sozomen [Note: [Col. 0749D] Book 4, ch. 17.] and Socrates [Note: [Col. 0749D] Book 2, ch. 37.] testify—but always with the false and unjust purpose of the heretics. For Lucifer declares that he heard Constantius say, “I desire peace to be made,” when the Pope’s legate was presiding over the council; and Liberius, writing to Lucifer shortly after that same council, begins his letter on p. 2 (col. 766) as follows: “Although, under the appearance of peace, the enemy of the human race seems to have raged more violently against the members of the Church, yet you, etc.”

For this reason, then, I find that Constantius issued two Edicts [Col. 0749C]. The first commanded bishops absent from the council to subscribe to the Arian sentence against Athanasius. Athanasius himself intimates this:

> How many bishops, as it stands in the sacred writings, were brought before governors and kings and heard this sentence from the judges: “Either subscribe, or withdraw from the churches; for the Emperor has commanded that you be removed from the churches” [Note: [Col. 0749D] In the *Letter to the Solitaries*.].

But Lucifer does not write about this edict, since he indicates that it was of such a kind as to embrace a new formula of faith. The other was designated by Sulpicius Severus as an “epistle”; this is the one Lucifer had in view when composing his books, and the things charged by Lucifer against it suit it exactly.

For Sulpicius relates [Note: [Col. 0749D] *Sacred History*, book 2.] that an epistle, issued by Valens and Ursacius under the Emperor’s name, was filled with every sort of perversity, with this purpose: if the people approved it, they might put forth what they desired under public authority; but if not, all odium would fall upon the Emperor, who, not yet baptized, could not know the mysteries of the faith. “When the Epistle was read in church, the people rejected it; Dionysius, because he had not agreed, was expelled from the city,” etc.

Lucifer himself declares [Col. 0750A; Note: [Col. 0750D] *On Not Associating with Heretics*, p. 17 (col. 780).], and repeatedly confirms [Note: [Col. 0750D] The same, in *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, pp. 241, 245, 261 (cols. 1011, 1015, 1031).], both how cunningly, elegantly, and ornately it was written, and what impious and blasphemous content it contained against the Catholic faith. “For your word,” he says, “by which you creep like a cancer, you compose with a false, painted-up swelling of knowledge, maintaining that you are the destroyer of your Edict, stained with every crime, a harvest of every error.” Again: “Your novel preaching, and new religion—a blasphemy put forth by you under the pretext of faith, for the destruction of your salvation.” And again: “You have endeavoured to preach the blasphemy uttered by the sacrilegious mouth of your Arius, now through your agents, now through your Edict, now through your mouth filled with unclean spirits.”

That Lucifer denotes this epistle by the name “Edict” may be confirmed, first, by Athanasius’s example. He writes to the Orthodox that letters of the Prefect of Egypt concerning the installation of George in Athanasius’s own place were publicly posted in the form of an Edict—provided that these letters are assigned, with Pagius and Valesius [Col. 0750B; Note: [Col. 0750D] Book 1 of the *Observations on Volume 2 of the Ecclesiastical Historians*.], to the year 356, against Baronius’s opinion, who thinks they were written concerning Gregory, likewise intruded into the Alexandrian see, and assigns them to 342. It may be confirmed, secondly, by the authority of Hieronymus a Prato, who agrees with us in a note appended to Sulpicius’s testimony; and finally, because Lucifer himself [Note: [Col. 0750D] *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, p. 198.] says that it was despised by him and his fellow bishops: “You would rightly call me insolent, if we had not rightly despised your sacrilegious Edict.” He testifies in *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, p. 244 (col. 1014), that this occurred at Milan in the palace, when he told the judges, while Constantius listened behind a curtain, that even if all the weapons of imperial power were turned against himself and his colleagues as despisers of the sacrilegious decree, he would never depart from his resolution to defend the Catholic faith.

Hilary too had these matters concerning Constantius’s Epistle or Edict [Col. 0750C] in mind when he wrote [Note: [Col. 0750D] *On the Synods*, no. 78.] what we cited in the note appended to p. 17 (col. 780) of this edition, and what Pratensis transferred from the same passage into another annotation on Sulpicius:

> Previously, in darkness and corners, the Lord Christ was denied to be the Son of God according to nature, and was proclaimed to have received, together with creatures, an origin from things that did not exist, being devoid of the Father’s essence. But now heresy, breaking forth in a profession sanctioned by public authority, gloried as a victorious power in what formerly had been done secretly.

The Maurist editors of St Hilary’s works likewise refer to this testimony of Lucifer from the book *That One Must Die*, etc., produced a little above. Certainly, then, Arian heresy, for the first time supported by the authority of emperors, openly broke out victorious over the Roman world at the Council of Milan [Col. 0750D]. Before this, it had not deemed itself sufficiently safe and concealed itself by cunning and fraud. Lucifer often charges Constantius with this: that by his imperial rule and power the Arian poison had been diffused through every part of the earth.

It remains to inquire whether another testimony of our Lucifer from the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, p. 172 (col. 940), ought likewise to be referred here. It runs thus:

> Will you deny that you invited us to embrace idolatry? If you think it should be denied, the expositions of the bishops of your sect—your fellow-blasphemers, that is—will convict you; the pamphlets recited by you and given at Rome even to Catholic bishops will convict you, namely, so that your blasphemy might be strengthened in every place.

The author of the first *Dissertation on the Deeds of Liberius*, prefixed to the works of St Damasus, § 10, p. 117 (col. 320), cited these words of Lucifer from Book I *For St Athanasius*; the passage is presented by us more correctly below. That author thinks that Lucifer here marks and signifies the formula of Rimini—or rather the Acacian formula—and rejects Tillemont’s opinion that [Note: [Col. 0751D] Article 63, “On the Arians,” no. 6.] Lucifer wrote this concerning the Sirmian Formula of 357. In that year Constantius was at Rome; there, he says, a pamphlet was read by the Emperor, distributed through the city, and presented by imperial command to Catholic bishops, in order to test their minds and opinions concerning the formula of faith that was shortly to be published at the Sirmian assembly [Col. 0751B].

But before examining these questions more closely, it should be noted—as we also observed in the notes on p. 56 (col. 821), where an error must be corrected which slipped in through inadvertence, when the *Dissertation on the Deeds of Liberius* prefixed to the works of Pope St Damasus was attributed to Hieronymus a Prato—that Lucifer uses the terms “perfidy,” “blasphemy,” and “idolatry” in the simpler sense to signify Arian heresy itself, although these words may sometimes be understood of the Edict of Milan, of which we have just spoken.

But in the present passage three things must be distinguished: the words “idolatry” and “blasphemy”; the expositions of Arian bishops; and the pamphlets recited and given at Rome by Constantius to Catholic bishops [Col. 0751C]. The terms “blasphemy” and “idolatry,” therefore, indicate Arius’s heresy itself, which Constantius wished to strengthen everywhere and have accepted by all through Arian expositions of faith and the aid of impious pamphlets, which he ordered especially to be distributed at Rome. Arian heresy was rightly called a new kind of idolatry, and Arians idolaters, by other Fathers—Athanasius, Basil, both Gregories, Nazianzen and Nyssen, and Cyril of Alexandria—because, as Petavius observes from them [Note: [Col. 0751D] Book 2, ch. 12, no. 6.], they professed to worship one whom they admitted to be a creature, and thus differed in no respect from pagans.

The term “blasphemy,” moreover, cannot denote one Sirmian Formula alone, but all the heretical formulas of the Arians; the editors of Hilary’s works affirm that he too used it in this way [Note: [Col. 0752D] In book 4 *On the Trinity*, no. 12.]. “But,” says the aforementioned author of the *Dissertation* [Col. 0751D] against Tillemont, “when Lucifer writes that pamphlets were recited by Constantius and handed about through the bishops, so that his blasphemy might be strengthened everywhere, the reader readily understands that he is treating not of a blasphemy merely premeditated, but of one already brought to light and promulgated. Further, no one will readily grant that the blasphemy which everyone knows was afterwards composed at that clandestine and accidental gathering at Sirmium could already at that time have been formulated, read to Catholic bishops, and handed about.”

This is correctly said concerning the Sirmian formula; yet it conflicts with that author’s own view. For the formula of Rimini and that of Seleucia, or Acacian formula, which he believes Lucifer denotes, had still to be promulgated; indeed, they were issued three years later if, with Petavius, you assign Constantius’s Roman triumph to 356, or two years later if, with Pagius, Valesius, and others, you assign that triumph to 357 [Col. 0752A]. Moreover, the formula of Rimini too had been secretly and furtively drafted by Valens. As for the formula to be framed at Seleucia, how many divisions and disputes arose among the heretical bishops before they eventually approved the formula of Rimini by their votes!

Nor were only these formulas written after Constantius distributed those pamphlets at Rome. For Eudoxius, at a council held at Antioch in 358, together with bishops who favoured the same opinion, rejected both the term “like in substance” and even the word “consubstantial,” as Sozomen states [Note: [Col. 0752D] Book 4, ch. 12.]. Therefore nothing certain can be established from those words of Lucifer, which, as the same author writes, may appear somewhat obscure to us who are far removed from those times.

But, to state our own opinion as well, we hold that Lucifer does not allude to this or that particular exposition of faith. Rather, he reproaches Constantius solely for having attempted, by however many and various expositions of faith after the Council of Milan, impiously to overthrow the Nicene faith and to strengthen Arian blasphemy everywhere. He again makes this charge against Constantius in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, as we note there.

The pamphlets recited by Constantius at Rome and given even to Catholic bishops [Col. 0752C] were undoubtedly those he mentions in the same book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, p. 220 (col. 990), in these words: “So far as lies in your power, you have handed him over—that is, the Son of God—concerning whom you also gave written books.” They were consequently writings in which the Arian doctrine was impiously defended, but cleverly composed by Arian bishops—perhaps by Eudoxius himself, then bishop of Germanicia, who was staying with Constantius at Rome—in order fraudulently to draw the Roman populace and Catholic bishops into error. Indeed, it is much more likely that they set out the same impious expressions and blasphemous propositions contained in the Milanese Epistle or Edict. We may discuss these matters conjecturally, since no ancient writer besides Lucifer has recorded anything about this deed of Constantius [Col. 0752D].

But I do not sufficiently see how this entire testimony of Lucifer assists the opinion of the aforementioned author about Liberius’s twofold exile, which he defends. We do not pursue the matter further, since that question does not concern us. We observe, however, that the same author’s opinion concerning the sense of the word *blasphemy* was appended by us on p. 56 (col. 821) to Lucifer’s first book *For St Athanasius*, where the word *idolatry* slipped in for *blasphemy*, because there we noted from Lucifer certain points concerning the meaning of that word and other related terms which might shed light on the other passages of our Lucifer [Col. 0753A]. Otherwise, that author’s words and judgment truly pertain to Lucifer’s own testimony, which has just been explained. Enough on these points. We must now turn to Lucifer’s deeds; and readers will find in the annotations appended to this edition whatever may concern either the history of that age or, in some degree, the meaning of the words and the mind of Lucifer.

## § VI

When the Emperor Constantius had died at Mopsucrena near Tarsus, on 3 November in A.D. 361, after being baptized by the Arian bishop Euzoius, as Socrates says [Note: [Col. 0753D] Book 1, ch. 46.], shortly before his death—despite Lucifer’s vain urging that he seek the saving laver of regeneration through Athanasius or his fellow bishops [Note: [Col. 0753D] Book 1 *For St Athanasius*, p. 109 (col. 876).]—Flavius Claudius Julian, surnamed the Apostate, free from fear and alone took up the reins of the Roman [Col. 0753B] Empire to govern. He had first seized them in the preceding year at Lutetia of the Parisians by the favour of the soldiers, and then in Dacia with the same soldiers’ approval, while Constantius was still alive.

At the very threshold, as it were, of his reign, this most crafty Emperor gained great praise among all upright people by restoring the peace vainly sought and desired under his predecessor amid the Church’s disturbed affairs. He permitted all bishops formerly punished with exile by Constantius to return to their churches [Note: [Col. 0753D] “All bishops who had been driven from their own sees returned to their churches through the favour of the new ruler.” Jerome, *Against Lucifer*; Socrates, book 3, chs. 1 and 5; Sozomen, book 5, ch. 5; Theodoret, book 3, ch. 4; Baronius, under A.D. 361, no. 13.]; decreed that goods seized from them by heretics should be restored; and ordered that no one should thereafter be harassed on account of the faith [Note: [Col. 0753D] “By a law he restored their property to those who had been proscribed; and he publicly forbade the peoples of the cities either to injure Christians or to insult them, or to compel the unwilling to sacrifice.” Sozomen, in Valesius’s translation, book 5, ch. 5. See Julian himself, Letters 7 to Artabius, 43 to Hecebolius, and 52 to the people of Bostra. For Julian’s deceitful purpose in these measures, see Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration 2 against Julian*; Sozomen, book 5, ch. 4; Socrates, book 3, ch. 1; Theodoret, book 3, chs. 6 and 17; Evagrius, *Lives of the Fathers*, under Apollonius, ch. 7.].

Accordingly Lucifer, released from exile through Julian’s favour in the consulship of Taurus and Florentius, as A.D. 361 drew to its close [Note: [Col. 0753D] Chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine, in Canisius, vol. 1, *Treasury of Monuments*, p. 293; and Petavius, *The Reckoning of Time*, under the succession of Roman consuls, vol. 2, p. 466 [Col. 0754D].], left the Egyptian wilderness. Restored to the Catholics, he gave most timely aid to the afflicted state of the Church and, with Eusebius of Vercelli, his companion in the apostolic mission, travelled throughout the provinces of the East with great labour, striving to recall to the bosom of the Catholic Church those who had yielded to Arian heresy [Col. 0753C; Note: [Col. 0754D] From Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration in Praise of Basil*, and Baronius, under A.D. 362, no. 58.].

I think Lucifer completed these journeys from the time of the Edict by which Julian restored Orthodox bishops to their sees—that is, from the end of November 361—until the convening of the Council of Alexandria in the following year, 362, after the death of George of Cappadocia, the Arian bishop of Alexandria, and the return of the great Athanasius to that see [Note: [Col. 0754D] See Nazianzen, cited above, and Baronius, ibid., no. 171.].

Lucifer turned aside from these journeys when he learned, through letters of Pope Liberius, that he had been appointed to calm the disturbances at Antioch and cleanse that Church of the dregs of Arian heresy [Col. 0754A; Note: [Col. 0754D] Baronius, ibid., no. 177.]. At the same time Liberius had sent Eusebius of Vercelli as a legate, so that he might aid the Church of Alexandria at the council already summoned. Thus, while Eusebius devoted himself wholly with Athanasius to the Alexandrian Council, Lucifer hastened to the Catholics at Antioch, troubled by internal dissensions and suffering under Arian persecution. Since he himself could not go to the Alexandrian synod, he sent in his own name two deacons, Herennius and Agapetus, as delegates, as is apparent from the subscriptions to that council:

> “I, Athanasius, and likewise the other bishops who assembled, signed; and there were also sent by Lucifer, bishop of the island of Sardinia, two deacons, Herennius and Agapetus.” [Note: [Col. 0754D] Vol. 2 of the Councils, Venice edition of 1728, pp. 947 ff.; and vol. 1 of the Works of St Athanasius, Paris edition of 1627, p. 580.]

Hence Rufinus is plainly mistaken when he writes that only one delegate of Lucifer attended that council [Note: [Col. 0754D] Book 8, ch. 27. See Baronius, cited above, no. 180.], unless we wish to say that he named Herennius alone as the principal delegate, not excluding but passing over Agapetus. I would suppose this is also what the author of the *Life of St Eusebius of Vercelli* [Col. 0754B; Note: [Col. 0754D] In the additions to the Council of Alexandria from Baluze’s new collection, vol. 2 of the same edition of the Councils, p. 951.], Hieronymus a Prato [Note: [Col. 0754D] See notes on Sulpicius Severus, vol. 2, p. 244.], and other modern writers did when, neglecting his companion, they named the more distinguished man.

Before Lucifer went to Antioch, the cited writer of Eusebius’s life wishes him to have remained for some time at Alexandria with Athanasius and Eusebius, in these words:

> Blessed Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, having taken leave of Athanasius and Eusebius, was sent by them to Antioch to strengthen the churches concerning the consubstantiality of the Godhead. He left his deacon with them at Alexandria, to act in his stead at the council, through whom he declared that he would regard as ratified whatever should be established by the council’s ordinance.

Yet these statements openly conflict with what follows in the same place:

> But when Lucifer was entreated by Eusebius—because both had been banished in regions neighbouring Egypt—to proceed with him to Alexandria to see Athanasius and, in common deliberation with the bishops who survived, determine the condition of the Church, he declined to be present, sent his deacon as delegate in his place, and himself pressed on with fixed purpose to Antioch [Col. 0754C; Note: [Col. 0754D] In the Bollandists, 25 May, vol. 5.].

For if Lucifer took leave of Athanasius and Eusebius and was sent by them to Antioch, he surely lodged with them at Alexandria, where he is said to have left his deacon. But if he was entreated by Eusebius to go with him to Alexandria to visit Athanasius; if he refused to go; if he sent his deacon there—then it is wholly evident that he neither entered Alexandria [Col. 0755A], nor saw Athanasius, nor left his deacon there to attend the synod in his name.

Therefore, the compiler of that life, being entirely inconsistent with himself, must be said not to have attended to historical truth. I myself would believe that account was drawn partly from Rufinus’s history and partly invented by an anonymous author, and consequently contradicts itself manifestly. For the words, “But when Lucifer,” etc., which we cited last, are copied exactly and in full from Rufinus, Book I, chapter 27. We must therefore believe, as we indicated above, that Lucifer went directly to Antioch; that he did not meet Athanasius at Alexandria; and that, separated from Eusebius and having sent his delegates to the Alexandrian synod, he hastened to provide assistance and consolation for the Antiochenes.

## § VII

[Col. 0755B]

At that time the condition of the Church of Antioch was as follows. Two bishops occupied one and the same see: Meletius, exiled because of the Catholic faith, and Euzoius, appointed by the Arians as Meletius’ successor. What disturbances then existed at Antioch! With Constantius favoring them, what did not the Arians dare against the orthodox in defending Euzoius? The Catholics, however, were divided into two parties. The Eustathians utterly rejected Meletius—who had at one time seemed to adhere to the Arians but, having withdrawn from them, had been driven into exile and was absent from Antioch—as one polluted by heretical communion, suspect, and hated. Others, on the contrary, obedient to Meletius and more zealously favoring his cause, avoided the Eustathians and regarded Meletius alone, though in exile, as the lawful and true [Col. 0755C] shepherd of the Church of Antioch.

In order to calm these storms, Lucifer, as soon as he came to Antioch, directed all his mind and strength, with the authority he possessed, toward reconciling the parties, joining their hearts in a friendly covenant, and restoring peace to that Church. [Note: [Col. 0755C] Rufinus and Baronius, in the places cited; and Cassiodorus, *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 19.]

Lucifer therefore conceived the plan that, first Euzoius the Arian being rejected, and then Meletius the Catholic bishop being excluded, the dissenting orthodox might agree upon some third person: one approved by all the Antiochenes for unimpaired faith and holiness of life, and accepted as bishop by their common [Col. 0756A] wishes and efforts. Accordingly, having summoned two other prelates, Cymatius of Paltus and Anatolius of Beroea, [Note: [Col. 0755C] Bollandists, vol. 4, May, under 20 May, chapter 5, no. 34.] he set Paullinus over them—a man endowed with those qualities and, above all others, worthy of the see of the Church of Antioch. [Note: [Col. 0755D] Socrates, Sozomen, Baronius, in the place cited; Chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine, in Canisius, vol. 1, *Thesaurus Monumentorum*, p. 293: “Lucifer, with two confessors added, makes Paullinus—presbyter of Bishop Eustathius, who had never polluted himself by communion with heretics—bishop of the Catholic party at Antioch.”] He was the second Paullinus of that name in the succession of Antiochene prelates.

Baronius [Note: [Col. 0755D] Place cited, no. 180.] and Valesius [Note: [Col. 0755D] Notes on Socrates, book 3, chapter 5.] held that Paullinus was raised to the Antiochene see before the Synod of Alexandria. But, with Hermant in his *Life of St Athanasius*, [Note: [Col. 0755D] Book 10, chapter 9.] Pagi, [Note: [Col. 0755D] In his critique of Baronius for the same year, no. 23.] Bosch, [Note: [Col. 0755D] *Chronological History of the Patriarchs of Antioch*, in *Acts of the Saints*, vol. 4, July, p. 58, Venetian edition.] and the editors of the works of St Athanasius, [Note: [Col. 0755D] Notice, vol. 1, part 2, no. 4, p. 770.] we rather adopt the opinion that Paullinus was given to the Antiochenes as bishop by Lucifer while the Alexandrian Synod itself was still in session.

Meanwhile Paullinus, the new Antiochene prelate, as lawful bishop sent his deacons Maximus and Calimerus [Col. 0756B] to the Council of Alexandria to attend it in his name. They sat among the Fathers of the Council and approved the decrees of that Synod by their subscriptions. [Note: [Col. 0755D] In the Synodical Letter cited: “But from Paullinus, Maximus and Calimerus, who are themselves also deacons.”] And indeed the Synod of Alexandria recognized Paullinus as the true and lawful bishop of the Antiochenes, both by admitting his delegates and by receiving their subscriptions.

Moreover, the Fathers seem in their Synodical Letter to exhort the Antiochenes, laying aside partisan attachments, to obey Paullinus alone: “Then welcome those who have returned from the Arians to you; receive them as fathers and accept them as teachers and guardians, meanwhile being joined to our beloved Paullinus and his associates.” And, sending the Synodical Letter itself to the absent Paullinus for subscription, they wished that he too should attest in a formal document his profession of faith. [Note: [Col. 0755D] In the same Synodical Letter: “I, Paullinus, hold this view, as I received it from the Fathers: that the Son is and subsists perfect,” etc.]

[Col. 0756C] Thus Athanasius, together with the bishops of Egypt, and Epiphanius, together with all the churches of Cyprus, communicated with Paullinus and assented to his election. [Note: [Col. 0755D] Richard, vol. 1, *Universal Dictionary*, under “Antioch,” p. [Col. 0756C] 264, col. 2: “Athanasius and all Egypt communicated with Paulinus; Epiphanius with the island of Cyprus; the Bishop of Rome with the Westerners.”] Indeed, he also won approval from Liberius, Roman Pontiff, as the father of ecclesiastical annals demonstrates; [Note: [Col. 0756D] Place cited, no. 231 and following.] nor does he seem to have been less acceptable to Damasus, who wrote letters to Paullinus both concerning Vitalis, suspected and accused of the heresy of the Apollinarians, [Note: [Col. 0756D] Severinus Binius observes that a letter of Damasus falsely inscribed to Paullinus of Thessalonica was fabricated and attached by Theodoret through a deceptive heading to the Synodical Letter of the Third Roman Council; see the following note from vol. 2 of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1015.] and against the errors of Apollinaris, Arius, Sabellius, Macedonius, Eunomius, and Photinus. [Note: [Col. 0756D] This Synodical Letter belongs to the Third Council of Rome and was given to Paullinus, bishop of Antioch. Theodoret deceitfully prefixed it to Paullinus of Thessalonica in book 5, chapter 11. For it is certain that at that time Acholius, a most holy man, presided over the Thessalonians; Theodoret himself, forgetful of his own account, reports this from the Synodical Letter of the Council of Constantinople. Severinus Binius suspects, in notes on this letter, vol. 2 of the Councils, p. 1065, Venetian edition, that Theodoret—hostile to the Paullinian party—did this so that Paullinus himself might not appear united in Catholic communion to Pope Damasus. On the communion of Damasus [Col. 0757D] with Paullinus, see also St Basil, Epistle 214, otherwise 359, and Epistle 216, otherwise 272; and Sarazanius, on the *Short Works and Acts of Pope St Damasus*, chapter 10, no. 2.]

It is true that the Eastern bishops rejected Paullinus’ election [Col. 0757A] and always adhered to Meletius; and thus the schism at Antioch endured until peace was concluded between Meletius and Paullinus, on the condition—and after the parties, especially Flavian and Theodore, had sworn—that no successor should be appointed upon the death of either. [Note: [Col. 0757D] From Socrates and Gregory Nazianzen; Petavius, *Rationarium Temporum*, part 1, book 6, chapter 7, p. 281.] But the Eastern bishops did not abide by the agreement: after Meletius’ death, they appointed Flavian to the Antiochene see, and the schism broke out afresh for many years.

Now the alleged cause of disagreement between Lucifer and Eusebius—namely, Eusebius’ disapproval of Paullinus’ election by Lucifer—is not to be accepted, although it is supported by the testimony of Rufinus, Socrates, and Sozomen. For Eusebius himself, at the Alexandrian Synod, and Athanasius and the other Fathers had ratified it; Eusebius could not condemn what he had himself solemnly [Col. 0757B] approved. [Note: [Col. 0757D] Baronius, place cited, no. 215.] I would certainly believe that Eusebius did not disapprove Lucifer’s act as such, but was singularly displeased by Paullinus’ hasty and ill-timed election. He complained of it amicably to Lucifer when, upon arriving at Antioch, he found Catholic affairs not merely unsettled but more bitter, and saw new and graver disturbances arising among the orthodox.

For Meletius’ supporters, after their return from exile to Antioch, had joined themselves to him and begun to hold assemblies separate from the Paullinians. They recognized Meletius alone as Antiochene bishop and considered him worthy of the high priesthood: though he had at one time fallen into communion with the Acacians and Eudoxians, they believed him made illustrious by his subsequent glorious confession; indeed, if perhaps he had fallen from his rank, [Col. 0757C] they said that he had been restored to it by the solemn decree of the Alexandrian Synod concerning those who had truly repented after falling away and were to be restored to their former honors and dignities.

Since Eusebius foresaw the divisions and scandals that would result, he could not refrain from complaining privately to Lucifer, in some sense the author of the dissension. He wholly disapproved Lucifer’s plan in that precipitous election of Paullinus, pregnant with most disastrous consequences.

## § VIII

Accordingly, as we have said, when Eusebius arrived at Antioch, having already received news of Paullinus’ election, and discovered that the concord intended by Lucifer had not merely failed to be achieved but that fresh dissensions had arisen among the Catholics, he condemned Lucifer’s excessively hasty judgment [Col. 0757D] and endeavored to ensure that the affairs of the Church of Antioch might be provided for in the best manner possible. Therefore, once Antioch had been granted some sort of peace, Eusebius turned his attention and concern to ordering the other churches of the East.

[Col. 0758A] But when Lucifer perceived that Eusebius regarded his appointment of Paullinus as rash, he bore Eusebius’ judgment with difficulty. The decrees of the Council of Alexandria concerning the reception of those who had truly repented after falling away—provided they had not been the authors of heresies—and their restoration with rank to their sees, increased this bitterness already conceived in his mind. [Note: [Col. 0757D] Councils, vol. 2, as above; Rufinus, book 2, chapter 28; Baronius, place cited, no. 182.] This was especially so because he suspected that, contrary to his own view—that those returning from heresy to the orthodox faith should indeed be admitted to communion but deprived of their former honors—it had been done at the instigation of Eusebius and Athanasius.

Accordingly, Lucifer, inflamed with indignation, rejected the decrees of that Council; judging that he ought not communicate with bishops restored to their rank, he separated himself from them and from the other Fathers of the Alexandrian Synod. By this deed [Col. 0758B] he gave occasion and a name to a dangerous schism. Those who adopted his opinion were called Luciferians, and St Jerome afterward pursued them in outstanding writings when they disgracefully lapsed into heresy.

Meanwhile, while considering his return to Italy, Lucifer needed to stay at Caesarea in order to bring to peace the cities subject to that Church in Cappadocia, which were divided among themselves over the election of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea. We judge, with the great father of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, that this happened at the beginning of the second year of Julian Augustus—that is, at the end of January 363. [Note: [Col. 0757D] Under the year 363; and *Acts of the Saints*, vol. IV, May, under 24 May, chapter 5, no. 45.]

When these matters had been completed, Lucifer at last returned from the East to Italy in the same year of Christ 363, in the fourth consulship of Julian Augustus and that of Sallustius Promotus. In order at length to attend to his own rest after so many labors undergone, he withdrew to Sardinia. There are those who say that before Lucifer returned to Cagliari, he landed in Campania, avoided Zosimus, the pseudo-bishop of Naples, whom the Arians had appointed after driving Maximus into exile, [Note: [Col. 0758D] See Mazochi, on the ancient marble martyrology of Naples, chapters 1 and 4, under 11 January; Sabbatini, *Ancient Neapolitan Calendar*, vol. 5, p. 26; Muratori, on the Chronicle of John the Deacon; Coletti, *Italia Sacra*, on the archbishops of Naples, vol. 6; *Sardinia Sacra*, cited place, where the note says: “I observe that in Baronius, perhaps through the fault of copyists, Maximus is said to have been appointed in Zosimus’ place. I am surprised that the most sharp-sighted Mansi did not correct this error in the Lucca edition, although Coletti himself, vol. VI of *Italia Sacra*, noted that it should be corrected.”] and met Pope Liberius in Rome. But since all these matters seem doubtful and rest especially upon the suspect testimony of the Luciferians Faustinus and Marcellinus, [Note: [Col. 0758D] *Book of Petitions*, in Sirmond, place cited.] we willingly pass them over.

For about eight years from his return, Lucifer devoted himself to governing the Church of Cagliari, having fallen upon very difficult times under Valens, the Arian emperor of the East. At last, when Valentinian the Elder was directing the reins of the Western Empire, in the year of Christ 371 begun, the eighth of his reign, under the second consulship of Gratian Augustus and that of Sextus Anicius Probus—or at least toward the end of the preceding year, the seventh of Valentinian, A.D. 370—Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, died in that city.

His death is recorded thus in Jerome’s Chronicle: “Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, dies; he, together with Gregory of the Spains [Col. 0759A] and Philo of Libya, never mingled himself with Arian perversity.” [Note: [Col. 0759B] And from this, Petavius, place cited, chapter 7, p. 281.]

There is no pleasure in refuting here the glaring error of John Fara, who placed Lucifer’s death in A.D. 390, the seventeenth year of the reign of Valentinian the Younger, [Note: [Col. 0759B] *On Sardinian Affairs*, book 1.] an opinion accepted, without concern for chronology, by Dimas Serpi [Note: [Col. 0759B] *Chronicle of the Saints of Sardinia*, book 2, chapter 3.] and Seraphinus Esquirrius. [Note: [Col. 0759B] *Sanctuary of Cagliari*, book 2, chapter 1.]

Whether Lucifer renounced the schism before his death and returned himself to Catholic communion is uncertain and remains undecided. Besides Socrates, Sozomen, and Nicetas, the following wrote in Lucifer’s defense: Papebroch, [Note: [Col. 0759B] *Acts of the Saints*, vol. IV, May, under 20 May.] Ruinart, [Note: [Col. 0759B] Notes on book 4 of Victor of Vita, p. 188, Venetian edition, 1732; and *Sacred Cemeteries*, book 4, part 1, chapter 3, p. 366.] Thomassin, [Note: [Col. 0759B] Dissertation 5, on the Synod of Rimini, no. 25, p. 82, Lucca edition.] Machin, [Note: [Col. 0759B] *Defense of the Sanctity of Blessed Lucifer*, Cagliari edition, 1699.] Methodius, [Note: [Col. 0759B] In the manuscript Life, in the Bollandists, place cited.] Macedo, [Note: [Col. 0759B] *On the Tutelary Gods of the Christian World*, p. 215 and following.] Ferrarius, [Note: [Col. 0759C] *Catalogue of the Saints*, 18 June, p. 35.] Spondanus, [Note: [Col. 0759C] *Epitome of Baronius’ Annals*, under A.D. 362, Paris edition, 1622, p. 464.] and other modern writers.

Against him, however, argued Ambrose, [Note: [Col. 0759C] Book 1, *On the Death of St Satyrus*, vol. 2 of the Works, no. 47, col. 1127.] Augustine, [Note: [Col. 0759C] Works, vol. 2, Epistle 185, otherwise 50.] Isidore, [Note: [Col. 0759C] *On Origins*, book 8, chapter 5, p. 105, Paris edition, 1601.] Baronius, [Note: [Col. 0759C] Under A.D. 362, no. 225.] Natalis Alexander, [Note: [Col. 0759C] Vol. IV, *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, chapter 3, article 13.] Tillemont, [Note: [Col. 0759C] Vol. VIII, *Ecclesiastical History*, no. 4, p. 764, Venetian edition, 1732.] Sbaralea, [Note: [Col. 0759C] *Against the Defenders of Cyprian*, dissertation 1, chapter 1, no. 2.] Labbe, [Note: [Col. 0759C] *History of the First Council of Constantinople*, in *Collection of Councils*, p. 1092, Venetian edition, 1728.] [Col. 0759B] Jerome de Prato, [Note: [Col. 0759C] Notes on Sulpicius Severus, vol. 2, book 2, p. 245, Verona edition, 1754.] Severinus Binius, [Note: [Col. 0760B] On the Life of St Liberius, Pope, from the *Liber Pontificalis* of Pope Damasus, vol. 2 of the Councils, cited edition.] and many other distinguished critics. To those of uncertain opinion we add Rufinus and Sulpicius Severus.

Archbishop Machin gathered much material in a large volume for Lucifer’s defense, and brought forward the proceedings concerning the discovery of his body—which Papebroch also published—the iconography of certain churches, [Col. 0760A] and inscriptions excavated at Cagliari. But what if we should say that this body belonged to another, younger Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, who suffered martyrdom in the Vandal persecution under King Huneric? [Note: [Col. 0760B] Victor of Vita, in the *Notice of Africa*, under the province of Sardinia, which in the ninth century, according to Leo the Wise, belonged to Africa; its metropolis, Cagliari, was numbered among the cities of Mauretania Secunda, under the most glorious eparch of Africa. In 484, after the Catholic bishops of Africa, among them Lucifer, had been summoned to Carthage, they were sent into exile to cut timber useful for the royal ships. Since they were oppressed by extreme need and so many hardships, St Symmachus, supreme pontiff, provided them annually with money and clothing, as Anastasius says, [Col. 0760C] *Bibliotheca*, vol. 3, p. 222.] What if we should maintain, with the archbishop of Torres, that those inscriptions were fabricated by the people of Cagliari?

Nevertheless, adhering with the reverence due to the decrees of Urban VIII, supreme pontiff, of 20 June 1641, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, and of Innocent X, supreme pontiff, of 17 October 1647, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, we neither approve nor reject any of these matters with the learned Matthaeus. [Note: [Col. 0760C] *Sardinia Sacra*, cited place: “I neither approve nor reject these particulars, but set them forth merely as a historical narrative, as though reported by others. For I confess that I hold in the highest veneration the decree by which Urban VIII, on 20 June 1641, commanded all and each, etc., that henceforth, until His Holiness or the Holy See should otherwise ordain, they should not dare publicly to treat, dispute, or contend concerning Lucifer’s sanctity, cult, and veneration, nor attack or defend it in writing or in print. It is printed in Benedict XIV’s work *On the Beatification and Canonization of Saints*, vol. 1, book 1, chapter 40, which discusses the cult of Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, in such a way as to show that it has not hitherto been duly approved by the authority of the Roman Pontiff.”] We have set them forth only by historical narration, as if reported by others, without disguise or contention, supporting neither side by our judgment.

If, however, following the example of other writers and the ancient Milanese manuscript [Col. 0760B] in which the *Faith of St Lucifer the Bishop* is transcribed, we have given Lucifer the designation “Saint” at the very beginning of his works and in the title of each book, we declare that we have given it only in the sense entirely consistent with the published decrees of Urban VIII on this matter.

[Col. 0759]

# LETTER OF JOHN TILLIUS TO PIUS V, SUPREME PONTIFF, PRINTED AT THE HEAD OF LUCIFER’S WORKS EDITED BY TILLIUS IN 1568

To Pius V, Most Holy Supreme Pontiff: John Tillius, Bishop of Meaux, sends greetings.

[Col. 0759D]

I should never have dared, Most Blessed Father, to approach you by letter, had I not been admonished by the example of the most weighty and holy men of old in the Church, who always had recourse to your Apostolic See, whether they needed counsel or were pressed by other great affairs. For Your Holiness cannot be unaware of the calamities amid which we now live in France; and in such adversity we could find no better consolation in God than in your prudent fatherhood. While, according to the measure of our strength, we endeavor to dispel these most hostile and foul winters and mists, I confess, Most Blessed [Col. 0761A] Father, that through our own fault the contempt and disdain directed against our order are so miserable that we possess scarcely any authority left; and indeed we do not deserve it.

Therefore I have recourse to our first Fathers, nearer to the times of Christ the Lord, and turn over and investigate their writings, in order to show how they applied themselves to the treatment of that doctrine which, in the progress of time, they had learned from him and his Apostles; and by what means they sustained both themselves and Christ’s cause against the assaults of enemies. Among them this Lucifer shone upon me as a most brilliant star, reflecting the light of the sun. He brings into the open and elucidates that worst heresy of Arius—greatest of all since humankind began—the mother of Antichrist.

I desire this splendor to appear under the name of Your Holiness, whose elevation neither friends nor enemies throughout the whole world could disapprove or despise, nor could they desire in a shepherd greater care and labor for the Church’s good. I do this chiefly for two reasons. The first is that I may reproach my own order—formerly most upright in France and most devoted and faithful toward God and the prince—for being in these times so unhappy and deplorable that, though our Most Christian king is a boy descended from Most Christian kings who have deserved well of us, not even one person was found to preserve religion for him whole and unharmed. This is especially so since we have seen with our own eyes chairs set against chairs, profane tables erected against altars, and faithful servants of God—even bishops themselves—judged by heretics and faithless men and oppressed in every way. Shall I dare mention the climax? That atheism in practice and every forgetfulness of God are common, and the blood redeemed by Christ’s benefit is being poured out everywhere; yet not even one voice among us has barked out.

But because we were so cowardly in the past, now that under your favor and example we may breathe again, we shall encourage our brother bishops likewise and recover our strength, being prepared to meet death rather than allow the beautiful Church, the friend and bride of our Lord Jesus Christ, to be further torn and violated in this manner. The trumpet of this most weighty confessor and evangelical herald will sufficiently encourage them to this end.

The other reason that moved me is that I have much at stake in this [Col. 0761D] book. For although the whole volume seems to me to be a work addressed in one continuous course to Emperor Constantius, the author himself divided it into little books. One of these maintains that it is not lawful for us to meet with heretics or to have anything in common with them. When we were at Poissy, I did not speak so freely; I said only that it was a crime to establish a public conference and disputation with heretics, as though we were summoning the word of the Lord into a theater and a game. From this nothing could arise except scandal to many and, finally, [Col. 0762A] what I then very much feared: comedy would turn into tragedy.

Thus I alone remained in my opinion and withdrew myself from that disputation, which seemed criminal to me; and I was greatly grieved that sacred matters were there being handled after the fashion of profane ones. Therefore some regarded me as almost a seditious man and a heretic. But how sad, indeed how dreadful, the outcome of events was afterward became known to everyone. It not only brought grief upon our own godly people but may also cause great sorrow to posterity.

It remains to relate whether the author of this work, as is said to have happened to many most learned men and even to Solomon himself, most skilled in divine wisdom, lapsed near the end of his life into an erroneous opinion, since some number his disciples, the Luciferians, among heretics. It is not mine to pronounce judgment upon such great men. Yet I shall say frankly that the integrity of the Church at that time was such that it overlooked no contention without immediately marking it. This was not because it condemned notable men as heretics on account of some fancy or opinion, unless their assertion in a serious matter was wholly contrary to the doctrines of the Fathers. Yet it was so zealous for the Church’s concord and peace that it did not permit even the slightest occasion to be given for seditions and divisions.

Accordingly, nothing is more charged against this great confessor than excessive harshness and severity toward the customary indulgence and forbearance of our mother the Church: namely, that he withdrew from those who received to honor and their former office in the Church bishops and clerics who had fallen [Col. 0762C] into heresy and were returning to the Catholic faith which they had abandoned. Ecclesiastical histories recount how these things happened and the cause of the disagreement between him and Eusebius of Vercelli. Since, wherever heresies and schisms prevail most, no place is left for discipline and morals become more corrupted, he and his followers, under this pretext, as though to avoid vices and vicious persons, separated themselves from the society of the faithful.

One of the more elegant books of St Jerome, directed against them, still survives. What excuse, then, will the heretics of our own age offer, who boast that they follow the same footsteps? St Augustine too inveighs rather sharply against this very Lucifer as excessively exacting and difficult, because he agrees well with Catholics concerning Christ, who is the head of the Church, but not likewise concerning the body, which is called the Church; nor, however, [Note: [Col. 0761D] Augustine in his book *On Heresies* does not recount Lucifer’s opinion, but that of the Luciferians, concerning the nature of the soul, and attributes it to them because they say that the soul is generated by transmission. Certainly nothing of the sort is read in Lucifer’s books, nor did any of the ancients recognize this error in Lucifer.] does Augustine wholly condemn his view concerning the generation of souls.

Later writers, to whom less trust and authority are given and who could by no means have stated anything so certain concerning him, have invented whatever they pleased. Thus, in place of one person they reckon two: one bishop of Smyrna and the other of Sardinia, the former indeed a heretic, the latter a good and devout man. Whatever [Col. 0763A] the case may be, he was regarded not only by his contemporaries and men of the immediately succeeding generation as eminent and holy—“saint” then being a common epithet for all the faithful of the Church militant throughout the world—but after his death he was also called “blessed.” Great Athanasius, Ambrose, and Hilary hold him in the highest honor and speak splendidly of him.

His style seems common to me and to that age itself: it is so rough and unpolished that he himself calls it rustic. Yet whoever weighs it carefully will find it weighty and full of thought, the product of a man of powerful intellect. For his rendering of passages from the sacred volume shows that it was certainly the common version and not, as it later became, revised and corrected.
