For he says below: “Of people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, supposing that godliness is gain: withdraw [**Note: [Col. 0787D]** With Greek, *aphistaso apo tōn toioutōn* (ἀφίστασο ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων), omitted by the Ancient Version and Sabbatier.] from such persons” (ibid. 5).

How could we be with you, when in the conclusion of this letter he urges us to flee you, who have fallen from the faith? “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of speech and the objections of falsely named knowledge, which some, professing, have fallen away from the faith” (ibid. 20). We were bound to avoid you as one uttering profane novelties of speech, since we recognized that at the devil’s prompting you had uttered that sacrilegious saying—namely, the saying by which you expressed the poisons of your dogma: “There was [Col. 0787C] when he was not; he was made from nothing; and the Father and Son are not one power.” [**Note: [Col. 0787D]** These formulas were set out in Constantius’s letter or edict, discussed a little above.] It was not the Holy Spirit who uttered these things through you, but that unclean devil.

How, then, could we have kept the deposit in accordance with the Apostle’s command if we had remained with you in your accursed [**Note: [Col. 0787D]** That is, the Milanese council, as we have observed elsewhere.] council? For we have resolved to hold the apostolic faith until death—namely, that faith which we retain as written at Nicaea against your blasphemy and against the execrable attempts of all your heretics. How could we Christians have been Arians in your council? [**Note: [Col. 0787D]** “Of the Arians.” Vatican manuscript.] We had read that our predecessors and fellow-servants were separated from those who had worshiped idols according to the edict of your fellow-tyrant Antiochus: “But Judas Maccabaeus, who was the tenth, withdrew into the wilderness, and there lived in the mountains with his companions, living with the wild beasts and feeding on grass, lest they should be partakers of defilement” (2 Macc. 5:27). [**Note: [Col. 0787D]** The verb “we had read,” or something similar, is absent. Tilius. “We had read.” Latin.]

You recognize from this one testimony that we ought to withdraw from you, lest we too be partakers of defilement. How could we join ourselves to you, when the Lord likewise says to the Apostles: “Take heed of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (Matt. 16:6)? And, in order to make clear to us that leaven was unsound doctrine—the doctrine advanced then by those Pharisees or Sadducees, and now by you heretics of every sect—the Scripture continues: “Then they reasoned among themselves, saying, ‘We have no bread’ [**Note: [Col. 0787D]** “We have not taken loaves.” Ancient Version.].” While they were reasoning, Jesus said [**Note: [Col. 0787D]** With many manuscripts cited by Sabbatier. Ancient Version: “But Jesus, knowing [it], said.”]: “Why do you reason among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand or remember the five [Col. 0788B] loaves and the five thousand men, and how many baskets you took up; nor the seven loaves and seven thousand men, and how many hampers you took up? Why do you not understand that I did not speak of bread, when I said, Take heed of the [**Note: [Col. 0788D]** Sabbatier reads “of the leaven,” with the Ancient Version, the Cambridge manuscript, and our Vatican manuscript.] leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees?” Then they understood that he did not say they should beware of the leaven [**Note: [Col. 0788D]** “The leaven of loaves.” Ancient Version. “Of loaves” is absent from the Corbie and Cambridge manuscripts, as from Lucifer.] of loaves, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees [**Note: [Col. 0788D]** “Of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Ancient Version.].

Likewise, when the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, deigns to instruct us to withdraw from you heretics and from all foreigners, how could your heart—variable and changeable in everything, but in this wickedness firmly established by a vast strength hostile to its own salvation—have presumed that we could have peace with you or your followers? “Do not draw the yoke with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement [Col. 0788C] has Christ with Belial [**Note: [Col. 0788D]** With the Greek. Ancient Version: “Beliab.”]? Or what share has the faithful with the unbeliever? What consent has the temple of God with idols? For you [**Note: [Col. 0788D]** Thus Greek: *hymeis gar naos Theou este zōntos* (ὑμεῖς γὰρ ναὸς Θεοῦ ἐστε ζῶντος). Ancient Version: “For we are the temple of the living God; for God says.”] are the temple of the living God. For it is written: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their
God, and they shall be my people; therefore, come out from their midst and be separated, says the Lord; do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you, and I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty (II Cor. 6:14). Since your commands plainly arose in opposition to these promises of the Lord, how could we believers have remained with you unbelievers? How could we, running on the way of light, stand with you—men completing a journey on a road filled with the darkness of every error? For who is so foolish that, when he hears God say, “For I shall dwell in them, and walk among them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people; therefore come out from their midst and be separated, says the Lord; do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you, and I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty” (II Cor. 6:16)—who, we say, is so foolish as not to wish God to dwell within him? Who would not wish to consider himself received by God among those whom He deigned to call sons? May it not escape you that you have been made unclean through your heresy.

It did not seem right to us to be one with you, since it is not right for human beings to remain with serpents. Or will you deny that the deniers of the only Son of God are called serpents in the sacred Scriptures? If you cannot deny it, observe that we did right to flee from you serpents. You have read the Apostle saying to Timothy: “Avoid profane novelties of speech; for they advance greatly toward impiety, and their word spreads like a cancer” (II Tim. 2:16). Did you suppose that men of God could be with you, whose word is like a cancer?

Likewise blessed John commands that you be avoided, saying: “I rejoiced greatly because I found some of your children walking in truth, just as we received a commandment from the Father. And now I ask you, lady, not as writing a new commandment to you, but that which we have had from the beginning: that we love one another. And this is love: that we walk according to His commandments. This is the commandment, as you heard from the beginning, that you should walk in it. For many deceivers have gone out into the world, who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. These are deceivers and antichrists. Watch yourselves, lest you lose what you have accomplished, but that you may receive a full reward. Everyone who departs and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God; but he who remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, and do not say ‘Hail’ to him; for he who says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (II John 4).

[Note: Col. 0789D: “In the flesh,” in Sabatier.]

How could it have happened that we, soldiers of God, should be with you and yours, soldiers of Antichrist? Especially since the Holy Spirit, giving these commands through the blessed Apostle, did not even permit us to greet you. But perhaps you will dare to say: “Do I deny that the Son of God came in the flesh, so that I should now be called one of the antichrists?” Certainly not, Emperor Constantius: you do not deny that the Son of God came in the flesh; but you say that He whom we confess to have come in the flesh is a creature. You say that He was made from nothing, thereby maintaining that He is not the true Son of God.

But we, who keep the tradition of this blessed Apostle, believe in the true Son of God; we believe that the Father and this His only Son possess one Godhead. The Lord himself makes this clear in His sacred Gospels, saying: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9–10); and, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me”; and, “I and the Father are one” (ibid., 10:30).

[Note: Col. 0789D: With the Greek, which lacks *meum* (“my”), found in the old version.]

[Note: Col. 0789D: “The Father is in me.” Old version. Irenaeus, Book III, agrees with Lucifer.]

We have often said that, although Father and Son are two persons, yet He says, “I and the Father are one” (ibid.); “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (ibid. 14:9); and, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (ibid. 10). By this He intended us to understand nothing other than that the eternity of the Father and Son is one, their glory one, their power one, and their greatness one.

[Note: Col. 0789D: “And one.” Latin.]

For this reason the Apostle also says in this Second Epistle: “Everyone who departs and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God; but he who remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son” (II John 9): so that, by gathering the teaching of the sacred Gospels, we might believe that God the Father and His only Son possess one Godhead. Whoever so believes has God. But whoever departs from this teaching—that is, from “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), which, although expressed in the plural, nevertheless shows two persons and the one power of those two persons, namely Father and Son—the Apostle therefore says: “He who departs and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God; but he who remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son” (II John 9). Thus we should believe the Son of God when He says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30): namely, that the Godhead of Father and Son is one.

It is therefore evident that you, who do not hold as the Lord delivered to the apostles and the apostles to the bishops, do not have God. For the Apostle, wishing to make manifest the single divinity of Father and Son, said: “He who departs from His teaching does not have God; but he who remains in His teaching has the Father and the Son” (II John 9). We know that we did entirely rightly to flee from you, I say—from you, established without God, possessing neither Son nor Father—since it would not have been fitting for those who have God to remain with the enemies of His divine majesty.

[Note: Col. 0789D: “We know.” Latin.]

[Note: Col. 0789D: “To remain.” The same source.]

But recognize how hateful you are to God: we were not even permitted to say “Hail” to you. How could we Christians have been with you Arians, when the Apostle Paul says: “Avoid foolish questions, genealogies, disputes, and quarrels about the law; for they are useless and vain. Avoid a heretical person after one correction, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned” (Titus 3:9).

[Note: Col. 0789D: “After one correction and two.” Old version. Lucifer agrees with Irenaeus, Book III, and Cyprian, Epistle 55.]

[Note: Col. 0790D: “Such a person is perverted.” Old version.]

We could not assemble with heretics self-condemned, lest that utterance strike us also, as it strikes the Galatians in blessed Paul: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Gal. 5:7).

[Note: Col. 0790D: Sabatier reads “you,” with the old version, which here also has “to obey.”]

Knowing you to be enemies of the only Son of God, we fled your impious counsels, obeying the Apostle’s voice: “‘That you have consented to no one,’ he says, ‘your persuasion is from God who calls you. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass?’” (Gal. 5:9).

[Note: Col. 0790D: For *obtemperantes*, “obeying,” and so frequently.]

[Note: Col. 0790D: “That you have consented to no one”: these words are read only in the Codex Boernerianus in Sabatier; elsewhere they are absent.]

[Note: Col. 0790D: “Is persuasion from him?” Old version; and where Sabatier reads “you” in Lucifer, does he read “we”?]

[Note: Col. 0790D: “Do you not know” is absent from the old version.]

We, servants of Christ, did not wish to admit you, the worms of Arius, into fellowship, lest we be consumed by the devil’s poison by which you are consumed. We did not wish to go with you—with men, that is, who still appear to be outside the knowledge of God, still placed under the devil’s power. We did not wish, living persons, to be joined to the dead, because you are known to be such as we ourselves were before we believed in the only Son of God.

The Apostle makes this clear when writing to the Ephesians: “And you, when you were dead in your offences and sins, in which you once walked according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit which now works in the children of unbelief; among whom we too all once lived in the desire of our flesh, doing the wills and counsels; and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:1).

[Note: Col. 0791D: “According to the course of this world, and according to the prince,” etc. Old version.]

[Note: Col. 0791D: With the Greek, *thelēmata* (“wills”); old version: “pleasures”; in which, “we were by nature,” etc.]

Since you are still such as the most holy Apostle reports that we were before we believed, you were certainly to be avoided: men in whom, and through whom, the rulers of the power of this air perform every desire of their own. You were to be fled as children of unbelief, children naturally of wrath, lest by clinging to you we should be brought back to what we had formerly been.

We did not wish to be with you because you had not yet obtained the mercy of God, which we have now received. We did not wish to have fellowship with you, who were led by the counsel of the flesh, just as this most blessed Paul was led before he believed. We remember him saying: “Let no one deceive you with empty words; because of this the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Therefore do not become their partners. For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light. For the fruit of light is in all goodness, righteousness, and truth, proving what is acceptable, and do not share in the fruitless works of darkness, but rather rebuke them” (ibid. 5:6).

[Note: Col. 0791D: “For this.” Old version.]

[Note: Col. 0791D: “Acceptable to God.” Vatican manuscript: “What pleases God … but rebuke them.” Old version.]

Because we had received these commands, we did not wish to remain with you, led by your empty words, lest wrath come upon us, just as it has come—and will come—upon you, upon you and yours, you children of unbelief. We did not wish to become partners in darkness. For, now believing in the only Son of God and desiring to obey the commands of His majesty, having escaped that darkness we have become light in the Lord. Therefore we did not obey your dark commands, because it would have been wicked for children of light to do the work of a man of darkness; for the fruit of light is to walk in righteousness and truth and in every goodness.

[Note: Col. 0791D: That is, a man of darkness.]

You say that we act wickedly because we refused to accept your heresy, because no enduring friendship was fixed between us and you and yours. Consider what Moses did concerning foreigners, at the time when God deigned to command him to send a specified number of Israelites and destroy by the sword the five kings of Midian and Moab. When those sent to battle had killed all the males, Moses rebuked the sons of Israel because they had spared the women who came in their way; he commanded that these likewise be killed before him, maintaining that they could entice the minds of the people to the worship of idols.

If, then, we likewise detest your heresy as Moses detested idolatry; if we likewise desire, indeed, to kill with God’s sword the heresies of all you erring persons, just as Moses killed those enslaved to idols; if we flee you, enemies of God’s religion, as he fled worshippers of idols—how do you suppose that we do not act rightly in withdrawing ourselves from you? For how could we have associated with you, when he says to the Philippians: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers” (Phil. 3:2)? Who among God’s servants would not flee you dogs, you evil workers, unless he had forgotten that he was a Christian?

Could we, servants of Christ, have been joined to you, adversaries of God’s religion, when the glorious Apostle Jude, brother of the Apostle James, exhorts us to avoid you and those like you, and to remain in the faith we have received until death’s end? “Jude, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, to those beloved in God the Father, preserved and called in Jesus Christ: mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you. Beloved, while making every effort to write to you concerning our common salvation, I urge you to contend earnestly for the fellowship once delivered. For certain men have entered secretly, men long ago marked out for this judgment: impious men who turn the grace of God into shamelessness and deny Him who is our ruler and Lord, Jesus Christ” (Jude 1:1).

[Note: Col. 0792D: Sabatier reads: “who are beloved in God the Father, preserved and called.”]

It would have been sinful to associate with you blasphemous deniers, since Jude, setting before us the examples of those who transgressed the Lord’s commandments, urges our hearts to remain in that faith in which he himself appears to have remained. “Therefore I wish to remind you,” he says, “although you know all things: that God saved His people from the land of Egypt, but afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not keep their own order but abandoned their dwelling, He has kept under darkness in the bonds of holy angels for the judgment of the great God. Sodom also and Gomorrah, and the cities around them, which in like manner committed adultery and followed other flesh, have been set forth as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire. Likewise these dreamers also defile the flesh and despise dominion” (ibid. 5).

[Note: Col. 0792D: “A second time.” The same source.]

[Note: Col. 0792D: As in the Greek, *toutois* (“these”); Sabatier reads “these [cities].”]

[Note: Col. 0792D: “And followed other flesh, have been set forth,” etc. Latin, according to the sense of the Vulgate.]

And below: “Woe to them, because they have gone in the way of Cain, have poured themselves out in the seduction of Balaam for reward, and have perished in the contradiction of Korah. These are stains in your love-feasts, governing themselves without fear, clouds without water, driven about by every wind, autumnal trees without fruit, dead, uprooted from the roots; savage waves of the sea, foaming out their own shamefulness; deceptive storms, for whom the time of darkness has been reserved forever” (Jude 1:11).

[Note: Col. 0792D–0793A: Greek: *en tais agapais hymōn*, “in your love-feasts.” Sabatier reads: “stains at their own feasts, feasting without fear, feeding themselves.” Here the Greek has the same sense as *agapai*, the love-feasts, or banquets of the early Christians.]

[Note: Col. 0793A: “Twice dead.” Latin from the Vulgate.]

[Note: Col. 0793A–0794A: With the Greek, *eis ton aiōna*, “forever.” Sabatier reads: “the eternal time of darkness.”]

And below: “But you, brothers, remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of Jesus Christ; for they said: ‘In the last days there will be mockers, going according to their own ungodly desires. These are those who separate themselves, sensual persons, not having the Spirit’” (ibid. 17).

[Note: Col. 0794A: “Separating themselves.” Latin according to the sense of the Vulgate.]

Since you, Constantius, have been found to be involved in all these evils, we avoided your friendships, which strive to destroy us, lest we be hurled with you into those places of torments, into which he whose course you follow relates that all those persons were cast headlong.

[Note: Col. 0794A: That is, the Apostle Jude, whose authority he has cited.]

[Col. 0793]

**One Book of Our Holy Father Lucifer, Bishop of Cagliari, *On Apostate Kings*, Addressed to the Emperor Constantius.** (C)

[Col. 0793B] Since you deign to hold the customary claim—that unless you both believed rightly and the things you are doing against us were pleasing to God, you would already have been destroyed—I have wished to set forth the deeds of a few kings your equals in apostasy and cruelty, so that your assertion may be buried, which says: “Unless the faith of Arius—that is, my own—were catholic, unless it pleased God that I persecute that faith which they wrote against us at Nicaea, I certainly would not still be flourishing in imperial power.”

I do not mention those kings who were strangers to the knowledge of God; I deal only with those known to have reigned in Judaea. In the Book of Judges we find Jerobbaal, son of Joash, chosen by God, and told: “Go in this your strength, and you shall save Israel from the hand of Midian. Behold, have I not sent you?” (Judg. VI.14).

[Col. 0793C] And below: “I will be with you, and you shall strike Midian as though one man” (ibid. 16). [Note: This agrees with the Vulgate. Old Latin: “For the Lord will be with you; and … as one man.” Others, with Lucifer, have from the Greek: “I will be with you,” ἔσομαι μετὰ σοῦ.] Scripture says that Midian had a multitude like the sand of the sea. But when everything which God had promised Gideon was fulfilled—when he saw himself raised from lowliness, enriched from poverty, and made king though of common condition—what did he immediately do? Clearly, he said to the people: “Let each of you give me an earring from his spoil” (ibid. VIII.24).

When he had received a weight of gold earrings amounting to seventeen hundred shekels, besides bracelets, collars, coverings, and the purple garments which were upon the kings of Midian, and besides the golden collars which were on the necks of the camels of the enemy (ibid. 26), what does Holy Scripture say Gideon did? Gideon—

[Col. 0794B] [Note: With the Vatican manuscript. Earlier editions: “a gold earring.” Old Latin: “The weight of the gold earrings which he had requested was seventeen hundred shekels of gold … and the purple coverings which were upon the kings of Midian, besides the collars which were on the necks of their camels.”]

[Note: “And Gideon made them into an ephod and set it in his city, in Ephra. Vatican manuscript; Old Latin: “And Gideon made it into an ephod and … in Ephra. And all Israel prostituted itself after it there,” etc.]

—who was also Jerobbaal—made an ephod and set it up in his city Ephrath; and the children of Israel prostituted themselves there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house (ibid. 27). Did he delay for some days before carrying out this wicked work against God? When he undertook to do this, could he remember what God had said to him: “Go; I will be with you” (ibid. VI.16)?

[Note: With the Latin text we correct it thus; earlier editions: “had done.”]

[Note: “Go” is absent from the Old Latin.]

Where is that act by which, according to God’s command, he demolished Baal and cut down his sacred groves, and offered sacrifice to God?

[Col. 0794C] Where is what he said to God’s messenger, who said to him, “The Lord is with you, mighty in strength”: “I pray you, Lord, if the Lord is with us, why have all these evils overtaken us? And where are his wonders, which our fathers told us of, saying: ‘Did not God bring us up from Egypt? Yet now the Lord has rejected us and delivered us into the hand of Midian’” (ibid. 11)?

[Note: “Mighty in strength,” from the Hebrew. Old Latin: “mighty in fortitude.”]

[Note: Something appears to be missing: “And Gideon said to him: ‘I pray you,’” etc. Old Latin: “My lord … and why have all these evils befallen us,” etc.]

[Note: “Did not?” Latinus, as in the Greek.]

When he attempted to act against God, did he recall the time when those evils had befallen them because of idolatry? Yet after they had been rescued, so as to live without fear of enemies, from all those evils by which, he said, he and all the people were oppressed, he immediately performed the deed through which both he and all the people together were handed over to their enemies because of idolatry.

[Col. 0795A] He had heard [Note: “God had happened”; it seems one should read either “God had brought [these evils],” or “these evils had happened because of God,” or even, “for he had heard that,” etc.] that all those evils had befallen them because they had served idols and abandoned God; he remembered the prophet’s words; and yet, on the day when their enemies had become as nothing before them, that king—whose madness you deign to resemble—judged that idols rather than God, who had granted him these things, ought to be served.

For Scripture says: “The children of Israel did evil before the Lord God, and he delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years. And the hand of Midian prevailed greatly against Israel; and Israel made for itself, before Midian,

[Col. 0795B] caves in the mountains, caverns, and tombs. And it came to pass, when Israel sowed, that Midian and Amalek and the children of the East came up against him; and they encamped against them and devastated the borders of the land as far as Gaza. They left nothing for Israel to live on: neither sheep nor calf nor ass. For they and their beasts came up; they brought their tents and drove their camels; they came like locusts in multitude, for they were without number, and they came upon the land to destroy it. And Israel was impoverished before Midian; and the children of Israel cried to the Lord because of Midian.”

[Note: Hollow and hidden places in the mountains. For κρύπτειν means “to hide” and “to conceal”; caves are σπήλαια. Tilius and La Cerda add: “Let the learned endure it; we sometimes scatter such notes for everyone’s understanding.” Gregory of Tours, Book X, final chapter: “and through crypts and hiding-places with a few Christians converted by him,” etc.]

[Note: Sabatier reads “they came,” and below omits “for this Israel.”]

[Note: “The children of Israel cried to the Lord; and it came to pass, because the children of Israel cried to the Lord because of Midian.” Vatican manuscript, which accords more closely with the Hebrew and with another translator in Origen’s Hexapla, as published by Montfaucon. Likewise Codex Alexandrinus, as cited by Sabatier.]

“The Lord sent a man, a prophet, to the children of Israel, and said to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I am he who brought you up from

[Col. 0795C] Egypt, and led you out of the house of bondage; I took you from the hand of the king of Egypt and from the hand of all who persecuted you; I drove them out from before you and gave you their land. And I said to you: I am the Lord your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; and you did not obey my voice’” (ibid. 1).

[Note: Sabatier reads “you shall fear.”]

[Note: “My voice.” Vatican manuscript, corruptly.]

What does Jerobbaal, also called Gideon, do after this rebuke of the Lord? As soon as he sees his enemy reduced to nothing; as soon as all those adversaries, said to have been like the sand of the sea, are slaughtered—not by a great number of Israelites but by three hundred men; as soon as he sees all the foreign kings killed—he fashions the thing by which the children of Israel may sin against God. Yet he is found to have reigned in Israel for forty years even after committing so great a crime.

[Col. 0795D] Therefore it will not be surprising if you too, sacrilegious man, still remain alive, when you see that Gideon lived forty years after committing idolatry and held his kingdom. For Holy Scripture says that the Israelites rested forty years, that no adversaries at all were allowed against them, and that no foreigner held dominion over them, because they had cried out to God.

[Col. 0796A] God bestowed such benefits upon your fellow sacrilegious men, showing himself wholly powerful, yet showing them unworthy to attain rest: they had not chosen to serve, even for one day after receiving rest from such dangers, him who had granted them so great a mercy. Although the Israelites were such, God spared them in his mercy even while they continued their idolatry after these events. He did not immediately repay them; but at the time that pleased him, he nevertheless repaid them. The guilt of idolatry could not pass from them unpunished.

So also he will exact payment from you, Constantius, unless meanwhile you take heed for yourself.

If the Israelites, serving demons and abandoning God, though they had become strangers to the knowledge of God, were nevertheless heard and delivered from the hand of Midian and from all their persecutors as soon as it entered their hearts that he is the all-powerful God who had brought their fathers out of Egypt, what do you suppose that we Christians may hope—that we can be delivered from your hands, or not? Do you not clearly know that we worship the same great God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of all the prophets, apostles, and martyrs?

[Col. 0796B] Believe me: we have been heard and shall be heard, so that you, with all your fragile exaltation, may lie beneath the feet of all his servants. And if there is some delay, so that he does not at once grant his holy Church complete security of peace after you Arians have been destroyed, the reason is that it is fitting for you, while the adversary rages, to come as a test for all.

[Note: “To come,” or “to be found.” Latinus.]

You say: “If I had acted wrongly, if I held heresy, God would already have taken vengeance upon me.” Hear Holy Scripture say that the Lord spared even a foreign people for a long time, yet later they received what their deeds deserved.

Samuel said to Saul: “The Lord sent me to anoint you king over Israel; now hear the voice of the Lord’s word. Thus says the Lord Almighty: Now I will punish what Amalek did to you, Israel—how he opposed you on the road when you came up from Egypt. Now go and strike Amalek and all that belongs to him. Do not desire anything of theirs, but utterly destroy him; devote him and all that is his to destruction; do not spare him, but kill all that is his, from man to woman and from infant to nursing child” (1 Sam. XV.1).

[Note: Sabatier reads “by which.”]

And below: “Saul came as far as the city of Amalek, approached, and laid siege to Amalek at the torrent. Saul said to the Kenite: ‘Go, withdraw from the midst; withdraw from Amalek, and do not join yourself with him, because you showed mercy to the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt.’ And the Kenite withdrew from the midst of Amalek. Saul struck Amalek from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt; Saul captured Agag king of Amalek alive, and killed all his people with the edge of the sword” (ibid. 5).

[Col. 0797A] Do you see how, though late, they received the consequence of their crime? And you say: “Unless I acted well, I would never reign long”? We also find that Saul acted against the Lord’s command, was rejected, and nevertheless reigned long after his rejection—after God said to Samuel: “I repent that I have anointed Saul king” (ibid. 11).

[Note: Lucifer repeats the same thought a little later, but in other words. Optatus of Milevis, Book II against the Donatists, and other Greek books have a similar expression: μεταμέλομαι ὅτι ἔχρισα, “I repent that I anointed.” See Theodoret, Question 33.]

And you say: “Unless I had right belief, unless I lived in the way pleasing to God, I certainly would not still be ruling now.”

[Col. 0797B] To drink in fully what we say concerning Saul, consider what he did against the Lord’s command: “Saul and all his people took Agag the king, and the good things of the flocks and herds, foods, vineyards, and every good thing; they would not destroy all the good things, but preserved every valuable work, while they destroyed what was worthless. And the word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: ‘I repent that I appointed Saul king, because he has turned away from me and has not upheld my words.’ Samuel was grieved and cried out to God all night; and before dawn Samuel went to meet Israel” (ibid. 9).

[Note: Thus with Sabatier; printed editions absurdly read “of kings.”]

And below: “Samuel came to Saul, and behold, Saul was offering a burnt offering to the Lord, the firstfruits of the spoil which he had brought from Amalek. Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him: ‘You are blessed by

[Col. 0797C] the Lord; I have carried out everything that the Lord spoke.’ Samuel said: ‘What then is this sound of sheep in my ears and this sound of oxen that I hear?’ Saul said: ‘I brought them from Amalek—the best of the flock and oxen which the people took as spoil—in order that they might be sacrificed to the Lord your God, the king; but the rest I destroyed and exterminated.’

[Note: For “the people took as spoil,” and “plundered Amalek,” as he had previously said, Tilius uses *iaculavit* for *iaculatus est*, “he took as spoil.”]

[Note: “To the Lord your God.” Vatican manuscript, as in the Greek. Latinus removes “the king” from Saul, as does the Greek.]

“Samuel said to Saul: ‘Were you not, though small in your own sight, leader of the sceptred tribes of Israel? The Lord anointed you king over Israel, and the Lord sent you on a mission and said: “Go and destroy Amalek, those who sin against me; wage war against them until you consume them.” Why did you not obey the Lord’s voice, but rush upon the spoil and do what is evil before the Lord?’

“Saul said: ‘Because I listened to the people, I went on the mission upon which God sent me, brought Agag king of

[Col. 0797D] Amalek, and destroyed Amalek. The people took the spoil, the first of the flocks and herds that I destroyed, in order to sacrifice before the Lord our God at Gilgal.’

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “on a mission,” as in the Greek; likewise a little below, although the Greek there has τῇ ὁδῷ, “on the way.”]

[Note: Sabatier reads “into which.”]

[Note: The same source reads “that they may sacrifice.”]

“Samuel said: ‘Does the Lord desire burnt offerings

[Col. 0798A] and sacrifices more than obedience to the Lord’s voice? Behold, I say: obedience is better than sacrifice, and submission than the fat of rams. For sin is an abomination; you have brought pains and groanings upon yourself. Because you treated the Lord’s word as of no account, the Lord will treat you as of no account, so that you may not reign.’

[Note: Earlier editions: *dicito*, “say.” Vatican manuscript: *dicto*, “having said.”]

“Saul said to Samuel: ‘I have sinned, because I transgressed the word of the Lord and your word, because I feared the people and listened to their voice. Now take away my sin. Return with me; I will worship the Lord your God.’ Samuel said to him: ‘Today the Lord will tear your kingdom in Israel from your hand and give it to your neighbor, who is better than you’” (ibid. 28).

[Note: Old Latin: “The Lord has torn … the kingdom from Israel … [and will give it] to your good neighbor above you.”]

And below: “Samuel did not again see Saul until the day of his death, because Samuel mourned for Saul, and the Lord repented that he had made Saul king over Israel” (ibid. 35). The Lord said to Samuel: “How long do you mourn for Saul? Behold, I cast him out so that he may not reign over Israel. Fill your horn with oil and come; I will send you to Jesse in Bethlehem, for I have heard of one among the sons of Jesse for myself as king” (ibid. XVI.1).

[Col. 0798B] [Note: In Book I for St Athanasius he says “I have seen,” which Latinus thought should also be restored here.]

You can now understand, Constantius, that even a man rejected by the Lord and destined for eternal death may reign long after committing a grave sin. For you see that although the glorious son of Jesse, David, had afterward been anointed king, Saul nevertheless reigned long and had power even to persecute him whom God had chosen for himself as prophet and king. The evil man persecuted the good, the unjust man the just; the man hated by God persecuted him whom God loved.

Since this is so, do not boast that, after committing so great a crime, you are still alive, as Saul lived. Rather consider the sort of punishment brought upon Saul, which may also be brought upon you unless you provide for yourself. For if the Lord was so angry with him—first, because he took spoil contrary to the prohibition; second, because he persecuted David, God’s own man—how much more must the vengeance of his anger proceed against you, whose crimes are so immense that you have even incurred the guilt of sacrilege.

You say: “If I had acted wrongly, if, as Lucifer says, I were a heretic, God would already have taken my kingdom from me.” Consider also that Solomon survived after committing idolatry, and understand that you too are such as he was after his idolatry (3 Kings XI.14).

[Col. 0798C] [Note: This testimony differs slightly in Sabatier, where, instead of “an adversary to Solomon, Ader, Saba, adversaries to Solomon,” there is read: “adversaries to Solomon, Hadad, Soba, adversary to Solomon.” In these readings Lucifer almost agrees with the Septuagint.]

“And the Lord raised up an adversary to Solomon,

[Col. 0798D] Hadad the Edomite, and Rezon son of Eliadah in Ramathad; Hadadezer king of Zobah, his lord; and men gathered around him, and he became leader of the band. He seized Damascus,

[Col. 0799A] sat in it, and reigned in Damascus; and they were adversaries to Solomon and Israel all the days of Solomon.”

We have proved to you that Solomon also reigned for some years after his idolatry and, certainly, while no longer serving God but the devil, the world, and devilish men, was marked as having attached himself to them. So you also cling to your fellow sacrilegious Arians. Although you are still bodily alive and still remain in power, you are found to be such as Solomon was after abandoning God and following idols.

[Note: “Serving,” whence Pontius in Latinus; but the construction seems clearer if corrected thus: “while serving the devil, the world,” etc.]

You wished us to attach ourselves to persons such as those to whom Solomon caused the Israelites to attach themselves. Where was that love of God which Holy Scripture says Solomon possessed, at the time when he deigned to follow idols and abandon God? How could this be, unless he had become altogether a man estranged from sober understanding?

[Col. 0799B] I do not want you to applaud yourself because, though blasphemous and a destroyer of God’s religion, you still possess the kingdom and are proud after your sacrilege, when we find that Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, though practising idolatry, lived in his kingdom for twenty years. For Holy Scripture says of him (3 Kings XI.43): “King Solomon slept with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Rehoboam reigned in his place in Jerusalem. He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty years in Jerusalem.”

[Note: Sabatier places these words out of sequence in the Old Latin at 3 Kings XII. The earlier part somewhat agrees with the Vulgate, as noted in the margin. But the full testimony cited by Lucifer is found in the Septuagint, 3 Kings XII, after verse 24, and, together with what follows through verse 25, is absent from the Vulgate and from some Septuagint manuscripts. In other manuscripts it is marked as repeated, transposed, confused, and poorly connected; so Nobilius says at this point. Theodoret also used it, besides Lucifer, who differs little from the Greek; there, instead of “twenty years,” is δώδεκα ἐτῶν, “twelve years.”]

And below: “He did evil before the Lord, and did not walk in the way of David his father.”

[Note: This testimony is absent from the Vulgate, though it corresponds in some respects to 3 Kings XIV.22 and 2 Chronicles XII.14. But in full, as stated and as Sabatier notes, it appears in the Septuagint, chapter XII, after verse 24.]

Therefore, although both Solomon, from the time when he deigned to enslave himself to idols, and his son Rehoboam, who was always serving idols, did not walk in David’s ways, they nevertheless lived in the kingdom,

[Col. 0799C] and both, reigning, reached the last day of life. Why do you then wonder concerning yourself, and, after committing an abominable crime, remain in that wickedness and boast as king because neither kingdom nor life is taken from you by God? You see that Jeroboam too attempted, as you have, utterly to overthrow the Lord’s religion; nevertheless he lived many years, and remained in that crime, as it is written:

[Note: Sabatier places this testimony out of sequence in the Old Latin. It does correspond to the Vulgate, as marked in the margin; but in the Septuagint it occurs twice, agreeing with the Vulgate in chapter XI.26, and in chapter XII in the same words as in Lucifer. Nobilius rejects the latter, together with the preceding passage, as repeated and confused. Sabatier reads *Sarira* for *Sariram*.]

“There was a man from Mount Ephraim, Solomon’s servant; his name was Jeroboam, and his mother’s name was Sariram,

[Col. 0800A] a prostitute” (ibid. 26).

And elsewhere (ibid. XII.20): “It came to pass when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned from Egypt, they sent and summoned him in the assembly and made him king over Israel.” [Note: That is, they caused him to reign in Israel; they established him as king over Israel. Tilius and La Cerda.]

And below (ibid. 26): “Jeroboam said in his heart: ‘Now the kingdom will return to David, if this people goes up to offer sacrifice in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem; and the heart of the people will turn to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah.’ Then Jeroboam took counsel and went away. He made two golden calves and said to the people: ‘It is enough for you to have gone up to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.’ He placed one in Bethel and set one in Dan. This thing became sin; and the people went before one calf as far as Dan.

[Col. 0800B] They made houses on high places, and he made priests from some portion of the people who were not of the sons of Levi. Jeroboam made a festival in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, corresponding to the festival of Judah. He went up to the sanctuary which he had made in Bethel, to sacrifice before the calves which he had made, and he appointed in Bethel priests of the high places which he had made. He went up to the sanctuary which he had made on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, on the festival day which he had devised from his own heart, and he made a festival for the children of Israel.”

[Note: Sabatier adds from material copied from Lucifer: “and he went up to the sanctuary to sacrifice.” But these words occur below, on page 38 of this edition, column 803, where some things are altered in this very text.]

Therefore I do not want you to boast because, though practising idolatry, you yet live and possess the glory of royal power. You see that this Jeroboam made golden calves and turned the people of Israel to idolatry; yet he was not only not destroyed at once when he sinned, but was allowed to live a long time.

[Note: “Therefore I do not want you to boast because, though practising idolatry, you live while possessing royal glory, when you see that this Jeroboam made golden calves, turned the Israelite people to idolatry, and yet was not only not destroyed immediately upon sinning, but was allowed to live a long time.” You understand what this means; but I wished you to consider the expression, for there is much of this sort of expression. For below: “when therefore he had practised idolatry for thirty-five years,” and immediately: “I say, do not from this boast to yourself, because you are doing these things.” I pass over *iaculavit*, *depraedavit*, *pepercitum*, *tinnibunt*, and a thousand others with which he is full. La Cerda.]

Could not God remove those same idolatrous kings?

[Col. 0800C] But it has been shown how ungrateful you are to God: though so greatly exalted, you not only forget him who exalts you, but still persecute that same God in his servants, desiring to remove his religion from the midst.

[Note: That is, “you forget him”: you are unmindful of him and of his commands. Later likewise, *persequimini* is used for *persequamini*. Tilius.]

Recognize that this is so from the deed of that king Jeroboam. Though he was the son of a servant-woman, though he remembered that he sprang from a prostitute, though he received the kingdom of his lord Solomon in dishonor of that same Solomon, nevertheless—though Jeroboam knew that God had given him the kingdom because his lord Solomon had followed idols—he accounted all this as nothing and resolved to make idols, and, with all the people who served God, to be enslaved to them rather than to the living God, who had made him, the son of a prostitute, possess the kingdom of his lord Solomon.

[Col. 0801A] Therefore do not wonder that God spares you while you are ungrateful and sin against him. Rather, I urge you to see that, though late, if you remain in this wickedness, you will receive what all your predecessors in sacrilege received. We urge you to deign to rescue yourself from such great evils; moreover, you have this additional fact: you are not the first to commit them.

[Note: An obscure passage, which I interpret thus: “We urge you to rescue yourself from such great evils, especially since you are not the first to perpetrate these crimes, but examples have been set before you against which you should chiefly guard. You have, besides, this: you are not the first to do these things.”]

We see also that this Jeroboam regarded the Lord’s warning as nothing (3 Kings XI.29): “It came to pass at that time that Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, and Ahijah the Shilonite prophet met him on the road. Ahijah was clothed in a new garment, and they were both in the field. Ahijah seized his new garment which he wore and tore it into twelve pieces. He said to Jeroboam: ‘Take ten pieces for yourself, for thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand and give you ten sceptres. Two sceptres shall remain to him for the sake of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city which I chose from all the tribes of Israel, because Solomon abandoned me and worshipped Astarte, the unclean idol of the Sidonians, Chemosh, the idol of Moab, and their king, the religion of the children of Ammon; and he did not walk in my ways to do what is right before me, as David his father did.

[Col. 0801B] I will not take the whole kingdom from his hand in the days of his life, for the sake of my servant David, whom I chose, for I will act against him throughout all the days of his life. But I will take the kingdom from his son’s hand and give you ten sceptres; to his son I will give two sceptres, so that my servant David may have a station always before me in Jerusalem, the city which I chose for myself in order to put my name there. I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires; you shall be king in Israel. And if you keep all that I command you, walk in my ways, do what is right in my sight, and keep my precepts and commandments, as my servant David did, I will be with you and build you a faithful house, as I built David’s.’”

[Note: Sabatier reads “I will put.”]

[Note: “And I will be with you.” Vatican manuscript, as in the Greek.]

When this man, born of a prostitute and remembering that he was born of servile stock,

[Col. 0802A] heard these things from God, did he obey him who had promised him so much after everything which the Lord had promised was fulfilled? Did he not, as soon as he saw himself exalted, begin to act against God? Was not every effort immediately made through Jeroboam that God might be abandoned by all his worshippers?

We tell you that unless you amend yourself, unless you begin to be in ways pleasing to God, you will perish by a new example; yet you remain in your wickedness and persist in your sacrilege. For it was no new thing for that king Jeroboam that God caused the things already mentioned to be conveyed through his own man; and when his son was held by a severe sickness, he sent to one of God’s household, heard what was to come, and yet, while seeing even the evils promised to him fulfilled,

[Col. 0802B] acted more and more against God and desired God’s house to be destroyed (ibid. XIV.1).

[Note: Perhaps one should add: “and God,” etc.]

“And there was,” it says, “a slender man, and his name was Achiabeth; he was sixty years old, and the word of the Lord was with him.”

[Note: Sabatier collated this testimony in the Old Latin from Lucifer, as it is also found placed at the head of this chapter in the Hexapla and in the Codex Regius cited by Montfaucon, though somewhat altered. In the Roman edition of the Septuagint it is inserted nearly word for word in chapter XII. Latinus corrects Lucifer’s wording thus: “And there was a man in Shilom, and his name was Achia, and he was sixty years old.” Nearly so the Septuagint: καὶ ἄνθρωπος ἦν ἐν Σηλὼμ, καὶ ὄνομα αὐτῷ Ἀχιὰ, καὶ οὗτος ἦν υἱὸς ἑξήκοντα ἐτῶν, “And there was a man in Shilom, and his name was Achia, and this man was sixty years old.” Our Vatican manuscript has *ex ilon* corruptly; since Tilius had also noticed this in his manuscript, he rightly thought it should be corrected to “he was from Shiloh.” In the text of Lucifer, however, we retain *exilis* [“slender”], as Sabatier also did.]

“Jeroboam said to his wife: ‘Arise and take in your hand, for the man of God, bread and cakes for his children, grapes, and a jar of honey.’ The woman arose and did as her husband told her. Achiab was a very old man, and his eyes were dim so that he could not see. The woman arose from Baria and went away. When she entered the city to Achiab the Shilonite, Achiab said to his servant: ‘Go now to meet Anna, Jeroboam’s wife, and say to her: “Come in and do not remain standing, because thus says the Lord: I send hard things against you.”’

[Note: These words, through “and Achiab,” partly agree with the Septuagint in the Hexapla and partly with the Roman Septuagint.]

[Note: The Septuagint in the Hexapla has the same words both in verse 1 and here in verse 4.]

[Note: That is, his sight was hindered by the dimness of his eyes. Tilius.]

[Note: Sarira. Latinus, as in the Roman Septuagint.]

[Note: What follows here agrees entirely with the Roman Septuagint edition, inserted in chapter XII.]

“Anna went in to the man of God; and Achiab said to her: ‘Why

[Col. 0802C] have you brought me bread, grapes, cakes, and a jar of honey? Thus says the Lord: Behold, you shall depart from me; and behold, when you enter the gate of the city Arira, your maidservants will come out to meet you and say to you: “The child is dead.” For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will destroy of Jeroboam every male who urinates against a wall. Jeroboam’s dead shall be in the city and dogs shall eat them; his dead shall be in the field and the birds of heaven shall eat them.’”

[Note: Sabatier has “why,” and below omits “thus says the Lord.”]

[Note: Sarira. Latinus, with the Septuagint.]

It is not new, I say, if you persist in this obstinacy, when you know that this Jeroboam was not deterred by all these things. For as soon as the man of God had spoken, when the woman entered the city, their son died. Yet Jeroboam did not perceive what God was about to inflict upon him because he had abandoned God and caused the people to perish with him;

[Col. 0803A] nor did he fear, from his son’s death, that the remaining things might follow him. Instead, he grew old in his cunning. Jeroboam had become so utterly bereft of understanding after he had departed from him who had given him the kingdom that, though he said, “Go to the man of God and learn whether our son is going to die” (3 Kings XIV.2–3), and learned through the man of God that not only their son would die but dangers also threatened his whole kingdom, he nevertheless preferred, as he had once resolved, to serve the devil.

[Note: This testimony, in respect of its sense, is taken from the Vulgate and from the Roman edition of the Septuagint, chapter XII, and is placed by Montfaucon in the Hexapla at verse 2, chapter XIV. Sabatier omits it.]

He sends to inquire of the man of God concerning the future, yet despises the one whose man he sends to consult; in contempt of his majesty he makes calves and makes the people worship them with him. He did these things, yet was not immediately destroyed, but survived a long time in his kingdom. And you say:

[Col. 0803B] “If I were a heretic, if, as Lucifer, Pancratius, and Hilary say, I were attacking God’s religion, vengeance would already have been taken upon me?”

[Note: See above, page 1 of this edition, column 765, and the Life of Lucifer.]

Consider further what happened to this king Jeroboam; yet see how not even so did he turn to God, but persevering more firmly, died in his crime and perished in his sacrilege (ibid. XII.32): “Jeroboam made a festival in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, corresponding to the festival day of Judah. He went up to the sacrifice which he made at Bethel, to sacrifice before the calves which he had made, and appointed in Bethel priests of the high places which he had made. He went up to the sanctuary which he had made on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, on the festival which he had devised from his own heart; he made a festival for the children of Israel and went up to the sanctuary to sacrifice.

[Col. 0803C] And behold, a man of God came from Judah by the word of the Lord to Bethel; Jeroboam stood at his altar to sacrifice. The prophet cried out against the altar by the word of the Lord, saying: ‘O sanctuary, sanctuary, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born in the house of David, and Josiah shall be his name. He shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who sacrifice upon you, and shall burn human bones upon you. On that day he shall give the sign which the Lord has spoken: behold, the sanctuary shall be torn apart, and the fat which is in it shall be poured out.’

[Note: Sabatier argues that *in te*, “upon you,” should be read for *inter*, “among.”]

“When the king heard the words of the man of God crying out against the altar which was at Bethel, he stretched out his hand toward the altar and said: ‘Seize him!’ The king’s hand, which he had stretched out against him, became withered, and he could not draw it back to himself. The sacrifice was torn apart, and its fat was poured out from—”

…the sanctuary, in accordance with the sign [Note: [Col. 0803D] The sign is omitted above in the book *On Not Associating with Heretics*.] which the man of God spoke by the word of the Lord. And [Col. 0803D] the king answered and said to the man of God: “Entreat the face of the Lord your God, that my hand may return to me.” And the man of God entreated the face of the Lord, and the king’s hand returned to him and became as it was at first [Note: [Col. 0803D] “As it was at first” is also read above in the book *On Not Associating with Heretics*. But Sabat. here has, “as it had been before.”] (ibid. XIII.1).

When he had seen these signs fulfilled, which had been uttered by the mouth of the man of God, and when the impious arm stretched out to kill God’s man was suddenly withered in terror, then immediately, through the prayer of God’s worshipper, made sound again—did he destroy the idolatry which he himself had established? Did he at last remove from the midst the feast day which he himself had devised out of his own heart? By no means; rather, he is found, in that stubbornness of his presumption, to have received the day of death. Therefore we cannot wonder if, God avert it from you, you too think that in your heresy you may receive the day of death, since even by signs and wonders your earlier fellow-sacrilegists could not be recalled to worship God alone. For Holy Scripture says of Jeroboam (ibid. 33): “After this Jeroboam did not turn back from his wickedness, but he turned [Note: [Col. 0804D] Thus the Greek; but Sabat., in place of “but he turned,” reads the reverse: “and he made.”] and made priests of the high places from among part of the people. Whoever wished, he raised up [Note: [Col. 0804D] It differs entirely from the Greek and Latin texts, in which is ἐπλήρου, ‘he filled.’] his hand, and became a priest in the high places. And this matter became sin to the house of Jeroboam, unto destruction and extermination from the face of the earth.”

Lest these things be said also of you, I beg you, rescue yourself from the abominable company of the Arians. I beg you, become again the Christian you were before you became an Arian; and do not resent our comparing your deeds with those of Jeroboam. Rather, I entreat you, recognize that I set before you all these things as instructions for your salvation rather than as rebukes. For we compare you with Jeroboam in our own times because, just as he attempted to make the people of Israel apostate from the worship of God, so you have attempted to turn all people away from God.

I do not wish you to promise yourself any hope from this—that, though you act wickedly, you nevertheless reign—when you see that Jeroboam also reigned for a long time in his crime, and that Solomon’s son likewise, practicing idolatry, died in the same crime; and likewise his son Abia [Note: [Col. 0804D] Abijah, in the Latin.], concerning whom I find it written (ibid. XV.3): “He walked in the sins of his father, which he had committed before him; and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father.” Yet, while they served idols, they remained in royal power, died in that dignity, and handed down royal authority to their sons.

Do not therefore exult even in this, because your father handed the kingdom down to you, saying: “Unless my father had done well in joining himself to the Arians, we his sons would not reign.” [Note: [Col. 0804D] See the notes on this matter in Book I *For Saint Athanasius*.] Do not say: “If I were a heretic, I would never exercise such great power; God would never have allowed me still to remain in the kingdom,” when you see that Baasha [Note: [Col. 0804D] Baasan, in the Latin.] son of Ahijah reigned over Israel for twenty-four years, concerning whom you have found written in the Third Book of Kingdoms (ibid. 34): “He did evil before the Lord, and walked in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sins, by which he sinned [Note: [Col. 0804D] Greek: ἐξήμαρτε τὸν Ἰσραήλ, ‘caused Israel to sin.’] in Israel.”

Surely King Baasha ought to have feared that he would be struck down as Jeroboam was, if he departed from the ways of the Lord. But such are you who turn aside from God: when it pleases you to undertake the office of idolatry in insult to God, you cannot [Note: [Col. 0805D] “Can,” Latin.] even be terrified by the example of those already judged, nor turn to God. [Note: [Col. 0805D] “Terrified,” ibid.; but the sense stands correctly: “you could neither be frightened by their example nor converted to God.”]

It is also written concerning King Zimri [Note: [Col. 0805D] Zambri, ibid.] (III Kings XVI.25): “He did evil in the sight of the Lord, and acted more wickedly than all who were before him, and walked in every way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, in his sins.” Yet this man, said to have sinned more than the kings before him, was not extinguished as soon as he abandoned God; nor was he afflicted by some severe illness, so that he might seem to have been destroyed by a more grievous punishment, though he is described as having sinned more grievously.

You see, Constantius, that although it may befall you to pass this temporary life in the height of prosperity, you ought all the more to fear because you are reserved for God’s judgment. And although even those who are immediately destroyed, upon whom some punishment is divinely inflicted here, are nevertheless always tormented after their descent below, yet if you are snatched away from here while living in the height of happiness, consider how vengeance will proceed against you, since you are found in so great a crime.

Do not therefore attribute to yourself any happiness because, though you deny the only Son of God and persecute his household, your spirit nevertheless still remains in that executioner’s body. Consider also that the son of Asa reigned among the Jews for thirty-five years, though he was sacrilegious as you are; and you have read written of him (ibid. XXII.43): “He walked in the ways of Asa his father and did not turn aside from them, to do what was right in the sight of the Lord; but they did not abstain from the high places, and they sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.” [Note: [Col. 0805D] These words are absent from the Hexapla and Vulgate, but occur in the Septuagint, Roman edition, ch. XVI after v. 28, and concern Jehoshaphat king of Judah. Latinius reads “son of Asa” for “son of Baasha”; Asa was Jehoshaphat’s father. The same words are repeated in the Septuagint edition, ch. XXII, v. 43, where they are also placed in the Vulgate. Latinius noted an error in the number of years, for both the Septuagint and the Vulgate assign Jehoshaphat twenty-five years of reign. But see what we have considered necessary to investigate concerning this passage in the Preface. Latinius also suspects that something is missing after the words “in the sight of the Lord”; but nothing may lawfully be added, since the Septuagint likewise reads thus in ch. XVI.28.]

Behold, this king too is described as having fallen asleep in peace. Therefore, though he practiced idolatry for thirty-five years, do not take this as glory for yourself and say: “This is why I am not struck by any blow; this is why I have not already been extinguished, but still live and possess the kingdom of the Roman Empire: because I believe rightly, because Arius’s faith is correct, because I did well to remove bishops and appoint others such as Arius desired.”

Do not, I say, glory in this—that though you do these things, you are nevertheless proud—when you see that this king held the kingdom for thirty-five years and was removed in peace [Note: [Col. 0806D] That is, died; as a little later “removed” means “dead.”]. If, therefore, the crime of idolatry could pass without punishment for those because they were thus removed, it can do so also for you, Constantius.

Turn therefore to the Lord, lest you be found such as Ahab was found, concerning whom I read: “Ahab did evil in the sight of the Lord, and acted more wickedly than all who were before him. It was not enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, but he also took as wife Jezebel, daughter of Baal and Hela [Note: [Col. 0806D] Ethbaal, in the Latin from the Vulgate.] king of the Sidonians; and he went and served Baal and worshipped him. He set up Baal’s sanctuary in the house of his worship, which he had built in Samaria; and Ahab made a grove, in order to provoke God and destroy his own soul; and he acted more wickedly than all the kings of Israel who were before him” (ibid. XVI.30).

Do not any longer allow yourself to remain among the Arians; cross over to us Christians, to whom all heresies are as Baal was. You are now heretics to us just as those who sacrificed to idols were to God’s worshippers in those times. Believe me: through this heresy of yours, you are in our times such a person as Ahab was. Do not be pleased with yourself because God has not immediately repaid you, when you see that Ahab and his wife Jezebel, who even killed the prophets of the Lord and were found immersed in such great crime that they allowed no one confessing himself a servant of God to remain in the land of Israel, were spared for a very long time.

Do not look to this—that, though you do evil, you are nevertheless proud in your crimes—but, I beseech you, see this: unless you turn, just as the recompense of their deeds was at last rendered to them, so it can be rendered to you. Do not say: “I have long been in the kingdom; I am powerful because I hold the true faith, because I rightly persecute those who believe according to the faith set forth at Nicaea.” Do not say these things; rather, I pray you, see that you are still proud after so many deaths caused by you, so that either, hearing us priests of God, you may turn yourself to God, or else receive the deserved recompense of your deeds at that time when you will be unable to say that you erred in ignorance.

Recognize that these things are so, warned by the example of Ahab—the murderer of the prophets of the Lord and worshipper of all demons. Understand that this exceedingly wicked man was preserved in the kingdom for a long time after so many crimes so that he might at last turn if he wished: he not only did not receive immediately the recompense of his evil deeds, but was even helped in distress, undoubtedly so that he might conclude that he had not been avenged by Baal and the other demons whom pagans call gods, but by the God of Israel, whose prophet he saw speaking with him and declaring to him how God would reduce the enemies of the Israelites to nothing.

For King Ben-hadad [Note: [Col. 0806D] That is, Ben-hadad, ibid. from the Vulgate; likewise below. In the Septuagint, ch. XXI.1, υἱὸς Ἄδερ, ‘son of Ader.’] besieged Samaria with thirty-two other kings, boasting as though the Israelites were nothing, as though he alone could defeat the whole multitude of Israelites [Note: [Col. 0807D] Perhaps one should add *he believed* or *he said*.]. God made this foreigner as nothing before Israel. For which king did God win the victory? Surely for Ahab—for the man who had abandoned him, who had caused Israel to serve Baal and all demons—because [Note: [Col. 0807D] Perhaps one should read *who*, that is, God.] he helped him for this purpose: that he might believe that this God alone, whose people Israel was, is God, and that there is no other besides him who had given him victory; so that Ahab might see that it was fitting that he should at last correct his errors as soon as the enemy began to construct a siege against the city of the Israelites.

“And behold,” says Holy Scripture, “a certain prophet approached the king of Israel and said: ‘Thus says the Lord: Have you heard this great sound? Behold, today I will deliver him into your hands, and you shall know that I am the Lord.’ And the king said: ‘By whom?’ And the prophet said: ‘By the young men of the provincial rulers.’ And the king said: ‘Who will begin the battle?’ And the prophet said: ‘You’” (III Kings XX.13). And below: “The young men of the provincial rulers went out from the city, and the army behind them; and each struck the one whom he found beside him, and the Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them” (ibid. XX.19).

How do you say, Constantius: “If I did not serve God well, if I did not believe rightly, I would never have seen the Roman Empire placed under my power, nor would I have lived so long in the kingdom,” when you see that to Ahab king of Israel—living after the manner of the Gentiles and turning God’s people away from God, just as you do—there was said by him against whom he sinned and whose commands he treated as nothing: “I deliver him into your hands, that you may know that I am God”?

Therefore, just as he rescued Ahab from the son of Jader, king of Syria, so he has rescued and does rescue you from all who seek to destroy you, precisely that you may be able to know that he is the God of the patriarchs and martyrs; that you may conclude that victory has not been granted you for the merits of your faith and life, since you are like King Ahab in every respect, but that mercy has been shown you, contrary to your merits, by him whom you abandoned, just as it was shown to Ahab. For if you say that you conquer your enemies because you believe rightly, Ahab too, the worshipper of idols and murderer of holy prophets, could have said the same.

Do you not see that you have been preserved in order to correct your errors? [Note: [Col. 0807D] “You will correct,” Vatican manuscript.] As soon as you occupied Italy [Note: [Col. 0807D] Namely in A.D. 354, when he came from Gaul into Italy; he attended the Council of Milan in 355. “When he was at Milan,” Athanasius says in his letter *To the Solitaries*, “he did everything at the counsel and suggestion of the heretics—or rather, they themselves, having obtained power against all, did whatever they wished.” He then relates more fully how many disturbances were stirred up in Italy by Constantius’s arrival, especially in order that the judgment of the council might fall in accordance with the heretics’ opinions.], you attempted to overturn his Church. You said that God the Father is not the true God the Father, denying his only Son and affirming that he is not the true Son. You maintained [Note: [Col. 0807D] Although the name Pneumatomachians was preeminently assigned to the Macedonians, since they denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit, the Arians nevertheless held much more shameless views than they did regarding the Holy Spirit. They did not hesitate to call him, no less than the Son, a creature, and therefore made from nothing. Thus Lucifer reproaches the Arian emperor with this blasphemy against the Trinity, concerning which the Arians at times disputed with the Semi-Arians and Macedonians, who were somewhat less shameless and excluded the Holy Spirit both from participation in divinity and from the category of creature. See Petavius, Book I, *On the Trinity*, ch. 14.] that the holy Paraclete Spirit too was fashioned from nothing; you attempted to defend the view that he came down from nothing, that the only Son of God existed when he did not exist. With all your strength you labored to remove the apostolic and evangelical tradition from the midst; you caused bishops appointed by God’s judgment to be removed by your authority; you judged that heretics should be installed in their places, so that they might proclaim your heresy. You fought against the Church in Alexandria by military force [Note: [Col. 0808D] This refers to the events following the Council of Milan, which Athanasius recounts at length in his letter *To the Solitaries* and in the *Apology to Constantius*. See also Hilary, in his one book *Against Constantius*.]; you sent very many bishops into exile, to the mines, and into prison; you also killed a fixed number from among all God’s worshippers.

Though you have done these things, do you nevertheless say: “Unless I acted well and believed soundly, God would never still permit me to reign?”—as though God was patient toward Ahab and your other fellow-idolaters because they held the right way. Since, then, in his tireless mercy he is patient with your sins, as he was with King Ahab, do you suppose that you do not sin, but that you are spared because of your merits? You imitate Ahab also in this: you love those who advise you evil, but destroy those who tell you what is true for your salvation.

For just as those four hundred false prophets told Ahab that every prosperity would come to him, while God’s prophet Micaiah said, on the contrary, that every evil would come upon him, and Ahab loved those false prophets more than the true prophet of the Lord, so too [Note: [Col. 0808D] I think that *and* should be read.] you love your fellow-heretics, the Arians; you obey their words and curse all of us priests of the Lord. First, because we confess God’s Son as the true Son of God; second, because we do not flatter you, because we declare that you are in danger, and say that unless you turn to God you will come to eternal punishment.

And so that you may believe that God’s people have always been hated by apostate men, while the enemies of God’s religion—that is, worshippers of the devil—have been loved, learn whom Ahab loved and whom he hated. Jehoshaphat king of Judah said to the king of Israel: “Inquire of the Lord today.” And the king of Israel assembled all the prophets, about four hundred men, and King Ahab said to them: “Shall I go to Ramoth of Gilead for battle, or refrain?” And they said: “Go up” (ibid. XXII.5).

And below: Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel: “Is there not here a prophet of the Lord, that we may inquire of the Lord?” And Ahab king of Israel said to King Jehoshaphat: “There is one man through whom we may inquire of the Lord, but I hate him, because he does not speak good things concerning me” (ibid. 7). Likewise, after Micaiah the prophet of the Lord had told him not to go up, because if he went up he would not return: “The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: ‘Did I not tell you that this man prophesies not good things concerning me, but rather evil?’” (ibid. 18). [Note: [Col. 0809D] What follows here down to the words “The king said,” etc., seems in some measure to correspond to Sabat., verse 17, and may be referred to the order of this chapter. But these are Lucifer’s words, in which he comprises what is read there concerning the prophet Micaiah from verse 13 to verse 17.]

Those things which were said by God’s servant seemed evil to the senseless man already besieged by the devil, and those things spoken by the devil’s servants were judged good. Nor is it surprising, therefore, that Ahab listened to those whom the devil made his own slaves so that he would listen to them, and refused to listen to those whom God showed to be his servants both by their endurance of suffering and by the constancy of their confession. The false prophets were enriched, honored, and dismissed by the king; but Micaiah, the prophet of the Lord, was shut up in prison, and it was said: “Let him eat the bread of affliction until I return” (ibid. 27). [Note: [Col. 0809D] I do not know why Sabat. omitted these words, which belong to the ancient version and differ little from the Greek in the Septuagint: εἶπον … ἐσθίειν αὐτὸν ἄρτον θλίψεως … ἕως τοῦ ἐπιστρέψαι με, etc., “they said … let him eat bread of affliction … until I return,” etc.] Yet, in accordance with the saying of God’s servant, he did not return at all.

You act likewise, Constantius: you love those who draw you with themselves to everlasting death, who lead your soul to utter destruction; and you deign to hate those who desire you to become God’s friend. Do not glory because, while doing such great things, you nevertheless flourish in royal glory and still possess this fragile life. For the sacred writings relate that Jeroboam son of Joash reigned in Israel forty-one years in Samaria—having forsaken God and served idols, and not departing from the wicked acts of Ahab king of Israel or from Jeroboam’s sacrifices.

“You say, ‘If I had acted wickedly, God would already have removed me from the kingdom,’” as though the son of Amaziah, because he did not depart from vain things, was not struck with leprosy, yet reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. But you are superior to King Uzziah in this: you have no elephantiasis, which can consume all your limbs, but that which can utterly stain the soul. Mourn for yourself with us and shed tears for yourself. See how this visible elephantiasis stains the body, how the poison of leprosy consumes the limbs. Understand that in this way your Arian heresy, your elephantiasis, stains all those inward things within you; observe that it makes your inner person such as this disease makes those whom you see steeped in elephantiasis. [Note: [Col. 0809D] Perhaps *visibly* should be read.] [Note: [Col. 0809D] “Elephantiasis,” Latin.]

Do not say: “Unless I acted well, I would never have ruled for so long; I would never still have been permitted to live.” For you see Manasseh son of King Hezekiah, king of Judah, receiving the kingdom when he was sixteen years old and reigning fifty-seven years [Note: [Col. 0810D] Latinius corrects this to fifty-five years, here and below, as in the Vulgate and Septuagint. Sabat. retains the figure fifty-seven; but I suspect an error entered either into the manuscripts or printed editions, since no biblical manuscripts hitherto give this number.]. When you hear what is written of him, you will certainly find that you are his imitator; and you will cease to wonder that, though you act wickedly, you are nevertheless still spared, when you see Manasseh—than whom you are no less in cruelty and sacrilege—holding the kingdom for fifty-seven years while committing such deeds.

“And Hezekiah,” Scripture says (IV Kings XX.21), “slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David; and Manasseh his son reigned in his place. Manasseh was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-seven years in Jerusalem; and his mother’s name was Ebsibas. And he did evil before the Lord according to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord cast out before the children of Israel. He rebuilt the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed; he built a sanctuary to Baal and made groves, as Ahab king of Israel had done; he worshipped all the host of heaven and served them. He built a sanctuary in the two courts of the house of the Lord; he made his sons pass through fire, practiced divination, made mediums and many diviners, in order to do what was evil in the eyes of his soul and provoke the Lord God. And he made carved images of groves in the house of which the Lord said to David and Solomon his son: ‘In this house and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever, and I will no more cause Israel’s foot to be moved from the land which I gave them—if they will hear me in all that I commanded them, and according to the law which Moses my servant commanded them.’ But they did not hear [Note: [Col. 0810D] “They would hear” above is erroneous.].

“And because Manasseh greatly despised, and Manasseh led them astray so that they did evil beyond all the nations whom the Lord removed before Israel, the Lord spoke by the hand of his servants the prophets: ‘Because Manasseh king of Judah made images according to all that the Amorite did who was before him, and caused Judah to sin by his idols, therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I bring evils upon Jerusalem and Judah; everyone who hears of them, both his ears shall ring [Note: [Col. 0810D] For *shall ring*: “their ears shall perceive a sound,” Til. and La Cerda.]. I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria and the weight of the house of Ahab; and I will wipe out [Note: [Col. 0810D] Sabat. reads “I will wipe out.”] Jerusalem as a box is wiped from a doorpost before its face. I will give them into the hands of their enemies, and they shall become plunder and burning for all their enemies, because they have been cast away from behind me and were behind me [Note: [Col. 0810D] The same editor omits “and were behind me,” and reads “provoking exceedingly” for “provoking.”], provoking me from the day when their fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day.’
