“Eli,” Scripture says (ibid., 21), “was very old, and his sons had gone on in their ways, and their way was evil before the Lord. And it came to pass in those days that the foreigners assembled for battle against Israel” (1 Kingdoms 4:1).

And below:

“The battle turned, and the men of Israel fell before the foreigners; and four thousand men were wounded in battle on the field. The people came into the camp, and the elders of Israel said: ‘Why has the Lord caused us to fail today before the foreigners? Let us take the ark of the Lord our God [Col. 0833D] from Shiloh, that it may come into our midst and deliver us from the hands of our enemies.’ The people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the Lord, where the Cherubim sat; and both sons of Eli, Hophni [Note: [Col. 0833D] “Ophne” in Sabatier.] and Phinehas, went with the ark of God” (ibid., 2).

And below:

“They defeated them, and the men of Israel failed before the foreigners, and each fled to his own tent. The slaughter was very great: thirty [Col. 0834A] thousand men of Israel fell; the ark of God was captured; and both sons of Eli died” (ibid., 10).

And below:

“A man hastening came to Eli and said to him: ‘I am the man who came fleeing from the camp, from battle today.’ Eli said: ‘What has happened, my child?’ The man answered [Note: [Col. 0833D] “The man” is absent from Sabatier.] and said: ‘Israel fled before the foreigners, there has been a great slaughter among the people, both your sons are dead, and the ark of God has been captured.’ And when he heard, ‘The ark of God has been captured,’ he fell backward from his seat beside the gate; his back was broken, [Note: [Col. 0834D] That is, it was broken and bruised by the fall. Tillemont and La Cerda.] and he died, for he was an old and heavy man, and he had judged Israel for twenty years” (ibid., 16).

If these evils came upon Eli, priest and judge of the Israelites, in one day because he had not chastised his sons as was fitting, I have judged it proper to demonstrate here what you, the destroyer of God’s religion, see is coming upon you.

For you will not deny that you said it happens by God’s will that we, his servants, are subjected to you, our persecutors: “Unless our faith—that is, this faith which Lucifer calls Arian—were Catholic, I should never have received power over all peoples.” If this is so, then perhaps someone among those Philistines who captured God’s ark might have been better than a worshipper of God. Certainly, you say that your faith, which we know to be heretical, bestowed this upon you. But Maxentius, Nero, and all those persecutors of God’s house likewise said that, by the power of their gods, Christians had come under their rule.

Review what befell those who rejoiced that they had seized God’s ark, who said that by the power of their gods they had conquered the Israelites, [Col. 0834C] and you will find yourself one of those who persecuted God’s house.

“The foreigners took the ark of God from Ebenezer and brought it to Ashdod. The foreigners took the ark and brought it into the house of Dagon, and placed it beside Dagon. When the men of Ashdod rose early in the morning and entered Dagon’s house, they saw, and behold, Dagon had fallen upon his face before the ark of God. They lifted Dagon and set him in his place. The hand of the Lord was heavy upon Ashdod: he afflicted them and struck them in their houses, in Ashdod and its regions. And when they rose before dawn, Dagon had fallen upon his face before the ark of the Lord’s covenant; Dagon’s head and both the marks of his hands had been removed separately, and both joints of his hands had fallen [Col. 0834D] upon the threshold” (1 Kingdoms 5:1).

And below:

“The hand of the Lord was heavy upon Ashdod, and he brought mice upon them; a great confusion of death arose in the city. The men of Ashdod saw that it was so and said: ‘Let not the ark of the Lord God of Israel remain with us, for his hand is hard upon us and upon Dagon our god.’ They sent and summoned the remaining [Note: [Col. 0834D] “The remaining” is erroneously written, as Nobilius and Sabatier observe; it should be corrected to “the satraps,” Greek σατράπας. And a little below Lucifer himself repeats “the satraps.”] Philistines’ rulers to them and said: ‘What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?’ The people of Gath said: ‘Let the ark of the God of Israel pass [Col. 0835A] to Gath.’ After the ark of God was transferred, the hand of the Lord came upon the city, and there was a very great disturbance. He struck the men of the city from the least to the greatest; mice swarmed in their dwellings, and the men of Gath made themselves leather seats, and they sent the ark of God to Ashkelon. When the ark of the God of Israel entered Ashkelon, the people of Ashkelon cried out: ‘Why have you sent the ark of the God of Israel to us, to deliver us and our people to death?’ They sent and summoned the rulers of the Philistines and said: ‘Send back [Note: [Col. 0835D] Sabatier: “send back,” singular. Greek is plural, but with another verb: ἐξαποστείλατε, “send away.”] the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its place, that it may not deliver us and our people to death.’ For grievous confusion had overtaken the entire city, exceedingly grievous, when the ark entered; and those who lived and did not die were afflicted in their dwellings; and the cry of the [Col. 0835B] cities rose to heaven” (ibid., 6).

You see, Constantius, how our God permits his religion to appear humbled by you foreigners—humbled indeed to this point: until even you, persecutors of the true religion, see that there is no God besides our God.

But, to return once more to Athanasius’ case: did you not know that it is written in the first book of Kingdoms, “Samuel judged the people Israel in all sanctifications” (ibid., 7:16), that you should think it ought to be commanded that an innocent man be condemned through the Lord’s priests? You read that Samuel judged God’s people in every holy matter; and because we refuse to depart from this just way of judging, we suffer persecution from you.

Yet this is nothing new, when Saul persecuted the righteous Samuel because he spoke the truth to him—indeed, the very man by whom Saul had been anointed king, through whom the Lord had raised him to such glory. Saul persecuted the Lord’s prophet and priest because he was out of his mind. For how, if sane, could Saul persecute the man whom he knew to be God’s minister, full of God’s Spirit? He persecuted the man whom he knew continually to have groaned for the persecutor’s salvation.

Scripture says in the first book of Kingdoms that the Lord said to Samuel:

“How long do you mourn for Saul? Behold, I cast [Note: [Col. 0836D] Sabatier reads “I cast,” as in the book *On Apostate Kings*. See above, p. 33, where certain other variants occur in this text.] him out, that he may not reign over Israel. Fill your horn with oil and come; I shall send you to the house of Jesse, as far as Bethlehem, for I have seen among Jesse’s sons one for myself as king.” Samuel said: “How shall I go? Lest Saul hear and kill me” (1 Kingdoms 16:1).

Saul sought to destroy the man whom he remembered had already shown himself to be God’s man in many ways. The man of God did not cease to seek pardon for his persecutor, while Saul, made a son of pestilence, sought to take his life. Indeed, Saul proved so great a persecutor of Samuel, the Lord’s priest, that when the Lord said to him, “Come, I shall send you,” he replied, “How shall I go? Saul will hear and kill me” (ibid.).

You see, Constantius, that when you depart from God you are reckoned not as human beings but as wild beasts, monsters, and robbers. Or are you not comparable to Saul in this, that you unjustly persecute Athanasius? For you desire to slaughter the innocent Athanasius just as Saul desired to kill not only Samuel but David also. Saul, indeed, threatened to kill those with whom he knew God was.

“Saul,” Scripture says, “saw that the Lord was with David, and that all Israel loved him; and Saul further began to fear David” (ibid., 18:28). “Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, to kill David” (ibid., 19:1).

Answer, most shameless emperor: can one who has God’s Spirit do these things? At what time did Saul begin to do them? Surely at the time when he was cursed and rejected through Samuel. For at that same time it is written that [Col. 0836B] the Lord departed from him, but was with David. By these things it is proved that you Arians are without God’s Spirit, since you persecute Athanasius, a man full of the Holy Spirit.

“David,” it says, “was wise in all his ways, and the Lord was with him; and all Israel and Judah loved David” (ibid., 18:34).

Therefore, so that you may recognize that you act toward Athanasius as Saul acted toward David, hear what is written:

“Jonathan son of Saul loved David greatly; and Jonathan told David, saying: ‘Saul seeks to kill you’” (ibid., 19:1).

And below:

“Jonathan spoke to his father, saying: ‘Do not sin, O king, against your servant David, for he has not sinned against you, and his deeds are very good. He put his life in his hands and killed the foreigner, and the Lord wrought salvation in Israel; [Col. 0836C] all Israel saw and rejoiced. Why do you sin against innocent blood and wish to kill David without cause?’ Saul heard the voice of Jonathan his son, and Saul swore, saying: ‘As the Lord lives, David shall not be put to death’” (ibid., 4).

And below:

“War again arose, and David prevailed and defeated the foreigners; he struck them with a great slaughter, and they fled before David. An evil spirit came upon Saul, and he slept [Note: [Col. 0836D] “Sat.” Latinus, with the Greek and Vulgate.] in his house with a spear in his hand; and behold, David was playing with his hands. Saul sought to strike David with the spear; he struck, but David turned aside from Saul, and the spear struck the wall. David fled and escaped. That night Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him, that he might kill him in the morning” (ibid., 8).

“David fled and escaped, and came to Samuel at Ramah, and told him all that Saul had done” (ibid., 18).

And below:

“Saul became very angry with Jonathan” (ibid., 20:30).

And below:

“He said: ‘Send these things; take the youth, for he is a son of death.’ Jonathan answered his father: ‘Why shall he die? What has he done?’ Saul lifted his spear against Jonathan to kill him” (ibid., 31).

Whom would Saul spare when he would not spare his own son for telling him the truth? Such are you, who pass over God’s commands [Col. 0837A] and establish your own. Finally, we do not wonder that, because it is said, “One absent cannot be condemned,” you persecute the Lord’s priests, when we see that Saul persecuted those who served God in this manner.

Scripture says:

“The king said: ‘You shall surely die, Abimelech, you and all your father’s house’” (ibid., 22:16).

And below:

“The king said to his runners who stood by him: ‘Bring forward and kill the priests of the Lord, for their hand is with David; for they knew that David was fleeing and did not uncover it to my ear.’ But the king’s servants would not put forth their hands against the priests of the Lord” (ibid., 17).

[Note: [Col. 0837D] “Not” is absent from Sabatier’s reading.]

What do you say, most equitable king? If those servants of a king are reported to have refused obedience to the king’s command, if they are shown to have disregarded Saul’s orders lest they act against God’s commands, was it fitting for us bishops, trampling upon the Lord’s commands, [Col. 0837B] to carry out yours, sacrilegious murderer? Therefore you deem us worthy of persecution because we do not place your commands before the Lord’s.

Saul also did these things, as Holy Scripture proves in saying:

“Saul said to Doeg: ‘Turn yourself against the priests of the Lord.’ Doeg the Syrian turned and put the priests of the Lord to death; on that day he killed three hundred and five men, all wearing the ephod. And he killed Oben, the city of the priests, by the edge of the sword—man and woman, infant and nursing child” (ibid., 18).

[Note: [Col. 0837D] That is, he handed them over to death, punished them with death, and killed them, as he himself explains in the following line: “and on that day he killed three hundred and five men.” Hence the word “putting to death,” which he uses below: “because you are sons of putting to death,” that is, sons of death—worthy, namely, to have death inflicted upon you because you did not preserve your Lord, the Lord’s Christ. Tillemont and La Cerda.]

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Such proper names, as here, all differ from those in our Bibles; nor do they agree in the passages following. From this it may readily be seen that they then possessed a far different common translation from ours, which was subsequently corrected. The same editors.]

You have now attempted, and still attempt, in like fashion to tear the bodies of those whom you see resist your command because they remember God’s commands. We therefore cannot wonder if you persecute us, when we see that Saul, because they had not delivered the Lord’s servant David into his hands, destroyed not only three hundred and five priests but an entire city.

Saul persecuted David, although David, when he had him in his power, often nevertheless spared him. Scripture says:

“When Saul had returned from pursuing the foreigners, they reported to him: ‘Behold, David is in the wilderness of Gaddi.’ Saul took with him three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to seek David and his men before the place of the deer-hunt. He came to sheepfolds beside the road, [Note: [Col. 0837D] Thus it is found in an ancient manuscript, although the text should have said “which.” Tillemont.] and there was a cave there. Saul entered to relieve himself, while David and his men sat in the innermost part of the cave. David’s men said to him: ‘Behold, this is the day of which [Note: [Col. 0838D] Sabatier punctuates: “The Lord said to you: I will give,” etc. The Complutensian Greek has Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ δίδωμι, “Behold, I give,” which corresponds to our reading.] the Lord said: “I shall give your enemy into your hands, and you shall do to him what is pleasing in your eyes.”’ [Col. 0838A] David arose and secretly cut off the edge [Note: [Col. 0838D] That is, he secretly and covertly removed the edge of Saul’s cloak. Here David’s supreme goodness is recognized: although he could have killed Saul, he nevertheless spared him. Tillemont and La Cerda.] of Saul’s cloak. After this David’s heart smote him because he had cut off the edge of the cloak; and
And David said to his young men: “May it never happen to me from the Lord that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, to lay my hand upon him; for he is the Lord’s anointed.” And David restrained his men with words and did not permit them to rise up and kill Saul. And Saul rose up, went down into the road, and David went out after Saul, saying: “My lord the king.” Saul looked behind him, and David bowed with his face to the ground and did him reverence. And David said to Saul: “Why do you listen to the words of people saying, ‘Behold, David seeks your life’? Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the Lord delivered you today into my hands in the cave [Note: [Col. 0838D] That is, in a cavern, a hidden and hollow place. Thus he very often uses whole Greek words, mixing them into Latin, as he previously said *thlipsen*, θλίψιν, for “affliction.” From this it is easy to understand that this was how people spoke at that time: even in those islands, on one of which this author had his seat, and at the imperial court, Greek was spoken. Til.], and I was unwilling to kill you, [Col. 0838B] but spared you and said: ‘I will not lay my hand upon my lord, because he is the Lord’s anointed.’ See: I have taken the fringe of your cloak in my hand; I cut off the hem of your cloak, yet did not kill you. Know and see today that there is neither malice nor injustice in my hand, and that I have not sinned against you, though you seek to take my life. May the Lord judge between me and you, and avenge me upon you; but my hand shall not be against you. As the ancient proverb says, ‘Out of the wicked comes wickedness’; but my hand shall not be against you. Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog, or a single flea. Let the Lord be judge and avenger between me and you; let the Lord see and judge my cause, and vindicate me from your hand” (Ibid. XXIV, 2).

Such is the custom of God’s worshippers: to reserve everything for [Col. 0838C] God, knowing that it is a great thing to be avenged by him. Meanwhile, as I said above, observe what Saul says when he is in his right mind; and when he becomes beside himself, how he thirsts for the blood of David, righteous and innocent:

“And it came to pass,” Scripture says, “when David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said: ‘Is this your voice, my son David?’ And Saul cried aloud and wept; and he said to David: ‘You are righteous [Note: [Col. 0838D] Greek: δίκαιος, “righteous”; in Sabatier, *more righteous*.] more than I, because you have returned good to me, whereas I have rendered evil to you. Today you have reported to me the good things you did for me, since the Lord shut me up in your hands and you did not kill me. And as a man finds his friend and sends him forward on a good road, so may the Lord repay you good for what you have done for me today. And now, behold, I know that you shall indeed reign [Note: [Col. 0838D] *Regnando* (“by reigning”) is omitted by Sabatier, but it is in the Greek, Βασιλεύων.] and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand. And [Col. 0839A] now swear to me by the Lord that you will not root out my seed after me, nor destroy my name from my father’s house.’ And David swore to Saul” (Ibid. 17).

After this Saul ought certainly by now to have changed; yet he still does not cease to pursue, nor does David cease to spare. “And Saul,” Scripture says, “rose up and went down into the shady wilderness, with three thousand chosen men from Israel, to seek David” (Ibid. XXVI, 2). And below:

“David sent scouts and learned that Saul had come to Sicelet. David rose secretly and went to the place where Saul slept, and Abner son of Ner, commander of his army. Saul slept on splendid bedding, and the people were around him. And David said to Amalek the Hittite and to Abessa son of Sarvia, brother of Joab: ‘Who will go in with me to Saul’s camp?’ And Abessa said to [Col. 0839B] David: ‘I will go with you.’ David and Abessa entered among the people by night, and behold, Saul was sleeping on costly bedding, with his splendid spear fixed at his head, while Abner slept around him. And Abessa said to David: ‘Today God has shut up your enemy in your hands; now I will strike him with the spear, pinning him to the earth with one blow, and I shall not strike him again.’ But David said to Abessa: ‘Do not touch him; for who shall lay his hand upon the Lord’s anointed and be guiltless?’ And David said: ‘As the Lord lives, unless the Lord himself strikes him, or his hour comes and he dies, or he goes down into battle and is swept away, may it never be mine from the Lord to lay my hand [Note: [Col. 0839D] “My hand.” Vatican manuscript, as in the Greek.] upon the Lord’s anointed. Now take the spear that is at his head and the vessel of water, and let us depart.’ David took the spear and the vessel [Col. 0839C] of water from his head, and they went away. There was no one to see or know, and no one was awake; for they all slept, because the fear of the Lord had fallen upon them. David crossed over and stood on the summit of the mountain at a distance, with a great space between them. David called to the people and to Abner, saying: ‘Will you not answer, Abner?’ Abner answered and said: ‘Who are you that call to me? What is it?’ David said to Abner: ‘Are you not a man? And who is like you in Israel? Why have you not guarded your lord the king? For one of the people entered to destroy your lord the king. This thing that you have done is not good. As the Lord lives, you are sons of death, because you did not guard [Note: [Col. 0839D] “You guarded.” Vatican manuscript.] your lord the king, the Lord’s anointed. And now see where the king’s spear is, and the vessel of water that was at [Col. 0839D] his head.’ Saul the king recognized David’s voice and said: ‘Is this your voice, my son David?’ ‘Your servant, my lord king.’ And David continued: ‘Why does my lord thus pursue his servant? What have I done wrong, and what evil is there in me? Now let my lord the king hear his servant’s words: if [Note: [Col. 0839D] “If the Lord your God moves you against me, may he smell an offering.” [Col. 0840D] Latin from the Vulgate and Greek: “The Lord God moves.” Vatican manuscript omits *your*, as in the Greek.] the Lord your God moves you against me, may he accept a sacrificial offering; but if it is the sons of men, cursed are they [Note: [Col. 0840D] Οὗτοι, “these,” in the Greek; omitted by Sabatier.] before the Lord, because today they have driven me out so that I am not established in the covenant of the Lord, saying: “Go, serve foreign gods.” And now let not my blood fall to the earth before the Lord, [Col. 0840A] for the king of Israel has come out to seek one flea, as an owl pursues in the mountains.’ Saul said: ‘I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I shall no longer deal maliciously with you, because today my life has been precious in your eyes. On this day I have acted foolishly and have been greatly ignorant.’ David answered and said: ‘Behold the king’s spear. Let one of the young men come over and take it. May the Lord repay each person according to his righteousness and faithfulness, since he delivered you today into my hands and I was unwilling to lay my hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Behold, as your life was exalted today in my eyes, so may my life be esteemed in the sight of the Lord, and may he snatch me away and rescue me from all tribulation.’ Saul said to David: ‘Blessed are you, my son; you shall both accomplish and prevail mightily’” (Ibid., 4).

I have inserted these things so that at last you may infer [Col. 0840B] that you persecute unjustly—whether me, Athanasius, or us; that you render service toward the destruction of your own salvation; and that you incur before the Godhead the perils of death, just as Saul incurred them through these deeds. If this is not so, say why you persecute us. Surely it is because we do not shed innocent blood. Whom do you wish us to imitate—you or David? For of David I find it written: “And David reigned over Israel, doing judgment and justice for all his people” (II Kings VIII, 15); but we see you to be an unjust judge and a killer of God’s worshippers. Why do you persecute us? Surely because we have refused to become apostates as you are, because we have refused to deny the only Son of God. David speaks plainly of the perfect Trinity and declares one Godhead of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but you are found to be an apostate. Whom, I ask, [Col. 0840C] should I follow—you or David? That worshipper of the Lord, lover of mercy, or you, sacrilegious man and executioner? What man of wisdom persecutes Athanasius?

I would be astonished that you do these things, if King Ahab had not also persecuted Elijah and the other prophets of the Lord in this manner. I would be astonished that you persecute a man of God, if I did not see that in all things you are Ahab. In short, we say to you what God’s household said to him: “Do not worship Baal; do not serve idols, but God. Serve the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob; serve the God of Israel.” If you remember that Elijah and the other prophets of the Lord said such things to Ahab the apostate king, recognize that similar things are said to you by those to whom the Lord has given authority to teach. Constantius, do not fight with the Arians against God’s house; do not introduce Arius’s idolatry [Col. 0840D] into the Church; do not deny the only Son of God; cease persecuting the apostolic and evangelical faith. Because we say these things, we seem enemies to you; so those who spoke truth to the king seemed enemies to him.

Let us then run through what occurred and was done between Elijah, the prophet of the Lord, and Ahab, your fellow-apostate; and you will find that today you are Ahab. “As the Lord lives,” Elijah says, “before whose presence I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years except by the word of my mouth” (III Kings XVII, 1). When this was fulfilled, that madman ought surely to have recognized that no one except the one whom Elijah served was the true God, alone powerful over [Col. 0841A] all things. What does Ahab do? For three years and more he sees that there is no rain, yet he serves idols all the more and desires all the more to kill Elijah. The prophet of God hears from the mouth of the sacrilegious Ahab: “Are you he who overturns Israel?” (III Kings XVIII, 17). So you too say to Athanasius or to us—for we [Note: [Col. 0841D] He says *we are overturning* in Greek fashion for “we do not overturn,” and *we overturn* for “we overthrow,” as he says a little below: “We do not overturn God’s house, but you”; that is, we do not disturb or throw God’s house into confusion, nor cause God’s people to sin, as you Arians do. Further below he uses *to overturn* in the sense of “to turn back,” saying: “Nor after so many things does he deign to turn himself to God”; that is, to turn to God and implore him to be merciful. Yet note that the text itself was printed, “we are,” etc.; we retain this wording because both punctuation and sense require it. Perhaps a copyist’s error entered Tillemont’s note, where *not* was printed instead of *we*.] do not overturn God’s people—whereas you are summoning Christians to embrace your heresy. But you hear from us what that worshipper of idolatry, Ahab, heard from glorious Elijah: “It is not we who overturn God’s house; rather, you and your father’s house overturn it.” Or will you deny that you think of nothing except making all of us your fellow-apostates? But to continue the account I began of the deeds of Elijah and Ahab:

“Elijah said: ‘I do not overturn Israel; rather, you and your father’s house overturn it, [Col. 0841B] because you have forsaken the Lord our God and gone after Baal. And now send and gather to me all Israel on Mount Carmel, and the four hundred and fifty prophets of shame, and the four hundred prophets of groves, who eat and drink at Jezebel’s table.’ King Ahab sent to all Israel and gathered all the prophets on Mount Carmel. Elijah came near to them all and said: ‘How long will you limp in your understanding? If the Lord is God, go after him; but if Baal is, go after him.’ The people answered him not a word. Elijah said to the people: ‘I alone remain [Note: [Col. 0841D] For *I remain*, that is, I alone remain and survive among God’s true prophets, and I shall overcome you, the four hundred false prophets of Baal. Til. and La Cerda.] the sole [Note: [Col. 0842D] The Latin omits *sole*. But the word should be retained, since, joined to *one*, it admirably expresses the force of the Greek μονώτατος, as though one said “most utterly one.”] prophet of the Lord, while Baal’s prophets are four hundred and fifty men, and the prophets of the groves four hundred. Let two oxen therefore be given us. Let them choose one for themselves, cut it in pieces, and place [Col. 0841C] it upon the wood, but put no fire beneath it; and I will prepare the other ox and put no fire beneath it. Call upon the names of your gods, and I will call upon the name of my God; and whichever God answers us by fire, he shall be God.’ All the people answered and said: ‘The word Elijah has spoken is good.’ Elijah said to the prophets of shame: ‘Choose one calf for yourselves and prepare it first, because you are many; call upon the names of your gods, but do not put fire beneath it.’ They took the calf and prepared it, and called on Baal’s name from morning until evening, saying: ‘Hear us, Baal, hear us.’ But there was neither voice nor hearing. Elijah the Tishbite added, saying: ‘Cry out together with a loud voice; perhaps he is occupied, or perhaps he is asleep and will be awakened.’ [Col. 0842A] They called on him in a loud voice and cut themselves, according to their custom, with swords and razors until blood flowed over them. They prophesied until noon had passed; and when [Note: [Col. 0842D] For *when*; Tillemont and La Cerda.] it was time to offer [Note: [Col. 0842D] Sabatier: *ascend*, following the Greek ἀναβῆναι.] the sacrifice, Elijah the Tishbite spoke to the prophets, saying: ‘Depart now, and I will make the burnt offerings.’ They departed and went away. Elijah said to the people: ‘Come near to me.’ All the people came near to him. Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of Israel, as the Lord had said to him: ‘Israel shall be your name.’ He built with the stones and restored the altar of the Lord that had been broken down. He made a trench around the altar capable of holding two measures of seed, and he piled the split wood [Note: [Col. 0842D] That is, he gathered the *schizae*, namely the wood that he had cut and split upon the altar. For σχίζειν means “to split” or “to cut,” and σχίζα means wood cut and divided into pieces. Til. and La Cerda.] upon the altar he had made. He cut up the burnt offering and [Col. 0842B] placed it upon the split wood, arranging it on the altar. Then he said: ‘Bring me four jars of water and pour them over the burnt offering and over the wood.’ He said: ‘Bring them again.’ They brought them again. He said: ‘Do it a third time.’ They did it a third time; water ran around the sanctuary and filled the trench. Elijah cried to heaven and said: ‘Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, hear me, Lord; hear me today by fire, that all this people may know [Note: [Col. 0842D] In agreement with the Greek γνώτωσαν; Sabatier reads the singular, “that this people may know.”] that you are the Lord God of Israel, that I am your servant, and that because of you I have done these works; and that you have turned [Note: [Col. 0842D] For *turned away*, as though he said: “Because of the people’s wickedness, you have turned their heart back from yourself.” This interpretation more closely approaches the Hebrew version. Til.] the heart of this people backward.’ Fire fell from the Lord out of heaven and consumed the burnt offerings, the split wood, and the water that was on the altar; the fire licked up the stones and the earth. All the people fell upon their faces and said: ‘Truly the Lord himself is God.’ Elijah [Col. 0842C] said to the people: ‘Seize the prophets of Baal; let none of them escape.’ They seized them, and Elijah led [Note: [Col. 0842D] “They led.” Vatican manuscript.] them down to the torrent of Kishon and killed them there. Elijah said to Ahab: ‘Eat and drink, for there is the sound of the feet of rain.’ Ahab went up to eat and drink, while Elijah went up to Carmel, bowed himself to the ground, and put his face between his knees. He said to his servant: ‘Go up and look toward the way of the sea.’ The servant looked and said: ‘There is nothing [Note: [Col. 0842D] In Greek fashion, for “there is nothing” or “there is not anything.” Til. and La Cerda.].’ ‘Turn about seven times.’ On the seventh time, behold, a little cloud, like a man’s footprint, bringing water from the sea. Elijah said to him: ‘Go up and tell Ahab: Harness your chariot and go down, lest the rain overtake you.’ And here and there the sky grew dark [Note: [Col. 0842D] That is, the sky became dark and overcast, as happens when rain approaches. Ibid.] with clouds and winds, and there was a great rain. Ahab wept and went [Col. 0843A] to [Note: [Col. 0843D] Jezreel. Latin and Sabatier, as in the Greek and Vulgate.] Israel, and the hand of the Lord was upon Elijah” (III Kings XVIII, 18).

You recognize the perversity in which you now remain, the same in which Ahab remained. For after so many signs and wonders had been displayed, he does not deign to rejoice with the people, but grieves because Elijah dared to kill the priests and prophets of idols. Nor after so much does he deign to turn himself to God; rather, he continues to persecute God’s worshipper. He sees that God is with Elijah, yet seeks his life all the more. He sees that the prophets of Baal and the groves were worshippers of demons, yet loves them, even after they are killed, more than the one whom in so many ways he had observed to be a member of God’s household. So you too deign to love those whom you see to be adherents of the Arian heresy, while you persecute God’s worshippers with the greatest severity.

For this reason I have thought it necessary to set before you [Col. 0843B] a few of the many deeds between Ahab and Elijah: that you may know [Note: [Col. 0843D] For “to recognize” or “to know.” Til.] that, since you abandon God, neither signs nor miracles easily turn you back to him; rather, persisting in your errors, you rage like savage beasts against the flock of God’s worshippers. We beseech you, Constantius, do not deign to remain any longer in these evils of yours, but emerge rather from the whirlwinds of the devil, lest those evils which overtook Ahab and Jezebel overtake you also. Do not call yourself fortunate because you have power to persecute God’s people. You see that Ahab and Jezebel could have been destroyed at Elijah’s request, yet they were spared, so that both the endurance of Elijah, God’s man, might be more fully blessed and the measure of their impiety fulfilled. As though Elijah could not have asked God to burn the persecutors of his religion, those worshippers of idols! He asks for fire to be given from heaven to consume the sacrifices; immediately it descends. Rain, withheld for three years [Col. 0843C] and six months, is immediately given when he asks. Very many signs occur. Could God’s enemies not be destroyed at Elijah’s request, when descending fire at Elijah’s word also consumed those honored captains of fifty? You see that today, because you persecute Athanasius or us, you could be destroyed by lightning or in any other way [Note: [Col. 0843D] It seems that *to destroy* should be read.], but are preserved for this purpose: either that you may be converted, or that the full measure of all your iniquity may be completed.

King Ahab persecuted Elijah as you now persecute Athanasius. After Jezebel had learned through Elijah of those mighty acts, and that the prophets of shame and priests of false religions had been killed, she said to the prophet of the Lord: “May the gods do these things to me and add these things to me, if tomorrow at this hour I do not make your life like the life [Col. 0843D] of one of them” (Ibid. XIX, 2). [Note: [Col. 0843D] This verse too is omitted by Sabatier; it differs somewhat from the Greek and nearly agrees with the Vulgate.] But what does Elijah hear from God after his celebrated fast of forty days and nights? Namely, that he should anoint kings through whom Ahab and his associates would be destroyed. God’s mercy is with Elijah; Elijah knows that he is loved by God. By contrast, Ahab, Elijah’s persecutor, is so miserable that he has always remained in the devil’s power.

You commanded Athanasius to be punished just as Jezebel did Nabutheus [Note: [Col. 0843D] For *Noboth*. Thus also Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 8, chapter 13, from three manuscripts—Vatican, Henneberg, and Busbecq—in Havercamp’s edition.] the Israelite. You produced true witnesses against Athanasius as they produced those to whom Jezebel had written, saying: “Proclaim [Note: [Col. 0843D] Ancient Version: “And set Nabuthe at the head of the people, and set . . . men of iniquity opposite him, that they may bear false witness . . . ‘He has cursed God and [Col. 0844D] the king’; then bring him out and stone him.” Lucifer’s wording is more fitting with the Greek: Ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῦ λαοῦ, “at the head of the people”; παρανόμων, “of lawless men”; καταμαρτυρησάτωσαν αὐτοῦ, “let them testify against him”; and he adds “let him die,” as does the Greek, καὶ ἀποθανέτω.] a fast, and seat Nabutheus at the head of the people. Set two men, sons of iniquity, against him, and let them testify against him, saying: ‘You have cursed the Lord and the king.’ Then lead him out, let him be stoned, and let him die” (Ibid. XXI, 9).

Such are now your deeds, Arians: you call us accused, bring many charges against us, and have no need of false witnesses, for you yourselves are false witnesses in every respect. Thus you Arians, sons of perdition, attempt to kill Athanasius as Jezebel killed Nabutheus, [Col. 0844B] as though you could escape the hand of him who sees all things. You know that God avenged Nabutheus’s blood and required his death from the hands of his murderers; and do you suppose that God will not require from your hands the blood of Athanasius, his priest?

“And the Lord said to Elijah the Tishbite: [Note: [Col. 0844D] Sabatier omits this verse, “And the Lord said to Elijah the Tishbite,” though it agrees with the Greek and Vulgate.] ‘Arise and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria; for behold, he has gone down into Nabutheus’s vineyard to possess it. You shall say to him: Thus says the Lord: Because you killed Nabutheus and took possession of his vineyard, therefore thus says the Lord: In the place where dogs and swine licked Nabutheus’s blood, dogs shall lick your blood there, and harlots shall wash in your blood.’ Ahab said to Elijah: ‘Have you found me, my enemy [Note: [Col. 0844D] Greek: ὁ ἐχθρός μου, “my enemy.” Sabatier reads “an enemy to you.”]?’ Elijah said: ‘I have found you, because you have devised evil before the Lord in order to provoke him.’ [Col. 0844C] Thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I bring evils upon you; I will kindle fire after you and destroy from you, Ahab, everyone who urinates against a wall, the despised and the remnant in Israel. [Note: [Col. 0844D] That is, everything belonging to you, down to “the one who urinates,” etc.] I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because of all the provocations by which you provoked me and made Israel sin.’ And the Lord spoke concerning Jezebel: ‘Dogs shall eat her before the wall of Israel [Note: [Col. 0844D] Jezreel. Vatican manuscript, with the Greek.], and birds of heaven shall eat your dead in the city’” (Ibid. 17).

What do you, Constantius, say to these things? Do you maintain that your sins are less than those of Ahab and Jezebel? They persecuted God’s priests, killed members of God’s household, abolished God’s religion, established idolatry, and turned the people away from God—and you have done and still do all these things. So you call us your enemies, [Col. 0844D] just as Ahab called Elijah his, when he heard the Lord’s indignation from the prophet’s mouth and said: “Have you found me, enemy of King Ahab?” (Ibid. 20). Surely because Elijah said: “Do not serve idols, but the God alone of Abraham, [Col. 0845A] Isaac, and Israel.” And now, because you are told, “Do not be a heretic, but be a Christian,” you call enemies those who lay before you, as you promulgate idolatry, the same things that were brought before King Ahab through Elijah. [Note: [Col. 0845D] “May be brought before.” Ibid.] Certainly Ahab would have loved Elijah if the Lord’s prophet had judged that his idols should be served and God abandoned. You cannot deny this: had we chosen to be what you yourself are, you would have loved us with singular affection. From these things you are understood to be a son of pestilence, a source of darkness, a whirlpool of every evil, head of all wickedness, sewer of all blasphemers, fuel of heretics, root of bitterness; a tree destined for fire, indeed bearing deadly fruit; enemy of God, foe of the Church, corrupter of truth, contriver of depravity, lover of injustice, adversary of justice; [Col. 0845B] wholly turned into darkness, and indeed inextricable darkness; or rather made a temple of all demons, at whose prompting you have perpetrated and still perpetrate all these evils, like Ahab.

But unless you turn to God, you cannot long remain unpunished, since you see what Ahab and Jezebel received. If Ahab perishes, as had been promised him through Elijah’s mouth, and dogs devour Jezebel, will you go unpunished for such great crimes? You who not only do not grieve that you have killed persons consecrated to God, but still glory in it, believing that you have done well. Nor is it strange, since he who foreknows the future, whom you deny, said in the Gospel: “The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is doing service to God; but they do these things because they know neither the Father nor his only Son” (John XVI, 2). [Note: [Col. 0845D] Ancient Version: “My hour will come, that everyone who kills you may suppose that he performs a service to God; but they do these things to you because they have known neither the Father nor me.” Lucifer agrees with Cyprian, Epistle 56, down to the words “but they do these things,” etc.]

Knowing this, while living without knowledge of God, you persecute Athanasius, who speaks truth to you and loves God with his whole heart. So too Ahab persecuted Elijah. But observe Elijah’s end and that of his enemy Ahab. See Elijah translated to enjoy [Note: [Col. 0845D] See what we have discussed on this matter in the Preface.] eternal fellowship with God; and now Ahab is tormented in the outer darkness. Elijah rejoices in God’s friendship, while Ahab pays everlasting penalties. Without doubt Athanasius will be at the banquet where Elijah is, and you, unless you provide for yourself, will be in that place of torments where Ahab is held, whom you are found [Note: [Col. 0845D] “You are found.” Latin text.] to imitate in all things. Is this wisdom—to choose the eternal misery of King Ahab rather than enjoy the perpetual blessedness attained by Elijah? Scripture speaks of Elijah’s translation in the Fourth Book of Kings, saying: “While [Col. 0845D] they were going and speaking, behold, a fiery chariot and fiery horses separated the two; and Elijah went up in a commotion, as though into heaven. Elisha saw and cried out: ‘Father, father, charioteer of Israel!’ And he saw him no more” (IV Kings II, 11).

It cannot seem new to us, heretic, if you [Col. 0846A] persecute us, the priests of the Lord, since in the Second Book of Chronicles we find that Jeroboam and his sons did these things. “The sacred Scripture says: Judah and Benjamin, and the Levites and priests who were in all Israel, assembled from every border, because the Levites abandoned their tabernacles and their possessions and went to Jeroboam [Note: [Col. 0846D] Rehoboam. Ibid., and rightly; in Greek, Πρὸς Ἰούδα εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, “to Judah, to Jerusalem,” where Rehoboam reigned.], because Jeroboam and his sons drove them away so that they might not serve the Lord. He established there priests for the high places, for images, demons, and the calves which Jeroboam had made. He cast them out from [Note: [Col. 0846D] “From the children of Israel” is removed by the Latin text and absent from the Greek and Vulgate.] the children of Israel, and from the tribes of Israel, those who had given their heart to seek the Lord God of Israel” (II Chronicles XI, 12).

It will therefore not be surprising if you persecute us or those divinely entrusted to us, if you drive us from the charge committed to us, if finally you install in our places ranks [Col. 0846B] hostile to God—those who, with you, have abandoned God—when you see that you are fulfilling what Jeroboam did. For what does it mean to say, “Condemn the creed drawn up at Nicaea and accept mine,” except what Jeroboam said: “Abandon God and serve my images”? What sort of man are you to say, “Condemn one absent, unheard, innocent”? Certainly one who had already denied the apostolic and evangelical faith; indeed, one who had destroyed, as far as lay in you and yours, the tradition of the blessed apostles. Thus it came about that you fell into such madness, because, like Jeroboam, you were without God. But if you had God, if you remembered yourself to be his worshipper, you would never say: “Condemn the innocent; strike the unheard, absent man—your fellow priest.”

And so that you may see that you are not in [Col. 0846C] God—and that this is why you order such deeds—consider a king whom God attended according to his merits; consider also his exhortation to the priests of the Lord, whom he urged to render righteous judgment to God’s people. Observe also the judgment of your own officials, established by you against the Church [Note: [Col. 0846D] “Judges.” Vatican manuscript.], and the deeds of that king’s ministers. Then you will be able to discern whether unclean spirits are not with you, as they were with Jeroboam.

“In the Second Book of Chronicles,” it says, “Jehoshaphat dwelt in Jerusalem; he went out again among the people, from Beersheba to Mount Ephraim, and turned them back to the Lord God of their fathers. He appointed judges in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city, and said to the judges: ‘See what [Note: [Col. 0846D] “You do.” Latin, as in the Greek, ὑμεῖς ποιεῖτε. Below: “You shall do.”] you do; for you judge not for man but for the Lord, and he is with you in the judgment. And now let the fear of the Lord be upon you, that you may keep and do what is right. For with the Lord our God there is neither injustice, nor respect of persons, nor acceptance of gifts.’ In Jerusalem Jehoshaphat also appointed Levites, priests, and chiefs of Israel for the Lord’s judgment and to judge [Note: [Col. 0846D] That is, for judging, and that they might judge Jerusalem’s inhabitants. Til.] the inhabitants of Jerusalem. He commanded [Col. 0847A] them, saying: ‘Thus shall you do in the fear of the Lord, with a perfect heart. Every case that comes before you from your brethren dwelling in their cities—between blood and blood, between law, commandments, ordinances, and judgments—you shall distinguish for them [Note: [Col. 0847D] Sabatier reads “them,” but the Greek has αὐτοῖς, “for them.”], so that they may not sin against the Lord and wrath may not come upon you and your brethren. Do this, and you shall not sin. Behold, Amarias the chief priest is over you in every matter of the Lord; and Jabadias [Note: [Col. 0847D] Zabadias son of Ishmael. Latin, with the Greek.] son of Zmabel, who is chief over the house of Judah, in every matter of the king; and the scribes and Levites are before you. Be strong and act; and the Lord shall be with the good’” (II Chronicles XIX, 4).

Did he say to the priests of the Lord, to the princes of his kingdom, or to the other judges: “Condemn the righteous; persecute the innocent; condemn and kill all [Col. 0847B] who believe in God”? Did he say: “Love what God does not love; hate justice; love injustice,” as you say? Or can you deny that you said: “Condemn Athanasius, absent and unheard”? Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah dedicated to God, says that judgment must be rendered according to the Lord’s law; but you, a king turned to apostasy, say: “Condemn one unheard.”

Suppose, meanwhile, Constantius, that King Jehoshaphat were alive in the body today, and that you both spoke to us: he, indeed, saying these words: “See what you do; for you judge not for man but for the Lord, and he is with you in the judgment. And now let the fear of the Lord be upon you, that you may keep and do what is right. For with the Lord our God there is neither injustice nor respect of persons” (Ibid. 6); while you, on the contrary, say that an unheard man is to be condemned—and one whom you yourself know to be innocent. To whom could we bishops of God [Col. 0847C] give obedience? We whom he had formerly promised to his people through Jeremiah’s mouth, saying: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed you, feeding you with discipline” (Jer. III, 15). To whom, I ask, should we have obeyed: you, or Jehoshaphat, the man dedicated to God, who compelled us to do what we remembered God had commanded to be done? If therefore you recognize that he fulfilled the Lord’s commands, while you have proved to be not only a destroyer of God’s commands but even an abandoner of God himself, it remains for you to see which of you was the man of God and which did the will of his mercy.

We read this written of him: “And the Lord was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the former ways of his father [Note: [Col. 0847D] “His father David.” Ibid., with the Vulgate.] and did not seek images, but the Lord God of his father; he walked in his commandments [Col. 0847D] and not according to [Note: [Col. 0847D] “As.” Ibid. and Til.] the works of Israel. The Lord established his kingdom, and all Judah gave gifts to Jehoshaphat; he had great riches and glory. His heart was exalted in the ways of the Lord, and he further removed the high places and [Note: [Col. 0847D] The particle “and” is absent in Sabatier, who reads “also from Judah” instead of “and the groves from Judah.”] groves from Judah. In the third year of his reign he sent his leaders and the sons of the mighty” (II Chronicles XVII, 3). And below: “With them were Elimasat and Joram, priests, and they taught Judah,”
and with them [Col. 0848A] the book [Note: [Col. 0847D] It was the book of the Law, according to Sabatier.] of the Law of the Lord; and they went through the cities of Judah and taught the people. And the fear of the Lord came upon the kingdoms of the land and upon those around Judah, and they did not make war upon Jehoshaphat; and foreigners brought [Note: [Col. 0847D] Thus the Greek: Ἀπὸ τῶν ἀλλοφύλων ἔφερον, “They brought from among the foreigners.”] gifts to Jehoshaphat, silver, and presents; and the Arabs brought him seven thousand seven hundred rams of sheep; and Jehoshaphat went on, becoming ever more great (ibid., 8).

What comparable thing do you do? You have, of course, sent throughout your whole realm instructions that we should all spurn God’s commandments and accept your decree, which attempts to assail the Lord’s commandment. Jehoshaphat sent the leading men of his kingdom, sent his counsellors, sent Levites and priests of the Lord, beseeching that all in his realm should be worshippers of the Lord, that all with one accord should offer themselves to God alone as servants; [Col. 0848B] he also sent the book of the sacred Law handed down through glorious Moses, so that they might do nothing other than what God had commanded to be done [Note: [Col. 0848D] Tilletius reads *facerent* (“might do”) in his customary manner.].

You, however, are found not only to have assailed the Law of the Lord, which commands that the innocent and the just are not to be killed, but also to have abandoned God himself; for you do not hold the apostolic faith, but Arius’s faithlessness. He turned a people wandering among idols back to God; you have attempted to make a people consecrated to God apostate—what you yourself are, that is, sacrilegious. You have persecuted and still persecute Athanasius, thirsting for his blood.

But see what the Holy Spirit says in the ninth psalm, in which you seem to me to be portrayed especially:

> He has said in his heart: “I shall not be moved from age to age, without evil.” His mouth is full of cursing, [Col. 0848C] bitterness, and deceit; beneath his tongue are toil and sorrow. He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, that he may kill the innocent. His eyes watch the poor man. He lies in wait in hiding, like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor, to seize the poor until he draws him into his net. In his snare he has humbled him; he has bent down, and he shall fall while he rules over the poor. He has said in his heart: “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, that he may never see” (Ps. IX, 6, after 21).

[Note: [Col. 0848D] Old Latin version: “From generation to generation … in secret … in secret as a lion in his lair … when he drags away the poor man. In the snare he will afflict him … while he rules,” etc.]

And if you persevere in this wickedness, will it not rightly be said of you: “He has turned away his face, that he may never see” (ibid.)? Your slaughter is so great, Constantius, that when the tenth psalm speaks in the person of our people:

> In the Lord I trust; how do you say [Note: [Col. 0848D] Old Latin: “You will say.”] to my soul, “Flee to the mountain like a sparrow”? For behold, sinners [Col. 0848D] have bent [Note: [Col. 0848D] Old Latin: “They have stretched … their arrows in the quiver.”] their bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at those upright in heart (Ps. X, 2),

you appear to me to be described, together with your accomplices in crime. For we recognize you Arians as the antichrists of our time; or, if you are not one worthy to be counted among antichrists, consider yourself a denier of the only Son of God. [Note: [Col. 0848D] The Latin reads, and rightly, “yet you are”; but Tilletius says the phrase is rough, as though it meant: “You appear to me to be that one of whom the Psalmist speaks concerning antichrists”; or: “Consider whether you are one worthy to be numbered among antichrists—you who are found to deny the only Son of God.”]

The Holy Spirit says through [Col. 0849A] the prophet:

> The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord—his throne is in heaven. His eyes look upon the poor, and [Note: [Col. 0849C] “The Lord” is omitted in the Old Latin, but is read in the Greek and Vulgate.] his eyelids examine the children of men. The Lord examines the righteous and the wicked; but he who loves iniquity hates his own soul (Ps. X, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0849D] “And” is absent from the Old Latin and Vulgate.]

And you have decreed punishment for one whom you yourself had not found guilty, except only because, in resisting your blasphemy, he had thereby become guilty of death in your eyes. Hear the Spirit of God say: “But he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (ibid., 6); and yet you compel men to love iniquity more than justice. If it is not unjust to condemn a man unheard, then, with you heretics as accusers, convict the Catholic. For when I still find it written:

> He will rain snares upon sinners: fire and sulphur and a stormy wind are the portion of their cup; [Col. 0849B] for the Lord is righteous and loves righteousness; his face beholds equity (ibid., 7),

[Note: [Col. 0849D] “And” is omitted in the Old Latin and Vulgate, where *justitias* (“righteous deeds”) is read instead of *justitiam* (“righteousness”).]

I know that you and all who act with you belong to that portion. Fire and sulphur and a stormy wind shall surely come upon you unless you turn back to God; for this is the portion of your cup—you deniers of the only Son of God, persecutors devoted to the divine majesty of that Son. Though you know that God is righteous, loves righteousness, and loves equity, you have judged it right to condemn an innocent man and persecute the Lord’s most faithful priest.

“Love the Lord,” says the Holy Spirit in the thirtieth psalm, “all you his saints; for the Lord seeks truth and will repay those who act [Note: [Col. 0849D] Old Latin: “those who commit arrogance abundantly.”] with abundant pride” (Ps. XXX, 24). Yet you urged us to kill an innocent man, in order to secure your own pride. For you cannot deny that [Col. 0849C] you are proud, since you have laid murderous hands upon God’s worshippers, attempted to destroy the Gospel faith, and sought to establish heretical faith.

Had you not read in the thirty-second psalm:

> The Lord loves [Note: [Col. 0849D] “The Lord” is omitted by the Old Latin and Vulgate, where only “mercy” is read in place of “judgment and mercy.”] mercy and judgment, and the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy (Ps. XXXII, 5),

that you should command an absent man to be condemned? Learn from these deeds of yours how thoughtless you are, and how hostile to your own salvation: though you remember it written,

> Who is the man who desires life and loves [Note: [Col. 0849D] Old Latin: “desires … restrain … deceit. Turn away.”] to see good days? Restrain your tongue from [Col. 0850A] evil, and your lips from speaking deceit; turn away from evil and do good (Ps. XXXIII, 13),

you nevertheless find no rest while doing what God has forbidden you to do. This is to refuse to see good days; this is to refuse life; this is to seek for oneself the grant of death.

Since, therefore, you are such a man as runs to gain eternal death, you seem to me also to have been foreshown in the thirty-fifth psalm:

> The unjust man has spoken, that he may sin within himself [Note: [Col. 0849D] Old Latin: “to himself … that his iniquity might be found … he hated.”]: there is no fear of God before his eyes. For he dealt deceitfully in his sight, so that his iniquity and hatred might be found. The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he refused to understand in order to do good. He devised iniquity upon his bed; he stands in every way that is not good, and he did not hate malice (Ps. XXXV, 2).

Observe what sort of man you are, most just [Note: [Col. 0849D] This is said ironically, since he judges him utterly unjust and impious because he wished Athanasius, absent and—what is worse—innocent, to be condemned. Tilletius.] emperor, on whose account even those things [Col. 0850B] spoken concerning Judas Scariot [Note: [Col. 0849D] He says “Scariot,” with the *iota* removed; and he very often similarly corrupts proper names, as the populace then spoke. Tilletius. He halves *Ischarioten* with pleasure. Hence Arnobius has *striculus* for *histriculus*, *trionem* for [Col. 0850C] *histrionem*. Ancient glosses in Isidore: “*Strio*: a mime, almost a stage-performer.” St Odo, abbot of Cluny, also said “Scarioth,” in his sermon on Magdalene: “What Judas Scarioth indignantly said against this most holy woman.” Hence also *Spaniscus* for *Hispaniscus* or *Hispanicus*, as Anastasius says in the Life of Benedict III, “Spanish [hangings] which hang over the altar”; likewise, “a garment decorated with Spanish [work],” that is, with Spanish cloth. For just as there were Tyrian and Alexandrian fabrics, so also Spanish ones. La Cerda.] and the Jewish people were said.

How could we, Constantius, condemn an innocent man at the prompting of your pride, when we knew David had written:

> Extend [Note: [Col. 0850D] Old Latin: “Stretch out your mercy.” Greek with Lucifer: παράτεινον τὸ ἔλεός σου, “Extend your mercy.”] your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart. Let not the foot of pride come against me, nor let the hand of the sinner [Note: [Col. 0850D] Old Latin: “of sinners … all who work.”] move me. There all who work iniquity have fallen; they have been driven out and shall not [Note: [Col. 0850D] Here, with the Old Latin, “shall not be able”; but a little below, “were not able,” with the Greek δύνωνται.] stand (ibid., 11).

What do you say? Is God’s mercy and righteousness such that absent and unheard persons are condemned—indeed, innocent persons whom it is unlawful to punish even when present? But why should it be surprising that you commanded these things to be done, you who do not know God? Why surprising that, ignorant of his mercy and righteousness, you ordered perverse, inequitable, unjust acts? Could the Psalmist’s word not turn you away from so great a crime:

> There all who work iniquity fell; they were driven out and could not stand (ibid., 13)?

Nor could that other passage in the thirty-sixth psalm:

> Cease from anger and abandon [Note: [Col. 0850D] Old Latin: “Abandon indignation; do not emulate [others] so as to do wickedly, for those who act unjustly,” etc. Lucifer is nearer the Greek *thymon*, θυμὸν, “wrath”; “that you may act wickedly,” ὥστε πονηρεύεσθαι; “those who act wickedly,” οἱ πονηρευόμενοι.] wrath; do not emulate, so as to act wickedly, for those who act wickedly shall be destroyed (Ps. XXXVI, 8).

Reading these things, yet judging the Lord’s ordinances to be of no account, I therefore judge you to be the one of whom it was said:

> The sinner watches the righteous and gnashes [Note: [Col. 0850D] Greek with Lucifer: Βρίξει, “will gnash.” Old Latin: “will rage.”] his teeth against him; but the Lord will deride [Note: [Col. 0850D] Old Latin: “will mock him, because he foresees that his day is coming.” Sabatier likewise reads “because he foresees.”] him, because he foresees [Col. 0851A] that his day is coming (Ps. XXXVI, 12).

We count you among those of whom I see it said:

> Sinners have drawn the sword and bent [Note: [Col. 0851D] Old Latin: “And they have stretched [it] … that they may slay the upright in heart. A sword … into the heart.”] their bow, to cast down the needy and poor and to slay the upright in heart. Let their sword enter into their own hearts, and let their bows be broken. Better [Note: [Col. 0851D] That is, it is preferable to be just while possessing modest goods than to be unjust and possess immense riches with sinners. Tilletius. But perhaps more aptly: “better is a little belonging to the righteous,” that is, honestly acquired. Old Latin and Sabatier: “a little for the righteous.”] is a little of the righteous man than the many riches of sinners, for the arms of sinners shall be broken (ibid., 14).

You have been made an enemy of the Lord among those whom the Spirit of God describes further on:

> The enemies of the Lord, as soon as [Note: [Col. 0851D] The Old Latin reads “immediately” in place of “as soon as.”] they are honoured and exalted, shall fail away; like smoke they shall fail away (ibid., 20).

Consider at last that you, with all your exaltation, unless you correct yourself, will perish like smoke, since you are God’s enemy. I see further written of you that, unless you repent and turn back, you will come to nothing:

> I saw the wicked greatly exalted and raised up above [Note: [Col. 0851D] Old Latin: “like.”] the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold he was not there; I sought him, and his place was not found (ibid., 35).

You are, I say, that man, Constantius, of whom I see these words also spoken:

> The sinner watches [Note: [Col. 0851D] Old Latin: “considers … and to destroy him; the Lord will not abandon.” Greek: θανατῶσαι, “to put to death,” like Lucifer’s *mortificare*.] the righteous and seeks to put him to death; but the Lord will not abandon him into his hands (ibid., 32).

The prophet, full of the Holy Spirit, says:

> Do not emulate evildoers, nor be jealous [Note: [Col. 0851D] In the Old Latin, *aemulatus fueris* (“you will emulate”) for *zelaveris* (“you will be jealous”), and *cito* (“quickly”) for *velociter* (“swiftly”).] of those who work iniquity; for they shall swiftly wither like hay, and quickly fall like the green herbs (ibid., 1).

And you, Constantius, destroyer of God’s religion, say: “Imitate me”? Who would imitate you except one who wishes to wither with you like green herbs? Who, except one who wishes to be blotted out by God’s indignation? If indeed Scripture rightly says:

> Speak righteousness, [Col. 0851C] judge justly [Note: [Col. 0851D] Old Latin: “just things.”] , O sons of men (Ps. LVII, 2),

yet you rise up to kill an innocent man. Therefore no one can doubt that you belong to those to whom the Holy Spirit says:

> Indeed, in your heart you work iniquities; on earth your hands devise injustice. Sinners are estranged [Note: [Col. 0851D] Old Latin: “alienated … of serpents, like deaf [Col. 0852D] and stopped-up asps.”] from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly and have spoken falsehood. Their rage is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp stopping its ears, which did not hear the voice of charmers, of the charmer [Note: [Col. 0852D] Old Latin: “and of the enchanter who is enchanted,” etc. The Greek has the singular number, as in Lucifer’s version.] charmed by a wise man. May God crush [Note: [Col. 0852D] Old Latin: “He will crush their teeth in their own mouth; the Lord has shattered the molars of lions … they shall melt away like running water; he bends [his bow] … they shall be removed; fire fell upon [them], and they did not,” etc.] their teeth in their mouths; the Lord shall break the molars of lions. Coming to nothing, they shall run away like water; he has bent his bow until they are weakened. Like melted wax, let them be taken away; fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun (ibid., 3).

You hear that you and yours will come to nothing, as those whose imitator you have chosen to be have already come to nothing. You see [Col. 0852A] that you, persecutors of God’s servants and deniers of God’s only Son, are compared to serpents and asps; yet do you not at last fear to pass over into God’s household? Do you not shape yourself—you who are shown to be one of those asps—so as to tread upon the devil’s head, that you may be made worthy to reign among those whose glory John recounts:

> He came into his own [Note: [Col. 0852D] Old Latin: “into his own [place] … gave to them … to those who.”], and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God—to those who believe in his name (John 1:11)?

Did you not remember what is written in the fifty-eighth psalm:

> God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations; do not have mercy on any who work iniquity (Ps. LVIII, 6),

that you should command sentence to be passed upon an absent man? Nor had you learned that the Holy Spirit alike warns and rebukes in the sixty-first psalm by these words:

> How long do you rush upon a man? [Col. 0852B] You kill [Note: [Col. 0852D] Old Latin: “and to kill.” Greek Φονεύετε, “you kill,” with Lucifer.] all together (Ps. LXI, 4).

“Fear of the Lord,” says Solomon, “is the beginning of understanding; but the ungodly despise wisdom and instruction” (Prov. I, 7). Hence you despise instruction and wisdom, because you are without fear of God. Hence you are described by sacred Scripture as ungodly—ungodly, certainly, because you have not only yourself abandoned God, but persecute so fiercely those who worship [Note: [Col. 0852D] Vatican manuscript: “and worshipping.”] him.

Woe to you, because you are found among those of whom I read in Proverbs:

> My son, let not ungodly men deceive you, nor consent if they ask you, saying: “Come, share blood with us; let us unjustly hide a righteous man in the earth; let us swallow [Note: [Col. 0852D] Old Latin: “Let us indeed swallow him up alive like hell.”] him alive like the grave” (ibid., 10).

What pleased you, Constantius, in the followers of the Arians who imitate the Jews, that, hearing these impious voices of theirs, you followed them in shedding [Col. 0852C] the blood of God’s servants? Why did you not heed Solomon’s counsels when he said to you:

> Do not go in the ways with them; do not turn your foot toward their paths. For nets are not spread unjustly for birds; but they who share in murder store up evils for themselves. These are the ways of all who accomplish wicked things: by their own impiety they take away their own soul (ibid., 15).

And again:

> As long as the innocent [Note: [Col. 0852D] Old Latin: “the simple obtain … but the foolish, while eager for insults, having become impious hated understanding, and became subject … to rebukes.”] retain righteousness, they shall not be ashamed; but fools, while eager for insults, become ungodly, hate understanding, and are made subject to reproaches (ibid., 22).

You have sought these reproaches for yourself, Constantius; you have condemned yourself. Despising God’s commandments, you have judged it right to adhere to the Arian disciples of the accursed Jews, with whom you now deservedly hear these words:

> Because I called and you did not obey, and I stretched out [Col. 0853A] my words and you paid no attention; but you made my counsels void and did not attend to my rebukes: therefore I too shall laugh at your destruction and rejoice over you when sudden turmoil comes upon you, and destruction like a storm; when ruin comes upon you. For when you call upon me, I shall not hear; the wicked shall seek me and shall not find me. For they hated wisdom and did not receive the word of the Lord; they were unwilling to heed my counsels and despised my rebukes. Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way and fill their souls with their own impiety. For because they deceived the little ones, they shall be killed (Prov. I, 24).

We should indeed have deserved to be killed with you—and that by God—had we persecuted God’s man with you. But how could we have done so, when we knew it was written:

> Do not devise evil against your friend, against one who dwells with and trusts you. Do not pursue enmity against a man without cause, lest he do you some harm (ibid. III, 29)?

Or would it not have been without cause if, as the mad fury of your fellow-heretics ordered through you, we had passed sentence of death upon an innocent man? Woe to you, because I see it said of you, our persecutor:

> A scornful eye, a wicked tongue, hands [Note: [Col. 0853D] *Sunt* (“are”) is deleted by Sabatier.] shedding the blood of the righteous, a heart devising evil thoughts, and feet swift to do evil (ibid. VI, 17).

You read: “My son, honour the Lord, and you will be strong; fear no other besides him” (ibid. VII, 1); yet you wished yourself to be feared and God to be despised. For how could we be found to fear God alone, if, yielding to your threats, we condemned one absent, [Col. 0853C] unheard, and—indeed—one whom we knew to be righteous?

Solomon says:

> A deceitful balance is an abomination before the Lord, but a just weight is acceptable to him (ibid. XI, 1).

You, on the contrary, do not hesitate to command: “Condemn a man by an unjust judgment,” considering right that which is perverse. Solomon speaks further of you and those like you:

> The ways of fools are right in their own eyes, but the wise man listens to counsel (ibid. XII, 15).

“Condemn Athanasius,” you say; and where you could not prevail by the ingenuity of your detestable cunning, you began to use the powers of your imperial office. Therefore accept what is written of you:

> An evil man acts evilly with scorn (ibid. XIII, 10);

and again, that you have now killed yourself by this snare, adhering to Arians as Judas Scariot adhered to the Jews:

> The law is a fountain of life to the wise man, but the fool shall die in a snare [Col. 0853D] (ibid., 14).

Further it is said of you:

> A bold king shall fall into evils (ibid., 17).

Certainly you have fallen into these evils, because you have left no wisdom in yourself: denying the only Son of God, you have turned your whole self over to folly; and this has made you slaughter those dear to God. It is written:

> The wise man, through fear, turns away from evil; but the fool mingles confidently with iniquity (ibid. XIV, 16).

Had you not read what is written:

> He who insults the poor man [Col. 0854A] provokes him who made him (ibid., 31),

that you draw us into killing an innocent man with you? For if God is angered at one who insults, how much more at one who kills his priest! Did you not still remember what is written:

> The beginning of a good way is to do righteous things; and these are more acceptable before the Lord than sacrificing victims (ibid. XVI, 5),

that you should compel us to do unjust things? And elsewhere:

> He who calls [Note: [Col. 0853D] Old Latin: “judges … and the wicked man righteous, [he is] abominable.”] the righteous unjust, and the unjust righteous, is abominable before God (ibid. XVII, 15).

We should undoubtedly have been abominable if we had pronounced you righteous and judged Athanasius, a man acceptable to God, unjust. “To show partiality to the wicked,” he says, “is not good, nor to turn aside the righteous in judgment” (ibid. XVIII, 5). You say the opposite, being described in the person of the wicked:

> [Col. 0854B] “Condemn the innocent; imitate my unjust person.”

And although you have compelled us to do things that could make God angry with us, we nevertheless urge you, the enemy of our salvation, to become godly from ungodly, healthy from sick, alive from dead, religious from sacrilegious. “How,” you ask, “can I attain this? By what means?” Cease to persecute God’s house; cease to proscribe, exile, and kill his servants. Confess that you are a Christian; abhor with us the Arian horde, acquired by the devil’s contrivance. Believe as we believe—we who are bishops in succession from the blessed Apostles. Confess the only Son of God, as they confessed him and as we confess him; and you shall obtain forgiveness for so great crimes.

For you have read in Solomon: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (ibid., 21), [Col. 0854C] and in blessed Paul: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” [Note: [Col. 0853D] Old Latin: “unto salvation.”] (Rom. X, 10). You remember what is written: “A false witness shall not go unpunished, and he who accuses unjustly shall not escape” (Prov. XIX, 5); yet you dared to accuse Athanasius falsely. [Note: [Col. 0853D] That is, to charge Athanasius with a false crime and wrong him. Tilletius.]

For we had no dispute with your fellow Arians, since God’s power had already long ago, together with Arius at Nicaea—when the faith was set forth not only against your blasphemy but against all heresies—removed them from before us. I say, we had no dispute with those pseudo-bishops, God’s enemies, your teachers, such that we should fight them again after God had once driven them from his people. Therefore our business is now with you, because you have made yourself the author of the charge that Athanasius [Col. 0854D] was guilty. [Note: [Col. 0853D] The Latin and Tilletius formerly read *meus* (“my”).] Because we would not punish him unheard, you—who knew yourself to be a false witness—began, like a savage wild beast, to wish to punish us along with Athanasius, as though by your snarling [Note: [Col. 0854D] That is, rabid cries. A barbarous word from the Latin verb *frendo*: one is called *frendens* because in threatening he breaks his teeth; so Isidore, *Etymologies*.] you could overcome the steadfastness of God’s servants.

Although Solomon says:

> The threats of a king [Note: [Col. 0854D] Old Latin: “The threat of an unjust king is like a lion’s roar.” Another Greek translator in the Hexapla has βρυγμῷ, “gnashing,” in place of “roar,” and στεναγμῷ, “groaning,” closer to Lucifer’s version; a little below the Greek is ἀπειλὴ, “threat,” where the Old Latin has *ira*, “anger.”] are like the groanings of a lion (ibid., 12),

yet your leonine groanings can have no power against us. Why? Because you are the forerunner of antichrist, and we are Christ’s soldiers. Why? Because you, persecutor of his religion, cannot conquer God’s people. Likewise elsewhere he says: “There is no difference between the threats of a king and the anger of a lion” [Note: [Col. 0855D] Old Latin: “The anger of a king does not differ from the anger of a lion.”] (Prov. XX, 2). What is this to God’s servants, who have resolved that no one but God is to be feared, who remember that our souls are placed in God’s hand? Your fellow Arians may fear your roars, because they lack knowledge of God and are not clothed in the armour of God. [Note: [Col. 0855D] For “clothed in the armour of God,” he uses the accusative in Greek fashion. Tilletius. It is poetic. Again he says *coopertus judicium* for *judicio* (“covered with judgment” for “with a judgment”). La Cerda.]

But we, God’s household, laugh at your lion-like roaring. Why? Because, recognizing you as a beast whose roar is so described, we must laugh rather than fear when we see a rabid beast under a human form. But if you are not a beast hidden beneath the likeness of a man, say so. You read in Solomon:

> Mercy [Col. 0855B] and truth are a king’s protection, and the righteous surround his throne (ibid., 28).

Since, on the contrary, you are surrounded by the troop of malicious Arians, and we see you to be a punisher of mercy and an abominator of truth, what else shall we judge you to be but a beast and a wild creature? You rise against us like a roaring lion because we love mercy and truth, because we did not punish the innocent and righteous; and do you think yourself not to be a monstrous beast and most savage wild creature?

Yet I am utterly unable to see what will led you to perpetrate these things: to persecute with such ruin the Catholic bishop of all righteousness, the priest of the Lord. Did you not remember what is written:

> To do righteousness and be truthful pleases God more than the blood of sacrifices (ibid. XXI, 3)?

Athanasius displeases you because he keeps the tradition of the blessed Apostles, confesses himself a Christian, and does not wish to be your fellow apostate. It is not surprising, since we have Scripture: “But the holy man is unclean in the sight of the wicked” (ibid., 15). He who pleases God displeases you wicked men—especially you, rash and proud man. You are understood to be rash and proud because you stretched out your hand against God’s ordinance, judged apostolic tradition fit to be destroyed, and thought that bishops—under whose pastoral care you ought to have lived—were to be reduced under your dominion.

Understand, then, what you are, hearing through Solomon the name assigned to you as proud:

> The rash and proud man shall be called pestilence (ibid., 24).

Though you are a pestilent man, you cannot afflict us with your sickness, [Col. 0855D] because divine mercy provides us protection. You did indeed try, pestilent man, to make us fellow-pestilences with you; but he to whom we live consecrated did not allow [Note: [Col. 0855D] That is, God, to whom we live consecrated, did not permit your pestilential attempts to enter our upright hearts; he delivered us from your empty attempts. Here he uses *tentamenta* for “attempts.” Tilletius.] your attempts to enter upright hearts. For Scripture urges:

> Deliver those who are led to death, and ransom those who are being killed; do not spare [Note: [Col. 0855D] Sabatier reads “do not cease.”]. But if you say, “I do not know this man,” know that the Lord knows the hearts of all; and he who formed the spirit in all of them knows all things, and renders to each according to his deeds (ibid. XXIV, 11).

When you say, “Condemn God’s worshipper; abandon the apostolic faith; accept my faithlessness,” you plainly reveal yourself to be a pestilent man. God wishes to help us [Note: [Col. 0855D] *Subveniri* (“to be helped”). Latin manuscript.] when we are in distress and straits; yet you urge those whom it is fitting to benefit to do evil, indeed bringing forward things which you think can inspire fear. [Note: [Col. 0855D] *Timeri* (“to be feared”). Latin manuscript.] Consider now whether that sickness called pestilence is not in you—a sickness strong enough to make not only bodies but also souls diseased: namely, the souls of those willing to hear you [Col. 0856B] say, “Condemn the Lord’s bishop; reject the faith which the Church has always held; accept mine, which Arius handed down.”

Holy Scripture says:

> To show partiality in judgment is not good; and he who says that the wicked man is righteous shall be cursed among peoples and hated among nations.
