But those who rebuke shall hope for better things [Note: [Col. 0855D] “They shall appear better.” Latin manuscript, with the Greek Βελτίους [Col. 0856D] φανοῦνται.] , and upon them shall come the best blessing (ibid., 23).

And you thought that we could show partiality toward your person and condemn one whom even you knew to be innocent, whom you maintained guilty only because he had refused to deny that he was a Christian. Meanwhile, because we rebuke you as one following the path of death, because we correct you, see what reward is promised us:

> Open, says the Prophet, your mouth with the word of God, and judge all things with integrity; open your mouth and judge justly (ibid. [Col. 0856C] XXXI, 8).

And you say, “Condemn the innocent”? I indeed hold fast to [Note: [Col. 0856D] He uses *continens* for “being content” or “being held fast.” Tilletius and the Latin manuscript.] the sacred Scriptures: “Do not behave proudly before the king” (ibid. XXV, 6). But if you had wished to remain within the bounds of your authority, and I had acted proudly [Note: [Col. 0856D] It would have been clearer had he said, “and had I acted proudly against you”; yet he frequently transposes words and entangles expressions in this way. Tilletius.] against you, I myself would indeed condemn myself as a transgressor of the Law. But since we speak truth to you, a murderer and sacrilegious man, we shall certainly not deserve punishment as proud men; rather, we shall receive heavenly rewards because we did not spare you in your error.

It is written:

> A whip for a horse, a goad [Note: [Col. 0856D] “A goad and a rod.” Latin manuscript and Old Latin. The Old Latin governs “an ass.”] for an ass, but a rod for a foolish people [Note: [Col. 0856D] Old Latin: “an imprudent nation”; Theodotion has “foolish,” but joined to “body.”] (ibid. XXVI, 3).

We rightly call you, deniers of God’s only Son, foolish, seeing you engaged in such great sacrilege. For when I see it written that, “as a dog which returns to its vomit and becomes hateful, so a fool, returning in his wickedness to his sin” (ibid., 11), I judge this to have been said particularly of you. “Why?” you ask. Because in your letters [Note: [Col. 0856D] He alludes to letters written by Constantius to the Catholic people of Alexandria in 349, when Athanasius was restored to his church; in them he ordered all impious decrees against the most holy bishop to be revoked.] you swore to the Alexandrians that henceforth you would do Athanasius no harm, and now you seek to kill him.

[Col. 0857A] But you say: “My father [Note: [Col. 0857C] This occurred in 336, when Constantius the Great, deceived by the plots and frauds of the Eusebians, sent Athanasius—who had come to Constantinople to seek his aid—into exile in Gaul.] sent him into exile, and I was bound to obey my father’s decrees.” Suppose, as you wish, that Athanasius is a heretic. If he had rightly been sent into exile, why did you allow him, contrary to your father’s decrees, to recover the rank from which your father had thought he removed him?

“But,” you say, “it was done through the intervention of my brother Constans.” [Note: [Col. 0857D] Constans, Constantius’s brother, intervened for Athanasius’s return in 348; and because Constantius was hard pressed by the Persian war, he preferred to consent to this request lest Constans’s assistance be unavailable to him.] Yet you could have opposed Constans, saying: “Our father, who judged him a heretic, unless he correct himself, I cannot receive into the parts of my realm.” “But,” you say, “I feared [Note: [Col. 0857D] Constantius also feared that Constans, the Catholic emperor, might turn his arms against him.] that war would arise between us.” Therefore, since Sapor, [Note: [Col. 0857D] The Persian war was still active when Lucifer wrote this: with great preparations Constantius was equipping military forces against Sapor, king of the Persians, late in the year 360.] king of the Persians, is now waging war against you, if he should say to you, “Adopt my religions and I shall be at peace with you,” ought you, together with all who live in your empire, to pass over to the religions of demons? For Sapor sacrifices [Col. 0857B] to demons.

You see, then, that you did not act as God’s servant when you received and restored to his place one whom you remembered had been exiled on a matter of faith. First, because you judged God powerless, as though he could not protect you while you defended the truth and resisted heretics; secondly, because you wished Constans to be more favourable to you than God. If you remembered that Constans the king had become a heretic by supporting Athanasius, whom you had already judged sacrilegious, you ought to have set neither your kingdom nor even your own soul before God.

For you yourself are witness to your own conscience that he was sent into exile because of the faith which the Church has always held and still holds—because he would not condemn it, because, that is, he would not become an Arian. [Col. 0857C] For it did not escape you that your father held Athanasius in hatred [Note: [Col. 0857D] See what we have discussed more fully in the Preface on this matter.] on this account; since you too judge him worthy of persecution for the same cause for which your father persecuted him. Let him finally say that he is not a Christian; let him confess that he is an Arian, and he will be, in your eyes, most wise and great.

You have therefore rightly been compared to a dog returning to its vomit. For you were already thought a Christian and not an Arian, from the time when you restored Athanasius [Col. 0858A] with such letters, divinely entrusted to him. But now, since you have been proved an Arian and, desiring to find a place for your heresy, persecute a righteous man because he
Indeed, since he is striving with every effort to assail that same truth, you are rightly compared to a dog returning to its vomit. Likewise, even in that distinguished action of yours, you are rightly to be compared to a dog that returned to its vomit: for, having received the truth that Adoxius of Germanicia was not catholic—

> [Note: These events occurred in the year 358, when Eudoxius, having occupied the see of Antioch, adopted the new doctrine of Aetius. For this reason, having been accused before Constantius by the delegates of the council of Ancyra, he was removed from that see by the Emperor’s letters and decree. In 359, however, relying on the support of the Acacians, he returned to Constantius’s favour after the little council of Seleucia, convened in October of that year, when he had approached the Emperor at Constantinople and had deceitfully abjured Aetius’s teaching. In the following year, 360, he obtained the church of Constantinople. Lucifer was therefore writing these books about the beginning of 360. When he adds that Constantius approved Eudoxius’s heresy as though it were the catholic faith, understand the Arian heresy, in which the Eudoxians—so called from Eudoxius—were especially influential; nevertheless, Aetius’s doctrine differed from it. Or perhaps Lucifer held that the new blasphemies of Aetius, which Eudoxius defended until his death, had not been condemned by Constantius, since he knew well both that Eudoxius persisted in this view and that he still enjoyed Constantius’s favour. Constantius, however, never adhered to the Aetian error. Here Lucifer calls Eudoxius “of the Germanicians,” that is, their bishop, because, since he had violently seized the episcopate of Antioch contrary to the decrees of the canons and to the Emperor’s will, he had no right to be called by the title of that episcopate. Perhaps, when writing this, Lucifer had not yet heard that Eudoxius had been intruded into the see of Constantinople after Macedonius’s deposition, in January 360.]

—and had issued letters against that same man to the Antiochenes, you afterwards began to defend this same Adoxius as a teacher of truth, judging his very heresy to be the catholic faith. Why, Constantius, are you so fickle? Why, in the matter of faith, do you bend this way and that like a reed buffeted by winds? What wonder that you were so ready to summon all God’s priests to condemn Athanasius, when you do not hesitate, by your recklessness, to commit such acts even against the established order of religion?

You have boiled over, most pious king, to shed an innocent man’s blood, as though you did not remember what is written: “The throne of a king judging the poor in truth shall rise up as a testimony” (Prov. 29:14). Yet you thought yourself greatest precisely if you went against the divine Scriptures, if you did everything they forbid. You hate Athanasius because he is a Christian; because he refused to become, as you say, a disciple of Arius, you persecute him with the utmost hatred. Yet the Holy Spirit had long ago shown, through Solomon’s mouth, that you would behave thus toward him, saying: “A righteous man is an abomination to an unrighteous man” (Prov. 29:27).

Constantius, do not linger any longer in these evils; do not abuse God’s patience. Keep in mind what is written in the seventy-seventh Psalm: “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome with wine; and he struck all his enemies upon the back parts; he gave them everlasting reproach” (Ps. 77:65).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “My enemies backward.” Lucifer follows the Greek, αὐτοῦ εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω, “his [enemies] backward.”]

In the eighty-first Psalm the Holy Spirit says: “How long have you judged iniquity and accepted the persons of sinners? Judge the orphan and the needy; vindicate the humble and poor. Rescue the poor and needy; deliver them from the hand of the sinner” (Ps. 81:2).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “You judge … judge the orphan and needy.”]

But you say, “Kill with me the man dedicated to God,” desiring that we should be counted with you among those of whom it is said: “They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness” (Ps. 81:5).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “What they understood.” The Greek, with Lucifer, has οὐδὲ συνῆκαν, “nor did they understand.”]

God commands that we should not pronounce an unjust judgment; that, out of reverence for your person as a sinner, we should not allow you to punish the man whom you persecute unjustly. God commanded us to vindicate the humble, to rescue the poor, and to deliver the needy from your hand—the hand of an executioner. Yet you say, “Condemn him whom God has willed to be rescued from my sinful hand.” No wonder: you could not act contrary to your accursed designs.

The Holy Spirit says in the ninety-sixth Psalm: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. 96:10).

> [Note: The ancient version has “wickedness.” The Greek has πονηρόν, “evil,” as does Lucifer.]

Yet your commands show that you say, “Love what is evil.” For if it is evil in God’s sight to condemn an innocent man, to pass sentence against an absent man—and indeed a righteous man—what else do you compel us to do except what God hates? If, therefore, we did what God hates, we certainly would not be among those to whom it is said: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.” You do not hate evil precisely because you do not love the Lord; but we refuse to do what God hates precisely because we love him. You do these things because you are not the servant of him whose fear and love compel us to hate evil.

Nor are you found in the Lord’s Church—you, its persecutor—so that you might suppose the Prophet spoke to you in the Psalm: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.” For in the hundredth Psalm he also says: “He who acts proudly does not dwell in the midst of my house; he who speaks unjust things has not been set straight before my eyes” (Ps. 100:7).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “He did not dwell … he who spoke.”]

Therefore it is not said to you, who stand outside, but to us: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. 96:10). Indeed, we hate the evil which you love precisely because you are not in God’s Church. For how can you establish that you are in God’s Church, you who not only persecute the Church but deny him who founded it? Are you not proud? Can you dwell in the Lord’s house so long as you remain in this arrogance? Who could rightly be called proud if you could be judged humble—you who say, “Condemn an innocent man contrary to the divine commands; trample God’s precepts; keep mine”?

But perhaps you do not speak injustice, and can be found among Christians: you who deny the Father, deny his only Son, deny the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, found the Arian heresy, and destroy the apostolic faith; you speak no injustice with your venomous lips, and utter nothing unjust from that sacrilegious mouth! Did you not know that in the hundred and second Psalm the Holy Spirit said concerning the Lord: “The Lord performs mercy and judgment for all who suffer wrong” (Ps. 102:6)?

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “You perform the Lord’s mercies.” The Greek, with Lucifer’s translation, reads ποιῶν ἐλεημοσύνας ὁ Κύριος, “the Lord performing acts of mercy.”]

Did you not know this, when you commanded that judgment be rendered unjustly?

> [Note: “To judge,” in the Latin.]

Whose commands ought us priests of the Lord to obey: yours, you who have not yet been delivered from unclean spirits, or the Prophet’s, through whom the Holy Spirit warns that every share in injustice must be avoided by us worshippers of the true divinity?

> [Note: “You who have not yet been delivered”; a form of expression customary with Lucifer.]

Had you not read, Constantius, what God said to you kings: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not deal maliciously with my prophets” (Ps. 104:15), that you should dare stretch out your hands against God’s house? David, full of the Holy Spirit, says in the hundred and fifth Psalm: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at every time” (Ps. 105:3). Yet you say: “Commit injustice with me.” You persecute Athanasius—an impious man persecuting a pious one, a heretic persecuting a Christian. But pray tell, which of you can be acceptable to God: you, denier of the eternal majesty of God’s only Son, builder and founder of a false religion; or Athanasius?

You have read in Psalm 118: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him” (Ps. 118:1).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “They search and seek.”]

And say which of you seeks God, which faithfully renders service to his majesty: you, who persecute Athanasius because he confesses himself a Christian; or he, who wishes that you, his persecutor, may be rescued from the devil’s snares? You, destroyer of the catholic faith; or he, preacher of the apostolic faith? If you serve God, how does the Holy Spirit say below: “For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways” (Ps. 118:3)? You heretics, therefore, workers of iniquity, since you are not found in the Lord’s ways, plainly show by your works that you are in the devil’s way.

You have read: “Do not zealously seek death through the error of your life, nor acquire destruction by the works of your hands; for God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living” (Wis. 1:12). Or do you remember having read it? Why did you command that we should seek death for ourselves? If you have not read it, learn what you urged us to do—you who chose to be among those whose crimes the Holy Spirit describes through Solomon’s mouth, saying: “They did not hope for the reward of righteousness, nor judge there to be honour for holy souls; for God created man incorruptible, and made him according to the image of his own likeness; but through the devil’s envy death entered into the world. Therefore those who belong to his portion imitate him” (Wis. 2:22).

You see that you are an imitator of the devil and established in his portion. You recognize that you are procuring death for yourself—you who refused to remain in God’s image, as you were made by God, but have transferred yourself to him through whose envy death entered the world.

On the other hand, learn what great blessedness Athanasius desires to attain; this is why he refuses to become what you are, an apostate Arian. Learn also what blessedness those have attained whom you have already thought worthy of death because they called themselves Christians: “The souls of the righteous are in God’s hand, and no torment shall touch them.”

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “The torment of death”; “of death” is absent from the Greek, as it is from Lucifer. Sabatier reads “the torment of evil.”]

“They seemed, in the eyes of fools, to die, and their departure from the righteous way was reckoned an affliction. They went away into destruction, but they are in peace. For even if they suffered torments before men, their hope is full of immortality; and, having been chastised in a few things, they shall be abundantly rewarded, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself. Like gold in a furnace he tested them; like a sacrificial offering of whole burnt-offering he received them; and at the time of their visitation they shall shine forth like sparks and run through a bed of reeds; they shall judge nations and rule peoples, and their Lord shall reign for ever” (Wis. 3:1).

> [Note: The Greek has κάκωσις, “affliction.” The ancient version reads: “And the way which is from us, destruction; but they …” Yet the punctuation seems better as follows: “They departed from the righteous way; they went into destruction, but they are in peace.”]
>
> [Note: Greek: Καὶ γάρ, “for indeed.” The ancient version reads “if.”]
>
> [Note: “And” is absent from the ancient version. The Greek has καὶ ὀλίγα, “and in a few things.”]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads: “And as a whole burnt offering.” “A sacrificial offering of whole burnt offering” is also found in Lucifer, *On Not Being of One Substance with God’s Son*. Sabatier reads “a whole burnt offering.”]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads: “The righteous shall shine, and as sparks in a reed-bed.” This is also added by Latinius and in the Greek.]

You desire to kill Athanasius, thinking that if you slaughter him you can give him eternal evil, unaware of what is written: “A righteous man who has died condemns living ungodly men, and youth quickly completed condemns the long life of the unjust. For they shall see the end of the wise man and shall not understand what God has known concerning him, or why the Lord has protected him. They shall see and despise him, but the Lord shall mock them. After this they shall fall dishonoured and be in the reproach of death for ever, because he shall burst them, puffed up, without a sound; he shall shake them from their foundations, and they shall be deserted even to the uttermost; they shall be in pain, and their memory shall perish. They shall come trembling to awareness of their sins, and their iniquities shall confront and accuse them” (Wis. 4:16).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “He shall have thought … concerning him God … protected him … they shall despise him … reproach among the dead for ever … they shall be desolate and groaning.”]
>
> [Note: “Shall perish,” rather than “perishes,” just as earlier “shall go out” occurs for “goes out.” Til. The ancient version also reads “shall perish.”]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads: “In their own thought.”]

You see among whom your portion has been established; you see with what persons you have made yourself stand against God’s house. But you shall see Athanasius among those of whom, further on, it is written: “Then the righteous shall stand in great steadfastness against those who afflicted them and took away their labours. Seeing them, they shall be troubled with dreadful fear and shall be amazed at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation. They shall say among themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit: ‘These are they whom we once held in derision and made a likeness of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honour. How have they been counted among God’s children, and how is their portion among the saints!’” (Wis. 5:1).

> [Note: The ancient version and Sabatier read “afflicted them, and those who.”]
>
> [Note: The Greek has ἐροῦσιν, “they shall say.” The ancient version: “saying among themselves.”]
>
> [Note: Sabatier reads “acting [in repentance]”; the ancient version reads “acting and because of anguish.”]
>
> [Note: With the Greek εἰς γέλωτα, “for laughter.” The ancient version has “in derision”; Latinus and Sabatier, “for laughter.”]
>
> [Note: “How” is the reading of Sabatier and the ancient version.]

Unless you take counsel for yourself, you will say these things when you see yourself plunged into Tartarus. You will then say what Holy Scripture says Christ’s soldiers’ persecutors will say: “Therefore we strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us. We were wearied in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we travelled difficult wildernesses, but we did not know the Lord’s way. What profit did pride bring us? Or what did wealth with boasting contribute to us? All those things passed like a shadow and like a messenger running by” (Wis. 5:6).

> [Note: “You,” in the Latin.]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads: “The sun of understanding.” “Of understanding” is absent from the Greek.]
>
> [Note: That is, desolate, steep, and difficult places. Again, as he very often does, Lucifer uses the Greek expression. Til. and La Cerda. Greek: ἐρήμους; the ancient version: “ways.”]
>
> [Note: From Greek, Πλοῦτος μετὰ ἀλαζονείας, “wealth with boasting.” The ancient version reads: “Or what did the boasting of riches contribute?”]

By contrast, you shall see Athanasius among those whose glory the Holy Spirit recounts, saying: “But the righteous shall live for ever; their reward is with the Lord, and their care is with the Most High. Therefore they shall receive a kingdom of splendour and a diadem from the Lord’s hand, for his right hand shall protect them and his arm defend them” (Wis. 5:16).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “A diadem of beauty; and he shall cover them with his holy arm.” The Greek omits “his holy.”]

But if you remain in this obstinacy of mind, if you decide to end this fragile life among the Arians, you shall be among those to whom the Holy Spirit again speaks through the Prophet’s mouth: “Hear therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who hold multitudes in your power and take pleasure in crowds of nations, for authority was given you by the Lord and power by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize the thoughts of your kingdom. Since, though you were his ministers, you did not judge rightly, nor keep the law, nor walk according to God’s will, he shall appear to you terribly and swiftly, for a most severe judgment shall be given against those in authority. Mercy is granted to the lowly, but the powerful shall suffer powerful torments. For the Lord shall not pass over anyone’s person nor reverence anyone’s greatness, because he himself made both small and great, and his care is equally for all; but a stronger torment presses upon the stronger. Therefore my words are addressed to you, evil tyrants, that you may learn wisdom and not fall away” (Wis. 6:2).

> [Note: The ancient version reads “multitudes.”]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads: “He shall scrutinize their thoughts,” omitting “of the kingdom.” “Of the kingdom” is also omitted by Latinus and Sabatier.]
>
> [Note: “Ministers of his kingdom,” in the ancient version and Sabatier.]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads “the law of righteousness”; “of righteousness” is absent from the Greek.]
>
> [Note: The ancient version omits “against.”]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads: “For God shall not withdraw from anyone … nor shall he fear.”]
>
> [Note: “Small,” in Vaticanus and the ancient version.]
>
> [Note: As in the Greek, τύραννοι, “tyrants.” The ancient version reads “kings”; these words are addressed to them.]

Then, Constantius, if you do not yet listen to us, you shall see what now you are entirely unable to see because of your unbelief. You shall see it then, when you have been placed among your fellow tyrants in those places of torments: not only that you loved unjust judgments, but also that you wished to destroy God’s house, that you proved a denier of God’s Son, and that by your continuing power you decreed that the faith be preached otherwise than the Prophets and Apostles preached it.

> [Note: “Mad” in the Latin.]

Nor will you be able to say, “I am not among those whom the Holy Spirit describes through Solomon,” when you hear him say: “Therefore, O evil tyrants, my words are addressed to you” (Wis. 6:10). Thus you will be unable to deny that you are the leader of all your fellow tyrants, if only you look closely at your deeds.

“The keeping of laws,” says the Prophet, “is the confirmation of incorruption; and incorruption will make you near to God” (Wis. 6:19).

> [Note: Greek βεβαίωσις, “confirmation”; the ancient version has “completion.” Shortly below, it reads “makes,” for “will make.”]

To this you say: “Corrupt God’s law, as you have corrupted yourselves, our persecutors.” Who is so senseless as to wish to be corrupted by you and perish eternally, rather than, by remaining in integrity, to become near to God? Why did you yourself do these things, or dare to compel us to do them?

Had you not read Solomon saying to God in the Book of Wisdom: “God of the ancestors, and Lord of mercies, who made all things by your word and established man by wisdom, that he might rule the creatures made by you, that he might order the world in righteousness and equity, and render judgment in uprightness of heart” (Wis. 9:1)?

> [Note: The ancient version reads “of my fathers”; “my” is absent also from the Greek.]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads: “By your wisdom … that he might rule … uprightness of heart,” etc.]

And again: “By such works you taught your people that one must be just and humane, and you made your children of good hope” (Wis. 12:19).

> [Note: “And humane,” in the Latin and ancient version. Yet I fear that an error has entered, since Lucifer shortly below says, “how shall we present ourselves as righteous and humane?” This suggests that he wrote “the righteous and humane man.”]

I say that, if you had found these things written, you would not dare provoke us to such inhumanity. But how shall we be children of good hope? How shall we present ourselves before God as righteous and humane servants of his, when transgressors of the law are called neither righteous nor children of God? Learn, then, from what good you wished to drag us to death—and indeed to eternal death. For everyone who ceases to be among those whom God has called to the adoption of sons loses life and possesses everlasting death.

Since you Arians are inhuman, impious, cruel, and murderers, how can you be called Christians? And since you deny Christ, the only Son of God, and confess that you have believed in Antichrist, how or by what means can you prove yourselves Christ’s servants, when by your own confession you show yourselves to be Antichrist’s slaves?

> [Note: “When you show,” in the Latin.]

For Antichrist, in whom Arius believed, truly “was when he was not”; whereas our Saviour, Lord and God, the only Son of God, is not, as you wish, Constantius, a creature, but the Lord of creation. He is eternal and beyond estimation, as is he whose Son he is. Indeed, in the last days he assumed perfect humanity from a virgin’s womb; but even after assuming humanity, he remains unchangeable, incorruptible, ineffable, and immutable, just as is he whose Son he is. The humanity he assumed could not change him into anything other than what he always was, since he is in the form of God his Father and is the Son equal to the Father, as the most blessed Apostle relates: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

> [Note: The ancient version reads “having been constituted,” for “was.”]

For when it says that God, the only Son of God, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” it does not mean that he could become anything other than what he is—incorruptible, ineffable, and unchangeable—since he always remains in that state of eternal greatness in which his Father also remains. But we certainly understand what “he emptied himself” means: although the Son is like and equal to the Father, he nonetheless willed, for our salvation, to become man.

> [Note: Vaticanus reads “what it means.”]
>
> [Note: Some Arians said that Jesus Christ was like, ὅμοιος, only to the Father, without any mention of substance or *ousia*. But the Semi-Arians and Homoeusians, under Eusebius of Caesarea as teacher, affirmed that the Son was like the Father in all respects, κατὰ πάντα ὅμοιος. Yet since perfect likeness differs in no way from equality and identity of nature, the proposition “the Son is like the Father” could be judged catholic or Arian according to the speaker’s intention. Several Semi-Arians, after explaining their meaning, were therefore admitted among Catholics, since they acknowledged that ὁμοιούσιον, “of like substance,” was altogether the same as ὁμοούσιον, “of one substance.” Lucifer, therefore, calls the Son like the Father according to a perfect likeness, by which he is consequently equal and of the same nature as the Father; hence he also calls him equal, intending by the term “equality” to indicate perfect likeness. Hilary of Arles, however, regarded both ὁμοῖος and ὁμοιούσιος as highly suspect. Therefore, in his apologetic replies concerning his books *On the Synods*, he wrote to Lucifer: “It could be sufficiently and absolutely known, lord brother Lucifer, that I was unwilling to make mention of *homoiousios*. But because you proclaimed the likeness of the Son to the Father, its exposition had to be set forth by me without fault; this he himself supplies in many passages.”]

Since you have accepted Antichrist in place of Christ, because he truly “was when he was not,” with what face do you still resist Christians—unless with that with which adulterous women confront chaste ones? You dared to attempt to rule God’s people, wishing to subject God’s Church, which fears only its divine majesty, to your futile imperial power. You did this because you did not know what is written concerning you tyrants: “For this reason undisciplined souls went astray. For when the ungodly were persuaded that they could rule a holy nation, bound with chains of darkness and fettered in a long night, shut beneath roofs, they became fugitives” (Wis. 17:1).

> [Note: The ancient version omits “themselves”; it subsequently reads: “bound with chains of darkness and fettered in a long night.”]

You now see that you are among those persecutors of God’s people of whom you read that “all were bound together by one chain of darkness” (Wis. 17:17).

> [Note: The ancient version reads “were.”]

And again: “They were indeed worthy to lack the light and suffer the prison of darkness, who kept your children confined, through whom the incorruptible light of the law of life was beginning to be given to all” (Wis. 18:4).

> [Note: The phrase uses an accusative in place of an ablative: “to lack light and suffer ….” Til. and Latinus. Some emend to *carere lumine*, “to lack light”; La Cerda rejects this in the present author.]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads “kept confined.”]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads “the same … to be given to the age,” omitting “of life.”]

Will you deny that you keep God’s bishops in confinement?

> [Note: Perhaps “us” should be added. Latinus.]

And when you prevent us from preaching truth to God’s people, why do you keep us in prison? Why send us into exile? Is it not because you fear that, as the sacred Scriptures reveal, we shall expose you as Arian wolves, ravenous mad dogs, and the Antichrists of our time? For the sacred Scriptures prove from your actions that you are not God’s servants but plainly the devil’s sons.

For if you are not one of those whom the sacred Scriptures proclaim will be such, why, when you find written in Psalm 131: “Arise, Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification; let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131:8), did you desire an absent man to be condemned by us? Certainly it was so that we might lose the righteousness with which the Lord had clothed us. For when he says, “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness,” and you pressed us to commit injustice, what would we have been, if we had done what your malevolence wished, except your accomplices in crime, sources of every iniquity—men who, casting off the office of righteousness, would take up injustice in order to please you?

You persecute God’s house, Constantius, not knowing that you persecute God himself in his house. For God’s house is the Church, in which the Lord dwells, as is written in the same Psalm: “The Lord chose Zion; he chose it beforehand for his dwelling: ‘This is my rest for age upon age; here I shall dwell, for I chose it beforehand’” (Ps. 131:13).

> [Note: The ancient version reads “his,” and also has *praelegit* for *praeelegit*, “chose beforehand.”]

Since these things are so, see that when you punish one of us, you punish yourself; that when you oppose God, you persecute salvation—not us, concerning whom you hear God say that he deigns to rest in us. Therefore, you who attempt to violate the Lord’s temples, unless you are converted, may you perish in the manner of those of whom David says in Psalm 135: “He struck Egypt with their firstborn, for his mercy endures for ever; and led Israel out from their midst, for his mercy endures for ever; with a strong hand and an uplifted arm, for his mercy endures for ever; he divided the Red Sea into divisions, for his mercy endures for ever; and led Israel through its midst, for his mercy endures for ever; and cast Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea” (Ps. 135:10).

> [Note: The ancient version reads “for the age.”]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads “in division.”]
>
> [Note: As in the Greek, εἰς θάλασσαν Ἐρυθράν, “into the Red Sea.” The ancient version reads “in the Red Sea.”]

Why do I find these things written, except that I might believe that, when you attempt to oppress me, my God can, if you do not turn back, destroy you as he destroyed Pharaoh, and can rescue me from your hands as he rescued them from Pharaoh’s power? For this reason he says after every mighty work, “for his mercy endures for ever”: so that he might make known to me that the Lord’s mercy remains with me always, because I serve him alone, and that it cannot be with you, since you are his enemy, as Pharaoh also was.

We refused to condemn an absent man; we refused, concerning one whom we know is innocent and whom we know to be a preacher of the catholic faith, to pronounce a sentence according to your desire. Why? Because we Christians have extended our hope to God, not to you and your perishable kingdom. We refused to seek our pleasure in the glory of your kingdom, because we are to attain glory, awaiting it from him in whom alone we must trust and hope. David teaches this when he says in Psalm 145: “Do not trust in princes, nor in sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit shall go forth and return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish. Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them; who keeps truth for ever and renders judgment for those who suffer wrong” (Ps. 145:2).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “Nor in … their spirit.”]
>
> [Note: “And return to his earth” is absent from the ancient version but occurs in the Greek.]
>
> [Note: Latinus thinks that the words “Blessed is he,” etc., should be removed; but this is contrary to Lucifer’s evident meaning.]
>
> [Note: Vaticanus corruptly reads “we are to attain.”]

We refused unjustly to persecute with you a man full of the fruits of righteousness, lest, when vengeance began to overtake you, it might overtake us as well. We did not do what you unjustly commanded us to perform, lest we should come with you to that place described in Ecclesiastes: “And God will seek out him who suffers persecution” (Eccl. 3:15); and again: “I saw beneath the sun the place of judgment: there was the ungodly; and the place of the righteous: there was the godly” (Eccl. 3:16).

> [Note: This is the book which the Septuagint and Vulgate call *Ecclesiastes*. The book called *Ecclesiasticus* is the one entitled Σοφία Σειράχ in the Septuagint, that is, “Wisdom of Sirach.” Unless the text in this passage of Lucifer is corrupt, he uses the title *Ecclesiastes* for this book, a title not indeed customary among the ancients.]
>
> [Note: Lucifer, with the Greek, has ἐκεῖ ὁ ἀσεβής, καὶ τόπον τοῦ δικαίου, ἐκεῖ ὁ εὐσεβής: “there the ungodly; and the place of the righteous, there the godly.” The ancient version reads: “There is ungodliness, and the place of righteousness, there is iniquity.”]

We refused to join ourselves to you heretics; we refused to join hands with you in assaulting God’s house; we refused to embrace idolatry with you to God’s dishonour; we refused to mingle with your sacrilege, lest we too should deserve to hear with you what the priests, people, and king of Israel—who had all abandoned God and given themselves to idolatry—hear through the mouth of the prophet Hosea: “Hear this, priests; attend, house of Israel; and look, house of the king: judgment is for you, because you have become a snare for a watch-post, and like nets spread for the hunter’s bird-trap” (Hos. 5:1).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “House of the king, receive with your ears; for judgment is for you … because you have become a snare for the watch-post, and like a net spread over Itabyrium.”]

You surely knew that it is written in the prophet Amos, when you laid down a rule—namely, the example of condemning an innocent man: “He makes judgment on high and has placed righteousness upon the earth” (Amos 5:7).

> [Note: With the Greek Septuagint: Ὁ ποιῶν εἰς ὕψος κρῖμα, καὶ δικαιοσύνην εἰς γῆν ἔθηκεν, “He makes judgment on high and has placed righteousness on earth.” The ancient version reads “He makes.”]

You violator of God’s righteousness, did you not know that the prophet Micah said concerning Judah and its rulers: “They did not lift up their hands to God, but coveted fields and plundered orphans; they seized a house by force and plundered a man and his house, a man and his inheritance. Therefore the Lord says: ‘Behold, I devise evils against this people, from which you shall not lift up your necks’” (Mic. 2:1).

> [Note: The ancient version reads “desired … orphans, oppressed houses and seized them … therefore these things.”]
>
> [Note: “I devise,” in the Latin, with the Greek, ancient version, and Vulgate. Moreover, the ancient version reads: “against this tribe evils from which you shall not remove your necks.”]

But when you think yourself worthy to proscribe, deport, imprison, torture, and finally kill God’s worshippers, will no evils be brought upon you? We refused to mingle in your wicked actions, lest, condemned with you to eternal punishment, we should hear the words God speaks in Micah: “Hear therefore these things, rulers of Jacob’s house and remnant of Israel’s house, who abominate judgment and pervert all that is straight; you who built Zion and Jerusalem in blood and iniquities. Her judges judged for gifts, her priests gave answers for payment, and her prophets divined for money; yet they rested upon the Lord, saying, ‘The Lord is among us, and evils shall not come upon us’” (Mic. 3:9).

> [Note: The ancient version reads: “Hear these things, leaders … and the rest.”]
>
> [Note: “You who built Zion in blood and Jerusalem in iniquities,” in the Latin, from the Greek, the ancient version, and Vulgate. The ancient version reads “in bloods”; the Vulgate, “in iniquity.” Sabatier reads *aedificatis* (“you build”) in Lucifer.]
>
> [Note: The ancient version reads: “Her leaders in … for payment … her prophets in … and upon the Lord … ‘Is not the Lord …? Evils shall not come upon us.’”]

Had you not yet read in this most holy prophet that you should command a man dedicated to God to be condemned? “With what shall I come before the Lord?”

How shall I receive my God most high? Shall I receive him with burnt offerings, or with yearling calves? Or will the Lord accept thousands of rams, or ten thousand fat goats? Or shall I give my firstborn for my impiety, the fruit of my womb for the sins of my soul? It has been declared to you, O man, what is good, or what else the Lord has required of you: that you do judgment and justice, love mercy, and be ready to walk with the Lord your God (Mic. 6:6).

[Note: “Or” is removed from the Latin; it is absent from the Greek and the Ancient Version. “Receive.” Ancient Version: “May he accept . . . among thousands . . . or among ten thousand goats . . . or shall I give,” etc. Sabatier reads: “Shall I receive the Lord?”]

[Note: Greek: εἰ προσδέξεται, “whether he will accept,” without “or.” Ancient Version: “May he accept . . . among thousands . . . or among ten thousand goats . . . or shall I give,” etc. Sabatier reads: “Shall I receive the Lord?”]

[Note: With Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book 3. Ancient Version: “For impiety . . . for sin.” Sabatier: “For my impiety.”]

[Note: “Has it been declared to you,” etc. Latin: “It has been announced to you, O man, what is good.” Ancient Version: “What has he [Col. 0868D] also required,” Sabatier likewise.]

[Note: Ancient Version: “What does he require of you, except that you do judgment, love . . . walk with your God?”]

Had you not found written also in Habakkuk: “The wicked has oppressed the righteous by force” (Hab. 1:4)? Thus you had undertaken a criminal act that could make you wicked before God. Again, had you not found stated below: “Why do you look upon the despisers? Will you be silent because the wicked devours the righteous?” (Hab. 1:13). And therefore, seeing that you, a wicked man, had attempted to devour the righteous man, we not only have not been silent concerning your evil conduct, but we shall not be silent.

[Note: Greek: καταδυναστεύει, “oppresses by force.” Ancient Version: “The wicked prevails against the righteous.”]

[Note: With the Greek in the Roman and Complutensian editions: ἵνα τί ἐπιβλέπεις, “why do you look upon?” Ancient Version: “Why do you not look,” etc.]

[Note: Almost exactly with the Greek in the same editions: ἐν τῷ καταπίνειν ἀσεβῆ τὸν δίκαιον, “when the wicked devours the righteous.” Ancient Version: “When the wicked devours one more righteous than himself,” omitting “because of this.”]

For you are no different from him of whom it is said: “The self-pleasing and contemptuous proud man shall accomplish nothing; he has enlarged his soul like Hades, and he himself is insatiable like death” (Hab. 2:5). It cannot be said that this does not apply to you, if you will deign to remember with me the crimes of your deeds and are not slow to recount your murders. For who else in our days can be found self-pleasing, contemptuous, proud, accomplishing nothing, enlarging his soul like Hades, and capable of being reckoned insatiable as death, except you?

[Note: Ancient Version: “The arrogant man . . . brings nothing to completion . . . like Hades . . . and this one, like death, is not filled.”]

But see that you can accomplish nothing: God says this to you. Although you are a despis­er of God’s commandments, although, desiring to persecute his religion, you have enlarged your soul so far as to slaughter God’s worshippers, so that throughout the whole empire you refuse to cease harassing the Lord’s flock, nevertheless all your hostility accomplishes nothing. For all whom you persecute are, and ever shall be, servants of God. But you, unless you provide for yourself, will perish eternally: self-pleasing, contemptuous, proud, enlarging your soul like Hades in order to devour and swallow us up together because we resist your wrongdoing; made insatiable like death, you are driven by furies to bring about our death.

You are so wicked, Constantius, that when I find the prophet saying, “Woe to him who lays an evil foundation for his house, that he may set his nest on high” (Hab. 2:9), you and the inheritance of Antichrist, whom you favor, come before my eyes, as I recognize those sacrilegious purposes of yours. For it cannot be doubted that you have attempted, and continue to attempt, to establish your heresy throughout your whole empire and to destroy the catholic faith.

[Note: Ancient Version: “Woe to him who multiplies evil greed . . . that he may place [his nest] on high,” etc.]

And when I hear the prophet consecrated to God say: “Woe to those who build a city with bloodshed and prepare a city with iniquities” (Hab. 2:12), you seem to me to be the one who builds a den of thieves by the shedding of blood, by the killing of God’s servants.

[Note: “Builds and prepares a city.” Ancient Version.]

Or will you deny that your malignant council of Arians is a den of thieves? If you are not thieves, how are you found killing men consecrated to God? Those who build cities in blood have woe. Most prudent Emperor, did you not see that woe could be yours because you thought your heresy had to be rebuilt by the shedding of the blood of God’s people?

The Holy Spirit says through the prophet Zephaniah: “Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth; perform judgment, seek justice, and answer, so that you may be covered in the day of the Lord’s wrath.” You say: “Condemn the innocent; be murderers and sacrilegious men with me” (Zeph. 2:3). Are these not the things you command us to do? You ordered that the Lord’s priest be condemned; you also ordered that Arian perfidy be maintained and the faith drawn up at Nicaea rejected. Since you cannot deny that you commanded these things to be carried out, see that you wished to make us both murderers and sacrilegious men.

[Note: “And” is removed from the Latin and is absent also from the Ancient Version.]

[Note: Ancient Version: “So that you may be protected.”]

God says: “And it shall be in that day: I shall search Jerusalem with a lamp; I shall avenge myself upon men who are despisers and do not keep the commandments” (Zeph. 1:12). Yet you say that your own commandments and those of your fellow-blasphemers ought rather to be kept. How could we unjustly condemn the Lord’s priest, who is full of the fruits of righteousness, when we see what a threat has arisen against the rulers of the Jews—or against all their accomplices known to have done the things you do?

[Note: “I shall search” is said in place of “I shall inquire”; hence *scrutiny* is used among the ancients for inquiry and catechesis. Tillemont and La Cerda. Ancient Version: “In that day I shall search.”]

[Note: “I shall avenge myself.” Latin, with the Ancient Version, adding “and.”]

[Note: Ancient Version: “Who despise their safeguards.”]

“O illustrious and redeemed city, dove: she did not heed the voice; she did not receive instruction; she does not trust in the Lord and has not approached her God. Her princes within her roar like lions; her judges are like wolves of Arabia, not leaving anything for the morning. Her prophets are spiritual men, contemptuous men; her priests defile themselves and act impiously. But the Lord is righteous in her midst and will not act unjustly” (Zeph. 3:1).

[Note: Ancient Version: “O illustrious . . . she heard . . . she received . . . she did not trust . . . she approached. Her princes within her are like roaring lions.”]

[Note: “They left.” Ancient Version: “And her prophets, carrying spirit.” Sabatier reads in Lucifer: “They did not leave behind.”]

[Note: “Holy things.” Latin from the Greek, with the Ancient Version, which reads: “They defile holy things and act impiously against the law. The Lord . . . will not do iniquity.”]

Since this is so, and since it is by no means lawful for us to render an unjust judgment, one thing remains: make yourself one of God’s servants and learn to render judgment; or, if you wish always to be among God’s adversaries, issue your unjust judgment alone. Stop forcing us to do what you see has been divinely forbidden.

Stop now accusing Athanasius or us of destroying God’s house, when you find in Zechariah yourself and your fellow-tyrants described as those who would be persecutors of God’s inheritance, whom he says have arrogated to themselves excessive authority. For, recounting your cruelty, the Lord says: “I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy, and with great wrath I am angry against the nations that set themselves over you; because I was angry only a little, but they have joined themselves to evil” (Zech. 1:14).

[Note: “Who are imposed over [you], because I indeed . . . only a little; but they have set themselves over [you] in evil.” Ancient Version.]

Do you dare, lover of darkness and execrator of light, to say: “Condemn the innocent,” when God deigns to command us through Zechariah: “Judge righteous judgment; show kindness and mercy, each one to his brother; do not wrong by force widow, orphan, proselyte, and poor; and let no one remember in his heart the malice of his brother” (Zech. 7:9).

[Note: Ancient Version: “And let each one show mercy and compassion [Col. 0870C].”]

[Note: “Proselyte” is omitted by the Ancient Version but is present in the Greek. Ancient Version: “And do not oppress orphan and poor; and do not remember in your hearts the malice of each one’s brother.”]

These are heavenly commands; by whose authority, then, did you say, “Tear your fellow-servant to pieces”? If you say that you issued this command under God’s commandments, you cannot prove it, since no command of God that the innocent should be condemned can be found in the sacred Scriptures. Since, therefore, you have done what God’s law forbids, it is clear that you issued this command by the will of him who is called God’s enemy. Thus you must be compared with those to whom it is said through the prophet: “They refused to observe; they gave their back to folly; they made their ears and heart unpersuadable, lest they obey; they made them heavy, lest they obey my law” (Zech. 7:11). And below: “They did not heed; if they cry out, I shall not hear them, says the Lord Almighty” (Zech. 7:13).

[Note: Ancient Version: “They refused to attend, gave a disdainful back, made their ears heavy so that they might not hear, and made their heart disobedient so that they might not hear my law.” Sabatier reads in Lucifer: “unpersuadable,” and “they made [them] heavy.”]

[Note: For “my law,” as above *to lack light* for *light*: that is, “that they might not obey my law.” Tillemont.]

“Rest, souls: these are the words that you shall do: speak truth, each one to his neighbor; judge peaceful and righteous judgment in your gates. Let none of you devise in your hearts the evil of his neighbor; do not love a false oath, for I hate all these things, says the Lord Almighty” (Zech. 8:15).

[Note: In place of “rest”: “rest yourselves,” “remain in peace.” Tillemont. “Trust. These are the words which you shall do.” Ancient Version, without “souls.”]

[Note: Ancient Version: “With his neighbor; truth and judgment . . . let him not devise his neighbor’s evil . . . and do not love a false oath, because,” etc.]

Why do you compel me to do the things which the Lord Almighty says he hates? But the Lord, instructing concerning fasting, says: “Love peace and truth” (Zech. 8:19). How could we be lovers of peace and truth if we punished as guilty an innocent man overwhelmed by false accusations through you and yours? Or what peace would there have been, when by doing these things we might even have been excluded from the Lord’s peace? For the peace of the Lord who says, “I leave my peace to you; I give you my peace” (John 14:27), would not have remained in us if we had unjustly taken it away from another. Who does not know that, when discipline withdraws, grace withdraws also?

God says in Malachi: “A son honors his father and a servant his own lord. And if I am father, where is my honor?” says the Lord Almighty (Mal. 1:6). What fear and honor, then, would we have rendered to God if we had done what you commanded to be done? For those commands of yours strive to take away fear and honor from God’s devoted mercy.

[Note: Ancient Version: “Glorifies.”]

[Note: “His own lord will fear.” Ancient Version. “Will fear” is absent from the Greek Vatican manuscript, as from Lucifer.]

[Note: Ancient Version: “Where is my glory? And if I am Lord, where is my fear? says,” etc.]

And below, specifically exposing your activity, he says: “You provoke God with your words, and you say: ‘In what have we provoked him?’ In saying: ‘Everyone who does evil is good before God, and he will bless them;’ and, ‘Where is the God of justice?’” (Mal. 2:17). The prophet says, “Where is the God of justice?” against those who say, “He who does evil is good before God, and he will bless them.” Yet you give orders for righteous blood to be shed, and still call yourself God’s servant, though you are the destroyer of his law.

[Note: Sabatier reads better: “You have provoked.” Ancient Version: “You have provoked the Lord with your words . . . In what matter have we provoked [him]? . . . You say . . . he is good in the sight of the Lord, and in such persons he is pleased.”]

Is it just or unjust to condemn an absent man—and an innocent one at that? If it is not just, why do you compel us to do the deed for which we deserve to be punished by God?

[Note: Latin: “why.” *Because* is used for *why*; he very often uses one for the other, and also for *when*, as will be noted when it occurs. Tillemont and Galandius.]

Tobit says: “All the days of your life, my son, keep God in your mind; do not will to sin or transgress his commandments. Do justice all the days of your life, and do not walk in the way of iniquity; for, if you act in truth, regard shall be had for your works and for all who do justice” (Tob. 4:6).

[Note: Ancient Version: “Go in the way . . . regard in [his] works,” etc.]

Tell me, Constantius: does one who kills innocent people do justice? Does one who sheds the blood of God’s servants? If he does not do justice but rather iniquity, it follows that you should see yourself as a lover of iniquity and a maker of every unjust work. For when the sacred law exhorts us to do justice at every time, and you force us to do injustice, what else should I consider you but both a lover and perpetrator of injustice?

“All the days of your life, my son, keep God in your mind” (ibid.), when you have abandoned him by cleaving to the Arians. For we do not abandon him, who hold the apostolic faith. How do you not transgress his commandments, when you kill servants dedicated to his name and majesty, compelling them to abandon him and become your fellow-serpents and fellow-apostates?

We suffer hatred from you because we tell you the truth, because we desire you to live with us eternally. But you love those who have gone over to you, those who, though at first opposed you, afterwards preferred to serve your wicked designs rather than obey God’s commandments. You rejoice that, by enticing them with your cunning, you have brought them to accept your heresy; that you have all of them subject to you—those whom you had long seen count you as nothing, whom you saw trample the authority of your empire for the sake of truth.

[Note: “Opposed.” Latin and Galandius.]

[Note: “Lead.” Latin.]

But we want you to know that this is not new, but has often been done by faithless and heedless persons, by those whom the prophet Malachi, foreknowing things to come, pointed out in these words: “You have weighed down your counsels against me, says the Lord Almighty; and you have said, ‘In what have we spoken ill of you?’ Because you have said: ‘Vain is everyone who serves God; and what more is there? That we have kept his commandments and walked as suppliants before the face of the Lord Almighty. And now we magnify strangers; all those who do wicked things are renewed; they have resisted God and have been saved’” (Mal. 3:13).

[Note: Ancient Version: “You have made your words heavy against me, says the Lord. And you said: ‘In what have we spoken against you?’ And you said: ‘Vain is he who . . . What more, because we have kept . . . his commandments, and because we have walked as suppliants before [his] face . . . And now we call strangers blessed; all who do iniquity are built up . . . and have been saved.’”]

[Note: Sabatier omits “God” here.]

“Those who fear God spoke these reproaches, each to his neighbor; and the Lord attended and heard, and wrote a book of remembrance before himself for those who fear the Lord and reverence his name. And they shall be mine, says the Lord Almighty, on the day which I make, as a possession; and I shall choose them as a man chooses his son who serves him well. And when you have turned, you shall see how great the difference is between the righteous and the unrighteous, between one who serves God and one who does not serve him. For behold, the day of the Lord comes, burning like an oven, and it shall burn them; all foreigners and all who do wicked deeds shall be as branches; and the day of the Lord which comes shall set them aflame, says the Lord Almighty, and no root or vine shall be left of them” (Mal. 4:1).

[Note: Greek: κατελάλησαν, “they spoke against/reviled.” Ancient Version: “They spoke . . . and he attended . . . and he heard . . . a book of remembrance before him for those who fear . . . and reverence his name.”]

[Note: Ancient Version: “They shall be mine . . . as a possession; . . . as . . . his son who serves him. And I shall turn, and you shall see what [the difference is] . . . between the unrighteous and . . . the one who does not serve him.”]

[Note: “Of the Lord” is absent after “day” in both occurrences in the Ancient Version; there it reads “stubble” for “branches,” “in them” for “of them,” as in the Greek, and “branch” for “vine,” with several other very slight variants.]

Hearing God say these things, because you deign still to remain in your evils, I suppose that you even rejoice in this: that with transgressors, with those who abandon God, you will receive these things from him. Woe to you, murderer and sacrilegious man! Unless you repent of your deeds, you shall be, as you now are, among those whom God rebukes through Isaiah, saying: “Woe, sinful nation, people full of offenses, evil seed, lawless children: you have abandoned the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel” (Isa. 1:4).

[Note: Ancient Version: “Sins . . . wicked . . . criminal; you have abandoned . . . and stirred him, the Holy One, to indignation,” etc.]

You will always be one of those who, because of the wickedness of their pursuits, are compared with the rulers of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah, when it is said: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; heed the law of God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:10).

[Note: “Law of God,” as in the Greek. Ancient Version: “Word of the Lord, people,” etc.]

Unless you correct yourself, you shall be with those of whom you have read: “If you multiply prayers, I shall not hear you, for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:15).

[Note: Ancient Version: “If you multiply prayer.”]

Woe to you, Constantius, who have incurred such offense against God that you could not see what you ought to have guarded against. For when, through Isaiah’s mouth, he says to those killers of holy prophets and of all the righteous: “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove the wickedness from your souls before my eyes; cease from your wickedness; learn to do good; seek judgment; rescue one suffering wrong; judge for the orphan and vindicate the widow” (Isa. 1:16), you, to the contrary, order God’s worshippers to be slaughtered, God himself to be abandoned, and idolatry to be accepted. This, indeed, was to hear God’s admonitions and to be corrected.

[Note: “Souls.” Latin and Galandius, as in the Greek and Ancient Version: “Wickedness from your souls before the sight of my eyes . . . seek . . . rescue . . . judge for the orphan,” etc.]

For what reason do you compel us to do this, except because you desire us to be consumed with you by the sword? “And if you are willing,” God says, “and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the earth. But if you are unwilling and do not hear me, the sword shall consume you; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isa. 1:19).

[Note: Several slight readings that do not alter the sense vary here in the Ancient Version.]

Whom shall we obey: God, who says this, or you, his enemy? God tells the Jews now to abandon their errors, cast their wickedness from their hearts, learn to do good, and judge righteous judgment. You say: “Condemn unjustly.” Why do you urge me to do this, except because you want to make me the kind of person such as those to whom God said: “But you,” says God, “why do you burn up my vineyard, and why is the plunder of the poor in your houses? Why do you wrong my people and put the faces of the poor to shame?” (Isa. 3:14).

[Note: Ancient Version: “Why do you burn up . . . and the plunder of the beggar . . .? Why do you harm my people . . . [and shame] the faces of the poor?”]

And you do these very things, you conduct all affairs in this manner—the deeds for which he is angry with those who do them—as though you knew that you could not please yourself unless you had also burned up the Lord’s vineyard, established the plunder of the poor within your house, and inflicted injuries in many ways upon God’s servants. Or will you attempt to say that you have done none of these things? Did you not burn up the Lord’s vineyard when you compelled it no longer to know the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, the God of apostles, prophets, and martyrs, but rather the idolatry devised through Arius and exalted through yourself?

Is this not the plunder of the poor—the Christian servants of God—in your house, concerning whom you read: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3)? You know that you have proscribed those who resisted your sacrilege. Would you dare say: “I have not done, nor do I do, wrong to God’s people”? And who has ever done as great wrong as you, who do not cease either from inflicting every kind of torture or from imposing punishments in diverse ways?

[Note: For “do not cease to inflict,” where he has used the gerund for the infinitive. Tillemont. The passage does not appear mutilated, as Latinius judges, nor to us, nor to Galandius.]

We refused to punish an innocent man as guilty, lest that sentence, still prophesied through Isaiah’s mouth, should strike us also: “Woe to those who write wickedness; for they write wickedness while perverting the judgment of the poor and taking away the judgment of the needy of my people, so that the widow may be their prey and the orphan their plunder. And what will they do on the day of visitation? For tribulation shall come upon you from afar; and to whom will you flee?” (Isa. 10:1).

[Note: Latin: “on the day,” as Sabatier reads; it is also in the Greek.]

We did not comply with your poisonous counsel, desiring in all our tribulations and distresses to flee to him to whom that lover of righteousness, Job, fled in every trial. We did not obey your cruel command because we wished to be found imitators of that servant of God, Job, who says: “I delivered the poor from the hand of the mighty, and I was a helper to the orphan who had no helper. The mouth of the widow always blessed me. For I was clothed with righteousness, and judgment covered me; I was an eye to the blind and a father to the weak; but I broke the jaws of the wicked and tore their plunder from their teeth” (Job 29:12).

[Note: For “we did not comply.” Tillemont, Latinius, and La Cerda; as in book 2, “We would falsely have complied with the charge.”]

[Note: For “with judgment,” as earlier he said “clothed with weapons” for “with weapons,” in Greek fashion. Tillemont. The Ancient Version adds “like a cloak,” and has several other quite slight variants here.]

[Note: Sabatier reads “from [their] teeth.” Ancient Version: “An eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the weak. I sought out the judgment that I did not know. I broke the jaws of the wicked and pulled plunder from the midst of their teeth.”]

And below: “I have been placed in the balance of righteousness, and the Lord knows my simplicity, because my foot has never strayed from the straight way, nor has my eye looked” (Job 31:6).

[Note: Greek: ἕσταμαι, “I stand.” Ancient Version: “Let him weigh me in a most just balance.”]

[Note: Ancient Version: “But he knows . . . innocence . . . if my foot has declined from the way” (without “straight”; in Greek, ἐξέκλινεν, “has turned aside”), “and if my heart has followed my eye.”]

What is the straight way from which glorious Job declares that he did not depart? Certainly this: the way which neither kills the innocent nor knows another God, for he knows none but the God of angels and archangels—the God whom you believe cannot rescue us from your power. For when you say concerning the faith of the blessed Church, “If the catholic faith set down at Nicaea is [truly] faith, let him in whom they have believed rescue them from my power,” you say that we have no God able to rescue us from your hands, that you cannot be withstood; you assert that the God of the apostolic Church does not possess power sufficient to exclude your might.

What else does the blessed faith of the Church confess except that it believes in God the Father and in his only Son, born of the unbegotten and true Father, and in the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete? What else does the faith of the catholic Church confess except that the Trinity is perfect and that the Godhead of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one? What else does the blessed Church’s faith confess except that neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, assumed a human being, but the only Son of God did? What else does the faith of the glorious Church affirm except that the only Son of God is unchangeable, unconvertible, inestimable, immeasurable, eternal, as is he whose Son he is?

[Note: “Father, unbegotten.” Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: For “Godhead.” Tillemont and La Cerda.]

The holy Church has believed that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess one power and one sovereignty. This is the faith which you call heretical; and you maintain as catholic your own, which says that God does not have a true Son, which says that there was a time when he was not, which says that he was made from nothing—precisely the notions by which Rabshakeh, commander of the king of Assyria, reproached the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, because your God is unable to deliver you from the hands of the king of Assyria” (Isa. 36:14).

[Note: These are the formulas by which the Arians attacked the divinity of Jesus Christ.]

Thus you too, commander of Antichrist, say through your agents: “Let not the words of your bishops, who oppose me, deceive you, because the faith which they preach cannot deliver you.” Although they vary the wording, the matter nevertheless comes to this: you reproach God to us as powerless to rescue us, just as the king of Assyria reproached him: “Thus says the king of Assyria: If you wish to be blessed, come out rather to me; and each of you shall eat the fruit of his own vine and fig tree and drink water from his own cisterns, until I come and take you to a land like your own land, a land of wheat, wine, bread, and vineyards. Therefore do not let Hezekiah deceive you by saying, ‘God will deliver you.’” And below: “Who will deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” (Isa. 36:16, 20).

[Note: “For he is powerless.” Vatican manuscript.]

But because you have been shown to be like such a man, God says through Isaiah to Hezekiah: “You need not fear these words which you have heard, with which the messengers of the Assyrians reproached me. Behold, I shall send my spirit upon him; when he hears a report, he shall return to his own land and fall by the sword in his own land” (Isa. 37:6).

[Note: Sabatier corrects *my* to *him*, as in the Greek, εἰς αὐτόν, and reads “to his own region.”]

Now, Constantius, unless you take counsel for yourself, we see those same dangers standing around you which stood around the man who said: “Thus shall you say to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying: Jerusalem shall not be handed over into the hands of the king of Assyria’” (Isa. 37:10). You, blasphemer, are in dangers as he was, and do not see it; but we, God’s worshippers, see ourselves standing safe, defended, and unharmed. Why are we safe and defended? Because we hold the holy faith which patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs held—the faith you have judged heretical.

But, to return again to Athanasius, in whom you persecute this sacred faith: I ask you, did you not fear the Lord’s indignation pronounced against those who attempted to reproach most righteous Job, when you pursued God’s bishop with false accusations? Even now do you not fear lest God say to you what he said to that king who spoke against most holy Job: “You and both your friends have sinned, for you have said nothing true before me” (Job 42:7)?

[Note: Ancient Version: “Two.” “For [you have said] nothing . . . true.”]

Meanwhile, you Arians will be found superior to Athanasius before God only as those men were then found superior who reproached Job. It is advantageous for you, Constantius, to be a suppliant to God for your crimes through Athanasius, the Lord’s priest; through him direct your prayers, as those men did through Job; through Athanasius or his fellow bishops, strive to obtain saving baptism.

[Note: “Reproached.” Latin.]

[Note: Tillemont thinks this implies that Constantius, baptized by heretics, was to be rebaptized—or, more probably, that he had not yet been baptized. But from ecclesiastical history and St. Athanasius’s work *On the Synods*, we learn that he was baptized by the Arian bishop Euzoius shortly before his death, in A.D. 360; during the Persian expedition he died at Mopsuestia in Cilicia, on 3 October.]

Moreover, however you may choose to rage against Athanasius, you are found to be, as heretics, among the children of that serpent, that snake, fugitive, and deserter. Athanasius, however, is of God’s household, as Job was; he is among the children of light; he holds the very way of righteousness which God’s servant Job held; he possesses the faith by which Athanasius too is among Abraham’s children. Athanasius confesses the Son of God as Job confessed him. How was Job among Abraham’s children, except because he believed as Abraham believed?

If you do not know that these things are so, read through the blessed apostle Paul, not only in Romans but also in Galatians, and you will find true what I maintain. Or because the blessed apostle does not make particular mention by name of righteous Job, will Job be denied to be among Abraham’s children? If Job cannot be denied to be among the children of Israel, it cannot be doubted that he became so great and such a man because he believed in God as blessed Abraham believed. For the apostle reveals that believers are justified not by works of the law but through faith. Indeed, victory in those trials would not have been reckoned to him as righteousness unless he believed in God as Abraham believed. Or whence would he have conquered the devil, unless he had believed in God the Father, and in his only Son, born of the unbegotten and true Father, and in the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete?

[Note: The Apostle speaks of Abraham’s faith in Romans 3 and Galatians 3.]

[Note: “Father, unbegotten.” Vatican manuscript.]

Or, if you think that it was not always believed as we believe today, prove that the blessed apostles and martyrs could have overcome your fellow-torturers and, after conquering your friend the devil, obtained the heavenly kingdoms unless they believed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

[Note: That is, torturers such as you are. He very frequently uses such compounds: “your fellow-Arians,” “your fellow-pestilences,” “your fellow-blasphemers,” “your fellow-apostates,” and the like. Tillemont and La Cerda.]

Therefore, if those who believed after the advent of the Lord, the only Son of God, conquered by believing thus, believe that those who conquered the devil before his advent did not believe otherwise than we believe today. For Daniel would not have conquered the lions, nor the three youths the fires, unless they had believed as the Church believes today. Thus the apostle appeals to Abraham’s faith, proving by the authority of sacred writings that Abraham believed as Paul now believed—whereas Paul had formerly been an erring child of wrath when, with the Jews, he denied the only Son of God.

Since this is so, I beg you now to cease waging war against God’s house and receive the heavenly exhortations which can lead you to attain everlasting salvation. Receive from the mouth [of Isaiah] what God says to you: “Hear me, you who have lost your heart, who are far from righteousness” (Isa. 46:12).

[Note: “Your” is absent from the Greek and Ancient Version.]

Or if your heart is with you, if you are not far from righteousness, why do you say to us, God’s priests: “Condemn the absent man; punish the innocent”? For if you have not lost your heart and hold the way of righteousness, why do you not keep what is written: “Keep judgment; do justice. For my salvation is near to come, and my mercy to be revealed. Blessed is the man who does this, and the person who embraces it: keeping my sabbaths, not to profane them, and keeping his hands from doing [source ends mid-sentence]

[Note: He says *is near* in place of *has drawn near*, and *to come* in place of *has come*, the infinitive for the perfect; likewise shortly below, “they desire to approach God,” that is, they greatly desire to be near God, to approach God. Tillemont and La Cerda. In the Ancient Version: “For my salvation is near, that it may come, and my mercy, that it may be revealed.” But Lucifer follows Greek syntax throughout: Ἤγγικε γὰρ τὸ σωτήριόν μου παραγίνεσθαι, καὶ τὸ ἔλεός μου ἀποκαλυφθῆναι, “For my salvation has drawn near to come, and my mercy to be revealed.”]

[Note: Ancient Version: “These [things], and the man who keeps them: who keeps the sabbaths so as not to profane them and guards his hands from doing iniquity.”]
injustices. And again (ibid. 57:21): “There is no [Note: [Col. 0877D] The Ancient Version: “There is no joy . . . . . the Lord God. Cry aloud with strength, and do not spare; like a trumpet . . . . . their: for they . . . . . like a nation which . . . . . and which . . . . . They seek me . . . . . they desire to draw near to God.”] joy for the ungodly,” says the Lord. Cry out mightily; do not spare. Lift up your voice like a trumpet [Note: [Col. 0877D] Sabatier reads *trumpet* (*tuba*).], and declare to my people their sins, and to the house of [Col. 0877C] Jacob their iniquities. They seek me day by day and wish to know my ways, as though they were a people who had practised righteousness and had not forsaken the judgment of God. They ask of me now a just judgment, and desire to draw near to God (ibid. 58:1). What hope can you have, unhappy man, unless you repent of your evil deeds, when you hear God say (ibid. 57:21), “There is [Col. 0878A] no joy for the ungodly”? Or will you deny that you are an ungodly worshipper of God, when you do not deny that you are a shedder of blood?

Further, if God uttered rebukes of this kind against those who, during times of fasting, struck their subjects with their fists and injured them by other kinds of wrongs, what rebuke would he have uttered against us if, contrary to the commands of his divine majesty, we condemned one unheard, absent, and indeed innocent? “Not even if you bend [Note: [Col. 0877D] The Ancient Version: “Nor if you bend your neck like a circle . . . . . spread beneath yourself . . . . . will you call this a fast and an acceptable day.”] your neck like a hoop, and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath yourself, will you even then call it an acceptable fast” (ibid. 58:5).

By this threat we see how great God’s wrath against us could be if we condemned an innocent man. For if, during times of fasting, we strike our subjects with fists, the Lord is angered in such a manner; how much more so if we slaughter his worshippers! If I am not permitted to strike my subjects with fists [Col. 0878B] during a fast, can it be permitted at any time to strike down my fellow priest with the sword? “This is not the fast I have chosen,” says the Lord, but [Note: [Col. 0877D] Perhaps one should add: “but loose every bond of iniquity, but loose,” etc., as in the Ancient Version and in the Greek, since a little below he will cite this statement against Constantius: [Col. 0878C] “For how have you loosed every bond of iniquity?” etc., and will again produce the whole Isaian testimony in this form. Thus Cotelerius, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. 2, p. 90, and Galandius after him. The Ancient Version: “Is not this . . . . . fast which he chose? . . . . . but loose every fastening of iniquity, dissolve,” etc.] “loose the obligations of oppressive contracts” [Note: [Col. 0878D] More suitably, in accordance with the Greek συναλλαγμάτων, “transactions” or “contracts.” The Ancient Version: “of legal securities.”]; “release the crushed into remission, and tear up every unrighteous written bond; break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy [Note: [Col. 0878D] The Ancient Version: “The homeless poor . . . . . do not despise them.” A little below Lucifer himself has “the poor,” and “you shall not despise.”] who have no roof into your house. If you see one naked, clothe him, and do not despise those of your own seed” (ibid., v. 6).

What hope do you maintain, most prudent emperor, when you have turned all these things into their opposites? For how have you loosed every bond of iniquity, when, whether by your unbelief—having set yourself against us as you have done—you remain such a man and grow more and more in malice for our destruction; or whether, in your blasphemy, you have grown to be the author of sacrilege, and have even by edict [Note: [Col. 0878D] See what was said in the preface.] asserted that your blasphemy [Col. 0878C] is the Catholic faith, in the manner [Note: [Col. 0878D] By this comparison Lucifer indicates the craft and cunning of the Arians, who at first secretly fostered their heresy while outwardly professing themselves Catholics; afterwards, becoming bolder, they began openly to preach and defend their errors.
