[Note: Greek: ἔθεντο εἰς τήρησιν, “they put [them] in custody.” Old Latin: “They laid hands on them . . . [put] them in custody until the next day.”]

And below (ibid. 4:13): “Seeing the boldness of Peter and John, and discovering that they were uneducated and ordinary men, they marvelled; they also recognized them, that they had been with Jesus. Seeing the man who had been healed standing with them, they could say nothing in reply. But after ordering them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying: ‘What shall we do to these men? For that a notable sign has occurred through them is manifest to all who live in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. But lest these words spread further among the people, let us threaten them, that they may no longer speak in this name to any person.’ With all agreeing, they summoned them and ordered them not to speak at all or teach in the name of Jesus. But Peter and John answered and said: ‘Whether it is right before God to listen to you rather than to God, judge; for we cannot but speak what we have seen and heard.’ They, after threatening them, let them go, finding no way to punish them because of the people; for all were glorifying God for what had happened. For the man in whom this sign of healing had taken place was more than forty years old. When released, they went to their own people and reported all that the chief priests and elders had said to them. And when they heard it, with one accord they raised their voices to the Lord and said: ‘Lord, you are God, who made heaven and earth and sea and all things in them; who through the Holy Spirit and through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate empty things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ.” For Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the nations and the people of Israel, truly assembled in this city against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed, to do what your hand and counsel had predetermined. And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant your servants to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hands for healings and for signs and wonders to be done through the name of your holy Son Jesus.’ And when they had prayed, the place where they were gathered was shaken; they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with all boldness.”

[Note: With the royal manuscript. Old Latin: “The boldness . . . having learned that . . . they were uneducated and common . . . they recognized them,” etc.]

[Note: From the Greek, οὐδὲν εἶχον, “they had nothing [to say].” Old Latin: “He who had been healed—they had nothing against [them].” Sabatier reads *had been healed*.]

[Note: Old Latin: “Ordering them to go outside the council, they conferred with one another.” Greek: ἔξω τοῦ συνεδρίου, πρὸς ἀλλήλους, “outside the council, with one another,” as in Lucifer.]

[Note: Old Latin: “these men? For indeed . . . through them . . . manifest, and not,” etc. The royal manuscript with Lucifer has “it is manifest.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “But lest these words spread further among the people, let us threaten them, that they may no longer . . . in this name.”]

[Note: “But when all agreed, they ordered them,” with the Cambridge manuscript. These words are absent from the Old Latin, which reads: “And having summoned them, they ordered them absolutely not to speak.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “They said to them: If this seems right to you before God, to obey you rather,” etc.]

[Note: Old Latin: “Those things which.” *Those* is absent also from the Cambridge manuscript.]

[Note: Old Latin: “But they, further threatening . . . finding nothing . . . by which they might punish them, fearing the people . . . were glorifying . . . for this event.” The Greek with Lucifer has διὰ τὸν λαόν, “because of the people,” without “fearing,” and ἐπὶ τῷ γεγονότι, “for what had happened,” without “this.”]

[Note: “This sign.” Old Latin; *this* is absent also from Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 3.12.]

[Note: Entirely with the Cambridge manuscript. Old Latin: “But they . . . reported . . . to them,” etc.]

[Note: Nearly with the same manuscript except for “with one accord . . . to God . . . you are God.” Old Latin: “When they . . . heard, they with one accord raised their voice to God . . . you, God, made . . . that are in them.” Sabatier reads *had heard* for *heard*.]

[Note: As in Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 3.12. Old Latin: “Saying: Why?”]

[Note: As in the same passage there. “Above.” Old Latin.]

[Note: “People.” Old Latin.]

[Note: Old Latin: “Whatever . . . your counsel predetermined should be done . . . upon their threats.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “Since you stretch out your hand for healing, and signs and wonders are done . . . of your servant.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “And when they had prayed . . . with all boldness to everyone willing to believe.”]

If you have now gathered why we have set forth all these things, if you have fully absorbed the whole purpose of our defence, will you still dare to say that we are insolent? For you see that the blessed apostles neither yielded to the leaders of the Jews nor succumbed to their threats, but always carried out with boldness what had been entrusted to them. You see likewise that God’s people were not merely undismayed by the threats of unbelievers, but also prayed that God might deign to grant his apostles boldness in speaking and steadfastness in defending the truth.

If, therefore, this was done by the blessed apostles and by peoples consecrated to God, and they were called by God neither disobedient nor insolent because they resisted his enemies, how are we called by you proud, insolent, and insulting? We, though sinners, nevertheless hold the holy faith of the apostles and of those peoples who believed in the only Son of God. Are we, together with the apostles, therefore proud because, as apostates and sacrilegious soldiers of Christ, we count your voice and your terrors as nothing, and proclaim God’s Son to be the true Son of God, as the most blessed apostles proclaimed him?

Thus we seem to you obstinate, insolent, and proud, as the holiest apostles seemed to the Jews; had those apostles been alive in bodies today, you could have said to them what you deign to say to us. For we find that they were always commanded by the mouth of your fellow-blasphemers—the scribes, Pharisees, rulers, and high priest of the Jews—not to teach or preach the only Son of God. Yet learn further from what is written what they did, lest perhaps your heart, fed on darkness, may be brought to behold the truth:

“By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were performed among the people. They were all with one accord in Solomon’s portico; but none of the rest dared join them, although the people magnified them. And increasingly there were added to the Lord believers, multitudes of men and women, so that they even brought the sick out into the streets and laid them on beds and pallets, that as Peter came by, at least his shadow might overshadow one of them; and they were delivered from their infirmity. A multitude also came together from the neighbouring cities of Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted by unclean spirits; and all were healed. Then the high priest arose, and all who were with him, the sect of the Sadducees; they were filled with jealousy, laid their hands upon the apostles, and put them in custody. But an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, saying: ‘Go, stand in the temple, and speak to the people all the words of this life.’ When they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and taught. The high priest and those with him arrived, summoned the council and the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought. But the officers came and did not find them in the prison; returning, they reported: ‘We found the prison securely shut, with the guards standing at the doors; but when we opened it, we found no one inside.’ When the leaders and high priest heard these words, they were perplexed about them, wondering what this might be. Then someone came and reported to them: ‘Behold, the men whom you put in custody are standing in the temple and teaching the people.’ Then the captain went with the officers and brought them, though not by force, for they feared that the people would stone them. When they had brought them, they set them before the council; and the high priest questioned them, saying: ‘We strictly charged you not to teach in this name; and behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and wish to bring this man’s blood upon us.’ But Peter and the apostles answered: ‘Must one obey God or men?’” (Acts 5:12 ff.)

[Note: Old Latin: “Among the people . . . with one accord . . . assembled in the temple, in the portico.” Sabatier reads with the Old Latin: “But by the hands.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “Join themselves to them . . . the people [magnified] them.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “But more were added . . . of men also and women.” Sabatier reads in the Cambridge manuscript, and in Lucifer: “And the number of believers in the Lord increased still more,” etc.]

[Note: Old Latin: “The sick; they placed [them] before them . . . that even his shadow might overshadow someone . . . and they might be delivered from every illness they had.” Greek has simply ἡ σκιά, “the shadow,” as Lucifer. Sabatier reads *placed* and *might overshadow*.]

[Note: With the Greek, συνέρχετο δέ, “and there came together.” With the Cambridge manuscript: “and those afflicted by unclean spirits.” Old Latin: “Therefore a multitude from the cities adjacent to Jerusalem also came together, bringing with them . . . and those afflicted by unclean spirits; all were healed.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “And seeing these things”—words absent also from the Cambridge manuscript—“. . . the sect that was with him . . . they were filled with zeal.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “Their hands upon the apostles . . . [put] them in public custody.” *Their* is absent in some Greek manuscripts.]

[Note: Old Latin: “During the night he opened the doors . . . and after bringing them out, said.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “Speak to the people.” Vatican manuscript: “To the people.”]

[Note: Greek: ἀκούσαντες δέ, “having heard.” Old Latin: “Having gone out of prison . . . at daybreak into the temple . . . and all the elders of the children . . . to bring them.” Sabatier reads: “To the prison, that they might be brought.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “But the officers, arriving . . . [did not find] them in the prison . . . returning, announced.” Greek: ἀπήγγειλαν, “reported,” with Lucifer.]

[Note: From the Greek: Ὅτι τὸ μὲν δεσμωτήριον εὕρομεν κεκλεισμένον ἐν πάσῃ ἀσφαλείᾳ, “We found the prison shut with all security.” Old Latin: “With every diligence . . . at the door; but opening [it],” etc.]

[Note: With the Greek, τοὺς λόγους, “these words,” and with the Cambridge manuscript, “they were perplexed.” Old Latin: “The priests, captain of the temple, and chief priests began to marvel and were confused in mind over these matters, what this could mean.” Sabatier reads here in Lucifer: “The captain of the temple and chief priests.”]

[Note: As in the Greek, λέγων, “saying.” Old Latin: “He reported to them that behold . . . in the prison . . . the people.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “The captain in the temple”; Greek, simply στρατηγός, “captain.”]

[Note: Old Latin: “They set [them] in the council, and the high priest.”]

[Note: Thus the Greek, παραγγελίᾳ παρηγγείλαμεν, “We commanded by command.” Sabatier reads in Lucifer, as in the Vulgate: “Strictly commanding, we commanded.” Old Latin: “Did we not strictly command you . . . not to teach . . . your teaching . . . this man’s [blood]?” The interrogative οὐ is absent in certain manuscripts, as in Lucifer.]

If, therefore, God must be obeyed and not men, why do you call us disobedient, why injurious, when you see that we obey God’s commands? “When they heard this,” Scripture says, “they were enraged and plotted to kill them” (ibid. 5:33). So too you keep us in prisons and threaten to kill us, because you are possessed by the same spirit by which the Jews were held captive and are held captive. If you are not held captive by that unclean spirit, why do you forbid us to confess and proclaim the only Son of God?

The angel of God, bringing the apostles out of the prison of your despairing fellow Jews:

[Note: “As you and your Arians, who by their heresy profess Judaism, denying the divinity of Jesus Christ.”]

“Go,” he says, “teach in the temple the words of this life” (ibid. 20).

[Note: See a little above the same words, which he alters somewhat here.]

And you thought it right to take priests from the Church of God and cast them into prison, lest we preach the word of life.

[Note: In truth, as regards the very substance of the heresy, the Arians differed in no respect from the Photinians. Photinus, however, taught that Christ, the Son of God, was merely a man, so that he first came into existence when he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb; whereas the Arians proclaimed that he had been created before all creatures. Yet at the Council of Sirmium in the year 351 he was condemned by the Arians themselves ostensibly for this reason; but in fact, since Constantius, as Baronius observes under the year 357, was not second to Photinus in impiety, in order to display himself as pious and Catholic and an opponent of heretics, he brought Photinus forward as though in a theatrical performance, with Arian bishops against him. In the published formula of faith—the first Sirmian formula—they omitted the term οὐσίας (“substance”), and the terms “likeness” and “image,” while affirming that the Son was God from God and pronouncing an anathema against those who said that the Word was from non-existent things or from another hypostasis, or that there had ever been a time when he was not. Yet all these things were cunningly decreed in order to deceive and conceal their impiety. Here Lucifer unmasks this pretence when he calls Photinus Constantius’s companion and, as it were, his friend in impiety.]

Meanwhile, I ask you to answer what difference there is between you and your fellow-darkness, whom the Sirmians, reversing the proper order, call Photinus. Distinguish, if you are asked, what difference there is and in what way you differ.

[Note: That is, between one who, along with you and like you, dwells in darkness; for σκότος means “darkness.” By a contrary designation he alludes to the name Photinus. Til. It is an antiphrasis, certainly; for *Photinus* derives from φῶς, meaning “light.”]

[Note: We have corrected this from the Vatican manuscript, where previously “Smyrnians” was read, and below “Smyrnaeans.” For Photinus was bishop at Sirmium, although at the time when Lucifer wrote this he had been deposed from rank and office by the Arians themselves.]

If at that time the rulers, high priest, and whole council of the Jews said to the apostles, “You wish to bring upon us the blood of that man” (ibid. 28), Photinus likewise professes the Son of God to be only a man and says that he did not exist before blessed Mary.

[Note: “And says that he did not exist.” Galland.]

This too is your profession: that the Son of God existed indeed before all things—that is, before heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them—but that he was made from nothing and is a creature. What difference do you think exists between you and Paul of Samosata, or between him and his disciple, now your fellow-darkness, except that you place him before all things, whereas he places him after all things?

[Note: Paul of Samosata denied that the Lord Jesus was God and Son by the divine nature, attributing to him mere humanity. His error was condemned in the Synod of Antioch in 265 and again at a second synod held there in 270; he himself was condemned and expelled from the Church of Antioch over which he presided. Lucifer calls Photinus his disciple because he drew the poison of his impiety from him.]

[Note: “He who is with you in darkness”; σκότος, “darkness.” La Cerda.]

Yet you share one mind in cruelty and unbelief:

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “credulity,” i.e. “belief.”]

in maintaining that God has no true Son.

[Note: For, as the teaching of Paul, Photinus, and the Arians implied: if Christ, begotten from God’s substance, is not God, then the Father has no Son properly so called and is μονοπρόσωπος, “single-personed.”]

But see how the holy Church believes:

[Note: This is the Nicene Creed, or Nicene confession of faith, which Lucifer cites here, almost identical with that published from ancient codices in vol. 2 of the Venetian edition of the Councils.]

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, begotten from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made.”

[Note: “Maker of all things visible,” in the cited codices of the Councils.]

[Note: Thus from the Greek in Athanasius’s letter to Jovian. The other codices have “our Lord.”]

[Note: “Begotten from the Father, only-begotten.” The Greek and the same codices.]

[Note: With the Greek, οὐ ποιηθέντα (“not made”).]

… In one manuscript: “not created”; [it reads] “made,” [and] “of one substance with the Father,” which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), through whom all things were made, whether those in heaven or those on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down and was incarnate, and became man; suffered; rose again on the third day; ascended into heaven; and is to come to judge the living and the dead. [Note: The Colbert and Harduin manuscripts have “of the same substance with the Father.”] [Note: In both places the same manuscripts have “whether.”] [Note: The same manuscripts have “and became man.”] [Note: “And rose again”: the same manuscripts. In Gelasius of Cyzicus, *History of the Council of Nicaea*, book 2, chapter 26: “was buried, and rose again.”] [Note: Thus the Harduin manuscript; all the others, with the Greek, read “and ascended into the heavens.”] [Note: With the same manuscript, which adds “from there”: “from there he is to come.” From Gelasius: “and he will come again.” The Colbert manuscript: “from where he is to come.”] And we believe in the Holy Spirit. [Note: With the Colbert manuscript; “we believe” is absent from the others.]

You see that this faith is apostolic and evangelical: it maintains that the Son has always reigned and reigns with the Father; it confesses both that the divine Trinity is perfect and that it possesses one substance. Otherwise, what distinction would there be between the Church and you heretics—or Jews—if the blessed Church did not believe thus? This holy faith, so that you might know what the Church of the Lord punishes in you, said and says concerning you:

> But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten he was not,” and, “He was made from things that did not exist,” or who say that he is “from another substance or essence,” and call the Son of God mutable and changeable—these the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

[Note: The anathemas appended to the same Creed follow, directed against the principal propositions of the Arian heresy.] [Note: The Greek and other manuscripts read “there was once a time”; others have “there was a time.”] [Note: The Harduin manuscript has “from things that had no subsistence”; the Colbert manuscript, “from things that did not subsist.”] [Note: “Or from another substance or essence”: so the Harduin and Colbert manuscripts, with the Greek.] [Note: The Colbert manuscript has “mutable.”] [Note: “Or”: the Colbert and Harduin manuscripts, following the Greek.]

For this holy faith the apostles were shut up in prison, put in chains, and tormented with lashes from hour to hour, lest they reveal the truth to the world; nevertheless they chose to preach until they should even be slaughtered. And you say that we are people of extreme obstinacy because we keep the way of the apostles? Because we tell you that you have become a wanderer from the way?

What did the blessed John the Baptist do to Herod? “Herod the tetrarch, when he was reproved by him concerning Herodias, his brother’s wife, and concerning all the evils which Herod had done, added this also above all, and shut John up in prison” (Luke 3:19). [Note: “What did”: the Latin text and Gallandi read “did.”] [Note: “Concerning Herodias, his brother’s wife”: the Ancient Version adds this together with “and concerning all the evils which Herod had done.”] Why did Herod shut John up? Certainly because his deeds were rebuked. Thus you too deal with the servants of God because we say to you: Do not do what you do; do not be a murderer; do not persecute the Church of the Lord; do not reject the apostolic faith and approve the heretical one; do not introduce idolatry into the Church.

We judge that we say these things especially for your salvation. If you refuse to restrain yourself, you will undoubtedly seek eternal death for yourself, as Herod also sought it. For Herod could not harm John, whether by casting him into prison or by killing him, since you see John to be God’s friend, but Herod God’s enemy. You seek to harm us, although we desire eternal safety to be bestowed upon you; you persecute us in every way. Yet the force of your authority will not be able to harm the servants of God’s only Son, because you are found to be one of those whom he subjected to us who believe, saying: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and nothing shall harm you” (Luke 10:19). [Note: The Greek has δέδωκα, “I have given,” in certain manuscripts. The Ancient Version reads “I give,” and adds “and over all.”]

You say that I tell you the truth; which proud person do you wish me to be found? The servant who received one talent, hid it, and presented that talent alone to his master? Because he did not present it multiplied by investment, as his fellow servants did, he deserved even to lose the talent itself and to hear: “Wicked and slothful servant” (Matt. 25:26). [Note: The Colbert manuscript and the Ancient Version read “Wicked servant, evil and lazy.”] Or the one who presented the entrusted sum multiplied tenfold, and to whom it was said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful in a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:21)? [Note: The Ancient Version reads “over a few things … over many things.” Lucifer agrees with Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 11, except for “over many things,” which Sabatier also finds in Lucifer.]

But how could I hear this, if, fearing you, I were to do what pleased you? Look in the Gospel at what the Lord wished us to do, and stop calling us arrogant.

“A certain man was rich. He went into a far country to receive a kingdom and return. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “And he went into a far country to receive for himself,” etc.; “for himself” is absent from the other manuscripts cited by Sabatier, as from Lucifer. Sabatier here reads *longinquam* (“far”) for *longe* (“a long way off”).] And he called ten servants and gave them ten talents [Note: The Ancient Version reads “minas”] and said to them: ‘Conduct business until I come.’ But the citizens hated him and sent an embassy after him, saying: ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ And it happened, when he returned after receiving the kingdom, that he ordered the servants to be called to whom he had given the money, in order that he might know what each had gained by trading. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “But his citizens …”; “his” is absent from the other manuscripts, as it is from Lucifer. It also reads: “When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered …”; the Major Monastery manuscript has “and he sent,” together with Lucifer.]

“The first came, saying: ‘Lord, your talent has gained ten talents.’ [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “Your mina has gained ten minas.”] And he said to him: ‘Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ Another came, saying: ‘Lord, your mina has made five talents.’ [Note: The same version reads: “Your mina has made five minas”; Sabatier appears to read the same in Lucifer.] And he said to this one: ‘You also shall be over five cities.’ Another came, saying: ‘Behold, [Note: The Ancient Version adds: “Lord … your mina, which …”; Sabatier here has “which” rather than “whom.] your talent, which I kept stored in a cloth; for I feared you, because you are a severe man: you take [Note: The Ancient Version reads “you will take, and reap”; the other manuscripts likewise read this with Lucifer.] what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’ And the master said to him: ‘From your own mouth I judge you, faithless servant. You knew that I am a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow. Why then did you not give my money to the bank, so that, upon coming, I might certainly have demanded it with interest?’ [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “And he said to him: From your mouth … I am severe; I take …”; one Greek manuscript has Κύριος, “Lord,” as does Lucifer. Sabatier adds in Lucifer “faithless, wicked servant.”]

“And he said to those standing by: ‘Take the talent from him, and give it to the one who has ten talents.’ [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “The mina, and the ten minas.”] But I say to you: ‘To everyone who has, more shall be given; but from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away.’ [Note: The same version reads “shall be taken away from him”; “from him” is absent from other manuscripts, as it is from Lucifer.] Yet those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and kill them before me” (Luke 19:12).

Plainly, unless you change, you will be one of those ordered to be killed. [Note: “Change”: the Latin and Gallandi read “be changed.”] Is it for this that I seem proud to you—because I do not want you killed, because I desire that you too should be found in that entrusted sum which has been committed to me and which I desire to multiply? [Note: “In that”: the same manuscript and Gallandi.] Because we contend with you in this way, do we seem enemies to you—we who, keeping the command of the blessed apostle, unceasingly pour out prayer for your welfare?

“I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high position, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life, with piety and dignity. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “I exhort, therefore, first …”] For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:1). [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “before God … and in the knowledge.”] [Note: The Greek has ἤρεμον καὶ ἡσύχιον βίον, “a calm and quiet life.”] [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “that we may lead a life with seriousness and gravity, with piety and chastity.”]

We who desire you to attain the knowledge of truth seem enemies to you; you call me insulting because I say what contributes to your salvation and mine. But this assertion of yours also—that I do you an injury—shows you to be foolish. For if you had been prudent, first you would never have been found sacrilegious; then, rebuked by the authority of the sacred Scriptures, you would by now have shown yourself a changed man. But now, because you are foolish, when a bishop says to you, “Emperor, provide for your salvation: you are heavily burdened by the enormous loads of your crimes,” you say, “You insult me.”

“I charge you before God, and Christ Jesus, and the elect angels, to keep these things without partiality, doing nothing by turning to one side, but to maintain equity” (1 Tim. 5:21). [Note: Latinius thought the words “doing nothing by turning to one side” should be removed; to Gallandi they seemed to have the character of a gloss. They may have been written in the margin of the Luciferian exemplar to explain the preceding words and subsequently admitted into the text. Latinius rejects them because they are absent from the Vulgate; Gallandi’s judgment, however, is merely conjectural. The same words are also found in the Vatican manuscript.] [Note: The Ancient Version reads “without prejudice, and turning aside to another side.”]

And do you call insulting the person who, finding you entangled in such crimes, now rebukes you for having committed them, and now implores you, while there is opportunity, to rescue yourself from your evils, and to become such a person as God does not punish among those whom he marks as wicked and faithless, saying: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2)? [Note: Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 2; the Ancient Version reads “I generated them, and they rejected me.”]

Does this make me seem proud to you, because I desire you to be found among those whom God’s only Son invites into his kingdom, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34)? [Note: Cyprian, *On Works and Alms*, reads “possess … prepared … of this world.” Calmet, in his commentary on the Gospel of St. Matthew, reports that Lucifer reads: “Possess the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning”; this agrees with the Corbie manuscript produced by him.]

You suppose that you suffer an insult because true things are said to you. On the contrary, the glorious apostle commands: “Rebuke those who sin before all, so that the rest also may have fear” (1 Tim. 5:20). [Note: Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book 3, reads “that they may have”; the Ancient Version has the reading “and so that the others also may have,” as does Lucifer below.]

Whom ought I to obey? You, who say, “Allow me to destroy God’s religion, to turn his servants to Antichrist; allow me to establish everyone in this my sacrilege”? Or the blessed apostle, who commands me to rebuke you as a sinner before all?

But if you think that I ought to have spared you because you are emperor, in this too you are found foolish. For you hear the apostle say, “Rebuke those who sin before all, so that the rest also may have fear”; and you say, “You ought especially to have spared me because I was king of the Roman Empire.” And where was I to omit this charge? “I charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to keep these things without partiality, doing nothing by turning to one side” (1 Tim. 5:21). [Note: “Turning aside”: with the Ancient Version, which omitted it somewhat earlier.]

Surely this is why I seem insulting to you: because I have not placed your commands before God’s commands. In the Acts of the Apostles I read that the blessed apostles were seized by those whose associate you are not only in unbelief but also in cruelty, and were ordered not to teach in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. But let us consider together that very passage of sacred Scripture: whether the apostles yielded to the commands of the enemies of God’s only Son, or whether they pressed most urgently onward in the things they had undertaken to fulfill.

“They called the apostles, had them beaten, and dismissed them, ordering them not to speak to any person in the name of Jesus. Therefore they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the Name. And every day, in the temple and at home, they did not cease teaching and proclaiming our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 5:40). [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “They called … and, after beating them, ordered them … and dismissed them.”] [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “Therefore they went away … because they had been deemed worthy for the name of the Lord Jesus”; the Cambridge manuscript and certain Greek manuscripts simply read “for the name.” Sabatier adds “his” in Lucifer.] [Note: The Cambridge manuscript omits only “our.” The Ancient Version reads: “Every day … in houses … teaching and proclaiming Jesus Christ.”]

When sacred Scripture reports that the blessed apostles did these things, while you invite all hearts to deny the Son of God and labor earnestly to establish your heresy, ought we who preside over the churches of God to be silent, lest we be found to have insulted you—a blasphemer, murderer, and destroyer of God’s religion? Sacred Scripture says that the apostles feared neither lashes nor the threats of the children of pestilence, but taught continually; are we to have been taught to be broken by the force of your perishable kingdom, by which you may carry out all your wicked designs?

You judge us obstinate because we speak true things to you. Thus your fellow blasphemers judged the most blessed Stephen because he said to them: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers, because you received the law by the ordinance of angels and did not keep it” (Acts 7:51). [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “Uncircumcised … you resist … as your fathers did.” The words “and so do you” are absent from the Greek, as in Lucifer. Lucifer may have written “you resist” according to the Greek ἀντιπίπτετε. Sabatier likewise reads “you resist” in Lucifer.]

When the Jews heard these things, were they rightly angered against the most holy martyr Stephen, or wrongly? If wrongly, then recognize that you too are wrongly moved against those who desire your salvation. Observe that you stand against the Church of God on the side on which the Jews then stood and now stand: you too are stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears. Hence, just as they could not endure hearing the truth but rushed to kill a worshiper of God, so you too rush upon the complete and manifest death of us who speak to you.

“When they heard these things,” divine Scripture says, “they were enraged in their hearts and gnashed their teeth at him” (Acts 7:54). [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “When they heard these things, they were enraged in their hearts and gnashed their teeth against him.” “Their” is absent from certain manuscripts, as in the Greek and in Lucifer.] And later: “Crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and rushed upon him with one accord; and having cast him out of the city, they stoned him” (Acts 7:56). [Note: With the Cambridge manuscript. The Ancient Version reads “they closed,” and “with one accord.” It also reads “they cast him out … and stoned him”; the Cambridge manuscript adds “him” after “they stoned.”]

Thus you rage in heart and gnash your teeth against us for no other reason than that we call you a persecutor of God’s house, a destroyer of God’s religion, a shedder of the blood of Christ’s servants, and rightly call you sacrilegious—indeed blasphemous and heretical, because you assail the apostolic and evangelical faith. We do not do a thing hateful to God if, contending with you in this fashion, we say that you are what we understand you to be.

For we find that persons such as you acted thus against the glorious [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “glorious ones”; whichever reading one chooses, one must understand either Paul or the apostles. The scholars of Lyon thought the passage should be emended as follows: “If, acting in this way with you, we call you such as we plainly know you to be, we find that such persons acted in such things as you do against the glorious one.” But this is excessively bold; Lucifer’s sense is readily discerned: “If, acting in this way in which I contend with you, we tell you what we understand you to be.” We neither reject nor approve the rest.]

“While they were serving the Lord and fasting,” sacred Scripture says, “the Holy Spirit said: ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’ Then, fasting and praying, they laid hands on them and sent them away. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “And, laying hands on them, they sent them away.”] And they, sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia; [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “They indeed, having been sent out … to Seleucia, and from there … to Cyprus.”] and from there they sailed to Cyprus. [Note: The Latin text has “from there”; Sabatier reads *inde*, “thence.”] When they came to Salamis, they proclaimed the word of the Lord in the synagogues of the Jews; and they had John as an attendant. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “In Salamis … the word of God … having John with them as an attendant.” These words occur in Greek with Lucifer: Εἶχον δὲ καὶ Ἰωάννην ὑπηρέτην. In the Cambridge Greek manuscript reported by Mill, the reading is “they proclaimed the word of the Lord,” as Gallandi notes. Sabatier reads “Salaminam.”] [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “While they were ministering to the Lord … he said to them … separate … which I have called them.” Gallandi places “the word Lord” after “serving,” in agreement with the Greek.] Having passed through the entire island as far as Paphos, [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “Having passed through the whole island … a certain magician, a false prophet.”] they found a certain Jewish man, a false prophet, whose name was Bariesuban”—that is, “Prepared” [Note: The Latin, with the Ancient Version, has “Barjhesus,” which is interpreted as “Elymas.” Mill, in his *Prolegomena*, §774, adds: “Bariesuban,” he says, is a scribal error for “Barjesus,” which is found in the Cambridge manuscript; but perhaps either Lucifer himself or the translator whom he used read *Bar-shuman*, as it occurs in the Syriac interpretation.]—“who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a prudent man. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “This man, having summoned …, sought,” etc.] He summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. But Etaemus the Great (for thus his name is said to be interpreted) resisted him, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “Elymas resisted them … he sought … concerning the faith, because he willingly listened to them.”]

“But Saul, who is Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fixed his gaze upon him and said: ‘O man full of every deceit and fraud, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, do you not cease to pervert the straight ways of the Lord? And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is against you; and you shall be blind, not seeing the sun for a time.’ [Note: The Greek has ἀτενίσας, “having fixed his gaze”; the Ancient Version reads “and looking upon him.” Sabatier reads, with the same witness, “who is also Paul.”] Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking someone to lead him by the hand. [Note: The Ancient Version reads “he sought those who could lead him by the hand”; Sabatier reads “lead” rather than “bring down.”] Then the proconsul, seeing what had happened, believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “Then … what had happened, he marveled and believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord.” “He marveled” is absent from the Greek, as from Lucifer.]” (Acts 13:2).

[Note: The Greek word ἔτοιμος means “prepared” and “ready,” just as Bar-Jesus is also interpreted. Others explain that name as “evil-doer” and “magician”; and it appears that ἔτοιμος was read in place of ἐλύμας, which means “magician,” or “corruptor and pernicious one.” Tilius says that the words “Etaemus the Great” contain a fault in the Luciferian version, and that the old translator correctly rendered as “Prepared” the name Etaemus that he had read in Greek. Mill, in his *Prolegomena*, §774, attributes the error to corrupt Greek copyists, who substituted ἐτοίμος ὁ μέγας, “the great prepared one,” for ἐλύμας ὁ μάγος, “Elymas the magician.” In the Cambridge manuscript, as reported by Sabatier, the reading is ἐτοίμας. Sabatier therefore himself suspects that Lucifer read this in his manuscript, or that the common noun ἔτοιμος, “prepared,” was made into a name from ἔτοιμος. Yet the manuscript has “Elymas the magician.” Tilius, however, appears to be mistaken when he notes that some interpreted the name Bar-Jesus as “sorcerer” and “magician.” For in the Vulgate version we read “Elymas the magician,” for so his name is interpreted; and the sense is that the name Elymas signifies “magician,” as certain writers in the *Synopsis of Sacred Critics*, volume 4, believe, while they maintain that Elymas is an Arabic word. Ludovicus de Dieu, cited by Calmet in his commentary on Acts 13, derives Elymas from the Hebrew word *chalumam*, which means “healer”; hence Bar-Jesus was called Elymas, that is, “son of salvation,” and therefore one suited to healing, indeed a healer. The Greek Bodleian manuscript cited by Mill, §1025, has Βαριεσοῦς ὃ μεθερμενεύεται ἐλύμας, “Bar-Jesus, which is interpreted Elymas.” Lightfoot, in his *Hebrew Hours* on Acts, chapter 13, says that Bar-Jesus was called “son of pain,” with which Elymas agrees, since it is derived from the Arabic word *elima*, “to suffer pain.” Therefore the proper sense of the expression is that the name Elymas, not Bar-Jesus, signifies “magician.” We may also call him a healer with Ludovicus de Dieu, because people of this kind boasted that by magical arts and tricks they could cure diseases. It should nevertheless be noted that this magician, whom Ambrose in book 4, chapter 8 of the *Hexaemeron* calls Elymus, is called “Hymn” in the Carnutian manuscript of that work, “Etymus” in the Benignian manuscript, “Jeu” in the Bigotian and Gemeticensian manuscripts, “Hymenaeus” in the Cenomannian manuscript, and “Barjeu” in one Corbie manuscript.]

We believe that, instructed by this testimony, you will not say: “Lucifer insults me, the emperor.” What does it matter to me what you are, when I say to you what that man, recognized as a Jewish false prophet, heard from the apostle? For I regard you, Emperor Constantius, as such a man as the glorious Paul and Barnabas found the Jew Bariesuban to be. For you are found as contrary to the name of the Lord as he was; you resist the truth as he resisted it; you do not wish people to believe in God’s only Son; [the transmitted text is incomplete: “for you and that Jewish false prophet …”] because you too are driven by an adverse spirit, as he was.

For when you hear that the proconsul was a prudent man and desired to be instructed by the blessed apostles, so that he might grasp the way of truth, and that the man whose imitator you are resisted the apostles lest they bring the proconsul to believe in the Son of God, it is manifest that you are such as that Jewish false prophet was. [Note: The Vatican manuscript has “he” rather than “that one.”] Again, since holy Scripture says that Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, uttered that rebuke, you ought to understand that that Jewish false prophet was filled with an unclean spirit. Therefore, just as he, driven by an adverse spirit, opposed them, so you too, since you are found resisting at the adversary’s prompting, must judge that you are none other than Bariesuban, the Jewish false prophet.

Therefore, since you understand yourself to be another Bariesuban, a Jewish false prophet, do not take offense if, whenever your sacrilegious mouth says, “God does not have a true Son,” we say to you what the apostle said to your Jewish false-prophet predecessor: “Full of every deceit and fraud, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, you do not cease to pervert the straight ways of the Lord” (Acts 13:10). [Note: “Your sacrilegious mouth”: the same manuscript reads “that sacrilegious mouth of yours.”] [Note: Lucifer repeatedly presses Constantius and the Arians on their denial that the Son is the true Son of God and that God the Father has a true Son. His argument is that confessing Jesus Christ as the true Son entails that he is *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος), of one substance with the Father. The Arians, however, called Christ a true Son but not true God, treating his sonship analogically, like that of human beings called sons of God in Scripture, though with greater excellence than other creatures. They also called him God, but only equivocally (*homonymously*, ὁμωνύμως) and as though in a secondary rank of dignity. Hence Lucifer very often presses upon the Arians these expressions: that the Son is a true Son and true God. Petavius discusses this fully in book 2, chapters 4, 5, 9, and 10.]

If you are disturbed that these things are said to you which were said to him whose path of death you follow, you show yourself exceedingly foolish: you wish to be what that Jewish false prophet was, yet do not wish to be called by the names by which he too was called.

Again I exhort, implore, and warn you to take thought for yourself, lest eternal punishment overtake you. For if he deserved to be struck blind because he tried to resist, consider what evils may befall you, a murderer, a sacrilegious man, and a destroyer of God’s religion, both in this life and forever.

Receive still further evidence that we are not insulting but truthful. Those seven most glorious brothers resisted Antiochus, just as we now resist you. You have read what the fourth answered to your fellow pestilent man, though you deign to cry out that I insult you because I say that, unless you turn to God, you will perish eternally. He says: “It is better, when given over to death by men, to await the hope from God of being raised again by him; but for you there shall be no resurrection unto life” (2 Macc. 7:14). [Note: The Greek has ἀναστήσεσθαι, “to be raised”; the Ancient Version reads “to be raised again.”]

If you, a tyrant, hear from us that you will not receive resurrection unto life if you remain in this unbelief, and that you shall rise not to rest but to everlasting punishment, what insult is that? Likewise, when the fifth had been brought forward and tortured, Scripture reports that he said to the king: “Though you are corruptible, you have power among men and do what you wish; but do not think that our race has been abandoned by God. Endure patiently, and see his great power—how he will torment you and your seed” (2 Macc. 7:16). [Note: Sabatier reads “having power,” as in the Ancient Version.] [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “But you … and you will see his great power,” and Sabatier appears to have read “his” also in Lucifer.]

What do you think? Because God’s servant assailed your fellow tyrant with such constancy, will you, a worshiper of the devil, judge that worshiper of God to have been abusive? Will you deny that he who spoke true things was proud? Nor should you judge me insolent because I tell you that we are not abandoned by God, for whose sake I endure these things, while you, on the contrary, unless corrected, shall come to nothing with your corruptible glory. [Note: “For whose sake I endure these things, you … shall come to nothing”: the Latin and Poncius understand the sense in this way: “Because I tell you that we are not abandoned … while you, on the contrary, shall come to nothing.” The passage may also be emended: “I endure these things against you, who … shall come to nothing.”]

Consider also what the sixth said, and you will find that we resist you, a stormy tempest, with the same wedge with which they resisted: “Do not err in vain” (2 Macc. 7:18). “For we suffer these things for our own sake, having sinned against our God, and these astonishing things have occurred to us. But do not suppose that you shall go unpunished, since you have attempted to fight against God.” [Note: The Ancient Version reads “things worthy of wonder have occurred among us”; the Greek lacks “among us.” Lucifer also appears to read “wonder” in this place.] [Note: The Ancient Version reads “that it will be unpunished for you …”; Sabatier reads “for you” also in Lucifer, but it is absent from the Greek.]

The letters of my humble self and my books, though written in rustic speech, prove that I have often said that our sins indeed brought us into the hands of you, the forerunner of Antichrist; but that you fight against God, and therefore, unless you provide for yourself, you shall be destined, like that Antiochus, for eternal punishment, while the Lord will be propitious to us. [Note: No letters of Lucifer survive except one written to Florentius; it is especially lamentable that the others have perished through age.]

You are grieved because we reveal what you are—you who have been entrusted to us—and because you, the shadow of Antichrist, deserve to be trampled by all Christ’s soldiers. “Who,” you say, “could trample me?” Those whom, because they confess themselves Christians, you keep shut in prisons, strip of property, make exiles, torture, and kill. [Note: This alludes to the extremely severe persecution raised by Constantius against the Catholics; see the book *For St. Athanasius*.]

You judge us insolent because we entreat all committed to us to trample the devil’s head and, by the power of the sufferings inflicted on them for Christ, God’s only Son, to bring your sacrilegious attempts to nothing. Let that most glorious mother of these seven sons also seem insolent to you, because she deigned to urge her sons to conquer your fellow combatant Antiochus, saying: [Note: Poncius, cited by Latinius, reads “to overcome your combatant”; earlier it read “your effort.”] [Note: The Latin has “she deigned”; the sense requires “let her be considered to have deigned.”]

“I do not know how you appeared in my womb; nor did I give you spirit and life, nor did I myself compose the structure of each of your limbs. [Note: The Ancient Version reads: “Nor indeed did I give you spirit and soul … I did not form the limbs of each one.” “Soul” is absent from the Greek. Sabatier has “limbs” instead of “formation of limbs.”] But the Creator of the world, who formed the birth of humankind and searches out the origin of all things, will in mercy give you back spirit and life again, since you now despise yourselves for the sake of his laws” (2 Macc. 7:22). [Note: The Ancient Version reads “who discovers the origin of all things, and yourselves”; Sabatier also finds this reading in Lucifer.]

This devout mother, loving her sons bravely, did not cease to speak these things to them until she had seen them all killed. But were we, whom the prophet foretold would be shepherds for his flock when he said, “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed you with discipline” (Jer. 3:15), obliged to remain silent lest we seem insolent to you, a rabid wolf coming to slaughter God’s sheep?

That woman so inflamed her sons’ hearts with the love of God that she obtained the joyful victories of their deaths by the sword; and did you think it fitting for us to say to Christ’s soldiers: “Do not take up arms against Constantius, the devil’s satellite; do not resist the temple of all demons. Rather, do whatever he commands to be done”? What is this obstinacy of ours, if we strive to fulfill the duty entrusted to us by God—if, in short, we are found imitators of that woman?

You wish to please the devil, whose work you are found to celebrate; we do not. By doing these things you wish to become most acceptable to God, on the contrary. If you are still moved by the question why you are called by us what you are, receive also what the seventh son of this woman cried out against Antiochus:

“But Antiochus, thinking himself despised,” [Note: Ancient Version: “thinking himself,”]

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence and mid-note.]

…at the same time, the voice of her reproach being despised … not only by words did he exhort him, but also … that he would make him rich … and that, removed from the ancestral laws, he would have him as a friend … and would provide for him. “Thinking himself,” and “and himself rich,” are also read by Sabatier.] (II Macc. VII, 24), and, despising the voice of her who rebuked him, while the youngest still survived, he not only exhorted him with words [Col. 0983A], but even affirmed with an oath that he would make him rich and blessed, would remove him [Note: [Col. 0983C] “Removed from the ancestral laws”: in Sabatier and Galland. From the corrections appended to the Tilian edition we have adopted “would remove”; and we alter nothing at discretion.] from his ancestral customs, would have him as a friend and guest, and would entrust necessary resources to him. But [Note: [Col. 0983C] Ancient Version: “But when the young man was by no means inclined by these things, the king called the mother and urged her,” etc. Sabatier reads in Lucifer almost the same: “But when the young man paid no attention to these things, the king called,” etc. Perhaps, however, our edition should read: “the young man paying no attention.”] when the young man paid no attention to these things, he called the mother and urged her to act for the young man’s salvation. And when he had exhorted her with many [Note: [Col. 0983C] “Words … promised that she would persuade her son.” Ancient Version, and likewise Sabatier in Lucifer, omit *words*. “Words” and “her own” are not in the Greek.] words, she undertook to persuade her son. Therefore, bending toward him, she mocked [Note: [Col. 0983C] Ancient Version: “Mocking … she said … my son … nine months.” The Greek does not have “my” after “son”; and the manuscript of St. Theodotus and Cyprian’s Letter to Fortunatus prefer “ten months,” as does Lucifer. Sabatier has “nine.”] the cruel tyrant and said in her native tongue: “Son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for ten months, gave you milk for three years, nourished you, and brought you to this age. I beseech you, child, look [Note: [Col. 0983C] Ancient Version and Sabatier in Lucifer: “That you may look to heaven and earth and to all things in them, and understand,” [Col. 0983D] etc. Lucifer agrees with Cyprian’s Letter to Fortunatus, except for *I beseech* in place of *I ask*.] upon heaven and earth, and, having observed all things in them, understand that God made them, and the human race also, out of nothing. Thus it shall come about that you do not fear this executioner, but, made worthy [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Made a worthy participant with your brothers, receive … in that mercy with your brothers.” Ancient Version has “your” in both places, and *participant* is absent from the Greek, which, together with Lucifer, has ἀλλὰ ἐπιδέξασθαι, “but receive.” Sabatier reads “worthy of your brothers,” and likewise later “your brothers.”] of your brothers, receive death, so that in that mercy I may receive you again with your brothers.”

When she had said [Col. 0983B] these things, the young man [Note: [Col. 0983D] “While she was still speaking … by the king’s command, but by the command of the law, which,” etc. Ancient Version.] said: “Whom are you awaiting? I do not obey the king’s command, but I obey the command of the law given to us through Moses. But you, who have become the inventor of every evil against the Hebrews, shall not escape the hand of God. For if [Note: [Col. 0983D] “And if because of … the Lord our God [is angry with us] a little.” The same version. Sabatier likewise reads “And if.”] our Lord has been moderately angry with us while we live, for rebuke and correction (ibid. 33), he will again be reconciled to his servants; but you [Note: [Col. 0983D] “But you … with vain hopes … inflamed by them.” [Col. 0984C] The same version; yet we did not wish to alter anything in Lucifer’s text, as Galland printed *hopes* for *appearances*. See a little below.], O wicked man and most criminal of all human beings, do not vainly exalt yourself with empty appearances against his servants [Note: [Col. 0984D] “Puffed up against his servants.” Latin and Vatican manuscript, as also a little below.]; for you have not yet escaped the judgment of almighty God, who sees all things [Note: [Col. 0984C] Ancient Version: “And who observes all things.” Sabatier adds this as well.]. For our fathers [Note: [Col. 0984C] “Brothers.” Latin and Vatican manuscript, as in the Ancient Version: “My brothers … became subject to the covenant of eternal life … your pride.” *Your* is absent from the Greek, as from Lucifer, who agrees here in: ὑπὸ διαθήκην Θεοῦ, “under the covenant of God,” etc. Sabatier too seems to read “became subject to the covenant of eternal life,” both here and a little below.] have fallen again under God’s covenant of eternal life after enduring a brief pain; but you shall pay, under God’s judgment, the just penalties of your pride. But I, like my brothers [Note: [Col. 0984C] “My brothers, [I give] my soul and my body.” Ancient Version with Sabatier. The Greek does not have “my” after “body,” as Lucifer does.], surrender both soul and body for our ancestral laws, invoking God to become more swiftly gracious to our nation [Col. 0983C], and that you, amid tortures and scourges, may confess that he alone is God. But in me and in my brothers may the Almighty bring to an end [Note: [Col. 0984C] “The wrath of the Almighty shall cease.” Ancient Version, and Sabatier with it, in Lucifer. Greek: στῆναι, “to stand.” Vatican: “Almighty wrath.” Others: “to cease.” The author followed the letter, as [Col. 0984D] also in what immediately follows. Galland.] the wrath which has justly been brought upon our whole race.”

What more, Constantius, have you heard from us [Col. 0984A] than what was spoken by this faithful servant of God? If he said to Antiochus’ attendants, “Whom are you awaiting? I do not obey the king’s command, but I obey the command of the law given us through Moses” (ibid. 30), we too say to yours: “Why do you think that we Christians can become Arians at the will of Constantius, the precursor of Antichrist? As we are Christians, so we shall always be” (ibid. 31). If he said to Antiochus, “But you, who have become the inventor of every evil against the Hebrews, shall not escape the hand of God,” we also have said and continue to say to you that, because no persecutor of God’s holy law has ever been greater than you, you shall not escape God’s hand. If Antiochus hears that the Lord was then angry with his people for the sake of rebuke, and that he would again be reconciled with his servants, you hear us say these same things.

[Col. 0984B] If it was said to that king, “And you, O wicked man and most criminal of all human beings, do not vainly exalt yourself, puffed up by a vain [Note: [Col. 0984D] Greek, plural: ἀδήλοις ἐλπίσιν, “uncertain hopes.” A little above: “O wicked man … with vain appearances against his servants,” omitting “puffed up.”] hope against his servants; for you have not yet escaped the judgment of almighty God” [Note: [Col. 0984D] “God who sees all things.” Vatican manuscript, as a little above.] (ibid. 34), you too hear this from us: that you are wicked, most criminal of all people, since you do these things in order to make us your fellow-apostates; yet that you are vainly exalted, puffed up against us servants of God with a vain hope inspired by the devil, because you can neither accomplish your malignant attempts nor escape the judgment of God who sees all things and has power over all things. You hear from us, just as Antiochus hears through that illustrious young man: “For our brothers [Note: [Col. 0984D] Here he agrees with the Greek in these words: ἀδελφοὶ, “brothers,” πεπτώκασι, “have fallen,” or “have fallen again.” See the same words a little above, with the sense retained but wording changed. The Lyons editors, following the Vulgate, altered these and many other passages, as often elsewhere, with a policy not altogether to be praised. Galland.] endured little and fell again under the covenant of God’s eternal life, but you shall pay the just penalties of pride under God’s judgment” (ibid. 36). You hear from us also that we are thus prepared to be killed by you, executioner, as you have already killed our brothers: prepared to surrender our souls and bodies for Jesus Christ, the true and only Son of God; and furthermore we trust in his [Col. 0985A] unfailing mercy, that he will more swiftly rescue his entire flock from you, a ravening wolf, from you, a mad dog; but that you, unless you take heed for yourself, shall go forever into torments.

What more have I said to you, whether through Scripture or in person? I want you, tyrant of our time, to refute us. If I have called you an executioner, not only this most righteous young man but also his mother called your fellow-madman Antiochus one. If I have called you the inventor of every evil; if I have said that you shall not escape God’s hand; if I have called you wicked and most criminal of all people, because you shall not escape the judgment of him who has power over all and sees all things, but under God’s judgment shall pay just penalties: all these things had already been said by this devout young man to your colleague Antiochus.

You cry out that I am abusive [Col. 0985B] because you see that names appropriate to your deeds have been imposed upon you—the names which our predecessors, worshippers of the living God, already imposed upon your fellow tyrants. The blessed apostle Peter says: “Be sober, be watchful. Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, firm in faith, knowing that your brotherhood throughout this whole world undergoes these same sufferings” (I Pet. V, 8). [Note: [Col. 0985D] Sabatier: “Because your adversary … and goes about … and may devour.” But ὅτι, “because,” is absent from some manuscripts, as in our edition.]

If you think I am abusive because you hear that what you do is evil, in what respect am I found to resist the devil according to the apostle’s command? For see: this dragon, bringing you by his wine to every form of drunkenness, has sent you into all God’s flock so that, using your royal assistance, he may make them all drunk as you yourself are—that is, mad, senseless, and insane. Who indeed makes you drunk from the vine of Sodom [Col. 0985C], from the vineyard of Gomorrah, so that you do not see that you have committed fornication, just as the Jews committed fornication? How, I ask, shall we resist the devil if we do not go out to meet you, through whom he has armed himself to devour us? If you are not told by the sober that you are drunk, by the sound that you are sick, by the whole that you are wounded, by those who see that you are blind, by those who stand that you are overthrown, by the godly that you are ungodly, by God’s sheep that you are a ravening wolf, by the most kindly and mercy-loving that you are a cruel executioner, by those who glorify God that you are a blasphemer, by worshippers of God that you are sacrilegious, by Christians that you are an Arian heretic—if you are not told by us: “Depart, servant of our adversary; give honor to God”?

How shall we resist the devil if we spare you, the net of his will; if your drunkenness—that is, madness—is not disclosed to everyone; if finally [Col. 0985D] you are not made manifest to the entire world [Col. 0986A] by your savagery against us? From the things you do, you cannot be recognized as Christ’s servant, but plainly as the slave of him who is like a roaring lion against us. This is why we seem insolent to you: because we say that you have been made drunk by that wine by which those too were brought into the madness of every drunkenness—those of whom, or on whose account, it is said: “They sinned; they are not his children, but stained—a crooked and perverse generation. Have you repaid the Lord thus, foolish and unwise people?” (Deut. XXXII, 5). [Note: [Col. 0985D] “Nation,” as in most manuscripts in Sabatier, who reads differently from us here: “They sinned against him, and not his children in uncleanness, a generation,” etc. “Generation,” Ancient Version.] [Note: [Col. 0985D] With the same manuscripts. “Foolish people,” Ancient Version. Sabatier varies: “Do you repay the Lord thus, people,” etc.]

And below: “Jacob ate and drank wine and was filled [Note: [Col. 0985D] “And he was filled, and the beloved kicked … he became fat, grew thick, and became broad … from his salvation.” Ancient Version. Lucifer: “He was filled; he became fat,” with the Rheims manuscript; “he grew thick,” with the Corbie manuscript; “his Savior,” with the Greek, σωτῆρος αὐτοῦ.] and kicked; the beloved became fat, grew thick, became broad, and forsook God who made him, and departed from God his Savior” (ibid. 14). “They provoked me with strangers; with their abominations they stirred [Note: [Col. 0985D] Thus some manuscripts. “And they exasperated me,” Ancient Version. Sabatier adds “with foreign gods.”] me up; and they sacrificed [Note: [Col. 0985D] “They sacrificed … to gods whom … new and recent … their [fathers].” Ancient Version. Rheims and Corbie manuscripts: “gods”; Corbie manuscript, “at the present time,” with [Col. 0986D] Lucifer. Sabatier reads Lucifer otherwise: “To gods whom … new and recent ones came, whom their fathers did not worship; and you forgot the Lord your creator.”] to demons and not to God, to gods whom they had not known; new ones had lately come, whom their fathers did not know. You have forsaken the God who begot you, and forgotten the God who nourished you.”

Your faithlessness, which you proclaim, indeed proves that you have forsaken God, as did the Jews, and followed idolatry. But for now I thought it necessary to bring you to this alone: that you might see that we are not injurious, insolent, and proud because I tell you what you are, but truthful, and fearing no one but God.

The most blessed apostle John says: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out [Note: [Col. 0986D] “Beloved … because … have gone out into this world.” Ancient Version. Sabatier has *are* for *are from*.]” (I John IV, 1). You plainly appear to me to be one of these false prophets, since in denying the only Son of God you declare that you possess nothing but the spirit of Antichrist in [Col. 0986C] your sacrilegious mouth. Hence it follows that you cannot even hear us when we speak of the divine eternity of God’s only Son, since that spirit of Antichrist which remains in you cannot endure it and does not wish to be driven out from you, but desires to remain in you until it sees you carried off to those places where it itself will be forever. For it grieves to lose from itself you, its most faithful darling [Note: [Col. 0986D] He uses a singular not in ordinary use in place of a plural, “its most faithful delights,” as has very often been said elsewhere. Til.], you who comply with all its desires.

“Beloved,” he says, “do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world [Note: [Col. 0986D] Sabatier reads “into the world,” as in the Ancient Version.]. By this recognize [Note: [Col. 0986D] With the Greek, γινώσκετε, “recognize.” Ancient Version: “In this the spirit is recognized.”] the Spirit of God: every spirit which confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. And every spirit which [Note: [Col. 0986D] Ancient Version: “Which does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.” Lucifer, with Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 16, except that he has *destroys* in place of *dissolves*.] destroys Jesus is not from God, [Col. 0986D] and this [Note: [Col. 0986D] From the Greek: καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ τοῦ Ἀντιχρίστου, “and this is that of Antichrist.” Ancient Version with Sabatier: “And this is Antichrist.”] is what belongs to Antichrist” (ibid.). And below: “They are of the [Col. 0987A] world [Note: [Col. 0987C] “World,” and “world” in Sabatier, as in the Ancient Version: “They are of the world; therefore,” etc.]; therefore they speak of the world, and the world hears them. But we [Note: [Col. 0987C] Ancient Version: “We are from God … knows God … who is not … we recognize the spirit of truth and error.”] are from God. Whoever knows God hears us; but whoever is not from God does not hear us. By this we recognize the spirit of truth and the spirit of error” (ibid. 5).

It is clear, Constantius, that you bear the spirit of Antichrist and are led by the spirit of error. For just as those who said that the only Son of God did not take humanity from the womb of the blessed Virgin, who did not believe that he was incarnate and made man, are shown to possess the spirit of error and are called antichrists, so you Arians also, when you deny that the only Son of God was truly born of the Father—that is, from the Father’s substance—when you reject his being the true Son, and refuse to believe that he has always reigned with the Father, that the Son has never been without the Father, nor the Father without the [Col. 0987B] Son, and when you deny that the Father and his only Son have one Godhead: do you not make it manifest that you are full of the spirit of Antichrist? [Note: [Col. 0987C] Heretics who denied that God the Word and the Son of God became man are divided into two classes. Some held that there was no union whatsoever between humanity and the Word; their leaders were the Photinians and Samosatenes. Others taught an unreal and fictitious incarnation, displayed merely in appearance to human eyes. [Col. 0987D] Lucifer seems to refer to the former; for the history and doctrines of both groups see Petavius, Book I, *On the Incarnation*, chapters 2 and 4.]

For one who has God’s Spirit cannot say concerning the only Son of God, “There was [a time] when he was not,” and, “He was made from nothing,” when he believes that he has reigned with the Father without beginning and will reign without end. Therefore, when [Note: [Col. 0987D] Thus with Pontius in the Latin text. Formerly, “him.”] you say that he is not the true Son of God; when, finally, you attempt to destroy him as ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρί, as the Greeks say, but as we Romans [Note: [Col. 0987D] He calls himself Roman because, though Sardinian, he belonged to the Roman patriarchate. Til. On the origin of patriarchal power and jurisdiction see Bingham, vol. I, *Origines Ecclesiasticae*. Whether Sardinia was subject to the Roman patriarch or perhaps to that of Constantinople is discussed by Mattheius, *Sardinia Sacra*, chapter IV, dissertation on Sardinia and its churches. Yet it seems more likely to me that, when Lucifer calls himself Roman, he refers to the language used by Romans, namely Latin: thus what Greeks call ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρί, “of one substance with the Father,” Romans express in Latin. On the words ὁμοούσιος and *substantia*, see Petavius in several places in his books *On the Trinity*, especially Book V, chapter 7, no. 2, where he shows that Arians attacked the true generation from the Father’s substance. [Col. 0988C]] call “of one substance with the Father,” you are thereby declared to belong to those false prophets and to be among the antichrists. [Note: [Col. 0988C] “Declared,” with Pontius and Galland. Formerly, “to be declared.”]

You ought not judge me abusive because I say that you are led by an unclean spirit, because I call you a precursor of Antichrist. For your mouth reveals that you are this; [Col. 0987C] one who has God’s Spirit cannot assert such things as you Arians, or all your heretics too of the various [Note: [Col. 0988C] For the Arian heresy was divided into several sects, all of which thought wrongly concerning Christ’s divinity. Petavius lists them in Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 10.] sects, affirm. You deny that true God has a Son; you say he is adoptive [Note: [Col. 0988C] Arians and the other heretics who denied that the Son of God was ὁμοούσιος and truly begotten entirely eliminated natural sonship, regarding him only as adoptive, in an adoption common indeed with other human beings, [Col. 0988D] though more eminent and distinguished. Lucifer here reproaches Constantius with this error. On Christ’s adoptive sonship according to his human nature, see Petavius’ learned and learnedly documented treatment in Book VII, *On the Incarnation*, against the Felician heresy and certain distinguished theologians in Catholic schools.], and yet you judge yourself not to have been understood: for you have revealed yourself as one of those antichrists announced by John. [Note: [Col. 0988D] “You judge yourself.” Til. and Galland.] [Note: [Col. 0988D] “Announced.” The same.] I say that you have been revealed to be led by an adverse spirit.

This, finally, is why we have not believed you when you say concerning the Son, “He was made from nothing.” For we knew that no one could say these things except one possessing the spirit of a false prophet, a precursor of Antichrist, an attendant and slave of demons. We could not believe you when you said these things, since the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophets concerning the only Son of God: that he is the true Son of God, eternal and coeternal with the Father, and that neither has the Son ever been or is without the Father, nor the Father without the Son; and the blessed apostles handed down these same things. For the Holy Paraclete Spirit, who was in the prophets, also remained in the apostles. Since that holy Paraclete Spirit is in God’s Church and you are placed outside [Col. 0988B] God’s Church, and does not remain in you, you are surely proved to possess the spirit of Antichrist. That unclean spirit, lest you see what we urge upon you, covers your heretical hearts with the blind gloom of errors [Note: [Col. 0988D] With the Latin text and Galland, we judged that it should be corrected thus, where it formerly read “to be covered by the darkness of terrors.”], so that you may not be able to emerge from its snares.

You judge us abusive because we declare you to be what we see you are. Yet I find that the Lord said in the Gospel according to [Note: [Col. 0988D] That is, “according to.”] Matthew: “Behold, I send you as sheep among [Note: [Col. 0988D] Thus also the Corbie manuscript. Ancient Version: “in the midst of wolves.”] wolves” (Matt. X, 16). You seem to me to be one of those wolves; indeed, I see concentrated in you the fury of all wolves roaring against God’s flock. For what denier of God’s only Son would not rejoice and exult when he sees you so ravage Christ’s flock? I also regard you as one of those unbelievers, [Col. 0988C] one of those faithless people to whom it is said: “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? For each one speaks from the abundance of his heart. A good person brings forth [Note: [Col. 0988D] Greek: ἐκβάλλει, “casts out.” Ancient Version: “brings forth.”] good things from a good treasure, and an evil person brings forth evil things from an evil treasure” (ibid. XII, 34). [Note: [Col. 0988D] “Can you speak good things … for from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” Ancient Version.]

If the things you say are good, Constantius, you may have a good treasure. I am insolent because I tell you that darkness dwells in your heart; hence, from your utterly dark thoughts, you dare to bring forth impure and dark things, as you are yourself. See, if you hear also what was said to the blessed Peter by the Lord, you will undoubtedly call me abusive. The most holy Matthew says: “While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve [Note: [Col. 0989C] Ancient Version and Sabatier: “came, and with him a great crowd.”], came, and with him many crowds carrying swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders of the people. Now he who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying: ‘Whomever I kiss, that is he; seize him.’ And immediately approaching Jesus he said: ‘Hail, Rabbi’; and he kissed him. But Jesus said [Note: [Col. 0989C] “And Jesus said to him.” The same version. “Jesus said to him.” Sabatier here.] ‘Friend, why have you come?’ Then they came forward, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him. And behold, one of those who [Col. 0989B] were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, struck the servant of the chief priest, and cut off his ear. Then Jesus said to him: ‘Return your sword to its place [Note: [Col. 0989C] “In its place,” in Book II for St. Athanasius.]; for all who take the sword shall perish by the sword’” (ibid. XXVI, 47).

You must call me abusive when you hear that, if you use the sword, you shall perish by the sword. Or have you not used the sword [Note: [Col. 0989C] Something is found to be missing here. What if we read, “for the killing of Christians”? Certainly this or something similar seems required by the context. Galland.] against Christians? If you have killed no one by the sword, if you have persecuted no one unto death because he confessed that God’s only Son is the true Son, because he held the apostolic and evangelical faith, because he refused to be an Arian, then you can fail to perish by the sword. For you hear that it was said to the blessed Peter, and certainly by God’s only Son: everyone who uses the sword shall perish by the sword.

[Col. 0989C] I am abusive because I have said to you: Christians are not permitted to kill, because it is fitting for Christians to suffer wrong rather than inflict it, to be killed [Note: [Col. 0989D] Add: “and to be killed.”]; for Christ’s sake, you ought not to kill those who call themselves Christians. The Lord gave us these commands; if they are kept, then we shall remain Christians. But you, since you deem it worthy to persecute his servants with the sword, can no longer be called a Christian; you are plainly [Col. 0990A] a brigand or swordsman.

Meanwhile, since we have recounted how your fellow-madman Judas Iscariot betrayed the Lord, let us in this place thoroughly reconsider the causes of his sacrilege and yours, and you will find that you and Judas Iscariot are one. He betrayed the Lord to the Jews because he had not believed—just as your fellow citizen of Sirmium, the man who was called and is called, unworthily, Photinus, now believes. You betrayed him, indeed to the entire world, so that all might be able to deny his divinity. Which of you is greater in wickedness? I think it is you. “Everyone [Note: [Col. 0989D] Ancient Version: “And whoever speaks a word against … shall be forgiven … speaks against … shall be forgiven … neither in this age nor in the future.”] who sins against the Son of Man shall be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither here nor in the future” (ibid. XII, 32). And you have become the betrayer of that divinity, so that all can deny it. [Note: [Col. 0989D] Perhaps *may be able*, so that the sense is: “And you became a betrayer of that divinity so that all might be able to deny it.” Til.]

[Col. 0990B] So far as lies in you, you have betrayed him: you have issued written books concerning him [Note: [Col. 0989D] See the book *On Not Associating with Heretics* (here col. 780), and the notes on the book *One Must Die for the Son of God*.], and established preachers of your benevolent purpose everywhere. So that all might be able to deny that he is the true Son of God, you caused the apostolic and evangelical faith set forth against you heretics at Nicaea to be judged heretical, and your blasphemy to be called catholic.
