[Note: [Col. 0989D] These words must be understood of the Synod of Rimini, at which in A.D. 359, by the unanimous agreement of the fathers, the term ὁμοούσιος, established by the Council of Nicaea and serving as a badge of faith by which Catholics were distinguished from Arians, was omitted in silence. Hence Jerome, in *Against the Luciferians*, wrote of the proceedings of the Council of Rimini: “Then the condemnation of the Nicene Faith was loudly proclaimed. The whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian.” [Col. 0990C] Lucifer’s words may nevertheless be referred to the Council of Nicaea in the same year, to which very many Catholic bishops were forcibly brought and deceitfully outwitted by the Arians, and rejected the terms οὐσία and ὁμοούσιος. See Theodoret, *History*, Book II, chapter 21. In both synods the Son was declared similar to the Father in the deceptive Arian sense; at Rimini, however, through the fraud of Ursacius and Valens, these further formulae were proposed and subjected to the bishops’ anathema: they did not deny that the Son was a creature, but that he was similar to other creatures; consequently the Arian blasphemy seemed in some fashion to be approved. See also Baronius for this year.]

Yet that Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had worked his own destruction, was moved by repentance and returned the thirty silver pieces to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood.” But they said [Note: [Col. 0990D] “They said to him,” Ancient Version; but “to him” is absent also from the Greek.]: “What is that to us? See to it yourself.” And, casting down the silver pieces in the temple, he departed; he went away and hanged himself with a rope (ibid. XXVII, 3). Although he repented after a single moment and returned the price he had received, [Col. 0990C] what such thing have you done? When you are reproved by his servants for committing sacrilege, not only have you not repented, but you have grown still more obstinate. What such thing have you done—you who give all the resources of your kingdom in order to establish your sacrilege; who have corrupted by immense rewards from your wealth those whom you could not otherwise corrupt from the truth; who have enriched a certain number of poor men so greatly that they can equal your counts [Note: [Col. 0990D] Counts were then the chief magistrates under Caesar. Til. But not correctly: they were nobles of the imperial palace, called counts because they accompanied the emperor wherever he went and never departed from his side. This title was also applied to those who presided over palace services and offices, though they exercised no magisterial function. Provincial counts did indeed exercise a magisterial office, but, as we infer from Du Cange’s *Glossary*, perhaps had not yet been established under Constantius. Lucifer refers here to the former, whose wealth was almost equaled by the most contemptible [Col. 0991C] scum of Arian men, enriched by Constantius with the property and resources of Catholics whom he punished by exile or death. We have noted some matters on this subject in Book II for St. Athanasius.] in the magnitude of their riches.

After Judas recognized his crime, he ended his life with a noose. What will you do, who deserve to be punished with a greater penalty in proportion to the greatness of your wrongdoing, when—though late—you come to recognize that you have acted wickedly? When your eyes, now poisoned with festering heretical venom, begin to see the things which they can now see least of all? And yet, if you are willing to believe, what you do in ignorance must be forgiven you, just as you see that it was forgiven the blessed apostle Paul. But if not, you will be like Judas, descending into infernal night, and then you will say to those who now compel you to do these things—namely, to your fellow Arians: “I sinned with you in denying God’s only Son; I sinned by granting you authority to deny his eternal mercy.”

Then, when you begin to know that we rightly confess one eternity of Father, Son, and [Col. 0991B] Holy Spirit; when you begin to see that there is one greatness and one power in the Father, in his only Son, and in the holy Paraclete Spirit—where then will be those who urged you to perpetrate this sacrilege, so that you might say to them: “I repent that I ran with you, enemies of God; that with you I persecuted God’s house”? They will undoubtedly be with you in Gehenna. Where then will be the wealth of your kingdom, which contributes not to your salvation but to your eternal destruction? We indeed pray that God may deign to reveal the truth to you, the enemy of your own salvation, and that you may emerge from such great dangers.

But it takes no effort to estimate how much more eminent than Judas Iscariot you are in wickedness, since you summoned the entire world to deny his divinity. [Note: [Col. 0991C] Namely, when the Synod of Rimini, attended by Western bishops, and the Synod of Seleucia, attended by Eastern bishops, were convened in the same year, 359, by Constantius’ command [Col. 0991D], in order that all disputes between Arians and Catholics might at last be settled. But by their habitual heretical frauds, through which they sought to overthrow the Nicene faith—what was done at the Council of Rimini we have already stated; at Seleucia the Semi-Arians prevailed and decreed that the Son was ὁμοιούσιος, “of like substance,” confirming the second formula of the Arian faith, issued from the Antiochene conventicle of A.D. 341.] Judas [Col. 0991C] betrayed the Lord only to those who had not yet believed in him; but you have even considered it fitting to incite to the denial of his divinity those who had already believed. Judas compelled no one to perish with him; but you, with military force, fight against us whom you know to believe as the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs believed. Surely it takes no great [Col. 0992A] effort to consider the distance between you and Judas.

You call me abusive because, desiring that neither I nor those entrusted to me should be wounded by your deadly doctrine, I say that you are full of disease and therefore must be avoided by God’s servants [Note: [Col. 0991D] “That you are.” Vatican manuscript.], lest, becoming diseased ourselves, we perish together through this single plague of yours. The apostle says to the Corinthians: “Would that you endured [Note: [Col. 0991D] Ancient Version: “Bore … my folly.” Greek in the Boerner manuscript, with Lucifer: μικρὸν τῆς ἀφροσύνης μου, “a little of my folly.”] a little of my folly—but indeed bear with me. For I am jealous [Note: [Col. 0991D] “For I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy.” Lucifer therefore appears to have read Ζηλῶν γὰρ ὑμᾶς θεῷ ζηλῶ. The Claromontane and Saint-Germain manuscripts in Mill likewise prefer this reading. Galland.] over you with God’s jealousy. For I determined to present you to one husband, as a chaste virgin, to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning [Note: [Col. 0991D] “By his cunning … from the chastity and simplicity that are in Christ.” Ancient Version. The Luciferian reading, “from chastity,” is also found in Ambrose, Augustine, Prosper, and Gaudentius, apparently as an interpretation of τοῦ ἁπλότητος, “simplicity.” See Mill on this passage. Galland. But in Greek Codex Colbertinus I, and then the Royal and Saint-Germain manuscripts in Sabatier, one reads ἁγνότητος καὶ ἁπλότητος; and in the Greek-Latin Boerner manuscript in the same editor, ἁπλότητος καὶ ἁγνότητος. Since ἁγνότης in Greek is “chastity” in Latin, those fathers who wrote “from chastity” [Col. 0992D] in the Pauline text took the expression not from an interpretation of τοῦ ἁπλότητος but from the Greek word ἁγνότης itself and from the Greek text. In the codex used by Lucifer perhaps τὸ καὶ ἁπλότητος, “and simplicity,” was lacking.] your minds should be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ Jesus” (II Cor. XI, 1). Therefore you seem to me to be…

Contumelious, because I fear that through your blasphemies you may corrupt the chastity which we have in Christ Jesus; because we fear lest, as your beloved serpent [Col. 0992B] by its craft deceived Eve, you may deceive us away from God and make us liable to death. You call me obstinate because I call you a deceitful worker, a pseudo-Christian. These charges were not first brought against you by me. For you hear the blessed apostle designate you a deceitful worker, a false apostle: “For such false apostles are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ. And no wonder; for Satan himself transforms himself as an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also transform themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end is according to their works.” Hence I seem proud to you because, knowing you from your deeds, I say that you are among those whom the Holy Spirit through the apostle foretold would be such.

If you are not a deceitful worker, refute me. For I know that [Col. 0992C] you pretend to be a Christian, though you are an Arian, and that you wished to make all of us servants of him whose attendant you are. [Note: For *satelles*, “attendant,” “minister,” as *prophetis* or *prophetes* for *propheta*, “prophet.” Til. and la Cerda.] If you are not a deceitful worker, prove us wrong. For we see that in some respects you pretend to be devout [Note: In almsgiving and sacred gifts, concerning which see Book I, against St Athanasius.], while you exercise all your impiety against us Christians. If you are not a deceitful worker, how was it that, while pretending to establish peace, [Note: More has been said on this in the book *On Not Meeting with Heretics*. But since the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God* was written after the Council of Rimini, perhaps Lucifer alludes to what we read in Socrates, Book II, chapter 37, ed. Valesius: namely, that Constantius, for the sake of concord, decreed those two councils, one held at Rimini and the other at Seleucia; but his design met with no happy success.] you attempted to destroy the whole Church of God and to dissolve the peace entrusted to it through the only Son [Note: “The Son of God.” Vatican manuscript.] of God?

For I could not thereafter possess the Lord’s peace, once I had done what you commanded me contrary to the Lord’s precept, once finally I had begun, as you deny him, to deny God’s only Son himself. If you have not transformed yourself into an apostle of Christ—who, as though the entire care of the Church truly belonged to you, are so solicitous, namely, that no Catholic bishop should preside over a church anywhere, and that no one should remain who can confess himself a Christian—[Note: Understand: “prove us wrong,” that is, prove it against us, if you have not transformed yourself, etc. Gallandius printed *in Apostolum Christi* and substituted *quia* for *qui*, to produce a coherent sense; but the sense is established by Lucifer’s own words, which we interpret thus: “Prove against us that you have not assumed the apostolic office wholly at your own discretion, you who,” etc. These words are plainly ironic and reproach Constantius for interfering in ecclesiastical affairs to the ruin of the Catholic faith.] you remove Catholic bishops, ordain heretics, and write dreadful threats lest perhaps a disturbance arise. Surely anyone ignorant of the facts, seeing you do these things, supposes you a Christian. But we, instructed by the blessed apostle, know that Satan, who carries out all these things against the holy Church through you, has transformed himself as an angel of light; therefore we cannot wonder [Col. 0993B] if we see you as his minister, transformed as though into a minister of righteousness, while we exhort you to righteousness. [Note: That is, we urge and invite you to uphold and preserve righteousness; we remind you of righteousness. Til. Gallandius appends to the words “we exhort [you] to righteousness” this note: “Let learned men judge how these words cohere with what precedes.” But they seem to cohere rightly thus: “If we exhort you, who wish to appear a minister of righteousness, to true righteousness.”]

Would that you would turn yourself to this, whereby you might be believed to be God’s servant, whereby you might be judged and understood to be a Christian. Whenever we tell you that you could not have become a denier of God’s only Son unless you were full of a hostile spirit, you are accustomed to say that we wrong you. Although I have already proved in many places that you come against God’s household with your hearts stirred up by unclean spirits, take still further from the Acts of the Apostles what happened.

“It happened, as we were going to prayer, that a certain girl having a spirit of Python met us, [Note: “Met us, who brought much gain,” etc. Old Version; the Cambridge manuscript has *reditum*, “return,” with Lucifer.] who by divination brought much profit to her masters. This girl followed Paul [Note: “Paul and us”; the Cambridge manuscript: “Paul and us she cried … These men … proclaim.” Old Version.] and us, crying out, ‘These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us [Col. 0994A] [Note: “To you.” Vatican manuscript, with the Greek ὑμῖν, “to you.”] the way of salvation.’ This she did for many days. But Paul, grieved by this, turned to the spirit and said, [Note: Old Version: “But Paul, grieved, and having turned, said to the spirit.”] ‘I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.’ And it came out that very hour. But when her masters saw that the hope of their profit had gone, [Note: “The hope of their gain … having seized Paul and Silas, they led [them] into the marketplace before the magistrates.” The same version uses *Silam* for *Sileam*, as does Sabatier here and below.] they seized Paul and Silas, dragged them into the marketplace before the magistrates, and brought [Note: “Bringing them before the magistrates, they said.” The same version.] them, saying, ‘These men disturb our city, being Jews, and they preach a custom [Note: “Customs which … it is not lawful [for us] … Romans established.” The same version.] which we Romans may neither receive nor practise.’ And the whole crowd rose up [Note: “The crowd rose … having torn [their garments] … they ordered.” The same version.] against them, and the magistrates, having stripped off [Note: “Torn off,” in the Latin, as in the Old Version. What these words mean here Millius frankly confesses that he does not know, *Prolegomena* §774. I would judge that Lucifer wrote *disruptis* or *diruptis tunicis*, “with their tunics torn apart.” Greek περιῤῥήξαντες, “tearing apart.” Galland.] their tunics, ordered them to be beaten with rods. And after they had inflicted many wounds upon them, [Note: “But having laid many stripes upon them, they sent them into prison … ordering [the jailer] to keep them.” Old Version.] they sent them to prison, commanding the keeper of the prison to guard them carefully. When he [Note: “When he had received such a command … [he put them] into the inner prison … and fastened [them] securely in the stocks.” Thus Sabatier reads in Lucifer. “Into the lowest part of the prison, and he fastened their feet in wood.”] had received such a command, he put them into the lowest prison and fastened [Col. 0994B] their feet in the stocks.

“But about [Note: “But about midnight,” with the Cambridge manuscript. “But at midnight Paul and Silas, praying, sang a hymn to God; and the prisoners heard them.” Old Version.] midnight, while Paul and Silas were praying and singing a hymn to God, the other prisoners heard them. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that [Note: “So that [the foundations] were shaken … and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds,” etc. The same version.] the foundations of the prison were shaken; and the doors were opened and all bonds were loosed. The keeper of the prison awoke, and when he saw the prison doors open, drew his sword to kill himself, [Note: “But the keeper, having awakened … and seeing the prison doors open, drawing his sword, began to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had escaped.” The same version.] thinking that the prisoners had fled. But Paul cried out with a loud voice: ‘Do yourself no harm; for we are all here.’ [Note: “Here,” with the Cambridge manuscript. “We are present.” Old Version. Sabatier also reads *sumus*, “we are,” in Lucifer. It also has *nihil* for *nil*.] On hearing this, the keeper of the prison asked for a light, entered, and trembling fell at the feet of Paul and Silas. [Note: The Old Version omits: “But asking for a light he entered, and, trembling, fell before Paul and Silas.” Greek ἐπὶ τοὺς πόδας, “at the feet,” with Lucifer.] And when he had brought them out, he said: ‘Lords, what must I do to be saved?’ [Note: Old Version: “And bringing them outside … may be saved.” Cambridge manuscript agrees with Lucifer.] But they said: ‘Believe in God Jesus, and you and your household shall be saved.’ [Note: “But they … in the Lord Jesus Christ … and all,” etc. Old Version; see slightly below.] And they spoke to him [Col. 0994C] the word of the Lord, together with [Note: Σὺν πᾶσι, “with all,” in certain Greek manuscripts. Old Version: “and all.”] all who were in his house. And taking [Note: “And taking them at that hour … he himself and all who belonged to him immediately.” Old Version. Sabatier reads “he washed their wounds” in Lucifer.] them in that hour of the night, he washed them from their wounds; and he [Col. 0995A] himself was baptized with all his household. And bringing [Note: “And when he had brought them into his house … he set a table before them, and rejoiced, believing in God.” Old Version. Sabatier reads here: “Into his house, he set a table before them, and he rejoiced.” The Cambridge manuscript has “with all his household,” as Lucifer does.] them into his house, he set a table before them, and they feasted [Note: “He feasted.” Latin.] with all his household, believing in the Lord.”

Therefore, just as that spirit of Python, hearing the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, was at once driven out of its dwelling, stirred up the whole populace of the city against the preachers of the majesty of God’s only Son, so those unclean spirits stirred you and your followers against us, his servants. Do not doubt that you are driven by the same spirits by whom those who rose against Paul and Silas were driven, when you see yourself made such a persecutor of God’s religion as was that mob, which had not yet believed in God’s only Son; it was such only because it did not possess God’s Spirit, as you also are proved to be.

For that you cannot have the Holy Spirit unless you believe [Col. 0995B] in God’s only Son is made manifest by the conduct of that keeper of the prison. Although he was certainly one of that opposing people, yet after he believed, because he was now governed by the Holy Spirit—the Spirit by whom Paul and Silas were governed—he embraced no course except that of those for whose sake he had seen the prison doors spontaneously opened. [Note: That is: it came about that, after he believed … he embraced, etc.] So you, now driven by a contrary spirit, unless you believe in God’s only Son as we also believe, can have within you nothing but the spirit of our adversary.

For that keeper said to the glorious Paul and Silas: “Lords, what must I do to be saved?” But they said: “Believe in our Lord Jesus, and you and your household shall be saved” (ibid. 30). It is therefore established that you are not saved, because you have not yet believed in the Lord Jesus. Nor can you maintain that you have believed in him while you persecute him. Or do you suppose that you do not persecute him himself in us? If you do not persecute him in us, how does he himself say to Saul: “Why do you persecute me? [Note: “Do you persecute [me]? I am Jesus, whom you persecute. It is hard,” etc. Vatican manuscript.] It is hard for you to kick [Note: “To kick against the goad.” Old Version.] against the goad” (ibid. IX, 4)?

What was Saul doing when he heard this from the Lord? Precisely what you are doing. For he denied God’s only Son just as you deny him. Paul, who was then a persecutor and later began to suffer persecution, [Col. 0996A] did not persecute Christians because they believed, as you believe, that there was a time when he did not exist, that he was made from nothing, and that he is a true [Note: “Is not.” Latin. Gallandius added the same particle *non*, “not,” without consulting the Luciferian text. For in this place Lucifer reproaches not merely the impiety but in a sense the very stupidity of the Arians, who taught that the Son of God was truly Son, but not ὁμοούσιος, that is, consubstantial; whereas he cannot be a true Son who is not of the same substance as the Father. Thus Lucifer mocks both them and Constantius, since they maintained that he was the Father’s true Son whom they said existed when he had not existed and was made from nothing. See Petavius, *On the Trinity*, Book II, chapter 10. The Arians, moreover, attached a deceptive appearance to their words and understood the word “Son” not in its proper and stricter sense, but in the looser sense in which the same term is transferred to rational creatures; hence human beings too are called sons of God.] Son. Rather, he persecuted them because they dared to confess God’s only Son and declared that they believed as Christians that the eternity of Father and Son is one, that the divinity is one, and that the power in Father and Son is one. Paul abhorred these things, thinking Christians mistaken; but after he was enlightened by him whom he denied, after he learned from the books of Moses and from all the volumes of the prophets, he immediately began to defend the things he had attacked—those things which those whom he persecuted had defended before he believed.

But who was ever so mad as you Arians are, or as Photinus of the Sirmians is—who is rightly called *Scotinus*—[Col. 0996B] as to believe in a creature, in one who existed when he did not exist, in one created from nothing? It is therefore clear that all of you who do not believe as the glorious Church believes are led by a hostile spirit. You cannot be freed from that hostile spirit unless you believe that he is the true Son of God.

“You bishops insult me,” you say. Why do we seem insulting to you? Surely because we say: “Why do you pretend to be a Christian? You are plainly an Arian; you are plainly an enemy of God’s religion.” For this reason we seem injurious in your eyes and those of your party. But see what the most blessed apostle said that we bishops should do against you wolves:

“You know, from the first day on which I entered [Note: “From the time when I came into Asia, how,” etc. Old Version; Cambridge manuscript: “how,” as Lucifer.] Asia, how I was with you the whole time, serving the Lord in [Note: “With, and in trials.” Old Version.] all humility and tears and [Col. 0996C] trials that befell me through the plots of the Jews; how [Note: Greek: Ὡς οὐδὲν ὑπεστειλάμεν τῶν συμφερόντων, “How I withheld nothing of the things that were profitable.” “I withheld what was profitable, so as not to proclaim … teach you,” etc., Old Version. The Cambridge manuscript also omits *vos*, “you.”] I withheld nothing of what was profitable, how I proclaimed [Note: Greek τοῦ ἀναγγεῖλαι, “to proclaim.” Moreover, Millius testifies that the negative particle μή, “not,” is absent also in the Cambridge manuscript, as in Gallandius’s note.] it to you and taught publicly and from house to house, testifying [Note: “Testifying also to Jews and Gentiles the things … and the faith which [is] in the Lord Jesus Christ,” Old Version. Greek, with Lucifer: Ἰουδαίοις τε καὶ Ἕλλησι τὴν εἰς τὸν Θεὸν μετάνοιαν, “to Jews and Greeks repentance toward God”; and in certain Greek manuscripts τὴν, “the,” is absent after πίστιν, “faith,” as is Χριστόν, “Christ.”] to Jews and Greeks repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus. And now, behold, bound [Note: “Behold, I … to Jerusalem … things to come,” Old Version. Sabatier also has “to Jerusalem.”] in spirit, I go to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that [Note: “But only that the Holy Spirit testifies to me, saying that … remain,” Old Version. In some Greek manuscripts, κατὰ πάσας πόλεις, “through all cities,” and εἰς Ἱεροσολύμοις, “in Jerusalem,” occur, with Lucifer.] the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying: ‘Bonds and tribulations await me in [Col. 0997A] Jerusalem.’ But [Note: “But I make account of no one; nor do I hold my life dearer, that I may finish my course with joy, and the ministry which … Jesus, to testify to the Gospel,” etc., Old Version. Cambridge manuscript: “My life dear to me, than to finish my course,” etc. Some Greek manuscripts read διακονίαν λόγου, “ministry of the word,” and Ἰουδαίοις καὶ Ἕλλησι, “to Jews and Greeks,” in the Cambridge and Stephanus manuscripts cited by Millius, with Lucifer; Sabatier reads “my life dearer.”] I count my life as nothing dear to myself, rather than fail to finish my course and the ministry of the word which I received from the Lord: to testify to Jews and Greeks the Gospel of God’s grace.” [Note: In our Tilian edition one reads “the Gospel of God’s grace”; hence Gallandius wrongly judges that the editors of the Paris Library of the Fathers copied from Tilius “the Gospel of God’s glory.”]

“And now I know that you all, among [Note: Old Version: “Through whom I passed, preaching the kingdom [Col. 0997D] of God.”] whom I travelled, preaching [Note: “I travelled preaching.” Vatican manuscript. The Cambridge manuscript cited by Millius prefers “the kingdom of Jesus,” τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.] the kingdom of the Lord Jesus, will see my face no more. Therefore [Note: Old Version: “Wherefore … on this day … of all of you.” Cambridge manuscript: “because of which,” as Lucifer.] I testify to you on this day that I am innocent of the blood of all; for I did not refrain [Note: “For I did not shrink back.” Old Version.] from proclaiming [Note: “So as not to announce to you the whole counsel of God.” The same version.] to you the whole will of God. Take heed [Note: “Take heed therefore to yourselves and to the whole flock.” The same version; Cambridge manuscript agrees with Lucifer.] to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit placed you as bishops to govern the Church of the Lord, [Note: Greek, with the Vulgate: “the Church of God.” Very many manuscripts and Fathers retain this reading; it is therefore to be preferred to Lucifer’s “of the Lord,” although the latter is known to occur in other manuscripts and is found in other ecclesiastical writers. See Millius on this passage. Galland. Old Version: “through his own blood.”] which he acquired by his own blood. I know [Note: “For I know this: that after my departure [they] will come,” etc. Old Version. *Hoc*, “this,” is omitted also in the Cambridge manuscript. Greek εἰσελεύσονται, “they will enter,” “come in,” with Lucifer. For *lupi graves*, “grave wolves,” Sabatier has *lupi rapaces*, “ravening wolves.”] that after my departure grievous wolves will enter among you, sparing not the flock. From [Note: “And from … men speaking … after themselves.” Old Version. Sabatier reads “draw away” for “draw.”] among yourselves men will arise and speak perverse things, to draw disciples after themselves. Therefore [Col. 0997B] be watchful, remembering [Note: “Keeping remembrance, and warning.” The same version.] that for three years, night and day, I did not cease with tears to warn every one of you” (ibid. XX, 18).

When you see these to be the apostle’s commands, what do you order me to do, so that I may not seem insulting to you? Surely you command me to be silent and allow you, one of those grievous wolves designated by him, to ravage God’s flock in whatever manner you please. We see you as the wolves whom the Holy Spirit deigned through the apostle, the chosen vessel, to foretell; wolves who have attempted to seize the whole flock of God. And are we, bishops [Note: Gallandius printed *nos episcopi*, “we bishops”; but the sense is “we, whom [he calls] bishops.”] whom the blessed apostle says the Holy Spirit appointed to govern [Note: “To rule.” Latin.] God’s Church, obliged to spare you, a wolf? Must we fear the diadem of your kingdom, your earring [Note: An ornament of the ears common to men and women alike, but much more customary for men in the East, especially rulers. Pliny, Book XI, chapter 37. Indeed, in the East, wearing gold in that place—that is, in the ears—is considered an adornment even for men.], and your right-hand ornament (*dextrocheria*) [Note: The word appears compounded from Latin and Greek, denoting an ornament worn on the right hand. Til. and la Cerda. It is plainly from Latin *dexter*, “right,” and Greek χείρ, “hand.” Du Cange in his *Glossary*, on the authority of Ugutio, calls it an ornament of the right arm; but if one considers the word’s derivation, it appears to be a kind of bracelet adorning the right hand. It was nevertheless common to men and women, especially in the East, since those peoples delight in ornaments of this kind.], must we honour the distinguished garments which you think yours, and [Col. 0997C] despise the Creator and Ruler of all things?

Who is more foolish than you, that you say: “I suffer injury from Lucifer—the emperor from a needy man”? You do not even deign to say, “from a bishop,” because you have been recognized as a wolf and have deserved rejection. You thought to burden me with such odium that you asserted God’s servant had insulted you, the emperor. If you think us injurious, hear what the blessed Paul answered the high priest who forbade the preaching of God’s only Son:

“Paul, looking intently, [Note: Greek ἀτενίσας, “having looked intently.” Old Version: “But looking intently at the council … I have lived before God unto this day.” Sabatier has *dicit*, “says,” for *dixit*, “said.”] said to the council, ‘Men, brethren, I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience until this day.’ But the high priest Ananias [Note: Our Tilian edition reads *Ananias* thus; in others it is corruptly *Annas*.] commanded those standing [Note: “Standing by him.” Vatican manuscript.] around him to strike Paul on the mouth. Then Paul said to him: ‘God will begin to strike you, whitewashed wall! And do you sit to judge [Note: “Judging me … and contrary to the law,” etc. Old Version.] me according to the law, and contrary to the law command that I be struck?’” (ibid. XXIII, 1).

Therefore, if the sacred law cannot judge the blessed Paul insulting because he said this to an unjust [Col. 0998B] judge, neither can you justly call me proud when I speak truth to you and call you what you are. You designate me guilty of insults; but I ask you, tell me to whom you can complain about me. To God? How can you complain to him whom you do not know? How, when you are alien to his house? Or if you complain to yourself, what will you do—a man who cannot in any way harm God’s servants? If you torture us, we are the more healed; if you torment us, we are the more refreshed; if you kill us, we shall live the more.

Because I dare call you the forerunner of Antichrist, you call me injurious. If your deeds do not show that you are this, examine with great care even the book of the most holy prophet Daniel, and you will find yourself to be one of those foretold persecutors of God’s religion. “In the first year of Belshazzar [Col. 0998C] king of the Chaldeans, Daniel saw a dream and visions [Note: Sabatier: “a vision.”] of his head upon his bed, and he wrote his dream: I Daniel was looking, and behold, the four winds of heaven were rushing [Col. 0999A] [Note: In the same edition: “They were contending on the great sea.” Our edition, with the Greek, προέβαλον εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν τὴν μεγάλην, “they broke forth upon the great sea.”] upon the great sea. And four beasts [Note: “Great beasts came up from the sea,” in Sabatier.] came up from the sea, each exceeding the other in size. The first was like a lion [Note: Sabatier: “The first [was] like a lioness and had eagle’s wings; I looked until its wings were plucked out. And it was lifted from the earth and stood upon feet like a human being,” etc. He rightly supplies what is lacking in our edition. But after “its feathers” one should read “as those of an eagle,” as in the Greek, καὶ πτερὰ αὐτῆς ὡς ἀετοῦ; and after “feet” it reads “of a human being,” ἀνθρώπου.] and had wings. It rose from the earth and stood upon human feet, and a human heart was given to it. And behold, another beast like a bear, [Note: “Like a she-bear.” Vatican manuscript.] and it stood on one side; and three ribs were in its mouth amid [Note: “And in the midst.” Sabatier. But *and* is absent from the Greek.] its teeth; and it was told: ‘Rise, and devour much flesh.’ After [Note: Sabatier: “After these things I was looking, and behold, a beast,” etc.] this beast I looked, and behold another beast like a leopard; it had four wings of a bird upon it, and the beast had four heads, and power was given to it. After [Note: With the Greek, ὀπίσω τούτου, “after this one.” Sabatier: “After these things I was looking.”] this I looked, and behold a fourth beast, terrible, wondrous, and exceedingly strong. Its iron teeth devoured and crushed, and it trampled the remainder under its feet; [Note: “It trampled.” The same edition.] and this beast was greater than the other beasts which had appeared before it, and it had ten horns. And I observed its horns, and behold another, smaller horn arose among [Col. 0999B] them, and three horns [Note: “The horns which were before it were uprooted,” etc. The same edition. Greek: ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ, “before it,” as in our edition.] which were before it were uprooted before it; and behold, this horn had human eyes and a mouth speaking great things.

“I looked until thrones were set in place and the Ancient of Days sat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool; his throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire. A river of fire shone before him; thousands upon thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court [Note: Gallandius judges that Lucifer wrote *judicium*, “court,” after the Septuagint, κριτήριον ἐκάθισε, “the tribunal sat.” We retain the Old Version.] sat, and the books were opened. Then I looked because of the sound of the great words which that horn spoke, until the beast perished and was destroyed, and its body was given to be burned. The dominion of the remaining beasts was taken away, and length of life was given them until [Note: Septuagint: ἕως καιροῦ καὶ καιροῦ, “until a time and times.” Through repetition of the word, an inattentive copyist omitted the latter words. Galland. But the reading accords with the Old Version.] a time. I saw in [Note: “In a vision.” Sabatier.] the vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven [Col. 0999C] came to the Ancient of Days; he came before him and was presented to him. And there were given to him kingdom, honour, and dominion; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues serve [Note: “Will serve.” Sabatier and Gallandius, from the Greek Septuagint δουλεύσουσιν, “they will serve.”] him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion which shall never pass away, and his kingdom shall never be destroyed.

“My spirit shuddered within me, and I Daniel [Note: Sabatier: “I Daniel was terrified in them.” Yet the words after “Daniel” are absent even from the Greek.] was troubled by the visions [Col. 1000A] of my head. I approached one of those standing by and sought from him the truth concerning all these things. He told me the truth and made known to me the interpretation of the words: ‘These four great beasts are four [Note: “Four kingdoms which shall arise upon the earth,” in Sabatier. The Roman Greek edition agrees with our edition. Gallandius, following the Septuagint, reads: “four kingdoms … which shall be removed from the earth.”] kingdoms which shall arise upon the earth; and the saints of the Most High God [Note: Latin judges that *Dei*, “God,” should be removed here and a little below, but without any reason, since it is read in the Greek except at the end.] shall receive the kingdom and possess it for ever.’ Then I diligently sought concerning the fourth beast, which was very terrible beyond the other beasts: its teeth [Note: Sabatier: “Its teeth and claws were iron.” Our edition, with the Greek: “its teeth were iron, and its claws bronze.”] were iron and its claws bronze; it devoured and crushed and trampled the remainder under its feet; and concerning its tenth horn, which was upon its head, and concerning the other horn which arose and struck down the first three horns, whose eyes and mouth spoke great things and whose appearance seemed greater than the others. [Note: Sabatier punctuates thus: “than the others. It seemed,” etc.] That horn made war upon the saints and prevailed [Note: So also Irenaeus, Book V, chapter 25. Sabatier: “prevailed.”] against them, until the Ancient of Days came [Col. 1000B] and gave judgment to the saints of the Most High God; and the time came, and the saints received the kingdom.

“And he said: ‘The fourth beast shall be a fourth kingdom upon the earth, which shall surpass all [Note: Sabatier: “all kingdoms, and it shall crush. Ten,” etc. “It shall crush. And its ten horns are ten kings.” Latin, in the sense of the Vulgate. The author follows the letter: ὑπερέξει πάσας τὰς βασιλείας, “it shall surpass all kingdoms.”] kingdoms, devour the whole earth, trample it down, and break it in pieces. Its ten horns shall be ten kings; ten kings shall arise, and after them another shall arise, who shall surpass in evil all who were before him, and shall humble three [Note: “Three kings.” Latin, with the Vulgate and Gallandius from the Septuagint.] and shall speak words against the Most High God, wear out [Note: As in the Roman Greek edition, παλαιώσει, and Theodotion in the Hexapla. Sabatier: “crush.”] the saints of the Most High God, and devise to change times and law. They shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time. And the court shall sit, and it shall remove his kingdom, to exterminate and destroy it unto the end. And kingdom and dominion and the greatness of the kingdoms [Note: “Of their kingdoms.” Latin. Old Version: “Of the kingdoms which are under all heaven … of the Most High; and his kingdom [is] an everlasting kingdom, and all authorities shall serve and obey him.” Irenaeus, Book V, chapter 34, agrees with our edition: “of the Most High God; and his kingdom [is] everlasting … obey.”] shall be given to the saints of the Most High God; and his kingdom is everlasting, and all shall [Col. 1000C] serve and obey him’” (Dan. VII, 1).

I ought indeed to have inserted only that part which declares, through your deeds, to which of the beasts you are like. But so that you might know that you shall be in that Gehenna into which the glorious Daniel reports that beast was cast, unless you correct yourself; and so that you might understand how those whom you persecute are to reign eternally, [Col. 1001A] established in the Lord’s kingdom—we append all these matters. Likewise, I judged that the whole revelation should be applied to this purpose: that you might satisfy yourself, at least by reading, that you tyrants and persecutors of God’s religion were called beasts. For I desire to clear myself before your conscience infected by the poisons of Arian doctrine: before you, not a religious man but a destroyer of religion, I am not—as you allege—insulting because I call you a wild beast or savage brute, when you see yourselves called thus and these names applied to you according to your deeds.

Moreover, it is evident that you bear the likeness of that fourth beast, and that you desire to fulfil what was foretold it would fulfil. It is written concerning Antichrist, whom you resemble [Col. 1001B] or are judged to be: “He shall speak words against the Most High Lord, wear out the saints of the Most High God, devise to change times and law, and they shall be given into his hand” (Dan. VII, 25). You have already done these things and are doing them. For when you say, “The Son of God is not true God, but was made from nothing,” you speak words against God. Since we Christians maintain one divinity for the Father and his only Son, and you attack this our confession, asserting of the Son that there was a time when he was not and that he was made from nothing, you surely prove yourself either Antichrist or at least his forerunner.

For you can be understood as none other than either the forerunner of Antichrist or Antichrist himself, you who dare call the apostolic and evangelical faith heretical and attempt to claim your own [Col. 1001C] blasphemy as Catholic faith. You feel that you suffer injury because we call you a beast. Yet you are found devising to change the faith—that is, that we should not believe as patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs believed, but should establish belief as your fellow-destroyed Arius did—and you say you are not rightly called a beast, when the most holy prophet called you a beast because you were going to do these things? Constantius, you are not less than Antichrist in unbelief; for with iron teeth you do not cease to devour God’s servants.

Why say more? Antichrist will do nothing except bring about the denial of God’s only Son. This is what your most unclean mind, fattened with folly, does. But however fiercely you rage, your times will pass, will pass; and there will come those in which you will see yourself, [Col. 1001D] unless you provide for yourself, set in that river of fire. You will then see those whom you cruelly persecute because they refuse to perish with you, not in the place of torments where you will be, but with the holy angels always rendering thanks and praises to God—while you are in that flaming stream. I do not wish you to wonder if the glorious Daniel calls you a beast.

… designated, when the blessed Paul too called your associates “Cretans”: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies” (Titus 1:12).

> [Note: “[Col. 1001D] Conelectis, or combestiis.” Latin. Whether something lies here that ought to be referred to history, when he calls them his own Cretans, cannot be guessed; certainly he means the Arians, to whom, like Cretans, the designation “beasts” and Paul’s words apply most aptly. “Collegis” for “associates.” Galland.]

And below: “For this reason rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, not giving heed to Jewish fables and lies—

> [Note: “[Col. 1001D] For which reason . . . commandments of men turning away, [Col. 1002D] etc.” Old Version.]

—of men who turn themselves away from the truth” (ibid. 13).

> [Note: “[Col. 1002D] Perhaps “commandments,” as in the Old Version, since a little later he uses this word in Paul’s sense.]

This is why we bishops seem injurious to you: because we rebuke and reprove you for daring to turn yourself away from the truth; because you chose, abandoning God’s commandments, to cling to the blasphemies and commandments of men; because, finally, abandoning God, you embraced idolatry. This is why I seem your enemy: because I want you to walk according to the apostle’s command and not according to the commandments of Arius and the Jews.

Against these most just charges of ours, seeing yourself overcome by truth, you are accustomed to say: “Holy Scripture commands that you be subject to kings and all who live in high station [Col. 1002B]; and do you dare, Lucifer, to bring such great and such things against me?” You observe these things; you understand those things which command that you be honoured. But those which command what you must do, you pretend not to know: those by which the Lord admonishes you to obey the priests; those which press upon you that you ought to show yourself one among all your fellow servants, and—if you wish to be found God’s servant—not to call yourself superior to anyone.

The blessed apostle says to Titus: “Speak these things, and exhort—

> [Note: “[Col. 1002D] Encourage.” Old Version.]

—and rebuke with all authority; let no one despise you” (ibid. 2:15). If you are a Christian, since you too are one of those on whose account he said, “Speak these things, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority; let no one despise you,” you must certainly hear me reproving you with all authority and not despise me. Then you will be a Christian, if [Col. 1002C] you do not despise me when I exhort you to persevere as a Christian. But if you despise me, you will be found no longer to belong among Christians; for, had you been a Christian, you would not have despised him whom God appointed to instruct His people, and to whom the apostle said: “Speak these things, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority; let no one despise you” (ibid.).

For what do I exhort you to do? Only this: not to be a murderer; not to persecute God’s house; to cease torturing, proscribing, deporting, confining in prison, slaughtering, destroying in various ways, and killing those whom you see to be Christians; finally, to cease blaspheming the only Son of God; to embrace the apostolic faith which you call heretical—namely, our faith, which the bishops set forth at Nicaea against you and all heretics [Col. 1002D]; to believe as we do, and to deign to reject the idolatry established through Arius, your teacher; to proclaim yourself a Christian, not an Arian; and—

> [Note: “[Col. 1002D] That is, that you cease bringing false charges against God’s priests, falsely accusing them; here he says *mittere* (‘to bring’) for *immittere* (‘to bring against’). Til. and, from him, Galland.]

—to cease bringing false accusations against God’s priests. This is my correction; this is my rebuke. The apostle tells me to rebuke you with all authority, and you say: “Lucifer wrongs me.” You do not say: “God’s priest [Col. 1003A] warns and exhorts me according to the precepts of the holy law, that I may be able to lead a life most acceptable to God.”

For because you say that we owe you obedience, know that we recognize ourselves as debtors in rendering obedience not to you alone but to all who live in high station.

> [Note: “[Col. 1003C] *Repraesentandis*.” Galland.]

For the apostle says: “Admonish them to be subject and obedient to rulers and magistrates—

> [Note: “[Col. 1003C] ‘Powers, and obedient.’” Old Version.]

—to be ready for every good work; to blaspheme no one; not to be contentious—

> [Note: “[Col. 1003C] ‘Not quarrelsome, but moderate,’ etc.” Same version.]

—but gentle, showing all meekness toward all men. For we too were once foolish and unbelieving—

> [Note: “[Col. 1003C] Sabatier reads ‘unbelieving.’]

—wandering, slaves to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another—

> [Note: “[Col. 1003C] ‘Each other.’ Old Version.]

—but when the kindness and humanity of God our Saviour shone forth, not by works of righteousness which we had done, but according to [Col. 1003B] His mercy He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom He poured out upon us—

> [Note: “[Col. 1003D] ‘Upon us.’ Same version.]

—abundantly—

> [Note: “[Col. 1003D] Greek: πλουσίως, ‘richly, abundantly.’ The Vulgate: *abunde*. But I change nothing. For this is the common rendering throughout, as also that of the Old Translator whom Lucifer follows. Wisdom 7:11: Καὶ ἀναρίθμητος πλοῦτος ἐν χερσὶν αὐτῆς (σοφίας): ‘And innumerable wealth is in her hands (of Wisdom)’; Latin: ‘And innumerable honourableness is through her hands (of Wisdom).’ Ibid., v. 13: Τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτῆς οὐκ ἀποκρυπτομαι: ‘I do not conceal her wealth’; Latin: ‘I do not conceal her honourableness.’ Likewise Sirach 11:14: Πτωχεία καὶ πλοῦτος παρὰ Κυρίου ἐστί: ‘Poverty and wealth are from the Lord’; Latin: ‘Poverty and honourableness are from the Lord.’ Ibid. 24:23: Καὶ τὰ ἄνθη μου, καρπὸς δόξης καὶ πλούτου: ‘And my flowers are the fruit of glory and wealth’; Latin: ‘And my flowers are the fruit of honour and honourableness.’ We omit the rest. Galland.]

—through Jesus Christ our Saviour, that, justified by His grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of life—

> [Note: “[Col. 1003D] ‘Of eternal life,’ Latin, as in the Old Version, the Vulgate, and Greek.]

—” (Titus 3:1).

The apostle therefore admonishes us to be subject in good works, not in evil ones. If it is a good work to kill one who is absent—

> [Note: “[Col. 1003D] Understand this of Athanasius, whose cause Lucifer here defends, as in the preceding books written to Constantius on his behalf.]

—to kill one crying out that he be allowed to clear himself though unheard—

> [Note: “[Col. 1004C] On this word see the beginning of Book I, *For Saint Athanasius*.]

—to punish with you, disregarding every consideration of mercy, one whom we know to be innocent; if it is a good work to deny the only Son of God; if it is a work acceptable to God to abandon the apostolic faith and embrace heresy: then you would rightly say that I acted contrary to the admonitions of Holy Scripture.

I add this: the apostle made mention of those rulers and magistrates [Col. 1003C] who had not yet believed in the only Son of God, so that surely—

> [Note: “[Col. 1004C] Unless Lucifer used *ni* for *ut* [‘so that’], I would suppose that he himself wrote: ‘so that they too.’ Galland. The sense is: that those unbelievers too, moved by our example [Col. 1004D], might believe.]

—by our humility and gentleness, our long patience amid adversities, and our very great obedience in fitting matters, they might be moved to believe. But if you, because you are emperor, pretending that you are one of us, compel us to abandon God and embrace idolatry, must we obey you so that the apostle’s precepts may not seem to have been disregarded?

And yet you, who pretend to be a Christian, tempt Christians to do what you yourself do—[Col. 1004A] that is, to become apostates; you who are still foolish and unbelieving, persisting in your malice, in which the apostle says that we too had been before recognition, before receiving the sacred faith. In what matters were we to yield to you, except in fulfilling what was lawful?

Or when you, blasphemous murderer, say: “Kill those who believe in the only Son of God; be with me persecutors of His house; with me deny Him; reject the apostolic faith; embrace my heresy, of which I have proved a lover with all the powers of my heart”—who is more wretched than you, so that he should not avoid you? Will not someone, recognizing you as a temple of demons when you urge these things, flee from you?

Because you hear these things, you say: “I suffer wrong from Lucifer, a wretched man, and yet an emperor”; but that blasphemous and defiled utterance of yours does not follow: “I hear what I deserve from Lucifer, the Lord’s [Col. 1004B] priest.”

To the Galatians the chosen vessel says: “I marvel that you are so quickly being transferred—

> [Note: “[Col. 1004D] ‘Being transferred from Him.’ Latin, as in the Vulgate and Old Version; in ‘the grace of Jesus Christ,’ but Tertullian too, in Book 5 against Marcion, omits ‘Jesus Christ.’ Greek: Ἐν χάριτι, ‘in grace,’ with Lucifer. Sabatier reads here: ‘You are being transferred. Who [has] you . . . ?’]

—from Him who called you in grace, to another gospel, which is not another, except that—

> [Note: “[Col. 1004D] ‘Except if.’ Old Version. Sabatier seems to read *turbant* for *conturbant* (‘trouble’ for ‘disturb’).]

—there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach—

> [Note: “[Col. 1004D] Thus also Tertullian, Book 5 against Marcion, and in the book *On Prescription*. Old Version: ‘should preach to you.’ Sabatier has *praeter id quod* (‘besides that which’) for *praeterquam* (‘contrary to that which’).]

—to you a gospel contrary to that which we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone should proclaim to you another—

> [Note: “[Col. 1004D] ‘Should proclaim to you [a gospel] other than that which.’ Old Version.]

—than that which you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:6).

And do you suppose that I can judge you to be anything other than accursed, when I find you preaching otherwise than the blessed apostles handed down? Therefore, when you hear from me that I hold you accursed for preaching otherwise than the apostles preached, if you call me injurious, you will be able to recognize that you are lying, if you bear anything human—

> [Note: “[Col. 1004D] Vatican: ‘You are something human,’ etc.; but this is obscure unless the particle *si* (‘if’) is placed before *aliquid* (‘something’). Therefore the reading *gestans* (‘bearing’) gives the clearer sense absolutely; thus in the book *One Must Die for the Son of God*: ‘You bear nothing human except bodily features.’]

—if indeed [Col. 1004C] you see that I call you accursed for this reason: that the blessed apostle has already pronounced you accursed.

You judge me injurious because I call you foolish. But how can I rightly be called injurious by you, when it is plain that I speak the truth—that you are foolish? If the Galatians hear from the blessed apostle, “O foolish—

> [Note: “[Col. 1004D] ‘Senseless.’ Old Version.]

—Galatians” (ibid. 3:1), why do you think that you ought not to be called by the name “foolish”? For if they were called foolish because they had obeyed false brethren—because, giving heed to the suggestions of your serpent-like associates, they had judged that they must keep sabbaths [Col. 1005A] and observe circumcision—how much more rightly are you called foolish, who have become a denier of the only Son of God!

Because I tell you, “Rescue yourself from the rabid Arian dogs; grieve that, by clinging to their malignant counsel, you yourself have become a dog,” you call me insolent. But perhaps you do not know that deniers of the only Son of God are called dogs, fat bulls, children of iniquity, adulterous seed and the seed of a harlot, children of perdition, and wicked seed. If you flee being called thus by God, hear Him Himself say through Isaiah to your fellow blasphemers, the Jews: “Come near here, children of iniquity—

> [Note: “[Col. 1005C] ‘Wicked [children], adulterers’ seed.’ Old Version.]

—adulterous seed and seed of a harlot. In what have you delighted—

> [Note: “[Col. 1005C] ‘Have you played? Against whom . . . against whom have you cast out,’ etc.” Old Version.]

—and against whom have you opened your mouth, and against whom have you thrust forth your tongue? Are you not children of perdition, [Col. 1005B] a wicked seed?” (Isaiah 57:3).

And elsewhere: “See that—

> [Note: “[Col. 1005C] ‘For they are all blinded; they have not all known; dumb dogs, unable to bark, dreaming [Col. 1005D] of a bed, loving slumber.’ Same version. Greek MS Alexandrinus has φρονῆσαι, ‘to understand,’ after ‘have known.’ The Complutensian Greek has πάντες κύνες, ‘all dogs.’ Greek, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Septuagint have νυστάξαι, ‘to slumber,’ with Lucifer.]

—all are blinded; they have not known how to understand; all are dumb dogs, which could not bark, dreaming of a couch—

> [Note: “[Col. 1005D] Sabatier reads *cubili*, ‘of a bed.’]

—loving to slumber; and shameless dogs—

> [Note: “[Col. 1005D] ‘Shameless souls, who have not known satiation . . . evil [men], not knowing understanding,’ etc. Old Version. Perhaps the author wrote *canes improbi anima* (‘shameless dogs [of] soul’). Galland.]

—souls not knowing satiety; and they are wicked, not knowing understanding; all have followed their own ways” (ibid. 56:10).

Who are those to whom, or on account of whom, these things are said? Clearly those whom the only Son of God, speaking through David’s mouth, accuses in the twenty-first Psalm: “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls beset me. They opened their mouth against me like a lion ravening and roaring” (Psalm 21:13). And below: “Many dogs surrounded me; the council of evildoers beset me; they pierced my hands and feet” (ibid. 17).

> [Note: “[Col. 1005D] ‘My feet.’ Old Version. Greek: πόδας, simply ‘feet.’]

Therefore, when you notice that your teachers in sacrilege are called calves, fat bulls, and dogs, you, one of the council of evildoers, cannot judge me insulting because I call you by the names by which your plague-ridden associates have been called and are called. For you are no less wicked, you who dare to say, “There was when He was not,” and, “He was made from nothing”; thus you are called by names appropriate to you. But do you wish not to be called by these names? Change your ways; correct your errors, as the most blessed Paul [Col. 1006A] and the others from that faithless people corrected theirs.

Because I tell you, “Rescue yourself from the council of evildoers,” I seem to you insulting. For what reason? Clearly because I profess myself a Christian, because I have refused to abandon God and go after your idolatry. We are not the first to be called insulting and proud by you sacrilegious men. All those too who resisted the deadly edicts of your fellow tyrants were so called.

To pass over the rest, at the close of my discourse I return once more to King Antiochus alone. Did he judge those who resisted him to be insulting and proud, or not? Without doubt, because he considered them insulting and proud, he persecuted those dedicated to God with such cruelty even unto death. It remains, then, for you to see what Antiochus did in addition to the things already known to you; and if you can rightly [Col. 1006B] say that they were proud and insulting toward Antiochus, then you can say the same of us—

> [Note: “[Col. 1005D] ‘And us toward you.’ Galland.]

—for we suffer from you the very things they suffered from Antiochus. We likewise cry out for faith and religion, as they cried out; we likewise profess that we serve the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, just as they confessed.

Scripture says that the king sent an old Athenian—

> [Note: “[Col. 1005D] ‘A certain Antiochene.’ Old Version, which omits ‘that they should not use’; Greek: Ἀθηναῖον, ‘Athenian,’ with Lucifer; and, after ‘laws,’ μὴ πολιτεύεσθαι, ‘that they should not govern themselves.’ The Lyons editors and Sabatier, contrary to the evidence of the Tilian edition, read ‘an old Antiochene,’ with the Vulgate.]

—to compel the Jews to depart from their ancestral laws and not use the laws of God; also to defile the temple in Jerusalem and name it after Olympian Jupiter, and Garizim—

> [Note: “[Col. 1005D] ‘And in Garizim, according as those there were.’ Old Version. The printed texts most wrongly give *Margarizin*. Perhaps in Lucifer’s exemplar *In Garizin* was written in larger letters, and someone added the letter M in the margin, signifying Mount Garizim, where another temple had been built. But an unlearned copyist, thinking that such a marginal letter belonged to the text and not sufficiently understanding Lucifer’s reading, produced from it the monstrous word *Margarizin*. [Col. 1006C–D] Galland.]

—according to the people inhabiting that place, after Hospitable Jupiter. But the insurrection of evils was grievous and burdensome to all—

> [Note: “[Col. 1006D] ‘Invasion.’ Old Version.]

—for the temple was full of the feasting of the Gentiles, [Col. 1006C] with harlots consorting with prostitutes, and women approaching within the holy precincts, moreover bringing inside what ought not to be brought in; the altar too was full of unlawful things forbidden by the law. Nor were sabbaths observed—

> [Note: “[Col. 1006D] ‘Kept, and ancestral days observed.’ Old Version. Greek: διαφυλάττειν, ‘to keep,’ after ‘ancestral days.’]

—nor ancestral feast-days kept” (2 Maccabees 6:1).

And below: “They were led with bitter—

> [Note: “[Col. 1006D] ‘With bitter necessity, on the day . . . to sacrifices . . . crowned with ivy, to parade for Liber.’ Old Version. Sabatier reads *absque miseratio erat* (‘without there was mercy’): ‘On the king’s birthday, to sacrifices.’ Greek, with Lucifer: εἰς τὴν κατὰ μῆνα, ‘monthly,’ and κισσοὺς ἔχοντες, ‘having ivy.’ After ‘the king’s birthday’ Greek reads ἐπὶ σπλαγχνισμὸν, ‘for sacrifice/visceration’; hence the Latin is corrected in Lucifer to ‘for visceration,’ or ‘there was visceration,’ that is, because on that day there was a disembowelling of sacrificial victims. But σπλαγχνισμός signifies both sacrifice and compassion, since sacrificial entrails are handled; hence in Lucifer, *miseratio* (‘compassion’). Yet Galland says that he would not suppose this reading of the editions first came from Lucifer’s hand.]

—necessity every month, on the king’s birthday; there was sacrifice; and when the rites of Liber were celebrated, they were compelled [Col. 1007A] to parade for Liber wearing ivy. A decree went forth to the neighboring Greek—

> [Note: “[Col. 1007B] With Greek Ἑλληνίδας, ‘Greek [cities].’ Old Version: ‘of the Gentiles . . . that they likewise . . . should do [this], that they should sacrifice.’ Here Greek has σπλαγχνίζειν where Lucifer has *misereri*: that is, to disembowel victims for sacrifice. But since σπλαγχνίζειν (‘to sacrifice’) and σπλαγχνίζομαι (‘to be moved with compassion’) are derived from σπλάγχνον (‘inward parts, entrails’), either Lucifer or the translator he used rendered it ‘to have compassion.’ Yet Galland says that he would not think this edition’s reading originated first from Lucifer’s hand. Sabatier reads: ‘of the Gentiles . . . that they should do this . . . and sacrifice.’]

—cities, at the instigation of the Ptolemies, that they should establish the same thing against the Jews: that they should act and sacrifice; but those unwilling—

> [Note: “[Col. 1007B] Greek, with Lucifer: Greek institutions, ἑλληνικά, and παρῆν, ‘there came.’ Old Version: ‘But those who would not [adopt] the customs of the Gentiles, they should kill.’]

—to pass over to Greek institutions should be killed. Thus there came a sight of misery. For two women were denounced for having circumcised their sons; their infants they hung from their breasts, and, after publicly leading the women through the city, they threw the women down from the wall.

> [Note: “[Col. 1008B] Old Version: ‘After hanging their infants from their breasts and publicly leading them through the city, they threw them down from the walls.’ Lucifer, following Greek, has *illas* (‘the women,’ αὐτάς) in ‘they led them around,’ and ‘from the wall,’ κατὰ τοῦ τείχους.]

Others fled to nearby lookout places and secretly observed the seventh day. When this was reported, they were burned alive, because they feared on the solemn day to render themselves glorious assistance (2 Maccabees 6:7).

> [Note: “[Col. 1008B] ‘They gathered in nearby caves . . . observing the sabbath day; when they were reported to Philip, they were burned with fire, because out of reverence for religion and observance they feared to help themselves with their own hands.’ Greek: τὴν ἐβδομάδα, ‘the seventh day,’ and συνεφλογίσθησαν, ‘were burned together,’ with Lucifer. Sabatier has: ‘They ran into nearby caves.’]

What do you think the worshippers of God ought then to have done? Ought they to have pleased God or Antiochus [Col. 1008A]?

> [Note: “[Col. 1008B] *Placendum* for *placere* (‘to please’), just as earlier he used *nocitum* for *nocere* (‘to harm’). Til.]

If you do not think that they ought to have pleased Antiochus, neither certainly ought we to please you, because you too—though in another way—wish to remove us from God and join us to the devil, as he wished to do to them. The same cruelty is carried out through you; you are as savage and unjust toward those who resist your deadly edict.

It remains, therefore, as has often been said, that you should grieve for having erred and, acknowledging yourself to be a murderer and a blasphemer, should present yourself, deserter of God, to the house—

> [Note: “[Col. 1008B] The house of God, that is, the Church, for repentance.]

—lest otherwise you have yourself to blame when you begin to see yourself there where all those your fellow tyrants now are.

[Col. 1007]

**One Book of Saint Lucifer, Bishop of Cagliari: That One Must Die for the Son of God, Addressed to the Emperor Constantius.** (C)

[Col. 1007C] It would indeed have been fitting, Emperor Constantius, to discuss the divine Scriptures with you no longer—since we have found you to be a falsifier of the truth, and have caught you by your deeds to be such a man as those who call themselves wise while in fact pursuing the path of folly. It would have been fitting, as we have said, after all that we have brought forward, now to be silent; especially since we remember what is written: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Prov. 26:4). And again: “Say nothing in the ears of a fool, lest, when he hears, he mock your prudent words” (ibid. 23:9). But because you still fear on account of the power of your arms and the empty dominion of your empire—

[Note: Col. 1007D: *Times*, “you fear.” Vatican manuscript: *tumes*, “you swell with pride.”]

—I understood that you were applauding yourself because you could violate those whom you ought by reason to have established in the position you had determined upon.

[Note: Col. 1007D: Perhaps: “I understood that you were applauding yourself”; or, if *times* is retained: “I understood that, defeated by the very Catholics whom you killed, you do not yourself trust in your arms; therefore I applaud and rejoice that you are miserable,” etc.]

In all those things in which you think yourself great, I wished especially in this book to make known to your mind, made fatal by sacrilege, that you are miserable, and that all the fury of your butchery is despised by the servants of God.

[Col. 1008C] For we wish you to hold as fixed and manifest this: that you will pass away with your temporal, perishable, frail, corruptible kingdom, and will come to eternal punishment unless, while there is still opportunity, you provide for yourself; whereas Christians will come to eternal rest and attain an incorruptible kingdom. Or will you attempt to maintain that through this heresy of yours you will attain the kingdom of heaven—you who, together with your pestilent Arians, fearing that the truth itself crying aloud might at some time compel you to yield to us Christians after you had been defeated, rejected debate and decided to resort to the force of your frail Arian arms?

[Col. 1008D, Note: *Armorum*, “arms.” Latinius rightly restores this reading; for it seems to refer to what was read a little earlier: “because you still fear on account of the power of your arms,” etc. Moreover, the restoration is confirmed by what the author immediately adds: “as though you could with frail arms,” etc. Nor indeed does either the title of the treatise, *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, or the whole tenor of the work suggest anything else. Galland.]

[Col. 1009A] As though, enemy of divine religion and forerunner of Antichrist, you could overcome with frail arms the religious servants of Christ, who are to attain immortal gifts—soldiers of God whom the only-begotten Son of God has deigned to invite into the eternal enjoyment of friendship with his divinity, saying: “Blessed are you when men hate you, and curse and persecute you and reproach you and say every evil thing against you. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven; for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.”

[Col. 1009C, Note: “When they curse you, and persecute you, and say … for righteousness’ sake.” Old Latin version; St. Germanus manuscript: “when men have hated you.” Floriac manuscript: “and reproach you,” with Lucifer; in which Sabatier reads: “have persecuted, reproached, and said.”]

[Col. 1009C, Note: “Because your reward is abundant in heaven.” Old Latin version. Greek Vatican manuscript: “great.”]

You thought that you could in every way drive these men from their rank; you thought that you could cast down those whom you see ready to be killed for the only Son of God precisely because they have chosen not to be tortured with you deniers in hell, but to attain the heavenly kingdom. By the empty authority of your kingdom you had thought that you would overcome them—

[Col. 1009C, Note: Read: “would overcome.”]

—though by their very confession of faith they are clearly the temples of God. For just as you Arians, by denying the Son of God, are designated by the utterances of prophets, apostles, and holy Gospels as houses of the unclean spirit, so we who confess the Son of God show that we are temples of God.

[Col. 1009C, Note: We read *ita qui*, “so we who,” in order that the comparison may be properly constructed. The printed editions have *itaque*, “therefore.” Perhaps *ita quum* was written in Lucifer’s exemplar, and the copyist, letting his eyes run on, read *itaque*. Galland. From the corrections of the Tilian edition we read: *ita qui*.]

Your cruel and sacrilegious mind, yielding to the suggestions of your fellow-heretics, had presumed that soldiers of God could succumb to your butchery—though God calls us his temples in these words: “For I shall dwell in them and walk among them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people” (1 Cor. 7:16). You had judged that you could conquer those whom the apostle urges to bear God and carry him in their bodies; you had thought that you could subdue them with the futile arms of your kingdom.

[Col. 1009C] But you see—

[Col. 1009D, Note: Perhaps the text should read: “you are subjected,” since in your palace, etc. Galland reads *perspicue*, “clearly,” for *perspicis*, “you see,” or reads “a clear answer.”]

—that, though standing behind a curtain within your palace, you received from me the answer that, for the preservation of salvation, all the servants of God, trampling upon your frivolous authority, agree in mind, will, zeal, courage, and speech.

[Col. 1009D, Note: Here Lucifer indicates with what constancy he resisted Constantius at the Council of Milan. Admitted to the palace and to the emperor’s inner chamber, he himself, in the name of the Catholic bishops, as it were the legate of Pope Liberius and president of the council, denied that either he or the others could assent to the judgment and will of Constantius and the Arians. He did so with such freedom of speech that the Emperor, standing behind the curtain by which the inner chamber was closed off, could hear him answering the Arian bishops and the Emperor’s officials. Concerning the curtains by which the inner rooms of princes’ residences were screened from the doors, Caspar Sagittarius treats at greater length in his *On the Doors of the Ancients*, chapter 24. Emperors chiefly used them either to present a certain greater appearance of majesty, when standing behind a curtain they gave answers as though from a sacred recess, or to listen unnoticed to matters proposed for determination in council or judgment. Both purposes are confirmed by this passage of Lucifer, where he says that Constantius, standing behind the curtain, received his answer, etc., and by another passage a little below, where he writes that he spoke to the judges while Constantius listened with the curtain drawn. Yet both passages escaped Sagittarius’s diligence. Jerome Magius, *Miscellanies*, book 2, chapter 13, teaches that a curtain was interposed in judicial proceedings when more serious cases were brought under examination; such certainly was Lucifer’s case, concerning the defense of the Catholic faith and Athanasius’s innocence.]

[Col. 1010A] You observe how your perishable dominion, the more it deigns to rage against us, is thereby judged all the more weak, contemptible, empty, feeble, and abject. For as often as your hand, stirred up by fury and wickedness, has prevailed in killing us, so often we remember that we have increased and emerged more and more victorious. You slaughtered very many in Alexandria, tore apart steadfast persons throughout the whole world, and destroyed those resisting you in various places; but all these, though you are entirely unwilling to hear it, are martyrs. We believe that all those most blessed persons slaughtered by your sword are in Paradise.

[Col. 1010C–D, Note: Since the citizens of Alexandria adhered with the utmost constancy to Bishop Athanasius and would not tolerate anyone, especially an Arian bishop, being substituted in his place, Constantius’s fury frequently blazed against them. This happened especially when first Gregory and then George—two monsters of the Arians—were substituted after Athanasius had been driven into exile. The Catholic Alexandrians refused to hold any communion in religion with them, ready to endure anything whatsoever rather than agree with Arians. Hence a fierce persecution was stirred up against them, which cruelly spread through all Egypt until Constantius’s death, although it sometimes ceased, but only briefly. See Athanasius’s *Apologies* and his Letter to the Solitaries, together with the notes which we appended to Lucifer’s own books in defense of St. Athanasius. Indeed, throughout almost the whole world, whether by Constantius’s command or with his connivance, Arian cruelty raged so fiercely against Catholics that very many persons, especially bishops, underwent glorious martyrdom. Lucifer, most eager to attain the same glory, indicates this here and elsewhere in this work.]

[Col. 1010D, Note: Perhaps read *quin*, “indeed,” rather than *qui*, “who.” Galland.]

Believe me: we have determined that it is better to be killed by you—

[Col. 1010B] —for we see that it is better through all ages to have God as a lover than to be punished with you, an imitator of Judas Scariot among the Jews. Therefore, Constantius, not fearing the serpent’s bites inflicted by you, we are ready to undergo every death. We can never repent of our counsels if we who seem thus far to have resisted your cruel hands are slaughtered by you. For the death which you threaten to inflict on us is prepared for all; but such blessedness as the holy martyrs attained, as we see, no one has attained except those who conquered death by dying for the only Son of God.

You torture, kill, and destroy persons devoted to God; yet you cannot give reasons for the hatred which makes you do these things, because you are in error. You are even angry with us because we hold the true way; and although you might correct yourself by our saving admonition, you heap your errors still further with cruel deeds—

[Col. 1010C] —wrenching consecrated minds from the disembowelled bodies of those who have resolved to keep faith with God until the final course of life is run.

[Col. 1011A] You see that this is so—and not without your deepest distress—when you perceive that you have no power to turn us away from this religion, which alone is true, or draw us back from that course in which we press toward the prize of the upward calling.

[Col. 1011D, Note: *Sursum*, “upward,” with Latinius, where *rursum*, “back,” had formerly been read. Lucifer adheres to the words of the text: ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως, “toward the prize of the upward calling.” Galland.]

You cannot do so when you openly make yourself our enemy, nor when you pretend to be our friend.

[Col. 1011D, Note: By promises and flatteries with which he tried to draw Catholic bishops into his designs, as we shall note below.]

For it appears that the deceiver of Eve is in you.

[Col. 1011D, Note: We have corrected the reading thus with Galland, where formerly *non*, “not,” was read.]

For when you compose your word—by which you spread like a cancer—with a false and painted swelling of knowledge, asserting yourself to be the repealer of your edict stained with all your crimes—

[Col. 1011D, Note: Discussed at length in the *Life*.]

[Col. 1011D, Note: That is, by showing yourself to be one who, with an edict stained by all your crimes, repeals sound doctrine and reaps and gathers every error.]

—the harvest of all errors, although you yourself are the fountain of all error, you claim to be a bearer of light, though you are beset by every darkness.

[Col. 1011B] Therefore, although you are wholly devoid of understanding, yet, seeing yourself despised at least in part, you can at last see, most savage Emperor Constantius, that we cannot by any means be turned away from the path of truth. For we Christians know this to be the distinctive task of faith: not to be removed from one’s rank either by prosperity or adversity, and not to be drawn away from a purpose once embraced with resolve. We see that every crime is excluded by this one religious utterance: “I am a Christian; I do not wish to be as you are, Constantius, an apostate.” By this one utterance, we see, the protection of salvation, the bond of liberty, and honor are bestowed. We see that by this confession there is given us a shield of protection, a weapon against the devil raging against us through you; and you say: “Deny that you are Christians!”

That we may stand firm against the danger that opposes us, that we may not dread your cruelty as you torture us, and that we may be encouraged rather than grieve, is brought about by this consciousness: it remembers that the only Son of God offers the presence of his divinity in order to protect his own and make them victorious. Hence it comes about that by the punishment through which you think us extinguished, we are given life. For we who believe that he for whose sake we suffer is with us take as an increase of strength that which you, our executioner, hoped would aid torture. Hence, when your evils shake us, we are not broken; and the more we are afflicted in diverse ways by continual cruelty, the more firmly we are strengthened.

[Col. 1011C] For he is with us who protected in the furnace of fire the Hebrew youths who believed in him. He himself strengthens our minds, he himself directs our understanding, he himself kindles our hearts with his divine love and encourages us to endure holy suffering.

[Col. 1012A] Therefore none of us thinks of the death which you threaten to inflict, but of immortality; not of the temporary punishment inflicted by you, but of everlasting glory. For the holy Scriptures thus declare that God’s martyrs are consecrated by tortures and crowned by the very testing of their suffering: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). And: “Though in the sight of men they suffered torments, their hope is full of immortality; and, having been afflicted in few things, they shall be well ordered in many; because God tested them and found them worthy of himself. He tested them as gold in a furnace, and accepted them as a sacrifice of whole burnt offerings; and in due time there shall be regard for them. They shall judge nations and rule peoples, and their Lord shall reign for ever” (Wis. 3:4, 8).

[Col. 1011D, Note: The Old Latin version omits “and.” See certain variants in Book I in defense of St. Athanasius, p. 95 [here col. 861], and our notes there.]
