[Col. 1011D–1012D, Note: “A sacrificial victim of whole burnt offering.” Latinius, as in Book I in defense of St. Athanasius, p. 95 [col. 861, line 7]; Old Latin: “a victim of whole burnt offering.” According to Galland, St. Cyprian cites this entire passage in book 3 of the *Testimonies*, chapter 15, and in *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 12; in both places, however, he reads *holocausta hostiae*, “sacrifices of victims of whole burnt offering,” which I judge also to be Lucifer’s genuine rendering. Nobilius nevertheless observes, on this passage in the Book of Wisdom, that many Cyprianic manuscripts prefer the reading “a sacrificial victim of whole burnt offering,” which Latinius, Galland himself, and others insert into Lucifer. Sabatier has: “a victim of whole burnt offering.”]

[Col. 1012D, Note: “And in the time.” Latinius, as in the Old Latin version and the Vulgate.]

[Col. 1012B] Those, then, who expect and rejoice in attaining such happiness through the greatness of God must necessarily, as they think of future joys, trample underfoot the present evils which you inflict. The divine voice of the only Son of God says: “He who loves his life in this world shall lose it; but he who hates his life for my sake shall preserve it unto eternal life” (John 12:25).

[Col. 1012D, Note: Old Latin: “He who loves his life shall lose it, and he who hates his life in this world … shall preserve it.” Cyprian, Epistle 81, with Lucifer: “in this age,” and “shall preserve.”]

Clinging to this divine command, we Christians, though your claw, Constantius, should strike back against the wounds of our bodies, stand and shall stand unmoved, stronger than you and all your punishments, considering only this within ourselves: that this butchery of your cruelty is useful to us for everlasting glory.

The barbarians often spare the conquered; even amid arms there is room for mercy, yes, even among those who live with a savage manner of life.

[Col. 1012D, Note: In place of *ferino*, “savage.”]

[Col. 1012C] But what you do against us is indescribable—you against whom we have wished well, and whose welfare we desire to come about, and for whom we do not cease continually to beseech God. You despoil, proscribe, slaughter with the sword, punish in diverse ways; you do not even permit the bodies which you have ordered torn apart to be buried.

[Col. 1012D, Note: This happened especially at Alexandria, when George of Cappadocia, by Constantius’s order, occupied that church by force and arms in 356. See the notes in the books in defense of St. Athanasius.]

You forbid almsgiving; you have filled every mine and every place considered suitable to be called a place of exile with the multitude of us who resist your cunning. You do not cease to banish innocent persons and afflict them with hunger, thirst, and nakedness. These evils you inflict upon persons who desire to attain eternal blessedness.

And yet, most cruel emperor, whatever your cruelty has inflicted upon us or shall inflict, observe that it is falsehood; for even death inflicted by you upon holy martyrs who preceded us is not death, nor loss, nor damage, but an investment of faith.

[Col. 1013A] We Christians are always tortured by you tyrants in a perverted inquiry during persecution.

[Col. 1013D, Note: Thus we have corrected and punctuated the passage with Latinius and Galland, where the Tilian edition gave it as follows: “But an investment of faith always Christian: by you tyrants,” etc.]

For by the same kind of procedure by which guilty persons are compelled to confess, we are compelled to deny Christ, the only and most true Son of God. But as they, having confessed according to their deserts, are condemned, so we, because we do not deny the Son of God, are crowned; for us condemnation inflicted by you is victory. You remove from the midst those before whom you do not dare to blaspheme. For by the single utterance of a soldier of Christ, he who remains in you against our religious confession is cast down. He speaks through you, thirsting for our blood; he who has besieged your mind trembles at the presence of worshipers of God and cannot bear it when we dissent from you—

[Col. 1013B] —you who say that the Son of God is from nothing—when we stand against your threats and trample upon every cruelty of your butchery, helped and protected by his power.

You undoubtedly feel yourself reproved by the constancy and endurance of his servants, for he says: “Do not fear him who can kill the body; rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell” (Matt. 10:28).

[Col. 1013D, Note: Old Latin: “Fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy the soul,” etc. Cambridge manuscripts: “rather him who can,” and, with Lucifer, “fear.”]

We are also encouraged by the exhortations of his most blessed apostle Paul to trample upon you, the tyrant of all tyrants: “We are children of God. But if children, then heirs: heirs indeed of God and fellow-heirs of Christ, provided that we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified together” (Rom. 8:16).

[Col. 1013D, Note: “But if children, then heirs: heirs indeed of God … provided that we suffer with him … that we may be glorified together.” Old Latin. Cyprian, Epistle 55, with Lucifer: “But if children of God, also heirs of God, and fellow-heirs of Christ.”]

And again: “I judge that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (ibid. 8:18).

[Col. 1013D, Note: With Cyprian, book 3 of the *Testimonies*, except for “for the glory which is to come.” Old Latin: “For I judge that they are not worthy,” etc.]

[Col. 1013C] As we think upon the glory of that brightness, it is fitting for us servants of Christ to endure all afflictions and persecutions inflicted not only by you, through the devil, but also by all his human agents. For though they are many, we are delivered from them all—we who believe that the Son of God is truly Son, and who, though we remember that the Father and Son are two persons, nevertheless ascribe one divinity to the Father and his only Son.

When he who has besieged your mind hears these our just and invincible arguments, since he cannot bear the truth, he incites your savage spirit to afflict us most bitterly and torture us with carefully devised forms of punishment because we refuse to abandon the saving path. Therefore your excessive cruelty mocks our bodies because we value faith greatly—

[Col. 1014A] —and do not deny that we are worshipers of God. You press upon us with the full force of your butchery, thinking that you harm us, while ignorant that we rejoice in the occasions of our testing. We deem this our greatest happiness: that, in this contest for righteousness, it may happen that we are cut down by your executioner’s hand for the Son of God. With a religious mind we stand firm against your madness, because he for whose sake we suffer conquers in us whatever insult to his divine majesty you profanely cast out in empty speech, futile talk, and perverse intention.

[Col. 1013D–1014D, Note: Latinius has *in injuriam*, “as an insult.” But perhaps Lucifer wrote *injuriae*, in the dative case, with the same sense, in his characteristically less exact style. For the author himself acknowledges, at the end of the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, that his books were written in rustic speech. Galland.]

All these things your hard mind and the savage ferocity of your heart bring forth toward the destruction of your own salvation, while you dissent from the religion of God, led by madness, carried away by fury, and tormented by every kind of savagery. At once urged on and striking, you are resisted, beast that you are, by him whom you deny protecting us against your savagery, just as opposing masses resist when the sea is wont to be turned back.

[Col. 1014B] Though diabolical waves strike through you and the far-ranging storms of the world beat upon us, our strength will be more and more immovable, as it is; we shall not succumb, overwhelmed by the foaming waves of your assaults, but shall always stand upright against every danger. For the Christian spirit is not abject, to be overthrown and tossed about toward vices; rather, it is so high-born and noble that it remains unmoved and victorious against all temptations.

We are not Christians because we think to enjoy the sweetness of this present frail life; rather, we desire to attain the glory of eternal security and happiness, the possession of perpetual blessedness. The religious voice of the blessed apostle John exhorts us, so that, despising earthly things, we may desire to follow heavenly things: “The world passes away, and its desire; but he who does the will of God remains for ever, just as God remains for ever” (1 John 2:17).

[Col. 1014D, Note: With the Greek, ἐπιθυμία, “desire.” Old Latin: “desires,” and “as he himself remains for ever.” Cyprian, book 3 of the *Testimonies*: “as God,” omitting “and.”]

Since these things are so, I want you to know that you, with all your tricks and frauds and with the utterly immense cruelty of your savagery, lie beneath the feet of God’s servants; that all the glory of your empty dominion is regarded and held by us as nothing; and that, with all the strength and authority of your empire, you are perceived by us as nothing other than an empty breath.

Perhaps some one of your flatterers will say that we boast in saying these things. Do you not remember, Constantius, that I said to the judges, while you listened with the curtain drawn—

[Col. 1014D–1015D, Note: We corrected this passage, on the authority of Pontius in Latinius, where it had previously been wrongly read *te vel omisso audiente*, “you listening, with ‘curtain’ omitted.” The sense refers to what we noted a little above. Galland confirms the same point; in both places Lucifer speaks of the curtain which removed the Emperor’s or judge’s appearance from the sight of those standing by. Cotelerius, on book 2 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 52, and Mazochius, on the ancient marble calendar of the Church of Naples, p. 384, also noted certain matters concerning these curtains. From the latter, note that the ancients customarily heard more serious cases—such as Lucifer’s case—behind a drawn curtain, but lighter ones with the curtain removed.]

[Col. 1015A] —that even if you had decided to hurl all the weapons of your kingdom, your whole army, upon us, the detesters of your blasphemy, and that all should dash their weapons against us as contemners of your sacrilegious decree—

[Col. 1015D, Note: Thus we corrected the text with Latinius; formerly it read “as contemners of your sacrilegious decree.”]

[Col. 1015D, Note: *Nec sic*, “not even thus,” Latinius and Galland.]

—yet not even then could we depart from our purpose? But in your celebrated prudence you thought your soldiers were men destined to die for you in every war, whereas you decreed that Christians ought to become deniers of God. And certainly your men feel the pain of wounds; they grieve that they have perished, they grieve to lose this light. But we, first, cannot feel the torments of punishments in which Christ suffers, in which Christ works eternal salvation. Then, because we account present things as nothing and shall always be in that everlasting light, how is it possible that we should not choose to be killed by your hands, made fatal by sacrilege, for Christ the Son of God, the giver of eternal life?

[Col. 1015D, Note: Vatican manuscript: *quin*, “indeed,” but corruptly.]

[Col. 1015B] How could we please God the Father otherwise, when summoned by you to deny his only Son, unless even through death itself we confessed him to be the true Son of God? Your detestable mind takes offense because we say that Christ, the Son of God, is the Word of God, the Wisdom of God, the Power of God: true God from true God, born from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—light from light, born not made, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of the same substance”); through him all things were made, and the Father was never without him.

[Col. 1015D, Note: Here he cites the beginning of the Nicene Creed, which he copied out in full in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*.]

You, worm of Arius, take offense because we maintain that the brightness, power, greatness, eternity, and divinity are one and the same for the Father and his only Son.

[Col. 1015D, Note: Latinius and Galland read: “and divinity.”]

What we ambassadors affirmed in your palace is not new; and we do not cease always to establish that Christians have so believed and do so believe, just as at Nicaea the holy faith appears to have been written against your Arian heresy and—

[Col. 1015D, Note: Concerning Lucifer’s embassy at the Council of Milan, see what is narrated in his *Life*.]

[Col. 1015C] —against all errors. If at last you open the eyes of your heart, pierced by the bites of the serpent, you will find that the Church holds and defends this faith, which she recognizes as handed down to her through the blessed apostles. If you could traverse all nations in a moment, most foolish emperor, you would find Christians everywhere believing as we do and, persevering in this defense of the Son of God, desiring to die as we do.

But your novel proclamation and recent religion, a blasphemy put forth by you under the pretext of faith for the ruin of your salvation—

[Col. 1015D, Note: Understand an edict, or letter, issued in Constantius’s name by the Arians at the Council of Milan, concerning which see Lucifer’s *Life*. Galland would prefer to read “a blasphemous religion.”]

[Col. 1016A] —has not yet been able to pass through the Roman world, although you have exerted yourself enough; and where it had attempted to take root, it withered, since all God’s servants withdrew from you, while only your few supporters remained with you—those whom the Lord foretold to be tares sown among the wheat.

[Col. 1015D–1016D, Note: That is, at the Council of Milan itself, from which it might have spread widely through Italy and the West; but the effort of Constantius and the Arians was futile. From this you may see, says Baronius under the year 356, no. 71, how greatly the Arians, through Constantius’s favor—and Constantius himself by all the Arians’ efforts—disturbed the whole Christian world in order to sow Arian heresy in the Church after expelling the Catholic faith.]

All this has been supplied to you, and is being supplied, by the skilful maker of deceit and death, who through you ensnares and deceives very many by crooked flatteries. Though guilty of the whole crime, he suggests to that most bitter heart of yours that you should punish us as though we were guilty of some crime.

But look at last; open the eyes of your heart, in which there is no light for you, but only all darkness and immense shadows. You will find that death inflicted by your frail power restores a more whole life, that it leads us rather to glory through fires, swords, chains—

[Col. 1016B] —and beasts, through whatever your frenzy, most pious emperor—

[Col. 1016D, Note: Said ironically.]

—has decided to inflict for our death. With God protecting us, we are not merely not extinguished; rather, we are made more and more alive, since we remember that nothing is above us except God. Therefore a soul devoted and enslaved to God blushes to succumb, through your blasphemy, to you who are dead—to a dog barking against truth, crawling with the worms of Arius.

Whenever the souls of Christ’s servants carefully examine the true force of tortures, they consider that there is no greater torment than for a servant of Christ to be overcome by you, the servant of our adversary. We remember that the Lord said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up [his cross and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life shall lose it; but whoever loses his life—

[Col. 1016D, Note: “For whoever wishes to lose his life,” etc. Old Latin and the St. Germanus manuscript in Sabatier, with Lucifer, except that Lucifer has *nam*, “for,” where the other has *autem*, “but.”]

[Col. 1016C] —for my sake shall find it. For what does it profit a man if he gain the whole world but suffer loss of his life? Or what shall a man give in exchange for his life?” (Matt. 16:24).

[Col. 1016D, Note: From the Greek, τὸν ὅλον κόσμον, “the whole world.” Old Latin: “this world.”]

The dignity of martyrdom compels us Christians to despise life in the face of death—

[Col. 1016D, Note: Latinius and Galland have “purchase it in exchange for death,” but less correctly, although the sense remains.]

—since a new kind of salvation has been granted through the Son of God: to perish lest I perish.

[Col. 1016D, Note: The Tilian edition does not contain the reading “to perish lest I perish,” as Galland affirms; but it clearly reads “to perish lest I may perish.” The Lyons editors, however, most wrongly and without any reason printed: “to perish lest I be able.”]

We know that this discipline has been handed down to us by God: that without any terror we should defend the force of warfare for so great a name, since the desire for eternal remembrance has long since drawn us away from longing for this light, and fellowship with Christ has separated us for trampling upon all earthly things.

The battle of your cruelty grows, Constantius; but observe that glory too grows for Christ’s soldiers. We are not, therefore, held back from the battle-line by fear of tortures; rather, by your very tortures we are provoked all the more to battle.

[Col. 1016D–1017D, Note: Cyprian has a similar statement in Epistle 8 of Baluze’s edition, to the Martyrs and Confessors: “The battle grew, and the glory of those who fought grew also; you were not kept from the battle-line by fear of tortures, but by the very tortures you were provoked more and more to battle.” In Lucifer’s text we have printed, from Latinius’s correction, “we are not held back” in place of “we are held back.”]

[Col. 1017A] You cannot deny that these things are so when you see Christians throughout the world encouraged to enter the contest with equal and like ardor of courage; when you see that the soldier of Christ’s uncorrupted firmness of faith is not deceived by your detestable flatteries, frightened by the threats of your fury, or overcome by the torments and tortures of your cruel butchery. For he remains in us and is always with us who said to the blessed apostles: “I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

[Col. 1017D, Note: Again Cyprian in the same place: “Now I have learned … that all … are encouraged with equal and like ardor of courage to engage in the contest … so that neither flatteries deceive the uncorrupted firmness of faith, nor threats terrify it, nor sufferings and tortures overcome it; because he who is in us is greater than he who is in this world.”]

He is present everywhere because he is almighty—

[Col. 1017D, Note: Vatican manuscript: “of the Almighty.”]

—the all-powerful Son, whose eternity and divine power are one with the Father’s. But it cannot be said how great a darkness of unbelief has besieged you, or how great a cloud of shadows and errors has covered your heart—you who pretend to be a Christian, yet strive to remove the Christian name from the midst.

[Col. 1017B] Amid these things, you should see that readers will grant pardon if my modest talent in eloquence has been unable to portray you in terms sufficient to execrate you, in proportion to your impiety. For they saw that I had given a model to all who fear God and furnished material to those who would discuss how they might cut you down, a man planted without the roots of eternal life.

[Col. 1017D, Note: These words seem to refer to the book which he wrote to Constantius *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*.]

Nor should you say that you are reproached by us with abusive words, if you hear what you deserve from men who are unpolished, yet Christians.

[Col. 1017D, Note: “What you deserve to hear from unpolished persons,” etc. Galland.]

We know that one ought not curse, but rather pray for enemies; for the Son of God, though he is Lord of all things, when cursed did not curse in return.

[Col. 1017C] Besides, if the Lord of all things did curse in return, all things would surely collapse beneath the onset of so great a majesty. You say, no doubt, in reply: “The Lord wished you to be gentle, since you are his bishop, yet you show yourself obstinate toward me. Prophets, apostles, and the chorus of the Gospels teach that one must not kill; but you, on the contrary, deign to kill persons devoted to God.” We Christians know that, in order to appease him whom we worship, those things are necessary by which we know that he is delighted and rejoices. Therefore, if what you do is to be judged capable of pleasing God, we must all be murderers, sacrilegious persons, and blasphemers.

O Constantius, you see how immense your madness is. That subtle deceiver, the ensnarer of innocents, is seen to have established a seat for himself in your mind; and do you suppose that you have not yet been exposed? Do you still wrap yourself in a sheep’s skin, though you are a wolf—you whom the most holy prophets call a beast, and the most blessed apostles a dog and a ravening wolf; you who, being a worker of iniquity, are set forth as though a minister of righteousness? And do you think yourself a human being, when you bear nothing human except features and outward form?

[Col. 1018A] You grieve to be called a savage beast, to be said to bear nothing human except features and outward form. Tell me, I beg you: can you, a killer of innocent people, deservedly be called a Christian, rather than mad, dull, and senseless—an enemy, indeed, of God’s religion, in which piety, humanity, and every justice are found, in which one does not learn to repay evil for evil, in which we are taught not to kill but to be killed for the Son of God?

[Col. 1018B] You, considering your vain and despised dominion, apply tortures in your sacrilegious enterprise; but there is a protector—

[Col. 1017D, Note: Likewise Cyprian in the passage a little above.]
commended: “How joyful Christ was there . . . and the protector of the faith prevailed . . . he was present at his own contest—he raised up the fighters and defenders of his name.” The protector of the faith, the guide of salvation, the ruler of souls—whom you constantly compel us to deny—is always present with us in our contest, because he raises up the fighters and defenders of his divine name. Hence it is that, against those serving your injustice and your ministers—that is, your fellow-torturers—as they torture us, we stand the stronger; we are strengthened so that our limbs, beaten and torn by your claw, overcome it.

[Note: [Col. 1018D] With Gallandius: where the Tilian edition had *serviens* (“serving”), Latinius and the Lyons editions have *servientes* (“those serving”). Cyprian, in the cited letter: “Those tortured stood stronger than their torturers, and their beaten and mangled limbs overcame the claws that struck and tore them.”]

For how can a repeated and prolonged blow, however savage, overcome invincible faith, when every soldier of Christ knows that he for whom he suffers is present with him and rejoices in the endurance of his servants? We certainly stand, servants of Christ, strengthened by his majesty, with free speech and uncorrupted mind; naked indeed against your frail weapons, but clothed in those arms which the blessed apostle urged us to put on, saying: “Henceforth be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power” (Eph. 6:10). And: “Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the devices of the devil; for your struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day and, having accomplished all things, to stand: girding your loins with truth, putting on the breastplate of righteousness, and having your feet shod in readiness for the gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, by which you may extinguish all the glowing darts of the most wicked one; and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; praying at every time in the Spirit with every prayer and entreaty, and watching in him” (Eph. 6:11 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1018D] “Be strengthened, and in the power.” Antiochene Version. “Be strengthened”: the same reading occurs below in Lucifer.]

[Note: [Col. 1018D] “Snares.” The same version. See the notes in Book II *For Saint Athanasius* and a little below.]

[Note: [Col. 1018D] I have no doubt that Lucifer wrote “against principalities, against powers.” Gallandius. And that is indeed how it is read in Greek; but our author agrees well with the Antiochene Version in Sabatier, and therefore nothing should be altered arbitrarily.]

[Note: [Col. 1018D] “Stand in all works.” Antiochene Version. Lucifer follows the Greek text exactly. Gallandius. But it differs from Cyprian’s version both in Book III of the *Testimonies* and in Epistle 58, Oxford edition cited by Gallandius: for there it reads, “Therefore put on the armor of God, that you may be able to resist on the most evil day; so that, when you have accomplished all things, you may stand girded,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 1019C] “Readiness.” Antiochene Version.]

[Note: [Col. 1019C] We have corrected this from the Antiochene Version. Formerly it was read *cadentia*, “falling.”]

[Note: [Col. 1019C] With Cyprian, Epistle 56. The Antiochene Version has *salutaris*, “saving.”]

[Note: [Col. 1019D] Greek: *eis auto touto* (εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο), “for this very purpose.” Lucifer, together with other Fathers, did not express *to touto*; nor does the Vulgate translator acknowledge it, since it is known to be absent from several manuscripts noted by Mill. Gallandius. The Greek Codex Boernerianus in Sabatier has *eis auton* (εἰς αὐτόν), “in him,” with Lucifer. The Antiochene Version: “in him.”]

Therefore, since your cruelty and that of your father cannot overcome us when we are armed in such a fashion and fortified with so great a power, as has often been said, we have stood and stand, and, until you consume our bodies, we shall stand, protected by Christ’s saving shield, surrounded by the breastplate of his piety, guided by the Holy Spirit, immovable, and increasingly in all things masters, driving away every utterance of slavery.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] Gallandius incorrectly thinks that *immobile* is here used for *immobiliter*, “immovably.” From the Tilian corrections we read *immobiles*, as the Lyons editions also printed.]

[Note: [Col. 1019D] I take it that Lucifer, accustomed to Greek style, uses *auctores* for αὐθένται, ἐξουσιασταί, “masters, those having authority,” especially from what immediately follows: “driving away every utterance of slavery.” See the observations of learned men on Hesychius, s.v. Αὐθέντες; also Suicer, *Thesaurus ecclesiasticus*, same entry, § II, vol. 1, p. 574. Nor should you omit Du Cange, *Glossarium*, s.v. *Auctor*. Gallandius.]

For we are certain and confident that no snares of yours, no cunning, no quibbling, no frauds of yours can lead us away from the steadfastness of our purpose, since we know that the end of sins is death, and that life which is everlasting follows thereafter. Let us embrace the counsels of his blessed apostle and desire to be found his imitators and sharers, he who affirms that, “though our old man is corrupted, the one within is renewed” (2 Cor. 4:16). And: “if the earthly house of our body is dissolved, a heavenly building is built”; and that, while we are placed in the body, we are away from the Lord. With that apostle we shall be unable to render abundant praises to God in the heavenly kingdoms unless, first purified by death, we have come to receive immortal rewards.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] “But though our outward human being is corrupted, the inward one is renewed day by day.” Antiochene Version.]

[Note: [Col. 1020C] “And” is a conjunction by which he joins one testimony to another, as he often does; it does not properly belong to the testimony which follows, as Sabatier supposes. Antiochene Version: “If the earthly house of this our dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in heaven.”]

[Note: [Col. 1020C] Here too the conjunction has the same force, contrary to Sabatier’s reading. Antiochene Version: “While we are in the body, we are away from God”; likewise Lucifer in Book II *For Saint Athanasius*, col. 1020D, see p. 151, note 10. The Greek nearly agrees with Lucifer: Ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι, ἐκδημοῦμεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου, “being at home in the body, we are away from the Lord,” although in these three testimonies he appears to have expressed the sense rather than the Apostle’s exact words.]

Thus, when through you our bodies have been scattered and utterly dissolved, then let us suppose ourselves most whole; when death has been brought upon us through you, then we believe that we are able to live more truly. How do you still presume, Constantius—ever the most senseless emperor in the meantime—to inflict things that extinguish you but give life to us? You rise up with evil and wicked counsel to destroy us; you are swift to shed the blood of the servants of God’s only Son, not knowing that heaven is opened by our blood and the fire of Gehenna extinguished by our blood.

Worldly ambition instructs you; heavenly greatness instructs us, who fear losing eternal salvation. We know that we must die for God. For just as, unless you make the passage from the camp of the devil to the army stationed in the heavenly camp, fire in Tartarus will hold you forever, so we, if, scorning your threats and torments, we prefer to be slaughtered by you—most savage beast and monstrous brute—for the Son of God, shall rejoice in heaven. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10); and he did not say, “Blessed are those who inflict persecution.”

[Note: [Col. 1020D] With Latinus. Formerly: *jugulare*, “to slaughter.”]

We Christians know that we have been made soldiers of Christ for this purpose: that, confessing our leader on the battlefield of the unjust war imposed by you, we may die armed, so as to attain the triumph of victory. Hence, the more savagely you act toward us, the more merciful you appear, since you deem us worthy to kill a Christian confessing himself such.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] “Triumphs.” Vatican manuscript.]

But in this you are judged most criminal: that, under the guise of affection and of wishing to provide for us, you flatter us in order to cast us down, as though it profited us to be driven from our rank by you and preserved, but condemned by God.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] Thus Latinus, where formerly *cupientes*, “wishing [plural],” was read. Gallandius: *cupiens*, “wishing.” Lucifer often reproaches Constantius for this cunning of flattering Catholics in order to draw them to his own party. Hence Hilary, in his book *Against Constantius*: “We fight against a deceptive persecutor, an ingratiating enemy . . . who does not strike backs, but strokes bellies; who does not proscribe unto life, but enriches unto death; who does not thrust into prison for freedom, but honors within the palace for servitude; who does not torment sides, but occupies the heart; who does not sever the head with the sword, but kills the soul with gold; who does not publicly threaten fires, but privately kindles Gehenna.”]

We know that you fear lest, under all these punishments devised by your abominable ingenuity, we should die in this perseverance of faith; yet you apply diverse and harsh tortures. Thus you wish us, whom you persecute so fiercely, to be variously tortured and mangled, indeed at every moment; but you have decided that we are not to be killed, as though death alone made Christ’s soldiers blessed, and not also tortures which, the more grievous they are, yield the greater glory of courage.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] Hilary in the same book: “You carry out every savage cruelty without the odium that attends glorious deaths.”]

For we who know that the life of righteousness is richer and more enduring do not turn our backs in this field of war; nor do we make our way into your camp, enemy of God. Rather, placed amid these destructions inflicted by you, we desire to be presented to the sheepfold of God, from which the devil possesses you as one snatched away. Yet I say this not in order that you may spare us. For you shall find us Christians, just as you have already found those whom you killed: steadfast in faith, patient in pain, victorious under examination through him, namely, who does not abandon his confessors. Recognizing ourselves as his soldiers, as you see, we engage bravely and fight steadfastly.

We know that it is great glory, immeasurable exaltation, and singular holiness to adorn the life of eternal salvation with the honor of suffering; that it is the highest nobility to despise the torments of your power, not to shudder at treading upon you, and not to fear your frenzy—you who rage so madly against the innocent, you who, though a teacher of blasphemy, injustice, and every cruelty, nevertheless think that you can appear a pious, prudent, and just Christian, blind, dull, and ignorant of the truth.

[Note: [Col. 1021C] Again Hilary agrees with Lucifer in the same place: “Constantius confesses Christ in order to deny him . . . he suppresses heresies lest they be Christian . . . he honors priests lest they be bishops. You, Christ, he carries about in words, you upon his lips, and he does absolutely everything to prevent your being believed to be God as the Father is.”]

Consider, devourer of the innocent, that one in whom Christ keeps watch cannot be conquered by your torments: he conquers hunger, despises thirst, subdues the filth of prison and confinement, and the horror of punishments by the vigor of his strength; he tramples every penalty, crushes every torture, and does not fear the death which you threaten to inflict with such exertion. Do you think you can overcome one who remembers what is written: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:12, 15). And: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress? Or persecution, hunger, nakedness, peril, or sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death; all day long we are counted as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us” (Rom. 8:35 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1021C] “Will render.” Antiochene Version.]

[Note: [Col. 1021D] “Unto death.” The same version, in which these words “all day long” are joined to “we are put to death.” Irenaeus, Book II, chapter 22: “unto death”; and Book IV, chapter 16 joins “all day long” to “we are counted,” as in Lucifer, who nevertheless has in Book I *For Saint Athanasius*, p. 58: “We are killed all day long.”]

I cannot at all see what of yours can take us away from these saving precepts. For although you do not cease, in every impious exercise of your office, to elevate those who agree with your perversity in order to entice us—such as Epictetus and the rest, whom from servants of God you have made servants of yourself and satellites of your father—yet far be it from us to have such madness as to prefer falsehood to truth, or to let any prosperity offered us by you entice us to your kingdom. Keep your empty glory for yourself; retain for yourself and your equals all the wisdom of your most foolish heart—those with whom similarity of character has joined you. Leave us our folly: that we confess Christ, the Son of God, to be the true Son; that we maintain he is of one substance with the Father; that we profess our desire to be killed for his sake rather than deny his divinity. Leave us such folly.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Concerning him also in the book *On Not Associating with Heretics*. But from these words of Lucifer we understand that this man first belonged to the Catholic party, and then, driven by ambition, joined the Arians. Athanasius indicates this in Oration I *Against the Arians*: “For it is superfluous to speak of Cecropius, Auxentius, and the hypocrite Epictetus, since it is clear to everyone how, for what reasons, and through which enemies of the Church these too were promoted: namely, men who offered themselves as performers and actors in slanders against orthodox bishops, against whom plots were being made. Though they had been established only in the rank of presbyter and were not known to the people, they nevertheless procured for themselves the title of bishop through impiety.”]

[Note: [Col. 1021D] That is, of the devil, as a little above.]

Why do you labor that we should lose this? Why do you think truth can be assailed by you, ignorant that it prevails by its own force? Whence is it that you see the people of God resisting your savage rage and harsh torments with unconquered courage, except because this is the apostolic and evangelical faith which we defend? These are the people who resist your cruelty, who trample your frenzy: their hope is eternal immortality and heavenly life; their ardor is kindled with longing for perpetual light, and their salvation rejoices in promised blessedness.

So certain are we that we shall attain and enjoy eternal life that we gladly endure everything, since we profess that we consider not our own torments but your punishments as torturer. We Christians compensate bodily losses with gains of the soul; we count a crown in wounds; we triumph most joyfully in Christ over tortures and pains inflicted by you.

Remember, Constantius, the recent memory of your crimes which you branded upon yourself in the city of the Alexandrians: how many you caused to be hurled down precipices by one inked subscription; how many you caused to be cut down by the sword; how many to be consumed by hunger and thirst or killed in prisons; how many to be strangled by having their breath cut off. Yet, though in all these cruelties toward holy martyrs, whom your gladiatorial temper has killed, you raged against us, you rage more cruelly when you withhold the sword, when you take care that the swift remedy of death may not come more quickly.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] What Lucifer here recalls seems to refer to the year 360, when this book was written; nevertheless historians make no mention of this act of Constantius. Yet, if we understand by what Lucifer calls a “recent memory” the things which Constantius ordered to be cruelly done against the Catholic Alexandrians a few years earlier, perhaps one may infer that he narrates here what George the Cappadocian, returning from Constantinople to Alexandria around the year 357, impiously and most cruelly undertook against the Alexandrians by Constantius’s authority and edict. See Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 10, Valesius’s edition, and our Preface, § IV.]

[Note: [Col. 1022D] For George, having been expelled from Alexandria, fled to the emperor. Greatly inflamed with anger, the emperor sent a notary to Alexandria who, at Constantius’s command, subjected many Alexandrians to tortures and beatings. Not long afterward George himself returned, made more terrible because he had incited the emperor to afflict many persons, as Sozomen says in the same passage. Hence Lucifer writes that so many crimes were committed in that city by one inked subscription—that is, by one signature of an edict rashly and furiously made by Constantius at George’s instigation.]

[Note: [Col. 1022D] *Tincta subscriptionis una*, “one inked subscription,” for a single subscription made with dye or ink; *tincta* is a new noun. Tilian edition and La Cerda.]

We suffer our whole bodies to be torn and burned, proving that nothing better accords with the dignity and constancy of the wise than not to be driven from conviction and purpose by any terrors; that it is most beneficial to be tortured for God; that those dedicated to God cannot die; that perpetual torments are conquered; and that you are rather cast down and reduced to nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1022D] “Nothing more.” Gallandius.]

Receive what is set down in the twenty-sixth Psalm: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation: whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life: of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers draw near against me to eat my flesh—my enemies who trouble me—they themselves have grown weak and fallen. Though an army stand against me, my heart shall not fear. Though battle rise against me, in this I shall hope. One thing have I asked from the Lord, this shall I seek: that I may dwell in the house of God all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:1 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1023D] “In the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” Antiochene Version.]

Therefore, since the power of righteousness is perfected in these sufferings; since Christ suffers in us and we do not feel punishment, because where guilt is absent there is no penalty either, how did you think that you could conquer those consecrated and devoted to God by things to which invincible faith gives an increase of courage? I firmly believe—and truth does not deceive me—that, although you still exert all the strength of your butchery to tear apart our limbs, and although, raging for long, you as torturer might afflict our mangled limbs until our blood flows, you can nevertheless never conquer God’s household, never overcome Christ’s army, never subdue it under pains, never bend it under agonizing punishments.

We Christians refuse no tortures or death; we cannot tremble at your tyrannical commands or the swords of your judges, because armed with God’s sword we resist you. The blessed apostle says to the Ephesians: “Henceforth, be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power. Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the devices of the devil, because your struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual wickedness” (Eph. 6:10 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1023D] “In the power.” The same version.]

[Note: [Col. 1023D] With the royal manuscript in Sabatier. Antiochene Version: “snares.” See the note in Book II *For Saint Athanasius* and in this same book, p. 248.]

Since you cannot overcome those clothed in God’s armor—you through whom all demons rage for our death—we urge you at last to surrender yourself to us, lest with those whom the apostle describes you be tortured throughout all ages. Thus the sons of light cannot be conquered in the darkness of your prison by the son of darkness, as though those in whom he who is the creator of light deigns to dwell could feel darkness.

Courage must necessarily endure what mortal nature has been taught to bear. For if you attempt to consume our limbs with fire, we shall feel that you are burned more in our bodies than we are; for, running willingly and readily to death for the faith, we cannot lose life, but rather acquire it, and after a fragile life we anticipate one eternal. The point of your sword always stands drawn, ready for the slaughter of Christians; yet that blade of your sword seems to us more bent than any lead, as does the edge of your soul.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] “Drawn.” Latinus, and Gallandius following him.]

We endure everything securely in suffering, as though we inflicted the punishments that we suffer, because he who rages against us through you is overthrown by our faith. For we know that death cannot erase us into perpetual nothingness, since we have believed in Christ, the sole Son of God, bestower of eternal life. Rather, we believe and confidently expect that even the bodies which you now burn, torture, and tear will rise to light and everlasting life.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] “The only true [Son].” Vatican manuscript.]

For if, after being killed by you, we knew that we would be nothing, we should surely be most foolish not to provide for this life so that it might be as long as possible and full of every comfort. This could have happened to us had we thought it right to comply with you rather than God’s decrees. But now, since when this present life is taken away through you, an immortal one is received, it is necessary that his servants despise this present life with its goods for the sake of God’s Son, since every loss of this kind is repaid by immortality.

Consider, Constantius, how great was the courage, how great the strength of spirit, and what firmness of faith belonged to those whom you killed, and belongs to those who still resist your sacrilege. Consider that either those blessed martyrs whom we now see established by God’s power in heavenly kingdoms, or these whom you have not yet been able to kill, have stood against you, monstrous beast: you who never cease to threaten us with things lawful and unlawful, while always desiring, and being, more ready to dare against rival rulers than to allow those who confess Christ, the Son of God, to emerge victorious.

[Note: [Col. 1024D] Perhaps *multo* (“much more”) or *multos* (“many”). Tilian edition. *Multo*, Latinus and Gallandius. *Multis* is correct: that is, “with many things,” more tolerably, in his customary manner of writing.]

For it had pleased your heart, besieged by the darkness of every error, and your mind blinded by deep gloom, first, by converting us all from God through your heresy, to make us your dependents, and then your fellow-satellites. But truth, which had undertaken to devise this very scheme against you, conquered both you and itself within you; for it prevails by its own force.

[Note: [Col. 1024D] A participle used in place of a gerundive; he often writes thus: “by converting us, to make us your dependents.” Tilian edition and Gallandius. Latinus: *convertentes primos*.]

Finally, at every moment we await your adding torments still more atrocious than those already inflicted, appointing fiercer executioners and more savage avengers, who may attack with the sword, crucify, roast with fire, or tear our entrails and limbs by any unheard-of kind of punishment—us soldiers devoted to God and resisting your deadly edicts—so that through God’s mercy we may trample threats, sufferings, and tortures with the strength of faith. As we stand now immovable through the Lord, so we shall stand forever; for it is not we who conquer your gnashings, but he himself in us, by whose help we are governed and by whose power we are preserved.

[Note: [Col. 1024D] That is, more atrocious than these. Gallandius.]

For how great or what sort of man are you, that you can strip us of these goods divinely bestowed upon us? You seize us, banish us, make us needy, condemn us, overcome us, burn us, and even kill us by miserable methods; and yet you cannot overcome the unconquered faith of Christians.

[Note: [Col. 1024D] Latinus: *relegas*, “banish.”]

From this you ought to have understood that you too will receive punishments for your error and cruelty; and that, as against us, the exceedingly narrow path laid down through this difficulty leads on high to the reward of immortality. We cannot yield to your cruelty, since we know martyrdom to be a singular imitation of the Lord’s courage. The way of martyrs is indeed very full of labor and difficulty, and so steep that no one can fulfill it with human strength; but we, aided by the support of divine assistance, must always trample you, as we trample you now.

Hence it has pleased us not only not to fear you, adversary of God’s religion, but even to provoke you voluntarily. You are provoked, since you are always expected not to show pity, pitiless as you are, but to kill. Hence our happiness cannot be divided: even when we are killed for God’s Son, he himself lives in us by love—he who is in affliction and encouragement, strength in the battles of persecutions.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] “For you are provoked.” Gallandius.]

By whatever means you choose to display yourself against God’s worshippers, you will nevertheless never make void their marked virtue, since worldly torments neither entice nor terrify them. Since this is so, what else shall I call you, persecutor of God’s house, but wretched, since you obey the instigations of your plundering demons? Driven by their goads, you undertook to devise and carry out these deeds; by their persuasion, clinging to your heart, you willingly wander in your sacrilegious error.

Indulge your folly, unknown to yourself; and would that you wished to err and be foolish only with your fellow-blasphemers, the Arians! But you attempt to drag us also into partnership in your evils; you proscribe and despoil us. Yet we know that poverty sought for Christ’s sake is a supreme kind of blessedness. You bring death upon us, executioner; not only do we not draw back our necks, but we offer them, that we may be slaughtered for God’s only Son.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Better with Latinus and Gallandius; formerly *ignitae*, “fiery,” was read.]

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Perhaps *inferas*, “may you bring,” as a little above *faveas*, “may you indulge.” Gallandius.]

[Note: [Col. 1025D] “Death; but we,” etc. Latinus and Gallandius.]

[Note: [Col. 1025D] *Damus*, “we offer,” with the same editors, so that the sense is: “You bring death upon us, executioner; but we not only do not draw back our neck, but offer it.” Formerly *manus*, “hands,” was read.]

Why have I related these things? That you might know that your punishments have no force against Christ’s servants, and that we cannot fear what we always await as coming. You take it ill that you are called a heretic, and yet you dare to say that the Son cannot be compared or made equal to the Father. We, who maintain one divinity of Father and Son, say that the Son is equal to the Father. We believe as the blessed apostle Paul believed, who says of the Son: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not deem it robbery to be equal to God” (Phil. 2:6).

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Antiochene Version: “Established in the form of God.”]

What does “although he was in the form of God” mean, except that the Son, as God the Father is, is unchangeable, immutable, immeasurable, inexpressible, eternal, and perfect? What does “although he was in the form of God” mean, except that the Son inhabits that same inaccessible light which the Father inhabits; except that the divine sublimity of Father and Son is one?

The Holy Spirit, dwelling in the blessed apostle and already then seeing all your hearts of heretics, added an interpretation of what it is for the Son to be in the form of God: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not deem it robbery to be equal to God.” The blessed apostle calls the Son equal to the Father, declaring one divinity of Father and Son; and do you dare, with the satellites of your sacrilegious audacity and the sharers in your sacrilege, to say: “For we cannot make the Son equal or compare him to the Father”?

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Thus with Latinius. Formerly it was read: “The Father and Son and Holy Spirit, dwelling in the blessed Apostle.” See Preface, § 2.]

Or why do you suppose that the Lord said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), and, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), except because the power of Father and Son is one?

[Note: [Col. 1025D] With the Greek, simply τὸν πατέρα, “the Father.” Antiochene Version: “my Father.”]

You say that the Son has a beginning; but we say he is without beginning, since everything that has a beginning must be capable also of having an end. Therefore, since we believe God’s only Son to be eternal—that is, coeternal with the Father—and you enemies of God deny it, do we not most rightly call you mad, filled with every folly, sons of pestilence? Of you the blessed apostle cries out, as he then did of the Jews: “And as they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting” (Rom. 1:28).

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Antiochene Version: “are fitting.”]

And to the Philippians: “Be fellow-imitators of me, brothers, and observe those who walk thus, as you have our example. For many walk, of whom I often told you, and now tell you even weeping, as enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame: they set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. 3:17 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1025D] “Observe those who.” Antiochene Version.]

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Antiochene Version: “our example.”]

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Antiochene Version: “whom always.” The reading *quos*, “whom,” also occurs in Lucifer, Book II *For Saint Athanasius*. See p. 159 [here col. 926, line 17].]

[Note: [Col. 1026D] From the Greek, ἐν τῇ αἰσχύνῃ, “in shame.” Antiochene Version: “in their confession.”]

And to Timothy, concerning you, Constantius, and your dearly loved companions in perdition: “The Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons, in the hypocrisy of liars whose own conscience has been seared” (1 Tim. 4:1 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1026D] Greek: τῆς πίστεως, “from the faith.” Antiochene Version: “from the truth.”]

[Note: [Col. 1026D] Greek: Ἐν ὑποκρίσει, “in hypocrisy.” Antiochene Version: “in the dissimulation of liars.” Cotelerius, vol. I of *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, p. 337, observes that in Lucifer the two words should either be joined in accordance with the Greek construction, *mendaciloquentium*, “of lying speakers” (ἐν ὑποκρίσει ψευδολόγων, 1 Tim. 4), or one should read *mendacium loquentium*, “of those speaking falsehood.” We have joined them both according to the sense of the Greek expression.]

[Note: [Col. 1026D] Antiochene Version: “their mind and conscience.” *Mind* is absent from the Greek.]

The Holy Spirit still strikes and kills you through the mouth of that same blessed apostle: “In the last days perilous times will come. People will be lovers of themselves, greedy, proud, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, faithless, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, puffed up, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having an appearance of piety but denying its truth. Avoid such people” (2 Tim. 3:1 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1026D] “The Apostle Paul.” Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 1026D] With Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*. Antiochene Version: “avaricious . . . disobedient.”]

[Note: [Col. 1026D] Greek: ἀλαζόνες, ὑπερήφανοι, “boastful, proud.” The Vulgate: *elati, superbi*, “haughty, proud.” Lucifer’s *fastidiosi* may indeed be understood in the sense of “proud.” Cicero, *Philippics* X: “If they were arrogant, I could not bear their disdain.” Add that *fastidium* is sometimes used for *fastigium*, “height,” as Du Cange teaches us in the *Glossary*, s.v. *fastidium*. What, moreover, if Lucifer, frequently using a less Latin and almost uncultivated style, is said to have written *fastigiosi*? Gallandius. Nevertheless the Antiochene Version in Sabatier agrees with Lucifer.]

And further: “Just as Jamnes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these too resist the truth, men corrupted in mind and reprobate concerning the faith; but they will progress no further, for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (2 Tim. 3:8 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1027B] Greek: Ἰαννῆς; Vulgate: Jannes. But Saint Cyprian also reads Jamnes with Lucifer, *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 115, Oxford edition. See Cotelerius on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VIII, chapter 1, Gallandius. It is not ours to raise a question about this name. “With great variation,” Cotelerius says in the cited place, “Hebrew, Greek, and Latin authors pronounce and write the names of these magicians in approximately the following forms: Johane, Janne and Mamre, Jamre, Ἰαννής, Ἰάννης, Ἰαννῆς, Ἰαννίς, Ἰωάννης, Ἰάμνης and Ἰαμβρής, Ἰάμβρης, Ἰαμβρῆς, Ἰαμβρίς, Μαμβρής with the same accents, Μαμβρίς; in Glycas Ζαμβρῆς, perhaps with the first letter M reversed and thus changed to Z; Jannes, Jamnes, Johannes, and Mambres, Jambres,” etc. Sabatier reads *restiterunt* (“resisted”) for *resisterunt* (“they resisted”). Antiochene Version: Jannes.]

[Note: [Col. 1027C] The same version reads “resist, and corrupted in mind, reprobate,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 1027C] “For their folly,” etc. The same version.]

And further: “The time will come when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, with itching ears; and they will turn their hearing away from the truth and will turn aside to fables” (2 Tim. 4:3 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1027C] Sabatier reads *auribus*, “with ears.”]

Abandoning the apostolic faith, turned to fables, your discourse spreads like a cancer. Though the Holy Spirit had foretold through the apostle’s mouth, you call Catholics wanderers; and shortly afterward you say that the very faith which you called Catholic, and which you compelled us to accept, is blasphemy.

[Note: [Col. 1027C] Vatican manuscript: “which you compelled us to accept.”]

[Note: [Col. 1027C] Here Lucifer rebukes the emperor’s inconsistency: at will and according to the Arians’ desires, he at one time accepted and at another rejected confessions of faith put forward by them. He seems especially to indicate the statement of faith presented to Catholic bishops at the Council of Milan, which they were compelled to subscribe under force and threats, as we have often noted elsewhere. Constantius himself later rejected this confession, and repeatedly ordered new ones forged by heretics either to be accepted or rejected.]

Likewise—

[Note: [Col. 1027D] Eudoxius, whom Lucifer contemptuously calls Adoxius, after seizing the church of Antioch about the year 358, held a council there at the beginning of the following year, and there set forth a confession of faith.]
of the formula, rejected the terms *homoousios* and *homoiousios*; moreover, addressing the people from the episcopal throne, or in the council itself, he uttered the most impious blasphemies, which Hilary reports in Book I Against Constantius. But, accused through the hostile intrigues of Arians and Semi-Arians, both before the emperor—whose favor and authority he greatly enjoyed—he was deposed from his see at the Council of Seleucia, on 13 September 359. Yet again, relying on Acacius’ influence, he approached the emperor, verbally abjured his blasphemies, and, at the beginning of 360, in the assembly at Constantinople, was placed over the church of Constantinople by his supporters, with Constantius’ approval, Macedonius having been expelled [Col. 1028B]. These matters are related by Bosch in his *History of the Patriarchs of Antioch*, prefixed to volume IV of the July *Acta* of the Bollandists.

Whether Eudoxius also abjured the Antiochene formula seems uncertain, since the fathers at Seleucia decreed nothing against it, the council having dissolved without accomplishing its business. So far as one may infer anything certain from Lucifer’s words, I think that the Antiochene formula, ratified by Eudoxius, was approved by Constantius at Eudoxius’ persuasion; shortly afterwards Constantius, turned from this view by Eudoxius’ opponents, condemned both the formula and its author; and then, once more deceived by Eudoxius’ fraud—when the latter had attributed his own blasphemies to Aetius and pretended to abjure them—received Eudoxius into favor, without further concern for the Antiochene formula, and confirmed him as bishop of Constantinople [Col. 1028C].

This interpretation, however, may also be applied to the same words: Constantius may have appeared to approve that formula again when he raised its author to the summit of the Constantinopolitan episcopate, although he never ceased openly to profess both his formula and his blasphemies. Petavius assigned the Antiochene council to the year 360 in Book I, chapter 9, of *On the Trinity*; it is not our business to dispute this controversy. Whichever opinion you approve, since the Constantinopolitan council appointed Eudoxius head of this church at the beginning of 360, even if the Antiochene council followed shortly afterwards—as Petavius and others maintain—at which that formula of faith was published, it is certainly established that this book was written by Lucifer either toward the end of that same year or in the following year.

Indeed, this very passage of Lucifer accords with Bosch’s opinion, if we understand its sense correctly: namely, “The formula which you had approved when it was issued among the Antiochenes, you soon afterwards, roused against Adoxius, said was blasphemy; and now you again confirm it as catholic [orthodox], when you judge Adoxius, its author, worthy of the episcopate of Constantinople.” See Bosh in the history cited above, who distinguishes two Antiochene synods: one under Eudoxius before 360, in which the terms *homoousios* (“of the same substance”) and *homoiousios* (“of like substance”) were rejected; the other at the beginning of 361, in which, despite Acacian opposition, the formula of the Constantinopolitan synod was confirmed, together with the *homoiousia* of the Son with the Father—that is, likeness according to the Scriptures.

Shortly afterwards, the formula which you had then [Note: Then. Galland.] maintained to have been a blasphemy committed among the Antiochenes against Adoxius—you now again affirm to be catholic; hence you have judged Adoxius fit to be at Constantinople, because you have approved that very formula as catholic. Learn, then, from this very fact how great the difference is between truth and falsehood. For although you are, as it seems to you, learned, and have an appointed number of dictating secretaries [Note: That is, writers who take down dictation and write it out, as Du Cange thinks in his *Glossary*. I would rather understand certain men of Constantius’ court, trained in liberal learning, who dictated in polished and eloquent language the composition of his edicts, letters, judgments concerning the faith, and formulas, as he says a little below, calling them “helpers in letters.”], we see that you have been able to persuade no one except those who feared your butchery.

But we, for whom nature suffices to speak, strangers to all learning and therefore strangers to letters, are able to overthrow every heresy [Col. 1028B], because the thing itself and truth speak. You and your literary assistants have thereby increased another art full of artifices; we know only the sacred writings [Col. 1029A]. Our speech is ordinary; yours is polished and adorned, and even deserves to be called eloquent. Yet your sweet, carefully contrived rhetoric can persuade no Christian—unless he is not truly one, but only called one—just as you, though a wolf, are judged by the ignorant to be one of the sheep.

Who is so senseless, unless he has swallowed all madness as you have? Which servant of God would not wish to be honored by death in the service of devotion? Who does not desire to pour out his own blood for Christ, when such a death makes life more whole and gains eternal glory? We stand, as you see, protected by God’s power, shod with the precepts of the Gospel, immovable with firm step, so that our footsteps cannot through you be swept away in headlong ruin. We stand holding the shield of faith, so that the flaming missiles thrown by the enemy through you cannot [Col. 1029B] take hold at all, since they are always hurled back upon you. Our heads are fortified with the helmet of salvation; the word of the Lord is in our mouth, so that the enemy stationed in you may be struck down with the spiritual sword, overthrown and scattered alike.

You will discover that the holy faith which you compelled us to reject is the shield of our soul, strong, impenetrable, and a closely woven breastplate, which none of the devil’s missiles, brought against us through you, can pierce. Seeing such steadfastness in Christians, you say: “The Arian doctrine once adopted by me must also be defended.” You say such things, wandering with an honorable intention. For you understand that nothing in human affairs is more excellent than religion, and that it must be defended with all one’s power. You defend it by the sword; but we know that religion must be defended, not by killing, but by dying [Col. 1029C] for God and enduring all these evils which you inflict.

What cruelty of yours can conquer those who defend religion in this manner? For if any one of your soldiers, in this frail service of your empire, keeps faith with you—a mortal with a mortal—in some noble deed, he becomes more acceptable and dearer; and if he dies for you, an empty man, he gains the highest glory in your eyes because he fell in death for you, his leader. How much more must faith be kept with God, the eternal emperor, by us who are soldiers of his mercy! Since the duty of devotion undertaken compels us to do these things, you—because in your blindness you do not believe Christ to be the true God, the Son of the true God, and because you are simply wretched, having by no means escaped the darkness of eternal death—wished us too to return to our former blindness, so that, now [Note: “Already.” Latin.] not merely simply but detestably, we might see that we had lost prudence while possessing the light.

For since we know that one condemnation of death awaits you because you refuse to believe, and that the evil is doubled for us if, rejecting our faith, we choose to return to destruction, how did you presume that we could be separated from God’s love either by your false favors—which, while they entice, kill all the more—or by every kind of cruel torture? Who would reject such great happiness offered to him [Col. 1030A], unless he were more wretched than you, when he sees that by the confession of one utterance, “I am a Christian,” adversities are overcome, joys arise, kingdoms are opened, and eternal dominions prepared?

You say: “Deny the Son of God, or the power of my empire will kill you.” How much better to be killed by an enemy of Christ than by Christ! How excellent to be slaughtered by you, friend of Antichrist, and made alive by Christ! Who would not prefer to be found a participant and companion of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and all the righteous, rather than of Judas, whose imitator you have become? John the Baptist was punished in prison by your plague-bearing Herod; James was killed by Herod’s cruelty; the apostle John was banished to an island [Note: Perhaps the word “Patmos” should be added. Galland.]; blessed Peter was crucified; blessed apostle Paul was bound, shut [Col. 1030B] in prisons, scourged, often stoned, and finally killed.

But all these, by most gladly enduring those things, were made friends of God. We observe this, and we too prefer to be slaughtered by your cruel hand rather than yield to your executioners. Why do you hate us? Why do you persecute us with such savagery? Surely because we confess ourselves Christians. And those blessed men whom we have mentioned were killed by your fellow-tyrants for the one Son of God, because they called themselves his servants.

The Holy Spirit says through the mouth of devout David in the person of our people: “If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have stretched out our hands to a foreign god, will not God require [Note: The Antiochene version: “will require.”] these things? For he knows the hidden [Note: “Secret things, and we are put to death.” Same edition.] things of the heart; because for your sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43:21). And you, Constantius [Col. 1030C], emperor enslaved to Arian idolatry, say meanwhile: “Fear the gnashings of my madness, renewing itself for your death, and become apostates with me.”

Hearing this, you do not wish to heal your wounds, but proceed rather in blind and irrational frenzy, prompted by those spirits who insinuate themselves into your mind and incite you, unknowingly, to rage [Note: “They incite you, unknowingly, to rage.” These are the spirits, etc. Latin and Galland. With these changes—*spiritibus* for *spiritus*, *furere* for *furore*—we preserve the sense.], those spirits to whom you are known to sacrifice by denying God’s only Son. Because they can do us no harm by themselves—for we are protected by God’s greatness—they persecute us through you, their attendant. They recognize us as their most hostile enemies, and through you, their lover, they exercise as violently as possible the cruelty they can, thinking that through your intervention as executioner they will violate our faith.

The teaching of all sacred Scriptures is that faith in the Son of God is the first and complete righteousness [Col. 1030D]. Therefore, when you, the defeated inquisitor [Note: “Who conducts judicial examinations of us concerning the faith.”], are overcome, those demons are overcome in you; for victory is granted to us not by the strength of our frail bodies, but by his mercy. He alone supplies strength, so that amid every instrument of your butchery we endure immovably; we are not broken by the pain of wounds or the blows of interrogation, but are instead raised up. Hence true worship of God consists in this: the minds of worshippers present themselves to God as spotless sacrifices [Col. 1031A].

And do you suppose any worshipper of God to be so sluggish and foolish that the ardor of so great [Note: “Of such great.” Latin.] a desire does not awaken, arm, impel, spur, and finally set him ablaze with those fires of love by which the holy prophets, apostles, and martyrs were set ablaze? Which of us, I ask, is not driven in spirit to be killed by your cruel hands for Christ? Whom does not urge toward the glory and heights of martyrdom not merely these things which you administer, but even cruelties still greater? For your punishments are easily overcome if the glory of those very sufferings is set before one’s eyes. That which tears us is not considered where so great a reward of punishment is bestowed.

By incorruptible rewards, your tortures, Constantius, are overcome; anguish is crushed down [Col. 1031B]; death is subdued, and when it is inflicted, life is restored all the more [Note: Latin: “when [death] is inflicted”; earlier reading: “life is prepared to be avoided.”]. Emperor, the wounds inflicted through you would hurt if they did not immediately make us friends of God. And [Note: “But.” Same edition.], since we confidently expect then truly to live when we are punished by you for the Son of God, and then to lose nothing of salvation, how can it be that we should yield to your empty gnashings? You imagined that we could and can be subdued by your force; I believe you still imagine this in vain.

How long, then, will you abuse God’s patience, Constantius? Rather, I urge you: drive these things from your dark thickets, and let your tasteless mind receive meditations able to set you on the way that leads to God’s kingdom. Grasp gladly that which may lead you to the banquet of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, God’s friends—you who have dared, a man of every injustice, to judge yourself righteous [Col. 1031C], preferring yourself, by your own judgment, to all bishops appointed in the holy Church of God; rejecting the holy faith which the Church has always held and holds; and striving to preach the blasphemy uttered by the mouth of your sacrilegious Arius, now through your agents, now by your edict [Note: Concerning this, enough has already been said in the *Life of Lucifer*.], now from your own mouth filled with unclean spirits; and to call yourself a perfect worshipper of God and one who does everything holily—though no king now called a tyrant has been found more cruel, more detestable, or greater in [Note: “Greater in blasphemies.” Earlier reading: “of the greater.”] blasphemies than you.

Since I have already shown your folly that these things are so in the book entitled *On Apostate Kings* [Note: From this recognize that Lucifer wrote his books separately and at different times.], I now want you to know [Col. 1032A] that, unless you are speedily converted—unless you believe with us that the only Son of God has always reigned with the Father, that the Father was never without the Son, that the kingdom of the Father and his only Son is one, and that Father and Son possess one Godhead—you will perish eternally. For Arius, your master, called the Son of God a creature, and you have exalted his blasphemy to heaven with praises.

We press, entreat, and urge you to become most loving toward God; yet you complain that you suffer injury from us. Thus you uphold the empty authority of your rank, as if it could rescue you from everlasting torments. You raise your proud head above the Lord’s priests, not observing what is written: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” The Apostle says concerning the only Son of God, whom you persecute in us: “Though he was in the form [Col. 1032B] of God” [Note: So also Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book VIII. Antiochene version: “being established,” for “was.”], “he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being found in appearance as a man” [Note: Antiochene version: “made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man.” Greek: *en schēmati*], “he humbled [Note: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient,” etc. Antiochene version.] himself unto death, even death on a cross.”

He who always was, is, and will be in the Father’s form—being the true Son, immutable and unchangeable, because he is God, the all-powerful Son of the almighty—nevertheless deigned, for our salvation, to humble himself, so that he might raise and exalt us who lay fallen and cast down. Yet that holy humility of his has made you, a rabid dog, bark against his divine majesty: you see only those statements in the sacred Scriptures written concerning [Note: “Because of.” Latin and Galland.] his assumed humility, passing over those that relate his eternal divinity [Col. 1032C].

What do you answer to this, Constantius? Your Arian bishops frequently acclaim you “bishop of bishops” [Note: Thus they flattered Constantius, who intruded himself into decisions about controversies of faith. Bishops surpassing others in rank, virtue, or learning were given this title, as more honorific. See Bingham, *Origines Ecclesiasticae*, vol. I, Book II, chapter 2, §8. Hence Lucifer’s statement in *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, reproaching Constantius for meddling in ecclesiastical affairs and religious controversies: “as though all care of the Church truly belonged to you, you are so concerned,” etc. Constantius was a man who boasted of expertise in ecclesiastical doctrines and laws. Thus Lucifer writes of him in Book II *For St Athanasius*: “you wish to seem an expert in the law”; and near the beginning of that book: “I believe no sacred Scriptures escape you, for you could not give us distinguished commands unless you were skilled in the law.” This is ironic. And in *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*: “concerning him”—that is, Jesus Christ—“you have issued books written.” Such writings were published among the people by Arian bishops in the emperor’s name.] Do you believe or not believe that those dying for God’s only Son will possess the kingdom of heaven? If you believe it, why do you compel us to deny his eternity? Why do you not cease persecuting us who believe in him? Why are you so continually restless and hostile toward us, presenting yourself as a violent persecutor, but under the title of peace a deceitful enemy?

I grieve that you have acquired for yourself such great evils. I mourn that you are in every respect placed without hope of eternal life. Yet though you not only cut us apart with swords but even [Col. 1033A] gnaw us with your teeth, be certain that, protected by God, we shall overcome your madness. Nor should you despise us because you see that our bodies are frail; for in what chiefly matters, we are strong in sound and fortified wisdom [Note: Perhaps read “wisdom.”], possessing adornments and defenses in our hearts and minds.

Whence do we now see ourselves adorned? Whence do we feel ourselves fortified and secure? Whence do we know ourselves to be wise? Is it not because we both avoid your blasphemy and gladly hand over our mortal bodies to your sword for the Son of God, knowing that, though you may kill our earthly dwelling, you cannot kill the heavenly one which we possess? For this reason we know that good and evil have been set before us: that all the force of our prudence might lie in distinguishing goods from evils [Col. 1033B].

What is more foolish than truly to deny God, as you do? What wiser than to trample your impious head and thereby please God? Hence you see that, with all our strength, we stand ready in the contest of righteousness: with faith intact, devoted courage, and an uncorrupted mind, standing in battle array which you have proclaimed—fearless soldiers of God [Note: Either something is missing, or one should read “soldiers of God.”]. We also bear the shield of faith bravely; therefore, God protecting us, whatever the devil hurls by your hands is extinguished, because our feet are shod with evangelical teaching and armed with spurs.

Though you are Augustus, the serpent roaring for the destruction of us innocents is nevertheless trampled underfoot in you [Note: Galland: “Yet he is trampled underfoot in you,” who prints this in the Tilian edition; yet *in te obteritur* is correctly read there.]; for he cannot, through you as his executioner, prevail to bite and overthrow us. God wills that we be pressed through you, not so that [Col. 1033C] we may abandon the faith and way of the patriarchs, apostles, and martyrs, but so that, compelled by you to deny God’s only Son, we may not refuse even to undergo death.

We are not, like you, so foolish and perverse as to prefer to cast away saving things and embrace mortal ones. We do not flee the protection of heavenly medicine. We understand that although a physician cuts with iron, burns with the cautery, and by the burning of mustard brings the sick person to every pain, cutting, burning, consuming, and biting are not therefore hostile things; for they are good precisely because, through pains applied for healing, they remove useless pains [Note: Lucifer here, as Cotelerius observes in his note appended to Book II, chapter 41, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, imitates Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, chapter 5: “There is clearly, as it were, the cruelty of medicine—in the scalpel, the cautery, and the burning of mustard. Yet cutting, burning, stretching [elsewhere, ‘consuming and biting’] are not therefore evil because they bring useful pains.”].

God wills us to undo death by death, to drive away eternal torments by temporary sufferings, and to nullify future everlasting punishments by your punishments. We, that is, who, when you take life [Col. 1034A] from us, confidently expect life to be bestowed all the more—eternal life in exchange for temporary life, incorruptible and perpetual life in exchange for one that is fragile and perishing.
