You think it insufficient that those confessing themselves Christians be punished merely by the sword, unless you inflict every type of torture on their bodies. It matters nothing by what kind of death you deign to punish us, provided that through these things we are admitted to enjoy eternal life; provided that through them your madness is put to death and we, in contrast, are made alive. If you think it miserable that I prefer to be killed for God’s Son by any cruel punishment, then, leaving aside the eternal glory of blessed martyrs, I know that I must die by some manner of death. I can show you many who perish more cruelly in their beds, swollen by some internal suppuration and drawn tight by the pain of struggling sinews [Col. 1034B]. What matters is the cause for which I hang, not the beam from which I hang.

What do you say, most foolish king? Am I sent by you unjustly to these tortures, to this kind of punishment, or justly? If unjustly, the cross is yours—the cross of the one who fastens me—not mine, whom you have fastened to it. If justly, my own guilt for my crime, not your punishment, will begin to torment me. But as regards the outcome, it matters nothing whether I die through you by nail or spear; with hands bound behind my back or extended and spread; bent forward, bowed, or upright and raised. It makes no difference whether you kill me resting in a bed, cut my neck with a sword while I stand, remove my head with an axe, bind me to a stake or a cross, roast me with fire, bury me alive in the ground, cast me down from a rock, or drown me in the sea; whether, making a violent effort with the *labandago* [Note: A barbarous word for a kind of instrument employed with force. Hence among us the implement by which ballistae are tightened is called *bendage*. Tilianus and La Cerda. Du Cange, in the *Glossary*, disagrees, maintaining that the French *bendage* has another meaning. He thinks the reading should be *an a pendigine*, “or from the rest of the body”; for *pendigo* is the same as Greek *pēgma*, “a fastening, frame.” The word could therefore be understood in two ways: either as a wooden machine or platform, also called *pēgma* by the Greeks, from which the head is violently struck a long distance away; or as the very joining of the rest of the body from which the head is torn. I think *labandaginis* should be retained: it is the name of a machine highly suitable for violently severing the head, though its use is unknown to us. Perhaps one should not dismiss the conjecture that the name was taken from the place where this machine was first invented: namely Alabanda, a city of Caria, whence the Alabandians and the Alabandensian people in Strabo and Pliny; Pliny praises Alabandensian hemp in *Natural History*, Book XIX, chapter 9.], with one [Col. 1034C] enormous blow, you strike my head far away from me; or whether, with a dart subtler than every subtle thing, you toy for a very long time while piercing my body. Though your cruelty devise a hundred thousand forms of punishment, from them all only immortality will reach me through the death inflicted upon me by you.

I cannot but rejoice when you inflict such things, since through these sufferings I know that every punishment can come to an end. For I judge that those things which are external and which, I believe, may happen through your perpetual [Note: Tilianus and Latin edition: “perpetual”; earlier reading: “through your cruelty.”] savagery do not concern me at all: whether birds or dogs tear my body and cling to it; whether beasts, while you wait with cruel eyes [Note: “Watching.” Latin edition.], leap upon it; whether, lying on the ground, I am reduced by claws and teeth to the bone—provided that after all this I am safe with God.

For when, by such acts, you have consumed my body through the forces of your beastly [Col. 1035A] inhumanity, the Creator of all things will restore and renew it, indeed from corruption into eternal incorruption. But you, our most unjust persecutor, should know that unending punishment awaits you. Do not suppose that you will escape with impunity, you who have judged the name of the only Son of God to be put beneath your footsteps and trodden down impiously and wickedly.

It is the voice of the blessed apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming [Note: As in Cyprian in several passages. Antiochene version: “future.” See above p. 243, note 3 (here col. 1013, note d), where certain variants occur in this very text.] glory” (Rom. 8:28), which we shall possess if we choose to be killed by you rather than deny the Son of God. When that revelation and splendor has shone upon all us believers, we shall be blessed servants placed forever in his kingdom [Note: “We shall be.”]. You, by contrast, if you judge that you must persist in your perfidy, will be in outer darkness: a deserter [Col. 1035B] from the service and an assailant of truth, one who has done the devil’s will. Therefore, unless you draw yourself from his snares, you must be tortured with him in unquenchable fire, as is written.

We say these things not from ourselves [Note: “Not at all.” Latin.], but we read them set down by the most holy prophet concerning you transgressors, you blasphemers, who deny that God’s only Son is the true Son, and all who refuse to believe in him: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24). If you remain in this madness, you will always be in inextricable darkness. For as we who confess the Son of God, having received the rewards of immortality, shall enjoy everlasting light, so you, his denier, must be carried away to eternal [Col. 1035C] sunset and darkness. You will be led by the way you now hold—not, as the Arians lie to you, toward heaven, but toward the visible citadel of the world [Note: Galland: “to the hateful citadel of the world,” that is, the most fortified place of the lower world.], to the left of the wicked and to impious Tartarus. It is the way [Note: That is, “it is indeed the way.”] of that fugitive whose entire will you, his attendant, are found to fulfill; it is, I say, the way of that serpent who turned you from the heavenly road to hold this way of injustice.

This is the broad and spacious way of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “How broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction!” (Matt. 7:13) [Note: With the Clermont manuscript in Sabatier. Antiochene version: “because,” and “to destruction.” See no. 6, p. 122 (here col. 888, note o).] If, then, you refuse to take counsel for yourself, there can be no doubt that you are among those whom blessed John rebukes, saying: “Now the axe [Note: Antiochene version: “And the axe [is laid] at the roots.” Lucifer with the Cambridge manuscript; Greek: *pros tēn rhizan*, “at the root.”] is laid at the root of the trees; if [Note: Antiochene version: “But every tree not producing …”] anyone does not produce good fruit, he will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke 3:9).

Therefore you and all your associates, since you are most bitter trees bearing the fruit of death, sinning against God, unless you make your passage to the heavenly way, will be cut down and [Col. 1035D] cast headlong more swiftly than speech into the deep abyss. There you will undoubtedly see those whom you now unjustly persecute, just as [Col. 1036A] the rich man then saw Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, God’s friends, and of all the prophets, apostles, and martyrs.

You will not escape those punishments, Constantius, unless first of all you believe that God’s only Son is truly God’s Son; then, as has often been said, confess that he has always reigned and does reign with the Father—that is, without beginning or end—and transfer yourself from the abominable assembly of the Arians to the catholic Church, from death to life. Confess, as we catholic Christians confess, that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the perfect Trinity and possess one Godhead.

Thus you hate Christians and persecute them by every means, as if your malice could overcome those who have entered upon a hard and rough path. Though they are objects of contempt, mockery [Col. 1036B], and hatred in your sight, they nevertheless choose in all this present life to be poor, humble, unknown, and subject to your injuries. Believing and enduring for God all things known to be bitter, they expect to come to those excellent rewards which the apostle declares they will receive—things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor [Note: Antiochene version: “and which have not entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him.” Cyprian, Epistle 56, with Lucifer: “nor has it entered into the heart of man.”] entered into the heart of man, which the Lord has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

Therefore, since God will grant these things to those who love him, we who love God, though we displease you and are punished by you, are confident that we please God. Your deadly sentence can have no authority to punish us eternally, since you who condemn are yourself to be condemned—and condemned indeed so that you may suffer everlasting punishments. But we whom you torture, tear apart, and kill will receive eternal joys; vast and [Col. 1036C] immeasurable happiness and perpetual blessedness await us.

Know, then, that authority has rather been divinely given to us, so that while you think you condemn us, we condemn you; while you presume that you can punish us, we may punish you, sacrilegious Constantius. For he whom you deny has deigned to grant us, his bishops, authority so that whatever we bind on earth may be bound also in heaven. We endure temporary evils for God so that we may obtain eternal goods. We flee the temporary things which you offer us as goods, because eternal evils follow those goods of yours. Thus we choose to endure present things which you think harmful to us, so that, while glorious confession persists in us, we may deserve to obtain eternal and immortal goods; just as you, with those who, fearing you, are found to have obeyed your will [Col. 1036D] and abandoned God’s commands—because they have chosen present goods rather and despised future things—will incur immortal evils.

“For they are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb [Note: That is, the commands of God. Antiochene version: “For your servant … in keeping them.” Sabatier has in Lucifer, “in keeping those things.”]. For your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward” (Ps. 18:11). We know that this life, which you labor so greatly to take away, is exceedingly brief. We know that both this life’s goods and evils are brief, whereas the goods of that eternal life which we desire to obtain are everlasting. For we know that eternal evils will follow for you from these brief goods in which you delight and take pleasure; and that eternal goods will follow for us Christians, whom you despise and do not cease to tear apart with every power of your empire, from these brief evils [Col. 1037A].

You have read that these things are so in Psalm 125: “The Lord has done great things for them” (Ps. 125:2). And below: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Going forth they went and wept, scattering [Col. 1037B] their seed; but coming they shall come in exultation [Note: Greek: *en agalliasei*, “in exultation.” Antiochene version: “into exultation.”], carrying their sheaves” (ibid., v. 5). And in Psalm 128 [Note: This psalm is numbered 128 among the Hebrews; in the old and new Latin version, 127.]: “Blessed [Col. 1038A] are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. You shall eat the labors of the fruits [Note: “Of your hands.” Latin, from the Vulgate. Septuagint: *tous ponous tōn karpōn sou*, “the labors of your fruits.” Symmachus: *kopon cheirōn sou*, “the labor of your hands”; hence it is clear that the Septuagint also used *karpous* not for the receipt of fruits but for a part of the hand [Col. 1038B]. Scholiast: “They called *karpos* not ‘fruitfulness’ but a part of the hands.” St Jerome also noted this in his letter to Marcella (Epistle XXXV, alternatively CXLI, §5), because Latin books read “of your fruits.” Likewise, in 1 Kingdoms 5, *karpoi* is understood in the same sense as a part of the hand. The scholion cites Aquila: *kopon tarsōn sou*, “the labor of your palms.” Galland, from Nobilius in the Greek-Latin Septuagint edition. Sabatier adds in Lucifer: “because you shall first eat.”] of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:1).

It shall indeed be well forever with those who did not deny the Son of God, who shall attain their reward by the labor of their holy confession. But for you, if you judge that you must always remain in the madness in which you now live, it shall be ill forever, as you receive the things Judas Iscariot now receives. Then you will see us while you are a suppliant; yet every lament of your repentance will be ineffectual, because it is here that either eternal life or death is acquired.

We wish these things always to occupy our hearts [Note: I think “our hearts” should be read.]; we want you to know that we think on them by day and night: your everlasting punishments, and the eternal rewards and merits of God’s servants; what punishment he threatens you, the denier and persecutor of his name; [Col. 1038B] and, conversely, what he promises those who confess him for everlasting glory.

[Col. 1037]

# TWO LETTERS OF ATHANASIUS TO LUCIFER. (C)*

## LETTER I

[Col. 1037C]

Athanasius sends greetings in the Lord to his most beloved lord, brother Lucifer, bishop and confessor.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] This title was given to those who had endured either tortures or exile for the faith of Christ.]

By God’s favor, while we are well in body, we have again sent our most dear deacon Eutyches, so that your devout Holiness also may deign to give us the welcome and desired assurance of your own safety and of that of all who are with you.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] From this you may understand that this exchange of letters was not the first between these holy men. Papebroch.]

For we believe that, while you confessors and servants of God remain alive, the condition of the Catholic Church is being renewed, and that our Lord Jesus Christ is restoring in full through you what the heretics attempted to tear apart. For although the forerunners of Antichrist have employed every resource of this world’s power to extinguish the lamp [Col. 1037D] of truth, yet the Godhead, through your confession, has made its light shine more brightly, so that their deceit cannot remain hidden from anyone. Formerly they could at least pretend; [Col. 1038C] now they are called antichrists. For who would not abhor them? Who would not flee their communion as though it were a stain and the venom of a serpent?

Everywhere the Church mourns; every city groans; aged bishops suffer in exile; and the heretics dissemble. While denying Christ, they have made themselves tax-collectors, sitting in churches and demanding revenues.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] “Sitting in the church and demanding tributes.” Id.]

O new kind of men, and of persecution, devised by the devil: that he should employ these very ministers for wrongdoing, and use them with such cruelty!  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] “And use them …” Id. Nor correctly: the Tilian corrections read *his* (“these”), whence the sense is weightier and sharper: namely, that the same devil employed these very persons—that is, the Arians—as ministers for wrongdoing, and used them with such cruelty, that is, as persons so cruel.]

But although they do such great things and have extended their arrogance and blasphemies, your confession, devotion, and wisdom are no small but the greatest comfort and great consolation to the brotherhood.  
[Note: [Col. 1038D] Papebroch omits “and great.”]

For word has reached us that your Holiness has written to the Emperor Constantius; [Col. 1038D] and we marvel more and more that, though dwelling among men as among scorpions, you nevertheless exercise freedom of spirit, so as by warning, teaching, and correcting to bring those who err [Col. 1039A] to the light of truth.  
[Note: [Col. 1039C] Thus the Tilian edition, as also Montfaucon, *Works of Athanasius*, vol. I, part 2, p. 965. Baronius, however, under the year 356, no. 74, has “the one who errs.” Galland.]  
[Note: [Col. 1039C] Papebroch has “light.”]

Therefore I ask—and all the confessors ask with me—that you may deign to send us a copy, so that all may perceive, not merely by report but from your writings themselves, the virtue of your soul and the confidence and freedom of your faith. Those who are with me greet your Holiness; I greet all who are with you. May the Godhead always preserve you safe, vigorous, and mindful of us, most beloved lord and true man of God.

## LETTER II

Athanasius sends greetings in the Lord to his most glorious and, with good reason, most longed-for fellow bishop, Lucifer.  
[Note: [Col. 1039C] We have printed this letter from the copy published by Chifflet among his notes on Vigilius of Tapsus, pp. 109 ff., where that distinguished man writes: “Because in the ancient Cluniac, Parisian, Poitevin, and Pontigny manuscripts we found this letter joined to the Dialogue of Vigilius of Tapsus under the name of Athanasius against Arius, and considerably more correct than its published editions, we therefore give it here.” Thus he. Galland, who, following Chifflet, prefixed this heading to the letter: “Athanasius, to the most blessed and deservedly most glorious holy bishop Lucifer.” The Venetian manuscript likewise heads it so, merely transposing “bishop” and “Lucifer.” “Deservedly most longed-for.” Papebroch.]

Although I believe that news has reached your Holiness also of the persecution which the enemies of Christ have even now attempted to inflict upon our brotherhood, seeking [Col. 1039B] our blood, nevertheless our most dear brethren can report its details to your piety. They have dared to extend their rage so far through the soldiers that they not only drove out the clergy of the city, but also went out to the deserts and laid their deadly hands upon the *monazontes*—that is, those living the solitary life, monks.  
[Note: [Col. 1039D] “Our brotherhood.” Chifflet.]  
[Note: [Col. 1039D] The Venetian manuscript rightly has *heremias* [deserts]; for a little below he calls those who inhabited the wildernesses, that is, the deserts, *μονάζοντες*, “monks.” Chifflet also reads thus.]  
[Note: [Col. 1039D] So too the Saint-Germain manuscript in Montfaucon’s works of St Athanasius; the Venetian manuscript agrees with it. *Μονάζοντας.* The Royal manuscript in Montfaucon there has *Monachos*, “monks.” Chifflet.]

Accordingly, I too withdrew farther away, lest those who had received us should suffer trouble from those same men as well.  
[Note: [Col. 1039D] “So that I too …” Venetian manuscript.]

For whom would the Arians spare, when they have not spared even their own souls?  
[Note: [Col. 1039D] “For whom would the Arians spare, who have not spared even their souls?” Id.; where *nanis* is erroneous.]

And when can they withdraw from their impious acts, while they persist in denying Christ the Lord, the only Son of God?  
[Note: [Col. 1039D] “Christ the Lord.” Id.]

This is the root of their depravity: upon this sandy foundation they build their perverse paths, as we find written in the thirteenth [Col. 1039C] Psalm: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1).  
[Note: [Col. 1040C] “Urenoso,” in Id., erroneously.]

And immediately it follows: “They have become corrupt and abominable in their works” (ibid.).  
[Note: [Col. 1040C] “In their desires.” Old Latin version.]

Thus the Jews, denying the Son of God, deserved to hear: “Woe, sinful nation, people full [Col. 1040A] of offences, evil seed, lawless sons.” Whence are they lawless? Because “you have forsaken the Lord” (Isa. 1:4).  
[Note: [Col. 1040C] “Woe to the sinful nation, a people full of offences,” etc. Chifflet.]  
[Note: [Col. 1040C] “Full of sins, evil seed, wicked sons: you have forsaken the Lord.” Old Latin version. The Greek Septuagint translation: “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, evil seed, lawless sons.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1040C] “Whence lawless?” is omitted in the Venetian manuscript.]

Thus the most blessed Paul, once he had begun not merely to believe in the Son of God but also to preach his divinity, wrote: “I am conscious of no evil in myself” (1 Cor. 4:4).  
[Note: [Col. 1040C] “He said.” Chifflet.]  
[Note: [Col. 1040D] “I am conscious of nothing against myself.” Old Latin version.]

Likewise, in accordance with your confession, we too desire, holding fast the apostolic tradition, to live according to the commands of the divine law, so that we may be found with you in that choir in which the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs now rejoice.

Although Arian madness, together with foreign power, so stirred itself that the brethren were not even allowed, insofar as those men raged, freely to see the air, nevertheless, through your prayers and God’s favor, though with labour and danger, I was able to see the brother who customarily conveys both necessary things and letters from your Holiness and from others. We received [Col. 1040B] the letters and books of your most devout and wise soul. In them we perceived an apostolic image, prophetic confidence, instruction in truth, teaching of the true faith, the heavenly way, the glory of martyrdom, triumphs over the Arian heresy, the uncorrupted tradition of our fathers, and the straight rule of ecclesiastical order.

O truly Lucifer—“Light-bearer”—you who, in accordance with your name, bear the light of truth and have set it upon a lampstand so that it may shine for all.  
[Note: [Col. 1040D] From this perhaps one might suppose that this letter was written in Latin by Athanasius, since it plays upon a Latin word. Montfaucon.]  
[Note: [Col. 1040D] The words “in accordance with your name” seem to have the character of a gloss. Galland.]  
[Note: [Col. 1040D] Papebroch reads “light.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1040D] “So that you may shine.” Venetian manuscript.]

For who, except the Arians, does not discern from your teaching the true faith and the stain of the Arians?  
[Note: [Col. 1040D] “From your teaching, that you have indeed [shown] the true faith, but the stain of the Arians very greatly and admirably, as light from darkness, have separated truth from the craft and perversity of the heretics,” etc. Chifflet. But it seems to us that this passage should be punctuated thus: “Who … does not discern from your teaching the true faith, but the stain of the Arians? Very greatly,” etc. So also Papebroch, who reads *valide* (“powerfully”) for *valde* (“greatly”).]

Very greatly and wonderfully, as light is separated from darkness, you have separated truth from the craft and hypocrisy of the heretics; you have defended the Catholic Church; you have proved that [Col. 1040C] the words of the Arians are nothing but a phantom; and you have taught that the devilish gnashings of teeth are to be trampled underfoot.  
[Note: [Col. 1040D] “Governors.” Chifflet.]

How good and delightful are your exhortations to martyrdom; how most desirable you have shown death for Christ, the Son of God, to be; and how you have made known the love of the age to come and of the heavenly life!  
[Note: [Col. 1040D] “How most desirably you have shown that one must die for Christ.” Chifflet; Royal, Saint-Germain, and Venetian manuscripts.]

You appear to be a true temple of the Saviour, who, dwelling in you, himself speaks these things through you; he who granted such grace to your words. For formerly you were beloved by all; but now so great a love for you has been fixed in everyone’s minds [Col. 1041A] that they call you Elijah in our times.  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Truly.” Id.]  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] “These things” is feminine in the Saint-Germain manuscript.]  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Placed.” Venetian manuscript.]

Nor is this surprising. For if those who seem pleasing to God are called sons of God, how much more fitting is it that confessors who share in the prophets—and especially you—should be so called.  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] Chifflet, and the Royal, Saint-Germain, and Venetian manuscripts, read “when” or “how much”; earlier editions have “a participant.” Baronius: “You, who share in the prophets, confessors”; Poncius in Latinius: “to call you the prince of prophets, confessors, and martyrs,” etc.]

Believe me, Lucifer: it was not you alone who spoke these things, but the Holy Spirit was with you.  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] “We believe that it was not you,” etc. Chifflet.]

Whence comes such a memory of the Scriptures? Whence their sound and uncorrupted understanding? Whence such ordered composition of discourse?  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Was composed.” Venetian manuscript. Papebroch: “composed.”]

Whence such exhortations toward the heavenly way? Whence confidence against the devil and proofs [Col. 1041B] against the heretics, unless the Holy Spirit dwelt in you?  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] Papebroch has “against.”]

Rejoice, therefore, seeing that you are already in that place in which your predecessors, the martyrs, are now: that is, in the choir of angels.  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Now by faith.” Chifflet.]  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Predecessors.” Chifflet and the Royal and Saint-Germain manuscripts. Papebroch: “Your predecessor martyrs are now in the choir of angels.”]

We too rejoice in having you as an example of courage, endurance, and freedom.  
[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Having you as an example.” The same witnesses, with Papebroch and the Venetian manuscript, which reads “of courage, endurance,” etc., without the conjunction *and*.]

As for what you wrote concerning my name, I blush to say anything, lest I seem a flatterer. But I know [Col. 1042C] and believe that the Lord himself, who revealed every knowledge to your holy and devout mind, will render to you also a reward in the kingdom of heaven for this labour.  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] “But I also know, and …” Venetian manuscript.]

Since you are such a man, we ask that through your prayers you may be our intercessor with the Lord, that in his mercy he may now deign to look upon the Catholic Church and rescue all his servants from the hands of the persecutors. Thus all those who have fallen [Col. 1042A] through temporal fear may at last be able to raise themselves up and return to the path of righteousness, from which, deceived, they wander, not knowing in what pit they miserably lie.  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] “Through your prayers to the Lord.” Galland.]  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] “Have fallen away.” Baronius.]

I especially ask that, if anything has been said less adequately by me, you may deign to forgive it. For my inexperience could scarcely draw what it was capable of from so great a fountain.  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] “If anything is lacking.” Venetian manuscript.]  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] “My,” with Chifflet and the Royal, Saint-Germain, and Venetian manuscripts; earlier editions have “that.”]

And concerning our brethren, if I could not see them, I ask you again to forgive me. Truth itself is witness that I wished and desired to obtain this, and that I felt such grief because I could not. For neither did tears cease from my eyes nor groaning from my heart, because we are not permitted to see even the brethren.  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] “We are permitted,” with the Tilian edition. The Venetian manuscript has “we shall be permitted”; earlier editions, “we permit.”]

The Lord is witness that I have not been able to see even the parents whom I have, from the time that they began persecuting us. For what do the Arians not do? They watch the roads; they take care concerning those departing [Col. 1042B] and leaving the city; they search ships; they range through the deserts; they disturb houses; they harass the brethren; they contrive troubles for each individual.  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] The Saint-Germain manuscript reads “they take care.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] Chifflet incorrectly has “hermits.” Baronius: “they range through the deserts.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] “Troubles,” with Latinius, Chifflet, and the Royal, Saint-Germain, and Venetian manuscripts; earlier editions have “by troubles.”]

But thanks be to God: while they do these things, they are all the more hated and abhorred by everyone, and are recognized truly—as your Holiness says—to be slaves of Antichrist. Yet those wretches, though hated, persist in their malice until, at the death of their grandfather Pharaoh, they too are condemned.

Those with me greet your piety; deign to greet those with you. May the divine grace of God always preserve you safe and mindful of us: blessed man, deservedly a man of God, servant of Christ, sharer with the apostles, consolation of the brotherhood, teacher of truth, and in all things most longed-for.  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] “And always.” Papebroch.]  
[Note: [Col. 1042C] Chifflet: “but in all things most longed-for.” Papebroch: “most longed-for.”]

# APPENDIX

[Col. 1041]

## ON THE PROFESSION OF FAITH OF ST LUCIFER, BISHOP OF CAGLIARI

[Col. 1041D] We first learned of this very ancient Fragment, which we here append, from the *Italian Diary* of the celebrated Bernard de Montfaucon. He testifies that he saw it at Milan in the Ambrosian Library, in these words, p. 19:

> A codex of the eighth century, written in Lombardic letters, contains certain homilies of Chrysostom; some works of Eucherius of Lyons; a Confession of Faith of Lucifer; likewise a Confession of Athanasius, found among spurious works attributed to Vigilius; likewise the Faith of Ambrose.

[Col. 1042D] Accordingly, when by letter we requested a copy of it from the distinguished Balthasar Oltrocchi, Prefect of the Ambrosian Library, he most courteously sent it to us and voluntarily communicated what was necessary both for determining the age of the codex in which Lucifer’s *Faith* was copied and for conjecturing whether the work were genuinely that of the holy bishop.

The codex, then, consists of parchment leaves and is written in rounded Roman minuscule, with letters joined together within individual [Col. 1043A] words. It contains certain shorter works of St John Chrysostom—though the title “Saint” is not prefixed to his name in the codex—the portion of the book of Hermas called *The Shepherd*, several minor works of St Eucherius, and some professions of faith. They are: “The Faith of St Ambrose, Bishop”; “Likewise, the Catholic Faith”; “The Faith of St Lucifer, Bishop”; “The Faith which proceeded from the Council of Nicaea”; and “The Faith of Blessed Athanasius,” which differs altogether from the Creed commonly published under his name, and which Montfaucon states was published among works spuriously attributed to Vigilius. Finally, the titles themselves and the first line of each little work are written in red.

From these facts Oltrocchi infers that the entire codex is much older than that from which Antonio Muratori extracted the *Faith of Bacchiarius* and the *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*, or Creed, of Venantius Fortunatus, and published them among the *Anecdota* which he had gathered from the Ambrosian Library. And if Muratori says that his codex was written a thousand years ago, Oltrocchi professes himself more cautious than Muratori, [Col. 1043B] since he judges that the codex from which he transcribed Lucifer’s *Faith* must be assigned at least to the sixth century, although it may appear and be said to be older.

Thus Oltrocchi differs from Montfaucon both concerning the age of the codex and concerning the form of its writing. In the absence of the manuscript itself, which we are unable to view and examine carefully, we cannot subscribe to either opinion. Yet, if we considered only the antiquity of the codex, the judgment of those who thought that this document of Lucifer’s *Faith* had previously been written or dictated by Lucifer himself might perhaps not be rejected. But the Formula of Faith itself contains neither few nor slight features which prevent us from adopting such an opinion.

For, first, its very style and manner of composition differ greatly from Lucifer’s. Further, Lucifer employs no Formula of Faith other than the Nicene one, which he quoted in full in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God* and whose opening he repeats in the book entitled *That One Must Die for the Son of God*. Then too, the expressions [Col. 1043C] that he usually employs when discussing the divine nature of the Word differ markedly from those presented in this Formula of Faith. Moreover, the term *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος, “of one substance” or “consubstantial”) is omitted from it, although the same force and sense may be detected in it. Yet Lucifer himself expressly presses this word and its meaning in his books and throws it in the face of Constantius.

For *homoousios* was a sure watchword of faith for Catholics, and at that time it would have been wrong to omit it in formularies of faith and in books written against the Arians. Indeed, at what time or place Lucifer could have issued this Formula of Faith, it would be astonishing that this most learned bishop—who knew thoroughly every artifice, stratagem, and snare of the Arians and who fought so long and strongly to defend the proposition that God the Son is *homoousios* with God the Father, that is, consubstantial—should finally, in a public testimony of his faith, have abstained from the one term that established Catholic doctrine. It would be still more astonishing if he had used genuinely ambiguous expressions such as this Formula contains, when above all things it was necessary to avoid them in a matter [Col. 1043D] of such moment; and we can scarcely discover that Lucifer used such expressions.

Such, therefore, is the expression in which the Father is said to have “the Son made from himself, without beginning, not unto himself.” The Nicene Synod decreed that the word “made” must be rejected from the divine generation of the Son, whom it clearly taught to be begotten, not made. And the writer of this Faith does not entirely agree with himself, since shortly afterward he adds that the Son is begotten, not made.

Although a Catholic sense may be drawn from the accompanying expressions “from himself” and “without beginning,” the use of this word is certainly imprudent. It is sometimes read in the sacred books where the Son of God is the subject, but the Fathers teach, against Arian calumnies, that it is to be attributed to his human nature, as Petavius discusses in *On the Trinity*, book II, chapter 3.

Nor is the other expression, “from himself,” free from ambiguity. It can signify either an efficient principle or one that begets and brings forth. [Col. 1044A] The latter properly belongs to God the Father, who is in truth the principle begetting the Son; the former does not, since being made is opposed to the Son of God. Petavius argues against the Calvinists on this in book VI, chapter 11, where he warns that this is a futile hunting after words and syllables which nevertheless “does not aim at a simple or moderate evil” (as Basil says concerning these very little words in *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 2), “but has a deep and hidden design against piety.”

Hence, even if the participle “made” were referred to the latter words and not merely to “unto himself,” these expressions would still be suspect and should not be approved, especially in a public attestation of the Catholic faith. The Synodical Letter of the Council of Alexandria, to which Lucifer himself subscribed, also warned this.

Moreover, the Son is improperly called “without beginning,” since the Father is the principle of his divine generation. Yet in a mode of writing or speaking less usual among the ancients, “without beginning” means the same as “eternal”; and therefore the Son is called *anarchos* (ἄναρχος, “without beginning”), because he is eternal and his generation is eternal. [Col. 1044B] Petavius discusses this at length in book V, chapter 5. Lucifer too employed the expression “without beginning” in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, but directly opposed it to the Arian error which ascribed a beginning to the Son because those men said that he had been made and created by the Father.

But the words “not unto himself” are subject to an ambiguous interpretation. For the Father begets the Son “unto himself,” if one considers in the Son those things which are *schetika* (σχετικά), that is, relative: his being the Word, the image of the Father, and the very notion of Sonship. But the Son is not “unto the Father,” if the statement concerns those things predicated absolutely and according to substance of the Son of God. For the Son is God absolutely, and good, and wise, and so forth. In support of this view, the aforementioned Petavius investigates and explains much according to the sense of Augustine in book IV, chapter 10, and book VI, chapter 9, no. 8.

But perhaps the author of this Faith used these words to oppose the error of the Arians, who said that the Son, the Word, was a certain instrument of the Father, which he had employed for creating the other things. Both Eusebius of Nicomedia and Eusebius of Caesarea especially followed this impious [Col. 1044C] opinion, as Petavius testifies in book II, chapter 3, no. 16, and chapter 7, no. 7. Consequently they taught that the Father had made the Son for himself, subject to himself and an instrumental minister. Therefore this Formula of Faith professes, admittedly in an obscure sense of the words, that the Father has the Son “not made unto himself.” Yet you will scarcely find the use of the expression “unto himself” introduced in the period when Lucifer lived; it seems first to have begun to be used in the age of Augustine, and subsequently to have been extended by theologians to various senses and meanings.

Who, observing these things, could readily persuade himself that Lucifer could publicly testify to his faith in expressions so ambiguous and obscure? Add to this that, although this Formula of Faith says more concerning the Holy Spirit in a Catholic sense than other formulae published in Lucifer’s time, whether by Catholics or heretics, yet, although the Arians themselves held impious views concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, before [Col. 1044D] the Macedonian heresy neither councils nor Fathers made fuller definitions of it in words or propositions. For at that time no controversy had yet been raised by name concerning this matter, as Petavius says in book II, chapter 6, no. 4.

But after Macedonius’s error had been condemned by the Council of Constantinople in 381, people began to discuss the nature of the Holy Spirit more clearly and copiously, and the phrases which this Formula presents came into common use. An exception must be made, however, for the Council of Alexandria held in 362, whose Synodical Letter written to the Antiochenes expressly decreed that the Holy Spirit must be regarded as God, and that he is neither a creature nor alien from the substance of the Father and the Son, as Petavius notes in book I, chapter 14, no. 18.

Lucifer himself assented to this Council and its decrees, as was demonstrated in §7 of his Life. And since the Alexandrian Fathers further wished this to be confirmed from the Synod of Sardica—that no one should write or publish anywhere [Col. 1045A] any other profession of faith besides the Nicene—we certainly cannot persuade ourselves that so useful and holy a decree, which he himself had approved, was neglected and violated by Lucifer.

We do not deny, indeed, that Lucifer sometimes spoke of the Holy Spirit in his books and sharply attacked the impiety of the Arians in this respect also. But he did so in expressions and words unlike those put forward in this Formula, as is readily evident from our preface.

Finally, we add this argument also, by which it may be proved that this Formula should not be attributed to Lucifer as its author: namely, that no time can properly be determined at which he ought to have established his faith by public and written testimony. At the Council of Milan, at which he was present as legate of Pope Liberius, he professed before the Emperor Constantius the Nicene Formula of Faith alone, as he himself testifies in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God* in these words:

> We legates affirmed in your palace, and we do not cease to affirm it, that Christians have always believed and do believe thus, as the sacred faith appears to have been written at Nicaea [Col. 1045B] against your Arian heresy and every error.

Throughout the whole period of his exile, he publicly testified to the same faith in written books, using the very words of the Nicene Formula. After his return from exile, he devoted himself wholly to settling the dissensions in the Church of Antioch and in the province of Caesarea which had arisen over the election of their bishops. He then returned to his own Church in Sardinia. What cause could then have arisen for him to devise and publish a new Formula of Faith—why one different from the Nicene, why one in some respect ambiguous and obscure—no one may either guess or safely assert. These are our reasons for rightly judging that the author of this Formula was someone other than Lucifer.

But every doubt concerning its author was removed for us when we saw almost the identical Formula of Faith previously published by Paschasius Quesnel in volume 2 of the *Works of Pope St Leo*, in the *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*, etc., chapter 38; and published again in Venice [Col. 1045C] in volume 3 of the same works, p. 278. These works were elucidated by the brothers Ballerini with learned and scholarly labour against Quesnel’s errors.

This formula bears in its heading the name of Faustinus the Presbyter, and is the same as that which Mabillon, from the Augiensis manuscript, calls the *Brief Faith*, as the Ballerini testify. And, as we suppose, the Augiensis manuscript is the same codex which Mabillon indicates in his *German Journey* as having been seen by him at Reichenau (*Augia*): “A notable large folio book, containing all the Fathers’ expositions of the Lord’s Prayer, and also various confessions of faith.”

The Oxford manuscript, from which Quesnel published the *Code of Canons*, etc., supplies this heading: “The Faith of Faustinus the Presbyter, sent to the Emperor Theodosius.” Another, the Thuanus manuscript, reads: “Likewise, the confession of the true faith of Faustinus the Presbyter, which the aforesaid Theodosius the Emperor ordered to be written and transmitted.” In Dissertation 14, no. 6, Quesnel corrects this to “which was ordered to be written and transmitted by the aforesaid …,” conjecturing that this Faith was composed by Faustinus at Theodosius’s command and sent by Theodosius to [Col. 1045D] Damasus, afterward to be entered into the archives of the Apostolic See; whence it was transferred into the Roman Code.

But the Ballerini reject Quesnel’s opinion in the preface to their new edition of this Code. They judge that it was composed neither in Italy nor at Rome, but in Gaul; and from a Vienna manuscript of the same Code they cite this heading: “Likewise, the confession of the true faith of Faustinus the Presbyter, which the Emperor Theodosius ordered the presbyter to write and to be sent to himself.” The Ballerini note the readings “wrote” and “to himself,” etc.

Thus the three most ancient manuscripts attribute this Creed to Faustinus; and no other Faustinus occurs, as Quesnellus observes in the cited Dissertation, who could have been the author of this little work, besides that Luciferian presbyter Faustinus, who, having written seven books against the Arians and Macedonians for Flaccilla, wife of the Emperor Theodosius, and having presented to Theodosius himself, together with the presbyter Marcellinus, the *Libellus Precum* (“Petitionary Book”), could readily have sent the same Emperor a document attesting his faith [Col. 1046A]. We indeed agree with this opinion.

The reason why Faustinus published a statement of his faith is indicated by Quesnellus in the same place: namely, because he was harassed, together with his colleague, by Turbon, bishop of Eleutheropolis—the city in which Faustinus, having been driven from Rome with Marcellinus and Lucifer himself because of the schism of Ursicinus, was then residing—as though he were an adherent of the errors of Sabellius and Apollinaris. For Faustinus himself, in the name both of himself and of Marcellinus, complains bitterly of Turbon in the *Libellus Precum* sent from Eleutheropolis to the emperors—that is, Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius—as stated in the Preface to the *Libellus Precum*: “The distinguished Turbon, bishop of the city of Eleutheropolis, despising our lowliness . . . after he heard that some persons were joining themselves to the sound faith and that, through God’s grace, the cause of truth was increasing, threatens us with ruin and troubles us.”

Whether Faustinus offered his Creed to Theodosius voluntarily or by Theodosius’s command, Quesnellus places the time when he composed it no earlier than the year 379, to which the beginnings of Theodosius’s reign are assigned [Col. 1046B], and not long afterward. His reason is the profound silence in it about Macedonius and about the First Council of Constantinople, by which Macedonius was condemned in 381; likewise, its manner of speaking of error against the Holy Spirit is no different from that used against that heretic by the Fathers of the Alexandrian Council in their synodal letter of 362.

Lequien, in volume 3 of *Oriens Christianus*, in his account of the bishops of Eleutheropolis, seems to refer the beginnings of Turbon’s episcopate to roughly the same period. He says that Turbon held the episcopate until nearly the death of Theodosius, that is, until about 395; but the year in which Eutychius, bishop before Turbon, died is unknown. Since, then, the author of this Formula has been identified, as well as the time when it was written and the reason for writing it, let us see how little Quesnellus’s copy differs from ours.

Faustinus first prefixes a brief apology for having himself written another Creed besides the Nicene Creed, lest he seem to violate the decrees of the Council of Sardica, which had approved those of Alexandria, forbidding anyone thereafter to issue new formulas of faith [Col. 1046C]. This opening is absent from our copy taken from the Ambrosian manuscript. He then testifies to his faith in precisely the same words, except for the words, “begotten from himself without beginning, not made”; in the Ambrosian copy these contain a certain obscurity and ambiguity, as we noted above. Finally, in a few words he defends himself against the charge of Apollinarian heresy brought against him, and condemns those who confess three hypostases; this concluding section likewise is absent from the Ambrosian copy.

Quesnellus, however, makes this observation: Faustinus, like his colleague Marcellinus also, was infected by the Luciferian schism and therefore opposed the decree of the Alexandrian Council, by which it had been established that participants in the Arian communion under the Emperor Constantius—especially bishops—should be received back into favor and communion with Catholics. Hence he was suspected of Sabellian and Apollinarian error. For the Fathers of the Alexandrian Synod had decreed that those returning to the Church from the society of the Arians should also condemn the impious doctrines of Sabellius [Col. 1046D]; that they should confess that the Holy Spirit is not a creature nor alien, but proper to and undivided from the essence of the Father and the Son; and finally that they should abhor the foolish error of Apollinaris, who taught that the Word, the Son of God, had assumed for himself a body without a soul and devoid of sense and mind.

Accordingly, lest Faustinus should seem, while rejecting the decree concerning the reception of those who had returned from the Arians, to reject the Catholic doctrine set forth by the Alexandrian Fathers and approved by the consensus of the entire Church, he expressly condemns Sabellius and openly distinguishes the persons in the Trinity against Sabellius’s error. He confesses the divine nature of the Holy Spirit in almost the very words of the Synod and plainly detests the heresy of Apollinaris. But concerning the indulgence granted to the fallen he is wholly silent; and he absolutely denies that among Catholics there may be tolerated the use of “three hypostases,” concerning which those who had fallen had been accused as suspected of heresy before they obtained pardon, and the sound and Catholic sense of which they had demonstrated to the Synod [Col. 1047A].

This gave those who confessed three hypostases in the Trinity—that is, three persons—another reason to call him a Sabellian. For Sabellius maintained that God was *huiopator* (ὑιοπάτορα), that is, that the Father and Son are one person in God, as Athanasius says in his *Exposition of the Faith*. And Sabellius held concerning the Holy Spirit the same view as concerning the Son, so as to make them equal in honor (*homotimous*, ὁμοτίμους) and not separate them from the person of the Father, but establish one and the same, as it were primary, hypostasis, of which those two—the Son and the Holy Spirit—were manifestations in operation (*energeiai*, ἐνεργείᾳ), as Petavius says in Book I, chapter 6.

Yet the Greek term *hypostasis* (ὑπόστασις) was used by the ancient Fathers, especially before the Council of Nicaea, for *ousia* (οὐσία), or essence; and indeed it signifies both that which simply exists—that is, essence—and that which subsists through itself, namely an individual or person. On these points see Petavius, Book IV, chapters 1, 4, and 7. Subsequently the Greek Fathers used it in this latter, individual sense; and so did those who had returned from the Arians to the communion of the true faith [Col. 1047B]. For by “three hypostases” they did not mean three essences, three gods, or three principles, but three persons in the Trinity: the Father, who truly is and subsists; the Son, as existing and subsisting; and the Holy Spirit, as subsisting and existing. This is attested by the synodal letter of Alexandria.

Thus the disputes and quarrels which had arisen over the term *hypostasis*, particularly at Antioch, were settled—the disputes from which the Antiochene schism had arisen, as Basil testifies in Epistle 349 of the old edition, cited by Petavius, Book IV, chapter 4, no. 11. Writing to Count Terentius, Basil says that he did not regard as unimportant the questions over which the schism had originally been formed. In this passage one should note that this dissension first began among the Greek East, not between Greeks and Latins, as the Preface to the synodal letters of the Alexandrian Council asserts in volume 2 of the earlier Venetian edition of the Councils.

But at the time when Faustinus issued this Creed, the smoldering fire of controversy had again burst out more violently, and the Latins also fostered it with intense party zeal [Col. 1047C]. Some wished *ousia*—that is, essence or substance—to be understood by the term *hypostasis*; others meant person or personal subsistence. Interpreting *substantia* among themselves, the former as essence and the latter as subsistence, they contended over the actual force of the same words in Latin speech.

Therefore Faustinus, maintaining that the word *substance* signifies essence, denies that three substances are to be affirmed in the Trinity. For it followed that those who confessed three substances in that sense must confess three gods. Indeed, in setting forth the Creed itself, he seems almost deliberately to have repeated the term *substance*, insofar as it denotes essence. Those, on the other hand, who said that *hypostasis* denoted person accused Faustinus and his colleague Marcellinus of Sabellianism, because they seemed to them to defend one person in the Trinity.

From these matters one may infer that Faustinus also introduced into his Formula of Faith the mention of three substances in order to seek the favor of Damasus, bishop of Rome [Col. 1047D], toward whom he had been hostile in the schism of Ursicinus. For Damasus had imposed silence upon the controversy over three hypostases, as Baronius maintains under the year 372 from the letters of Cyril of Alexandria, and had adopted Jerome’s view, which disapproved the use of three hypostases.

[Col. 1048A] Although it is uncertain whether Faustinus was living at Eleutheropolis when he issued the Creed, as Quesnellus thinks, or in another city—certainly in the East, where controversy over the use and sense of “three hypostases” was still raging—this gives rise to the inference that his entire reason for composing the Creed was to defend himself against the charges of those who confessed three hypostases in the sense approved by the Alexandrian Synod. While they interpreted the force of the term to support their own position, they accused of Sabellianism all who understood it differently. Faustinus therefore presents his Creed to the Emperor in such a manner that it wholly agrees with the Catholic doctrine of the Synod, while he insists that the terms *hypostasis* and *substance* must be explained only according to his own interpretation. This is indicated by the opening of the Formula itself: “We set forth the confession of the original faith against Sabellius and against those who, under the name of Catholic faith, defend impious expressions [Col. 1048B], saying that there are three substances.”

And this is enough about Faustinus’s Formula. Anyone can readily see, merely by considering the words of the Creed itself and the purpose for which it was issued, whether these things suit Lucifer. But who could say that a Creed written by Lucifer was adopted by Faustinus into his own Formula, with an opening and conclusion added, so that it might be approved the more on account of the author himself? Faustinus would not have suppressed the name of Lucifer, whom he adorns repeatedly with so many praises in the *Libellus Precum*.

Finally, from what has thus far been said, it may rightly be concluded that the Formula of Faith which we here present from the Ambrosian manuscript is not to be attributed to Lucifer. Lucifer exclusively followed the Nicene Formula of Faith; he never wrote anything ambiguous or obscure concerning the Trinity; he confirmed by his assent the decrees of the Alexandrian Synod; he openly abhorred Sabellius’s errors in the book *On Not Communicating with Heretics*; and he was never brought under suspicion of the error of any heretic. Rather, the Formula was drawn from the Faustinian Formula either by some ignorant person or by a Luciferian sectarian, corrupted by the ambiguous expressions which we have noted, and either ignorantly or fraudulently ascribed to Lucifer. It was inserted into the Ambrosian manuscript around the fifth century, with Lucifer’s name subsequently prefixed [Col. 1048C].

It is pleasing to add the following from the Preface to volume I of Sirmond’s Works, Venetian edition, no. 2: “Some think that, together with the *Libellus Precum* of Marcellinus and Faustinus, a Confession of Faith was delivered to the emperors—the confession which, in the *Code of Canons and Constitutions of the Church of Rome*, published twenty years ago in the Appendix to the Works of St. Leo, edition of 1675, p. 138, is entitled *The Faith of Faustinus the Presbyter, Sent to the Emperor Theodosius*. But since in the Preface of that *Libellus*, which is the work of a schismatic, the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius are named, the *Libellus Precum* must be assigned to the year 383, when Arcadius was proclaimed Augustus, and cannot be placed later than 392, when Valentinian died. This cannot agree with the year in which the Creed was issued [Col. 1048D]. Others judge the *Libellus* to be several years later than the Confession of Faith, which seems more probable.”

Let us now place examples of both Creeds together for comparison.

[Col. 1049A]

From the parchment manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, shelf-mark I, 101, upper part. **HERE BEGINS** [Note: [Col. 1049C] These words, “Here begins the Faith of St. Lucifer the Bishop,” are written in red in the manuscript.] **THE FAITH OF ST. LUCIFER, BISHOP.** [Note: [Col. 1049] The *Incipit fides S. Luciferi episcopi* and the *Fides Faustini presbyteri* are printed in parallel in Migne.] (C, S)

[Col. 1049]

[Col. 1049B] We believe in the Father, who is not the Son, but has a Son from himself, without beginning, not made unto himself. And we believe in the Son, who is not the Father, but has a Father from whom he is begotten, not made. And we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is truly the Spirit of God. Therefore we confess one substance of the divine Trinity, because such as the Father is according to substance, such a Son has he begotten. And the Holy Spirit, not being a creature but the Spirit of God, is not alien from the substance of the Father and the Son, but is himself of the same substance with the Father and Son, just as of the same Godhead. End.

[Col. 1050A] From the *Code of Canons and Constitutions of the Holy Apostolic See*, in volume 3 of the Works of St. Leo, Venetian edition of 1757, col. 278. **THE FAITH OF FAUSTINUS THE PRESBYTER, SENT TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS.** (S)

The faith [Note: [Col. 1049C] That is, the Nicene Creed. He prefaces an apology for issuing a new Formula of Faith against the Alexandrian decree; [Col. 1049D] the decree particularly concerns the use of “three hypostases,” in these words: “Concerning those,” that is, those who had communicated with the Arians, “since some accused them of affirming three hypostases, because expressions of this kind are not found in Scripture and may therefore be suspected, we determined that they should inquire no further beyond the Nicene confession.”] composed against the Arian heresy was sufficient. But because, through perverse ingenuity, some alter impious expressions under the profession of that faith [Note: [Col. 1049D] The Thuanus manuscript: “mix.”], bringing reproach upon us as though we defended the heresy of Sabellius, we set forth in a few words the confession of the original faith against Sabellius [Note: [Col. 1049D] Perhaps “confession.”], and against those who under the name of Catholic faith defend impious expressions, saying that there are three substances; whereas the Catholic faith has always confessed one substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Col. 1050B].

We believe in the Father, who [Note: [Col. 1050C] He openly distinguishes the person of the Father from that of the Son, in order to show that he opposes the Sabellian error; whence one may infer that this Creed was written more to condemn that heresy than the Arian.] is not the Son, but has a Son begotten from himself without beginning, not made; and we believe in the Son, who is not the Father, but has a Father from whom he is begotten, not made; and we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is truly the Spirit of God. Therefore we confess one substance of the divine Trinity [Note: [Col. 1050C] He calls the substance one, no less in order to profess Catholic doctrine than to press upon his opponents the meaning of the term [Col. 1050D].]: for such as the Father is according to substance, such also has he begotten the Son; and the Holy Spirit, not being a creature but the Spirit of God, is not [Note: [Col. 1050D] This is taken almost word for word from the Alexandrian synodal letter.] alien from the substance of the Father and the Son, but is himself of the same substance with the Father and the Son, as of the same Godhead.

For those who think that we are [Note: [Col. 1050D] Concerning the heresy of Apollinaris and the three substances, see what we have said above.] Apollinarians should know that we abhor the heresy of Apollinaris no less than the Arian. Yet we wonder how those can be approved as Catholics [Col. 1050C] who confess three substances of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And even if they say that they do not believe the Son of God or the Holy Spirit to be a creature, nevertheless they think in accordance with an impious faith [Note: [Col. 1050D] Unless there is an error in both the Quesnellian and Venetian editions, and one should read *ipsam*, “that very,” the sense will be: “yet conversely they follow an impious faith; they think impiously.”], when they say that there are three substances. For it follows that those who confess three substances confess three gods. The Catholics have always abhorred this expression.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 397. ST. PACIAN, BISHOP OF BARCELONA.**

(From Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. VII.)

[Col. 1051]

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 1051A] I. Although Pacian was an outstanding glory of Spain, among ancient writers we know him only from Jerome, who has transmitted but a few facts about him to memory; from Jerome, it is evident, all later writers derived their accounts. We learn, then, from the greatest Doctor [Note: [Col. 1051C] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 106.] that St. Pacian flourished as bishop at Barcelona, beneath the ridges of the Pyrenees, in chastity and eloquence, and that, renowned alike for life and speech, he exchanged life for death in extreme old age under the Emperor Theodosius. Accordingly, the blessed bishop was especially distinguished around the year of Christ 370, since in 392, when Jerome wrote of him, he had already departed this life.

Elsewhere the holy Doctor sufficiently reveals the nobility of his family when he mentions Dexter—Pacian’s son, to whom he dedicated his own book *On Illustrious Men*—as still not raised to the priesthood [Col. 1051B], but eminent in public life and devoted to Christ’s faith [Note: [Col. 1051C] Jerome, same work, ch. 132.]. Referring again to this matter elsewhere, Jerome writes as follows [Note: [Col. 1051C] Jerome, Book II, *Against Rufinus*, §24.]: “Almost ten years ago, when my friend Dexter, who had administered the office of Praetorian Prefect, asked me to compose for him an account of the authors of our religion,” etc. Thus Jerome wrote in 402 concerning Dexter, Pacian’s son. Dexter, after being made *comes rerum privatarum* (“Count of the Private Estate”) under Theodosius the Great in 387, is reported finally to have held the office of Praetorian Prefect under Honorius in 395, as we gather from the prosopography of the Theodosian Code [Note: [Col. 1051C] *Codex Theodosianus*, vol. VI, part II, p. 49, latest edition.].

II. These, then, are the facts handed down to us by Jerome concerning Pacian’s distinguished family, integrity of life, administration of the episcopal office, praise for learning, and literary works. Jerome also left this testimony concerning him [Col. 1052A] [Note: [Col. 1052C] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 106.]: “Pacian,” he says, “wrote various little works, among which are *The Stag* and works against the Novatians.” The work first named here, entitled *The Stag*, has wholly perished. The holy Father mentions it in writings that still survive [Note: [Col. 1052C] Pacian, *Exhortation to Repentance*, §1. See below.]. At that passage we have noted some matters from Cange concerning the unusual title of the work; to these I should especially like added the observations of the learned Tillemont [Note: [Col. 1052C] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. VIII, p. 539.].

The other work mentioned by Jerome, Pacian’s work against the Novatians, survives: namely, his three letters to the Novatian Sympronianus. The first is entitled *On the Name Catholic*, the second *On the Letter of Sympronianus*, and the third *Against the Treatises of the Novatians*. The learned Tillemont argues from Pacian’s mention of the Apollinarians that the author wrote them after 377 [Col. 1052B] [Note: [Col. 1052C] Tillemont, same work.] [Note: [Col. 1052C] Pacian, Letter 1, §3. See below.].

These letters are followed by the truly excellent little work, the *Paraenesis*, or exhortatory treatise *On Repentance*. Finally there is added the *Sermon on Baptism*. Both, of course, are to be included among those various little works which, according to Jerome’s testimony, our bishop of Barcelona is said to have committed to writing.

We have carefully reviewed all these works of Pacian from the principal Tilian edition; divided them into chapters or sections, whereas previously they had been set forth rather inconveniently in an almost uninterrupted sequence; but we have directed our attention especially to restoring the text, corrupted in many places in earlier editions, to its original integrity, adding from time to time a few observations to confirm the correct reading.

[Col. 1051]

# THE THREE LETTERS OF ST. PACIAN TO SYMPRONIANUS THE NOVATIAN. (S)

## LETTER I. On the Name “Catholic.” Pacian to his brother Sympronianus, greeting.

[Col. 1051D]

I. If it is not a carnal intention but, as I judge, a spiritual calling, sir, that leads you to examine us concerning the faith of Catholic truth, you especially ought to have indicated what or how different a teaching you yourself followed. Since, as far as appears, you began far away from a little stream, you did not hold to the fountain and origin of the chief Church [Col. 1052D]. You ought to have disclosed what cause in particular had separated you from the unity of our body; for those parts requiring medicine must be uncovered. But now, with the bosom of your letter, so to speak, closed, we do not see which members especially need treatment.

For so many heresies have arisen from the Christian head that their names alone would fill a vast volume. To pass over the heretics of the Jews—Dositheus the Samaritan, the Sadducees, and the Pharisees—it would take too long to enumerate how many emerged in the times of the apostles: Simon Magus, Menander, Nicolas, and the rest whom obscure report has concealed. What of [Note: [Col. 1053D] “What of Ebion in later times?” In Cotelerius’s judgment, on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VI, ch. 6, these words of Pacian require a charitable interpretation. For the origin of the Ebionites seems, according to Epiphanius and Jerome, to be referable to the time of the Apostle John [Col. 1054D].] Ebion in later times, Apelles, Marcion, Valentinus, and Cerdon? Nor long after them came the Cataphrygians and [Col. 1053B] Novatians, not to mention newer swarms. Whom, then, must I first refute in writing? If you wish, a sheet itself would not contain all their names. Except that by your writings, which everywhere condemn repentance, you declare that you agree with the Phrygians.

Yet even among these, most dear sir, error is so manifold and diverse that not merely this one doctrine in them—their view against repentance—but, as it were, certain Lernaean heads must be cut off.

II. First, these rely upon very many authorities. For I suppose even Blastus the Greek belongs to them; Theodotus also and Praxeas at one time taught your people. Those more famous Phrygians themselves, who falsely claim that they are inspired by Leucius and boast that they were instructed by Proclus, followed Montanus, Maximilla, and Priscilla. How many disputes they stirred up concerning the day of Easter, the Paraclete, the apostles, and the prophets—and many other matters, including this matter of the Catholic name and pardon after repentance [Col. 1053C].

Therefore, if we wished to examine all these questions, we would need the presence of a willing learner. Even if I did not sufficiently instruct you on these particular points which you write about, yet, since those who wonder must be served in whatever way is possible, for your instruction let us briefly discuss the subjects on which you have deigned to write. If you wish to know more fully concerning our position, you ought to state your own more plainly, lest by consulting too obscurely you make us unable to know whether you are asking a question or issuing a challenge.

Meanwhile, so far as the present matters are concerned, before all else I ask you not to borrow authority for error from this very fact: that, as you say, throughout the whole world there is no one within who could refute you or [Col. 1053D] persuade you contrary to what you believe. Even if we are unlearned, the Spirit of God is most learned; and even if we are faithless, God is faithful, who cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13). Moreover, it was not permitted to continue long in contention by resisting the priests of God [Note: [Col. 1054D] “By resisting.” We have restored this from the context. The printed editions read “by prevailing.”]. “We,” says the Apostle, “have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16). “After one admonition” (Tit. 3:10), as you yourself know, a contentious person is left alone. And who can persuade anyone against his will?

The fault, then, brother, is yours, not theirs, if no one persuaded you of what was best [Col. 1054A]. For even today it is in your power to despise our writings also, if you prefer to conquer them rather than approve them. Moreover, very many resisted the Lord himself and his apostles, nor could truth be persuaded to anyone unless he assented to it by his own religious disposition.

Accordingly, sir, we too have written not with the confidence that we can persuade one who resists, but with the faith that we should not deny an entrance to good peace to one who is willing. If that is in your mind and heart, there need be no dispute about the name “Catholic.” For if our people receive it from God, the question need not be asked, divine authority having preceded; if from a human being, it must be discovered when it was adopted. Then, if the name is good, it does not admit hatred; if evil, it lacks grounds for envy.

[Col. 1054B] III. I hear that Novatians are called after Novatus or Novatian; yet in them I accuse the sect, not the name. Nor has anyone objected to Montanus or the Phrygians because of their name. “But under the apostles,” you say, “no one was called Catholic.” Let it be so; grant even that point. After heresies arose following the apostles and sought, under various names, to tear and divide into pieces the dove of God and the queen, did not the apostolic people require a designation of its own, by which it might distinguish the unity of the uncorrupted people, lest the error of some rend limb by limb the undefiled virgin of God? Was it not fitting that the principal head be marked by a distinctive name?

Suppose that today I entered a populous city and found Marcionites, Apollinarians, Cataphrygians, Novatians, and other such groups, all calling themselves Christians: by what designation could I recognize the congregation of my own people, unless it were called Catholic [Col. 1054C]? Come now: who bestowed so many names on the other peoples? Why does each of so many cities and nations have its own designation? The very man who questions the name Catholic will not know the origin of his own name if I ask from whom it was handed down to me. Certainly what has endured through so many centuries was not borrowed from a human being.

This name Catholic speaks neither of Marcion, Apelles, nor Montanus, and takes no heretics as its authors. The Holy Spirit has taught us much—the Spirit whom God sent from heaven as Paraclete and teacher to the apostles; much has been taught by reason, as Paul says, by propriety, and, as he says, by nature itself. What? Does the authority of apostolic men, of the earliest bishops, and of the most blessed Cyprian—martyr [Col. 1054D] and teacher—count for little with us? Or do we wish to teach the teacher? Are we wiser than he, and are we inflamed by the spirit of the flesh against one whom the noble shedding of blood and the crown of a most glorious passion have brought forth as a witness of the eternal God?

What of all the bishops of those regions whom one peace united throughout the whole world with Cyprian himself? What of so many aged bishops, so many martyrs, so many confessors? Come now. If they were not suitable authorities for adopting this name, shall we be suitable authorities for rejecting it? Will the Fathers follow our authority instead [Col. 1055A], and must the antiquity of the saints yield to correction, while times now decaying with vices erase the canons of apostolic antiquity?

IV. Yet do not be troubled, brother. “Christian” is my name; “Catholic” my surname. The former names me; the latter identifies me. By this I am approved; by that I am indicated. And if, finally, an account must be given of the word *Catholic* and its Greek meaning rendered in Latin: “Catholic” is so called where there is one whole, or, as the more learned think, the obedience of all—that is, obedience to the commands of God. Hence the Apostle says: “If you are obedient in all things” (2 Cor. 2:9). And again: “For as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many shall be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19). Therefore one who is Catholic is likewise obedient as a righteous person [Col. 1055B]. One who is obedient is likewise Christian; thus the Catholic is Christian.

Accordingly our people are distinguished from the heretical name by this designation when they are called Catholic. But if “Catholic” means “one everywhere,” as those mentioned above think, David himself indicates this when he says: “The queen stood in a garment of gold and many colors” (Ps. 44:10), that is, one in all places. And in the Song of Songs the Bridegroom says: “My dove is one, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, chosen by her who bore her” (Song 6:8). And again: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her” (Ps. 44:15). And still again: “Young maidens without number” (Song 6:7). Therefore she is one in all things and one above all things.

V. If you seek the reason for the name, it is evident. But concerning repentance: may God grant that it be necessary for no believer [Col. 1055C]; may no one, after the help of the sacred font, fall into the pit of death; and may priests not be compelled to offer or teach delayed remedies, lest, while they soothe the sinner with remedies, they open a path for sinning again.

But we disclose this indulgence of our God to the miserable, not the blessed; not before sins [Note: [Col. 1055D] “But sins.” It seems that one should read “but after sins.” The Lyons editors printed it thus.], but after sins; we announce medicine not to the healthy but to those who are ill. If spiritual wickednesses have no power over the baptized; if the serpent’s deceit, which first overthrew humankind and imprinted upon its descendants so many marks of condemnation, has no power; if it has departed from the world; if we have already begun to reign; if no crime creeps into our eyes, hands, or minds—then let this gift of God be cast aside, let help be rejected, let no confession of sins be made, let no groans be heard; let proud righteousness despise every remedy.

But [Col. 1055D] if the Lord has provided these things for his human creature; if he who has bestowed rewards upon those who stand has also bestowed remedies upon those who lie fallen: cease to accuse divine mercy, to erase by the objection of severity so many testimonies of heavenly compassion, or to prevent the free gifts of the Lord by unyielding harshness.

[Col. 1056A] “Return to me,” says the Lord, “with fasting, weeping, and mourning; rend your hearts” (Joel 2:12). And again: “Let the wicked forsake his ways and the criminal man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he shall obtain mercy” (Isa. 45:7). Likewise the Prophet cries in this manner: “For God is gracious and gentle and patient, [Note: [Col. 1055D] “And who turns back . . . imposed.” Following the old translator, the author renders this passage of Joel 2:13 here and below, in Letter 3, chapter 21, according to the Septuagint: *kai metanoōn epi tais kakiais* (καὶ μετανοῶν ἐπὶ ταῖς κακίαις), “and repenting concerning evils.” The Vulgate has “relenting over evil.” St. Cyprian likewise quotes the same words of Joel in the same manner, at the end of *On the Lapsed*, at the beginning of *On the Good of Patience*, and in Letter 55 to Antonianus, pp. 138, 211, and 111 of the Oxford edition. But everywhere, in place of *reflectat*, he reads *flectat*, “turns,” and in place of *irrogatam*, “imposed,” *irrogatas*, “imposed [evils]”; I myself would prefer this latter reading to the other Cyprianic one.] and turns back the sentence imposed against evils” (Joel 2:13).

Does the serpent possess poison so enduring, and Christ no medicine? Does the devil kill in the world, and can Christ not help here? Let it indeed grieve you to sin, but let it not grieve you to repent. Let it shame you to be in danger, but let it not shame you to be delivered. Who would take away a plank from a shipwrecked person lest he escape? Who would begrudge the healing of wounds?

Does not David [Col. 1056B] say: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6:7)? And again: “I acknowledge my sin, and I did not conceal my wrongdoing” (Ps. 31:5). And again: “I said: I will confess my transgression against myself to my God, and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (ibid.). Did not the prophet answer the penitent David, after the guilt of murder and adultery concerning Bathsheba: “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Kings 12:13)? Was not the Babylonian king, condemned after so many acts of idolatry, delivered by confession of sins?

And what does the Lord mean when he says: “Will not one who has fallen rise again, and one who has turned away return?” (Jer. 8:4). What answer all those illustrations in the Lord’s parables? That the woman finds the drachma and rejoices at finding it; that the shepherd carries back the wandering sheep [Col. 1056C]; that, when the son returns after [Note: [Col. 1056D] “Squandered.” Tertullian likewise, *On Modesty*, ch. 8: “The younger son, having squandered God’s substance, begs in a foreign land.”] squandering all his goods and wasting them in revelry with prostitutes and fornicators [Note: [Col. 1056D] “Wasting in revelry.” The Lyons editors incorrectly restored *epotata*, “drunk up.” Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 46: “Aristippus revels in purple under a great appearance of seriousness.” On this passage Havercamp notes that such a word was transferred from the extravagant *nepotuli*, or spendthrift youths. Cange will provide more in his Glossary.], the gracious father runs to meet him and reproves the envious brother by showing him the reason: “This son of mine was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32).

What of the man wounded on the road and passed by by Levite and priest? Is he not treated? Consider what the Spirit says to the churches (Rev. 2): he accuses the Ephesians of having abandoned love; charges the Thyatirans with sexual immorality; rebukes the Sardians for ceasing from works and the Pergamenes for teaching divergent doctrines; censures the wealth of the Laodiceans; and nevertheless invites them all to repentance through satisfaction.

What of the Apostle when he says to the Corinthians: “Lest, when I come, I mourn many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the fornication and impurity which they previously committed” (2 Cor. 12:21) [Col. 1056D]?
