What when he says again to the Galatians: “If anyone has been overtaken in any transgression” (Gal. 6:1)—that is, in any transgression whatever—“you who are spiritual, instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, taking heed lest you too be tempted.”

[Col. 1057A] Does the master of a household, in a great house, preserve only vessels of silver and gold? Does he not also deem worthy vessels of clay and wood, and certain vessels repaired and put together again? “Now I rejoice,” says the Apostle, “because you were made sorrowful unto repentance” (2 Cor. 7:9). And again: “For godly sorrow works a steadfast repentance unto salvation” (ibid., 10).

VI. “But repentance was not permitted.” No one commands toil without result: “For the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Matt. 10:10; Luke 10:7). God would never threaten one who does not repent, unless He forgave one who repents. “God alone,” you will say, “can do this.” True; but what He does through His priests is His own power. For what is the meaning of what He says to the Apostles: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever [Col. 1057B] you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19; John 20:23)? Why say this, if human beings were not permitted to bind and loose? Or is this permitted to the Apostles alone? Then baptism too is permitted to them alone; the giving of the Holy Spirit is permitted to them alone; and to them alone belongs the cleansing of the sins of the nations—for all this was commanded to none but the Apostles. But if in one place both the release of bonds and the power of the sacrament are given, then either everything has been transmitted to us from the pattern and authority of the Apostles, or not even that has been relaxed by their decrees. “I,” he says, “laid a foundation, but another builds upon it” (1 Cor. 3:10). Therefore we build upon what the teaching of the Apostles established as a foundation.

Indeed, bishops too are called apostles, as Paul explains concerning Epaphroditus: “My brother and fellow-soldier,” [Col. 1057C] he says, “but your apostle” (Phil. 2:25). If, therefore, the authority over the font and chrism—greater and far more extensive gifts—has descended thence to bishops, then the right both to bind and to loose has also belonged to them. Even if we presumptuously claim this for ourselves because of our sins, God nevertheless will not deny it to the holy men who occupy the chair of the Apostles—He who has even granted bishops the name of His Only-begotten.

VII. I would write more, brother, were I not pressed by the haste of the boy returning, and reserving fuller matter either for you in person or [Note: [Col. 1057] “On the whole subject.” Latinius’s conjecture, reading *de nomine* (“on the name”) instead of *de omni proposito*, is very pleasing, so that Pacian may here refer to the subject of the letter, entitled “On the Catholic Name.”] for one confessing concerning the whole matter. Let no one despise a bishop out of regard for the man. Let us remember that the Apostle Peter called our Lord a bishop: “But now,” he says, “you have returned to the bishop and shepherd of your souls” [Col. 1057D] (1 Pet. 2:25). What can be denied to a bishop in whom God’s name is at work? He will indeed render an account if he has done anything wrongly, or judged corruptly and impiously. Nor is God prejudged, so that He cannot undo the works of an evil builder. Meanwhile, if that administration is devout, it continues as a helper in God’s works.

See how the Apostle writes to laypersons: “If you forgive anything to anyone, so do I. For what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven for your sakes in the person of Christ, lest we be possessed by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices” (2 Cor. 2:10–11). But if the Apostle says that he himself has forgiven what laypersons forgive, how can what a bishop does be rejected? [Col. 1058A] Therefore neither baptism, nor forgiveness of crimes, nor renewal of the body has been granted to his holy authority—for nothing has been entrusted by private usurpation, and all this has flowed from apostolic right.

I know, brother, that this pardon of repentance is not given indiscriminately to everyone, nor granted before there has been either an interpretation of the divine will or perhaps a visitation. Only after great weighing and grave deliberation, after many groans and an outpouring of tears, after the prayers of the whole Church, is the forgiveness of true repentance not refused—yet in such a way that no one prejudges Christ, who is to judge. If you write more plainly what you think, brother, you will be instructed more fully.

## LETTER II. On the Letter of Sympronianus

[Col. 1058B] Pacian, bishop, to brother Sympronianus, greeting.

I. In this lengthy controversy I shall follow brevity as far as I can. Nor shall I repay you, brother, with any corresponding malice when, under the guise of a worthy question, you hurl hidden verbal weapons and bring forward accusations which you yourself contrive. We are commanded to pray for those who persecute us and to bless those who curse us (Matt. 5:44). Fraud belongs, as it were, to the little fox; violence, to the lion. Both are utterly alien to humanity; but fraud deserves the greater hatred. For when you believe that you are doing more harm, you question as though ignorant; when you imagine that you are teaching, you pretend to be taught. The Pharisees of old called the Lord “Rabbi” when they set before Him riddles from the Law; they called Him “Teacher” when they claimed all teaching for themselves. Whatever you do, brother, you will receive everything from me in simplicity. I prefer to be considered unlearned rather than malicious, foolish rather than crafty. Therefore, before I set forth the reason for our faith, concerning which you are troubled, receive a few remarks upon the letter which you prefixed to your treatise.

II. You say that you were refreshed by my earlier letters, and immediately add that what I wrote was a bitter reply. If bitter things refresh, I do not know what sweet things accomplish—unless it is because, as with medicinal draughts, bitterness is more commonly healing than sweetness. But I beg you, reread my letters: are they sprinkled with any gall? What proud or unpleasant thing did I answer? You say that I named several heresies about which no one had asked. Well then: what concern of yours was it, if you were not a heretic? Since you raised a question concerning our faith [Col. 1058D] and said that you wished to be taught, I wrote that the causes of ignorance are numerous, asking you especially to disclose which one held you, lest I should labour in unravelling too many.

I answered much, and gently, concerning the Catholic name. For I said that it makes no difference what anyone else may be called. And if you demanded the force of the name, that whatever it might be, it was wonderful: whether “one in all,” or “one above all,” or, what I had not said earlier, “the king’s son,” that is, the Christian people. Certainly it is not a name recently imposed upon us, for it has not fallen away through so many ages. I am indeed glad that, although you have placed others before us, you nevertheless agree with us concerning the name. What if you denied it? Nature itself would cry out. [Col. 1059A] Or if you still doubt, let us be silent. What we shall be called, that we shall be, with the antiquity of the name as witness. But if you demand it more stubbornly, beware lest that man of strength cry out to you: “Why do you ask my name? It too is wonderful” (Judg. 13:18).

You then added, to be sure, that one ought not to consider whence Catholics derive this name, since it is not usually counted against Valentinians if they are called after Valentinus, nor against Phrygians if after Phrygia, nor against Novatians if after Novatian.

III. At this you were violently stirred and rose up as though pierced by a goad; for in anger you cry out thus: “Does it harm holy Cyprian that his people bears the name ‘apostate,’ or ‘Capitoline,’ or [Note: [Col. 1059D] “Syndrean.” I think *συνέδριον* (“council, assembly”) should be read here. It is an insult derived from the name of a council and applied in disparagement of Cyprian. —Tilius.] ‘Syndrean’?” You revile, and behold, I am not moved. Have we been called by any of these names? Ask the age, brother, and every year in succession: whether this name has clung to us, or whether Cyprian’s people have been called anything other than Catholic. [Col. 1059B] I have never heard any name of this kind. Now consider whether anyone can be called by a name which he does not know has been applied to him.

What then? These are curses, not names: curses of angry and insolent people. I too can call you by any number of names, if anger is permitted. You call Cyprian holy, yet call his people apostate? How so? “If the first-fruits are holy, so is the lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches” (Rom. 11:16). [Note: [Col. 1059D] “If the first-fruits are holy, so is the lump.” Rom. 11:16: *Εἰ δὲ ἡ ἀπαρχὴ ἁγία, καὶ τὸ φύραμα.* Vulgate: “But if the offering of first-fruits is holy, so also is the mass.”]

Am I apostate, or Novatus? Novatus, I say: he who betrayed his father, deserted the Church, and cast out his wife’s pregnancy? Am I apostate, or Novatian—whom a letter fabricated as bishop while he was absent; who, though no one consecrated him, received a linen-covered [Col. 1059C] seat? But that later. Meanwhile, say yourselves what you are called. Do you deny that Novatians are called after Novatian? Whatever name you impose, that one will always cling to you. Search all the annals, if you please, and trust so many centuries: you will answer, “Christian.” If I inquire after the designation of the sect, you will not deny “Novatian.” Yet I do not accuse the name of your Novatian, which, though repeatedly sought, you enclose in circumlocutory lines and hide in a sort of covered fold. Confess simply: there is no crime in the name. Why do you conceal yourself when so often questioned? Why are you ashamed of the cause of your name? When you first wrote, I thought you a Cataphrygian. Do you confess it only in your second letter? You envy my name while avoiding your own? See whose cause is shameful: that which shrinks from being called what it is.

[Col. 1059D] IV. What are you criticizing and pursuing? Have we come, as it were, before a rhetorician, or is an art to be treated, or am I to expound lines of Virgil line by line? When I had named several heretics, I added: [Note: [Col. 1059D] “And those whom obscure report conceals.” The author wrote this in Letter I, §1. Shortly afterward, perhaps *Atquin* (“and yet”) should be read [Col. 1060D] instead of *ego*.] “And those whom obscure report conceals.” And how do you think that this was taken from a verse of Virgil, if you did not know Virgil at all? Yet I deny that I set down the verse in its proper order. I said, “whom obscure report [Col. 1060A] conceals,” as speakers commonly do: from the abundance of ordinary human speech they say something that has been said before. But you repeated the verse in its own order and structure. Did you love Virgil so much that you considered it almost sacrilege to break up his verse? Yet I had learned it in childhood. What wonder if I fell upon words I knew? Is your labour so great, brother, that only now you read things which you were once ashamed that others had read?

You should accuse one educated in Latin and speaking Latin just as you would a Greek speaking Greek, a Parthian speaking Parthian, or a Phoenician speaking Punic. Medes, Egyptians, and Hebrews have their own language, according to the abundance of the Lord, who modulated it into one hundred and twenty tongues. “A bishop used a poetic verse.” What then of the Apostle Paul? Is he ashamed when he both quotes and approves that Athenian verse? For in the Acts of the Apostles he says: “As certain even of your own poets have said: ‘For we are also His offspring.’ Therefore, since we are God’s offspring…” [Col. 1060B] (Acts 17:28–29). And again he said to Titus: “One of them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies’” (Titus 1:12–13). And he adds: “This testimony is true.”

Thus we sin by following an example. We are not rhetoricians, but we believe that every utterance belongs to God’s abundance. Latium, Egypt, Athens, Thrace, Arabia, and Spain confess God; the Holy Spirit understands every language. Why, then, do you yourself say, “I shall coat your letters with living cedar because of the worm-eaten enemies of the Muses”? Which Muses, I ask? Those who invented letters and wrote documents which moths pursue? Tell me, brother, I ask: did the Muses discover letters? Is not everything through the Lord and from God? Apart from those [Note: [Col. 1060D] “One hundred and twenty languages.” The author has indicated the same a little earlier. Cotelerius, however, on *Recognitions*, book II, chap. 42, conjectures that Pacian wrote “seventy languages,” whence the number 120 arose by a slight alteration.] one hundred and twenty languages, was there still another belonging to the Muses? Hesiod lied about this on Helicon, encouraged by the pursuits of the Athenians, who, as the Apostle says, had leisure for nothing except speaking (Acts 17:21). But, on the Apostle’s testimony, we maintain that the varieties of every sound and the kinds of every language are inspired by God (1 Cor. 14:10, 18).

Still, I pardon you, brother, if you too presume something from your own author and join to Hesiod’s authority the philosophy of Novatian, through which he incurred the shipwreck of religion. Nevertheless, you ought to have remembered the Apostle, who says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty seduction” (Col. 2:8).

V. What sort of assertion is this now, that you think it should be charged against Catholics if kings or governments have sometimes persecuted you? Then, conversely, it ought to be charged against you whenever Catholics endured the impiety [Note: [Col. 1060D] “Of kings and persecution.” Tilius supplies “impiety and persecution.” A little later, instead of *questi sunt* (“they complained”), he reads *queri debuerunt* (“they ought to complain”).] and persecution of kings, and pagan rulers persecuted our people. Have you endured hatred from Christians? But ours have complained more. Let him who did this consider with what mind and spirit he acted—whether he sought peace or discord. [Col. 1061A] But even if some of them sinned, he says, “does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?” (Rom. 3:3).

Yet you must not suppose that ours made a complaint. But when, through our faith, rulers began to be Christian, the rulers themselves, favouring the Catholic—that is, their own—party, were moved by personal grief. Unless Daniel is to be blamed because he was vindicated by Darius; or most holy Esther, because the king’s official was killed on her account; or the three youths, because, after their ordeal by fire, the king of Babylon threatened the profane and unbelieving on their account. Did not Peter confound Simon, [Note: [Col. 1061D] “With a judge assisting.” The distinguished Mazochius observes in his commentary on the Neapolitan calendar marble, vol. III, p. 872, that Pacian here touches upon Peter’s Roman conflict with Simon. He adds that “with a judge assisting” might refer to any judge presiding over the contest, were it not that Philastrius, in discussing Simon’s heresy, had written that the contest took place before the emperor Nero. Shortly afterward, following Latinius and Mazochius in the cited place, we have restored “not Elymas, or Elimas,” where [Col. 1062D] the printed editions have “now.”] with a judge assisting? Did not Paul blind Elymas, with Sergius favouring him? [Note: [Col. 1062D] “He would have been vindicated,” etc. This passage is rather obscure. —Tilius.] He would also have been vindicated at Jerusalem, if he had possessed any bond of faith.

Do you not know that authorities themselves serve the innocent [Col. 1061B] and minister for good to the holy fathers? As the Apostle says: “Rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Do you wish, then, not to fear authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it through the Lord; for it is God’s minister to you for good” (Rom. 13:3–4). Yet I have complained of no one and have been vindicated against no one. Nor do I think Novatians hinder me; if I wished, I could boast of their smallness and decline. Behold, no one accuses your people before the emperor, and you stand alone. Yet we must all stand before the judgment seat of God (Rom. 14:10; 2 Cor. 5:19). One thing I know: the Novatians would complain if their cause were pleasing to any rulers.

VI. You say it would be more useful to conquer than to please. But those led by the ardour of conquering make progress by contention. [Col. 1061C] The Apostle, however, says: “If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16). On the contrary, concerning the desire to please, he says: “I please all in all things, not seeking what is useful to myself, but what is useful to the many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:33). But you, while considering your own advantage rather than that of your brethren, prefer by conquering to crush rather than by pleasing to restore. To overcome evil with good is rational; but in any cause whatsoever, to wish to prevail is mad presumption. This is not according to apostolic right, but Greek custom, among whom all the manner of the Spartans is thought to have been inflamed by a desire to conquer. That muddy pig too, and the mad tiger—what else do they desire but to conquer rather than please? You write that you have leisure, and therefore contentious matters delight you. But I, occupied with Catholic affairs, received your letter nearly thirty days after it was sent, and it was recalled after another forty days.

VII. You say that I am angry. Far from it. I am provoked, perhaps, like a bee which sometimes defends its honey with a sting. But review both sets of letters, and you will see whether we have woven the page with darts or with flowers. The Apostle speaks of people of this kind, whom one must [Note: [Col. 1062D] *Indentari*: that is, be rebuked. Lucifer of Cagliari uses the same word in *For St Athanasius*, book II, chap. 40, as we observed at that passage, where we also cited this passage of Pacian. Thus the old translator rendered Paul’s text. See vol. VI of our *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 195, note I.] rebuke (Titus 1:11). But observe: we contend with you as doves, with the mouth rather than the tooth. Would that what you say—that you wish to be taught—were true! Then I myself would offer you with my own hands the ointments of the Holy Spirit.

“Do you love me?” I know that I have not injured you. But you would only then love me if you did not think differently and approached my work with favour. You are surprised that Cyprian’s letters please me. Why should they not—the letters of a blessed martyr and Catholic priest? You press Novatian upon me. I hear that he was a philosopher of this world, and I am not greatly surprised that he degenerated alive from the Church of God. I know that, envying Cornelius, he abandoned the root of the ancient law and the fountain of the old people; that he lent himself to the madness of Novatus; that he was made bishop without lawful consecration, [Col. 1062B] and therefore not made one at all, by a letter from men who pretended to be Confessors and tore apart the limbs of the one Mother. Brother, I shall establish these things for you from the confession and letters of your own people.

Thus this philosopher of yours, seeking to establish his own wisdom, as the Apostle says (Rom. 10:3), is not subject to God’s wisdom, since through its wisdom the world did not recognize God’s wisdom. As for your supposition that Novatian suffered earlier, and your addition that Cyprian said, “My adversary has gone before me,” see how plainly I reply. Novatian never underwent martyrdom, nor has this been heard or read from the words of most blessed Cyprian. You possess Cyprian’s letters, in which he reports that Cornelius, bishop of the City—whom Novatian then envied—resisted hostile rulers, confessed often, [Col. 1062C] was often harassed, became leader of many Confessors and likewise of many Martyrs, and was most gloriously crowned with many others, while Novatian was still alive and secure. Indeed, this was why he had withdrawn from Christ’s Church: lest the labour of confession press upon him. First pricked by envy, he could not endure Cornelius’s episcopate; then he had attached himself to Novatus, mocked by the letters of a few persons. Cyprian’s letters will teach you all these things about Novatian.

Moreover, even if Novatian suffered something, he was nevertheless not killed; even if killed, he was nevertheless not crowned. Why not? He was outside the peace of the Church, outside concord, outside that Mother of whom everyone who is a martyr must be a part. Hear the Apostle: “Though I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing. And though I distribute all my substance as food for the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, but have not love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2–3). But Cyprian suffered in the concord of all, in the common peace, among the company of Confessors; he confessed often amid repeated persecutions, [Col. 1063A] was harassed by many wounds, and at last was given the saving cup to drink. This was to be crowned.

Therefore let Novatian keep his letters for himself; let him keep his swelling pride, by which, while raised on high, he was dashed down; while sparing no one, he was poured out. Behold the man who blocks the way of salvation to his brethren by an inexorable religion! Behold the man who trusts that he can [Note: [Col. 1063D] “Carry the chaff openly.” Another reading: “remove the chaff,” less correctly in Latinius’s judgment.] carry the chaff openly and cleanse the Lord’s threshing-floor!

VIII. Have pity on yourself, brother Sympronianus. Do not let Novatian deceive you under this appearance, nor be thought more just because he despised everyone else in comparison with himself. Audacity often counterfeits confidence; and for desperate sinners, a false image of a good conscience is flattering. On the contrary, all humility is innocence—even humility that is indebted, even sinful humility, [Col. 1063B] even that which pleads for its own soul together with the sinner.

“Blot me out,” says Moses, “from the book which You have written” (Exod. 32:32), lest sinners should perish. “I could wish,” says the Apostle, “that I myself were accursed in Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. 9:3). Certainly both intercede for sinners; and for this reason neither Moses nor Paul offends God. Is Novatian better than they? A corrector of Prophets? A teacher of Apostles? Is he now, together with Christ, thought equal to Moses? Is he now, like Paul, raised on high into the third heaven? Is he, all others disregarded, now heard alone?

Let this suffice as an answer to your letter. But because you have argued at length that repentance is not to be performed, or is to be performed before baptism, and have filled the pages of your treatise with many chapters of examples, I shall answer each point in abundance. I shall not keep silent as to which faith has the truer claim. Since you have deigned abundantly to command our hearing, now grant a kindly return in hearing this treatise. Perhaps the Lord will grant that we, who have presented ourselves to you patiently, may reap some fruit from your patience as well. May the Lord deign to keep and protect you forever, grant that you live as a Christian and a Catholic, and bring you into concord with us. Amen.

## LETTER III. Against the Treatises of the Novatians

Pacian, bishop, to brother Sympronianus, greeting.

I. The entire treatise of the Novatians, which you, brother Sympronianus, have sent me, pressing arguments from every side, contains this: that one may not repent after baptism; that the Church cannot forgive mortal sin; indeed, that the Church itself perishes by receiving sinners. A splendid honour, singular authority, great constancy—to reject offenders, flee the touch of sinners, and put evil confidence in one’s own innocence. Who claims this, brother: Moses, Paul, or Christ? Moses wishes to be blotted out of the book for blasphemers (Exod. 32:32); Paul wishes to be accursed for his brethren (Rom. 9:3); and the Lord Himself prefers to suffer for the unjust. “None of these,” you say. Who then? Novatian commanded this.

Was he some immaculate and pure man—one who had not listened to Novatus; [Col. 1064A] who had never deserted the Church; who was made bishop by bishops; who was consecrated according to regular law; who obtained the vacant chair in the Church? “What is that to you?” you say. “Novatian taught this.” But when, brother, and in what times? Immediately after the Lord’s Passion? No: after the reign of Decius, that is, nearly three hundred years after the Lord’s Passion. What then? Did he follow prophets, like the Cataphrygians; or some [Note: [Col. 1064D] “Philomene.” Read *Philumena*. —Tilius.] Philumena, like Apelles; or did he alone receive such authority? Did he speak with tongues? Did he prophesy? Could he raise the dead? He ought to have possessed something of this kind in order to introduce the gospel of a new law. And yet the Apostle cries out against it: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than that which we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:8).

“Novatian understood it thus,” you say; “but Christ taught it.” Therefore, from Christ’s [Note: [Col. 1064D] “From Christ…” Supply: “coming.”] coming to the reign of Decius, was there no one who understood? Then after Decius every bishop was impatient; all the others were lax, who preferred to mingle with the lost, perish with the wretched, and be wounded by another’s wound? With Novatian as champion, justice is set free; with him as author, whatever had erred is corrected.

II. “Come,” you say, “let us contend with examples and fight with reason.” But until now I have been secure, content with the peace of the Church’s feast and of the ancient congregation. I learned no zeal for discord and sought no arguments for controversies. But after you separated yourself from the rest of the body and were divided from your mother, in order to give a reason for your deed you search every recess of books as an assiduous investigator: you disturb every hidden thing; whatever is secure in them [Col. 1064C] you unsettle. Our forefathers have argued nothing gratuitously; among us security itself is unadorned. What fortified matter have you brought from your side?

I do not know what Novatian did, what Novatus committed, what Evaristus presumptuously asserted, what Nicostratus proclaimed. Because I despise your weapons, I do not know them; see whether you are fighting unarmed truth. Yet let us wait to see what you object and what you say. Could bare truth, or innocence unskilled in argument, stand firm? You propose—and correctly—that the Church is a people renewed from water and the Holy Spirit, without denial of Christ’s name; the temple and house of God, the pillar and foundation of truth (1 Tim. 3:15); a holy virgin of most chaste dispositions; Christ’s bride from His bones and flesh (Eph. 5:30), having neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. 5:27), and preserving the complete ordinances of the Gospels. Who among us denies this? Indeed, we add that the Church is the queen in garments of gold and many colours (Ps. 44:10); a fruitful vine on the sides of the Lord’s house (Ps. 127:3); the mother of maidens without number (Song 6:7); the one beautiful dove of her mother, and perfect (Song 6:8); the mother of all, built upon the foundations of Prophets and Apostles, with Jesus Christ Himself as the cornerstone (Eph. 2:20); a great house enriched by the diversity of every kind of vessel.

III. But more of our own claims later; meanwhile, let us consider yours. [Col. 1065A] The Church is a people reborn from water and the Holy Spirit. Very well. Who has shut God’s fountain? Who has seized the Spirit? On the contrary, among us is the living water itself, which springs up from Christ. You, separated from the perpetual fountain—whence are you born? Nor has the Holy Spirit departed from the mother who is the source; how did He reach you? Unless perhaps He followed one in schism, abandoned so many priests, was content with an unconsecrated seat, and loved the worn-out pit of an adulterous fountain.

Whence does your people have the Spirit, when it is not sealed by an anointed priest? Whence its water, when it has departed from the mother-source? Whence renewal, when it has lost the cradle of wedded peace? The Church is a people without denial of Christ’s name. Are there no Confessors among us, proved by chains, fires, and swords? “There were,” you say, “but by receiving deniers [Col. 1065B] they perished.” Shall I not pass over the fact that Novatian himself, while he was still living in the Church, both wrote, recommended, and read aloud to the assembly a document concerning the reception of deniers or the fallen? Meanwhile, whom can you persuade that the entire Church collapsed because the fallen were received? That, when penitents were admitted, the people who admitted them became deniers? And if some people were more lax, did all the rest—who did not approve their action but followed custom and peace—lose even the Christian name?

Receive the word of Jeremiah: “In those days they shall no longer say, ‘The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’; but each shall die in his own sin” (Jer. 31:29–30). Nor does the Lord keep silent in Ezekiel: “As the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son, are Mine. Each shall die in his own sin” (Ezek. 18:4). Again below: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him” (Ezek. 18:20). You yourself offer this example: “Though these three men were in its midst—Noah, Job, and Daniel—they would deliver neither sons nor daughters; they alone would be saved” (Ezek. 14:16). Behold, those placed among sinners are themselves saved, though they cannot save others. You bind the whole world with the chains of a few; you condemn the entire Church for the weakness of a small portion.

What, in your view, of all the holy people whom Novatus instructs, whom Evaristus chose, whom Nicostratus taught, whom Novatian trained? You have fled thorns and thistles; your harvest has no tares; for you the grains have already been purified; to you the purifier will come without [Col. 1065D] a winnowing-fan (Matt. 3:12). You alone, among all people, will have no chaff?

IV. Come, state the rest: the Church is Christ’s body. It is a body, certainly—not a member: a body gathered into one from many parts and members, as the Apostle says: “The body is not one member but many” (1 Cor. 12:14). Therefore the Church is a complete body, [Note: [Col. 1065D] “And a body and solid.” I would judge either that the later conjunction should be deleted, or rather, that the first two words should be removed and the reading should be “and solid.”] a body and solid, now spread throughout the whole world. It is like a city whose parts are one whole—not like you Novatians, an insolent little portion and a gathered tumour [Col. 1066A] separated from the rest of the body.

The Church is God’s temple: certainly a spacious temple, a great house, having indeed vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthen ones—some for honour, and many magnificent vessels assigned to the varied uses of various works (2 Tim. 2:20). The Church is a holy virgin of most chaste dispositions, Christ’s bride. A virgin, truly—but also a mother. A bride, manifestly—but also a wife and spouse taken from her husband; therefore bone from his bones and flesh from his flesh (Gen. 2:23). Of her David said: “Your wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house; your children like young olive trees around your table” (Ps. 127:3).

Thus this virgin has abundant childbirth and innumerable offspring, by whom the whole [Col. 1066B] world is filled; by whom, in ever-flowing hives, the populous swarm teems. Great is this mother’s concern for her children, and tender her affection: the good are honoured, the proud corrected, the sick healed. None perishes; no one is despised. Her children are kept safe under their mother’s indulgence. The Church is without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27): that is, it has no heresies—no Valentinians, Cataphrygians, or Novatians. In these are certain spotted and wrinkled folds, begrudging the adornments of precious garments.

But a sinner or penitent is not a spot upon the Church, because [Note: [Col. 1065D] “So long as he sins, he is placed…” The passage seems to have been corrupted by a Novatian, unless perhaps it speaks of sinners who have fallen into heresy, as Bellarmine noted in *On the Church*, book III, chap. 9, on the seventh argument. —Brasich.] so long as he sins and does not repent, he is placed outside the Church. When he ceases to sin, he is already healthy. The heretic, however, tears, seizes, corrupts, and drenches the Lord’s garment, Christ’s Church. For, he says, “while there are schisms and contentions among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man?” [Col. 1066C] (1 Cor. 3:3). And “their word spreads like cancer” (2 Tim. 2:17): this is the spot of unity; this is the wrinkle. Finally, where the Apostle speaks of these matters, he brings forward Christ’s love and affection: “As Christ,” he says, “loved the Church and gave Himself for her” (Eph. 5:25)—in order to exclude heretics, since they do not know how to love. But why say these things to the wretched penitent? For he too desires both to love and to be loved.

V. The Church preserves the complete ordinances of the Gospels. Complete, certainly, because it is whole, because it is full: where reward is given to the faithful; where tears are not denied to the wretched; where the sick are healed; where arrogant health and proud righteousness claim nothing for themselves; where watchful love persists in all things, “believing all things, hoping all things, enduring all things” (1 Cor. 13:7). Hence the Apostle’s words: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). There the whole brotherhood bears its burdens, suffering together and made secure by mutual devotion. All bear with one another in love, earnestly seeking to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3).

This will be the Church, brother Sympronianus; this will be the people reborn in Christ from [Col. 1067A] water and the Holy Spirit. “I do not know,” you say, “whether sin can be forgiven by bishops, since the Lord said: ‘Whoever denies Me before men, I will deny him before My Father who is in heaven’” (Matt. 10:33). Why then did your Novatian recommend this while he was not yet even falsely a bishop or priest—long before Cornelius became bishop of Rome, before he envied Cornelius’s priesthood? You have Cyprian’s testimony, Cyprian whom not even you have ever been able to discredit. For in one place he wrote to Antonianus as follows: [Note: [Col. 1067D] “It was added,” etc. The passage occurs near the beginning of Cyprian’s Letter 52 to Antonianus, p. 69 of Baluze’s Paris edition.] “It was also added, while Novatian was then writing and reading aloud in his own voice what he had written, and while Moses, then a Confessor but now already a martyr, subscribed, that peace should be granted to the fallen who were weak and at the point of death. These letters were sent throughout the whole world and conveyed to the knowledge of all the churches.”

What do you say, brother Sympronianus? Novatian wrote this; and, to add the compliance of his own free will, he even read aloud what he had written. His right hand is witness; his hand that wrote is witness; his tongue that read it is witness. Cornelius, against whom all this hostility of yours burst forth, was not yet bishop. Much later, with many fellow-bishops, many Confessors, and soon Martyrs, as Cyprian himself writes, he assented to the counsel of the elders that peace might be granted. If access to repentance must be denied, Novatian is guilty—he who wrote, recommended, and read these things. Where then was that impatient rigour? Where that fierce censure? Had no one preferred Cornelius to you, the authority of the man who wrote would have remained. Now the entire judgment displeases you; now weapons are hurled against us, [Col. 1067C] supplied by the very persons through whose authority the cause of those weapons gained strength.

VI. But when did they begin to lapse into this very heresy of Novatian? [Note: [Col. 1067D] “When did they begin?” I think one must understand “to lapse.” TIL.] Listen, I beg you, and observe the entire sequence of your error. Cornelius had already been made bishop at Rome by sixteen bishops; he had taken possession of the vacant episcopal chair, and, with the virginal purity with which he was endowed, was enduring the repeated persecutions of an angry emperor. Then, by chance, a certain presbyter, Novatus, came to Rome from Africa—after defrauding widows in the church at Carthage, despoiling orphans, withholding the church’s money, casting his father out of the house, so that he died from hunger and was not buried, striking his pregnant wife in the womb with his foot and causing her to miscarry. And when, at Carthage, as the brethren pressed the matter in the church, the day of his trial was approaching, he hid there as well. Not long afterwards, he found this Novatian anxious over Cornelius’s episcopate—for Novatian had hoped for it himself—and wavering with a few supporters from his own party, as often happens in such a matter; he drove him onward, encouraged his hesitation, and urged him to hope for something great. He found certain persons among those who had escaped the storm of that persecution, and among them he stirred up this very hostility against Cornelius concerning the reception of the lapsed. He gave their letters to Novatian. On the authority of those letters, while a bishop was already seated at Rome, Novatian, contrary to the law of the singular priesthood, assumed for himself the title of another bishop. He accused Cornelius of communicating with the lapsed; he claimed innocence for himself. Against this man I must render an account; against him modesty must be defended; against him life must be vindicated.

VII. “But you too,” you say, “why do bishops approve such things?” Let another say this: you defend Novatian. Let this cause appear inexcusable to others, though it may be pleasing to you. Let whomever you consider guilty be innocent to you, if he supports you. Do not accuse another of a charge from which you cannot free yourself. Come then: let us bishops owe all modesty, because we have received the name of the apostles, because we are marked by the appellation of Christ. “The Lord,” you say, “denies one who denies him; yet you refuse to acknowledge that the denier has denied.” Who acknowledges him as denying? The one who compels him to penitence, rebukes him, exposes the offence, opens the wounds, recalls the eternal punishments, and corrects him by the destruction of the flesh? This is chastisement, not acknowledgment.

The Lord says to us: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5:13). Therefore we rightly salt by saying these things; and whoever has heard will not be good for nothing. [Note: [Col. 1067D] *Salimus* (“we salt”). Thus Latinius rightly corrects the editors’ error *psallimus* (“we sing psalms”).] You see that the Lord’s judgment is not trampled underfoot by us but approved; that severity is not cast aside, but his will is disclosed. “But,” you say, “you forgive sins to the penitent, although you are permitted to remit sin only once in baptism.” Certainly not I, but God alone—he who both forgives what has been committed in baptism and does not reject the tears of penitents. Moreover, what I do, I do not by my own right, but by the Lord’s: “We are God’s fellow-workers,” he says; “you are God’s building” (1 Cor. 3:9). And again: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase” (ibid. 6–7). Therefore, whether we baptize, compel persons to penitence, or grant forgiveness to penitents, we administer it with Christ as author. You must consider whether Christ can do this, whether Christ has done it.

VIII. “If remission of sins could be given to penitents,” you say, “baptism was unnecessary.” A most foolish comparison! Baptism is the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion; forgiveness for penitents is the reward of the one confessing. The former all may receive, because it is the gift of God’s grace—that is, a gratuitous gift. But this labour belongs to the few who rise again after a fall, who recover after wounds, who are aided by tearful cries, who come to life through the destruction of the flesh. You maintain that I introduced in vain the passage where God says: “I prefer the repentance of the sinner to death” (Ezek. 33:11). What if I had added Isaiah’s words: “When, having turned back, you groan, then you shall be saved and know where you had been” (Isa. 30:15, according to the LXX)? [Note: [Col. 1068D] “When, having turned back, you groan,” etc. This passage of Isaiah 30:15 is likewise cited from the Old Latin translation, according to the LXX, by St Cyprian, near the end of *On the Lapsed* and in Epistle 34, pp. 138 and 67, Oxford edition.] What if I had cited the Apocalypse: “Remember from where you have fallen, repent, and do the former works” (Rev. 2:5)? “These,” you say, “were spoken to the Gentiles before baptism.”

Listen to the Apostle: “We know that whatever the Law says, it says and speaks to those who are under the Law” (Rom. 3:19). Therefore those who lived without the Law will not be bound by the condition of repenting. Even if they had repented, they would have done it by free faith, not under a bond of repentance imposed by the Law. “Therefore,” you say, “even Jews who repented before baptism cannot repent after baptism.” Who taught you this, brother Sympronian? Who persuaded you that one who repented beforehand ought not to repent afterwards? But we shall consider that later. Meanwhile, if repentance is barred to Jews after baptism because they had rendered it beforehand, at least concede that Gentiles, who had not previously known the law of repentance, ought subsequently to repent. Yet do not be mistaken about the Jews. They had repented previously precisely because they had corrupted the old baptism, and they repented, as it were, after faith, because faith had been betrayed. Listen to the Apostle: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1–4). They had violated this baptism, and therefore they repented.

IX. Let us next see what you say: “If God repeatedly commands a person to repent, he permits him repeatedly to sin.” What are you saying? Does the one who repeatedly shows the remedy for an offence thereby show the offence? Does a physician, when he cures, teach a person to be continually wounded? God does not will a human being to sin even once, and yet frees him from sin. Certainly, when he frees, he does not teach sin; just as one who rescues from a fire does not point out the fire, nor does one who snatches a shipwrecked person from rocks drive him onto the rocks. It is one thing to be freed from danger, another to be forced into danger.

Perhaps I could allow this to be believed if penitence were thought a pleasure—a burden so great is imposed by it; destruction of the flesh is commanded; continual tears and unending groans are required. Will one who has been healed then wish to be cut again, burned once more? Will he wish to sin again and repent again, when it is written: “Do not add sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14)? And again: “I do not have mercy on one who sins continually” (Ecclus. 12:3). But if, as you say, one to whom the medicine of penitence is shown is compelled toward sin, what then will become of the person to whom penitence itself is barred, whose whole wound is covered over when the remedy is despaired of, [Note: [Col. 1069] “Is covered over.” Following Latinius’s conjecture, we have restored this reading where the editions give *aperitur* (“is opened”), contrary to the context.] and to whom access to life is utterly denied anew?

“In baptism,” you say, “we die once,” as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that all of you who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Therefore you were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead, so you too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:3–4). What is surprising? The Apostle taught that we should be new, so that no one might sin; yet it followed that the one who had sinned should repent. The one would live whole, the other healed; the innocent would receive a crown, the penitent forgiveness; the former a reward, the latter a remedy. Finally, the same Apostle says: “For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, now justified in his blood, we shall be saved through him from wrath” (Rom. 5:9–10)—from the wrath, certainly, due to sinners. If he did not permit the Gentile people to perish, much more will he not allow the redeemed to be extinguished. He will not reject those whom he redeemed at great cost, for the loss of his servants is no small matter to him. The one who rises will indeed die no more, as it is written (Rom. 14:4). But he himself is advocate with the Father; he himself intercedes for our sins—no contemptible patron of the miserable, nor an inadequate intercessor.

X. Answer, brother: can the devil overpower God’s servants, while Christ cannot absolve them? You say that Peter’s penitence took place before the Lord’s Passion? No one put that before you. Yet Peter had already been baptized; for the Lord had said to him: “One who has bathed once has no need to wash again” (John 13:10). Yet he later received Christ’s remedy, though he repented beforehand; and he was regarded as holy before he received the remedy. Nor would his repentance have been recorded for remembrance unless it had profited the penitent. “He wept bitterly,” it says (Matt. 26:75). Do you refuse to do faithfully what Peter did? Do you refuse to benefit us by what benefited Peter?

Come: did not my Thomas, after the Lord’s resurrection, doubt the resurrection? Was he not marked by the Lord as guilty of unbelief, when the marks of the nails, the pierced hands, and the wound in the side were shown him, and when the Lord said to him: “Do not be unbelieving, but believing” (John 20:27)? What then? Was he ashamed to repent? Was he not humbled? Did he not immediately confess his God and Lord? Does not this confession commend him?

XI. How cleverly now you dispose of that passage which I advanced: that power was given to bishops, so that what they bound on earth should be bound also in heaven. You say that this concerns not believers but catechumens: namely, that it was permitted to loose or retain offences in peoples who were still to be baptized. Finally, you join chapters from two Evangelists so that they seem one; and you add that John completed what Matthew had treated less fully. Thus, because in Matthew the Lord had said, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), he had fulfilled this in John by saying: “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven him; if you retain them, they are retained” (John 20:23). Thus, forgiving or binding appears to concern Gentiles who were to be baptized, because the first Evangelist had spoken beforehand of the Gentiles, while the latter had completed the matter concerning loosing and binding.

What are you saying? Did the two Evangelists report mutually incomplete and half-complete meanings? Did words or reasoning fail them in relation to one another? Or did the Holy Spirit not fill each of them completely, conveying the intended sense and defining the utterances fully? No one adds to a ratified human testament; will one tablet of God be altered by a different tablet? What eagerness for victory is this among you, that you dare such a thing?

Moreover, in Matthew himself, before his Passion, the Lord had said: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). The Lord foretold this in Matthew and made no mention there of Gentiles. Why then do you attach to it John’s chapter, where John set down his own passage and set it down so as to distinguish it from the Gentiles? If he had wished it to concern the Gentiles, he himself could have joined what he himself was setting down. Therefore you have the whole thing you seek in Matthew. Why did you not read all of it, you who teach a bishop? Recall the first section of this command. Matthew himself reports that, a little earlier, the Lord had spoken to Peter—to one person, in order that from one he might establish unity; then immediately he enjoined the same thing upon all in common, [Note: [Col. 1071D] “In what manner.” Perhaps, with Latinius, one should read *aequaliter*, “equally,” and punctuate thus: “enjoining it equally upon all in common, yet …”] though he begins with Peter: “And I say to you,” he says, “that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed in heaven” (ibid. 18–19).

Tell me, brother: did he speak this of Gentiles alone when he said, “Upon this rock I shall build my Church”? Does he call unbaptized Gentiles “the Church”? Is a person not yet reborn the body of Christ? What do I loose for Gentiles that is not bound? For if it has not been imputed, neither has it been bound. What do I bind when I constrain it by no right? A Gentile person is free from the Law. Consider now, conversely, whether both things apply to one baptized. He is loosed by forgiveness because he was held by sin; he is bound by anathema because he had been loosed by faith and set free through grace. But even if I grant that this authority to loose or bind concerned Gentiles, I shall prove much more strongly that it concerned the baptized. For if the one who had no bond could be loosed or bound, how much more the one whom the ordinances of faith had held?

XII. You say that Matthew wrote: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him alone, one to one” (Matt. 18:15), and that the Lord immediately added: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven”; so that it appears to concern an offence against a brother. Come now, do you not see that above he says, “If your brother sins against you,” but here adds, “Truly I say to you: whatever you loose on earth,” and so forth? The former he commanded to one person; the latter he granted to many. The former is forgiven by the person against whom the offence is committed; the latter by the Church. The former is without priest or brethren; the latter is obtained from all. “Whatever you loose,” he says: he excepts absolutely nothing. “Whatever,” he says: whether great or small. Notice that he tells Peter below that what is sinned against a person must be forgiven seventy times seven, showing that in other cases it may be forgiven even once. Yet the one who sins against Peter injures the Lord, just as he himself declares concerning Samuel: “They have not made you of no account, but me” (1 Sam. 8:7). Therefore the Church is granted even once what is commanded of us ourselves so many times.

XIII. Let us now return to the wandering sheep, that drachma, and the younger son. When I had touched upon these examples briefly in my earlier writing, you repeated them at length, teaching and demonstrating that the drachma, the sheep, and the younger son refer to tax collectors and sinners—that is, to the lowly people—and do not pertain to the image of the Christian people or the pattern of believers. I am glad to be taught; but I regret that I have not been understood.

For what shall I assert? I agree that whatever the Law says, it says to those who are under the Law (Rom. 3:19), and that this was principally said to the earlier people; but it was said in the figure of believers, in the image of those to come, as the Apostle says: “These things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). And again: “All these things were shadows for them of future good things” (Heb. 10:1). Certainly you yourself concede that these sayings concern tax collectors and sinners—that is, the lowly people, and therefore the younger. Tell me then: is the Christian people itself younger? Has it adhered to the root? Has it been joined to those members? [Note: [Col. 1072D] “Those members.” Latinius reads: “joined to *those* members.”] Has it been built, as it is written, “upon the foundations of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20)? Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also God of Gentiles? Indeed, also of Gentiles. For there is one God, who justifies the ungodly by faith and through faith (Rom. 3:29–30).

Certainly that lowly people, whom God compared to the drachma, the younger son, and the little sheep, was the Church—the source from which came the whole multitude of believers and the Christian people. To this body our members also are joined, and the entire portions of believers, so that they might be grafted into the good olive tree from the wild olive of the Gentiles, as the Apostle says: “They have become partakers of its richness” (Rom. 11:17); and thus we might all be one in Christ—Jew and Greek, slave and free (Gal. 3:28). Therefore, if we are one body with those lowly people, what the lowly of old heard was spoken also to us; and so whatever was proclaimed concerning a part of the body was announced to the whole body.

XIV. I shall speak more plainly. That later people, that poor and ordinary people, was an image of the Church: a humble and modest soul, a soul set free through Christ. The Lord came to save this soul; he did not leave it in the underworld. This is the sheep borne back upon his shoulders—that is, by the exertion and strength of patience. This is the drachma that is sought and, once found, shown to the neighbours. Do you see that its pattern corresponds to the likeness of penitents? Do you see mercy extended to this very time? Do you see that whatever was said to the Church at its birth belongs to the Church in its fullness?

Therefore there the Lord added: “So there shall be joy in heaven over one sinner repenting, rather than over ninety-nine righteous persons who had no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7). For if all those things were written to admonish us, to what people, I ask, can that lowly sinful people be compared except to a penitent people? And if the figures recur in sequence, the ninety-nine sound ones are the entire Church, while the one wandering sheep is a small portion of offenders; the lost drachma is the wretched sinner; and the son returning after his evil deeds is considered like that redeemed person. You now see that I was right, when treating the healing of penitents, to quote the Lord: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9:12). And rightly also: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). Whatever was said about tax collectors and sinners applies to all the sick and all the miserable.

XV. “It is written,” you say, “of martyrs alone: ‘Blessed are those who mourn.’” Does no one besides them lament his sins? Does David not cry: “Every night I shall wash my bed” (Ps. 6:7)? And again: “For I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10). Does Jacob not say: “The years of my life have been very hard” (Ps. 47:9)? Does the Apostle not say to Timothy: “Desiring to see you, remembering your tears” (2 Tim. 1:4)? Yet he was not speaking of a martyr. What now? Do wretched penitents have dry eyes? Do those who grieve that they have sinned not know how to weep? Have we ourselves, communicants and believers, no tears? Is any one of us pleased to rejoice while the world rejoices? You Novatians are already filled, have become rich, and have begun to reign without us (1 Cor. 4:8). Thus not everyone who is miserable thereby begins to deserve pity. [Note: [Col. 1073D] “Everyone.” Read: “as each person is miserable …”]

After this you bring forward and say that the Lord wrote: “Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to human beings; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:31–32). Either I am mistaken, or this example works against you. For if every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven, you see that forgiveness is not denied to penitents. Therefore every sin—even blasphemy itself. You have added according to Luke: “Whoever sins against the Son of Man shall be forgiven” (Luke 12:10). What more could be said concerning God’s mercy or the clemency of the judge? Is your eye envious because the householder is good (Matt. 20:15)? Is he not permitted to do what he wills? Indeed—who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own Lord; and God is able to make him stand (Rom. 14:4).

“But,” you say, “whoever blasphemes in the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven” (Matt. 12:32). You are accustomed to go through whole readings: why did you not read here what “in the Spirit” means? You have written above that, when the Lord drove out demons by a word and performed many miracles by particular power, the Pharisees said: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (ibid. 24). That is to have sinned against the Holy Spirit: to have blasphemed the things done through the Holy Spirit. In other sins we err, are broken by fear, or are overcome by weakness of the flesh. This is blindness: not to see what one sees, to attribute the works of the Holy Spirit to the devil, and to call the very glory of the Lord—by which the devil himself is overcome—the devil’s power. [Note: [Col. 1073D] “This, then, is …” Understand St Pacian’s words correctly: other sins are forgiven to good penitents, but not blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, because ordinarily and for the most part such a sin is not healed through perverse repentance, God justly abandoning and giving over to a reprobate mind those who sin in this way. See Bellarmine, *On Penance*, book 2, ch. 16. BRASICH.] This, then, is what shall not be forgiven; the rest, brother Sympronian, are granted to good penitents.

XVI. After this, concerning the branches and the vine, you offer the following: The Lord says in John, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will take away; and every fruitful branch he will prune” (John 15:1). You see, therefore, that fruit is required in the branches—that is, the good works of penitence, as John says: “Bear fruit worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:8). You see the branches pruned: these are losses of the flesh, losses of pleasure, losses of property, and the labours of life—acts properly belonging to penitents. You see also the Lord’s cultivation, in that he does not destroy even the branches themselves, but prunes and gathers them: some indeed for the fire, others for renewing and digging the vineyards.

“Eli the priest,” you say, “speaks and says: ‘If a man sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if someone sins against God, who will pray for him?’” (1 Sam. 2:25). John likewise says: “If anyone knows that his brother sins a sin not unto death, he shall ask for him, and God shall give him life. But there is a sin that leads unto death; I do not say that you should pray for that” (1 John 5:16). You see that this entire passage concerns sins that persist, not those who have sinned at some time and have begun to repent before anyone prays for them. It would take long to rehearse the examples. Consider all the sins with which the Lord threatens: you will see that they are present sins.

But if a person’s past righteousness does not profit him in the time of his iniquity, neither will an ungodly person’s abandoned iniquity harm him in the time of his righteousness (Ezek. 18:24), since it is written: “Let the ungodly abandon his ways, and the criminal man his thoughts; let him return to God, and he shall obtain mercy” (Isa. 55:7). But if God has even punished past sins and decreed penalty and punishment for matters transacted and passed over, [Note: [Col. 1074D] “And concerning matters transacted.” Latinius very aptly restores this against the editors’ erroneous reading, “concerning which transacted matter.”] come now: does he not have authority to change his sentence? Did he not deliver Rahab, King Nebuchadnezzar, the Gibeonites, the Ninevites, and Zoar from the foretold destruction? Did not the prophet Joel declare through him: “Turn to the Lord your God, with fasting, weeping, and mourning; because he is merciful, patient, long-suffering, and of great compassion, and repents of evils. And who knows whether he will turn and repent, and leave behind a blessing?” (Joel 2:12–14). Therefore, whenever you establish that a punishment was decreed for sinners, maintain either that it was decreed for sins persisting, or that God retained the freedom of changing the sentence for the better if you repent.

XVII. You further say that it is written: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cast it away from you” (Matt. 5:29). Moses, testifying in Deuteronomy, foretold what this means: “If your brother should entreat you”—for these are our eyes and hands—“or your daughter, or the wife in your bosom, or one equal to your own soul, saying: ‘Let us go and serve gods whom you have not known’” (Deut. 13:6). Then he added below: “You shall denounce him, and your hand shall be upon him to kill him.” You see, therefore, that this was said not about penitents, but about those who not only persist in crime themselves but do not cease to cause us to stumble. However dear they may be, these must be left; however useful, they must be forsaken.

You further advance that the Apostle Paul said: “Remove the evil one from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:13)—the evil one, certainly, who persists. Penitence, however, is not evil, since David says: “It is good to make confession [*exomologesis*] to God” (Ps. 111:2). Nor is one who repents in communion with me, or joined to the portion of the saints or to peace. But the Apostle says: “If anyone is called a brother and is a fornicator, or an idol-worshipper, or greedy, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even eat with such a one” (1 Cor. 5:11). You see that “and is” is not stated without reason: it means one who has not yet repented, who has not yet ceased to be wicked. And certainly it is said together concerning the greedy, drunkards, and revilers. Answer, brother: does no such person remain within your communion? Therefore it is also said through Isaiah: “Together the wicked and sinners shall perish” (Isa. 1:28)—not penitents, not those pursuing works of mercy, to whom God says again through the same Isaiah: “Even if your sins are like scarlet, I shall make them white as snow; and if they are like crimson, I shall make them white as wool” (ibid. 18).

XVIII. “Yet,” you say, “the Apostle condemned one who had gone astray.” For in the First Epistle to the Corinthians he says: “Though absent in body but present in spirit, I have already judged the one who committed such an offence: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you have all assembled in the power of God, to hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:3–5).

Notice first, brother, that he does not condemn those with whom this man communicates. The one alone who committed such an offence is handed over to Satan; he alone is excluded, while the peace of the saints remains safe. Do you condemn every church because of one sinner? Next, you see that this incestuous sinner himself is not handed over to death, but to Satan—for correction, for being buffeted, for repentance. Finally, he says, “for the destruction of the flesh,” but not of the soul or even of the spirit: only for the destruction of the flesh, namely temptations, bodily hardships, and loss of limbs, just as elsewhere he says concerning the intemperate: “Such persons will suffer tribulation of the flesh” (1 Cor. 7:28).

Do you wish to know this? In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, the same Paul absolves this very wicked man. For he says of him: “For such a person, the rebuke inflicted by the majority is sufficient; so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, lest one such as he be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm love toward him” (2 Cor. 2:6–8). Again below: “If you have forgiven anyone anything, so have I; for what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I did for your sakes in the person of Christ, lest he be possessed by Satan” (ibid. 10). Do you see the Apostle’s indulgence, tempering even his own judgments? Do you see the gentlest mildness, far removed from your haughtiness, unlike the countenance of Novatian, yet providing for the common life and salvation of all?

XIX. Yet you also launch a severe censure against us. You say that by heavenly law it is not permitted to loosen one of the commandments, nor to associate lambs with wolves; that every agreement in crime is culpable; and therefore whoever touches pitch is defiled (Ecclus. 13:1), nor can there be any fellowship of light with darkness, or of God’s temple with idols, or any concord between Christ and Belial (2 Cor. 6:14–15). David therefore says: “You saw a thief and ran with him, and set your portion with adulterers” (Ps. 49:18). Finally, you say that we abrogate the Lord’s commandments.

Do we bend one point of the Law? Or rather the Novatians, who have violated every right of the Church and every right of concord, who after so many years of peace and so many bonds of holiness have produced new laws for themselves, new institutions, new rites, pretending the secret of justice with an inexorable countenance? [Note: [Col. 1075D] “Do we … or rather the Novatians?” Following Latinius, we restore the passage, which the editions present in a disordered and corrupt form: “Do we bend one point of the Law? Or rather the Novatians, since they have violated every right of the Church and every right of concord; who, after so many years of peace and so many bonds of holiness, [have made] new laws for themselves,” etc. The following words support this restoration.] Have we admitted wolves into the Church, though we avoid the mouths of heretics? Or rather the Novatians, who, being themselves ravening wolves, fear even sheep that are somewhat more wretched? Do we consent to evils, touch pitch, cling to darkness, join ourselves to an idol and Belial? Or those who have received Evaristus, Nicostratus, and others withdrawing from the Church—polluted in tongue, hand, and conduct? Do we associate with adulterers and thieves? Or those who have preferred Novatus to their own life and head, after he had seized the money of orphans and widows, the murderer of his wretched father and of his wife’s unborn child—not merely unrepentant, but even glorying in it? Yet the Apostle Paul said: “Lay hands suddenly on no one” (1 Tim. 5:21). The same Apostle teaches that they are not to be denied either late or after repentance.

XX. But when Jericho was destroyed, Achan, son of Carmi, was killed for stealing a garment. [Note: [Col. 1076D] “Achan, son of Carmi.” The editions incorrectly have “Achan, son of Carini.” We restore the passage from the reading of Lucifer of Cagliari, *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, ch. 3. See volume VI of our *Library of the Fathers*, p. 221, note 3, where, from Cotelerius, it is demonstrated that Achan is the correct pronunciation of this name.] Come then: kill all the thieves of our money and books, and rage against the bones of Novatus. Take up again that yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear (Acts 15:10). Why do you hesitate, Novatians, to demand eye for eye and tooth for tooth (Deut. 19:21), to demand life, and to restore the practice of circumcision and Sabbath observance? Kill thieves; stone the licentious.

Do not read in the Gospel that the Lord spared even the adulteress who confessed, whom no one had condemned (John 8:11); that he absolved the sinful woman who washed his feet with tears; that he saved Rahab, a Phoenician, in the very city of Jericho; that he absolved Tamar from the patriarch’s judgment; that, though Sodom perished, he did not destroy Lot’s daughters, and would have saved their husbands also if they had believed the coming destruction. Come then: do you not care to say with David concerning the Lord, “With those who hated peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119:7)? Or to keep silent concerning Solomon’s judgment: “A brother helping a brother shall be exalted” (Prov. 18:9)? What does the Apostle say? “Brothers, even if a person is overtaken in some offence, you who are spiritual instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourselves lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and thus fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:1–2). And the passage I already quoted: “For I could wish to be anathema in Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. 9:3). And again: “I became all things to all people, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9:22): that is, to share groaning with the wounded, labour with the sick, death with the dying; to be able to unite the fall of brethren with one’s own standing, to surrender something of one’s own health, and apply medicine to those who fail.

XXI. What advantage is it to you to harden yourselves with proud and harsh brow, hold your necks high, turn your faces from the wretched, and shut your ears and eyes? Have you never fallen, I beg you [Col. 1077C]? Is there no stain in your minds? No speck in your eyes, I pray? “Who shall boast that he has a pure heart, or that he is clean from sins?” (Prov. 20:9, LXX). I suppose [Note: [Col. 1077D] “Credo . . . languorum.” Perhaps it should be read and punctuated: “Cedo . . . languorum?”] that you are righteous, kindly, temperate people, whose limbs are all sound, whose whole body is untouched, who have no need of a physician or of medicine for ailments. Enter heaven at once; penetrate the entrance of paradise, the flaming sword giving way; bar your gifts against the multitudes of our people who confess the one God.

But if matters stand very differently from the unyielding severity [Note: [Col. 1077D] “Rigor rerum.” Latinius deletes the latter word. But what if Pacian wrote *vestrum* through an accidental repetition? The following word *immanitas*, supplied by Tilius, is restored. ID.] and your cruelty lies, you now understand, Novatian, that God can have mercy; that even late medicine is open to wretched brethren confessing their past sin; that the man passed by, wounded by the Levite and priest [Col. 1077D], can be healed through Christ; that the prayers of the Church must not be denied to the humble; that the hands of priests must be extended to pitiable brethren.

But we understand—as you reproach us—that the Church of God is a dove, not bitter with gall, not violent with the tearing of claws, adorned also with small and slender feathers. [Note: [Col. 1077D] “With small feathers also, and slender ones.” Tilius supplies “shining white.” Then, following Latinius, we have restored “a well of living water,” where the editions read “that him.”] We know also that the well of living water and the sealed fountain [Col. 1078A] are not defiled by any pollution from a heretical whirlpool; and that the enclosed garden is full alike of large and small vegetables, cheap and precious. We know too the eight souls from the ark, among whom Ham also was; and those thousands of birds and beasts, by twos and by sevens, clean alike and unclean. But dry springs and clouds raised by whirlwinds we take to signify the barrenness of heretics and the assaults of frenzied voices.

Nor do we promise freedom while we ourselves are slaves to punishment; rather, having confessed our own crimes, we exhort the rest also to confess, and to believe in him who justifies the ungodly by faith (Rom. 3:26), who relents from the judgment pronounced against wickedness (Joel 2:13, LXX). We also guard ourselves against false prophets and ravening wolves when we beware of you (Matt. 7:15). We judge that Jannes [Col. 1078B] and Mambres resisted Moses in the same way that you resist Catholics. Thus the Apostle writes: “Just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: men corrupt in mind and rejected by God. But they will not make further progress; for their folly will become plain to all, as theirs also was” (2 Tim. 3:8–9). It is plain that this was spoken about you, who have been unable either to advance further or to conceal your folly.

XXII. “He who is baptized by a dead man gains nothing” (Ecclus. 34:30): certainly, one washed in a heretic’s font, and likewise one anointed with a sinner’s oil—that is, one filled with an unclean spirit. Thus you too will be children of blood. For you desire not the peace of brethren but blood. Your belief is false faith. The adulterous woman [Col. 1078C] is the heretical congregation; for the Catholic Church, from the beginning, has not departed from her husband’s bed and chamber, nor desired alien or strange lovers. You have painted an exiled form with a new color; you have separated your bed from the ancient marriage; you have departed from the body of your mother who shares but one couch, adorned with a novel manner of pleasing and new enticements of corruption.

For you set before me, as a witness for the contrary side, the most blessed Cyprian, because in the letter *On the Lapsed* he says that Moses [Note: [Col. 1078D] “Moses.” Either Pacian’s memory failed him, or rather the copyist, occupied with something else, made an error. Noah should apparently be restored in place of Moses, according to the Ezekiel passage cited below. Nor does St Cyprian write otherwise in *On the Lapsed*, p. 130 of the Oxford edition, to which the holy Father refers. This correction is confirmed by what occurs below in ch. 24.] and Daniel and Job prayed for sinners and did not obtain their request, the Lord saying: “Even if these three—Noah, Job, and Daniel—were in their midst, they would not deliver sons or daughters, but they alone would be saved” (Ezek. 14:20).

Would that you relied on Cyprian’s testimony; would that you accepted such salutary judgments. For when he compelled the lapsed to repentance—those unwilling to repent, who said that they had received peace from confessors or martyrs—he taught and showed that not even those patriarchs could obtain anything for those who did not repent. For who can deliver one unwilling? Who can humble himself for the proud? Who can obtain mercy for those who do not repent? In saying this, he was undoubtedly compelling them toward the remedies of repentance. Nor did a man of such gravity and merit say anything against himself [Col. 1079A]; rather, he taught that sinners must pour out prayers and cherish *exomologesis*—open confession. Yet Cyprian’s very examples move you: he recalls that Moses and the other saints, who prayed for sinners, did not obtain their request.

XXIII. Indeed? Do you not see for whom Moses did not obtain his request? Returning to the people, what did he hear in the camp? The voices of drunkards and songs offered to idols resounded. The people still persisted in wickedness, still remained in the very crime, and had not learned to repent. Yet which of us told you that Moses did not obtain his request? God had indeed said to him: “Whoever has sinned before me, I will blot him out of my book” (Exod. 32:33). He had said this with the authority of a judge and the power of the Lord [Col. 1079B]; but see how quickly he relented from the judgment pronounced against the people’s wickedness. Listen. The prophet immediately says in the same place: “Moses prayed in the presence of the Lord his God: Why, Lord, are you so angry with your people?” and the rest (ibid. 21). Again below: “And the Lord was appeased concerning the evil which he had said he would do to his people” (ibid. 14). Do you see God’s anger softened? Do you see the offense appeased? And did he not pray for the people, nor—for the following corrupt words are uncertain—for what the penitent had done? [Note: [Col. 1079D] “Nor for what the penitent had done.” Latinius conjectures that it should be read: “unless for what he had done while penitent.”]

XXIV. “But,” you say, “Noah, Daniel, and Job could not deliver sons and daughters.” The case is this: if they ask for people who do not ask; if they pray for one persisting in crime; if they defend not individuals, not a few, but many thousands. Yet Noah delivered his own household [Col. 1079C] from the public ruin; Job received back everything he had lost; and Daniel by prayer warded off the sword hanging over Babylon’s wise men. Lot, certainly, prays for the salvation of a city; Paul, for the passengers of a ship. Thus those who know how to repent are absolved by the righteous.

Finally, I consider also what the Scripture says: “They alone shall be saved” (Ezek. 14:20). Who are they? They themselves, certainly, who pray for sinners; they shall safely make petition for such persons. And why do you condemn the Church? Why forbid her to pray for penitents, if it is permissible even to ask for those for whom it is not permissible to obtain the request? Read my Cyprian, then, more carefully: read the entire letter *On the Lapsed*; read the other which he sent to Antonianus, where Novatian is pressed by every example. You will then know what he declares concerning the healing of penitents. [Col. 1079D] I speak of Cyprian, who attacks your doctrines and preserves Catholic rights. After his heresy—for you have taken much from it—you will hear Tertullian himself confessing, in his own letter, indeed in the very one which he published while Catholic, that the Church can forgive sins.

XXV. You see, therefore, that the Church is the queen “in a golden and variegated garment” (Ps. 44:10), composed, certainly, of the diversity of many bodies and many peoples.
