This picture is not of one color, nor does so great a diversity shine in one manner of dress. One part of the garment covers; another arranges. Some clings to the breast; some is dragged along in the lowest fold, and becomes soiled among the very footprints [Col. 1080A]. Some is compared with the purple of martyrs; some with virginal silk; some is stitched beneath a folded hem or repaired by the insertion of a needle. “One indeed thus, another thus” (1 Cor. 7:7); yet in all of them one queen is formed.

Therefore, this same fruitful and rich vine, having many branches and spreading more widely in the abundant tresses of its shoots—has none among these suffered winter cold? Has none endured harsh hail? Has none complained of scorching summers? One shoot is harder, another stronger, another purer; one spreads itself into fruit, another luxuriates only in leaves. Yet the vine is beautiful everywhere. This is the mother of maidens without number (Song 6:7). If you can, count the Catholic flocks and reckon on your fingers the swarms of our people. [Col. 1080B] Not only those spread throughout the whole world and filling every region, but also these, brother Sympronianus, which stand with you in the neighboring districts and nearby city. Consider how many of our people you see by yourself, how many multitudes of mine you encounter alone. Are you not swallowed up like raindrops by great springs, like some drop from the ocean? Tell me, tell me: are these maidens born from your people, or do you alone bear them? [Note: [Col. 1080D] “Do you bear these.” We have restored this from Latinius’s conjecture. The editions read, “you bear this.”] This, I say, is our queen, “chosen for her mother and perfect” (ibid. 8). For nothing is chosen unless it is better and greater than another thing; nothing can be perfect unless it is full.

XXVI. Consider also whether this is especially the Church built “upon the foundation of prophets and apostles, with Jesus Christ himself as the cornerstone” (Eph. [Col. 1080C] 2:20). If she began before you, believed before you, did not depart from the earlier foundations, did not migrate, did not separate herself from the remaining body to establish teachers of her own and her own scriptures; if she advanced no strange argument, discovered no new law, and pronounced a repudiation of peace upon her own body—then indeed she may appear to have departed from Christ, then to have placed herself outside the prophets and apostles.

This, therefore, will be the great house, rich in the diversity of all vessels, in which pure gold gleams and malleable silver shines; yet which also deigns to possess wooden and earthen vessels, as Scripture says (2 Tim. 2:20). For a great house serves many uses and requires diverse tasks. It does not seek silver alone, nor does it delight only in golden adornment. Often something humble is more fitting for greatness; and amid noble surroundings, small things too are pleasant. No craftsman despises his own works or considers worthless what he has made. And why do you suppose Christ suffered for sinners, except because he did not wish to destroy anything that he himself had formed? Why do you suppose he still intercedes today for the wretched, except because he does not reject even what is small and utterly despised, intending to lose none of those whom he has received? Though they be compared to wood and clay, he thus arranges every kind of vessel in his house [Col. 1080D].

XXVII. At last, brother Sympronianus, do not be reluctant to be with the many. At last, choose to despise the hangnails of the Novatians [Col. 1081A] and your own clippings; at last, look upon the Catholic flocks and the Church’s peoples spread so widely abroad. “Where one is,” you say, “there I also am; and where two are, there is the Church”—where one, however, is harmonious; where two are peaceable. Where one is, there is also the Church; how much more where there are many? “Two,” he says, “are better than one, and a threefold cord is not broken” (Eccles. 4:12). Hear David: “I will sing praise to your name in a great assembly” (Ps. 34:18). And again: “I will praise you among a weighty people” (ibid.). And: “The God of gods has spoken, and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Ps. 49:1). Why should Abraham’s seed, according to the measure of the stars and the number of grains of sand, be content with your poverty? “In you,” he says, “all tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Tell me: does Novatian fulfill these things? God did not redeem so little by his blood, nor is Christ so poor.

Recognize now, brother, the Church of God enlarging her tents and fixing the stakes of her curtains to right and left [Col. 1082A]. Understand that the name of the Lord is praiseworthy from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. 112:3). See, see, I beg you: while Novatians struggle over words, Catholic riches are carried throughout the whole world.

On every point about which you consulted me, I have instructed you. I have passed over no proposed heading or opinion. I have replied to the very details and words. If you sought this with the mind of one consulting, it has been lovingly shown; if with the mind of one challenging, it has been vigorously disputed. When I have leisure, I shall add another letter also, in which I shall not refute yours but set forth our own; if you read it kindly and without contempt, perhaps it will not offend you. Meanwhile, in this one, I ask you to review every point individually. Things rapidly read pass rapidly away. If you desire the better gifts and possess the spirit of sound instruction, you will not lightly despise matters so true [Col. 1082B]. May the Lord deign to keep and protect you forever, and make you live as a Christian unto spiritual concord. Amen.

[Col. 1081]

# THE PARAENESIS, OR EXHORTATORY TREATISE, OF SAINT PACIAN, ON REPENTANCE. (C)

[Col. 1081C] I. Although I have more than once, however tumultuously, spoken of the healing of penitents, I nevertheless remember the Lord’s solicitude: for the loss of a single little sheep he spared neither his own neck nor shoulders, restoring the delicate sinner to the flock made whole again. I shall endeavor, as I can, to set down in writing an example of such great virtue [Note: [Col. 1081D] “To set down.” Or perhaps “to season”?] and, a servant as I am, to imitate the diligence of the Lord’s labor in a measure fitting to my lowliness.

One thing I fear, beloved, lest, in urging what must be done upon those disposed to habitual opposition, I may call sins to mind more than repress them; and lest it might have been better, following the example of Solon of Attica, to be silent about great crimes than to warn against them. For our countrymen’s morals have advanced so far that they think themselves instructed when they are forbidden. This, I think, is what that recent Little Stag accomplished: the more strongly it was censured, [Col. 1081D] the more diligently it was practiced. The whole rebuke of a disgrace publicly performed and often repeated seems not to have restrained, but to have taught, debauchery. Wretched me! What crime have I committed? I suppose they did not know how to perform the Little Stag unless I had shown them by rebuking it.

[Note: [Col. 1081D] “That Little Stag . . . they performed the Little Stag.” In *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 106, St Jerome lists, first among Pacian’s various works, a work entitled *The Stag*, now long lost. In that work the holy Father evidently attacked a form of public spectacle; learned persons have written more on this subject. See especially both glossaries of Du Cange, under Κερβούκολος and *Cervula*.]

But let that be true. Those who have fled from God or placed themselves outside the Church have even been exasperated by the injury of correction, indignantly refusing, of course, that anyone could rebuke their conduct. And as mud usually smells worst when you stir it, fire burns more fiercely when you turn it over, and madness rages more violently when provoked, so they broke the goads of necessary rebuke with a contrary kick, resisting indeed not without their own harm and wound [Col. 1082C].

II. Yet you, beloved, remember what the Lord has declared: “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you; rebuke a fool, and he will hate you” (Prov. 9:8). And again: “Those whom I love I rebuke and discipline” (Rev. 3:19). Therefore believe that the gentle and earnest care of this work of mine, undertaken by me, your brother and priest, according to the Lord’s will, is love rather than severity. Follow it lovingly; do not resist stubbornly.

Moreover, let no one suppose that this discourse on the discipline of repentance has been arranged for penitents alone, so that anyone outside this rank may disdain what is said as though directed at others. For in this—as in a clasp binding together the discipline of the whole Church [Note: [Col. 1082D] Alternatively, “may be restrained.” ID.]—attention must be given to catechumens, lest they enter this state; to the faithful, lest they return to it; and to penitents themselves, lest they fail to labor toward reaching quickly [Col. 1083A] the fruit of this work.

Nevertheless, my discourse will observe this order. First, I shall discuss the kinds of offenses, lest anyone suppose that the highest severity is assigned to all sins without exception. Then I shall speak of those faithful people who are wrongly ashamed of their remedy, blushing to confess it, and who communicate with defiled body and polluted mind: most timid before human eyes, yet most shameless before the Lord; with profane hands and polluted mouth they contaminate the altar, dreadful even to saints and angels. Third, I shall speak of those who have properly confessed and openly revealed their crimes, but either do not know or refuse the remedies of repentance and the actual practices by which *exomologesis* is to be carried out. Finally, I shall endeavor most clearly to show what punishment awaits those who do not repent [Col. 1083B], or who are negligent and consequently die in their wound and swelling; and, conversely, what crown and reward belong to those who cleanse the stains of conscience by a proper and regular confession.

III. First, therefore, as we have said, let us reconsider the degrees of sinners, carefully investigating what are sins and what are crimes, lest anyone suppose that, because of the countless offenses from whose deceptions no one is immune, I bind the entire human race under an indiscriminate law of repentance. Under Moses and the ancients, men were tossed in the same estuary of misery even for the smallest sin and, so to speak, for a matter worth a single farthing. Those who violated Sabbaths, touched unclean things, presumed to eat forbidden foods, murmured, entered the temple of the supreme King with a corrupted wall or stained garment [Col. 1083C], or handled its altars with an offending hand or touched them with their garment—it would have been easier to ascend to heaven, or better to die, than to observe all these requirements.

From all these things, therefore, and from many further carnal faults, the blood of the Lord has delivered us, so that each may more quickly arrive at his appointed end: redeemed from the slavery of the Law and set free into the liberty of faith. Therefore the apostle Paul says: “You, however, have been called to liberty” (Gal. 5:13). This is that liberty: that we are not bound by all the things by which the ancients were held. But, with the forest of offenses pardoned, so to speak, and the indulgence of remedies provided, we have been confined to a few necessary matters—matters which believers could most easily keep and avoid. Thus he would most deservedly not refuse Tartarus [Col. 1083D] who, ungrateful for so great a gift, had not kept even these few. Let us see what they are.

IV. After the Lord’s passion, the Apostles considered and discussed all matters and delivered a letter to be conveyed to those from the Gentiles who had believed. The sense of that letter was this: “The apostles and presbyters, brethren, to the brethren from the Gentiles who are at Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings. Since we have heard that certain persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words” (Acts 15:24–25). Again below: “For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose upon you no further burden except this: you must abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and blood, and fornication. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell” (ibid. 28–29).

This is the whole summary of the New Testament [Col. 1084A]. The Holy Spirit, disregarded in many matters, has bequeathed these to us under the condition of capital danger. Other sins are healed by the compensation of better works; but these three crimes, like the breath of some basilisk, a cup of poison, or a deadly arrow, must be feared. For they know not merely how to corrupt the soul, but how to destroy it. Thus greed will be redeemed by kindness; abusive speech compensated by satisfaction; sorrow by joy; harshness by gentleness; frivolity by seriousness; perversity by integrity; and whatever is corrected by its contrary will make progress.

But what will the despiser of God do? What will the man of blood do? What remedy will the fornicator take? Can one who deserts the Lord placate him? Can one who has shed another’s blood preserve his own? Can one who has violated God’s temple by fornication restore it? [Col. 1084B] These, brethren, are capital sins; these are mortal. Now listen to John, and take courage if you can: “If anyone knows that his brother is committing a sin not leading to death, let him ask, and the Lord will give him life, if he has committed a sin not leading to death. But there is sin leading to death; I do not say that you should pray for it” (1 John 5:16).

V. But, if you wish, hear separately concerning each one. God addresses Moses, praying for the blaspheming people, thus: “If anyone sins before me, I shall blot him out of my book” (Exod. 32:33). And concerning the murderer, the Lord decrees this: “Whoever kills with the sword shall die by the sword” (Exod. 21:12). And concerning the fornicator the Apostle says: “Do not violate the temple of God, which you are. Whoever violates [Col. 1084C] the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17).

These things, beloved brethren, have been written and cut into everlasting monuments; written and engraved, I do not mean on wax, parchment, bronze, or by a pen, but in the book of the living God. “Heaven and earth will pass away; not one iota or stroke,” he says, “can pass away before all things are fulfilled” (Matt. 5:18). What then? Must we die? Many have fallen into these sins even in intention; many are guilty of blood, many enslaved to idols, many adulterers. I add that not hands alone are punished in homicide, but every plan that has driven another’s soul to death; nor only those who burned incense on profane tables, but absolutely every lust wandering outside the marriage bed and lawful embraces is bound under guilt of death. Whoever does these things after faith [Col. 1084D] shall not see the face of God.

Those guilty of such great crimes have despaired. “What have I done to you? Was it not in your power for it not to be done? Did no one warn you? Did no one foretell it? Was the Church silent? Did the Gospels say nothing? Did the Apostles threaten nothing? Did the priest ask nothing of you? Why do you seek late consolations? The proper time was when it was permitted.” This is a harsh utterance; but those who call you happy lead you into error and confuse the paths of your feet. Whoever flatters the guilty after their crimes shows the way of crime to the innocent.

VI. “Then,” someone will say, “are we to perish? And where is the merciful God, who did not devise death and does not delight in the destruction of the living? Shall we die in our sins? And what will you do, priest? By what benefits will you compensate for so many losses of the Church?” Receive the remedy if you have begun to despair; if you recognize that you are wretched; if you fear. One who is overly confident is unworthy. “Upon whom,” says the Lord, “shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet, and one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Therefore I first address you, brethren, who, after committing crimes, refuse repentance: you who are timid after shamelessness, ashamed after sin; who are not ashamed to sin and yet are ashamed to confess; who, with an evil conscience, touch God’s holy things and do not fear the Lord’s altar; who approach the priest’s hands and stand in the sight of angels under a confidence of innocence; who insult divine patience; who thrust upon the silent God, as though he did not know, a polluted soul and profane body. Hear what the Lord has done; then [Col. 1085B] what he has said.

When the Hebrew people were bringing the ark of the Lord back to Jerusalem, from the house of Aminadab, Uzzah—who touched the side of the ark without an examined conscience—was killed. Yet he had approached it not to take something from it, but to hold it fast when it was tipping toward a fall from the oxen (2 Sam. 6). Such was the divine concern for reverence that it did not tolerate rash hands even when assisting. The same Lord cries out and says: “Every clean person shall eat the flesh; but whatever soul touches the flesh of the peace-offering while uncleanness is upon it, that soul shall perish from among its people” (Lev. 7:12).

Are these ancient things, and do they no longer happen now? What then? Has God ceased to care for us? Or has he withdrawn beyond the sight of the world and looks down from heaven on no one? Is his patience ignorance? “Far be it,” you say. Then he sees what we do, but surely waits and endures; he grants time for repentance and allows his Christ to delay, lest those whom he redeemed perish quickly. Good: understand, sinner, that you are watched by the Lord; you can appease him if you wish [Col. 1085C].

VII. But suppose that this prohibition against the unclean approaching God’s table is ancient: turn to the Apostles and learn what is new. In the First Epistle to the Corinthians, Paul says: “Whoever eats or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27). Again below: “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. Therefore,” he says, “among you many are weak and sick, and many sleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged; yet when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world” (ibid. 29–32).

Have you trembled or not? “He shall be guilty,” he says, “of the body and blood of the Lord.” One guilty of a human life could not be acquitted; shall the violator of the Lord’s body escape? “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily,” he says, “eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” Awake, sinner; fear the judgment now present within you, if you have done any such thing. “Therefore,” he says, “among you many are weak and sick, and many sleep.” If anyone does not fear the future, at least let him dread present sickness and present death. “When we are judged,” he says, “we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world.” [Col. 1086A] Rejoice, sinner, if in this age you are cut off either by death or consumed by sickness, lest you be punished after this age. Understand how great a crime is committed by one who comes unworthily to the altar: when he suffers illnesses or is dissolved by death, this is reckoned to him as a remedy.

VIII. But if your own soul is cheap to you, spare the people; spare the priests. The Apostle cries: “A little leaven leavens the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6). What will you do, through whom the whole mass is corrupted, through whom the whole brotherhood must suffer? Will you live guilty of so many souls? Will you be excused when the innocent charge their communion to your account, when the Church calls you the author of her calamity? See again the Apostle’s words to the priest: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Tim. 5:22).

[Col. 1086B] What will you do, you who deceive the priest? You either mislead one who does not know, or confound one whose knowledge is incomplete because of the difficulty of investigation. Therefore I beg you, brethren, even for my own danger, by that Lord whom hidden things do not deceive: stop concealing a wounded conscience. Sensible patients do not fear physicians, even when they must cut or cauterize the hidden parts of their bodies. We remember some who, not ashamed even when their private bodily parts were exposed, endured knife and cautery and the exceedingly painful corrosive powder. Yet how great is what human beings have endured? Shall the sinner fear? Shall the sinner be ashamed to purchase eternal life by present shame, and withdraw badly concealed wounds from the Lord who offers his hands? Does one who has offended the Lord have anything about which to be ashamed before him?

Or is it somehow better for him to perish, so that you, timid from shame, may die without shame and, leaving no room for shame, gain more from his loss—he for whom it is better to perish in your stead? But if you are ashamed before the eyes of brethren, do not choose to fear companions in your misfortunes. No body rejoices in the suffering of its members; it suffers together and labors together for their remedy. In one and another, the Church is present; but in the Church, Christ. Therefore whoever does not conceal sins from brethren is absolved by Christ’s prayers, aided by the Church’s tears [Col. 1086C].

IX. Let the discourse now be directed to those who rightly and wisely confess their wounds under the name of repentance, yet do not know what repentance is or what medicine heals wounds. They are like those who open wounds and swellings and confess them even while physicians sit beside them, but, when told what must be applied, neglect it, and disdain what must be drunk. It is as though someone said: “See, I am sick; see, I have been wounded, [Note: [Col. 1085D] “But I do not wish to be cured—stomachache. This . . . what could be more foolish?” It seems, with Latinius, that the text should read: “But I do not wish to be cured. This was cause for indignation; but see what is more foolish.”] but I do not wish to be cured—stomachache.” This was cause for indignation; but see what is more foolish. Disease is even added to the cause, wound joined to wound, and every contrary thing applied; harmful drinks are administered.

This brotherhood especially suffers from this evil, adding new sins on top of old offenses. Thus it has broken out more gravely into vice, and is now tormented by a most destructive infection. What, then, shall I do, a priest compelled to heal? In such cases it is late. Yet if there is any one of you [Col. 1087A] who can endure cutting and burning, I still can help. See the prophetic scalpel: “Return,” he says, “to the Lord your God, with fasting, weeping, and mourning; and rend your hearts” (Joel 2:12–13).

Do not fear this incision, dearest ones. David endured it: he lay in filthy ashes, disfigured beneath a rough sackcloth. He who had once been accustomed to jewels and purple clothed his soul in fasting. The seas, forests, and rivers served him, and the earth, giving birth, brought forth promised riches; yet he consumed in tears those eyes by which he had seen the glory of God, and confessed himself unhappy and wretched—the father of Mary, ruler also of the Jewish empire.

That Babylonian king, deserted, performs *exomologesis* and is wasted by seven years of squalor. In him, an uncombed mane and savage roughness surpass the manes of lions; his dreadful hands, with long-curving nails, imitate eagles, while he eats grass in the manner of an ox, a pale chewer of herbs. Yet this punishment commends him to God and restores him to his former kingdoms. God received the man whom human beings dreaded, making him happy by that very calamity of severe treatment. See the incision I promised: whoever can endure it will be healed.

X. I shall apply also the fires of apostolic cautery; let us see whether you can bear them. “I have judged,” he says, “when you are assembled and my spirit is present, in the power of the Lord Jesus Christ, to hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:3–5). What do you say, penitents? Where is the destruction of your flesh? Is it because, in repentance itself, you always go about more luxuriously [Col. 1087C], stuffed with feasting, polished by baths, and finely dressed? I see one who was sometimes frugal, sometimes poor, sometimes grimy in a cheap tunic; now he is well groomed, wealthy, and handsome, as though he reproached God because he had been unable to serve him, and refreshed a dying soul by the pleasure of his limbs.

It is well that we are of moderate means; otherwise we too would do what some men and women are not ashamed to do: cover themselves in marble, burden themselves with gold, flow in silk, and glow red with scarlet. Perhaps you do not have iron-colored powder shining upon your brows, artificial brilliance glowing upon your cheeks, or forced blush sweating upon your lips. Yet you do not lack garden retreats or seaside retreats, more choice wine, more sumptuous feasts, and the refining of old age. Go on thus, believe thus [Col. 1087D]: how long will you live?

I can bear it no longer, brethren. Daniel with his companions, clothed in sackcloth and ashes and even drained by fasting, says: “We have sinned, committed iniquity, acted impiously, and transgressed your commandments and judgments” (Dan. 9:5). Likewise the divine Scripture says of Azariah: “Azariah stood and prayed, and opening his mouth made *exomologesis* to God together with his companions” (Dan. 3:25). David himself says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6:7).

But we—what do we do like this, what anything similar? I do not speak of those things which we heap up as an accumulation [Col. 1088A], by keeping taverns, trading, and plundering; hunting for gains abroad and lusts within; doing nothing simply, giving nothing to the poor, forgiving nothing to brethren. We do not keep even those practices which can be seen by a priest and praised with a bishop as witness; we do not keep even these daily practices: weeping before the Church, mourning a ruined life in filthy dress, fasting, praying, prostrating oneself. If anyone invites you to the baths, refuse the pleasures; if anyone asks you to a banquet, say: “Those things are for the happy; I have sinned against the Lord, and I am in danger of perishing eternally. What have I to do with feasts, I who have offended the Lord?” Moreover, hold the hands of the poor, entreat widows, throw yourself before presbyters, implore the Church, your intercessor; try everything before you perish.

XI. I know that some of your brothers and sisters [Col. 1088B] wrap their breasts in haircloth, lie upon ashes, and devise prolonged fasts; and perhaps they have not committed such sins. Why should I speak of brethren? Wild she-goats, as they say, know their own remedies: when pierced, I hear, by poisoned arrows, they range through the Dictean glades until, having stripped the stem of dittany, with the salutary, potent juice of its sap, they shake the embedded shafts from their bodies. We do not repel the fiery darts of the devil by any juice of repentance, by any herb of confession (*exomologesis*). The swallow knows how to restore the sight of her blinded young with her own celandine (*chelidonia*): shall we, having lost the lights of the mind, be healed by no root of harsh treatment? Behold, a human being is unlike either goat or swallow: he begrudges himself relief from his blindness and pain. Consider now, brethren, what we promised at the end: what fruit follows these works, or conversely, what outcome follows.

Upon self-indulgent sinners who do not repent [Col. 1088C] the Spirit of the Lord pronounces a threat and says: “They did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved; and therefore God will send them an operation of error, that they may believe a lie, that all may be judged who did not believe the truth, but take pleasure for themselves in injustice” (II Thess. II, 10, 11). Likewise the Apocalypse speaks thus concerning the harlot: “To the extent that she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her so much torment and mourning” (Apoc. XVIII, 7). And the apostle Paul says: “Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. II, 4, 5).

Therefore fear, most beloved, the just judgments; abandon error, condemn self-indulgence. The final time is already hastening on; Tartarus and Gehenna open their loosened bosoms for the ungodly. [Col. 1088D] After the timely punishments of souls, everlasting punishment is also reserved for their bodies when restored to life. Let no one believe in the liver of Tityus and the vulture of the poets. Eternal fire itself supplies its own material for the bodies that grow again. Give heed, if you do not believe: the surge of waters that rages with fires will be renewed as a punishment that nourishes itself. If you shrink back from confession because of its affliction, remember Gehenna, which confession will extinguish for you. Estimate its force even from present things: certain little furnaces of it boil vast mountains with subterranean fires. Sicily’s Etna [Col. 1089A] and Campania’s Vesuvius seethe with tireless balls of flame; and, to prove to us the perpetuity of judgment, they burst asunder and are swallowed up, yet are never ended by any succession of ages. Consider, in the Gospel, the rich man still suffering the punishments of his soul alone. What, then, will be the punishment when bodies return? What gnashing of teeth will there be? What weeping of eyes?

> [Note: [Col. 1087D] “Sicilian Etna and Ves.” Baluzius, in his edition of Cyprian, p. 568, Paris edition, restored the corrupt reading of the editors, “Etna and Lisaniculus and Ves.,” as we have reproduced it, from an old book of the Grande Chartreuse [Col. 1088D]. Latinius had previously conjectured that this was the reading. GALLAND.]

XII. Remember, brethren, that in the underworld there is no confession (*exomologesis*); nor can repentance then be granted, once the time for repentance has been spent (Eccles. IX, 10; Ecclus. XIV, 17). Make haste while you are alive, while you are travelling with your adversary. See how we fear worldly fires and dread the torturers’ claws: compare with these the eternal hands that torment, and the pointed flames that never die through any age. I entreat you, brethren, by the faith of the Church; by my concern [Col. 1089B], by the souls common to all, I beseech and implore you: do not be ashamed of this work; do not be reluctant to seize, as soon as possible, the timely remedies of salvation—to cast down your mind in grief, wrap your body in sackcloth, pour ashes over yourself, be worn down by fasting, consumed with sorrow, aided by the prayers of many. To the degree that you have not spared yourselves punishment, God will spare you. For he is gentle and patient and rich in mercy, and one “who relents from the sentence imposed against evils” (Joel II, 13, according to the LXX).

> [Note: [Col. 1089B] “And who relents from the sentence,” etc. On this passage of Joel, cited according to the LXX, see what we observed above [Col. 1089C] on Epistle 1, no. 5. ID.]

Behold, I promise and pledge: if you return to your Father with true satisfaction, straying no further, adding nothing to your former sins, and saying something humble and [Col. 1090A] tearful also, “We have sinned in your sight, Father; we are no longer worthy of the name of sons” (Luke XV, 22), immediately that unclean herd and the ugly food of carob-pods will depart from you. Immediately, upon your return, you will be clothed in a robe, a ring will honor you, and your Father’s embrace will receive you again.

> [Note: [Col. 1090B] “Clothed in a robe.” From the context it appears that, with Tilius, one should read *stola vestiet*, “he will clothe [you] in a robe.” ID.]

Behold, he himself speaks: “I do not will the death of the sinner so much as that he should return and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 23; XXIII, 11). And again: “Will not he who has fallen,” he says, “rise again? And will not he who has turned away return?” (Jer. VIII, 4). And the Apostle says: “God is able to make him stand” (Rom. XIV, 4). The Apocalypse also threatens the seven Churches unless they repent. Surely it would not threaten those who do not repent unless it pardoned those who repent. God himself also says: “Remember, then, from where you have fallen, and repent” [Col. 1090B] (Apoc. II, 5). And again: “When, having turned back, you groan, then you shall be saved, and you shall know where you were” (Isa. XXX, 15, according to the LXX).

Let no one despair so greatly because of the baseness of a sinful soul as to believe himself no longer needed by God. The Lord wills none of us to perish: even the small and least are sought out. If you do not believe, look: behold, in the Gospel, a drachma is sought and, once found, shown to the neighbors. The little sheep, to be carried back upon his shoulders, is no burden to the shepherd. Over one sinner doing repentance, the angels rejoice in heaven and the heavenly choir exults. O sinner, do not cease to pray: you see where joy is taken at your return. Amen.

[Col. 1089]

# SERMON OF SAINT PACIAN ON BAPTISM. (C)

[Col. 1089C]

I. I wish to explain how we are born in baptism and how we are renewed. Certainly, brethren, I shall speak in his own words, lest perhaps you think that I have exulted in style for the polish of my expressions; and so that you may be able to understand the mystical matter. Would that I could impress it upon you: I do not seek glory [Col. 1089D], for glory belongs to God alone. I am concerned only for you, and especially for these candidates, that I may somehow make known the measure of so great a blessedness. I shall therefore explain what Gentile life was before, what faith bestows, and what baptism forgives. If this penetrates your hearts as I understand it, brethren, you will judge that no preaching has yet benefited us more greatly. Receive, then, most beloved, the condition of death in which a person stands before baptism.

You surely know that ancient fact: Adam was set over the earthly origin.

> [Note: [Col. 1089D] *Praestitutus*, “set over.” Latinius reads *restitutus*, “restored.”]

This condemnation, of course, imposed upon him the law of eternal death; and from him, upon all [Col. 1090C] his descendants whom that one law held, this death ruled over the entire race, from Adam to Moses (Rom. V, 14). Yet through Moses only one people was chosen—the seed, that is, of Abraham—if it had been able to keep the commands of righteousness. Meanwhile we all [Col. 1090D] were held under sin, so that we might be the fruit of death: destined for the food of carob-pods and the keeping of beasts—that is, for unclean works—under evil angels. While they ruled, it was not permitted either to do righteousness or to know it; for the very fact of the matter compelled obedience to such masters. Consider how we have been delivered from these powers and from this death.

II. After Adam sinned, as I have related, when the Lord then said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19), he was consigned to death. This consignment flowed down into the entire race. For all sinned, nature itself now pressing upon them, as the Apostle says: “Because through one man [Col. 1091A] sin entered, and through transgression death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12). Sin therefore ruled, by whose bonds we were dragged, like captives, to death—namely, everlasting death.

Before the times of the Law, however, this sin was not even understood, as the Apostle says: “For until the Law was laid down, sin was not accounted in the world,” that is, it was not seen; at the coming of the Law it revived (Rom. V, 13). It was revealed so that it might be seen; but in vain, because almost no one kept it. For the Law said: “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not covet”; yet covetousness persisted with all its vices. Thus, before the Law, this sin killed humanity with a hidden sword, while the Law stood drawn. What hope, then, was there for a human being? Without the Law he perished [Col. 1091B] because he could not see sin; and under the Law, because he fell into the very thing that he saw. Who could deliver him from destruction? Hear the Apostle: “Therefore, most wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Grace,” he says, “through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. VII, 24, 25).

> [Note: [Col. 1091D] Elsewhere: “I.”]

III. What is grace? The forgiveness of sin—that is, a gift. For grace is a gift. Therefore Christ, when he came and assumed humanity, was the first to present that very humanity to God pure and innocent, free from the power of sin. Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin,” he says, “shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, before he knows either to utter evil or to choose good” (Isa. XIV, 15). And again concerning him: “He committed no sin, [Col. 1091C] nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. XLIII, 9).

Under the protection of this innocence, as soon as Christ began the defense of the Name in that very flesh of sin, that father of sinful disobedience—the one who had once deceived the first human beings—immediately began to hurry, rage, and tremble. For he was to be conquered by the annulment of the law of sin, by which alone he had either possessed humanity or could possess it. He therefore arms himself for spiritual battle against the immaculate one. First, by the very artifice through which he had conquered Adam in Paradise, he attacks him with an appearance of dignity; and, as though solicitous for his heavenly power, says: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (Matt. IV, 3), so that, while he is ashamed or unwilling to conceal that he is the Son of God, he might carry out the commands of the tempter.

Behold, he still is not silent, suggesting that, if he cast himself down from on high, he would be received [Col. 1091D] in the hands of angels, to whom the Father had commanded that they carry him upon their shoulders, lest perhaps he strike his foot against a stone—while he wishes to make the Lord prove that he is the one concerning whom the Father had commanded what the tempter urges. Finally, the serpent, having been thrown down, as though he were now yielding, promises the kingdoms of the world—the very things that he had taken from the first human being—so that, believing himself to have conquered humanity’s Advocate, he might make him, having received the dominion he defended, bow down before the dignity proposed by the ungodly man, and thus at last commit sin.

But in all these things the enemy is overcome and dissolved by heavenly power, as the Psalmist says to the Lord: “That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger, [Col. 1092A] because I shall see the heavens, the work of your fingers” (Ps. VIII, 3, 4).

IV. The devil ought to have yielded; yet he did not cease. He incites the scribes and Pharisees and that entire band of the impious with familiar snares and drives them into fury. Thus, after diverse artifices and deceitful intentions, by which they had tried, in the serpent’s manner, to deceive the Lord by feigned compliance, had accomplished nothing, they finally assailed him with open robbery and the most cruel kind of suffering. Their purpose was that, either through the indignity of what was done or through the pain of the punishments, he might do or say something unjust and thereby destroy the human being whom he bore, and his soul might be left in the underworld, whose one law was to hold the sinner: “For the sting of death is sin” (I Cor. XV, 56).

Christ, then, stood firm [Col. 1092B] and committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (I Pet. II, 22), as we have said; not even when he was led to the sacrifice. This was victory: to be condemned without sin. For the devil had received power over sinners, which he claimed for himself over the immaculate one; and so he himself was conquered, decreeing against the Just One what was not permitted him by the law which he had received. Hence the prophet says to the Lord: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L, 6). And so, as the Apostle says, having led away the powers, Christ condemned sin in the flesh by fastening it to the cross and cancelling the written bond of death (Col. II, 14, 15).

Hence God did not abandon his soul in the underworld, nor did he allow his Holy One to see destruction (Ps. XV, [Col. 1092C] 10). Hence, having trampled down the stings of death, on the third day he rose again in the flesh, reconciling it to God and restoring it to eternity, sin having been conquered and erased.

V. But if he alone conquered, what did he confer upon the rest? Listen briefly. Adam’s sin had passed into the entire race: “For through one man,” as the Apostle says, “transgression entered, and through transgression death; and so it passed into all human beings” (Rom. V, 12). Therefore Christ’s righteousness must likewise pass into the race; and as Adam destroyed all his offspring through sin, so Christ through righteousness must give life to all his race. The Apostle presses this point when he says: “As through the disobedience of one many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many may be made righteous; and as transgression reigned unto death, so likewise [Col. 1092D] may grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life” (ibid., 19, 21).

VI. Someone may say to me: “But Adam’s sin rightly passed to his descendants, because they were begotten from him. And have we been begotten from Christ, so that we can be saved through him?” Do not think carnally: you will now see how we are begotten with Christ as parent. In the last times Christ received a soul together with flesh from Mary; this he came to save, this he did not leave in the underworld, this he joined to his Spirit and made his own. And these are the Lord’s nuptials, joined to one flesh, so that, according to that great [Col. 1093A] mystery, Christ and the Church might become two in one flesh (Eph. V, 32).

From this marriage the Christian people is born, when the Spirit of the Lord comes from above; and, as soon as heavenly seed is poured and mingled in, we grow within the womb of the mother as the substance of our souls, and, poured forth from her belly, are made alive in Christ. Hence the Apostle: “The first Adam [became] a living soul; the last Adam, a life-giving spirit” (I Cor. XV, 47). Thus Christ begets in the Church through his priests, as the same Apostle says: “But I begot you in Christ” (I Cor. IV, 15). And so Christ’s seed, that is, God’s Spirit, sets the new human being in motion in the mother’s womb and, received in the birth of the font, pours him forth through the priest’s hands—yet with faith as bridesmaid.

For one who has not believed will not be considered grafted into the Church; [Col. 1093B] nor one who has not received the Spirit, begotten by Christ. Therefore it must be believed that we can be born. For Philip says: “If you believe, you can” (Acts VIII, 37). Christ must be received so that he may beget, because the apostle John says: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John I, 12). But these things cannot otherwise be fulfilled except by the sacrament of the washing, chrism, and bishop. For by the washing sins are cleansed; by chrism the Holy Spirit is poured upon us; and both of these we obtain by the hand and mouth of the bishop. Thus the whole human being is reborn and renewed in Christ, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so we too may walk in newness of life (Rom. VI, 4): that is, that, having put off the errors of the old life—slavery to idols, cruelty, fornication, luxury [Col. 1093C] and the other vices of flesh and blood—we may follow, through the Spirit, new ways of life in Christ: faith, modesty, innocence, chastity.

And: “As we have borne the image of the earthly human being, let us also bear that of him who is from heaven; for the first human being is from the earth, earthly; the second is from heaven, heavenly” (I Cor. XV, 49, 47). If we do this, most beloved, we shall die no more. Even if we are dissolved in this body, we shall live in Christ, as he himself says: “Whoever believes in me, though he die, shall live” (John XI, 25). Finally, we are certain, on the Lord’s own testimony, that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all God’s saints live. Indeed, concerning these very persons the Lord says: “All of them live; for God is God of the living, not of the dead” (Luke XX, 38). And the Apostle says of himself: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain; I would prefer to be dissolved [Col. 1093D] and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 21). Again: “While we are in this body, we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith, not by sight” (II Cor. V, 6, 7).

[Col. 1094A]

VII. This is what we believe, beloved brethren. Besides, “if we have hope in this age only, we are more miserable than all human beings” (I Cor. XV, 19). The life of the world, as you yourselves see, is either shared with us by cattle, wild beasts, and birds, or is longer than ours. What is proper to human beings is what Christ gave through his Spirit—that is, eternal life—but only if we sin no more. For as death is acquired by wickedness and avoided by virtue, so life is lost by wicked deeds and retained by virtue. “For the wages of sin are death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VI, 23).

Above all, hold fast to this, little ones: all nations were once, as we said above, handed over to the princes of darkness and the powers; now they have been delivered through the victory of Jesus Christ our Lord. [Col. 1094B] He is the one—he who redeems us, forgiving us all sins, as the Apostle says, and blotting out the written bond of disobedience that stood against us; for he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross. Having stripped himself of flesh, he led away the powers, triumphing freely over them in himself (Col. II, 13–15). He released those in chains and broke our bonds, as David had said: “The Lord raises up those who are cast down; the Lord releases those in chains; the Lord enlightens the blind” (Ps. CXLV, 7, 8). And again: “You have broken my bonds; to you I shall offer a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXV, 16, 17).

Released, therefore, from bonds, when through the sacrament of baptism we come to the Lord’s sign, we renounce the devil and all his angels, whom we formerly served, so that we may no longer serve them, having been set free by the blood and name of Christ. But if anyone [Col. 1094C] thereafter, forgetful of himself and ignorant of his redemption, returns again (Col. II, 18) to servitude to angels and (Gal. IV, 9) to those weak and needy elements of the world, he will be bound with those old shackles and chains—that is, with the bonds of sin—and his latter state will become worse than the former (Luke XI, 26). For the devil will bind him more fiercely, as one defeated in flight; and Christ will no longer be able to suffer for him, because he who rose from the dead will die no more (Rom. VI, 9).

Therefore, beloved, we are washed once, freed once, received once into the immortal kingdom. Blessed once for all are those “whose crimes have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1). Hold firmly what you have received; preserve it happily; be unwilling to sin any more. Keep yourselves henceforth pure and immaculate for the day of the Lord. Great and infinite are [Col. 1094D] the rewards laid up for believers, which “eye has not seen,” he says, “nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II, 9). That you may be able to receive these, obtain them through the labors of righteousness and spiritual vows. Amen.

ANNO DOMINI 397. QUINTUS JULIUS HILARIANUS.

(From Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. VIII.)

[Col. 1093]

[Col. 1093]

# PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 1093D]

I. It is certainly remarkable that none of the ancients mentions Quintus Julius Hilarianus, although from the surviving monuments of his writings we know that he flourished at the end of the fourth century [Col. 1094D]. For this author wrote two little books, in each of which he left a record of the time at which he composed it. He entitled the earlier one: *Exposition concerning the Day of Easter and the Month*; at its end he writes as follows:

> “We completed this laborious work on this third day before the Nones of March, after the consulship of Arcadius for the fourth time and Honorius for the third. Therefore we advise those who hastened to obtain these writings from us before they were corrected to endeavor to procure the work corrected according to this arrangement. For this reason we have now attached to this account both the day and the consuls, which we did not set down at first, so that henceforth anyone may know that this is the corrected work. Quintus Julius Hilarianus finished and corrected it on the third day before the Nones of March, Caesarius and Atticus being consuls.”

Hilarianus himself mentions this work in the later little book, *On the Duration of the World*. For there he says:

> [Note: [Col. 1095D] Q. Jul. Hilarianus, *On the Duration of the World*, §1. See below.]

> “For, as you yourselves know, I wrote some time ago, at your urging, concerning the calculation of Easter and the number of the years of the world; but I kept silence for some time for this reason: lest these little works of ours should be unreasonably composed with seasonings drawn from another’s wisdom. Therefore, having arranged matters better, we have already sent forth a little book concerning the most sacred day of Easter, in which we have demonstrated according to the Law which is the first month; thereafter, in this little work, we also set down, by calculation in its own order [perhaps, “each in its own order”], the course of the years from the creation of the world.”

These are his words. He himself defines the time at which he wrote this later booklet in these words:

> [Note: [Col. 1095D] Q. Jul. Hilarianus, ibid., §17. See below.]

> “But of the 470 years from the Passion of the Lord, 369 years had passed, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.”

On this passage Gerard Johannes Vossius observes:

> [Note: [Col. 1095D] Vossius, *On Latin History*, book II, ch. 12, p. 213.]

From the Passion of the Lord to the year 397, when Caesarius and Atticus were consuls, not 369 but 364 years had elapsed. Hilarianus must therefore have written it thus; for by an easy slip, X may have been substituted for V. Hence it is established not only in what order but also at what time our author composed his little books.

II. Now Pfaffius, Christopher Matthew, was the first to bring the earlier little work to light from parchment manuscript 840 of the Royal Library at Turin. After the distinguished Scipione Maffei, a specimen of it was published by the very learned men who catalogued and elucidated with observations the manuscripts of the same Royal Library at Turin.

> [Note: [Col. 1096D] Maffei, *Ecclesiastical Minor Works*, p. 5.]

> [Note: [Col. 1096D] *Manuscript Codices of the Royal Library at Turin*, part II, p. 272.]

The praised editor accordingly published that little work of Hilarianus, appended to the *Epitome of Lactantius’s Divine Institutions*, at Paris in 1712, employing the care and industry of the most learned Nicolas Nourry. Yet, although I sought for a long time and with the utmost zeal this edition of Pfaffius, from which the aforementioned work had to be transcribed, I was unable to obtain it anywhere. I had already almost abandoned all hope of ever acquiring it, when behold, the most distinguished gentleman JOSEPH VERNAZZA, an eminent citizen of Alba Pompeia and a most diligent cultivator of humane letters [Col. 1096A]—whom I had never known and who had consequently never been asked by me—of his own accord arranged for a copy of this much-desired edition, indeed as a gift, to be brought to me. Enriched by this splendid gift, offered with such kindness, I should surely be ungrateful if I did not declare myself under the greatest obligation to that most humane man, and at the same time render and feel the fullest thanks for such generosity, than which none more liberal could even be imagined in one’s wishes. For I shall never fail to strive, as I remember having declared elsewhere, that no one may justly complain that a kindness has been bestowed upon someone wholly ungrateful.

But since the aforementioned copy, sent only in the September just past, reached my hands only after the later little work of Hilarianus [Col. 1096B], *On the Duration of the World*—the only one then available to us—and indeed quite a number of works by other writers, allotted according to the exigencies of time, had already been committed to the press, this alone remained: that we should cast the earlier little book of the same Hilarianus into an Appendix at the end of this volume, together with certain others.

III. There survives besides, as we have taught above, another little book by the same author, *On the Duration of the World*, or, as the Viennese manuscript has it, *On the Course of Times*, which Peter Pithou first published. It will be pleasant to hear what Margarin de la Bigne, the celebrated theologian of the Sorbonne, says of this booklet:

> [Note: [Col. 1096D] *Library of the Fathers*, vol. VII, p. 258, Paris ed. 1644.]

> “For a long time,” he says, “and very much I hesitated whether I should give this author a place in this library [of the Fathers]: first, because he remains obscure and is known to no catalogue of ecclesiastical writers; next, because in calculating the totals and reckonings of times he seems not to be an authority of altogether unquestionable reliability; and finally, because he does not at all define Daniel’s weeks, as Jews rather than Christians desire, by the coming and age of Christ, and because toward the end of the work he may seem to incline even toward the delusions of the Chiliasts. But since I hope that he will be of great use in marking out and establishing chronology—than which no aspect of all history is described more variously by historians—I confess that I thought it a matter of religious scruple to banish so quickly from this library, or, what is no lighter a matter, to throw as though from a bridge a thousand years farther back, a polished writer scarcely yet born in this library, and that through Pithou’s benefit. Therefore, reader, embrace this gift of Pithou, which two hundred years ago Rodolfus the priest copied elegantly indeed, but, in my opinion, not accurately enough, as the following inscription written at the front of the manuscript testifies: ‘Rodolfus acquired this book for Saint Boniface in the year of the Lord 1360.’ Pithou, moreover, corrected it in many places. Accordingly, you should be indebted to Pithou on not one account only but on a second as well: that he gives you Quintus Julius Hilarianus, an ancient writer, corrected and adorned.”

These are his words. What remains is that I had nearly forgotten those things which the distinguished Mansi has recorded concerning our author and which I should like to transcribe here:

> [Note: [Col. 1097] Mansi, on Fabricius, *Medieval and Later Latin Library*, vol. III, p. 251.]

> “To this Quintus Julius Hilarianus,” he says, “I believe that the little work *On the Calculation of Easter*, by Agriustia, a citizen of the municipality of Timidensian Regia in the proconsular province of Africa, was addressed. A very ancient writer of a still unpublished work on Easter, which I copied for myself from the library of the canons of the major church of Lucca and which is to be published in due time, mentions this composition and its author. See my little commentary on a manuscript written in the time of Charlemagne, §15, in volume XLV of Father Calogerà’s minor works.”

[Col. 1097]

# CHRONOLOGY, OR LITTLE BOOK ON THE DURATION OF THE WORLD, OF QUINTUS JULIUS HILARIANUS. (C)

[Col. 1097B]

I. For however long, in the divine laws, the mind of anyone who fears God is attentive, by so much it will learn to choose what is true, so that through learning it may become wise, because the guide of the eyes of the heart in the Law is the Power and Wisdom of God the Father, Christ (I Cor. I, 24).

> [Note: [Col. 1097D] “To choose.” A suspect reading.]

And as though the gates of heaven had been opened, hearing God with God’s own mouth, he exults, learning something truly and wisely in the Law.

> [Note: [Col. 1097D] “With [God’s] own mouth.” Perhaps *from [God’s] mouth* (*ex ore*). “Truly and wisely.” Perhaps *of true wisdom* (*verae sapientiae*). And immediately below, *inde* in place of *unde*.]

Hence the wisdom of God does not allow a person to remain silent; compelled by truth itself, he speaks in order to make others wise. But one joined to wisdom could not envy.

> [Note: [Col. 1098D] “Who.” Perhaps “because.” Further on, *potest*, “is able,” perhaps for *potuit*, “was able.”]

Therefore the wise person, through the wisdom of God by which he was made wise, desires, having abandoned envy through which death rules and reigns (Wis. II, 24), that all people in the world should become wise. For he knows that it is foretold in the Law that “the multitude of the wise [Col. 1097C] is the health of the world” (Wis. VI, 26).

Accordingly, when a discussion from the Law, with wisdom as guide, had taken place before the brethren, and they themselves objected that the beginning of the world and its end could not be known by us at all—because some maintain that the world is already more than twenty thousand years old; others, unwilling to assign it either beginning or end; and others, though conceding its beginning, have held that it will be eternal—I say in reply: in establishing this by art, the philosophy of the world, and empty deceit, they have loved pomp of words and opinion more than truth, and have become lovers of these things.

> [Note: [Col. 1098D] “Truth.” Thus we have restored the reading in place of the editors’ *varitatem* [“variety”].]

For if we heed God’s command, which is faithful, we must accept whatever the divine Law has faithfully narrated to us. With the Lord’s assent, this will be related to you simply, if you permit. For there are those who think that the years in the Law were written down idly [Col. 1097D] or superfluously, as though unnecessarily; not knowing that such persons have little faith, since they do not believe that what the Law of God intimates is true. But they say: “Is it a great thing to bring something from the Law forward and commit it to writing?” Indeed it is, I say. For, as you yourselves know, I wrote some time ago, at your urging, concerning the calculation of Easter and the number of the years of the world; but for this reason I remained silent for some time: lest those little works themselves of ours should be irrationally composed with seasonings borrowed from another’s wisdom. Therefore, having arranged matters better, we have already sent forth a little book concerning the most sacred day of Easter; in it we have demonstrated according to the Law which is the first month. Thereafter, in this little work, we also record, by calculation in its proper order, the course of the years from the creation of the world.

II. In these promises, then, the brethren find sufficient delight in what we have more carefully established. For very many have written concerning this matter, not uniformly but diversely, so that the reader’s mind, left in uncertainty, cannot know [Col. 1098C] what is truer. I shall do as you wish, as I myself promised, with the Lord—that is, Christ God—showing the way. Therefore I shall follow up every part and rule of the years skillfully and more carefully, so that the exposition itself may seem to its readers, as they advance, like a pleasant road, level and smooth.

After the various constructions of earlier writers (especially those already regarded as carrying prejudged authority), it is impious or arrogant to say something; yet I shall say it. For reason compels it; and I do not believe it arrogant if, at a later time, someone brings forth something better from the Law. This the holy apostle Paul, seeking peace, testifies and says: “But if something better has been revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent” (I Cor. XIV, 30). And surely the Apostle said this concerning whatever discussion of the Law: whatever opinion anyone has held on a matter, however well he has held it, something better may be accepted. Now the question concerns the complete number of years, where no one can put an imperfect number in place of a complete one, nor exceed the complete [Col. 1099A] number itself, and maintain as true either what falls short of the complete number or what exceeds it. Therefore let us now come to the subject and relate all things in their order, so that it may be understood at what point I, wishing to attain this calculation, may have stated it fully.

> [Note: [Col. 1099D] “Or have stated it fully.” Perhaps, “or have not stated it fully.”]

III. Therefore, when this world was established by God the Creator, and he saw that all things had appeared from nothing at his command: the firmament with its ornaments—the sun, moon, and stars—shining with light for the cycles and signs of times; the earth, full of the verdure of every seed in its perfection and bearing flowers of diverse colors in a divine painting; the seas, enclosed by the barrier of shores and mountains, hemmed in as by a certain rampart so that they might not pass beyond them, and likewise first brought forth with movement in themselves and with every living soul—after this perfection of the world, it pleased almighty God to establish the human being, whom almighty God willed to be something above the other [Col. 1099B] animals. For he created those by his command and word; this one he formed with sacred hands (Gen. I, 27), and appointed him free and lord over all his creatures: those, that they might be governed by this one; this one, that, as a wise, rational, and intelligent animal, he might govern himself in the world.

From this person’s time and that of all his descendants, we have shown, in sequence, the generations down to our own age: how many years there have been since this world in which we dwell was made—a world which is now, according to the Gospel’s declaration, established at its end. Taking its origin from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which we have already expounded in the Easter treatise, by a calculation now proceeding, that this world was begun and made, we also related that the world existed five days without a human being, and that on the sixth day the human being was formed and given life by the breath of God [Col. 1099C].

IV. From the birth of the first-created man, Adam—that is—until the flood that occurred under Noah, there are [Note: [Col. 1099D] Better: 2237, for this is the total obtained.] 2257 years, which are reliably verified as follows through each successive generation. Adam, at the age of 230, begot Seth; Seth, at 205, begot Enos; Enos, at 170, begot Cainan; Cainan, at 170, begot Mahalaleel; Mahalaleel, at 165, begot Jared; Jared, at 162, begot Enoch; Enoch, at 165, begot Methuselah; Methuselah, at 182, begot Lamech. No one has seen, examined, or corrected by careful inquiry the first years of Methuselah, which an error of copyists has produced: that he lived 167 years [Note: [Col. 1099D] “And begot.” Perhaps better: “when he begot.”] and begot Lamech, and afterward lived 811 years. This cannot be true, since 811 years are shown to extend fourteen years beyond the flood. For no one survived the flood; [Col. 1099D] no one passed beyond it alive except in the ark. Therefore Methuselah lived 182 years and thus begot Lamech; after this he lived 787 years. For thus the true authority of divine Scripture demonstrates, which relates that Methuselah both lived and died before the flood.

V. Lamech, at the age of 188, begot Noah; for in Noah’s six-hundredth year the flood took place and was completed. From the time of the flood until Abraham’s [Note: [Col. 1100D] Better: 70th.] seventieth year, when he departed from his own land upon his sojourn, [Col. 1100A] there are 1012 years. Thus, in sequence, the second set of generations, beginning with Shem, Noah’s son, is displayed. But because Shem had completed [Note: [Col. 1100D] Better: 98.] 78 years at the completion of the flood, two years are necessary for the reckoning of the total that we have set out after the flood. For Shem himself was one hundred years old two years after the flood, and thus begot Arphaxad. The writers of this computation did not put these two years into the total number of years, because they failed to take them into account. Therefore, after the flood, Shem lived two years and begot Arphaxad. Arphaxad, at 135, begot Salah; Salah, at 130, begot Eber; Eber, at 134, begot Peleg; Peleg, at 130, begot Reu; Reu, at 132, begot Serug; Serug, at 130, begot Nahor; Nahor, at 79, begot Terah; Terah, at 70, begot Abram. Abram, at the age of 70, departed from his land, as we have said, for Harran. From Abraham’s sojourn until the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt into the wilderness, there are 430 years. [Note: [Col. 1100D] Thus. Read: “which are thus.”] These are then more certainly demonstrated by us.

VI. Abraham sojourned for thirty years and received Isaac, the son of promise. When Abraham desired to hear the word of the Lord concerning when [Note: [Col. 1100D] “May be able.” Perhaps: “might be able.”] his seed might inherit the land of Canaan, the sacrifice having been prepared toward evening, the Lord spoke to him, at once determining and declaring that his seed would still be strangers in the land of Canaan and in bondage to the Egyptians for 400 years, as divine Scripture testifies to Abraham himself in the book of Genesis: “Know certainly that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own; they shall be reduced to slavery, and they shall rule over them for 400 years. But the nation [Col. 1100C] whom they shall serve, I shall judge” (Gen. XV, 13–14).

And therefore Moses, the most wise lawgiver, by the authority of our God, says accordingly: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was 430 years” (Exod. XII, 40). Disputants concerning the years, paying too little attention to this, have vainly alleged that the children of Israel were in Egypt alone for 350 years, rather than for those 430 years. For, to show more fully—and thus more correctly—that the 430 years through Abraham’s seed were completed from Isaac’s birth until their departure from Egypt, not in Egypt alone but in the land of Canaan also, we set it forth by tracing their generations. Isaac, at the age of 60, begot Jacob. Jacob, when he was 130 years old, entered Egypt with his sons, grandsons, and all his offspring. Among [Col. 1100D] those grandsons was Kohath, son of Levi, who was Moses’ grandfather; therefore Amram was born in Egypt. Amram begot Moses; Moses himself departed Egypt with the children of Israel in his eightieth year. Consequently, from Isaac’s birth until Jacob’s entry into Egypt, they dwelt in the land of Canaan for 140 years, and they spent 210 years in Egypt. This is sufficient clarification of these years, concerning which very many who had spoken of them had hesitated.

[Col. 1101A] VII. Therefore, from the creation of the world until the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, there are 3,646 years. [Note: [Col. 1101D] Better: 3,000.] They were in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 1101D] “In the year.” Perhaps: “for forty years” or “in forty years.”] for forty years. Then, after Moses’ death, Jesus son of Nun brought the peoples across the channel of the Jordan on dry foot into the promised land; and, with divine favor, he conquered fierce nations and judged righteously.

Under the Judges there were also periods of captivity: from Jesus son of Nun to Samuel the prophet, who anointed Saul king, 561 years. Yet, that readers may recognize both that our total has been collected intact and that the apostle Paul stated the matter correctly in the Acts of the Apostles—namely, that after the land of Canaan had been apportioned by Jesus son of Nun to our fathers, the Lord God gave them judges for 450 years until Samuel the prophet—the Apostle, pursuing a different purpose and persuading them of something else in Acts [Col. 1101B] of the Apostles, named not the periods of captivity but only those periods in which they had judges and were governed by them: “And he gave them Judges,” he says (Acts XIII, 20). For when, because of their sins, they were delivered into captivity, they had not their own judges, but were oppressed by foreigners. Nor could the apostle Paul himself contradict the authority of the book of Judges, had he wished to trace the full extent of the periods. He named the judges given by God to the people because he wished to suggest faith in the Lord Christ; for he addressed the people as far as David, in order to relate that Christ had come from David’s seed, and proclaimed that those believing in him, if they wished, would have forgiveness of sins.

VIII. These periods of the Judges are thus displayed. Jesus son of Nun, with the elders, judged for thirty years. [Col. 1101C] After this, when they sinned, they were delivered to Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years; and the Lord raised up Othniel to help them. After killing Cufarsamoth, he judged Israel for fifty years. After him, when they sinned, they served Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years. Ehud killed Eglon, and Ehud judged for eighty years. When he died, the people sinned, and they served Jabin, king of the Canaanites, for twenty years. Against him the Lord raised up Deborah; after Jabin was killed, she judged for forty years. Sinning again, they were delivered to the Midianites for seven years. Against these Gideon arose and judged the people for forty years. After him his son judged for three years. After him Tola judged for twenty-two years. When Tola died, Jair was chosen by the people, and he too judged the people for twenty-two years. After his death, the people sinned and were delivered to the Ammonites for [Col. 1101D] eighteen years. Crying to the Lord because of oppression, they were given Jephthah, who judged for six years. And Sebon judged for seven years. Then the people sinned, and they were delivered to the foreigners (*allophyli*) for forty years. Turning again to the Lord, Samson was raised up for them; having defeated the foreigners, he judged for twenty years. After his death, [Note: [Col. 1101D] Semergar. Otherwise: Shamgar.] Semergar judged for one year. After him the people were at peace and had no ruler; but each did what pleased him, and they were their own judges for thirty years.

IX. After these years had passed, Eli [Col. 1102A] the priest judged for twenty years. Samuel, likewise a priest of God, succeeded him and judged for forty years, until he anointed Saul king. Thus the total number of years, as we have said, is 561. Those who think that the Apostle related something else concerning these years should observe more carefully that they themselves have failed to notice that the periods of the Judges alone, separated out—as the Apostle did—without the years of captivity, amount to 111 years. Therefore the total years from the creation of the world to Samuel, who anointed Saul king, are 4300.

Then came the periods of the Kings. They had kings for 514 years, from Saul to Zedekiah; Nebuchadnezzar put out Zedekiah’s eyes and killed him in the mill. The years of the kings are verified thus: Saul reigned forty years; David forty years and three months; Solomon forty years; Rehoboam [Col. 1102B] seventeen years; Abijah three years; Asa forty-one years; Jehoshaphat twenty-five years; Joram eight years; Ahaziah one year; [Note: [Col. 1101D] “Godolias.” Better: Athaliah, mother of Ahaziah.] Godolias six years; Joash forty years; Amaziah twenty-nine years; Uzziah fifty-two years; Jotham seventeen years; Ahaz fifteen years; Hezekiah twenty-nine years; Manasseh fifty-five years; Amon two years; Josiah thirty-one years; Jehoahaz three months; Jehoiakim eleven years; Jehoiachin three months and twenty days; Zedekiah eleven years. Therefore, as we have said, the years of the Kings are 514.

X. From the creation of the world, then, until Zedekiah, when Jerusalem was overthrown and the people were transported to Babylon, there are 4814 years. After Zedekiah’s eleventh year, Jerusalem was overthrown by King Nebuchadnezzar, and the Jewish people were transported into Babylonian captivity. That captivity lasted seventy years. How these years were completed [Col. 1102C] will be shown more clearly than daylight when we come to Daniel’s weeks, so that it may be most carefully established from what time and where these weeks were fulfilled.

For Daniel, in his tenth vision, while he was wholly intent upon prayer to God with an attentive mind and anxious concern, wishing to know whether the condition of Jerusalem and its people, after the Babylonian captivity, would suffer no further evil from enemies, was visited by an angel of God, who said: “Daniel, I have now come forth to show you understanding; for the Lord’s command went forth, and I have come to reveal it to you. For you are a man of desires. Consider therefore the command and understand the vision: seventy weeks have been cut off for your people and for the city Jerusalem” (Dan. XI, 22–24).

[Col. 1102D] XI. Therefore the angel sets forth to Daniel the total in seventy weeks, and again divides them in their order, stating when and how they are fulfilled. The angel continues concerning the same matter: “To blot out the things that have been received, to bring sins to completion, [Note: [Col. 1102D] “And to pray away injustices.” According to the LXX: καὶ τοῦ ἐξιλάσασθαι ἀδικίας, “and to make atonement for injustices.”] to make atonement for injustices, to abolish transgressions, to devise everlasting righteousness, to bring vision and prophecy to a conclusion, and to anoint the Holy of Holies; and do you rest and understand [Note: [Col. 1102D] “Concerning the coming forth,” etc. I suspect the passage is corrupt. LXX: Ἀπὸ ἐξόδου λόγου τοῦ ἀποκριθῆναι, “From the going forth of the word to give answer.”] concerning the coming forth of the Saints, or the command to be answered, and the rebuilding of the city Jerusalem, [Col. 1103A] until Christ the leader, seven weeks” (Dan. 24–25).

These weeks are forty-nine years, and they belong to the full period of Jerusalem’s seventy-year captivity. For Daniel saw the vision in the first year of King Darius, who reigned over the Chaldean kingdom and who also killed King Belshazzar; and it was the twenty-first year of Jerusalem’s captivity. For Nebuchadnezzar lived eighteen years after despoiling Zedekiah and Jerusalem, and his son Belshazzar reigned three years; in his third year he was killed, and Darius received the kingdom. In Darius’ first year the angel spoke to Daniel concerning the seventy weeks. Dividing them, the angel first named seven weeks, which, as has been said, are forty-nine years. These are joined to the twenty-one years of captivity [Col. 1103B] when Daniel saw the vision, producing seventy years, which were completed in Babylon, so that the vision and prophecy of Jeremiah might be fulfilled. After these years Cyrus, king of the Persians, in the first year of his reign commanded the peoples to go to Jerusalem, so that Jerusalem might be built and the Holy of Holies anointed—that which was most sacred in God’s Temple.

XII. The peoples therefore return from Babylon, having with them as leader Zerubbabel, of whom the angel spoke to Daniel: “until Christ the leader, seven weeks.” For every king of God’s people is called *christus*, “anointed one,” in the divine law. Thus the prophet Zechariah, speaking to the people of him as a future king, says: “The hands of Zerubbabel founded this house, and his hands will complete it; [Col. 1103C] and you shall know that the Lord Almighty sent me to you. For who has despised you in the days of small things? They shall rejoice in you and shall see the tin-stone in Zerubbabel’s hand” (Zech. IV, 9–10)—a thing which emperors today seem to carry in their right hand, as though representing the people.

The angel repeats and says to Daniel [Note: [Col. 1103] Better: “after sixty-two weeks the Lord is to be killed.”] “sixty-two weeks [the Lord],” that is, the period in which, after Temple and city of Jerusalem had been restored, they served the Lord with their offerings. These sixty-two weeks are 434 years, completed in the time of the Maccabees, in the 141st year of the Greek kingdom. For at that time Antiochus ruled the Greeks with a proud mind.

XIII. Although this order of years from the divine law, beginning with the world’s establishment, is sufficient in itself, nevertheless, that we may seem to satisfy the reader’s mind, we also show, tracing through the kings of Persia [Col. 1103D] from the histories of public records, that the sixty-two weeks were fulfilled from Cyrus to this Maccabean period. Cyrus reigned over the Persians thirty years; Artaxerxes nine years; Argus nine months; Darius thirty-six years; the second Artaxerxes nineteen years and two months; Sogdianus seven months; Xerxes the elder son twenty years; Artaxerxes seventy-two years; Artabus seven months; Darius Nothus twenty-nine years; Olus twenty-two years; Arser seventeen years; Darius six years. Alexander the Great of Macedon killed this man. From Alexander’s time the history of the Maccabees [Col. 1104A] traces the Greek years in divine narration. Thus the whole total of the Persian kings’ years is 263; and from Alexander of Macedon until Antiochus’ time—that is, until the 141st year of the Greek kingdom—the sixty-two weeks, as we have said, were completed, namely 434 years.

XIV. “After sixty-two weeks,” says the angel, “the anointing and the holy things shall be destroyed.” Therefore, after seven and sixty-two weeks, one week remains, making seven years to complete the total of seventy weeks. In this week, indeed, the wickedness of the Gentiles grew, as had already been declared by the angel, so that in the middle of that same week King Antiochus removed sacrifice from the holy place. The Holy Place itself was polluted by a woman’s affront; the Abomination [Col. 1104B] of Desolation was established upon the altar; and a statue of Jupiter, called Olympian, was placed there.
