This Antiochus also, bearing in his perverted mind an image of Antichrist, attempted to make one people and one sacrilegious nation under his rule. He allowed apostate men to build a *gymnasium*—that is, a school—in Jerusalem; and where Almighty God had commanded that he establish for himself a temple solely for prayer to him and the offering of holy sacrifices to him, Antiochus desired to pollute it with idolatrous spectacles.

XV. Therefore, when the seven and sixty-two weeks had been completed, in this first remaining week, as stated above, he commanded the Jewish people to burn the books of the Law, sacrifice to images, and eat unclean things. This continued until the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month in the [Col. 1104C] 148th year of the Greek kingdom. In that year all seventy weeks, which the angel set out in sequence to Daniel, are completed—the weeks concerning the disturbance of the city Jerusalem and the overthrow of the people, the matter about which Daniel himself had desired to inquire of the Lord.

XVI. From that point until the 174th year of the Greek kingdom, at which time Lucius Licinius Lucullus, Roman consul, gave letters concerning alliance and friendship to Simon, brother of Judas Maccabaeus, there are twenty-six years. For, tracing the annual consuls from this consulship onward, we find that 179 years were completed until the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, up to the sixteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Consequently, from the creation of the world until the passion of Christ our Savior, there are [Col. 1104D] 5530 years. Therefore 470 years remain to complete six thousand years. For just as the children of Israel, 470 years after the promise made by the Lord God to Abraham, received the promised land, so we Christians too shall have the first resurrection after the same number of years. For the Jewish people bear our figure in all things: “Upon whom the ends of the ages had come together” (I Cor. X, 15). Therefore, from Christ the Lord’s passion—at which time the Son of God promised resurrection to those believing in him by faith—470 years must necessarily be completed, in order that the total of six thousand years may be concluded. When the seventh [Col. 1105A] and thousandth year begins, those who believe with true faith shall be delivered from the world; for then shall be the first resurrection of all the saints.

XVII. Of the 470 years from the Lord’s passion, 369 have passed by the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April. There remain, therefore, 101 years for the six thousand years to be completed. These six thousand years cannot be completed unless, first, near the end, ten kings arise in the world and remove from the midst of the world the daughter of Babylon who now holds power. Then one powerful ruler shall suddenly arise over them, who is called the Dragon in the Apocalypse; he shall possess the ten kings, destroy some of them, while the others remain under his rule. Then shall be revealed that impious one, the son of perdition, who is exalted above everything called God [Col. 1105B] or worshipped, so that, sitting in God’s temple, he shows himself as though he himself were God (II Thess. II, 8, 4). This will be Antichrist himself. That most powerful Dragon, to whom the ten kings have yielded, shall hand over to him his force and power, and all mortals shall marvel.

The times of Antichrist—which must be mortal times—will resemble those when Antiochus attempted to make one people apostate under his rule. Yet, because it was not his time, such things did not happen to Antiochus as Antichrist will attempt to bring about. When he comes, he shall come for the destruction of unbelievers. His time shall be grievous and abominable; the Lord Christ alone shall kill him by the spirit of his mouth and nullify him by the manifestation of his coming (ibid., 4).

XVIII. Once Antichrist has been overcome and killed, [Col. 1105C] and the total of six thousand years completed, the resurrection of all the saints shall occur while the world still remains. A thousand years will then run their course, during which that ancient dragon (Apoc. XX, 3), the Devil and Satan, shall be bound and confined in the abyss so that he may deceive no one, until three years are completed. These three years shall be reckoned among those who remain under the sign of Antichrist; [Col. 1106A] all of these shall marry and be given in marriage, and shall die. Upon them the plagues described in the Apocalypse shall come, and this world shall thereafter be struck in its regions.

For the saints of God, in the resurrection, there shall be one day; and this day of the saints shall be extended in light for as long as one thousand years are counted for the impious living in the world in punishment. This is the seventh day, the eternal and true sabbath, of which the temporal sabbath prescribed in the Law of Moses bears the image and figure. For just as the Jewish people were told: “For six days perform the works of the world; but on the seventh day, called sabbath, rest from your works” (Exod. 23, 12), so for all the saints who have existed from the beginning of the world, and who now believe in Christ with true faith, once the six days—that is, [Col. 1106B] six thousand years—in which they had labor and suffering have passed, the seventh day and the true sabbath comes.

XIX. Therefore the Lord Christ warned every soul in the Gospel that it must hasten to believe in him before that time when eternal punishment must be rendered to the impious and good reward to the saints according to each person’s merits: “Pray,” he says, “that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath” (Matt. XXIV, 20). After the seventh and thousandth year Satan shall be released from his prison and go out to deceive the nations Gog and Magog. Gathering them against the camp of the saints as though to fight, fire shall descend from heaven and all human beings shall be consumed. Then there shall be the second resurrection of all flesh, and all shall be judged by God’s just judgment because they did not believe but pleased themselves [Col. 1106C] in their own righteousnesses. After this, this heaven and this earth shall be removed; and that city described in the Apocalypse, prepared in heaven, shall descend with God’s riches, and the righteous shall dwell in it. There shall be a new heaven and a new earth, and both shall endure forever: the impious in eternal burning, but the righteous with God in eternal life. Amen.

[Col. 1105]

[Note: [Col. 1105D] See above, Prolegomena, chapter 9, §§ 1 and 2.] **QUINTUS JULIUS HILARIANUS** [Note: [Col. 1105] This *Expositum* is printed by Gallandius in the appendix to the volume containing Hilarianus.] **EXPOSITION ON THE DAY OF PASCHA AND THE MONTH.** (C)

[Col. 1105D] I. Brothers, some servants of God and I have often met together to discuss certain matters from the divine Scriptures. There, at their request, having spoken briefly for the time being concerning the PASCHAL CYCLE, I promised that I would provide a full explanation. The command of the brothers has repeatedly and frequently reminded me of my promise: that what we formerly discussed gradually and patiently concerning the calculation of Pascha should now be defined in my writing. That is: since the Lord God named no month to Moses except the first, and commanded Pascha to be celebrated in it, saying, “This month shall be the beginning of months; it shall be [Col. 1106D] for you the first among the months of the year. Speak therefore to the whole synagogue of the children of Israel, that they may celebrate Pascha, beginning on the fourteenth of this month at evening until the twenty-first” (Exod. XII, 2, 3, 18, according to the LXX)—the divine Scripture has not declared to us by an entirely clear answer where this first month begins or where it has its end.

Why, then, is the first lunar day today sought by us from the third day before the Nones of March until the [Note: [Col. 1105D] MS: “third.”] fourth day before the Nones of April, [Note: [Col. 1105D] MS: “fourth.”] or why is it established that the fourteenth [Note: [Col. 1106D] MS: “day.”] falls from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April until the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May? Wherever the day of Pascha then occurs within this period, we celebrate it lawfully, as we have learned was celebrated and handed down by our Fathers.

Now the time has come to treat all things in sequence in my discourse according to the rationale of the Law, [Note: [Col. 1107D] Read: *affabre*, “skillfully.”] maintaining, of course, that Pascha was commanded to be celebrated not from the beginning of the world but by the sacred word through Moses; and that the first month [Note: [Col. 1107D] Namely, that the first month must be determined for us.] is not to be reckoned as the Egyptians begin their first month from the fourth day before the Kalends of September, or as the Romans begin theirs from the Kalends [Note: [Col. 1107D] MS: “January.”] of January. Rather, by the authority of divine law, in every year the moon, in its course, produces for us the first month. But in order lawfully to identify this first month for our Pascha, we are compelled to return by certain calculation to the origin of the world, so that [Col. 1107B] we may be able to know the day on which the luminaries were made and what sort of moon God made for the world—although in the world’s construction we must believe nothing other than that Almighty God established all things equal, full, and perfect.

II. First, therefore, it must be demonstrated what day it was when the world’s creation began and Almighty God, by creating light, established it. Secondly, we shall show what kind of moon God made at evening [Note: [Col. 1107D] Namely, made, and where.] and where, indeed, its year reaches its end. Then we shall explain [Note: [Col. 1107D] MS: “we have narrated.”] why the first lunar day is sought by us from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April, or why, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, the fourteenth must be sought in order to celebrate Pascha completely, so that [Col. 1107C] every avenue may be closed [Note: [Col. 1107D] MS: “is,” as often.] to those who delight in objections, lest they suppose that we have defined the calculation inadequately in any respect. [Note: [Col. 1107D] MS: “defined.”]

III. Before the law had been given by the Almighty Lord, people often disagreed about the course of the moon. Some called the first moon the full-orbed moon, such as had arisen for the world at God’s command; others thought otherwise. Therefore, reckoning months only by thirty-day units, they completed the course of twelve [Note: [Col. 1108D] MS: *epagomenos*.] months in 360 days, just as Scripture in Genesis shows that during the flood a month ran for thirty days. The five days remaining to complete the year were called vacant in remembrance of God’s creation. For the world was created in five days; but the human being was made on the sixth day, after all else. From that day, the count for passing through twelve months was 360 days, ending on the day before that day which God first established. Then there were five [Note: [Col. 1108D] *Vacivi*. Perhaps read *vacui*, “vacant,” as shortly above; likewise below.] vacant days until the day before the birth of that same first-created human being. [Col. 1108A] From this custom or tradition, it is known that the practice remained among some peoples—for example, among the Egyptians, who have these five vacant days, which they call ἐπαγόμενοι (*epagomenoi*, “added days”). Some Roman writers who wished to record the calculation of days likewise called them “dark” and intercalary days.

Thus in ancient times no one, because God had not yet disclosed the course of sun and moon, grasped the seasons of spring and summer, the boundaries of autumn and winter, or calculated the increases [Note: [Col. 1108D] MS: “diminishments.”] and decreases of days and nights—things which these luminaries were commanded by God’s decree to unfold in their own seasons until the end of time. Hence Almighty God, among many words of rebuke, also admonished that most holy and blessed Job concerning this, saying: “Tell me this also: do you know the course of sun and moon?” (Job XXVIII, 19). At the time when we know that the Law was given by the Lord our God to Moses for the celebration of Pascha, he gave Moses the calculation of months and years through the moon’s course, so that he might be able to identify, from [Note: [Col. 1108D] MS: “months.”] the *neomenia* [Note: [Col. 1108D] MS: *eomeia*.]—that is, the new moon—the first month and the others. This is now gathered from the tradition of the Law, if the person who wishes to gather it investigates most carefully. Applying ourselves to this matter, we set out each point, beginning, as we said, from the first day of the world.

IV. “In the beginning,” Moses says, “God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters. And God said, ‘Let light be,’ and light was made. [Col. 1108C] And God saw the light, that it was good, and divided between light and darkness. And God called the light day, and he called the darkness night. And evening came, and morning came: one day. And God divided between light and darkness”—that is, he balanced day and night (Gen. I, 1–5, according to the LXX).

For at God’s command the light so cut through darkness that an equal course between the two appeared; and from that point day and night began, by alternating turns, to receive their increases and [Note: [Col. 1108D] MS: “diminishments.”] decreases and to mark the seasons. For just as Almighty God at the outset immediately commanded earth and seas to bring forth every living soul in its full prime according to its kind, as well as all the fruits of the earth, perfect and with their seeds, so afterward he first established the span of light and darkness in an equal course. This first day is therefore known [Col. 1108D] to be that which was made at the beginning, on which the Lord God made light and night equal, in the season [Note: [Col. 1108D] Read: “of spring.”] of spring, which Almighty God intended to be the head of the year.

V. At this time, then, he created the world. [Col. 1109A] Before all other seasons, the Lord deigned first to establish this season, which is pleasant above the others and balanced in the quality of its air. In it, when the torpor of icy winter has passed and the cheerful air of spring has arrived, all things growing from the earth burst forth into diverse flowers and seeds of different kinds, so that they too, in some fashion, may celebrate the praises of the Lord Creator with human festivals, through the most welcome abundance and sweetness of fertile first fruits. In this season too the first equinox, established by the Lord, now occurs; according to the Roman names [Note: [Col. 1109D] MS: “months.”] of the months, it is found on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Taking our beginning from this point, therefore, we shall proceed through everything we have proposed.

VI. We have briefly set out our discussion of the world’s first day. Let us now come to the calculation of the moon. After three days had passed, on the fourth day—that is, the fifth day before the Kalends of April—the luminaries were established, not simultaneously, for signs and seasons, days and years. Although they were made on one day, Almighty God established the sun in the morning, so that he might make the day bright for us. As night approached, he established the moon, revolving in varying course through numbers and seasons, as the monthly measure. This moon was made at evening fourteen [Note: [Col. 1109D] The manuscript plainly appears to require reading *dodrans*, “three quarters.” The same form will be found below with the same meaning.] and three-quarters days old, for the reason that it might illuminate all the darkness of the first night and traverse the whole night; and so that, for the new human being, for whom the Lord God made these things, on the sixth day, just as the sun was made for the day, another work—the moon, serving the night—might appear to proceed, lest humanity, when the light and the sun’s brightness had departed, suffer unexpected [Col. 1109C] or solitary darkness.

For at that time the sun, rising in the morning, sees such a moon toward the west; and at the beginning of night, after the withdrawal [Note: [Col. 1109D] MS: “withdrawal.”] of light and the completion of the sun’s course, the moon advances, shielded with the strength of its own light. Not without reason did the Lord God also command his people through Moses in Exodus that Pascha should be celebrated from the full fourteenth moon of the first month at evening until the twenty-first. For the Lord wished the week [Note: [Col. 1110D] MS: *ebdomadum*, likewise below.] of Pascha to begin with the full fourteenth moon at evening, so that, at the dawn of the day of Pascha—the first day of that same week—the fifteenth day of the first month might be for them the day of unleavened bread. For in Leviticus the Lord declares this, saying: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, in the midst of the evenings, is Pascha to the Lord; and on the fifteenth of this month is the feast-day of unleavened bread to the Lord” (Lev. XXIII, 5–6, according to the LXX).

Lunar days begin at evening [Note: [Col. 1110D] MS: “evening,” likewise below.] and end at evening, because the moon received the beginning of its birth from the evening of the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in order that by its light it might moderate night’s darkness for humanity still unformed. It completed the course of its first day on the following evening [Note: [Col. 1110D] MS: “another evening.”]—that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April. Therefore we, taught by God and preserving the lunar course, celebrate the Paschal vigils when evening begins. [Col. 1110A]

VII. We have explained what kind of moon the Lord made at evening on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. Now we shall also show where it completed its year. For this year set a limit for all other years. But the Lord God himself testifies that the moon, by its course through *neomeniae*—that is, new moons and the first days [Note: [Col. 1110D] Read: “of months.”] of months, which the moon produces—marks months and years, as mentioned above. For it is written: “And the Lord God spoke to Moses, saying: On the first day of the new moon of the first month, you shall dedicate [Note: [Col. 1110D] MS: “you have dedicated.”] the tabernacle of testimony” (Exod. XL, 1–2, according to the LXX). And elsewhere, speaking of sacrifices and when and how they should be offered, he says: “You shall also offer sacrifices in [Col. 1110B] the new moons, month by month, throughout the months of the year” (Num. XXVIII, 11, 14, according to the LXX).

It is also said in the book of Kingdoms: “When David hid himself, fearing King Saul, the new moon came, and the king entered to the table to eat, and his customary guests came with him. But David did not enter with him, and his place was visible; and Saul said nothing that day. And on the morrow, on the second day of the month, it happened …” (I Reg. XX, 24–26, according to the LXX). Likewise in the Psalms it is said: “God made the moon for seasons” (Ps. CIII, 19).

Therefore the moon completes a month in twenty-nine and a half days. Why? Because it does not end with its light entirely diminished. Otherwise it would already be another work, not that which Almighty God made at first. On the thirtieth day, therefore, the moon is hidden in a half-day of deficiency. Twelve times twenty-nine and a [Col. 1110C] half consequently make 354 days.

VIII. Thus on the fifth day before the Nones of March this same moon, in completing its course, completed its year. We can prove this through each month of that lunar year. For it completed its first month on the second day before the Ides of April, because God made it full [Note: [Col. 1110D] MS: “full.”] for the world and commanded it to proceed.

The second month it completed on the fourth day before the Ides of May. The third month it completed on the third day before the Ides of June. The fourth month on the sixth day before the Ides of July. The fifth month on the fifth day before the Ides of August. The sixth month on the seventh day before the Ides of September. The seventh month on the Nones of October. The eighth month on the Nones of November. [Col. 1110D] The ninth month on the Nones of December. The tenth month on the third day before the Nones of January. The eleventh month on the fourth day before the Nones of February.

It assigned its twelfth month, indeed, to the fifth day before the Nones of March; but on the fourth day before the Nones of March, after the fifth day before those same Nones had passed through twelve moons—that is, twelve months—the birth of that same moon appeared.

IX. Accordingly, the moon completes its year in 354 days [Col. 1111A], whereas the sun does so in 365 days and a quarter. That is, there are eleven days and a quarter which the lunar reckoning seems, as it were, to have fewer than the solar reckoning: the twelve half-units, constituting six days of the moon’s *cavaturae* [deficiencies]; the five days which, in commemoration of God’s creation, were called vacant days, and which Roman arrangement has now distributed among certain months, calling them intercalary days; [Note: [Col. 1111D] The manuscript reads “to it.”] and that quarter-day, which properly belongs to the solar reckoning. When this quarter-day is counted in addition, it makes a whole day through the additions of four years, and is added to the course of the sun as the twice-sixth day before the Kalends of March [i.e. leap day].

But since sun and moon, day and night, have a discussion joined one to another, the lunar year consists of 353 days; these eleven days and the leap-year quarter are added, and thus the year of the sun is recognized to contain [Col. 1111B] 365 days and a quarter. Therefore, because the moon completed its first year—that is, on the fifth day before the Nones of March—the third day before the Nones of March appears to belong to the first month.

X. Yet since divine mercy has ordained that the solemnity of Easter must beyond doubt be celebrated only in the first month, for that reason we do not seek the first moon from the fourth day before the Nones of March, on account of [Note: [Col. 1111D] The manuscript reads “reckoning.”] the reckoning of Easter. For on that day, when the first year was turning, the moon appeared not as a full unit but as a half-unit; whereas on the following day, that is, the third day before the Nones of March, it is known to have been first at a full unit. Hence [Note: [Col. 1111D] The manuscript reads “we understand.”] we understand that its increase toward the birth of that same moon must be reckoned from the fourth day before the Nones of March, so that the third day before the Nones of March may more correctly meet us as the first moon.

Therefore, when the first moon falls on the fourth day before the Nones of March, we set it aside, because the unit itself is completed in twenty-four hours of night and day; and it begins its increase from the day of the final month of its completed year—the fifth day before the Nones of March—toward its full unit, lest the first moon of the first month appear to have the beginning of its increase in the final month. We retain this fourth day before the Nones of March as an intermediate day, so that it may stand between [Note: [Col. 1111D] Read “the day.”] the day of the final completed month and the third day before the Nones of March; thus the first moon that falls on the third day before the Nones of March has the beginning of its increase from the fourth day before those same Nones. For if, on that day—that is, the third day before the Nones of March—the moon is first, without any difficulty concerning the year, it is found to be first on the day of the first month, and from the day of the first month it receives its increase toward its birth.

[Col. 1111D] XI. Therefore, from this third day before the Nones of March until the fourth day before the Nones of April, we must seek the first moon; for on whichever day within these twenty-nine days the moon is first, the first lunar month begins from that point. From the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April until the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, it is established by true calculation that the moon is legally to be the fourteenth. [Note: [Col. 1111D] The manuscript reads “day.”] Proceeding from there, when the most holy day of Easter occurs, Easter ought rightly and without any interruption to be celebrated in that same first month which the moon has produced.

For thus the Lord testifies and says concerning this matter in Exodus: “You shall observe the feast day of Passover; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the season of the month of new things. For in it you came out from the land of Egypt” (Exod. 23:15, according to the Septuagint).

Likewise, in Leviticus the Lord commanded and says: “In the first month, on the fourteenth of the month, in the midst of the evenings, is the Passover of the Lord; and on the fifteenth of this month is the feast day of unleavened bread to the Lord” (Lev. 23:5–6, according to the Septuagint).

Likewise, in Numbers: “The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the second year of their departure from Egypt, in the first month, saying: Speak, and let the children [Note: [Col. 1112D] The manuscript reads “Istrael”; likewise often elsewhere.] of Israel keep the Passover at its appointed time. On the fourteenth day of the first month at [Note: [Col. 1112D] Read “evening.”] evening you shall perform it according to its times, according to its law, and according to its ordinance [corporationem] [Col. 1112B] you shall perform it.” And Moses spoke to the children of Israel to keep the Passover in the wilderness of Sinai; and as the Lord commanded Moses, so the children of Israel did (Num. 9:1–5, according to the Septuagint).

And a little later the Lord commanded with a threat and says: “The man who is clean and is not on a distant journey, and yet neglects to keep the Passover, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he did not offer the gift to our Lord at its appointed time; that man shall bear his sin” (ibid., 13).

Likewise, in Deuteronomy Moses addresses the people, saying: “Observe the month of new things, and you shall keep the Passover for the Lord your God, because in the month of new things you came out by night from the land of Egypt; and you shall sacrifice the Passover of the Lord your God” (Deut. 16:1–2, according to the Septuagint).

Moreover, in the first book of Esdras it is written more plainly: “And Josiah kept the Passover to the Lord in Jerusalem [Col. 1112C], and sacrificed the Paschal offering on the fourteenth moon of the first month at [Note: [Col. 1112D] The manuscript reads “evening.”] evening” (1 Esdras 1:1, according to the Septuagint; Vulgate, 2 Chron. 35:1).

XII. But why do we range over so much material, when it is stated in all the sacred Scriptures that Easter ought to be [Note: [Col. 1112D] Read “celebrated.”] celebrated in the first month? Yet this moon does not have this first month fixed and securely bounded so that it always occurs on the same day. Rather, the twenty-nine days mentioned above—from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April [Note: [Col. 1112D] That it may be, as elsewhere.]—are those in which, after the first year from the creation of the world had elapsed, it displayed its first month. Thus, whenever it is first on one day among these, it thereby produces the first month for us.

This calculation produces embolismic and common years. For whenever, in the twelfth month, before the third day before the Nones of March, after the days of its year mentioned above have been completed, that moon appears first, it is necessary that it complete a thirteenth month and make an embolismic year. But if, when its year has been completed at its proper time—that is, on the days which appear to belong to the first month—after its twelve months have elapsed, the moon is first, a common year results.

These twenty-eight days thus make embolismic and common years manifest. There are eleven days [Col. 1113A] from the third day before the Nones of March to the day of the Ides of the same month. If the moon is first on these days, because it will appear to have been born after twelve months, this shows that the years past were common, while it indicates that the present years, in which its birth makes the first month, are embolismic. There are eight days from the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April to the tenth day before the Kalends of April. If the moon appears first on these days, it signifies that both the past and the present years are common. There are, further, ten days from the eighth day before the Kalends of April to the third day before the Nones of the same month. If the moon is first on these days, it makes the past years embolismic and shows the present years to be common. These common years contain 354 days: either the lunar reckoning has eleven days fewer than the solar reckoning and makes a common year, or it exceeds by ten and nine [days] and makes [Col. 1113B] an embolismic year.

XIII. Thus, from year to year, by this variation, the days of the lunar years do not seem to agree with the days of the sun, which completes its year in 365 days and a quarter. We have accordingly shown this also, so that it may appear to all that their days are equal to one another, that they have run from the beginning of their course in this order, and that the same moon has made good in embolismic years the losses of common years.

Let us set forth the calculation of eight years, which appears to be complete. In eight years the moon has five common years and three embolismic years. Therefore, five times 354 [Note: [Col. 1113D] The manuscript has a sign in place of the word “make,” apparently indicating it. PFAFF. — The number 354 multiplied by five yields 1,770; therefore the character reported by the manuscript seems to be read as CIC. The editor or printer evidently omitted this CIC notation for a thousand. My Gallicioli observed this correctly.] make 1,770, and three times 384 [Note: [Col. 1114D] “Make” is absent from the manuscript.] make 1,152; together they make 2,922 days. Then let us likewise gather into one the total of the sun’s eight years: [Col. 1113C] eight times 365¼, 2,922. Thus it brought together the courses of sun and moon with the days written above.

XIV. We have explained what was the day of the world on which almighty God, in creating, established light; what the moon was made like at the beginning of the night; where it first completed its year; why the first moon is sought by us from the third day before the Nones of March; and from which days the fourteenth moon is determined. We have also set out the calculation of embolismic and common years in full detail, so that our descendants may, through endless years, calculate this lunar course together with the days of Easter, and more easily and truthfully investigate the times to come: on what numbered Kalends or Ides it might fall; what day or what numbered moon might occur in the first month. [Col. 1113D] Thus this little work of ours has been made available to all without labor, since the true calculation has been set forth above, and so that the days of Easter themselves may be known in their own season without effort or any stumbling-block of falsehood by many who are uncertain or ignorant.

For our Easter is one thing; that of the Jews is another. Our sacrament, moreover, is very different [Col. 1114A] from theirs; nor do we celebrate the Passover for the Lord as they do, as is shown by clear reasoning in the following discussion.

XV. In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, the Lord Christ, being about thirty years old, began his ministry upon receiving John’s baptism. The Evangelist attests this. Accordingly, for one year he preached to the Jewish people to whom he had come. In that year he not only foretold that the kingdom of heaven was drawing near, but also showed himself to be the Lord manifest in mighty works, so that they might believe. This continued until the sixteenth year of the reign of Tiberius [Note: [Col. 1114D] The manuscript reads “Caesarian.”] Caesar, in which year Christ the Lord himself, rather than—as was customary in the Jewish solemnity—a sheep from the flock, was sacrificed for us, so that we who believe might be delivered not from Egypt but from the world and its vices.

For in that year, as the reliability of calculation shows and calculation itself persuades, that same Lord Christ suffered on the fourteenth moon, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the sixth weekday [Friday]. But on the third day, as the first weekday dawned—the day after the Jewish Sabbath, the Lord’s day, that is, our Sabbath and the true Easter—[Col. 1114B] that same Lord Christ, by rising after conquering death, sanctified our Easter: that is, he effected the passing-over of the living and the dead from the judgment of the old human being unto deliverance. And for those who fear the Lord and believe in Christ, the true sun of righteousness rose, with healing in its wings.

Therefore we Christians today, in remembrance of our deliverance, celebrate Easter for the Lord no longer as the Jews do, with a slain lamb, unleavened cakes of fine flour, and on whatever day it may be; rather, in likeness of the resurrection of that same Lord of ours, on the first weekday—that is, Sunday—retaining from the Law only the first [Col. 1114C] month, which the moon produces as it runs through its numbers. As it is written: “From the full fourteenth [day] until the twenty-first at evening, in unleavened bread of sincerity and truth”—that is, in purity [Note: [Col. 1114D] The manuscript reads “purity.”] of mind—we celebrate Easter for the Lord.

## Epilogue

With God’s favor, we have explained in due course everything that had to be said concerning the calculation of Easter. Let us now bring our discourse to an end here. We completed this laborious work on this third day before the Nones of March, after [Note: [Col. 1114D] The manuscript reads “the consulship of Arcadius.”] the fourth consulship of Arcadius and the third of Honorius. Therefore we admonish those who hastened to obtain these writings before they had been corrected by us to endeavor to obtain the work corrected according to this order. For this reason we have now fixed to this calculation the day and the consuls, which we did not include at first, so that henceforth anyone may know that this is the corrected work.

Quintus Julius Hilarianus completed and corrected it on the third day before the Nones of March, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.

## A.D. 398. Saint Siricius, Pope

[Note: [Col. 1115B] **Siricius.** After an interregnum of twenty-one days, in the year of Christ 385, on the day before the Ides of January, Siricius was appointed in Damasus’s place, not without disturbance from the schismatic Ursicinus. He presided over the Church under the emperors Valentinian II, Theodosius the Elder, Arcadius, and Honorius. Near the beginning of Siricius’s pontificate, that imperial Jezebel, Justina, persecuted Ambrose. The Antiochenes threw down the statues of Theodosius; Chrysostom and Flavian pleaded against the punishment consequently imposed—imprisonment and deprivation of privileges. Saint Monica, Augustine’s most devout mother, was called to the blessed life, concerned with one matter only: that the saving sacrifice be offered for her. “Only this,” she said, “I ask of you: remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you may be.”

Dissensions arose between Epiphanius of Constantia in Cyprus and John, bishop of Jerusalem, on the occasion of Origen’s heresies, which the latter had unhappily undertaken to defend with Rufinus and many others. Which heresies emerged in his time and which councils were held will be evident from the notes on the councils and letters. He sat fifteen years—thirteen years, one month, and fourteen days. For on the eighth day before the Kalends of March in the year 398, he departed this life. If the duration of Siricius’s pontificate is calculated from the beginning of his see down to this point, the assigned number of years, months, and days will be found. Because he did not respond sufficiently quickly to the Church’s peril through the Origenists—whom Marcella had exposed at Rome, as we shall say below in the notes on the Alexandrian council held under Anastasius—he was removed from this life very swiftly.

He decreed that no presbyter should celebrate Mass during the week unless he had received the consecrated *fermentum* from the bishop of the place. What the *fermentum* is and what its use is, we have said above in the notes on the life of Melchiades, under the words “He did this”; likewise in canons 14, 32, and 49 of the Council of Laodicea. These wonderfully explain what is subscribed here. He discovered Manichaeans whom he had deported. The pontiff enacted these measures against the Manichaeans because they could with difficulty be distinguished from Catholics. They held only secret meetings and, reinforcing their claims by oaths and lies, asserted that they were Catholics. Convicted of lies, heresy, and perjury, they feigned repentance and outwardly denounced their heresy, while inwardly continuing to be Manichaeans. To avoid detection, they frequented the Catholic church and shared the sacred Eucharist with Catholics. Rightly and deservedly, when discovered, they were punished by exile; or, if they performed penance, they were admitted to receive the sacred Eucharist only at the end of life.

It is probable that, at the request of Pope Siricius, the rescript of Emperor Theodosius extant in Book XVIII, *On Heretics*, of the Theodosian Code was promulgated. By it, adherents of the aforesaid heresy were ordered to be banished not merely from the city but from the whole world. Since, in honor of sun and moon, they fasted on Sunday and the second weekday, and, worshipping the sun as a divinity, turned toward the east in superstitious adoration—and since Catholics did the same with pious and holy intent—Catholics and orthodox Christians could not be distinguished from Manichaeans by any sign. Saint Leo I therefore suspended this manner of praying for a time, lest the faithful people have anything in common with heretics, and so that they might instead be distinguished by this sign most plainly. Baronius, year 443, nos. 4 and 5.]

[Col. 1115]

## Prolegomena

[Col. 1115A]

## The Life and Reign of Pope Siricius

*(From the Pontifical Book, Labbé’s Councils, vol. II, col. 1015.)*

SIRICIUS, a Roman by nationality and son of Tiburtius, sat fifteen years, eleven months, and twenty-five days. He issued a decree for the whole Church and against all heresies, and disseminated it throughout the entire world and through all provinces, so that it might be preserved in every archive of the Church, for defense against all heresies. He decreed that no presbyter should celebrate Mass throughout the week unless he received the consecrated and designated portion from the bishop of the place, which is called *fermentum*. He discovered Manichaeans and deported them into exile. [Col. 1115B] And he decreed this: that they should not share communion with the faithful, [Col. 1116A] because with a polluted mouth they were not permitted to profane the holy body of the Lord.

He also decreed that, if anyone converted from the Manichaeans returned to the Church, he should by no means receive communion, but should remain subject only to confinement in a monastery for the days of his life, so that, worn down by fasts and prayers and tested by every examination until the final day of his passing, the Church in its mercy might grant them the viaticum. He decreed that heretics be received and reconciled by the laying on of hands in the presence of the whole Church.

He held five ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: thirty-one presbyters, sixteen deacons, and thirty-two bishops for various places. He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. And the [Col. 1116B] episcopate was vacant for twenty days.

*From Coustant, Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, vol. I, col. 621.*

[Col. 1117A]

Siricius assumed the government of the Roman Church at the end of the year 384, though on what day is uncertain; and in 398 he departed this life. In some copies of the *Pontifical Book* he is recorded as buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, in others on the ninth. The Hieronymian Martyrology, supported also by Bede’s Martyrology, records his death thus on 26 November: “At Rome, the deposition of Bishop Siricius.”

Thus, although Siricius administered the Church for only fourteen years, and indeed not even the entirety of those years, if nevertheless the end of 384 and the greater part of 398 are counted, as often happens, as two years, it is not falsely said in the ancient catalogues of Roman pontiffs that he sat for fifteen years. The ancient epitaph of this pontiff agrees:

> He who ruled the people in love for three times five years  
> Now enjoys rest, having obtained the heavenly kingdoms.

From this we also learn that he ruled the people more by love than by authority. Jerome portrays him as simple-minded, judging others according to his own disposition (Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus*, book III). Yet the writings of his that have reached us breathe the highest zeal for the Catholic faith and for maintaining canonical discipline.

*From Schoenemann, vol. I, p. 306.*

Siricius, a Roman, born of the father Tiburtius, was first a presbyter of the Roman Church and then, after the death of Damasus in A.D. 384, was chosen bishop of the Roman see with such unanimity [Col. 1117C] of all votes that Emperor Valentinian was immediately won over to him by this very judgment concerning his integrity and virtues. This is attested by the emperor’s reply to Pinianus, prefect of the City, concerning his election:

“Since,” he says, “they have desired the religious Siricius, a bishop of holiness, to preside over the priesthood in such a way that by their acclamations they assailed the wicked Ursinus, let the aforesaid bishop remain with our rejoicing; for it is a great example of innocence and uprightness that in one acclamation he himself should be elected and the others rejected.”

Nor did Siricius fail to live up to this reputation. For although by nature he possessed a gentle disposition, joined with remarkable simplicity of character, he allowed none of his predecessors to appear his equal in vigilance and zeal for preserving and defending the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical discipline. At the very outset of his office, concern for ecclesiastical discipline occupied him. For a certain Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, uncertain what counsel to adopt concerning various practices of the churches in Spain, had asked Damasus by letter and requested help with advice. After Damasus had meanwhile died, these letters were delivered to Siricius. He convened a synod of his fellow bishops and presbyters, reviewed them, and gave a response by the common decision of the synod, with the provision that Himerius was forbidden to depart from it unless he wished to be separated from the communion of that body.

Not long afterward, having learned that the errors of Priscillian were spreading more widely in Gaul, he urged by letter the tyrant Maximus, then holding power there, and obtained from him also that he should neither allow himself to be led away from the Catholic faith nor permit the license of the Priscillianists. This proved fatal to Priscillian and some of his companions, yet it could not confine their teaching within narrower bounds.

Further, in 389 he condemned Jovinian by a synodal decision and expelled him from the city. When Jovinian fled to Milan, Siricius anticipated him by letters to Ambrose and the other bishops gathered there, lest he deceive either them or Theodosius, then residing there, by a feigned case. He acted more unjustly toward Flavian, bishop of Antioch: after Paulinus’s death, he so refused communion with Flavian that he pressed Theodosius—though in vain—about removing him from the bishopric of Antioch. At last, only a few months before the end of his life, he was won over by Chrysostom’s skill and entered into communion with him. Why he refused to pronounce judgment in the case of Bonosus is unclear. He died on 2 November, certainly near the end of A.D. 398.

## Writings and Editions of Pope Siricius’s Works

*From Schoenemann, as above.*

### 1. Writings

Six letters of Siricius survive, although it does not appear that all can be ascribed to him with sufficiently certain credibility.

[Col. 1118C] The first, to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, is especially celebrated because it is the first—or at least the first that has reached us—of the decretal letters in which Roman bishops answered inquiries from various churches. It was written in the very year of his election, 385.

The second is to Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica. Its date cannot be fixed with certainty. It is nevertheless clear that it was sent before anything concerning the case of Bonosus had been heard at Rome; otherwise Coustant thinks Siricius would not have been silent about it:

“And not without reason,” he says, “shall we refer to the year 385 those letters by which Siricius entrusted to Anysius the task of learning what was being done in the churches of Illyricum.”

But he sent these second letters before he could yet know whether the first had been received. It follows that these second letters belong at least to A.D. 386.

The third, to the bishops of Africa, was written A.D. 386, 6 January. Mention of it is already found in Ferrandus the deacon, in his *Summary of Canons*, articles 6, 130, 138, and 174. Blondel, Papebroch, and others nevertheless called its authenticity into doubt; Quesnel did so with very strong arguments. [Note: [Col. 1117D] In the appendix to the works of Leo the Great, Dissertation 15.] Schelstrate and Baluze defended it against them [Note: [Col. 1117D] In a separate dissertation on the Council of Telepte against [Col. 1118D] Quesnel, reprinted at the end of the 1704 edition of the book *On the Harmony of Priesthood and Empire*, p. 1339.]; yet they were altogether unable to free it from every suspicion raised by Quesnel.

[Col. 1119A] The fourth is to various bishops. Its true superscription is lacking. It appears to have been written directly to the bishops of Italy, but to have reached us from a copy delivered to bishops in other provinces. Regarding its date, Coustant considers it not much later than the preceding letter.

The fifth is to various bishops, against the heretic Jovinian and his associates, who were to be removed from the Church. Coustant aptly observes that its date can be elicited from Ambrose’s answering letter to Siricius. For since Jovinian and his companions are said there to have been expelled from Rome and to have fled to Theodosius at Milan, and since Theodosius arrived there in August or September of 388 but is said to have come to Rome on the Ides of June, it is clear that this letter could not have been written before the latter part of 388. Coustant therefore assigns it to 389.

The sixth, to Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica, and the other bishops of Illyricum, concerns Bonosus. It was written shortly after the Council of Capua—that is, after the sixth day before the Kalends of December 391—and before Valentinian’s murder—that is, before the Ides of May 392. It was falsely attributed to Damasus and Ambrose. Justellus, supported by others, rightly vindicated it for Siricius. [Note: [Col. 1119D] In notes on Canon 48 of the Code of the African Church.]

Several other letters of his have been lost: for example, the letter to Emperor Maximus, written in 385; that concerning the case of the Ithacians, in 386; that to Emperor Theodosius against Flavian; and that to Rufinus in 398. Coustant discussed all these, as well as those falsely attributed to Siricius.

### 2. Editions

It would not, I think, be worth our labor to enumerate the individual letters of Siricius scattered through various collections of canons and [Col. 1119C] councils, as they have been printed at different times and places. It will suffice to indicate the collected editions by Coustant and Gallandius.

Coustant, then, in his *Collection of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs* (vol. I, Paris, 1721), pp. 622–711, presents Siricius’s letters in the same order in which we have enumerated them, but with various related documents by others inserted. Copious historical observations are added to all of them, and introductory notices where needed. He was not content merely to reproduce them from the principal printed collections of councils and canons, but was aided also by many manuscript codices. He edited ten letters.

I. The letter to Himerius, found in all collections of canons, is enlarged from the Corbie, Colbert, and Saint-Germain manuscripts by a threefold appendix to the Decree, which Dionysius Exiguus did not know and which Coustant considers perhaps to belong to another rescript of Siricius.

II. The letter of Emperor Valentinian to Pinianus, prefect of the City.

III. The letter of Emperor Maximus to Pope Siricius.

IV. The letter to Anysius. This was once published by Lucas Holstenius in the bipartite Roman Collection (Rome, 1762, octavo), Part I, p. 43.

V. To the bishops of Africa. It was preserved through the Council of Telepte. Various and very ancient collections of conciliar and pontifical letters present it as it was read at that council. Four of these were formerly kept in the Colbert Library, two in the Royal Library, one in the Saint-Germain Library, and others elsewhere; Coustant used most of them. Nor is it absent from the codex that Quesnel published under the name *Code of Canons of the Roman Church*, although in that codex it occupies the last place and is additionally thought to have been added later. Coustant argues against this opinion and, from the superscription supplied by the Corbie codex, endeavors to free the Council of Telepte from every suspicion.

VI. (no. 4) Letter to various bishops.

VII. (no. 5) Letter to various bishops. He collated both against the manuscript codices of the Colbert Library and printed editions.

VIII. The letter or rescript of Ambrose and other bishops to Pope Siricius concerning the case of Jovinian.

IX. Letter to Anysius. Holstenius published it in 1662 in the *Bipartite Collection*, Part II, p. 189. It is also found among Ambrose’s letters. Coustant had several manuscript books at hand in revising it.

X. Or, the canons of the Roman synod to the bishops of Gaul, which Sirmond added from the Fossat manuscript, later the Colbert manuscript, and another Pithoean collection, at the end of volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*. There follows an account of other writings relating to Siricius.

1770. Venice, Albrizzi, folio. *Letters and Decrees of Pope Saint Siricius.* Some items relating to the same pontiff are interwoven: in Gallandius’s *Library of the Fathers*, vol. VII, pp. 533–549. Besides Siricius’s six letters, it contains no. VI, Ambrose’s rescript, and no. VIII, the canons of the Roman synod. Critical notes, especially, are selected from Coustant. Concerning the individual letters Gallandius, following Coustant’s tracks, discusses them in chapter 13 of the *Prolegomena*, p. XVIII ff.

*From Coustant, Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, col. 699.*

### 1. Account of Other Writings Relating to Pope Siricius

#### I

1. **In the year 385: Siricius’s letter to Emperor Maximus.** At the beginning of his pontificate Siricius judged that he ought to write to Emperor Maximus, both to induce him to undertake the protection of the Catholic faith and to bring back into order a certain Agricus, who had improperly entered the rank of presbyter. There is no doubt that he also indicated his intention at the same time to announce the beginnings of his pontificate and to discharge the customary duties of greeting. Maximus, replying to him, praised Siricius’s letter (Letter III) as suited to the Catholic faith and to the dignity of the most splendid city.

#### II

2. **Proceedings against the Priscillianists.** To the letter which Maximus wrote back to Siricius, the emperor had appended the most recent proceedings against the Manichaeans—that is, the Priscillianists—by which the crimes they committed were known from their own confession (Letter III). But these proceedings have been lost.

#### III

3. **Siricius’s letter to Anysius.** Not long after the beginning [Col. 1121A] of Siricius’s pontificate should be placed his letter to Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica, delivered through the agency of Bishop Candidianus. By it Siricius entrusted to Anysius his authority throughout Illyricum (Letter IV), and expressly commanded that in those regions no one should be permitted to ordain bishops without Anysius’s consent.

#### IV

4. **After the year 386: Siricius’s letters concerning the case of the Ithacians.** Ithacius, as Sulpicius Severus relates, bishop of Sussuba—or rather of Ossonoba—in Lusitania, carried away by unconsidered zeal against Priscillian’s heresy, had persuaded Emperor Maximus to punish the chief leaders of this heresy with death in 385. Pope Julius had already noted that such a course of action was contrary to the evangelical law and had written to the Eusebians who maintained it (Letter I, no. 22): “O beloved, ecclesiastical judgments are now decreed not according to the Gospel, but unto penalties of exile and death.”

Accordingly, holy and Catholic bishops, abhorring the cruel deed of Ithacius and his companions, rejected communion both with them and with Felix, whom they had ordained bishop of Trier in 386. Felix, indeed, was, according to Sulpicius (*Life of St Martin*, book II), a most holy man and entirely worthy to become a priest in a better time. Yet because his ordination could not be approved by those who disapproved the deeds of Ithacius and his companions, a schism arose from this. To settle it, Siricius wrote letters which are mentioned and approved in canon 6 of the Council of Turin, held about 398, in these terms:

> “Further, the holy synod decreed that, since the bishops of Gaul who communicate with Felix have sent delegates, those who wish to separate themselves from his communion shall be received into the fellowship of our peace, according to the letters formerly issued by Ambrose, bishop of venerable memory, or by the bishop of the Roman Church, which were read in the council in the presence of the delegates.”

These letters must be acknowledged to have been sent sufficiently long before the Council of Turin, yet not before 386, since they are later than Felix’s ordination.

#### V

5. **Siricius prescribes the conditions under which peace is to be restored to Priscillianists.** Nor did Siricius fail those who wished to return from Priscillian’s heresy to the Church. For the Spaniards, in the proceedings appended to the First Council of Toledo, commend a letter of Ambrose written after the Council of Saragossa—that is, after 381—and then promise peace to Priscillian’s followers “if they condemned what they had wrongly done and fulfilled the conditions contained in the prescribed letters of Ambrose, with the additions advised by Pope Siricius of holy memory.” From this it may be inferred that Siricius wrote letters prescribing and advising what the Priscillianists had to do in order to be admitted to the communion of the Church.

#### VI

[Col. 1122A]

6. **In the year 392: letters of Anysius and his associates to Siricius.** The Council of Capua had entrusted the investigation of the case of Bonosus, bishop of Sardica, who was accused of heresy, to Anysius and the other bishops of Illyricum (Letter 9, nos. 1 and 5). But they, either deterred by the gravity of the case or through modesty and their singular reverence for the Apostolic See, sent Siricius letters asking his judgment concerning that bishop. To the same letters they attached certain proceedings, and specifically reported that Bishop Bassus had given Senecio to share in the governance of the Church. What Siricius replied to them, his ninth letter teaches us.

#### VII
7. Siricius’ Letters to the Emperor Theodosius against Flavian. [Col. 1122B] —Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 24, recounts the conflict which existed between the Romans and the Easterners concerning the church of Antioch, some supporting Paulinus, others Flavian, the successor of Meletius; nor was it extinguished by the death of Paulinus. For when Evagrius had been appointed in his place, “the Westerners and Egyptians,” says the same Theodoret, “attempted to gain access to the ears of the Emperor Theodosius against Flavian. Frequently importuned, he summoned Flavian to Constantinople and commanded him to proceed to Rome. But Flavian, pleading the winter season and promising that he would do as commanded at the beginning of spring, returned to his own country. Thereupon, since not only the admirable Damasus, bishop of Rome, but also his successor Siricius, and Anastasius after Siricius, had sharply reproached the pious emperor, saying that he was crushing tyrants who rose against himself, but was allowing those who insulted the law of Christ to exercise tyrannical condemnation, he again summoned him to Constantinople and undertook to compel him to sail to Rome.”

8. Theodoret’s account is indeed mistaken in many respects. Damasus died before the ordination of Evagrius, and the Emperor Theodosius did not live to see the time of Pope Anastasius. Moreover, Ambrose’s Letter 56 to Theophilus establishes that the case of Flavian and Evagrius was entrusted by the synod of Capua not to the bishop of Rome, but to Theophilus of Alexandria and the Egyptian bishops, “because, being joined in communion with neither party, they would incline through no partial favor.” Hence Theodoret is again corrected, since he represents the Egyptians as hostile to Flavian. Yet in what he says of imperial orders disregarded by Flavian, and of the leave which he obtained from Theodosius to return home, that writer agrees in some measure with Ambrose. Ambrose reports that Flavian refused either “to appear before the judges appointed by imperial decrees” or “to present himself at the assembly of bishops”; indeed, he says that Flavian “again had recourse to the help of entreaties and the support of imperial rescripts” (Ambrose, Letter 56, nos. 3–4).

We may therefore reasonably believe that it was then that Siricius, informed of Flavian’s various evasions, wrote to Theodosius the severe letter mentioned by Theodoret, asking him to compel Flavian to present himself not at Rome but at Alexandria before the appointed judges. Certainly, one who refused, even when asked, to pronounce his own judgment concerning Bonosus, because the synod of Capua had entrusted that matter to those who asked him, was far from arrogating to himself the hearing of a cause committed by the same synod to the bishops of Egypt. Indeed Ambrose, who had attended the synod of Capua and shared in everything transacted in this affair, urges Theophilus not to refer the case entrusted to him back to the Roman bishop, but himself to meet with Flavian and, “if he persists in thinking that he ought not to come” (*ibid.*, nos. 6–7), to deliver such a judgment as will not displease the bishop of the Roman church, to whom Ambrose considers that judgment should be referred.

[Col. 1123B]

9. If, therefore, we compare Ambrose’s writings with Theodoret’s statements, we learn from them that the case of Flavian and Evagrius was brought before the council of Capua; that there it was decided that, peace having been granted to each side, Theophilus and the Egyptian bishops should determine—to the preservation of the decrees of the Nicene synod—to which claimant the bishopric of Antioch ought to be adjudged; and that Flavian, refusing altogether to abide by this decree of the council of Capua, evaded ecclesiastical judgment and again sought imperial rescripts. Hence Siricius was under a certain necessity to intervene against Flavian’s efforts. This accounts for the severe letters mentioned by Theodoret to Theodosius, which we may reasonably judge to have been written not long after the synod of Capua, and therefore in the year 392.

VIII.

[Col. 1123C]

10. About the year 396. Letters of Theophilus against Epiphanius. —Palladius, *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*, ch. 15, pp. 150–151, charges Theophilus of Alexandria with inconsistency in the following manner: “He who had reproached blessed Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, who presided over the Church for thirty-six years, as a heretic or schismatic under Damasus or blessed Siricius, later, in his letter to Pope Innocent criticizing blessed John, calls Epiphanius most holy.” If he refers here to a letter written by Theophilus to Damasus or Siricius, although it may seem uncertain to which of the two this letter is to be attributed, it is nevertheless not uncertain that it can apply to Siricius alone, since the controversy between Theophilus and Epiphanius began only under that pontiff. Socrates, book IV, ch. 7, and Sozomen, book VIII, ch. 14, explain of what heresy Epiphanius was accused: they report that Theophilus denounced him as an Anthropomorphite.

IX.

11. About the same time. Letters of Epiphanius to Siricius. —Letters of Epiphanius himself, bishop of Salamis, to Pope Siricius against John of Jerusalem are more than once cited by Jerome. At the end of what was formerly Letter 61, now 38, Jerome speaks thus: “There are several letters of Epiphanius at hand: one to John himself, others to the bishops of Palestine, and recently one to the pontiff of the city of Rome, in which he says that, although he accused John of Jerusalem before many witnesses, he did not deserve a response.” Earlier in the same letter Jerome demonstrates the emptiness of John’s boast that Epiphanius had admired his words and declared them Catholic, in these terms: “The letters of Epiphanius to Pope Siricius prove it; if you read them, you will see how he admired your statements and declared them Catholic.”

For in some assembly, when John had spoken beforehand against the Anthropomorphites, Epiphanius, taking up and pursuing his address, had said: “What our brother has spoken before the assembly—my son in age—against the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, he has spoken well and faithfully; I too condemn it with my voice. But it is fitting that, just as we condemn this heresy, so also we condemn the perverse doctrines of Origen.” It is therefore clear that Epiphanius approved what John had set forth against the Anthropomorphites in such a manner that he wished the perverse doctrines of Origen to be condemned by him on the same principle. Indeed, because John delayed to condemn them, Epiphanius “openly called him a heretic in letters sent abroad, and charged him with eight heads of questions concerning the hope of Christian faith,” which Jerome expounds in the same Letter 39, and which perhaps were touched upon in the aforementioned letter of Epiphanius to Siricius. These letters seem to be dated both after 394, when the disagreement between Epiphanius and John began, and nearer to that part of 396 in which John sent Theophilus his defense.

X.

[Col. 1124C]

12. In the year 397. Letter of the Africans to Siricius. —On 28 August 397, the Africans, assembled at a council in Carthage, decreed in canon 28: “Concerning the Donatists, it seemed good that we should consult our brothers and fellow bishops, Siricius and Simplicianus, concerning only those infants baptized among them, lest the error of their parents—an error which they did not commit by their own judgment—should hinder them, when they have been converted to the Church of God with a saving purpose, from being advanced as ministers of the sacred altar.” This canon was inserted into the *Code of Canons of the African Church*, ch. 47.

13. Reply of Siricius to the Africans. —From the same Code, ch. 56, we infer that Siricius, together with Venerius, responded to this consultation and denied what the Africans sought. There we read that the Africans, again at Carthage on 16 June 401, decreed that an embassy of an energetic bishop should be sent to Anastasius and Venerius, the successors of Siricius and Simplicianus, to set forth forcefully the needs of the African church and the extreme lack of clergy, and thus to obtain permission from them to advance into the clergy infants baptized among the Donatists. The following reason for this petition is then given: “For from those sees this had been forbidden.” That is, as no prudent person will deny, the matter had first been asked of Siricius and Venerius.

Paschasius Quesnel did not sufficiently consider this when, in Dissertation XV on the works of Leo, ch. 3, no. 6, he asserted: “It is certain that in Siricius’ time the Africans administered their churches according to the canons of their own synods, and did not permit laws of ecclesiastical discipline to be imposed upon them from overseas regions.” For it is clear here that they did permit such laws to be imposed upon them, and that they did not dare do anything contrary to them even under pressing necessity, unless with the consent of those who had imposed them.

14. Why the bishop of Milan is joined with Siricius in the aforesaid letters. —If the matters discussed in this paragraph are joined to those explained in the fourth and fifth, a question arises: whence came that agreement among the Gauls, Spaniards, and Africans by which they declare that they consult, follow, or await the judgment concerning ecclesiastical matters not only of the Roman bishops but also of the bishops of Milan? For we have heard that the Ithacians were received at the council of Turin in accordance with the letters of Ambrose of Milan and Siricius, bishop of the Roman church. Likewise, in the published acts of the First Council of Toledo, we read that peace was promised to the Priscillianists provided they fulfilled the conditions prescribed by Ambrose and Siricius. Finally, concerning infants baptized among the Donatists and to be promoted to the clergy, the Africans consult Siricius and Venerius, Ambrose’s successor; nor do they venture to undertake anything contrary to their judgment until the agreement of the same sees is obtained.

To state briefly what I think concerning this: perhaps this happened because Siricius was accustomed to consult Ambrose concerning ecclesiastical affairs and to send Ambrose’s letters together with his own to the churches; those churches subsequently began to write not to Siricius only, but also to Ambrose, and became accustomed to regard Ambrose’s successors as holding the same position. Or rather, this deference was secured for Ambrose and his successors by the emperors’ residence in the city of Milan, from which the authority of the bishops of that city began to increase considerably. Certainly, from the fact that the Africans, when sending an embassy to the emperors, write, “Letters are also to be sent to the bishop of the Roman church for the recommendation of the envoys, or to others wherever the Emperor may be” (*Code of Canons of the African Church*, ch. 93), the custom then prevailing is not obscure.

XI.

15. In the year 398. Siricius’ courteous letter to Rufinus. [Col. 1125D] —Having heard of the reputation of the presbyter Rufinus, Siricius sent him an honorable letter, earnestly requesting that he remain at Rome and adorn the city by his presence. Rufinus was accustomed to set this letter against another, less favorable one which Siricius’ successor Anastasius later wrote concerning him. Accordingly Jerome, *Apology*, book III, addresses him thus, as he calls Anastasius’ letter into question: “Whether it was written by him or not written, you declare that it does not concern you; you who, out of love for your little town, scorned the testimony of his predecessor, beseeching you to come to Rome that you might adorn it by your presence.” And after a few intervening words: “You produce a letter of Siricius, who sleeps in the Lord, and despise the words of Anastasius, who is alive.”

XII.

[Col. 1126A]

16. Other letters of communion to the same man or to his associates. —About the same time, either Rufinus or his associates, who approved the book *On First Principles* (*Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) of Origen, recently rendered into Latin by Rufinus, obtained letters of communion from Siricius. Jerome notes this in Letter 16 to Principia: “Seeing that the heretics were kindling very great conflagrations from a small spark, and that the flame long laid beneath had now reached the rooftops, they request and obtain ecclesiastical letters from Siricius, so that they might appear to have departed from the City as communicants of the Church. Not much time intervened: an eminent man, Anastasius, succeeded to the pontificate, etc.”

17. In thus noting Siricius’ easiness of disposition, Jerome at the same time guarded against anyone suspecting him of having assented to heresy. He attributes the favor bestowed by Siricius upon Origen’s followers not to any inclination toward perverse doctrine but to simplicity, because Rufinus “was deceiving the simplicity of the Roman bishop, who judged others according to his own character.” Rufinus more easily obtained from Siricius letters full of kindness and goodwill for himself and his associates because, illustrious in reputation for virtue and learning, he had not yet acquired an evil name.

If Siricius is to be blamed in this matter, how much more blameworthy were Augustine and others who did not refuse similar letters to Pelagius when he was already suspected of heresy—letters which he abused at the Synod of Diospolis to remove from himself the charge of heresy! Christian simplicity does not readily turn to unfavorable suspicion, nor does it love to judge anyone harshly, especially someone concerning whom it finds in its mind nothing that would make it think ill. At times it even judges that something should be overlooked, so that by soothing the erring person through anticipatory acts of kindness it may draw him to the truth.

XIII.

18. Embassy carrying to Rome the decree of John’s ordination at Constantinople. —On 28 February 398 John was ordained bishop of the Church of Constantinople; thereafter an embassy was decreed to announce his ordination at Rome. This embassy may therefore be assigned to the time of Siricius, especially if that pope lived until November 398. It is not likely that John delayed until the next year to inform the Roman pontiff of his ordination. Palladius, *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*, ch. 4, p. 39, and ch. 6, pp. 50–51; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 23; and Sozomen, book VIII, ch. 3, mention this celebrated embassy. Although they confuse certain matters, especially Theodoret, they agree in reporting that Acacius, bishop of Beroea, was the leader of this embassy. Palladius speaks specifically of him at p. 39: “Who was more gray-haired, or more modest in appearance, than Acacius of Beroea . . . whose very nostrils had long gray hairs, when he came to Rome carrying the decree of the ordination of Bishop John?”

19. The same embassy reconciles Flavian of Antioch to the Roman pontiff. —Acacius was chosen not merely to carry the decree of John’s ordination, but also to reconcile Flavian, bishop of Antioch, to the Roman pontiff. For this purpose Theophilus of Alexandria, at John’s own request, joined to the embassy the venerable Isidore, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, formerly ordained by Athanasius. Sozomen recounts the matter as follows: “At the very beginning of his episcopate, while the Western and Egyptian bishops were still divided from the Eastern bishops on account of Paulinus, John requested Theophilus to lend him his assistance and reconcile the Roman bishop with Flavian. When this was approved, Acacius, bishop of Beroea, and Isidore were chosen for the business—the latter being the person on whose account Theophilus had opposed John’s ordination.”

Palladius, conversing in his *Dialogue* with Theodore, deacon of the Roman church, says of this same Isidore: “You yourself also know the man: when he came with Acacius, he brought communion between Flavian and Theophilus, broken off for twenty years on account of blessed Evagrius.” Nor should we pass over what Theodoret says concerning that embassy: “Flavian sent certain distinguished bishops to Rome together with several presbyters and deacons of the church of Antioch. The leader of them all was Acacius, bishop of the Syrian city of Beroea . . . Coming to Rome with the rest, he calmed the long-standing quarrel, which had lasted seventeen years, and established peace between the churches.”

Theodoret adds immediately: “At that time Innocent presided over the Roman church.” But, as Valesius observes, this quarrel had begun with Flavian’s ordination, which occurred in 381. It follows that, if it was calmed after seventeen years through the benefit of the aforementioned embassy, the embassy itself must be assigned to the year 398, and thus before Innocent presided over the Roman church. Theodoret therefore seems to confuse it with another event that occurred under Innocent. For the peace of the Antiochene church which began in 398 was completed and made full under Pope Innocent, when, after the death of Flavian and his successor Porphyry, Alexander also united to himself the Eustathians, who until then had refused to agree with the rest. It is clear from this that what the synod of Capua had decreed, and what Ambrose had specifically required of Theophilus, was carried out when, through Theophilus’ agency—although perhaps with no preceding judicial examination—the peace of the Antiochene church was so arranged that the Roman pontiff did not hesitate to ratify it.

XIV.

20. Pacifying letters of the Roman bishop to Flavian of Antioch. —“The pacifying letters to Flavian of Antioch must therefore be attributed either to Siricius or to his successor Anastasius.” Boniface I, Letter 15, no. 6, notes them in these words: “When the church of Antioch suffered for a long time, so that frequent journeys were made from there for this very reason, first under Meletius and afterward under Flavian, it is evident that the Apostolic See was consulted; and no one doubts that, after many actions taken by our church under its authority, Flavian received the favor of communion, of which he would have been deprived forever unless letters concerning this matter had issued from here.”

Then several Western bishops, imitating the Roman bishop—as Ambrose had foretold would occur (Letter 56, no. 7)—gave similar letters to the envoys of the Antiochene church. Sozomen, book VIII, ch. 3, merely indicates this generally when he says that Acacius, returning from Rome to Syria, brought Flavian pacifying letters from the Egyptians and Westerners.

## 2. Examination of certain decrees attributed to Pope Siricius in the *Liber Pontificalis*

1. Siricius’ constitution against all heresies. —Although the authority of the *Liber Pontificalis* is slight and questionable, both in many matters generally and in those which it reports to have been decreed by Roman pontiffs, what it attributes to Siricius should not be passed over in silence, especially because these matters are not wholly inconsistent either with his period or with his practice. First, we read concerning him in this book: “He made a constitution concerning the whole Church and against all heresies, and distributed it throughout the whole world and through all provinces, that it might be preserved in every church archive as a defense against all heresies.”

But these words seem merely to designate the preceding Letter 5, which, we suppose, was called “against all heresies” by a less accurate writer because he had read in its conclusion: “Therefore, brethren, if these things are observed by all with complete vigilance, ambition will cease, dissension will be quieted, heresies and schisms will not arise, and the devil will find no place for raging.”

[Col. 1128C]

2. *Fermentum* sent by the bishop to presbyters. —The same book adds: “He decreed that no presbyter should celebrate Masses throughout the whole week unless he received the consecrated portion designated by the bishop of the place, called the *fermentum*.” But that same book attributes the establishment of this practice to Melchiades; by now referring it to Siricius as well, it is shown to err against exact historical truth in more than one respect, as we observed above, pp. 339–340. What we noted there persuades us that the aforesaid practice is later than Siricius.

3. Manicheans banished. —The following statement, “He found Manicheans, whom he transported into exile,” contains nothing contrary to historical truth if the words “by the authority of Theodosius” are understood. For on 17 June 389 Theodosius decreed against those heretics “that they be expelled from the whole world indeed, but especially from this City” (*Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 5, law 18).

[Col. 1128D]

4. Manicheans not to receive communion with the faithful; converts to be tested in monasteries and to receive viaticum at the end of life. —To the same period may be referred what is subsequently recorded in the same book: “And he decreed that the Manicheans should not partake of communion with the faithful, because it was not lawful for them, with polluted mouths, to profane the holy body of the Lord. He also decreed that, if anyone converted from the Manicheans returned to the Church, he should by no means receive communion, but should remain subject to confinement in a monastery for the days of his life, so that, worn down by fasts and prayers and tested under every examination until the final day of his passing, the Church’s mercy might grant them viaticum.”

Two points should be noted here: first, the confinement of heretics in monasteries so that the sincerity of their conversion may be tested there; secondly, the postponement of sacred communion until the end of life. Siricius’ first letter, chs. 3, 5, and 6, proves that this latter measure was customary with him. Whether the former likewise belongs to his period—that is, whether in Siricius’ age it had become customary to confine heretics in monasteries—I leave others to investigate.

5.
