Finally, this last decree which the same book attributes to Siricius—“He decreed that heretics be received and reconciled under the imposition of hands in the presence of the whole Church”—seems to refer to what this pope answers in Letter 1, ch. 1, when consulted whether Arians ought to be rebaptized: “These, along with Novatians and other heretics, as established in the synod, we unite to the fellowship of Catholics by the sole invocation of the sevenfold Spirit and the imposition of a bishop’s hand.”

## 3. Other decrees incorrectly attributed to the same pope

1. In a certain manuscript written about seven hundred years ago, once belonging to Herovallius, then to Petit, and finally bequeathed by the will of that most distinguished man to our Germain Library, several chapters occur under ninety-two titles. They are excerpted, not always with the greatest fidelity, from various councils and letters of Roman pontiffs. Among them are inserted certain items as though from Pope Siricius’ letter to Genesius.

Specifically, under title 54 we read:

> “In the letter of Pope Siricius to Bishop Genesius, ch. XII. If a healthy man has taken a leprous wife, or if leprosy afterwards comes upon her, they should be separated, lest children conceived be contaminated by leprosy. For it is lawful that one who is clean be joined to one who is clean.”

Likewise under title 18:

> “In the letter of Pope Siricius to Bishop Genesius, ch. [read: chapter] XIII. A presbyter who says that he does not know whether the person who ordained him was a bishop, and who celebrated Masses for some time, but afterward, having abandoned his office, took a wife—who can doubt that this pseudo-presbyter is detestable? He must therefore be removed in every way and confined in a monastery for penance throughout the whole time of his life.”

[Col. 1129D]

And under title 23:

> “In the letter of holy Pope Siricius, HR [read: chapter] XIV. A presbyter who baptizes in wine in the nearest necessity [thus the manuscript here and below; Hardouin, however, reads ‘in the greatest necessity’], so that a sick person may not be endangered, is to be charged with no fault for such an act. But if water was available and no such necessity pressed, he is to be deprived of communion and subjected to penance; yet that infant, if baptized in the Holy Trinity, is to remain in that baptism.
>
> “HR [or chapter] XV. If, in the nearest necessity, he baptizes an infant in danger with a vessel or with his hands, and in the name of the Holy Trinity, it will remain valid, especially when necessity requires this.
>
> [Col. 1130A] “Concerning the presbyter who does not know the Lord’s Prayer. HR [or chapter] XVI. A presbyter who does not know the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, or the Psalms—if the person who blessed him was a bishop—must first of all lose the rank which he unlawfully presumed to assume, and live in a monastery under strict penance throughout the whole time of his life. But the infants whom he baptized in the Holy Trinity are to remain baptized.
>
> “HR [or chapter] XVII. Those, however, who baptize in this manner, saying, ‘In the name of the Father I immerse; in the name of the Son I immerse; and of the Holy Spirit I immerse’: those baptized in this manner, although rudely, have nevertheless been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity.”

7. John Hardouin notes, in his *Question concerning Baptism in Wine*, p. 35, that the same decrees occur in the same form in two other copies, namely the Pithoean and the Tours manuscripts. But they are nothing other than the responses of Pope Stephen II, IX, X, XI, XII, XIII, and XIV, published by Jacques Sirmond in vol. II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 16, from the manuscript of St Mary of Laon—responses truncated or altered with complete freedom by the person who excerpted them.

The reason why, in the compilation of the aforesaid unskilled collector, they came to be ascribed to Siricius was undoubtedly this: in Sirmond’s text, according to the Laon manuscript, Stephen II’s Response VIII immediately precedes them, expressed in these words:

> “Concerning a woman who, after her husband’s death, had worn the veil for some time and afterwards takes a husband: in the letter of Pope Siricius addressed to Bishop Himerius of Tarragona, ch. 5, the following is contained: ‘Concerning those who, having done penance, return like dogs and swine to their former vomit and wallowings, and to the belt of military service, etc.,’”

up to these words:

> “We judge that this rule must also be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves to such defilements.”

Immediately afterward follows:

> “Therefore, in accordance with the judgment of this venerable man, we decree that the same woman, who has been joined in such a wicked marriage after casting off the monastic habit, and has not persevered in what she promised to God, be sent without delay to a monastery, in order that she may end her life there in her penance.”

These words are immediately followed by “If a healthy man has taken a leprous wife,” and the remainder cited above. Since Stephen customarily supports his responses by some authority, and fortifies the first with the testimony of Pope Leo, the fifth and sixth with that of Innocent, the seventh with that of the Council of Chalcedon, the eighth with that of Siricius, the fifteenth with that of the Synod of Antioch, the sixteenth with that of Carthage, the seventeenth with that of Neocaesarea, and the nineteenth again with that of Pope Leo, the imprudent compiler imagined that chapters set forth with no cited author were expressed from the judgment of the same person whose testimony had just been cited.

He therefore concluded that Responses IX, X, XI, XII, XIII, and XIV, which follow Response VIII and lack any supporting authority, belonged wholly to the same Siricius from whose judgment and expressly quoted words Response VIII had been composed. Nor should it move us that he cites them not from the letter to Himerius but from a letter to Genesius. Through corruption of the word *Himerium*, an inattentive copyist could easily have produced *Genesium*, especially since in many manuscripts the letters *r* and *s* have the same form. Hence it is not surprising that *nerium* and *nesium* should be confused. The copyist, therefore, reading *e* for *i* and for the first stroke of the letter *m*, and omitting the letter *H*, as often happens, had *Jenesium*, and thence *Genesium*.

8. Whether those responses suit Stephen II is not the matter at issue here. We merely observe that Siricius’ judgment “concerning those who, having performed penance, again sought the belt of military service, theatrical spectacles, new marriages, and unlawful sexual unions” is applied to the woman “who, after her husband’s death, had worn the veil for some time and afterward took a husband,” because Siricius intends what he declares concerning men to be understood also of women who sin in like manner. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that the kind of offense concerning which Siricius gives judgment differs from that proposed to Stephen II.

[Col. 1131]

# LETTERS AND DECREES OF SAINT POPE SIRICIUS

(*Constant, Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, col. 623.) (C, G, S)

## LETTER

> [Note: [Col. 1131C] It is found in all ancient collections of canons. It is cited by Innocent I, Letter 6 to Exsuperius, no. 2; by the Council of Agde, canon 9; by Pope John II in his letter to Caesarius; by Cresconius in the *Canonical Breviary*; and by other later collectors of canons. It is also mentioned by Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 3. Dionysius Exiguus divided it into fifteen chapters, prefixing the same number of titles; in most copies of the letter these titles are placed both together at the beginning of the letter and separately before their respective chapters. We retain those titles, supplying in square brackets what is somewhat lacking for clarity. The division is no different in the canon-law manuscript published by Quesnel, as is evident also from its prefatory Index, where it is entitled, “Letter of Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, responding to fifteen chapters,” although at the head of the letter itself it is marked, “Letter of Siricius, etc., under sixteen titles.” For the instruction directing Himerius to make known to the other bishops the replies to the fifteen chapters is given the name of a sixteenth title. Although this is the first surviving decretal letter in which Roman bishops answer consultations from various churches, it is not the first written for that purpose. Jerome would not have mentioned, in his letter to Ageruchia, that he assisted Damasus in replies to consultations from East and West, unless this practice had previously been received.]  

# I. POPE SIRICIUS TO HIMERIUS, BISHOP OF TARRAGONA

[Col. 1131B]

I. Concerning Arians [the Spanish collection adds: “by Catholics”] not to be rebaptized. —II. That baptism is not to be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost, save in necessity. —III. Concerning apostates [the Spanish collection adds: “to be separated from the Church”]. —IV. That it is not lawful to take another’s betrothed woman in marriage. —V. Concerning those who have in no way observed [the Spanish collection adds: “the penance undertaken”]. —VI. Concerning monks and virgins who do not keep their profession. —VII. Concerning incontinent clerics [Spanish collection: “concerning ministers”]. —VIII. What sort of persons ought to attain the office of the clergy. —IX. Concerning the conduct of clerics, or the age at which they are to be promoted. —X. Concerning elderly persons [Spanish collection: “concerning those who turn to sacred service in old age”]. —XI. That a cleric who takes a second wife is to be deposed [Spanish collection: “concerning clerics who enter second marriages, that they are to be deposed”]. —XII. What women ought to live with clerics. —XIII. Concerning the promotion of monks [Spanish collection: “concerning their proposal for the clergy”]. —XIV. That a penitent is not to become a cleric [Spanish collection: “that clerics are not to receive penance through the imposition of a priest’s hand”]. —XV. That, if through ignorance penitents, bigamists, or husbands of widows have become clerics, they are not to be promoted further [Spanish collection: “concerning penitents, bigamists, and husbands of widows, that they are not to be permitted admission to clerical order”].

SIRICIUS [Note: [Col. 1132D] Merlin: “to Cumerius.” One manuscript: “to Hiemerius.” Another: “Hiero.” Gerundensis: “to Eumerius.” In an ancient Corbie manuscript, the letter *m* in the word *Himerio* has a transverse stroke.] TO HIMERIUS, bishop of Tarragona [Note: [Col. 1132D] Dionysius here added “greetings,” which was retained by those who followed his collection.].

1. Siricius duly announces his ordination; his concern, and the assistance he receives from Peter. —The report of your brotherhood, sent to our predecessor Damasus of holy memory, found me already established in his see, because the Lord so ordained. When we carefully read it in the assembly of the brethren, we found as many things worthy of censure and correction as we should have wished to find deserving of praise.

Since we necessarily had to succeed to the labors and concerns of him to whom by God’s grace we succeeded in honor, after first giving the due notice of my elevation, we do not refuse to give a fitting response to each of your inquiries, insofar as the Lord has deigned to inspire us. [Note: In the printed editions, except Merlin’s, *pro* is prefixed here; it is absent from the manuscripts.] For, in view of our office, we have neither the right to conceal nor the liberty to keep silent—upon us especially rests a zeal for the Christian religion greater than upon all others. We bear the burdens of all who are burdened; indeed, blessed Apostle Peter bears these burdens in us—he who, as we trust, protects and defends us in all things as heirs of his administration.

## Chapter I—2. Decrees of Liberius. The manner of receiving heretics into the Church.

Thus, at the head of your letter, you indicated that very many persons baptized by the impious Arians are hastening to the Catholic faith, and that some of our brethren wish to baptize those same persons again [Note: In one manuscript *velle* (“wish”) is lacking. In the Regius, however, there stands: “or that it is not lawful to wish this,” whereas *cum hoc* is found.]. This is not lawful, since both the Apostle forbids it (Eph. 4:5), and the canons oppose it; and, after the Council of Rimini had been annulled, the general decrees sent to the provinces by my predecessor Liberius, of venerable memory, prohibit it. In accordance with what was established in the synod, we admit them, together with Novatians and other heretics, to fellowship with the assembly of Catholics by the invocation alone of the sevenfold Spirit and the imposition of a bishop’s hand [Note: At the Council of Nicaea, here referred to simply as “the synod,” the text reads ὥστε χειροθετουμένους, “so that they receive the laying-on of hands.” The old translator, followed by Pseudo-Isidore, seems to have read ὥστε χειροτονουμένους, which he rendered in Latin, “that they be ordained.” But Siricius’s words here make clear that, with Dionysius Exiguus, “receiving the imposition of hands” is to be preferred. The same interpretation is confirmed by Innocent I, Letter 16, no. 10, where he cites and reproduces the Nicene canon in full. Even before the Council of Nicaea, it was customary to receive heretics baptized in the name of the Trinity by imposition of hands; see above, pp. 227 ff., in the Dissertation on Stephen I’s judgment concerning the reception of heretics. There, especially on pp. 241–42, we showed the agreement of these words of Siricius with ancient writings and with the ancient blessing to be pronounced over those returning from heresy. We also indicated [Col. 1133C] the distinction between this imposition of hands and the sacrament of Confirmation, while not denying that similar modes of expression may have led some to understand the imposition of hands prescribed for returning heretics as the sacrament of Confirmation. Pseudo-Isidore indeed appears to have understood it so in the statements which he published as though excerpted from the synodal acts of Pope St. Sylvester. He says: “He established that an Arian priest who came to his senses should not be received unless the bishop of that place reconciled him and confirmed him with the grace of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be conferred by heretics, through the sacred chrism and the imposition of the bishop’s hand.”]; and this practice is observed by the whole East and West. From this course you also ought by no means henceforth to depart, if you do not wish to be separated from our synodal fellowship by judgment.

## Chapter II—3. Times and rites for receiving baptism. Those to whom baptism must be given at once.

There follows, moreover, a blameworthy and corrigible confusion concerning the candidates for baptism, according to each person’s preference [Note: The old collection of Hadrian: “There follows concerning the different times for baptizing, according to …” Pseudo-Isidore: “There follows concerning the different times for baptizing, according to …”; this latter form was preferred in the Roman edition and in the collections of councils. We restore the more genuine reading from manuscripts of Dionysius and others of better authority.], which, as we say with distress, is presumed by our fellow bishops not on the ground of any authoritative rule but through mere rashness (De Consecratione, distinction 4, canon 11): namely, that everywhere and freely, at the Nativity of Christ or the Apparition [Epiphany], and likewise on feasts of Apostles or martyrs, countless multitudes, as you assert, receive the mystery of baptism [Note: One manuscript has *episcopi* (“of the bishop”) in place of *Christi*. Moreover, the term “Apparition” denotes the feast which we still call, with the Greeks, Epiphany.]. Yet the Lord’s Pascha, especially together with its Pentecost, claims this privilege for itself both among us and in all churches [Note: Dionysius, Hadrian, and older manuscripts read “together with its Pentecost.” Tertullian expressly attests, in *On Baptism*, chapter 19, that these two days had from the earliest centuries of the Church been consecrated to the solemn administration of baptism: “Easter provides a more solemn day for baptism … After it, Pentecost affords the widest space for administering the laver.” In order that this custom might remain unviolated, not only the supreme pontiffs Siricius, Leo, Gelasius, and others, but also very many councils laboured; nevertheless, they could not prevent its repeated violation and the solemn administration of baptism in different regions on principal feasts.

Gregory’s testimony concerning the Nativity of the Lord is particularly clear. Writing to Eulogius, Indiction 1, Book VIII, Letter 30, he says: “At the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, which occurred in this first Indiction, more than [a number omitted in the supplied text] thousand English people were reported to me as baptized by that brother and fellow bishop of ours [Augustine].” Avitus, bishop of Vienne, records in his letter to King Clovis himself that Clovis was solemnly regenerated on that same day. That this custom was received in Gaul appears from Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 69 and 76, and *History of the Franks*, Book VIII, chapter 9. This final passage of Gregory of Tours also suggests the same conclusion concerning the birthday of St. John the Baptist.

There are many ancient testimonies for Epiphany. The Sicilians especially liked to be baptized on that day—a practice reproved by Leo, Letter 18, nos. 2 and 9. Gregory of Nyssa delivered his address to candidates for baptism on that very day. Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 40; John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 214; and Ratherius of Verona, Sermon I on Lent, confirm the same custom. Indeed, Gregory Nazianzen in the aforementioned Oration 40 strongly maintains that baptism may be received on any day and should not be postponed, explicitly refuting those who say: “I am waiting for the day of Lights [that is, Epiphany]; I value the feast of Pascha more; I shall wait for Pentecost.” It is better, he says, to be baptized with Christ on Epiphany, to return with Christ to life on the day of resurrection, and to honour the coming of the Spirit.

Sozomen, Book II, chapter 26, after recounting the dedication of the Jerusalem church under Constantine the Great, immediately adds: “From that time the church of Jerusalem has celebrated an annual solemn festival with great splendour, so much so that the sacraments of baptism also are celebrated on that day.” From this it may be inferred that baptism was also conferred on the anniversary of a dedication, indeed on any most solemn day, so that its administration belonged to the festal celebration. Finally, after Siricius, Leo bears witness in Letter 156, to the bishops established throughout Campania, Samnium, and Picenum, that many sought baptism on the feast-days of individual martyrs. The Second Council of Mâcon, held in 585, likewise complains in canon 3 that Christians, neglecting the lawful day of baptism, baptized their children almost every day and on the birthdays of martyrs, so that scarcely two or three were found at holy Pascha who were regenerated through water and the Spirit.

It should nevertheless be noted that Siricius claims this privilege for the days of Pascha and Pentecost not absolutely but especially. “Besides,” says Tertullian in *On Baptism*, chapter 19, “every hour and every time is suitable for baptism: if there is a difference as to solemnity, there is none as to grace.” Augustine likewise teaches in Sermon 210, part 2, that baptism may be received on every day. Then, adding that a larger multitude gathers for baptism on Easter Day, drawn not by a more abundant grace but by greater solemnity, he indicates that baptism was in fact customarily received on other days also [Col. 1135B]. Although the grace of baptism, whenever received, is in itself equal, the mysteries celebrated on Pascha and Pentecost more expressly portray baptismal grace, and are in themselves certain lessons concerning what is either done in the baptized or ought to be done by them. Hence the rites with which those two feasts are customarily celebrated contribute not a little both to instructing or strengthening faith and to shaping morals.

Moreover, the first fathers of the churches were persuaded how important it was that no one should approach the grace of baptism without suitable preparation, and therefore only after those days appointed for more diligent preparation of souls—as Siricius immediately teaches in explicit words. Accordingly, when Gregory I heard that very many Jews were flocking to the Christian faith, he adopted this moderation: he allowed them to be baptized outside the Paschal season, after first imposing forty days’ penance. Thus he wrote concerning them, in Indiction 1, in May, to Fantinus the defender: “If, however, it seems long or burdensome to them to wait for the Paschal solemnity, and you know that they are now hastening to baptism, then—lest, God forbid, a long delay should turn their minds back—speak with our brother, the bishop of that place, so that, after penance and abstinence have been imposed for forty days, he may baptize them, protected by the mercy of almighty God, either on Sunday or, should some particularly celebrated feast occur, on that feast-day.”].

Therefore Pascha with its Pentecost is to be maintained as possessing this special privilege; on those days alone in the year, for all who flock to the faith, the general sacraments of baptism ought to be administered—only to those chosen persons who have enrolled their names forty days or more beforehand and have been purified by exorcisms, daily prayers, and fasts. Thus may that apostolic command be fulfilled (1 Cor. 5:7): “When the old leaven has been purged out, a new batch may begin to exist.”

Accordingly, just as we say that reverence for the sacred Pascha ought in no respect to be diminished [Note: Quesnel, with three Colbert manuscripts and one Pithoean manuscript, omits *sacram*, “sacred.”], so we wish that aid be given with all speed, through the sacred water of baptism, to infants who cannot yet speak because of their age, or to those who in any necessity require it. Otherwise, if the saving font is withheld from those who desire it, each person departing from the world may lose both the kingdom and life, to the ruin of our souls.

Likewise, whoever falls into danger of shipwreck, invasion by enemies, the uncertainty of siege, or the desperation of any bodily illness [Note: In Merlin, as in the manuscripts, “the desperation of illness.” It would have been expressed more clearly: “any bodily illness that is despaired of.” Until the end of the eleventh century, many supreme pontiffs, councils, bishops, and kings took care that baptism should not be administered outside Pascha and Pentecost; yet none of their decrees failed to admit an exception of this kind.], and seeks help in the one aid of faith, shall receive the benefits of the regeneration he seeks at the very moment at which he asks for them.

Let the error hitherto committed in this matter suffice. Now let all priests keep the aforesaid rule, if they do not wish to be torn away from the solidity of the apostolic rock upon which Christ built the universal Church (Matt. 16:18).

## Chapter III—4. Apostates are to be cut off from Christ’s body, but pardon at the end of life must not be denied to the penitent.

It was also added that some Christians have passed over into apostasy—an abomination even to name—and have been profaned by the worship of idols and the defilement of sacrifices. We order that they be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, by which they had formerly been redeemed through rebirth [Note: Four manuscripts read *quod dudum* (“which formerly”), through a not uncommon scribal lapse, especially among those taking down the words of a speaker, who readily add a letter where words of similar sound meet. But far more and better manuscripts, with the editions, have *quo dudum* (“by which formerly”). Accordingly, both the author of the Spanish collection and Pseudo-Isidore must be corrected, since they summarize this chapter, contrary to Siricius’s intention, as “Concerning apostates to be cut off from the Church.” For if Siricius had said only “from the body of Christ,” it might reasonably be supposed that he meant cutting off from the Church; but since he adds “and the blood by which they had been redeemed,” he should be understood to speak only of the Eucharist. In this Eucharist, it should be noted, he does not hesitate to say that the blood by which we were redeemed, and whose fruit we receive in being reborn, is offered to us. To those, however, to whom he afterwards grants the grace of reconciliation at the end of life, he should rightly be held to grant what he had previously denied: namely, participation in the Eucharist.].

But if at some time they repent and turn to lamentation, they must perform penance as long as they live, and at their final end the grace of reconciliation is to be granted them. For, as the Lord teaches, we do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he may turn and live (Ezek. 18:23) [Note: Thus the manuscripts, except that three have merely “that he may return.” The Roman edition and collections of councils read, “but that he may be converted.”].

## Chapter IV—5. No one may take another’s betrothed woman as wife.

You have also asked concerning marital veiling [Note: Merlin and Crabbe read “prohibition”; later editions of the councils, with the Roman edition, read “violation,” against the manuscripts. In two manuscripts *nuptae*, “married woman,” occurs in place of *nupturae*, “a woman about to marry,” and in one *nupturis … violentur*, “may be violated by those about to marry.” What Siricius means by *desponsata*, “betrothed woman,” is not entirely clear. In Gratian, 27, question 2, canon 12, the gloss on a similar decree attributed to Gregory distinguishes a betrothed woman from a wife in that the former has not been carnally known, whereas the latter has. Yet Jerome, at the beginning of Book I against Jovinian, proves that even a woman not carnally known is sometimes called a wife.

In accordance with our own custom, Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 11, understands a betrothed woman as one initiated by betrothal but not yet bound to a man by the ceremonies of marriage; he teaches that the veil is bestowed at the actual ceremonies of betrothal. First he says: “Betrothed women indeed have the example of Rebecca, who, when unknown, was led to an unknown bridegroom”; and immediately adds: “But if they are veiled at betrothal.” Yet Siricius here speaks of the marital veiling to which priestly blessing was attached. Later, in Letter 5, no. 3, he testifies that priests attend marriages and give the veil to those marrying; and Ambrose says, Letter 19 to Vigilius, no. 17: “Marriage itself ought to be sanctified by the priestly veil and blessing.” Therefore nothing prevents us from understanding a *desponsata* here as one sanctified by priestly veil and blessing, and from interpreting Siricius’s phrase, “the blessing which the priest lays upon the woman about to marry,” in the sense of Ambrose’s statement in *Exhortation to Virginity*, chapter 6, no. 1: “Clouds, therefore, are those heavy clouds which have married … Finally, they are covered as clouds when they receive the veils of women about to marry.” The plain sense of Siricius’s words, however, requires rather that these matters be understood of the first pledge of betrothal, by which the Fathers prove from the Gospel that even a virgin may be called a spouse.]: whether a man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to another (27, question 2, canon 50). We forbid this by every means, lest it occur. For the blessing which the priest lays upon a woman about to marry is, among the faithful, akin to a sacrilege if violated by any transgression.

## Chapter V—6. Rules concerning penitents.

Concerning those who, after performing penance, return like dogs and swine to their former vomit and wallowing-place [Note: Quesnel alone reads “to vomit and wallowing-places.” Both here and in canon 12 of the Council of Nicaea, the distinguished Claude Fleury attempts, under the year 826, p. 355, to prove that military service and the other matters listed here are forbidden only during the actual course of penance. His opinion is supported not only by the cited Nicene canon 12 but also by canon 8 of the First Council of Tours, composed after the model of these words of Siricius. Canon 3 of Vannes, canon 11 of the First Council of Orléans, Dionysius Exiguus, and Pseudo-Isidore in their summaries of this chapter also favour it.

Yet the compiler who summarized this chapter in the old Colbert manuscript 3368, in agreement with Pithoeanus, understood Siricius differently: “Those who, AFTER PENANCE HAS BEEN PERFORMED, return like dogs to their vomit.” This is indeed the sense of Siricius’s own words. He speaks of men who “have performed penance,” not of those said to be “performing penance”; he rebukes their incontinence from children begotten not during the course of penance itself but after absolution, when they no longer have recourse to penance. He also speaks of women who have bound themselves to similar pollutions after penance, not during its performance [Col. 1138C]. Moreover, this may be gathered from Leo, Letter 2 to Rusticus, queries 10, 11, 12, and 13: persons who have once professed penance were subject to the same regulations concerning military service, marriages, and so forth, whether during or after penance.], your belovedness rightly believed that the apostolic see should be consulted (33, question 2, canon 12; Ivo, part 13, canon 17). They have again sought the soldier’s belt, theatrical pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden sexual relations; and children begotten after absolution have revealed their professed lack of self-control.

Because they now have no recourse to perform penance, we have judged that the following must be decreed concerning them: they are to be joined with the faithful in the Church only in prayer; they are to be present at the sacred celebration of the mysteries, though they do not deserve it; but they are to be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table. Thus, corrected at least by this strict discipline [Note: An older Corbie manuscript reads “distinction.”], they may themselves chastise their errors within themselves and provide an example to others, so that they may be drawn back from shameful desires.

Yet because they fell through the weakness of the flesh, we wish them, when they begin to depart to the Lord, to be strengthened by the gift of viaticum through the grace of communion. We judge that the same rule is to be observed concerning women who after penance have bound themselves to such defilements (Pope Zachary, Letter 7, chapter 36).

## Chapter VI—7. Monks or nuns who violate their resolution of chastity are to be punished.

[Note: In the cited Colbert manuscript 3368, with which Pithoeanus agrees, the following summary is prefixed to this chapter: “If monks or nuns marry.” Another Colbert manuscript has: “Concerning the fall of monks or nuns.”]

Furthermore, you report that certain monks and nuns, having cast aside their resolution of holiness, have sunk into such wantonness that at first, secretly and as though under the pretext of monasteries, they joined themselves in unlawful and sacrilegious defilement [Col. 1137C]. Afterwards, driven by despair of conscience into open abandonment, they freely begot children from unlawful embraces. Both public laws and ecclesiastical laws condemn this.

We therefore command that these shameless and detestable persons be removed from the company of monasteries and the assemblies of churches, so that, shut up in their own houses of confinement, they may lament such a great crime without ceasing and be purified by the cleansing fire of penance. Thus, at least at death, pardon may come to their aid through the grace of communion, solely in view of mercy.

## Chapter VII—8. Incontinence of clerics.

Let us now come to the most sacred orders of clerics, which, to the injury of venerable religion, we find—according to your charitable report—so trampled down and thrown into disorder throughout your provinces [Note: Two Colbert manuscripts read “trampled-down canons.” For this reading to be admissible, “by whom” would first have to be substituted for “which.”] that we must speak in the words of Jeremiah: “Who will give water to my head, or a fountain of tears to my eyes? And I shall weep for this people day and night” (Jer. 9:1).

If, then, the blessed Prophet said that tears could not suffice him for mourning the sins of the people, with how great a sorrow may we be struck when we are compelled to lament the crimes of those who belong to our body—especially we upon whom, according to blessed Paul, the daily pressure and unceasing care of all the churches rests. “For who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

For we have learned that very many priests of Christ and Levites, after long periods since their consecration, have begotten offspring both by their own wives and even by shameful intercourse (Distinction 82, canon 3; Ivo, part 6, canon 50), and defend their crime by this pretext [Note: Older manuscripts read *perscriptione*, “prescription” or “pretext.” Siricius appears here to censure persons also noted by Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book I, chapter 50, no. 258: “I have not passed this over because in many more remote places, while they discharged the ministry [that is, the diaconate], or even the priesthood, they begot children; and they defend this as an old custom, when sacrifice was offered at intervals of days.” See by what reasoning he refutes them.]: that in the Old Testament priests and ministers are said to have been granted the liberty of procreation.

### 9. The authority of the Old Testament is pleaded in vain.

Let any follower of lust and teacher of vices tell me now: if he thinks that in the Law of Moses the reins of sensuality were everywhere relaxed by the Lord for sacred orders, why does God warn those entrusted with the Holy of Holies, saying: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 20:7) [Col. 1138C]? Why were the priests also commanded to live in the temple, far from their homes, during the year of their course? Clearly, this was so that they could not have carnal intercourse even with their wives, and so, shining with integrity of conscience, might offer an acceptable gift to God.

When their period of service was completed, the use of wives was relaxed solely for the purpose of succession, because no one except one from the tribe of Levi had been commanded to be admitted to God’s ministry.

### 10. Priests and deacons are bound by an indissoluble law of continence.

Therefore, after the Lord Jesus had enlightened us by his coming, he declares in the Gospel that he came to fulfill the Law, not to abolish it. Accordingly, he wished the Church’s form of chastity, of which he is the bridegroom, to shine with splendour (Matt. 5:27) [Note: The Roman edition and collections of councils read, “the Church whose bridegroom is beautiful in form”; this is corrected from Quesnel and the manuscripts.], so that, when he comes again on the day of judgment, he may find her without spot or wrinkle, as he established through his Apostle (Eph. 5:27).

By these ordinances all priests and Levites are bound with an indissoluble law: from the day of our ordination, we must devote both our hearts and our bodies to sobriety and chastity, so that in all these sacrifices which we offer daily we may please our God [Note: An older Corbie manuscript reads, “our bodies, so that in these things we may please the Lord our God.” Peter de Marca considers that the first law and obligation of continence binding bishops, presbyters, and deacons in the West began with this decree of Siricius and the subsequent decree of the African council. Yet he does not deny that these three grades had long before been bound to that discipline by the custom of the universal Church. He cites as witnesses to the custom Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book I, chapter 9; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 59.4; Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book I, final chapter; Jerome, Book I against Jovinian; and elsewhere.

Accordingly, he understands the statement of the African bishops at the Second Council of Carthage in 390, canon 2—“When in the previous council the rule of continence and chastity was discussed, these three grades were bound by a certain written obligation of chastity in connection with their consecrations … so that what the Apostles taught and antiquity itself observed, we too may keep”—to mean that they suitably extended, by an interpretation drawn from practice and custom, the continence and chastity prescribed by the Apostle for bishops to the form of continence which they required of the higher clergy.

He himself draws this distinction between law and custom: custom, when violated, punishes offenders with shame; law deprives the obstinate of their grades. Yet it will be difficult to persuade anyone that such a custom, unless established either by enacted law or apostolic tradition, could have had such force that no example may be found in the West of bishops, presbyters, or deacons permitted to depart from it with impunity.

At the end of the mixed Questions on both Testaments, printed in the appendix to Part I of Volume III of Augustine and attributed by many to Hilary the deacon, an adherent of the Luciferians’ schism, p. 142, the author asks himself: “If marriage is lawful and good, why are priests not allowed to have wives—that is, why are those already ordained not allowed to have intercourse?” He answers: “Who does not know that each thing has its own law?” He then immediately adds: “And not only is intercourse forbidden to this man [the priest], but even to his minister, that is, to the deacon.”

Jovinian confirms that this was not said of a rule based on mere custom. For this enemy of continence, in Jerome’s Book I against him, is compelled to acknowledge that a man who fathers children while a bishop cannot be a bishop; otherwise, if caught, he is condemned not as a husband but as an adulterer. According to the opinion of the distinguished writer, he would merely have been put to shame, rather than condemned as an adulterer, had he sinned only against custom. But Jovinian acknowledges that he must be condemned, and condemned in such a way that he could no longer be bishop [Col. 1140B]. There seems no doubt that he there had in view what was practiced in the Church even before Siricius’s time.

The same must be said of Augustine’s observation, *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book II, final chapter, that clerics were very often compelled unexpectedly and by force to accept clerical rank, and that the law and necessity of continence was imposed upon them even against their will. Siricius himself punishes those who lament that they fell through ignorance not merely with shame but also with a penalty, since he forbids them any increase of rank. Indeed, he signifies that he was permitted to inflict a more severe penalty, since he declares that he is decreeing against them not what strict right demands but what mercy and indulgence recommend. Accordingly, he deprives of their ranks those who, sheltering behind the example of priests and Levites under the old Law, refused obedience.

Having thus voluntarily acknowledged that Siricius knew no decree of either his predecessors or councils commanding continence for the aforesaid grades [Col. 1140C], I should not without reason judge that he wished to vindicate not a mere custom but a law established by God and handed down by the Apostle. For he derives this law both from the Old Testament itself, in which priests are commanded, “Be holy,” and in which, during the year of their course, they were commanded to dwell far from their homes, and therefore from their wives, so that afterwards the use of wives was relaxed for the sole purpose of succession; from the will of the Lord, who came to fulfill and perfect the Law also in this matter; and, finally, from the institution of the Apostle, who declared this will of the Lord.

After setting out these matters, when he adds, “By these ordinances all priests and Levites are bound by an indissoluble law,” he indicates not that he is making a new law but that he is vindicating one enacted by God and the Lord and instituted by the Apostle. He further commends the necessity of this law on the ground that priests of the new covenant offer sacrifices to God daily, and therefore are commanded by divine law to preserve continence daily [Col. 1140D]. Finally, in Letter 5 sent to the Africans, when about to renew this same law and others, he declares that he is sending a letter not to impose any new commands, but to ensure the observance of matters neglected through some persons’ sloth and indifference, though they were established by apostolic and patristic ordinance. This decree of Siricius concerning the continence of the aforesaid grades is confirmed by the First Council of Toledo, chapter 1.].

“For those who are in the flesh,” says the vessel of election, “cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. 8:8–9). And where can God’s Spirit dwell, as we read, except in holy bodies?

### 11. Those who fell through ignorance retain their rank; others do not.

Since some of those of whom we speak, as your holiness reported, lament that they fell through ignorance (Distinction 82, canon 4; Ivo, part 6, canon 50), we say that mercy must not be denied them on this condition: that, without any increase of rank, they continue for as long as they live in the office in which they were discovered, provided that henceforth they endeavour to show themselves continent [Note: Two manuscripts read *opere*, “in work,” awkwardly. What Siricius establishes here is commanded to be followed by Innocent I, Letter 6 to Exsuperius, and by canon 9 of the Council of Agde. In agreement with these are the rulings of canon 8 of the Council of Turin, canon 24 of the First Council of Orange, and canon 2 of the First Council of Tours.].

But those who rely on the excuse of an unlawful privilege, claiming that this was allowed to them by the old Law, must know that by the authority of the apostolic see they have been deposed from every ecclesiastical rank which they have unworthily exercised. They can never touch the venerable mysteries, of which they have deprived themselves by longing after shameful desires.

And since present examples warn us to be on guard for the future, any bishop, presbyter, or deacon who, though we do not wish it, is hereafter found to be such, must understand that every avenue to indulgence has now been closed to him by us. For wounds that have not felt the healing of poultices must necessarily be cut out with iron.

## Chapter VIII—12. A twice-married man is not to be ordained priest or deacon.

We have also learned that men of unexamined life, even those who have had numerous marriages, freely and without restraint aspire to the aforesaid dignities, according to each one’s own pleasure [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads *libenter*, “willingly.” With the other witnesses, *licenter* should be retained, that is, “with impunity and without anyone opposing.” In the oldest Corbie manuscript the following summary is prefixed to this chapter: “Let the metropolitan be held accountable when someone has been unworthily ordained by him.”]. We attribute this not so much to those who attain these positions through excessive ambition [Note: Labbe reads, “who pervert these things by excessive ambition,” contrary to the other books.] as especially to metropolitan bishops, who, by conniving at forbidden audacities [Note: Quesnel reads “unlawful.” In the older Corbie manuscript: “who do not restrain forbidden impulses.”], so far as lies in them, despise the commands of our God.

And, not to mention what we suspect more deeply, where is that which our God established in the Law given through Moses, saying: “My priests shall marry once” (Lev. 21:13–14)? And elsewhere: “A priest shall take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not a divorced woman, not a prostitute” (Ezek. 44:22). Following this, the Apostle, transformed from persecutor into preacher, commanded that both priest and deacon should be the husband of one wife (1 Tim. 3:2).

All these requirements are treated with such contempt by the bishops of your regions as though they had been established rather for the opposite purpose. Since we must not neglect such usurpations, lest the just voice of the angered Lord rebuke us when he says: “You saw a thief and ran with him, and placed your portion with adulterers” (Ps. 49:18), we decree by a general pronouncement what henceforth must be followed and what avoided by all churches.

### Chapter IX.—13. The Age of Those to Be Ordained

[Note: The same manuscript gives the following summary of this chapter: “How long clerics ought to remain [in the grades] in order to attain the episcopate.” In Pithou and Colbert the following is prefixed to it: “Through how many grades an acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, or bishop is made.”]

Therefore, whoever from childhood devotes himself to the service of the Church ought, before the years of puberty, to be baptized and enrolled in the ministry of readers (Distinction 77, canon 3; Ivo, part 6, canons 91 and 92). When he reaches adolescence, he must remain an acolyte and subdeacon until his thirtieth year, provided that he has lived commendably and is content with one wife only—the one whom he received as a virgin by the common blessing through a priest. Afterwards he shall advance to the rank of deacon, if he has first proved himself worthy through the practice of continence. If there he ministers laudably for more than five years, he may fittingly attain the presbyterate. Thereafter, after ten years, he may obtain the episcopal chair, provided that throughout these periods the integrity of his life and faith has been approved.

[Note: The printed editions read, “who from the onset [*ab accessu*] of adolescence.” The preposition *ab* has been deleted on the authority of eleven better manuscripts. This onset of adolescence was reckoned at the twentieth year of age, as may be gathered both from Zosimus, Epistle 9 to Hesychius, chapter 3: “If he has given his name to ecclesiastical ministries from infancy, let him remain among the readers in uninterrupted observance until his twentieth year”; and from that Irish canon, book 1, chapter 9, in the *Spicilegium*, vol. IX: “But a boy dedicated from infancy to ecclesiastical ministries shall remain a reader or exorcist until the twentieth year of his age.”]

[Note: Emperor Justinian indeed prohibited, in Novella 123, the ordination of readers before their eighteenth year; but earlier it had been customary in both the Eastern and Western Church to confer this office upon boys. Of the Eastern Church, although many examples could be offered, that of Euthymius will suffice: Otreius, bishop of Melitene, received him as a boy, baptized and tonsured him, and made him reader of the church entrusted to himself, as Cyril relates in the Life of Euthymius himself, *Analecta Graeca*, vol. I.]

[Note: Of the Western Church, besides Siricius, Zosimus, and the Irish canons, Paulinus of Nola bears witness, singing of St. Felix: “From boyhood he began to serve God . . . and served as reader in his earliest years.” Augustine is a witness, as we shall see in Epistle 1 to Celestine, no. 3; Ennodius is a witness in the Life of St. Epiphanius, p. 360, where he reports that Epiphanius undertook the office of reader at about eight years old; and finally, to omit others, Victor of Vita, book I, chapter 9, who, when he reports that the Carthaginian clergy condemned to exile exceeded five hundred in number, adds: “Among them there were very many little-boy readers.” Hence in the Second Council of Toledo, chapter 1, the words, “Concerning those whom the will of their parents has devoted to the office of cleric from the first years of infancy, we decree that the following be observed: as soon as they have been tonsured or entrusted to the ministry of the elect,” there is strong reason to suspect that, in place of the immediately preceding word *electorum* (“of the elect”), *lectorum* (“of readers”) should be restored.]

[Note: A very ancient Corbie manuscript, together with one Colbert manuscript and another from Laon, reads: “he must be an acolyte and subdeacon for five years.” Then the Corbie manuscript alone has: “And after his thirtieth year [he proceeds] to the grade of deacon.”]

[Note: The Irish canon in the *Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 4, seems to reproduce these words of Siricius, though not fully understood. It reads: “But whoever, having reached adolescence, has lived commendably until his thirtieth year, being content with one wife only, shall be a subdeacon for five years and a deacon for five years; in his fortieth year, a presbyter; in his fiftieth, a bishop.”]

[Note: It must be observed that this synod departs from Siricius’s meaning in two ways. First, it distinguishes three classes of candidates for ordination: one of a boy dedicated from infancy to ecclesiastical offices, another of a young man who is the husband of one wife, and a third of an elderly layman. Secondly, concerning the first it determines that he shall be porter and subdeacon for four years, deacon for five, presbyter at thirty, and bishop at thirty, forty, or fifty; while concerning the second it decrees that he shall be subdeacon at thirty, deacon at thirty-five, presbyter at forty, and bishop at fifty.]

[Note: For it is plain that Siricius here recognizes only two classes of those to be ordained: namely, those trained as readers from infancy, who, when they had reached puberty, were compelled either to take wives or to profess continence, as the Third Council of Carthage, canon 19, directs; and elderly men. He wishes one dedicated to the Church’s services from boyhood to perform the duties of acolyte and subdeacon, upon reaching adolescence, until his thirtieth year; then to attain the deaconate in that thirtieth year, the presbyterate in the thirty-fifth year—wherein Justinian’s Novella 123, chapter 13, agrees with him—and the episcopate in the forty-fifth year.]

[Note: Most ancient canons, however, determine that deacons may be ordained in their twenty-fifth year and presbyters in their thirtieth. This is attested by the Synod of Neocaesarea, canon 2; the Quinisext Council, canon 14; and the Third Council of Carthage, canon 4; the Council of Agde, canons 16 and 17; the Second Council of Toledo, canon 1; the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 20; and the Fourth Council of Arles, canon 1. Jerome also supports this in his Epistle against the Errors of John of Jerusalem. The usual reason given for refusing to ordain a priest before his thirtieth year is that Christ began preaching at that age.]

[Note: Yet Caesarius of Arles, though he presided over the Council of Agde just mentioned, is reported in his Life, book I, chapter 28, when on the point of death, to have said that no deacon should ever be ordained in his church before the thirtieth year of his age—read *ordinaret* (“should ordain”) for *ordinarit*. From this it may be inferred that he complied with these decrees of Siricius and, so far as lay in his power, wished them to be observed.]

[Note: From what has been said one may also understand what we read in the Life of Boniface of Mainz, in Surius under 5 June: when Willibrord wished to make him bishop, Boniface declined the burden because he had not yet fully reached, according to the norm of canonical rectitude, his fiftieth year. Although Louis Thomassin, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 68, no. 1, says that he does not clearly perceive what this canonical norm was which required that age, it is required not only by the Apostolic Constitutions, book II, chapter 1, but also, as we have seen above, by the statutes of the Irish synod, which Boniface probably had before his eyes.]

### Chapter X.—14

But if someone already advanced in age, prompted by conversion to a better purpose, hastens to pass from lay life into the sacred service, he shall obtain the fruit of his desire only if, at the time when he is baptized, he is immediately joined to the number of readers or exorcists—provided it is established that he has had, or has, one wife, and that he received her as a virgin. Once initiated, after completing two years, he shall become an acolyte and subdeacon for another five years; and thus, if he has been judged worthy during those periods, he shall be advanced to the deaconate. Thereafter, as time advances, he shall deservedly receive the presbyterate or episcopate if the election of clergy and people has singled him out as pre-eminent.

[Note: The Roman edition and the collection of Hadrian’s manuscripts read *conversatione* (“way of life”). With the other books we prefer *conversione* (“conversion”), that is, a change from a former purpose to another and better one. In former times it was customary in our monasteries to call *conversi* (“converts”) those who, already advanced in years, renounced the world and embraced monastic life; by this designation they were distinguished from others who had been offered to monasteries from childhood.]

[Note: Here again the Irish synod seems to adapt itself to this decree of Siricius; in the *Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 4, it determines: “But if he is an elderly layman and it is necessary that he become bishop, let him be reader for two years, subdeacon for five, deacon for five, and after twelve years—that is, from the time he began to convert—let him be appointed presbyter or bishop.”]

[Note: Thus the Pithou manuscript, together with an old Colbert manuscript written in Lombardic letters, reads; in this manuscript moreover the same word, *edecumarit*, as though singular, is noted in the margin. The Corbie manuscript, written in the sixth century, supports this: after its first three letters have been erased, it retains *cuimaneret*, doubtless in place of *edecumaverit*. The Colbert copy of the manuscript published by Quesnel has *sequatur* (“shall follow”). The royal copy of the pure Dionysian collection has *existerit* (“shall have been”), whence *fuerit* (“shall have been”) seems to have passed into one Colbert manuscript, with *pro* having previously been inserted before *eum*. In copies of the Hadrian collection, *evocarit* (“shall have summoned”) has been substituted, and was thereafter retained.]

[Note: The word *edecumaverit*, which means much the same as “he shall have selected, as meritoriously surpassing the rest, one out of ten”—ten being used in place of all—is most suitable to Siricius’s purpose and entirely free from suspicion of being a fabricated reading. In the Greek-Latin Glossary published by Labbe one reads: “ἀποδεκατῶ” (“I tithe”); *edecumatus*, “ἀδέκαστος, ἀδωροδόκητος” (“incorruptible, not accepting gifts”). Du Cange explains *edecumatus* in his Latin Glossary as “pure, distinguished, excellent, outstanding, pre-eminent,” like a judge who is not corrupted by gifts.]

[Note: Du Cange likewise observes there that in Festus, through Paul the Deacon, *edecumata electa* (“selected as outstanding”) should be restored in place of *edecimata electa*; similarly in Papias, *edecumatus electus* for *edicumatus ejectus*; and in Valeran, in the letter prefixed to the work of St. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, On the Diversity of the Sacraments, *edecumatos* in place of *edocumatos*. Hence we too think that in Aurelius Symmachus, Siricius’s contemporary, book III, letters 49 and 51, where we read *viros decumatae virtutis* (“men of tithed virtue”), *edecumatae* should be preferred, as the old Benignian manuscript has it noted in the margin of letter 51.]

[Note: What Symmachus means in letter 49 to Eutropius by the words, “I have nothing burdensome in this, that you associate with my friendship men of outstanding virtue,” he explains more plainly in letter 51 to the same man, which begins: “I indeed give abundant thanks to my zeal—perhaps read ‘to yours’—because you procure for me the acquaintance of every most approved person.” It is therefore evident that for him *edecumatus* means “most approved,” especially since later in the same letter 51 he asks Eutropius to find him one or two persons of equally tithed—or, more accurately in the Benignian manuscript, outstanding—honesty.]

[Note: Siricius accordingly teaches that the man to be chosen is the one who excels the others; that is, as the Roman synod says in Epistle 10, no. 18, the worthiest. Thus he anticipated Leo, Epistle 12, chapter 6, where that pope determines that the best person is to be promoted, and the Council of Trent, session 24, chapter 18, whose decree commands that the one chosen be he who, among those approved by the examiners, is more worthy. Therefore *edecumare* must not be confused with *decumare* or *decimare*, by which every tenth person, as chance may determine, is understood to be taken.]

### Chapter XI.—15

Any cleric who marries either a widow or, indeed, a second wife shall immediately be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical rank, with lay communion alone granted to him. He may retain even that only if he afterward commits nothing by which he would lose it.

### Chapter XII.—16

We do not permit any women to be in clerics’ houses except those alone whom the Synod of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely on account of ties of kinship (canon 3; see Third Council of Carthage, canon 17).

### Chapter XIII.—17

We also desire and decree that monks, provided that the gravity of their morals and the holy formation of their life and faith commend them, be joined to the offices of clerics. Those who are below their thirtieth year shall be promoted, as time increases, through each individual grade among the minor orders; and thus, by consecration at a mature age, they shall arrive at the distinctions of the deaconate or presbyterate. Nor shall they ascend by a leap to the summit of the episcopate unless the same periods which we have prescribed above for the individual ranks have been observed in their case.

[Note: Isidore, and after him the Roman edition and the collections, read “They are worthy,” adding on their own authority *digni* (“worthy”), which is more correctly absent from the earlier collections. This confirms what was decreed in no. 3: namely, that the deaconate is not to be conferred upon anyone before he has reached his thirtieth year. Here *intra* means “below,” as does *infra*. Nor is it obscure that the subdeaconate is there counted among the minor orders.]

[Note: One Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript read “nor immediately to”; the royal manuscript, with two other Colbert manuscripts, “nor at least to”; another royal manuscript, with certain Hadrian copies, “nor by leaps to.” Hence Isidore, and after him Merlin and Crabbe, read “nor by leaps to.” Other printed editions, with two manuscripts, read “nor immediately by a leap.” The very ancient Corbie manuscript, the Coislin manuscript, that of Laon, and many others read “nor by a leap to”; this reading, being simpler and closer to the readings of the other manuscripts, is preferred.]

### Chapter XIV.—18. No Cleric Is Allowed to Do Penance

[Note: One Colbert manuscript and another of Pithou state the chapter’s summary as follows: “Those who were formerly vessels of vices shall not attain the honor of the clergy.”]

It was also fitting that we should provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layperson whatsoever may attain the honor of the clergy. For although they have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, those who were formerly vessels of vices ought nevertheless not to receive the instruments for administering the sacraments.

[Note: It may properly be asked here from what clerics Siricius exempts public penance. Canon 11 of the Fifth Council of Carthage states: “It has been confirmed that if presbyters or deacons are convicted of some graver fault by which they must be removed from ministry, hands are not to be imposed upon them as upon penitents or lay believers.” Leo agrees, writing in Epistle 2 to Rusticus, no. 5: “It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated in presbyteral honor or in the rank of deacon should receive, through imposition of hands, a remedy of penitence for any crime of their own; this undoubtedly descends from apostolic tradition.”]

[Note: Siricius seems to approach this view when he indicates that he is speaking of clerics to whom belongs the receiving of instruments for administering the sacraments. For, as the Second Council of Carthage, canon 2, teaches, bishops, presbyters, and deacons handle the sacraments. Yet it should be noted that Siricius speaks not only of clerics who handle the sacraments, but also of those who receive the instruments for administering the sacraments. His statement denying penance to any cleric is no less general than his statement excluding every layperson after penance from every grade of the clergy.]

[Note: But, according to the testimony and interpretation of Innocent, Epistle 40, the canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest clerical offices. The Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 68, likewise excludes them; and Innocent, Epistle 16, nos. 8 and 11, maintains that this has been received in the Roman Church by law and custom. This is also confirmed by Gelasius, Epistle 11, chapter 2. It follows that, in Siricius’s view, every cleric is to be exempted from public penance. Felix II, however, departed from this position in Epistle 15, no. 6, expressly subjecting lower clerics to public penance.]

### Chapter XV.—19

And since the sole excuse pleaded for all these practices that incur censure is ignorance, which for the time being we must mercifully forgive out of regard for piety alone: any penitent, any bigamist, any husband of a widow, who has improperly and unlawfully entered the sacred service, shall understand that pardon is granted him by us on this condition: he must regard it as a great benefit if, all hope of advancement having been taken from him, he remains permanently and securely in the rank in which he is found.

Let the chief bishops of all provinces know that henceforth, if they think anyone of such persons should be admitted to holy orders, a fitting sentence will be issued from the Apostolic See both concerning their own status and concerning the status of those whom they have promoted contrary to the canons and our prohibitions.

[Note: Thus the older manuscripts. Other books read “of promotion.” See Fourth Council of Carthage, canons 68 and 69. The “chief bishops of provinces” here are those called “metropolitans” above in no. 12. Although Gaudentius, in his sermon at his own ordination, Pope Innocent I, Leo, and others indiscriminately call any bishops “chief priests,” it is nevertheless agreed that the chief bishops of provinces are the metropolitans.]

[Note: Someone may perhaps wonder why Siricius, both here and above in no. 12, thinks metropolitans ought to be punished for the faults mentioned in each place. They were indeed liable to blame if anything contrary to the canons was done in the ordinations of bishops, since none of these was performed without their consent. But in the other orders, which bishops conferred without consulting them, the bishops alone seem liable to punishment, just as the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 68, in fact punishes them alone. Nevertheless, since it belonged to metropolitans to ensure and provide that the canons were observed in their provinces, and since for that reason they were commanded to hold councils twice a year, the severity of this discipline toward them cannot appear unjust.]

[Note: In a very ancient Corbie copy, a note is inserted here and, as often happens when something omitted is supplied, repeated in the margin of the book in Merovingian script: a new chapter, or decree, hitherto unpublished. The Colbert manuscript 1868 likewise presents it interpolated in the very text of the letter, before the next word, “We have explained.” The same passage, interpolated in the same manner, is cited in Siricius’s name in an old collection of canons written more than eight hundred years ago and preserved in our German library. Moreover, another old collection, recently given to the same library, likewise cites it in Siricius’s name in a shorter form. We shall append this decree, which Dionysius did not know and which perhaps belongs to another writing of Siricius, at the end of the letter, in the manner of an appendix, under these three forms.]

### 20. That Himerius Should Make These Decrees Known to Other Churches

We have explained, I think, dearest brother, everything set forth in complaint; and concerning each matter which you referred, through our son Bassianus the presbyter, to the Roman Church as the head of your body, we have supplied answers sufficient, as I think.

Now we urge the mind of your brotherhood more and more to observe the canons and to maintain the decretal enactments, so that you may cause these replies which we have written to your inquiries to be brought to the knowledge of all our fellow bishops—not only of those established in your diocese, but also of all the Carthaginians, Baeticans, Lusitanians, Galicians, and those in the provinces on either side adjoining your borders. Let the provisions which we have established by salutary ordinance be sent to them under cover of your letters.

And although no priest of the Lord may be free to be ignorant of the statutes of the Apostolic See or the venerable decisions of the canons, it may nevertheless be especially useful and, in view of the antiquity of your priesthood, very glorious for your affection if the matters written to you generally under your particular name are, through the care of your unanimity, brought to the knowledge of all our brethren. Thus the measures which we have established, not rashly but prudently, under the greatest caution and deliberation, may remain inviolate; and every avenue of excuse, which can now be open to no one before us, may be barred for the future.

[Note: Thus Quesnel, with the very ancient Corbie manuscript. The Reims manuscript reads “Gauls.” The other books read “Gallic.” Labbe wrote in the margin, “Gallicans; II, Galicians.” Again, in Leo’s Epistle 17 to Turibius, no. 23, we shall encounter “Lusitanians, Gallic”; by the latter designation the bishops of Gallaecia are undoubtedly meant. We think that from *Gallaecos* arose *Gallecos*, and then, after *e* was altered into *i*, the form *Gallicos* prevailed.]

Given on the third day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto.

[Note: 2 February 385. Three sound manuscript witnesses read “IV Ides”—that is, 10 February. The printed editions then add “most illustrious men, consuls.” The words “most illustrious men” are absent from the older manuscripts, and Dionysius Exiguus did not read them either, as is shown by his uncorrupted copy preserved in the royal library. Later, in the collection sent by Hadrian to Charlemagne, “vv. cc.” was rashly added before “consuls,” and from there passed into others. Yet among all forms of the collections there is none which does not exhibit that consular date.]

[Note: Tillemont therefore rightly considered Papebroch’s conjecture slight and suspicious: moved by this date, Papebroch suspected that the remainder of the letter was not entirely pure and genuine. The principal reason that moved him disappears once the words “most illustrious men” are removed. But even if he is still troubled because, when Arcadius is named, the title *Augustus* is omitted, he will doubtless be satisfied when he observes that Prosper and Marcellinus, in their chronicles, date the same year by “Arcadius and Bauto, consuls,” likewise without adding *Augustus*. Nor should the learned man have been more troubled by the fact that Siricius’s predecessors had not hitherto used a consular date on their letters, especially since it is clear that this practice was afterward common with Innocent and his other successors.]

## Appendix

### From a Very Ancient Corbie Manuscript

And because whenever religion is at issue bishops ought to judge: if a dispute should arise between two churches, the ecclesiastical cause shall be brought before a synod or before the metropolitan. It shall not be permitted for anything to be brought before the emperor on any pretext; rather, what is conducted among bishops shall be concluded by the judgment of bishops.

If it should happen that a church has a successor bishop who is simple-minded, such that the things acquired or bestowed by the former bishop are taken away through the sluggishness of this simplicity, and the church loses through the simplicity of its bishop what it had acquired through the prudence of its predecessor; whenever a dispute of this kind has arisen between church and church, if at some time a more prudent successor succeeds, he shall not be denied access to make representation. For, according to the statutes of the canons, one church never prejudices another; nor can charity be divided, which is united and diffused throughout the whole world.

### The Same Chapter Interpolated, as It Appears Both in German Manuscript 424, Chapter 21, and in Colbert Manuscript 1868, Attributed to Siricius

If a dispute should arise between two churches, the ecclesiastical cause is brought before a synod or before the metropolitan. No one may, on any pretext, bring it before the emperor; rather, what is conducted among bishops shall be concluded by the judgment of bishops.

[Note: The material enclosed in brackets belongs to the law of Arcadius published by Jacques Sirmond in the appendix to the Theodosian Code, p. 5, and constitutes its opening.]

[“As veneration is due to blameless priests, so also moderate punishment is due to those who are troublesome and degraded. For just as those who serve God and shine with the integrity of the divine priesthood furnish not only an ornament proper to their own life but also an example to the people subject and obedient to them, so those whose sins are more unworthy under the profession of integrity, if they are found guilty and deposed by bishops,”] shall by no means be received by other bishops.

If it should thus happen that a church has a successor bishop who is simple-minded, such that the things acquired or bestowed in that church by the former bishop are taken away through the sluggishness of the simple man, and the church loses through the simplicity of its bishop what it had acquired through the prudence of its predecessor; whenever a dispute of this kind has arisen between church and church, if at some time a more prudent successor succeeds, he shall not be denied access to make representation. For, according to the statutes of the canons, one church never prejudices another; nor can charity be divided, which is united and diffused throughout the whole world.

### The Same, Expressed Briefly and Summarily, as Cited in Another Old Collection of Canons

[Note: This collection was not long ago left by testament to the German library by the lord Petit, almoner of the church of La Rochelle.]

**IN THE LETTER OF POPE SIRICIUS**

If the possessions of a church have been lost through a simple-minded bishop, access to make representation shall not be denied to his successor; and, according to the judgment of the canons, no prejudice shall ever be done to a church, because it is one and diffused throughout the whole world.

## Letter II. Of Emperor Valentinian to Pinianus, Approving the Election of Siricius, Bishop of Rome. (C, G)

[This letter has already been presented by us in the *Ancient Monuments Pertaining to the Doctrine of the Arians*, above, col. 593.]

## Letter III. Of Emperor Maximus to Pope Siricius. (C, G)

Maximus promises concern for the Catholic faith. He also promises that the case of Agriciius, whom Siricius had written to have been improperly promoted to the rank of presbyter, will be examined in a synod. He again professes his zeal for the Catholic faith and sends the proceedings in which the recently exposed crimes of the Manichaeans, or Priscillianists, are recorded.

[This letter also has been placed by us in the *Ancient Monuments Pertaining to the Arians*, above, col. 589.]

## Letter IV. Of Pope Siricius to Anysius, Bishop of Thessalonica

### That No One in Illyricum Shall Ordain a Bishop Without the Consent of Anysius

[Note: This is one of the various letters once read in the Roman council under Boniface II and eventually published through the efforts of Lucas Holstenius. To this letter, or to another written earlier by Siricius, or to both, refer Innocent I, Epistle 1—where he recalls that Siricius and Anastasius granted so much authority to Anysius that they entrusted to him for examination all matters transacted in those regions—and Leo, Epistle 3, no. 2.]

[Note: Leo, entrusting the churches of Illyricum to Anastasius as his representative, does so after the example of Siricius of blessed memory, who, he says, first entrusted this by a definite arrangement to Anysius, your predecessor of holy memory, deservedly for his good service to the Apostolic See at that time and afterward approved by events. Although we cannot determine with certainty when this letter was written, it is nearly certain that it was sent before anything had been heard at Rome concerning the case of Bonosus; otherwise Siricius would not have been silent about it.]

[Note: Nor would it be unreasonable to assign to the year 385 the letter in which Siricius entrusted to Anysius the examination of affairs transacted in the churches of Illyricum. He sent these second letters when he could not yet know whether the first had been received. It follows that these second letters belong at least to the year 386; and the “long ago” which Siricius mentions as lying between the two refers not to an interval of years but of several months, since to one who desires something, that which is delayed beyond expectation seems long.]

To the most beloved brother **ANYSIUS**, SIRICIUS.

Even long ago, dearest brother, through Bishop Candidianus, who has gone before us to the Lord, we had sent letters of this kind: that no one should presume to ordain bishops in Illyricum without your consent. Whether these reached you I have not been able to learn. For many things have been done there amid contention by bishops in performing ordinations, as your charity knows better.

Therefore you ought to act diligently, lest, as has happened, men should presume in rivalry to ordain unworthy persons in one church and thus appear to have made, as it were, three bishops. Your vigilance ought to be alert to restrain every audacity of this kind, with the Holy Spirit fervent within you. Either you yourself, if you can, or those bishops whom you judge suitable, should be sent with letters granting consent, so that in the place of one who has died or been deposed they may ordain a Catholic bishop, approved in life and morals, according to the statutes of the Synod of Nicaea, or a worthy cleric from the clergy of the Roman Church.

[Note: Celestine I, Epistle 2, and Sixtus III, Epistle 8, confirm this same privilege of the bishop of Thessalonica in such a way that Sixtus reserves to the metropolitans, after consultation with him, the right to ordain the bishops of their provinces. Siricius, however, derogates from this right below when he charges Anysius either to ordain bishops himself or to have them ordained through such bishops as he chooses.]

[Note: Siricius seems to allude to what occurred in the church of Antioch in 362. For when there were already two bishops there, namely Euzoius and Meletius, Paulinus was imprudently established as a third by Lucifer of Cagliari. Subsequently Vitalis was added by the Apollinarians to Meletius and Paulinus. Siricius probably adduces the example of this church because, when Flavian had not long before succeeded Meletius and Evagrius Paulinus, the dissensions had revived and, as Ambrose says in Epistle 56, no. 1, “a grievous discord stood throughout the whole world.”]

[Note: This exception confirms the general rule requiring that a bishop be selected from the clergy of the particular church for which he is to be ordained; at the same time it indicates a certain special right of the Roman Church in the provinces of Illyricum.]

## Notice on the Following Letter

### I. The Following Letter Ascribed to Siricius by Some, Denied Him by Others, and Held Doubtful by Certain Persons

It would be a long task to report the diverse opinions of learned persons concerning this letter and the arguments by which each defends his own view. Yet I cannot remain entirely silent about them either.

Blondel, in *Pseudo-Isidore*, p. 550, was, so far as I know, the first to sow certain seeds of doubt concerning its genuineness. He acknowledges that Deacon Ferrandus mentions this letter in the *Breviatio Canonum*, articles 6, 130, 138, and 174, and that Ferrandus, having lived to the year of the Lord 547, is qualified to establish its authority. Nevertheless, he raises two objections against it: first, that no mention of it exists in an old Roman Church codex; secondly, that it is almost copied word for word in Innocent’s letter to Victricius. He then leaves the matter to the reader’s judgment.

Papebroch considers the consular date an addition. Paschasius Quesnel, in Dissertation 15 in his edition of Leo’s works, argues at length that both this letter and the African council in which it is said to have been read are mere fabrications of an impostor. Emanuel de Schelstrate defends the genuineness of both writings in *Ecclesiastical Dissertation* 3, chapter 12. Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont, vol. X, p. 793, after setting out the points that move him, leaves everything, with his characteristic modesty, to the judgment of learned persons, preferring, after the example of Baluze, to leave the matter unresolved rather than rashly define anything.

Later, however, Étienne Baluze, at the end of the edition of the book *On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire*, reprinted in 1704, p. 1339, added a separate dissertation against Quesnel on the Council of Telepte. In it he shows himself neither doubtful nor uncertain in this matter, but vigorously defends the genuineness of our letter.

### II. Asserted on the Authority of Ferrandus
