In this dissertation, having first refuted the conjectures by which Quesnel seeks to make Ferrandus’s little work suspect of interpolation, Baluze does not hesitate to affirm that “hardly any work of the ancient writers is so sound, so complete, and one into which the hands—not, I would say, of impostors, but even of unskilled copyists—have intruded less”; and accordingly that it is “free from the stains with which Quesnel has attempted to bespatter it.”

He then adds that even if certain errors and obscurities in Ferrandus’s collection were certainly proved, it would not follow in the least that every occurrence of a reference to a letter of Siricius must immediately be expunged. Otherwise, if such license once prevailed, the authority of nearly all ancient writers would be at an end.

He next especially charges Quesnel with carelessness because, near the end of chapter 1, Quesnel says of Chifflet: “He mentions a Troyes codex which calls the same synod Zellensian that others call Telensian; but it is one against countless others.” For apart from the Troyes manuscript, there are not countless copies of Ferrandus’s *Breviatio*, but only one Corbie manuscript. Yet the age of this codex—since it is more than eleven hundred years old—gives no slight authority to Ferrandus’s published work.

Therefore, since Quesnel himself admits in chapter 2, no. 1, that “the genuineness of the Telensian or Zellensian council and of the letter attached to it could safely be pronounced upon if the integrity of the *Breviatio* itself were established,” Baluze rightly pronounces both that council and the letter read in it genuine after vindicating Ferrandus’s *Breviatio* from every suspicion of corruption.

### III. That it was read at the Council of Telepte.

Quesnell’s second argument against the authenticity of this letter is drawn from the name of the council to which it is attached. “For it is certain,” he says in chapter 3, “that it is everywhere written *Telense*, and that it is not so written through scribal error. Moreover, it is clear that there is only one city of Teles, situated in the proconsular province; but that Donatian, bishop of Telepte in Byzacena, held a synod in the proconsular province is the dream of an impostor, who lacked sufficient acquaintance both with ecclesiastical discipline and with the regions of Africa to weave his fraud skillfully.”

Here we cannot sufficiently wonder how greatly the force of a preconceived opinion misleads each person. For, leaving aside the old Vatican manuscript, in which the aforesaid council is called *Thelescense*, and two Royal manuscripts, in one of which it is called *Telenense*, in the other *Telinense*: in the very Thuan manuscript, now Colbert manuscript no. 932, which Quesnell possessed and repeatedly cites in his Code, one reads in the general index, chapter 62: “Constitutions of the Council of Telepte, that is, in Africa, together with the decretal letter of Pope Siricius”; and then at the head of the council itself: “Here begins the Council of Telepte concerning the Tractoria of holy Cyricius, pope of the city of Rome, throughout Africa … a council having been assembled in the Church of the Apostles of the people of Telepte.”

How could that threefold repetition of the word *Teleptensis* escape a man with eyes? Or did he omit to consult those passages? But if he neglected even to read the manuscript in his possession, what trust should be placed in his pronouncement: “It is certain that *Telense* is written everywhere, and not through scribal error”?

Moreover, another Colbert manuscript, no. 3368, contains two copies of the same council. In the first it is called *Telense*; in the second, *Telenense*, with the addition at the end: “Here end the Thelensian canons.” Donatian, moreover, is called in the first copy bishop of the city of Teleptina, and in the other bishop of the city of Teles. Since it is undisputed that Donatian was bishop of the church of Teleptina or Telepte and primate of the province of Byzacena in the year 417—as both his subscription at the Second Council of Milevis, held in 416, proves—and since he is nevertheless called bishop of the city of Teles through an obvious scribal slip, why should we not likewise believe that through scribal error the council which in some manuscripts we read as *Teleptense* was written in others as *Telense*?

Baluzius thinks that the same council was called *Zellense* by Ferrandus because it was in fact held at Zella, but *Teleptense* by others because Zella belonged to the diocese of Telepte: “in the same manner in which Loaisa called Tarraconensian the council which was held in the time of King Sisebut at Egara in the province of Tarraconensis; while Sirmond called Magalonensian that which met at Juncariae in the territory of Magalona.”

### IV. That its agreement with another letter of Innocent does nothing against its authenticity.

Another objection, drawn from the close agreement of Siricius’s letter with another letter of Innocent to Victricius, is answered by this observation of Hincmar of Rheims, vol. II, p. 461: “For this is the custom of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See: they place the words of their predecessors in their letters as though they were their own.” Hincmar of Laon, in the same work, pp. 624 and 631, confirms that this observation is entirely true.

Although perhaps their observation rests upon no other basis than that they found the same things frequently repeated in letters fabricated by Isidore. At least this is certain, as Baluzius adds: Innocent himself, in his letter to Exsuperius, chapter 1, copies out his own words from chapter 9 of his letter to Victricius. Hence it should seem less strange if he likewise copied the writings of his predecessor, which in some sense had become his own together with that predecessor’s see.

Indeed, on comparing the two letters, I am persuaded that Innocent’s letter was drawn from Siricius’s, not this one from that. And I trust that those too will be persuaded who observe that what requires explanation in Siricius’s letter is for the most part supplied in Innocent’s letter; so that Siricius plainly appears to be the author of his words, and Innocent the interpreter of Siricius. For it is not likely that someone who wished to compose a letter from Innocent’s words and attribute it to Siricius would omit certain words of Innocent which seem necessary for clarity of meaning.

Some of these passages ought now to be indicated, were it not more convenient to reserve this for the notes. As for Innocent, by incorporating into his letter several rules already prescribed by Siricius, he suitably answered Victricius, who requested nothing new from him but sought a book of rules by which he might be instructed “what discipline is observed in the churches of the city of Rome.”

### V. The alleged motive for forging it is rejected.

Nor is there any basis here for the suspicion of the most distinguished man, who thinks that someone perversely devoted to the grandeur and authority of Rome, seeing that the Roman pontiffs Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine had failed in their efforts to introduce into the African provinces the right of appeals to the Apostolic See, resolved to forge these letters of Siricius and invent a celebrated African synod receiving them, so that the memory of that unfortunate result might be effaced.

Certainly, suspicions of this sort are dispelled and removed as easily as they are introduced. Indeed, anyone devoted to the Roman name ought at that time to have been deterred from inventions of this kind, when the Africans had recently demonstrated their diligence in scrutinizing matters thrust upon them under the name of councils. Who, moreover, was so dull as to hope that the memory of a matter recorded in so many proceedings and inserted into the very Code of Canons of the African Church could be effaced?

But even if someone had been so zealous for Roman greatness that for its sake he would not fear to invent false writings, he would undoubtedly have expressed the right of that see in clearer and more magnificent words than those used by Siricius in no. 2.

### VI. That Siricius did not absurdly use words of exhortation and request in persuading persons to do what had been commanded.

But, says the cited author in chapter 5, no. 7, “these words of chapter 9, ‘We advise that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives,’ as also these, ‘I exhort, admonish, beseech,’ etc., make manifest either the malice or the ignorance of the impostor.”

Yet we freely confess that nothing of the kind appears to us in these words. For we do not understand them as the learned man represents them, “as though priests and Levites were not bound by a law of continence,” but as exhorting, admonishing, beseeching, and advising them to observe the law by which they were bound. Is there room for exhorting, admonishing, beseeching, and advising only in matters dependent upon the free choice of the will and required by no necessity of command?

Siricius himself, from the prologue of his letter onward, indicates that the matters to which he repeatedly exhorts are not mere counsels but commands—indeed, commands binding all the more because they are not new but ancient enactments. Therefore, after setting them out, he adds: “If anyone, puffed up by the mind of his flesh, should wish to wander away from this rule of the canon, let him know that he is excluded from our communion and shall suffer the penalties of Gehenna.” Surely no one would think that a person ought to be excluded from communion or liable to the punishments of Gehenna for neglecting counsels.

Further, as Baluzius has already observed, Innocent, Letter 3 to Exsuperius, no. 3, citing Siricius’s words on the law of continence, calls them “the admonitions of Siricius, a man of blessed memory,” not commands. Siricius himself also, in Letter 4, no. 5, strongly condemns something done “contrary to apostolic commands,” and, to prevent its happening thereafter, forbids it by a word of admonition thus: “I admonish that this be done no longer.” And in Letter 10, no. 6: “I admonish, religious reverence itself so persuading, that men who are defiled and unbelieving … ought not to believe the mystery of God.”

### VII. The Africans’ reverence toward the Apostolic See.

Quesnell had already stated in chapter 3, no. 3: “It is certain that in that age the Africans administered their churches according to the canons of their own synods, and did not permit laws of ecclesiastical discipline to be imposed upon them from overseas regions.”

But what he treats as certain cannot at all be reconciled with what took place under Siricius’s successors Anastasius, Innocent, and Boniface, if Siricius’s letters are to be rejected because they are said to have been read in an African council. For the Africans then decreed, as Baluzius also notes (Code of Canons of the African Church, c. 36), that a letter should be written and an envoy sent to Anastasius, bishop of the Apostolic See, and to Venerius, priest of Milan, to request that they moderate a decree which the condition of the African Churches at that time did not permit to be observed.

Soon afterward, when the same Anastasius’s letter had been read in their council, they gave thanks to God “because he had deigned to inspire in that most excellent and holy bishop such pious care for the members of Christ, though established in different lands, yet in one framework” (ibid., c. 65). They themselves also again send letters to the same pope, reverently explaining what they had decreed concerning the reception of Donatists.

Then, when Innocent’s letter providing “that bishops ought not easily to go overseas” had likewise been read to them (ibid., c. 94), they confirmed this very rule by their own decisions. Finally, after publishing the canon of Scripture, they decree “that this too be made known to our brother and fellow-priest Boniface, or to other bishops in those regions, for the confirmation of this canon” (ibid., c. 24). Indeed, they considered Siricius himself and Simplician to be consulted on whether it was permitted to promote to ministries of the sacred altar infants baptized among the Donatists (ibid., c. 47).

Since the Africans were thus disposed toward the Apostolic See, who would wonder that in 418 they ordered Siricius’s useful letters, full of sound regulations, to be read in their council? Nor, properly speaking, were laws imposed by those letters, since they did not issue new commands but confirmed ancient ones.

### VIII. That the following letter was written for Italians and on account of Italians.

The remaining objections against the authenticity of the following letter are dispelled with equal ease. For this purpose it will be especially helpful to observe that the letter was written not for Africans, but for those who had been summoned to the Roman council and could not come, and that it was later sent to Africans in much the same way as we have seen Damasus’s third letter, written for the bishops of Illyricum, afterward sent to and addressed to the Easterners.

Just as, in the copy of that letter transmitted to the Easterners, matters suitable to be said only to the bishops of Illyricum were retained—for example, no. 2: “Hence your sincerity perceives … that Easterners who acknowledge themselves Catholic, and Westerners, glory with us in this faith”—so in the copy of Siricius, written for Italians but transmitted to Africans and read by them in their council, matters said only of Italians were not altered.

Hence the words, “especially on account of those who at present could not be present either because of illness or because of enfeebled age,” which Quesnell, interpreting them of Africans, judges wholly absurd, are found to fit Italians—of whom alone they are spoken—most suitably.

The interpretation of the first chapter or decree also depends on the same observation, a matter over which the aforesaid author labored in vain. Had he observed this, he would have been far from saying in chapter 4 that “the first argument for *notheia* [spuriousness] is drawn from the absurdity of this first decree,” because “however one reads it, one cannot adapt it either to common usage, to the laws of grammar, or to African discipline and custom.” Rather, he would freely have confessed that it is so aptly adapted to African custom and discipline that he would already cease, on this ground alone, to doubt the authenticity of the entire letter and of the Council of Telepte.

### IX. It has reached us only through the copy transmitted to the Africans.

It should next be observed that this letter has reached us from no source other than the proceedings of the Synod of Telepte. Various and very ancient collections of councils and papal letters present it as it was read in that council; four of these are preserved in the Colbert Library, two in the Royal Library, one in our Germanensis library, and others elsewhere. Nor is it absent from the manuscript which Quesnell designated the Code of Canons of the Roman Church.

There it occupies the last place, from which he conjectures that it was added later. But if that argument is admitted, the canons of Constantinople, Laodicea, and Antioch, which immediately precede it, must likewise be regarded as additions. The same judgment must be made concerning Damasus’s letter to Paulinus, which in that manuscript alone is placed as chapter 55, after the letters of Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, and so forth.

But whoever first transcribed this letter from the proceedings of the Council of Telepte took care only that its source should not be unknown. Nor should it be counted a fault in him that he omitted the remaining proceedings of that same council—just as no one will blame us for presenting here letters of Roman pontiffs read in various councils while omitting the synodal proceedings. For just as it is not our purpose, so it was not the purpose of those who collected ancient canons and decrees of the Apostolic See, to append synodal proceedings to their collections.

Therefore, from their having copied from those synods only the letter read there, it does not follow that nothing else occurred in them. Nor should Quesnell have inferred “that no business of greater importance was to be dealt with in that Synod of Telepte than the reading of Siricius’s letter or letters.” The preface itself, which ancient books place before this letter of Siricius, indicates that the pope’s letters were read only incidentally, after the business for which the synod had assembled had been completed, and with the council’s approval.

I have thought it worthwhile to place before all eyes this preface, transcribed here from the Colbert manuscript, with variants from other copies noted in the margin. The said manuscript reads as follows.

### X.

“Here begins the Council of Telepte concerning the *Tractoria* [Corbie MS: “Telesim per tractatus” (a corrupt or uncertain reading)] of holy Cyricius, pope of the city of Rome, throughout Africa. After the consulship of the most glorious Honorius for the eleventh time and Constantius for the second, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, a council having assembled [in the Church of the Apostles] of the people of Telepte [same MS: ‘a council of the people of Teles,’ omitting the intervening words], the blessed father, Donatian, bishop of the first see of the city of Telepte, having taken his seat, with Januarius, Felix, Secundus, Cyrius, Secundianus, Geta [same MS: Zeta], Eunomius, Maximianus, Donatus, Cresconius, Jocundus, Sopratus [another Colbert MS: Sopatrus], Restitutus, Julianus, Maximinus, Romanus, Teriolus, Nilicus, Maximus, Donatianus, Basilius, Papinianus, Januarius, Porphyrius, likewise Porphyrius, Donatus, Julianus, Tutus, Fortunius [two MSS: Fortinus, Quantianus], Quintianus, Capio, and the other bishops seated with him; and also Vincentius and Fortunatianus, envoys of the Proconsular province sent to the Byzacene council, and the rest”—that is, the things transacted in the synod, which the copyist intentionally omits in order to come to Siricius’s letter—“Vincentius and Fortunatianus said: ‘When we were also at Thusdrum [Corbie MS: Thosdrum; another Colbert MS: Thiodrum], as your recollection of the proceedings recalls with me, and had caused letters of Siricius, of holy memory, bishop of the Apostolic See, to be read, from which, when the holiness of our brother Bishop Latonius was reading one, our petition indicates that we should now present both. Please allow them to be read.’

“The bishops said: ‘Let the letters of holy [two MSS: sacred] Siricius, of venerable memory, be read, that we may know what their text contains.’

“And when they were handed over, Privatus the notary said: ‘A copy of the *tractatoria* [some MSS: ‘an example of the tractoria,’ or *tracturia*] of the bishop of the city of Rome. To the most beloved brethren,’ etc.”

Here perhaps someone may suspect the statement that the council of Telepte was held “in the Church of the Apostles” to have been invented in imitation of Siricius’s words, who says in his preface that they assembled “at the relics of blessed Peter.” Yet this suspicion will seem all the more unjust, since churches dedicated to the Apostles are by no means unusual in any part of the world.

### XI. That the Council of Telepte is undeservedly called suspect of forgery.

Having duly considered these matters, let each person judge whether it is permissible, upon mere conjectures, to reject as spurious an African council preserved in very ancient copies, particularly the Corbie manuscript, which is not later than the middle of the sixth century, and supported by the authority of Ferrandus, an African deacon flourishing at the beginning of the same sixth century. I mean a council in which are recorded the day and consuls under which it was held, the place where it was celebrated, the bishop who presided, and the other bishops who attended it; although among all these particulars nothing is discovered which either disagrees with or contradicts historical truth.

Certainly, from the Conference of Carthage we know that Donatian was bishop of the Church of Telepte in the year 411. His subscription appended to the Second Council of Milevis bears witness that he was at least from the year 416 primate of the province of Byzacena; and the Code of Canons of the African Church, c. 127, expressly confirms this. A general synod of Africa, held on the Kalends of May in the same year 418, as is read in Labbe, vol. II, p. 1578, assures us that he was also alive in the year 418, to which the Council of Telepte is assigned.

Nor is it inconsistent that a provincial synod should be held somewhat before a general one, whether on account of its own business or to prepare matters to be referred to the general synod. Further, we learn both from the Second Council of Milevis, c. 27, and from the Code of Canons of the African Church, cc. 97 and 127, that Vincentius and Fortunatianus, who speak at Telepte as legates of the Proconsular province, performed the same office elsewhere as well.

### XII. What is meant by the name *tractoria*.

The term *tracturia*, *tractoria*, or *tractatoria*, by which this letter is designated—and in the rendering of which the ancient manuscripts of Augustine show the same variation—was transferred from civil law to ecclesiastical usage. In the Theodosian Code, book VIII, title 6, there is a special title, “On *tractoriae* and *stativae*,” where a *tractoria* is a letter by which persons discharged from military duties were sent home, as is also clear from book VII, title 18, law 11.

Elsewhere it means a diploma granting authority to receive public provisions or a travel allowance. The Africans commonly use it to denote ecclesiastical letters. In Augustine, Letter 43, nos. 8 and 9, the word denotes a letter by which bishops were summoned to a synod; but in Sermon 2 on Psalm 36, nos. 19 and 20, the synodical letter of the Maximianists sent throughout Africa is called *Tractatoria* or *Tractoria* both by Augustine himself and by the Maximianists.

By the same word, Augustine, Letter 43, no. 8, means letters sent throughout the whole world concerning persons who either had been convicted or stubbornly refused to answer charges brought against them. In the same sense Marius Mercator, in the *Commonitorium*, calls *Tractoria* the letter of Zosimus concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius, addressed to all churches.

## LETTER V. OF BLESSED POPE SIRICIUS TO THE BISHOPS OF AFRICA

Siricius, with a synod, having set forth how great a concern bishops ought to have for the purity of the Church, and seeking to restore ancient regulations already neglected by some, decrees how bishops are to be ordained; that a cleric may not marry a widow, nor may one who has married a widow be admitted to the clergy, nor one who after remission of sins has worn the belt of secular military service; that no one may ordain a cleric from another church. Likewise, concerning those who have been cast out, that they are not to be received. Concerning Novatians and Montensists who return to the Church. Concerning the continence of priests and Levites. That a judgment of mercy must not be lacking.

To the most beloved brethren and fellow bishops throughout Africa, SIRICIUS.

> Note [Col. 1155C]. Three Colbert manuscripts, together with the Fossat and Corbie manuscripts and Merlin, immediately append after the word *Siricius*: “Although diverse, into one.” Here one must carefully retain what we have previously noted: namely, that this letter was first written to the bishops of a Roman synod and later sent through various provinces, specifically to the Africans, with its original address altered and adapted to them; it has reached us only from the proceedings of the Council of Telepte, into which it had been inserted.

[Col. 1155C]

### 1.

When many brethren had assembled together at the relics of the holy apostle Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ had their beginning,

> Note [Col. 1155C]. Quesnell alone reads *placuit*, omitting the conjunction *-que*. [Col. 1155D] Such pleonasm is especially familiar to Gregory, in whom, according to the manuscripts, after a question has been set forth, *ideoque* is commonly added for simple *ideo* (“therefore”). One Colbert manuscript has *placeretque* (“and it might please”). The rest, as in Merlin, have *placueritque* (“and it may have pleased”). Although this entire opening seems to Quesnell, Dissertation 15, chapter 5, no. 3, to suggest an unannounced synod, Baluzius rightly proves that it fits a council previously convened.

it also pleased us, because of the many matters that had arisen—which in some persons were not matters but crimes—that thereafter every person in the Church should be solicitous to exercise such care, as the apostle Paul teaches that a Church must be presented to God “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27), lest our conscience should appear defiled by the breath of some diseased sheep.

> Note [Col. 1155D]. Quesnell lacks “our conscience.” The Corbie manuscript does contain *conscience*, but lacks *our*. Immediately afterward, the editions, except Merlin’s, read *hac de re* (“on this matter”), where other books have *qua de re*, that is, “wherefore” or “for which reason.” In the same sense, in the following letter, no. 3, we shall see *qua de re videt* (“for which reason he sees”), and in Letter 7, no. 3: *Qua de re necessarium fuit* (“for which reason it was necessary”). We note this so that the fact that these three letters have one author may be confirmed even from this.

For this reason, a better counsel was adopted. Especially on account of those who at present could not be present because of bodily illness or enfeebled age,

> Note [Col. 1155D]. Quesnell prefixes the particle *prae* here. [Col. 1156C] But the difficulty which he brings from this passage as a supposedly certain argument for forgery entirely vanishes when these words are understood to concern bishops subject to the Roman synod.

it pleased us to send such letters, so that a permanent form of this sort might be observed,

> Note [Col. 1156C]. Thus Merlin, with the manuscripts. The other editions of the councils, with the Roman edition, read *perpetuo* (“perpetually”). In Quesnell the word *quo*, “so that,” together with the following phrase *perpetua istiusmodi forma servetur*, is omitted.

not letters imposing any new commands,

> Note [Col. 1156C]. In the manuscripts, as in Merlin, “but those things.” In Quesnell: “but because those things.”

but letters by which we desire to have observed those things which through the ignorance and negligence of some have been neglected, but which have been established by the constitution of the apostles and fathers,

> Note [Col. 1156D]. Quesnell: “by the apostolic sanction of the fathers.” But the manuscripts read: “by the constitution of the apostolic fathers,” or “of the apostles and fathers.” The received reading is supported by the Second Council of Carthage, canon 2: “that what the Apostles taught and antiquity itself observed, we also may keep.”

as it is written: “Stand firm and hold fast our traditions, whether by word or by letter” (2 Thess. 2:14).

This certainly ought to move your minds more strongly, most beloved brethren: that, free from every stain of this world, we may come confidently and securely into the presence of God. For we shall not be exempt because we preside over peoples,

> Note [Col. 1156D]. Thus the three better manuscripts and Merlin. Two others, with Crabbe, read “we who preside.” The remaining books: “who also preside.”

since it is written: “To whom much has been entrusted, more will be required from him” (Luke 12:43). Therefore, because we are compelled to render an account not only for ourselves but also for the people entrusted to us, we must instruct the people in humble divine discipline.

> Note [Col. 1156D]. The word “humble” is lacking in Quesnell. Merlin has “to prefer divine discipline”; other printed editions here add “and humble.” In the Fossat manuscript and one Colbert manuscript one reads “the humble discipline of God”; in another Colbert manuscript, “divine discipline humbly.” We follow two other Colbert manuscripts agreeing with the Corbie manuscript.

For there have arisen some who, not keeping the statutes of the elders,

> Note [Col. 1156D]. The Roman and council editions read: “despising the elders”; the other books oppose this.

have violated the chastity of the Church by their own presumption, following the will of the people and not fearing God’s judgment.

### 2.

Therefore, lest by similar conduct we seem silently to wink at and lend consent to such persons, and thereby incur the punishments of Gehenna, the Lord saying, “You saw a thief and ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Ps. 49:18): these are the matters which henceforth it is expedient for all Catholic bishops to observe in view of divine judgment.

> Note [Col. 1156D]. Fossat manuscript: “henceforth Catholics,” omitting the intervening words. Here, by the word “all,” are understood the bishops to whom the letter was first addressed.

[Col. 1157A]

### I. First: that no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the Apostolic See—that is, of the primate.

> Note [Col. 1157A]. In one manuscript, corruptly: “this is the first attestation.” In two others: “that is, of primates.” Quesnell, suppressing “that is,” retained “primates.” More correctly, in the very ancient Corbie manuscript and other manuscripts, as in the Roman and council editions: “that is, of the primate.”
>
> In my judgment, the original wording at the Roman council, written on account of Italian bishops, was: “First, that no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the Apostolic See,” with the word “bishop” understood. But when this letter was brought to the Africans, they adapted the same decree for the use of their church, adding an explanation to the words “Apostolic See,” namely, “that is, of the primate.” In this they departed in no way from Siricius’s meaning.
>
> For there is no doubt that if this pope had written this letter directly for Africans, he himself would have framed the decree differently: “First, that no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the primate.” Thus Innocent, a fitting interpreter of Siricius, afterward adapted and moderated it to Gallican discipline in Letter 2 to Victricius of Rouen: “First, that no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop.”
>
> That right of the Roman pontiff, by which it was not permitted in Italy, or in churches subject to his synod, to ordain bishops without his knowledge, seems to be noted and confirmed by canon 6 of the Council of Nicaea. There the synod wills that the bishop of Alexandria should possess, according to custom, through Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis, a right similar to that held by the Roman bishop in the suburban churches, as Rufinus calls them.
>
> The Africans explain and establish their own custom concerning episcopal ordinations at the Council of Carthage, canon 12. When Bishop Numidius said, “Some bishops, in a certain usurpation, think that, disregarding the primate of their own province, they may ordain a bishop at the desire of the people,” all said: “It pleases all that no one should so readily presume, without consulting the primate of any province, even with many bishops, to ordain a bishop in any place without his direction, as has been said. But if necessity requires, three bishops, wherever they may be, ought to ordain a bishop by command of the primate.” See also the Code of the African Church, chapter 13.
>
> Augustine conformed to this discipline when he arranged for a bishop to be ordained in the fortress of Fussala, as we shall see in his first letter to Pope Celestine, no. 3. With respect to other provinces, the common rule prevailed, which the Nicene synod explains in canon 6: “It is generally clear that if anyone has been made bishop contrary to the judgment of the metropolitan, the great synod has decreed that he ought not to be bishop.”
>
> Therefore Siricius, writing to bishops subject to his synod, said, “That no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the Apostolic See.” If he had issued this decree primarily for Africans, he would undoubtedly, as we have said, have written, “That no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the primate”; if for Gauls or Spaniards, he would have altered his style just as Innocent later did and said, “That no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop.”
>
> For from the beginning he professes that he wishes not to impose new commands but to restore ancient enactments. And indeed the aforesaid threefold custom comes to the same thing. For the Roman bishop in the suburban churches, and the primate in each province of Africa, were what the metropolitan was in other regions of the Christian world.
>
> This certainly was the understanding of Ferrandus the deacon in the *Breviary*, no. 4, where he writes: “That a bishop be ordained by three, with the others consenting in writing and with confirmation of the metropolitan or primate: Council of Nicaea, title 4; likewise title 6; Council of Antioch, title 18; Council of Laodicea, title 12; Council of Carthage under Bishop Genethlius, title 10; Universal Council of Carthage, title 48; Council of Zella, from the letter of Pope Siricius.”
>
> Thus he understands and teaches that in the letter of Siricius or the Council of Zella nothing else is decreed than what is taught in the councils noted above. So too, concerning episcopal ordinations, Ferrandus does not doubt that the right claimed by Siricius in the churches to which he originally directed this letter belongs either to the primate in Africa or to the metropolitan in other provinces.
>
> Hence there is here a certain argument not of *notheia* [spuriousness] but of *gnesiotēs* [genuineness], both of this letter and of the Council of Telepte. For no one except Africans would have thought to add to the words “Apostolic See” the explanation “that is, of the primate.” And from this it follows no less certainly that this letter was not drawn from Innocent’s other letter, but Innocent’s letter from this letter of Siricius. A crafty forger would by no means have substituted Innocent’s clear words for words which are obscure and less suited to the purpose for which Quesnell raises his suspicion.

For the judgment is sound which is confirmed by the decision of the greater number.

> Note [Col. 1158B]. Thus the Corbie manuscript, with two Colbert manuscripts, and likewise Innocent. Two other manuscripts read “may follow.” Quesnell alone reads “is consecrated.” Other editors read “follows.”

### II. Let not one bishop presume to ordain a bishop through arrogance, lest a benefit bestowed in secret appear to have been granted. For this was established and decreed in the Council of Nicaea (canon 4).

> Note [Col. 1158B]. The word “bishop” is absent from the very ancient Corbie manuscript, not only here but also in Innocent’s Letter 2 to Victricius. Ferrandus the deacon altered and interpolated these words of Siricius in the *Breviary*, no. 6, as follows: “That one bishop should not ordain a bishop, except for the Roman Church.” Baluzius explains in the cited Dissertation, p. 1352, how that exception may be understood.
>
> Moreover, at the Council of Chalcedon, act 11, p. 693, Bassianus is said to have been made bishop of the Ephesians by Olympius alone, bishop of Theodosiopolis, and thereafter to have been admitted to communion by Proclus and other bishops. But Olympius himself, asserting that he had suffered compulsion, testifies that he then objected: “Because it is contrary to the rule of the canons for one bishop alone to dispose of a church, especially of so great a metropolis.”
>
> Indeed, whether he said this truly or falsely, he did not properly ordain Bassianus; rather, he merely enthroned him in the see of Ephesus. Bassianus had already been ordained bishop of Evazorum by Memnon, as is explained in the same council, p. 688. This concerns the assertion of Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 23, that Evagrius was ordained contrary to ecclesiastical rules because Paulinus alone had chosen him, whereas the canons forbid anyone’s ordination without three bishops.
>
> Thus the bishops assembled at the Synod of Regensburg, after first consulting Leo III, defined that chorepiscopi were not bishops chiefly for this reason: they were neither assigned to an episcopal see of a city nor canonically ordained by three bishops. This is repeated in the Aachen Capitular of 803, chapters 4 and 6, pp. 381 and 383.
>
> Quesnell’s inference in chapters 5 and 6 from the words “through arrogance” against the authenticity of this letter is of less weight: “As though,” he says, “it were permitted, provided it were done without arrogance.” For this kind of argument proves no more than the argument by which some, in Siricius’s own age, wished to infer from Matthew 1:25—“And he did not know her until she bore her firstborn son”—that Mary was known by Joseph after Christ’s birth. But Siricius’s chief reason for confirming this decree was that it had been enacted by the Nicene synod.

III. Likewise, if anyone after the remission of sins—namely, that received through baptism—has worn the belt of secular military service, he must not be admitted to the clergy.

[Note: The remission in question is evidently that received through baptism. Therefore Ferrandus the deacon, in his *Breviary*, no. 3, citing this decree as though from the Council of Zella, judged that it should be expressed more plainly thus: “Whoever, after baptism, has entered secular military service is to be excluded from ordination.” Likewise the Council of Toledo held in 400, canon 8, decreed: “If anyone after baptism has served as a soldier and has assumed the military cloak or belt, even if he has not committed graver offenses, if he has been admitted to the clergy, he is not to receive the rank of deacon.” The reason for this discipline is given in canon 4 of the canons sent to the Gauls, which Sirmond and others attribute to Innocent, while we ourselves think should be attributed to Siricius: “Regarding one who, already a believer, has served in secular military service, it is known that he enjoys public freedom; for who can guard him? Who can deny that he may have attended spectacles, or that, prompted by pecuniary advantage, he could not have remained free from violence and injustice?” For this reason Siricius, in Epistle 1 to Himerius, nos. 13 and 14, admits no one to the clergy unless he either from childhood or at a more advanced age, at the very time when he received baptism, enrolled in sacred service among the readers or exorcists. So irreproachable did our fathers wish anyone to be who was consecrated to God’s service.]

IV. A cleric is not to take a woman—that is, a widow—as his wife.

[Note: Quesnel suppressed “that is.” Ferrandus likewise cites this decree in no. 3: “A cleric is not to take a woman as wife”; and Innocent inserted it in precisely these words into his letter to Victricius. Hence there is suspicion that the words “that is, a widow” slipped from a marginal note into the text.

The word *mulier* is indeed ambiguous and is sometimes understood of a woman who has not known a man; more often, however, it denotes a married woman. Thus Jerome, Epistle 83 to Oceanus, after adducing many Scriptural testimonies on this point, adds: “In all these testimonies understand *mulier*, that is, γυνή (*gynē*, ‘woman/wife’), according to the ambiguity of Greek speech.” He then observes that “husband of one wife” may be understood as “husband of one woman” in such a way that it refers more to sexual intercourse than to marriage documents. Likewise Ambrose, although in *On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 5, no. 36, argues that the term *mulier* is not a mark of corruption but a designation of sex, nevertheless does not deny that common usage signifies something else. To this common usage he himself, with other bishops, adapts his language below, Epistle 8 to Siricius, no. 3, where one reads: “Through woman care came; through a virgin salvation came.” In the same sense he writes to the Vercellians, Epistle 69, no. 33: “Through man and woman flesh was expelled from paradise; through a virgin it was joined to God.”]

V. A man who, while a layman, married a widow is not to be admitted to the clergy.

VI. No one is to presume to ordain a cleric belonging to another Church (Council of Nicaea, canon 7; Antioch, canon 22; Sardica, canons 18 and 19).

VII. A cleric cast out is not to be received by another Church (Council of Nicaea, canon 5; Antioch, canon 6; Sardica, canon 16).

VIII. Those coming from the Novatians or Montenses are to be received by the laying on of hands, except those whom they rebaptize.

[Note: Fossat manuscript: “Montanists.” Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, ch. 13, observes that the Novatians at Rome were called Montenses (μοντησίους, “mountain people”). Apparently on no authority other than this letter and another of Innocent, he considered the names Montenses and Novatians, mentioned in both places, synonymous. Baronius, at the year 254, no. 38, traces the first origin of the name Montenses to the fact that the schismatic Felicissimus began gathering his followers in the hills. He thinks Cyprian’s Epistle 38 supports that opinion, where the bishop relates that Felicissimus threatened that those who wished to obey us—that is, Cyprian—would not commune with him on the mountain. But whether Cyprian or the schismatic Felicissimus speaks there of a mountain, it was situated not at Rome but at Carthage.

A trustworthy witness that the Donatists at Rome were customarily called by this name is Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 69, where he says of them: “Those heretics in the city of Rome are called Montenses.” So too in Epistle 165, elsewhere numbered 153, no. 2: “They sent someone ordained from Africa, who, presiding over a few Africans in the city of Rome, propagated the designation Montenses, or Cutzupitani.” Thus Jerome in the *Chronicle*, at the year 360, reports that they were called from the church which they first began to possess at Rome on a hill—not on the hill’s actual summit, but in its hollow, as Optatus explains in Book II: “They had no place in Rome where they could assemble. So they enclosed with steps a certain cave outside the city, where at that time they could hold a meeting; hence they were called Montenses.” Accordingly Emperor Honorius, *Theodosian Code*, Book XVI, title 5, law 42, decrees: “All things [enacted] against the Donatists, who are also called Montenses,” etc.]

[Note: Quesnel: “because they rebaptize.” Our manuscripts likewise read, “because they rebaptize,” except that one has “they may rebaptize,” and another “they may be rebaptized.” The true reading and meaning of this passage must be sought from Innocent’s Epistle 2, no. 11. From both we learn that not only the Montenses or Donatists, but also the Novatians, customarily rebaptized those coming over to them. This is confirmed both by the author of the commentary on Ambrose, I Corinthians 1:14, and by Cyprian at the beginning of Epistle 73 to Jubaianus, cited by Augustine, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book III, ch. 10. Those who had been rebaptized, however, Innocent in the cited passage admits only after prolonged penitential satisfaction, and therefore excludes from the clergy. Nor does the Fifth Council of Carthage, canon 11, permit them ever to be promoted to clerical rank. Leo, Epistle 16 to Januarius, and Felix II, Epistle 11, ch. 5, no. 8, decree the same.]

3. Moreover, we urge what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied in the service by the daily necessities of ministry. For Paul writes thus to the Corinthians: “Abstain yourselves, that you may have leisure for prayer” (I Cor. 7:5). Therefore, if abstinence is commanded even to laypeople so that their prayers may be heard, how much more must a priest be ready at every moment, secure in the purity of cleanliness, lest he be compelled either to offer sacrifice or to baptize? If he has been defiled by carnal desire, what is he to do? How will he excuse himself? With what modesty, with what mind, will he undertake it? With what conscience, by what merit, does he believe that he will be heard, when it has been said: “To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus 1:15)? On this matter I exhort, admonish, and entreat: let this reproach be removed, one which even the pagans may rightly denounce. Perhaps this is believed permissible because it is written: “the husband of one wife” (I Tim. 3:2). He did not say this of one persisting in the desire to beget children, but with regard to future continence. For he did not exclude those who were unmarried when he said: “I would that all men were as I myself am” (I Cor. 7:7). And he explains more plainly when he says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8:8).

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “we urge priests and Levites”; two others, “we urge what priests and Levites [should do].”]

[Note: So one Colbert manuscript, supported by the others. The old Corbie manuscript has: “in the ministry of ministry in daily [matters].” Two others, with Fossat and followed by Merlin, read: “in the ministry, ministers in daily [matters].” Quesnel, omitting *ministri*, retained “in the ministry in daily [matters].” Crabbe, contrary to the authority of the old codices, replaced that word with *divino* and read: “in the divine ministry in daily [matters]”; this reading thereafter prevailed in the Roman edition and the councils. It would not be objectionable [to read]: “because these are ministers of the daily ministry.” Simpler and clearer is Innocent, Epistle 2, no. 12: “because they are occupied by the daily necessities of ministry.” Among those necessities imposing a rule of continence upon the ranks mentioned, Siricius in Epistle 10 includes this: that we may please our God in the sacrifices which we offer DAILY, and in which deacons minister. On the same matter the Second Council of Carthage, canon 2, says: “It is fitting that the most holy bishops and priests of God, likewise Levites, or those who serve the divine sacraments, should be continent in all things, so that they may simply obtain what they ask from God.” Incidentally, one should observe that this council expressly includes presbyters under the designation “priests of God,” by which bishops are commonly denoted among the ancients.]

[Note: “Yours” is absent from all manuscripts, but appears in Innocent’s Epistle 2.]

[Note: Quesnel, who reads “who offers” here, in Dissertation 15, ch. 5, no. 9, lightly ridicules this passage, as though it said that a priest could at any moment be compelled to offer sacrifice; whereas its natural meaning is that a priest ought to be ready at any moment to offer sacrifice or baptize. There is nothing absurd or false in this understanding, if there is no moment at which he may be compelled to baptize.]

[Note: One manuscript: “What can he do to excuse himself?” It would not be objectionable to read: “What can avail to excuse him?” supplying “him.” Another: “What will he do? What will he excuse?” Another: “How will he excuse himself?”]

[Note: The word “this,” omitted in the printed editions, is restored by the authority of all manuscripts: as though it were said, “Perhaps this, which we declare unlawful, is believed permissible.” Innocent also expressed it thus in Epistle 2, no. 12: “But perhaps he believes this permissible, because it is written.” From this passage and similar ones it is clear that Innocent acted as Siricius’s interpreter and sought to express a little more fully and clearly what Siricius had written briefly and obscurely; hence Siricius truly preceded Innocent, not the latter Pseudo-Siricius. But what we read here in Quesnel has the flavor of a gloss: “Perhaps it is believed that a presbyter can, or rather ought, to have a wife, because it is written.” Certainly we find nothing similar in our manuscripts or even in the exemplars of the codex which he published.]

[Note: The Roman edition and the councils, contrary to Merlin, read “persisting.” Other books correctly read “future,” that is, he said or understood [this]—a manner of speaking in which Ambrose, Epistle 63 to the Vercellians, no. 62, says: “For he said ‘having children,’ not ‘begetting [them].’” It concerns the future continence by which a man seeking the priesthood is not permitted to repeat marriage; or, if he has repeated it, to hope for this dignity. See Ambrose’s letter just cited.]

4. Therefore, brothers, if these things are observed by all with full vigilance, ambition will cease, dissension will rest, heresies and schisms will not arise, the devil will find no place for raging, unanimity will remain, iniquity, overcome, will be trampled down, charity will burn with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will agree with the will: namely, the peace of our God, which the Savior himself, when his passion was near, commanded to be preserved (John 14:27), and left to us as an inheritance, saying: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (Phil. 2:2–3); and [let us observe] the Apostle’s saying (I Thess. 2:4), that, being of one mind and thinking the same thing, we may remain in Christ, claiming nothing for ourselves through contention or empty glory, but pleasing not human beings but God our Savior. If we faithfully wish to obey all these precepts, the Lord will guard our bodies and souls until the day when he will render to each according to his works (Phil. 4:7; Rom. 2:5). But if anyone, puffed up by the mind of his flesh, wishes to stray from the rule of this canon, let him know that he is excluded from our communion and will suffer the punishments of Gehenna.

[Note: Quesnel: “canons.” But all the other books read “canon,” or, erroneously, “canons.”]

5. Moreover, mercy must be joined with judgment. For such persons, when they are falling, ought to be offered a hand, provided that they do not drag into ruin one who is thus running [the course prescribed] by the canon.

[Note: One Colbert manuscript, with Quesnel, reads “which … may drag.” More correctly the other books read “who … may drag.” We are admonished that mercy, by which a hand is offered to the falling, should be joined with judgment, by which care is taken that those to whom a hand is offered do not drag into ruin one running according to the rule of the canon, and do not bring destruction upon the canon itself.]

Given at Rome, in a council of eighty bishops, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, after the consulship of Augustus Arcadius and the vir clarissimus Bauto.

[Note: To Quesnel’s objection in Dissertation 15, ch. 5, no. 10—“I do not recall ever reading a letter of any ancient Roman pontiff that was marked at its end as given at Rome, or in a council of bishops”—Stephen Baluze, p. 1354, recalls examples: the letter of Hormisdas to Emperor Anastasius, sent through Theopompus and Severianus; the letter of John II to Emperor Justinian; and two other letters of Gregory the Great, marked at the end as given at Rome. Moreover, just as this letter, first written to the Italians and later sent to the Africans, is marked at its end as given at Rome in a council of eighty bishops, so another similar letter of Damasus, Epistle 3, first written to the bishops of Illyricum and later sent also to the East, is prefaced, as we read, “Copy of the synod held at Rome of ninety-three bishops.” What prevents one letter from bearing this information at its beginning and the other at its end? Especially since a notice placed at the beginning to establish authority establishes it equally if moved to the end.

Papebroch, however, in the *Propylaeum*, p. 60d, taking it as certain that new consuls were often announced before the beginning of the year and therefore could not have been unknown to Siricius on January 6, does not hesitate to reject these chronological notices as spurious. Tillemont, vol. X, p. 791, refutes him, showing from the examples of Ausonius, Saturninus, and others that consuls were then selected only around the end of the year and could easily have been unknown at Rome on January 6. If this happened in other years, it must be granted that the announcement was by no means hastened in 386, when Honorius, an infant of four months, and Evodius, attached to the tyrant Maximus, were created consuls. We shall also see below, in Innocent’s Epistles 29 and 31, that although written on January 27, 417, they are dated after the consulship of Theodosius VII and Junius Quartus. This indicates that Innocent at that time did not know the new consuls Honorius and Constantius.]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

### I. To whom it was primarily written

This letter is found not only in manuscripts of the Isidorian collection, but also in those of another, older collection which we call the Spanish. What we read in no. 2, “Let candidates for ordination come even from afar, so that they may be approved as worthy both by the judgment of the people and by ours,” indicates that it was written to those bishops who were not permitted to ordain “without the knowledge of the Apostolic See”; that is, to those to whom the preceding Epistle 5 was primarily addressed. Yet the present inscription of that letter is not false merely because it is not the primary one. For by the same right by which the following letter could be addressed “to brothers and fellow bishops throughout Africa,” this one could be addressed “to orthodox [bishops] throughout the provinces.” Siricius, being convinced that the care of all churches belonged to him, imitated his predecessors, especially Liberius, of whom he himself recalls in Epistle 1, no. 2, that “general decrees were sent to the provinces.” Whenever he had issued responses in the case of some Church which he thought could contribute to the benefit of others, he took care that they were brought to those Churches’ knowledge. His own Epistle 1 bears witness to this, for there he orders that what he wrote in reply to Himerius be “conveyed to the knowledge of all fellow bishops.” Therefore no one should be disturbed that the inscription bears the title “pope.” For it should be believed to have been assigned not by Siricius himself, but by the person who noted that his letter had been sent to various provinces.

### II. Agreement of this letter with the preceding one; it may be the very letter read at Thusdrus and Telepte

It would be desirable to possess it copied from the original sent to the bishops of Italy, rather than from a copy subsequently given to bishops of other provinces. Yet, although passages remain which seem to require correction from some more accurate exemplar, there is no reason to doubt that it is a product of Siricius. Its agreement with the preceding letter is very great. Both have the same aim: that provisions established by the apostolic constitution of the Fathers, especially concerning ordinations, should be observed. In both occur not only the same thoughts but the same expressions, such as *qua de re* (“on which matter”) for *quare* (“wherefore”), “the disposition of the ecclesiastical canon,” and “the belt of secular military service.” Just as fear of divine judgment and zeal for preserving traditions are urged at the beginning of both, so Christian charity and concord are commended on the same grounds at the end of both. Perhaps also the letter said in no. 3 to have “previously circulated with the consent of many brothers” is none other than the preceding letter, known to have been composed by a large synod in defense of the Nicene canons. If so, there seems to be scarcely any doubt that the letter under discussion is the very one which, as we learned from the preface of the Council of Telepte itself, was first read at the council of Thusdrus and afterwards at Telepte.

### III. When it was written

As to its date, Siricius’s statement concerning certain ambitious persons “who,” he says, “frequently press themselves upon my ears in order that they may become bishops,” and on whose account “the matter has sometimes been contested,” indicates that by then he was no novice in carrying episcopal burdens. But if the letter which Siricius says at the beginning of no. 3 had “previously circulated” is the preceding one, this letter may be considered not much later than it. For he simply says that it had previously circulated, without adding “long ago” or another particle indicating a longer interval. Thus it could easily have happened that those two letters, as relating to the same persons and issued in closely successive councils, were sent together to Africa and read there first at Thusdrus and then at Telepte. The differing addresses of the letters do not oppose this conjecture, since the preceding letter alone reached us from the acts of the African council, while this one came to us from another source.

## EPISTLE VI OF POPE SIRICIUS TO VARIOUS BISHOPS

### I. No unworthy person is to be made bishop. — II. The priesthood is not to be given to unknown persons. — III. Neophytes or laypeople are not to become priests.

Pope Siricius to the orthodox throughout the various provinces.

### CHAPTER I

1. **Siricius’s care for all Churches.** As we consider, dearest brothers, the fear of divine judgment, and that after this life each person will receive according to what he has done, it was not permitted us to keep silent about what comes as a complaint; necessity commanded us to speak, as the prophet says: “Lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). And if I dissemble, I who have care of all the Churches, I shall hear the Lord saying: “You reject the commandment of God, that you may establish your traditions” (Mark 7:9). For what else is it to reject God’s commandment than, by private judgment and human counsel, freely to take pleasure in establishing novel practices?

[Note: Isidore: “You have rejected.” Below, Epistle 10, no. 2: “and supporting.”]

2. **The ordinances of the elders must not be violated. Great care is required in clerical ordinations.** It has therefore come to the knowledge of the Apostolic See that persons presume contrary to the ecclesiastical canon and introduce certain new practices of their own, although these matters were so ordained by the elders that they ought not to be violated even by the slightest whisper; passing over the foundation, they wish to build upon sand. The Lord says: “Do not move the boundaries which your fathers established” (Prov. 22:28). The holy Apostle also, preacher of the New and Old Testament, in whom Christ spoke, admonishes: “Stand fast,” he says, “and hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word or by letter” (II Thess. 2:14). Therefore your sincerity sees how great care and diligent solicitude priests ought to exercise in sacred ministries and in your ordinations. Accordingly he says to Timothy: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (I Tim. 5:22). This is mentioned so that, after examination, the man called forth to receive the high priesthood may be the more commended by uprightness of life and ecclesiastical labor: approved by judgment, not favor; accepted by truth, not partiality; supported by apostolic order, not by precipitous will.

[Note: For greater clarity, supply here: “contrary to those things.”]

[Note: In the manuscripts: “to establish.”]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. But printed editions: “you shall not cross.”]

[Note: Printed editions after Crabbe: “be observed.” More correctly Merlin and the manuscripts: “ought to observe,” that is, how great a vigilance the solicitude of priests ought to employ.]

[Note: A Noyon manuscript has “by apostolic order,” then, with the others, “supported,” except that the Navarre manuscript has “having discharged secondary duties,” and the Rouen manuscript, now belonging to the Capuchin Fathers, formerly of Saint Sergius at Angers, likewise has “supported by secondary duties.” The printed editions prefer *functus* (“having discharged [duties]”); but *fultus* (“supported”) is preferable. This correction is supported by Leo, Epistle 1, ch. 5, where he confirms the decrees of his predecessors, by which it was beneficially established that no layperson, “supported by any votes,” should ascend to the first, second, or third rank in the Church before arriving at that merit through lawful stages. We should not suppose lightly that Leo there refers especially to this passage of Siricius. “Apostolic order” means apostolic ordination, especially that by which Paul forbade the ordination of a neophyte. “High priesthood” likewise means the episcopal rank. In this sense St. Gaudentius of Brescia, in the sermon on his own ordination, calls those by whom he had been elected “high priests.”]

3. **Siricius does not yield to the ambitious.** Concerning this matter, dearest to me, letters of this kind had previously gone forth to your sincerity with the consent of many brothers and fellow priests, so that, confirmed by your subscription, the ordinance of the ecclesiastical canon treated at Nicaea might remain, firmly established according to its merit: namely, that persons such as apostolic authority commands should be permitted to approach ecclesiastical rank—not, I say, those who were once bound by the belt of secular military service. After they have exulted in secular pomp, or desired to serve in affairs of state, or to manage worldly business, they frequently press themselves upon my ears, supported by the laying on of hands of certain persons and surrounded by the favor of their associates, in order that they may become bishops—though by tradition and evangelical discipline they cannot be so. With what exertions has this sometimes been contested! Yet nothing of the sort could be extracted which reason does not compel. Let candidates for ordination come even from afar, so that they may be approved as worthy both by the judgment of the people and by ours.

[Note: The two words “dearest to me” have hitherto been separated by a comma in printed editions, but a similar expression in Epistle 7, no. 3—where we shall read “most beloved to me”—suggests that they can be joined; and the sequence of the argument requires it. Siricius indicates that he had previously not merely received letters, but sent them with the consent of many brothers. It is therefore almost beyond doubt that “previously to your holiness” should be restored nearby; the preposition *ad* was easily dropped by copyists. What follows concerning these letters fits the preceding letter very well: it was composed with the consent of many bishops, namely eighty, concerning the rules to be observed in clerical ordinations; its decrees accord with Nicaea, and it expressly excludes from the clergy anyone who has worn the belt of secular military service. Nor does it appear that it was sent to those who could not attend because of ill health or advanced age for any other reason than that they might ratify the synodal constitution by their subscription and that such a standard might be preserved forever by all.]

[Note: Merlin and the manuscripts read “be elicited.” We interpret the passage thus: “None of those things which reason does not compel could be elicited from me.” Here Siricius explains more clearly than in the preceding letter that by those who have worn the belt of secular military service he means not only men who have served in military camps, but also those bound by public affairs.]

[Note: That is, I think, from Sicily, Sardinia, and other regions belonging to the Roman pontiff’s diocese or synod, called suburban. But if anyone should imagine that Siricius meant that every candidate for the episcopate, from wherever he came, should come to Rome, Siricius’s own words refute him. In this letter he commands that the ecclesiastical canonical constitution treated at Nicaea remain firmly established. But by the ordinance and prescription of the Council of Nicaea, canons 4 and 6, authority to ordain bishops in each province belongs to the metropolitan. This decree therefore resembles chapter 1 of the preceding letter.]

### CHAPTER II

4. **Wandering monks are ordained by bishops in order to spare expenses.** The unlawfulness of this cannot be measured: that some should be unwilling to assist at their own expense travelers—whether they pretend to be, or are, monks, as they call themselves—whose life we cannot know, whose baptism, faith, and character are unknown and untested, but should hasten immediately to make them deacons or ordain them presbyters, or, what is graver, should not shrink from appointing them bishops. In their eyes it is costlier to provide maintenance for a traveler than to confer the priesthood. Not being detained so that they may be examined, they are then exalted into pride, and then quickly fall further into unbelief, because they are not said to have learned the true faith while wandering among the Churches throughout the world.

[Note: The word [*est*, “is”] had been deleted by Crabbe and is restored from Merlin and the manuscripts. It is to be referred not to *sumptum* (“expense”) but to *charius* (“costlier”), thus: “In their eyes it is costlier to provide maintenance for a traveler than to confer the priesthood”; that is, they value the priesthood less than a traveler’s maintenance. The printed editions then read, “than the priesthood not retained.” This must be understood as follows: those monks are not detained in order that their faith and morals may be tested, but are immediately dismissed with priestly rank; from this they are exalted into pride.]

### CHAPTER III

5. **What necessity has extorted once or twice is not to be treated as law.** Certainly this too was not to be passed over: that what the necessity caused by heretics had introduced once or twice against apostolic commands should not begin to be presumed, as though lawful by statute—namely, the inconsiderate ordination as presbyter or deacon of a neophyte (I Tim. 3:6), or of a layman who has exercised no ecclesiastical office—as though such men were better than the Apostles, whose command they dare to alter. And one who has not learned is already compelled to teach. Is no suitable cleric to be found? Is there no one among the deacons or among the other clerics judged worthy of the priesthood, but a layperson is demanded to the condemnation of the Church? That this may not happen any longer, I admonish and proclaim that, having one faith, we ought also to think one thing in tradition, showing ourselves united and concordant, peaceful in Christ, and maintaining charity in apostolic observances. Therefore, through the Father, his only-begotten Son, the Holy Spirit, and the Trinity of one divinity, I entreat that in these matters the Catholic faith and our discipline may remain. Let no one suppose that ordinations are made as though they were earthly, since the priesthood is heavenly, so that the faithful may retain the glory of this dignity and thereafter have nothing for which to accuse themselves before Christ’s tribunal.

[Note: The printed editions lack *coepisse* (“to have begun”), which we supply from manuscripts of the Spanish collection. We would prefer *coepisset* (“had begun”), and would read the entire passage thus: “It was not to be passed over that what the necessity caused by heretics had introduced once or twice should have begun to be presumed by some as lawful by statute, contrary to apostolic commands—namely, [the ordination of] a neophyte or …” What is said here of the ordination of a neophyte or layman, introduced by the necessity of heretics, seems to apply especially to Ambrose’s ordination. Siricius prudently guards against anyone’s using this or another similar example to abolish a law received in the Church.]

[Note: Celestine I treats this argument more fully in Epistle 4, no. 4. See also Zosimus, Epistle 9, no. 2, and Felix II’s letter to Caesarius of Arles. Accordingly Gregory I customarily concludes his command to any visitor appointed to preside over the election of bishops with these words: “Take care above all that lay persons of whatever manner of life or merit do not presume to aspire to this, lest you incur, which God forbid, the peril of your ordination.” He also customarily addresses the electors thus: “Know without doubt that all among you who are found to have aspired from lay status are to be excluded from office and communion.”]

[Note: That is, an injury and insult to those devoted to the service of the Church—in a word, to ecclesiastics.]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

### I

We have collated this letter with old exemplars of different collections: namely, the codex published by Quesnel; another collection no less ancient, preserved in the Colbert Library; and also the Spanish and Isidorian collections. Yet in none did we find the title given it by Quesnel: “Of Pope Siricius to all bishops of Italy concerning the condemnation of Jovinian and the other heretics who disparage virginity.” Isidore, bishop of Seville, mentioning it in Book 3, ch. 3, of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, reports that it was sent to various bishops; and all our manuscripts agree, in which it is marked as sent through various bishops. The title which we present was copied from manuscripts of the Spanish collection. Isidore Mercator retained the same title, but added from his own resources the salutation: “Pope Siricius sends greetings to the orthodox bishops throughout the various provinces.” In place of this salutation, Crabbe and subsequent editions read: “Siricius [to] the Church of Milan.” But that new address, in my opinion, rests upon no other basis than the fact that this letter was sent to Milan and that Ambrose with his colleagues replied to it. Mabillon, however, in *Italian Journey*, p. 69, notes that in a codex in the Vallicellian Library at Rome this letter is addressed not to the bishop of Milan but to all bishops. He meant only to note that it is addressed not to the Church of Milan, as circulated in the printed editions, but to various bishops. For that codex does not differ from ours, which with strong agreement read “various bishops,” not “all bishops.” Such slips may be forgiven to those who briefly inspect a foreign library and, after returning home, record from memory what they found there worthy of note.

Jerome and Augustine appear to indicate this letter. Jerome does so when, at the beginning of his book *Against Vigilantius*, he teaches that Jovinian was condemned “by the authority of the Roman Church,” and when, at the beginning of Book III *Against the Pelagians*, he repeats that Jovinian’s opinions were “formerly condemned at Rome and long ago in Africa.” Augustine does so in *Retractations*, Book II, ch. 12: after stating that Jovinian’s heresy had greatly prevailed in the city of Rome, he adds, “The holy Church which is there resisted this monstrosity most faithfully and courageously.” Siricius himself testifies that he wrote this letter so that bishops would not be ignorant of what had been done at Rome in Jovinian’s condemnation.

### II

The date at which it was written may be determined from what follows. In it he rather clearly implies that Jovinian and his companions, driven from Rome, fled to Milan to Emperor Theodosius. Now Theodosius, after defeating Maximus—which some place in August and others in September of 388—is said first to have come to Milan; historical records attest that he came thence to Rome on the Ides of June 389 and, after celebrating a triumph there, returned to Milan on the Kalends of September. It follows that, if this letter is placed before Theodosius’s triumph, it cannot be earlier than the end of 388; if it is placed afterwards, it should be considered as preceding the end of 389 by no great interval.

## EPISTLE VII OF POPE SIRICIUS, SENT TO VARIOUS BISHOPS AGAINST THE HERETIC JOVINIAN AND HIS ASSOCIATES, WHO ARE TO BE REMOVED FROM THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH

It publicly exposes the perverse teaching of Jovinian and his associates, and announces by name the condemnation of its principal authors.

### Jovinian’s Doctrine, the Devil Being Its Author

1. I would always wish, most dearly beloved brethren, to report to the sincerity of your charity and peace matters of joy, so that, as letters pass back and forth, those joys might be aided by news of your well-being. [Note: Crabbe: “might communicate indications”; Merlin: “might be aided by indications”; Quesnel: “might be aided by an indication”; other editions: “we might be aided by an indication.” But the manuscripts, with great agreement, read “might be aided”—that is, the joys—“by an indication.”] Yet because the ancient enemy, a liar from the beginning, the enemy of truth and rival of humankind, does not permit us to be at rest, free from his attacks—he who, in order to deceive humankind, first deceived himself; the adversary of chastity and teacher of luxury, who feeds upon cruelties, must be punished by abstinence, hates fasts, and, while his ministers preach, declares them superfluous—having no hope in things to come, struck down by the Apostle’s saying: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Cor. 15:32).

[Note: Quesnel reads “is tormented”; other editions, “is punished,” corrected from the better manuscripts.]

[Note: The Roman edition after Crabbe reads “says the same,” against the manuscripts. Ambrose, Epistle 63, §7, writes of Sarmatio and Barbatianus, followers of Jovinian’s errors, that they were empty talkers, saying that abstinence has no merit, frugality no merit, virginity no grace, and that all are valued at an equal price; he says that those who discipline their flesh by fasts are mad.]

2. **How pernicious while it remained concealed.**—O unhappy audacity! O cunning of a desperate mind! The previously unknown discourse of heretics was already creeping through the Church like a cancer, so that, taking possession of the breast, it might hurl the whole person into death. And unless the Lord of Sabaoth had broken the snare which they had prepared, the public exposure of so great an evil and hypocrisy would have drawn many simple hearts into ruin. For the human mind is easily led over to the worse side, preferring to flutter through broad spaces rather than traverse, with labor, the path of the narrow way.

[Note: Crabbe, followed by the Roman and conciliar editions, reads “had prepared,” and then “had drawn,” contrary to the manuscripts.]  
[Note: The Roman edition reads “preferring”; other conciliar editions, following manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, read “willing rather.” In the more reliable books *magis* (“rather”) is omitted, which is not unusual in ancient writers. The Roman edition then reads “to walk through broad places”; Merlin and other conciliar editions, with the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, “to walk by the broad way.” One Colbert manuscript reads “than the path of a narrow life.”]

3. **How it was detected and condemned. Priests attend marriages.**—For this reason it was altogether necessary, beloved, to send to your knowledge what has occurred here, lest the ignorance of any priest should allow the Church to be defiled by the contagion of utterly wicked persons invading it under a religious name. As the Lord says in Scripture: “Many will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves; by their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. 7:15–16).

[Note: Quesnel reads “ignorance,” incorrectly. Siricius takes care that bishops should know what had been done at Rome against the new heretics, lest, if anyone were ignorant of it, the Church should be defiled by the contagion of the worst men—and this under a religious name, since Jovinian was still boasting, as Jerome writes against him, that he was a monk.]

These are plainly those who subtly boast that they are Christians: under the veil of a pious name they proceed, enter the house of prayer, and pour forth the discourse of serpentine disputation, “that they may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:3); by turning people away from Catholic truth, they lead them after the manner of the devil into the frenzy of their own doctrine, and rob the simplicity of the sheep.

[Note: In the Pithoean manuscript and one Colbert manuscript: “These are plainly those, as if by the usefulness of Christ.” In the other Colbert manuscript: “These are plainly those who, as if by some usefulness of Christ”; correcting this, Quesnel substituted: “These are plainly those who [proceed] under the cheapness of their garments.” This correction at one time pleased our editors of Ambrose. But, besides lacking even clear manuscript authority, it is plainly opposed by Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, I, after the middle: the heretic, although boasting that he was a monk, after a filthy tunic, bare feet, bread for food, and water for drink, turned to white clothing, a polished skin, sweet wine, and elaborate meats. Hence in Book II, around the middle, Jerome addresses him thus: “Formerly you went barefoot; now you are not merely shod but adorned. Then you wore a rough tunic and a black undergarment; now you walk clothed in linen and silk garments, adorned with apparel from Arras and Laodicea.” And near the end: “All whom I see handsome, all whom I see curled, with arranged hair and reddened cheeks, belong to your herd.” Must Jovinian be said to have changed his first clothing later, while retaining it at the beginning of his perverse preaching? This might be imagined, unless both his teaching and the softness of life criticized by Siricius opposed those affectedly filthy garments. Therefore the received reading, confirmed not only by manuscripts of Isidore but also by the Hispanic collection, is rightly preferred to an insufficiently secure conjecture.]

We have learned, and have proved by experience, the malignity of many heresies from the apostles until now. Yet never have such dogs wearied the mystery of the Church with their barking as these enemies of the faith, suddenly springing up, with a teaching of perfidy burgeoning forth, whose disciples they are made known by the fruits of their words.

[Note: The older manuscripts and Quesnel read “from the apostles until now”; the other books read “from apostolic times.”]  
[Note: Baronius, as in the Roman edition, reads: “such as these, suddenly springing up, polluted with a doctrine of perfidy, enemies of the faith, who [show] whose [disciples] they are.” Our reading is that of the other books, except that one Colbert manuscript has *polluta* and three others *pollutorum* for *pullulata* (“burgeoning forth”).]

For whereas other heretics, by wrongly understanding individual kinds of questions, have proposed to overthrow and tear apart matters belonging to divine ordinances, these men, who have no wedding garment (Matt. 22:12), wound Catholics, pervert the content of the New and Old Testaments, as I have said, and interpret it in a devilish spirit. By seductive and feigned speech they have already begun to devastate certain Christians and join them to their madness, keeping the poison of their wickedness within themselves.
