[Note: In manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, as in Crabbe, *interpretantes* (“interpreting”) is absent. The same word, and also the words “and in a devilish spirit,” are absent from the Roman edition and Baronius; they are restored from the other books. The phrase “the content of the New and Old Testament” may aptly mean what is contained and taught in the New and Old Testament. Jerome uses *continentia* in this sense in Epistle 61 to Pammachius, where he reports that John of Jerusalem was accused of allegorizing Paradise so as to take away the truth of the history, “and to overthrow the whole CONTENT of Paradise by a tropological interpretation.” The false interpretation which Siricius notes is particularly evident in the argument by which, according to Augustine, *Retractations* II.12, Jovinian pressed consecrated virgins: “Are you therefore better than Sarah, better than Susanna, than Anna?” He named other women most highly commended by the testimony of Holy Scripture, women whom those virgins could not regard themselves as better than, or even equal to.]  
[Note: Instead of “Christians,” Quesnel reads “Romans,” against the other books. Yet Augustine, *Retractations* II.12, suggests that Siricius may here refer to what happened specifically at Rome: “Jovinian’s heresy, by equating the merit of consecrated virgins with marital chastity, gained such force in the city of Rome that it was said to have brought even certain nuns, concerning whose chastity no suspicion had previously existed, down into marriage … In this way also, by mentioning the fathers and comparing them, he undermined the holy celibacy of holy men.”]  
[Note: Quesnel, and from him the new edition of Ambrose, reads “not keeping within themselves,” with an added negative particle, though no authority of any manuscript appears. The reading of the other books is supported by Augustine, *Retractations* II.12: “These disputations remained in the conversations and whispers of certain persons, which no one dared to advocate openly.” The sequence of the sentence requires the same reading.]

But, as chosen men, they publicly brought forth their blasphemies in a rash written composition; driven by the fury of a desperate mind, they published them everywhere in favor of the Gentiles.

[Note: Merlin and Crabbe, as in manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, read “as if chosen.” Labbe, from Crabbe’s margin and in some editions of Ambrose, reads “but chosen.” Two older Colbert manuscripts and one Pithoean manuscript read “but ensnared.” We have scarcely any doubt that “but detected” should be restored: those who kept the poison of their wickedness within themselves, as soon as they realized that it could no longer remain hidden, began publicly to defend in writing the blasphemies which they had previously whispered secretly. Yet we did not wish to impose a reading supported by no certain authority. Quesnel’s “but their chosen ones” seems suspect of interpolation and falsity, as though Jovinian and his companions, like the Manichaeans, had had their own “elect”; no one has recorded this. No less interpolated is the Roman edition: “the poison, setting themselves forward as if chosen, nevertheless made their blasphemies public by a rash composition.”]  
[Note: Most and the oldest manuscripts, with Merlin, read “in fury”; two others read “fury,” without *in*; Quesnel, “fury.” “In favor,” with the Roman, Crabbe, and Ambrosian editions, is preferable, because *furore* (“by fury”) immediately precedes and because Jovinian’s teaching in fact strongly favors Gentile customs. Thereafter the Roman edition alone reads “they put themselves forward” instead of “they published.”]

But from most faithful Christians—men excellent by birth and distinguished in religion—a horrific written composition was suddenly brought to my lowliness, so that, once exposed as contrary to the divine law by priestly judgment, it might be destroyed by a spiritual sentence.

[Note: Quesnel reads: “But their madness seems suddenly to have been reported by the most faithful … through an honorable written composition,” an interpolated reading not conforming to Siricius’s meaning. One Colbert manuscript, as also the Reims and Pithoean manuscripts, reads *scriptura honorifica* (“honorable writing”), and Merlin *honorificata*; but *scriptura horrifica* (“horrific writing”) is to be preferred with the other books—namely, the very composition which a little earlier was called a rash writing. It is now called horrific both because it was strewn with blasphemies and because of the barbarity of its style. For Jerome, *Against Jovinian* I, observes that the writing of this heretic is so barbarous and his foul speech so confused with so many defects that, he says, “I could understand neither what he says nor by what arguments he wishes to prove what he says.” Nor is the reading in Baronius, as in the Roman edition, more acceptable: “they seem to have been reported by a horrific writing,” so that the words “once exposed” are deleted. Among those most faithful Christians who brought Jovinian’s horrific writing to Siricius, Pammachius was foremost. Jerome therefore addresses him in Epistle 50: “Through your action, after the Lord, he was condemned because he dared to compare marriage to perpetual virginity.”]

Certainly, we do not receive marriage vows with contempt; we attend them with the veil. But we honor with greater distinction virgins whom marriage produces and who are devoted to God. Therefore, when the presbyterium had been assembled, it was established that this teaching was contrary to our doctrine—that is, to the Christian law.

[Note: Labbe reads “not despising marriages.”]  
[Note: Such is the manuscript reading. But the Roman edition and Baronius read: “we have attended at your veiling, but we honor the marriages of virgins devoted to God …”; Merlin and Crabbe: “we have attended with the veil,” and then Merlin alone: “but virgins devoted to God,” omitting “whom marriage produces.” Labbe reads “we venerate” for “we reward,” though “reward” more fittingly conveys the recompense owed to virginity as it possesses greater merit. Crabbe’s conjecture *vero animo* (“with a true mind”) for *velamine* (“with the veil”) must not be accepted. For Ambrose, Epistle 19 to Vigilius, §17, writes that marriage itself should be sanctified by the priestly veil and blessing. Thus Siricius rightly answers Jovinian, who preached that marriages were despised by those preferring continence to them.]  
[Note: The Reims manuscript has “the law of Christ.” Then the old Colbert manuscript: “that certain things were contrary.” The Roman and conciliar editions, with some manuscripts, read “that [they] were contrary.” The older Pithoean manuscript, as well as the Navarre and Capuchin manuscripts, more truly reads “that it was contrary”—namely, the writing which Pammachius and his companions had asked, by submitting their petition, to be condemned if it were found contrary to the divine law. Accommodating his judgment to that petition, Siricius first declares the writing brought forward to be contrary to Christian law, and then proscribes and condemns it as such. Therefore Quesnel’s “that their opinion was contrary” has the character of a gloss and is found nowhere else. “Therefore, when the presbyterium had been assembled” means “therefore, when the assembly of the clergy had been gathered,” as we have already observed in Liberius’s Epistle 11, who uses *presbyterium* in the same expression and sense. Surviving ancient records show how customary it was for Roman pontiffs to deliberate on ecclesiastical affairs with this assembly, to which even visiting bishops were customarily admitted.]

4. **The promoters of the new heresy are condemned.**—Therefore, following the Apostle’s command (Gal. 1:9), because they proclaimed something other than what we had received, know that there was one judgment of us all—presbyters, deacons, and indeed the entire clergy—that Jovinian, Auxentius, Genialis, Germinator, Felix, Plotinus, Martianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus, who were found to be promoters of the new heresy and blasphemy, should remain forever condemned outside the Church by the divine sentence and by our judgment.

[Note: Quesnel, with two manuscripts, reads “those [who proclaimed] something else,” and then, with no manuscript authority known to me, adds after “proclaimed,” “we excommunicated.”]  
[Note: Thus read the two older Colbert and Pithoean manuscripts, with Quesnel. But Crabbe and Merlin, following manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, read “it is established that one judgment was made.” The Roman edition reads “there was one total judgment”; Labbe, “one judgment was raised.” It is evident from this that the assembly called *presbyterium* from its more distinguished rank sometimes consisted not only of presbyters but also of deacons and the remaining clergy.]  
[Note: In manuscripts, as in Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 3, and in Merlin: Auxentius.]  
[Note: The manuscripts agree closely with the Roman edition and Quesnel in reading Plotinus. But the Reims and Ambrosian manuscripts read Prontinus; Baronius, Pontinus, with Frontinus in the margin.]  
[Note: The old manuscripts of the Hispanic collection—those of Laon and Noyon—and most manuscripts of the Isidorian collection, with Merlin and Crabbe, read *accentores* (“assistants”); Reims, *actores* (“agents”); the two older Colbert manuscripts and Pithoean manuscript, with Quesnel, *auctores* (“authors”).]

Not doubting that your holiness will observe this, I have sent these writings through my brethren and fellow-presbyters Crescens, Leopardus, and Alexander, who can fulfill the religious duty of faith with fervent spirit.

[Note: Baronius, as in the Roman edition, reads “presbyters.” The reading “fellow-presbyters,” found in the other codices, is confirmed by ancient usage. Indeed, Augustine, even when addressing deacons, called them fellow-deacons. Thus in Epistle 149 to Paulinus, §1, one reads: “concerning the very prosperous arrival of our brother and fellow-presbyter Quintus”; and shortly afterward, “on the occasion of our son and fellow-deacon Rufinus.” At the end of the same letter: “Our fellow-deacon Peregrinus … has not yet returned … We greet fellow-presbyter Paulinus.” Epistles 191, to fellow-presbyter Sixtus; 492, to fellow-deacon Celestine; and 222 and 224, to fellow-deacon Quodvultdeus, bear these forms of address. Likewise Orosius is called fellow-presbyter by the Council of Carthage at the beginning of its letter to Innocent I. Baronius notes that Leopardus was a presbyter of the title of Pastor, from which Siricius too had been raised to Peter’s see, and that his name is still preserved on a marble tablet.]

## EPISTLE VIII

[Note: In the Roman edition it had been reproduced from the commonly circulated manuscripts of Ambrose. It is preserved in the old exemplars of the text published by Quesnel, chapter 31, and in several others. It was written in reply to Siricius’s preceding letter not long afterward, while the Emperor Theodosius was at Milan—thus in 388 or 389, as we demonstrated in the Notice on the preceding epistle.]

### Or Reply of Ambrose and Other Bishops to Pope Siricius Concerning the Above-Mentioned Matter. (C, G)

They recount and refute the errors of Jovinian and his companions: first, because they abolish degrees of merit and equate marriage with virginity; then, because they deny Mary’s virginity in childbirth; next, because they oppose fasts. Finally, having observed that their teaching concerning Christ’s birth supports the Manichaeans, they subscribe to Siricius’s judgment condemning them.

See Ambrose’s letter in the works of that same holy Father, vol. XVI of our *Patrologia*, col. 1123.

## Notice on the Following Epistle

I. **What must be investigated.**—There is more than one question concerning this epistle. Scholars do not agree even about its author. Nor is there greater agreement concerning Bonosus, on whose account it was written. They debate what his error or crime was, what see he held, and whether he was himself the person called by the ancients the leader of the Bonosiacs. To clarify these matters, it will first help to know when the epistle itself was written.

II. **When it was written.**—The epistle itself bears no obscure indication of the time when it was written. For in it the Council of Capua is mentioned as having been held recently. Now this synod has been shown, in the latest edition of Ambrose—where the sequence of Epistle 56 is established—to have been celebrated after Theodosius’s return to Constantinople, that is, after 26 November 391, and before Valentinian’s death, that is, before 15 May 392. It follows that this epistle too is rightly considered to have been written in 392, before May; especially since the disturbances in Italy following Valentinian’s death do not permit it to be dated later.

III. **It is falsely attributed to Damasus.**—Accordingly, the view of Nicholas of Cusa, *On Catholic Concord* II.18; James Almain, *On the Authority of the Church*; Cajetan, *On the Comparison of the Authority of Pope and Council*; and Robert Cook, Book III, ch. 14, who ascribe this epistle to Damasus, cannot be defended. That pope had already died in 384, so that his successor Siricius answered Himerius’s inquiries at the beginning of 385. They did not adopt this opinion on the authority of any manuscript assigning the epistle to Damasus, but were misled by the order in which they saw it placed among Ambrose’s letters. They observed that it was positioned immediately before what is now Ambrose’s Epistle 17, in which Damasus is mentioned as still alive, but did not even suspect that this letter concerned Damasus’s successor. How much more probable would this opinion have appeared to them if they had read in Marius Mercator, Baluzian edition, p. 165, that Bonosus was “previously condemned by Damasus”! Yet Mercator did not call Bonosus previously condemned by Damasus in any other sense than that in which we may say that Socinus was previously condemned by the Council of Nicaea and by Damasus himself. Mercator refers to the confession of faith which Damasus sent to Paulinus, especially to this statement: “We anathematize Photinus, who, renewing the heresy of Ebion, confesses the Lord Jesus Christ to be only from Mary.” For Bonosus too was reported to renew the same error.

IV. **Nor is it Ambrose’s.**—Not only the old editions of Ambrose, but also the Colbert manuscript, the manuscript of Carolilocum, and some others, attribute the same epistle to Ambrose. But Baronius, at the year 389, proves that it is not Ambrose’s, since at §2 Bonosus is said to have consulted “our brother Ambrose.” Our brethren who prepared Ambrose’s edition observed, to be sure, that this could have been said by Ambrose not in his own name but in the name of a synod over which he presided; they also noted the great affinity of this little work with Ambrose’s undisputed writings, such as *On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 5, and Epistle 63 to the Church of Vercelli, §109. But if Ambrose speaks in this epistle in the name of a synod, it ought to be entitled in the name of that synod as well, not in Ambrose’s; consequently, the authority of the title in those codices—which is clearly false—is weak. For this reason the aforementioned brethren, although placing it among Ambrose’s letters, published it without a heading and in a different typeface.

V. **It is rightly restored to Siricius.**—Justellus, in his notes on canon 48 of the African Ecclesiastical Code, thinks it should be assigned to Siricius; and the men mentioned above in §3—Cusanus and others—support him insofar as they take it for certain that it belongs to some Roman pontiff. Had it been shown to them that it was written in Siricius’s time, they would not have hesitated immediately to adopt the same opinion. Finally, Luca Holstenius restored it to this pope in the Roman bipartite collection. Launoy approves and praises that restoration in vol. I, his letter to Samboeuf, where he also discusses this epistle at length. Labbe subsequently restored it to its place among Siricius’s letters. Holstenius died before his work was printed and could not record in which manuscript he had found this epistle with its sounder title. But there is no room to doubt that he did not invent that title himself—one which no one can deny is entirely fitting—but copied it on the authority of some ancient exemplar. For there was no reason for him to publish it anew among the letters of Roman pontiffs, which he was first publishing either newly or in better texts, unless the title itself, newly found and supported by an ancient codex, had persuaded him that it was rightly to be regarded as better and, in some fashion, new. Its agreement with the cited writings of Ambrose, especially from §3 onward, must nevertheless not be denied. But either Ambrose may have lent Siricius his assistance in this matter, or Siricius may have thought fit to use Ambrose’s arguments against Bonosus’s reported error, arguments advanced in the Synod of Capua or elsewhere.

VI. **Different opinions concerning Bonosus.**—Baronius, at the year 389, Petavius, *Ecclesiastical Dogmatics*, vol. IV, Book XIV, and others admit that they do not know over which Church this Bonosus presided. In his notes on Avitus, Sirmond conjectures that he was bishop of Naissus in Dacia. His conjecture undoubtedly rests on Innocent’s Epistle 16 to Marcianus, bishop of Naissus; and Holstenius therefore defends the same view in his geographical notes on the Roman patriarchate, pp. 122–123. But John Garner, in his commentaries on Marius Mercator, relying on Mercator’s own authority, affirms that Bonosus presided over the metropolitan see of Sardica. Hence Tillemont, vol. X, p. 755, readily admits that Bonosus was bishop either in Macedonia or in a neighboring province, and proposes the question whether two Bonosi should be distinguished: one, bishop of Naissus, of whom Siricius and Innocent speak; the other, bishop of Sardica, whom Marius Mercator and other writers make leader of the Bonosiacs. In his characteristic modesty, he testifies that he does not dare to be the first to assert this distinction, but does not conceal that he sees nothing opposed to it.

VII. **Whether two Bonosi must be distinguished.**—He further supports this distinction by observing that Siricius and Innocent refer to a Bonosus whom they suggest was accused rather of canonical crimes than of any heresy; in particular, Innocent required no profession of faith from clerics ordained by him. But we are surprised that this escaped a man outstanding in diligent scholarship. For Siricius teaches that the Bonosus of whom he speaks was “rightly reproved concerning Mary’s sons,” and observes that, by asserting this, he “asserts nothing other than the perfidy of the Jews, who say that he”—Christ—“could not have been born from a virgin.” And Innocent, Epistle 16 to Marcianus, writes that it had been decided concerning clerics ordained by Bonosus that, if, “having condemned his error, they wished to be joined to the Church, they should gladly be received, lest perhaps those who were worthy of recovering salvation should perish in the same error.” Since, therefore, the Bonosus of whom Siricius and Innocent speak is known to have been stained by error, it remains to inquire whether the error for which Siricius says he was accused differed from that attributed by others to the leader of the Bonosiacs. But the other authorities agree that the leader of the Bonosiacs renewed the heresy of Ebion, Paul of Samosata, and Photinus.

These are Marius Mercator’s words concerning him: “Marcellus of Galatia followed the philosopher Ebion, as did Photinus, and in later times Bonosus, who was previously condemned by Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome.” For this reason Pope Gelasius, Epistle 33, §4, condemns Photinus and Bonosus, “who fell away through a similar error.” Likewise the Fathers of the Second Council of Arles, having spoken in canon 16 concerning Photinians and Paulianists, declare in canon 17 that they judge the Bonosiacs to come “as it were from the same error.” Gennadius likewise held no other view; in *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 14, he mentions a book by Audentius directed principally “against the Photinians, who are now called Bonosiacs.” He says similar things about them in *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 22, or 52. Gregory the Great also, Book XI, Epistle 67 to Quiricus, includes the Bonosiacs among those who stray from the faith of the Trinity, insofar as, as Avitus, bishop of Vienne, more plainly explains in Epistle 3, p. 29, “they take away from Christ the honor of divinity.” Augustine also appears rightly to speak of the leader of these heretics when, replying in Epistle 242 to Elpidius, who denied Christ’s divinity and directed him to Bonosus as a person capable of persuading him of the same opinion, he writes: “I most gladly embrace your goodwill in having thought me worthy, as you write, to send me even across the sea to Bonosus and Jason, most learned men, to bring back abundant fruits from their disputations.” From this it may also be inferred that the heresiarch was still alive when Augustine wrote this.

Certainly, these varied testimonies establish that there was a Bonosus who gave his name to the sect of the Bonosiacs; that they were classed with the Ebionites and Paulianists; and that they were called new Photinians because, just as those groups did, they deprived Christ of divinity. But this error is none other than the perfidy of the Jews which Siricius attributes to Bonosus. Therefore the leader of the Bonosiacs should not be considered different from the Bonosus reproved by the same pope. Accordingly, Ambrose, in *On the Institution of Virgins*, refuting from chapters 5 through 9 the objections of Bonosus—whom he does not name but indicates clearly—and defending Mary’s perpetual virginity, proceeds in chapters 10 and 11 and in the middle of chapter 12 to refute those attacking the equality of the Trinity and the divinity of the Son; finally, in the latter part of chapter 12 itself, he returns to the defense of Mary’s integrity. He adds nothing indicating that he is refuting different heretics. The fall was indeed easy for one who had once proclaimed that children were born from Mary: he could go so far as to preach, with Ebion and the Jews, that Christ too was born no differently, and thus that he was “an ordinary man, born from Mary and Joseph.”

VIII. **Bonosus should be considered bishop of Sardica.**—Now, if there was only one Bonosus, why should we not regard him as bishop of Sardica rather than of the Church of Naissus, since we have the explicit authority of Marius Mercator, who lived in his time and calls him Sardican? Against testimony so explicit and weighty, nothing can be opposed except a bare conjecture: because Bonosus is said to have ordained clerics of Naissus, and the canons prohibit ordaining clerics of another Church. But that conjecture is all the weaker because Bonosus, in order to acquire more adherents, as Innocent testifies in Epistle 17, §12, “performed unlawful ordinations everywhere and without any examination.” The canons would also have required that, if Bonosus had been bishop of Naissus, his case be referred to the bishop of Sardica, his metropolitan, rather than to neighboring bishops. For the supreme pontiffs entrusted to the bishop of Thessalonica, acting in their stead, the examination of cases that might arise in the Churches of Mediterranean Dacia, Riparian Dacia, Moesia, and so on, provided that this was done “with their primacy preserved,” as Innocent expressly testifies in Epistle 13 to Rufus, §3. But the case of the bishop of Sardica, metropolitan or primate of the province of Dacia, ought to have been heard by the bishop of Thessalonica, who was established as “first among the primates,” as Innocent says in the passage cited. The Council of Capua therefore preserved intact this right of Anysius when it referred Bonosus’s case to him. At the same time, the synod complied with the canons which require that judges of bishops be selected not from a distant province but from a neighboring one—especially Antiochene canon 14 and Sardican canon 7—when it ordered that “particularly the Macedonians” be joined with Anysius as judges in this matter.

IX. **Anysius’s judgment against the Bonosiacs.**—We learn from Innocent’s Epistles 16 and 17 what Anysius’s judgment was. He condemned Bonosus in such a way that those ordained by him, if “having condemned his error, they wished to be joined to the Church, should gladly be received.” From this judgment the Second Council of Arles rightly observed, canon 17, that it was clear that the Bonosiacs were “baptized in the Trinity.” Accordingly, although the same council recognizes Photinians or Paulianists and Bonosiacs as coming “from the same error,” it nevertheless decreed that Photinians or Paulianists “must be baptized,” but that Bonosiacs, “if, when questioned, they have confessed our faith with their whole heart, are to be received in the Church with chrism and the laying on of hands.” Bonosus, however, did not abide by this solemn judgment. He continued to ordain new clerics from every quarter, indeed to defile through repeated ordination some who had already been ordained in the Catholic Church. As we shall see there, this was the cause and occasion of Innocent’s Epistles 16 and 17, and of fresh disturbances. Perhaps we seem overlong in these matters; but we considered it worthwhile to explain a question not yet adequately untangled by scholars, so that light may also be shed on the aforementioned letters of Innocent.

## EPISTLE IX: Pope Siricius to Anysius of Thessalonica and the Other Bishops of Illyricum. (C)*

Asked for a judgment concerning Bonosus, Siricius does not wish to pronounce one, but orders the judges appointed for him by the Synod of Capua to discharge their duty. Meanwhile, he confirms that Bonosus was rightly reproved, and was an object of horror, for his error concerning Mary’s children.

To the most beloved brethren Anysius and the other bishops established throughout Illyricum, Siricius.

[Note: In the Beauvais manuscript and other manuscripts, no superscription or salutation is prefixed. One Colbert manuscript and another formerly belonging to Thou have: “Ambrose to Theophilus”; in early editions of Ambrose, “and to Anysius” is added to these words. We suspected that copyists added this superscription in imitation of Ambrose’s Epistle 56 to Theophilus. Reading there that the Synod of Capua had entrusted Theophilus and the Egyptian bishops with examining the case concerning the see of Antioch between Evagrius and Flavian, they inferred that the same synod entrusted to the same Theophilus the examination of Bonosus’s case and that Ambrose now wrote to him concerning it. But their error is manifest. Innocent’s epistles make it certain that examination of this case was entrusted to Anysius, not Theophilus; and this very epistle teaches that the Council of Capua joined to Anysius, particularly, Macedonian bishops, not Egyptian bishops, in this matter. Certainly that synod was too knowledgeable in ecclesiastical discipline to appoint judges as remote from the see of the accused or of the accusers as the Egyptians were.]  
[Note: Hence it may be inferred that Anysius was permitted to associate with himself in this judgment others from Illyricum besides the Macedonians. Thus “particularly the Macedonians,” not the Macedonians alone, are said shortly afterward to have been appointed as judges.]

1. Judges appointed for Bonosus and his accusers.—I have received your letters concerning Bishop Bonosus, by which, whether out of zeal for truth or for moderation, you wished to ascertain our judgment.

> [Note: In the new edition of Ambrose, on the authority of ancient manuscripts, the beginning of this letter has been restored thus: “You have sent concerning Bishop Bonosus.” The fuller reading of the other editions, with which Holstenius agrees, seemed preferable and more elegant.]

But since the judgment of the Council of Capua was such that judges neighboring Bonosus and his accusers were to be assigned, especially the Macedonians, who, together with the bishop of Thessalonica, were to investigate his deeds—or at least examine them—we recognized that the proper form of passing judgment did not belong to us.

> [Note: In the Longpont manuscript *scriptis* (“writings”) is added here. In some others, however, *vel* (“or”) is absent. We suspect that both the addition and the omission arose from the rashness of copyists who did not grasp Siricius’s meaning. For his meaning, if I am not mistaken, is this: that they should concerning his deeds, if they did not pass judgment or pronounce a definitive sentence, at least investigate them. Nor should Bonosus’s case be thought to have been entrusted by the Council of Capua to Anysius and the bishops of Illyricum on terms other than those on which the case of Evagrius and Flavianus was entrusted to Theophilus and the Egyptian bishops. Ambrose addresses Theophilus in Letter 56 in such a way as to indicate that an inquiry, rather than a determinative judgment, was delegated to him and his colleagues. Among other things he writes to him: “We think that the matter should indeed be referred to our holy brother, the priest of the Roman Church, since we presume that you will judge those things which could not displease him either . . . so that, when we learn that what has been done has undoubtedly been approved by the Roman Church, we may joyfully obtain the fruit of such an EXAMINATION.” Certainly Innocent, in Letter 1 to Anysius, indicates that, following the example of Damasus and Siricius, he entrusts to him the examination of all matters arising in those regions, so that they may either be concluded by Anysius himself or, if they cannot be concluded, reserved for the judgment of the Apostolic See upon his report; as we also learn from Letter 9 of the same pope to Rufus.]

For if the synod were still intact today, we should rightly determine the matters contained in the sequence of your written report. It is therefore for you, who have undertaken this judgment, to pronounce sentence on all matters, and to give neither the accusers nor the accused opportunity to evade or escape. For you have assumed the role of the synod, since the synod chose you for examination.

2. Bonosus, contemplating forcing his way into the church forbidden to him, is dissuaded by Ambrose.—Finally, when Bishop Bonosus, after your judgment, sent someone to our brother Ambrose to consult his opinion as to whether he ought to force his way into and enter the church forbidden to him, he was answered that nothing should be rashly attempted, but that all things should be conducted modestly, patiently, and in proper order; nor should anything be attempted contrary to your sentence. Rather, you should determine what seemed to you consonant with justice, since the synod had granted you this authority.

> [Note: One must supply “whether he ought,” or something similar. This seems to refer to a prior judgment by which the bishops of Illyricum, excluding Bonosus from his church until they had more fully investigated his case, entrusted its administration to Bassus and Senecio.]

Therefore it is right that those should judge first to whom the power of judging has been given. For you decide, as we have written, in the place of the entire synod; it is not fitting for us to judge, as it were, by the authority of the synod.

3. Bonosus’s error concerning Mary’s children favors the Jews.—Certainly, we cannot deny that he was rightly reproved concerning Mary’s children, and that your holiness rightly recoiled from the assertion that another birth had issued from the same virginal womb from which Christ was born according to the flesh. For the Lord Jesus would not have chosen to be born through a virgin if He had judged that she would be so lacking in continence as to defile with the seed of human intercourse that generative shrine of the Lord’s body, that hall of the eternal King.

> [Note: Thus Holstenius. But in Ambrose: “seed.”]

Whoever asserts this asserts nothing other than the unbelief of the Jews, who say that He could not have been born of a virgin. For if they receive this authority from priests, so that Mary appears to have borne many children, they will strive with greater zeal to overthrow the truth of the faith.

4. Refutation.—And where is that which is written, when the Lord said to His mother concerning John the Evangelist, “Woman, behold your son,” and again to John concerning Mary, “Behold your mother” (see Ambrose, *On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 7, no. 46; John 19:26–27)? What does this mean: that when the Lord, placed upon the cross, was taking away the sin of the world, He also pronounced concerning His mother’s integrity? Or what else is said except that unbelief may shut its mouth and be silenced, lest it dare to assail the Lord’s mother with any reproach?

Thus the same witness is also the arbiter, the same defender of maternal chastity: she was betrothed only to the man Joseph, yet knew no marital intercourse or rights of the marriage-bed (Matt. 1:18). For He would not have wished to separate her from companionship with her husband if she were to bear children by Joseph. But if this is insufficient, the Evangelist added his testimony, saying that the disciple took her into his own home (John 19:27).

> [Note: Holstenius reads *in suam*, “into his own [house].” More correctly, Ambrose has *in sua*, “among his own things,” and he himself reads this passage no differently both in *Exhortation to Virginity*, ch. 5, no. 33, and in *On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 7, no. 48, where he explains it thus: “Certainly Christ was not effecting a divorce, nor was Mary leaving her husband. But with whom should the virgin LIVE, rather than with him whom she knew, as the son’s heir, to be the guardian of her integrity?”]

Did He then effect a divorce? Did He lead her away and take her from her husband? How then can one who reads this in the Gospel stagger and be tossed about like a shipwrecked man? This, therefore, is the son’s testament concerning his mother’s integrity; this is Mary’s abundant inheritance of unblemished chastity; this is the completion of the whole matter. Finally, He spoke thus and gave up the spirit, bringing every mystery to completion in the good end of devotion.

5. Administration of the Church entrusted.—We have also read and considered everything concerning both the appointment of Senecio as associate to our brother and fellow bishop Bassus in administering the Church, and the other matters on which we await the standard of your judgment.

> [Note: That is, the Church of Sardica, from which Bonosus had been excluded. The Senecio mentioned here may perhaps be the man whom Innocent, in Letter 13 to Rufus, praises as a man of the highest maturity. We also possess a letter of Celestine to the bishops of Illyricum, among whom Senecio’s name is listed.]

## Notice concerning the following canons

### I. Their origin and source

The following canons were first published through the efforts of Jacques Sirmond from the Fossatensis manuscript, now preserved in the Colbert Library, and likewise from the ancient collection of the Pithoean manuscript. Since he could not establish with certainty when they were composed, he judged that they should be placed at the end of volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*. But having demonstrated their antiquity in these words—“That they are wholly most ancient is shown both by the antiquity of the copies and especially confirmed by the very subjects of the decrees, which accord with the early centuries of the Church”—he finally proposed his conjecture about their author as follows:

> “Both the form of the decrees and their style do not differ from the letters of Pope Innocent. Therefore, perhaps the opinion would not be empty if someone were to conjecture that he was their author.”

Following this conjecture of so great a scholar, Labbe was the first to append these canons to Innocent’s letters. Thus, since we could by no means omit them altogether, no place at first appeared more suitable for presenting them.

### II. Their author is earlier than Leo

Certainly, it is evident that they are decrees or responses of the Apostolic See, which the Gallic bishops had first consulted; and on that account they belong to our undertaking. Nor is the following uncertain: the Roman pontiff from whom they proceeded was earlier than Leo. For, as is clear from no. 5, these canons were composed when the Roman Church bound only bishops, presbyters, and deacons among the clergy by the law of continence. Yet in Leo’s time, as Leo himself testifies in Letter 14 to Anastasius, no. 7, “not even subdeacons are permitted carnal marriage.”

Indeed, the pope speaks in that passage in such a way that he is understood not to have first enacted the law of continence for subdeacons, but to have confirmed a law enacted by others and already accepted in practice. Moreover, in chapter 4 of the *Code of Canons of the African Church*, Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Potentia and first legate of Boniface I and then of Celestine, is recorded as having said in the African council:

> “It is pleasing that a bishop, presbyter, and deacon, or those who handle the sacraments, guardians of chastity, should abstain from their wives.”

If we join to these words those of chapter 25 of the same Code:

> “It has been decided—as has also been confirmed in various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, and deacons and presbyters, and also bishops, should abstain from their wives according to the earlier statutes,”

Faustinus will appear to have held, according to the prescription and practice of the Roman Church, that subdeacons too ought to be bound by the law of continence. Yet it must not be concealed that in canon 3 of the Fifth Council of Carthage, from which the immediately preceding words were transferred into the said Code, no mention is made of subdeacons; rather, it simply reads:

> “It has been decided that bishops, presbyters, and deacons, according to the proper—or earlier—statutes, should also abstain from their wives.”

Be that as it may, it remains at least unquestionable that carnal marriage was by no means permitted to subdeacons in Leo’s age. That same law, by which presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons were forbidden to take wives, is shown to have been approved and received in practice among the Gauls from the fifth century onward by the Council of Vannes, held in 465, canon 2; Agde, canon 39; Orléans III, canon 2; Orléans V, canon 4; Tours II, canon 10; and Auxerre, canon 20.

### III. The canons may be attributed either to Innocent or to Siricius

Now, if we compare the appended canons with the writings or decrees of the supreme pontiffs who preceded Leo, we shall find that they agree with none more closely than with Innocent, or even with Siricius. Certainly, both in canon 5 of these canons and in Innocent’s Letter 2, no. 12, the same law of continence is prescribed for priests and deacons. The same is likewise commanded concerning veiled or unveiled virgins who have fallen away from their resolution, both in canons 3 and 4 here and in the aforementioned letter, nos. 15 and 16.

Likewise, just as the author of these canons judges unworthy of the priesthood both “one who, already a believer, has served in secular military service” and “those who have exercised the law of the world,” so Innocent, in Letter 3, nos. 8 and 10, denies admission to the honor of the clergy to “those who, after receiving the grace of baptism, have been engaged in forensic practice,” or “who have served as soldiers after baptism.” Again, what is decreed in the same letter, no. 6, against certain persons who had usurped the power of ordaining bishops in other churches accords very closely with the matters censured below in no. 18.

Yet these arguments are not so peculiar to Innocent that they do not apply no less fittingly to Siricius. If anything may also be inferred from the place which these canons occupy in the archetype, since they immediately follow the Council of Télèpte or Telepte—that is, the letter of Siricius read in that council—this adds some weight for attributing them either to Siricius or to Innocent.

### IV. They should be attributed to Siricius

As to which of the two they should be attributed, we had initially left this to the judgment of scholars. Indeed, because the opinion of Sirmond and Labbe favored Innocent, we had judged that they should be placed at the end of this pontiff’s writings, without heading them with his name, until something more certain should emerge. But when we came to examine each one, we found so many things specifically appropriate to Siricius that we became wholly convinced that they cannot be denied to him.

First, these canons begin, just as Siricius’s Letter 6 does, with a commendation of traditions; and in both places the same passage, Matthew 5:9, is employed against those who introduce novel observances. Next, just as Siricius in Letter 5, no. 1, again commending traditions, declares that he imposes no new precepts but confirms what has been established by apostolic and patristic ordinance, so here ancient traditions, not new enactments, are said to be supplied in answer to the individual questions.

Third, expressions are repeatedly found in these canons that are characteristic of Siricius: *qua de re* in place of *quare* (“for which reason”); *charissimi mihi* (“my dearest”) rather than simply *charissimi*; and *remissio peccatorum* (“remission of sins”) for baptism. Moreover, Siricius usually induces observance of traditions by admonishing and entreating rather than commanding. “That this may no longer happen,” he says in Letter 6, no. 5, “I admonish.” And in Letter 5, no. 3: “But to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean. Therefore I exhort, admonish, and entreat: let this reproach be removed.”

The following in canon 6 agrees with this manner: “Therefore, my dearest ones, I admonish you that, religion’s own reverence so persuading, the mystery of God ought not to be entrusted to persons of this kind, defiled and unbelieving.” Again, who declares in canon 9:

> “Apostolic discipline has established that Catholic bishops ought to have one confession. If, therefore, faith is one, tradition too must remain one; if tradition is one, one discipline must be preserved throughout all churches”?

Does he not appear to be Siricius himself, who states the same point more tersely in Letter 6, no. 5: “I declare that, having one faith, we ought also to hold one mind in tradition”?

It would take too long to set forth here all the points in which these canons and Siricius’s other letters agree. It will suffice to have indicated these few, so that each reader may more easily attend to discovering the rest. Those matters which these canons have in common with Siricius and Innocent, whether in wording or in meaning, are referred with better right to Siricius, because he preceded Innocent and because it is established that this pope borrowed much from him.

### V. Whether these canons settle the question which Innocent says had not yet been settled by the elders

The following may cause difficulty: how could Innocent, in Letter 6, chapter 3, when asked about those who after baptism held public office and either merely employed torture or even pronounced a capital sentence, reply, “We read that nothing concerning these persons has been settled by the elders,” if we attribute these canons to Siricius, in which a similar question seems to be settled in no. 13?

Yet, on closer examination, there is no slight difference between the two questions. For in Innocent’s letter the question concerning those who held office is whether they may be admitted to communion, whereas in these canons the question is whether they may be admitted even to episcopal dignity. Moreover, in these canons we are taught that they are to be admitted to the altar only after performing penance, not expressly because they exercised a judicial office, but because they attended or even presided over superstitious games and spectacles. Furthermore, the differing manner of response readily indicates that the two writings do not have one author. For Innocent dares to define nothing; in these canons, however, nothing is left undefined.

### VI. With what caution they have been corrected

Therefore, although the unskilled hand of the writer has greatly disfigured the appearance of this composition, it has not so deformed it that it cannot be recognized at all. Sirmond desired more correct manuscripts by which to cleanse it; but lacking their help, he could not refrain from attempting to repair certain passages by his own hand. Yet his effort was not successful in every respect. Accordingly, compelled to return to the authority of the archetype, we have thought it sufficient to indicate in their places which reading seemed preferable. We found not only many errors, but also suspected that certain passages had been displaced, especially the question in no. 14 concerning one who has married his uncle’s wife.

### VII. The agreement between matters treated in the Second Synod of Arles and the decrees set forth in this letter should be noted

Canon 6 of that synod concerns one made bishop without the metropolitan’s knowledge; canon 7, those who mutilate themselves; canon 8, those who presume, after prohibition, to receive someone excommunicated by another—whether cleric or layman; canon 52, girls who have vowed themselves to God but voluntarily pass to earthly marriages.

## Letter X, or Canons of the Synod of the Romans to the Gallic Bishops

> [Note: In the Fossatensis manuscript, after the Council of Télèpte or Telepte has been prefixed, the following is appended: “The canons of the Council of Télèpte end. The chapters of the Synod of the Romans begin. Letter of the synod.” Then, after the six following titles—which, Sirmond observes, are the only ones recognized in the ancient collections, although he himself judged that the entire letter should be divided into sixteen chapters—there follows: “The canons of the Romans begin. Among the other things, the Lord,” etc. We present at the head the only titles found in the ancient books. We suppose that they are called “Canons of the Romans” because they were composed in a Roman council.]

I. Concerning a virgin who has already been veiled in Christ, and likewise one not yet veiled.—II. That priests should be examples of good works to the people; concerning the chastity and continence of priests; and concerning one who has served in the secular sphere.—III. Concerning the custom of the Roman Church in admitting persons to the clergy; and that Catholic bishops ought to have one confession and one discipline.—IV. Concerning the sacrament of baptism, exorcised oil, and one who has taken his wife’s sister as wife.—V. Concerning those who have attained secular authority; one who has taken his uncle’s wife; the ordination of clerics; and clerics belonging to another church.—VI. Likewise concerning a bishop who crosses his proper boundaries; laypersons excommunicated and made clerics by another bishop.

1. Knowledge of truth must be sought; it is attained by prayers.—Among His other saving commands by which the Lord exhorts and admonishes His disciples, the apostles, toward the hope of life, as the Gospel words also teach us, He commands this as well: that we should labor diligently to attain knowledge of the truth. And first we should understand that unknown things are to be investigated not through empty progress, but through labor and diligence; and things not yet known are to be sought by prayers.

Those things which are more familiar, yet difficult, He commanded to be sought persistently; things which are closed should be requested in prayer to be opened by the power of faith through knocking. For it is written: “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). Certainly, no one who does not ask receives; no one who does not seek finds; and to one who has not knocked it cannot be opened. Therefore, because what is asked in faith is granted; because what was obscure is, when investigated, acquired in clear understanding—or perhaps “opened”; and because what was closed to us is revealed by more frequent knocking, that is, by asking:

> [Note: Sirmond and Labbe read “is revealed; thence the same . . . but necessary for you.” The passage is restored on the authority of the archetype.]

“For everyone who asks receives, and one who seeks finds, and to one who knocks it shall be opened” (ibid.). Thus it is not burdensome for me to repeat the same things, for they are necessary for you.

2. By changing traditions one falls into heresy. Traditions are supplied in answer to the questions proposed.—We know, dearest brothers, that many bishops in various churches have hastened, by human presumption, to alter the tradition of the Fathers, to the worst disrepute of their own name; and through this cause have fallen into the darkness of heresy, while they take greater pleasure in the glory of human beings than in seeking to possess God’s rewards.

Now therefore, since your holiness has deigned to inquire from the authority of the Apostolic See concerning both knowledge of the law and traditions, not for the purpose of investigation but for the confirmation of faith, wishing us to explain more freely the questions proposed, which you seek sincerely and with desire:

> [Note: Thus the Colbert manuscripts. The printed editions read, “and desire to hear,” supplying “as much as.”]

Hear as much as divine condescension will supply. Though I speak in modest language, I shall set forth matters to be maintained with forceful meaning, for the correction of all the diversities in which arrogance alone has presumed to disagree. For divine Scripture says: “You have rejected the commandment of God, in order that you may establish your traditions” (Matt. 5:9). If, therefore, you desire to recognize the true observances with an undivided faith, deign gladly to give heed to what I say.

First, a question is put to me concerning modesty and chastity. Then many accumulated questions are presented. Therefore, traditions must be supplied in their order to the individual propositions.

### Chapter 1

3. What has been judged concerning a veiled virgin who has changed her resolution.—A question is asked concerning veiled virgins who have changed their resolution: what has been judged in this matter.

If a virgin, already veiled in Christ, who has professed integrity by public testimony and received from a priest, after prayer had been offered, the veil of blessing, either has secretly committed incest or, wishing to conceal her crime, has given an adulterer the name of husband—taking away the members of Christ and making them members of a prostitute (1 Cor. 6:15)—so that she who had been the bride of Christ might be called the wife of a man: in such a woman there are as many charges as offenses. Her resolution of integrity has been changed; her veil has been lost; her first faith has been corrupted and rendered void.

> [Note: Sirmond reads “has committed incest or theft,” where Labbe notes that *furtum* (“theft”) ought, in his opinion, to be deleted. The archetype has *commiserit furtum* without the particle *seu* (“or”). It is certain that *furtim* (“secretly”) should be read from Innocent, Letter 2, no. 15: “Those who have been spiritually married to Christ and have deserved to be veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or secretly defile themselves.” Thus here one should say *furtim*, as there—and in Siricius’s own Letter 1, no. 7—one finds *clanculo*, “secretly.” Gelasius, Letter 11, ch. 20, likewise calls such unlawful unions of girls consecrated to God incestuous and sacrilegious.]

What kind and how great a satisfaction is necessary here! How great the penance of one who has incurred the destruction of the flesh!

> [Note: That is, one who has perished through sins of the flesh.]

It is no small fault to have left God and gone after a man. Therefore she must mourn for very many years, so that, after producing the worthy fruit of repentance, she may at some time attain pardon—if indeed she performs the acts required of one repenting.

> [Note: Labbe observes that *non* (“not”) should be added here. Yet *poenitenda* may be understood: the things which a penitent must do are prescribed, namely the works by which she may make satisfaction for and expiate her offense—in a word, the worthy fruits of repentance.]

4. What is to be done concerning a girl not yet veiled who has likewise fallen away from her resolution.—Likewise, a girl who has not yet been veiled, but had resolved to remain so, although not veiled in Christ, nevertheless, because she made the resolution and is not veiled in marriage, has entered what are called clandestine marriages, since, through desire hastening her into the blindness of lust, she has not kept the command of the heavenly marriage.

> [Note: In the Colbert manuscript: “has not kept the heavenly command, desire hastening toward the blindness of lust.” We would prefer: “has not kept the resolution—or promise—of heavenly marriage.” Innocent likewise says, in Letter 2, no. 16, that such a girl is bound to perform penance, because her promise was held by God and she violated the pledged faith made with God.]

And a period for the performance of penance must be established for these also. For whether abducted or willing, she consented to go to a man in a perverse manner, and neither she nor such persons maintained with chaste modesty the customary order for receiving the solemn veil, supported by the testimony of relatives and priests; rather, they acted contrary to the command of the Old Testament.

> [Note: The sequence of the sentence requires “and for this girl.” But the mode of expression repeatedly changes here, so that what had been stated generally of girls is immediately expressed concerning one girl in the singular. A girl who, even though abducted and subjected to force, consented to go to a man is declared guilty and liable to penance for two reasons: first, because she did not observe the customary order for receiving the solemn veil; second, because, contrary to the command of the law, she did not protest against one doing violence to her. The first reason is illustrated by the Second Council of Milevis, canon 26: “If any bishop, because the virgin’s chastity is endangered, when a powerful suitor or some abductor is feared . . . or at the request of parents, or of those to whose care she belongs—namely, bishops—veils a virgin below the years of age prescribed by the Third Council of Carthage, canon 4, the decree of this council shall not prejudice him.” The second is supported not only by the precept of the old law, but also by a constitution of Emperor Constantine, Theodosian Code, book IX, title 24, law 1, which decrees: “If consent of will is discovered in the virgin, she shall be punished with the same severity as the abductor.”]

> [Note: Sirmond and Labbe read “whom.” The archetype has “which.” The sequence of the sentence requires “those whom,” referring both to the girl and to the man joined to her. Of them Deuteronomy 22:24 commands: “They shall be stoned with stones: the girl because she did not cry out when she was in the city; the man because he humiliated his neighbor’s wife.” The words of Constantine’s constitution concerning the matter have just been cited. For the penalties decreed by Gallican canons upon girls who, abandoning their resolution, proceed to marriage, see the Council of Valence, 374, canon 2; Tours I, canon 6; Orléans V, canon 19; Mâcon I, canon 12. It should be noted that the girls whose clandestine marriages are censured here are represented as bound to God as by a true marriage; therefore, after breaking faith, they are considered adulteresses and liable to the punishment of adulteresses. Consequently, no one should doubt that this Roman synod intended their new marriage to be held no more valid than that of a woman who, while her husband lived, married another.]

Those whom the law commanded to be stoned (Deut. 22:24) are now, that punishment having ceased, struck spiritually, so that they cannot enter the Church except as dead persons. Yet there is room for them to perform penance; they do not quickly obtain pardon. For if the girl had cried out according to the law and had steadfastly maintained herself, she would certainly have been free from guilt.

> [Note: In the manuscript, “if she had maintained continence”; that is, if I am not mistaken, if she had preserved continence.]

It is therefore expedient for both to be suspended from communion for the same determined period, to perform worthy penance, and to redeem the offense committed through weeping, humility, fasting, and mercy.

### Chapter II

5. Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are bound by the law of continence.—And indeed, our discourse concerning such persons has often spread through many churches, especially concerning priests, whose office requires that they be examples of good works to their people.

> [Note: The Colbert manuscript reads: “Concerning these, such is the discourse.” Here a question concerning incontinent clerics, previously put to the Apostolic See, seems to require supplementation; so that, just as at the beginning of chapter 1 there is prefixed, “A question is asked concerning veiled virgins,” etc., so here should be prefixed, “A question is asked concerning priests, presbyters, and deacons who do not observe continence,” etc. Siricius’s discourse on this subject spread through many churches, as Innocent himself testifies in Letter 6, no. 4.]

But as I understand it, since Scripture says, “Speak into the ears of those who hear,” we shall pour instruction into their ears.

> [Note: The same manuscript reads, “of those to be instructed.”]

When the same things are often repeated which individuals hold in neglect, truly this is what was said concerning the adulterous sex: “Always learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3:7).

> [Note: Since the Colbert archetype reads *adulterum sexum*, “the adulterous sex,” Sirmond printed *adulter sexus*, “an adulterous sex.” It seemed preferable to retain the archetype’s reading and add the preposition *ad* (“to”), which, because of the similar following syllable, appears to have fallen out through a copyist’s frequent kind of omission.]

For when what is usefully admonished is not observed, apostolic commands are despised as though unknown. Yet judgment concerning the things they have committed cannot be changed.

> [Note: The Colbert manuscript reads, “by changing it, concerning priests.” The phrase “concerning priests” appears to have slipped from the margin into the text.]

This applies to priests. First, it has been decreed concerning bishops, presbyters, and deacons, who must attend the divine sacrifices, through whose hands both the grace of baptism is given and the body of Christ is consecrated. Not only we, but divine Scripture also, compels them to be most chaste; and the Fathers likewise commanded that they ought to observe bodily continence. We should therefore not pass this matter over, but state its reason.

For with what modesty would a bishop or presbyter dare to preach or commend integrity or continence to a widow or virgin, or urge her to preserve a chaste marriage-bed, if he himself devoted himself more to begetting children for the world than to God?

> [Note: We have already read this phrase, “with what modesty,” in Siricius’s Letter 5, chapter 9. Ambrose, by a similar argument in Letter 63 to the Church of Vercelli, no. 64, teaches that one who has entered a second marriage is rightly excluded from the clergy: “For how,” he says, “can he console a widow, honor her, exhort her to preserve widowhood and keep faith with her husband, when he himself has not preserved it for his former marriage? For the life of a priest ought to prevail, just as grace prevails.”]

Adam, who did not keep the command, was cast outside Paradise and lost the kingdom (Gen. 3:23); and do you think that a transgressor can reach the kingdoms of heaven? For this reason Paul says: “You are no longer in the flesh but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8:9); and again: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7:29). Or would he who exhorts the people, and graciously addresses Levites and priests, grant permission to perform a carnal act, while he himself says: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14); and elsewhere: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:7)? How can one who serves Christ, who sits in the teacher’s seat, fail to keep the discipline of that service?

[Col. 1185B] **6. Worshippers of idols, about to sacrifice to demons, imposed continence upon themselves.** Concerning these three ranks which we read of in the Scriptures, ministers of God are commanded to observe purity, since necessity is always at hand for them. For either baptism must be administered or sacrifices offered (see Siricius, Epistle 1, ch. 7, and Innocent, Epistle 6, no. 2). Would an impure person dare to defile what is holy, when holy things are for the holy? Indeed, those who offered sacrifices in the temple remained there throughout the whole year merely by virtue of the observance, knowing nothing at all of their homes, so that they might be clean.

> [Note: [Col. 1185C] We have already heard Siricius, Epistle 1, no. 9, discussing the same matter for the same reason: “Why were priests also commanded to live in the temple, far from their homes, during the year of their turn? Clearly for this reason: that they might not even be able to have carnal intercourse with their wives, so that, shining in the integrity of their conscience, they might offer to God an acceptable gift.”
>
> What follows concerning the continence of pagan priests also illustrates what the same pope says in Epistle 5, no. 3, against incontinent ministers of Christ: “Let this reproach be removed, for which even paganism may justly accuse us.”
>
> What he now explains more openly is confirmed both by these words of Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book III, p. 446: “Those who worship idols abstain from foods and sexual intercourse . . . . More especially, those who worship angels and demons are careful to abstain at once from wine, living creatures, and sexual matters”; and by these words of Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, Book IV: “The time required for the complete performance of sacred rites comprises a number of days: in one case forty-two, in another shorter or longer than this fixed limit. Yet among them seven days are never omitted, during which they [Egyptian priests] must wholly abstain from living creatures, likewise from every vegetable and pulse; but above all from intercourse with women.” See Julian the Emperor, Oration 5, p. 325.
>
> From this alone, moreover, everyone may observe how great is the agreement between Siricius’s Epistle 1, likewise his fifth, and these canons.]

Certainly idolaters, in order to practise impieties and sacrifice to demons, impose upon themselves continence from women; and they even desire to purify themselves from foods. Yet you ask me whether a priest of the true God, who is about to offer spiritual sacrifices, ought to be continually purified, or whether, wholly given over to the flesh, he ought to make provision for the flesh?

[Col. 1186A] If sexual union is defilement, then surely the priest must stand ready for his heavenly office, since he is to plead for the sins of others, lest he himself be found unworthy. For if laypeople are told, “Abstain for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5), and they indeed serve the created order through generation, priests may have such a name, but they cannot possess its merit.

> [Note: [Col. 1185D] In Siricius: “generation.” We retain, with the archetype, *generatione*, and understand the word *creaturae* in the dative case.]

If this is so and the presumption persists, bishops, presbyters, or deacons must already be taught not to associate themselves with the life of tax collectors.

> [Note: [Col. 1185D] Thus the archetype, except that it has twice *discine cum publicanorum*. Sirmond printed the passage thus: “Bishops, presbyters, or deacons must now be told not to associate themselves with the life of tax collectors.” It would have been more fitting to present it, corrected in accordance with the mind of the synod, thus: “the distinction between bishops, presbyters, or deacons and the life of tax collectors must now be associated.” That is: if incontinence is permitted to bishops, presbyters, or deacons, they must be associated with tax collectors in the same manner of life. Below, no. 8, “tax collector” means one free from the law, and is opposed to one who observes the law.]

Therefore, my dearest ones, I warn you—religion’s own reverence urging it—that the mystery of God ought not to be entrusted to persons such as these, defiled and faithless, in whom the holiness of the body appears polluted by filth and incontinence.

> [Note: [Col. 1186C] In place of the word *charissimi* (“dearest ones”), the archetype has the notation *cc.*, which Sirmond interpreted otherwise and was thus compelled to alter and interpolate the whole passage as follows: “There is no concern about such defiled and faithless persons, in whom bodily holiness seems polluted through filth and incontinence, that the mystery of God ought not to be entrusted to such persons”—the last three words being his own addition.
>
> In our reading, however, since it exactly follows the archetype, nothing remains to be desired. That we have not rashly read here, “my dearest ones,” is suggested by Siricius’s Epistle 6, no. 3: “Concerning this matter, my dearest ones, previously,” etc. That this manner of speaking is characteristic of Siricius is confirmed by a similar passage in his Epistle 7, no. 3: “For this reason, dearest ones to me, it was quite necessary [to report] what was done here.”
>
> Just as a single *c* may rightly be interpreted as *charissime* (“dearest one”), so doubled *cc* should be understood as standing for *charissimi* (“dearest ones”). For scribes commonly use a letter which, singly, signifies a word in the singular, doubled to signify the same word in the plural. Thus in consular abbreviations a single *v* is customarily written for *vir* (“man”), a double one for *viri* (“men”).]

For right reason itself separates such people. Let them certainly hear: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, nor shall corruption inherit incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:50). And does a presbyter or deacon dare, like animals, to submit to corruption—that is, of the flesh?

> [Note: [Col. 1186D] Supply “to corruption,” namely, that of the flesh. Sirmond substituted *contentioni* (“contention”) for *contendere* (“to submit/strive”), contrary to the archetype and the sense of the sentence.]

**7. One who, though a believer, serves in secular employment is not immune from injustice.** Likewise, concerning one who, already a believer, has served in secular service, it is known that he enjoys public freedom. For who can keep watch over him? Who can deny that he may have attended spectacles, or that, driven by the advantage of money, he could not remain immune from violence and injustice?

> [Note: [Col. 1186D] Sirmond supplied the negative particle, missing in the manuscript. See Innocent, Epistle 2, no. 11.]

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 1187A] **8. One baptized who has fallen into fornication is not to be admitted to the clergy.** The Roman Church especially observes this: if anyone, baptized as a child, has preserved bodily integrity, he may be admitted to the clergy; or if anyone has been baptized when older and remained chaste, the husband of one wife, he may become a cleric, provided he is bound by no other chains of crimes.

But one who has corrupted the sacraments of water by carnal vices—how, after fornication, even if he takes a wife, can he stand in ministry for the remission of sins, when he has returned to the blindness of his former life? How is this saying to be understood: “Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor others such as these, shall possess the kingdom of God” (2 Cor. 6:9), if there is no distinction between good and evil, between just and impious, between licentious and chaste, [Col. 1187B] between one who observes the law and a tax collector?

> [Note: [Col. 1187C] The word *intersit* (“there is a distinction”) is likewise missing in the manuscript. If one considers both the reason why, in the preceding chapter, no. 7, one who has served in secular employment is excluded from the clergy, and what is required in this chapter of those baptized either as adults or as children if they are to be promoted to the clergy; and if these matters are compared with what Siricius explains in Epistle 2, nos. 12 and 13, then the agreement of these canons with Siricius’s teaching will become ever clearer, and it will become manifest how solicitous the Church has always been concerning the integrity of its ministers.]

Such men will become ministers or priests, not of Christ but rather of Antichrist. And where is what the holy apostle Paul—who laid down the standard for a bishop—previously commanded when describing the man to be ordained: “Blameless, sober, and chaste,” etc. (1 Tim. 3:2)? How is the man blameless who could not preserve the sacrament of baptism? O novel presumption! The priesthood is entrusted to one to whom repentance alone is due, so that through a lengthy satisfaction he may wash away the benefits of pardon that have been stained.

**9. There must be one faith and one tradition.** Apostolic discipline has established—or perhaps reminded us—that Catholic bishops ought to have one confession. [Col. 1188A] If, then, faith is one, tradition also must remain one. If tradition is one, one discipline must be maintained in all churches. Churches have indeed been founded in diverse regions; but throughout the whole world she is called one through the unity of the Catholic faith. For we also read: “My dove is one, my perfect one is one, one to her mother” (Song 1:8). Therefore I am not now writing concerning the manner of baptism, but concerning the person of those who administer it.

> [Note: [Col. 1187C] Sirmond reads, “one to my mother.” We restore the archetype’s reading, which is supported not only by our Vulgate, but also by Cyprian near the beginning of his book *On the Unity of the Church*, where he elegantly explains how the Church is also one, though she extends more broadly into a multitude through the increase of fruitfulness.]

## CHAPTER IV

**10. Presbyters may confer baptism outside Easter; deacons are not granted the same authority.** At Eastertime, presbyters and deacons customarily give remission of sins and fulfil the ministry throughout the parishes, even in the bishop’s presence; [Col. 1188B] they themselves also descend into the font. They serve in the office, but the supreme responsibility for the act is assigned to his name.

> [Note: [Col. 1187C] Labbe, following Sirmond and the Colbert manuscript, reads *repromissionem* (“promise again”). We prefer, with the ancient Angers collection, *remissionem* (“remission”). Here remission of sins is meant, which is conferred through baptism. In this sense it is said shortly afterward that a presbyter outside Easter and Pentecost may give pardon of sins.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 1187D] The Colbert manuscript reads *nomen* (“name”); it is corrected from the ancient Angers collection, which also previously prefers “of the bishop” in place of “his,” for greater clarity. That the right of baptizing properly belongs to the bishop is the teaching of the ancients. Hence Ignatius writes to the Smyrnaeans: “It is not lawful to baptize without the bishop.” Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 17: “The chief priest, who is the bishop, has the right of giving [baptism]; thereafter presbyters and deacons do, but not without the bishop’s authority.” Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*: “Whence comes it that without the bishop’s command neither presbyter nor deacon has the right to baptize?”
>
> Accordingly, when the bishop happened to be absent, the customary solemn administration of baptism on the days of Easter and Pentecost was omitted, as our Edmund Martène proves at length, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, vol. I, p. 14 ff. Since presbyter and deacon are said immediately before to descend into the font even in the bishop’s presence, “and at his command” must be understood—as when the Second Council of Seville, held in 619, decrees in canon 17 that presbyters may not enter the baptistery in the bishop’s presence, nor baptize an infant while the bishop is present, unless he himself commands it. Thus decrees seemingly in conflict are reconciled and shown to accord with ancient discipline. Quite rightly, moreover, the bishop’s name is here given the highest responsibility for the act, because by his command presbyter and deacon act as his ministers.]

At other times, however, when necessity arising from illness compels a person, the presbyter is specifically permitted through the grace of saving water to grant pardon of sins, since he is also permitted to offer the sacrifice for purification. But no such permission is found to have been granted to deacons. If they have perhaps once presumed to do this, they are said to be excused by necessity; but afterward, when conditions are secure, they must not presume to do so.

> [Note: [Col. 1188C] We have judged that this should be corrected thus, whereas it was formerly read as *commissum* (“committed”). Here a particular authority of presbyters is vindicated where some circumstance calls for the baptism either of sick persons or infants; and the presumption of deacons, who claimed equal authority for themselves, is restrained. Nevertheless, the capacity to confer baptism when necessity presses is not denied them.
>
> For then, as Tertullian says in *On Baptism*, ch. 17: “Even laypersons have the right . . . Accordingly, baptism also, being equally God’s possession, can be performed by all.” Nor can it be denied that, at the very beginning of the Church’s birth, this sacrament was conferred by Philip the deacon. But care is taken lest deacons suppose that what is permitted them when necessity requires it is permitted them by a special right of their own.]

**11. Whether the anointing with exorcised oil should be repeated.** Concerning exorcised oil, whether a short or a long number of days is to be undertaken in receiving it, speech contributes much in this matter. For a person is wholly purified by faith.

> [Note: [Col. 1188D] The Colbert exemplar reads *cupiendusne* (“whether it is to be desired”). The whole passage could be restored in accordance with the mind of our synod as follows: “In receiving it [*capiendo*, that is, accepting it], neither a small nor a large number of days is efficacious, but rather the prayer by which this oil is blessed.”
>
> As Cyril of Jerusalem explains, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 2: “This exorcised oil, through the invocation of God and prayer, receives such power that it not only cleanses away the traces of sins by burning, but also puts to flight all the invisible powers of evil spirits.” Those anointed with exorcised oil were, as the same Cyril testifies in the same place, led to the holy bath of divine baptism. Then each was asked whether he believed in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and, after confessing this, was immersed three times.
>
> Therefore this anointing with exorcised oil is understood to belong to the rite of the final scrutiny and to have been administered on the very day of baptism. Since the same order of rite is noted in this decree, and since the candidate for baptism is expressly said to be anointed with exorcised oil at the third scrutiny, it follows that in the ancient Roman Church not seven scrutinies, as people generally suppose, but only three were performed; and the last of these was celebrated not on the Wednesday before baptism but on the very day of baptism.]

For if chrism poured upon the head imparts its grace to the whole body, nevertheless, if one examined at the third scrutiny has been touched with oil, God works by his power at the appropriate time—not often, but once.

> [Note: [Col. 1189C] The Colbert manuscript reads *contractus* (“contracted”), correctly emended by Sirmond. Here we are taught two things: first, that one anointing suffices; second, that it is neither necessary nor customary at Rome or in Gaul for the whole body to be drenched with it.
>
> In this way those are refuted who believed that such anointing must be repeated at every scrutiny; and at the same time the Greek rite is shown to be unnecessary, concerning which Cyril of Jerusalem says in *Mystagogical Catechesis* 2 to the newly baptized: “Having now been stripped, you were anointed with exorcised oil from the crown of the head down to the lowest parts, and were made participants in that fruitful olive tree, Jesus Christ.” Chrysostom, *Homilies on Colossians* 6: “He is anointed as an athlete entering the stadium . . . not as priests of old, on the head alone, but he is wholly anointed.”
>
> That the Gauls followed Roman custom and did not wish the anointing with exorcised oil to be repeated is clear from the fact that in 441 the First Council of Orange, canon 2, decreed: “No minister who has undertaken the office of baptizing ought anywhere to proceed without chrism,” so that, if the necessity of baptizing anyone arose, the rite of anointing might by no means be omitted. Hence in the same place they also direct that, regarding anyone who for any necessity had not been chrismated in baptism, the priest should be reminded at confirmation.
>
> More directly relevant is what they establish there: “It has been agreed among us that anointing with chrism should be done once.” They add this reason: “For among all persons this is agreed: that there is only one blessing of chrism itself,” not as prejudging anything, but so that repeated chrismation may not be regarded as necessary. By these words they declare that they do not wish the anointing repeated, not because repetition harms, but because it is by no means necessary.
>
> They repeat the first part of this canon in the Second Synod of Arles, canon 27. Nor should it trouble anyone that the Gauls, in the passage just cited, speak of chrism, whereas this Roman synod speaks of oil. For it is clear from Innocent, Epistle 2, no. 6, that the Romans also called exorcised oil “chrism.” There he first says: “Presbyters may anoint those baptized with chrism,” and subsequently adds: “yet they may not sign the forehead with the same oil.”]

**12. It is not permitted to marry one’s wife’s sister.** Concerning one who has married his wife’s sister: it is written in the law of the Old Testament that, to raise up offspring for a deceased brother, one ought to take the wife, provided, however, that he had left no children by her (Deut. 25:5).
