> [Note: [Col. 1190C] Thus the Colbert manuscript. Sirmond, however, reads “by the same [brother],” which I do not deny is supported by what follows immediately, because it concerns a brother who had left children.]

This is why John the Baptist opposed Herod: because it was not lawful for him to take the wife, since the brother had left children (Matt. 14:4). Yet the provision of the Law commanded a man to do this for the sake of male offspring; nowhere has anything been read concerning women, though perhaps this has been presumed.

[Col. 1189B] For the Law says: “Cursed is he who lies with his wife’s sister” (Lev. 18:18). Does Jacob, who at one time had two wives who were sisters, as a mystery, as well as concubines, and whose descendants were all called patriarchs—is a Christian now no longer permitted to have them? Or those who had wives and concubines? But the Testament does not now permit this to occur, since it treats more fully of integrity and, Christ teaching, praises chastity, when he says: “Not all receive the word of God, but those to whom it is given” (Matt. 17:11).

> [Note: [Col. 1190C] Sirmond reads “Christians,” and above, “Does he have two wives?” and below, “Does he have wives?”, omitting *qui* in both places contrary to the archetype. But if “because” is substituted for “those,” the sentence will be complete as follows: “Does Jacob, because he had two wives . . . and concubines, and because all who were born from him were called patriarchs, therefore mean that a Christian is now permitted to have them? Does this mean that because others had wives and concubines, now . . . ?”
>
> But even if the words themselves are obscure, the sense of the argument and Siricius’s view are not obscure: namely, that certain things were granted to the ancients which are prohibited to Christians.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 1190C–D] To this question, concerning one who has married his wife’s sister, should apparently be joined another—likewise concerning one who has married his maternal uncle’s wife—with its attached answer, which is found at the beginning of no. 14. That these have been displaced from their proper location is clear from the fact that the second part of the same no. 14 coheres not with what immediately precedes it, but with the final words of no. 13.]

## CHAPTER V

**13. Those who have exercised secular jurisdiction are not to be admitted to the ministry of the altar. Simoniacal stain and popular favour must be avoided in elections.** Furthermore, it is manifest that those who, having acquired secular power, have exercised secular jurisdiction cannot be immune from sin.

> [Note: [Col. 1190D] Thus the Colbert archetype. Sirmond reads: “have conducted the business of this world.” The discussion here chiefly concerns those charged with administering justice—those who, as Innocent says in Epistle 6, no. 6, “after baptism administered public affairs and either inflicted tortures only, or even pronounced capital sentence”; or those whom the same pope, Epistle 2, no. 14, calls persons occupied with any public functions.
>
> Although in Epistle 6 that pope does not deny that men of this kind may be free from sin, he nevertheless teaches in Epistle 2 that they are freed from it with the greatest difficulty: “For it is established,” he says there, “that in those offices they also present entertainments, which there is no doubt were invented by the devil, and either preside over or attend the apparatus of games or public shows.” Therefore these canons no more conflict with Innocent’s Epistle 6, where those judges are excused, than with his Epistle 2.]

For while the sword is drawn, or unjust judgment rendered, or tortures administered because cases require it, or while they take care to provide entertainments or attend them once prepared, they again associate themselves with those things which they renounced and alter the discipline of observance handed down to them. They do much for themselves if they do not aspire to the episcopate; but, after doing penance for all these things and completing the appointed time, they may deserve to be admitted to communion with the altars.

[Col. 1190B] When the Council of Nicaea—by the assent of the divine Spirit—had rightly confirmed the confession of faith, the bishops assembled together also wished apostolic traditions to come to the knowledge of all. Among other things, they decreed (canon 1) that a mutilated man should not become a cleric, because “the mutilated and the effeminate shall not enter into the sanctuary of God” (Deut. 23:1). Then, after the grace of baptism and [Col. 1191A] pardon of sins, they decreed that one who had gloried in secular service, or delighted in purple and the fasces, should by no sudden intrusion be admitted to the priesthood.

> [Note: [Col. 1191B–C] There is an agreement not only of thought but also of words with these words of Siricius, Epistle 6, no. 3: “Those who formerly gloried in being bound by the belt of secular service, who afterwards exulted in secular pomp—again associating themselves with the things they had renounced—or desired to serve in affairs of state or manage worldly business, supported by the assistance of certain persons and surrounded by the favour of relatives, are repeatedly brought to my attention as candidates to become bishops.”
>
> The question is where the Nicene Fathers commanded that such men should by no sudden intrusion be admitted to the priesthood. What is prescribed in Nicene canon 2 against newly converted persons may seem also to have been said against them. But if there “sudden intrusion” means excessively hasty speed, we shall not doubt that Sardican canon 13 is referred to here; we observed this canon inscribed “Nicene” also in an old manuscript of the monastery of Morbach.
>
> In this canon, which is the tenth among the Greek canons, we read: “If perhaps a wealthy man, a learned man from the forum, or one from public administration is requested to become bishop, he is not to be ordained until . . . his life has been examined over a long period and his merits have been proved.” The same Council of Sardica likewise notes the corruption of simoniacal stain in canon 2: “Since it is manifest that a few could have been corrupted by reward and payment . . . so that they might cry out in the church and appear to request that very man as bishop.”]

For men approach the summit of such dignity through merits and observances of the law; no one can attain it through Simon’s money, favour, or popular support. For the question is not what the people may want, but what evangelical discipline requires. The people then bear witness whenever they grant it to the merit of some worthy person, rejecting the breath of favour.

> [Note: [Col. 1191C–1192C] It appears that the passage should be restored: “whenever they grant this to the merit of some worthy person, rejecting the breath of favour.”
>
> The words “whoever has presumed to act contrary to the apostolic canons,” with what follows, should be moved back, as stated above, after the question set forth in no. 12. Once the text is restored here, the argument of Hincmar, *Book of Fifty-Five Chapters*, ch. 24, p. 473, is greatly weakened. He thought he could prove that Gregory the Great received the Chalcedonian canons, except the thirty-eighth, because that pope says in *Homilies on the Gospels* 17, no. 13: “The sacred canons condemn the Simoniacal heresy and command that those who seek payment for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood.”
>
> The archbishop’s subsequent claim—that no synod except the Council of Chalcedon issued a judgment on this subject—is refuted by this passage. Those guilty of Simoniacal heresy are likewise deprived of the priesthood by Apostolic Canon 30, which is 28 among the Greek canons. Yet I would think that not this canon, but rather the rule and pattern which the apostle Peter prescribed for the Church to follow by sharply rebuking Simon’s wickedness, is here designated by the name “apostolic canons.”
>
> Above, we heard Nicene canons called apostolic traditions because they rest on apostolic writings or examples. The Nicene Fathers themselves, in canon 2, forbidding for the future what has been done contrary to ecclesiastical rule in the ordination of persons recently converted to the faith, whether through necessity or other pressure from men, give this reason for their decree: “For the apostolic Scripture is clear, which says: ‘Not a novice.’”
>
> The same Fathers, in canons 9 and 10—to pass over similar passages—remove from the clergy persons convicted of a crime, because “the rule does not admit such persons.” They teach that such persons are not admitted by the rule, or ecclesiastical rule, because the Catholic Church maintains what is blameless, in accordance with the Apostle’s precept requiring a bishop to be blameless. In this way, for both the Nicene and this Roman synod, “rule,” “ecclesiastical rule,” “apostolic Scripture,” “apostolic traditions,” and “apostolic canons” are synonymous.]

**14. It is not permitted to marry one’s maternal uncle’s wife.** Likewise, concerning one who has married his maternal uncle’s wife: it is not permitted to marry one’s maternal uncle’s daughter, because the analogous relationship is separated and purified through the degrees of an unrelated father in procreation; but it is not lawful to return backwards. For one who has presumed to violate the bed of father or mother, this is called not marriage but fornication.

[Col. 1191B] Whoever, however, has presumed to act contrary to the apostolic canons must be deprived of the priesthood if he is obstinate. But if he corrects himself, what has been presumptuously done is to be annulled, so that, once reconciled, he may have fellowship with us.

**15. Laypersons are not to be promoted to the episcopate.** In ordinations it must especially be observed that bishops are always chosen from among the clergy.

> [Note: [Col. 1192C] That is, bishops are to be taken from the body of clergy, where they may be proved over a long period, and not from the crowd of laypersons. In agreement are the prescriptions of Nicene canon 2, Sardican canon 13, and Siricius, both Epistle 1, nos. 13 and 14, and especially Epistle 6, nos. 2 and 5. For how Ambrose, made bishop from a layman, excuses his own ordination, see his Epistle 63 to the church of Vercelli, no. 65.]

For it is written: “Let these also first be proved; then let them minister” (1 Tim. 3:10). How can a man not proved by serving for a preceding period in a lesser office be placed over the clergy? It has never been heard that a recruit, not yet trained, has received command of soldiers. Therefore he ought to be made bishop whom age, time, merit, and life commend. Or why does the Apostle prohibit a novice (ibid., v. 6), and not permit hands to be laid hastily upon anyone (1 Tim. 5:22)?

**16. One is not to transfer from church to church.** Likewise, it has been commanded concerning those who move from one church to another that they are to be regarded as though, having left their wife, they had gone to another’s. Such a deed cannot go unpunished. They ordered that such a bishop, an invader of another’s chastity, be deprived of the episcopate.

> [Note: [Col. 1192C–1193D] Sardican canon 1 appears to be indicated here as well. For although Nicene canon 15 provides that no bishop transfer from city to city, that synod by no means commands that a transferred bishop be deprived of the episcopate; rather, it directs that he be restored to the church in which he was ordained. Sardican canon 1, however, commands that such a man should not even have lay communion.
>
> Jerome, Epistle 83 to Oceanus, seems also to refer to this canon—regarded as Nicene—when he writes that the Fathers decreed in the Nicene Synod that a bishop should not be transferred from one church to another, “lest, having despised the companionship of a poor virgin, he seek the embrace of a wealthier adulteress.” There that Doctor certainly echoes the words of Hosius in the canon just mentioned: “Since no bishop has been found in this matter to transfer from a greater city to a lesser.”
>
> Rufinus indeed translated Nicene canon 15 into Latin as follows: “Let no one, whether bishop or another, seek to transfer from an inferior city to a greater church.” But no one can deny that the words “inferior” and “greater” were added by him, or rather repeated from Sardican canon 1. See Julius I, Epistle 1, no. 5.
>
> That churches are called the wives of pontiffs has always been an accepted usage in the Church. Jerome teaches this expressly in the cited letter; our Roman synod confirms it. For this reason Cyprian calls Novatian an adulterer and an opposing head in Epistle 2 to Cornelius, no. 1, and an adulterous and foreign bishop in Epistle 52 and elsewhere, because he wished to seize the Roman Church from her lawful spouse Cornelius.
>
> For the same reason Chrysostom, in Innocent, Epistle 4, no. 2, complains against Theophilus of Alexandria because he dealt with the Church of Constantinople as though she were a widow and had no bishop. Hence bishops who either invaded another’s church or, abandoning their own, occupied another were called adulterers. Examples may be read in the Council of Constantinople under Mennas, Act 1, p. 19, and in Pope Vigilius, Epistle 19, etc. But particularly illuminating on this matter is the passage from the Alexandrian synod held in 340, cited above, p. 364, note a.]

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1193A] **17. Clerics rejected by their own bishop are not to be received or promoted by others.** Likewise, the matter of clerics belonging to another bishop has frequently been discussed and settled by synod; and sound reason compels the conclusion that clerics rejected from the Church by their own bishop cannot receive even lay communion in another church. This has been confirmed and made evident, since even an innocent man, without letters from his own bishop or a *formata* [letter of commendation], cannot minister in another church (see Siricius, Epistle 5, chs. 5–6).

But if anyone presumes to do this to the injury of a priest, and wishes to receive or promote a condemned cleric, let him know that he has shared in another’s sins and incurred the Apostle’s judgment, who says that guilty are not only those who act contrary to the law, but also those who consent to persons doing so (Rom. 1:32). Therefore the decision must be left to the conscience of him who judged his own cleric, knowing that God will judge his judgment hereafter. Hear the Lord saying: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same also to them” (Matt. 7:12). Why do you arm yourself to injure a brother and fellow priest?

For when a rejected cleric is not only received but even promoted, the bishop is judged unjust. Whoever does this should know that he is excluded from the fellowship of Catholics and can no longer have communion with the Apostolic See.

> [Note: [Col. 1193D] Sirmond reads: “a cleric of another [bishop] . . . Whoever does this.” From the Colbert archetype we restore: “a rejected cleric . . . Whoever,” as though *hoc quisquis*. That clerics rejected by their own bishop should not be received by others is established by Nicene canon 5 and Sardican canon 16. Likewise, Nicene canon 17 and Sardican canons 18 and 19 prohibit a cleric of another bishop from being promoted or ordained without that bishop’s consent and refuse to regard such an ordination as valid.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 1193D] Printed editions read “excluded.” We restore from the manuscript, “separated.” In the preceding Epistle 5 of Siricius, no. 4, we read: “But if anyone, puffed up by the mind of his flesh, should wish to wander away from this rule of the canon, let him know that he is separated from our communion.”]

**18. It is not permitted to conduct ordinations in another’s territory.** Furthermore, it is a sufficiently serious matter, and contrary to the episcopal moderation of the Apostolic See, to exceed one’s own boundaries, proceed hastily to another’s region, and celebrate ordinations, the metropolitan bishop not permitting it in his own diocese, together with neighbouring bishops. As the 318 bishops confirmed, three or more bishops ought to ordain a bishop or install the worthiest candidate (see Siricius, Epistle 1, no. 14).

> [Note: [Col. 1194C–D] In place of *praeceptis* (“by commands”), which the archetype incorrectly presents, Sirmond substituted *prae ceteris* (“before the rest”). With equal right one might restore *praesertim* (“especially”) or *praesumere* (“to presume”). Then it appears that one should read: “the metropolitan bishop not permitting it.” Unless someone prefers *admittere* (“allow”) instead of *permittere*.
>
> At the beginning of the fourth century in Gaul, the abuse in ordinations now restrained was frequent, as the Synod of Turin, held between 398 and 403, testifies in canon 3, where four bishops are called to account for a usurpation in the ordination of priests. See the Second Council of Arles, canons 5, 6, and 42.]

Certainly, if anyone invades the borders of another’s possession, he is judged guilty of violence. Why this running? Why this haste, that ecclesiastical rule may be trampled underfoot? Human laws are observed, and divine commands despised. The present sword and temporal punishment are feared; but divine vengeance, which has the eternal flames of Gehenna, is disregarded.

> [Note: [Col. 1194D] The word *neglegitur* (“is disregarded”), absent from the archetype, is borrowed from Sirmond. Or else it is clear that “is not feared,” “is scorned,” or something similar has fallen out through the scribe.]

Consider what presumption has done. If anyone henceforth dares to presume to perform an ordination in another diocese, let him know that he may endanger his own position, since he has presumed to invade another’s church. This is not a secular matter; these are not worldly promotions. Let us hear the Apostle saying: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others; keep yourself chaste” (1 Tim. 5:22).

> [Note: [Col. 1194D] Related to this is what Siricius writes near the end of Epistle 6: “Let no one think that ordinations are, as it were, earthly, since the priesthood is heavenly.”]

If writings are read and divine fear is within us, [Col. 1194B] all scandals can be removed, and peaceful unanimity, full of charity, may endure among all the brethren.

19. That laymen excommunicated by their own bishop are not to be promoted to the clergy by another. — Furthermore, laymen are said to have been excluded from communion after their cases were examined, and then made clerics by another bishop. This is now evil beyond all measure. Therefore, when those who have dared to do such things are summoned, let them correct the matter, so that those upon whom an order has unworthily been conferred may be removed; or let their names be reported to us, that we may know from whom we ought to abstain (Council of Nicaea, canon 5).

20. Let your sincerity therefore know that, if all these things are observed in their proper order, as they have been established:

> [Note: [Col. 1194D] Not unlike these are the words in Siricius, Letter 5, no. 4: “Therefore, brethren, if these things are observed by all with complete vigilance, ambition will cease, dissension will subside, heresies and schisms will not arise.”]

then God is not offended, schisms are not produced, and heresies do not arise; but the nations will say that

[Col. 1194C]

Christ our Lord is truly God among us, he who lives and reigns

> [Note: [Col. 1194D] Thus the Colbert manuscript; but the printed editions read, “with the Father and with.” Siricius, Letter 5, no. 5, invokes the Trinity in this manner: “With the Father in the midst, and his only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit.”]

with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto eternal ages of ages. Amen.

Furthermore, there are two familiar letters of Ambrose, bishop of Milan—namely, Letters 85 and 86—addressed to Siricius. From them one might establish how great a friendship existed between that prelate and our pope, if

[Col. 1195A]

it were certain that the Siricius of Rome to whom he writes was not some other person bearing the same name. Yet, since it is by no means unclear that this Siricius was a bishop,

[Col. 1196A]

from the fact that Ambrose calls him “father” in the earlier letter, it is not implausibly believed that he was the one who presided over the Roman Church.

## ADDENDA

[Col. 1195]

## SYNODICAL LETTER

> [Note: [Col. 1195] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### From the Synod at Constantinople

(From Gallandius, taken from THEODORET, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 9; translated by HENRY VALESIUS.)

[Col. 1195]

Their churches’ ordinances did not permit them to be absent from them farther away; and for this reason, as well as because of the shortness of the appointed time, they did not come to the Roman synod. They ask that the Westerners also ratify by their approval the ordinations of bishops made or accepted by them.

[Col. 1195]

[Col. 1195B] To the most honored and most devout lords, brothers, and fellow ministers—Damasus, Ambrose, Britto, Valerian, Ascholius, Anemius, Basil, and the other holy bishops assembled in the great city of Rome—the holy synod of orthodox bishops assembled in the great city of Constantinople sends greetings in the Lord.

> [Note: [Col. 1195D] Valesius here and below reads *megalopolis*, “the great city.” —Ed.]

It may perhaps be superfluous to instruct your piety, as though it were ignorant, and to recount the multitude of sufferings inflicted upon us by the power of the Ariomaniacs. For we do not suppose your godliness so indifferent to our affairs that you need to be informed of matters over which you ought to grieve with us. Nor have the storms surrounding us been so insignificant as to escape notice, especially since the time of the persecutions is recent and still preserves a vivid memory,

[Col. 1195C]

not only among those who suffered, but also among those who through love make the sufferings of the afflicted their own.

For only yesterday, so to speak—indeed, the day before yesterday—some, released from the chains of exile, returned to their own churches through countless afflictions; while the remains of others, who had even died in exile, were brought back. Some, even after returning from exile, fell upon the still-boiling fury of the heretics and endured at home harsher things than they had suffered in a foreign land, being stoned to death by them after the example of blessed Stephen. Others, mangled by various tortures, still bear in their bodies the marks of Christ and their bruises.

Who could enumerate losses of property, assessments imposed on cities, the confiscations of individuals,

> [Note: [Col. 1196D] Sirmond reads *dēmeuseis*, “confiscations.” —Ed.]

plots, insults, and prisons?

[Col. 1195D]

For truly all afflictions were multiplied against us beyond number,

[Col. 1198A]

perhaps because we were paying the penalties of our sins,

> [Note: [Col. 1198D] Sirmond reads *etisamen*, “we paid.” —Ed.]

perhaps because the God who loves humankind was training us through the multitude of sufferings. For these things thanks be to God, who through so many afflictions disciplined his servants and, according to the abundance of his mercies, brought us forth again into refreshment.

Yet we needed much leisure, much time, and labor for the restoration of the churches, so that, as though nursing the body of the Church back from a long illness through gradual treatment, we might restore it to the ancient health of godliness. For although we seem at last to have been delivered from the violence of persecutions

[Col. 1198B]

and to be recovering the churches long held by the heretics, nevertheless grievous wolves, even after being driven from the fold, plunder the flocks in the valleys, dare to hold rival assemblies, stir up popular uprisings, and shrink from nothing harmful to the churches. Therefore, as we have said, it was necessary for us to devote a longer time to these matters.

But since, displaying brotherly love toward us, you assembled a synod at Rome by God’s will and summoned us also, as your own members, through the letters of the emperor beloved by God, so that, because at that time we alone were condemned to suffer afflictions, now, in the harmony of the sovereign emperors concerning godliness, you might not reign without us but we also, according to the apostolic saying,

[Col. 1198C]

might reign together with you: it was our desire, if possible, to leave all the churches together and yield to longing—or necessity. For who will give us wings like a dove? Then we would fly and find rest with you.

> [Note: [Col. 1198D] Sirmond reads, “But since this …” —Ed.]

But since this would entirely strip the churches, which were only now beginning to be renewed, and the undertaking was wholly impossible for most of us—for we had assembled at Constantinople in response to last year’s letters sent by your reverence to the emperor Theodosius, beloved by God, after the synod at Aquileia; we had prepared only for this journey as far as Constantinople, and had obtained the consent of the bishops remaining in the provinces only for this synod; we neither anticipated the need of a longer journey

[Col. 1198D]

nor had heard anything at all about it before assembling in Constantinople; and, in addition, the shortness of the deadline allowed time neither to prepare for a longer journey nor to notify all the bishops in communion in the provinces and obtain their consent—since these things, together with many others, prevented the arrival of the greater number, we did what was second-best, both for the restoration of affairs and for demonstrating your love toward us:

[Col. 1199A]

we earnestly asked our most reverend and most honored brothers and fellow ministers, the bishops Cyriacus, Eusebius, and Priscianus, to undertake the labor of travelling to you. Through them we demonstrate both that our intention is peaceful and directed toward unity, and that our zeal for the sound faith is manifest.

For whatever persecutions, afflictions, imperial threats, cruelties of rulers, or any other trial we endured from heretics, we underwent them for the evangelical faith confirmed at Nicaea in Bithynia by the three hundred and eighteen fathers. This is the faith which ought to please both you and us, and all who do not pervert the word of the true faith: a faith most ancient indeed, and

[Col. 1199B]

consonant with baptism, teaching us to believe in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. That is, we believe in one deity, power, and substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; in equal dignity and co-eternal sovereignty, in three perfect hypostases—that is, three perfect persons—so that neither the disease of Sabellius may find room, through the confusion of the hypostases, that is, the removal of their distinctive properties; nor may the blasphemy of the Eunomians, Arians, and Pneumatomachians prevail, by dividing the substance, nature, or deity and introducing, alongside the uncreated, consubstantial, and co-eternal Trinity, some nature later in time, created, or of another substance.

We also preserve without distortion the doctrine of the Lord’s incarnation, admitting neither a fleshly economy without soul nor mind,

[Col. 1199C]

nor an incomplete one; but knowing that the Word of God, wholly perfect before the ages, became wholly perfect man in the last days for our salvation.

Such, in summary, are the matters of the faith preached by us without reservation. You may be more fully instructed concerning them if you deign to consult both the *Tome* issued at Antioch by the synod assembled there,

[Col. 1202A]

and that issued last year at Constantinople by the ecumenical synod. In these documents we have expounded the faith more fully and have set down in writing an anathema against the heresies recently innovated.

Concerning the particular administration of the churches, the ancient rule, as you know, has prevailed, as has the ordinance of the holy fathers at Nicaea: in each province the bishops of that province—and, if they wish, the neighboring bishops together with them—are to perform ordinations as is expedient. In accordance with this, you know that the other churches among us are administered and that the bishops of the most distinguished churches have been appointed.

Accordingly, for the newly established church at Constantinople—which, as one might say, by God’s mercies we snatched from the very mouth of the lion of heretical

[Col. 1202B]

blasphemy—we have ordained the most reverend and God-beloved Nectarius as bishop at the ecumenical synod, with common unanimity, in the presence of the emperor Theodosius, beloved by God, with all the clergy and the whole city giving their assent.

For the most ancient and truly apostolic church at Antioch in Syria, where the honored name of Christians was first used, the bishops assembled from the province and the Diocese of the East canonically ordained the most reverend and God-beloved bishop Flavian; the whole church voted with them, honoring the man as with one voice. The assembly of the synod also accepted this lawful ordination.

For the church at Jerusalem, mother of all churches, we recognize the most reverend

[Col. 1202C]

and God-beloved Cyril as bishop: he was canonically ordained long ago by the bishops of the province, and has fought many contests against the Arians in various places.

Since these things have been lawfully and canonically established among us, we ask your reverence also to rejoice, spiritual love intervening and the fear of the Lord suppressing every merely human partiality, while making the edification of the churches more important than personal sympathy or favor toward any individual.

> [Note: [Col. 1202D] Sirmond reads *synētheias*, “customary attachment.” —Ed.]

For thus, when the doctrine of the faith has been agreed upon and Christian love established among us, we shall cease to say what was condemned by the apostles: “I am of Paul; I am of Apollos; I am of Cephas.”

[Col. 1202D]

But, being shown to be all Christ’s—Christ who is not divided among us—by God’s grace we shall preserve the body of the Church undivided, and shall stand with confidence before the tribunal of the Lord.

### Of the Council of Constantinople to Pope DAMASUS and the Western Bishops

(From Gallandius, taken from THEODORET, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 9; translated by HENRY VALESIUS.)

[Col. 1196]

Their churches’ ordinances did not permit them to be absent from them farther away; and for this reason, as well as because of the shortness of the appointed time, they did not come to the Roman synod. They ask that the Westerners also ratify by their approval the ordinations of bishops made or accepted by them.

[Col. 1195]

[Col. 1196B] To the most beloved and most devout lords, brothers, and fellow ministers—DAMASUS, AMBROSE, BRITTO, VALERIAN, ASCHOLIUS, ANEMIUS,

> [Note: [Col. 1195D] Perhaps Bassianus, namely the one called bishop of Audensis in the subscriptions to the Council of Aquileia. The sees of the other persons named above, except Britto, are known: Damasus was bishop of Rome, Ambrose of Milan, Valerian of Aquileia, Ascholius of Thessalonica, and Anemius of Sirmium. COUTANT.]

BASIL, and the other holy bishops assembled in the great city of Rome—the holy synod of orthodox bishops who assembled in the great city of Constantinople sends greetings in the Lord.

I. It may perhaps be superfluous to recount to your reverence, and to report as though you were ignorant, the multitude of evils inflicted upon us

> [Note: [Col. 1195D] Epiphanius: “by Arian power.” Sirmond: “by the power of the Arians.” Valesius: “by the fury and power of the Arians.” We judged it permissible to imitate Hilary and Phoebadius of Agen, who, after the Greek manner, call Arians *Ariomanitae* in Latin. On this term see the new edition of Hilary, p. 919, note d. On the passage which follows, Theodoret, book V, chapter 8, makes this observation: the Easterners wrote a letter to the Westerners in which they both indicated the storm raised against the churches and obscurely hinted at the Westerners’ former negligence. COUTANT.]

by the power of the Ariomaniacs. For we do not think that your godliness makes so little of our affairs that you need to learn matters over which you ought to grieve. Nor were the storms by which we were troubled such that their smallness could conceal them. Moreover, the recent time of the persecutions

[Col. 1196C]

still preserves a vigorous memory, not only among those who suffered but also among those who, through charity, regard the calamities of others as their own.

For yesterday, as we may say, and the day before yesterday, some, freed from the bonds of exile, returned to their own churches, not without innumerable hardships. The remains of others, who ended their lives in exile, were brought back. Some also, after returning from exile, when the fury of the heretics was still raging, suffered at home harsher things than they had endured among strangers, being overwhelmed by stones cast by them, after the example of blessed Stephen (Acts 7:57). Others, torn by various tortures, still carry in their bodies the marks of Christ and their welts.

And who can enumerate losses of money,

[Col. 1196D]

assessments inflicted upon cities,

> [Note: [Col. 1196D] Valesius finally judged that this passage should be rendered in Latin thus, and that the Greek *protimēseis* should be restored, although at first he had not approved Sirmond’s interpretation, namely “fines imposed on cities,” preferring “removals from cities,” because one suffering persecution is compelled to change his residence and prefer foreign regions to his homeland. Christophorson translated “losses of the cities in which they lived”; Epiphanius, “deprivations of honor.” —Ed.]

the proscriptions of individuals,

[Col. 1197A]

plots, insults, and prisons? In truth, all hardships against us have multiplied beyond number—whether because we are paying the penalties of our sins, or because the gracious God wished to train us through this multitude of evils. Therefore, for these things we give thanks to God, who instructed his servants through so many and such great calamities and, according to the greatness of his mercies, again brought us forth into refreshment.

II. But for the restoration of the churches we needed long respite, much time, and labor, so that, gradually restoring the body of the Church, as though from a prolonged sickness, by careful treatment, we might bring it back to its former health of godliness. For although we seem to have been wholly freed from the violence of persecutions, and to have perfectly recovered the churches

[Col. 1197B]

long possessed by heretics, nevertheless wolves trouble us. After being driven from the sheepfolds, they ravage the flocks of sheep in the wilds; they do not hesitate to hold rival assemblies, stir up popular seditions, and refuse no undertaking aimed at the ruin of the churches. Therefore, as we said, we needed a long time in which to devote ourselves to this business.

III. But since, in showing brotherly love toward us, you summoned us also as your own members by the letters of the most pious emperor, to the synod which by God’s will you are assembling at Rome—so that, because at that time we alone were condemned to endure hardships, now, when the emperors agree in the cause of godliness, you might not reign without us, but, according to the apostolic

[Col. 1197C]

word (2 Cor. 4:8), we also might reign with you—it was indeed our wish, if possible, that all of us together should leave the churches and yield to longing, or rather necessity. For who will give us wings like a dove (Ps. 54:7), that we may fly and find rest with you?

But because this would utterly leave the churches bare, though they are now only beginning to be renewed, and because most people could in no way do it—for we had assembled at Constantinople according to letters sent by your reverence to the most pious emperor Theodosius in the preceding year, after the Council of Aquileia; we were equipped only for this journey as far as Constantinople, and brought the consent of the bishops who were in the provinces concerning this synod alone; we neither had any suspicion of undertaking a longer journey nor had heard anything at all about it before

[Col. 1197D]

we had assembled at Constantinople; and in addition the shortness of the appointed time was inadequate both for preparation for a longer journey and for informing all our bishops in communion who were in different provinces and receiving their consent—since these and many other matters besides prevented the greater number from coming, we did what was second-best, both to restore affairs and to declare our love toward you. We entreated our most reverend

[Col. 1200A]

and most beloved brothers and fellow ministers, Cyriacus, Eusebius, and Priscianus, willingly to undertake the labor of going to you. Through them we show both that our intention is peaceable and directed toward unity, and that our zeal for sound faith is manifest.

IV. For whatever persecutions, imperial threats, cruelty of rulers, or any other temptation we endured from heretics, we endured it for the evangelical faith which was confirmed at Nicaea in Bithynia by the three hundred and eighteen fathers.

> [Note: [Col. 1199C] Valesius here adds in the Greek *hagioi theophoroi*, “holy God-bearing [fathers],” but does not add “holy God-bearing” in the Latin translation. Yet, while admitting that this addition is not found in Nicephorus, he merely observes that it is a customary epithet by which later Greeks commonly designate the bishops of the Nicene Council. That is certainly no adequate reason for adding the same epithet to a monument of the fourth century. Epiphanius Scholasticus long ago, and Sirmond in our own age, certainly did not know it. COUTANT.]

This faith ought to be approved by you, by us, and by all who do not pervert the word of the true faith:

> [Note: [Col. 1199D] Sirmond removed the words enclosed in brackets and did not render them in Greek. But Valesius objects that they occur in all his manuscripts, as well as in the Basle edition, Nicephorus, and Epiphanius. Yet Nicephorus’s translator agrees with Sirmond; nor is Epiphanius found to agree with Valesius. In Epiphanius one finds, “which we know to be most ancient.” From this it may be inferred that he read in Greek, *hēn eidomen presbytaten* (“which we have recognized as most ancient”). Such a reading accords much more closely with the council’s purpose than Valesius’s. For “which at last we scarcely retain” plainly conflicts with what was just said, namely, that the Easterners professed themselves always steadfast in the Nicene faith. Moreover, no expression in the Greek text corresponds to Valesius’s words “we hold and preserve.” —Ed.]

(a faith which we barely retain and preserve at last), since it is most ancient and

[Col. 1200B]

consistent with baptism, teaching us to believe in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: namely, believing in one deity, power, and substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; likewise in equal dignity and co-eternal sovereignty in three perfect hypostases, or three perfect persons. Thus the pestilence of Sabellius has no place, by which the hypostases are confused and their properties removed; nor does the blasphemy of the Eunomians, Arians, and Pneumatomachians prevail, which divides substance, nature, and deity, and adds to the uncreated, consubstantial, and co-eternal Trinity some subsequent, created, or differently-substanced nature.

We also preserve the doctrine of the Lord’s incarnation uncorrupted, admitting no dispensation of flesh devoid of soul,

[Col. 1200C]

devoid of mind, or incomplete; but knowing that the Word of God was wholly perfect before the ages and became wholly perfect man in the last days for our salvation.

This is, as it were, the summary of the faith constantly preached by us. If you desire anything further on the matter, you will be fully satisfied if you deign to read the *Tome*

> [Note: [Col. 1199D] Valesius seems less aptly to have rendered the Greek word *tomos* by the Latin *libellus* (“little book”). Nevertheless, he has understood its meaning very well. He observes that in canon 5 of the Council of Constantinople the term *tomos* denotes Damasus’s synodical letter, of which the preceding Letter 2 provides a portion. Nor is it unusual for synodical letters to bear the title *tomus*. In Athanasius, the letter of the Alexandrian Synod of 362 is entitled “Tome to the Antiochenes”; and Leo’s letter to Flavian, because it contains a summary of the faith, is commonly called Leo’s Tome in ancient monuments. Therefore, retaining the name *tome* with Epiphanius and Sirmond, we understand with Valesius that the Tome here mentioned was composed in 379 at the celebrated Synod of Antioch mentioned above at the end of Letter 2. We also agree with him in thinking that what is called “the Tome of the Westerners” in canon 5 of the Council of Constantinople is nothing other than the document of the Roman synod, fragments of which above in Letter 2 bear this title: “Letter or Exposition of the Roman Synod held under Pope Damasus and sent to the East.” Therefore we reject the opinion of Zonaras and Balsamon, who interpret the Tome of the Westerners as the canon of faith promulgated at the Council of Sardica; of Petit, who in *Various Readings*, book III, chapter 2, wishes “Antiochenes” to be substituted for “Westerners”; of Baronius, who for the year 381 thinks the cited letter of Damasus is the letter to Paulinus; and of Peter de Marca, book I, *On Concord*, chapter 4, no. 5, who understands this Tome of the Westerners as some letter of the Westerners declaring that they embrace communion with the Antiochenes because they profess the right faith, though afflicted by the schism of Meletius and Paulinus. COUTANT.]

issued at Antioch by the synod

[Col. 1201A]

held there, as well as that issued in the preceding year at Constantinople by the ecumenical synod. In these tomes we have expounded our faith more fully and pronounced a sentence of anathema upon heresies recently arisen.

V. Concerning the particular administration of churches, however, the ancient ordinance has prevailed, as you well know, as has the rule of the holy fathers assembled at Nicaea: that in each province the bishops of that province—and, if it pleases them, the neighboring bishops together with them—should perform ordinations as may be useful. In accordance with the prescription of these laws, know both that the other churches are administered by us and that priests have been appointed for the most illustrious churches.

Thus for the church of Constantinople, newly founded, so to speak,

[Col. 1201B]

which we recently rescued by God’s mercy from heretical blasphemy as though from a lion’s jaws, we ordained as bishop the most reverend and devout Nectarius, in an ecumenical council, with the common consent of all, in the presence of the most devout emperor Theodosius, with all the clergy and the whole city assenting.

For the most ancient and truly apostolic church of Antioch in Syria, in which the venerable name of Christians was first heard (Acts 11:26), the bishops of that province and of the Diocese of the East, gathered together, canonically ordained the most reverend and devout bishop Flavian; the whole church consented and, as it were, praised the man with one voice. This lawful ordination the whole synod also accepted.

[Col. 1201C]

For the church at Jerusalem, which is the mother of all churches, we declare the most reverend and devout Cyril to be bishop. He was canonically ordained long ago by the bishops of the province, and he endured many contests against the Arians in various places.

VI. Since these have been established lawfully and canonically, we exhort your reverence likewise to rejoice, with spiritual love acting as mediator and the fear of the Lord restraining every human partiality, while preferring the edification of the churches to private benevolence or favor toward individual persons. For in this way, once the word of faith has been established by common consent and Christian charity confirmed among us, we shall cease to say what was condemned by the Apostles: “I am of Paul,”

[Col. 1201D]

“but I am of Apollos,” “and I of Cephas” (1 Cor. 1:12). But when we all appear to belong to Christ—who is not divided among us—we shall, with God’s help, preserve the body of the Church whole and without any division, and shall stand with confidence before the judgment seat of the Lord.

[Col. 1201]

## CRITIQUE OF THE DECREES ATTRIBUTED TO POPE DAMASUS I

1. **What Damasus is alleged to have enacted in a Roman synod.** — In the recently mentioned Sarazani collection, p. 21,

[Col. 1202D]

there appears: “Life of Blessed Damasus, copied from a manuscript codex of the archive of the canons of St Peter,” in which the following is said of him:

[Col. 1203A]

“I. In those days, having summoned bishops from various parts of the world, he held a council in which he condemned Macedonius, who denied the Holy Spirit, Eunomius and Donatus, followers of Arian blasphemy; he also condemned Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, against whom he decreed: ‘If anyone should say that the Son of God, who was truly God as he was truly man, possessed anything less either of humanity or of deity, let him be judged alien to the Church.’ He also ordered this ruling to be confirmed at the holy second synod, held at Constantinople by his command and authority.

“II. Damasus further commanded priests to deny holy communion and entry into churches to all sacrilegious persons who had seized ecclesiastical property, and especially to those who did not pay tithes.

“III. He also judged that those who engage in lending at interest and usury should be expelled from the house of God, saying that there is no difference between a robber and a usurer.

“IV. Likewise, those who remain in churches and occupy themselves with frivolous and idle talk: for he said, ‘If it is a house of prayer, as the Lord says, no one is permitted in it except to pray, sing psalms, confess sins, and implore pardon.’

“V. He also judged that those should be anathematized who, forgetful of the divine law, engage in sorceries, superstitions, and vain incantations. … Therefore,” he says, “we command that whoever observes divinations, auguries, or lots which they falsely claim to be those of saints,

[Col. 1203C]

or listens to magicians or enchanters, shall by no means be counted among Christians.

“VI. We also wish those women to be expelled from churches who, deceived by the illusions and phantasms of demons, believe that in the silence of night they ride with Herodias and an innumerable multitude of women, etc.,” down to “he leads [them] through every byway,” as in Gratian, 26, question 5, canon 12, and in Augustine, *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 28, with a few words altered.

“VII. It was also renewed in the same council what had been established at Nicaea: that if anyone should dare on the Lord’s Day to sing Mass after the third hour, and on other days from the middle of the fourth hour until the ninth hour, let him be anathematized.

“VIII. Then St Damasus also established that

[Col. 1203D]

psalms should be sung day and night in all churches. He further ordered that at the end of every psalm there should be appended: ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit; as it was in the beginning, and now, and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.’”

Baronius, under the year 384, approves and commends these same decrees as genuine. Thus he seems also to accept the acts from which they were excerpted. But both what precedes and what follows those decrees in these acts—and indeed what is asserted in the decrees themselves—deprive them of all credibility.

2. **The unskilled architect of the forged Acts of Damasus makes Meletius and Paulinus heresiarchs.** — From what follows, it will suffice to bring forward this passage:

[Col. 1204A]

“For in those same parts of the East, while Valens reigned—of whose tyranny mention was made above—there were three heresiarchs: Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus, who hastened to draw the Church, divided into three parts, to themselves.”

Who, hearing this, could tolerate the ignorance of the author of these Acts, who so absurdly calls Paulinus a heresiarch—Paulinus, I say, whom Damasus addresses in his letter so modestly and honorably (Damasus, Letter 5), and concerning whom the fathers of the Council of Italy wrote to Emperor Theodosius in 381 (*in Sirmond, Appendix to the Theodosian Code*, p. 103): “The bonds of communion, maintained without offense from our forefathers, testify that this man has remained in our communion”?

Or who could patiently hear Meletius branded with the same title of heresiarch, he who won for himself the veneration of the whole East, who deserved to be called both “great” and “divine” by orthodox writers, and whom the fathers of the Council of Italy just cited testify they consider to agree with them in faith?

Not even Vitalis was a heresiarch while Valens reigned; only after that emperor’s death was he revealed to be a disciple of Apollinaris the heresiarch. It is quite clear that inventions of this kind arose from a perverse understanding of Jerome’s words in the preceding Letter 11, no. 2: “The Church, split into three parts, hastens to draw me to itself. … Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus say that they adhere to you.” If one wishes to continue examining the same Acts, one need not proceed much farther to discover similar fabrications. First one encounters several fragments of Jerome’s preceding Letters 10 and 11 to Damasus, corrupted by interpolations

[Col. 1204C]

which one will seek in vain in genuine copies. Then, after setting out the petitions explained by Jerome in those letters, it adds: “Blessed Damasus suitably granted these petitions”—a fact of which we have no knowledge from any other source.

3. **Further fables concerning the Council of Rimini, Liberius’s exile, and so forth.** — If we return to the material prefixed to the decrees mentioned above, there too the impostor’s unskilled deception reveals itself no less plainly. For Lucifer, Pancratius, and Hilary, who are known to have been sent by Liberius to Constantius in 354 and exiled from the Council of Milan in 355, are fictitiously represented as envoys to this emperor after the Council of Rimini, which was held in 359, in order to admonish him concerning the wickedness committed at that council.

Then, according to these same Acts,

[Col. 1204D]

Constantius ordered Liberius “to be conveyed outside the city, as if into exile; and he lived outside, at the third milestone, in the cemetery called Noella, on the Via Salaria”; and “when he was led into exile, he left Damasus as his deputy in the city.” At that time “it came about that all the bishops whom ignorance or fear had caused to go astray at the Council of Rimini returned to the Catholic faith through Damasus’s persuasions.” And after a few intervening words, it adds: “At the same time, when the solemnity of Easter was approaching, at which very many desired to be reborn in Christ, Liberius summoned all ranks of Catholic clergy; and, seated in the aforesaid cemetery, Noella, he began to speak as follows, etc.”

Everyone sees how utterly all this conflicts with the true course of events.

[Col. 1205A]

For it is established from Theodoret and Sozomen that Liberius was banished to Beroea in Thrace, where he had no power to summon clerics. There Liberius himself, already broken and bent to the will of the Arians, attests that he accepted the creed set before him by Demophilus, bishop of Beroea (Liberius, Letter 8, no. 6). Nor is it less certain that Liberius had not only been taken from but had also been restored to the Roman Church before the Council of Rimini. Hence Hilary, writing against Constantius immediately after that council, no. 11, addresses the emperor thus: “You then turned your warfare even upon Rome; you took its bishop away; and—wretched man that you are—I do not know whether you acted with greater impiety in banishing him or in restoring him.”

Thus the story that, while Liberius was in exile, Damasus labored to bring back those who had fallen at Rimini is mere fiction. The same judgment must be made concerning the office of deputy which he is simultaneously alleged to have exercised, and concerning the other things stated there.

4. **Many grounds for suspecting forgery in the decrees.** — In the remaining Acts, which narrate the foregoing, there is likewise a medley of similar absurdities. We therefore cannot sufficiently wonder how the learned father of the *Annals* could have attributed such authority to Acts of this sort as to accept as genuine a Roman synod otherwise unknown, and the decrees alleged to have been issued in it—especially since there is no appearance of truth even in the decrees themselves.

5. **Donatus is represented as a follower of Arian blasphemy.** — First, who is this Donatus, alleged to have been a follower of Arian blasphemy and condemned in the first decree together with Macedonius,

[Col. 1205C]

Eunomius, and Apollinaris? It is probable that the man here indicated is the author and leader of the infamous schism in Africa; and that he is called a follower of Arian blasphemy because the Arians, assembled at Philippopolis in 347, sent him a synodical letter inscribed with the name of the Council of Sardica. But he neither lived to Damasus’s time nor was described as a follower of Arian blasphemy. Only a report had spread that “the Arians, after separating from Catholic communion, attempted to associate the Donatists in Africa with themselves,” as Augustine, having been informed by Alypius, writes in Letter formerly 163, now 44, no. 6.

6. **Damasus is fictitiously said to have ordered the Second Synod to confirm his decrees.** — It is vainly said that this synod was assembled by his command. Further, the addition, “He ordered this ruling to be confirmed also in the holy second synod,” is refuted by the acts and decrees of that second synod, in which there is no mention of Donatus, of anyone acting as Damasus’s representative, or of anyone commanding anything in his name.

Damasus gives only this instruction concerning that council in Letters 8 and 9 to Acholius and his colleagues: that they should take care that a bishop without reproach be ordained at Constantinople. “Because,” he says in Letter 8, no. 3, “I have learned that a council is to be held at Constantinople, let your sincerity take care that a bishop be chosen for the said city who has no reproach.” Here one should also note that he says, “I have learned that a council is to be held at Constantinople,” not,

[Col. 1206A]

“I have commanded a council to be assembled at Constantinople.” This refutes the assertion that “the holy second synod was held at Constantinople by his command and authority,” and confirms the judgment of Antonio Pagi under the year 381, no. 7, and of others who deny that this synod was convoked by Damasus.

7. **Most of the decrees reflect discipline customary in the fifth and sixth centuries.** — The remaining decrees generally reflect the discipline prevailing in the fifth and later centuries. There is reason to suspect that they were drawn from the writings either of Fathers or of Gallican councils. The second decree agrees with canon 4 of the Council of Agde, which provides that those who have taken possessions of the Church are to be “excluded from the churches until they restore them.”

Alongside this and other sources should be compared Sermons 276 and 277 of Caesarius of Arles, concerning the payment of tithes; Sermon 278, concerning auguries; and Sermons 283 and 286, concerning the avoidance of idle talk in church, found under Augustine’s name in the appendix to volume V. In the latter Caesarius specifically addresses his hearers in no. 6 as follows: “When you come to church, do only what ought to be done: namely, either pray or sing psalms, so that by praying you may receive forgiveness of sins and by singing psalms may attain spiritual joy.” Closely related to this is the statement in the fourth decree above: “If it is a house of prayer, as the Lord says, no one is permitted in it except to pray, sing psalms, confess sins, and implore pardon.”

8. **Lots of the saints.** — Likewise, closely related to the next decree against those who observe divinations, auguries, and “lots of the saints”

[Col. 1206C]

is the provision of canon 30 of the First Council of Orléans: “If any cleric, monk, or layperson believes that divination, auguries, or lots—which they falsely claim to be those of saints—are to be observed or made known by any means whatsoever, let them be expelled from the communion of the Church.” Similar enactments occur in canon 16 of the Council of Vannes, canon 42 of Agde, and canon 4 of Auxerre.

At Auxerre, “lots of the saints” are said to be made “from wood or bread”; at Vannes and Agde, by “any inspection of the Scriptures.” To this pertains the chapter reported by Sirmond in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 157, under the year 789: “Let no one presume to cast lots in the Psalter, the Gospel, or other things, nor observe any divinations.” Among the enactments of Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, in *Spicilegium*, volume

[Col. 1206D]

IX, p. 66, chapter 33 is expressed thus: “If any priest or cleric observes auguries, divinations, dreams, lots, or phylacteries—that is, writings—let him know that he is subject to the penalties of the canons.” Here it is worthy of note that lots and phylacteries are treated as synonyms.

This practice, by which omens of the future were taken from the inspection of the Scriptures, although repeatedly forbidden from the beginning of the sixth century onward, nevertheless persisted long afterwards and was still common at the beginning of the twelfth century. Hence arose that prognostication mentioned by Abbot Guibert of Nogent in book II of his *Life* and book III, chapter 4, and by William of Malmesbury, book I of *On the Bishops of England*, folio 121: namely, that, upon opening a sacred codex, they inferred the future character of a chosen bishop or

[Col. 1207A]

abbot. Our Edmond Martène proves this custom to be most ancient in volume II of *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, p. 331.

9. **Women deceived by demonic illusions.** — What we read in Decree 6 concerning women deceived by demonic illusions is also found in the appendix to volume VI of Augustine, *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 28, and is cited as though from canon 1 of the Council of Ancyra by Burchard, book X, chapter 1; Ivo, part 11, chapter 30; and Gratian, 26, question 5, canon 12. To whom it should be attributed is not easy to determine.

As for the aforesaid book *On Spirit and Soul*, since it is almost a mere patchwork compiled from various excerpts gathered from everywhere, the entire passage about the deceived women should rightly be thought borrowed from another source. Yet it does not appear among the canons of the Council of Ancyra.

It would therefore remain to judge that the compilers of canons just named took it from the Acts of the Roman synod praised in the Life of Damasus, were it not for two obstacles. First, none of them attributes it either to Damasus or to a Roman synod. Second, in their works the passage is fuller and more complete, whereas in the Life of Damasus it appears more meager and manifestly truncated; thus there it flows pure from the source, while here it flows corrupted.

A briefer but wholly similar decree is cited by Burchard, book X, chapter 29, and Ivo, part 11, chapter 54, as from canon 4 of the Council of Agde, though it is likewise absent from that council:

[Col. 1207C]

“It must be investigated whether there is any woman who claims that, by certain sorceries and incantations, she can alter the minds of persons—that is, turn hatred into love or love into hatred, or curse or steal away people’s goods; and whether there is any woman who claims that, transformed into the likeness of women together with a company of demons, she rides on certain nights upon certain beasts and is numbered among their company. Such a woman, having been thoroughly beaten with whips, is to be expelled from the parish.”

10. On the hour for celebrating Masses.—Decree 7, concerning the hours at which Mass may lawfully be celebrated, seems no less spurious than the Nicene canon whose renewal it professes. Among the matters which Isidore Mercator falsely ascribed to the earliest pontiffs is this under the name of Pope Telesphorus: “At other times [than the night of the Lord’s Nativity], celebrations of Mass are by no means to be held before the third hour”; [Col. 1207D] and we proved its falsity when treating of Telesphorus himself, p. 59.

11. Whether Damasus was the author of chanting psalms antiphonally.—Decree 8, which says that St Damasus ordained “that psalms should be sung day and night throughout all churches,” and, as Anastasius adds, commanded this “to priests and bishops or monasteries,” may be understood in two ways: either that they were simply to be sung, or that they were to be sung antiphonally. Yet those learned in antiquity judge that the practice of simply singing psalms in churches did not begin with Damasus, but had prevailed continuously from the Church’s beginning. Socrates, Book VI, ch. 8, relates that St Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, established in his church the practice that certain hymns should be sung by alternating choirs, [Col. 1208A] and that this custom passed from the Church of Antioch alone to the others. Pliny too, in Epistle 102 to Trajan, writes that he had learned from Christians “that they were accustomed to assemble on a fixed day before dawn and sing a hymn to Christ as to a god, alternately among themselves.”

Nor is this authority at all diminished because Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 2, omits the phrase “among themselves” (*invicem*) and is content to say that Pliny wrote to Trajan that he had discovered “nothing else concerning their rites [those of the Christians] except pre-dawn assemblies for singing to Christ and God.” For Tertullian, reporting Pliny’s meaning rather than his exact words, was free to make such an omission. From a reciprocal comparison of Pliny’s and Tertullian’s wording, [Col. 1208B] Lombert’s conjecture appears nearly certain: in Tertullian, *Christo et Deo*, “to Christ and God,” should be restored as *Christo ut Deo*, “to Christ as God.” For who would fail to see that Tertullian wished to express Pliny’s *Christo quasi Deo*, “to Christ as to a god,” and therefore should have written *ut*, “as,” rather than *et*, “and,” in place of *quasi*, “as if”? Certainly, in ancient books *et* is frequently read in place of *ut*. I thought this worth observing here, so that what had been incidentally noted above on p. 59 concerning the same passage in Tertullian, on the basis of a report not sufficiently exact, may be corrected accordingly.

But, to return to the point from which the discussion had digressed: Pliny here, no less than Socrates above, mentions only certain hymns, not psalms generally, as sung antiphonally in Christian assemblies. Most, however, interpret the cited decree as concerning antiphonal chanting of psalms, [Col. 1208C] and for no other reason make Damasus the author of this practice. This was so firmly believed by the ancient writer cited by our Mabillon in the preface to Part II of the fourth century of the *Acta Benedictina*, no. 210, that in the Chronology of Lérins, concerning St Agricolaus—who had been taken from the monastery of Lérins to the episcopal see of Avignon, and wished to introduce antiphonal chant there—he transmitted the following:

> “He also wished that henceforth the canonical hours and divine offices should be recited in that church in the same manner as was customary in monasteries, namely by antiphonal chants. For in those regions that custom, which the Supreme Pontiff Damasus had introduced some years earlier, had not yet become established.”

12. Ambrose was the author of this practice in the West; [Col. 1208D] Flavian and Diodorus in the East.—Nevertheless, Cardinal Bona, *De divina psalmodia*, ch. 16, no. 1, charges with error those who assert that Damasus was the author of antiphonal chant in the West, since all who write in the Latin Church concerning sacred rites ascribe the credit for introducing this custom to Ambrose, relying on Augustine’s testimony. Augustine, in Book IX of the *Confessions*, ch. 7, recorded the matter as follows:

> “Not long before, the Church of Milan had begun to practise this manner of consolation and exhortation, with great zeal of brethren singing together with voices and hearts. It was, to be sure, a year, or scarcely more, since Justina, mother of the boy-emperor Valentinian, was persecuting your servant Ambrose because of the heresy by which she had been seduced [Col. 1209A] by the Arians. The devout people kept vigil in the church, prepared to die with their bishop, your servant. . . . Then it was instituted that hymns and psalms should be sung after the manner of the Eastern regions, lest the people waste away through the weariness of grief; and from that time it has been retained until the present day, being imitated by many, indeed by almost all your flocks, and in the other parts of the world.”

In the East, however, as Theodoret testifies, Book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 24, Flavian and Diodorus, while still laymen, “first divided the choirs of singers into two parts and taught them to sing Davidic hymns alternately. This practice first began at Antioch, then spread thence to the rest, and was carried even to the furthest bounds of the earth.”

13. It cannot be said that it was confirmed by Damasus. [Col. 1209B] It spread through the devout emulation of churches.—Thus the aforementioned Cardinal affirms that this devout practice was first introduced into the West by Ambrose, but thinks that it was afterwards confirmed by Pope Damasus through pontifical authority, and supposes that the error of certain historians who consider Damasus its author arose from this. But this opinion too is not free from error. For if this custom began only at the time when Justina persecuted Ambrose, which happened in 386, how could Damasus have confirmed it, when Siricius’s own letter to Himerius proves that Damasus died in 384 and that Siricius had succeeded him at least from the beginning of 385?

Indeed, although Augustine says that the custom spread in a short time through almost the whole world, he is wholly silent about this alleged confirmation [Col. 1209C] by Damasus. It is much more likely that individual churches adopted it through a certain holy emulation rather than by any pontifical authority. Certainly, when St Agricolaus undertook the government of the Church of Avignon, it had not yet prevailed there, as we saw above. The same must be said of the Church of Arles when Caesarius was placed over it. When at last he obtained the admission of this custom there also, unable to contain his joy, he expressed it in a special sermon, now found as no. 284 in the appendix to vol. V of Augustine:

> “For many years,” he says, “my soul had been ardently concerned about this matter and desired with the whole intentness of its heart that the merciful Lord might inspire you with that custom of psalm-singing. . . . Since I desired you to sing psalms in the way [Col. 1209D] in which they were sung in other neighbouring cities, God so prepared your hearts that, with the Lord’s assistance, you may perform this even better.”

Surely, if a general command on this subject from the supreme pontiff had preceded it, churches so distinguished and situated on the frontier of Italy would not have delayed so long in obeying it. Nor would Caesarius, acting as representative of the Apostolic See in Gaul, have omitted to commend an authority so weighty, in order more quickly to obtain what he so ardently desired. Yet he does not say, “Since I desired you to sing psalms in the way commanded by decree of the Apostolic See,” but only, “in the way in which they were sung in other neighbouring cities.” In the preceding passage from the Chronology of Lérins it should also be noted [Col. 1210A] that the words, “For in those regions that custom, which the Supreme Pontiff Damasus had introduced some years earlier, had not yet become established,” are by no means words of St Agricolaus, but of the chronicler.

14. Whether Damasus ordained that “Glory be to the Father,” etc., should be added to psalms.—Must at least the final part of the last decree be accepted, by which Damasus is said to have ordained that *Gloria Patri*, etc., should be added at the end of every psalm? Cardinal Bona, *De divina psalmodia*, ch. 16, no. 2, admits that many otherwise trustworthy writers refer to Damasus the rule that this doxology be sung at the end of psalms, and hold that this pope enacted it at Jerome’s urging and instigation. But he warns that they were deceived by a forged letter which Isidore Mercator attributed to Jerome, [Col. 1210B] in which one reads:

> “Therefore your client prays that this voice of those singing psalms may be sung day and night in your Roman see, and that by order of your apostolate there may be joined at the end of every psalm, whether at the morning or evening hours: ‘Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit; as it was,’ etc.”

Certainly, in 529, as may be inferred from canon 5 of the Second Council of Vaison, held in that year, the practice of adding the verse *Sicut erat*—“as it was”—to the doxology *Gloria Patri* had not yet been received in Gaul, although it had already prevailed in other regions. For the council speaks thus:

> “Because not only in the Apostolic See, but also throughout all the East and all Africa and Italy, on account of the cunning of heretics who blasphemously assert that the Son of God was not always with the Father but began in time, in all conclusions, after ‘Glory,’ ‘As it was in the beginning’ is said, we too decree that this shall be said in the same way in all our churches.”

Here the word “psalms” is not expressed after “in all conclusions,” [Col. 1210C] but it is plainly understood from these words of Pope Vigilius, Letter I to Profuturus, bishop of Braga, no. 3: “We judge it to be an innovation and error that, whereas at the end of psalms it is customarily said by all Catholics, ‘Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,’ etc.” If Gaul was later than the whole East in adding the verse *Sicut erat*, it certainly far preceded it in the practice of singing *Gloria Patri*. Cassian, in Book II of the *Institutes of the Coenobia*, believed to have been composed before 416, ch. 8, writes:

> “We have also seen in this province [Gaul] that, when one person sings at the conclusion of a psalm, all standing sing together aloud, ‘Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit’; this we have heard nowhere in the whole East.”

This being so, it must be admitted that the practice of singing the doxology *Gloria Patri*, with the addition of the verse *Sicut erat*, at the end of every psalm is ancient, having been devised to restrain the Arian heresy and gradually received throughout the whole Church; but there is no reason to attribute it to Damasus.

15. Damasus’s decree concerning the rite of singing *Alleluia* in the City.—Besides the eight decrees above, attributed to Damasus as though issued in a Roman synod, Gregory I ascribes to him another concerning the rite of singing the word *Alleluia* in Rome. A certain person, coming from Sicily, [Col. 1211A] complained to this pope that he followed in every respect the customs of the Church of Constantinople, or of the Greeks, specifically “because he had caused *Alleluia* to be said at Masses outside the season of Pentecost.” The devout and modest pontiff repelled even this unjust complainant, not without an adequate answer. But, as he himself wrote in October of the second indiction to John, bishop of Syracuse: “I replied that in none of those matters [which he criticized] have we followed another church”; and he then adds: “For the practice that *Alleluia* should be said here [the old Royal and Colbert manuscripts read ‘should not’] is handed down as having been drawn from the Church of Jerusalem, by the tradition of blessed Jerome, in the time of Damasus of blessed memory. And therefore in this matter we have rather abolished that custom.” What Gregory means in this passage must be examined, so that from it may be understood what he himself decreed, and what he says was decreed by Damasus.

16. The first interpretation of Gregory’s words set forth.—Cardinal Bona, *De divina psalmodia*, ch. 16, interprets it thus: when *Alleluia* was sung only during the Paschal season, then, at Jerome’s urging, Damasus decreed that it should also be used outside that season. Tillemont, vol. VIII, p. 420, likewise accepts this Cardinal’s interpretation. From this those two most distinguished men observe that the tradition commended by Gregory is not very certain, since, they say, the practice of singing *Alleluia* in Rome during Damasus’s age was so frequent that it was heard even at funerals, according to Jerome’s testimony in Fabiola’s epitaph. Tillemont adds [Col. 1211C] that it is not even certain whether Jerome had visited Jerusalem before Damasus’s death.

But even if their interpretation were admitted, and it were granted that Jerome had not visited Jerusalem before going to Damasus, nothing in the reasons adduced would disprove the tradition mentioned by Gregory. First, they speak only of singing *Alleluia* within Masses, not of using the same word outside Mass and at funerals. Secondly, Fabiola’s funeral occurred after Damasus’s death and thus after the introduction of the new practice. Finally, since it is known that Jerome lived in Syria before travelling to Rome, there is no doubt that he could have become acquainted there with the customs of Jerusalem.

17. The second interpretation is to be preferred.—[Col. 1211D] But Isidore Mercator followed an interpretation wholly opposite to that of the praised men. For, except on the occasion of Gregory’s cited words, he introduced Jerome as writing to Damasus as follows: “But in the Church the practice of saying *Alleluia* is to be confined to the fifty-day period from the holy Resurrection until holy Pentecost.” It is evident from this that he understood Gregory to mean that, whereas *Alleluia* had formerly been sung outside Pentecost, Damasus, at Jerome’s urging, decreed that it should be said only within Pentecost.

This interpretation of Gregory’s words agrees exceedingly well both with his language and with historical truth. For it is certain that in Augustine’s time there were some churches in which *Alleluia* was sung only during the Paschal season. Accordingly, the same Doctor writes in Letter formerly numbered 119, now 55, ch. 17: “That *Alleluia* should be sung in the church only during those fifty days is not everywhere observed; for on other days it is sung in different places in different ways.” Moreover, it may not rashly be inferred from Sozomen, Book VII, ch. 19, that among the churches which sang *Alleluia* only during Paschal time, the Roman Church was one. [Col. 1212A] He was indeed mistaken when he wrote, “At Rome *Alleluia* is sung once each year, on the first day of the Paschal festival,” and Nicephorus Callistus, copying his words, became an author of the same error, Book XII, ch. 34. But no other cause of this error appears likely than that, since Latin writers use *Pascha* indiscriminately both for the whole Paschal season and for the one day of the Lord’s resurrection, he heard that *Alleluia* was sung at Rome only at Pascha and construed as referring to one day what had been said to him of the whole Paschal season.

18. The same interpretation also coheres no less aptly with Gregory’s wording. He first states that someone had complained to him “because he had caused *Alleluia* to be said at Masses outside the season of Pentecost.” It follows that previously it was said only within the season of Pentecost. Then, to the charge that he had introduced Greek customs into the Roman Church, he replies: “In none of these things have we followed another church.” Thereupon, according to the Royal and Colbert manuscripts, he aptly adds: “For the practice that *Alleluia* should not be said here”—understand, outside the season of Pentecost—“is handed down as having been drawn from the Church of Jerusalem, by the tradition of blessed Jerome, in the time of Pope Damasus of blessed memory. And therefore in this matter,” in which we have ordered that it be said also outside the season of Pentecost, [Col. 1212C] “we have rather abolished that custom, which had been transmitted here by the Greeks.” Certainly, once his entire statement is thus explained, nothing fails to suit Gregory’s purpose most aptly. By contrast, if the received reading, “For the practice that *Alleluia* should be said here,” is similarly supplemented “outside the season of Pentecost,” the pontiff’s statement becomes not only obscure and devoid of all intelligibility, but absurd.

19. How the tradition cited by Gregory may stand.—Given these points, it remains to ask whether what Gregory writes as “drawn from [Jerome’s] tradition” can at least stand. Does not such a [Col. 1212D] tradition conflict with the same Doctor’s refutation, at the beginning of his book against Vigilantius, of that heretic’s assertion that “*Alleluia* must never be sung except at Pascha”? Or with his addition, in Fabiola’s epitaph, after recalling the whole city’s thronging to her funeral: “Psalms resounded, and the gilded ceiling of the temples, echoing on high, was shaken by *Alleluia*”? Indeed, even not long before Gregory’s time, *Alleluia* was customarily sung and frequently used outside Pentecost, at least in the churches of Italy, as is shown by the Rule of St Benedict, well known and familiar to Gregory. Chapter 15 directs: “That every Sunday outside Lent the canticles of Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, and None be said with *Alleluia*”; while on the other days [Col. 1213A] “from Pentecost until the beginning of Lent, on every night, [*Alleluia*] is to be said only with the last six psalms at Nocturns.”

Yet the mentioned tradition may be reconciled with these facts if the observation made by us above be admitted: namely, that it concerns saying *Alleluia* at Masses. Thus what the Rule of St Benedict ordains in the cited passage concerning responsories—“Responsories, however, are never to be said with *Alleluia*, except from Pascha until Pentecost”—also prevailed at Rome before Gregory’s time in Masses: they were never said with *Alleluia* except from Pascha until Pentecost. Gregory thought himself permitted to abolish the custom which, according to common report, had begun at Rome with Damasus, and to restore what had been abolished by that pope.

20. Five decrees attributed to Damasus.—[Col. 1213B] In Crabbe’s edition of the councils, and afterwards in the others, five further decrees collected from the compilations of Gratian and Ivo were published under Damasus’s name.
