The first is given by Gratian, II, question 3, ch. 2, as follows: “If the accuser fails in his accusation, let him receive retaliation in kind.” It was excerpted from the Isidorian letter, forged under Damasus’s name, to Bishop Stephen, ch. 7; its very words are cited by Gratian himself, IV, question 3, ch. 4. What is prescribed there agrees with Theodosian Code, Book IX, title I, law 14, and title 10, law 3.

21. The second is given thus: “If anyone attacks or accuses a bishop, priest, or deacon with false charges and cannot prove them, we judge that communion is not to be given him even at the end.” But this, cited by Gratian, II, question 3, ch. 4, as Damasus’s, and by Ivo, Part VI, ch. 240, after Burchard, Book II, ch. 195, as canon 5 of the Council of Carthage, belongs to neither; it is canon 75 of the Council of Elvira.

22. The third, which Gratian, X, question I, ch. 15, produces, is as follows:

> “We wholly forbid this custom, which seems to be growing contrary to the holy Catholic Church: that offerings made within the holy Church should under no circumstances be held under the control of laymen; but that only priests, who are seen to serve the Lord daily, may eat and drink of them. For in the Old Testament [Leviticus II and XXIV] the Lord forbade the children of Israel to eat the holy loaves, except Aaron alone and [Col. 1213D] his sons. Those loaves were far inferior to these loaves now offered in the holy Church, because those were under the shadow of the Law, whereas those which are now under the grace of the Holy Spirit, with the Gospel shining forth over the whole world, appear more splendid. With what face or what conscience do you wish to receive offerings, when you can scarcely offer prayers to God for yourselves, much less for others? For it is wicked and contrary to the Lord’s command, and brings loss upon his own soul, for anyone to attempt what is granted to him on no ground whatever. Since it pleased all our holy fathers and predecessors that this ordinance be made, we likewise wish to persevere in the same rule: let no one dare make void what has been established, if he does not wish to remain [Col. 1214A] in everlasting condemnation. But if anyone, as a rash presumptuous person, acts against this our rule and against the rule of the 318 holy Fathers, who ordained this in the Council of Nicaea, and hereafter seeks to remove offerings from sacred churches, let him be bound and condemned under the bond of anathema.” All replied: “Let it be done, let it be done.”

23. Concerning this decree I observe first that it appears to be nothing other than the fabrication of the man who composed the letter printed in the new edition of Jerome, vol. V, p. 420, under the title *Jerome to Damasus concerning altar offerings*, in which that Doctor is made to write to this pope thus:

> “Let your holy authority know, venerable Pope, concerning the question which you proposed to your client [Col. 1214B] and to which you sent fitting answers by letter—namely, concerning loaves offered on the altar by the faithful, who ought lawfully to use them—that I have taken care to write back to you briefly, so far as I have been able to investigate the matter from the principal Doctors of the Church. The competent witnesses whom I have summoned [read: consulted] to establish this matter are these: Gregory Nazianzen, that wonderful Doctor; Cyril, Athanasius, Theophilus, Anatolius, John Chrysostom, Eustachius, Eusebius the chronicler, and our Hilary. All of them, with one voice and one consent, as true instruments of the Holy Spirit, judge that those who have transferred the loaves of offerings to the use of laymen are to be smitten by the sword of anathema, because they are due wholly to priests alone—unless perhaps laymen, for religious reasons, receive them from the priest’s hand as a blessing.

> “Moreover, our Fathers enacted this not only concerning loaves in church, but concerning everything offered to the altar, saying and teaching that it is a great crime, and that wherever it occurs it is done in every respect with diabolical presumption; and that it is utterly intolerable to the holy Church [Col. 1214C] that it should remain without the punishment prescribed by the holy canons. Thus Chrysostom, in his commentaries on Matthew [Matthew XII.1], where the disciples plucked ears of grain on the Sabbath and the Pharisees rebuked them, says: ‘If David and his men, still under the shadow of the Law, were not permitted to eat the loaves of presentation when, driven by hunger, he asked Abimelech for loaves, how now, when the Gospel shines forth, should laymen be persuaded to seize for their own use the offering of loaves offered to God?’ For the Apostle likewise says: ‘Those who serve at the altar partake of the altar’ [X, question 1, ch. 13].

> “Therefore, since priests customarily pray for all those whose alms and offerings they receive, with what face do laymen presume either to eat offerings which Christians offer for their sins, or to grant them to others, when they themselves ought not to pray for the people? For this reason, glorious Pope, those presumptuous persons ought to be subjected to perpetual excommunication, so that the rest may fear and that such things may no longer occur in the Church.”

24. Both works are the work of an impostor.—Concerning this letter, it was noted in the most recent edition of Jerome that its fabricator “piles up the names of authors from whom he nevertheless adduces nothing, because he had read none of them; he specifically cites Chrysostom’s commentaries, although St Jerome was entirely unacquainted with Chrysostom.” He certainly did not know Chrysostom’s commentaries on Matthew while Damasus lived. For that pope died in 384; Chrysostom, however, only began preaching when he was ordained priest in 386. Nor did we find, despite searching, the words here cited as though from Chrysostom’s commentaries on Matthew XII.1. Moreover, if we compare this letter with the preceding decree, we shall discover that they are the work of one and the same artificer, who assumes now the character of a counsellor whom one consults, now that of a judge pronouncing sentence. The presbyter Gregory, known under the name Polycarp, and Gratian excerpted both from the same source.

Many other features also reveal the impostor. For when, in 502 under Pope Symmachus, a document of the king of the Heruli was read before a council—a document by which he attempted to attribute a certain right over the Church’s property to kings—the whole council protested against a thing unheard of until then; and Bishop Eulalius specifically said [Col. 1215B] (*Symmachus*, Epistle V, no. 11): “No power of disposing in any way of ecclesiastical property is ever found to have been attributed to laymen, however religious.” Accordingly, in the times of Damasus, and still more in those of the Nicene synod, there was no need to restrain laymen from appropriating ecclesiastical offerings. This wicked custom, which the impostor complains was increasing and growing daily, has rather the flavour of the beginning of the ninth century. Therefore the bishops assembled in 836 at the Second Council of Aachen confirmed, by testimonies from Scripture, the Fathers, and councils in three books sent to King Pippin, what they had earlier written to that king “against those who said that there was no distinction if they used for their own necessities things offered to God.”

25. Both may plausibly be attributed to Isidore Mercator.—Both writings, then, aptly fit the time in which the impostor Isidore lived. Neither indeed occurs in his large collection; but nothing prevents us from judging that, after the publication of that collection, a genius so fertile in falsehoods produced something new. Certainly, he who wrote to Damasus in Jerome’s name concerning adding the verse *Gloria Patri* at the end of every psalm, “Therefore your client prays,” now seems to address the same man under the same name: “Concerning the question which you proposed to your client.” The man who, in both writings, wishes a recent ordinance to be heard as though it were an ancient rule of the holy Fathers—is he not recognized as the very man accustomed to sell his own opinions as decrees of the ancients, and to introduce the earlier Roman pontiffs as defenders of decrees promulgated only by later persons? Finally, it is characteristic of him to commend his inventions by the fictitious authority of the Council of Nicaea. To make this succeed more readily, from the very preface of his collection he labours with utmost zeal to persuade readers that the Council of Nicaea formerly possessed far more canons than are extant. Hence repeatedly, and especially in the pseudo-Julian letter, he does not fear to attribute to that council many decrees wholly foreign to it. To whom, then, should we assign the decree against those who seek to remove offerings from sacred churches—a decree most falsely trumpeted to us as an ancient Nicene rule of the 318 Fathers—if not to the notorious father of such falsehoods?

26. On violators of canons.—In editions of the councils the fourth decree is given thus: “Voluntary violators of canons are severely judged by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift they were dictated; since they seem not incongruously to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, etc.” Yet this was not unpublished. For Gratian, XXV, question I, ch. 5, transcribed it from the letter which Isidore Mercator attributed to Damasus as writing in reply to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and placed at the head of his collection. It may be seen published in Labbe, vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 863, and elsewhere.

27. On metropolitans who neglect to request the pallium.—The last runs as follows:

> “Since certain metropolitans, refusing to set forth their faith to the holy Apostolic See according to ancient custom, neither request nor receive the use of the pallium, and in consequence the consecration of bishops for vacant churches is dangerously delayed: it has pleased us that any metropolitan who, within three months of his consecration, has not sent to the Apostolic See to set forth his faith and receive the pallium, shall lose the dignity entrusted to him. Other metropolitans, after a second and third admonition, shall have permission, with the counsel of the Roman pontiff, to assist vacant churches by ordaining bishops [Ans.: ‘a vacant church . . . by ordaining a bishop’]. But if through the negligence of the bishop to be consecrated a church remains vacant beyond three months, let him be deprived of communion until he either yields the place or does not delay to present himself for consecration. But if through his own negligence he keeps the church vacant beyond five months, let him receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere; rather, let him yield to the judgment of his metropolitan [Ans.: ‘withdraw’].”

This is attributed to Damasus by Anselm, Book VI, ch. 80; Burchard, Book I, ch. 25; Polycarp, Book II, title 10; and the author of the *Panormia*, Book III, ch. 11. But Ivo, Part III, ch. 136, and Gratian, Distinction 100, ch. 1—whom Innocent III also follows, Book I, Epistle 117 to the archbishop of Bourges, beginning *Ne si universi*—attribute it to Pelagius. The same Innocent, cited in *Extra*, *De translatione episcopi*, ch. 2, §1, cites its final words as from a canon: “Nor is that to be overlooked which is read in the canon concerning the elect: if through his own negligence he keeps the church vacant beyond six months—note that ‘six,’ not ‘five,’ is read there—let him receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere; rather, let him yield to the judgment of his metropolitan, etc.”

28. But it accords neither with Damasus nor with Pelagius I or II, since it asserts and safeguards a discipline introduced only in the eighth century. This may be inferred from the council over which Boniface, bishop of Mainz, presided in 742, and concerning which he himself writes in Epistle 105: “We decreed in our synodal assembly, and confessed, that we would preserve to the end the Catholic faith, unity, and submission to the Roman Church; that we wished to be subject to St Peter and his vicars; [Col. 1217A] and that metropolitans should seek pallia from that see.” Hence it is plain that, at least in Gaul, no law had yet been imposed on metropolitans in 742 compelling them to seek pallia from the Apostolic See. Indeed, from Pope Zachary’s Letter 5 to Boniface and Boniface’s reply to him, we learn that the Franks did not immediately obey the aforesaid decree and that metropolitans later still deliberated whether they should seek pallia from the Apostolic See.

But if by the middle of the eighth century the custom that metropolitans should seek pallia from the Apostolic See had not yet fully prevailed, who would not judge the decree far more recent—a decree plainly issued [Col. 1217B] when the long-established practice was that metropolitans not only sought the pallium from the Apostolic See, but could neither discharge their office nor ordain bishops until they had received it? The most recent editors of Gratian have noted that, where the heading of the cited decree reads “Pope Pelagius,” two Vatican manuscripts have “John VIII, from the Third Council at Ravenna.” No one will deny that it aptly fits the times of this pope, whom Gratian likewise cites, Distinction 100, ch. 4, as writing thus to Wilbert, bishop of Cologne: “We have been unable now to confer upon you the pallium you requested, because we have found the statement of your faith to contain less than it ought.”

I observe in passing that, although in Pope Zachary’s time the custom had not yet prevailed that all metropolitans were bound to seek the pallium from the Apostolic See, those to whom it was then granted nevertheless customarily set forth their faith first to the Apostolic See. Thus the same pope writes in Letter 4 to Boniface: [Col. 1218B] “We have sent them instructions concerning the custom of the pallium and how those who are permitted to use the pallium ought to set forth their faith.”

[Col. 1217]

## TWO POEMS ALSO ATTRIBUTED BY SOME TO POPE DAMASUS. (C, S)*

### EPITAPH OF THE PRIEST SISENNIUS

(Gruter, p. 1172, no. 9.)

[Col. 1217B]

Here the priest Sisinnius wished to lay down his limbs,  
Beloved by every people and a priest worthy of his office;  
One who knew how to preserve the covenants of his holy mother;  
[Col. 1217C] Ever gentle in God’s love, knowing how to live,  
Content with his own lot, and knowing nothing of the prince’s court.

### TO REPROVE A CERTAIN BROTHER

[Note: This little letter is thus entitled by the copyist.]

(From the parchments of the Passionei Library, now the Angelica Library of the Augustinian Hermits.)

[Note: Parchment manuscript, eleventh century, fol. 31, shelf-mark no. LXXXVII.]

Tityrus, reclining beneath the faithful shelter of Christ,

[Col. 1218B] You sing divine utterances [Note: It denotes psalms, I think.] with sacred voice.

You do not vainly meditate upon false tales [Note: The first syllable of *fabulas* is shortened inelegantly.];

For in the latter is contained the glory of the blessed life,

But for the former endless and everlasting punishments will follow.

[Col. 1218C] Therefore beware, brother, lest you submit yourself to empty cares,

Lest the grim Tartarus of hell snatch you away in misery.

Rather, remember to breathe the sacred Scriptures in your heart,

Which may make hearts pure through chaste nourishment.

May the grace of the Lord always preserve you safe.

[Col. 1217]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING CALENDAR

(From Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 163.)

[Col. 1217] This Calendar of the Saints whom the Church of Carthage formerly commemorated annually may be called African. Of all calendars hitherto published in print, it is, I think, the most ancient and rarest. By a happy chance we found it in a very ancient codex of the celebrated monastery of Cluny, containing the Commentaries of Blessed Jerome on Isaiah—or rather, attached not to the codex itself but to the worm-eaten wooden cover of the codex, which had been gnawed by moths and worms. It was worthwhile to tear the very ancient, half-eaten parchment away from the decayed wood. The front part of the cover contained the beginning of the Calendar, the back part the remainder. The script is Roman, written in capital letters, and is no later than the seventh century.

This is an ancient calendar, since no saints occur in it later than those—still less Fulgentius the bishop—who suffered in the Vandal persecution under King Huneric. The saints then honored in Africa by annual observance were for the most part natives of the region; some, however, came from Italica and from Spain, besides the apostolic men. There is no feast of the Mother of God, concerning whom Augustine has no treatise or sermon. The year begins on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, that is, after Easter; it ends on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March. There is no feast throughout the whole month of March—that is, throughout the whole of Lent. It seemed worthwhile to give these general notices. The title of the old parchment is worded as follows: “Here are contained the birthdays of the martyrs and the depositions of bishops which the Church of Carthage celebrates annually.”

[Col. 1219]

## MOST ANCIENT CALENDAR OF THE CHURCH OF CARTHAGE. (C)

[Col. 1219A] [Note: Thus runs the title in the manuscript.] Here are contained the birthdays of the martyrs and the depositions of bishops which the Church of Carthage celebrates annually.

XIII Kalends of May: of the martyr Mappalicus. [Note: [Col. 1219A] XIII Kalends of May: of the martyr Mappalicus. He is the very same man whom Lucian celebrates with his companions in the letter to Celerinus, which is letter 22 among Cyprian’s letters; and Cyprian himself in letter 23, to the martyrs and confessors, and in letter 9, to the Roman clergy, where he says among other things: “A voice full of the Holy Spirit burst forth from the martyr’s mouth, when the most blessed Mappalicus said to the proconsul amid his torments: ‘Tomorrow you shall see the contest’; and what he said with the testimony of courage and faith, the Lord fulfilled.” Then the same most holy bishop exhorts his own flock, by the example of the martyrs Mappalicus [Col. 1219B], that those whom, he says, “the bond of confession and the hospitality of prison have joined together, may also be joined by the consummation of courage and the heavenly crown.” In Ado, who reports these words, and in the old Roman Martyrology published by Rosweyde, as well as in Usuard and Notker, Mappalicus is praised on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. Wandalbert’s metrical calendar agrees. His bare name is read in the third volume of the Bollandist April.]  

III Kalends of May: of the martyr Pudens. [Note: [Col. 1219B] III Kalends of May: of the martyr Pudens. Not, indeed, that Pudens, the Roman senator, whom Paul mentions in the Second Epistle to Timothy—the father of Novatus and also of the virgins Praxedes and Pudentiana—whose house on the Viminal was converted into a church, which thereafter received the title of Pastor; but rather Pudens, the soldier, an *optio* and officer in charge of the prison, who, as Saint Perpetua says in the Acts written by herself and Saint Felicity, “held us in high regard and began to understand that there was great power in us; he admitted many persons to us, so that both we and they might refresh one another” [Col. 1219C]. Or perhaps Pudens, the martyr of Alexandria, whose commemoration is made on this very day by the continuators of the Bollandists.]  

II Kalends of May: of the martyr Claudius. [Note: [Col. 1219C] II Kalends of May: of the martyr Claudius. It is uncertain who this Claudius was, unless he is the Claudius counted among the other Alexandrian martyrs on this day in certain copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology, according to the Bollandist associates.]  

III Nones of May: deposition of Bishop Gratus. [Note: [Col. 1219C] III Nones of May: deposition of Bishop Gratus. The bishop of Carthage, who attended the Council of Sardica with other African bishops and presided over the first Council of Carthage in the year 348, where he opposed the efforts of Donatus; he also undertook an embassy to Emperor Constans. The Bollandist continuators have nothing concerning him on this day.]  

[Col. 1220A] II Nones of May: of the martyrs Marinus and James. [Note: [Col. 1219C] II Nones of May: of the martyrs Marinus and James. Baronius calls him Marianus, from the Acts which he copied from Surius’s April volume, under the year 262, no. 34. These holy martyrs suffered in Numidia in the same year, regarded as the last year of that persecution. They are commemorated on the day before the Kalends of May in the Roman Martyrology, in Rosweyde’s old Martyrology [Col. 1220A], and in Ado, who briefly recounts their Acts. Surius recounts these Acts on the same day, as do the Bollandists.]  

Nones of May: deposition of Bishop Geneclus. [Note: [Col. 1220A] Nones of May: deposition of Bishop Geneclus. He is undoubtedly Genethlius, whom Augustine, in the letter to Eleusius and others, letter 44 of the new edition, calls the bishop of Carthage of blessed memory before Aurelius. The Bollandist associates have nothing concerning him.]  

V Ides of May: Saint Majulus. [Note: [Col. 1220A] V Ides of May: Saint Majulus. Notker writes on this day: “In Africa, Majolus, Victorinus, Fortunatus, and other soldiers.” The commonly circulated Martyrology of Jerome agrees [Col. 1220B], as published by our Acherius in the fourth volume of the *Spicilegium*, and the second volume of the Bollandist May, p. 625.]  

III Ides of May: of the martyr Secundianus. [Note: [Col. 1220B] III Ides of May: of the martyr Secundianus. In the commonly circulated Martyrology of Jerome and in Notker, the following is commemorated on the day before the Kalends of May: “In Africa, the birthday of Saint Secundianus, Quartus, Victorianus,” etc. Some copies among the Bollandists have “Secundianus, bishop and martyr.” There was also another Secundianus, bishop of a place called Thambes, mentioned in the Council of Carthage held by Cyprian concerning the rebaptism of heretics. Augustine also mentions him in Book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 44. Thambes, moreover, was a mountain situated at the far end of Numidia, called Thabeis by others; hence perhaps the city Thabena in Caesar, and the place which received the name Tabba in Ptolemy.]  

II Ides of May: Saints Felix, Cecilius, and their companions. [Note: [Col. 1220B] II Ides of May: Saints Felix, Cecilius, and their companions. That is, Saint Felix, to whom Cecilius, together with others, is joined as a fellow martyr in the second volume of the Bollandist May, but on the Nones of May, p. 136.]  

XI Kalends of June: Saints Castus and Aemilius. [Note: [Col. 1220C] XI Kalends of June: Saints Castus and Aemilius. The Martyrologies of Bede, Rabanus, and Notker fittingly read here: “XI Kalends of June, in Africa, Castus and Aemilius, who consummated their martyrdom through the fire of suffering,” as the blessed Cyprian writes in the book *On the Lapsed*. Usuard has the same, and Wandalbert’s metrical calendar agrees. Augustine delivered a sermon, published among the miscellaneous sermons, on the birthday of the martyrs Castus and Aemilius, as Possidius testifies in chapter 9. Another Castus, a deacon, was examined in the Acts of Cirta, in Baronius under the year 303, no. 26.]  

X Kalends of June: Saints Lucius and Montanus. [Note: [Col. 1220C] X Kalends of June: Saints Lucius and Montanus. Flavianus, Julianus, Victorius, and other confessors, disciples of Cyprian, are joined with Lucius and Montanus, African martyrs; Baronius published their letter and the Acts of their passion after Surius, under the year 262. The Martyrologies of Jerome and Notker place them on this very day. Montanus is praised in Celerinus’s letter to Lucian, letter 21 among Cyprian’s letters; Lucius in letters 68, 69, 78, and 80.]  

[Col. 1221A] VIII Kalends of June: Saint Flavianus and Septimia. [Note: [Col. 1221A] VIII Kalends of June: Saint Flavianus and Septimia. There is no doubt that this Flavianus is the same man who, the illustrious fellow martyr of Saints Lucius and Montanus, met death two days after them. For no other African martyr of that name is to be found; and from the Acts of Lucius and his companions themselves it is clear that, at the request of his friends, Flavianus’s execution [Col. 1221B] was delayed for two days, so that in this way the martyr’s unconquered endurance might be broken—which did not happen. But whence came Septimia the martyr? On the sixth day before the Ides of May the Martyrology of Jerome praises, at Rome, among many others, Septimia the martyr; but we seek another here.]  

II Kalends of June: Saints of Timida. [Note: [Col. 1221B] II Kalends of June: Saints of Timida. If the Acts of the martyrs of Timida ever existed anywhere, they have disappeared. Perhaps among their number was that distinguished Confessor Faustus of Timida-regia, also mentioned by Augustine in *Against Cresconius*, Book VII, chapter 22. This Faustus gave his judgment at the Council of Carthage held under Cyprian in support of the baptism of heretics. Timida-regia was situated in the proconsular province of Africa; its bishop, named Benenatus, was deported to Corsica by King Hunneric.]  

III Nones of June: Saint Perseverans, martyr. [Note: [Col. 1221B] III Nones of June: Saint Perseverans, martyr. The Hieronymian Martyrology mentions Perseverans, martyr of Terracina, on the Kalends of November; I find no other.]  

Nones of June: Saint Systus. [Note: [Col. 1221C] Nones of June: Saint Systus. He appears to have been a bishop, but of what place is not clear; he must certainly be distinguished from Pope Xystus, listed shortly afterward.]  

III Ides of June: Saint Gallo. [Note: [Col. 1221C] III Ides of June: Saint Gallo. The Martyrology attributed to Jerome praises Gallo, a martyr of an uncertain place, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March; and Galanus, a martyr from Africa, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December.]  

XIII Kalends of July: Saints Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs. [Note: [Col. 1221C] XIII Kalends of July: Saints Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs. Their passion and cult were famous at Milan, and perhaps were brought from there into Africa through Augustine, who was a witness to the discovery of their bodies by Saint Ambrose, as appears from Book IX of the *Confessions*, chapter 7.]  

VIII Kalends of July: Saint John the Baptist. [Note: [Col. 1221C] VIII Kalends of July: Saint John the Baptist. Here are two sermons of Saint Augustine on his nativity, besides those of other Fathers.]  

Saint … and Rogatus, martyr. [Note: [Col. 1221C] … Saint … and Rogatus, martyr. Rogatus is numbered among the most renowned martyrs of Aluta in Baronius under the year 303, no. 26.]  

[Col. 1222A] … July: Saint E… , martyr. [Note: [Col. 1221D] … July: Saint E… , martyr. The Calendar is mutilated at this point. Perhaps it should be read: “Saint Elaphus, martyr in Africa,” who is recorded on the fourth day before the Kalends of July in the commonly circulated Hieronymian Martyrology, with Sabianus, Felix, and others.]  

… July: Saints … Apostles. [Note: [Col. 1221D] … July: Saints … Apostles. Undoubtedly Peter and Paul, who receive an entry on the third day before the Kalends of July in all Martyrologies. Possidius, in chapters 9 and 10 of the *Index*, mentions Augustine’s treatises delivered on their birthday.]  

… July … [Note: [Col. 1221D] July … The Calendar is likewise defective at this point; it would be irreverent to guess.]  

The Ides of July: Saint Catulinus, martyr. [Note: [Col. 1221D] The Ides of July: Saint Catulinus, martyr. The African martyr Catulinus is known from no other source than Augustine’s miscellaneous sermon delivered on Catulinus’s birthday. I read that Calus was admitted among the African martyrs, through a copyist’s error for Catulinus, who is mentioned on this day in the Martyrologies of Jerome and Usuard. [Col. 1222A] Jerome: “In Africa, in the city of Carthage, the birthday of the holy martyrs Catolinus the deacon and the rest of the martyrs, who rest in the basilica of Saint Fausta.” Ado and Usuard read “in the basilica of Faustus,” and enumerate his companions. In Victor of Vita the “basilica of Faustus” is read twice in Book II and once [Col. 1222B] in Book III of *The Persecution*. Ancient writers, through ignorance, often wrote *Faustae* for *Fausti*, as above, “Saint Felicis,” and similarly throughout this Calendar.]  

XV … Kalends of August: Saints of Scilli. [Note: [Col. 1222B] XV … Kalends of August: Saints of Scilli, or, as printed books have it, Scylitani. Having been arrested in the year of Christ 202, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, as their Acts in Baronius state, they were executed within four days. Possidius, chapter 9 of the *Index*, records Augustine’s sermon delivered on the birthday of the holy martyrs of Scilli. Is it the very sermon which in printed editions is called the sixth sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*? In the manuscript of the Cistercian monastery of Holy Cross in Jerusalem at Rome, it is said to have been delivered in the basilica of the holy martyrs of Scilli. Usuard’s Martyrology, together with the Acts, enumerates twelve altogether on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, on which day at Carthage occurred the birthday of the holy martyrs of Scilli: Speratus, Nartalus, Cythinus, Beturius, Felix, Aquilinus, Laetatius, Januaria, Generosa, Bessia, Donata, and Secunda, under the prefect Saturninus. After their first confession they were sent to prison [Col. 1222C], fixed upon the wood, and then beheaded with the sword. The Acts enumerate the same number of martyrs, though with names slightly altered; Bede’s Martyrology likewise, where there are eleven martyrs of Scilli, and Jerome’s, where only seven are numbered. Wandalbert calls them a people of twelve. Victor mentions them in Book I: “And, to speak of what is necessary, the larger basilica, where the bodies of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity are buried, that of Celerina, or of the Scillitan martyrs, and others which they did not destroy, they appropriated to their own religion by tyrannical license.”]  

XIII Kalends of August: deposition of Saint Aurelius, bishop. [Note: [Col. 1222C] XIII Kalends of August: deposition of Saint Aurelius, bishop. Bishop of Carthage, a most celebrated man and contemporary of Augustine, whose name I do not find in the martyrologies.]  

XI Kalends of August: Saints of Maxula. [Note: [Col. 1222C] XI Kalends of August: Saints of Maxula. The African city of Maxula, in the proconsular province, produced a band of martyrs; it is regrettable that their Acts have disappeared. Among Augustine’s published sermons are two on the holy martyrs of Massilia, namely miscellaneous sermons 42 and 43 [Col. 1222D], where perhaps “Maxula” should be restored. Nor do manuscript codices reject this. Yet Victor of Vita, in Book I, writes “the Massilian shore.” Carcadius, bishop of Maxula, exiled to Corsica by Hunneric, is attested in the *Notice of the Provinces and Cities of Africa*.]  

… Kalends of August: deposition of Saint Capreolus, bishop. [Note: [Col. 1222D] … Kalends of August: deposition of Saint Capreolus, bishop. After Aurelius, with Quodvultdeus in between, he was bishop of Carthage. He wrote a letter to the Fathers at Ephesus, published in the councils; likewise another to the Spaniards Vitalis and Constantius, or Tonantius, which the eminent Jacques Sirmond published from the manuscript of Hérivaux.]  

III Kalends of August: the holy women of Tuburbo, and Septimia. [Note: [Col. 1222D] III Kalends of August: the holy women of Tuburbo, and Septimia. There was one Tuburbo the Greater and another the Lesser. Victor of Vita mentions the city of Tuburbo the Greater in Book III. Tuburbo the Lesser was in Zeugitana; its bishop was Victor in the Conference of Carthage, and Maximus [Col. 1223A] was his adversary. Tuburbo the Greater was a city of proconsular Africa; its bishop Benenatus is listed in the *Notice of Africa*. Notker calls the place where the martyrs suffered Tuburbo-Lucernaria. Most ancient and modern writers ordinarily mark two companies of holy female martyrs of Tuburbo: namely Perpetua and Felicity, who suffered on the Nones of March; and the virgins Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, who consummated their martyrdom at Tuburbo on this third day before the Kalends of August. No one denies that the latter suffered at this date; and it is established by the unanimous agreement of ancient authorities, who entered [Col. 1223B] their names in the sacred diptychs on this day, that they are indicated here. Whether Perpetua and Felicity also shed their blood at Tuburbo in Mauretania or at Carthage is open to doubt. Ancient authors support both views. Pseudo-Bede, Notker, Usuard, and the rest who followed them have Tuburbo. Prosper in the Chronicle published by Labbe, Bede in *On the Six Ages*, Freculf, Regino and Hermann, Rabanus, and others prefer Carthage. The late Henri de Valois, of most illustrious memory, adopted the latter opinion. In the preface to the Acts of these martyrs published at Paris, having weighed the arguments on both sides, he proves by weighty arguments that they were killed at Carthage rather than Tuburbo. The matter itself would be settled by the authority of this Calendar, if it covered the month of March—when the martyrs suffered—as it does the other months. For no one would doubt that it would record them on the Nones of March, as other martyrologies do. But because at that time in Africa no commemoration of martyrs [Col. 1223C] was celebrated throughout the whole Lenten season and the Paschal feasts, it follows that from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May the name of no saint is entered here, much less that of Perpetua and Felicity. Whether they were transferred to the third day before the Kalends of August and received their feast together with the virgins of Tuburbo is for others to judge. Certainly, anyone who reads through the sermons of Blessed Augustine concerning those two martyrs will plainly see that they were celebrated by a distinct feast and cult. The Martyrology attributed to Jerome adds sixteen others to the martyrs of Tuburbo—Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda—among whom Septimia, praised here, is numbered.]  

[Col. 1223A] Kalends of August: Saints Maccabees. [Note: [Col. 1223C] Kalends of August: Saints Maccabees. From this alone it is clear that the feast of the Maccabees is exceedingly ancient in the Church; Saint Bernard gives its rationale in letter 98. Earlier still are the homilies of the Fathers concerning the Maccabees themselves: Gregory Nazianzen, John Chrysostom, and others who followed.]  

VIII Ides of August: Saint Systus, bishop and martyr of Rome. [Note: [Col. 1223C] VIII Ides of August: Saint Systus, bishop and martyr of Rome. His commemoration may therefore have been especially precious among Africans in preference to Saints Stephen and Cornelius [Col. 1223D], because he settled the controversy concerning the baptism of heretics. Hence Pontius, in the Life of Saint Cyprian, calls him a good and peace-making priest.]  

IV Ides of August: Saint Lawrence. [Note: [Col. 1223D] V Ides of August: Saint Lawrence. The illustrious martyr of Rome, whom all praise on this day; Augustine too, among the Fathers, delivered a sermon on the birthday of Saint Lawrence the martyr. Possidius records it in chapter 9 of the *Index*.]  

II Ides of August: Saint Marinus. [Note: [Col. 1223D] II Ides: Saint Marinus. I remain uncertain who this Marinus was. Among the bishops who were *traditores* mentioned by Optatus, I find Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae; but whether he was entered among the saints, or whether—as may be the case—he is the person designated here, I would not venture to guess. I also know Marinus, bishop of Arles, who is the first to subscribe the synodal letter to Pope Sylvester in the Donatist case. Did he obtain a place for that reason?]  

Ides of August: Saint Hippolytus. [Note: [Col. 1223D] Ides of August: Saint Hippolytus. The very famous Roman martyr, [Col. 1224A] concerning whom, among others, Prudentius wrote in Hymn 11, *Peristephanon* (*On the Crowns*).]  

… Kalends of September: Saints of the White Mass. [Note: [Col. 1224A] … Kalends of September: Saints of the White Mass. Three hundred African martyrs of the White Mass are counted; Pontius describes their noble martyrdom in the Acts of Saint Cyprian, Prudentius in Hymn 13, and Augustine in his exposition of Psalm 49 and in Miscellaneous Sermon 112, which Possidius records in chapter 9 of the *Index*. They are mentioned in the martyrologies on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, but in the commonly circulated Martyrology of Jerome on the fifteenth day before those Kalends.]  

[Col. 1224A] … Kalends of September: Saint Quadratus. [Note: [Col. 1224A] … Kalends of September: Saint Quadratus. I find Quadratus, defender of the Christian religion, in the time of Emperor Hadrian, after Publius, bishop of the Athenians. I would not suppose that he is recorded in an African Calendar. Possidius, in chapter 9, indicates a sermon of Augustine delivered on the birthday of the martyr Quadratus; this sermon, not yet known among the published works, was excerpted by Bede in his genuine exposition of Paul’s epistles, compiled from various works of Augustine, such as the copy we found in the library of Saint-Sithiu. A fragment of it quoted by Bede will shortly be brought to light in the new edition of Augustine. Yet it is not thereby clear who this Quadratus was, the bishop celebrated both by Augustine and in our Calendar. It is not permissible to bring in Quadratus, the bishop who attended the Conference of Carthage, since during Augustine’s lifetime he could not yet have been enrolled among the saints, much less celebrated by a sermon of Augustine. In the commonly circulated Martyrology of Saint Jerome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, the birthday of Saint Quadratus, bishop, is numbered among others; perhaps he is meant here. Nor should it object that [Col. 1224C] Quadratus is there mentioned on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, whereas the martyrs of the White Mass are generally noted in the martyrologies on the ninth day before those Kalends. For from the fading numerical letters of our Calendar we have been unable to determine what day was assigned to them; and Timothy, who is placed everywhere on the eleventh day before the Kalends, is set down here after Quadratus, not to mention after the martyrs of the White Mass.]  

… Kalends of September: Saint Timothy. [Note: [Col. 1224C] … Kalends of September: Saint Timothy. In ancient martyrologies, including the genuine Martyrology of Bede, Timothy the martyr is praised on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September; he had come from Antioch to Rome in the time of Pope Miltiades and was beheaded there.]  

… Kalends of September: Saint Genesius the actor. [Note: [Col. 1224C] … Kalends of September: Saint Genesius the actor. At Rome, Genesius the actor, or master of the art of mime, is commemorated under Emperor Diocletian in most martyrologies with Genesius of Arles on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. In the Martyrology of Jerome, however, Genesius of Arles is recorded on the following day and is also praised by Prudentius in Hymn 4.]  

IV Kalends of September: deposition of Bishops Restitutus and Augustine. [Note: [Col. 1224D] IV Kalends of September: deposition of Bishops Restitutus and Augustine. The Roman Martyrology, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, mentions Saint Restitutus, bishop and martyr of Carthage. But those who call him a martyr lack Augustine as their authority; Possidius, chapter 10, lists Augustine’s treatise entitled *On the Deposition of Bishop Restitutus*, without the designation “martyr.” On him see Baronius under the year 303, no. 75. Augustine says remarkable things concerning another Restitutus, a presbyter of Calama, in Book XII of *The City of God*, chapter 24. I also read of several African bishops of that name, both in the letters of the Council of Carthage and in the *Notice of the Provinces of Africa*; but they do not concern this passage, since here the Restitutus in question is placed before Augustine and was therefore older than he.]  

III Kalends of September: Saints Felix, Eva, and Regiola, martyrs. [Note: [Col. 1224D] III Kalends of September: Saints Felix, Eva, and Regiola, martyrs. They were martyrs of Aluta in Numidia, joined with many others, whose Acts Baronius supplies [Col. 1225A] under the year 303, no. 35, where in some printed editions *Fua* is written through a typographical error for Eva. The day is unknown from the Acts; but it is certain to be after the fifth day before the Kalends of August, on which day Augustine, in the *Brief Record of the Conference*, third day, chapter 17, says that they suffered under the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian, on the day before the Ides of February—although the martyrologies commemorate them on the third day before the Ides, and this Calendar on the third day before the Kalends of September.]  

[Col. 1225A] … Ides of September: Saint Ampelius. [Note: [Col. 1225B] … Ides of September: Saint Ampelius. Ampelius likewise occupies fourth place among the martyrs of Aluta; I do not know whether he is the same as the Ampelius listed here, who is not at all called a martyr. Ampelius is twice named among the Fathers of the Council of Carthage, both when they write to Pope Innocent and when Innocent’s reply is sent to them; but I have not yet been able to discover the episcopal see which he held.]  

XVIII Kalends of October: Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage. [Note: [Col. 1225B] XVIII Kalends of October: Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage. His name, doctrine, and sanctity are held in esteem, and deservedly so, among all, but especially among Africans. Victor of Vita, Book I, reports that in his own time there were two outstanding and spacious basilicas bearing Cyprian’s name at Carthage: one where he shed his blood, the other where his body was buried, a place called Mappalia.]  

XVI Kalends of October: Saint Euphemia. [Note: [Col. 1225B] XVI Kalends of October: Saint Euphemia. Euphemia, virgin and martyr of Chalcedon, suffered in the year 311 on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October. Asterius describes her clothed in a dark robe and cloak, declaring Philosophy as her profession [Col. 1225C]. The day suits this place.]  

… Kalends of October: Saint Januarius, martyr. [Note: [Col. 1225C] … Kalends of October: Saint Januarius, martyr. I think that the Januarius recorded here is the African martyr who in the year 302 received the crown of martyrdom with Paulus Gerontius and six others. Unless Januarius is the bishop of Benevento, who suffered at Naples in Campania under Maximian, with the martyr Sossius, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, and of whom the Calendar speaks immediately afterward.]  

… Kalends of October: Saint Sossius. [Note: [Col. 1225C] … Kalends of October: Saint Sossius. In the year 305 Sossius, deacon of the church of Misenum, was arrested with Januarius, bishop of Benevento, and others; under the prefect Dracontius, after various tortures, he was beheaded. He is commemorated in Rosweyde’s old Roman Martyrology on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. Is he the one in the Hieronymian Martyrology on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the words: “And elsewhere, Januarius, Sossius,” etc.?]  

VI Ides of October: Saint Quintasius. [Note: [Col. 1225C] VI Ides of October: Saint Quintasius. In the same Martyrology of Jerome, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, Quintasus is recorded among others in this fashion: “In Africa, Heraclius, Dionysius,” etc.; “and elsewhere, Caius, Quintasius,” etc., whose day seems to correspond to this place [Col. 1225D]. Several bishops subscribe to the letter of the Fathers of Arles given to Pope Sylvester; among them it is beyond doubt that not a few came there from Africa. Quintasius is included among these, though his see is unknown to us. Moreover, among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis summoned with the rest to Carthage by Hunneric, Quintasius of Mutecita holds a place.]  

[Col. 1226A] III Ides of October: Saint Luke, evangelist and martyr. [Note: [Col. 1225D] III Ides of October: Saint Luke, evangelist and martyr. Two details here do not agree with the rest: namely, the day and the designation “martyr.” Luke is customarily recorded on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, and he does not generally bear the title of martyr. Yet Gregory Nazianzen suggests it in Oration I against Julian, and Paulinus and Gaudentius state it openly. Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 43, describes the manner of his martyrdom, saying that Luke was hanged from an olive tree because there was no supply of dry timber from which a cross might be made. Gaudentius, in Sermon 17, or the treatise *On the Dedication of the Basilica of the Holy Forty Martyrs*, identifies the place as Patrae, a city of Achaea [Col. 1226A].]  

XVI Kalends of November: Saints of Volitana. [Note: [Col. 1226A] XVI Kalends of November: Saints of Volitana. Volitana—or Bolitana, as others write—was a city of the proconsular province. It had Boniface as bishop under King Hunneric, by whom he was exiled to Corsica. There a company of martyrs died, whom Augustine simply calls the martyrs of Bolitana in the title of Sermon 13 [Col. 1226B] *On the Words of the Apostle*, which he delivered in the Basilica of Gratian on the birthday of the holy martyrs of Bolitana.]  

… Kalends of November: Saints Leucius and Victorinus, martyrs. [Note: [Col. 1226B] … Kalends of November: Saints Leucius and Victorinus, martyrs. Baronius, under the year 262, recounts the Acts, or the outstanding letter, of Lucius, Victoricus, and other martyrs in Africa. Hardly any more notable monument of that period is to be found. Cyprian mentions Victoricus in two places, namely letters 54, to Cornelius, and 68, to the Spaniards; Pamelius observes that he was called “of Thabraca.” On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, the Martyrology of Jerome commemorates in Africa Lucius, Victor, Dasius, Leucius, Victoricus, etc. But the Roman Martyrology places them on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.]  

… Kalends of November: Saint Victoria. [Note: [Col. 1226B] … Kalends of November: Saint Victoria. Victoria the martyr is joined with the martyrs of Aluta; but I do not think her birthday is written here. Why, indeed, should she be separated from Eva and Regiola, mentioned above? The Martyrology of Jerome mentions among many others Saint Victoria, martyr in Mauretania, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, and another Victoria in Africa on the preceding day [Col. 1226C]. We also read of two other Victorias from Africa in the Martyrology of Jerome on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, and another two on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December. Among these, I do not doubt, a place must be given to that renowned Victoria who, as Book III of Victor of Vita testifies, was continually burned while hanging in the city of Culusita, yet was healed by an angel. In two manuscript codices there is a sermon indeed ascribed to Augustine for the birthday of Saint Victoria, which has been pieced together from two others concerning Saints Perpetua and Felicity. If, however, Augustine were its author, it would refer not to Victoria of Culusita, who suffered after Augustine, but to another.]  

IV Kalends of November: Saint Felicianus and the saints of Vaga. [Note: [Col. 1226C] IV Kalends of November: Saint Felicianus and the saints of Vaga. I find Felicianus, an acolyte, mentioned in Cyprian’s letter to Cornelius concerning Fortunatus and Felicissimus; likewise another, a bishop of the Maximianist party at Mustis, whom the advocate Titianus petitioned by memorial to expel from his see. The martyrs of Vaga are known nowhere else, so far as I know. More familiar is the Council of the Donatists at Bagai, or Vagai [Col. 1226D]. The African *Notice* mentions Fulgentius, bishop of Vaga in Numidia. Ptolemy and others locate the city of Vaga opposite Cirta. Perhaps Catholics of Vaga or Bagai, killed in a riot stirred up by the Donatists, were regarded as martyrs; for their Acts sufficiently indicate that the Donatists caused disturbances there.]  

Kalends of November: Saint Octavius. [Note: [Col. 1226D] Kalends of November: Saint Octavius. Is he the Octavius named in two letters of Augustine among the Fathers of the Council of Carthage, who wrote to Pope Innocent against Pelagius and Caelestius, namely letters 175 and 181 of the new edition?]  

… Ides of November: Saints of Capita. [Note: [Col. 1226D] … Ides of November: Saints of Capita. Which martyrs these Capitani were, and what place Capita was, is not clear to us. Nothing more likely concerning the place occurs than the city of Capsa, or the Capsitani, mentioned by Pliny and also by Cyprian in letter 53. According to Pamelius, manuscript codices read *Capensem*, or perhaps Carpitana, the place whose bishop Felix, of the proconsular province [Col. 1227A], was exiled to Corsica by Hunneric, as the *Notice of the Provinces of Africa* teaches. See Augustine *Against the Donatists* [Col. 1227B]. Are the Four Crowned Martyrs of Rome meant here, whom the martyrologies commemorate on the sixth day before the Ides of November? Or rather Heraclius, Dionysius, Septimia, and others who suffered in Africa on that very day according to the Martyrology of Jerome?]  

[Col. 1227A] Ides: Saint Valentinus. [Note: [Col. 1227B] Ides: Saint Valentinus. The name of Valentinus, bishop of Arles, is celebrated in the councils; yet it is by no means likely that he is recorded here. Rather, it is Valentinus, bishop of Castellum Medianum in Mauretania Caesariensis, suggested to us by the *Notice of the Provinces of Africa*.]  

… Kalends of December: Saint Clement. [Note: [Col. 1227B] … Kalends of December: Saint Clement, pope and martyr.]  

… Kalends of December: Saint Chrysgonus, martyr. [Note: [Col. 1227B] … Kalends of December: Saint Chrysgonus, martyr. A most celebrated martyr at Rome, commemorated in various martyrologies on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.]  

… Kalends of December: Saint Andrew, apostle and martyr. [Note: [Col. 1227B] … Kalends of December: Saint Andrew, apostle and martyr. We could not read the day. It may readily be supplied from the other martyrologies, which assign the day before the Kalends of December.]  

Nones of December: the holy martyrs Bili, Felix, Potamia, Crispina, and their companions. [Note: [Col. 1227C] Nones of December: the holy martyrs Bili, Felix, Potamia, Crispina, and their companions. The Cluniac parchment expressly has the name Bili, in place of which other ancient records prefer Juli or Julius. The first three martyrs suffered at Thagura in Numidia. Crispina, however, frequently mentioned by Augustine, underwent martyrdom at Thebeste in the same province. The most illustrious Cardinal Baronius lamented that her Acts had apparently been lost. Were that great man alive, he would now have cause to rejoice with us at their recovery. For this is supplied by a very ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Theoderic near Reims, such as we here publish. Usuard and Ado commemorate Crispina with others on this day. Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, companions of Crispina, are praised in her Acts.]  

IV Ides of December: Saint Eulalia. [Note: [Col. 1227C] IV Ides of December: Saint Eulalia. In the same year, 303, in which the martyrs just mentioned were praised, the virgin Eulalia suffered at Emerita in Lusitania; Prudentius celebrated her in a sacred hymn, namely Hymn 3.]  

III Ides of December: the holy martyrs of Eron. [Note: [Col. 1227D] III Ides of December: the holy martyrs of Eron. They are unknown to us. Might they be from the metropolitan city of Eroina, under the patriarch of Constantinople?]  

XVI Kalends of January: the holy martyrs Felix, Clementianus, Honoratus, and Massaria. [Note: [Col. 1227D] XVI Kalends of January: the holy martyrs Felix, Clementianus, Honoratus, and Massaria; that is, Clementianus, Honoratus, and Massaria. Among the many Felixes in Africa who suffered martyrdom, two suffered with Saint Cyprian; Felix was condemned to the mines with his colleagues by Valerian; Felix, bishop of Tiberita, became a martyr because he would not surrender the books; and there was another of the same name—not to mention Felix and seven other Numidian martyrs. Yet among the associates of all these I nowhere read Clementianus, Honoratus, and Massaria. Thus I readily conclude that their Acts have perished, and that they shed their lives with an unknown Felix in an unknown place. Perhaps they belong to the number of those martyrs whom the Martyrology of Jerome commemorates on this day: “In Africa, Victor, Victorianus … and thirty-nine others together.”]  

X … Kalends of January: Saint Nemesianus. [Note: [Col. 1227D] X … Kalends of January: Saint Nemesianus. Nemesianus, bishop of Tubunae in Numidia, is the very man to whom [Col. 1228A] Cyprian addressed three letters. There also survives a letter to Cyprian from him and from Dativus, Felix, and Victor, bishops who had been condemned with him [Col. 1228B] to the mines; it is found as no. 78 among Cyprian’s letters. I would believe that Nemesianus survived the persecution and died in the peace of the Church, since here he is not at all granted the title of martyr, although in some places in this Calendar the designation “martyr” is also absent for those known from elsewhere to have been martyrs.]  

VIII Kalends of January: our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God. [Note: [Col. 1228B] VIII Kalends of January: our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God. That is, the Nativity.]  

VII Kalends of January: Saint Stephen, the first martyr. [Note: [Col. 1228B] VII Kalends of January: Saint Stephen, the first martyr. From this it is evident that the Church had honored Saint Stephen on this very day from ancient times onward.]  

VI Kalends of January: Saint John the Baptist, and James the Apostle, whom Herod killed. [Note: [Col. 1228B] VI Kalends of January: Saint John the Baptist, and James the Apostle, whom Herod killed. The designation “the Baptist” should be noted; in its place the Church, according to ancient custom, celebrates John the Evangelist on this day. Is this a scribal error?]  

V Kalends of January: the holy Innocents whom Herod killed. [Note: [Col. 1228B] V Kalends of January: the holy Innocents whom Herod [Col. 1228C] killed. From this passage the antiquity of this feast is apparent; but an account of it is far older in Origen, Homily 2 on Matthew. The most illustrious …

Cardinal Baronius, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, mentions several sermons of Augustine for the feast of the Holy Innocents; among them, two sermons delivered on their octave, and he cites Possidius’ index. Now Possidius, in chapter 10, lists two treatises of Augustine *On the Octaves of the Infants*. But it is certain that these were delivered on the octave of Easter, which was called the octave of the infants newly baptized at Easter. One of these treatises is Sermon 160 *De tempore*, for the Sunday in the Octave of Easter; in chapter 2 of that sermon one reads: “Today is called the octave of the infants,” etc. Possidius undoubtedly referred to this passage.]

The Nones of January: the deposition of the holy bishops Deogratias and Eugenius.

[Note: [Col. 1228C] The Nones of January: the deposition of the holy bishops Deogratias and Eugenius. Both were bishops of Carthage under Geiseric and Huneric, renowned for their merits and confession; Victor of Vita, among others, writes of them—of Deogratias in Book I, and of Eugenius, his successor, in the other two books [Col. 1228D].]

The eighth day before the Ides of January: holy Epiphany.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] The eighth day before the Ides of January: holy Epiphany. This was celebrated among the Africans, who, as Victor of Vita testifies in Book II, blessed the fonts on that very day, so that those coming to the faith might be baptized. Augustine composed seven treatises on the Epiphany, as Possidius’ index testifies in chapter 10.]

The sixth day before the Ides of January: the deposition of Bishop Quodvultdeus.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] The sixth day before the Ides of January: the deposition of Bishop Quodvultdeus. There is no doubt that he too was the bishop of Carthage expelled by Geiseric, praised by Victor of Vita in Book I, and predecessor of Bishop Deogratias. For other bishops of the same name, see Augustine’s letter to Innocent and the *Notitia of the Provinces of Africa*.]

The third day before the Ides of January: Saint Salvius, martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] The third day before the Ides of January: Saint Salvius, martyr, bishop of Membresa. Augustine writes outstandingly of him against Cresconius and likewise against Parmenianus; and, according to chapter 3 of Possidius, he also delivered a sermon on the birthday feast of Saint Salvius the martyr, and, according to chapter 10, one treatise on the feast of Saint Salvius.]

The nineteenth day before the Kalends of February: Saint Felix of Nola.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] The twelfth day before the Kalends of February: Saint Felix of Nola. He was very well known not only in Africa but throughout all nations; on his feast Augustine delivered a sermon on Psalm 127, as Ado thought.] [Col. 1229A]

The sixteenth day before the Kalends of February: the holy Rubrenses.

[Note: [Col. 1229A] The sixteenth day before the Kalends of February: the holy Rubrenses. Their acts have escaped me. Were they perhaps martyred at Rubicaria, a city of Mauretania Caesariensis, whose bishop Paulinus is listed in the *Notitia of the Provinces of Africa*? In the Martyrology of Jerome, on this day in Africa, Miea, Victor, and Mistrianus are commemorated with others [Col. 1229B]. Elsewhere Mucus is named; in Bollandus, on this day, Rubentius is joined to others from an Irish manuscript. Were they called Rubrenses from this source? I think the name was rather derived from some place. I read of a Lake Rubrensis in Gaul, but what has that to do with the present passage?]

The fourteenth day before the Kalends of February: the holy Tertullenses and Ficarienses.

[Note: [Col. 1229B] The fourteenth day before the Kalends of February: the holy Tertullenses and Ficarienses. I think these are those commemorated by Notker on this day: “In Africa, Paul, Quintus, and very many martyrs.” This perhaps is the first group, the Tertullenses; then: “At Carthage, Picaria, Pia, and thirty-eight others.” This is the second group, perhaps from Ficaria, a small island adjoining Sardinia; or perhaps from the city of Fice in the province of Mauretania Sitifensis, whose bishop Abus is read in the *Notitia of Africa*.]

The thirteenth day before the Kalends of February: Saint Sebastian, martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1229B] The thirteenth day before the Kalends of February: Saint Sebastian, martyr. Or rather, he is well known by his own name. Sebastian, a count in Africa during the Vandal persecution, mentioned by Victor of Vita in Book I, was worthy of that name.]

The twelfth day before the Kalends of February: Saint Agnes, martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1229C] The twelfth day before the Kalends of February: Saint Agnes, martyr. The illustrious martyr’s name is customarily declined thus among the ancients; elsewhere it is *Agna*, as in Prudentius, Hymn 14.]

The eleventh day before the Kalends of February: Saint Vincent, martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1229C] The eleventh day before the Kalends of February: Saint Vincent, martyr—the Spaniard, whom everyone knows. This saint too, another from Spain, was venerated in Africa after Eulalia, of whom above. Possidius, in chapters 9 and 10, indicates two treatises of Augustine on the feast of Saint Vincent.]

The eighth day before the Kalends of February: Saint Ageleus, martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1229C] The eighth day before the Kalends of February: Saint Ageleus, martyr. Augustine delivered a sermon to the people on the feast of Saint Ageleus, as Possidius testifies in chapter 9. Do not suppose that this Ageleus was that bishop of the Novatian sect at Constantinople whom Socrates reports to have died in extreme old age in the year 384. But who this our Ageleus was, I do not discover.]

The Kalends of February: Saints Lucian and Vincent, martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 1229C] The Kalends of February: Saints Lucian and Vincent, martyrs. It is uncertain whether Lucian was himself the martyr whom Cyprian somewhat reproves in Letter 23 because, being insufficiently skilled in understanding the divine reading of Scripture, and troublesome through his own easy-going disposition, he was granting pardon indiscriminately to the lapsed; or rather Lucian, Cyprian’s successor; or another Lucian, who was crowned with martyrdom together with Vincent—of whom we have been unable to learn anything. Or was he Vincent who, together with Cyprian, wrote Letter 68 [Col. 1230A], to the Spaniards?] [Col. 1230A]

The fourth day before the Nones of February: the holy Carterienses.

[Note: [Col. 1230B] The fourth day before the Nones of February: the holy Carterienses. Cartennae was a city of Mauretania Caesariensis, whose bishop Lucidus appears in the *Notitia of Africa*. Were these martyrs called Carterienses from that place, or from Carteia, a city of Baetica in Spain mentioned by Ptolemy—which Holstenius identifies as Cartagena—or finally from the island Carteria near Smyrna, according to Pliny? I would rather call them Africans, whom Possidius shows to have been famous in Africa in his index, where in chapter 9 he indicates a sermon of Augustine delivered on the feast of the Cartherienses. The Martyrology ascribed to Jerome praises several martyrs of Africa on this day. Allatius, in his annotations on the Roman Martyrology: “In Africa, Victor and Honoratus.”]

The Nones of February: Saint Agatha, martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1230B] The Nones of February: Saint Agatha, martyr. She is too well known to be elucidated in this place, or to require it.]

The fifth day before the Ides of February: Saints Felix, Victor, and Januarius.

[Note: [Col. 1230B] The fifth day before the Ides of February: Saints Felix, Victor, and Januarius. The common edition of Jerome’s Martyrology records these martyrs, with seven others, on the third day before the Ides of February. See Bollandus on the tenth day of that month.]

The fourteenth day before the Kalends of March: the holy martyrs Macrobius and Lucilla, Nundinarius, Caeciliana, and the Petrenses.

[Note: [Col. 1230C] The fourteenth day before the Kalends of March: the holy martyrs Macrobius and Lucilla, Nundinarius, Caeciliana, and the Petrenses. Macrobius and Lucilla, together with many others, are listed on this day in the Martyrology called Jerome’s; the names of the others are absent there. Cyprian was buried in the burial-ground of Macrobius Candidus; but whether this Macrobius was a martyr is a matter for inquiry. In the Acts of the Cirtense martyrs, Nundinarius and Lucilla are named, but without the title of martyr. Were the Petrenses from Petra in Palestine or Arabia, or from the islands called Petræ in Italy, which are Ptolemy’s Sirenussae? Others will conjecture better.

Thus far the Carthaginian Calendar. We first inspected a copy of it in the Cluniac Library this year; thereafter we received that very copy from there through the kindness of the Reverend Father Joachim Lestinois, most courteous Prior of that sacred house, to whom we owe many other things. But the learned world ought at least to know this one fact.]

[Col. 1229]

## DISSERTATION ON THE SANCTITY OF POPE SIRICIUS

To the Most Eminent and Most Reverend Cardinal Girolamo Casanate, when the question was raised in the Congregation of Sacred Rites whether the Mass and Office of that Pontiff should be granted to the Canons of the Basilica of St John Lateran; including a discussion of the Paschal letters of St Theophilus of Alexandria.

Most Eminent and Most Reverend Lord,

[Col. 1229D] Cardinal Baronius, under the year 397, finds fault with Siricius because, when Rufinus had translated Origen’s *Periarchon* into Latin at Rome and had thereby instilled Origenist errors into many persons, he did not immediately oppose the emerging sect by an Apostolic pronouncement. He adds that, for this reason, Siricius was more speedily—that is, in the following year, 398, on 22 February—removed from this life by God’s avenging hand: “By fearful examples,” he says, “it has been shown that those Pontiffs who dealt somewhat too slowly with the cause of the faith and attended to the matter too remissly were swiftly taken from this life by Christ, the chief Shepherd of all.”

He cites St Jerome, Epistle 16, in the epitaph of Marcella, praising her because she alone opposed the Origenist heresy, when it deceived the simplicity of the bishop—that is, Siricius—who, upon Rufinus’s departure, even gave him letters of communion as one professing Catholic doctrine, as Jerome himself testifies in his *Apology against Rufinus*. Hence he praises Siricius’s successor, Pope Anastasius, [Col. 1231A] who in the following year, 399, together with Theophilus, Patriarch of Alexandria, struck the Origenists with an anathema in a synod. I shall briefly show that these matters cannot detract from Siricius’s sanctity.

The Fathers contemporary with Siricius, and later Popes, repeatedly commended his doctrine, piety, care, and diligence in safeguarding the Church entrusted to him. Besides the testimonies reported in the published collections for restoring his cult, St Innocent I should be heard in his letter to Anysius, Primate of Thessalonica, from p. 45 of Holstenius’s *Collectanea*: “To him,” he says, “my predecessors also—men such as these and so great, namely Damasus, Siricius, and the above-mentioned man, Anastasius, of holy memory—showed such deference,” etc. “For it would not have been lawful for me to attempt to oppose the judgment of such great and good men,” etc.

Thus St Innocent joins Siricius with Damasus and Anastasius in equal praise and commendation, so that it hardly seems permissible to maintain that Siricius was inferior to either of them and to imagine that divine power was angry with him alone. St Leo the Great, in his letter to Anastasius, p. 145 of the cited *Collectanea* of Holstenius, writes that he confers upon him primacy over all the churches of Illyricum, “following the example of Siricius of blessed memory,” etc. Thus Siricius’s care in governing the Church had both a great admirer and an imitator in Leo. At the First Council of Toledo, held in the year 400, shortly after Siricius’s death, the letters of Ambrose of holy memory are praised, as likewise Siricius of holy memory, whose watchful zeal is said to have kept the Catholic cause safe and sound in the provinces of Spain.

Nor is Siricius’s reputation harmed by the statement that Rufinus and his Origenist associates deceived his simplicity, or that he gave letters of communion to Rufinus when the latter departed from Rome. For heretics, wolves hiding under sheepskins, more than once deceived holy Pontiffs at the outset. Praxeas at first imposed upon Pope St Anicetus, as Tertullian testifies in chapter 1 of *Against Praxeas*. Marcellus, Bishop of Ancyra, infected with the Sabellian heresy, [Col. 1231C] initially deceived Pope St Julius and the Synod of Sardica; yet Julius’s successor Liberius later condemned him. I shall shortly adduce St Basil’s testimony concerning this deception by which Pope Julius was misled.

Caelestius, the ringleader of the Pelagian heresy, deceived Pope Zosimus and his Roman synod so thoroughly by ambiguous language that Zosimus sharply rebuked the African bishops for having condemned him as a heretic. Zosimus’s letters survive; St Augustine often refers to them, especially in Book II to Boniface, chapter 3, and in his book *On Original Sin*. It has seemed worthwhile to mention these instances.

Here I shall briefly set forth the example of St Damasus, Siricius’s predecessor; it is both close in time to, and very similar to, Siricius’s action. Vitalis, an Apollinarian hiding beneath a Catholic cloak and irregularly intruded by certain persons as bishop of the church of Antioch, went to Rome to Pope St Damasus so that, fortified with letters of the Apostolic See, he might return more safely to Antioch. He presented Damasus with a statement of faith. Damasus understood its words in a Catholic sense and sent him back to the East furnished with letters of the Apostolic See.

This judgment of Damasus, deceived by the cunning of a heretic, so angered the most holy bishops of the East that Basil, almost their chief spokesman, wrote the following in Epistle 10 to St Gregory Nazianzen concerning the Western bishops and their foremost representative, Pope Damasus:

> “They neither know the truth nor tolerate learning it; but, hindered by false opinions, they are now doing those things which they formerly did in the case of Marcellus”—the heretical Sabellian Bishop of Ancyra, defended by Pope Julius and the Synod of Sardica. “I myself wished to write to their leader, namely Pope Damasus, without the usual formalities of letters: nothing concerning ecclesiastical matters except in riddles, since they neither understand our truth nor embrace the way by which they could learn it.”

Basil wrote this against Damasus, who had been deceived, in an agitated temper and an angry style. But Gregory Nazianzen judged Damasus more gently in Epistle 2 to Cledonius. After saying that Vitalis had used equivocal language, he adds that “Damasus himself, when he had later been more correctly instructed and had at the same time heard that they persisted in their former explanations, expelled them from the Church and annulled their statement of faith together with its anathema.” He adds also that Damasus took very badly the deception into which he had fallen through simplicity, etc. As Vitalis the Apollinarian initially deceived the simplicity of St Damasus, so Rufinus the Origenist likewise deceived the simplicity of Siricius.

They will reply that Damasus, as the cited Gregory testifies, was deeply grieved by the simplicity through which he believed Vitalis Catholic and sent him away fortified with Apostolic letters; and that nothing similar is recorded of Siricius. Yet I would ask them why God did not immediately remove Damasus from the living after he had been deceived by a heretic, as they suppose happened with Siricius. Pope Julius lived five years after acquitting Marcellus, Bishop of Ancyra, although Liberius subsequently condemned him.

From Jerome’s very words from which the rebuke of Siricius is fashioned, his defense is also drawn. He writes as follows in Epistle 16, in the epitaph of Marcella:

> “The heretics, seeing that great conflagrations had arisen from a small spark, that the fire secretly kindled long ago had now reached the rooftops, and that what had deceived many could not remain concealed, sought and obtained ecclesiastical letters, so that they might be seen to have departed in communion. Not much time intervened: an eminent man, Anastasius, succeeded to the pontificate.”

Thus, according to Jerome, Rufinus departed Rome because he feared that the errors of the Origenist work could not remain concealed any longer, and therefore he feared Siricius. Had he hoped Siricius favourable to him, he could safely have disregarded with deaf ears the outcries of the rest.

Rufinus remained two years at Aquileia, enjoying the friendship of St Chromatius, bishop of that city. At Chromatius’s urging, too, he translated Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* into Latin in the year 400; and Chromatius likewise endeavoured by letters to reconcile Rufinus with Jerome. Nor did these services harm Chromatius’s sanctity. Indeed, it is fairly clearly gathered from the Pope’s letter to John of Jerusalem that Venerius, Bishop [Col. 1232C] of Milan, also wrote to Anastasius on Rufinus’s behalf. Moreover, the aforementioned Jerome relates that Siricius survived only a short time after Rufinus’s departure. Therefore it was not slowness or negligence, but an earlier death, that prevented Siricius from publicly pronouncing an anathema upon the Origenists. From the words “could not remain concealed” it is clear that these errors had not yet been publicly disseminated, but were asserted only secretly. What wonder if they escaped Siricius’s notice?

Moreover, the adverse judgment drawn from Siricius’s comparatively early death because he did not immediately condemn the Origenists will, when referred to a more exact chronology, appear wholly false. I shall first set out Baronius’s opinion. He writes that Rufinus crossed from the East into Italy with Melania in the year 397. It is scarcely credible that they traversed the sea in the violence of winter; rather, they must have done so at the beginning of spring, when the sea was opened. Let us grant that they reached Rome about May.

Rufinus did not immediately set hand to translating the work *Periarchon*, but did so only when asked by Macarius, who suspected Rufinus’s doctrine, as Rufinus himself testifies in his first *Invective against Jerome*. The Latin autograph translation could not so quickly have been distributed in several copies that this could have happened before about summer.

But Baronius says that Siricius died in the immediately following year, 398, on 22 February; and he writes that Origen’s errors were condemned in 399, in the Alexandrian synod by Theophilus and in the same year at Rome by St Anastasius. He proves that the Alexandrian synod took place in 399 in vol. V, p. 85, of the Roman edition of 1594:

> “We infer that these things were done in this year because St Jerome, writing to Pammachius and Marcella—namely in Epistle 78—reports that, one year before Theophilus’s first Paschal letter was written, this general letter had been written from the synod.”

The same author, lower down on p. 90, writes that Jerome mentions five letters of Theophilus which he translated into Latin, namely the first [Col. 1233A] synodical letter, issued from the synod against the Origenists in 399. He then adds: “The second, called Paschal, written particularly against Origen and his disciples, is also missing; and this is the one concerning which Jerome himself writes to Pammachius and Marcella, when he says: ‘If anything has here been said too little against Origen, it is contained in the letter of the preceding year.’”

But Baronius says that the second Paschal letter is the one beginning, “The divine discourse of the august solemnity,” etc., which is read first in the codex of St Jerome. He says that the beginning of the third Paschal letter is, “Christ the Lord of glory,” etc.; and that the fourth begins, “Now also the living wisdom of God,” etc. Finally, he observes that the first Paschal letter, which is now missing, was written in 400 for the following year, 401; the second in 401 for 402; the third in 402 for 403; and the fourth in 403 for 404. For, since Paschal letters were published at Alexandria on the feast of the Epiphany, announcing the day of the Pascha to come in that year, etc., they were composed in the preceding Julian year.

Yet it is established that St Jerome translated only three Paschal letters of Theophilus. Before demonstrating this, I assume that we are here speaking of Theophilus’s Paschal letters against the Origenists, rendered into Latin by St Jerome. For Theophilus published Paschal letters every year of his episcopate. Thus, in Act I of the Council of Ephesus one reads: “From the fifth Paschal letter of Theophilus, most holy Bishop of Alexandria”; and later: “Likewise from the sixth Paschal letter of the same.” Therefore the present discussion concerns only the Paschal letters found in volume IX of the works of St Jerome, of which there are only three. A fourth is introduced alongside these three by their erroneous ordering.

### The First Paschal Letter Indicates Easter in 402

In the cited codex of St Jerome, the earlier Paschal letter begins: “The divine discourse of the august solemnity,” etc. It is divided into four parts. In the first, Theophilus exhorts the faithful to celebrate the Paschal feast more devoutly. In the second: “Let the disciples of Apollinaris cease,” etc., he attacks the errors of Apollinaris. In the third: “Let them therefore know [—of this solemnity…],” etc., he refutes Origen’s errors, calling Origen the hydra of all heresies. Finally: “And lest, being occupied,” etc., he exhorts them to repentance.

Jerome, in Epistle 78 to Pammachius and Marcella, writes: “At the beginning of spring I send the Alexandrian treasures,” namely the aforementioned Paschal letter of Theophilus, which, he says, “you should know is divided into four parts. In the first he exhorts believers to celebrate the Lord’s Pascha; in the second and third he slays Apollinaris and Origen; in the fourth, that is, the final part, he exhorts heretics to repentance. But if anything has here been said too little against Origen, it is contained in the letter of the preceding year.”

Baronius rightly observed that this earlier Paschal letter, beginning “The divine discourse of the august solemnity,” etc., was sent by Jerome with Epistle 78 to Pammachius. But this otherwise most learned man did not observe the Paschal cycle explained at the end [Col. 1233D] of that same letter. For it announces that Pascha was to be celebrated in that year on the eleventh day of the month Pharmuthi. The Egyptian months preceded the Latin months by five days. St Ambrose, in his letter to the bishops throughout Aemilia, vol. IV, p. 306, says: “For among the Egyptians the first month is Pharmuthi; it begins on the sixth day before the Kalends of April and ends on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.” Hence he teaches that Pascha in that year—namely, A.D. 387—was to be celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, which is the thirtieth day of Pharmuthi. He shows this by several other examples, as does St Proterius, Bishop and Martyr of Alexandria, in his letter to St Leo the Great.

Therefore, the Pascha announced in this letter of Theophilus as falling on the eleventh day of Pharmuthi was celebrated by the Latins on 6 April, as indeed occurred in A.D. 402, in the nineteenth solar cycle, fourth lunar cycle, letter E. St Augustine, in Epistle 236, writes to Xantippus, Primate of Numidia: “When there were one hundred days until the Lord’s Pascha, which will fall on the eighth day before the Ides of April,” namely 6 April in the year 402, when Xantippus was Primate.

### The Second Paschal Letter in Jerome’s Codex Indicates Easter in 401

The letter which follows second in the ordering of Theophilus’s Paschal letters in Jerome’s codex begins: “Christ Jesus, the Lord of glory,” etc. In it Theophilus refutes Origen’s errors at greater length.
