At its end Pascha is announced for celebration on the nineteenth day of Pharmuthi: that is, 14 April among the Latins, the day on which the Paschal feast was indeed celebrated in the Roman Church in A.D. 401, in the eighteenth solar cycle, third lunar cycle, letter F.

From these Paschal characteristics, which are the most certain indicators of years, it is evident that the collectors placed these two letters in reverse order. The second, which indicates Easter in 401, was written and published by Theophilus before the other, which [Col. 1234B] announces Easter in the following year, 402. Therefore, when Jerome, sending the Paschal letter beginning “The divine discourse of the august solemnity,” etc., which announces Easter in 402, writes in Epistle 78, “If anything has here been said too little against Origen, it is contained in the letter of the preceding year,” he means the Paschal letter of the preceding year, 401, which begins “Christ Jesus,” etc. It is wrongly read as second in the sequence, though it was in fact the first.

Baronius, failing to notice this reversed order, invented and inserted another earlier letter, said to have been the fourth translated by Jerome and now missing, when Jerome’s “letter of the preceding year against Origen” was in fact the earlier of the three letters that survive. To be sure, St Leo the Great, in Epistle 97 to the Emperor Leo, chapter 8, says: “From the Paschal letter of St Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, which he sent through Egypt,” and there inserts a lengthy testimony from the Paschal letter of 402. Lower down he says: “Likewise from another Paschal letter of the same against Origen,” where he cites words from the Paschal letter of 401. The words are in St Jerome’s translation. Thus in the time of Pope Leo perhaps the letters were read in reverse order in the Roman codex; hence St Leo the Great there called the second letter the first, and the first the later. Yet order is not always preserved in citing testimonies.

### The Third Paschal Letter Marks Easter in 404

Baronius also noticed this from the year 404, in whose month of January St Paula had died, vol. V, under the year 404, p. 222; but the Paschal indicator makes it still more certain. At the end of the letter Pascha is announced for the twenty-second day of the same month, namely Pharmuthi: that is, 17 April among the Romans, on which day Pascha was celebrated in the leap year 404, in the twenty-first solar cycle, sixth lunar cycle, letter C.

Blessed St Proterius, in his letter to Leo the Great, says: “On the twenty-second Lord’s day of the new month Pharmuthi, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, or 17 April,” though he is there speaking of the Pascha of another year. From this we conclude that Jerome did not translate a Paschal letter for the year 403, as Baronius said, assigning to that year the Paschal letter beginning “Christ Jesus, the Lord of glory,” etc., listed second in Jerome’s codex. For that letter, as I have said, indicates Easter in 401 and should be placed first of all in correct order.

From the matters more fully explained above, we infer the year of the Alexandrian synod held by Theophilus against the Origenists. It was not held in 399, as Baronius and others thought, but in the following year, 400, since Theophilus pursued the Origenists condemned at the recent synod only in the Paschal letter for 401. For Jerome, in Epistle 78, sending the Paschal letter for 402, says: “If anything has here been said too little against the Origenists, it is contained in the letter of the preceding year.” And indeed, if Origen’s errors had been condemned in advance at a synod in 399, Theophilus would by no means have spared them in his Paschal letter of 400.

Socrates adds further confirmation. In Book VI, chapter 6, he narrates that the riot and slaughter connected with Gainas occurred in the consulship of Stilicho, A.D. 400; and in chapter 7 he testifies that at the same time disturbances of the Origenists also arose in Egypt, which Theophilus suppressed with great exertion.

That the Origenists were condemned at Rome by St Anastasius only in 401 is very clearly demonstrated from Jerome. First, because Epistle 78, which sends the Paschal letter for 402 and refutes Origen’s errors, says: “May the chair of Peter the Apostle confirm by its preaching the preaching also of Mark the Evangelist. Although it has been widely published in public discourse that the blessed Pope Anastasius, by the same favour and because he was led by the same Spirit, persecuted the heretics lurking in their holes; and his letters teach that what was condemned in the East has been condemned in the West.”

Thus, at the beginning of spring, when that letter was written in 402, Jerome had not yet received word that the Origenists had been condemned at Rome in synod by Pope Anastasius, though they had already been condemned by the chair of Mark, in which Theophilus sat. The letters of Anastasius mentioned there were written against Rufinus in 401, as I shall shortly explain.

Moreover, Jerome says in the later *Apology against Rufinus*: “I have translated two of his letters, synodical and Paschal—namely, those of Theophilus—against Origen and his disciples, and others against Apollinaris and the same Origen, during this period of almost two years. I do not know that I have translated any other work of his.” Thus he says that he translated only two Paschal letters of Theophilus: the earlier one in 401, and the other in 402, in which the errors of Apollinaris and Origen are refuted. He adds, “during this period of almost two years,” namely 401 and 402. In the latter year, as Baronius rightly observes, the second *Apology* was written; for in 402 Jerome sent to Rome, in Latin, the Paschal letter against Apollinaris and Origen, addressed to Pammachius and Marcella. Therefore no Paschal letter is missing, as Baronius supposed, for we still possess both letters which Jerome says he translated.

In 401 St Anastasius, intending to handle the case of the Origenists in synod, summoned Rufinus, the leader of so many disturbances, to Rome to state his case. When Rufinus pleaded fatigue, Anastasius condemned him in his absence, in letters addressed to John of Jerusalem which still survive. Jerome writes of these in the *Apology* of 402, refuting Rufinus, who published that the letter criticizing him had not been written by Pope Anastasius but by some rival’s hand:

> “Grant that I forged the letter of the preceding year: who sent the recent writings to the East”—namely, the letter to John of Jerusalem—“in which Pope Anastasius adorns you with such great flowers of praise,” etc.

Since Jerome wrote this in 402, the letter of the preceding year against Rufinus, leader of the Origenists, was issued by St Anastasius in 401; consequently, in the same year, the *Periarchon* of Origen translated into Latin by Rufinus was condemned by Anastasius. Certainly, from Jerome’s cited testimony we have that nothing against Rufinus was written by the aforementioned Pope before 401.

Again, in the same place Jerome writes: “Therefore the blessed bishops Anastasius, Theophilus, Venerius, and [Col. 1236A] Chromatius,” etc., “declare him,” namely Origen, “a heretic.” When the Popes at Rome condemned heretics in synod, they sent circular letters to the metropolitans concerning the completed condemnation of the persons, and these in turn published them afterwards in their dioceses. Hence Pope Anastasius sent letters concerning the condemnation of the Origenists to Venerius of Milan and Chromatius of Aquileia, metropolitans of Italy.

But Venerius was newly bishop at Milan at the beginning of September 400. For in the First Council of Toledo, convened in Era 438, that is, A.D. 400, the following is read in the definitive sentence under 11 September: “Waiting in like manner to see what answer the Pope who now is, St Simplicianus, Bishop of Milan, and the other priests of the churches will make.” In the ancient ecclesiastical registers St Simplicianus’s death is marked on 13 August. Therefore Venerius began to sit at Milan in the summer of 400 as it drew to a close, from which it follows that only in 401 did Venerius publish in his diocese the letters received from Anastasius concerning the condemnation of the Origenists.

At the Council of Carthage after the consulship of Flavius Stilicho, in 401, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, the African Fathers sent a legate to Pope Anastasius and Venerius, Bishop of Milan. Therefore, if the day of Simplicianus’s death is correctly placed in the ecclesiastical registers, he died in 400; nor had his death become known to the Spanish bishops in September of that same year.

Concerning letters which he had sent to Venerius about the books of Origen translated by Rufinus, Anastasius writes to John of Jerusalem:

> “Therefore know what a letter our lowliness sent, written with more diligent care, to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius; and I have made this a matter of conscience to myself, that I should not labour through superfluous alarm or be troubled by empty fear.”

He adds that he will endeavour by letters sent everywhere that no origin of a profane translation may creep in, attempting by the darkness it brings to unsettle devout minds. From these words it may seem that Venerius had suggested to the Pope something in defence of Rufinus’s translation. But it is certain that the letter to John of Jerusalem was written in 402, as I have shown from Jerome.

From this chronology concerning the year of the Alexandrian synod against the Origenists and likewise the year of their condemnation at Rome by St Anastasius, Baronius’s doubt concerning Siricius’s slowness or negligence in proscribing Rufinus’s Latin rendering of the books is resolved. For according to Baronius’s own calculations, Siricius survived only a few months after Origen’s *Periarchon* had been rendered into Latin. His successor Anastasius, however, condemned Rufinus with the other Origenists after almost three years of his pontificate, so that he would plainly be chargeable with a longer negligence than his predecessor Siricius.

Yet Anastasius first summoned Rufinus repeatedly by letters from Aquileia to Rome to state his case, as Jerome says in the *Apology*, before striking with an anathema one who pleaded empty reasons for delay. In that postponement no fault of negligence can be censured; rather, a more careful examination of the entire case deserves commendation.

DAMASUS, born at Rome, 113. As a boy, while a reader in the Basilica of Saint Lawrence, he collects the Acts of the holy martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, ibid. He is made deacon by Pope Julius, 114. He is vindicated against the slander of the schismatics Faustinus and Marcellinus, ibid. Whether he himself procured Felix’s election during Liberius’s exile, 115. He sends Evagrius, presbyter of Antioch, to Basil, and why, 158. He confirms Ambrose’s ordination, 172. He suspends his judgment in the dispute between Meletius and Paulinus, 160. He confirms Peter of Alexandria in the episcopate, 186. He promulgates the Confession of Faith addressed to Paulinus of Antioch, 197. This differs from another letter to Paulinus, 200. The accusation of adultery against him is false and fabricated, 205, 208. He refuses Priscillian access to his presence, 232. He responds to the Easterners, and his letters are explained, 257, 369. He has the statue of Victory removed; his letter to Ambrose on that subject, 233. His testimony for Symmachus to Emperor Valentinian, 259. He expels Helvidius from the Church, 263. His love and study of the sacred Scriptures, ibid. Many of his poems inscribed to martyrs have perished, 267. He dies, 260. His praises, 262. The site of his tomb, supposedly discovered, 261. DEMOPHILUS: whether Arian or Semi-Arian by sect, 288. Whether he attended and was condemned by the Council of Rimini, 289. His character according to Saint Basil, 289 ff. He attends the synod convoked by Damasus—what was done and in what year, 163. He returns to the East with letters to Basil, 167. He plans a second journey to Rome, 170. He undertakes it together with the most holy presbyter of Antioch, 172. He brings Damasus letters from Basil, which are explained, 173. He attends the third synod under Damasus, 175. He vigorously pleads Meletius’s cause before Damasus and is rebuffed by Peter of Alexandria, 178. DOROTHEUS, executioner of the holy martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, professes Christ’s name, 262, 396.

## E

Office of the defenders of the CHURCHES, 126. Imperial EDICTS were not customarily read in churches, 140. EPHESIUS, pseudo-bishop of the schismatics, is expelled from the City, 251. When BISHOPS were ordained, they customarily received from the ordainer a codex of the canons, 172. Bishops throughout Italy and Gaul who evade the Roman Pontiff’s judgment are ordered by the emperor to be sent to Rome, 228. On more solemn festivals they customarily sent letters wishing prosperity to kings, 268. Those who had been condemned were not received into communion before the pope’s judgment, 334. When bishops were deposed in a synod or died meanwhile, a successor was appointed by the same synod, 221. EVAGRIUS, presbyter of Antioch, comes to Italy with Eusebius of Vercelli, 128. He defends Damasus’s innocence before Emperor Valentinian, ibid. He is sent by Damasus to Saint Basil—what year and for what reason, 157 ff. Basil’s letters to him are explained, 159. His dispute with Flavian concerning the bishopric of Antioch is discussed at the Council of Capua, 339 ff. EUDOXIUS passes from the Semi-Arians to the strict Arians, 288. He slanders the Westerners for having accepted the Sirmian blasphemy, 302. Whether he was deposed at the Council of Rimini, 289. He is ordered by Emperor Constantius to be expelled from the see of Antioch which he had occupied, 296. Eunomius’s blasphemous words against the Holy Spirit, 358, note e; 362, note d. Pope EUSEBIUS praised by Damasus, 270, 311, 385. For the same reason as Pope Marcellus, he is banished to Sicily under Maxentius, 271. He dies there in exile; the place of his death is indicated conjecturally, 271, 272, 385, note g. The title-church of Saint Eusebius is dedicated to him, 315. Eusebius, a bishop, founder of the title-church, 385, note g. The Acts in circulation of Eusebius, presbyter and martyr, are wholly fabricated, perhaps constructed from the genuine Acts of Pope Eusebius, 272, 310 ff. The anonymous annotator on Bossuet is refuted and criticized, 311. Office and rank of an EXCEPTOR (official shorthand writer), 409.

## F

The calumnies of FAUSTINUS and MARCELLINUS against Damasus are refuted, 114, 124, 245 ff., 251; likewise against Liberius, 310. Whether those presbyters were Luciferians or rather Ursinians, 249, 250. In what year their petitions were composed and offered to Theodosius, 252. FELIX of Nola was also famous at Rome: whether Damasus went to Nola to Felix’s tomb in fulfillment of a vow, 128, 129, 388. Pope FELIX is intruded after Liberius’s exile, 115. He is expelled and withdraws, 310. The FERMENTUM was sent, even before the age of Melchiades, to cemeteries and suburban sacred buildings, 275. FLAVIAN of Antioch’s oath concerning the bishopric of Antioch, 190, 221, 230. He comes to Constantinople with Meletius for the synod, 221. At that synod he is ordained bishop of Antioch, 222, 223, 238, 335. His ordination causes schisms in the Church, 230. He loses communion with the Westerners, 335. He avoids the Council of Capua, to which he had been summoned, 339. He also declines the judgment of Theophilus of Alexandria, to whom the case had been entrusted, 340. On this matter, Ambrose’s—or Siricius’s—letter to Theodosius, ibid. FLORENTIUS, bishop of Puteoli, deposed by Damasus, and in what year, 203. FORTUNATIANUS of Aquileia: in what year he died, 347, note a. FOUNTAINS brought by Damasus into the Vatican Basilica, 281. [Col. 1241] Enlarged and adorned by Longinianus, Prefect of the City, 412, note a; also conveyed to the Basilica of Saint Lawrence, 410, note g.

## G

GEORGE of Alexandria’s two tyrannical incursions into that see, 318. GORGONIUS the martyr mentioned by Damasus is different from the Gorgonius mentioned by Eusebius, 276. GRACCHUS, Prefect of the City: in what year, 187. He destroys Mithras’s cave, 187, 188. Laws inscribed upon it and variant readings of them, 187. Emperor GRATIAN orders Novatians, Donatists, Luciferians, and Ursinians allied with them expelled from the City, 166. He permits free religious practice to sects, except Eunomians, Photinians, and Manichaeans, but later rescinds that permission, 189. He restores bishops exiled under Valens for the Faith, ibid. Letter to him from the fourth Roman Council under Damasus, 202; likewise from the Council of Aquileia on the same matter, 224. His rescript to Aquilinus, vicarius, in Damasus’s favor, 226. He is regarded by Damasus as a son, 259, 369. His law 2 of the Theodosian Code, *That Holy Baptism...*, is explained, 204. He hears Ursinus, who approaches him in Gaul while in exile, 225. GREGORY NAZIANZEN favors Paulinus over Flavian, 222. In what year he came to Constantinople, 199. He resigns, and when, 223. A passage from Oration 5 is explained, 199; likewise one from Oration 14, 190; another from Oration 13, 220. When and on what occasion each of the latter two orations was delivered, ibid. He disapproves Flavian’s ordination, 220, 221. His zeal for religion after resigning the episcopate of the imperial city, 255. In what year his letters to Cledonius were written, 344. A passage from the second is cited and explained, 359, note c. GREGORY OF NYSSA declines a journey to Rome, 171, 172. He communicates with the Marcellians as though Catholics and defends himself for doing so, 148, 149.

## H

HELVIDIUS expelled from the Church by Damasus, 263. HERACLIUS, Prefect of the City under Maxentius, 271. Leaders of HERETICS returning to the Church were received on the condition that they brought back with them those whom they had severed from it, 355, note d. JEROME: in what year he departed for the East, 158. In what year he wrote to Damasus concerning the hypostases; the letters are cited and explained, 180. The ancient reading is retained in the first of them, 184. Why that question was then raised against him, 181. He returns to Rome and is retained by Damasus, 241. His minor works at Damasus’s urging, 263. The passage in his *Chronicle* concerning Liberius’s fall is doubtful, 309. He is inconsistent with himself in the same question in *On Illustrious Men*, 310. He chooses communion with Paulinus, 182, 183. Whether he regarded Vitalis of Antioch as Catholic, 183. HILARY’S testimonies vindicating Liberius from heresy, 284. The Arian “perfidiousness” which he reproaches this pontiff with is nothing other than the Sirmian exposition against Photinus, 285–287. Hilary’s passages from *On the Synods*, sections 3 and 28, are cited and explained, 291 ff. Another of his passages, from the same book and from *Against Constantius*, 304, 305, 306. He considers the Sirmian faith or exposition truly Catholic, 307. Why in the *Fragments* he rejects it as though it were perfidy: several reasons are adduced, and another, apparently truer, is proposed, 307, 308. HILARY the deacon: whether he is author of the Commentary on Saint Paul’s Epistles, and whether he returned from the Luciferians to the Church under Damasus, 253. *HOMO DOMINICUS* (“the Lordly Man”), 243, 355, note f. Whether the Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata rejected *homoousios*, 304. The force of the terms *homoousios* and *homoiousios* is at times one and the same among Catholics and strict Arians, 302, 304, 305, 322. Why the question of *hypostasis*, long previously settled, was later raised again against Jerome at Antioch, 183; why it reappeared at the First Council of Constantinople, ibid. The term was appended by Theodoret as a gloss to the letters of Damasus and the Illyrian synod, 184.

## I

The Spaniards, without any right, claim as their own Irene, consecrated virgin and sister of Damasus, 278, 405.

## J

Jericho fell by the trumpets of the priests: a figure of heresy overthrown by the voice of bishops assembled in synod, 350.

## L

The obstinacy of the Lapsed under Popes Marcellus and Eusebius, 270, 271, 385. Saint LAWRENCE the martyr was born at Rome and was a Roman citizen, 114, 280, 281. Boy READERS, 113. LIBERIUS never resigned the pontificate, 115. He is sent into exile, 116. At his departure the Romans swear not to choose another pontiff, 115. He is in communion with Meletius of Antioch, 146. [Col. 1242] Whether he was ever condemned by Damasus, 252, 253, 311, 312. He writes that he accepted the Sirmian Faith, and what that faith was, 282, 284. The testimonies of Athanasius, Hilary, and Jerome on that matter are cited and weighed, 283, 307, 308. At the end of 357 he had not yet left Beroea, 292. His letters in exile to Basil of Ancyra, Ursacius, and Valens are mentioned, 297. He is recalled from exile through Basil of Ancyra’s efforts, 298. In Emperor Constantius’s presence he condemns the Anomoeans, 302. Whether he then subscribed a new formula of faith, or rather the Ancyrene exposition alone, ibid. He returns to Rome, arriving in August, 298. The whole sequence of events is set out, ibid. His entrance into the City is explained and Anastasius’s inventions rejected, 310, 311. Whether he ever condemned *homoousios*, 301. He is vindicated against the calumnies of Bossuet’s anonymous annotator, 312. He was not present at the Council of Rimini, and why; Bossuet’s French translator is criticized and refuted, 315. He annuls the decrees of the Council of Rimini, 319. He is forced again to withdraw and hide, 319, 320. Whether he truly departed from Athanasius’s communion, 316. A passage of LUCIFER from *Against Constantius* is cited and explained, 320. No civil law prohibited the sect of the LUCIFERIANS, provided they did not rebaptize, 166, 249.

## M

MACARIUS, a Roman presbyter of Ursinus’s faction, is expelled from Rome, 249, 250. The MACEDONIAN heresy, which had begun under Liberius, breaks out openly under Damasus and is suppressed, 199. Two kinds of Macedonians, 359, note a. Damasus expels both from the Church with a twofold anathema, 363, note b. During Valens’s lifetime, Macedonians are united with the truly Catholic, 199. At what time and in what year they first began to be called Macedonians, 198, 358, note e. MANICHAEANS, at Damasus’s instigation, are restrained by a law issued by Valentinian, 155. They are also called Venustians and Paternianians, and why, 156. The heresy attributed by Basil to MARCELLUS of Ancyra, 146, 174, 175. He is vindicated from it, 148 ff. The formula of faith of Marcellus and the Marcellians, offered to the Alexandrian synod, and in what year, 146, 147. Saint Basil considers the MARCELLIANS genuinely Catholic in his last years, 148. Pope MARCELLUS is exiled for canonical discipline against the lapsed, 270, 384. He establishes twenty-five title-churches because of baptism and penance, and the meaning of this, 270, 276. The Acts of Saint Peter attributed to Marcellus are spurious, 269. MAXIMUS, or Maximinus, Prefect of the Annona, is hostile to Damasus, 127. MAXIMUS THE CYNIC: whether Apollinarian, 211; whether identical with the recipient of extant letters from Athanasius and Basil, 212. He is condemned by canon 3 or 4 of the Second Council of Constantinople, 221. Before that time he had not come to Italy, ibid. Damasus removes him from the episcopate, 211, 365. Whether he attended the Council of Aquileia, 324 ff.; whether he attended an Italian council and was received by it into communion, 327 ff. In what year he came to Italy, 327. Damasus’s letters against his ordination, 322, 365. Emperor MAXIMUS, having seized power, turns his attention to the Church, 260. He replies to Siricius in the Priscillianist case, ibid. MELETIUS OF ANTIOCH is commended to Damasus by Basil, 146. The division in the Church of Antioch between him and Paulinus, ibid. His reconciliation and sworn agreement with Paulinus, 190. This is confirmed by Damasus, 197, 212, 221, 222. He sends Acacius, bishop of Beroea in Syria, to Rome with the acts of the Antiochene synod which he had held, 191, 195 ff. Author of canon 5 of the First Council of Constantinople, p. 93. He is received into full communion with the Roman See and the Westerners, 219. He convenes a synod from his patriarchate; the proceedings of this synod, 190, 191. Nazianzen refers to him as present with the presbyter Flavian, 221. Disturbances arise after his death, 222. Beginnings of the schism of MELETIUS OF LYCOPOLIS, 317. The location in Rome of Mithras’s CAVE, 187, 188. Pagans customarily abused Mithraic rites, ibid.

## N

NECTARIUS is ordained bishop of Constantinople, 238. Confirmation is sought from Damasus, 239 ff. What is determined concerning him at the fifth synod under Damasus, 247, 334, 335. In what year and for what reason Nazianzen’s letters to him were written, 255.

## O

By “WESTERNERS,” the Easterners designate the Roman Pontiff as metropolitan and head of the West, 235, 334. OLYBRIUS, Prefect of the City, follows the advice of Maximinus, Prefect of the Annona, disregarding Aginatius the vicarius, 127. Valentinian’s rescripts for Damasus are addressed to him, ibid. The order of the first three sees was established before the pontificate of Gelasius, 241. Anciently appointed TIMES for sacred orders, 113. [Col. 1243] Only Eastern bishops are summoned to the First Council of Constantinople, 368, note e. They report to Damasus what they had done there, 238. They excuse themselves for not coming to the Roman council and send legates to it, 238, 239. They ask Damasus to expel Timothy from the Church, 255. His letters to them are explained, 257, 370. Their frequent appeals to the Apostolic See, 144, 162, 163, 173, 174, and elsewhere. They attempt to seize the bodies of the holy Apostles and transfer them to their own region, 268, 269.

## P

The bishop of PARMA, deposed in a Roman synod, retains the church by force, 263. Who he was, ibid. He obeyed the Roman bishop and depended on him, not the bishop of Milan, 228. Whether the order of the three PATRIARCHAL sees was established before Gelasius, or rather by Damasus, 246, 247. PAULINUS OF ANTIOCH is ordained bishop by Lucifer, 146. He is denounced by Basil to the Apostolic See concerning Marcellus’s heresy, 174, 351, note a. He is confirmed in the episcopate by Damasus’s letters, 168 ff. He is excommunicated by Timothy, disciple of Apollinaris, 176. His cause is preferable to Meletius’s, 168, 176, 182, 183. He has serious disputes with Vitalis of Antioch, 185. He attends the holy Roman synod under Damasus, 241. The pontiff’s letters to him are explained, 168 ff., 197, 354, 357. He is vindicated against Montfaucon’s criticism, and a passage of Chrysostom concerning him is explained, 344, 345. Strangers were not enrolled in the Church’s ministry before being tested, 113. PETAVIO: whether this city was formerly called Patavium and is now called Passau, 224, note e. The sacred pledges of the Apostles PETER and PAUL are miraculously preserved at Rome, 267. Gregory the Great’s testimony on this is confirmed by Damasus’s verse, 267, 268. The Acts of the holy martyrs PETER and MARCELLINUS are committed to writing by Damasus, 113, 396. PETER, bishop of Alexandria, succeeds Athanasius, 161. Two persecutions against him; because of one he flees to Rome, and in what year, ibid. He is kindly received by Damasus, 162. He attends Damasus’s third synod, 175 ff. His contention with Dorotheus, presbyter of Antioch, 178. Upon returning to Alexandria, he promulgates the Roman synod’s decrees against the Apollinarians, ibid. PRISCILLIAN, condemned by the Council of Saragossa, flees to Rome to clear himself, 232. Damasus denies him access to his presence, ibid. He is condemned by Damasus’s fifth synod, 248. DUPIN is refuted and criticized, 232, 296, 323.

## Q

QUESNEL’s inventions, 232, 253, 323, 360, note e.

## R

The faith of the ROMAN CHURCH is unfailing from Peter onward, 194. Connection of the Churches of Rome and Milan, and its origin, 232. The Roman Pontiff was once the sole metropolitan of the West, 214, 334. He is the first to receive expelled bishops into communion, 334. He hears episcopal cases, at what are called first instance, throughout Italy and Gaul, 228, 229. Bishops of the principal sees cannot be received from heresy into communion unless their acts have first been transmitted to and confirmed by him, 239. The right and origin of establishing apostolic vicars throughout the West, 215. His supreme authority is often acknowledged by Easterners, 144, 162, 163, 174, 181, 194, 255; confirmed by emperors, 194, 228, 236. The great modesty and restraint, at this supreme height of affairs, of several Roman pontiffs down to the still-living most holy BENEDICT XIV, 120. The recent French writer of the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, printed at Amsterdam, is refuted and criticized, 116, 119, 125, 145, 179, 210, 229, 260, 322. “Roman” often has the same force as “Latin,” 139. RUFINUS: in what year he departed for the East and arrived at Alexandria, 157. His judgment on suburban churches, 143. He is uncertain concerning Liberius’s fall, 298.

## S

The SABBATIANS, an offshoot of the Novatians: when they arose, 165. They are expelled from the City with the Donatists and Luciferians, with whom they were associated, 166. Canon 7 of the First Council of Constantinople, dealing with them, belongs to a later time and synod, 165. SABINUS, deacon of the Church of Milan, is sent by Damasus to Athanasius and Basil, and why, 151. In what year he arrives at Alexandria, 152. From there he goes to Basil, bringing him letters, ibid. On returning to the West he brings Damasus letters from Basil, which are explained, 155. Yet they are not approved by the same pontiff, and why, 157. Catholics are sometimes called SABELLIANS by calumny; Damasus removes that accusation from them by an anathema promulgated against the Sabellians, 358, note f. [Col. 1244] The Canon of sacred SCRIPTURES is enlarged by various pontiffs according to the needs of the times, 241. Christian SENATORS are numerous under Damasus, 234. Saint SILVESTER, accused by Donatists before Constantine, clears himself, and the reason for the accusation, 204. SIMPLICIANUS, presbyter of the Roman Church, is sent by Damasus to Ambrose, 171. SIMPLICIUS, vicarius of the City: Valentinian’s directive against rebaptizers is addressed to him, 165. The second SIRMIAN formula: in what year it came to light, 290; written in the first or second month of 358, 291. Whether it issued from a synod and may be called synodical, 285, 292. Whether it was promulgated in the East as in the West, 296. Demophilus could in no way have expounded it to Liberius, ibid. Ursacius and Valens are compelled to abjure it, 297, 298. What the Sirmian “perfidiousness” is in Hilary, 285 ff. A passage from Sozomen, book IV, chapter 24, explained, ibid.; again book IV, chapter 18, 315. Pope and martyr STEPHEN praised by Damasus, 270, 383. The authenticity of his Acts is confirmed by Damasus’s testimony, 270. What the SUBURBICARIAN regions are, and whether they are identical with suburban churches, 141.

## T

The commander TERENTIUS is asked to restore concord among the Catholic Antiochenes, 169. He withdraws from Valens’s court, why and when he returns to it, 170. THARSI­CIUS, martyr: whether perhaps a deacon, 276. He dies in preserving the discipline of the secret, 276. THEODORE and THEODOLUS are often one and the same name, 147. THEODORET is often more hostile to Paulinus of Antioch, 222. His gloss upon the letters of Damasus and the Illyrian bishops, 184. Theodosius the Great’s book II of the Theodosian Code, *On the Catholic Faith*, is cited and explained, 194. He summons Eastern bishops to the Roman synod, 235. He sends his own legates to it, and why, 236, 240. He restrains the Apollinarians by laws, 257; again, and why, 344. He orders Flavian to go to the Council of Capua, 339. Ambrose’s—or Siricius’s—letter to him in this case, and his reply, 339 ff. Damasus asks him for a tutor for the boy Arcadius, 254. He summons only Eastern bishops to the First Council of Constantinople, 367, note b. TILLEMONT is rejected, 182, 191, 201, 215, 218, 223, 254, 300, 336, 352, note f. TIMOTHY, disciple of Apollinaris, is sent to Rome for the sect, 175, 255. Whether he was bishop of Berytus, 255. Damasus receives him into communion on a feigned profession of faith, 176, 177. The same pope condemns him with his master Apollinaris when he comes to Rome again, 255. Returning to the East, he excommunicates Peter of Alexandria, Basil, and Paulinus of Antioch, 177. Leader of the Apollinarians after Apollinaris, 255. Author of the letter under Pope Julius’s name to Prosdocium, 256. Banished by order of Theodosius, 257. All basilicas or sacred buildings are called TITLES; what title-churches established by Pope Marcellus for baptism and penance additionally were, 280. TRANSLATIONS disapproved by Damasus, 360, no. 369, note g. Catholics are called TRITHEISTS by calumny, 363, note c.

## V

VALENS, Arian pseudo-bishop of Petavio, is deposed at the Council of Aquileia, 208. He is expelled by clergy and people from the see he had occupied by force, 224. As a fugitive he hides in Milan and allies himself with Ursinus, antipope, 208, 225. In what year he flees to that city, 208. VALENS and URSACIUS, Arian bishops: while Liberius is still exiled, after abjuring the Sirmian blasphemy, they are compelled to profess the Ancyrene exposition, 297. After the Sirmian blasphemy, of which they had been authors, Gallic bishops exclude them from communion, 290, 291. They had long before been condemned by Damasus, 131. Constantius grants them power to compel Western bishops to profess the formula promulgated at Constantinople and at Rimini, 320. In what year they left that city to return West with this command, 321. They persuade the emperor to order Hilary to return to Gaul, ibid. Emperor VALENTINIAN’S rescripts for Damasus against Ursinus the antipope, 124, 126, 127. His law addressed to Damasus, 140. Rescripts to Maximus, or Maximinus, Prefect of the Annona, in favor of the Ursinians, 120, 121. Letter to Arian bishops on behalf of the Catholic faith, 137. Law against Manichaeans, 155. Law 20, title 36, book XI of the Theodosian Code is cited and examined, 164. His rescript to Simplicius, vicarius of the City, is explained, 165, 226. He establishes Damasus’s innocence, 206. VALERIAN of Aquileia: in what year ordained, 347, note a. VENUSTIANS, heretics identical with Manichaeans, and why so called, 156. [Col. 1245] A passage from VICTORINUS, *On Faith against the Arians*, is explained, 305. VINCENTIUS, bishop of Capua, praised by Damasus, 349. Whether Liberius’s legate to Emperor Constantius was a prevaricator and departed from Athanasius’s communion, 135. VITALIS, presbyter of Antioch, gives himself over to Apollinaris, 167. He opposes Bishop Paulinus, and why, ibid. Accused of heresy, he is summoned to Rome by Damasus; presenting a deceitful formula of faith, he obtains communion and is dismissed with letters to Paulinus, 167, 168. Apollinaris consecrates him bishop of Antioch for his sect, 167, 185. Whether Jerome regarded him as Catholic in his letters to Damasus, 185. He is condemned by that pontiff, 360, note d. The Council of Capua considers him after he is again denounced to the Apostolic See, 343. A passage of Chrysostom is explained, 344. VITALIANUS and VICTOR, bishops at the first Roman synod under Damasus, 347, note b. [Col. 1246] URSINUS, or Ursicinus, antipope: his election examined, 118 ff. He is ordained on an unlawful day, 120. He is expelled from Rome by Juventius, Prefect of the City, ibid. He and his followers are recalled from exile by Praetextatus, then expelled again, 125. Whether he was bishop of Naples, 166. In exile, he incites Romans against Damasus, 202, 203, 225. Residing at Milan, he allies himself with Valens of Petavio, an Arian, 225. In exile in Gaul, ibid. He approaches Gratian, ibid. He again stirs disturbances against Siricius, 251. Number of URSINIANS from the Roman clergy, 122. They are expelled from Rome, 126.

## X

Companions of Saint XYSTUS in martyrdom, 408 and in the addenda.

## Z

ZANOBIUS, bishop of Florence, 139.

[Col. 1245]

# ANALYTICAL INDEX OF THE WORKS OF LUCIFER OF CAGLIARI

[Note: [Col. 1245] This index refers only to the works of Lucifer of Cagliari in columns 767 to 1050.]

## A
Adoxius, by antiphrasis for Eudoxius. See Eudoxius. The Church of Alexandria harassed by Emperor Constantius, pp. 808, 813. The Alexandrians complain to Emperor Constantius about George of Cappadocia, 830; those who recoiled from communion with George were cruelly punished by Constantius himself, 910, and by his commander Syrianus, 916. They steadfastly followed the cause of Athanasius, 921; were persecuted by Constantius, 1009, 1012; and savagely killed, 1022.

The Arian heresy is called idolatry, 824, 825, 828, 832, 840, 843, 874, 879, 880, 893, 905, 910, 919, 937, 940, 946, 947, 950, 963, 965, 1002, 1003, 1006, 1030. Arians compared with Judas Iscariot, 777; sons of pestilence and darkness, 778; what they thought concerning the Trinity, 781; likened to the Jews, 782; a perverse generation, 784; members of the harlot, 785, 786; serpents, 789; compared with the Midianites and Moabites, 792; what they thought concerning the Holy Spirit, 808; they are antichrists, 848; disciples of the Jews, 852; condemned at Nicaea, 854; not Christians but servants of Antichrist, 863; wolves, dogs, and sons of the devil, 865; robbers, 869, 882; what they thought concerning the Son of God, 875, 987; compared with harlots, 878; extraordinarily loved by Constantius, 879; sons of the devil, 904, and of the Harlot, 910; they accuse Athanasius at the Council of Sardica, ibid.; they differ in nothing touching the very substance of the heresy from the Photinians, 972, nor from the heresy of Paul of Samosata, ibid.; anathematized by the Council of Nicaea, 973; filled with the spirit of Antichrist, 987; divided into several sects, ibid.; they confessed the Son of God to be merely adoptive, ibid.; wolves designated by the Apostle, 996, 997, 998; rabid dogs, 1005; a dwelling of the unclean spirit, 1009; they call Emperor Constantius “bishop of bishops,” 1032; chattels of Antichrist and grandsons of Pharaoh, 1042.

Athanasius (St.), persecuted at Alexandria by Emperor Constantius, 813. Defended by St. Lucifer in two books, 817, 881. Constantius vainly attempts to have him condemned while absent and unheard at the Council of Milan, 819, 894, 895. He is driven from the Alexandrian see and George of Cappadocia introduced in his place, 829, 1010. Compared with Samuel, 836; Elijah, 840, 843; Naboth, 844. He suffers persecution from Constantius, 849, 854, 860. Sent into exile by Constantine the Great, he is restored to the Alexandrians by Constantius through the intercession of Constans, 857, 910. Compared with Job, 876. Falsely accused by the Arians, 884, and by Constantius, 892. Likened to Susanna, 894 ff., and to Abel, 905. He does not attend the Council of Milan, fearing that the Arians are laying snares for him, 909. Accused at the Council of Sardica, he is acquitted, 910. He sends the deacon Eutychetes and a letter to Lucifer, requesting that the books written by him against Constantius be sent to him, 1037. He sends him another letter, informing him of the persecution and thanking him for the books sent, 1039 ff.

Auxentius the Arian occupies the Church of Milan after Dionysius has been expelled, 894.

## B

Bonosus reports to Emperor Constantius the two books for St. Athanasius, acknowledged by Lucifer, 935.

## C

What imperial *comites* are, 990. The Council of Milan held in the year 355, 765. What the Arians attempted there, 775. How many bishops attended, 998. The Arian Council of Arles, 778. Council of Sardica, at which Athanasius, accused by the heretics [Col. 1246], is acquitted, 910. Council of Sirmium, at which the Arians condemn Photinus, 972.

Emperor Constans procures Athanasius’s restoration to the Alexandrians, 857. Emperor Constantine the Great condemns Athanasius to exile, ibid.

Emperor Constantius, to whom Lucifer writes his books, 765. He attempts to unite Catholic bishops to the communion of the Arians, 773. Compared with Ahab, ibid. He feigns peace in order to ensnare Catholics, 775. He presents to the people of Milan an edict, or letter, full of Arian poison, 780, 821, 878. What he thought concerning the Trinity, 781, 859. He invents a sacrilegious expression against the Son of God, 787. Like Antiochus, ibid.; called Antichrist, 789; like Gideon the idolater, 793 ff.; Saul, 796, 797; Solomon after his idolatry, 798, 799; Rehoboam, 799; Jeroboam, 799–804; Abijah and Baasha, 804; Zimri and Jehoshaphat—on the latter, see the Notes—805; Ahab and Jezebel, 805, 809. As soon as he occupied Italy, he overturned the Church, 807, especially at Alexandria, 808. Compared with Joash and Uzziah, 809; Manasseh, 809, 810, 811, 812. What he boasts of concerning himself, 813, 814, 815. He orders Athanasius condemned unheard, 817. Compared with the serpent that deceived Adam, 818, 819; with Judas Iscariot and the Jews, 824, 850. Accursed, 825, 828. He cannot judge bishops, 826. He thrusts George of Cappadocia into the Church of Alexandria after expelling Athanasius, 829. He receives letters from the Alexandrians against George, 830. He vainly strives to have George’s election approved by Catholics, 831. Compared with Eli, 833; with those who captured the Ark of God, 833, 834; Saul, 835–840; Ahab and Jezebel, 840–845; Jeroboam, 846. Unlike Jehoshaphat, who restored the worship of the Lord in the kingdom of Judah, 846, 847. He persecutes Athanasius, 849, 850, 854, 860. Proud and heedless, 849. Compared with asps, 852. Impious, ibid. Like Judas Iscariot, 853, 990, 991, 1038. Forerunner of Antichrist, 855. He roars like a lion, ibid. Proud, reckless, and pestilential, ibid. Through Constans’s intercession he restores Athanasius to the Alexandrians, 856, 910. He wages war with Saporinus, king of the Persians, ibid. A dog returning to its vomit, 857. He persecutes Eudoxius by letters sent to the Antiochenes, then receives him back into favour, ibid. Persecutor of the Church, 859. Imitator of the devil, 860. He persecutes Catholic bishops, 865, 867. Like Pharaoh, 866. He rebuilds his heresy by the shedding of blood, 868. Compared with the Sodomites and Gomorrites, 873; with the Jews, ibid.; and with Rabshakeh, 875. Leader of Antichrist, ibid. Shortly before his death he is baptized, 876. Impious, 878. Cruel toward Catholics, 878, 879. He extraordinarily loves the Arians, 879. He expends the property of Catholics upon the poor of his own party, 882. He persecutes Catholics, 881. A robber, 882. Son of the devil, 884. He brings false charges against Athanasius, ibid. He mistreats Catholics, especially bishops, ibid. Destroyer of the pasture of the Lord’s flock, 885. Compared with Herod, 886, 902. Coming into Italy from Gaul, he pretends to be a sheep instead of a wolf, 889. Foolish, 890, 891. A liar against Athanasius, compared with Ananias and Sapphira, 892, 893; and with the elders who attempted to violate Susanna, 894–898. He drives Dionysius, bishop of the Milanese, into exile and substitutes the Arian Auxentius, 894. He appears as a heretic at the Council of Milan, 894, 895. Forerunner of Antichrist, 895, 899, 903, 911, 957, 981, 984, 988, 998, 1009. He summons bishops to condemn Athanasius at Milan, 898. A beast, 900. Agent of the devil, 904. Compared with Cain, 905. Slave of Antichrist, 906. Member of the devil, 908. He refuses to hear Athanasius himself, 969. He himself commends Athanasius by letter to the Alexandrians, ibid. Then, after Athanasius has been driven out [Col. 1247], he cruelly punishes the Alexandrians who recoiled from communion with George of Cappadocia, 910. Like the Jews who killed the prophets, 913. A serpent, 916, 917, 930, 931. He sends Syrianus to compel the Alexandrians to receive George, 915, 916. Compared with the Jews, 919, 920. Thief of Christ’s sheep, 921. He drives Catholic bishops from their sees, 927. A wolf, 928, 957, 958. A pagan, a Jew, and a follower of Antichrist, 929, 930. Compared with the devil tempting Adam and Eve, 930. He has the two books for St. Athanasius examined to determine whether they are truly by Lucifer, 935. Compared with the Israelites slain by Moses, 937, and with those slain by Phinehas, 938. What he attempted at Rome, by memorials presented even to Catholic bishops, 940. Compared with Achan, 940, 941, 942; Saul, 942, 943; Ahab, 944. A murderer, ibid. Like Amaziah, ibid.; King Uzziah, 946; the Jews harshly punished by Josiah, 947, 948, 949; likewise the Jews under Amaziah, 950, 951; Sennacherib, 951, 952; the Jews rebuked by Ezekiel, 953, 954; and Holofernes, 955, 956. Compared with Antiochus, 958, 959, 960. He denies Lucifer the glory of a completed martyrdom because Lucifer desired it, 962. Called “pious” (*pius*) by Lucifer ironically (*εἱρονικῶς*), ibid. One of the antichrists, 964. Like the Jews under Mattathias and Ezra, 964, 965, 966, 967; and like the Jews who enjoined silence upon Peter and John, 967, 968, 969. Like Photinus and Paul of Samosata with respect to the substance of his heresy, 972, 996. Compared with Herod, 974. Imprudent, 976. Like the Jews persecuting the Apostles and Stephen, 977, 978; and like Bar-Jesus, 978, 979, 980; Antiochus, 981–985 and 1006–1008. A wolf and dog, 985. Drunk with the vine of Sodom and the vineyard of Gomorrah, 985. Minister of the devil, ibid. A false prophet and possessing the spirit of Antichrist, 986, 987. A wolf and brood of vipers, 988. He promulgates the Arian heresy through written books and preachers, 990. He ensures that the Nicene faith is judged heretical, whether at Rimini or at another Nicene synod, ibid. He convenes the synods of Rimini and Seleucia in order to deny the divinity of the Son, 991. Worse than Judas, ibid. Like the serpent tempting Eve, 992. A false apostle, ibid. He removes Catholic bishops and introduces heretics, 993. Possessing the spirit of the devil, like the Jews who persecuted Paul and Silas, 993, 994, 995. Like Paul before his conversion, 995. One of the wolves designated by the Apostle, 996, 997, 998. Like Ananias, 998; and the persecutors of religion foretold by Daniel, ibid. and 999, 1000. Either Antichrist or his forerunner, 1001. Compared with the lying Cretans, 1002. A temple of demons and an anathema, 1004. Foolish, ibid. and 1005. Like the Jews whom Isaiah calls dogs, bulls, and calves, ibid. Standing behind the curtain, he hears Lucifer at Milan deny that he or the others can yield to the Arian opinion, 1009, 1014. He persecutes Alexandrians and other Catholics, 1010. He pretends friendship for Catholics in order to deceive them, as the serpent deceived Eve, 1011, 1020. He persecutes Catholics so severely that he does not even permit them burial, 1012. The most savage of all tyrants, 1013. A beast, 1014, 1020. The worm of Arius, 1015. He vainly attempts to spread his heresy by his edict, ibid., 1031. A wolf and dog, not even a human being, 1016. He savagely kills Alexandrians, 1022. Executioner, 1025. He now received, now rejected formulas of faith according to the Arians’ wishes, 1027. So too the formula of faith which Eudoxius issued at Antioch, 1028. A wolf, ibid. Friend of Antichrist, 1030. Imitator of Judas, ibid. Rabid dog, 1032. Called “bishop of bishops” by Arian bishops, ibid. He will be like the rich man who saw Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom, 1036.

## D

What dictators are, 1028. Dionysius (St.), bishop of Milan, deceived into condemning Athanasius, 894. Driven from his see and sent into exile by Emperor Constantius, ibid. Dydimas, a presbyter, from Catholic became Arian, 917.

## E

What Constantius’s edict is, 780, 821, 878, 940, 1011, 1015, 1031. Epictetus, Arian bishop of Centumcellae and intimate of Emperor Constantius, 777. He subscribed against St. Athanasius at the Council of Milan, ibid. Seduced by Constantius, he becomes an apostate, 1021. Bishops who had deserted the Nicene faith are denoted under the name of angels turned into apostasy, 947. Lost letters of Lucifer, 981.

Eudoxians, so called from Eudoxius, bishop of Germanicia, among the Arians, 858. Eudoxius, Arian bishop of Germanicia, is called Adoxius by Lucifer through antiphrasis, 830, 1028. He was in exile there with the same man [Lucifer], 830. Persecuted by Emperor Constantius because he followed the doctrine of Aetius, he afterward returns to favour, 858. He occupies the see of Antioch, then that of Constantinople, ibid., 1027. What formula of faith he issued at the Council of Antioch [Col. 1248], and whether he abjured it, 1027, 1028.

Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, is invited to the Council of Milan by legates of the Apostolic See, 765. Compared with the Apostle Peter, ibid. He assists St. Dionysius, bishop of Milan, who had been deceived into condemning Athanasius, 893. Eutychetes, deacon, is sent by Athanasius to Lucifer, 1037. Euzoius, an Arian bishop, baptizes Emperor Constantius, 876.

## F

Whether the presbyter Faustinus issued the formula of faith circulated under Lucifer’s name, 1045 ff. Catholic faith drawn from the Nicene Creed, 898, 973, 1015. Florentius, Master of Offices, asks Lucifer whether he wrote the two books for St. Athanasius, 935. Lucifer answers him affirmatively, ibid.

## G

George of Cappadocia, introduced by Constantius into the Church of Alexandria after Athanasius has been expelled, 829, 910, 1010, 1012. Called monstrous by Nazianzen, 829. Like Arius, Valens, Ursacius, and Eudoxius, 830. Accused by the Alexandrians before Constantius, ibid. Not regarded as a bishop by Catholics, especially by Lucifer, 831. Compared with the sons of Eli, 831, 832. Killed, 881. Hated by the Alexandrians, 921. A thief and robber, ibid. What he did to the Alexandrians at Constantius’s command, 1022.

## H

Hilary, legate of Pope Liberius, invites Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, to the Council of Milan by letter, 765. He declares that Constantius attacks the religion of God, 803.

## L

Memorials read at Rome by Emperor Constantius and given by him to bishops, even Catholic bishops, 940. Pope Liberius writes to the exiled Lucifer and others, 765.

Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari and legate of Pope Liberius, 765, 1015. By letter he invites Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, to the Council of Milan, 765, 899. While in exile he receives a letter from Pope Liberius, 765. He writes to Emperor Constantius the book *On Not Associating with Heretics*, 767, and does so at Germanicia, where he was in exile, 775, 830, 831. He writes to the same Constantius the book *On Apostate Kings*, 793; Book I *For St. Athanasius*, 817; and Book II, 881. He resisted the introduction of George of Cappadocia into the Alexandrian see and is therefore compelled to live in exile at Germanicia, 831, 881. In what year he wrote Book I *For St. Athanasius*, 858. What he thought concerning the divinity of the Son, 863, 864, and concerning the Trinity, 875, 934. He receives Florentius’s letter about the two books *For St. Athanasius* and replies that he did indeed write them, 935. He writes the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, 935. He is called abusive by Constantius, 937 ff., and proud, 962 ff. He wrote letters that have perished, 981. He calls himself a Roman, 987. He sends Emperor Constantius a book entitled *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, 1007. Before Constantius at Milan, he confidently denies that he or the others can yield to the Arian opinion, 1009, 1014. He receives through Eutychetes a letter from Athanasius, requesting that he send him the books written against Constantius, 1037; and another letter, informing him of Arian persecution and of the books received, 1039 ff. Called Elijah by Athanasius, 1041, and greatly praised by him, ibid. Whether he is the author of a certain profession of faith circulated under his name, 1041 ff.

## M

Macedonians less extreme than Arians in their teaching on the Holy Spirit, 807, 808. Machetas, or Achetas, a presbyter who from Catholic became Arian, 917. Marcion disseminated his heresy about the year 134, 780. Condemned, ibid.

## P

Pancratius, presbyter and legate of Pope Liberius, invites Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, to the Council of Milan by letter, 765. He declares that Constantius attacks God’s religion, 803. Paul of Samosata, condemned at the Council of Antioch, 780, 972. He differed in nothing from Arius with respect to the substance of the heresy, 972. Photinus, bishop of Sirmium and disciple of Paul of Samosata, is condemned at the Council of Sirmium, 780, 972. Called Scotinus by antiphrasis, 972, 990, 996. He differed in nothing from Arius with respect to the heresy, ibid. A disciple of Paul of Samosata, 972, 973. Like Judas Iscariot, 990. Profession of faith wrongly attributed to Lucifer [Col. 1249], 1041 ff.; more suitably to the presbyter Faustinus, 1045 ff.

## S

Sabellius first began to teach his errors in the year 257, 779. Condemned, ibid. Soporis: see Soporinus. Saturninus, Arian bishop of Arles and friend of Constantius, 778. He communicates with the Arians at the Council of Arles, ibid. He joins Valens and Ursacius against St. Athanasius at the Council of Milan, ibid. He was responsible for Bishop Hilary of Poitiers being driven into exile, ibid.

Semi-Arians less extreme than Arians in their doctrine on the Holy Spirit, 808. They affirmed that the Son was *ὅμοιον* (“like”) to the Father *κατὰ πάντα* (“in all respects”), 863. They triumph at the Synod of Seleucia, 991.

Soporinus, king of the Persians, wages war against Emperor Constantius, 857. Nicene Creed, 973, 1015. [Col. 1250] Syrianus, commander, at Constantius’s command harasses the Catholic Alexandrians, 915.

## U

Ursacius, Arian bishop of Singidunum and friend of Emperor Constantius, 777. What he does with Valens at the Council of Milan, ibid. He produces Constantius’s edict to be read to the people of Milan, 780. Like George of Cappadocia, 830.

## V

Valens, Arian bishop of Mursa, compared with Simon Magus, 765. Intimate of Emperor Constantius, 777. He takes the leading role at the Council of Milan against St. Athanasius, ibid. He produces Constantius’s edict to be read to the people of Milan, 780. Like George of Cappadocia, 830. The curtain by which the emperor’s inner chamber was enclosed, 1009, 1014.

[Col. 1249]

# INDEX OF MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## ST. POPE FELIX II

[Col. 1249] Biographical notice on St. Felix, 9.

**LETTERS AND DECREES**, 11. Letter of St. Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops to Felix, ibid. Letter I of Felix to the bishops assembled in the Alexandrian synod.—Many matters are treated relating to ecclesiastical discipline, but especially to the immunities of bishops, 17. Letter II of Felix to the same persons and to the rest of the Lord’s priests.—On patiently enduring persecutions and tribulations, 25.

## THE PRESBYTERS FAUSTINUS AND MARCELLINUS

**PROLEGOMENA**, 29. On Faustinus and Marcellinus, from Galland, ibid. On Faustinus, from Schoenemann, 34. **FAUSTINUS’S BOOK ON THE TRINITY**, ibid. Preface to Empress Flaccilla, 37.

CHAPTER I.—On the impious profession of the Arians, 38.

CHAPTER II.—On the statement of the heretics: “God made a Son for himself from nothing,” 49.

CHAPTER III.—That the Son of God is almighty; that the omnipotence of Father and Son is one, as their divinity also is one; and on the Incarnation, 62.

CHAPTER IV.—On the Son’s saying: “The Father is greater than I,” 67.

CHAPTER V.—On what is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Therefore let all the house of Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ,” 69.

CHAPTER VI.—On Solomon’s words: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works,” 75.

CHAPTER VII.—On the Holy Spirit, 76.

**FAUSTINUS’S CREED PRESENTED TO EMPEROR THEODOSIUS**, 79.

**THE PETITION OF FAUSTINUS AND MARCELLINUS TO EMPERORS VALENTINIAN, THEODOSIUS, AND ARCADIUS**, 81. Preface.—On the schism of Ursinus, ibid. The Petition begins, 83.

**THE RESCRIPT OF THEODOSIUS FOR MARCELLINUS AND FAUSTINUS**, 107.

## ST. POPE DAMASUS

**PROLEGOMENA**, 109. Dedicatory letter, ibid. Notice to the reader, 111. **ON THE WRITINGS AND DEEDS OF ST. DAMASUS**, ibid.

CHAPTER I.—I. The lineage and native country of St. Damasus. A reader from boyhood in the Basilica of St. Lawrence. II. As deacon he follows Liberius into exile, and why he later returns to the City. III. Whether he was ordained presbyter by Liberius or rather by Felix; Baronius’s view. IV. The preface to the *Petition* of Faustinus and Marcellinus is convicted of falsehood, and Damasus defended. V. What position and esteem he enjoyed under Liberius after the latter’s restoration to his see, ibid.

CHAPTER II.—I. Damasus is elected Roman pontiff, but Ursicinus is imposed as antipope by a faction. II. Contemporary writers are compared, and the true sequence of events is therefrom collected and set forth. III. The preface to the *Petition* of Faustinus and Marcellinus is again charged with falsehood. IV. Ursicinus is exiled, restored, and again expelled, and the reason why. V. Baluzius is rejected, 118.

CHAPTER III.—I. Emperor Valentinian approves the renewed exile of Ursinus and his schismatic associates, and orders the one basilica retained by the Ursinians to be restored to Damasus. II. The slaughter committed in the Church of St. Agnes, maliciously alleged as a crime against Damasus: the grave danger thereby created for the innocent pontiff; explained by the testimony of Rufinus and Jerome. III. Evagrius of Antioch approaches the emperor on Damasus’s behalf; the emperor pronounces him innocent, and on this occasion Jerome is introduced and elucidated. IV. Damasus fulfils a vow to St. Felix, apparently Felix of Nola, and to other martyrs, 126.

CHAPTER IV.—I. The first synod under Damasus against Auxentius, pseudo-bishop of Milan. II. Why it is assigned to this year. III. What was done in it. Its synodal letter explained. IV. On Vincentius of Capua, 129.

CHAPTER V.—I. The Illyrian synod which followed this Roman synod is discussed, together with letters written by it and by Emperor Valentinian. II. The evidence is adduced and assessed. III. On Zenobius, bishop of Florence. IV. On Valentinian’s law addressed to Damasus and inserted in the Theodosian Code; Baronius is defended, 136.

CHAPTER VI.—I. The Ursinians are recalled from the exile to which they had been confined: the suburban provinces; Rufinus’s opinion concerning suburban churches. II. Letters written this year by St. Basil the Great to St. Athanasius and Damasus are explained; the Anonymous Writer of Amsterdam is refuted. III. Other reasons why Basil wrote to Damasus are set out; on that occasion the Antiochene dissension between Meletius and Paulinus, and Marcellus of Ancyra, are discussed. IV. Marcellus is cleared of heresy; it is shown that Basil, having at last learned better, abandoned his prejudiced opinion against him, 141.

CHAPTER VII.—I. Dorotheus, deacon of Antioch, comes to Rome with letters addressed to Damasus by Eastern bishops and, his business completed, returns East with Sabinus, deacon of the Church of Milan, who carries in Damasus’s name letters to Athanasius and the Easterners. II. Sozomen is compared with these sources and assessed. III. Sabinus returns West with Basil’s letters to Damasus and the Westerners; they are explained and restored to their proper date. IV. On Theodosian Code, Book III, title 3, law 3, and, on that occasion, on the Venustians, mentioned in the *Praedestinatus*, 150.

CHAPTER VIII.—I. Damasus arranges for the letters brought by Sabinus to be sent on to Basil through Evagrius of Antioch, and for others to be written according to the formula prescribed at Rome; in what year Evagrius returned East. II. Why Basil’s letters did not please Damasus, and what he seems to have wanted in them. III. What Basil himself and Eusebius of Samosata thought concerning the requests then made by Evagrius. IV. On Athanasius’s death, Peter of Alexandria’s election, and his flight to Rome, 157.

CHAPTER IX.—I. Basil and the other Eastern bishops send Dorotheus, presbyter of Antioch, to Damasus with letters, which are produced and elucidated. II. A synod convened by Damasus, and its letters to the Easterners, brought after Dorotheus’s return, are explained. III. The year of this synod is established. IV. Theodosian Code, Book XI, title 36, law 20, is examined. V. Simplicius, deputy of the City, to whom the law is addressed. Theophanes is explained in his treatment of the Sabbatians; the petition of Faustinus and Marcellinus is again examined, 162.

CHAPTER X.—I. On Vitalis the Apollinarian, his journey to Rome and its reason; on the profession of faith which he presented to Damasus, communion obtained by fraud, and the three letters written on that occasion by Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch. II. The last of these causes unrest among the Catholic Antiochenes, as reported from Basil. III. For this reason Dorotheus contemplates a third journey to Rome and consults Basil. IV. Simplicianus, afterward Ambrose’s successor, a presbyter of the Roman Church; Baronius is defended, 166.

CHAPTER XI.—I. Dorotheus, setting out for Rome with another Antiochene presbyter, brings to Damasus letters written by Basil and the Easterners; these are assessed, and the entire sequence of events between Damasus and Basil is set forth. II. The same pontiff, with a synod attended by Peter of Alexandria, complies with Eastern wishes and answers them. III. At this same synod Apollinarius and Timothy are condemned. IV. On the case of Meletius, discussed before Damasus, his standing with that pontiff, and what the pontiff thought of him. Dupin is refuted. V. The astonishing thoughtlessness or bad faith of the Anonymous Writer of Amsterdam, 172.

CHAPTER XII.—I. Jerome’s letters to Damasus concerning the three hypostases are explained. What caused this revived controversy. II. Damasus’s reply to Jerome. III. The ancient reading of Jerome’s letter is retained and defended. IV. Whether Jerome regarded Vitalis as Catholic. V. Peter, restored to his see by Damasus’s letters, returns to Alexandria, 180.

CHAPTER XIII.—I. Gracchus, prefect of the City this year, destroys the cave of Mithras; Damasus’s role in the affair. II. A Roman council and its surviving letter to Gratian are mistakenly assigned to this year, 186.

CHAPTER XIV.—I. The Antiochene schism ended by mutual agreement between the parties; Theodoret is criticized. II. A synod held at Antioch under Meletius: what was done and decided there. Its acts sent to Damasus. III. On the date of this synod and the year of St. Basil’s death, 189.

CHAPTER XV.—I. Theodosian Code, *On the Catholic Faith*, law 2, is introduced. II. Acacius, bishop of Beroea in Syria, comes to Rome, apparently as Meletius’s legate with the acts of the Antiochene synod. III. A synod under Damasus. IV. On Damasus’s celebrated letter to Paulinus, and proof that it was written by this synod. When the Pneumatomachians first began to be called Macedonians. V. A passage of Pope Vigilius is examined, from which it is inferred that Ambrose attended this council, 194.

CHAPTER XVI.—I. The letter of the Roman council to Gratian, published by Sirmond in the appendix to the Theodosian Code, is discussed, assessed, elucidated, and attributed to this very council. II. It is compared with the letter of the Council of Aquileia, so that one may understand why the Fathers of this Roman council then wrote for Damasus against Ursicinus; and why this same letter should be considered written this year and attributed to Ambrose. III. It is shown that Damasus was never accused of adultery; the rashness and ignorance of the Anonymous Writer of Amsterdam are noted, 202.

CHAPTER XVII.—I. Damasus declares void the ordination of Maximus the Cynic, in letters to Acholius of Thessalonica; these are assessed and elucidated. II. On the Thessalonican vicariate. III. Whether Damasus, having later changed his mind, defended that Cynic’s ordination with an Italian council, 210.

CHAPTER XVIII.—I. The Council of Constantinople is discussed in matters concerning Damasus, and the defender of Gallican propositions is rejected. II. What is the Tome of the Westerners? III. Some matters concerning the third or fourth canon by which Maximus the Cynic’s ordination was rejected. IV. On the ordination of Flavian of Antioch and what was done at that time, 216.

CHAPTER XIX.—I. On the Council of Aquileia and its synodal letters; the first two, to Gratian, are reviewed. II. Gratian’s rescript to Aquilinus, deputy. Nentonus is criticized, and the impudence of the Anonymous Writer of Amsterdam rebuked. III. The third letter of the same Council of Aquileia is assessed and explained. IV. Priscillian comes to Rome to clear himself. Quesnel and Dupin are refuted, 224.

CHAPTER XX.—I. Damasus opposes pagan senators seeking restoration of the Altar of Victory, in letters to Ambrose. II. He holds at Rome the celebrated council which he had convened in the preceding year. III. The principal reasons for convoking it. IV. The Easterners excuse themselves for not attending; their letters are assessed in light of the sequence of events. V. Why they reported to Damasus concerning Cyril of Jerusalem and Nectarius’s election. VI. Who attended this council. Basnage’s erroneous opinion, 233.

CHAPTER XXI.—I–II. What was decided at that Roman council, and on confirmation of the Council of Constantinople. III. Then on fragments published by Holstenius. IV. Baronius’s conjectures assessed. V. Dadulus’s testimony concerning the same council adduced, 242.

[Col. 1252]

CHAPTER XXII.—I. The petition of Faustinus and Marcellinus is examined insofar as it concerns Damasus. II. Whether these two presbyters were Luciferians or rather Ursinians. Who Bassus, prefect of the City, was, and whether he was Christian. III. On Ephesius, the Ursinians’ pseudo-bishop in Rome, and his expulsion. IV. On the little tale of Liberius condemned by Damasus. V. On Hilary, Roman deacon: whether he returned to the Church, and whether he authored the commentaries circulated among Ambrose’s works. VI. On Arsenius, Roman deacon, tutor of Arcadius and most holy monk, 249.

CHAPTER XXIII.—I. In what year and on what occasion Damasus’s letter to the Easterners was written, and on Timothy the Apollinarian. II. On the Creed in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus attributed to the Council of Nicaea, 254.

CHAPTER XXIV.—Damasus’s letter to Valentinian on behalf of Symmachus; on Priscillian and the Council of Bordeaux. The death of this pontiff, the place of his burial, and his epitaphs, 259.

CHAPTER XXV.—I. The writings of Damasus are catalogued. Why Marius Mercator said that Pope Damasus had condemned Bonosus beforehand; whether the Bonosiacs were Photinians or only suspected of that heresy. II. Damasus wrote many works now known to have perished; several epigrams among those surviving are elucidated, a few others are assigned to Damasus, and still others are printed as an appendix. III. On Damasus’s works: the site of the basilica built by him on the Via Ardeatina, and its cemetery. On the Basilica of St. Lawrence in Damaso; on this occasion titles are discussed, and a passage of Anastasius on Marcellus is adduced and explained, 278.

**TWO DISSERTATIONS ILLUSTRATING CERTAIN ACTS OF THE POPES LIBERIUS AND DAMASUS**, 281.

**FIRST DISSERTATION.—On the deeds of Liberius in exile**, ibid.

§ I.—Contemporary writers on the deeds of Liberius in exile are adduced; the author proposes them alone as his judges in this celebrated controversy, ibid.

§ II.—Hilary’s testimonies are extensively examined to establish the Sirmian creed accepted by Liberius. No Arian synod could have been held at the city of Sirmium in 349, contrary to some opinions, 284.

§ III.—Hilary’s testimonies concerning the Sirmian creed accepted by Liberius are likewise examined, 285.

§ IV.—On the heresy of Demophilus, bishop of Beroea in Thrace. It is proved that he was always a Semi-Arian and a most vigorous opponent of the Arians; whether he attended the Council of Rimini, 288.

§ V.—In what year and with what intention may the Sirmian blasphemy have been composed and sent into Gaul? Various opinions on the question. Hilary is introduced and explained, and the controversy is decided by his testimony, 290.

§ VI.—The complete course of Liberius’s actions is set forth, and his letters to the Easterners and to Ursacius and Valens are explained. The sequence is confirmed by Sozomen’s authority, by Acacius, and by a previously unnoticed testimony of other Arians assembled at Constantinople, 297.

§ VII.—The question first raised by Tillemont is examined: namely, whether Liberius merely did not mention the *ὁμοούσιον* (“of one substance”), or even condemned it. Hilary and Victor are adduced and explained, having been incorrectly understood by Tillemont, 300.

§ VIII.—It is demonstrated that Hilary’s curses from the celebrated passage of the *Fragments*, customarily brought against Liberius, ought to carry no weight whatsoever, 307.

§ IX.—Liberius’s return to the City is described, along with the events which followed it. An anonymous annotator, cited in defence of the propositions of the Gallican clergy, is refuted, 310.

§ X.—An inquiry into the character Liberius actually displayed after returning to his see, and during the time of the Council of Rimini. Athanasius’s letter to the bishops of Egypt is elucidated, as is a passage of Hilary in Liberius’s favour, 315.

**SECOND DISSERTATION.—Whether Damasus ever supported Maximus the Cynic against Gregory Nazianzen; and on two letters published by Sirmond under the name of an Italian council**, ibid.

§ I.—Basnage is refuted. Writers are adduced, both those who say that Maximus the Cynic’s appeal to Damasus and the Westerners was void and regarded as nothing by the Easterners, and those who believe that it was not without effect and that Maximus was received into Western communion. Both parties rely upon one letter of a certain Italian council, which is produced. Those who have doubted its authenticity, ibid.

§ II.—The sequence of events devised by those who regard that letter as genuine is presented: in what year Maximus the Cynic came to Milan; what other council he attended in order to defend his ordination there. The opinion of Pierre de Marca, Valesius, and others on this matter is shown to be erroneous, 325.

§ III.—Tillemont’s opinion is adduced, assessed, and rejected. Arguments drawn from the same letter itself and from other contemporary records are presented, proving that the letter could not have belonged to any Italian council, could not have been genuine, and could not have been by Ambrose, 329.

§ IV.—The other letter published by Sirmond under the name of an Italian council is discussed. It is genuine and written by Ambrose, or perhaps even by Siricius. The occasion and date are investigated, and it is assigned to the Council of Capua as a kind of supplement. On this occasion the date of Gregory Nazianzen’s letters to Cledonius is discussed; a passage of Chrysostom is also adduced and explained; and Paulinus of Antioch is defended against the forced and prejudicial interpretation of the latest edition of that Father’s works, 339.

**Prolegomena.** 1115

**Letters and Decrees of Siricius.** 1131

**Letter I.**—On Arians not to be rebaptized; that baptism should not be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost; on apostates to be separated from the Church; that it is not lawful to marry another man’s betrothed; on those who have by no means maintained penitence; on monks and virgins who do not observe their obligation; on incontinent clerics; what persons ought to attain the office of the clergy; on the conduct of clerics; on those of advanced age who turn to sacred service; etc., etc. Ibid.

Appendix to Letter I, from the Corbie manuscript. 1147

**Letter III.**—Emperor Maximus promises care for the Catholic faith. He undertakes that the case of Agricius, whom Siricius had written to have been improperly promoted to the rank of presbyter, shall be examined in a synod. He again professes his zeal for the Catholic faith and sends the records in which the recently disclosed crimes of the Manichaeans or Priscillianists are set forth. Ibid.

**Letter II.**—Emperor Valentinian approves the election of Siricius as pope. 1148

**Letter IV.**—Siricius orders that no one in Illyricum be ordained bishop without the consent of Anysius. 1143

Notice on the following letter. 1149

**Letter V.**—Siricius, with a synod, after setting forth how great a concern bishops ought to have for the purity of the Church, and seeking to restore ancient rules already neglected by some, determines how bishops are to be ordained; that no cleric may marry a widow, and that no man who has married a widow, or who after the remission of sins has worn the belt of secular military service, may be admitted to the clergy; and that no one may ordain a cleric from another church. Likewise, on persons who have been cast out and are not to be received; on Novatians and Montanists who return to the Church and are to be received; on the continence of priests and Levites; and that merciful judgment must not be absent. 1155

Notice on the following letter. 1162

**Letter VI.**—Writing to various bishops, Siricius directs that no unworthy person be made bishop, that the priesthood be not bestowed upon persons unknown, and that neophytes or laymen not be made priests. 1164

**Letter VII.**—Siricius publicly exposes the perverse doctrine of Jovinian and his associates, and announces by name that its principal authors have been condemned. 1168

**Letter VIII.**—Ambrose and other bishops, replying to Siricius, enumerate and refute the errors of Jovinian and his associates: first, that they abolish degrees of merit and equate marriage with virginity; then, that they deny Mary’s virginity in childbirth; next, that they oppose fasts. Finally, having observed that their opinion about Christ’s birth supports the Manichaeans, they subscribe to Siricius’s judgment concerning their condemnation. 1172

Notice on the following letter. Ibid.

**Letter IX.**—Asked for a judgment concerning Bonosus, Siricius does not wish to pronounce one; rather, he directs the judges whom the Synod of Capua had appointed for him to perform their duty. He confirms that Bonosus was rightly held in abhorrence because of his error concerning Mary’s children. 1176

Notice on the following canons. 1178

**Letter X.**—Canons of the Roman synod addressed to the bishops of Gaul. 1181
